In 1921 General Manuel Fernández Silvestre crossed the Ameqqran River with 60,000 men despite Abd el-Krim's warning that this would be an act of war. In June a Riffian force killed 179 of an estimated 250 Spanish troops at a post in the Abarran foothills. Silvestre committed suicide when defeat became clear, and in three weeks of battles 13,000 Spanish and colonial troops were killed. The defeat at Annual damaged the Restoration regime in Spain, and Miguel Primo de Rivera installed a dictatorship in September 1923.

After Abd el-Krim invaded French-occupied Morocco in April 1925 and reached as far as Fez, France sent a force under Marshal Henri Philippe Pétain which, with a Spanish army, made more than 250,000 soldiers backed by aircraft and artillery. After ten months of fighting, in which the French and Spanish used chemical bombs against the population, he surrendered to the French on 26 May 1926 at Targuist.

He was exiled to Réunion from 1926 to 1947. On the way to the south of France in 1947 he was freed by Moroccan nationalists and taken to Cairo, where he supported Arab nationalism, corresponded with Ho Chi Minh and backed the Algerian National Liberation Front. He refused Mohammed V's invitation to return after Moroccan independence in 1956 while French forces remained in North Africa, and died in 1963. His guerrilla methods, including the first use of tunnelling in modern warfare, are said to have influenced Ho Chi Minh, Mao Zedong and Che Guevara.
abdallah-al-mahdi-billah: The origin and early history of the founder of the Fatimid Caliphate are obscure, and even his name and birthplace are disputed. According to his official biography he was born in Askar Mukram in Khuzistan on 31 July 874; other traditions give Baghdad, Kufa or Salamiya. His name was most likely Sa'id ibn al-Husayn. His father died in 881/2, and he was fostered by his uncle at Salamiya, the base of the family's secret Isma'ili missionary network, the da'wa.

In the mid-890s Sa'id took over the leadership of the da'wa. His claim that he and his ancestors held the imamate themselves, rather than acting as trustees of a hidden imam, led to a schism in 899, when the Qarmatians split off. A Bedouin uprising in Syria in 902-903 drew the attention of the Abbasid authorities to him. He fled to Ramla, then to Fustat in Egypt, and finally to Sijilmasa, where he lived as a merchant until his missionary Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i led the Kutama Berbers to overthrow the Aghlabid dynasty of Ifriqiya.

Abu Abdallah, who ran the new regime while his master was still in Sijilmasa, entered the Aghlabid palace of Raqqada on 25 March 909. Once al-Mahdi had taken power in Ifriqiya he claimed the right to conquer the world in the name of God. He soon fell out with Abu Abdallah and other leading missionaries, who were disappointed that he was not the semi-divine mahdi they had been propagating for, and he purged them. He also had to overcome revolts, some against the exactions of the Kutama, who were the backbone of his power.

The state he built was underpinned by a messianic ideology but was otherwise conventionally organised, and relied on personnel of the previous Aghlabid regime. Two invasions of Egypt were beaten back by the Abbasids, leaving only Cyrenaica in his hands, and the war with the Byzantine Empire in southern Italy brought raids for plunder and slaves without lasting success. In the west the Umayyads of al-Andalus challenged his attempts to rule the Berbers. In 921 he moved his court to the newly built palace city of Mahdiya on the Tunisian coast.

He died in 934 and was succeeded by his only son, al-Qa'im. Whether his claims of descent from Ali were true has been debated since the early 900s and has no definite answer. Marius Canard wrote that, whoever he may have been, he laid the foundations of the dynasty in North Africa. Michael Brett points out that building a state left him little time to develop Isma'ili doctrine into a full creed of the imamate, which was achieved under the fourth Fatimid imam-caliph, al-Mu'izz.
abdallah-ibn-yasin: Abdallah ibn Yasin was born in Tamanart, in the tribe of the Jazulah, a Sanhaja sub-tribe. His mother, Tin Izamarren, came from Temamanaout, at the edge of the desert bordering Ghana. A theologian of the Maliki school, he was a disciple of his relative Waggag ibn Zallu al-Lamti and studied at his ribat, Dar al-Murabitin, in the village of Aglu, near present-day Tiznit.

In 1046 the Gudala chief Yahya Ibn Ibrahim came to the ribat asking for someone to teach Islam to the Berbers of the Adrar, in present-day Mauritania, and Waggag chose Abdallah ibn Yasin to go with him. The Sanhaja were only superficially Islamized and held to many pagan practices, so he preached to them an orthodox Sunnism.

After a revolt of the Godala, ibn Yasin withdrew with his followers, and in alliance with Yahya ibn Umar, the leader of the Lamtuna, he put the rebellion down. He then formed the Almoravid alliance of the Lamtuna, Masufa and Godala tribes, with himself as spiritual leader and Yahya ibn Umar in military command. In 1054 they conquered Sijilmasa, ruled by the Maghrawa. Ibn Yasin introduced orthodox rule: wine and music were forbidden, non-Islamic taxes were abolished and one fifth of the spoils of war went to the religious experts. This rigorous application of Islam provoked a revolt in 1055.

Yahya ibn Umar was killed in 1056 in a new revolt of the Gudala in the Sahara, and ibn Yasin appointed Yahya's brother Abu Bakr Ibn Umar as military leader. Abu Bakr destroyed Sijilmasa but could not bring the Gudala back into the alliance. He took Sus and its capital Aghmat, near modern Marrakesh, in 1058.

Ibn Yasin died on 7 July 1059 while trying to subdue the Barghawata on the Atlantic coast. Sulaiman ibn Haddu replaced him and was in turn killed, and no successor was named. His grave lies south of Rabat, near Aïn El Aouda, above the Krifla River. A mosque and a mausoleum were built over it and the site survives.
abdallahi-ibn-muhammad: Abdallahi was born into the Ta'aisha Baqqara tribe around 1846 at Um Dafuq and trained as a preacher and holy man. His father, Mahommed et Taki, meant to take the family to Mecca but was prevented by the unsettled region, and died after advising his son to take refuge on the Nile.

Around 1880 Abdallahi met Muhammad Ahmad, who claimed to be the Mahdi, and became his follower. The Mahdi named him Khalifa in 1881, and he commanded a large part of the Mahdist army in a series of victories over the Anglo-Egyptians. He fought at El Obeid, where William Hicks's army was destroyed on 5 November 1883, and was a principal commander at the siege of Khartoum, from February 1884 to 26 January 1885.

After the Mahdi's unexpected death in June 1885, Abdallahi succeeded him as Khalifat al-Mahdi, usually rendered Khalifa. He had to suppress revolts in 1885–1886, 1888–1889 and 1891, mainly by the Ashraf, before emerging as sole leader. The state was at first run on military lines as a jihad state, with courts enforcing Sharia law and the Mahdi's precepts, and later under a more traditional administration. Khartoum was deserted on his orders and Omdurman became his capital.

He believed expansion into Ethiopia and Egypt would keep internal problems small. He invaded Ethiopia with 60,000 Ansar troops and sacked Gondar in 1887, destroying nearly every church in it, and repulsed the Ethiopians at the Battle of Metemma on 9 March 1889, where Emperor Yohannes IV was killed. He suffered a crushing defeat in Egypt, and in the 1890s crop failures strained the state while Italian, French and British forces surrounded it.

In 1896 an Anglo-Egyptian army under General Herbert Kitchener began the reconquest of Sudan. The Khalifa's army was defeated at the Battle of Atbara River on 8 April 1898, and at the Battle of Omdurman on 2 September 1898 his army of 52,000 men was destroyed. He fled south and was killed by Reginald Wingate's Egyptian column at Umm Diwaikarat in Kordofan on 25 November 1899. Described as devout, intelligent and an able general and administrator, he could not overcome tribal dissension to unify Sudan and had to employ Egyptians as administrators and technicians.
abdeen-palace: The palace stands on the site of a small mansion owned by Abdeen Bey, after whom it is named. Ismail Pasha built it to replace the Citadel of Cairo, the seat of Egyptian government since the Middle Ages, as the official government headquarters, and it was also used for state events and ceremonies. Construction began in 1863 and lasted ten years. It was designed by the French architect Léon Rousseau with many Egyptian, Italian, French and other European decorators.

The palace covers 24 feddans and has 500 rooms, adorned with paintings and many clocks, most of them decorated with gold. Joseph Urban added a new wing in 1891, and Sultan Fuad I laid out its garden on another 20 feddans in 1921. Building cost £E700,000, and furnishing a further £E2 million; for four palaces King Fuad spent more than 18 million French francs with a single Paris furniture maker, Linke & Cie. Later rulers spent more on altering and maintaining it. It stands in the Abdeen district, part of the Khedival Cairo area west of Historic Cairo.

After the 1952 revolution it became one of the presidential palaces. The upper floors, once the royal family's living quarters, are kept for visiting foreign dignitaries, while the lower floors hold the Silver Museum, the Arms Museum, the Royal Family Museum and the Presidential Gifts Museum. The Historical Documents Museum opened in January 2005; among its papers are the Ottoman firman that established the rule of Muhammad Ali and his family and a certificate of the Order of the Iron Crown of the Kingdom of Araucanía and Patagonia.
abdel-hakim-amer: Amer was born on 11 December 1919 in Samalut, in the governorate of El Minya, into an affluent family. His father was a landowner and village mayor, and his maternal uncle, Mohammed Haidar Pasha, served as minister of war under King Farouk. After school he attended the Egyptian Military Academy, graduated in 1938 and was commissioned into the Egyptian Army in 1939. He served in the 1948 Arab-Israeli War in the same unit as Gamal Abdel Nasser.

Amer played a leading role in the military coup of 1952 that overthrew King Farouk and brought General Muhammad Naguib and Colonel Gamal Abdel Nasser to power. The following year he was promoted straight from major to major-general, bypassing four ranks, and made Chief of the General Staff. In 1956 he became commander-in-chief of the joint military command established by Egypt and Syria, and he led Egyptian forces against Israeli and allied British and French forces in the Suez war.

Afterwards he accused Nasser of provoking an unnecessary war and then blaming the military for the result. As Nasser's representative in Syria he was detained by rebels during the coup of 1961 and sent back to Cairo. In October 1959 he had become Syria's governor, holding presidential authority. He later served as Minister for Defense and Vice President, and in March 1964 became first vice-president and deputy supreme commander, with power to rule for 60 days if the president was incapacitated.

Egypt's defeat by Israel in the Six-Day War of June 1967 ended his career. Historians including Hazem Kandil place much of the responsibility on Amer, whose control of the military fitted Nasser's policy of making institutions the fiefdoms of those most loyal to him; the war in North Yemen, where nearly half of the Western-trained officer corps were serving, is also seen as a cause. On 6 June, when he heard of the fall of Abu-Ageila, he is said to have panicked and ordered all units in Sinai to retreat, which turned the retreat into a rout. On 17 June he was relieved of all duties and forced into early retirement.

In August 1967 Amer, over 50 officers and two former ministers, among them Shams Badran, were arrested for allegedly plotting a coup against Nasser, and Amer was kept under house arrest at his villa in Giza. He died on 13 September 1967. The official Egyptian position was that he swallowed poison pills when officers arrived to question him. Another version holds that officers gave him the choice of a trial for treason or an honourable death by poison. In September 2012 his family filed a case to investigate his death, claiming that he was murdered.
abdelhamid-ben-badis: Abdelhamid Ben Badis was born in Constantine in 1889 into a prestigious family of ulama and notables that descended from the Zirid dynasty, 11th-century rulers of Ifriqiya. His grandfather Si Makki ben Badis was a qadi and his father, Muhammad Mustafa, an adjunct judge and a member of the financial delegations, the colonial parliament. He memorised the Quran at thirteen. His tutor Hamdan Lounissi, a defender of the rights of the Muslim inhabitants of Constantine, made him promise never to enter French service. He was also influenced by Jamal al-Din al-Afghani and Muhammad Abduh and read Rashid Rida's monthly al-Manar.

In 1908 he went to Tunis and studied at the Ez-Zitouna University, where Sheik Mohammed Al-Nakhli convinced him of the need to purge Muslim communities of the cult of saints and Sheik Muhammed Al-Taher Ben Achour deepened his appreciation of Arabic. He took a degree in 1912, taught there for a further year and in 1913 returned to Constantine, where he began teaching at the Sidi Lakhdar Mosque in early 1914.

He took part in founding the Algerian Muslim Congress and led the Association of Algerian Muslim Ulema, which set up institutions where thousands of Algerian children were educated. Its monthly journal, al-Chihab, modelled on al-Manar, set out its ideas on religious reform. He and the Association criticised maraboutic practices and sought to save Algerian culture from being eclipsed by French values.

Ben Badis died on 16 April 1940 after a long struggle with diabetes. 8,000 people, including 1,000 women, attended his burial. He is regarded as the leading Algerian Salafi educator, Islamic reformer and figurehead of cultural nationalism in colonial Algeria, and the Association later had a great influence on Algerian Muslim politics up to the Algerian War of Independence. Ahmed Menour's 2019 novel For Both Their Sakes, I Lived is about his life.
abdirahman-ahmed-ali-tuur: Tuur was born in Burao, in the British Somaliland Protectorate, on 6 November 1931, and came from the Muse Arreh sub-clan of the Habar Yoonis. His name, also written Tur or Tour, means hunchback. One of the best students of the protectorate's first intermediate school, he won a scholarship in 1948 to the Hantoob Secondary School in Sudan, where he befriended future Sudanese leaders such as Jaafar Nimeiry, Sadiq Al-Mahdi and Hassan Al-Turabi and excelled at football and athletics. A further scholarship took him to the University of Exeter.

He began as an administrative officer in Borama in 1956, became district commissioner in 1959, governor of the Eastern Region at Burao in 1961 and of the Western Region at Hargeisa in 1964. He then joined the Ministry of Foreign Affairs and served as ambassador to Sudan, Ethiopia, East Germany and the UAE between 1964 and 1983.

He went on to lead the Somali National Movement, a guerrilla force drawn mainly from the Isaaq clan, which sought to overthrow the military regime of Siad Barre. Founded with a unionist constitution, the movement later turned to secession, and under his leadership the northwestern territories declared independence on 18 May 1991.

After his presidency he renounced the separatist platform in 1994 and called for reconciliation with the rest of Somalia in a federal system with shared power, speaking for many Isaaq who opposed secession; he also gave some support to the UNOSOM mission in the south. The government of Mohamed Haji Ibrahim Egal sentenced him to death in absentia for treason. He joined the government of Mohamed Farrah Aidid in Mogadishu, then after disagreements lived in London until 2001, when he returned to Somaliland and declared that he accepted secession. In the 2003 presidential election he campaigned for Dahir Riyale Kahin. He died on 8 November 2003 and was buried in Burao.
abdirashid-ali-shermarke: Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke was born on 8 June 1919 at Harardhere in the Mudug region of Somalia. His father belonged to the Osman Mohamud Majeerteen branch of the Darod clan and his mother to the Habar Gidir clan. He was raised in Mogadishu by his mother, attended Qur'anic schools and finished elementary education in 1936.

He then worked as a trader and as a civil servant in the Italian colonial administration. In 1943 he joined the new Somali Youth League, and the next year he entered the British administration's civil service. He completed secondary school in 1953 and went on a scholarship to the Sapienza University of Rome, where he took a degree in political science.

Returning from Italy in 1959, Sharmarke was elected to the Legislative Assembly. British Somaliland became independent on 26 June 1960 and joined the Trust Territory of Somaliland, formerly Italian Somaliland, on 1 July 1960 to form the Somali Republic. On that day President Aden Abdullah Osman Daar appointed him the first Prime Minister. He travelled widely in pursuit of a non-aligned and neutral foreign policy, and remained in office until March 1964, when the first general elections returned him to Parliament as a member. In the presidential election of 1967 he defeated Daar and was sworn in as the second President on 6 July 1967.

In 1968 Sharmarke narrowly survived an assassination attempt when a grenade exploded near the car carrying him from the airport. On 15 October 1969, during an official visit to Las Anod, he was shot dead at the guest house by one of his own bodyguards, who fired an automatic rifle at close range. Observers suggested personal rather than political motives. On 21 October 1969, the day after his funeral, the Somali Army under Major General Siad Barre seized power in an almost bloodless coup. His son Omar Abdirashid Ali Sharmarke, born in 1960, later became Prime Minister of the Somali Transitional Federal Government.
abdul-rahim-khan-i-khanan: Abdul Rahim, popularly known as Rahim, was born in Lahore on 17 December 1556, the son of Bairam Khan, Akbar's trusted guardian and mentor. After Bairam Khan was murdered in Patan, Gujarat, his first wife and the young Rahim were brought safely to Delhi and presented to Akbar, who gave him the title Mirza Khan and married him to Mah Banu, sister of Mirza Aziz Kokah. Akbar later married Bairam Khan's widow Salima Sultan Begum, Rahim's stepmother, which also made him Akbar's stepson.

Rahim became one of the nine important ministers of Akbar's court, known as the Navaratnas, and received the title Khan-i-Khanan, meaning Khan of Khans. He was also a general, sent to deal with the rebellions in Gujarat and later overall commander in the campaigns in Maharashtra. In 1580 Akbar made him chief of Ajmer and sent him against Maharana Pratap of Mewar. Rahim left his family in Sherpura and advanced; Pratap's son Prince Amar Singh captured the women of Rahim's family, but Pratap rebuked him and ordered that they be returned with honour.

Rahim was known for giving alms with his eyes lowered. Tulsidas sent him a couplet asking why he gave so, with hands held high and eyes low, and Rahim replied that the Giver was another, and that because people credited him, he kept his eyes down.

Rahim was known for his Hindustani dohe, or couplets, and for two Sanskrit books on astrology, Khetakautukam and Dwatrimshadyogavali. He translated Babur's memoirs, the Baburnama, from Chagatai into Persian, completing it in 1589–90. He died on 1 October 1627. His tomb in Nizamuddin East, Delhi, near Humayun's Tomb, was built by him for his wife in 1598, and his body was placed in it in 1627. In 1753–54 marble and sandstone from it were used to build Safdarjung's Tomb. The Aga Khan Trust for Culture restored it over six years and opened it to the public in 2020.
abdul-razak-hussein: Abdul Razak was born on 11 March 1922 in Kampung Pulau Keladi, a village northwest of Pekan in Pahang. He was the first of two children of Hussein Awang bin Mohd Taib and Fatimah binti Daud, and an aristocratic descendant who held the title Orang Kaya Indera Shahbandar. He studied at the Malay College Kuala Kangsar and joined the Malay Administrative Service in 1938. A scholarship took him to Raffles College in Singapore in 1940, but the Second World War ended his studies.

During the war he helped organise the Wataniah resistance movement in Pahang and, according to the account given of him, served as an informant inside the Japanese administration. In 1948 he went to Britain, and in 1950 he qualified as a barrister at Lincoln's Inn in London.

After returning in 1950 Razak joined the Malayan Civil Service and became youth chief of the United Malays National Organisation. In February 1955, at 33, he became Chief Minister of Pahang. He won a seat in Malaya's first general elections in July 1955 and was appointed Education Minister, and he was instrumental in drafting the Razak Report, which formed the basis of the Malayan education system. He was a key member of the mission to London in February 1956 that sought independence for Malaya. From 1957 to 1970 he was deputy prime minister, and he held the defence portfolio, later also national and rural development. In 1965 he took part in the negotiations for the independence of Singapore.

After the riots of 13 May 1969, Prime Minister Tunku Abdul Rahman was criticised by Malay nationalists within UMNO for his accommodating attitude towards non-Malays. During the state of emergency of 1969 to 1971 Razak led the National Operations Council, which ruled in place of the elected government, and the Tunku resigned in 1970. Some contest the official account of these events.

As prime minister Razak launched the New Economic Policy to reduce socioeconomic disparity between ethnic communities, and in 1974 he set up the Barisan Nasional coalition. Malaysia joined the Non-Aligned Movement in 1970 and signed the ZOPFAN declaration in 1971, and relations with China began with his state visit in 1974. He died in London on 14 January 1976 while seeking medical treatment, and is called the Father of Development.
abdullah-ahmad-badawi: Abdullah bin Ahmad Badawi was born on 26 November 1939 in Kampung Perlis, Bayan Lepas, Penang, into a prominent religious family. His paternal grandfather, Syeikh Abdullah Badawi Fahim, was a religious scholar of Hadrami descent and a founding member of Hizbul Muslimin, which later evolved into the Pan-Malaysian Islamic Party, and became the first Mufti of Penang after independence. His father, Ahmad Badawi, was a religious teacher and active member of UMNO. He graduated from the University of Malaya in 1964 with a degree in Islamic Studies and joined the Malaysian Administrative and Diplomatic Corps.

Abdullah resigned from the civil service in 1978 to become Member of Parliament for Kepala Batas, a seat his father had also held. He served as a deputy minister and, from 1981, as a minister without portfolio responsible for the Look East policy. He was later minister of defence and, from 1991, of foreign affairs under Mahathir Mohamad. In January 1999 he replaced Anwar Ibrahim as deputy prime minister and acting deputy president of UMNO after Anwar was removed from government, expelled from the party and arrested.

He became prime minister after Mahathir resigned in October 2003. He shelved several costly projects begun under Mahathir, created a royal commission on police corruption and required ministers to declare their assets. His Barisan Nasional won 198 of 219 seats in the 2004 election. He then introduced Islam Hadhari, a moderate interpretation of Islam calling for religious tolerance and modernity. Malaysia ended the ringgit's peg to the US dollar in 2005. A series of scandals and public protests damaged his standing, and in March 2008 the coalition lost its two-thirds majority and control of four state governments.

On 10 July 2008 Abdullah announced that he would step down, and on 3 April 2009 he was succeeded as prime minister by Najib Razak. The King conferred on him the title Tun. He was also known as a poet, and his poem I Seek Eternal Peace was translated into more than 80 languages. Abdullah died in Kuala Lumpur on 14 April 2025, aged 85, and was buried at the Heroes' Mausoleum.
abdullah-i-of-jordan: Abdullah was born in Mecca on 2 February 1882, the second of four sons of Hussein bin Ali, Sharif of Mecca. In 1910 he persuaded his father to stand for Grand Sharif of Mecca, and in the following year he became deputy for Mecca in the Ottoman parliament. In 1914 he made a clandestine visit to Cairo to meet Lord Kitchener, seeking British support for his father's ambitions. In 1915 he encouraged his father to correspond with Sir Henry McMahon about Arab independence, which led to the Arab Revolt.

During the Revolt of 1916 to 1918 Abdullah commanded the Arab Eastern Army. He began by attacking the Ottoman garrison at Ta'if on 10 June 1916, which he besieged, and then joined the siege of Medina. In early 1917 he ambushed an Ottoman convoy and captured £20,000 in gold coins meant to bribe the Bedouin.

After French forces took Damascus in July 1920, Abdullah moved his forces from the Hejaz into Transjordan intending to liberate it. Winston Churchill invited him to Cairo in 1921 and persuaded him not to attack Britain's French allies. Abdullah established the emirate on 11 April 1921. A legislative council set up in 1928 was only advisory, and he ruled as an autocrat. In the Second World War he was a faithful British ally.

The Hashemite Kingdom of Transjordan was proclaimed independent on 25 May 1946, and Abdullah was crowned king in Amman; it was renamed Jordan on 26 April 1949. He dreamed of a Greater Syria under a Hashemite throne, which made many Arab states distrust him. On 15 May 1948 he joined the all-Arab intervention, and the Arab Legion fought around Jerusalem. In 1950 Jordan annexed the West Bank, which angered Syria, Saudi Arabia and Egypt.

On 20 July 1951 Abdullah was shot dead at the entrance of the Al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem, during Friday prayers, by Mustafa Shukri Ashu, a Palestinian tailor's apprentice. His grandson Prince Hussein, beside him, survived when a medal deflected a bullet. The assassin was shot by the king's guards. Abdullah was succeeded by his eldest son Talal, and then by Talal's son Hussein.
abdullah-khan-ii: Abdullah Khan was born in 1533 or 1534 at Afarinkent, on an island between two arms of the Zarafshan River. After the death of Abdulaziz Shaybanid there was a struggle for the throne. After Abdullatif of Samarkand died in 1551, Barak Khan of Tashkent took Samarkand and was declared supreme khan of the Uzbeks as Newroz Ahmed Khan. Abdullah Sultan, then governor of Kermine, led the resistance with his uncle Pir Muhammad Khan of Balkh, who was proclaimed supreme ruler after Newroz Ahmad died in 1556.

In 1557 Abdullah Sultan captured Bukhara with the support of Sufi sheikhs. In 1561 he proclaimed his father Iskander supreme khan, though his father, more interested in religious rites, left the conduct of state to him. He set out to combine Bukhara, Samarkand, Tashkent and Balkh in one state, which took many years: a long war for Tashkent, the conquest of Fergana, the taking of Balkh in 1573 after a long siege and of Tashkent in 1576, and a single state only in 1582. After his father's death in 1583 he was declared ruler of the Uzbeks and the state was called the Bukhara Khanate.

He seized Badakhshan in 1584 and Khorasan in 1588, and in 1593–94 his troops conquered Khorezm. A war with Iran lasted from 1587 to 1598, and a non-aggression pact with the Mughal Emperor Akbar, recognising Akbar's rule in Kabul, left him free to fight it.

His monetary reforms, including a 1583 reform centred on Bukhara with copper coins for daily trade, ended a monetary crisis and stopped currency leaking out of the state. He encouraged trade with Russia and India and built madrasas, caravanserais, reservoirs and bridges, including the Kosh-Madrasah in Bukhara. His court included the poet Abd al-Rahman Mushfiqi and the historian Hafiz Tanish, and he wrote poems under the name Avaz Gazi.

He died in 1598 and was buried at the mausoleum of Bahauddin Naqshbandi near Bukhara. His only son Abd al-Mumin was soon killed by rebels, and Baqi Muhammad, a son of Abdullah's sister, defeated and killed Pir Muhammad II in battle. With this the Shaybanid dynasty ended and Baqi Muhammad became the first khan of the Janid dynasty.
abdur-rahman-khan: Abdur Rahman Khan, a Pashtun, was born in Kabul in the 1840s, the only son of Mohammad Afzal Khan and grandson of Dost Mohammad Khan, founder of the Barakzai dynasty. He spent most of his youth at Balkh. When Dost Mohammad died on 9 June 1863 after naming Sher Ali Khan his successor, Afzal Khan rose in revolt in the north, beginning a struggle among Dost Mohammad's sons that lasted nearly five years. Abdur Rahman fled across the Oxus into Bukhara after Sher Ali grew suspicious of him.

After Sher Ali's death he asked the Russians for leave to enter Afghanistan as a claimant, and was at first refused. They allowed it after Yaqub Khan's abdication and the British occupation of Kabul. He annexed Badakhshan and soon held all of Afghan Turkestan.

At a durbar on 22 July 1880 the British recognised him as Amir, promising arms and money and aid against unprovoked foreign aggression, provided he aligned his foreign policy with theirs. Ayub Khan, a son of Sher Ali, defeated his troops at Kandahar that July but was beaten there by General Frederick Roberts on 1 September 1880. Backed by British arms and money, Abdur Rahman consolidated his hold over the country, repeatedly facing revolts such as those of the Ghilzai. One source counts over 40 rebellions during his reign.

His government was a military despotism, resting on a well-appointed army, a widespread system of espionage and officials subservient to him. He also held open courts for petitioners. A British official called his rule a reign of terror, and up to 100,000 people are said to have been judicially executed in his 21 years. He moved troublesome Durrani and Ghilzai tribes to northern areas populated by Uzbek and Tajik communities. In 1895 and 1896 he directed the invasion of Kafiristan and the conversion of its people to Islam, and the region was renamed Nuristan.

In 1893 Mortimer Durand negotiated with him the agreement that fixed the frontier between Afghanistan and British India, the Durand Line. Habibullah Khan confirmed it in 1905 and Amanullah Khan in the Treaty of Rawalpindi in 1919.

Abdur Rahman died on 1 October 1901 in his summer palace, and his son Habibullah Khan succeeded him. He wrote an autobiography and treatises including one on jihad. Afghans hold mixed views of him. Many Pashtuns remember him as a ruler who began modernisation and kept the country from Russian occupation, though he depended on British arms and money to stay in power. His great-grandson Prince Abdul Ali Seraj said he united Afghanistan under one king and one flag.
abdyl-frasheri: Abdyl Frashëri was born on 1 June 1839 in the village of Frashër in the Vilayet of Janina, the eldest son of Halit Bey, a Tosk Albanian bey of a Muslim family with Bektashi affiliations. His younger brothers included the writers Naim Frashëri and Sami Frashëri. As a young man he served as a captain in his father's irregular Albanian militia, which kept order in Rumelia. After his father died in 1859 and his mother two years later, he became head of the household and moved the family to Ioannina.

In Ioannina he studied with the Albanian scholar Hasan Tahsini, learning Arabic, Persian, French and Greek, as well as science, philosophy and mathematics. Of the six children born to him and his wife Ballkëze, only a daughter, Emine, and a son, Mit’hat Frashëri, survived.

Frashëri sat for Yanina in the first Ottoman Parliament of 1876–1877. In a speech on 14 January 1878 he blamed the empire's lack of progress on despotism, ignorance and incompetent officials and called for widespread education. At the end of 1877 he founded and chaired the Central Committee for Defending Albanian Rights in Istanbul, which argued for an autonomous Albanian state under Ottoman suzerainty, or at least a single Albanian vilayet. In 1879 he was a founding member of the Society for the Publication of Albanian Writings.

At the League of Prizren he led the radical wing and chaired its Foreign Affairs Committee. He visited Bektashi tekkes to win southern Muslim Albanians to the cause, organised the Assembly of Preveza in January 1879, which helped keep Çameria from being ceded to Greece, and in the spring of 1879 travelled with Mehmet Ali Bey Vrioni to Rome to petition the Great Powers. In early 1881 he became foreign minister of the provisional government formed in Prizren under Ymer Prizreni.

After the Ottoman army under Dervish Pasha crushed the League, Frashëri was sentenced to death by a special court. Sultan Abdul Hamid II reduced the sentence to hard labour, and he was held in the castle jail of Prizren from 1882 to 1885. Released for reasons of health in 1886 on condition that he abandon politics, he still corresponded with the Italian prime minister Francesco Crispi, proposing an autonomous Albania within a Balkan confederation. He died in Istanbul on 23 October 1892. In 1978, on the centenary of the League, his remains were brought to Tirana, and the communist regime proclaimed him a Hero of Albania.
abeche: Abéché lies in central-eastern Chad, surrounded by savanna. By road it is 749 kilometres northeast of the national capital, N'Djamena, 164 kilometres northwest of Adre on the border with Sudan, and roughly 90 kilometres southeast of Biltine. Its rainy season runs from June to September, and the hottest months are March to June. Its climate is hot and arid, and it is the hottest major city in Chad. The city stands on the trans-Saharan trade route, along which Islamic scholars and merchants travelled, and it is an important centre of cattle raising.

From the early 19th century Abéché was at the centre of the Islamic slave trade in Chad and an important city in the development of the religion in the region. It became the capital of the Wadai Sultanate in the 1890s, after the wells at Ouara, the former capital, had dried out.

In 1909 French troops invaded the kingdom and established a garrison in Abéché, forcing the sultan to renounce his throne. At that time Abéché was the largest city in Chad, with 28,000 people, but major epidemics reduced the population to 6,000 by 1919. In 1935 the French government ordered the sultanate restored, and Muhammed Ouarada, heir to the throne after his father became king, took up the title.

Abéché is the capital of the Ouaddaï Region and one of the largest cities in Chad. It contains the remnants of the old capital, including palaces, mosques and the tombs of former sultans. The Grand Mosque on the Place de l'Indépendance, built in the 19th century, is one of the oldest and most significant mosques in the country. The city's market is the principal one in Chad for camel exports and rugs, and camel-hair blankets are made in the area.
abeid-karume: Abeid Amani Karume was born on 4 August 1905, in Nyasaland according to some reports and in the village of Mwera in Zanzibar according to others. He had little formal education and worked as a seaman. He travelled to places including London, where contact with African thinkers such as Hastings Banda of Malawi shaped his understanding of geopolitics, and he later built up control of the Afro-Shirazi Party and its ties with the Tanganyika African National Union.

On 10 December 1963 the United Kingdom gave Zanzibar full independence under a sultan who was a constitutional monarch. Karume was on the mainland on 12 January 1964, the night of the revolution, which was led by a previously unknown Ugandan, John Okello, and deposed the last sultan, Jamshid bin Abdullah. Between 2,000 and 4,000 Zanzibaris, mostly Arabs and Indians, were killed, and many more were raped. The revolution ended some 500 years of Arab domination of the island.

Okello invited Karume back as President of the People's Republic of Zanzibar and kept the title of Field Marshal. In the three-month struggle that followed, Karume brought Tanganyikan police to Zanzibar and barred Okello from returning from a trip abroad. In April 1964 he agreed with Julius Nyerere that Zanzibar would unite with Tanganyika, and became first vice-president of the new Tanzania. The union kept the country from aligning with the Soviet bloc, as the Marxist Abdulrahman Mohammad Babu had urged, and Karume pushed Babu aside.

In 1970 four young Persian girls refused to marry the 64-year-old Karume, and he had ten of their male relatives arrested. Under Nyerere's pressure he dropped the charges, but months later four other girls were forced to marry members of his Revolutionary Council, and eleven relatives were imprisoned and flogged.

On 7 April 1972 four gunmen shot Karume dead as he played bao at Afro-Shirazi Party headquarters in Zanzibar Town. Reprisals followed, and Babu was charged with masterminding the killing. Karume had nationalised land owned by Arabs and Indians and redistributed it to poor Zanzibaris, and set up free education and health services and cheap housing. His son Amani Abeid Karume was elected president of Zanzibar in 2000 and 2005, and 7 April became a public holiday.
abel-king-of-denmark: Abel was the son of Valdemar II and his second wife, Berengaria of Portugal, and a brother of the later kings Eric IV and Christopher I. In 1232, when his elder brother Eric was elected co-ruler and heir of their father, Abel was chosen to succeed Eric as Duke of Schleswig. In 1237 he married Matilda of Holstein, daughter of Adolf IV of Holstein, and for several years acted as regent for her underage brothers John I of Holstein-Kiel and Gerhard I of Holstein-Itzehoe.

In early 1241 Abel took part in the Votia campaign against the Novgorod Republic and Finnic pagans, but suspended it on his father's death. Eric then became King Eric IV, and Abel fought him for years to gain independence for Schleswig. He raided north as far as Randers and moved into Funen, and Eric struck back by surprising Abel's garrison at Schleswig. A truce arranged by their sister Sophie held until 1250, when Eric was murdered while a guest at Abel's residence at Schleswig. His chamberlain Lage Gudmundsen and others killed him and dumped his headless body in the Schlei.

Abel and twenty-four noblemen swore an oath that he had no part in it, yet it was widely believed that Eric died at his brother's bidding, and people said, Abel by name, Cain by his deeds. He was proclaimed king at the Viborg assembly on 1 November 1250. In 1252 he raised an army to punish the peasants in Frisia, led by Sicko Sjaerdema, who had refused to pay a tax. He was killed on Husum Bridge near Eiderstedt by a wheelwright named Henner on 29 June 1252. His brother Christopher I was crowned on Christmas Day 1252 in Lund Cathedral.

Most people at the time saw his sudden death as God's judgment for his brother's murder. Tradition holds that the monks heard strange sounds in Schleswig Cathedral where his body lay, so it was taken outside and put in a marshy grave near Gottorp Castle with a wooden stake through the chest. Tales of Abel's wild hunt over the moors of Schleswig lasted long after. His descendants, the Abel family, ruled the Duchy of Schleswig until 1375 and kept up a lasting problem for the Danish crown, as their rule meant the eventual separation of Frisia, Holstein and most of Schleswig from the rest of Denmark.
abel-muzorewa: Abel Tendekayi Muzorewa was born on 14 April 1925, the eldest of a lay preacher's five children, and was educated at the United Methodist School at Old Umtali, near Mutare. He taught at Mrewa from 1943 to 1947, worked as a lay preacher at Mtoko, and studied theology at Old Umtali Biblical College from 1949 to 1952. He was ordained in 1953. He studied at Central College in Fayette, Missouri, and took a Master of Arts at Scarritt College in Nashville, meeting segregation in both places. Consecrated Bishop of Rhodesia of the United Methodist Church at Masera, Botswana, in 1968, he became a national figure in 1971.

In 1971 the British government made a deal with Ian Smith for a transition to majority rule in exchange for an end to sanctions. Muzorewa and the Reverend Canaan Banana formed the United African National Council to oppose it. The proposed referendum was withdrawn, and Muzorewa became a national leader. When ZANU and ZAPU turned to guerrilla war, the UANC was the only legal black party, since it rejected violence. On 3 March 1978 Muzorewa, Ndabaningi Sithole and other leaders signed an agreement paving the way for an interim government. A new constitution reserved 28 seats in the House of Assembly for the white minority; a nearly whites-only referendum approved it in January 1979 with 85 per cent in favour.

After the elections that followed Muzorewa became prime minister of Zimbabwe Rhodesia, and held office for less than a year. The war continued, Robert Mugabe and Joshua Nkomo rejected the settlement, and United Nations Security Council Resolution 423 declared it illegal and unacceptable. At the Lancaster House conference of 10 September to 15 December 1979 Muzorewa accepted fresh elections, and his government dissolved itself on 11 December. In the elections of 1980 ZANU won a majority and the UANC took only three of 80 seats reserved for Africans.

Muzorewa visited Israel on 21 October 1983 and was arrested on 1 November on a charge of conspiring against Mugabe; he went on hunger strike from 3 to 11 November. He stood against Mugabe in the 1996 presidential election, pulled out after the Supreme Court refused to postpone it, and won 4.8 per cent of the vote. He died of cancer at his home in Harare on 8 April 2010, aged 84, and is buried at the Old Mutare Mission Station. Forbes Matonga cited his role in the transition to independence, the Methodist Church and the founding of Africa University.
abellinum: Before the Roman conquest, the ancient Abellinum was a centre of the Samnite Hirpini on the Civita hill, about 4 km outside the current town of Avellino, in what is now Atripalda. It could correspond to the ancient Velecha, known from coins found in the area. The later Roman town lay on the left bank of the river Sabato.

The Romans conquered Abellinum in 293 BCE, and over the following centuries it changed name several times: Veneria, Livia, Augusta, Alexandriana and Abellinatium. A true Roman town, however, was built only after Lucius Cornelius Sulla's conquest in the civil wars in 89 BCE. He razed the old site and in 82 BCE founded the colony Veneria Abellinatium. The new city had massive walls and an orthogonal Hippodamian layout. In 7 CE Augustus renamed it Livia Augusta, for his wife Livia Drusilla, who owned the territory between Abellinum and Aeclanum. In the 3rd century Alexander Severus expanded the colony with a massive immigration of oriental settlers, which helped to spread Levantine cults such as Sol Invictus in the territory.

Economic crises in the 3rd and 4th centuries, violent earthquakes in 346 and disastrous volcanic eruptions in 472 followed. The town was Christianised around 500 and became an episcopal seat. The Goths invaded between 535 and 555, and after the Lombard conquest of southern Italy the ancient city was abandoned in 568, though historians dispute whether completely or partly. A new settlement grew on the Terra hill, where modern Avellino stands.

The ruins of Abellinum lie near the village of Atripalda, 4 km east of Avellino. They include the forum, faced by temples, baths, parts of the Serino aqueduct and a patrician domus, as well as an amphitheatre. Avellino itself is the capital of its province in Campania, with 51,819 inhabitants, about 47 km east of Naples.
abenaki: The name Abenaki derives from Wôbanakiak, meaning People of the Dawn Land, and the Abenaki also call themselves Alnôbak, Real People. Their homeland, Ndakinna, once covered most of northern New England, southern Quebec and the southern Maritimes. Ethnologists divide them into Western Abenaki, in the Connecticut and Merrimack valleys, along Lake Champlain and in Quebec, and Eastern Abenaki, in Maine and New Brunswick. They did not historically have a centralized government and formed a post-contact community after their original tribes were decimated by colonization, disease and warfare.

In 1524 the Portuguese explorer Estêvão Gomes kidnapped 58 Abenaki to sell into slavery in Europe. Bartholomew Gosnold made the first English contact in 1602, and Samuel de Champlain met them in 1604 along the Maine coast and the Kennebec River. In 1675 the Abenaki joined the Wampanoag in King Philip's War and fought along the Maine frontier in the First Abenaki War, which ended in a treaty in 1678. In Queen Anne's War they allied with the French and raided English settlements in Maine over ten years, killing about 300 settlers, and in 1704 raided Groton and Deerfield in Massachusetts.

English settlement and frequent violence drove many Abenaki into Quebec. They settled at Sillery between 1676 and 1680, then for about twenty years on the Chaudière River, before settling at Odanak and Wôlinak in the early 18th century. A museum at Odanak, managed since 1960 by the Odanak Historical Society, is one of the largest Indigenous museums in Quebec.

Abenaki lifeways resembled those of the Algonquian-speaking peoples of southern New England. They farmed, hunted, fished and gathered. Women tended the fields and grew corn, beans and squash together as the three sisters, while men hunted bears, deer, fish and birds. Unlike the Haudenosaunee, they were patrilineal, and each man had hunting territories inherited from his father. Most of the year they lived in dispersed bands of extended families and gathered at seasonal villages near rivers or the coast, with villages averaging about 100 people. Most lived in dome-shaped bark-covered wigwams. Their language, a polysynthetic Algonquian one, has come close to extinction, and members are working to revive it at Odanak and elsewhere.
abeokuta: Abeokuta lies on both banks of the Ogun River, in fertile wooded savanna broken by masses of grey granite, 77 kilometres north of Lagos by railway. The city stands below Olumo Rock, which has caves and shrines and carries spiritual significance. Its name already refers to several rock formations in the neighbourhood. Mud walls 29 kilometres long once surrounded it, and remnants still stand. Palm oil, timber, natural rubber, yams, rice, cassava, cotton and shea butter were the chief articles of trade, and the city exports cocoa, palm products and kola nuts. Rice and cotton were introduced by missionaries in the 1850s.

Accounts of the foundation differ in detail. All agree that Abeokuta was founded by Egba people around 1830 on and around Olumo Rock, at what had been a small farming village, as a refuge for displaced Yoruba during the collapse of the Oyo Empire and the wars that followed, and from slave hunters sent by Dahomey. One version says it replaced Orile Egba, a confederacy of towns said to date from about the 13th century. Another says the Egba withdrew from Ibadan after a chief named Lamodi shot an Ife chief named Ege, and took Sodeke as their leader. Other Egba and many Owu refugees soon joined them, but the groups did not fuse: Abeokuta was a federation of communities within a town wall.

Dahomey grew hostile because of the palm oil trade. In the Battle of Abeokuta in 1851 the Egba defeated King Gezo, and they beat back Dahomey again in 1864. In 1867 they expelled missionaries and traders after friction with the British at Lagos. In 1893, during the Yoruba Civil Wars, the alake of the Egba signed an alliance with the British governor, Sir Gilbert Carter, which formalised the Egba United Government. The Egba lands joined the colony of Nigeria in 1914 with Abeokuta as provincial capital. The Adubi War of 1918 resisted taxation and indirect rule, and the Abeokuta Women's Union led a revolt against unfair taxation in the 1940s.

Abeokuta has been the capital of Ogun State since 1976. The railway from Lagos, 77 kilometres long, was completed in 1899. Ake, the traditional residence of the alake, and Centenary Hall of 1930 stand in the Egba Alake's territory, and the Federal University of Agriculture, Abeokuta, was established in 1988. The census of 2006 counted 449,088 people in its two local government areas.
aberdeen: Aberdeen stands between two river mouths, and the city has little natural exposure of bedrock. It appears to sit on an inlier of Devonian Old Red sandstones and silts, while the outskirts spread onto older metamorphic and igneous rocks. The Rubislaw quarry supplied granite for much of the Victorian city. The name means mouth of the river Don: it is recorded as Aberdon in 1172, and its first element is the Pictish aber, 'river mouth'. The climate is oceanic, with winters milder than the northern latitude suggests, and very short days at the winter solstice, about 6 hours 41 minutes between sunrise and sunset.

The city began as two separate burghs: Old Aberdeen at the mouth of the Don, and New Aberdeen, a fishing and trading settlement where the Denburn waterway entered the Dee estuary. The earliest charter was granted by William the Lion in 1179 and confirmed rights granted by David I. During the Wars of Scottish Independence the city was under English rule, so Robert the Bruce besieged Aberdeen Castle and destroyed it in 1308. Edward III of England burned the city in 1336, but it was rebuilt.

5 per cent of the population. The city went bankrupt in 1817 after expensive infrastructure works but recovered with shipbuilding and fishing. By 1933 Aberdeen was Scotland's top fishing port. In the Second World War a raid on 21 April 1943 killed 98 civilians and 27 servicemen. Oil was discovered in the North Sea in 1969.

Aberdeen is the third most populous Scottish city, with 198,590 people in the main urban area in 2020. The University of Aberdeen, founded in 1495 as King's College, is the fifth oldest university in the English-speaking world and stands in Old Aberdeen. The harbour, established in 1136, is the largest in the north of Scotland and has been called the oldest business in Britain.

Local grey granite, which sparkles because of its high mica content, gives the city the nickname the Granite City. Its arms show three silver towers on red, a motif dating from at least the time of Robert the Bruce. The local dialect of Lowland Scots is known as Doric.
aberdeenshire: The Aberdeenshire council area covers 6,313 square kilometres, about 8 percent of Scotland. It borders Angus and Perth and Kinross to the south, Highland and Moray to the west and the city of Aberdeen to the east. It takes its name from the historic county, whose boundaries were substantially different. The council area includes the historic counties of Aberdeenshire and Kincardineshire, except the part forming Aberdeen City, together with part of Banffshire.

Many rivers and burns cross it, among them the Dee, the Don, the Ury and the Ythan. Lying in the rain shadow of the Grampians, it is generally dry for a maritime region, and coastal areas are subject to haar, a coastal fog. Since medieval times traditional paths such as the Causey Mounth and the Elsick Mounth have crossed the Mounth, a spur of mountainous land, from the Lowlands to the Highlands.

The area has many Neolithic and Bronze Age sites, including Longman Hill, Kempstone Hill and the Catto Long Barrow. The Beaker culture settled it, arriving from the south around 2000 to 1800 BCE, and stone circles and cairns were mostly built in that era. In the Iron Age hill forts were built. Around the 1st century CE the Taexali, who left little history, were believed to live along the coast. The Picts were the next documented inhabitants, and the Romans left signs at Kintore. There were Celtic monasteries at Old Deer and Monymusk.

Macbeth fell at Lumphanan in 1057. Edward I of England crossed the area twice with his army, in 1296 and 1303, and in 1307 Robert the Bruce was victorious near Inverurie. Other families, such as the House of Balliol, Clan Bruce and Clan Cumming, arrived with the Anglo-Norman penetration. Rivalry grew worse after the Protestant Reformation, the Gordon family adhering to Catholicism and the Forbes family to Protestantism. King's College in Old Aberdeen was founded in 1494 and Marischal College in 1593. The 17th century brought fighting under the Marquess of Montrose and in the Wars of the Three Kingdoms, but also trade with Germany, Poland and the Low Countries. The Rising of 1745 ended the ascendancy of Episcopalianism and the feudal power of landowners.

The historic county ceased to be used for local government in 1975; the present council area was created in 1996. Council headquarters are at Woodhill House in Aberdeen, which makes it the only Scottish council with its headquarters outside its jurisdiction. Fishing, farming and forestry have long been the traditional basis of the economy, joined by the oil and gas industry. The area has many castles, among them Balmoral, Dunnottar, Crathes, Drum, Huntly and Kildrummy, and part of the Cairngorms National Park.
aberdyfi: Aberdyfi, also called Aberdovey, is a village and community in Gwynedd, Wales, on the northern side of the estuary of the River Dyfi. It lies within Snowdonia National Park, with steep green hills behind it, and its centre lies around the original harbour, jetty and beach. The Welsh Language Commissioner recommends Aberdyfi as the standard form in both English and Welsh, though Aberdovey remains in use.

The site's strategic place in mid-Wales made it the setting of several conferences between the princes of north and south Wales, in 540, in 1140 and, in 1216, at the Council of Aberdyfi. In 1597, during the Spanish Armada, the Bear of Amsterdam entered the estuary by accident and could not leave for ten days because of the wind. An English fleet captured her off the Cornish coast. The village grew in the 1700s, with inns that survive, copper mined on Copperhill Street and lead at Penhelig.

In the 1800s Aberdyfi was at its peak as a port, exporting slate and oak bark. Seven shipyards at Penhelig built 45 sailing ships between 1840 and 1880. The railway arrived in 1863, and a jetty was built in 1887 to connect with the rail line. Livestock from Ireland came in through it. The SS Dora, one of the last ships trading with Liverpool, was scuttled by a German submarine in 1917. The wharf carried coal until 1959. The first Outward Bound centre opened in the village in 1941.

Aberdyfi is now a seaside resort, and the community had 878 people at the 2011 census. It is linked to the legend of the lost kingdom of Cantre'r Gwaelod beneath Cardigan Bay, whose bells are said to be heard under the water, and to the song The Bells of Aberdovey. In 1936 ten bells tuned in A flat were installed in the tower of St Peter's Church so that the tune could be played, and in 2011 a bronze Time and Tide Bell was hung beneath the pier, rung by the sea at high tide.
aberffraw: Aberffraw is a village and community on the south-west coast of the Isle of Anglesey, on the west bank of the River Ffraw, nine miles from the county town Llangefni. Its name is often shortened to Berffro in local Welsh. It is one of the oldest Mesolithic sites in Wales, about 9,000 years old. At Trwyn Du in Aberffraw Bay a Bronze Age kerb cairn of about 2000 BCE was excavated in 1977 and found to stand on a deposit of 7,000 flint tools and two axes from about 7000 BCE. Nearby is Din Dryfol, a Neolithic chambered tomb of about 3000 BCE, and the remains of stone hut circles and roundhouses lived in from the Iron Age until the Roman period.

In Welsh mythology Aberffraw is the setting of the wedding feast of Branwen and Matholwch. The court is said to have been founded in the 5th century by Cadwallon Lawhir ap Einion. Cadwallon ap Cadfan moved the royal court to Caernarfon in the 7th century, and Rhodri the Great rebuilt the residence in 873 and returned the capital of Gwynedd to the Aberffraw cantref. His son Anarawd ap Rhodri founded the Royal House of Aberffraw, whose members ruled as kings of Gwynedd and were eventually titled princes of Wales. Llywelyn ab Iorwerth re-established the palace as a residence in 1201.

Vikings raided Wales between 852 and 919 and again between 950 and 998, including a raid on Aberffraw in 968, and King Maredudd ab Owain paid the ransom for the Welsh they had enslaved. The court was dismantled in 1317 for building materials. On 6 December 1331 a sandstorm buried 186 acres between Aberffraw and Rhosneigr and drove families south to Llanddwyn and Newborough. Around 1500 the Meyrick family of Bodorgan received the Crown lease of the cantref's manor lands.

The community had 597 residents at the 2021 census, and 67.5 per cent of the population could speak Welsh in 2011. Near the village are the Barclodiad y Gawres Neolithic burial chamber and part of the Anglesey Coastal Path. St Beuno's Church in the village dates from the 12th century and is Grade II* listed, and the 12th-century St Cwyfan's Church stands on the tidal island of Cribinau. The Aberffraw dunes, 357 hectares, are a site of special scientific interest and part of a Special Area of Conservation.
aberystwyth: Aberystwyth is the largest town in Ceredigion, 16 miles from Aberaeron, the county's other administrative centre. The name means the mouth of the Ystwyth. It stands on Cardigan Bay on the west coast of Wales, near the confluence of the River Ystwyth and the Afon Rheidol. The seafront, with a pier, runs from Constitution Hill at the north end of the Promenade to the harbour at the south, and the castle divides the beach. The town lay in the historic county of Cardiganshire and forms a cultural link between North Wales and South Wales.

Flint was worked at Tan-y-Bwlch at the foot of Pen Dinas by Mesolithic hunter-gatherers, and the remains of a Celtic fortress on Pen Dinas show the site was inhabited before 700 BCE. South of the present town, across the Ystwyth, are the remains of a medieval ringfort believed to be the castle from which Princess Nest was abducted.

The fortified town was laid out from 1277 onwards and was administered from then as a borough. It was first called Llanbadarn Gaerog, meaning fortified Llanbadarn, and the name Aberystwyth is first recorded around 1400. It remained part of the ecclesiastical parish of Llanbadarn Fawr until the late 19th century. The Vale of Rheidol Railway, built between 1901 and 1902 to carry lead down from Devil's Bridge, opened for passengers in December 1902 and came to rely on tourism, as lead mining was in deep decline by its completion.

The town grew as a Victorian seaside resort and became more anglicised than the rest of the county. The 1891 census found 52.5 per cent of those answering the language question bilingual, 26.4 per cent Welsh monoglots and 21.1 per cent English monoglots.

Aberystwyth is a university and seaside town. University College Wales, now Aberystwyth University, was founded in 1872, when Wales had very limited degree-awarding capacity beyond St David's College, Lampeter, founded in 1822. Its Old College was built in 1865 as a hotel and sold to the university in 1867 after the owner's bankruptcy. The town also holds the National Library of Wales and the Aberystwyth Cliff Railway, which climbs Constitution Hill. Ysgol Gymraeg, opened in 1939, was the first designated Welsh medium school in Wales.
abgaal: The Abgaal belong to the Mudulood, one of the divisions of the Hiraab, with the Habar Gidir, Sheekhaal and Duduble. The clan is regarded as relatively young, its founder dating from the 1500s. A tradition recorded by the Italian scholar Enrico Cerulli makes the founder, Ali Isman, the son of Osman Darandolle of the Hiraab and of Faduma Sarjeele, a woman of the Gareen house that headed the Ajuran Sultanate.

According to the story, Faduma's father was warned that the boy's descendants would drive out his own and tried to poison him, but the mother drank the poison by mistake. The boy hid behind a camel and called the camels his grandfather, whence the name Abgaal, camel-grandfather. Cerulli read the story as a memory of fighting between Abgaal pastoral nomads coming from the north and the Ajuran.

Clan traditions say that the Abgaal Darandoolle began to arrive in the hinterland of Mogadishu in the sixteenth century, while the Muzaffar dynasty ruled the town, and manuscripts from Mogadishu record Abgaal nomads in the interior at about the same time. Towards the end of the seventeenth century an imam of Abgaal descent settled in the Shangaani quarter. His lineage, the Yaaquub, intermarried with merchant families of Yemeni origin and became known in the trade between the coast and the interior, and by the 1700s it ruled most of the town.

Traditions of the fall of the Ajuran speak of heavy taxes and of a quarrel over watering rights, after which the Darandoolle killed the Ajuran imam at a well called Ceel Cawl. According to oral tradition as reported by Lee Cassanelli, the Hiraab Imamate that followed was an alliance of related groups that ruled from the Shabelle valley to the arid lands of Mudug for at least two centuries. Mogadishu was its capital, and the port of Hobyo its commercial centre.

The Abgaal are divided into three main branches: the Harti, the eldest, the Wacbudhan and the Waceysle, the youngest. The imam of the Mudulood and of the Hiraab traditionally comes from the Abgaal, from the Owbakar sub-clan, while the ugaas of the Mudulood comes from the Reer Ugaas sub-clan. Mogadishu is regarded as Abgaal territory, and they form the majority of its population. Three presidents of Somalia, Ali Mahdi Muhammad, Sharif Sheikh Ahmed and Hassan Sheikh Mohamud, have been Abgaal, as was Daud Abdulle Hirsi, the first commander-in-chief of the Somali National Army.
abgar-v: Abgar V, called Ukkāmā, meaning the Black in Syriac and other dialects of Aramaic, was king of Osroene with his capital at Edessa and was described as king of the Arabs. The Roman historian Tacitus, a near-contemporary source, gave him that description. The Armenian historian Movses Khorenatsi, writing in the 5th century or later, depicted him as an Armenian, but modern scholars agree that the Abgarids were an Arab dynasty. Khorenatsi names Queen Helena of Adiabene as Abgar's chief wife, whereas Josephus says she was the wife of King Monobaz I of Adiabene.

Abgar is said to be one of the first Christian kings, converted by Thaddeus of Edessa, one of the seventy disciples. Eusebius recorded that the Edessan archives held a correspondence between Abgar and Jesus: Abgar wrote asking Jesus to come and heal him, and Jesus replied that he would send one of his disciples after he had been taken up. Some versions add that he also sent a portrait of himself. A Syriac text of the letters survives, along with an Armenian translation, two Greek versions and several inscriptions on stone. Egeria, who stayed at Edessa around 384, wrote that the copy there was fuller than the ones at her home.

The exchange was popular in the East and West during the Middle Ages. The letter of Jesus was copied on parchment, inscribed on marble and metal, and used as a talisman. On 15 August 944 the letter and the Mandylion reached the Church of St Mary of Blachernae in Constantinople. Abgar is counted as a saint, with feasts on 11 May and 28 October in the Eastern Orthodox Church. Scholars dispute details, such as whether he suffered from gout or leprosy.

Critical scholars place the story's origins outside historical record. Walter Bauer argued that it was written without sources to reinforce orthodoxy and apostolic succession, though several sources that were not in contact claimed to have seen the letters in the archives. Most scholars now hold that the texts concern the relationship between church and state power more than the Christianisation of Edessa, and that the third-century controversies, especially the response to Bardaisan, shaped the story. Supposed letters between Abgar and the emperor Tiberius also appear in the Teaching of Addai, and Ilaria Ramelli argues for their possible historicity.
abha: Abha stands high, well over two thousand metres up, in the Asir Mountains of south-western Saudi Arabia, on the western edge of Mount Al-Hijaz and near Jabal Sawda, the highest peak in the country. The high ground gives the city a mild climate for its latitude. It seldom sees temperatures above 35 °C and averages 278 millimetres of rain a year, most of it falling between February and April, with a smaller wet season in July and August. Snow falls occasionally on the higher ground, and the city harvests some of its irrigation water from rain. Saudis sometimes call it the Bride of the Mountain.

Abha was the capital of the Prince of Asir Ibn Ayde, who ruled under Ottoman authority until the First World War. In 1918 the prince Yahya bin Hasun Al Ayde, a grandson of Ibn Ayed, returned to the family throne at Abha with complete independence. In 1920 Asir was conquered by the Ikhwan tribesmen of Nejd, loyal to Ibn Saud, during the unification of Saudi Arabia. Many of the tribes of the surrounding region, among them Bani Shehr and Bal-Qarn, belong to the Azd, whose tribes are said to have migrated after the Marib Dam collapsed for the third time in the third century CE.

The city has four quarters, the largest of which contains a fortress, and hilltop forts are a characteristic feature. Shadda Palace, built in 1927, is now a museum of local handicrafts and household items. A coastal road linking Jeddah and Abha was completed in 1979, and the airport, designed by Dutch engineers, began flights in 1977.

Abha is the capital of Asir Province and a popular summer destination for Saudis, with a summer festival held there. King Khalid University, a public university, was founded in 1998 by merging two earlier institutions. The head office and main printing presses of the daily Al Watan are in the city.
abi-eshuh: Abi-Eshuh was the eighth king of the 1st Dynasty of Babylon and the son and successor of Samsu-iluna. His titles included 'descendant of Sumu-la-El, princely heir of Samsu-iluna, eternal seed of kingship, mighty king, king of Babylon, king of the land of Sumer and Akkad, king who makes the four quarters be at peace', a state of affairs presumably achieved by two aggressive military campaigns. His fourth year-name records that he subdued the army of the Kassites. The Chronicle of Early Kings recalls that he dammed the Tigris River in a vain attempt to capture Ilum-ma-ili, the founder of the Sealand Dynasty. Early in his reign the Elamites under their king Kutir-nahhunte I raided into Babylon and sacked 30 cities.

Two copies of a building inscription commemorate his work at Luhaia, a town founded by Hammurabi on the Arahtum canal north of Babylon, and an onyx eye stone is dedicated to the goddess Ningal. A clay cylinder fragment from Kish is tentatively assigned to him because the events it commemorates coincide with three of his year-names: the damming of the Tigris, the fashioning of a mace for Marduk and the digging of the Zubi canal. Cylinder seal impressions attest his officials, among them a diviner, a priest of the goddess Ninisina and an overseer of the merchants.

Abi-Eshuh died about 1684 BCE. His son Ammi-ditana called him the great champion in an inscription, and he appears in the genealogy of his descendant Ammi-saduqa. The Uruk List of Kings and Sages records that Gimil-Gula and Taqis-Gula were the scholars of his reign.
abidjan: Abidjan lies on the south-east coast of Ivory Coast, on the Gulf of Guinea, around the Ébrié Lagoon, which divides it into a northern and a southern half. Le Plateau is the business district, and Port Bouët in the south holds the airport and main seaport. According to the oral tradition of the Tchaman, the name came from a misunderstanding: an old man cutting leaves, asked the name of the village by a European, fled shouting a phrase in Ebrié meaning 'I just cut the leaves'.

Abidjan was originally a small Atchan fishing village. In 1896, after deadly yellow fever epidemics, French colonists who had settled at Grand-Bassam decided to move to a safer place, and in 1898 they chose the site of Abidjan. It officially became a town in 1903, while nearby Bingerville served as capital of the colony from 1900 until 1934. The city grew quickly after a new wharf was built in 1931, and the Vridi Canal later made it an important sea port.

Abidjan became a municipality in 1956, with Félix Houphouët-Boigny as first mayor. At independence in 1960 it became the country's administrative and economic centre, and its population grew from 180,000 in 1960 to 1,269,000 in 1978. In 1983 Yamoussoukro was designated the official political capital, but many government institutions and all foreign embassies stayed in Abidjan.

Abidjan is the largest city of Ivory Coast and its economic capital, with 6,321,017 inhabitants in the Abidjan Autonomous District at the census of 14 December 2021. It is the most populous French-speaking city in West Africa; about sixty languages are spoken, the traditional language of the region is Ebrié, and Dioula has long been the trading lingua franca. Christians and followers of Islam make up nearly equal shares of the population. The African Development Bank is headquartered there.
abimael-guzman: Manuel Rubén Abimael Guzmán Reinoso was born on 3 December 1934 in Mollendo, a port in the province of Islay, in the Arequipa region. He was the illegitimate son of an accountant who had ten children with five women, and his mother died when he was five. He completed degrees in philosophy and law at Arequipa, then a doctorate.

In 1962 the rector of San Cristóbal of Huamanga University in Ayacucho, the anthropologist Efraín Morote Best, recruited him as a professor of philosophy, and he studied Quechua. He attended a cadre training course in China in 1965 and returned there in 1967, during the Cultural Revolution, which made a large impression on him.

He took a pro-Chinese line when the Peruvian Communist Party split, and emerged as the leader of the faction called the Shining Path, a phrase taken from Mariátegui. He adopted the name Comrade or Chairman Gonzalo, and his followers called him the Fourth Sword of Communism after Lenin, Stalin and Mao.

On 17 May 1980 the group began its war by burning ballot boxes at Chuschi, near Ayacucho, to disrupt Peru's first democratic elections since 1964. It came to control large rural areas of central and southern Peru and attacked the army, police, officials, other leftists such as the Túpac Amaru Revolutionary Movement, and peasants who cooperated with the government. The Truth and Reconciliation Commission estimated that about seventy thousand people died, around half at the hands of the Shining Path and a third at the hands of the state. A car bomb on Tarata street in Lima in 1992 caused many casualties; Guzmán denied responsibility.

Police under President Alberto Fujimori watched a house in the Surco district of Lima, used as a ballet studio, and on 12 September 1992 raided it and arrested him with eight others. A military tribunal tried him in secret and sentenced him to life imprisonment. On 1 October 1993 he publicly declared peace with the government, and about 6,000 guerrillas accepted this as defeat and surrendered. His retrial began in November 2004 and he was again sentenced to life on 13 October 2006. In 2018 he received a second life term for the Tarata bombing, in which 25 people died.
He died on 11 September 2021 at the Callao Naval Base, aged 86. His body was cremated on 24 September and his ashes dispersed in a secret place, to prevent a monument to him.
abkhaz-people: Some scholars say the ancient Heniochi tribe were the progenitors of the Abkhaz. This warlike people came into contact with the Greeks through the Greek colonies of Dioskourias and Pitiuntas. In the Roman period the Abasgoi, or Abasgi, are mentioned as inhabiting the region, and Procopius described them as warlike worshippers of three deities.

The Abasgi lived within the Lazian Empire, also called Egrisi, a state in western Georgia. Their monarch was appointed by the Laz king with the approval of the Byzantine emperor. After Egrisi declined, the Abasgian prince Leon I acquired it with Byzantine support in the 7th century, and Abasgia became a kingdom with its capital at Kutaisi. It soon adopted Georgian in place of Greek, and in 978 Abkhazia united with the eastern Georgian kingdom through dynastic succession, forming the Kingdom of Georgia.

Christianity became the dominant religion of the Abkhaz in the 6th century, under the Byzantine emperor Justinian I, and was followed under the kings of Georgia in the High Middle Ages. The region came under the Ottoman Empire in the 16th century, which introduced Islam, and the population gradually became Muslim in the 16th and 17th centuries.

The Russian conquest, from the 1810s to the 1860s, was accompanied by a mass expulsion of Muslim Abkhaz to the Ottoman Empire; Christian Abkhaz were largely spared. A strong policy of Russification followed, and Russian replaced Georgian as the second language of the Abkhaz, which alienated them from Georgians despite their common heritage. As a result the Abkhaz diaspora is estimated at no less than twice the number living in Abkhazia. Some Abkhaz fought for Greece during the Greco-Turkish War of 1919 to 1922, and thousands then fled persecution to Greece. The war in Abkhazia of 1992 and 1993 left the Abkhaz an ethnic plurality of about 45 percent.

The Abkhaz language belongs to the Northwest Caucasian family, also called Abkhaz–Adyghe or Pontic, and the Abkhaz are closely related to Circassians and Abazins. There are three subgroups: the Bzyb, living by the Bzyb River; the Abzhui, living by the Kodori River, whose dialect is the basis of the literary language; and the Samurzakan in the southeast. The traditional economy rests on cattle breeding, beekeeping, viticulture and agriculture.

The Abkhaz are divided mainly between Orthodox Christian and Sunni Muslim of the Hanafi school, prevalent in Abkhazia and in Turkey respectively, though indigenous non-Abrahamic beliefs have always been strong. Many Abkhaz villages, some 250 Abkhaz-Abaza ones by one estimate, lie in Turkey, and the community there is believed to be larger than that in Abkhazia. In Egypt the Abaza family, which originated in Abkhazia, has contributed to political and literary life since the reign of Muhammad Ali Pasha.
abo-blood-group-system: Karl Landsteiner was working at the Pathological-Anatomical Institute of the University of Vienna when he noticed in 1900 that red blood cells clumped together, or agglutinated, when mixed in test tubes with sera from different persons. He recorded it in a two-sentence footnote, which left open whether it reflected inborn differences between individuals or some damage of bacterial kind.

It was the first evidence that human blood varies, since all humans had been believed to have similar blood. In 1910 Ludwik Hirszfeld and Emil Freiherr von Dungern introduced the term 0 (null) for his group C and AB for the fourth type, and were the first to explain how the groups are inherited.

The system is controlled by a single gene, the ABO gene, on the long arm of the ninth chromosome. Its three classical alleles are IA, IB and i, and the gene encodes a glycosyltransferase, an enzyme that modifies the carbohydrate content of the red blood cell antigens. The IA allele gives type A, IB gives type B and i gives type O.

Because A and B are codominant, a type A and a type B parent can have an AB child. Felix Bernstein demonstrated the pattern of multiple alleles at one locus in 1924. The A type has about 20 subgroups, of which A1 makes up about 80 per cent of all A-type blood. Rare variants include the Bombay phenotype and cis-AB.

Naming caused trouble for years. In 1907 the Czech serologist Jan Janský independently classified blood with the Roman numerals I to IV, while the American physician William L. Moss used the same numerals for a different order. Moss's system was adopted in Britain, France and the US, and Janský's in most European countries, which created confusion and danger in medical practice. A joint recommendation of 1921 favoured Janský's but was not followed where Moss's had been used.

In 1927 Landsteiner, by then at the Rockefeller Institute for Medical Research in New York, proposed the letters O, A, B and AB, and by the early 1950s they were universal. The American physician Reuben Ottenberg first used blood typing in transfusion in 1907, and large-scale use began in the First World War, once citric acid was used to prevent clotting.
abolition-of-the-ottoman-sultanate: The Ottoman Empire entered the First World War on 11 November 1914, and the Armistice of Mudros of 30 October 1918 ended its Middle Eastern war. British, French and Italian forces occupied Istanbul on 13 November 1918. After British troops occupied key buildings and arrested nationalists in March 1920, the Ottoman parliament prorogued itself, and Sultan Mehmed VI dissolved it on 11 April 1920, leaving the Istanbul government to act without a parliament.

The Treaty of Sèvres of 10 August 1920 finalised the partition of the empire. The Turkish national movement under Mustafa Kemal had set up the Grand National Assembly in Ankara on 23 April 1920, and it fought the Turkish War of Independence against the Istanbul government, whose Army of the Caliphate, armed by the British, was defeated.

The Allies invited both the Constantinople and Ankara governments to the Conference of Lausanne, but Mustafa Kemal was determined that only Ankara should be represented. On 1 November 1922 the Grand National Assembly declared that the Constantinople government was no longer the legal representative of the nation and that the sultanate was abolished, which ended the Ottoman Empire and the dynasty of Osman I that had ruled since 1299. On 11 November 1922 the Conference of Lausanne recognised the sovereignty of the Grand National Assembly. Mehmed VI left Constantinople on 17 November aboard the British warship HMS Malaya, and the remaining ministers accepted the new situation. No official document records a capitulation: the system dissolved itself.

The Treaty of Lausanne was signed on 24 July 1923. A list of 600 names, a who's who of the Ottoman Empire, was presented at the conference for declaration as personae non gratae, and negotiations reduced it to 150. The Grand National Assembly proclaimed the Republic of Turkey on 29 October 1923. The caliphate, held by the Ottoman dynasty since Selim I, passed to Mehmed's cousin Abdülmecid II and was abolished in March 1924, ending the last remnant of the monarchy. An exile list of 120 adherents of the deposed dynasty took effect on 23 April 1924.
abomey: Abomey, also called Agbome, was founded in the 17th century as the capital of the Kingdom of Dahomey, on the site of the former village of Kana. Traditional legends say the town was founded by Do-Aklin, a son of the king of Allada who ventured north to found his own kingdom.
