The name is thought to come from Danhomé, meaning belly of Dan, Dan being the original chief of the village.

Dahomey expanded rapidly in the 1700s, absorbing many surrounding kingdoms and growing rich from the slave trade. In the late 18th century a dry ditch alone surrounded Abomey, while the royal palaces had a mudbrick wall 20 feet high. By the 1840s it had an estimated population of 24,000. The French conquered the kingdom on 16 November 1892, and King Béhanzin torched the city and fled northward. The town then declined, as the French built a new administrative centre at Bohicon, to the east.

Abomey is the capital of the Zou Department of Benin and remains a centre for crafts. It houses the Royal Palaces of Abomey, earthen structures built by the Fon people between the mid-17th and late 19th centuries. UNESCO states that twelve kings ruled from 1625 to 1900, each building a palace within the same cob-wall area, except Akaba. Under Béhanzin the palaces covered some 44 hectares behind a wall 10 metres high and 4 kilometres long; only two of the twelve palaces survived the burning of 1892. The site became a World Heritage Site in 1985. Fifty of the 56 bas-reliefs of King Glèlè's palace have been replaced on the rebuilt structure.
aboriginal-australians: Archaeological evidence indicates that the ancestors of Aboriginal Australians first migrated to the continent 50,000 to 65,000 years ago. They reached it when it formed part of the Sahul continent, joined to New Guinea by a land bridge, though the journey still required crossing the sea at the Wallace Line. A 2021 modelling study suggests the first people may have landed in the Kimberley about 60,000 years ago and settled across the continent within 6,000 years.

Rising seas at the start of the Holocene, about 11,700 years ago, flooded large areas of the continental shelf where Aboriginal people had lived, separating Tasmania from the mainland. Aboriginal Australians and Papuans, who shared Sahul, became genetically distinct about 37,000 years ago. Aboriginal people may have one of the oldest continuous cultures on earth: in Arnhem Land the Yolngu have passed on oral histories through hundreds of generations.

Over the millennia Aboriginal people formed as many as 500 linguistic and territorial groups and developed trade networks, law and religion. At the time of European colonisation they spoke more than 250 languages. The population at first European settlement is estimated at no fewer than 314,500. After contact it declined until it reached a low in 1921, then recovered and passed the pre-contact figure by the end of the 20th century.

Before British colonisation there were perhaps five to sixteen languages in Tasmania, and the last speaker of a traditional Tasmanian language, Fanny Cochrane Smith, died in 1905. English-based creoles have arisen since contact, Kriol among them. In the 1970s and 1980s the outstation movement saw Aboriginal people move to small remote settlements on traditional land.

Languages and their groups are connected with stretches of territory known as Country, with which Aboriginal people have a profound spiritual connection. The anthropologist Harry Lourandos describes three main cultural areas, Northern, Southern and Central; the first two, richer in marine and woodland resources, were more densely populated. Group names include Koori in New South Wales and Victoria, Murri in Queensland and Noongar in southern Western Australia.

Traditional beliefs are passed on through dancing, stories, songlines and art, which together express the Dreaming, an account of ancient creation and daily life. Aboriginal identity has varied over time and place, with family lineage, self-identification and community acceptance of differing importance.
aboriginal-tasmanians: Aboriginal Tasmanians crossed into what is now Tasmania about 35,000 years ago, in the Late Pleistocene, when low sea levels in the Last Glacial Period exposed the Bassian Plain, a broad land bridge to the mainland. Rising seas later formed Bass Strait and left the island's communities isolated from the other Aboriginal groups of the mainland.

Before British colonisation in 1803 they kept distinct languages, cultural traditions and regional identities, organised in family groups and clans tied to particular territories and seasonal movements. A clan had a name of its own and comprised 40 to 50 people. They were mainly nomadic, following the seasons' supplies of seafood, land mammals, vegetables and berries. Estimates of the population before colonisation generally range from 3,000 to 15,000.

British and American sealers began visiting the Bass Strait islands in the late 1790s, and the first significant European presence on the main island was a small military outpost at Risdon Cove in September 1803. Conflict came in phases. Between 1803 and 1808 it concerned common food sources such as oysters and kangaroos, and from 1808 to 1823 farmers, sealers and whalers traded in and abducted Aboriginal women. Disease also took a toll; historians differ over how soon and how far, with Geoffrey Blainey and Keith Windschuttle naming introduced disease as the main cause of the decline.

Pastoral expansion and the loss of game brought armed resistance from 1824. In 1826 the government gazette began to report acts of atrocity, and a proclamation of 1828 established military posts and then declared martial law. Aboriginal people needed passes to cross settled districts, and bounties of £5 for an adult and £2 for a child were offered for those captured without one, which often led to organised hunts.

Between 1830 and 1835 most survivors were removed to the Wybalenna Aboriginal Establishment on Flinders Island. The first 51 had been brought in late 1831 to The Lagoons, which was exposed and had little water, and children aged 6 to 15 were taken from their families. In October 1847 the 47 survivors were moved to Oyster Cove.

Colonial writers and popular media wrongly described Aboriginal Tasmanians as extinct after the deaths of Truganini in 1876 and Fanny Cochrane Smith in 1905, each presented as the last. The community survived through descendants of Aboriginal women and European sealers in the Bass Strait islands, and thousands of people in Tasmania identify as Aboriginal Tasmanian. Historians continue to debate whether the events of colonisation amounted to genocide under the United Nations Genocide Convention.

The original languages are no longer spoken fluently. They survive in fragmentary wordlists recorded in inconsistent spellings by visitors and colonists, from which Palawa communities have built palawa kani, a reconstructed composite language.
abraha: Abraha, also called Abraha al-Ashram, was an Aksumite viceroy of Himyar in the 6th century. He took part in the Aksumite invasion of Himyar between 525 and 530, then overthrew the Himyarite king Sumyafa Ashwa and crowned himself ruler. Accounts of his background differ. The Byzantine historian Procopius calls him the former slave of a Roman merchant in Adulis, while the Muslim historian al-Tabari says he was related to the Aksumite royal family. Al-Tabari makes him commander of the second army sent by King Kaleb of Axum after the first, under Ariat, had failed.

According to Procopius, Abraha took Yemen with the support of dissident Aksumite soldiers who wanted to settle in South Arabia, an army sent by Kaleb joined him, and a second was defeated, so that Kaleb had to accept him in fact. His reign is documented in inscriptions. The most detailed, dated 548, records the suppression of a rebellion by Yazid, the governor of Kinda, and by Sabaean and Himyarite princes, the repair of the Marib Dam and an international conference at Marib attended by delegations from Aksum, the Sasanian and Byzantine empires, the Lakhmid Kingdom and the Ghassanids.

An inscription of 552 describes campaigns against the Banu Amir and the Ma'add in central Arabia, with hostages given at Haliban. Another inscription claims that he took the Arabs of Ma'add, Hagar, Khatt, Tayy, Yathrib and Judham.

He styled himself the Agazian King as well as using the long titles of the Himyarite kings. His sons, who succeeded him, lacked his ambition and left no known inscriptions, and the empire did not last long. The last dated Himyarite text, of 559 to 560, belongs to his reign. Christian Robin argues that Abraha probably died by 570.

Islamic tradition tells of a campaign against Mecca with elephants, the Year of the Elephant, which later served the people of Mecca as a starting point for dating events, and links it with Surah al-Fil. In that account he built a church called Al-Qalis at Sanaa, a man of the Kinana defiled it, and Abraha marched north with an elephant and about 13 in all, until birds dropped stones on his army. Outside Islamic tradition the expedition is not mentioned, not even in his inscriptions, and many historians regard the story as a later explanation of the surah. Iwona Gajda connects a newly found inscription with the expedition, dated to 552, and Christian Robin finds a failed expedition plausible.
abraham-accords: The Abraham Accords were preceded by earlier diplomatic milestones between Israel and members of the Arab League: peace treaties with Egypt in 1979 and Jordan in 1994, and relations with Mauritania in 1995. The Oslo Accords of 1993 and 1995 advanced the Israeli–Palestinian peace process, which later collapsed. The Arab Peace Initiative of 2002 offered normalisation of relations between the Arab world and Israel in return for a full Israeli withdrawal from the occupied territories, a settlement of the refugee question and a Palestinian state with East Jerusalem as its capital.

In the 2010s Israel and Sunni Arab states drew closer through shared concern about Iran, and by 2016 summits and contacts between officials and security services were openly discussed in major Arab media. In October 2018 the Omani foreign minister visited Jerusalem, and Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu visited Oman. In January 2020 the United States published a peace plan that foresaw Israeli sovereignty over parts of the West Bank.

When Netanyahu's cabinet considered annexing parts of the West Bank in mid-2020, the Emirati ambassador to the United States, Yousef Al Otaiba, warned in a newspaper article that it would end normalisation with the Emirates and other Arab states. At the end of June he told the American officials Jared Kushner and Avi Berkowitz that the United Arab Emirates would agree to normalisation if Israel declared annexation off the table. The agreement was announced on 13 August 2020, and annexation was postponed. Within hours Bahraini officials told Kushner and Berkowitz that they wanted to be next, and that deal was closed on 11 September 2020.

Netanyahu and the foreign ministers of the Emirates and Bahrain, Abdullah bin Zayed Al Nahyan and Abdullatif bin Rashid Al Zayani, signed the agreements on 15 September 2020 on the Truman Balcony of the White House, in a ceremony mediated by President Donald Trump. The name was chosen to reflect the shared heritage of the Abrahamic religions, Christianity, Islam and Judaism.

Israel and Sudan agreed to normalise ties on 23 October 2020. As part of that agreement the United States removed Sudan from its list of state sponsors of terrorism and gave it a loan of 1.2 billion US dollars, and Sudan agreed to pay 335 million dollars in compensation to American victims of terror. On 10 December 2020 Trump announced an agreement between Israel and Morocco, which came with American recognition of Moroccan sovereignty over Western Sahara. Governments in the Arab world expressed support, while public opinion in many countries remained opposed, particularly because the Accords made no progress on the Israeli–Palestinian conflict.
abraham-kuyper: Abraham Kuyper was born on 29 October 1837 in Maassluis, the son of Jan Frederik Kuyper, a minister of the Dutch Reformed Church. His father taught him at home, and he attended the Gymnasium of Leiden before studying literature, philosophy and theology at Leiden University. In 1862 he received a doctorate in theology for a dissertation comparing the church views of John Calvin and Jan Łaski, showing sympathy for the more liberal Łaski.

In 1863 he became minister at Beesd and married Johanna Hendrika Schaay. A correspondence begun in 1864 with the anti-revolutionary member of parliament Guillaume Groen van Prinsterer shaped his political and theological views. Around 1866 he turned to the orthodox tendency in the church, and he later served in Utrecht and, from 1870, Amsterdam. He founded the newspaper De Standaard in 1872.

Elected to parliament in a by-election in 1874, Kuyper took a special interest in the equal financing of public and religious schools. His programme Our Program of 1876 laid the foundation for the Anti-Revolutionary Party, which he led from 1879 and which he served as chairman until 1905. Suspended with about eighty members of the Amsterdam consistory in December 1885, he led an exodus from the Dutch Reformed Church in 1886, the Doleantie. In 1892 it merged with the churches of the Secession of 1834 to form the Reformed Churches in the Netherlands.

As prime minister from 1901 he also held the interior portfolio. He pushed harsh laws through parliament against the 1903 railway strike, improved the finances of religious schools and secured equal recognition of diplomas from faith-based universities after dissolving the Senate. His party lost the election of 1905. He became minister of state in 1908, sat in the Senate from 1913 and died in The Hague on 8 November 1920.

Kuyper developed neo-Calvinism and the principle of common grace. In his Stone Lectures at Princeton in 1898 he argued that Calvinism was a comprehensive worldview. He declared that over every square inch of human existence Christ cries: Mine. His concept of sphere sovereignty rejected both the popular sovereignty of France and the state sovereignty of Germany and gave schools, the press, business and the arts each authority in its own sphere.

His principle of antithesis divided religious from secular politics. He saw Catholics as allies and liberals and socialists as opponents, and he wanted every faith community to run its own schools and institutions with equal state funding. The Protestant Church in the Netherlands, created in 2004, largely undid the Reformed Churches he founded. In South Africa his ideas were taken up by Afrikaner Christian nationalists.
abraham-lincoln: Abraham Lincoln was born on 12 February 1809 in a one-room log cabin in Kentucky, the second child of Thomas Lincoln and Nancy Hanks Lincoln, and was raised on farms near Hodgenville. His father bought several farms but could not secure clear titles to any, and in 1816 the family moved to Indiana, where land titles were more reliable. His parents belonged to a Separate Baptist church whose members largely opposed slavery. His mother died of milk sickness on 5 October 1818, and his father married Sarah Bush Johnston the following year; Lincoln became close to his stepmother. He married Mary Todd on 4 November 1842.

Lincoln served four terms in the Illinois House of Representatives from 1834, as a Whig and supporter of Henry Clay, and championed the Illinois and Michigan Canal. He won election to the U.S. House of Representatives in 1846 and served from 1847 to 1849. The Kansas–Nebraska Act of 1854, proposed by Senator Stephen A. Douglas, brought him back into political life. His Peoria Speech of October 1854 opposed slavery, and he became a leader of the new Republican Party. He reached a national audience in the 1858 Senate campaign debates with Douglas and won the 1860 presidential election.

Secession followed. South Carolina adopted an ordinance of secession on 20 December 1860, and six other states had followed by 1 February 1861, forming the Confederate States of America. Lincoln refused to recognise the Confederacy and declared secession illegal. He closely supervised the Union's strategy, including the choice of generals and a naval blockade of Southern ports. On 1 January 1863 he issued the Emancipation Proclamation, declaring slaves in states 'in rebellion' to be free. He delivered the Gettysburg Address on 19 November 1863, and he promoted the Thirteenth Amendment, which abolished chattel slavery in 1865.

On the evening of 14 April 1865, five days after the Confederate surrender at Appomattox, Lincoln attended the play Our American Cousin at Ford's Theatre in Washington. John Wilkes Booth, an actor and Confederate spy, entered his box at 10:15 pm and shot him in the back of the head. Lincoln was taken to the Petersen House across the street and died at 7:22 am on 15 April. He was the first U.S. president to be assassinated. His body lay in state in the White House and the Capitol, then travelled by funeral train to Springfield, Illinois, where crowds gathered along the route. The Lincoln Memorial on the National Mall was dedicated in 1922.
abruzzo: Abruzzo lies roughly in the middle of the Italian peninsula, from the heart of the Apennines to the Adriatic coast, with its western border with Lazio 80 km east of Rome. The west is mountainous and wild, with the Gran Sasso at 2,912 metres and Mount Majella at 2,793 metres, and the east is a coastal strip of sandy and pebbly beaches. The name probably comes from Aprutium, a popular form of (ad) Praetutium, the land of the Praetutii, an Italic people around present-day Teramo, a derivation first proposed by the Renaissance historian Flavio Biondo. Another suggestion links it to Latin abruptus, steep.

Flint tools show that archaic humans lived in the region about 700,000 years ago, and Neanderthal remains come from caves at Calascio. By the end of the Iron Age several tribes lived there, among them the Oscan-speaking Pentri, Carricini and Frentani and the Aequi, Praetutii, Vestini, Marrucini, Marsi and Paeligni. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire and the Gothic War, the Lombards arrived, and around 572 they divided the area between the Duchy of Benevento and the Duchy of Spoleto, whose first duke was Faroald I of Spoleto.

In 1302 the Peace of Caltabellotta left the southern peninsula, Abruzzo included, to the Capetian House of Anjou. The people rebelled against the French invasion of 1798 and 1799, and in 1806 Napoleon's client kingdom split Abruzzo Ultra in two at the Gran Sasso. The Bourbons returned after the Congress of Vienna and founded the Kingdom of the Two Sicilies in 1816. Abruzzo joined the Kingdom of Sardinia in 1860 and the Kingdom of Italy in 1861, though some Bourbon supporters fought Garibaldi's volunteers and later joined in brigandage. In the Second World War the region lay on the Gustav Line, and the Battle of Ortona was among its most brutal fights.

Abruzzo is a region of Italy with a population of nearly 1.3 million, divided into four provinces named for L'Aquila, Teramo, Pescara and Chieti. L'Aquila is the regional capital and Pescara the largest city and major port. About half the territory is protected as national parks and nature reserves. The Museo Archeologico Nazionale d'Abruzzo in Chieti holds the Warrior of Capestrano, a statue from a necropolis of the 6th century BCE.
absalom: In the Hebrew Bible Absalom (Hebrew Avshalom, 'Father of Peace') is the third son of King David, born at Hebron to Maacah of Geshur. He is the only full sibling of Tamar, and both are described as exceptionally beautiful. He is also noted for his long hair. A verse in 2 Samuel records him saying that he had no son to keep his name in remembrance, and the text names a daughter, Tamar.

The narrative of 2 Samuel 13 begins when Tamar is raped by her paternal half-brother Amnon, David's eldest son. David is angered but at first does nothing, since Amnon is his heir. Absalom waits two years, then has his servants kill Amnon, who is drunk, at a feast to which all the king's sons were invited. He flees to his grandfather Talmai, king of Geshur, and is fully reinstated in David's favour only three years later.

Back in Jerusalem, Absalom built support by speaking to those who came to the king for justice, telling them their claims were good but that no one was deputed to hear them. He greeted petitioners with kisses and so, in the text's phrase, stole the hearts of the people of Israel. Some interpreters see in this a reflection of flaws in the judicial system of the united monarchy.

After four years he declared himself king and raised a revolt at Hebron, the former capital. All Israel and Judah are said to have flocked to him, leaving David with only the Cherethites and Pelethites and his bodyguard from Gath. The priests Zadok and Abiathar stayed in Jerusalem, their sons serving as David's spies. Absalom entered the capital, publicly took his father's ten concubines, and consulted the counsellor Ahitophel, who may, it has been suggested, have been moved by David's adultery with his granddaughter Bathsheba.

The revolt ended at the Battle of the Wood of Ephraim, where David's nephew and army commander Joab killed Absalom. Tamar is left, in the text's words, a desolate woman in her brother's house, guardian of his orphaned daughter. Rabbinic writers made his life a warning against false ambition and unfilial conduct, and held that his hair became his snare.

The story has been retold often. George Peele wrote a play on it, published in 1599, and John Dryden's satirical poem Absalom and Achitophel (1681) used it as an allegory for contemporary politics. Artists such as Guercino and Cabanel painted Tamar's story, and William Faulkner's novel Absalom, Absalom! takes its title from it.
absalon: Absalon was born around 1128 near Sorø on Zealand, the son of Asser Rig, a magnate of the Hvide clan from Fjenneslev, and Inger Eriksdotter. He was a kinsman of Archbishop Eskil of Lund. He grew up at his father's castle alongside his older brother Esbern Snare and the young prince Valdemar, later Valdemar I of Denmark. During the civil war after the death of Eric III in 1146 he studied theology in Paris, where he absorbed the Gregorian Reform ideal of the church's independence from monarchical rule, while Esbern fought for Valdemar's claim to the throne.

He first appears in Saxo Grammaticus's chronicle at the end of the civil war, helping to broker the peace between Sweyn III and Valdemar at Odense. He and Valdemar narrowly escaped assassination at Sweyn's banquet at Roskilde in 1157. After Valdemar won the throne, Absalon was elected bishop of Roskilde in 1158, the king's reward for Hvide support.

Absalon was Valdemar's close counsellor and the chief promoter of the Danish crusades against the Wends, whose raids had left a third of Denmark wasted and depopulated by Valdemar's accession. He formed a guardian fleet, built coastal defences and led his first expedition in 1160. The crusades lasted from 1164 for twenty years. In 1168 the fortress at Arkona on Rügen, with the sanctuary of Svantevit, was conquered, and the people of Rügen accepted Danish suzerainty and the Christian religion. At Charenza the garrison surrendered, and Absalon had the idol of Rugievit cut down and burned. In 1184 he defeated a Pomeranian fleet off Stralsund.

Absalon wished to free Denmark from entanglement with the Holy Roman Empire and warned against Valdemar's fealty to Frederick Barbarossa at Dole in 1162. In 1167 he was granted the land around Havn and built a castle there, from which Copenhagen grew. He held the first Danish synod at Lund in 1167 and commissioned Saxo's Gesta Danorum. In 1178, at the pope's order, he became archbishop of Lund, keeping Roskilde by dispensation. Under Canute VI, from 1182, he was the chief policymaker.

Absalon gave up military command in 1184 and in 1192 made his nephew Peder Sunesen bishop of Roskilde, while another nephew, Anders Sunesen, became chancellor and later his successor at Lund. He died at Sorø Abbey on 21 March 1201 and was buried there. He had given Copenhagen to the bishopric of Roskilde and left his holdings to the abbey. He is regarded as the foremost politician and churchman of 12th-century Denmark, and his expansion gave Denmark dominion of the Baltic for three generations.
absheron-peninsula: The Absheron Peninsula extends 60 kilometres eastward into the Caspian Sea and reaches a maximum width of 30 kilometres. Azerbaijan's outline is often compared to an eagle, with Absheron as its beak. The peninsula is technically the easternmost extension of the Caucasus Mountains, but its landscape is only mildly hilly, a gently undulating plain cut by ravines and dotted with salt lakes. It ends in a long spit of dunes called Shah Dili, the Shah Spit, the easternmost point of mainland Azerbaijan, now the Absheron National Park.

The climate is temperate and semi-arid, with warm, dry summers, cool and occasionally wet winters and strong winds throughout the year. Annual rainfall is about 200 millimetres or less, which makes it the driest part of Azerbaijan. The natural vegetation is dry steppe and semi-desert, and farming depends on irrigation. The ground consists of layers of clays, sandy clays, sands and limestones, and fresh groundwater is scarce because the thick clays hold highly mineralised water.

The name comes from the Persian ab shuran, meaning salty waters. Conrad Malte-Brun noted in 1810 that the peninsula also had the name Okoressa. Beginning in the 1870s Absheron was the site of some of the world's earliest petroleum production. The exploitation of its oil in the late 19th century drew large numbers of Iranian labourers to the Caucasus and Central Asia.

Absheron holds Baku, the most populous city of Azerbaijan, and the Baku metropolitan area with its satellite cities Sumqayit and Khyrdalan. It is divided into districts, two of them urban (Baku and Sumqayit) and others suburban, among them Absheron, Pirallahi and Khazar. Much of the landscape is still scarred with rusting oil derricks, and the petrochemical and refining industries have left their mark on the Caspian shore and the sea.
abu-al-abbas-al-saffah: Al-Saffah was born at al-Humayma, in present-day Jordan, in 721 or 722. He headed one branch of the Banu Hashim, a sub-clan of the Quraysh descended from Hashim, a great-grandfather of Muhammad, through al-Abbas, an uncle of the Prophet; hence the name Abbasid. This indirect link to Muhammad's clan was the basis of his claim to the caliphate.

Many believed, on the strength of hadith, that in the end times a leader or mahdi from Muhammad's family would deliver Islam from corrupt leadership. The Umayyad caliphs' half-hearted tolerance of non-Arab Muslims and Shi'as had failed to quell unrest, which produced a Shi'a revolt in Kufa under Zayd ibn Ali, put down in 740. The Abbasids chose to begin their rebellion in Khorasan, a remote but important military region.

In early October 749 al-Saffah's army entered Kufa. In February 750 it defeated the Umayyad caliph Marwan II at the Battle of the Zab, effectively ending a dynasty that had ruled since 661. Marwan fled and was killed in Egypt that August. Al-Saffah did not come forward to receive the people's pledge of allegiance until Marwan and many Umayyad princes were dead. He made Kufa his capital, ending the dominance of Damascus, and called himself al-Saffah, the Blood-Shedder, in his inaugural address in its Great Mosque.

Later tales say he invited the remaining Umayyads to a dinner and had them clubbed to death; the one survivor, Abd al-Rahman ibn Mu'awiya, reached al-Andalus, where Umayyad rule lasted three more centuries. Apart from his policy toward the Umayyads, historians widely regard him as a mild victor. Jews, Eastern Christians and Persians served in his government, and his army admitted non-Muslims and non-Arabs, whom the Umayyads had refused. In 751 Abbasid forces defeated the Tang army at the Battle of Talas, after the Karluk Turks changed sides; Muslim control of Transoxiana followed.

Al-Saffah died of smallpox on 8 June 754, on his way to Mecca. His own son was too young, so he named his brother Abu Ja'far as heir. His uncle Abd Allah ibn Ali, who had assembled an army for a campaign against the Byzantines, proclaimed himself caliph, claiming al-Saffah had promised him the succession. Abu Ja'far, who took the name al-Mansur, ruled until 775; he imprisoned his uncle in 754 and had him killed in 764.
abu-al-fida: Abu al-Fida was born in Damascus in November 1273. His father, al-Malik al-Afdal, was a brother of the emir al-Mansur Muhammad II of Hama and had fled there from the Mongols. He was an Ayyubid prince of Kurdish origin. In boyhood he studied the Qur'an and the sciences, but from his twelfth year he was almost constantly engaged in military expeditions, chiefly against the Crusaders. In 1285 he was present at the attack on a stronghold of the Knights of St. John, and he took part in the sieges of Tripoli, Acre and Qal'at ar-Rum.

In 1298 he entered the service of the Mamluk sultan al-Malik al-Nasir, who after twelve years invested him with the governorship of Hama. In 1312 he became prince with the title al-Malik al-Salih, and in 1320 he received the hereditary rank of sultan with a further title. He died on 27 October 1331.

His geography, Taqwim al-Buldan, written in 1321, draws on earlier works including those of Ptolemy and Muhammad al-Idrisi. A long introduction is followed by twenty-eight sections that list the chief towns of the world in tables, giving longitude, latitude, climate, spelling and observations usually taken from earlier authors. Parts were published and translated in Europe as early as 1650. It also contains the first known explanation of the circumnavigator's paradox: a person travelling westward round the world counts one day fewer than a stationary observer, and one travelling eastward one day more.

His Concise History of Humanity was written between 1315 and 1329 as a continuation of Ali ibn al-Athir's Complete History. It is in the form of annals from the creation of the world to 1329, in two parts, on pre-Islamic Arabia and on the history of Islam. Other Arab historians carried it on, Ibn al-Wardi to 1348 and Ibn al-Shihna to 1403. It was translated into Latin, French and English and was the main work of Muslim historiography used by 18th-century orientalists.
abu-al-hasan-ali-ibn-othman: Abu al-Hasan was the son of the Marinid ruler Abu Sa'id Uthman II, whom he succeeded in 1331. According to the chronicler al-Baydhaq his mother was a woman of Fes called Fatima, and his dark complexion earned him the name of the Black Sultan. He married Fatima, daughter of the Hafsid ruler Abu Yahya Abu Bakr II of Ifriqiya, sealing an alliance against the Zayyanid dynasty of Tlemcen.

In 1333, answering an appeal from Muhammad IV of Granada, he sent an army of 7,000 under his son Abd al-Malik across the strait to besiege Gibraltar, held by Castile since 1309. Its starving defenders, reduced to eating leather, surrendered on 17 June 1333. When Ibn Tashufin of Tlemcen attacked the Hafsids, Abu al-Hasan invaded in early 1335 and besieged Tlemcen for two years, turning his camp into a city beside it; Ibn Tashufin died in the final assault, and the conquest gave the Marinids control of the trans-Saharan trade.

In 1339 Yusuf I of Granada called on him against Castile. His fleet destroyed a Castilian squadron off Gibraltar on 5 April 1340, and in September his army joined Yusuf's to besiege Tarifa. A Portuguese and Genoese fleet cut his supply line, and Afonso IV of Portugal and Alfonso XI of Castile then defeated him; he made no further campaigns in Iberia, and Alfonso XI took Algeciras in March 1344. After the Hafsid sultan Abu Bakr died in 1346, Abu al-Hasan's army swept through Ifriqiya, and contemporaries compared his realm with that of the Almohad Caliphate.

His attempt to impose his authority on the Arab tribes led to their revolt. After the defeat of April 1348, his son Abu Inan Faris declared himself sultan in Fes, his fleet was wrecked by a storm off Bougie, and the Zayyanid princes beat him near the Chelif River. Defeated again by Abu Inan on the Oum er-Rebia in May 1350, he took refuge among the Hintata tribes of the High Atlas and abdicated in late 1350 or early 1351. He died there in May 1351, and Abu Inan had his body carried to the Marinid necropolis at Chellah.
abu-al-misk-kafur: Kafur was a black slave, most likely of Nubian origin: modern research places his homeland between the Nuba Mountains and the west of the White Nile, and the History of the Patriarchs of Alexandria says he was captured in the lands of Nubia. His name, meaning camphor in Arabic, contrasted the whiteness of camphor with his dark skin, while the kunya Abu al-Misk means Father of Musk.

Muhammad ibn Tughj, founder of the Ikhshidid dynasty, bought him in 923 for eighteen dinars, though other accounts say he was a gift. Noticing his intelligence, Ibn Tughj had him educated, freed him and made him tutor of his two sons, and Kafur took the nisba al-Ikhshidi. He led a military mission to Syria in 945, commanded campaigns in the Hejaz and took part in diplomatic exchanges with the caliph in Baghdad.

Named guardian of the two sons on Ibn Tughj's deathbed, Kafur helped the elder, Anūdjūr, secure the succession in 946 and the younger, ʿAlī ibn al-Ikhshīd, in 961, ruling behind them. He put down the rebellion of Ghalbūn in 947 and 948, averted an attempted coup by Anūdjūr in 954 and withstood Ismāʿīlī propaganda against him. Abroad he secured Damascus from the Hamdanids in 947 and checked Sayf al-Dawla of Aleppo, who came to recognise his lordship over parts of Syria, while holding off the Fatimids, Qarmatians and Nubians.

His administration avoided extortionate taxation and kept the gold coinage fairly stable despite a fire that devastated the business quarter of Fustat in 954, an earthquake in 955 or early 956 and repeated food-price inflation, at times with famine. He employed able administrators and merchants such as Yaqub ibn Killis, built two mosques, in Giza and on al-Muqattam, a hospital, palaces and the Kafuriyya gardens, and kept a luxurious court.

Kafur died in April 968 and was buried in Jerusalem beside the Ikhshidid emirs, near the Gate of the Tribes on the Haram al-Sharif. Later historians portrayed him as a just and moderate ruler, and his rise from African slave to ruler of Egypt and parts of Syria is one of the earliest examples in Islamic history of a sovereign of the lowliest origins. Much of his fame, however, comes from the satires of al-Mutanabbi, who turned on him after Kafur failed to give him the high office he wanted. No archaeological remains of his buildings have been found.
abu-bakr-al-siddiq: Abu Bakr was born in Mecca into a rich family of the Banu Taym, part of the Quraysh tribal confederacy. His father was Abu Quhafa and his mother Umm al-Khayr, and through his father's line his ancestry meets that of Muhammad at Murrah ibn Ka'b. His love of camels earned him the nickname Abu Bakr, father of the camel's calf. He was a wholesale trader in cloth. According to Ibn Kathir he was the first free adult man to embrace Islam, and several leading companions, among them Uthman ibn Affan, converted through his preaching.

According to Islamic tradition Muhammad was commanded in 613 to call people to Islam openly, and Abu Bakr delivered the first public address inviting people to offer allegiance to Muhammad. Young men of the Quraysh beat him until he lost consciousness. In 622 he accompanied Muhammad to Medina, and they took refuge in a cave on Jabal Thawr while the Quraysh sent out search parties. Muhammad appointed him amir al-hajj to lead about 300 pilgrims from Medina to Mecca in 630 or 631, and in his last illness told him to lead the prayers.

After Muhammad's death in 632, the Ansar gathered at the Saqifa of the Banu Sa'ida clan, and Abu Bakr succeeded as the first caliph. Revolts by several Arab tribes, known as the Ridda Wars or Wars of Apostasy, followed. Some were led by men who claimed prophethood, among them Tulayha ibn Khuwaylid and Musaylima. In 633 small forces were sent into Iraq and Palestine and captured several towns. After the Battle of al-Yamama Umar saw that some five hundred Muslims who had memorised the Quran had died, and Abu Bakr, at first hesitant, appointed Zayd ibn Thabit to gather the verses in writing.

On 23 August 634 Abu Bakr fell sick with a high fever and did not recover. He named Umar as his successor after consulting some companions, the first caliph to nominate one. He is buried with Muhammad and Umar in the Green Dome of the Prophet's Mosque in Medina. Sunni tradition regards him as the legitimate successor to Muhammad and the first of the Rightly Guided Caliphs. Shi'a tradition holds that Muhammad had designated Ali at Ghadir Khumm and that Abu Bakr's appointment bypassed Ali's rightful claim.
abu-bakr-ibn-umar: Abu Bakr belonged to the Banu Turgut, a clan of the Lamtuna Berbers. His uncle Yahya ibn Ibrahim, chieftain of the Lamtuna, had launched the Almoravid movement in the early 1040s with the Maliki scholar Abdallah ibn Yasin. When Yahya ibn Umar was killed at the Battle of Tabfarilla in the spring of 1056, Abdallah ibn Yasin appointed Abu Bakr military commander and amir of the Almoravids.

In late 1056 Abu Bakr recaptured Sijilmassa from the Maghrawa, then secured the routes of southern Morocco, taking the Draa valley and the Sous, with its capital Taroudannt, in 1057. An alliance with the Masmuda Berbers let the Almoravids cross the High Atlas and take Aghmat in 1058. When Abdallah ibn Yasin was killed among the Berghwata of western Morocco, Abu Bakr conquered them in a brutal campaign of revenge. Now sole leader, he claimed no religious authority and took the modest title amir al-Muslimin, Prince of the Muslims.

He married Zaynab an-Nafzawiyyah, the wealthiest woman of Aghmat, but found life in the town stifling. Around 1060 he and his lieutenants camped on the pastures by the Tensift River, and the camp grew into the city of Marrakesh, whose founding is credited to him. While his cousin Yusuf ibn Tashfin reduced the Zenata strongholds of the north, taking Fez in 1070, discontent spread among the desert clans. Abu Bakr went south to quell it, divorcing Zaynab, who then married Yusuf. When he returned in 1072, Yusuf persuaded him with gifts of gold and cattle to leave the north to him, though he kept Abu Bakr's name on the coinage.

Mauritanian oral tradition holds that he was killed by a poisoned arrow shot by an old, blind Gangara chieftain in the pass of Khma, on the way to Ghana, and places his grave at Maksam in the Tagant region; a Wolof tradition names a Serer bowman, Amar Godomat, near Lake Rkiz. The date of 1087 follows the chronicler Ibn Abi Zar and is supported by coins minted at Sijilmassa in his name until then. Oral tradition also makes Ndiadiane Ndiaye, founder of the Jolof Empire, his son, though the dates make a direct link impossible.
abu-firas-al-hamdani: Abu Firas, born al-Harith ibn Abi'l-Ala Sa'id, was probably born in Baghdad, where his father, a son of the Hamdanid family's founder Hamdan ibn Hamdun, held a distinguished place at the court of the Abbasid caliph al-Muqtadir. His mother was a Byzantine Greek slave concubine, a descent for which his Hamdanid relatives later taunted him. His father was killed in 935 in a dispute over Mosul with his nephew Nasir al-Dawla, and his mother fled to Nasir al-Dawla's brother Sayf al-Dawla. Raised at Sayf al-Dawla's court in Aleppo, among the philosopher al-Farabi, the preacher Ibn Nubata and the poet al-Mutanabbi, he was tutored by the grammarian Ibn Khalawayh.

At 16 he was made governor of Manbij, near the Byzantine frontier, and later of Harran too. He fought the Nizari tribes and joined his cousin's raids into Byzantine territory, and in 952 defeated a Byzantine force that tried to stop the refortification of Ra'ban and Mar'ash. The Arabic sources date his capture differently; most place it in 962, when he rode out with 70 men against a raid near Manbij led by the Byzantine general Theodore Parsakoutenos.

Sayf al-Dawla would not ransom him alone while thousands of other captives remained, and he was freed only in a general prisoner exchange at Samosata in 966. Named governor of Homs, he quarrelled after Sayf al-Dawla's death with the 15-year-old heir Abu'l-Ma'ali, his own sister's son, revolted, and was defeated and killed by the general Karghawayh on 4 April 968.

His early poems include qasidas praising the Hamdanids, the 225-line Hamdaniyyah the best known, shorter courtly poems on love, wine, hunting and friendship, and pro-Shia poems attacking the Abbasids. Encouraged by Ibn Khalawayh, a bitter opponent of al-Mutanabbi, he set himself up as the older poet's rival, though his work shows his influence. H. A. R. Gibb praised the qasidas for their sincerity, directness and natural vigour.

The scholar Sahib ibn Abbad wrote that poetry began with a king, Imru al-Qays, and ended with a king, Abu Firas. Ibn Khalawayh edited his collected works after his death with a commentary largely written by the poet himself, though other manuscript versions with significant variations also survived.
abu-hamid-al-gharnati: Abu Hamid al-Gharnati, in full Abu Hamid Muhammad ibn Abd al-Rahman ibn Sulayman ibn Rabi al-Mazini al-Qaysi, was born in Granada in 1080. His nisbas al-Mazini and al-Qaysi link him to Arab tribal lineages of the wider Qays confederation. His family is thought to have fled Granada to escape the rule of the Almoravid emir Yusuf ibn Tashfin. His kunya, Abu Hamid, means father of Hamid, after his first son, born in Baghdad.

He left Iberia for Egypt and Syria in 1106 and reached Alexandria in 1115 by way of Sardinia and Sicily, where he described Mount Etna. He settled in Baghdad in 1123. In 1130 he visited Abhar and Ardabil and Derbent in Dagestan, where the emir received him and took lessons in Islamic law from him. The next year he lived in Saqsin on the lower Volga, where local experts in jurisprudence brought him difficult legal cases.

From 1131 to 1150 he lived among the Volga Bulgarians, and from Bulgar he travelled to the Rus', noting the use of fur as money. In Kyiv he met Pechenegs who spoke a Turkic language, and led the Friday prayer for the Muslims there.

He went on to Hungary, where he served as an adviser at the court of King Géza II and dealt with the Muslim Pechenegs who formed an important part of the king's army. There he bought two enslaved girls, one of them a Byzantine child captured in the Hungarian wars against the Greeks. He left behind in Hungary an older son, established in the local Muslim community. He returned through Kiev to Baghdad in 1154, then lived in Mosul from 1161, Aleppo from 1165 and Damascus from 1169.

Al-Gharnati wrote of his journeys in the Arabic travelogue Tuhfat al-Albab, the Gift of Hearts, and of spectacular places and things in al-Mu'rib an ba'd aja'ib al-Maghrib, Praise of Some of the Wonders of the West, which also tells of his time in Hungary. These works combine geographical description, observation of the peoples he met and accounts of marvels, and they established the genre of books of wonders in Arabic. Many of the things he saw and reported are embellished with fantastic details.
abu-hanifa: Abu Hanifa came from Central Asia, though sources disagree on his birthplace, naming Kufa (the majority view), Kabul, Anbar, Nasa or Termez. They agree that he was born under the Umayyad Caliphate but differ on the year: 699 CE, held by the majority of classical scholarship, or 696, 689 or 680. His first name was Nu'man. He was born at least 60 years after the death of Muhammad, when some of the first generation of Muslims were still alive.

In his youth Abu Hanifa travelled to the Hejaz and studied in Mecca and Medina, and he later became established as a leading religious authority in Kufa. One of his main teachers there was Hammad ibn Abi Sulayman. He never held an official post as qadi. He kept an independent position toward political authority and was punished and imprisoned under both the Umayyads and the Abbasids because of his views and his refusal to accept the office of qadi in Kufa. He died in prison in Baghdad in 767 (AH 150).

The scholar Yusuf ibn Abd al-Rahman al-Mizzi listed 97 hadith scholars among his students, and Badr al-Din al-Ayni named another 260 who studied hadith and fiqh with him. His two best-known students were Abu Yusuf, who served as the first chief justice in the Muslim world, and Muhammad al-Shaybani, who taught the founder of the Shafi'i school, al-Shafi'i.

Abu Hanifa derived Islamic law, in order of preference, from the Qur'an, the authentic narrations of Muhammad known as hadith, the consensus of the Muslim community (ijma'), analogical reasoning (qiyas), juristic discretion (istihsan) and local custom ('urf). Modern scholarship regards him as the first to formally adopt analogical reasoning as part of Islamic law. Because Ali had moved the Islamic capital to Kufa and many first-generation Muslims settled there, the school came to be known as the Kufan or Iraqi school.

His school, the Hanafi, remains the most widely practised of the Sunni schools. Abu Hanifa received the honorific al-Imam al-A'zam, the highly venerated Imam. His tomb, surmounted by a dome erected by admirers in 1066, is still a shrine for pilgrims; the Ottoman ruler Suleiman restored it in 1535 after the Ottoman conquest of Baghdad.
abu-inan-faris: His father, Abu al-Hasan, had taken Tlemcen in 1337 and annexed Ifriqiya in 1347, briefly reuniting the Maghrib as it had been under the Almohads. When the Arab tribes revolted and defeated Abu al-Hasan's army near Kairouan in April 1348, Abu Inan, then governor of Tlemcen, returned to Fez, declared himself sultan and took the title Amir al-Mu'minin, commander of the believers. Abu al-Hasan, forced to come back from Ifriqiya by sea, failed to retake Tlemcen, was defeated by his son and died in May 1351.

After recapturing Tlemcen in 1352, Abu Inan reconquered the central Maghreb and took Béjaïa in 1353. The Nasrid rulers of Granada, fearing he would invade them once he held the whole Maghreb, backed a rebellion by his brother Abul Fadl, who had briefly governed Tunis; Sultan Abul-Hajjaj of Granada hired ships from Castile to carry the rebels to Sousse, where the rising was short-lived. Abu Inan took Tunis in 1357, but the intrigues of his vizier Faris bin Maymum forced him to withdraw from Tunisia the same year.

Abu Inan fell ill in November 1357. His vizier Hasan bin Umar al-Fududi, at odds with the heir apparent Abu Zayyan Muhammad, named the sultan's young son Abu Bakr Sa'id as successor instead. When Abu Inan began to recover, the vizier, fearing he would be punished for the nomination, had him strangled on 10 January 1358.

The Black Death and the rebellions of Tlemcen and Tunis under his rule marked the beginning of the decline of the Marinids, who proved unable to drive back the Portuguese and Spaniards; these began to settle on the North African coast under the Wattasids, who succeeded the Marinids. Abu Inan had his secretary Ibn Juzayy record Ibn Battuta's 29 years of travel, a rihla completed in December 1355. He built madrasas in Meknes and Fez in 1350 and another in Fez in 1357, and Mont Bouenan, south of Tetouan, was named after him.
abu-kamal: Abu Kamal, also called Al-Bukamal, is the administrative centre of the Abu Kamal District and Subdistrict. Just to the south-east is the Al-Qa'im border crossing to the town of Husaybah in Iraq's Al Anbar Governorate. Under Ottoman rule the place was called kışla, a Turkish word for military barracks, still pronounced locally as qashla. The name Al-Bukamal means the family of Kamal, the tribe that lives there, while Abu Kamal means the father of Kamal.

In the 17th century Abu Kamal was the seat of a sanjak of the Ottoman Empire in the Rakka Eyalet, and until the end of Ottoman rule in 1918 it was a kaza centre within the Zor Sanjak. In 1896 the old mud village was moved a mile upstream because flooding threatened it, and the new village was built of stone with wide streets. It was the centre of the Arab Uqaydat tribe and largely Sunni Muslim, with a small Christian community. Early in the 20th century it had eighty houses, a ferry and about 500 people. It became part of the French Mandate in 1921, when the French made it the seat of a large garrison, and part of independent Syria in 1946.

During the Iraq War, on 27 October 2008, four US helicopters raided the village of Sukkariyeh in Abu Kamal district, the first known US raid inside Syria. At least seven people were killed, four of them children, and the Syrian Foreign Minister Walid Muallem called killing civilians a terrorist aggression under international law. In the Syrian civil war the Free Syrian Army took the town in late July 2012, and the nearby Hamdan military airport on 16 November 2012. Islamic State forces captured it between late June and early July 2014, and it saw little fighting until 2017.

The Syrian Army began an operation against the town on 7 November 2017, backed by allied forces and Russian air strikes. Islamic State fighters retreated on 9 November, retook the town on 11 November, and the army and its allies regained complete control by 19 November. From late 2017 Iranian-allied militias occupied the town and countryside. The Al-Qa'im crossing reopened on 30 September 2019 after eight years of closure. On 27 October 2023 the US carried out air strikes on bases near the town, which it said were used by the Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps, and on 10 December 2024 Syrian opposition forces announced that they had captured it.
abu-musa: Abu Musa is an island of 12.8 square kilometres in the eastern Persian Gulf, near the entrance to the Strait of Hormuz. Its highest point is Mount Halva, at 110 metres. Because of the depth of the sea, oil tankers and other large ships have to pass between Abu Musa and the Greater and Lesser Tunbs, which makes the islands one of the strategic points of the Gulf. The climate is hot and humid, the soil and water are poor for farming, and fishing is the main local industry. Arabic sources derive the name from Abu Musa al-Ash'ari, a companion of Muhammad who stayed there in 643 CE.

Iran ruled the Persian Gulf region, Abu Musa included, in the pre-Islamic era. In the early Islamic period the island was ruled by the Umayyad and Abbasid caliphates until the Iranian Buyid dynasty conquered it in 935. Local rulers of southern Iran later managed these islands and ports with varying independence. A 13th-century account by Yaqut al-Hamawi gives what may be the first mention of the island. The Portuguese captured it in the 16th century and Iran retook it in 1622.

By common consent the island was later under the Al-Qasimi ruler of Sharjah and was covered by a protection treaty between the Gulf rulers and Britain of 1819. The first recorded dispute came in 1904, when Iranians replaced a flag of the Trucial States with their own, and British authorities opposed this. In 1964 Iranian forces occupied it for 20 days.

After Britain announced in 1968 that it would leave the Gulf, Iran moved to attach the island politically to the mainland. On 30 November 1971 Iran and Sharjah signed a memorandum of understanding that let Iranian troops be stationed on the island and left Sharjah a police station, and divided the island's energy resources. The United Arab Emirates took its claim to the United Nations Security Council on 9 December 1971, which deferred consideration of the matter. In 1992 Iran expelled foreign workers who ran a school, clinic and power station sponsored by the UAE.

The island is administered by Iran as part of Abumusa County in Hormozgan province, and the United Arab Emirates claims it as part of its Sharjah emirate. Abu Musa city is the island's centre. Most native residents speak the Bandari dialect of Persian, and the island has a regional airport.
abu-muslim: Sources differ on Abu Muslim's name and origin, and the suggestions that he descended from Persian heroes or from the Abbasids or Alids are all doubtful. He was most likely Persian, born in Merv or near Isfahan, in 718/9 or sometime between 723 and 727. He grew up in Kufa as a slave and saddler of the Banu Ijl clan, and there he met Shi'a Muslims.

Kufa was a centre of unrest against the Umayyad dynasty, whose policies favoured Arabs over non-Arab converts. In 737 he was accused of associating with ghulat sectarians and imprisoned. Abbasid missionaries freed him in 741/2, and Muhammad ibn Ali ibn Abdallah, head of the Abbasid clan, sent him in 745/6 to direct the missionary effort in Khurasan.

Khurasan, far from Syria and home to many Arab settlers and native converts who disliked the centralising tendencies of Damascus, offered fertile ground. When Abu Muslim arrived the province was in turmoil from the Third Fitna. In 747 he began the open revolt and took Merv in December 747 or January 748, defeating the governor Nasr ibn Sayyar and the Kharijite Shayban. He also defeated Bihafarid, leader of a syncretic Persian sect.

He then directed the Abbasid advance across the Iranian plateau into the Levant, which ended Umayyad authority and led to the proclamation of the Abbasid Caliphate. As governor of Khurasan he put down a Shi'a uprising in Bukhara in 750/1. His conciliatory policy toward Shia, Sunnis, Zoroastrians, Jews and Christians made him very popular.

The first caliph, Abu al-Abbas al-Saffah, trusted him in general but was wary of his power. His brother al-Mansur urged more than once that Abu Muslim be killed, and after becoming caliph he asked him to crush the rebellion of his uncle Abdullah ibn Ali, which he did. Relations then broke down over the spoils and over a transfer to Syria and Egypt, outside his power base. Reassured by al-Mansur's promise to keep him as governor of Khurasan, and by aides some of whom had been bribed, Abu Muslim went to meet him at al-Mada'in in 755. Al-Mansur listed his grievances, including a charge of heresy, and his guards killed him. His body was thrown into the Tigris.

His murder caused resentment and rebellion in Khurasan. Several leaders, including Ishaq al-Turk, the Zoroastrian cleric Sunpadh and al-Muqanna, revolted in his name, some claiming he had not died and would return. Legends and forms of veneration of him exist in Central Asia, Iran and Afghanistan, and at least three epic romances were written about him.
abu-said-bahadur-khan: Abu Sa'id Bahadur Khan was born on 2 June 1305 near Ujan, Tabriz, to Öljaitü and Hajji Khatun of the Oirat. He became his father's heir after the deaths of his elder brothers, and in 1315 he was assigned to govern Khorasan and Mazandaran, with the Uyghur noble Amir Sevinch as his guardian. His coronation, delayed by a conflict between the emir Chupan and Sevinch, took place in the spring or summer of 1317. He was the ninth ruler of the Ilkhanate, which covered present-day Iran, Azerbaijan, Georgia and Armenia and parts of Iraq, Turkey, Afghanistan and Pakistan.

When Sevinch died in January 1318 the young khan was left in the hands of Chupan, who became the de facto ruler after the vizier Rashid-al-Din Hamadani was executed on 13 July 1318 on an accusation of poisoning Öljaitü. In 1319 Özbeg of the Golden Horde invaded Azerbaijan and Keraite emirs rebelled. Abu Sa'id won a decisive victory at Mianeh on 20 June 1319 and received the titles Baghatur and al-Sultan al-Adil. Thirty-six emirs and seven khatuns were executed.

In 1322 Chupan's son Timurtash rebelled, claiming to be the Mahdi. Abu Sa'id fell in love with Chupan's daughter Baghdad Khatun, who was married to Hasan Buzurg, and on 25 August 1327 had one of Chupan's sons, Demasq Kaja, killed. Chupan marched against him but was deserted by many emirs, retreated to Herat, and was strangled there in 1327 on Abu Sa'id's orders. Baghdad Khatun was forced to marry the khan.

Now ruling personally, he made Ghiyas al-Din, son of Rashid al-Din, his vizier. In 1320 he signed a commercial treaty with Venice and a treaty with Mamluk Egypt. According to Ibn Battuta he was one of the most beautiful of God's creatures, and he was the only Ilkhan to compose poetry as well as music.

Another invasion by Özbeg took Abu Sa'id north in 1335, and he died on the way, in Karabakh, and was buried at Soltaniyeh. Ibn Battuta wrote that Baghdad Khatun had poisoned him from jealousy, while modern historians suggest bubonic plague. He left no heir or appointed successor, and clashes followed between the Chupanids, Jalayirids and Sarbadars. Ibn Battuta wrote of his amazement, on returning to Persia after twenty years, that so mighty a realm had dissolved so quickly. It became a collection of small kingdoms ruled by Mongols, Turks, Persians and Arabs.
abu-said-mirza: Abu Sa'id was born in 1424, the second son of the Timurid prince Muhammad Mirza, a son of Miran Shah and grandson of Timur. On his deathbed Muhammad Mirza placed the boy's hand in that of his cousin Ulugh Beg, governor of Transoxiana, as a sign of protection. Abu Sa'id served at Ulugh Beg's court and received his daughter in marriage, but when Ulugh Beg became sultan he turned against his benefactor. In 1449 he attacked Samarqand while Ulugh Beg was suppressing his son Abdal-Latif's rebellion. Abdal-Latif then defeated and had Ulugh Beg assassinated, and defeated and captured Abu Sa'id as well. He escaped in 1450 and fled to Bukhara.

With the aid of the Uzbek ruler Abu'l-Khayr Khan, Abu Sa'id defeated Abdullah Mirza in June 1451 and entered Samarqand unopposed, rewarding his ally with rich presents and Ulugh Beg's daughter in marriage. After he annexed Balkh in 1454, a truce with Abul-Qasim Babur of Herat set the Amu Darya as the border.

He later conquered Khorasan and made Herat his capital, defeated three Timurid princes at the Battle of Sarakhs in 1459, and extended his rule to Mazandaran and Sistan and to Badakhshan, where Timur himself had held only nominal suzerainty. He had the dowager Gawhar Shad executed, a deed contemporary chroniclers viewed negatively. Rival Timurid princes, notably Sultan Husayn Bayqara, kept raiding his lands, and Muhammad Juki's rebellion required a siege of Shahrukhiyya from November 1462 to September 1463.

At home he relied on the Arghun tribe and on the religious classes, and under the influence of the Naqshbandi shaikh Ubaydullah al-Ahrar he re-instituted Sharia law in Samarqand and Bukhara and removed taxes on commerce that could not be reconciled with religious doctrine. His rule brought stability but with considerable bloodshed. He favoured agriculture and irrigation, and the Juy-i Sultani Canal was built north of Herat.

In February 1468 Abu Sa'id launched a campaign against the Aq Qoyunlu, hoping to check Uzun Hasan's rise and reclaim the western lands once held by the Qara Qoyunlu. He advanced without all his troops, and his supply lines back to Khorasan, over 1200 miles long, were cut by Uzun Hasan's raids. Heavy losses at the Battle of Qarabagh followed, and he was taken prisoner.

He was executed on 5 February 1469 by Yadgar Muhammad Mirza, in vengeance for Gawhar Shad. Timurid lands west of Khorasan were lost, and the rest was divided among his sons and Husayn Bayqara, who ruled from Herat. Within forty years nearly all his territories were lost, which eventually pushed his grandson Babur to conquests in India and the foundation of the Mughal Empire.
abu-simbel: Abu Simbel lies on the western bank of Lake Nasser in the Aswan Governorate of Upper Egypt, near the border with Sudan, about 230 km southwest of Aswan. The temples stand at the Second Nile Cataract, the border between Lower Nubia and Upper Nubia. Nubia was a major source of gold and other precious trade goods and was controlled by Egypt, so it mattered greatly to the Egyptians.

Ramesses II carried out an extensive building programme in Egypt and Nubia. He built several grand temples in Nubia in order to impress upon the Nubians Egypt's might and to Egyptianize the people of Nubia. Work at Abu Simbel began in the 13th century BCE and lasted for about 20 years. The complex was known as the Temple of Ramesses, Beloved by Amun. It has two temples: the Great Temple, dedicated to Ra-Horakhty, Ptah and Amun and to the deified Ramesses himself, and the Small Temple, dedicated to the goddess Hathor, personified by his chief wife Nefertari.

Over time the temples fell into disuse and a sand dune came to cover most of the Great Temple. By the 6th century BCE the sand already covered the statues of the main temple up to their knees. The site remained unknown to Europeans until March 1813, when the Swiss researcher Johann Ludwig Burckhardt found the small temple and the top frieze of the main temple.

The Great Temple is entered between four seated statues of Ramesses II, each 20 m high, with smaller figures of his family beside his legs. The facade behind them is 33 m high and 38 m wide. The complex was moved in 1968 to higher ground, under an artificial hill, to keep it from being submerged by Lake Nasser, within the International Campaign to Save the Monuments of Nubia. Abu Simbel is part of the UNESCO World Heritage Site known as the Nubian Monuments, and is open to visitors.
abu-tahir-al-jannabi: Abu Tahir Sulayman was an Arabized Persian, born in June or July 906 at Ganaveh on the coast of Fars. His father, Abu Sa'id, a tribal leader taught by Hamdan Qarmat of Kufa, had begun the militarization of the Qarmatians.

Most Arabic sources agree that Abu Sa'id named his eldest son, Abu'l-Qasim Sa'id, as heir and that Abu Tahir revolted against him and usurped power. Another tradition, reported by the Kufan anti-Isma'ili polemicist Ibn Rizam, holds that Sa'id was only a regent and handed over power in 917/918, when his brother was barely ten. It is likely that power was nominally shared among all the sons, with Abu Tahir dominant. Abu'l-Qasim was not executed and lived until 972.

In 926 he led his army as far north as Kufa and made the Abbasids pay large sums for him to leave. On his return he built palaces at Ahsa and declared it his permanent capital. In 928 Caliph al-Muqtadir sent against him the generals Yusuf ibn Abi'l-Saj, Mu'nis al-Muzaffar and Harun, who were beaten and driven back to Baghdad.

At Mecca in 930 he was at first refused entry, invoked the right of all Muslims to enter and swore that he came in peace. Once inside, his men rode into the Masjid al-Haram, massacred the pilgrims, set fire to the Kaaba and threw bodies into the Zamzam Well. The attack was believed to be meant to prompt the appearance of the Mahdi and followed millenarian excitement over the conjunction of Saturn and Jupiter in 928.

The Mahdi he recognised in 931, Abu'l-Fadl al-Isfahani, a prisoner who claimed descent from the Sasanian kings, restored the veneration of fire, burned religious books and had members of Bahrayn's notable families executed. In one account Abu Tahir's mother exposed him and his brother Sa'id killed him after eighty days; in others Abu Tahir denounced him as a false Mahdi and had him executed.

Abu Tahir took back control of the state and resumed his attacks on pilgrims crossing Arabia. He rejected the attempts of both the Abbasids and the Fatimids to persuade him to return the Black Stone. He died of smallpox in 944, aged about 38, and was succeeded by his three surviving sons and his nephews. According to the historian al-Juwayni the stone came back in 951, thrown in a sack into the Great Mosque of Kufa with a note: "By command we took it, and by command we have brought it back." Its removal had broken it into seven pieces.
abu-ubayda-ibn-al-jarrah: Abu Ubayda was born around 583 into the al-Harith ibn Fihr clan of the Quraysh, settled in the lower quarter of Mecca. His full name was Amir ibn Abd Allah ibn al-Jarrah. His father, Abd Allah, was among the Quraysh chiefs in the Fijar War against the Hawazin nomads. According to traditional accounts, he was the ninth person to accept Islam, embracing it with Uthman ibn Maz'un and Abd al-Rahman ibn Awf before Muhammad began preaching from the house of al-Arqam. After the migration to Medina he was bound in brotherhood to Muhammad ibn Maslama.

Abu Ubayda fought at Badr in 624, where his father fought on the Quraysh side; commentators say Quran 58:22 was revealed about him after he killed his father there. At Uhud in 625 he stayed beside Muhammad when most of the army fled, and lost two front teeth drawing iron links of Muhammad's helmet or armour from his cheeks. He took part in all the major campaigns, led the Expedition of al-Khabt, and in 630 commanded the Muhajirun and Ansar in the Expedition of Dhat al-Salasil. Muhammad also sent him to instruct a Christian delegation from Najran, calling him trustworthy.

Traditions place him with Abu Bakr and Umar in the intervention that won the Ansar's allegiance to Abu Bakr at the Saqifa in 632. Al-Baladhuri denies that Abu Bakr sent him to Syria; modern historians date his dispatch to Umar's reign, around 636, as commander of reinforcements, with Khalid ibn al-Walid then holding supreme command. Khalil Athamina holds that Umar appointed him to the supreme command after the Muslim victory at the Yarmuk. He led the army that took Jerusalem in 636 and took Damascus, Homs, Antioch and Aleppo, then administered them.

During the drought of 638, Umar asked the governors for aid. Abu Ubayda sent caravans, and 4,000 camels loaded with food reached Medina first; Umar put him in charge of distribution and offered 4,000 dinars, which he refused. He died of the plague of Amwas in 639 and left no descendants. From the 13th century his tomb was traditionally held to be at Ammata in the Jordan Valley, which became known as Ghawr Abi Ubayda, though Tiberias and Beisan were also named. The Jarrahs, who claimed descent from him, kept the tomb and were exempt from taxes by the Ottoman authorities.
abu-yaqub-yusuf-i: Abu Yaqub Yusuf was born in 1135, the son of Abd al-Mu'min, the first Almohad caliph. His mother was Safiyya bint Abi Imran, a Masmuda woman from Tinmel and the daughter of Abu Imran Musa ibn Sulayman al-Kafif, a companion of Ibn Tumart. He supported Almohad doctrine and, like his predecessors, favoured the literalist Zahiri school of Islamic jurisprudence. He was a religious scholar in his own right and was said to have memorized the Sahih Bukhari and Sahih Muslim.

Yusuf reigned from 1163 until 1184 from Marrakesh. He continued his father's conquest of al-Andalus into Valencia and Catalonia, and in 1171 he established himself in Seville. He ordered numerous buildings there, including the Alcázar of Seville, the Buhaira Gardens and the fortress of Alcalá de Guadaíra, and he was responsible for the Giralda, part of a new grand mosque. Respected men of letters such as Ibn Rushd and Ibn Tufayl were entertained at his court. He favoured the Córdoban polymath ibn Maḍāʾ as his chief judge, and the two oversaw the Almohad reforms that banned religious material written by non-Zahiris. His son al-Mansur later went further and burned non-Zahiri books.

Yusuf was wounded at the Siege of Santarém in 1184 and died on the road to Seville, near Évora, on 14 October 1184. His body was taken from Seville to Tinmel and buried there. His buildings in Seville remained, and the Giralda in particular is attributed to him. The arrival of the zealous Almohads is also described as having ended the golden age of Jewish culture in Spain.
abu-yusuf: Abu Yusuf lived in Kufa and Baghdad in the 8th century. His genealogy has been traced to Sa'd ibn Habta, a youth in Medina in the time of the Prophet Muhammad, and his birth date is estimated from the date of his death, around 729. Anecdotes say he was raised poor but with a great appetite for knowledge. His mother wanted him to learn a trade, tailoring according to some sources, and stories suggest he did so while continuing his studies. Abu Hanifa recognised his talent and became his mentor. He studied religious law and traditions in Kufa and Medina under Abu Hanifa, Malik ibn Anas, al-Layth ibn Sa'd and others.

Abu Yusuf lived in Kufa until he was appointed qadi in Baghdad. It is unclear whether al-Mahdi, al-Hadi or Harun al-Rashid appointed him. One story says he gave sound advice to a government official, who rewarded him and recommended him to the caliph. Harun al-Rashid drew him into his inner circle and granted him the title of Grand Qadi, which had never before been conferred in Islamic history. It began as an honorific, but the caliph consulted him on legal matters and financial policy and gave him the ability to appoint other qadis, which made the post like that of a modern chief justice. He held it until his death in 798.

Ibn al-Nadim's Kitab al-Fihrist of the 10th century lists many titles by Abu Yusuf, but only the Kitab al-Kharaj, a treatise on taxation written at the caliph's request, survives from that list. Others that survive include the Kitab al-Athar, a collection of Kufian traditions, a comparison of the opinions of Abu Hanifa and Ibn Abi Layla, and a refutation of the Syrian scholar al-Awza'i on the laws of war. Excerpts from lost works were preserved by his disciples, among them Muhammad al-Shaybani.

In the Kitab al-Kharaj he advised the caliph on conducting financial policy in accordance with religious law. The caliph took some suggestions and ignored others, but the overall effect was to limit the ruler's discretion over the tax system. He favoured a proportional tax on produce over fixed taxes on property as an incentive to bring more land into cultivation, and a centralised tax administration to reduce corruption. His main legacy was affirming Hanafi law as the predominant legal thought of the empire.
abu-yusuf-yaqub-ibn-abd-al-haqq: Abu Yusuf Yaqub was the fourth son of the Marinid founder Abd al-Haqq I and of Oum el-Iman bint Ali el-Bethary, a Zenata woman. When his brother Abu Yahya died in July 1258, the Marinids held Fez and eastern and northern Morocco, while the Almohads kept the south around Marrakesh. Abu Yahya had named his own son as heir, but Abu Yusuf, then governor of Taza, displaced his nephew and was acknowledged as emir.

In September 1260 a Christian fleet, probably Castilian, seized Salé, which Abu Yusuf retook after a fourteen-day siege. His first assault on Marrakesh in 1262 failed, and the Almohad chieftain Abu Dabbus, whom he then backed, turned against him and drew in Yaghmorassan of Tlemcen. Abu Yusuf defeated the Abdalwadids by the Moulouya in 1268 and took the title Prince of the Muslims, never claiming the caliphal title. The Draa valley submitted in 1271, Ceuta and Tangiers in 1273 and Sijilmassa in 1274, a siege in which Ibn Khaldoun records what seems to be one of the first uses of powder cannon.

In 1275, answering an appeal from Muhammad II al-Faqih of Granada, he crossed the straits, took Tarifa and Algeciras and defeated Castilian armies at the Battle of Écija and the Battle of Martos. He crossed again in 1277, 1282 and 1285, shifting alliances between Granada, the Banu Ashqilula and Alfonso X of Castile. His son Abu Yaqub won the Battle of Algeciras on 21 July 1279. In October 1285 Sancho IV of Castile agreed a five-year truce and handed over Arabic books seized from Andalusian libraries. Abu Yusuf fell ill and died at Algeciras in March 1286 while negotiating with Granada, and was buried in the Marinid necropolis at Chellah, which he had built.

Although Abd al-Haqq or Abu Yahya are often named as founders of the dynasty, Abu Yusuf is regarded as the founder of the Marinid state: he ended the Almohads, unified Morocco, built Fes el-Jedid, first called the White City, opposite the old Idrisid city, and gave the Marinids a foothold in Spain. He left the state fragile, however. The Arabs and Maqil of the south were only half subdued, the Sanhaja of the High Atlas unconvinced, and Tlemcen still a threat. Without the religious prestige of the Almoravids or Almohads, the Marinids remained at root a tribal dynasty.
abubakar-tafawa-balewa: Abubakar Tafawa Balewa was born in December 1912 in the village of Tafawa Balewa, in Lere district of Bauchi province in the Northern Nigeria Protectorate. His father, Yakubu Dan Zalla, was a Gerawa man who married a Fulani woman, Fatima Inna. He studied at a madrasa in Bauchi, then at Bauchi Government Provincial School, and from 1928 to 1932 at Katsina Higher College, after which he became a secondary school teacher.

In 1944 he was headmaster of Bauchi middle school, and two years later he went to the University of London Institute of Education, where he obtained an overseas teacher's certificate. Back in Nigeria he worked as an educational assistant and then as inspector of schools in Bauchi Province.

Balewa was elected to the Central Legislative Council in 1947. When the Northern People's Congress (NPC) was founded in 1951 he became a member; in 1952 he moved to Lagos as a member of the central house of representatives and minister of works. In 1954 he lost the election for president general of the party to Ahmadu Bello but became its vice-president. After the NPC won a plurality of votes in 1957 he became Chief Minister and designated Prime Minister, and formed a coalition with the National Council of Nigeria and the Cameroons, led by Nnamdi Azikiwe, inviting the Action Group into an all-party cabinet.

He moved the motion for independence on 18 January 1959 and was reelected in 1964. A constitution of 1963 abolished the monarchy and made Azikiwe President. His term was turbulent, with regional factionalism constantly threatening his government, and the treason conviction of Obafemi Awolowo and the violent 1965 election in the west deepened the strain.

Balewa was overthrown and murdered in a military coup on 15 January 1966, as were other leaders including Ahmadu Bello. His body was found at a roadside near Lagos six days after he was ousted, and the circumstances of his death remain unresolved. He was buried in Bauchi, and news of his killing led to riots in Northern Nigeria and to the counter-coup of July 1966. In 1933 he had written the Hausa novella Shaihu Umar, published in 1934, which deals with the trans-Saharan slave trade and Islamic themes of submission to God. He was knighted in January 1960, and a university and an airport in Bauchi bear his name.
abul-fazl-bayhaqi: Abu'l-Fazl Muhammad ibn Husayn Bayhaqi was born in the village of Haresabad in Bayhaq, in Khorasan, to a Persian family. He studied at Nishapur, a major cultural centre, and in 1020/1 joined the secretariat of the Ghaznavid Sultan Mahmud, where he worked for nineteen years as assistant and pupil to the chief secretary Abu Nasr Mushkan.

After Mushkan's death in 1039/40 Sultan Mas'ud I appointed Bayhaqi as minister to Abu Sahl Zawzani, Mushkan's successor as chief secretary. Mushkan had urged that Bayhaqi succeed him, but Mas'ud is supposed to have said that Bayhaqi, then 46, was too young. Zawzani was a poor manager and bad-tempered, and Bayhaqi sent the sultan a secret letter of resignation, which Mas'ud refused. Mas'ud died soon afterwards, deserted by his army after a defeat by the Seljuq Turks, who then conquered Khorasan.

During the reign of Abd al-Rashid, from 1049 to 1052, Bayhaqi was chosen as chief secretary but soon removed. According to Ibn Funduq a judge of Ghazni jailed him over an unpaid obligatory fee to a wife, while according to Aufi his enemies' plots were the cause. In 1052 the slave-soldier Toghrul seized Ghazni, had Abd al-Rashid killed and moved Bayhaqi to a stronghold. Toghrul reigned fifteen days before loyalists killed him and put Farrukh-zad on the throne, and Bayhaqi was released.

According to Ibn Funduq, Bayhaqi served Farrukh-zad as secretary and at the end of that reign withdrew from the bureaucracy and settled in Ghazni to write the Tarikh-i Bayhaqi. A Seljuq chronicle says he drew up the 1058 peace treaty between the Seljuqs and the Ghaznavids.

The Tarikh-i Bayhaqi took twenty-two years to write and was finished in thirty volumes, of which five and half of a sixth survive. It is a key source on the Ghaznavid era, and its Persian prose influenced later writers. Modern scholars praise its frankness, precision and elegant style, and Julie Scott Meisami places Bayhaqi among the historians of the Islamic Golden Age. He died on 21 September 1077, and his tomb is in his birthplace.
abul-fazl-ibn-mubarak: Abu'l-Fazl was born in Agra on 14 January 1551, the second son of Shaikh Mubarak, who had been born in Nagaur and moved to Agra in 1543, where he set up a madrasa teaching philosophy. His elder brother was the poet Faizi. The family's ancestors were said to have come from Yemen and had settled in Sindh. Abu'l-Fazl began with Arabic, and by the age of five could read and write. He found conventional learning hard and sank into a state of depression, from which a friend rescued him.

In his own account he recalled repairing a dictionary eaten by white ants by joining blank paper to the surviving fragments; the original, when found, differed from his draft in only two or three places. He came to Akbar's court in 1575 and helped make the emperor's religious views more liberal in the 1580s and 1590s.

Abu'l-Fazl served as grand vizier of the Mughal Empire from 1579 until his death. His best-known work is the Akbarnama, a history of Akbar's reign and of his ancestors from Timur to Humayun in three volumes, which runs to the 46th regnal year (1602) and includes an administrative report of the empire, the Ain-i-Akbari. He also wrote letters and despatches, collected after his death as the Ruqaʿāt and the Inshā-i-Abu'l Fazl, and made a Persian translation of the Bible.

In 1599 he received his first office in the Deccan, where he led the imperial army in its wars against the Deccan sultanates. In the Ain-i-Akbari he argued that a king was sent by God as his agent for the welfare of his subjects, and that his sovereignty was not tied to any one faith: a king who discriminated by religion, caste or class would not be just. This was the doctrine of Sulh-i-Kul, universal peace.

Abu'l-Fazl was assassinated in 1602 on his way back from the Deccan, between Sarai Vir and Antri near Narwar, by the Bundela chief who later became ruler of Orchha. The plot was contrived by Akbar's eldest son, Prince Salim, the future Emperor Jahangir, because Abu'l-Fazl was known to oppose his succession. His severed head was sent to Salim at Allahabad, and he was buried at Antri. His son Shaikh Afzal Khan was made governor of Bihar by Jahangir in 1608. A shrine and mosque named in his honour was completed in Kabul around 2010.
abul-khayr-khan: Abu'l-Khayr was born around 1412, a descendant of Genghis Khan through Shiban, the fifth son of Jöchi, and a bey of the White Horde. At his birth the ulus of Shiban had divided into separate nomadic groups, one led by Jumaduq Khan. He served in Jumaduq's army and was taken prisoner when Jumaduq was killed in battle in 1427. He and his family loved literature and ordered some works translated from Persian into Turkic.

Released in 1428, he began to consolidate the nomadic groups of the old Shaybani ulus around Tyumen and the Tura River. After defeating and killing Kazhy Mohammed, Khan of the Khanate of Sibir, near the Tobol River, he was proclaimed Khan of Western Siberia, and spent four years strengthening his control. The Manghits and Vaqqāṣ Bej, a grandson of Edigü, assisted him. In 1430 and 1431 he and Vaqqāṣ attacked Khwarezm and occupied its capital Urganj, but retreated in the summer of 1431 and defeated two khans near Astrakhan.
