They attacked Khwarezm again in 1435 and 1436 and raided Astrakhan some years later.

From 1446 he invaded the Syr Darya region and won some lands from Timurid control, making Sighnaq his capital, from which he raided Mawarannahr. In 1451 he helped the Timurid Abu Sa'id defeat 'Abdullah at Samarkand, but Abu Sa'id locked the gates against the Uzbeks and bought them off with presents. In Samarkand he married a daughter of Ulugbek, Rabiya Sultan-Begim, mother of Kuchkunji Khan and Suyunchkhodja Khan. In 1452 the sultans Kerei and Janibek, descendants of Urus Khan, separated from his authority with groups of nomads and migrated to Moghulistan, where Esen Buqa Khan gave them lands near the Chu River, an important stage in the formation of the Kazakh Khanate.

In 1468 he launched a campaign against the groups led by Kerei and Janibek but died before reaching them. Some sources give 1469 or 1470 for his death. His state disintegrated, and many of his followers joined the Kazakh rulers. His son Sheikh Khaidar succeeded him, and afterwards two separate lines controlled the twin Uzbek states of Mawara al-Nahr and Khwarezm. In the first decade of the 16th century his grandson Muhammad Shaybani united the Uzbeks and established the short-lived Shaybanid Empire, centred on Samarkand.
abulkhair-khan: Abu'l-Khair, in full Mirza Abū'l-Khair Muhammed Khan bin Qājı Abdūllah Sultan, was the second son of Hajji Abdullah Sultan, a Kazakh mirza, or aristocrat, who rose to royal rank after making the hajj to Mecca. He too began as a mirza, which makes him one of the few documented khans of the Kazakh Khanate not descended from Janibek Khan or Kerei Khan; his father's connections with the royal family probably brought him to the throne.

He took the throne in 1718, during the Kazakh-Dzungar Wars, which the Little jüz fought chiefly to avenge the Dzungar invasion remembered as the Great Disaster. Under his leadership Kazakh forces defeated the Dzungars at the Bulanty river in 1726 and at the Battle of Anrakai in 1729. To gain Russian help he swore allegiance to the Russian crown in 1731, yet he went on raiding Bashkir and Kalmyk settlements until 1740, and he fostered a strong Sunni Muslim identity among the Kazakhs to keep any from going over to the Dzungars.

He also tried to limit Russian influence, wishing his realm to remain an independent Islamic state. A 2019 study concluded that neither Kazakhs nor Russian officials thought of the relationship as annexation, but as an alliance.

For his part in reuniting the Kazakhs and defeating the Dzungars he was given the Persian title Shah-i-Turan, King of Turan. Some Kazakhs, however, saw his submission to Russia as treachery, and in 1748 his rival Baraq Sultan beheaded him for what Baraq considered treason against the Kazakh people.
abylai-khan: Born Waliullah Abu'l-Mansur, Abylai belonged to the senior branch of the descendants of Janybek Khan, the 15th-century founder of the Kazakh state. His father was Korkem Wali Sultan. He spent his childhood and part of his youth in exile, and after losing his father to political rivals at the age of thirteen he worked as a herdsman. He was called Sabalak, the beggar, a name he kept so that his father's rivals would not notice a descendant of Janybek. At fifteen he began to fight the Dzungars in the Kazakh militia during the Kazakh-Dzungar War of 1723-1729. Shoqan Walikhanov wrote that the future sultan won universal attention, first as an ordinary warrior, for his courage and strategic insight.

In 1741 an Oirat army under Septen invaded the Middle Jüz. Abylai, commanding a reconnaissance detachment of 200 men, charged into the main Dzungar force and was captured with his companions. He was held at the headquarters of Galdan Tseren, where he learned the Oirat language and script and met the Khoit noyan Amursana. During negotiations he was at times shackled to pressure Kazakh envoys. By the late 1740s the Dzungar Khanate was in decline, and in 1751 the defeated noyan Dawachi fled to Kazakhstan. When the Dzungar khan Lama Dorji demanded the extradition of Dawachi and Amursana, Abylai replied that they had come of their own accord, and the Kazakh camps moved north, closer to the Russian frontier.

In 1755 a Qing army of about 200,000 conquered Dzungaria. Amursana, left with about two hundred warriors, took refuge in Abylai's camps. The Qing emperor then ordered his commanders either to persuade the Kazakhs to withdraw or to secure recognition of his suzerainty by force. Abylai refused to comply and marched against the Qing forces with the Middle Jüz militia. He also campaigned against the Kyrgyz and the Kokand ruler Irdana, and in 1779 led an army of about 12,000 against the Kyrgyz, taking prominent families hostage.

In the spring of 1780 Abylai moved to the area near Tashkent. In the autumn he fell seriously ill and died shortly afterwards, near Tashkent; the exact date is unknown. He was buried with great honours in the Mausoleum of Khoja Ahmed Yasawi at Turkistan, and more than 5,000 people attended the funeral feast. The Kazakhs raised Wali Sultan to the position of khan.

Abylai sought to unite the fragmented Kazakh tribes and was among the first to recognise the suzerainty of the Russian Empire voluntarily. Assessments of him vary widely: some portray him as a cunning barbarian, others admire his political and military work, and Soviet and Chinese publications have often treated him in a politicised way. He is important in the historiography of Kazakhstan.
academia-sinica: The National Government of the Republic of China established Academia Sinica in Nanjing in April 1928 as the country's highest research organisation. Its first president was the philosopher Cai Yuanpei and its first director-general the scholar Yang Xingfo. The historian James Reardon-Anderson called it by far the best-funded research organ in Republican China. Before the Second World War it received a third of all government research spending. Cai took European and American institutional models, including the election of academicians, and wished to save the nation through scholarship and science. Under Cai and Yang it worked independently of the Kuomintang government, and by 1931 ten institutes were at work, from physics to philology to zoology.

In the Second Sino-Japanese War Cai died in 1940 and the geologist Chu Chia-hua succeeded him, moving the academy's artefacts out of Kunming as fighting there grew. In October 1946 the first 81 academicians were elected, among them Shiing-Shen Chern, Hua Luogeng, Li Siguang, Fu Ssu-nien and Chen Yinke. On 19 December 1948, because of the Chinese Civil War, all the institutes voted to move to Taiwan, but only the Institute of Mathematics and the Institute of History and Philology could do so, and only nine of the 81 academicians went. The rest of its property and affiliates on the mainland were absorbed into the Chinese Academy of Sciences.

The academy was re-established in Taiwan in 1949 and, short of funds, reopened with the Institute of History and Philology in December 1954. Its main campus at Nangang, Taipei, was built that year. The second convocation met in 1957. Today it is the national academy of Taiwan, with institutes in three divisions: mathematics and physical sciences, life sciences, and humanities and social sciences. Academicians are elected every two years, and election is regarded as a national honour. Its presidents have included Hu Shih and the Nobel laureate Yuan T. Lee.
academie-francaise: The Académie grew from an informal literary group that came out of the salons held at the Hôtel de Rambouillet in the late 1620s and early 1630s. It met at the house of Valentin Conrart and then had nine members. Cardinal Richelieu made himself its protector, and new members were appointed in 1634. On 22 February 1635, at Richelieu's urging, King Louis XIII granted letters patent establishing it; those registered at the Parlement de Paris on 10 July 1637 charged it to give exact rules to the language and make it capable of treating the arts and sciences. Richelieu's model was the Accademia della Crusca, founded in Florence in 1582.

The National Convention suppressed all royal academies: in 1792 the election of replacements for dead members was prohibited, and in 1793 the academies were abolished. In 1795 a single body, the Institut de France, replaced them. Napoleon Bonaparte, as First Consul, restored the academies in 1803 only as divisions of the Institut. When Louis XVIII came to the throne in 1816 each class regained the title Académie, and since then its existence has been uninterrupted. The head of state has been the Académie's protector since Louis XIV took the role in 1672, after Richelieu and Pierre Séguier. It met at the Louvre from 1672 to 1805, and since 1805 at the Palais de l'Institut.

The forty seats are numbered, and candidates apply for a particular seat. A new member is elected by the Académie itself, and must deliver a speech that includes a eulogy of the predecessor. Members are called les immortels after the motto À l'immortalité on Richelieu's seal. They hold office for life but can be dismissed for grave misconduct; the first dismissal, in 1638, was for theft, and 20 members have been expelled in all, four of them at the end of the Second World War for association with the Vichy regime.

Marguerite Yourcenar was the first woman elected, in 1980. The Académie publishes the Dictionnaire de l'Académie française, whose first edition appeared in 1694, and awards more than sixty prizes, almost all created in the twentieth century.
academy-of-gundishapur: The Academy of Gondishapur, also called Gondishapur University, was a Sassanid-era centre of education in Khuzestan, Iran, founded by King Shapur I. It first offered education and training in medicine, philosophy, theology and science, and it also included a hospital and a library. According to Richard Frye, the name is a corrupted form of Veh-Andiukh-Shapur, meaning better than Antioch, built by Shapur.

Ibn al-Nadim writes that Ardashir I collected scattered ancient Persian books from India and China for the royal treasury and that Shapur I continued this, gathering texts translated into Middle Persian and compiling the Avesta into a single book. Khosrow I later built a library for the university at Gundishapur. The available historical information is insufficient for a precise picture, and Islamic-era accounts of the scholarly past often border on legend.

In 489 the Byzantine emperor Zeno ordered the East Syriac Christian school at Edessa closed, and it was absorbed into the School of Nisibis, then under Persian rule. There Nestorian scholars and Hellenistic philosophers banished from Athens by Justinian in 529 worked on medicine, astronomy and mathematics. Under Khosrau I (531-579) Gondishapur became known for medicine and learning. He gave refuge to Greek philosophers and to Syriac-speaking Nestorian Christians fleeing Byzantine persecution, and had them translate Greek and Syriac texts on medicine, astronomy, philosophy and useful crafts into Middle Persian.

He also sent the physician Borzouye to invite Indian and Chinese scholars, who translated Indian texts on astronomy, mathematics and medicine and Chinese texts on herbal medicine and religion. Almost all the physicians were Persians, but they wrote in Syriac, because medicine had a literary tradition in that language.

In 832 al-Ma'mun strengthened the House of Wisdom in Baghdad, which was staffed with graduates of Gondishapur and copied its methods. The intellectual centre of the Abbasid Caliphate had moved to Baghdad, and references to Gondishapur became few. The last known head of its hospital died in 869, and al-Muqaddasi, about 1000, described it as falling into ruins.

The hospital of Gondishapur combined treatment with medical training, and according to most sources on the history of medicine it transmitted Greek, Iranian and Indian medical knowledge into the Islamic world, whose first hospitals were modelled on it. Students worked in the hospital under the supervision of the whole medical faculty rather than with one physician, and graduates may have had to pass examinations. Notable physicians include Borzuya, Bukhtishu, Masawaiyh and Sabur ibn Sahl. In 1955 Jondishapur University and its twin, a medical university, were founded near Ahvaz in its memory, and the ancient site is now an archaeological site.
acadians: The settlers whose descendants became the Acadians came mainly from west-central France, such as the rural areas of Poitou-Charentes, and in the early 17th century about 60 French families were established in Acadia, one of the five regions of New France. Acadian culture first emerged in and around Port-Royal, present-day Annapolis Royal in Nova Scotia. The settlers built dikes along the Bay of Fundy to reclaim farmland from the sea and developed relations with the peoples of the Wabanaki Confederacy, particularly the Mi'kmaq.

Living in a borderland contested between French Canada and New England, the Acadians were drawn into six wars over 74 years, among them Dummer's War and Father Le Loutre's War. Under British rule they refused for decades to sign an unconditional oath of allegiance, fearing it would commit them to fight France, deny their Catholic faith or expose their villages to attack by the Mi'kmaq. The priest Jean-Louis Le Loutre preached against the British from 1738 until his capture in 1755, and some Acadians kept up supply lines to the French at Louisbourg and Fort Beauséjour.

After the Battle of Fort Beauséjour, from August 1755, Lieutenant Governor Lawrence expelled about 11,500 Acadians, three-quarters of those in Nova Scotia; families were separated, lands confiscated and homes sometimes burned. Scattered from New England to Georgia, many were imprisoned or put to forced labour, and about a third died of disease and drowning. Thousands were later taken to France, from where the Spanish Crown carried many on five ships to Louisiana. Others returned to the Maritime provinces, mainly to New Brunswick, as the British barred them from their old lands in Nova Scotia.

Acadians speak Acadian French, with regional accents such as Chiac and Brayon in New Brunswick, and most also speak English. In 1881 the First Acadian National Convention at Memramcook chose 15 August, the feast of the Assumption of Mary, as their national day, marked by a noisy parade called the tintamarre. Their anthem, Ave Maris Stella, and their flag, the French tricolour with a golden star for Mary as Star of the Sea, were adopted at Miscouche, Prince Edward Island, in 1884.

Henry Wadsworth Longfellow's poem Evangeline, loosely based on the 1755 deportation, helped activists revive a distinct Acadian identity in Canada and Louisiana. In 2003 Queen Elizabeth II, as Queen of Canada, issued a Royal Proclamation acknowledging the deportation and set 28 July as an annual day of commemoration.
acajutla: Acajutla is a seaport city in Sonsonate Department, El Salvador, on the Pacific coast of Central America. It is one of seventeen districts of Sonsonate and the country's principal seaport. A large part of the nation's exports of coffee, sugar and Balsam of Peru is shipped from it. As on the whole Pacific coast of Central America, the climate is continuously hot and humid, with daytime highs usually between 32 and 34 °C; it is classed as a tropical savanna climate.

Pedro de Alvarado, a Spanish conquistador under Hernán Cortés, had conquered Mexico and Guatemala before he came to the vicinity of Acajutla. There he met heavy resistance but defeated the indigenous people in 1524 and conquered all of present-day El Salvador at the Battle of Acajutla. After El Salvador's complete independence in 1838 its economy became increasingly dependent on coffee exports. The growth of this cash crop led to profound socio-economic changes and drew foreign investors and local plantation owners to Acajutla, where infrastructure was needed to carry the crop from the interior and load it onto ships.

During the peasant uprising of 1932 two destroyers of the Royal Canadian Navy, HMCS Skeena and HMCS Vancouver, anchored off Acajutla at the request of the British Consul, who feared for British nationals and assets. Armed Canadian sailors briefly landed against the wishes of the Salvadoran government and prepared to go on to San Salvador, but the situation improved and the British no longer thought an armed presence necessary. During the civil war of 1980-1992 the oil refinery at Acajutla, then the only one operating in El Salvador, was a target for anti-government rebels.

The port was built in its first phase at a cost of 25 million colones. Its breakwater of 338 metres began operations in August 1961, and it is managed by the Executive Commission of Autonomous Port (CEPA). The deepwater harbour handles a large part of the country's major exports, coffee making up 40 percent of its cargo, and the oil refinery, the nation's largest, mainly refines petroleum imported from Venezuela. The town holds its traditional festivals from the last days of May to 2 June, and on 24 October fishermen celebrate in honour of San Rafael Arcangel. Between March and April people decorate the streets with sand brought from the beach and enact the passion of Christ.
acamapichtli: Acamapichtli, whose name means handful of reeds, was the first tlatoani of the Mexica of Tenochtitlan and the founder of the Aztec ruling dynasty. Chronicles differ on the dates of his reign. He was not a native of Tenochtitlan. After the death of Tenoch, the elders of the Mexica calpultin chose to elect a tlatoani who could secure the new city through ties to powerful groups, and they sent a delegation to the leaders of Culhuacan. Acamapichtli was the child of one of the unions between Culhua and Mexica: his father Opochtli Iztahuatzin was a Mexica leader, and his mother Atotoztli was a daughter of King Coxcoxtli of Culhuacan. The Culhua nobility claimed descent from the Toltecs, which made his lineage prestigious.

Acamapichtli began as cihuacoatl, or governor. He was then 20 and living in Texcoco with his mother, and he entered Tenochtitlan with great pomp. He married Ilancueitl, daughter of the ruler of Culhuacan, and took a wife from each Tenochtitlan calpulli to bind the city together. His city fell quickly into the Tepanec orbit and became a tributary of Azcapotzalco, paying a tribute said to be oppressive and capricious, and Mexica forces fought for Azcapotzalco against Chalco and other cities before they were allowed to wage war on their own. He avoided trouble with the more powerful ruler Tezozómoc by paying what he demanded; when Tezozómoc asked for a chinampa of flowers, the Mexica raised one and floated it across the lake to him.

Within the city, Acamapichtli expanded the chinampa system and captured lakeshore chinampas from Xochimilco and other cities. The earliest excavated level of the Great Pyramid, Temple II, dates to his reign. The city was divided into four districts, Moyotlán, Zoquipan, Cuecopan and Atzacualco, houses of cane and reeds gave way to stone ones, and the first Aztec laws are said to have been made then.

His first wife bore him no children. Huitzilíhuitl, his son by Tezcatlan Miyahuatzin, succeeded him, and another son, Itzcóatl, who became tlatoani in 1427, was the son of a noble but enslaved woman Acamapichtli had bought in the market of Azcapotzalco. Before his death he asked the chiefs of the four districts to elect his successor, and they chose Huitzilíhuitl. Tlatoani was not strictly a hereditary title, but candidates came from a small class of princes, and all later Aztec rulers descended from Acamapichtli.
acapulco: Acapulco lies on the Pacific coast of Mexico in the state of Guerrero, 380 km south of Mexico City, on a deep, semicircular bay. The municipality is 40 percent mountainous, 40 percent semi-flat and 20 percent flat, with elevations from sea level to 1,699 metres. The climate is tropical wet and dry, and Pacific hurricanes and tropical storms are a threat from May through November. The name comes from the Nahuatl Aca-pol-co, meaning where the reeds were destroyed or washed away, or at the big reeds, which inspired the city's seal, a glyph of two hands breaking reeds.

By the 8th century a small culture existed around the bay, first dominated by the Olmecs, who had two sites there, and then by others, including Teotihuacan and later Maya influence. In the 11th century Nahua migrants, ancestors of the Aztecs, came through. In the later 15th century, after four years of fighting, Acapulco became part of the Aztec Empire under Ahuizotl, but only transitorily: the Yopis, who controlled the territory, kept defending it until the Spanish arrived in the 1520s.

Europeans are said to have found the bay in one of two ways. Either explorers sent by Hernán Cortés subdued the area after 1523 and Captain Saavedra Cerón was authorised to found a settlement, or a small ship under Santiago Guevara found it on 13 December 1526.

Acapulco is a port of call for shipping and cruise lines running between Panama and San Francisco and the largest city of Guerrero. It rose to prominence between the 1940s and the 1960s as one of Mexico's oldest beach resorts. It was the eastern end of the trans-Pacific sailing route to Manila, then in a Spanish colony.
acarnania: Acarnania lay in the westernmost part of central Greece, along the Ionian Sea, west of Aetolia and north of the gulf of Calydon, the entrance to the Gulf of Corinth. It was reckoned the most westerly province of Greece and covered about 4,070 square kilometres, with the Ambracian Gulf and Amphilochia to the north and the Achelous River as its boundary with Aetolia under the Romans. It had a rocky coastline, a rugged strip of mountains along the coast, and plains between the mountains and the Achelous. The soil was fertile but little cultivated, and the chief wealth of the inhabitants lay in herds and flocks pastured in the meadows of the lower Achelous. Pliny mentions iron mines and a pearl-fishery off Actium.

In Greek mythology the land was founded by Acarnan, son of Alcmaeon. Its early inhabitants were said to be the Taphii, the Leleges and the Curetes. In the 7th century BCE Corinth settled Anactorium, Sollium and Leucas, and Kefalonia settled Astacus, driving the earlier inhabitants into the interior. By the Peloponnesian War the Acarnanians, who lived mostly in dispersed villages and made good light-armed troops and slingers, were bound in the Acarnanian League, whose meetings were usually held at Stratus. It had a council, a general assembly and a general at its head.

Hatred of the Corinthian settlers led them to side with Athens, and about 432 BCE they joined it in restoring the Amphilochians to Argos. In 426 BCE they won a victory under Demosthenes over the Peloponnesians and Ambraciots at the Battle of Olpae. They later joined the Second Athenian League in 375 BCE and fought with Athens and Thebes against Philip II of Macedon at Chaeronea. In 314 BCE, at the order of Cassander, settlements near the Aetolian border were merged into fewer, larger ones, and about 250 BCE the territory was divided between the Aetolian League and Epirus.

Acarnania then drew close to the Antigonid kings and stayed loyal to Philip V in his war with Rome, submitting only after the capture of Leucas and the Battle of Cynoscephalae. In 191 BCE they were persuaded by Mnasilochus to side with Antiochus III, and after 168 BCE Thyrreion replaced Leucas as capital. In the 1st century BCE the country suffered from pirates and Roman civil wars, and Augustus moved the inhabitants of several towns to his new city of Nicopolis.

In 395 Acarnania became part of the Eastern Roman Empire. After the Fourth Crusade in 1204 it passed to the Despotate of Epirus, in 1348 it was conquered by Serbia, and in 1480 it fell to the Ottoman Empire. It has been part of Greece since 1832 and forms the western part of the regional unit of Aetolia-Acarnania.
accademia-della-crusca: The founders were first known as the brigata dei Crusconi, a circle of poets, men of letters and lawyers. They met on convivial occasions to recite cruscate, discourses in a merry and playful style that have neither beginning nor end. With humour, satire and irony they set themselves apart from the pedantry of the Accademia Fiorentina, which enjoyed the protection of Grand Duke Cosimo I de' Medici, and from its severe classical style.

The founders are traditionally identified as Giovan Battista Deti, Antonio Francesco Grazzini, Bernardo Canigiani, Bernardo Zanchini and Bastiano de' Rossi, each with a nickname. Lionardo Salviati joined them in October 1582. Under his leadership, at the beginning of 1583, the group took a new form, aiming to demonstrate and conserve the beauty of the Florentine vernacular, modelled upon the authors of the Trecento.

Agnolo Monosini was one of the earliest scholars to influence the academy's work. He contributed greatly to the first edition of the Vocabolario degli Accademici della Crusca, published in 1612, especially on the influence of Greek on the Florentine idiom. With that work the academy gave up its jocular meetings for a normative role. Its title was reinterpreted: the academicians would separate the farina, the good and pure part of the language, from the crusca, the bran. In 1636 Cardinal Richelieu created the Académie Française on the model of the Crusca.

The academy's purism drew opposition from Cesare Beccaria and the brothers Pietro and Alessandro Verri, whose journal Il Caffè attacked its archaisms as pedantic. Its activities continued with high and low points until 1783, when Pietro Leopoldo and several academicians left to create the second Accademia Fiorentina. After a third Accademia Fiorentina was founded in 1808, a decree signed by Napoleon on 19 January 1811 re-established the Crusca with its own autonomy, statutes and aims. A decree of 11 March 1923 removed the Vocabolario from it, and from 1955 Bruno Migliorini and others discussed returning the dictionary to it.

The academy's emblem is a sifter, with the motto Il più bel fior ne coglie, a line by Petrarch. It is the oldest linguistic academy in the world and a research institution for the Italian language, based in Florence. In February 2016 it approved the word petaloso, suggested by an eight-year-old boy.
accra: Accra lies on the southern coast of Ghana, on the Gulf of Guinea. The name comes from the Akan word Nkran, meaning ants, a reference to the soldier ants and the anthills of the countryside around it. In the Ga language the town is called Ga, the same name as the Ga people. The historian Carl Christian Reindorf proposed a link between the martial qualities and migratory behaviour of the ants and those of the Ga. Anthills were sacred places, seen as points of contact between the known world and the world of the dead. The Danes spelled the name Akra.

By the 15th century the kingdom of Accra ruled the area from its capital at Ayawaso. Local inhabitants destroyed a Portuguese fort in 1576. In the 17th century the Dutch built Fort Crèvecœur, later called Ussher Fort, and the British built James Fort; Christiansborg also stood there. In 1677 the Akwamu ruler Ansa Sasraku sacked Ayawaso and beheaded the king, Okai Koi. The king's son Ofori retreated to Small Accra, the town beneath Fort Crèvecœur, and was driven into exile in Fetu in 1681.

Britain gradually acquired the other powers' interests, beginning in 1851 when Denmark sold Christiansborg; the Netherlands was the last to sell, in 1871. In 1877, at the end of the second Anglo-Asante War, Accra replaced Cape Coast as capital of the British Gold Coast, because its climate was drier. After a bubonic plague epidemic in 1908 the native-only neighbourhood of Adabraka was created to relieve crowding. A bridge over the Korle Lagoon in 1923 spurred settlement to the west, and cocoa became the largest export.

Accra is the capital and largest city of Ghana, and the Greater Accra Region has about 5.46 million people. Kwame Nkrumah, Ghana's first Prime Minister from 1957, drew up his own plan for the city. Its architecture ranges from 19th-century colonial buildings to modern towers. The Parliament, the Supreme Court and Black Star Square are there, and the city has an international airport and railway links to Tema, Sekondi-Takoradi and Kumasi.
aceh: The first evidence of human habitation in Aceh comes from a site near the Tamiang River, where shell middens and stone tools suggest occupation from around 10,000 BCE. Before Islam, Hindu-Buddhist culture existed in the area. Aceh is thought to have been one of the earliest centres of Islam in Southeast Asia: Marco Polo found Peureulak a Muslim town in 1292, and the gravestone of Sultan Malikussaleh, first Muslim ruler of Samudra, is dated 1297.

The Sultanate of Aceh was established by Sultan Ali Mughayat Syah in 1511, and in the early 17th century it was the wealthiest, most powerful and most cultivated state in the Strait of Malacca. The Dutch colonial government declared war on Aceh on 26 March 1873, citing pirates operating from Aceh. The campaign quickly drove out the sultan, but local leaders fought on in about four decades of guerrilla war marked by high levels of atrocities.

Aceh was incorporated into North Sumatra in 1950, which led to the Acehnese Rebellion of 1953–59. In 1976 Hasan Muhammad di Tiro proclaimed independence, and the Free Aceh Movement took up the struggle. On 26 December 2004 the Indian Ocean tsunami killed over 170,000 people in Aceh. It helped bring about the Helsinki Agreement of 15 August 2005, under which Aceh received special autonomy and the movement disarmed.

Aceh is a province of Indonesia on the northern end of Sumatra, with Banda Aceh as its capital and largest city. It is the only Indonesian province to officially integrate Islamic law. The Acehnese, the largest of ten indigenous groups, speak a language of the Aceh-Chamic group that was traditionally written in Arabic script. The 2020 census counted 5,274,871 people. Gunung Leuser National Park protects the Sumatran tiger, orangutan and Sumatran elephant.
aceh-war: For much of the 19th century the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1824 guaranteed Aceh's independence. In the 1820s the sultanate supplied half of the world's pepper, and under Sultan Alauddin Ibrahim Mansur Syah (1838–1870) it extended its rule down the east coast, where it met the Dutch advancing north. After the opening of the Suez Canal, the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of Sumatra of 1871 ended British claims to the island. When Acehnese envoys discussed a possible treaty with the American consul in Singapore early in 1873, the Dutch treated it as a breach of the 1871 agreement and resolved to annex Aceh by force.

The first expedition, under Major General Johan Harmen Rudolf Köhler, bombarded Banda Aceh in April 1873 but was repulsed with the loss of Köhler and 80 troops. A second, of 8,500 men under General Jan van Swieten, arrived amid a cholera outbreak that killed thousands on both sides; in January 1874 Sultan Mahmud Syah abandoned the capital and the Dutch took the palace and declared Aceh annexed. The Acehnese proclaimed the young Muhammad Daud sultan and fought on from the hills, and by 1884 the Dutch had pulled back to a fortified line around Banda Aceh.

From the mid-1880s religious scholars such as Teungku Chik di Tiro led the resistance, preaching holy war, prang sabi, through poems known as hikayat. The chief Teuku Umar took Dutch money and weapons and in 1894 Dutch aid to raise an army, then two years later turned it against them. On the advice of the Islamic scholar Christiaan Snouck Hurgronje, who urged the Dutch to win over the hereditary chiefs and destroy the ulema, J. B. van Heutsz became governor in 1898 and waged a counter-insurgency with light Marechaussee units and scorched earth tactics. In the 1904 campaign Colonel Gotfried Coenraad Ernst van Daalen's troops killed at least 2,922 Acehnese, 1,149 of them women and children, for 26 Dutch dead.

The historian Adrian Vickers estimates that 50,000 to 60,000 Acehnese died of violence and disease in the whole war, while about 2,000 European and allied soldiers were killed in combat and more than 35,000 soldiers and labourers died of disease; some 10,000 Acehnese fled to Malaya. Van Heutsz was hailed in the Netherlands as the Pacifier of Aceh and became governor-general in 1904. Resistance in the highlands went on until 1942, and suicide attacks on Dutch personnel, known as the Atjeh-moord, forced the Dutch to keep large forces in the province.
achaea: Achaea lies in the northwestern part of the Peloponnese peninsula and forms a regional unit in the region of Western Greece. It is bordered by Elis to the west and southwest, Arcadia to the south and Corinthia to the east and southeast, with the Gulf of Corinth to the northeast and the Gulf of Patras to the northwest. The mountain Panachaiko, 1926 metres high, dominates the coast near Patras, and higher peaks lie in the south, among them Aroania at 2341 metres and Erymanthos at 2224 metres.

The Achaean League was a Hellenistic confederation of city states in Achaea, founded in 280/281 BCE. It grew to include most of the Peloponnese and much reduced Macedonian rule there. After Macedon's defeat by the Romans in the early 2nd century BCE, the League defeated a heavily weakened Sparta and took control of the whole peninsula. As Roman influence grew it revolted in the Achaean War, was defeated at the Battle of Corinth in 146 BCE, and was dissolved by the Romans. In 51/52 CE Lucius Junius Gallio Annaeanus was proconsul of Achaea; the Acts of the Apostles shows him presiding over the trial of Paul at Corinth.

Achaea remained a Byzantine province after the fall of the Western Roman Empire. Slavs reached the Peloponnese in the 6th and 7th centuries, but the coastal cities stayed largely Byzantine and a siege of Patras in 805/807 failed. After the Fourth Crusade the Principality of Achaea was founded in 1205, with the Barony of Patras, the Barony of Vostitsa, the Barony of Chalandritsa and the Barony of Kalavryta in the region. Patras, under its Latin Archbishop, became a semi-autonomous domain under the protection of Venice and the Holy See. The principality fell to the Byzantine Empire in 1430 and became part of the Despotate of the Morea, which fell to the Ottoman Empire in 1460. Venice held Achaea from 1687 to 1715.

In the Greek War of Independence Aigio was one of the first cities liberated, and all of Achaea was freed by the end of 1821. Tens of thousands of refugees from Asia Minor were settled around Patras after the Greco Turkish War of 1919-1922.

Achaea is one of the regional units of Greece, with its capital at Patras, the third largest city in the country. About two thirds of its people live near Patras, and the regional unit holds about one third of the population of the Peloponnese. Its five municipalities are Aigialeia, Erymanthos, Kalavryta, Patras and West Achaea. The Agia Lavra monastery lies a few kilometres west of Kalavryta.
achaemenid-empire: The empire takes its name from Achaemenes, credited as the progenitor of the dynasty, a minor seventh-century ruler of Anshan in south-western Iran and a vassal of Assyria. By the 7th century BCE the region of Persis had been settled by Persian people. From Persis Cyrus rose. He revolted against the Median Empire in 553 BCE and in 550 BCE defeated the Medes, captured Astyages and took the Median capital, Ecbatana. By inheriting Astyages' empire he also inherited its conflicts with Lydia and the Neo-Babylonian Empire, both of which he went on to defeat.

Cyrus's son Cambyses II used the army in Egypt against Psamtik III, while Cyrus himself died fighting a local Iranian insurgency. Darius I reinforced the empire, expanded Persepolis as a ceremonial capital and established the first Persian royal navy. The empire was repulsed from Scythia in 513 BCE and from Greece in 492–490 BCE and 480–479 BCE. The Ionian Revolt of 499 to 493 BCE began when Aristagoras, tyrant of Miletus, incited Ionia against Darius.

In 343 BCE Artaxerxes III invaded Egypt with 330,000 Persians and 14,000 Greeks. Artaxerxes IV Arses was poisoned by the eunuch Bagoas, who set Darius III on the throne. In 334 BCE Alexander the Great invaded Asia Minor, and in 330 BCE the empire was conquered in its entirety. Later Persian rulers in Fārs, the Frataraka, acted for the Seleucids and then became independent kings of Persis under the Parthians.

Cyrus founded the empire as a multi-state realm governed from four capitals: Pasargadae, Babylon, Susa and Ecbatana. It was divided into satrapies, between 20 and 30 at different times, each with a satrap, a general and a state secretary. Darius I introduced the daric, a gold coin, and the silver siglos, and a tax system tailored to each satrapy: Babylon was assessed at 1,000 silver talents, while Egypt supplied 120,000 measures of grain and 700 talents of silver.

The Immortals were a unit of 10,000 trained soldiers, and a postal system ran through relay stations. Elamite was the language of the chancellery while the court sat at Susa, and Aramaic gained in importance under Artaxerxes I. The Hebrew Bible reports that Cyrus released the Jewish people from the Babylonian captivity and helped rebuild the Temple in Jerusalem. Four kings are buried at Naqsh-e Rostam, and Cyrus's tomb at Pasargadae is a World Heritage Site.
achalpur: Achalpur, formerly Ellichpur, is a city and municipal council in the Amravati District of the Indian state of Maharashtra. The camp of the town is known as Paratwada, and the two stand as twin cities in the lap of the Satpuda hills at an average elevation of 369 metres, between the Sapan and Bicchhan rivers, tributaries of the Chandrabhaga.

According to the Prakrit text Vasudeva-hindi, Achalpur and Vatsagulma, modern Washim, were the chief cities of the Abhira kingdom. It was the earliest capital of a branch of the Rashtrakuta dynasty, which emerged in the 8th century, and the site of a battle between the Rashtrakutas and the Kalachuris in the 9th century. It was first mentioned reliably in the 13th century among the cities of the Deccan. Tributary to the Delhi Sultanate after 1294, it stayed under Hindu administration until 1318.

In 1347 it passed with Berar to the Bahmani Sultanate, and in 1490 Fathullah Imad-ul-Mulk proclaimed his independence, founded the Imad Shahi dynasty of the Berar Sultanate and made Ellichpur his capital. After the Mughal occupation the governor of the province moved to Balapur.

In the 18th century Berar came under the Nizam of Hyderabad. The British took over its administration in 1853, though it remained formally part of Hyderabad until 1903, when Berar was joined to the Central Provinces. In 1867 East Berar was split and Ellichpur became the headquarters of its own district, which was merged into Amravati district in 1905. In 1901 the town had 29,740 people, with ginning factories and a considerable trade in cotton and forest produce. After the States Reorganisation Act of 1956, Amravati District was transferred to Bombay State, renamed Maharashtra in 1960.

The town keeps many relics of the sultans of Berar. Its railway station is the northern end of the narrow-gauge line known locally as the Shakuntala railway, which joins the main Mumbai–Kolkata line at Murtajapur.
achelous-river: The Achelous rises at about 2,000 metres on the eastern slope of Lakmos mountain in the Pindus range, near the village of Anthousa. One of its first tributaries is the Aspropotamos, meaning the white river. It flows generally southwards and forms part of the boundary between Epirus and Thessaly, and later between Aetolia-Acarnania and Evrytania. Below the Kremasta reservoir it turns southwest, runs through the lowlands west of Agrinio and empties into the Ionian Sea 29 kilometres west of Missolonghi. Its waters are a whitish yellow or cream colour, which gave it the later name Aspropotamo.

In antiquity it was the largest and best known river in Greece. It was said to have been called Thoas, Axenus and Thestius in earlier times. It entered the plain of Acarnania and Aetolia near Stratus and reached the sea near the Acarnanian town of Oeniadae. The plain of its lower course was called Paracheloitis after the river and was known for its fertility, though much of it was marsh, formed in part by the river's floods. Herodotus compared its shoreline-transforming power to that of the Nile, noting that it had already turned half the Echinades islands into mainland. Its spirit was venerated as the river god Achelous.

In 1359 the Battle of Achelous was fought near the river between Albanian forces under Peter Losha and the Despotate of Epirus under Nikephoros II Orsini. Nikephoros was defeated and killed, and two new states arose in the area, the Despotate of Arta and the Despotate of Angelokastron and Lepanto.

The river is 220 kilometres long. Dams now regulate it: the Kremasta Dam was completed in 1965, the Kastraki Dam in 1969 and the Stratos Dam in 1989. The Kremasta Dam, built of concrete, flooded part of the western prefecture of Eurytania and supplies electricity to western and central Greece. Parts of the river are used for rafting in spring and canoeing in summer and autumn.
achilles: In Greek myth Achilles was the son of Thetis, a Nereid, and Peleus, king of the Myrmidons. According to one account, Zeus and Poseidon had both courted Thetis until Prometheus warned Zeus of a prophecy that she would bear a son greater than his father, and the two gods had her wed Peleus. Achilles was raised in Phthia with his companion Patroclus and educated by the centaur Chiron.

The story that Thetis dipped him in the river Styx, leaving him vulnerable only at the heel, comes from the Achilleid of Statius, written in the first century CE. No source before Statius mentions general invulnerability: in the Iliad Achilles is wounded at the elbow.

According to the Iliad, Achilles came to Troy with 50 ships, each carrying 50 Myrmidons. On the way he wounded King Telephus of Mysia, a wound that would not heal until Achilles healed it, as an oracle had said. His most notable feat was the slaying of the Trojan prince Hector outside the gates of Troy.

The Iliad does not present his death, but other sources agree that Paris killed him near the end of the war with an arrow. His tomb in the Troad was venerated through antiquity by Thessalians, by Persian expeditionary forces, by Alexander the Great and by the emperor Caracalla. Dedications from Greek colonies on the Black Sea attest a heroic cult from the sixth century BCE, and in the third century CE stelae at Olbia name an Achilles Pontarches, invoked as protector of the city. Aeschylus wrote a trilogy about him, of which only fragments survive.
achterhoek: The Achterhoek (in Achterhooks, Achterhook) is a cultural region and COROP area in the Eastern Netherlands. Its name means rear corner, which fits its position in the easternmost part of Gelderland, where it protrudes into Germany. It lies east of the IJssel and borders Germany to the southeast and the province of Overijssel to the northeast. The region is also called de Graafschap, Dutch for county or earldom, because it coincides with the historical County of Zutphen. In 2015 the Achterhoek had a population of 389,682. The region is predominantly rural, with much open space, forests and farms, and the area around Winterswijk is regarded as noteworthy.

Two of its towns, Doesburg and Zutphen, are old Hanseatic cities, and both have centres with well-preserved historical buildings. The largest places are Doetinchem, Winterswijk and Zutphen. Grolsch beer was first brewed in Groenlo in 1615. The eleven municipalities include Aalten, Berkelland, Bronckhorst, Brummen, Doesburg, Doetinchem, Lochem, Montferland, Oost Gelre, Oude IJsselstreek, Winterswijk and Zutphen. Cycling routes include the 80-year-war route and the Arfgoodroute.

The original languages of the Achterhoek are Achterhooks and Kleverlandish, varieties of Low Saxon that are also classified as Low Franconian dialects. The dialect differs from town to town: a speaker of the Groenlo variant pronounces words differently from a speaker in Winterswijk, only 10 kilometres to the east, though they will probably understand each other. The number of people whose only language is Achterhooks has declined greatly since World War II. Children are raised with Dutch at school, the dialect is spoken only sometimes at home, and many old words have been forgotten and replaced by Dutch ones.

Agriculture still supplies exports, among them meat, dairy products, fruit and potatoes, and technological products make up over 25 percent of export value. The shrinking of farming has helped rural tourism to grow, with cycling, hiking, canoeing and stays at recreation lakes such as Stroombroek, Slingeplas and Hilgelo. Most visitors come from other European countries, among them Germany, Belgium, Denmark and Ireland.
acoma-pueblo: Acoma is a Keres pueblo whose old village, Sky City, stands on a mesa 365 feet high, about 60 miles west of Albuquerque; with Acomita, Anzac and McCartys it makes up the village of Acoma Pueblo. Its people descend from the Ancestral Puebloans, the Mogollon and other earlier peoples. The pueblo emerged by the 13th century, though the Acoma themselves date Sky City to the 11th century. The site's isolation sheltered the community from raids by neighbouring Navajo and Apache peoples. The name comes, through Spanish, from the Acoma word for a person from Acoma Pueblo; it does not mean sky city.

Estevanico, an enslaved man of Moroccan birth, was the first outsider known to visit, in 1539. In 1540 Hernando de Alvarado of Francisco Vázquez de Coronado's expedition described the place as one of the strongest he had seen, reached only by a hand-built stairway and holes cut in the rock. Later Spanish parties came in 1581 and 1582. In December 1598 the Acoma killed Juan de Zaldívar, Juan de Oñate's nephew, and eleven of his men; Acoma oral tradition says the fighting began when the soldiers attacked Acoma women. In the assault of January 1599 led by Vicente de Zaldívar, the Spanish burned most of the village, cut off the right foot of men over 25 and forced survivors into slavery for 20 years.

Survivors rebuilt the town between 1599 and 1620. Between 1629 and 1641 the Acoma were made to build the San Esteban del Rey Mission, hauling about 20,000 tons of adobe, stone and mud up the mesa and pine beams from Mount Taylor, more than 40 miles away. The Acoma took part in the Pueblo Revolt of 1680, kept their own religion in secret beside Catholicism, and suffered smallpox and raids by Apache, Comanche and Ute. Railroads ended their isolation in the 1880s, and by 1922 most children had been sent to boarding schools.

About 300 two- and three-storey adobe buildings stand on the mesa, which has no electricity, running water or sewage system; a few dozen people live there permanently. The pueblo is a National Historic Landmark, and the Acoma hold a reservation of about 500,000 acres of their traditional land. Each September the feast of Saint Stephen opens the mesa to the public, and Acoma pottery is made in a tradition more than 1,000 years old.
acrocorinth: Acrocorinth, in Greek the acropolis of ancient Corinth, is a monolithic rock overlooking the ancient city. George Forrest judged it the most impressive acropolis of mainland Greece. It has a secure water supply, and its fortress was repeatedly used as a last line of defence in southern Greece because it commanded the Isthmus of Corinth and kept foes from entering the Peloponnese by land. The Upper Pirene spring lies within the encircling walls. According to a Corinthian myth told by Pausanias in the 2nd century CE, the giant Briareus judged between Poseidon and Helios, awarding the Isthmus to Poseidon and Acrocorinth to Helios.

The rock was continuously occupied from archaic times to the early 19th century. In the Hellenistic period it formed, with Demetrias and Chalcis, one of the three so-called Fetters of Greece, fortresses garrisoned by the Macedonians to secure their control of the Greek city-states. The archaic acropolis was already easy to defend because of its shape. The Byzantine Empire fortified it heavily when it became the seat of the strategos of the thema of Hellas and later of the Peloponnese. Leo Sgouros defended it against the Crusaders for three years. Afterwards it was a fortress of the Frankish Principality of Achaea, the Venetians and the Ottoman Turks.

Three circuit walls formed the man-made defence of the hill. The highest peak held a temple to Aphrodite, which was converted into a church and then into a mosque. The American School's Corinth Excavations began work on Acrocorinth in 1929, and it is now one of the most important medieval castle sites of Greece.
acropolis-of-athens: The Acropolis is a flat-topped rock that rises 150 metres above sea level in the city of Athens and has a surface of about 3 hectares. It is a klippe made of two rock units: the soft reddish Athens schist and the overlying Acropolis limestone, thrust over it by tectonic forces. The limestone is unstable and prone to rock slides. The marble of its buildings came from the quarries of Mount Pentelicus, northeast of the city. In ancient times the hill was also called Cecropia, after the first Athenian king Cecrops.

Habitation of the hill is evidenced as early as the 4th millennium BCE. A Mycenaean megaron palace probably stood there in the late Bronze Age, with a Cyclopean wall 760 metres long. Athena Polias had a temple, the Hekatompedon, built between 570 and 550 BCE. Around 500 BCE it was dismantled for a grander building, the Older Parthenon, which was still unfinished when the Persians sacked the city in 480 BCE. The Athenians built parts of it into the new northern wall, where they can still be seen.

Under Pericles, in the so-called Golden Age (460–430 BCE), the Parthenon and other temples were rebuilt, with the sculptor Phidias and the architects Ictinus and Callicrates responsible. Mnesicles began the Propylaea in 437 BCE, and the Erechtheion was built between 421 and 406 BCE. In the Byzantine period the Parthenon served as a church of the Virgin Mary. In 1687, during the Morean War, a Venetian bombardment hit the gunpowder the Ottomans kept in the Parthenon, and the explosion severely damaged it.

After Greek independence most Byzantine, Frankish and Ottoman additions were cleared from the site. The Parthenon mosque was demolished in 1843. The Acropolis Restoration Project, begun in 1975, reassembled original fragments with titanium dowels and used new Pentelic marble sparingly. The Acropolis Museum stands on the southern slope, 280 metres from the Parthenon.

In antiquity the Great Panathenaea, held every four years, ended with a procession to the Acropolis, where a new robe was placed on the statue of Athena. Since at least the mid-18th century the Acropolis has often been invoked as a symbol of the Greek legacy and of classical Greece.
act-of-abjuration: Philip II inherited the Seventeen Provinces in 1555 not as one state but as the holder of each province's feudal title, Duke of Brabant, Count of Holland, Count of Flanders and the rest. When provinces rose against him from 1568, the rebels kept up the legal fiction that they fought his viceroys, not the king. By 1579 the southern Union of Arras and the northern Union of Utrecht had divided the provinces, and William the Silent looked for a new overlord who could bring foreign allies. The rebel States General offered sovereignty to Francis, Duke of Anjou, while Holland and Zeeland looked to William himself.

On 14 June 1581 the States General decided to declare the throne vacant. A committee of four, Andries Hessels, Jacques Tayaert, Jacob Valcke and Pieter van Dieven, was charged with drafting the act, though the text itself seems to have been written by Jan van Asseliers. Signed in The Hague on 26 July 1581, it banned Philip's name and seal in legal matters and his name or arms on coins, released magistrates from their oaths to him and prescribed a new oath to the States of their province.

Its long preamble, an indictment of Philip based on Vindiciae contra tyrannos by Philippe de Mornay, held that a ruler who oppressed his subjects and violated their ancient rights forfeited his throne. Pieter Geyl noted that its principles came from Calvinism, though it lacked a purely religious argument.

Philip did not recognise the act, and many magistrates resigned rather than take the new oath. Anjou, dissatisfied with his limited powers, attacked Antwerp in the French Fury and was discredited; William was assassinated in 1584 before he could take the title of Count of Holland, and under the Treaty of Nonsuch Elizabeth I of England sent aid without accepting sovereignty. After the Earl of Leicester left in 1587 the States General assumed sovereignty themselves. The form of the act resembles the American Declaration of Independence, giving rise to speculation that Thomas Jefferson was partly inspired by it.
act-of-independence-of-lithuania: Lithuania had a centuries-long tradition of statehood going back to the coronation of Mindaugas. After the last Partition of the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1795 it was annexed by the Russian Empire, and Lithuanians rebelled in 1830 and 1863. Their first real opportunity came when Russia and Germany were weakened by the First World War. After the Russian Revolution of 1917 Germany allowed the Vilnius Conference, hoping that it would proclaim a closer relationship with Germany. Held on 18–23 September 1917, the conference instead resolved that an independent Lithuania should be established, with any closer relationship conditional on German recognition, and it elected a Council of Lithuania of twenty members.

The German Empire pressed the Council to form an alliance. The Act of 11 December 1917, drafted first by the German foreign ministry, proclaimed independence but asked for German protection and a firm and permanent alliance; it was adopted by fifteen votes to three, with one abstention. On 8 January 1918 the Council amended the text, adding democratic principles and a Constituent Assembly and omitting the alliance, but the German military administration rejected the changes, and four members resigned in protest.

On 16 February 1918 all twenty members met at 30 Didžioji Street in Vilnius, a building now called the House of the Signatories. The Act proclaimed the restoration of an independent State of Lithuania, governed by democratic principles, with Vilnius as its capital, and ended the ties binding Lithuania to other states. It was approved unanimously, though the four who had resigned were uneasy that the Constituent Assembly would decide Lithuania's foundation and foreign relations finally.

German newspapers printed the text on 18 February, but German authorities forbade its publication in Lithuania, and the editor Petras Klimas hid about 60 copies of the Council's newspaper, Lietuvos aidas. Little changed until Germany lost the war; on 2 November 1918 the Council adopted a provisional constitution.

The Act is the legal basis of modern Lithuania, in the interwar period and since 1990, when the Act of 11 March 1990 stated that it had never lost its legal effect. The original disappeared after 15 June 1940, when Lithuania received a Soviet ultimatum, and was reported found in the political archive of the German foreign office in Berlin in March 2017.
act-of-settlement-1701: After the Glorious Revolution the succession was governed by the Bill of Rights 1689, which treated the flight of James II to France as an abdication and named his daughter Mary II and her husband William III as his successors. The line was to pass next to Mary's sister Anne and her descendants, and finally to any children of William by a later marriage. During the debate the House of Lords tried to add Sophia, Electress of Hanover, and her descendants, but the amendment failed in the Commons.

The need for a further act came with the death of Prince William, Duke of Gloucester, the son and heir of the future Queen Anne, and with the perceived threat from the remaining Roman Catholic members of the House of Stuart.

The act gave the throne to Sophia, a granddaughter of James VI and I and a niece of Charles I, and to her Protestant descendants. It excluded for ever anyone who was reconciled to the Church of Rome, held communion with it, professed the Popish religion or married a Papist.

Eight further provisions were to take effect only on the death of both William and Anne. The monarch was to join in communion with the Church of England. If a person not native to England came to the throne, England would not wage war for territories not belonging to its Crown without the consent of Parliament, a clause that mattered because a Hanoverian king kept the Electorate of Hanover. Judges were to hold office for good behaviour rather than at the monarch's pleasure.

The Tory administration that had replaced the Whig Junto in 1699 steered the act through Parliament, and it passed with little opposition, although five peers voted against it in the Lords. Many shared their dislike of a foreign king, but the feeling was summed up as better a German prince than a French one. Sophia died two months before Anne, and her son became King George I. The Parliament of Scotland had not been consulted, and answered with the Act of Security 1704, reserving the right to choose its own successor to Anne.

England responded with the Alien Act 1705 and the Act of Union 1707, and through Article II of the Treaty of Union the act became part of Scots law as well. The clause on judges' tenure was later taken into many United States state constitutions and into Article III of the federal constitution of 1787. On 26 March 2015, following the Perth Agreement, legislation took effect across the Commonwealth realms that removed the disqualification arising from marriage to a Roman Catholic and instituted absolute primogeniture.
acts-of-the-apostles: Acts is the second part of a two-volume work, Luke–Acts, whose first part is the Gospel of Luke. Together the two volumes make up 27.5 percent of the New Testament, the largest share attributed to a single author. The author is not named in the text. Church tradition from the 2nd century identifies him as Luke, a companion of Paul, and the first-person passages in Acts 16 to 27 have led many to read him as a participant in Paul's journeys. Critical opinion on the traditional attribution has been roughly evenly divided, and some scholars point to differences from Paul's own letters. The title was first used by Irenaeus in the late 2nd century and was not given by the author.

Most scholars date the work to 80 to 90 CE, because it uses the Gospel of Mark, looks back on the destruction of Jerusalem and shows no awareness of Paul's letters. Others allow an early 2nd-century date, while some argue against a late date because the book says nothing of the burning of Rome or of Paul's trial before Nero.

Acts has 28 chapters and moves from Jerusalem to Rome. It begins with the ascension of Jesus and the replacement of Judas Iscariot by Matthias. At Pentecost the Holy Spirit descends on the apostles, and the first believers share their property. After Stephen is stoned, persecution scatters the community, and the message reaches the Samaritans and the Gentiles. Saul of Tarsus, a persecutor, is converted by a vision. Peter preaches to the centurion Cornelius, and at Antioch the followers of Jesus are first called Christians.

The second half follows Paul. The Gentile mission, promoted from Antioch, is confirmed at a meeting in Jerusalem. Paul travels through western Asia Minor and the Aegean, founding churches. After a mob attacks him in Jerusalem he is imprisoned, claims his right as a Roman citizen to be tried in Rome and is sent there by sea. He spends two years under house arrest, proclaiming the Kingdom of God. The book ends without recording the outcome of his legal troubles.

Acts was read as a reliable history of the early church well into the post-Reformation era. The debate over its historicity was most vehement between 1895 and 1915, when Ferdinand Christian Baur argued that the author had rewritten history to present a united Peter and Paul. Most scholars now treat it as ancient historiography, with a theological purpose, and a middle range of scholars judge it relatively reliable by the standards of Hellenistic history writing. Its account agrees with Paul's letters on the outline of his career, though it differs on details.
acts-of-thomas: The Acts of Thomas belongs to the New Testament apocrypha, within the subgenre of Acts of the Apostles. It was originally a work of Syriac literature, composed in Edessa before 240 CE, and complete versions survive in both Syriac and Greek. The surviving Syriac manuscripts have been edited to purge them of the most unorthodox, overtly Encratite passages, so the Greek versions reflect the earlier tradition.

The earliest external reference, about 225, is in Origen's Exegesis on Genesis; that text is lost, and the citation survives through later works such as Eusebius of Caesarea's Ecclesiastical History. Fragments of four other cycles of romances about Thomas survive, but this is the only complete one. It should not be confused with the Gospel of Thomas.

The work is a series of episodic Acts said to have occurred during the mission of Judas Thomas, Judas the Twin, to north-west India. In the first episode the apostles cast lots to see where each will go; Thomas is assigned India and refuses, even after the Lord speaks to him.

Jesus then appears in human form and sells Thomas, skilled as a carpenter, to the Indian merchant Abbanes, and only then does Thomas accept the mission. He enters the service of the Indo-Parthian king Gondophares and is bidden to build a palace, but spends the royal grant on charity, laying up treasure in heaven. The later episodes concern a serpent, a colt, a devil in a woman, the wife of Charisius and baptisms of Mygdonia and Iuzanes.

In one episode a young man kills his lover, and when he comes to the eucharist his hand withers; Thomas forgives him because his motive was good, and brings the woman back to life. The Acts end with Thomas's martyrdom: he is pierced with spears after earning the ire of the monarch Misdaeus, thought to be Abdagases I, because he converted Misdaeus's wives and a relative, Charisius. Embedded in some manuscripts is the Syriac Hymn of the Pearl.

The Hymn of the Pearl is older than the Acts and gained great popularity in mainstream Christian circles. The Anchor Bible Dictionary describes the work as combining popular legend and religious propaganda to entertain and instruct, its poetic and liturgical elements giving important evidence for early Syrian Christian traditions. Its view of Jesus has been read as docetic, since Thomas is Jesus's identical twin, perhaps signifying his earthly side. Mainstream Christian tradition rejects the work as pseudepigraphical and apocryphal, and the Roman Catholic Church declared it heretical at the Council of Trent.
acts-of-union-1707: England and Scotland shared a monarch from 1603, when James VI of Scotland inherited the English throne from Elizabeth I and became James VI and I. He announced an intention to unite the two realms, but the English Parliament feared an absolutist structure like Scotland's, and he withdrew his proposals while taking the title King of Great Britain. Union was tried again in 1606, 1667 and 1689. Religion kept the churches apart: the Church of Scotland was Calvinist, and attempts by James and Charles I to impose policy led to the Wars of the Three Kingdoms from 1639. Some Presbyterian leaders later saw union as a way to secure free trade and a Presbyterian kirk.

By the early eighteenth century the Scottish economy was weak: largely agrarian, with chronic deflation and tariff wars over linen. Colonial trade led to the failed Darien scheme. Queen Anne had favoured deeper integration since she came to the throne in 1702, and in 1705 both parliaments agreed to new negotiations.

Each country named 31 commissioners, led on the Scottish side by the Duke of Queensberry and the Earl of Seafield. Most Scots favoured union, while England's included many Whigs and only one Tory. They met at the Cockpit in London from 16 April to 22 July 1706. Within days England had a guarantee that the Hanoverian dynasty would succeed Anne to the Scottish crown, and Scotland had a guarantee of access to colonial markets.

In the Scottish Parliament the debate began on 3 October 1706. About 100 of its 227 members supported the Court Party, aided by some 25 of the Squadrone Volante. The opposing Country party included the Duke of Hamilton, Lord Belhaven and Andrew Fletcher of Saltoun. The Court party had significant funding from England, and included many in debt after the Darien Disaster. Article 1 passed by 116 votes to 83 on 4 November 1706, and the treaty as a whole was ratified on 16 January 1707 by 110 votes to 69. The Parliament of England then passed an equivalent act, and both took effect on 1 May 1707.

The Treaty of Union had 25 articles, 15 of them economic. It joined the two kingdoms in an incorporating union as Great Britain, with Queen Anne as sovereign and one parliament at Westminster, to which Scotland sent representative peers to the House of Lords. It created a customs and monetary union and restated the Act of Settlement 1701, barring Roman Catholics from the throne. The Church of Scotland remained the established church, the Court of Session stayed within Scotland and Scots law remained in force. A separate act secured the Presbyterian church, after which the church ended its open opposition. In 1708 English treason law was extended across Great Britain.
acts-of-union-1800: Ireland had been in personal union with England since 1542, when the Irish Parliament proclaimed Henry VIII King of Ireland. Ireland gained effective legislative independence from Great Britain through the Constitution of 1782, but access to power remained restricted to the Anglo-Irish of the Protestant Ascendancy. Frustration among the Catholic majority helped lead to the rebellion of 1798, which involved a French invasion and was crushed with much bloodshed. Union was motivated partly by the belief that it would ease the political rancour behind the rebellion, and partly by fear in London that a Catholic majority in an Irish parliament might break away and ally with France.

Many members of the Irish Parliament, notably Henry Grattan, guarded its autonomy. A motion for union was rejected in 1799, and in the Irish House of Commons the first attempt lost by 109 votes to 104. In 1800 it passed by 158 to 115, in part, according to contemporary accounts, through bribery with peerages and honours. Wealthy Catholics were strongly in favour, hoping for rapid emancipation. The two acts passed on 2 July and 1 August 1800 and came into force on 1 January 1801. Together they ratified eight articles that created one parliament, with 100 Irish members in the Commons and, in the Lords, four Church of Ireland bishops in rotation and 28 representative peers elected for life.

The articles also united the Church of England and the Church of Ireland and created a customs union, with some duties kept for ten years. Ireland was to contribute two-seventeenths of the expenditure of the United Kingdom.

The first parliament of the United Kingdom of Great Britain and Ireland met on 22 January 1801. The 100 Irish members were chosen from the last Irish House of Commons, and 84 Irish boroughs were disfranchised, their patrons receiving £15,000 compensation. The Irish army was merged into the British Army. The expected Catholic emancipation was blocked by George III, who argued it would breach his coronation oath, and came only with the Roman Catholic Relief Act 1829. The Union Flag added the Saltire of St Patrick, and the royal title dropped the claim to the throne of France.
ada-of-caria: Ada was a daughter of Hecatomnus, satrap of Caria, and a sister of Mausolus, Pixodarus, Artemisia and Idrieus. The identity of her mother is less clear. One view makes her Aba, daughter of Hyssaldomos and a sister of Hecatomnus, but scholars who consider the Hecatomnid sibling marriages purely symbolic challenge this. Four of the siblings intermarried: Mausolus wed Artemisia, and Ada was married to her brother Idrieus, while Pixodarus married outside the family. Every child of Hecatomnus governed Caria at some point.

Idrieus and Ada ruled together for seven years, until his death. The joint regents kept close ties to the Hellenic world; they were mentioned as donors to the Temple of Athena in Tegea and seem to have been major patrons of Delphi. After Idrieus died, Ada was sole satrap of Caria, until her brother Pixodarus expelled her in 340 BCE. When Pixodarus died in 335 BCE he was succeeded by his son-in-law, the Persian Orontobates. Ada fled to the fortress of Alinda, where she maintained her rule in exile.

When Alexander the Great entered Caria in 334 BCE, Ada adopted him as her son and surrendered Alinda to him. Alexander accepted, and gave her formal command of the Siege of Halicarnassus. After the city fell he returned Alinda to her and made her queen of all Caria. Arrian records that he did not reject the title of son and gave her command of the whole country. Her popularity with the people in turn ensured the Carians' loyalty to Alexander. She was under the protection of Asander, the Hellenistic satrap of Lydia.

Turkish archaeologists have said that the tomb of Ada has been discovered, though the claim remains unresolved, and her remains are said to be displayed in the archaeological museum of Bodrum. She appears as a character in Eleanor Herman's young adult book Voice of Gods, published in 2015.
adad-nirari-i: Adad-nirari I ruled Assyria in the Middle Assyrian period, in 1305 to 1274 BCE by the middle chronology or 1295 to 1263 BCE by the short one. His name, written ideographically in nearly all inscriptions, means Adad is my helper. In his inscriptions from Assur he calls himself the son of Arik-den-ili, though two king lists name Enlil-nirari as his father, probably in error. His annals survive in more detail than those of most of his predecessors.

He boasted of defeating the armies of the Kassites, Qutu, Lullumu and Shubaru. The defeat of the Kassite king Nazi-Maruttaš at the town of Kar Ishtar was remembered in the epic of Tukulti-Ninurta I, which says his army fell on the Kassite camp like a devastating flood and carried off the royal standard. The victory moved Assyria's border into southern Mesopotamia. Nazi-Maruttaš's successor Kadašman-Turgu then seems to have agreed to a humiliating treaty.

Adad-nirari then turned to the former Mitanni lands. Hanigalbat, the southern remnant of Mitanni, had become a vassal of the Hittites. According to Adad-nirari, its king Shattuara attacked first and was defeated, captured and taken to Assur, where he swore fealty and paid tribute for the rest of his reign. Adad-nirari then called himself king of the universe, in imitation of Shamshi-Adad I, and addressed the Hittite king as a fellow great king. Mursili III replied angrily, asking why he should call him brother. When Shattuara's son Wasashatta rebelled, Adad-nirari sacked a number of cities, destroyed Taite, captured Wasashatta at Irridu and deported him and his family to Assur. He annexed Hanigalbat, enslaved its people and appointed an Assyrian governor.

Mursili III's successor Hattusili III accepted the conquest as a fait accompli. He asked Adad-nirari to curb raids from the frontier town of Turira against Carchemish, a Hittite vassal, and complained that Adad-nirari had failed to send gifts when he became king. He also wrote about Adad-nirari's request for iron, sending a dagger blade because good iron was not yet ready. Taite may have been the seat of Assyrian rule, and Adad-nirari rebuilt buildings at Assur, including the Step Gate of the temple of the god Ashur, city walls and the temple of Ishtar. A bronze sword of his is in the Metropolitan Museum of Art, and inscriptions on brick moulds found at Qasr Shemamok refer to a palace he built at Kilizu.
adad-nirari-ii: Adad-nirari II's name means Adad, the storm god, is my help. His father was Ashur-dan II, whom he succeeded after a minor dynastic struggle. The accession probably encouraged revolts among Assyria's nominal vassals in nearby regions of Anatolia, the Levant and Iran. He began the first renewed period of major expansion after the Middle Assyrian Empire, which had begun in 1365 BCE under Ashur-uballit I and had ended after the death of Ashur-bel-kala in 1053 BCE.

Adad-nirari II firmly subjugated areas that had been only nominally under Assyrian vassalage. After a battle at the junction of the Khabur and Euphrates rivers in 910 BCE he conquered and deported troublesome Arameans. He then subdued Neo-Hittite and Hurrian populations in eastern Anatolia. In the same year he twice attacked and defeated Shamash-mudammiq of Babylonia, annexing a large area north of the Diyala River and the towns of Hit and Zanqu in central Mesopotamia, and later in his reign he made further gains against Nabu-shuma-ukin I.

To the west he subjugated the Aramean cities of Kadmuh and Nisibin and their territories, collected vast amounts of treasure and secured the Khabur river region. His reign was a time of returning prosperity in the Middle East, with the expansion of Phoenician and Aramaean trade routes linking Anatolia, Egypt, Mesopotamia and the Mediterranean.

His son Tukulti-Ninurta II continued to expand Assyrian territory and wage war against Assyria's enemies. Full eponym lists survive from Adad-nirari's reign down to the middle of the reign of Ashurbanipal in the 7th century BCE, so year one of his reign in 911 BCE is perhaps the first event in ancient Near Eastern history that can be dated to an exact year.
adad-nirari-iii: Adad-nirari III was a son and successor of Shamshi-Adad V, and his name means Adad, the storm god, is my help. He was apparently quite young at his accession, because for the first five years of his reign his mother Shammuramat was highly influential, which gave rise to the legend of Semiramis. It is widely rejected that she acted as regent, but she was surprisingly influential for the period. He was the father of the kings Ashur-nirari V, Shalmaneser IV and Ashur-dan III. Tiglath-Pileser III described himself in his inscriptions as a son of Adad-nirari, but it is uncertain whether this is true.

His youth, and the struggles his father had faced early in his own reign, had seriously weakened Assyrian rulership over Mesopotamia and made room for the ambitions of officers, governors and local rulers. According to his inscriptions he led several campaigns to regain the strength Assyria had enjoyed under his grandfather Shalmaneser III. The eponym canon records that he campaigned in all directions until the last of his 28 years of reign, 783 BCE, and he built the temple of Nabu at Nineveh.

Among his actions was a siege of Damascus in 796 BCE, in the time of Ben-Hadad III. It led to the eclipse of the Aramaean kingdom of Damascus and allowed the recovery of Israel under Jehoash, who paid the Assyrian king tribute at this time, and Jeroboam II. Despite his vigour, Assyria entered a period of weakness lasting several decades after his death.
adal-sultanate: Adal was a general term for a region of lowlands inhabited by Muslims, east of the province of Ifat, in the area stretching from Zeila to Harar. In 1288 it was conquered by the Ifat Sultanate, though it kept some independence under Walashma rule, and in 1332 the Ethiopian emperor Amda Seyon I invaded it. In 1415 Sabr ad-Din III, eldest son of Sa'ad ad-Din II, returned from exile in Arabia to restore his father's throne. He proclaimed himself king of Adal and made Dakkar his capital. The kingdom was founded on the Harar plateau after the fall of the Sultanate of Ifat.

Sabr ad-Din III's brother and successor Mansur ad-Din invaded the royal seat of the Solomonic Empire and drove Emperor Dawit I to Yedaya, where, according to al-Maqrizi, he destroyed a Solomonic army and killed the emperor. Under Sultan Badlay the polity controlled territory from Cape Guardafui to the port of Suakin. After Badlay died at the Battle of Gomit, his successor Muhammad ibn Badlay submitted to Emperor Baeda Maryam I and paid annual tribute. Adal's emirs saw this as a betrayal, and Emir Laday Usman of Harar seized power in 1471, leaving the sultan a ceremonial post.

In 1529 Imam Ahmad ibn Ibrahim al-Ghazi began the conquest of Abyssinia and won a decisive victory at the Battle of Shimbra Kure. By 1535 he controlled the east and centre of Abyssinia, and Emperor Dawit II became a hunted fugitive. In 1559 Nur ibn Mujahid, emir of Harar, invaded the Ethiopian Empire and killed Emperor Gelawdewos at the Battle of Fatagar. Sultan Barakat ibn Umar Din was then defeated and killed by another Ethiopian army, ending the Walashma dynasty. Oromo migrants invaded, Nur's army was defeated at the Battle of Hazalo, and a famine struck Harar. Nur died in 1567, and in 1577 the capital moved to Aussa.

Adal had a string of ports and inland cities, among them Harar, Zeila, Berbera and Dakkar, with courtyard houses, mosques, shrines and cisterns, integrated into the trade networks of the Red Sea and the Indian Ocean. It traded millet, cattle, fruits, slaves, gold, barley and ivory, and its cities imported glass bracelets and celadon ware from the Ming Dynasty. Its people included Somalis, Afars, Argobba and Hararis, and Arabic served as a lingua franca. Under Imam Ahmad the army was reorganised into three flexible units, and matchlocks and cannons were used in the conquest of Abyssinia.
adalard-of-corbie: Adalard was born about 751 at Huise, the son of Bernard, a son of Charles Martel and half-brother of Pepin. He was educated in the Palatine School at Charlemagne's court in Aachen and, while still very young, was made Count of the Palace. At the age of twenty he entered the monastery of Corbie in Picardy, founded by Queen Bathild in 662. Seeking greater seclusion he went to Monte Cassino, but Charlemagne ordered him back to Corbie, where he was elected abbot.

Charlemagne made Adalard chief minister to his son Pepin, King of Italy. As a senior court administrator he attended meetings on military planning, and his De ordine palatinii describes in some detail a well-developed system of intelligence by the end of Pepin's reign. When Pepin died in Milan in 810, Adalard became tutor to Pepin's twelve-year-old son, Bernard of Italy.

When Bernard reached for the imperial crown, Emperor Louis the Pious suspected Adalard of sympathy with him and banished him to the island of Noirmoutier, then called Hermoutier, while his brother Wala was made to become a monk at Corbie. Louis later recalled him and made him one of his chief advisers. Adalard had several hospitals built, and with Wala he founded Corvey Abbey, New Corbie, in Westphalia. Corvey became an imperial abbey whose lands stretched from the bishopric of Paderborn to the duchy of Brunswick, and its abbot later sat in the imperial diet at Regensburg.

Adalard fell ill three days before Christmas while returning from Corvey to Corbie, and died early in January 827 at the age of seventy-three.
