Soon afterwards Paschasius Radbertus, who greatly admired him, wrote his life, the Vita Adalhardi. He is recognised as a saint in the Roman Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches and is the patron saint of many churches and towns in France and along the lower Rhine.
adalbert-of-hamburg: Adalbert was possibly born at Goseck Castle in Saxony, the son of Count Frederick of Goseck, a Saxon count palatine from 1038, and Agnes of Weimar. He prepared for a church career, becoming subdeacon to the archbishop of Hamburg-Bremen in 1032 and later provost of Halberstadt Cathedral. He became archbishop himself later, with supremacy over the Scandinavian Peninsula, a great part of the Wend lands and all territory north of the Elbe.

Adalbert accompanied Emperor Henry III on a campaign of conversion in 1045 and went with him to Rome in 1046. Adam of Bremen reports a rumour that Adalbert refused candidacy for pope, leading to the election of Clement II, so that he could continue the conversion of the Wends. He worked to increase his see's influence, and the empire's, but met competition in Scandinavia from missionary bishops sent from England and elsewhere. When King Sweyn II of Denmark appealed to the emperor and Pope Leo IX for an archbishop of his own, the matter was cut short by the deaths of the pope in 1054 and the emperor in 1056.

Adalbert then lost his hold on the imperial court, where the young Henry IV fell under the influence of Archbishop Anno of Cologne. He gained control of Henry's education and replaced Anno in his confidence, but retired from court again in 1066, returning later. He was a papal legate and one of the regents for Henry IV. Adam of Bremen called him generous, prudent and zealous, but marred by indomitable pride. He died at Goslar on 16 March 1072.
adam-ferguson: Adam Ferguson was born in 1723 at Logierait in Atholl, Perthshire, the son of a minister of the same name. He was educated at Logierait Parish School, Perth Grammar School, and the universities of Edinburgh and St Andrews, taking his M.A. in 1742. In 1745, because he knew Gaelic, he was appointed deputy chaplain of the 43rd regiment, later the 42nd, the Black Watch. He became principal chaplain in 1746 and remained with the regiment until 1754, when he left the clergy to devote himself to literary pursuits. Historians debate whether he fought in the ranks at the Battle of Fontenoy.

In January 1757 Ferguson succeeded David Hume as librarian of the Faculty of Advocates. In 1759 he became professor of natural philosophy at the University of Edinburgh, and in 1764 he moved to the chair of pneumatics and moral philosophy. In 1776 he published an anonymous pamphlet on the American Revolution, opposing Richard Price and sympathising with the British legislature, and in 1778 he was secretary to the Carlisle Peace Commission, which tried without success to negotiate with the revolted colonies. In 1780 he wrote a long history section for the second edition of the Encyclopædia Britannica.

He published his History of the Progress and Termination of the Roman Republic in 1783 and resigned his chair in 1785. His lectures appeared in 1792 as Principles of Moral and Political Science. He died at St Andrews on 22 February 1816 and is buried against the east wall of the cathedral churchyard.

The Essay on the History of Civil Society of 1767 drew on classical authors and contemporary travel literature to analyse modern commercial society and its abandonment of civic and communal virtues. Ferguson was sympathetic to traditional societies, such as the Highlands, for producing courage and loyalty. He stressed conflict, political participation and military valour, and, like Adam Smith and Hume, the spontaneous order that arises from the uncoordinated actions of many individuals.

He was a leading advocate of the Idea of Progress but also thought commercial growth could foster a decline in virtue and lead to a collapse like Rome's. As a devout Presbyterian he placed both in a divinely ordained plan. He argued that civilisation consists largely of laws that restrict independence but give liberty as security, and that representative institutions could keep an expanding state from tyranny. He has been called the father of modern sociology, and his critique of commercial society influenced Hegel and Marx.
adam-olearius: Adam Olearius, born Adam Ölschläger or Oehlschlaeger, was born at Aschersleben, near Magdeburg, to the tailor Adam Oehlschlegel and his wife Maria Porst. His family name refers to the trade of oil millers. He grew up in modest circumstances, but with the money his mother and sisters earned by spinning wool he enrolled at Leipzig University in 1620 to study theology, and he also studied philosophy and mathematics. He became a Magister of Philosophy in 1627, and later taught at the Old St Nicholas School and the Thomas School.

Olearius became a court official of Frederick III, Duke of Holstein-Gottorp, who planned economic ties between northern Germany and Russia. In 1633 he was appointed secretary to the ambassadors Philipp Crusius and Otto Brüggemann, sent to Muscovy and Persia in the hope of making the duke's new city of Friedrichstadt the terminus of an overland silk trade. A second embassy, with Olearius again as secretary, left Altona on 22 October 1635 with the traveller Johan Albrecht de Mandelslo and the poet Paul Fleming. It travelled down the Volga, was shipwrecked on the Caspian in November 1636, and wintered at Shamakhi, where Olearius made astronomical observations and learned Persian. It reached Isfahan on 3 August 1637 and was received by Shah Safi on 16 August.

The mission failed largely because of the arrogant behaviour of its members, above all Brüggemann, and it left on 21 December 1637 without any result. Brüggemann was held responsible for the failure and publicly executed on 5 May 1640. Back at Gottorp, Olearius became the duke's librarian, and in 1649 keeper of his cabinet of curiosities. In 1654 he constructed the Globe of Gottorf, 3.01 metres across, which was given to Peter the Great in 1713. He died at Gottorp on 22 February 1671.

Olearius is best known for his narrative of the embassies, the Beschreibung der muscowitischen und persischen Reise (Schleswig, 1647), later enlarged and translated into French, English, Dutch and, in part, Italian. He also wrote a history of Holstein, a catalogue of the Gottorp cabinet and a translation of Saadi's Gulistan, published in 1654 as Persianisches Rosenthal. By his lively writing he introduced Germany and the rest of Europe to Persian literature and culture, and Montesquieu relied on him for local colour in the Lettres persanes.
adam-opel: Adam Opel was born on 9 May 1837 in Rüsselsheim, the son of Wilhelm, a locksmith, and studied with his father until the age of 20, when he received his travel pass. It allowed him to work as an apprentice locksmith in Liège and Brussels, and then in Paris, where he arrived in mid-1858. There he became interested in the sewing machine, and in 1859 he took a job with a maker of them to see the new technology at close hand. His younger brother George also came to Paris to learn it. In 1862 Opel returned to Rüsselsheim.

An uncle offered Opel an unused cow stall in Rüsselsheim in which to set up a workshop and build his own sewing machine, and in 1863 George came back from France to help with the slow production. In 1867, just as he was preparing to build a two-storey factory near the railway station, his father died. Opel married Sophie Scheller, whose dowry went into the plant, and her two sisters invested as well, so that a steam engine could be bought. A machine named Sophia, after his wife, appeared in 1870.

Production rose steadily in the 1880s, and by 1899 more than half a million machines had been made. Opel also became interested in bicycles after seeing a high-wheeled one in Paris. He ordered parts from England, tried the finished machine with disastrous results and swore off these bone breakers, but they sold easily at a greater profit than sewing machines, and his sons begged for them. By 1886 the Opels had made a bicycle of their own, and serious production of cycles began by the end of 1887.

Opel died on 8 September 1895, before the company built any automobiles. His will reorganised the firm, with his widow Sophie holding the main interest and his two eldest sons smaller shares. She and the five sons, Carl, Wilhelm, Heinrich, Friedrich and Ludwig, led the company on the road to motor vehicles. A sudden collapse of the bicycle boom in 1898 was its first crisis, but it carried on with more than 1,500 employees.

The bicycle plant later became the largest of its kind, with a capacity of 4,000 cycles a day by the mid-1920s, and with innovative equipment such as automatic painting and plating. Between 1929 and 1931 the family sold Adam Opel AG to General Motors, and in 1936 the bicycle plant went to NSU of Neckarsulm, after about 2.5 million bicycles had been produced.
adam-smith: Adam Smith was born in Kirkcaldy, Fife, Scotland. His father, Adam Smith senior, was a Writer to the Signet who also served as comptroller of the customs in Kirkcaldy, and he died two months before the birth. His mother, Margaret Douglas, was the daughter of Robert Douglas of Strathendry. Smith was baptised on 5 June 1723, a date often treated as his birthday, but his actual date of birth is unknown. He attended the Burgh School of Kirkcaldy from 1729 to 1737, learning Latin, mathematics, history and writing.

At 14 he entered the University of Glasgow and studied moral philosophy under Francis Hutcheson. In 1740 he was the graduate scholar presented to study at Balliol College, Oxford, under the Snell Exhibition. He thought the teaching at Glasgow far better than that at Oxford, which he found intellectually stifling, and he is reported to have had a copy of David Hume's A Treatise of Human Nature confiscated there.

After his studies Smith delivered a successful series of public lectures at the University of Edinburgh, which led to a collaboration with David Hume during the Scottish Enlightenment. He then obtained a professorship at Glasgow, where he taught moral philosophy and wrote The Theory of Moral Sentiments. Later he took a tutoring position that allowed him to travel throughout Europe and meet intellectual figures of his era. He never married and lived with his mother after his return from France; she died six years before him. At his request his personal papers were destroyed after his death.

The Theory of Moral Sentiments was published in 1759 by the co-publishers Andrew Millar of London and Alexander Kincaid of Edinburgh. Smith kept revising it until his death and is believed to have considered it a better work than The Wealth of Nations.

An Inquiry into the Nature and Causes of the Wealth of Nations appeared in 1776 and is regarded as his magnum opus, marking the start of modern economic scholarship as a comprehensive system. In response to mercantilism, the policy of protecting national markets by reducing imports and increasing exports, he laid the foundations of classical free-market theory. He developed the concept of division of labour and argued that rational self-interest and competition can lead to economic prosperity. He explained the distribution of wealth and power by natural, political, social, economic, legal, environmental and technological factors rather than divine will. He was controversial in his day, and writers such as Horace Walpole satirised his approach and style. He died on 17 July 1790.
adams-onis-treaty: Pinckney's Treaty of 1795 had set the borders between the United States and Spanish Florida, but expansion by American settlers led to continuing disputes, and the Louisiana Purchase of 1803 added arguments over whether the boundary to the south ran along the Sabine River or the Rio Grande. The Peninsular War and the Spanish American wars of independence undermined Madrid's hold on its American territories, and between 1810 and 1813 the United States annexed West Florida as far east as the Perdido River.

During the first Seminole War of 1817–1818 it occupied the rest of Florida, which gave John Quincy Adams, then Secretary of State, an opening to negotiate. By 1819 Spain was ready to accept the loss of Florida in exchange for a firm border in Texas.

Negotiations were held in Washington, D.C., between Adams and the Spanish ambassador Luis de Onís, and produced an agreement of 16 articles. Article 2 transferred East and West Florida to the United States, and Article 3 defined the southern border between the two countries, while Spain withdrew its historic claims to the Oregon Country. The United States renounced claims to Spanish Texas. Under Article 11 it set up a commission to handle claims by American citizens against Spain, which distributed around five million dollars before its dissolution in 1824.

The US Senate approved the treaty unanimously on 24 February 1819, but Madrid delayed ratification until October 1820, hoping to dissuade the United States from supporting anti-Spanish revolutionaries. The Senate voted again, and Henry Clay and others demanded the cession of Texas as well, a proposal that was defeated. Spain recognised Mexican independence in the Treaty of Córdoba on 24 August 1821, and Mexico accepted the boundary in the Treaty of Limits of 1828.

For the United States the treaty extended its claimed territory from the Mississippi to the Pacific. For Spain it preserved Texas and a buffer between California and New Mexico and American territory. Many historians count it a great achievement for the United States, since Adams's vision of trade with the Orient across the Pacific was later borne out. The treaty was formally terminated in 1902.
adana: Adana lies on the Seyhan River, 35 km inland from the northeastern shores of the Mediterranean Sea, on the 37th parallel north. It occupies the centre of the Cilician plain, called Çukurova in Turkish, a relatively large stretch of flat, fertile land south-east of the Taurus Mountains. Cilicia was important in the classical world because it lies by a pass in the Taurus Mountains, used for military campaigns and trade routes.

The name has been used for over four millennia. One theory derives it from an Indo-European expression a danu, meaning on the river. According to the Hittite inscription of Kava, Kizzuwatna, inhabited by Luwians and Hurrians, ruled Adana under Hittite protection by 1335 BCE. After the collapse of the Hittite Empire around 1191 to 1189 BCE the Denyen sea peoples took control until around 900 BCE. After the Greek migration into Cilicia in the 8th century BCE the region was unified under the Mopsos dynasty, with Adana as capital.

At the Battle of Sarus in April 625 Heraclius defeated the Sasanian forces of Shahrbaraz on the east bank of the river, after a charge across the bridge built by Emperor Justinian, now the Taşköprü. The Umayyad Caliph Abd al-Malik conquered Cilicia in 704. Suleiman ibn Qutulmish annexed Adana in 1084, and Armenian forces captured it in 1132. Under the Armenian Kingdom of Cilicia it remained a centre of handicrafts and trade, and Venetian and Genoese merchants came for goods imported through the port of Ayas.

Ramazan Bey made Adana the capital of the Ramadanid Emirate, which was de facto independent through the 15th century until Selim I incorporated it into the Ottoman Empire in 1517. The Ramadanid beys held the administration of the Sanjak of Adana until 1608, when the Ottomans began direct rule. Under the Convention of Kütahya of 14 May 1833 Cilicia passed to Egypt, whose ruler's son Ibrahim Pasha demolished Adana Castle and the city walls in 1836, and the Convention of Alexandria of 27 November 1840 returned it to Ottoman rule. From the 19th century Adana was a major centre of cotton production.

Adana is a large city in southern Turkey and the administrative seat of Adana province, with a metropolitan population of 1,816,750 across its four districts: Seyhan, Yüreğir, Çukurova and Sarıçam. It remains a centre of regional trade. Among its landmarks are the Taşköprü, a 2nd-century Roman bridge, and the Ulu Cami, built in 1541 in the Ramadanid era. Adana kebabı, made from minced meat, is the city's best-known dish.
adat: The word adat comes from the Arabic ʿādā́t, the plural of ʿā́da, meaning custom or habit, and is treated as a synonym of urf, something commonly known or accepted. It describes local customary practices and traditions regarded as compatible with Islam among Muslim communities in the Balkans, the North Caucasus, and Central, South and Southeast Asia. In a broader sense it covers the norms, prohibitions and sanctions that guide a person's conduct as a member of a community.

Before Islam arrived, the peoples of the North Caucasus and Central Asia already had long-established legal and civil codes, which in the Islamic period came to be called adat. In Central Asia councils of Aqsaqals, respected elders, guided it. In the North Caucasus the Teip, or clan, was the chief reference for loyalty, honour, shame and collective responsibility.

In Southeast Asia the concept was first formulated in the Islamised Malay-speaking world, apparently to distinguish non-Islamic from Islamic practices. In the fifteenth century the Melaka empire produced a code of international shipping law, the Undang-Undang Laut Melaka, and a civil and commercial code, the Undang-Undang Melaka, heavily Islamic but with extensive adat influences. These later spread to sultanates such as Brunei, Johor, Pattani and Aceh.

Malay society is divided into two traditions. Adat temenggung is patrilineal and found in most Malay states. Adat perpatih is matrilineal, tied to a kinship-based political structure, and confined almost entirely to Negeri Sembilan, where descendants of Minangkabau immigrants from West Sumatra live. Malay culture also distinguishes several kinds of adat, among them adatullah, the natural order created by Allah, and adat muhakamah, the laws that rulers compiled into legal codes, often blended with Islamic law. The earliest example of the latter is the Terengganu Inscription Stone of 1303, which sets out ten basic laws.

In the early twentieth century the study of adat became a specialised field in the Dutch East Indies. Scholars such as Cornelis van Vollenhoven, Ter Haar and Christiaan Snouck Hurgronje compared its systems, and the colonial government used adatrecht as a legal term. The customs of all ethnic groups, non-Muslims included, were collectively called adat, and the Dutch divided the East Indies into at least nineteen adat law areas.

In the Russian Empire, the colonial administration left local legal practice to councils of aqsaqals and teips, as did the Bolsheviks in the first years after 1917, until Soviet authorities banned adat in the early 1930s and replaced it with civil law. After the dissolution of the Soviet Union it was revived in Central Asia in the 1990s. Adat is still enforced as personal law in the courts of Brunei, Malaysia and Indonesia in certain respects.
adda-river: The Adda, known in Latin as Abdua or Addua, is a tributary of the Po, 313 kilometres long. It rises in the Alpisella valley near the head of the Fraele glen, in the Rhaetian Alps near the border with Switzerland, and several smaller streams join it near Bormio. The highest point of its drainage basin is the summit of La Spedla, a subpeak of Piz Bernina, at 4,020 metres. It flows southwest and then west through the Valtellina, past Tirano, where the Poschiavino joins it from the right, and Sondrio, where the Mallero joins. This east to west run is unusual in northern Italy.

The river enters the northern end of Lake Como and contributes much of the lake's volume. It leaves by the lake's southeastern arm at Lecco, crosses the Lombardy Plain, receives the Brembo and the Serio from the left and joins the Po near Castelnuovo Bocca d'Adda, a few kilometres upstream of Cremona. Towns along it include Bormio, Tirano, Sondrio, Bellagio, Lecco, Brivio and Lodi.

The lower Adda historically marked the border between the Republic of Venice and the Duchy of Milan, as established by the Treaty of Lodi in 1454. Several battles were fought on its banks. In 1705 Prince Eugene of Savoy and the French fought at the bridgehead of Cassano d'Adda, where Alexander Suvorov led his forces across the river in 1799. At Lodi in 1796 Napoleon defeated Austrian forces. The Trezzo sull'Adda Bridge, built in 1377, had a single arch of 72 metres, the longest bridge arch built before metal was used in bridge construction.
addis-ababa: Addis Ababa lies in the Ethiopian Highlands, on the western edge of the Great Rift Valley, at an elevation of 2,355 metres, which makes it the highest capital in Africa. It stands at the foot of Mount Entoto and forms part of the watershed of the Awash. The high elevation moderates temperatures, and no month has a mean temperature above 22 degrees.

The name is Amharic for new flower; in Oromo the place is called Finfinnee, meaning fountain of hot mineral water. The city is surrounded by the Special Zone of Oromia, and the Constitution of Ethiopia says that the special interest of the State of Oromia in Addis Ababa, in social services and natural resources, is to be respected.

Menelik II, Negus of Shewa, founded the city in 1886, after finding Mount Entoto unpleasant two years earlier. It was then a resort town, and its many mineral springs drew nobles of the empire, who settled permanently, followed by artisans, merchants and foreign visitors. Menelik formed his imperial palace in 1887, and in 1889 Addis Ababa became the empire's capital, after which international embassies opened. Urban development began in the 20th century without prior planning. The Oromo left the area after Menelik's conquest and were physically removed from near the city under Haile Selassie and the Derg.

The city saw an economic boom in 1926 and 1927, with stone houses filled with imported European furniture, imported automobiles and expanded banks. During the Italian occupation a masterplan increased urbanisation and modernisation, in the hope that Addis Ababa would become a more colonial city. French and British consultants drew later master plans from the 1940s onwards.

Addis Ababa is the capital and largest city of Ethiopia and a federally chartered city. It is the headquarters of the African Union and the United Nations Economic Commission for Africa. Addis Ababa University is there. All Ethiopian ethnic groups are represented, the largest being the Amhara, Oromo and Gurage, and Amharic is the most common mother tongue.
addu-atoll: Seenu Atoll, historically known as Addu Atoll, is the southernmost atoll of the Maldives and lies 540 kilometres south of Malé. With Fuvahmulah, 40 kilometres to the north, it extends the Maldives into the Southern Hemisphere. Unlike other atolls, its lagoon is a natural anchorage, reached by four channels: the Kuda and Maa channels on the north, the Gan channel on the south and the broad Villingili channel on the southeast.

Barrier reefs protect the islands from storms and high waves, coconut palms grow almost everywhere, and small lakes, wetlands and marshy taro fields are found nowhere else in the country. Addu City, one of the four cities of the Maldives, covers the inhabited islands of Hulhudhoo, Meedhoo, Maradhoo, Feydhoo and Hithadhoo; Gan, with its airport, lies outside it.

The name Addu is believed to come from the local words ah, eight, and dhoo, island, because eight islands were traditionally inhabited. British mapmakers anglicised it as Addou. Some of the earliest known settlements in the country are on Meedhoo, in the far north of the atoll. Long ago families appointed by the sultans in Malé ruled Addu, and it may have had a matrilineal system of inheritance.

During the Second World War the Royal Navy built a secret base there, HMS Haitan, to use the deep anchorage and sheltered harbour. Oil tanks and storage facilities, an airstrip and a flying boat base were built on Gan, and the base stayed unknown to the Axis in the early years of the war. In 1957 it passed to the Royal Air Force as RAF Gan and closed in 1976. The island is now the site of Gan International Airport. When Addu declared independence as the United Suvadive Republic, the Malé dialect rather than the Addu dialect was used in its official correspondence.

Addu people speak the Addu dialect, which resembles the Mulaku dialect of Fuvahmulah but differs somewhat from official Dhivehi; it was traditionally a lingua franca among the educated of three southern atolls, while the written language is common throughout the Maldives. The white tern is found in the Maldives only on Addu Atoll and is seen as a symbol of the islands. Addu was also the only part of the Maldives untouched by the coral bleaching of 1998.
adel-shah: Not much is known of the life of Ali-qoli Khan before he took the throne. He was the eldest son of Ebrahim Khan, a brother of Nader Shah, and he attended Nader Shah's coronation on 8 March 1736. In 1737 he was given the governorship of Mashhad and married Ketevan, a daughter of the Georgian king Teimuraz II; in 1740 he also married a daughter of Abu al-Fayz Khan, ruler of the Khanate of Bukhara, which the Afsharids had recently subjugated.

From 1743 to 1747 he commanded Nader's troops against the Yazidis of Kurdistan, the Karakalpaks and Uzbeks of Khwarazm, and in Sistan. He then fell into trouble with his uncle, who decided to levy 100,000 tomans on him and was suspicious of him. In April 1747, together with rebels of Sistan, he occupied Herat and induced the Kurds to rebel.

Nader Shah, marching against the insurgents, was murdered on 21 June 1747 by a group of his officers, who offered the crown to Ali-qoli. His death left a power vacuum, and his empire was divided among various sovereigns: Uzbek and Afghan rulers seized the east, and Ahmad Khan of the Abdali fled to Kandahar, took the title Durr-i Durran and renamed his tribe Durrani. In Mashhad the governor and superintendent of the Imam Reza Shrine, Mir Sayyed Mohammad, drove out the Afghans and secured the city for Ali-qoli Khan, who may have had a hand in his uncle's murder.

On 6 July 1747 Ali-qoli ascended the throne as Soltan Ali Adel Shah. His men captured the fortress of Kalat and massacred sixteen descendants of Nader Shah, among them three of Nader's sons. Nader's grandson Shahrokh, then 14, was spared in case his Safavid lineage proved useful, and was imprisoned at Kalat. Adel Shah ruled a considerably smaller realm than Nader, and his rule was secured only in eastern Iran. Preferring to revel in Mashhad, he made his younger brother Ebrahim Mirza governor of Isfahan, and Ebrahim declared independence.

Adel Shah marched against his brother but lost many men to desertion and was defeated in June 1748. He fled to Tehran, where its governor, Mirza Mohsen Khan, captured and blinded him and handed him to Mir Sayyed Mohammad. Taken back to Mashhad, he found that a group of Turkic, Kurdish and Arab tribal leaders had taken advantage of his absence to declare Shahrokh shah on 1 October. Adel Shah was executed at the request of Shahrokh and of the mother of Nasrollah Mirza. Ebrahim Afshar, who had established his rule in western Iran, had by then declared himself shah.
adela-of-normandy: Adela was the youngest daughter of William the Conqueror and Matilda of Flanders, and the favourite sister of King Henry I of England. She is generally believed to have been born between 1066 and 1070. Educated and high-spirited, she knew Latin and was probably schooled at a monastery, probably the Abbey of Sainte-Trinité in Caen. With three older brothers and one younger, she could not inherit her father's honours, but her blood was a valuable asset in marriage.

Between 1080 and 1083, at about fifteen, she married Stephen Henry, son and heir of the count of Blois, at Chartres Cathedral. He was nearly twenty years her senior. The marriage linked the two most powerful families in northern France. Stephen inherited Blois, Chartres and Meaux in 1089, and the couple had six or eight children who survived infancy. They decided matters together, and Adela helped lay the foundations of the county of Champagne.

Stephen joined the First Crusade in 1096 with his brother-in-law Robert Curthose, and Adela acted as regent. She granted charters, corresponded with Ivo of Chartres, toured the lands settling disputes and promoting economic growth, and commanded knights to go to battle with the king. Stephen's letters to her give an intimate view of the Crusade's leaders. According to Orderic Vitalis, when he returned to France in 1100 she berated him constantly and urged him back to the Holy Land. He returned for the crusade of 1101 and was killed in a last stand after the Battle of Ramla in 1102.

Adela continued as regent through the early rule of her son Thibaud until her retirement in 1120, and went on issuing charters and ruling jointly afterwards. In 1105, after Anselm visited her during an illness, she carried his threat of excommunication to Henry I. Orderic praised her as a wise and spirited woman. In 1107 she replaced her eldest son William as heir with Theobald. Her son Henry, pledged to Cluny Abbey at two as an oblate child, became Abbot of Glastonbury and Bishop of Winchester.

In 1120 Adela retired as a nun to the monastery at Marcigny, near her son Henry at Cluny, and kept in contact with her children and the churchmen of her former lands. That year her daughter Lucia-Mahaut drowned in the wreck of the White Ship. In 1111 her son Stephen had gone to London to join Henry I's court, and on Henry's death in 1135 he seized the English throne in preference to Empress Matilda, beginning a civil war of nearly twenty years. Adela lived to see him king and died at Marcigny in 1137. She is a saint of the Roman Catholic Church, with a feast day on 24 February.
adelaide: Adelaide lies on the Adelaide Plains, north of the Fleurieu Peninsula, between Gulf St Vincent in the west and the Mount Lofty Ranges in the east. The city stretches about 20 kilometres from the coast to the foothills. Its climate is a hot-summer Mediterranean one, with hot, dry summers and cool winters, and most rain falls in winter. The traditional owners of the region are the Kaurna, and in the Kaurna language the name Tarndanya refers to the city centre and the surrounding Park Lands. Aboriginal people have lived in the area for a very long time, and archaeological evidence of Aboriginal culture at Hallett Cove Conservation Park dates back 40,000 years.

Edward Gibbon Wakefield's ideas about colonial reform lay behind the project of a new colony, which Robert Gouger petitioned the British government to create. The South Australia Act 1834 followed. The first British colonisers arrived in February 1836, and colonial government began on 28 December 1836, when the governor made a proclamation near the Old Gum Tree in what is now Glenelg North. The date is still commemorated in South Australia as Proclamation Day. The city was named in honour of Adelaide of Saxe-Meiningen, wife of King William IV, and was founded as the planned capital of a freely settled British colony.

Colonel William Light, the first surveyor-general of South Australia, designed the city centre as a grid with five squares, ringed by parkland known as the Adelaide Parklands. His choice of site was at first unpopular with the early settlers and with the first governor, John Hindmarsh, because it lay far from the harbour at Port Adelaide and had little fresh water. The colony was founded on a vision of religious tolerance, which attracted many faiths and earned Adelaide the name City of Churches. Although it was English in culture, it drew German and other European nonconformists early on. The first German Lutherans arrived in 1838 and brought vine cuttings that founded the wineries of the Barossa Valley.

Adelaide was Australia's third largest city for most of the 20th century. Electric street lighting arrived in 1900 and electric trams in 1909, and 28,000 men were sent from the state to fight in the First World War.

Adelaide is the capital of South Australia and the seat of its government, with a bicameral Parliament made up of the House of Assembly and the Legislative Council. Its early buildings were often made of local bluestone. North Terrace, the cultural precinct, holds institutions built when the city was still Australia's third largest, among them the State Library of South Australia and the South Australian Museum. Light's plan of the Parklands survives, and the Parklands are now listed as national heritage.
adelaide-del-vasto: Adelaide del Vasto was the daughter of Manfred del Vasto, a brother of Boniface del Vasto, marquess of Western Liguria, and of Anselm del Vasto. Her paternal grandparents were Teto II del Vasto and Bertha of Turin. In 1089 she married Roger I of Sicily, as his third wife, while her sister married Roger's illegitimate son Jordan.

Roger I died in 1101, and Adelaide ruled as regent for her young sons Simon and Roger II. During her regency the emir Christodulus rose to preeminence at court and Palermo was settled as the capital. Rebellions broke out almost at once in parts of Calabria and Sicily, and the monk Orderic Vitalis writes that she ended them severely.

Alexander of Telese called her a most prudent woman who exercised the cares of government, and a Greek and Arab charter of 1109 names her the malikah of Sicily and Calabria and protector of the Christian faith. Latin Christians and Muslims lived side by side in cities with their own governmental and judicial bodies.

Simon was enthroned at about eight or nine but died in 1105, so Adelaide was regent again until Roger II reached his majority in 1112. Her signature appears on documents after 1112, which suggests she continued to play a central role in governing the island.

In 1112 the Latin Patriarch of Jerusalem, Arnulf of Chocques, suggested that Baldwin I of Jerusalem marry Adelaide. Baldwin's Armenian wife Arda was still alive, although he had sent her to a convent around 1105. Adelaide demanded that a son of the marriage inherit Jerusalem, and that otherwise the kingdom pass to Roger II. No heir came, the king was blamed for bigamy and Arnulf was deposed.

Pope Paschal II agreed to reinstate Arnulf in 1116 on condition that the marriage be annulled. The annulment was performed at Acre in 1117 and Adelaide sailed back to Sicily. She died on 16 April 1118 and was buried in Patti. According to William of Tyre, Roger II never forgave the Kingdom of Jerusalem.
adelaide-of-italy: Adelaide was born at Orbe Castle in the Kingdom of Upper Burgundy, the daughter of Rudolf II of Burgundy and Bertha of Swabia. Her father fought Berengar I for control of northern Italy, and the people of Lombardy appealed to Hugh of Provence, who succeeded in taking the Burgundian throne when Rudolf died in 937. To control Upper Burgundy, Hugh married his son Lothair II, the nominal King of Italy, to the 15-year-old Adelaide in 947. Their daughter Emma, born about 948, later became queen of West Francia by marrying King Lothair of France.

According to the calendar of saints, Lothair was poisoned on 22 November 950 at Turin by Berengar II of Italy. Berengar tried to force Adelaide to marry his son Adalbert. She refused, fled to the castle of Como and was imprisoned for four months at Garda. Her biographer Odilo of Cluny relates that she escaped, was rescued by a priest and reached a fortress, probably Canossa, from which she sent to the East Frankish king Otto I for protection. They met at Pavia and married on 23 September 951.

She accompanied Otto on his second expedition to Italy, and on 2 February 962 Pope John XII crowned both of them in Rome, the first time an empress was crowned. A new ordo was created for her anointing. Between 962 and 972 she appears as an intervenient in seventy-five charters, and Gerbert of Aurillac and her daughter Emma asked for her help. Otto I died in May 973. After conflict with her son Otto II, who expelled her from court in 978, she was reconciled with him, and in 983 he named her his viceroy in Italy.

Otto II died in 983, and Adelaide worked with her daughter-in-law Theophanu to secure the succession of her grandson Otto III. When Theophanu died in 991 Adelaide became regent until he came of age in 994. She then devoted herself to charity and to founding and restoring religious houses, and she kept close ties with Cluny. She died at Selz Abbey in Alsace on 16 December 999 and was canonised by Pope Urban II in 1097. Her feast day, 16 December, is still kept in many German dioceses. Operas by Sartorio, Porpora, Handel and Rossini draw on her life.
adelaide-of-saxe-meiningen: Adelaide was born on 13 August 1792 in Meiningen, the eldest child of Georg I, Duke of Saxe-Meiningen, and Luise Eleonore of Hohenlohe-Langenburg. In 1817 the death of Princess Charlotte of Wales, the Prince Regent's only legitimate child, left the British succession without a legitimate heir, and the sons of George III sought quick marriages. Prince William, Duke of Clarence, already had ten illegitimate children by the actress Dorothea Jordan, who were barred from the succession. Adelaide seemed the ideal wife: amiable, home-loving and willing to accept the children as part of the family. They married on 11 July 1818 at Kew Palace in a double wedding with William's brother Prince Edward, Duke of Kent.

Adelaide had several pregnancies, but all the children died in infancy or were stillborn. A daughter, Charlotte Augusta Louise, lived only a few hours in 1819, and a second daughter, Elizabeth Georgiana Adelaide, born on 10 December 1820, died on 4 March 1821. Twin boys were stillborn in 1822. The couple lived first in Hanover, where living was cheaper, and then at Bushy House. When William became king in 1830 they were crowned together at Westminster Abbey on 8 September 1831. Parliament set her a dower annuity of £100,000, and she gave a large part of her household income to charity. She was admired for piety, modesty and charity.

She was strongly Tory and said little about politics in public, but the press and courtiers assumed she worked against the Reform Act 1832, and it is unclear how far she influenced William. She treated her niece Princess Alexandrina Victoria, the future Queen Victoria, with kindness despite the open hostility between William and Victoria's mother, the Duchess of Kent.

William died on 20 June 1837 and Adelaide became queen dowager, the first for over a century. She was often ill and travelled in search of better health, to Malta in 1838, where she paid for St Paul's Pro-Cathedral in Valletta, and to Madeira in 1847. She funded the first village school in Great Witley. She died on 2 December 1849 at Bentley Priory and was buried at St George's Chapel, Windsor, having asked for a private and quiet funeral. The capital of South Australia, Adelaide, was named after her in 1836, as were Adelaide in the Eastern Cape and Sir Benjamin D'Urban's short-lived Queen Adelaide Province.
adelaide-of-susa: Adelaide of Susa was born in Turin to Ulric Manfred II of Turin and Bertha of Milan, and little is known of her early life. When her father died in December 1033 or 1034 she inherited the bulk of his property, including land in the counties of Turin, especially the Susa Valley, Auriate and Asti. Her mother probably acted briefly as regent.

Because a margrave's duties were chiefly military, Emperor Conrad II arranged in 1036 or 1037 for her to marry his stepson Herman IV, who was invested as margrave of Turin and died of plague in 1038. To secure her possessions she married Henry, Marquess of Montferrat, probably in 1041, and after his death around 1045 she married Otto of Savoy in 1046. They had three sons, Peter I, Amadeus II and Otto, and two daughters, Bertha, who married Henry IV of Germany, and Adelaide, who married Rudolf of Rheinfelden.

After Otto's death, around 1057/60, Adelaide ruled the March of Turin and the County of Savoy alongside her sons Peter and Amadeus. In 1070 she captured and burned Asti, which had rebelled against her. When Henry IV came to Italy to submit to Pope Gregory VII and Matilda of Tuscany at Canossa, she supported him through Bertha's intervention, received Bugey in return for passage through her lands, and went to Canossa as a mediator. She founded the monastery of Santa Maria at Pinerolo in 1064. Peter Damian and Gregory VII relied on her to enforce clerical celibacy, while Pope Alexander II reproached her for dealing with the simoniac Archbishop of Milan.

Adelaide died in December 1091, the last of the Arduinici. A later legend says she was buried at Canischio after living there in secret for twenty-two years, a story the historian Charles William Previté-Orton called absurd. A statue of her at prayer stands in the cathedral of Susa. She is sometimes compared with her second cousin Matilda of Tuscany.
aden: Aden lies on the north coast of the Gulf of Aden, near the eastern approach to the Red Sea and about 170 km east of the Strait of Bab al-Mandab, which makes it a gateway between the Red Sea and the Arabian Sea. The highlands of Jabal Shamsan rise in the south, with peaks above 500 metres, and like the rest of Yemen's highlands they are of volcanic origin. Aden encloses the eastern side of a vast natural harbour that forms the modern port.

The Greeks called Aden Arabia Emporion, the Arabian trading port, and in the 1st century BCE it was known as Eudaemon, a transshipping point for the Red Sea trade. According to the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea, it fell on hard times in the 1st century CE when ships began to cross directly to India. The Book of Ezekiel names Aden among the merchants of Sheba.

The British Empire held the city from 1839 until independence in 1967. By 1920 it was a major commercial centre of the Arabian Peninsula and supplied coal and salt to passing ships. The oil refinery began operating in 1954, and British Petroleum ran it and the port until the South Yemeni government took them over in 1978. Aden was the capital of South Yemen from 1967 until the union with North Yemen in 1990.

Aden is the principal city of Aden Governorate, which has eight districts. Its airport and the main offices of Aden University are at Khormaksar, on the isthmus that links the peninsulas to the mainland.
aden-protectorate: The protectorate grew in the hinterland of the port of Aden and in the Hadhramaut after the Bombay Presidency of British India conquered Aden in January 1839. British expansion there was meant to secure the port, which was then governed from British India. It began with informal arrangements of protection with nine states of the immediate hinterland: Abdali, Alawi, Amiri, Aqrabi, Aulaqi, Fadhli, Haushabi, Subeihi and Yafa. From 1874 these arrangements existed with the tacit acceptance of the Ottoman Empire, which kept suzerainty over Yemen to the north, and the nine polities became known as the Nine Tribes or Nine Cantons.

The British began to formalise protection with a treaty with the Mahra Sultanate of Qishn and Socotra in 1886. More than thirty major treaties followed, the last signed in 1954, together with minor agreements. In exchange for protection the rulers agreed not to make treaties with, or cede territory to, any other foreign power. In 1917 control passed from the Government of India to the Foreign Office, and in 1937 the territory was divided for administration into the Western Protectorate, with a Political Officer at Lahej, and the Eastern Protectorate, with one at Mukalla.

From 1938 Britain signed advisory treaties with the Qu'aiti sultan and later with twelve other states, which allowed a Resident Advisor in each. The treaties stabilised the rulers' status and succession but encouraged official corruption, and aerial bombardment and collective punishment were sometimes used against tribes that defied the rulers. King Ahmad bin Yahya of Yemen, who did not recognise British suzerainty and wished to form a Greater Yemen, was involved in skirmishes along the Violet Line, a demarcation made in 1914.

On 11 February 1959 six rulers signed an accord forming the Federation of Arab Emirates of the South. Nine more joined, and on 18 January 1963 Aden Colony merged with it to make the Federation of South Arabia, while the states outside, mostly eastern, became the Protectorate of South Arabia. A state of emergency was declared on 10 December 1963. Two rival groups, the National Liberation Front and the Front for the Liberation of Occupied South Yemen, fought the British and each other, and the British left Aden by the end of November 1967.

Rulers kept a large degree of autonomy. Their flags flew over government buildings, they governed in their own names, and their states kept a distinct international personality, unlike the Colony of Aden. The boundaries and number of polities changed over time, and some, such as the Mahra Sultanate, barely had a functioning administration. The territory now forms part of Yemen.
adhemar-of-le-puy: Adhemar, also known as Adémar, Aimar or Aelarz, was born around 1045 into the family of the Counts of Valentinois and became bishop of Puy-en-Velay before 1087. He was an advocate of the Gregorian Reform, and his supporters included the future Pope Urban II and Raymond of Saint-Gilles, Count of Toulouse. He is said to have gone on pilgrimage to Jerusalem in the 1080s. His brother William Hugh of Monteil also took part in the First Crusade. Adhemar most likely met Urban II when the pope visited Puy in August 1095.

At the Council of Clermont in 1095 Adhemar showed great zeal for the crusade, and there is evidence that Urban had conferred with him before the council. On 27 November 1095 Urban named him apostolic legate and appointed him to lead the expedition. He spent the next year raising money and recruiting men, and on 15 August 1096 he left with Raymond of Toulouse's army. Raymond and the other leaders often quarrelled over leadership, but Adhemar was always recognized as the spiritual leader. In Pelagonia, Pecheneg mercenaries beat and robbed him until crusaders noticed the disturbance and saved him. He then fell ill at Thessalonica and rejoined the army later.

He negotiated with Alexius I Comnenus at Constantinople, restored some discipline at Nicaea and played a crucial part at the Battle of Dorylaeum. At the siege of Antioch he sustained morale with fasts and observances, among them a three-day fast after an earthquake, and ordered the crusaders to shave and wear a cross so that they would not attack one another by mistake. During the siege by Kerbogha he had the gates locked so that panicking crusaders could not leave. He was sceptical of Peter Bartholomew's discovery of the Holy Lance, since such a relic was already held at Constantinople, but allowed the army to believe in it if it raised morale.

Adhemar fell sick in June 1098 and, after Kerbogha's defeat, organized a council to settle the leadership disputes. He died on 1 August 1098, probably of typhus, and was buried in the Basilica of St Peter in Antioch. The disputes among the nobles went unresolved and the march to Jerusalem was delayed for months, though the ordinary soldiers continued to regard him as a leader. Several crusaders reported visions of him. Peter Bartholomew claimed he had spent days in hell for his scepticism, and Peter Desiderius said that at Jerusalem Adhemar told him to have the crusaders fast and process around the walls. Jerusalem was taken in 1099.
adib-shishakli: Adib Shishakli was born in the Hama Sanjak of Ottoman Syria into a Sunni family. His mother was of Kurdish origin, from the Barazi family, and his father was a Syrian Turkmen. He was commissioned in 1930 as an officer in the colonial military of the French Mandate, studied at the Military Academy of Damascus and became an early member of the Syrian Social Nationalist Party (SSNP), founded by Antun Saadeh to promote a Greater Syria.

In the 1948 Arab-Israeli War he commanded the 2nd Yarmouk Brigade of the Arab Liberation Army and launched its first major operation in Palestine, an abortive assault on Qal'at Jiddin, which earned him a following among Syrian officers.

Shishakli joined the officers connected to the SSNP who overthrew Husni al-Za'im in 1949 and put Sami al-Hinnawi in charge. In December 1949 he launched the year's third coup, arresting Hinnawi to break Hashemite influence, and he ordered the killing of the air force commander, Colonel Mohammad Nasser. On 28 November 1951 he arrested Prime Minister Maarouf al-Dawalibi and his cabinet and the pro-Iraq politicians, and Hashim al-Atassi resigned. His right-hand man Fawzi Selu became figurehead head of state, though real power lay with Shishakli.

He dissolved all political parties, banned newspapers that were not pro-Shishakli and persecuted Communist Party, the Baath Party and the Muslim Brotherhood, banishing the Baath leaders Akram al-Hawrani, Michel Aflaq and Salah al-Bitar to Lebanon. He relied on radio, built a cult of personality and set up an information ministry. In August 1952 he founded the Arab Liberation Movement, boycotted by figures such as Atassi, and in mid-1953 staged an election to make himself president. In 1954 he shelled Druze strongholds in Jabal al-Druze to put down resistance.

Opposition centred on Atassi and the Druze leader Sultan al-Atrash. A coup on 23 February 1954 overthrew Shishakli, with Atassi's family, Druze officers, the Syrian Communist Party and Ba'ath Party members taking part. He refused to drag Syria into civil war and fled to Lebanon, then Brazil. A coup he planned with funds provided by Iraq before the union with Egypt in 1958 was foiled, and he was sentenced to death in absentia. On 27 September 1964 Nawaf Ghazaleh, a Syrian Druze seeking revenge for his parents' deaths during the bombardment of Jabal Druze, assassinated him in Ceres, Brazil.
adige: The Adige rises near the Reschen Pass, at 1,504 m, close to the borders with Austria and Switzerland, and flows through the artificial Lake Reschen. A church tower marks the site of the former village of Alt Graun, which was evacuated and flooded in 1953 after the dam was finished. Near Glurns the Rom joins it from the Swiss Val Müstair. It then runs eastward through the Vinschgau to Merano, where the Passer joins from the north. The section between Merano and Bolzano is called the Etschtal.

South of Bolzano the Eisack joins and the river turns south through a valley that has always been one of the major routes through the Alps, connecting the Reschen and Brenner passes; the Brenner, at 1,370 m, is considered the easiest of the main Alpine passes. Near Trento the Avisio, Noce and Fersina join. The river then crosses Trentino and Veneto, passing Rovereto, Verona and Rovigo, and reaches the Adriatic across the north-eastern Po Plain. In the delta the Adige and the Po run parallel without properly joining. The Mori–Torbole tunnel, an underground canal built for flood prevention, links the Adige with Lake Garda.

The origin of the name is unknown. Nineteenth-century theories, such as a derivation from Proto-Celtic meaning the water and a link with the River Tees, were never accepted by Celtic specialists and are now obsolete. The Chiusa di Salorno narrows the valley at Salorno and marks the southernmost part of the predominantly German-speaking province of South Tyrol. The Adige was named in the Lied der Deutschen of 1841 as the southern border of the German language area. Germany adopted the song as its national anthem in 1922, although Italy by then controlled the whole river. The marble trout, native to the river, is now far less common than before, partly because stocked brown trout interbreed with it.
adil-shahi-dynasty: The origin of the founder, Yusuf Adil Shah, is uncertain. He may have been a Georgian slave bought by the Bahmani statesman Mahmud Gawan, while other historians call him Persian or Turkoman. The historian Firishta made him a son of the Ottoman sultan Murad II, which modern historians dispute. Under the Bahmani sultan Muhammad Shah III he became governor of the province of Bijapur, and in 1490 he made it a de facto independent state, formally independent with the Bahmani collapse in 1518. In 1503 he proclaimed Shi'a Islam the official religion, following Isma'il I of the Safavids. Bijapur remained the capital throughout.

The sultanate fought constantly with its neighbours. The Portuguese took Goa in 1510, the year Yusuf died, and Vijayanagara's ruler Krishnadevaraya defeated his son Isma'il at Raichur in 1520. Ali Adil Shah I, who restored Shi'a Islam in 1558, joined the sultans of Golconda, Ahmednagar and Bidar to defeat Vijayanagara at Talikota in 1565, after which Vijayanagara was sacked. By 1576 his conquests had doubled the sultanate's holdings. His nephew Ibrahim Adil Shah II came to the throne aged nine in 1580 and presided over prosperity and patronage, with population estimates for the capital as high as one million.

The sultanate reached its peak under Muhammad Adil Shah, who ruled from 1627. After Shah Jahan's failed siege of 1631 a treaty of 1636 made Bijapur tributary to the Mughals, and its borders then reached from the Arabian Sea to the Bay of Bengal. Strained relations with nobles and the revolt of Shivaji weakened it. Aurangzeb invaded in 1657, Ali Adil Shah II lost ground to the Marathas, and the last sultan, Sikandar Adil Shah, was four years old when he took the throne. A Mughal siege begun in April 1685 ended on 12 September 1686, and Sikandar was taken captive.

Adil Shahi architecture is a Deccani variant of Indo-Islamic building, marked by large domes, turrets and calligraphic designs. The great Jami Masjid was commissioned in 1576 and the Ibrahim Rauza was completed in 1626. Muhammad Adil Shah's mausoleum, the Gol Gumbaz, had a dome that was the largest in the Islamic world when it was nearly finished in 1656.

The sultans also fostered miniature painting, which spread widely under Ali Adil Shah I, and writing in the Deccani language. Ibrahim II wrote the Kitab-i Nauras, and Firishta composed his history of the medieval Deccan, the Tarikh-i Firishta, in his service.
adnan-menderes: Ali Adnan Menderes was born in 1899 in Koçarlı, Aydın, to a wealthy landowner of Crimean Tatar origin. He studied at the American College in İzmir and, in the Turkish War of Independence, fought the invading Greek army and received the Medal of Independence. In 1930 he organised a branch of the short-lived Liberal Republican Party in Aydın, and after it dissolved Atatürk himself invited him to join the Republican People's Party (CHP); he was elected deputy for Aydın in 1931.

Under İsmet İnönü he opposed statist policy. In June 1945 he joined Celâl Bayar, Fuat Köprülü and Refik Koraltan in the Motion with Four Signatures, which demanded more political freedom, and by September three of them had been stripped of CHP membership. The four founded the Democrat Party (DP) on 7 January 1946.

The DP won 52 percent of the vote in the first free elections in Turkish history, on 14 May 1950, and Menderes became prime minister. He won again in 1954 and 1957. Turkey fought in the Korean War and was admitted to NATO in 1952. With Marshall Plan aid, agriculture was mechanised and transport, energy and education advanced, though the economy slowed in the mid-1950s. He campaigned in 1950 on legalising the Arabic call to prayer, which had been banned.

His government instituted press censorship, had journalists arrested and tried to control the opposition parties and the universities. In September 1955, after a bomb exploded near the Turkish consulate in Thessaloniki, mobs in Istanbul destroyed thousands of shops, houses, churches and graves of the Greek minority, killing over a dozen people. Several sources link the government to the Istanbul pogrom, and Menderes later apologised and offered compensation.

A military coup on 27 May 1960 deposed the government. Menderes was tried on the island of Yassıada for violating the constitution, embezzlement and ordering the Istanbul pogrom, and was sentenced to death. He attempted suicide with sleeping pills, and appeals from Cemal Gürsel, İsmet İnönü and foreign leaders did not save him. He was hanged on İmralı on 17 September 1961, with the ministers Fatin Rüştü Zorlu and Hasan Polatkan. The Turkish Parliament pardoned all three on 17 September 1990, and his grave was moved to a mausoleum in Istanbul. Adnan Menderes University in Aydın and Adnan Menderes Airport in İzmir bear his name.
adolf-frederick-king-of-sweden: Adolf Frederick was born on 14 May 1710 at Gottorf Castle, near Schleswig, a member of a junior line of the House of Holstein-Gottorp. His father, Christian August, had been Protestant Prince-Bishop of Lübeck since 1705 and acted during the Great Northern War as administrator of Holstein-Gottorp for his underage nephew, Duke Charles Frederick. His mother, Albertina Frederica of Baden-Durlach, descended from earlier Swedish royalty.

From 1727 to 1750 he was prince-bishop of Lübeck, ruling a fief around Eutin. After Charles Frederick died in 1739 he became administrator of Holstein-Kiel for the duke's orphan son, Charles Peter Ulrich, who was soon invited to Russia by his aunt, Empress Elizabeth, and was later Peter III of Russia.

In 1743 the Hat faction elected Adolf Frederick heir to the throne of Sweden, wanting better conditions from Empress Elizabeth at the Treaty of Åbo. In 1744 he married Louisa Ulrika of Prussia, a sister of Frederick the Great. On the death of Frederick I on 25 March 1751 he became the first Swedish king from the House of Holstein-Gottorp, and he was crowned in Stockholm Cathedral on 26 November 1751.

Real power lay with the Riksdag of the Estates, often distracted by party strife. Twice he tried to free himself from its control. In 1756, urged on by Louisa Ulrika, he took part in a coup to abolish the rule of the Riksdag and restore absolute monarchy, and nearly lost his throne. In the December Crisis of 1768, guided by his eldest son Gustav, he overthrew the Cap senate but could make no use of the victory.

The reign saw a long period of internal peace, but finances stagnated under the mercantilist policies of the Hat administration. In the parliament of 1765–1766 the opposition took over the government and enacted reforms towards economic liberalism, as well as a Freedom of Press Act that ended censorship, keeping punishment only for libelling the monarch or the Church of Sweden.

Adolf Frederick died suddenly in Stockholm on 12 February 1771, with symptoms resembling heart failure or poisoning. Stories that he died of an enormous meal are considered propaganda by modern writers. His son Gustav III seized power in a military coup in 1772 and restored absolute rule. The king was regarded as dependent on others and lacking the talents of a statesman, but was reported to be a good husband and a gentle master. He had a talent for astronomy, music and military matters, and his favourite pastime was making snuffboxes. He and Louisa Ulrika had five children, among them Gustav III and Charles XIII.
adolf-hitler: Adolf Hitler was born on 20 April 1889 in Braunau am Inn, a town in Austria-Hungary close to the border with Germany. He was the fourth of six children of Alois Hitler and his third wife, Klara Pölzl, and three siblings died in infancy. Alois was the illegitimate child of Maria Schicklgruber and bore her surname until 1876, when he took the name Hitler. Adolf's refusal to accept school discipline led to conflict with his father, who beat him; his mother tried to protect him. He moved to Germany in 1913.

In July 1919 Hitler was sent by the army to infiltrate the German Workers' Party (DAP), which he joined as member 555, the party having begun its count at 500 to seem larger. The party became the Nazi Party, and in 1921 he was appointed its leader. A coup attempt at Munich in 1923 failed; he was sentenced to five years in prison, served just over a year, and dictated the first volume of Mein Kampf there.

The Great Depression gave the party its opening: it won 107 seats in 1930, and after the elections of November 1932 it held the most seats in the Reichstag without a majority. Franz von Papen and other conservatives persuaded President Paul von Hindenburg to appoint Hitler chancellor on 30 January 1933. The Enabling Act of 23 March began the change to Nazi Germany, and after Hindenburg died on 2 August 1934 Hitler became head of state. Unemployment fell from six million in 1932 to fewer than one million in 1936. He ruled by the Führerprinzip, giving contradictory orders to set subordinates against one another.

Germany invaded Poland on 1 September 1939, and Hitler ordered the invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941. By January 1942 he had decided that the Jews, Slavs and other deportees considered undesirable should be killed.

On 29 April 1945 Hitler married Eva Braun in the Führerbunker in Berlin, and the next day they killed themselves to avoid capture by the Soviet Red Army. Few Germans mourned him. The historian Ian Kershaw calls him the embodiment of modern political evil.

According to R. J. Rummel, the Nazi regime was responsible for the killing of an estimated 19.3 million civilians and prisoners of war, in addition to about six million Jews murdered in the Holocaust. A further 28.7 million soldiers and civilians died from military action in the European theatre. Germany suffered wholesale destruction, described as Stunde Null, or Zero Hour.
adolf-ii-prince-of-schaumburg-lippe: Adolf was born on 23 February 1883 in Stadthagen, the only town of the principality apart from the capital Bückeburg, the eldest son of the hereditary Prince Georg and Princess Marie Anne of Saxe-Altenburg. He was born in the reign of his grandfather Prince Adolf I, whose death on 8 May 1893 made his father prince and the ten-year-old Adolf heir apparent. In 1904, while studying at the University of Bonn, he joined the student corps Corps Borussia Bonn.

Adolf succeeded his father on 29 April 1911, at the age of 28. During his reign he developed the spa of Bad Eilsen and was responsible for many of its buildings. The German revolution forced him to abdicate on 15 November 1918, when the principality became the Free State of Schaumburg-Lippe, and he went into exile at Brioni in Istria.

On 10 January 1920 in Berlin he married the actress Elisabeth Franziska (Ellen) Bischoff-Korthaus, who had been married from 1918 to 1919 to Prince Eberwyn of Bentheim and Steinfurt. Both were killed on 26 March 1936 when their Ford Trimotor, flying from Mexico City to Guatemala City, crashed between two volcanoes near Zumpango; all fourteen people on board, ten tourists from Europe and four crew, died. The New York Times of 27 March 1936 reported it as the worst air crash in Mexico.

Adolf's youngest brother, Friedrich Christian, an adjutant to Joseph Goebbels, spoke out against burying Ellen beside her husband in the Bückeburg Mausoleum because, as he put it, she was not of Aryan origin. Adolf had no children, and his younger brother Prince Wolrad succeeded him as head of the House of Schaumburg-Lippe.
adolf-luderitz: Franz Adolf Eduard Lüderitz was born on 16 July 1834 in Bremen, the son of the tobacco merchant Adolf Lüderitz and his wife Wilhelmine. After the merchants' school in Bremen he trained in his father's business. Between 1854 and 1859 he travelled among the tobacco exchanges of North America and took a post in Mexico, where his employer went bankrupt and the tobacco farm he then bought was destroyed in the Reform War. Back in Bremen, his marriage in 1866 to the wealthy Emilie Louise made him independent, and in 1878 he took over his father's firm.

A trading post he set up at Lagos in 1881 failed. With the Bremen merchant Heinrich Vogelsang he then planned a German colony in South West Africa, still unclaimed by any colonial power, as an alternative for the many German settlers emigrating to North America. In May 1883 he bought the anchorage at Angra Pequena and the land five miles around it from Captain Josef Frederiks II of Bethanie for £100 in gold and 200 rifles, and on 25 August a strip between the Orange River and the bay for £500 and 60 rifles.

The contract gave its width as 20 geographical miles, which both Lüderitz and the witness, the Rhenish missionary Johannes Bam, knew the chief would take for English miles. The deal became known as the Mile Swindle, and Lüderitz was nicknamed Lügenfritz.

Otto von Bismarck at first hesitated to protect the purchases, but when Lord Derby ordered the Cape Colony to take the coast he agreed, and on 7 August 1884 the German flag was raised at Lüderitzbucht. Lüderitz went on buying land until he owned the coastal strip from South Africa to Angola, about 580,000 square kilometres, but his mining engineers found neither gold nor diamonds, and in April 1885 he sold his enterprise to the German Colonial Society for 500,000 marks.

Seeking an income from his lands, he set off in July 1886 with three others to explore the Orange River, carrying two small boats to Nabasdrift. His boat was never found, and the last night the party was reported was 21 to 22 October. In 2013 Namibia renamed the Lüderitz constituency ǃNamiǂNûs, its original name, and in April 2018 Berlin decided to rename the street called after him in Wedding.
adolfo-lopez-mateos: Adolfo López Mateos was born in 1909, according to official records in Atizapán de Zaragoza in the State of Mexico, the son of a dentist and a teacher. In 1929 he graduated from the Scientific and Literary Institute of Toluca, where he was a student leader of José Vasconcelos's campaign for the presidency. After Vasconcelos's defeat he studied law at the National Autonomous University of Mexico and shifted his allegiance to the National Revolutionary Party. He was a senator for the State of Mexico from 1946 to 1952 and then Secretary of Labor under President Adolfo Ruiz Cortines, from 1952 to 1957. He was chosen as the party's presidential candidate and won easily against weak opposition.

López Mateos took office on 1 December 1958 and described his government as the administration of the constitutional left. Railway workers under Demetrio Vallejo and Valentín Campa struck from July 1958 and brought a major strike in Holy Week 1959. The government arrested the union's leaders, who received long prison sentences for the crime of social dissolution, as did the muralist David Alfaro Siqueiros. In 1960 the electrical industry was nationalised, and 16 million hectares were redistributed in land reform. The Institute for Social Security and Services for State Workers was created, and in 1959 the National Commission for Free Textbooks. The National Museum of Anthropology opened in Chapultepec Park. In 1962 the army murdered the peasant leader Rubén Jaramillo.

In foreign policy he held to non-intervention and refused to join the isolation of Cuba organised by the United States. He received President John F. Kennedy in July 1962, and the Chamizal dispute with the United States was settled in Mexico's favour. An electoral reform of 1963 gave opposition parties seats in the Chamber of Deputies. Former president Lázaro Cárdenas pressed him from the left and appealed for the release of the jailed union leaders, but later supported his choice of Gustavo Díaz Ordaz as successor in 1964.

After leaving office López Mateos briefly headed the committee that organised the 1968 Summer Olympics in Mexico, but had to resign because of failing health. He suffered from migraines and was found to have cerebral aneurysms, and he died in Mexico City on 22 September 1969. Admirers praise his land redistribution, nationalisation and health and education programmes, while critics point to his repression of unions and political opponents.
adolfo-suarez: Adolfo Suárez González was born on 25 September 1932 in Cebreros, in the Province of Ávila, the eldest son of the lawyer Hipólito Suárez Guerra. Both his parents supported the Republicans during the Spanish Civil War. He studied law at the University of Salamanca, worked for the municipal government of Ávila from 1955, and joined Opus Dei. In 1958 he became personal secretary to the civil governor of Ávila, Fernando Herrero Tejedor, and rose with him through the Movimiento Nacional. He was programme director of the state broadcaster RTVE in 1965, sat in the Francoist Cortes from 1967 and, as its director general from 1969, became a close friend of Prince Juan Carlos.

After Franco's death Suárez became secretary-general of the Movimiento in December 1975. In July 1976 King Juan Carlos asked for the resignation of Carlos Arias Navarro and chose the relatively obscure Suárez as prime minister, at 43 the youngest of the 20th century. His Francoist ties won the trust of the right, while reformists were dismayed. The Political Reform Act, establishing universal suffrage and a bicameral parliament, passed the Francoist Cortes in November 1976 and a referendum in December. Between February and April 1977 the PSOE and the Communist Party were legalised, trade unions recognised and the Movimiento abolished. The legalisation of the Communist Party provoked fury in the military, and Suárez responded by sacking hardliners.

His Union of the Democratic Centre won the 1977 election. A new constitution making Spain a constitutional monarchy was approved by referendum in December 1978, and Suárez negotiated the creation of the autonomous communities. His coalition won again in 1979, but economic recession, violence by ETA, demands for regional autonomy and divisions in his own party eroded his power. He survived a no-confidence motion in May 1980 and announced his resignation in January 1981.

In February 1981, as parliament voted on his successor Leopoldo Calvo-Sotelo, Lieutenant-Colonel Antonio Tejero and about 200 Civil Guards stormed the chamber and held the deputies for some 22 hours. Suárez, with two others, stayed calmly seated. In 1981 the king made him Duke of Suárez, and he received the Prince of Asturias Concord Award in 1996. He founded the Democratic and Social Centre in 1982 and retired from politics in 1991. Alzheimer's disease ended his public life in 2003. He died on 23 March 2014 in Madrid, was given a state funeral, and is buried in the cloister of Ávila Cathedral.
adolphe-grand-duke-of-luxembourg: Adolphe was born on 24 July 1817, a son of William, Duke of Nassau, and Princess Louise of Saxe-Hildburghausen. He became Duke of Nassau in August 1839 at the age of 22, and in 1841 took up residence in the newly built Stadtschloss at Wiesbaden, by then the capital of the duchy. On 4 March 1848 he consented to the population's nine Demands of the Nassauers, but a few years later revoked his liberal views and took a strongly conservative course. He was nevertheless seen as a popular ruler. In 1844 he married Grand Duchess Elizabeth Mikhailovna of Russia, who died within a year, and he built the Russian Orthodox Church of Saint Elizabeth in her memory.

In Luxembourg, the Treaty of London of 1839 had made the grand duchy independent but in personal union with the Netherlands. Luxembourg followed Salic law, which barred women from succession, so when William III of the Netherlands died in 1890 his daughter Wilhelmina took the Dutch crown while Luxembourg passed to Adolphe under the Nassau Family Pact. He was 73 and knew little of Luxembourgish politics. He left day-to-day government to Prime Minister Paul Eyschen, who had held office since 1888, which set a convention that the monarch stay out of the politics of the day. In 1902 he named his son William Lieutenant-Representative.

Adolphe died in 1905 at his summer home, Schloss Hohenburg in Lenggries, and was succeeded by his son William IV. In 1953 he was buried in the crypt of the church at Schloss Weilburg. With his second wife, Princess Adelheid-Marie of Anhalt-Dessau, whom he married in 1851, he had five children, of whom two lived beyond eighteen. In 1842, at his castle at Biebrich, the Adelsverein, a society for German immigrants in Texas, was organised under his protection, and its Nassau Plantation in Fayette County, Texas, was named after him. In 1892 he gave the Luxembourg title of Count of Wisborg to his Swedish nephew Oscar.
adolphe-sax: Antoine-Joseph Sax was born on 6 November 1814 in Dinant, in what is now Belgium, the first of eleven children of Charles-Joseph Sax and Marie-Joseph Masson. He was called Adolphe from childhood. In 1815 the family moved to Brussels, where his father, a joiner and cabinet maker whose factory had closed, opened an instrument-making workshop and was later appointed instrument maker to the Dutch royal court. Adolphe studied flute, harmony and solfège at the Royal School of Music and clarinet privately with Valentin Bender, but chose his father's workshop over a career as a performer.

Sax's first important invention was an improved bass clarinet, patented when he was 24. He settled permanently in Paris in 1842 and began work on valved bugles. He did not invent the type, but his instruments, called saxhorns, were more successful than his rivals' and were made in seven sizes. Hector Berlioz arranged in February 1844 for one of his pieces to be played entirely on saxhorns. The family laid the ground for the modern euphonium, and the British brass band movement adopted it exclusively.

On 28 June 1846 he patented the saxophone, intended for orchestras and military bands. By then he had designed saxophones from sopranino to subcontrabass, though not all were built. It did not become a standard orchestral instrument, but its ability to play technical passages like a woodwind while projecting like a brass instrument led to its use in military bands in France and elsewhere. During the Crimean War he designed two machines that were never built, a locomotive-powered organ meant to be heard across Paris and a giant cannon, the Saxocannon.

Sax began teaching at the Paris Conservatory in 1857 and led its new saxophone course. Rival makers attacked his patents for more than twenty years, and he sued them for infringement. He went bankrupt three times, in 1852, 1873 and 1877. He was made a Chevalier of the Legion of Honour in 1849 and won the first Grand Prix de la Facture Instrumentale at the Paris International Exposition of 1867. He died of pneumonia in Paris on 7 February 1894, in poverty, and was buried in the Cimetière de Montmartre.
adolphe-thiers: Adolphe Thiers was born out of wedlock in Marseille on 15 April 1797, during the rule of the Directorate. His father, Pierre-Louis-Marie Thiers, a businessman and occasional government official under Napoleon, married his mother, Marie-Madeleine Amic, on 13 May 1797, which made Adolphe legitimate, but he soon disappeared. He contacted his son only in 1825, when Adolphe was becoming well known in Paris journalism, to ask for money. Thiers replied that his only loyalty was to his mother, who had raised him alone, though he later supported his father and half-brothers. On his mother's side he had Levantine ancestry: his maternal grandfather Claude Amic had worked in Constantinople and married a Greek-speaking woman there.

Thiers was a key figure in the July Revolution of 1830, which replaced Charles X with Louis Philippe, and in the Revolution of 1848, which ended the July Monarchy. He was prime minister in 1836 and 1840, dedicated the Arc de Triomphe, and arranged the return of Napoleon's remains from Saint Helena. He was first a supporter and then a vocal opponent of Louis-Napoléon Bonaparte, and was arrested and briefly expelled from France when Napoleon III seized power.

Thiers opposed the Franco-Prussian War, but after France's defeat he was elected chief executive and negotiated its end. In March 1871 the Paris Commune seized power, and he gave the army the orders to suppress it. The National Assembly named him president of the Republic in August 1871, when he was seventy-four. His chief accomplishment was the departure of German soldiers from most of French territory two years ahead of schedule. Opposed by monarchists and by the republican left, he resigned on 24 May 1873 and was replaced by Patrice de MacMahon. He died on 3 September 1877, and Victor Hugo and Léon Gambetta led the procession at his funeral.

Thiers was also a popular historian. His ten-volume history of the French Revolution, published from 1823 to 1827, was the first large-scale history of it in French. It condemned the Terror and radical leaders such as Marat and Robespierre and praised moderates such as Mirabeau and Lafayette, and it did much to undermine support for the last Bourbon king. He followed it with a twenty-volume Histoire du Consulat et de l'Empire, helped by his access to Talleyrand and Napoleon's surviving generals. He was elected to the Académie Française in 1834.

He built the ring of fortifications around Paris known as the Thiers Wall, whose line now marks the city limits, and completed the column on the Place Vendôme. Judgements of him depended on the politics of those judging him: Karl Marx attacked him in 1871, while Gustave Flaubert wrote that no one had summed up France better.
adolphus-frederick-vi-grand-duke-of-meck: Adolphus Frederick was born in Neustrelitz on 17 June 1882, the eldest son of Adolphus Frederick V, Grand Duke of Mecklenburg-Strelitz, and Princess Elisabeth of Anhalt. He attended a gymnasium in Dresden, studied jurisprudence in Munich and served in the Prussian army, and he became Hereditary Grand Duke on the death of his grandfather, Grand Duke Frederick William, on 30 May 1904. He and his younger brother Duke Karl Borwin are said to have agreed that he would devote himself to painting while Karl Borwin continued the dynasty, but Karl Borwin was killed in a duel with Count George Jametel in 1908.

He succeeded his father on 11 June 1914, a few weeks before the outbreak of World War I. The soprano Mafalda Salvatini was his mistress from 1908 until his death, though research has disproved claims that he fathered her two sons. His heir, his cousin Duke Charles Michael, lived in Russia and had said he wished to renounce his rights, and without a male heir the grand duchy would merge with Mecklenburg-Schwerin. Daisy, Princess of Pless, proposed Princess Benigna Reuss of Köstritz as a bride, and his Minister-President Heinrich Bossart opened negotiations, but the match never came about, reportedly because of a relationship he first had to end.

He took his own life at Neustrelitz on 23 February 1918. Grand Duke Friedrich Franz IV of Mecklenburg-Schwerin became regent until the end of the German monarchies that year, and Charles Michael's renunciation arrived only in 1919. Adolphus Frederick left his fortune, estimated at 30 million marks, to Friedrich Franz's second son Duke Christian Ludwig, on condition that he become Grand Duke of Mecklenburg-Strelitz and live in Neustrelitz; otherwise the inheritance would fall to 3 million marks.
adomnan: Adomnán, also known as Eunan, was born about 624 into the Northern Uí Néill lineage Cenél Conaill, a relative of Columba on his father's side. His father was Rónán mac Tinne and his mother Ronat, of the Cenél nÉnda. He was probably born in or near Raphoe, in what became County Donegal. He may have begun his monastic career at a Columban monastery such as Druim Tuamma or Durrow and probably joined the Columban federation of monasteries around 640. He attained a level of learning rare in early-medieval Northern Europe.
