In 679 he became the ninth abbot of Iona after Columba, and he enjoyed a friendship with King Aldfrith of Northumbria, who stayed with him on Iona in 684. In 686 he went to Northumbria at the request of King Fínsnechta Fledach of Brega to secure the freedom of sixty Gaels captured in a raid two years earlier. Bede suggests that his visits to Northumbria led him to adopt the Roman dating of Easter, which caused a rift with the brethren of Iona; Jeffrey Wetherill sees his long absences as having undermined his authority to persuade them.

In 697, according to general belief, Adomnán promulgated the Cáin Adomnáin, the Law of Adomnán or Lex Innocentium, at the Synod of Birr, before a gathering of Irish, Dál Riatan and Pictish notables. It was a set of laws meant, among other things, to guarantee the safety and immunity of non-combatants in warfare.

His best-known work is the Vita Columbae, the Life of Columba, probably written between 697 and 700. Modelled in part on Sulpicius Severus's Life of Saint Martin of Tours, it groups stories about Columba by theme rather than chronology and presents him as comparable to a hero of Gaelic mythology. It is by far the most important surviving work written in early-medieval Scotland and a vital source for the Picts. He also wrote De Locis Sanctis, On Holy Places, drawing on the Frankish bishop Arculf, who had visited Egypt, Rome, Constantinople and the Holy Land and then came to Iona; Adomnán gave a copy to Aldfrith.

Adomnán died in 704 and became a saint in Scottish and Irish tradition, commemorated on 23 September. With Columba he is joint patron of the Roman Catholic Diocese of Raphoe. In 727 his relics were taken to Ireland to renew the Cáin Adomnáin, and they were returned to Iona in 730. Donegal institutions bear his name, among them the cathedral in Letterkenny and an Anglican cathedral in Raphoe.
adonijah: According to the 2 Samuel, Adonijah was the fourth son of King David, and his mother was Haggith. He was born at Hebron during the long conflict between David and the House of Saul. After the deaths of his elder brothers Amnon and Absalom he considered himself heir to the throne, and he acquired chariots and a large entourage.

In 1 Kings, with David old, in failing health and in a different city, Adonijah won the support of the army commander Joab and the priest Abiathar. The priest Zadok, Benaiah, the head of the king's bodyguard, and the prophet Nathan did not take his side. Adonijah invited his brother princes and court officials to a sacrifice at which to announce his claim, but not Solomon or his supporters. The Jewish Study Bible reads this exclusion as a sign that he knew he was usurping the throne.

Nathan warned Bathsheba, Solomon's mother, and advised her to remind David of a promise to make Solomon his successor. Lillian R. Klein finds in Nathan's offer to confirm her words a hint that there may have been no earlier definite promise. Persuaded by Bathsheba and Nathan, David ordered that Solomon be proclaimed king. Adonijah's supporters fled and he took refuge at the altar, and Solomon pardoned him on condition that he showed himself a worthy man. Later Adonijah asked to marry Abishag from Shunem, who had served David on his deathbed, and asked Bathsheba to plead for him. Solomon took this as a second attempt on the throne and Adonijah was put to death.

In some interpretations his death was the last of the punishments laid on David for his adultery with Bathsheba and the murder of her husband Uriah. When David judged the rich man of Nathan's parable he said that the lamb must be restored fourfold, and four of his sons died in reparation: the infant son of Bathsheba, Amnon, Absalom and, after David's death, Adonijah.
adonis: The Greeks considered the cult of Adonis to be of Near Eastern origin. His name comes from the Canaanite word adon, meaning lord. Most modern scholars consider the story of Aphrodite and Adonis derived from a Levantine version of the earlier Mesopotamian myth of Inanna and Dumuzid. Ezekiel 8:14 mentions Adonis under his earlier East Semitic name Tammuz and describes women mourning his death near the north gate of the Temple in Jerusalem.

The earliest known Greek reference is a fragment of Sappho, in which a chorus of girls asks Aphrodite how to mourn Adonis, and she answers that they must beat their breasts and tear their tunics. When the cult entered Greek culture is disputed. In Cyprus the cult of Adonis gradually superseded that of Cinyras.

Later sources tell the myth. In Ovid's Metamorphoses Adonis is the son of Myrrha, who was cursed by Aphrodite with desire for her father, King Cinyras of Cyprus, and who was changed into a myrrh tree but still gave birth to him. Aphrodite took the baby to the underworld to be fostered by Persephone, who also fell in love with him. Zeus decreed that he would spend a third of the year with each goddess and a third with whomever he chose; he chose Aphrodite.
While hunting, Adonis was wounded by a boar and bled to death in Aphrodite's arms. Versions differ on who sent the boar: Ares, jealous, or Artemis, or Apollo. Anemones grew where his blood fell.

The festival of Adonia was held by Greek women every year in midsummer. It was already observed on Lesbos in Sappho's time and seems to have become popular in Athens in the mid-fifth century BCE. The women planted gardens of Adonis, quick-growing plants such as lettuce, fennel, wheat and barley in baskets or broken pottery, and set them on rooftops in the summer sun, where they sprouted and quickly withered. They then lamented loudly, tearing their clothes and beating their breasts, and carried a statuette of Adonis on a bier, with the withered plants, to the sea.
adoptionism: Adoptionism is closely associated with dynamic monarchianism, and it holds that Jesus was adopted as the Son of God at his baptism, his resurrection or his ascension. It does not affirm the virgin birth. Bart Ehrman argues that the New Testament contains both a low, adoptionist Christology, in which God exalted Jesus by raising him from the dead, and a high one, in which Jesus was a pre-existent divine being who became human. Scholars disagree about which came first. Some hold that the earliest followers of Jesus were adoptionists, while a majority argue that high Christology existed before the letters of Paul, and Michael Bird holds that adoptionism first emerged in the second century.

Theodotus of Byzantium, who lived in the late second century, was its most prominent early exponent. According to Hippolytus of Rome he taught that Jesus was a man born of a virgin who was not God until after his resurrection. The Jewish Christians known as the Ebionites also held an adoptionist view, according to Epiphanius, who wrote that Jesus was chosen for his sinless devotion to God. The doctrine was declared heresy at the end of the third century and was rejected by the Synods of Antioch and the First Council of Nicaea.

Spanish Adoptionism arose in the eighth and ninth centuries in the Iberian Peninsula, beginning with the claim of Archbishop Elipandus of Toledo that Christ was, in his human nature, the adoptive Son of God. Felix of Urgel was another leading advocate. Beatus of Liébana opposed it in Iberia, and in Carolingian territory Pope Hadrian I, Alcuin of York and Agobard condemned it, officially at the Council of Frankfurt in 794. Its advocates used adoptivus only of Christ's humanity, which, once the divine Son had taken the form of a servant, was adopted as divine.

Peter Abelard revived a form of adoptionism in the 12th century, and in the 14th century Duns Scotus and Durandus of Saint-Pourçain admitted the term filius adoptivus in a qualified sense. A form of it surfaced among the Polish Brethren in the 16th and 17th centuries and in the views of Joseph Priestley in the 18th. John C. Cavadini has challenged the older view that Spanish Adoptionism was a minor revival of Nestorian Christology, arguing that it should be read in its own Spanish and North African context.
adud-al-dawla: Fanna Khusraw, later known by his honorific Adud al-Dawla, meaning pillar of the dynasty, was born in Isfahan on 24 September 936, the son of Rukn al-Dawla and nephew of Imad al-Dawla and Mu'izz al-Dawla. His uncle Imad al-Dawla, who had no heir, chose him as successor, and when Imad al-Dawla died in December 949 he became ruler of Fars at the age of thirteen. Daylamite officers rebelled against him, and Rukn al-Dawla defeated them and put him on the throne at Shiraz. He asked the Abbasid caliph for the title Taj al-Dawla, crown of the state, but Mu'izz al-Dawla objected that it implied superiority over the Buyids, so the title Adud al-Dawla was chosen instead.

Adud al-Dawla annexed Kerman in 967 and conquered Oman between 966 and 974, taking its port Sohar, which secured Buyid influence over the trade routes of the Persian Gulf. After Rukn al-Dawla died on 16 September 976, his cousin Izz al-Dawla, the emir of Iraq, stopped recognising him and allied with the Hamdanids of Mosul. Adud al-Dawla defeated him at Ahvaz on 1 July 977, and on 29 May 978 he defeated him again near Samarra; Izz al-Dawla was captured and executed. Adud al-Dawla then took Mosul and became sole ruler of the Buyid dynasty, taking the ancient Iranian title Shahanshah, King of Kings.

In Baghdad he banned public demonstrations and polemics to end sectarian violence, and he built the al-'Adudi Hospital. He also built caravanserais and dams, among them one between Shiraz and Istakhr that irrigated some 300 villages. In 982 his envoy Abu Ishaq ibn Shahram concluded a ten-year peace treaty with the Byzantines.

Adud al-Dawla died at Baghdad on 26 March 983 and was buried in Najaf. His son Abu Kalijar Marzuban kept the death secret at first to secure his succession and then took the title Samsam al-Dawla, but another son, Shirdil Abu'l-Fawaris, challenged him, and civil war followed.

He kept the Abbasids at Baghdad but showed more interest than earlier Buyids in the pre-Islamic culture of Iran. He visited Persepolis with the Zoroastrian chief priest Marasfand, left an inscription there and claimed descent from the Sasanian king Bahram V Gor. He still preferred Arabic authors, wrote Arabic verse and studied science in Arabic. He patronised an observatory at Isfahan where Azophi worked, and he did not follow a uniformly Shiite religious policy.
adulis: Adulis stood on the Gulf of Zula, about 40 kilometres south of Massawa, and its ruins lie within the modern Eritrean town of Zula. One theory derives its name from the Saho words ado lay, white or clear water, used for settlements with reliable sources of clean water. The town seems to have lain some distance from its harbour, about 20 stades away, and the main anchorage may have been at a site called Gabaza, which archaeologists have proposed placing in the Galala Hills to the south, where two ancient circular watchtowers survive.

Excavation has found a late prehistoric settlement beneath the town, dating from the mid-2nd to the early 1st millennium BCE, and Adulis may correspond to Wddt, a region of the Land of Punt in the geographical lists of Egypt's Eighteenth Dynasty. Pliny the Elder, the earliest European writer to name it, called it the principal market of the Troglodytae and the people of Aethiopia, and the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea lists ivory, hides and enslaved people among the exports of the interior shipped from it. Roman merchants used the port in the second and third centuries, and in 97 the envoy Gan Ying, according to the Houhan Shu, visited a place called Dou-le, believed to be Adulis.

In 520 Cosmas Indicopleustes visited the town under King Kaleb of Axum and copied two inscriptions there, one on the elephant wars of Ptolemy Euergetes and the Monumentum Adulitanum, in which an Aksumite king boasts of victories in Arabia and northern Ethiopia. Adulis also had a bishop. Its end is uncertain: Yuri Kobishchanov argued that Muslims destroyed it, and tradition dates an Arab expedition against it to 640, but the evidence is inconclusive. The port was abandoned sometime around the 8th century.

A French mission under Vignaud and Petit surveyed the site in 1840, and in 1868 men of Napier's campaign against Tewodros II exposed the foundations of a church. Richard Sundström carried out the first scientific excavations in 1906, uncovering a large building he called the palace of Adulis, and Roberto Paribeni followed in 1907, finding dwellings, pottery and wine amphorae from the area of modern Aqaba. Francis Anfray's expedition of 1961 and 1962 found a destruction layer. Among the finds is a flask stamped with Saint Menas between two camels, perhaps brought by a pilgrim. The National Museum of Eritrea has asked Ethiopia to return finds from these excavations.
advance-australia-fair: Peter Dodds McCormick (1833–1916), a Scottish-born Australian composer, published the song in early December 1878 under the pen-name Amicus. It was first sung by Andrew Fairfax, with a concert band conducted by McCormick, at a function of the Highland Society of New South Wales in Sydney on 30 November 1878, Saint Andrew's Day. In a letter of 1 August 1913, McCormick said he had attended a concert at Sydney's Exhibition Building where various national anthems were played and felt aggravated that there was not one note for Australia. He wrote the first verse on the bus home and set it to music, and said the words and music came with ease.

The song grew in popularity, and an amended version was sung by a choir of around 10,000 at the inauguration of the Commonwealth of Australia on 1 January 1901. In 1907 the Australian Government awarded McCormick £100. The Australian Broadcasting Commission used it to announce its radio news bulletins from 1942 to 1952.

The original song had four verses. The second edition of 1879 begins Australia's sons let us rejoice, For we are young and free, and its second verse told of Cook raising Old England's flag, while its later verses spoke of Britannia and of rousing to arms against a foreign foe.

For the 1984 adoption the text was cut to two verses. The first was kept largely as the original, with the first line changed to Australians all let us rejoice, and the second is a modified form of the third verse sung at Federation in 1901, which begins Beneath our radiant Southern Cross. On 1 January 2021 the word young in the second line was replaced by one, in recognition of the legacy of Indigenous Australians.

The Whitlam government replaced God Save the Queen with Advance Australia Fair as the official national anthem in 1974, after an indicative opinion survey. The Fraser government restored God Save the Queen in January 1976 alongside three national songs: Advance Australia Fair, Waltzing Matilda and Song of Australia. A plebiscite in 1977 to choose the national song preferred Advance Australia Fair, and the Hawke government proclaimed it the national anthem in 1984. God Save the Queen became the royal anthem.

The song has drawn criticism for its archaic word girt and for a melody some call dull. It has also been criticised for failing to acknowledge Indigenous peoples; the line for we are young and free was said to ignore their long history. Versions in the Dharug language have been written, by Jacqueline Troy in 2003 and by Richard Green, performed in 2010. The version most often performed at official functions is a 1986 arrangement by Thomas Tycho.
adygea: Adygea lies in the foothills of the north-western Caucasus, with plains in the north and mountains in the south, the highest point being Chugush Mountain at 3,238 metres. Forests of European beech, oak and maple cover almost 40 per cent of its territory. The Kuban River, about 870 kilometres long and one of the major navigable rivers of the Caucasus region, forms part of its northern border, and the Bolshaya Laba River part of the eastern one. The Sukhoy Kurdzhips River flows near the archaeological site at Mezmaiskaya cave. The territory is rich in oil and natural gas and also holds gold, silver, tungsten and iron.

The Cherkess (Adyghe) Autonomous Oblast was established within the Russian SFSR on 27 July 1922, on territory of the Kuban-Black Sea Oblast settled mainly by the Adyghe, and was renamed Adyghe (Cherkess) Autonomous Oblast on 24 August 1922. Krasnodar was at first its administrative centre. In 1924 it was transferred to the newly created North Caucasus Krai, and in July 1928 it became the Adyghe Autonomous Oblast. In 1934 it passed to the new Azov-Black Sea Krai, and Maykop became its administrative centre in 1936. When Krasnodar Krai was established on 13 September 1937, the oblast became part of it.

On 3 July 1991 the oblast was raised to the status of a republic within the Russian Federation. Its first president, Aslan Dzharimov, was elected on 5 January 1992, and its constitution was adopted on 14 May 1995.

Adygea is a republic of Russia, entirely surrounded by Krasnodar Krai. Its capital and largest city is Maykop, which holds about a third of its population of roughly half a million. Russians are a majority, and the Adyghe, the indigenous Circassian people, form about a quarter, with smaller Armenian and Ukrainian communities. The official languages are Adyghe, a member of the Northwest Caucasian family, and Russian. The National Museum of the Republic of Adygea in Maykop is its largest museum.
aedan-mac-gabrain: Genealogies make Áedán a son of Gabrán mac Domangairt, and much of what is known of him comes from hagiography, above all Adomnán of Iona's Life of Saint Columba. He was about forty when he became king on the death of his uncle Conall mac Comgaill in 574. His succession may have been contested: Adomnán says Columba had favoured his brother Eoganán, yet claims that Columba ordained Áedán as king, the first known ordination in Britain and Ireland. As chief king he ruled over lesser kin groups, among them the Cenél Loairn of northern Argyll and the Cenél nÓengusa of Islay.

At the convention of Druim Cett in 575, Áedán and Áed mac Ainmuirech of the Uí Néill agreed that the fleet of Dál Riata would serve the Uí Néill but that no tribute would be paid, a pact probably aimed at the threat from Báetán mac Cairill of Ulster. The annals record Áedán raiding Orkney about 580 and fighting on the Isle of Man about 583. Against the Miathi, probably the Maeatae of the upper Forth, he won a victory in which his sons Artúr and Eochaid Find were killed. He was defeated by the Picts in Circinn in 599 or after, and Welsh traditions remember his plundering of Alt Clut and wars with King Rhydderch Hael.

Áedán had already lost his son Domangart fighting the Bernicians before Degsastan. Bede says only that he was alarmed by Æthelfrith's advance, and wrote that from that day no king of the Irish in Britain had dared to fight the English. Æthelfrith's brother Theodbald was killed in the battle, and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle places Hering, son of King Hussa of Bernicia, on Áedán's side.

The annals say nothing more of Áedán until his death some six years later, perhaps on 17 April 609, the date given by the Martyrology of Tallaght; the Annals of Tigernach make him 74. The Prophecy of Berchán says he was no longer king when he died, and the 12th-century Acta Sancti Lasriani says he was expelled. John of Fordun believed he was buried at Kilkerran in Kintyre. His son Eochaid Buide succeeded him, and the main line of the Cenél nGabráin descended from Eochaid through Domnall Brecc.
aedui: The name Aedui is the Latin form of the Gaulish Aiduoi, meaning the Ardent, from a Celtic stem for fire. The Aedui held a central position in eastern Gaul, on the watershed between the Mediterranean, Atlantic and Channel drainage basins. The Loire separated them from the Bituriges, and the Saône from the Sequani. Their clients included the Segusiavi to the south and the Mandubii to the north, and the river ports of Cabillonum (Chalon-sur-Saône) and Matisco (Mâcon) controlled traffic on the Saône. Their principal oppidum, Bibracte, stood on Mont Beuvray in the Morvan, where sanctuaries lay on the highest points, aristocratic residences and the market on the plateau, and the craft quarters lower down.

Before the Roman conquest the Aedui were one of the major powers of central Gaul, contending for preeminence with the Sequani, Bituriges and Arverni. A senate, probably of the great families, conducted affairs, and an annual magistrate, the vergobret, handled current business and justice. Around 150 to 140 BCE they concluded an equal treaty with Rome, which gave mutual military assistance and the right of hospitality, and according to Tacitus they alone among the Gauls bore the title fratres populi Romani. The alliance brought lasting Roman influence, shown by a silver coinage modelled on the denarius and Roman-style building at Bibracte.

In the Gallic Wars the Aeduan noble Diviciacus, a Druid whom Cicero had received at Rome, was Caesar's trusted intermediary, while his brother Dumnorix led the anti-Roman faction and was killed in 54 BCE after refusing to embark for Britain. The Aedui supported Caesar most of the time but joined the revolt of 52 BCE briefly, and afterwards kept their laws and their title.

As allies the Aedui were not conquered but received Roman citizenship directly. Their capital moved from Bibracte to a new town, Augustodunum (Autun), created on the order of Augustus at the end of the 1st century BCE and enclosed by a wall about 6 kilometres long. In 48 CE a delegation of Gallic notables petitioned Claudius for a senatorial career, and the Senate granted it to the Aedui alone, who became the first Gauls to sit in it. In 269 to 270 CE Augustodunum, which had declared for Claudius II, was besieged for seven months and sacked, and the notables were proscribed. The city was restored under the Tetrarchy and Constantine, and in 312 it was renamed Flavia Aeduorum in honour of Constantine.
aegidius: According to Priscus of Panium, Aegidius was born in Gaul, and he is likely to have belonged to an old aristocratic family. Modern scholars propose that it was the family known as the Syagrii, from the name of his son Syagrius, although there is no strong evidence. Priscus reports that he served under Aetius when Aetius was magister militum of the Western Roman Empire, as did the emperors Avitus and Majorian, both also of Gallo-Roman origin. Priscus adds that Aegidius had considerable influence with Majorian.

Gregory of Tours claims that Aegidius was made magister militum in Gaul after Majorian became emperor, and many scholars place this around 458. Paulinus of Périgueux describes him leading Roman forces in a besieged city on the Rhone, which many historians take to be Arles, held against the Goths of Aquitania under King Theodoric II. The date and place are uncertain.

After Ricimer had Majorian killed in 461 and set up Libius Severus, Aegidius refused to recognise the new emperor. He may have pledged allegiance directly to the Eastern emperor Leo I. Priscus notes that the government in Italy feared his army, but his conflict with the Goths kept him from invading Italy. In 463 he repulsed an invasion by the Aquitanian Goths at the Battle of Orleans, where his forces, apparently largely Frankish, killed Frederic, the brother of Theodoric. He also besieged Chinon at an unknown date.

Gregory of Tours reports a story that Aegidius became king of the Franks while the Frankish king Childeric was in exile. Modern scholars are sceptical that a Roman could be called rex of the Franks, but several think it may reflect a real memory. Guy Halsall suggested that Aegidius took the Frankish title to legitimise his position after refusing Severus. Hydatius records that in May 464 Aegidius sent an embassy by sea to the Vandal king Gaiseric, probably to find an ally against Ricimer. He also records a lasting enmity with the Gallo-Roman Agrippinus, whom Aegidius had accused of planning to hand parts of the empire to barbarians.

Hydatius writes that Aegidius died soon after an eclipse dated to 464, some saying by ambush or treachery and others by poison, without naming anyone responsible. The Goths then invaded the regions he had been defending in the name of Rome. His son Syagrius succeeded him, and Gregory of Tours describes Syagrius as King of Romans, based at Soissons, which Aegidius had held before him. Syagrius was defeated by Clovis I, the son of Childeric, in the 480s, a major step in Clovis's creation of a unified Frankish state. The sources give Aegidius many contradictory titles, among them magister militum, rex, comes and, in one version of the Liber Historiae Francorum, a Roman tyrant.
aegukga: The first anthem of the Korean state came before the present song. After the Gabo Reform of 1894 and the founding of the Independence Club in 1896, about ten patriotic songs were written in the private sector, and their lyrics began to appear in the Independence Newspaper. After the Korean Empire was proclaimed, Emperor Gojong wanted a national anthem as a state symbol. The German musician Franz von Eckert came to Korea on 19 February 1901 and completed an anthem on 1 July 1902, based on traditional Korean musical scales. It was proclaimed on 15 August 1902. After Japan annexed Korea in 1910 it was banned, and after liberation it was not readopted because of Eckert's part in the composition of Japan's Kimigayo.

The lyrics of the present Aegukga are of uncertain authorship. Theories name Yun Ch'iho, Ahn Chang-ho or Min Young-hwan, but the National Institute of Korean History holds that the author remains unknown.

The words were first sung to the tune of the Scottish song Auld Lang Syne, and that version was sung before the founding of South Korea and by dissidents under Japanese rule. The composer Ahn Eak-tai (1906–1965) met the lyrics during the March 1st Movement of 1919. Regretting that they were sung to a Scottish melody, he decided that a Korean should compose the tune, and he did so in 1935. His melody was adopted as the national anthem of the Korean exile government, which existed during the Japanese occupation from the early 1910s to the mid-1940s.

The song was customarily called the national anthem until it was established as such after the founding of the government on 15 August 1948. It has four verses, but at public events such as baseball and football matches only the first is sung, followed by the chorus.

Because Ahn died in 1965, the copyright in the music would not have expired until 2036 at the earliest. Two professional football clubs were sued by a copyright holders' group for playing it in December 2003. On 16 March 2005 Ahn's widow Lolita Ahn and her family gave all rights in the song to the South Korean government, and it has since been in the public domain. In 2018 the music director Park In-young recomposed it, adding brass and woodwind instruments while keeping Ahn's original version. The word aegukga is also a general term for any patriotic song, official or not.
aegukka: The song was composed in 1945 as a patriotic piece celebrating independence from Japanese occupation, and it was adopted as the state anthem in 1947. The words were written by Pak Se-yong and the music was composed by Kim Won-gyun. Before it, the Korean exile government in Shanghai (1919–1945) had used a patriotic song of a similar name, Aegukga, sung to the tune of Auld Lang Syne. After the Second World War South Korea kept those words and gave them a new tune, while North Korea briefly used them with Auld Lang Syne before adopting the newly written piece in 1947.

The song is also known by its first line, Ach'imŭn pinnara, meaning Let Morning Shine, and as the Song of a Devotion to a Country. The word aegukka names any patriotic song, official or not, and is distinct from gukka, an official national anthem.

The complete version has two verses. On official occasions, when only the first verse is played, it is customary to repeat the last four bars; if both are performed, the last four bars of the second verse are repeated instead. In the early 1980s Kim Jong Il sought to reduce its importance in favour of the Song of General Kim Il Sung. That song and the Song of General Kim Jong Il later took the place of de facto national anthems at home, while Aegukka was kept to represent North Korea abroad, when foreign dignitaries visit and when its athletes compete internationally. Unlike most North Korean patriotic songs it praises neither the Workers' Party of Korea nor the Kim family, but Korea itself.

In 2024 the phrase three thousand ri, a reference to the length of the Korean peninsula, was replaced in the lyrics by this world, and the anthem was renamed National Anthem of the Democratic People's Republic of Korea.
aelfgifu-of-northampton: Ælfgifu came from an important noble family of the Midlands. She was a daughter of Ælfhelm, ealdorman of southern Northumbria, and his wife Wulfrun. Ælfhelm was killed in 1006, probably on the orders of King Æthelred the Unready, and her brothers Ufegeat and Wulfheah were blinded. When Swein Forkbeard, King of Denmark, invaded England in 1013–14, the northern peoples submitted to him, and he married his young son Cnut to Ælfgifu to seal their loyalty.

After Swein died in February 1014 and Cnut fled to Denmark, her family, seeking peace with Æthelred, sent her and her infant son Svein to Denmark with Swein's body. Harold Harefoot was born in 1015 or 1016. When Cnut married Emma of Normandy after conquering England in 1016, there is no evidence that Ælfgifu was put aside; her marriage had been made by handfasting, a custom that allowed a second wife to be taken.

After the death of Olaf II of Norway, Cnut sent Ælfgifu and Svein to rule Norway in 1030. Their rule was so harsh that the Norwegians rebelled and drove them out, and Svein died of wounds in Denmark soon after, probably in 1036. In Norway, where she was called Alfífa, the period was remembered as Alfífa's time, a byword for heavy taxation; a verse attributed to the skald Sigvatr says the people then ate ox's food and, like goats, rind.

After Cnut died at Shaftesbury in 1035, Ælfgifu worked to make Harold king while Emma's son Harthacnut was at war in Scandinavia. An assembly at Oxford chose Harold as regent, and Ælfgifu was to hold Wessex for him from Winchester. By August 1036 Emma's daughter Gunnhild had heard that Ælfgifu was winning nobles over with feasts and gifts.

Frank Stenton judged that Ælfgifu was probably the real ruler of England for part or all of Harold's reign, but others note that the few sources show Harold ruling on his own. The Encomium Emmae Reginae, written for Emma, makes her an accomplice in the murder of Alfred Aetheling and calls Harold a servant's son. She is not recorded after 1036, and the date of her death is unknown.
aelia-capitolina: Hadrian visited Judaea in 129 to 130 CE. Jerusalem, once heavily rebuilt by Herod the Great, was still in ruins from the siege of 70 CE in the First Jewish–Roman War, and the emperor resolved to refound it as a Roman colony dedicated to Jupiter. The name Aelia came from Hadrian's own Aelia gens, and Capitolina meant that the city was dedicated to Jupiter Capitolinus, whom the Romans believed had vanquished and replaced the God of the Jews. Mary E. Smallwood thinks the foundation was likely an attempt to combat resurgent Jewish nationalism, and Martin Goodman describes it as a deliberate effort to end Jewish rebelliousness by erasing the city.

Ancient sources disagree on whether the foundation caused the Bar Kokhba revolt of 132 to 135 or followed it. Cassius Dio says that Jews objected to gentiles being settled in their city and foreign cults established there. Eusebius of Caesarea presents the colony as a punishment after the defeat. Coins of Aelia Capitolina struck before the revolt have convinced most modern historians that the foundation came first.

The city was rebuilt on a Roman plan with a cardo and a decumanus, adapted to the western hill and the Temple Mount, and its two cardines met near the Damascus Gate, where a columnar monument gave the gate its Arabic name, Bab el-Amud. Hadrian placed the main forum at the junction of the main roads and built a large temple to Venus beside it, on a site later used for the Church of the Holy Sepulchre. The colony had no walls, and a detachment of Legio X Fretensis guarded it.

Its population, about 4,000 by one estimate, was mainly legionaries, veterans and other non-Jewish settlers. Jews were barred on pain of death except on Tisha B'Av, and a pilgrim from Bordeaux in 333 saw them gather yearly to anoint a perforated stone and mourn. Under Constantine, in the early 4th century, the Church of the Holy Sepulchre began the city's change into a Christian centre, and it became the fifth patriarchate. The ban on Jews lasted until the Muslim conquest of 636. In Arabic the name survived as Ilya.

The Roman street pattern is preserved in the Old City of Jerusalem. Substantial remains of the western cardo have been exposed near Suq el-Bazaar, and walls of Hadrian's temple to Venus have been found beneath the Church of the Holy Sepulchre.
aelia-eudoxia: Eudoxia was a daughter of Flavius Bauto, a Romanised Frank who served as magister militum in the Western Roman army during the 380s. Bauto was last mentioned as consul with Arcadius in 385 and was dead by 388. Some historians consider her mother to have been Roman, but the primary sources are silent on her maternal ancestry. According to Zosimus, she began her life in Constantinople as a member of the household of Promotus, magister militum of the East, and she is presumed to have been orphaned at the time. She was educated by Pansophius, later bishop of Nicomedia.

After Theodosius I died on 17 January 395, Arcadius succeeded him in the East under the control of Rufinus, the Praetorian prefect, who is reported to have intended to marry his own daughter to the emperor. The eunuch Eutropius instead arranged the marriage with Eudoxia, which took place on 27 April 395 without Rufinus's knowledge. For Eutropius it was an attempt to increase his influence. She was given the title of augusta on 9 January 400, wore the purple paludamentum and appeared on Roman coinage. She and the general Gainas are considered to have played a part in the fall and execution of Eutropius in 399, though how far is disputed.

Eudoxia became a patron of the Nicene faction of the Church and financed nighttime anti-Arian processions. Her conflict with John Chrysostom, Patriarch of Constantinople, began after he protested over the execution of Eutropius, and she assumed that his denunciations of extravagant dress were aimed at herself. An alliance of Eudoxia, Theophilus of Alexandria and others held the Synod of the Oak in 403, which deposed and banished John. Arcadius recalled him almost at once, but when a silver statue of her was dedicated near the cathedral John spoke against her harshly, comparing her to Herodias, and he was banished again.

Eudoxia's children included Pulcheria, Arcadia, Marina and her only son, the future emperor Theodosius II. Her last pregnancy ended in a miscarriage or, according to the hostile pseudo-Martyrius, a stillbirth, and she died of an infection on 6 October 404. She was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles in a porphyry sarcophagus. Historians disagree about her influence: Philostorgius thought her more intelligent than her husband, Zosimus thought eunuchs manipulated her, and the Cambridge Ancient History reports her dominating the government from 400 to 404.
aella-of-northumbria: Ælla became king of Northumbria after Osberht was deposed. His reign is traditionally dated to 862 or 863, but the evidence for Northumbrian royal chronology is unreliable before 867, and it may have begun as late as 866. His ancestry is unknown. Almost nothing is known of his reign. Symeon of Durham states that Ælla seized lands at Billingham, Ileclif, Wigeclif and Crece, which belonged to the church. Most sources describe him as a tyrant and an illegitimate king, though one source calls him Osberht's brother. An Anglo-Norman genealogy gives him a daughter, Æthelthryth, through whom he was grandfather of Eadwulf of Bamburgh, who died in 913.

The Great Heathen Army, made up mostly of Danish, Norwegian and Frisian Vikings, landed in Northumbria in mid-866 and had captured York by 21 November. According to the Historia Regum Anglorum, the dissension between Osberht and Ælla was allayed by divine counsel and other Northumbrian nobles. They united their forces and came to York on 21 March 867.

Most of the Vikings seemed to flee, and the Christians, seeing this, attacked but found the Vikings the stronger party. Surrounded, the Northumbrians fought fiercely until both kings were killed, and the survivors made peace. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle says both kings were slain on the spot. The Vikings then installed a puppet king, Ecgberht.

Norse sources tell a different story. According to Ragnarssona þáttr, Ælla captured Ragnar Lodbrok, a figure of Norse tradition, and put him to death in a pit of snakes, and the army of 866 was led by Ragnar's sons, Hvitserk, Björn Ironside, Sigurd Snake-in-the-Eye, Ivar the Boneless and Ubba, who avenged him by killing Ælla with the blood eagle.

Roberta Frank argued that the saga authors misunderstood kennings alluding to leaving foes face down on the battlefield, their backs torn by scavenging birds, so that the blood eagle may describe his death in battle. Ælla also appears in Chaucer's The Man of Law's Tale and was played by Frank Thring in the film The Vikings in 1958.
aelle-of-sussex: Ælle is known from two early sources. Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English People, written in 731, lists him first of seven kings who held imperium, overlordship, over all the provinces south of the Humber, and notes that he was not a Christian. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, assembled in Wessex around 890, about four hundred years after the events, has three entries for him.

It is not known where its annalists found this material. The Chronicle calls the native Britons Welsh, a Saxon word meaning foreigner. Historians are divided on the detail of his life and even his existence, because this was the least documented period in English history of the last two millennia.

According to the Chronicle, in 477 Ælle and his three sons, Cymen, Wlencing and Cissa, arrived with three ships at Cymen's shore, believed to be the rocks off Selsey Bill known as the Owers, killed many Welsh and drove some into the wood called Andredes leag, the Weald. In 485 he fought the Welsh near Mearcred's Burn, and in 491 Ælle and Cissa besieged Andredes cester and killed everyone there.

This is thought to be Anderitum, the Roman fort at Pevensey, though Henry of Huntingdon's account does not fit its geography and William Camden suggested Newenden. The Chronicle later lists him in 827 as the first of eight bretwaldas, Britain-rulers, though there is no evidence that this was a contemporary title.

Place names support an early settlement of Sussex: names ending in -ing, such as Worthing and Angmering, are densest from west of Selsey Bill to east of Pevensey, with about forty-five in Sussex. Historians suggest he may have been a war leader whose battles ran from west to east over fourteen years and whose control reached Hampshire and the upper Thames, but not all of England south of the Humber as Bede claims.

Guy Halsall argues that Ælle belongs to the mid sixth century and that the Chronicle moved him back a century to give Sussex a foundation story. His death is not recorded. Highdown Hill is the traditional burial place of the kings of Sussex.
aeneas: In Greek and Roman mythology Aeneas was the son of the Trojan prince Anchises and the goddess Aphrodite, known to the Romans as Venus. Anchises was a first cousin of King Priam of Troy, which made Aeneas a second cousin to Priam's children, among them Hector and Paris. The Homeric Hymn to Aphrodite tells how Zeus put desire for the mortal Anchises into Aphrodite, who bore Aeneas near Mount Ida and gave him to the nymphs of the mountain to raise.

In Homer's Iliad Aeneas is a minor character, the leader of the Trojans' Dardanian allies and a principal lieutenant of Hector. The gods twice save him from death, as if for a destiny not yet known. Aphrodite and Apollo rescue him from Diomedes, and Poseidon saves him from Achilles, noting that though from a junior branch of the royal family, he is destined to become king of the Trojan people.

Virgil's Aeneid tells the Roman form of the story. Aeneas is one of the few Trojans not killed or enslaved when Troy fell. Commanded by the gods to flee, he gathered the group known as the Aeneads, among them his father and his son Ascanius, and carried the household gods of Troy to Italy. Anchises died at Drepanum in Sicily. A storm brought the fleet to Carthage, where Aeneas had an affair with its queen, Dido. Mercury was sent to remind him of his mission and he left in secret. Dido cursed him, a curse said to set Carthage against Rome in the Punic Wars, and killed herself.

In Latium King Latinus welcomed the exiles. Turnus, king of the Rutuli, to whom Latinus's daughter Lavinia had been promised, made war on Aeneas at the urging of Juno and was killed, and there Virgil's account ends. According to Livy, Aeneas founded the city of Lavinium, named after his wife, and after his death Venus asked Jupiter to make him immortal, and he was recognised as the god Jupiter Indiges.

His son Ascanius, also called Iulus, founded Alba Longa. In the Aeneid, Romulus and Remus descend from Aeneas through their mother Rhea Silvia, and the Julian family of Rome, among them Julius Cæsar and Augustus, traced its lineage to him and so to Venus.
aeneid: The myth of Aeneas' adventures after the fall of Troy predates Virgil by centuries. Aeneas was already a character in the Iliad, and as Greek settlements spread from the sixth century BCE, colonists in Magna Graecia and Sicily linked their new homes to Troy. Virgil took the disconnected tales of Aeneas' wanderings and his vague association with the foundation of Rome and made of them a national epic. The poem tied Rome to the legends of Troy, explained the Punic Wars, glorified traditional Roman virtues and presented the Julio-Claudian dynasty as descended from the founders, heroes and gods of Rome and Troy.

The poem has 9,896 lines in dactylic hexameter, in twelve books. The first six tell of Aeneas' journey from Troy to Latium and are associated with the Odyssey; the last six tell of the war in Latium and mirror the Iliad. It opens with Arma virumque cano, Of arms and the man I sing, and explains the resentment of the goddess Juno against the Trojans. King Latinus is told by oracles to marry his daughter Lavinia to the foreigners and not to Turnus, ruler of the Rutuli, and Juno sends the fury Alecto to stir up war.

Its themes include pietas, the dutiful respect Aeneas shows his father, whom he carries from burning Troy, and the gods; divine intervention, especially in Book 4, where Dido's love delays his voyage; and fate. The shield of Aeneas shows Augustus' victory at Actium in 31 BCE. The poem ends abruptly, and scholars have speculated that Virgil died before finishing it.

According to tradition Virgil fell ill after meeting Augustus in Athens, and died in Brundisium harbour on 21 September 19 BCE, leaving a wish that the manuscript be burned. Augustus ordered his literary executors, Lucius Varius Rufus and Plotius Tucca, to disregard it and publish the poem with as few changes as possible. Critics disagree about its tone: some read it as pessimistic and subversive of the Augustan regime, others as a celebration of the new dynasty. The first full and faithful rendering into Scots was the Eneados of Gavin Douglas, completed in 1513.
aeolipile: The name comes from Ancient Greek and the Latin word pila, and means the ball of Aeolus, the Greek god of the air and wind. Both Hero of Alexandria and Vitruvius draw on the much earlier work of Ctesibius, who lived from 285 to 222 BCE, an inventor and mathematician in Alexandria in Ptolemaic Egypt.

Vitruvius mentions aeolipiles by name in De architectura, describing them as hollow brazen vessels with a small opening, which are filled with water. Little wind comes out before the water is heated, but once it boils a violent wind issues forth. Hero, who lived from about 10 to 70 CE, took a more practical approach and gave instructions for making one in his entry titled The Steam-Engine. Many sources credit him with the invention, though at least one credits Vitruvius as the first to describe it.

An aeolipile usually consists of a spherical or cylindrical vessel with oppositely bent nozzles projecting outward, set to rotate on its axis. When it is pressurised with steam, the gas escaping from the nozzles produces thrust by the rocket principle, and the thrusts combine into a torque that spins the vessel.
As Hero described it, the water is heated in a simple boiler that forms part of the stand, joined to the rotating ball by two pipes that also serve as its pivots.

It is not known whether the aeolipile had any practical use in ancient times, or whether it was seen as a pragmatic device, a novelty or an object of reverence. One source calls it a mere curiosity for the ancient Greeks, a party trick. Hero's drawing shows a standalone device, presumably meant as a temple wonder like many devices in his Pneumatica. Vitruvius mentions it for demonstrating the physical properties of the weather, saying that a simple experiment of this kind shows the causes and effects of the great operations of the heavens and the winds.

In 1543 Blasco de Garay, a captain in the Spanish navy, allegedly demonstrated to Charles V a boiler and paddle wheels that could drive large ships without wind. Spanish authorities denied the claim. The aeolipile is neither a practical source of power nor a direct predecessor of the Industrial Revolution's steam engines, and it is the symbol of the US Navy's Boiler Technician rating.
aeroplane: Stories of flight are old: the Greek legend of Icarus and Daedalus, and the Vimana of ancient Indian epics. Around 400 BCE Archytas was reputed to have built a bird-shaped model propelled by a jet of what was probably steam, said to have flown some 200 m. Among the earliest recorded attempts with gliders were those of the 9th-century poet Abbas ibn Firnas and the 11th-century English monk Eilmer of Malmesbury; both experiments injured their pilots. Leonardo da Vinci studied the wings of birds and designed a man-powered aircraft in his Codex on the Flight of Birds (1502).

In 1799 George Cayley set out the concept of the modern aeroplane as a fixed-wing machine with separate systems for lift, propulsion and control. He built and flew models from 1803 and a successful passenger-carrying glider in 1853. Otto Lilienthal, between 1867 and 1896, made well-documented, repeated gliding flights, and his work heavily inspired the Wright brothers. In 1894 Sir Hiram Maxim tested a 3.5-ton steam-powered craft on overhead rails; it had enough lift to take off, but he abandoned the project because of its instability.

An aeroplane is a fixed-wing aircraft. Its wings deflect air downward as it moves forward and so generate lift, and a fuselage joins the other parts of the airframe. A vertical fin and rudder control yaw, and a horizontal tailplane with elevators controls pitch. The word comes from the French aéroplane, which was first attested in English in the late 19th century and originally referred only to the wing. In the United Kingdom and most of the Commonwealth the word is aeroplane. In the United States, airplane became standard after the National Advisory Committee for Aeronautics adopted it in 1916.
Early aircraft were usually made of wood with fabric wing surfaces. As speeds rose, more parts became metal, and by the end of the World War II all-metal aircraft were common.

The Wright brothers flew the Wright Flyer in 1903, recognised as the first sustained and controlled heavier-than-air powered flight. Aircraft saw limited use in the First World War and were present in all the major battles of World War II. The first jet aircraft was the German Heinkel He 178 in 1939. The first jet airliner, the de Havilland Comet, entered service in 1952, and the Boeing 707, the first widely successful commercial jet, flew commercially from 1958 to 2019. Aeroplanes are used for recreation, for carrying people and goods, for military purposes and for research.
aeschines: Aeschines was born in Athens, though the records of his parentage and early life conflict. It seems probable that his parents, though poor, were respectable. His father Atrometus was an elementary schoolteacher and his mother Glaukothea assisted in religious rites of initiation. After helping his father in his school, he tried acting with indifferent success, served with distinction in the army and held several clerkships, among them that of clerk to the Boule. He took part in campaigns at Phlius in 368 BCE, the Battle of Mantinea in 362 BCE and Phokion's campaign in Euboea in 349 BCE.

The fall of Olynthus in 348 BCE brought Aeschines into politics, and he was sent on an embassy to rouse the Peloponnese against Philip II of Macedon. In the spring of 347 BCE he urged the assembly of the Ten Thousand at Megalopolis to unite against Philip. In the summer he joined the peace embassy to Philip and, to counter prejudice stirred up by his opponents, described Philip to the Athenian assembly as entirely Greek. His slowness on the second embassy of 346 BCE, sent to ratify the peace, led Demosthenes and Timarchus to accuse him of high treason.

Aeschines answered by arguing that Timarchus had forfeited the right to speak before the people because of his youthful conduct. The suit succeeded, Timarchus was sentenced to atimia, and Aeschines was cleared. His speech Against Timarchus is valued for the many Athenian laws it cites. In 343 BCE Demosthenes renewed the attack in On the False Embassy, and Aeschines was again acquitted. In 339 BCE, as an Athenian deputy to the Amphictyonic Council, he made a speech that brought about the Fourth Sacred War.

In 336 BCE Ctesiphon proposed that Demosthenes be rewarded with a golden crown, and Aeschines accused Ctesiphon of breaking the law. The case lay unresolved until 330 BCE, when the rivals delivered Against Ctesiphon and On the Crown. The result was an overwhelming victory for Demosthenes.

Aeschines went into voluntary exile at Rhodes, to avoid the jury's judgement, which was likely to be a large fine, and opened a school of rhetoric there. He later moved to Samos, where he died at the age of 75. His three speeches, called by the ancients the Three Graces, rank next to those of Demosthenes. The twelve letters published under his name are not genuine.
aeschylus: Aeschylus was born around 525 BCE in Eleusis, a small town about 27 kilometres north-west of Athens. His family was wealthy and well established, and his father, Euphorion, was said to belong to the ancient nobility of Attica, though this might be a fiction invented by the ancients to account for the grandeur of the plays. As a youth he worked at a vineyard. Pausanias, writing in the 2nd century CE, reported that the god Dionysus visited him in his sleep and told him to turn to tragedy. His first performance took place in 499 BCE, and he won his first victory at the Dionysia in 484 BCE.

Ancient sources attribute between seventy and ninety plays to him, and only seven survive complete: The Persians, Seven Against Thebes, The Suppliants, the three plays of the Oresteia, and Prometheus Bound, whose authorship has been doubted since the late 19th century. He tended to write connected trilogies in which each play is a chapter in one narrative, and the Oresteia of 458 BCE is the only complete trilogy of Greek plays still extant.

The Persians, performed in 472 BCE, is the only extant Greek tragedy on a recent historical event, the Persian defeat at Salamis, and it blames that defeat on the pride of King Xerxes. According to Aristotle, Aeschylus expanded the number of characters and allowed conflict among them, where earlier characters interacted only with the chorus.

In 458 BCE Aeschylus returned to Sicily for the last time and visited Gela, where he died in 456 or 455 BCE. Valerius Maximus wrote that a tortoise dropped by an eagle, which mistook his head for a rock, killed him, a story that may be a legend. His gravestone inscription commemorates only his part in the Greek victory at Marathon and says nothing of his plays. After his death his tragedies were the only ones allowed to be restaged in competitions.
aesop: Details of Aesop's life are scattered through ancient authors, including Aristotle, Herodotus and Plutarch, and the scholar Martin Litchfield West judged it far from certain that a historical Aesop ever existed. The earliest Greek sources, Aristotle among them, place his birth in the Greek colony of Mesembria. Later writers of the Roman imperial period, including Phaedrus, who adapted the fables into Latin, say he was born in Phrygia, and Callimachus called him Aesop of Sardis.

Aristotle and Herodotus describe him as a slave on Samos, owned first by a man named Xanthus and then by Iadmon. He must eventually have been freed, since he later appeared as an advocate for a wealthy Samian. A highly fictional biography, The Aesop Romance, composed around the 2nd century CE from older material, makes him an extremely ugly Phrygian slave who gains his freedom through clever storytelling. Scholars long dismissed it, and widespread study of the work began only toward the end of the 20th century.

Aesop may not have written his fables. Herodotus calls him a writer of fables, and Aristophanes speaks of reading Aesop, but that may mean a compilation of fables ascribed to him. Sophocles referred to the tale of the North Wind and the Sun, and Socrates, while in prison, turned some of the fables into verse. Demetrius of Phalerum made what may have been the earliest collection, now lost. Phaedrus rendered the fables into Latin in the 1st century CE, and at about the same time Babrius put them into Greek verse.

The fables went on being revised and translated through the centuries, with material added from other cultures, so that the body of fables known today bears little relation to those Aesop originally told. Many are characterised by animals that speak and act like people.

Aesop is said to have met his end at Delphi. Plutarch tells that he came there on a diplomatic mission from King Croesus of Lydia, insulted the Delphians, was sentenced to death on a false charge of temple theft and was thrown from a cliff. In 1965 the scholar Ben Edwin Perry judged that the stories linking him to Croesus and the Seven Sages of Greece were literary fiction, while later research found a mission for Croesus consistent with the year of his death.

Ancient sources mention statues of Aesop by Aristodemus and Lysippus, none of which survive. Later ages pictured him in many ways, usually as an ugly slave, and a tradition from the Byzantine scholar Planudes in the 13th century made him an Ethiopian, based on a mistaken derivation of his name. The Versailles labyrinth, finished in 1677 for Louis XIV, carried fountains depicting his fables.
aethelbald-of-mercia: Æthelbald belonged to the Mercian royal line, although his father Alweo was never king. Alweo's father was Eowa, who may have shared the throne for some time with his brother Penda. In Æthelbald's youth Penda's dynasty ruled Mercia, and Ceolred, a grandson of Penda, drove him into exile, according to Felix's Life of Saint Guthlac. In the fens he and his men visited the hermit Guthlac of Crowland, who was sympathetic to his cause, and Æthelbald later dreamed that Guthlac prophesied greatness for him and, once king, gave him a shrine. When Ceolred died of a fit at a banquet, Æthelbald returned and became king, ending Penda's line.

His reign began a resurgence of Mercian power that lasted until the end of the eighth century. Apart from the short reign of Beornrad, Mercia was ruled for eighty years by Æthelbald and Offa, long reigns at a time when eleven kings ruled Northumbria, many dying violently. At his accession Wessex and Kent had stronger kings, Ine and Wihtred, but Wihtred died in 725 and Ine abdicated in 726 for a pilgrimage to Rome. By 731 the contemporary chronicler Bede could write that all the provinces south of the Humber, with their kings, were subject to Æthelbald. A charter of 736, the Ismere Diploma, calls him king of the South English and in its witness list Rex Britanniae.

He went to war to keep his overlordship. In 733 he captured the royal manor of Somerton in Wessex, and Cuthred of Wessex fought him in 740 and, by one version of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, put him to flight at Burford in 752. In 740 he ravaged Northumbrian lands while its king Eadberht was away. London passed from the kings of Essex to Mercian control in his time.

About 745–746 Boniface and seven other bishops sent Æthelbald a letter reproving him for stealing church revenue, violating church privileges, imposing forced labour on clergy and fornicating with nuns. It strongly coloured later opinion of him, though it also praised his faith and alms-giving. A council at Clovesho followed, which he attended and perhaps presided over, and in 749 at Gumley he issued a charter freeing church lands from all obligations except building forts and bridges.

Æthelbald was killed at Seckington in Warwickshire in 757, 'treacherously murdered at night by his own bodyguards' according to a later continuation of Bede, with no reason recorded. Beornrad succeeded him briefly, and Offa soon took the throne. He was buried at St Wystan's Church, Repton, where the crypt can still be seen. A carved figure of a mounted warrior on a cross shaft from Repton may be a memorial to him, which would make it the earliest large-scale pictorial representation of an English monarch.
aethelberht-of-kent: Æthelberht was the son of Eormenric, whom he succeeded as king. Bede traces the Kentish royal line, known as the Oiscings, back to Hengist. Eormenric's name, with an element common among Frankish nobles, hints at links across the Channel, and Gregory of Tours records that Æthelberht's father was king of Kent. One other relative is known, his sister Ricole, mother of Sæberht, king of the East Saxons.

Kent later shows a system of joint kingship, divided between east and west Kent, with Canterbury the chief town of the east and Rochester of the west. Some forged early charters imply that Æthelberht ruled jointly with his son Eadbald, but he held authority throughout the kingdom. The dates of his birth and accession are debated, since Bede and the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle are inconsistent with each other.

Bede lists Æthelberht third among the kings who held imperium over the kingdoms south of the Humber, and the Chronicle calls such kings bretwalda. His authority was clearest in Essex, where his nephew Sæberht accepted Christianity and where Æthelberht, not Sæberht, built and endowed St Paul's in London. Over Rædwald of East Anglia his hold seems to have been weaker, and a passage of Bede on the point can be read in two ways.

Kent was rich, with strong trade ties to the Continent. Kentish workshops made glass beakers and jewellery, and goods from Kent turn up in cemeteries across the Channel. It has been suggested that Æthelberht took trade from the aristocracy and made it a royal concern, and the first English coinage since Roman times, gold shillings, probably circulated in his reign. A slave trade is thought likely.

In 597 nearly forty monks under Augustine landed on the Isle of Thanet. According to Bede, Æthelberht distrusted them enough to meet them in the open air, so that they could not use sorcery. He allowed them to settle in Canterbury and to preach. It is not known exactly when he became a Christian.

Some time after the mission arrived, perhaps in 602 or 603, Æthelberht issued a law code of ninety sections. It sets fines for offences at every level of society, the amount depending on the victim's rank, and it is the earliest surviving code in any Germanic language. Its only early manuscript is the twelfth-century Textus Roffensis. Alfred the Great later drew on it for his own laws.

Æthelberht died on 24 February 616. His son Eadbald, who was not a Christian, outraged the church by marrying his stepmother. A revolt against Christianity and the expulsion of missionaries from Kent followed, perhaps in part a reaction against Kentish overlordship. Æthelberht came to be regarded as a saint, and is venerated by Catholic and Eastern Orthodox churches.
aethelflaed: Æthelflæd was born around 870, at the height of the Viking invasions of England, the eldest child of Alfred the Great and his Mercian wife Ealhswith. By 878 most of England was under Danish rule, but Alfred's victory at Edington that year was followed by the rule of English western Mercia by Æthelred, Lord of the Mercians, who accepted Alfred's overlordship. In the mid-880s Alfred married Æthelflæd to Æthelred to seal the alliance. A charter of 887 first records her as his wife. Æthelred was much older, and their only known child was a daughter, Ælfwynn.

Æthelred and Æthelflæd fortified Worcester at the end of the ninth century and shared lordship rights over the city with its church, which in return promised psalms and masses for them. They also built a new minster at Gloucester. Her husband's health probably failed early in the next decade, and she was then mainly responsible for governing Mercia. When he died in 911 she became Lady of the Mercians. The historian Ian Walker calls her succession the only case of a female ruler of a kingdom in Anglo-Saxon history. Her brother Edward the Elder then took control of London and Oxford.

Edward and Æthelflæd extended Alfred's network of fortified burhs, and she built defences at Wednesbury, Bridgnorth, Tamworth, Stafford, Warwick, Chirbury and Runcorn. In 917 her army took Derby, the first of the Five Boroughs of the Danelaw to fall to the English, and in 918 Leicester surrendered without a fight. The Viking leaders of York then offered her their loyalty.

Æthelflæd died at Tamworth on 12 June 918, and her body was carried to Gloucester and buried with her husband in St Oswald's Minster. Her daughter Ælfwynn succeeded her, but in December Edward took control of Mercia and carried Ælfwynn off to Wessex.

The West Saxon version of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle calls her only Edward's sister, while the Mercian Register calls her Lady of the Mercians and the Annals of Ulster call her a queen of the Saxons. William of Malmesbury called her a woman of enlarged soul. Historians disagree whether Mercia was independent under Æthelred and Æthelflæd, but they agree that she played an important part in the conquest of the Danelaw.
aethelfrith-of-northumbria: Æthelfrith was the son of Æthelric and grandson of Ida, and he apparently succeeded Hussa as king of the Bernicians in 592 or 593, with his capital at Bamburgh. His accession may have involved dynastic rivalry and the exile of Hussa's relatives. The genealogies attached to some manuscripts of the Historia Brittonum say that he ruled Bernicia for twelve years and Deira for another twelve, which can be read as Bernicia alone from about 592 to 604. His predecessors are obscure, and he is the earliest Bernician ruler about whom significant details are known. The historian Frank Stenton wrote that the continuous history of Northumbria, and indeed of England, begins with his reign.

Bede praises his successes against the Britons while noting his paganism, and says he conquered more territory from them than any other king, making them tributary or driving them out and planting English in their places. It may have been Æthelfrith who destroyed the British army at the Battle of Catraeth, about 600, described in the poem Y Gododdin. In 603 Áedán mac Gabráin of Dál Riata led a great army against him, and according to Bede Æthelfrith won a crushing victory at Degsastan with an inferior force, though his brother Theodbald was killed.

About 604 he gained control of Deira; the circumstances are unknown, though the exile of Edwin, son of the former king Ælla, suggests conquest. D. P. Kirby suggested instead a formalisation of an existing relationship between the two kingdoms. His son Oswald was born about 604 to Acha of Deira, Edwin's sister.

Probably between 613 and 616 he attacked the kingdom of Powys and won the Battle of Chester, in which the Powysian king Selyf Sarffgadau was killed. Before the battle he massacred the monks of Bangor-Is-Coed, who had assembled to pray for the Britons; Bede gives about 1200 dead and fifty escaping. Historians have debated its importance, and John T. Koch says the older view that it split the Britons of Wales from those of the north is now outdated.

Edwin sought safety in several kingdoms and finally in East Anglia under King Rædwald. Æthelfrith sent messengers with money and threats to have him killed or handed over. Rædwald at first agreed but was dissuaded by his wife, and instead raised an army. About 616 Æthelfrith was defeated and killed at the Battle of the River Idle; Bede says his army was the smaller, because Rædwald gave him no time to gather all his forces. Edwin was placed on the throne, and Æthelfrith's sons took refuge in Dál Riata. His line was restored to power in the 630s.
aethelred-i-of-wessex: Æthelred was the fourth of five sons of King Æthelwulf of Wessex, and his mother Osburh was of West Saxon royal descent. His grandfather Ecgberht had become king of Wessex in 802. In 853 the future Alfred the Great was sent to Rome, and a confraternity book of San Salvatore at Brescia names both Æthelred and Alfred, indicating that both brothers went. Æthelred first witnessed his father's charters as king's son in 854, and in 862 and 863 he issued charters as King of the West Saxons, probably as deputy for his elder brother Æthelberht.

Æthelred succeeded Æthelberht in 865. His wife Wulfthryth is known from one charter of 868, where she is styled regina, a title rarely given to West Saxon kings' wives. They had two sons, Æthelhelm and Æthelwold. When Alfred asked for his share of their father's property, Æthelred said he had found it too hard to divide and would leave the whole to Alfred on his death. After Alfred succeeded, the supporters of Æthelred's infant sons complained, and Alfred had the will read to the witan to prove his right.

In 865 the Great Heathen Army arrived in East Anglia and went on to conquer Northumbria. When King Burgred of Mercia, his brother-in-law, appealed for help, Æthelred and Alfred besieged the Vikings at Nottingham, but Burgred bought them off. In December 870 the Vikings occupied Reading, and Æthelred and Alfred were defeated there in early January 871. About four days later they won the Battle of Ashdown, where Asser, stressing Alfred's part, says Æthelred stayed in his tent to hear Mass. Defeats at Basing and Meretun followed, and at Meretun the West Saxons lost many important men, including Heahmund, Bishop of Sherborne. Æthelred also adopted the Mercian Lunettes design for his coins, creating a common coinage across southern England for the first time.

Æthelred died shortly after Easter 871, which fell on 15 April, and was buried at the minster of Wimborne in Dorset. Because his sons were still young, Alfred succeeded him, bought off the Vikings and won a decisive victory at Edington in 878. Æthelwold later disputed the throne with Edward the Elder, launching his rebellion partly from Wimborne. Æthelred's descendants played an important part in governing England in the late tenth and early eleventh centuries.
aethelred-lord-of-the-mercians: Æthelred's ancestry is unknown, though his name suggests possible descent from earlier Mercian kings. Ian Walker sees him as a royal ealdorman whose power base lay around Gloucester in the former kingdom of the Hwicce, while Alex Woolf suggests he was the son of King Burgred of Mercia and Æthelswith, Alfred's sister. Thomas Charles-Edwards identifies him with Edryd Long-Hair, who led a Mercian invasion of Gwynedd in 881 and was defeated by the sons of Rhodri Mawr at the Battle of the Conwy, ending Mercian ambitions in north Wales.

By 883 he had accepted Alfred's lordship. Alfred's burhs were extended into Mercia, and at Worcester Æthelred worked with the bishop and used the standing Roman walls. In 886 Alfred handed him London, where the area now called Queenhithe was then known as Æthelred's Hythe. In 893 he led Mercians, West Saxons and Welsh kings against a Viking army at the Battle of Buttington. With Æthelflæd he gave land to Much Wenlock Abbey and founded a new minster at Gloucester, later St Oswald's Priory, in what seems to have been their main seat.

His status is disputed. West Saxon sources call him ealdorman, Mercian ones Lord of the Mercians and Celtic ones sometimes King of Mercia, and he issued some charters in his own name. In the Handbook of British Chronology David Dumville lists him as King Æthelred II.

Some historians believe his health collapsed in the decade from 899 and that Æthelflæd became the effective ruler, Cyril Hart and Maggie Bailey dating this by 902, though Simon Keynes's summary of 2014 and Martin Ryan's account do not mention a decline. The future King Æthelstan was brought up at the couple's court. Æthelred died in 911 and was buried with Æthelflæd at St Oswald's Priory; she ruled after him, but London and Oxford were taken by King Edward the Elder.
aethelred-of-mercia: Æthelred was the son of Penda of Mercia. His likely mother was Penda's queen, Cynewise, named by Bede, though this is not certain. His date of birth is unknown, and nothing is known of his childhood. He had brothers, Wulfhere and Peada, and sisters, Cyneburh and Cyneswith. Mercia in his time occupied the English midlands, with Northumbria to the north, East Anglia to the east and Wessex to the south. By the early 670s Wulfhere had become the most powerful king in southern Britain, but in 674 Ecgfrith of Northumbria defeated him, took Lindsey and imposed tribute. Wulfhere died in 675, possibly of disease, and Æthelred became king.

In 676 his armies ravaged Kent and destroyed Rochester, seat of the bishops of West Kent; the reason is not recorded. The bishop Putta retired and his successor Cwichhelm gave up the see because of its poverty. In 679 Æthelred defeated his brother-in-law Ecgfrith at the Battle of the Trent. Ecgfrith's young brother Ælfwine was killed, but Archbishop Theodore arranged a peace with the customary compensation. Æthelred took Lindsey, and it stayed Mercian until the Viking invasion of the 9th century. The battle effectively ended Northumbrian involvement south of the Humber, though he could not restore the dominance of his predecessors in the south.

Æthelred was known as a pious king, more famed for piety than skill in war, and granted lands to the church, including at Tetbury, Long Newnton and Somerford Keynes. During his reign Archbishop Theodore divided the great Mercian see into five dioceses. When Bishop Wilfrid of York was driven into exile in 692, Æthelred made him bishop of the Middle Angles and defended him at the Council of Austerfield in about 702. His wife Osthryth, daughter of Oswiu of Northumbria, was murdered in 697 by Mercian chieftains, according to Bede.

In 704 Æthelred abdicated, becoming a monk and abbot at Bardney, which he and Osthryth had founded, and left the throne to his nephew Coenred. He still gave advice afterwards: Stephen of Ripon records him urging Coenred to make peace with Wilfrid. The date of his death is not recorded, but he was buried at Bardney, and he and Osthryth were later revered there as saints. His son Ceolred became king in 709 after Coenred left for Rome.
aethelred-the-unready: Æthelred was the younger son of King Edgar and Queen Ælfthryth. Little is known of his early life; he was born during his father's reign. He came to the throne in 978, after his older half-brother Edward the Martyr was killed on arriving to visit Ælfthryth and Æthelred at Corfe in Dorset on 18 March. No perpetrator is named in sources from before the Norman Conquest. Later chroniclers and some historians blame Ælfthryth, while Ann Williams suggests an accidental affray. Æthelred was at most twelve and too young to be suspected, but he began in a weak position and was crowned only after more than a year. His nickname Unræd, 'ill counsel', puns on his name and is first recorded in the early thirteenth century.

The country was governed by his father's advisers, including his mother, until he came of age in the mid-980s. He then took new advisers and granted them church property, but by the early 990s regretted this and saw Viking raids as God's punishment. Raids that were minor in the 980s became large attacks from the 990s. As the English were rarely victorious, the king and his advisers paid the Vikings tribute. The 990s and early 1000s were the most successful period of his reign, with able advisers and a monastic revival. In 1002 he ordered the St Brice's Day massacre of Danes, which historians see as a sign of increasing paranoia. By 1009 Eadric Streona had become his most powerful adviser.

In December 1013 Swein Forkbeard of Denmark conquered England and Æthelred fled to Normandy. When Swein died in February 1014 he returned and drove out Swein's son Cnut. In early 1015 civil war began when Eadric murdered close allies of Æthelred's son Edmund Ironside. Cnut came back soon afterwards, and suspicion between father and son hampered their resistance.

Æthelred died on 23 April 1016 and was buried in Old St Paul's Cathedral in London, where his tomb was destroyed in the Great Fire of 1666. Edmund was chosen king by the Londoners and Cnut at Southampton. Edmund was beaten at Assandun on 18 October, agreed to divide the kingdom with Cnut and died on 30 November, leaving Cnut king of all England. The main chronicle account of the reign was written after the Danish conquest and attributes the defeat to incompetence and cowardice, and historians since the 1970s distrust it as coloured by hindsight. Writers from the Norman Conquest to the late twentieth century judged him a bad king, until a reassessment stressed the achievements of the 990s and early 1000s.
aethelstan: By the ninth century the early kingdoms had been consolidated into four: Wessex, Mercia, Northumbria and East Anglia. Mercia had been the strongest in the eighth century, but Wessex became dominant under Æthelstan's great-great-grandfather Egbert. The Great Heathen Army invaded in 865, and by 878 the Vikings had overrun East Anglia, Northumbria and Mercia and nearly conquered Wessex. Alfred the Great fought back and won the Battle of Edington. Over the following decade Edward the Elder and Æthelflæd of Mercia conquered Viking Mercia and East Anglia, and in 918 Edward took direct control of Mercia.

Æthelstan was the oldest son of Edward the Elder by his first consort Ecgwynn, of whose rank the sources disagree. Edward died at Farndon on 17 July 924. Mercia accepted Æthelstan; Wessex may have chosen his half-brother Ælfweard, who died within three weeks. There was opposition in Wessex, particularly at Winchester, and he was crowned only on 4 September 925 at Kingston upon Thames, by Archbishop Athelm, in a new ordo in which the king wore a crown rather than a helmet. He never married. In 927 he took York, the last Viking kingdom, and in 934 he invaded Scotland and forced Constantine II to submit. In 937 an alliance of Scots and Vikings invaded and he defeated them at Brunanburh.

He created the most centralised government England had yet seen. Between 928 and 935 all charters were written by a single scribe, known to historians as Æthelstan A. He summoned leading figures to his councils, where Welsh kings acknowledged his overlordship, and more legal texts survive from his reign than from any other tenth-century English king. He was pious and collected relics. He died at Gloucester on 27 October 939 and, by his own wish, was buried at Malmesbury Abbey, where he had buried his cousins killed at Brunanburh.

After his death the men of York chose the Viking king of Dublin, Olaf Guthfrithson, and Anglo-Saxon control of the north collapsed. His half-brothers Edmund (939 to 946) and Eadred (946 to 955) spent their reigns regaining it. Modern historians regard Æthelstan as the first King of England, and Frank Stenton and Simon Keynes compare him with Alfred. The title is problematic, since rex Anglorum was not closely tied to the area of England; Charles Insley sees his hegemony over Britain as fragile. The sources are limited: the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle is largely silent, historians are cautious about William of Malmesbury, and the first biography appeared in 2011.
aethelthryth: Æthelthryth was probably born at Exning, near Newmarket in Suffolk, one of four daughters of King Anna who became saints; her sisters Wendreda and Seaxburh of Ely also left secular life and founded abbeys. The earliest account of her is in Bede's Ecclesiastical History, which calls her the virgin mother of many virgins. In about 652 she married Tondberct, prince of the South Gyrwe, keeping a vow of perpetual virginity throughout the marriage. After his death in 655 she withdrew to the Isle of Ely, which he had given her as a morning gift.

In 660 she was married for political reasons to Ecgfrith of Northumbria, then fourteen or fifteen. Soon after he became king in 670 she wished to become a nun, which fed Ecgfrith's quarrel with Wilfrid, bishop of York and her confessor. One account says that about 672 Ecgfrith asked Wilfrid to enforce his marital rights; the bishop persuaded him to let her live for a time as a sister of Coldingham, the nunnery of his aunt Æbbe. Fearing to be carried off by force, she fled back to Ely with two nuns, escaping capture partly thanks to a rising tide.

A later legend tells of her staff growing into an ash tree at Stow on the journey. According to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle she founded the double monastery at Ely in 673; it was destroyed in the Danish invasion of 870.

Bede says she died of a tumour of the neck, which she took as God's way of freeing her from guilt for wearing heavy necklaces in her youth. In 695 Seaxburh, her sister and successor, moved her remains from a common grave to the new church; the body was found uncorrupted and laid in a white marble coffin taken from the Roman ruins at Grantchester. More medieval lives of her were written in English than of any other native female saint. The Church of England keeps her festival on 17 October or 23 June, and from St Audrey, her common name, comes the word tawdry, after the cheap lace sold at her fair in Ely.
aethelwulf-of-wessex: Æthelwulf was the son of Ecgberht, who was king of Wessex from 802 to 839, and of Osburh, daughter of Oslac, described by Asser as King Æthelwulf's butler. In 825 Ecgberht defeated King Beornwulf of Mercia at the Battle of Ellandun in Wiltshire, ending a long Mercian ascendancy over southern England. He then sent Æthelwulf with Eahlstan, Bishop of Sherborne, and Wulfheard, Ealdorman of Hampshire, and a large army into Kent to expel the Mercian sub-king Baldred. Æthelwulf became sub-king of Kent, with Surrey, Sussex and Essex, and governed there through Kentish ealdormen, advancing their interests, which won local support that Mercian rulers governing from a distance had lacked.
