When he succeeded in 839 he was the first son to follow his father as West Saxon king since 641. He gave Kent and the south-east to his son Æthelstan and governed Wessex and Kent as separate spheres. Janet Nelson says he ran a Carolingian-style family firm of plural realms.

Viking raids increased in the 840s: in 843 he was defeated by the crews of 35 ships at Carhampton in Somerset, and in 850 Æthelstan and Ealdorman Ealhhere won a naval victory off Sandwich. In 851 a fleet of 350 ships took London and Canterbury and defeated King Berhtwulf of Mercia, but Æthelwulf and his son Æthelbald defeated the Vikings at the Battle of Aclea in Surrey, after which the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle records the heathen army's heavy losses.

In 853 he joined a Mercian expedition to Wales, and his daughter Æthelswith married King Burgred of Mercia. In 855 he made a pilgrimage to Rome, first giving a decimation, a tenth of his property, and leaving Æthelbald to act as king of Wessex and Æthelberht to rule Kent. He spent a year in Rome. On the way back he married Judith, daughter of Charles the Bald, in 856. Æthelbald refused to give up the West Saxon throne, and Æthelwulf agreed to divide the kingdom, taking the east.

Æthelwulf died on 13 January 858, leaving Wessex to Æthelbald and Kent to Æthelberht; Judith then married Æthelbald. Æthelbald died two years later and the kingdom was reunited. In the 20th century historians thought him excessively pious and impractical, and saw his pilgrimage as a desertion of duty. Historians now see a king who consolidated and extended his dynasty's power, commanded respect on the continent and dealt with the Vikings more effectively than most of his contemporaries. His youngest son Alfred the Great laid on this base his own success. A ring inscribed Æthelwulf Rex, found in Wiltshire about 1780, is now in the British Museum.
aetolia: The Achelous River separates Aetolia from Acarnania to the west, and the region also bordered Epirus, Thessaly and Ozolian Locris. Together with Achaea on the opposite shore, it forms the entrance to the Corinthian Gulf. In classical times Old Aetolia lay in the west, from the Achelous to the Evenus and Calydon, and New or Acquired Aetolia in the east. The coast is level and fruitful, the interior mountainous and unproductive.

The mountains were known in myth as the scene of the hunt for the Calydonian Boar. The mountain tribes included the Ophioneis, Apodotoi, Agraeis, Aperantoi and Eurytanes, and they worshipped Apollo, Artemis and a warlike Athena. After the 7th century the shrine of Apollo Thermios at Thermos became a significant religious centre.

In 426 BCE the Aetolians defeated an Athenian force under Demosthenes, and in 338 BCE they took Naupaktos with the help of Philip II. Their Aetolian League was organised in the reign of Philip II and by the 270s BCE was one of the leading military powers of Greece, a rival of the Macedonian kings and the Achaean League. Aetolians helped defend the sanctuary of Delphi against the Gauls under Brennus and then founded the Sotiria Games in honour of Zeus the Saviour. The Social War against the Achaean League was fought between 220 and 217 BCE.

The Aetolians allied with Rome against Philip V, whose army destroyed the temple of Apollo Thermios, but they sided with Antiochus III against Rome, and after his defeat in 189 BCE they became virtually subjects of Rome. After 146 BCE the region belonged to the province of Achaea. Polybius, from the rival Achaean centre of Megalopolis, doubted their Greek heritage, and he is now thought to show a heavy anti-Aetolian bias.

In the Middle Ages Aetolia was part of the Byzantine Empire and, after 1204, of the Despotate of Epirus. The Ottoman Empire conquered it in the 15th century and called it Karli-Eli. The area of ancient Aetolia corresponds to the eastern part of the modern regional unit of Aetolia-Acarnania, whose seat is Missolonghi and whose largest city is Agrinio, and to parts of Evrytania, with its seat at Karpenisi.
aetolian-league: The Aetolians were a recognised ethnic group with a religious centre at Thermos from at least the seventh century BCE. Their mountain tribes, among them the Ophioneis, Agraeis and Eurytanians, impressed ancient historians with their primitive lifestyle, and Polybius doubted their Greek heritage. The League of the Aetolians was founded sometime in the 4th century BCE, but when is uncertain. One suggestion credits Epaminondas in 367 BCE, while Grainger places it later, around the rise of Philip II of Macedon. After Philip's death the Aetolians joined the Thebans against Alexander the Great, and the league was reconstituted over the next decade.

About 301 BCE the Aetolians took control of Parnassus, including Delphi, which they held for over a century, and in 280 BCE took Heraclea in Trachis, controlling the pass at Thermopylae. In 279 BCE they resisted the Gallic invasion, and the whole population, old people and women included, joined the defence, using skirmishing tactics against the Gauls. At its peak the league held much of Central Greece. It fought the Achaean League and Macedon in the Social War of 220 to 217 BCE and was the first Greek ally of Rome on the Greek mainland, in the First Macedonian War.

In the Second Macedonian War it helped Rome defeat Philip V at Cynoscephalae in 197 BCE, but grew hostile to Roman involvement and in 192 BCE urged Antiochus III to oppose Rome in Greece. After his defeat the league made peace with Rome. Rome's demand for an indemnity of a thousand talents was lowered to 200 talents plus 300 over six years, and Aetolia became a client state required to minister to the power and empire of the Roman people.

The league was federal, able to raise armies and conduct foreign policy in common, with taxes, a common currency and uniform weights and measures, while member communities kept substantial autonomy. It met twice a year, at the Panaetolika and the Thermica festivals. From 278 BCE it sent delegates to the Delphic Amphictyony, eventually holding a majority of the seats. Its official texts used a Northwest Doric koine. Aetolians were known more for light infantry than for hoplites. Polybius gave the league a reputation for piracy and brigandage, a charge some modern historians accept and Grainger doubts, noting that the accusations came from political opponents.
afanasy-nikitin: Afanasy Nikitin, son of Nikita, was a merchant in Tver. Before his great journey he had probably traded over long distances and had travelled to the Ottoman Empire, the Grand Duchy of Lithuania, Moldavia, Wallachia, Georgia and Crimea. He left Tver on a commercial trip planning to trade around the Caspian Sea as far as Shirvan, and travelled down the Volga through Uglich, Kostroma, Plyos and Nizhny Novgorod, where he joined the caravan of Hasan Beg, the returning ambassador from Shirvan.

Near Astrakhan his party was robbed by Nogais and again by Kaitags on the Caspian coast, and some of his companions were taken prisoner. The Shirvanshah rescued them at Shemakha but would not give them the means to return home, so the merchants dispersed. Some went home, others stayed at Shemakha or worked at Baku.

Hoping to recoup his losses, Nikitin went on to Derbent and Baku and crossed the Caspian into Persia. He stayed six months at Chapakur and passed through Sari, Amol, Kashan and Yazd to reach Hormuz, spending two years in Persia in all. Muslim merchants told him of India's riches, and he sailed from Hormuz, reaching the port of Chaul six weeks later.

He observed the markets, ways of life and courts of the Bahmani Sultanate and the Vijayanagara Empire, visited the sanctuary of Parvattum, which he called the Jerusalem of the Hindus, and dealt in horses. After almost three years he concluded that further travel would bring no great profit. He returned by way of Muscat, Somalia and Trabzon, sailed to Caffa in November 1474 and probably wrote his narrative there. He died near Smolensk in the spring of 1475. Other merchants took his notes to Vasily Mamyrev, secretary to Grand Prince Ivan III of Moscow, and they entered state chronicles.

Nikitin's narrative, A Journey Beyond the Three Seas, describes India's population, political structure, agriculture, trade, customs and ceremonies. He noted that the countrymen were very poor while the boyars were rich, and he described the four months of rain he spent at Junnar. Historians have used it as a dependable source for 15th-century India, though some of his accounts of everyday life are exaggerated and he accepted legends such as that of a monkey prince with armed followers.

Because he transliterated Muslim prayers into Cyrillic and kept Muslim fasts, Gail Lenhoff and Janet Martin speculated that he converted to Islam. The editor Yakov Lurye doubts this, noting that a convert would hardly have tried to return to Rus', and calls his piety a peculiar syncretism. Nikitin himself wrote of shedding tears for the Christian faith and longing to go home.
afar-triangle: The Afar Triangle, also called the Afar Depression, is a geological depression formed at the Afar triple junction, part of the Great Rift Valley in East Africa. It borders Eritrea, Djibouti and the whole Afar Region of Ethiopia. The Ethiopian Plateau and escarpment lie to the west, the Danakil block to the north-east, the Somali Plateau to the south and the Ali-Sabieh block to the south-east. It contains the lowest point in Africa, Lake Assal in Djibouti, at 155 metres below sea level. The northern part is known as the Danakil Depression, where Dallol is one of the hottest places on Earth by year-round average temperature. Rainfall averages only 100 to 200 millimetres a year.

The Awash River, the main source of water, provides a narrow green belt for plants, animals and the Afar, a nomadic people. It ends about 128 kilometres from the Red Sea in a chain of salt lakes, where it evaporates as fast as it arrives. About 1,200 square kilometres are covered by salt deposits, and mining salt is a major source of income for many Afar groups.

The recent geological history began about 33 million years ago with the eruption of the Ethiopian Flood Basalts, caused by a rising mantle plume. Rifting started in the Afar about 28 million years ago. The region lies where the spreading ridges of the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden meet the East African Rift, driven by the movement of the Arabian and Somalian plates away from the Nubian plate. Volcanic and tectonic activity is still strong, and geologists predict that in about 10 million years the East African Rift will be submerged and form a new ocean basin.

The Afar has been called the cradle of human evolution by some palaeontologists. The Middle Awash region and the sites of Hadar, Dikika and Woranso-Mille have yielded the earliest fossil hominins and some of the world's oldest stone tools. Hadar is the site of Lucy, a specimen of Australopithecus afarensis, and Dikika of Selam, a fossilised child. In 1994 Tim D. White found 4.4-million-year-old Ardipithecus ramidus, a nearly complete female skeleton named Ardi, which took almost 15 years to excavate, preserve and describe.

The vegetation is desert scrubland of drought-resistant small trees, shrubs and grasses. Its wildlife includes Grévy's zebra, Soemmerring's gazelle and the last viable population of the African wild ass, and the Mille-Serdo Wildlife Reserve lies in the southern part of the plain.
afghanistan: Afghanistan is a landlocked country at the crossroads of Central and South Asia, occupying 652,864 square kilometres. It is predominantly mountainous, dominated by the Hindu Kush range, which ends in the west-central highlands and separates the plains of the north, the Turkestan Plains, from those of the southwest, the Sistan Basin. The highest point is Noshaq, at 7,492 metres. Its longest border, the Durand Line, is with Pakistan.

People lived in what is now Afghanistan at least 50,000 years ago, and farming communities there were among the earliest in the world. Urban civilisation is believed to have begun as early as 3000 BCE, and Mundigak, near Kandahar, was a centre of the Helmand culture; an Indus Valley site has been found at Shortugai on the Oxus River. After 2000 BCE successive waves of semi-nomadic people from Central Asia, among them many Indo-Iranians, moved south.

By the middle of the 6th century BCE the Achaemenids had overthrown the Medes and incorporated Arachosia, Aria and Bactria, and the tombstone inscription of Darius the Great lists the Kabul Valley among the 29 countries he conquered. Because of its conquests and periods in both the Iranian and Indian cultural spheres, the area was a centre for Zoroastrianism, Buddhism, Hinduism and later Islam.

The modern state began with the Durrani Empire in the 18th century under Ahmad Shah Durrani, although Dost Mohammad Khan is sometimes considered the founder of the first modern Afghan state. The name Afghanistan became a state designation only during the colonial interventions of the 19th century. Afghanistan was a buffer state in the Great Game between the British and Russian empires. The British were repelled in the First Anglo-Afghan War, but won the Second. After the Third Anglo-Afghan War in 1919 the country became free of foreign political hegemony, and the independent Kingdom of Afghanistan emerged in 1926.

Since the late 1970s warfare has dominated Afghanistan's history. In 1973 King Zahir Shah was overthrown by his cousin Mohammad Daoud Khan, and a communist revolution in 1978 killed Daoud Khan. The Soviet Union invaded in 1979 and withdrew in 1989 after the mujahideen won the Soviet–Afghan War, and a civil war followed. The Taliban controlled most of the country by 1996, were overthrown in the 2001 United States invasion, and returned to power in 2021. The population is estimated at between 35 and 50 million, and about 70.4% live in rural areas.
afgooye: Afgooye lies about 30 kilometres from Mogadishu, in the Lower Shebelle region, and the Shabelle River passes through the middle of the town. It is identified with the historical settlement of Lama Jiidle, "two roads" in Somali, which Lee V. Cassanelli describes as the centre of Silcis administration. In Somali the name Afgooye means split mouth. It is one of the oldest towns of the lower Shebelle valley.

In the medieval period the Silcis, a section of the Ajuran, governed the district from Lama Jiidle. They limited themselves to controlling the caravan routes and collecting taxes and tribute, and imposed a daily measure of grain on each household of the Geledi. Oral accounts say that when the sultan's daughter Imbia came to collect the tribute, the Geledi beat her instead. Her father, the sultan 'Umur Abukar Abroone, exclaimed "waa la i afgooye", "they have cut off my mouth", and the town took its name from the event. The Geledi, under Ibrahim Adeer, a general who had served the Ajuran, drove the Silcis out and established the Geledi Sultanate.

Under the Gobroon dynasty Afgooye reached its golden age as a trading hub between the coast and the interior, with caravans bringing ivory, leopard skins and aloe in exchange for cloth, sugar, dates and firearms. In the early nineteenth century its population is estimated to have exceeded 80,000, and it was surrounded by a wall with five fortified gates. At the turn of the twentieth century Afgooye was incorporated into Italian Somaliland; the Italians occupied the town in 1908 and abolished its slave market, and a station on the Mogadishu–Villabruzzi Railway served it. After civil war broke out in 1991 parts of the town sheltered many internally displaced people, and on 25 May 2012 Somali government forces backed by AMISOM tanks recaptured it from Al-Shabaab.

The town has about 79,400 inhabitants, and the wider Afgooye District is inhabited mainly by the Geledi and Garre clans, sub-clans of the Digil and Rahanweyn. It is the site of Lafoole College, the first college of education in Somalia, built on the site of the Battle of Lafoole of 1896. Afgooye is also known for the Istunka, an annual mock stick fight marking the New Year, which developed in the Ajuran period and was expanded by Sultan Ahmed Yusuf into a tournament of teams with poets and dancers. The Afgooye datum, based on the Krasovsky ellipsoid, is a geodetic datum used in Somalia.
afonso-de-albuquerque: Afonso de Albuquerque was born around 1453 in Alhandra, near Lisbon, the second son of Gonçalo de Albuquerque, Lord of Vila Verde dos Francos. His father held an important position at court and was connected by remote illegitimate descent with the Portuguese monarchy. He was educated in mathematics and Latin at the court of Afonso V, where he befriended Prince John, later King John II.

He was present at the conquest of Tangier and Arzila in 1471, fought at the Battle of Toro in 1476, and joined the campaign of 1480 to help Ferdinand I of Naples repel the Ottoman invasion of Otranto. When John became king in 1481, Albuquerque was made master of the horse, a post he held throughout the reign.

On 6 April 1503 Albuquerque sailed on his first expedition to India with his cousin Francisco de Albuquerque. They fought the forces of the Zamorin of Calicut and secured the king of Cochin on his throne, who allowed the Portuguese to build Fort Immanuel. In 1506 he sailed again in the fleet of Tristão da Cunha, carrying a sealed letter naming him to replace the viceroy Francisco de Almeida two years later. He took Muscat in July 1507 and reached Hormuz on 25 September; it agreed to become a tributary of the Portuguese king.

On 4 November 1509 he became the second Governor of Portuguese India. An attack on Calicut in January 1510 turned into a defeat when Marshal Coutinho attacked the Zamorin's palace against his advice and was killed. Soon after he assembled 23 ships and 1,200 men and, relying on surprise, took Goa from the Sultanate of Bijapur.

In 1513 he led the first European fleet into the Red Sea, but his siege of Aden failed when his scaling ladders broke, and sickness and lack of water forced a retreat. He sent expeditions that made contact with Ayutthaya, Pegu, Timor and the Moluccas. Camões praised his achievements in The Lusiads of 1572 but depicted the muses frowning on his harsh rule.
afonso-i-of-kongo: Afonso, born Mvemba a Nzinga around 1456, was a son of Nzinga a Nkuwu, the king of Kongo who took the name João I on conversion. As a young man he ruled the province of Nsundi, in the northeast of the kingdom. The first Portuguese reached the capital, Mbanza Kongo, in 1491, and Mvemba took quickly to Christianity, took the name Afonso and studied for ten years with Portuguese priests. Around 1495 his father turned against Christianity and pushed the priests out of the capital, but Afonso welcomed them into Nsundi.

After João died in 1506 Afonso, whose mother had kept the news secret while he gathered followers in the capital, prevailed against his half-brother Mpanzu a Kitima in the Battle of Mbanza Kongo. Kongo was an elective monarchy.

Afonso centralised government at Mbanza Kongo, curbed the rural nobility and expanded Kongo's borders to the south and east; captives were enslaved, and conquered lands paid tribute in iron, palm cloth and ivory. He made Christianity the royal faith, paid for the church from taxes and founded schools; by 1516 more than 1,000 students attended the royal school.

Trade with Portugal grew, and with it the slave trade, which Portuguese demand from the colony on São Tomé drove up. By the 1510s Afonso received Portuguese military help in exchange for a share of the captives of his wars. By the mid-1520s nobles were illegally exporting slaves and even kidnapping freeborn Kongolese. In 1526 Afonso wrote to the king of Portugal: "Each day the traders are kidnapping our people." He threatened to end the trade and set up a committee to judge the legality of enslavement, which for a time slowed the enslavement of free Kongolese.

In 1540 plotters, among them Portuguese residents, made an unsuccessful attempt on his life. He died around the turn of 1542 to 1543 and was succeeded by his son Pedro, who was overthrown by Afonso's grandson Diogo in 1545. Descendants of three of Afonso's daughters supplied many later kings. Almost everything known about Kongo in his time comes from his long series of letters to the Portuguese kings Manuel I and João III.
afonso-i-of-portugal: Afonso was the son of Theresa, an illegitimate daughter of King Alfonso VI of León, and Henry of Burgundy, together rulers of the County of Portugal. His birth year is given as 1106, 1109 or 1111, and his birthplace is disputed among Guimarães, Viseu, Coimbra and places elsewhere. Henry died on 22 May 1112, and Theresa ruled as a widow. She allied with the powerful Galician count Fernando Pérez de Traba, which the Portuguese nobility disliked, and she exiled Afonso in 1120, while he was still a boy.
In 1128 Afonso and his supporters defeated her and Fernando Pérez at the Battle of São Mamede, near Guimarães, and he exiled his mother to Galicia and took over the county.

Afonso then turned against the Moors in the south. On 25 July 1139 he won a decisive victory at the Battle of Ourique and was proclaimed King of the Portuguese, possibly unanimously, by his soldiers, although the first reference to his royal title dates from 1140. The Cortes of Lamego, supposed to have given him the crown, is a 17th-century embellishment of Portuguese history. After his victory at Valdevez, the Treaty of Zamora of 1143 established peace with Alfonso VII of León, who recognised Portugal as fully independent.

He married Matilda of Savoy in 1146 and seized Santarém and Lisbon from the Moors in 1147. In 1169 he was possibly disabled in an engagement near Badajoz and captured by soldiers of his son-in-law Ferdinand II of León, an event called the Disaster of Badajoz; Portugal gave up most of its conquests in Galicia as ransom. In 1179 the papal bull Manifestis Probatum, issued by Pope Alexander III, recognised him as king and Portugal as an independent kingdom.

Afonso died on 6 December 1185 and was succeeded by his son Sancho I. His tomb is in the Santa Cruz Monastery in Coimbra. The Portuguese revere him as a hero and the founder of their nation, and call him the Conqueror, the Founder and the Great.
afonso-iii-of-portugal: Afonso was born at Coimbra, the second son of King Afonso II of Portugal and Urraca of Castile. As a second son he was not expected to inherit the throne, which was destined for his elder brother Sancho. He lived mostly in France, where in 1238 he married Countess Matilda II of Boulogne and so became count of Boulogne, Mortain, Aumale and Dammartin-en-Goële by right of his wife.

By 1245 the conflicts between King Sancho II and the Church had become unbearable, and Pope Innocent IV ordered Sancho removed and replaced by the Count of Boulogne. Afonso accepted and marched to Portugal. Sancho was not a popular king, the order was not hard to enforce, and he fled into exile at Toledo, where he died on 4 January 1248. Until then Afonso held the title Visitador, Curador e Defensor do Reino. To take the throne he gave up his rights to Boulogne in 1248, and in 1253 he divorced Matilda to marry Beatrice of Castile, an illegitimate daughter of Alfonso X of Castile.

Afonso paid special attention to the merchants and small landowners of the middle class. In 1254, at Leiria, he held the first session of the Cortes to include the nobility, the middle class and representatives of all municipalities. He made laws to restrain the upper classes from abusing the less favoured, founded several towns, granted the title of city to others and reorganised public administration. He also ended preventive arrests, so that every arrest had to be presented to a judge, and negotiated extraordinary taxes with the merchants and taxed the Church directly instead of debasing the coinage. These measures may have led to his excommunication by the Holy See.

Once secure on the throne, Afonso made war on the Muslim communities of the south, and in his reign the Algarve became part of the kingdom with the capture of Faro. Castile considered the new lands to be its own, which led to a series of wars. The Treaty of Badajoz, signed in 1267, set the southern border between the two kingdoms at the River Guadiana, where it still runs. Afonso died at Alcobaça, Coimbra or Lisbon; the sources differ. His son Denis came to the throne prematurely, at the age of 18.
africa: Africa covers about 30.3 million square kilometres, including adjacent islands, around 20% of Earth's land area. It straddles the equator and the prime meridian and is joined to Asia by the Isthmus of Suez, 163 kilometres wide. Its coastline is 26,000 kilometres long, and the absence of deep indentations means that Europe, a third of its size, has a longer one. The climate ranges from tropical to subarctic on the highest peaks: the northern half is primarily desert or arid, the centre and south hold savanna plains and rainforest, and 60% of the land surface consists of drylands and deserts. Algeria is the largest country by area.

Africa is widely accepted as the place of origin of humans. The earliest hominids and their ancestors have been dated to around 7 million years ago, and Homo sapiens is believed to have originated there 350,000 to 260,000 years ago, before the Out of Africa II migration of about 50,000 years ago.

African societies have generally recorded their history through oral tradition, which anthropologists have termed oral civilisations. The continent saw the rise and fall of many kingdoms and empires, among them Ancient Egypt, Makuria, the Fatimids, Mali, the Asante, Kongo, the Luba, Great Zimbabwe and the Zulu, although many societies were heterarchical and stateless. Slave trades created diasporas, especially in the Americas.

From the late 19th century to the early 20th century most of Africa was conquered and colonised by European nations, except Ethiopia and Liberia. Colonies were maintained for the economic exploitation and extraction of natural resources. Most present states emerged from decolonisation after the Second World War, and in 1963 they established the Organisation of African Unity, the predecessor of the African Union. The new countries decided to keep their colonial borders, using traditional power structures in governance to varying degrees.

The continent has 54 fully recognised sovereign states, and the African Union, which succeeded the Organisation of African Unity in 2001, has 55 member states and is headquartered in Addis Ababa. Africa's population was estimated at 1,394 million in 2021, up from 229 million in 1950, and it is the youngest among the continents. Bantu-speaking peoples are the majority in southern, central and southeast Africa.
african-americans: African Americans are Americans of wholly or partly sub-Saharan African descent. In the sense of an ethnic group the term generally denotes the descendants of Africans enslaved in the United States. Most were taken from several Central and West African ethnic groups in the transatlantic slave trade, captured by European traders in coastal raids or sold to them by West African traders or by half-European merchant princes. Most African Americans are of West African and coastal Central African ancestry, with varying amounts of Western European and Native American ancestry.

Enslaved Africans were put to work on plantations, particularly in the southern colonies. A few gained freedom through manumission or escape and founded independent communities before and during the American Revolution.

Africans, enslaved and free, took part in the American Revolutionary War on both sides; patriots included James Armistead, Prince Whipple and Oliver Cromwell, and around 15,000 Black Loyalists left with the British, most becoming free people in England or its colonies, among them the Black Nova Scotians and the Sierra Leone Creole people. After the United States was founded most Black Americans remained enslaved, mainly in the South, and four million were liberated only after the Northern victory in the Civil War of 1861 to 1865.

During Reconstruction African Americans gained citizenship and adult men the vote, but belief in White supremacy left them second-class citizens, and Reconstruction ended in 1876. By the late 1890s Southern states had enacted Jim Crow laws enforcing segregation and disenfranchisement. The Great Migration of the first half of the 20th century carried many to the North and West, where they met discrimination in work and housing; the Red Summer of 1919 brought race riots in more than three dozen cities. Legal segregation was eliminated through the civil rights movement.

African Americans formed their own congregations, schools and civic associations, and the historically Black churches remain central to the religious life of the community. African-American culture has influenced the English language, literature, politics, cuisine, sports and music, and most American popular music, including gospel, blues, jazz, rock and roll, R&B, soul, funk, disco, hip-hop and house, has its origins partly or entirely in the community. In 1967 Thurgood Marshall became the first African American Supreme Court Justice, and in 1968 Shirley Chisholm the first Black woman elected to Congress.
african-national-congress: The African National Congress was founded in Bloemfontein on 8 January 1912 as the South African Native National Congress, and took its present name in 1923. It was a successor of the Cape Colony's Imbumba Yamanyama organisation. Its founders were Pixley ka Isaka Seme, Sol Plaatje, John Langalibalele Dube and Walter Rubusana, who, like much of the early membership, came from the conservative, educated and religious professional classes of black South African society. Xhosa chiefs did not take part but showed great support, and King Jongilizwe donated 50 cows at the founding. Around 1920 the organisation moved partly away from the politics of petitioning towards a programme of passive resistance aimed chiefly at the pass laws.

In the 1940s Alfred Bitini Xuma revived some of Gumede's programmes, and in 1944 a left-wing Youth League formed under Walter Sisulu, Nelson Mandela and Oliver Tambo. After the National Party came to power in 1948 on a platform of apartheid, the new generation pushed through a Programme of Action advocating African nationalism and the sustained use of strikes, stay-aways and boycotts. This culminated in the Defiance Campaign of 1952–53, organised with the Indian Congress and the coloured Franchise Action Council. In June 1955 the Congress of the People at Kliptown ratified the Freedom Charter, which became a fundamental document of the struggle.

The Charter was used as a pretext to prosecute hundreds of activists in the Treason Trial. After the Sharpeville massacre on 21 March 1960 the government banned the ANC, and it remained banned until February 1990. Increasing state repression forced it into exile. Headquartered in Lusaka, Zambia, it pursued sabotage and guerrilla warfare through its military wing, uMkhonto weSizwe, founded in 1961 with the South African Communist Party. It became a key player in the negotiations to end apartheid that began after the ban was lifted. The first post-apartheid election in 1994 resulted in Nelson Mandela being elected President of South Africa.

Every member belongs to a local branch, and branch members choose policies and leaders mainly by electing delegates to the National Conference, held every five years. Between conferences an 86-member National Executive Committee leads the organisation. It has three autonomous leagues, for women, youth and veterans, and leads the Tripartite Alliance with the South African Communist Party and the Congress of South African Trade Unions, formalised in mid-1990. Its flag has black, green and gold stripes.
african-union: The historical foundations of the African Union lie in the First Congress of Independent African States, held in Accra, Ghana, from 15 to 22 April 1958, which aimed to establish Africa Day to mark the African peoples' wish to free themselves from colonial rule. Later attempts at unity included the Organisation of African Unity, established on 25 May 1963 in Addis Ababa by 32 signatory governments, and the African Economic Community in 1991. Critics argued that the Organisation did little to protect citizens' rights from their own political leaders and dubbed it the Dictators' Club.
The Sirte Declaration of 9 September 1999 called for an African Union. The bloc was launched on 9 July 2002 in Durban, South Africa, and the Organisation of African Unity was disbanded that day.

The most important decisions are made by the Assembly, a meeting of the heads of state and government of its member states. The Pan-African Parliament sits at Midrand, near Johannesburg, and its secretariat, the African Union Commission, is based in Addis Ababa, in a headquarters complex inaugurated on 28 January 2012 and built as a gift from the Chinese government. The Peace and Security Council can authorise peace support missions and impose sanctions after an unconstitutional change of government, and the Constitutive Act allows intervention in grave circumstances: war crimes, genocide and crimes against humanity.

All United Nations member states on the African continent belong to the Union, together with the Sahrawi Arab Democratic Republic. Morocco withdrew from the Organisation of African Unity in 1984 over the Sahrawi Republic's admission and was readmitted on 30 January 2017.

The Union's objectives include greater unity and solidarity, the defence of its members' sovereignty and territorial integrity, and the integration of the continent. At its July 2007 summit in Accra the principal topic was a Union Government, aiming at a United States of Africa, and member states divided between those who wanted a common government with an army and those who preferred strengthening existing structures. In 2018 the Union adopted a Free Movement Protocol. Its emblem shows the silhouette of Africa drawn without internal borders to symbolise unity.
african-union-mission-to-somalia: A foreign force for Somalia had been debated since 2005, when the Transitional Federal Government was divided over it and the rising Islamic Courts Union warned that any foreign peacekeepers would face death. The African Union adopted a plan to deploy troops on 14 September 2006, and on 6 December the UN Security Council issued a six-month mandate for the force first planned by IGAD, the regional body. States bordering Somalia were barred from it, so the mission was widened to other African Union members. After Ethiopian troops deposed the Islamic Courts Union in a large invasion in late 2006, the AU's Peace and Security Council created AMISOM on 19 January 2007, and the Security Council approved it on 21 February.

The first troops landed at Mogadishu airport on 6 March 2007 as fighting raged between Islamist insurgents and Ethiopian and government forces. A Burundian advance force followed in December 2007. In July 2010, after deadly bombings in Kampala, AU ministers allowed pre-emptive strikes against al-Shabaab. After four years of urban fighting, Ugandan and Burundian troops forced the militants out of the capital in the Battle of Mogadishu of 2010–2011. Kenyan forces, who had crossed into Somalia on 15 October 2011, were brought into the mission under Security Council resolution 2036 of 22 February 2012, which raised its strength to 17,731.

Between 2012 and 2015 the mission and Somali forces retook a number of towns in the hinterland, though most rural clans remained under al-Shabaab. The mission suffered heavy losses: according to SIPRI, 1,039 of its soldiers were killed between 2009 and 2013, and on 15 January 2016 al-Shabaab overran a Kenyan base at El Adde, where around 150 soldiers were later reported to have died.

The head of mission was the Special Representative of the Chairperson of the African Union Commission. The force was organised in sectors: Sector 1, based in Mogadishu and held mainly by Ugandans, covered Banadir and the Shabelle regions, while Sector 2, based in Kismayu under Kenyan command, covered Gedo and the Juba regions. The United States trained the Ugandan and Burundian contingents and an army unit in Djibouti. The civilian staff worked from Nairobi from 2008 and moved to Mogadishu on 16 May 2011. The mandate ended on 31 March 2022.
afrikaans: Afrikaans is a West Germanic language that emerged during the late 19th century as a fusion of Dutch dialects, mainly Hollandic and Zeelandic, spoken by Dutch settlers in South Africa since the 17th century, and the Dutch-based creole languages spoken by the Khoisan, Nguni and Coloured peoples. Its name comes from the Dutch word Afrikaansch, meaning African. It was previously called Cape Dutch, or the derogatory kitchen Dutch, from its use by slaves of colonial settlers in the kitchen.

For a long time the Eastern Border Hypothesis of the linguist Christo van Rensburg was regarded as the scientific consensus. More recent research concludes that the development was more gradual and diverse. South Africa had a highly diverse linguistic landscape until the early twentieth century, from communities where Dutch differed little from Dutch in Europe to communities for whom Dutch was a second or third language.

An estimated 90 to 95 per cent of the vocabulary is of Dutch origin, although Afrikaans has also adopted words from German, Malay and Khoisan languages. It differs from Dutch in its more analytic morphology and grammar and in some spellings, and the two languages are largely mutually intelligible, especially in writing. Many consonants of the earlier Dutch spelling are dropped: Dutch slechts becomes slegs, and zuid becomes suid. A particular feature is its double negative, which is absent from the other West Germanic standard languages.

Afrikaans is an official language of South Africa and a recognised national language of Namibia. Before independence in 1990 it had equal status with German as an official language in Namibia. Contrary to popular belief, the majority of its speakers today are Coloured people, not Afrikaners or Boers.

In South Africa it shares its status with ten other official languages and has lost the preferential treatment of earlier times in education and media. Even so, it remains more prevalent in radio, newspapers and television than any other official language except English, and more than 300 book titles are published in it annually.
afrikaners: The Dutch East India Company established a victualling station at the Cape of Good Hope in 1652 as a watering point for ships bound for East Asia. Company officials did not favour permanent European settlement, but supplying garrisons and passing fleets led the administration to free some of its employees and oblige them to farm independently. In 1657 the first of these free burghers, the vrijburgers, received farms, and the white population was only about 134. The company offered free passage to Dutch families from 1685 to 1707, and in 1688 it sponsored the settlement of 200 French Huguenot refugees, in the hope that people used to Mediterranean agriculture would succeed with vines and olives where the Dutch had not.

German soldiers returning from Asia in company service added to the colonists. By 1691 over a quarter of the white population was not ethnically Dutch, and a count at the start of British rule put 26,720 permanent settlers at 50 per cent Dutch, 27 per cent German, 17 per cent French and 5.5 per cent other. Their descendants also include a smaller number of Flemish, Danish, Norwegian, Swiss and Swedish settlers and of indigenous Africans. The first recorded marriage across lines of descent was in 1664 in Cape Town, between a Khoi woman, Krotoa, and a Danish surgeon, Peder Havgaard.

Early colonists were called Christians, colonists, or ingezeetenen, inhabitants, and their sense of being rooted in Africa, unlike the company's expatriate officials, found wide expression only in the late eighteenth century. Dutch rule at the Cape lasted about 140 years, and the colony became British after 1806. In the 20th century Afrikaner nationalism took the form of political parties and closed societies such as the Broederbond. The National Party was founded in 1914 to promote Afrikaner interests, won the general election of 1948 and enacted apartheid, a system of racial segregation, and in 1961 declared South Africa a republic. Afrikaners dominated the country's politics until the first non-racial elections of 1994.

Afrikaans, the mother tongue of Afrikaners, evolved from the Dutch dialect of South Holland. The settlers came from Protestant Europe, and the Boer republics were founded on the principles of the Dutch Reformed Church, whose congregations were centres of frontier communities. In 1985, 92 per cent of Afrikaners identified as members of the Reformed churches. The language is promoted by the Afrikaanse Taal en Kultuurvereniging, and the Voortrekkers is a youth movement. Afrikaners are concentrated in South Africa, especially around Pretoria, and in Namibia, with a diaspora mainly in Australia and New Zealand. About 100 black families who identify as Afrikaners live at Onverwacht, founded in 1886.
afsharid-empire: The dynasty took its name from the Turkoman Afshar tribe, which had migrated from Turkestan to Azerbaijan in the 13th century; in the early 17th century Abbas the Great moved many Afshars to Khorasan to guard the frontier against the Uzbeks. Nader, born Nadr Qoli into a humble semi-nomadic family of the tribe's Qereqlu branch, rose as a local warlord after the Ghilzai Mahmud Hotak overthrew Shah Soltan Hoseyn in 1722, while Russia and the Ottomans seized Iranian land.

Allied with Hoseyn's son Tahmasp II, Nader drove the Afghan leader Ashraf from Isfahan in 1729, deposed Tahmasp in favour of the infant Abbas III in 1732, and won back the Caucasus. At a qoroltai on the Mughan plain he was proclaimed shah, and was crowned on 8 March 1736.

Under Nader, Iran reached its widest extent since the Sasanian Empire. In 1738 he destroyed the last Hotak stronghold at Kandahar, then invaded the Mughal Empire and crushed Muhammad Shah's army at the Battle of Karnal on 13 February 1739. When Indians in Delhi killed Iranian troops on a rumour of his death, he had the city sacked, and 20,000 to 30,000 people were killed in one day. He carried off the Peacock Throne and the Koh-i-Noor and Daria-i-Noor diamonds, and the plunder let him suspend taxes in Iran for three years. He went on to subdue Khiva and Bukhara, took Bahrain and Oman, and built a navy.

In his last years Nader grew despotic and paranoid. He had his son Reza Qoli Mirza blinded on suspicion of an attempt on his life and ordered the killing of many suspected enemies. He sought a form of Shi'ism, which he called Ja'fari, acceptable to Sunnis, and banned the cursing of the first three caliphs. After his assassination by a faction of his officers in 1747, his nephew Adel Shah killed his sons and grandsons, sparing only Shahrokh. Ahmad Shah Abdali founded the Durrani Empire in the east, and Erekle II made eastern Georgia independent in all but name.

Shahrokh, blinded, reigned from Mashhad over little more than the city and its surroundings, and fell under Durrani overlordship. In 1796 Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar seized Mashhad and tortured him to reveal the whereabouts of Nader's treasure; Shahrokh died of his injuries soon after, ending the dynasty. The Qajars restored Iranian rule over much of the lost territory. Shahrokh's descendants bear the surname Afshar Naderi.
afsluitdijk: The Zuiderzee had been a large bay giving maritime access to five provinces and, in the Dutch Golden Age, a protected route for Amsterdam's harbour. The opening of the North Sea Canal in 1876 gave Amsterdam a shorter route, and overfishing had depleted the bay. In 1886 a few notables founded the Zuiderzee Society to study reclamation, and the civil engineer Cornelis Lely, one of its prominent members, designed the first plan for closing and reclaiming the Zuiderzee in 1891. As Minister of Water Management in 1913 he saw land reclamation included in the government programme. The flood of 1916 and the famine of 1918 changed opinion, and work began in 1927.

The dyke runs for 32 kilometres from Den Oever in North Holland to Zurich in Friesland. Its core is mostly sand, covered on the seaward side by boulder clay, dredged from the bottom of the Zuiderzee, and basalt boulders. Work started at four points, two on the mainland sides and two on artificial construction islands, Kornwerderzand and Breezanddijk. The physicist Hendrik Antoon Lorentz calculated the force of the tides as the gap narrowed. At the end ten thousand workers, 27 large dredges, 13 floating cranes, 132 barges and 88 tugs were at work. The last gap, the Vlieter, was closed on 28 May 1932, two years earlier than expected, and the IJsselmeer began, though still salty.

The dyke was officially opened on 25 September 1933, with a monument by Willem Marinus Dudok marking the closing spot and a road linking Friesland and North Holland. Two lock complexes, the Stevin locks at Den Oever and the Lorentz locks at Kornwerderzand, together hold 25 discharge sluices to release water from the IJsselmeer into the Wadden Sea.

A storm in December 1936 showed that the crest height had been set on too little data about wave run-up, and it was later raised several times, particularly after the North Sea Flood of 1953. On 12 and 13 May 1940 Fort Kornwerderzand was the one Dutch line of defence to withstand a German attack. In the 1970s a reserved railway line was used for a second carriageway, making the highway the four-lane A7. Major upgrade works began in 2018, and improvement of the main dyke body was completed in 2022.
afyonkarahisar: Afyonkarahisar lies in the mountainous country inland from the Aegean coast, about 250 kilometres south-west of Ankara on the Akarçay River. Its name means opium black fortress in Turkish, since opium was widely grown there and a castle stands on a black rock. The city was called Afyon until the Turkish Parliament changed the name to Afyonkarahisar in 2004. In antiquity it was known as Akroinon.

The top of the rock has been fortified for a long time, and the Hittites knew it as Hapanuwa. In the Iron Age it was occupied by Phrygians and Lydians, then by the Achaemenid Persians until Alexander the Great conquered it. It was later ruled by the Seleucids, the kings of Pergamon, Rome and Byzantium. Akroinon became an important fortress in the Armeniakon theme and was first mentioned in Byzantine history when Arab invaders attacked it in 716 and 732. After his victory over Arab besiegers in 740, Emperor Leo III renamed it Nicopolis, city of victory.

After 1071 the town lay in the frontier zone between the Byzantine Empire and the invading Turks. It was still Byzantine in 1112, but it had been lost to the Sultanate of Rum by 1146, when Manuel I Komnenos won a victory there. The Turks could not firmly control it until about 1210, and they renamed it Kara Hissar, black castle. After the dispersal of the Seljuqs the town was occupied by Sahib Ata and then by the Germiyanids. The Ottoman Sultan Beyazid I conquered the castle in 1392, it was lost in the invasion of Timur in 1402, and it was recaptured in 1428 or 1429.

Lying on the caravan route between Smyrna and western Asia and Armenia and Georgia, it became a place of extensive trade and during the Ottoman Empire a wealthy centre of opium production. A fire in 1902 burned for 32 hours and destroyed parts of the city. During the First World War British prisoners captured at Gallipoli were held in an empty Armenian church at the foot of the rock. Greek forces occupied the city in the Greco-Turkish War, and it was recovered on 27 August 1922, a key moment in the Turkish counter-attack.

Afyonkarahisar is the administrative centre of its province and a junction of railway and road routes between İzmir, Konya, Ankara and Istanbul. It has hot springs and spas, and it is known for its marble: Docimaean marble from the region, including the purple-veined Pavonazzetto, was valued by the Romans and used under Augustus, Trajan and Hadrian for buildings such as the Pantheon. Raw opium production ended in the late 1960s under international pressure, and poppies are now grown under licence for morphine and other opiates.
aga-khan: The title combines agha, from an Old Turkic and Mongolian word for an elder that came to mean master or lord, and khan, meaning king or ruler in Turkish and Mongolian languages. Together they mean commanding chief, lord or master. According to Farhad Daftary, Aga Khan was an honorific given to Hasan Ali Shah (1804 to 1881), the 46th imam of the Nizari Ismailis, by the Iranian monarch Fath-Ali Shah Qajar. The third Aga Khan stated in a legal proceeding in India that it was not a title but an alias given to the first when he was a young man.

The Aga Khan is the religious head and temporal leader of the Nizari Ismaili Shia community, and his followers believe each Aga Khan to be a descendant of Muhammad. The office is also the Pir of the community.

During the First Anglo-Afghan War of 1841 to 1842, Hasan Ali Shah and his cavalry officers helped General Nott in Kandahar Province and General England in his advance from Sindh. The British Raj recognised him as a prince, as it did other landowners and tribal chiefs who made themselves useful. He was unusual in that his claim to nobility rested on leading an entire sect of Islam. The British saw the value of having the head of a major Shia sect under their patronage, one who might even counterbalance the Ottoman caliph. He was the only religious or community leader in British India given a personal gun salute.

In 1866 the High Court of Bombay decided the Aga Khan Case in his favour, securing the British government's recognition of the first Aga Khan as imam of the Ismaili Khoja community. In 1887 the Secretary of State for India, acting through the Viceroy of India, formally recognised the title.

Four men held the title in the following century and a half. Hasan Ali Shah Mahallati was imam from 1817 to 1881. Shah Ali Shah, the 47th imam, led from 12 April 1881 to 17 August 1885. Sir Sultan Mohammed Shah (1877 to 1957), the 48th, was imam from 1885 until 11 July 1957. Shah Karim Al-Hussaini (1936 to 2025), the 49th, led the community until 4 February 2025, when his son Shah Rahim Al-Hussaini became the 50th imam and Aga Khan V.
aga-of-kish: Aga, written Agga or Akka in some sources, was king in the first dynasty of Kish in the Early Dynastic I period, around 2700 BCE. The Sumerian King List counts him as the 23rd king of Kish and many sources name him as son of Enmebaragesi. His name is Sumerian and rarely attested in early texts, which makes him easy to spot. It probably means made by a god. He appears in the Stele of Ushumgal, where he is a Great Assembly official, and in the Tummal Inscription, which records that he made the Tummal pre-eminent.

The Sumerian King List says that Kish held the hegemony of Sumer and that Aga reigned 625 years, a figure that cannot be taken literally, before Uruk defeated him. His rule probably covered Umma and Zabala, a dependency of Umma; he appears as king of Umma in the Gem of King Aga. There is some scant evidence that the rulers of Kish, like the later Ur III kings, courted the authorities in Nippur to legitimise a claim to leadership over Sumer or part of it. Archaeology shows Kish flourishing in the Early Dynastic II period, with influence beyond its own territory, and declining rapidly in the Early Dynastic III period.

The Sumerian poem Gilgamesh and Aga tells how Aga, treating Gilgamesh of Uruk as his vassal, demanded labour to finish wells and irrigation works at Kish. Gilgamesh put the demand before the city fathers, who refused, and then to the able-bodied men, who declared him lugal. After ten days Aga besieged Uruk. Birhurtura, Gilgamesh's guard, went out, was captured and tortured. When Gilgamesh looked over the wall his radiance terrified the Kishite army, and Enkidu and the men of Uruk captured Aga in the midst of it. Gilgamesh addressed him as his superior, recalling Aga's past help, and set him free to return to Kish.
agadir-crisis: France's pre-eminence in Morocco had been upheld by the Algeciras Conference of 1906, after the First Moroccan Crisis. On 9 February 1909 France and Germany agreed that France would have exclusive political control while each upheld the other's economic interests. In 1911 a rebellion broke out against Sultan Abd al-Hafid. After forcing him to request help, the French prepared to send troops to Fez, on the pretext of protecting European lives and property, though the danger was remote, and dispatched a flying column at the end of April. The German move was aimed at testing the relationship between Britain and France and at winning compensation for accepting French control.

The French finance minister Joseph Caillaux told German diplomats in May that France was prepared to make concessions elsewhere. On 1 July the gunboat SMS Panther arrived at Agadir under the pretext of protecting German trade, and the cruiser SMS Berlin followed days later. On 15 July Germany demanded, as compensation for a French protectorate, the whole French Congo from the Sangha River to the sea.

Britain at first thought France largely responsible and urged it to avoid hasty measures. The prospect of a German naval port on the Atlantic changed this, and Foreign Secretary Sir Edward Grey told the German ambassador that Britain would respond forcefully; battleships were sent. Chancellor of the Exchequer David Lloyd George gave his Mansion House speech in July, bypassing the majority of the Cabinet, which favoured non-intervention. Germany was also hit by financial turmoil: the stock market fell by 30 per cent in a day and the Reichsbank lost a fifth of its gold reserves in a month. Secret talks between Caillaux and the Germans produced the Franco-German Accord of 4 November 1911.

Under the accord Germany accepted France's position in Morocco in return for 275,000 square kilometres of the Middle Congo, which became Neukamerun, part of Kamerun. Germany ceded a small area to the French colony of Chad. Caillaux's negotiations were leaked and he fell from office on 21 January 1912. By the Treaty of Fes of 30 March 1912 France established a full protectorate over Morocco, which lasted until 1956. Neukamerun returned to France in 1916.

The crisis strengthened the Entente between Britain and France, increased Anglo-German estrangement and led to a secret naval agreement between Britain and France. It also led Winston Churchill to conclude that the Royal Navy must convert from coal to oil.
agamemnon: In Greek mythology Agamemnon was a descendant of Pelops, son of Tantalus. According to the common story, told in Homer's Iliad and Odyssey, he and his younger brother Menelaus were the sons of Atreus, king of Mycenae, and Aerope, daughter of the Cretan king Catreus. His father Atreus murdered the sons of his twin brother Thyestes and fed them to him. Thyestes' son Aegisthus then killed Atreus and took the throne of Mycenae. Agamemnon and Menelaus took refuge with Tyndareus, King of Sparta, who brought them back to Mycenae, where they drove out Thyestes.

In Sparta, Agamemnon and Menelaus married Tyndareus' daughters Clytemnestra and Helen. Menelaus succeeded Tyndareus as king of Sparta, while Agamemnon, with his brother's help, drove out Aegisthus and Thyestes to recover his father's kingdom, and he extended his dominion by conquest to become the most powerful prince in Greece. In Aeschylus' Oresteia he has a son, Orestes, and two daughters, Iphigenia and Electra.

Agamemnon gathered the Greek forces to sail for Troy. At Aulis, in Boeotia, the army incurred the anger of the goddess Artemis, and plague and a lack of wind stopped the fleet. The prophet Calchas announced that the goddess could be appeased only by the sacrifice of Agamemnon's daughter Iphigenia, and the classical dramatists differ on how willing father and daughter were.

The Iliad tells of his quarrel with Achilles in the final year of the war. Agamemnon took Chryseis as a war prize and, when Apollo sent a plague, reluctantly returned her, then seized Achilles' prize Briseis in compensation. Achilles withdrew from the fighting. Agamemnon later sent ambassadors to Achilles with offers of riches and his daughter's hand, which Achilles refused until his companion Patroclus was killed by Hector. They were reconciled in Book Nineteen. He is described as a representative of kingly authority, whose chief fault was haughtiness, and as one of the three best warriors on the Greek side.

After the fall of Troy, Cassandra, the daughter of Priam, fell to Agamemnon as a prize. On his return he was killed. In the oldest versions he was slain by Aegisthus, and in Homer's Odyssey Aegisthus ambushes him at a feast. In Pindar and the tragedians he is killed in a bath by Clytemnestra, as in Aeschylus' Oresteia. Orestes later avenged him by killing Aegisthus and his own mother, and was pursued by the Erinyes until he was absolved. In Sparta he was worshipped as Zeus Agamemnon, and his tomb was pointed out among the ruins of Mycenae and at Amyclae.
agartala: Agartala lies in the plain of Tripura on the banks of the Haora (also written Saidra) River, about 2 kilometres east of the border with Bangladesh and about 2,499 km from New Delhi. The river flows through the city and floods each year in the monsoon. The climate is humid subtropical, with long, hot and wet summers from April to October and a short, mild winter from mid-November to early March. The name combines agar, the perfume and incense tree of the genus Aquilaria, with tala, 'underneath', a reference to the density of agarwood trees in the region.

Tripura served as the capital of several Hindu kingdoms. No timeline of rulers has been found, but records name as many as 179 Hindu rulers, from the mythological King Druhya to Kirit Bikram Kishore Manikya, the last king. Tripura also came under Mughal rule, and under British governance in 1808. The older capital of the princely state, then called Swadhin Tripura, was at Rangamati on the Gomati River, in what is now Udaipur. Its move to the present Old Agartala, called Haveli, is dated to 1760 and credited to the Manikya rulers.

The founding of the capital city of Agartala is dated to 1838, under Maharaja Krishna Kishore Manikya, and the shift from Old Haveli to New Haveli, the present Agartala, to 1849. The reasons given are frequent invasions by the Kukis and the wish for easy communication with British Bengal. The Ujjayanta Palace, the palace of the Tripura kings, was named by the poet Rabindranath Tagore, who visited Tripura many times. It served as the meeting place of the Tripura Legislative Assembly until 2011 and is now a museum. In 1941 the city had 17,693 inhabitants.

Agartala is the capital and largest city of the Indian state of Tripura, and it is governed by the Agartala Municipal Corporation, which was formed on 21 January 2014. Bengali is the dominant language, with Kokborok also spoken, and the population is mainly Bengali and Tripuri. The Bengali influence reflects royal patronage and the arrival of Bengalis from Comilla, Sylhet, Noakhali and Chittagong. Hinduism is the main religion and Christianity widespread. Durga Puja and Saraswati Puja are major festivals, and the Tripuri festivals Kharchi and Garia are also known. Its 2011 census population was 400,004.
agatharchides: Agatharchides is believed to have been born at Cnidus, from which his name comes, and he flourished in the 2nd century BCE. The evidence for his life is meagre. Photius describes him as a threptos, a kind of assistant of servile origin, to Cinnaeus, who served as a counsellor to Ptolemy VI, and states that he was later a secretary to Heraclides Lembus, who is best known for negotiating the treaty that ended the invasion of Egypt by Antiochus IV in 169 BCE.

At the end of On the Erythraean Sea he apologises that he cannot complete the work, because disturbances in Egypt meant that he could no longer reach the official records. Two occasions are possible: 145 BCE, when Ptolemy VIII purged Alexandria of intellectuals who supported his rivals, and 132 BCE, when Ptolemy returned after a rebellion in Alexandria had driven him out and took reprisals on the city. Most scholars have favoured the later date, while Stanley M. Burstein argues for the earlier.

Agatharchides wrote Affairs in Asia in ten books and Affairs in Europe in forty-nine, but only a few fragments of either survive. His On the Erythraean Sea, in five books, is better preserved: almost the entire fifth book, a geographical treatise on the Horn of Africa and the lands around the Red Sea, survives almost intact. Burstein judges that its comparative soberness and the wealth of information in it brought quick recognition as a valuable summary of the results of Ptolemaic exploration.

The fifth book describes the way of life of the Sabaeans in Arabia, the Ichthyophagi or fish-eaters, the catching of elephants, and the working of the gold mines in the mountains of Egypt near the Red Sea. Diodorus Siculus copied his account of the Ichthyophagi and the mines. Strabo, Pliny the Elder, Aelian and Josephus also quote the work, directly or indirectly. Photius found a copy in the 9th century and preserved extensive extracts in his Bibliotheca. He states that Agatharchides wrote in the Attic dialect and imitated Thucydides in his speeches. He appears to have been the first to discover the true cause of the yearly flooding of the Nile.

Josephus quoted a passage in which Agatharchides said that the Jews failed to defend their city against the army of Ptolemy I Soter because the attack fell on Shabbat. Some scholars see this as antisemitic, but it appears to belong to his critique of superstition, which also uses the example of a Hellenistic princess. A crater on the Moon is named after him.
agathias: Agathias was a native of Myrina in Mysia, an Aeolian city in western Asia Minor. His father was Memnonius, and he had a brother and a probable sister, Eugenia. He mentions being in Alexandria as a law student when an earthquake destroyed Berytus, the seat of one of the empire's three official law schools. The earthquake of 551 sent its students to Sidon, and since he would have been in his early twenties, his birth is placed around 530.

He left Alexandria for Constantinople soon afterwards, visited Kos and saw the earthquake's damage there. In his fourth year of study he and three fellow students, Aemilianus, John and Rufinus, made a joint offering to Michael the Archangel at Sosthenium. He returned to Constantinople in 554 to finish his training and practised in the courts as an advocatus, which is why he is called a scholasticus. He also served as pater civitatis of Smyrna, effectively a magistrate.

Literature was his favourite pursuit and he is best known as a poet. Only the introduction survives of his Daphniaca, nine books of short hexameter poems on love and romance. He published over a hundred of his own epigrams together with those of friends in the Cycle of New Epigrams, probably early in the reign of the emperor Justin II. It largely survives in the Greek Anthology.

His Histories, in five books, were begun in Justin II's reign. They continue Procopius, whose style they imitate, and are the chief authority for the years from 552. They deal chiefly with the struggles of the imperial army under the general Narses against Goths, Vandals, Franks and Persians. Agathias says he wrote because he would not let momentous events of his own times go unrecorded. He gathered information from eyewitnesses rather than from high office, and he describes the customs and religion of foreign peoples as well as earthquakes, plagues and famines. The work seems incomplete, and the historian Menander Protector continued it.

Agathias is the only authority for the story that Justinian closed the Platonic Academy at Athens in 529, which is sometimes cited as the end of Antiquity. His Histories also give the earliest substantial evidence for the Iranian Khvadhaynamagh tradition and the earliest description of the rules of backgammon, in a story of an unlucky game played by the emperor Zeno. Agathias' contemporaries knew him more as an advocate and poet than as a historian, and Myrina raised statues to him, his father and his brother.
agathocles-of-syracuse: Agathocles was a son of Carcinus, who came from Rhegium and settled at Thermae Himeraeae, in the Carthaginian part of Sicily. In 343 BCE, when Agathocles was about eighteen, the family moved to Syracuse in answer to a call from Timoleon for new citizens. The sources say Carcinus was a potter and that Agathocles followed him, though modern historians generally think he must have been wealthy and owned a workshop. Agathocles later advertised his low origins as a ruler. After Timoleon's death he rose to be a chiliarch under the general Damas, and he married Damas's widow, which made him one of the richest men in Syracuse.

Syracuse was then ruled by an oligarchic club called the Six Hundred, and Agathocles sided with the democrats. After accusing the oligarchs Sosistratus and Heracleides of seeking tyranny, he left the city and led a mercenary life in southern Italy. He later defeated a Syracusan force at Rhegium, which led to the oligarchs' fall, but the Corinthian commander Acestorides exiled him again. He returned and was elected commander in chief in 319 or 318 BCE, swearing an oath that he would not establish a tyranny.

In 317 BCE he used a loyal force to launch a coup. His men massacred leading members of the oligarchy, and according to Diodorus Siculus more than 4,000 people were killed. He then secured election as general with unlimited power, the title Dionysius I had used, and announced a cancellation of debts and a redistribution of land. He brought many Sicilian cities under his hegemony. War with Carthage followed, and after defeat on the Himera River in 311 BCE he was besieged in Syracuse.

In August 310 BCE he landed at Cape Bon and defeated the Carthaginians. He allied with Ailymas, king of the Libyans, and later killed him, and he had Ophellas of Cyrenaica killed after luring him into the campaign. He was finally defeated in 307 BCE and fled secretly to Sicily, leaving his army and two sons, who were murdered. He made peace with Carthage in 306 BCE, which left him control of Sicily east of the Halycus, and took the royal title in 304 BCE.

His last years were marked by ill health and an attempt by his grandson Archagathus to seize the throne. Diodorus states that Agathocles was poisoned, but Justin and most modern historians say he died a natural death. Machiavelli cited him in The Prince as a man who gained a principality through crimes.
agaw-people: The Agaw speak the Agaw languages, also called the Central Cushitic languages, a part of the Cushitic branch of the Afroasiatic family. They are first mentioned in the Monumentum Adulitanum, an Aksumite inscription of the third century recorded in the sixth century by Cosmas Indicopleustes, which names a people called Athagaus, perhaps from ʿAd Agaw, meaning sons of Agaw, among those conquered by its unnamed king.

They appear again as the Atagaw in the Ezana Stone of the fourth century. Cosmas also noted that a major gold trade route passed through the region of Agau, west of the Tekezé River and south of the Semien Mountains, and that King Kaleb of Axum had a governor there to protect the caravan routes. According to Taddesse Tamrat, this governor probably had his seat in Lasta.

The Agaw formed and ruled the Zagwe dynasty of Ethiopia, from about 1137 to 1270. Later sources accused the Zagwe of being usurpers and belittled their achievements. Gebre Mesqel Lalibela, a Zagwe ruler, is credited with building the rock-hewn churches of Lalibela. The Zagwe were deposed by a Semitic-speaking Amhara dynasty, which claimed to resume the Solomonic lineage of the earlier Aksumite kingdom, though it gave the Zagwe rulers and their descendants the title of Wagshum so that they could govern their native regions of Wag and Lasta.

Travellers and outside observers noted that Agaw peoples practised what some called a Hebraic religion, while some followed Ethiopian Orthodoxy and many were Beta Israel Jews. Thousands of Agaw Beta Israel converted to Christianity in the 19th and early 20th centuries, both voluntarily and under force, and became the Falash Mura.

The Agaw consist of several linguistic groups living in scattered communities from Eritrea to Gojjam, and local traditions point to Lasta as the place from which they dispersed. The Northern Agaw are the Bilen, around Keren in Eritrea; the Western Agaw are the Qemant, around Gondar; the Eastern Agaw are the Xamir; and the Southern Agaw are the Awi, who live around Dangila south of Lake Tana.

Many Agaw also speak Amharic, Tigrinya or Tigre, and Amharic has influenced their languages. The Agaw varieties differ among themselves more than the Romance languages do, while Amharic speakers differ little, which points to a recent spread of Ethio-Semitic languages through the Agaw homeland.
age-of-discovery: The Age of Discovery is dated c. 1418 to c. 1620. Its background lay in trade. For centuries the Republic of Venice and neighbouring maritime republics held the monopoly of European trade with the Middle East, and the silk and spice trade made them very rich. Muslim traders dominated the Indian Ocean routes, with Calicut a main emporium, and the overland routes into Asia were blocked by wars and banditry as the Mongol states disintegrated. The Crusades, though not a military success, had brought Europe into contact with the Middle East and its goods.

The Portuguese began systematically exploring the Atlantic coast of Africa in 1418 under the sponsorship of Prince Henry the Navigator, and in 1488 Bartolomeu Dias reached the Indian Ocean by that route. Portugal had rejected Christopher Columbus's plan to reach India by sailing west in 1485 and 1488, its experts judging his estimate of the distance too low.

In 1492 the Catholic Monarchs of Spain funded Columbus's Atlantic crossing, and he reached a continent unmapped by Europeans, though the Norse had explored it 500 years earlier. The Treaty of Tordesillas, ratified by Pope Julius II, divided the zones of exploration between Portugal and Castile. In 1498 Vasco da Gama established a sea route to India. Vasco Núñez de Balboa became the first European to see the Pacific from the New World on 25 September 1513, and the Magellan expedition of 1519–1522 under Juan Sebastián Elcano completed the first circumnavigation.

Spain's conquistadors, who were more like soldiers of fortune than an army, conquered Mexico (1519–1521) and Peru (1532–1533) and formed alliances with some indigenous peoples. In 1565 Andrés de Urdaneta found the return route across the Pacific, reaching Acapulco on 8 October 1565 after 130 days, and the Manila galleon trade linked the Americas and Asia until 1815. France, the Netherlands and England did not recognise the Treaty of Tordesillas and challenged Iberian power. Russia, meanwhile, moved into Siberia.

Contact between the Old and New Worlds produced the Columbian exchange of plants, animals, people, including slaves, diseases and culture. Cattle, horses and sheep went west, and tobacco, potatoes, tomatoes and maize came east. The era began the global silver trade between the Americas, Europe and China. It also brought the enslavement, exploitation and conquest of Indigenous peoples, and European diseases such as smallpox decimated indigenous populations.

The term itself has been scrutinised. J. H. Parry called the period the Age of Reconnaissance and stressed its expansion of geographical knowledge and empirical science, while Edmundo O'Gorman, as Anthony Pagden reports, argued that Europeans' effort to fit the new knowledge into their worldview mattered more than the encounter, in what he called the invention of America.
age-of-enlightenment: The Enlightenment emerged from and built upon the Scientific Revolution of the sixteenth and seventeenth centuries, which established new methods of empirical inquiry through the work of Galileo Galilei, Johannes Kepler, Francis Bacon, Pierre Gassendi, Christiaan Huygens and Isaac Newton. Its philosophical foundations were laid by René Descartes, Thomas Hobbes, Baruch Spinoza and John Locke, whose ideas about reason, natural rights and empirical knowledge became central to it. The beginning of the period is often dated to the publication of Descartes' Discourse on the Method in 1637. The movement emerged in Western and Central Europe in the late seventeenth century, reached its peak in the eighteenth, and spread into the European colonies in the Americas and Oceania.

The Enlightenment emphasised reason, empirical evidence and the scientific method, and promoted individual liberty, religious tolerance, progress and natural rights. Its central doctrines were individual liberty, representative government, the rule of law and religious freedom, set against absolute monarchy and the persecution of faiths other than the established one. Other currents argued for Deism and atheism and for secular states. Ideas circulated through new institutions: scientific academies, literary salons, coffeehouses, Masonic lodges, and an expanding print culture of books, journals and pamphlets. Among its figures were Denis Diderot, Émilie du Châtelet, David Hume, Immanuel Kant, Montesquieu, Jean-Jacques Rousseau, Adam Smith and Voltaire.

Science was prominent in Enlightenment thought. The experiments of Antoine Lavoisier were used to create the first modern chemical plants in Paris, and in 1783 the Montgolfier brothers launched the first manned flight in a hot air balloon. The Scottish thinkers Adam Ferguson, John Millar and William Robertson developed a science of man, from which modern sociology largely originated.

The movement took on a local character in each country. In France it became associated with anti-government and anti-Church radicalism, and the government was hostile: the philosophes fought its censorship and were sometimes imprisoned or driven into exile. In Germany it reached deep into the middle classes without threatening governments or established churches. European rulers such as Catherine II of Russia, Joseph II of Austria and Frederick II of Prussia tried to apply Enlightenment thought on religious and political tolerance. In Poland the Enlightenment began in the 1730s and 1740s and peaked under King Stanisław August Poniatowski.

The Enlightenment also faced criticism in its own time, later termed the Counter-Enlightenment. It has long been seen as a foundation of modern Western political and intellectual culture, and it paved the way for the political revolutions of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries. Liberalism, socialism and neoclassicism trace their intellectual heritage to it. In Haiti, Toussaint Louverture had read Guillaume Thomas François Raynal's critique of European colonialism.
ageladas: When Ageladas worked has been much discussed, because the ancient writers who name him seem to contradict each other. Pausanias says he cast a statue at Olympia of Cleosthenes, victor in the chariot race of the 66th Olympiad, with chariot, horses and charioteer, and made statues there of Timasitheus of Delphi, put to death by the Athenians in 507 BCE, and of Anochus of Tarentum, who according to Eusebius won in the 65th Olympiad. If Ageladas was born about 540 BCE, he could well have taught Phidias.

Pliny, however, says that Ageladas flourished with Polykleitos, Phradmon and Myron in the 87th Olympiad, and a scholiast on Aristophanes describes a statue of Heracles by Ageladas the Argive at Melite, set up during the great pestilence of that Olympiad. Some scholars have argued that Pliny's date is wrong and that the Heracles was made long before it was set up; others that Pliny is right and the victor statues were made many years after the victories.

Friedrich Thiersch proposed what has been called the most probable solution: that there were two artists of the name, an Argive born about 540 BCE who taught Phidias, and a native of Sicyon who flourished at Pliny's date and whom the scholiast confused with his Argive namesake. Other scholars accept two artists called Ageladas but hold that both were Argives.

Ageladas the Argive made one of a group of three Muses representing the presiding geniuses of the diatonic, chromatic and enharmonic styles of Greek music; Canachus and Aristocles of Sicyon made the other two. He may also have taught the sculptor Ascarus.
agen: The name Agen comes from Occitan Agen, recorded in 1197, itself from Latin Aginnum, which appears in the Itinéraire d'Antonin of the 3rd century. It derives from a Celtic root agin- meaning rock or height. Aginnum was the capital of the Celtic tribe of the Nitiobroges, and extensive Roman ruins attest its importance under the Roman Empire. Its bishopric was founded in the 4th century, and Saint Caprasius of Agen, a Christian martyr, and the bishop Phoebadius of Agen, who died around 392, belong to that century.

Agen changed hands more than once in the course of the Albigensian wars. At their close a tribunal of inquisition was established in the town and inflicted cruel persecution on the heretics. The first Jews settled there in the twelfth century. They were expelled in 1306, a number returned in 1315, and a Rue des Juifs has been documented since then. During the religious wars of the 16th century Agen took the part of the Catholics and openly joined the League in 1589. The Hôtel de Ville was completed around 1666.

Agen is the prefecture of the department of Lot-et-Garonne, on the east bank of the Garonne in the region of Nouvelle-Aquitaine, about 135 kilometres south-east of Bordeaux. The Canal des Deux Mers, joining the Mediterranean with the Atlantic, crosses the river there on a canal bridge. Agen Cathedral, dedicated to Saint Caprasius, dates from the twelfth century and is one of the few large churches in France with a double nave. The art museum holds works by Goya, Bonnard and Seurat.

Louis Arthur Ducos du Hauron, a pioneer of colour photography, lived and worked in Agen. He patented his three-colour principle in 1868 and published it in 1869, and his View of Agen of 1877 is the most widely reproduced of his surviving colour photographs. Agen is called the capital of the prune, a local product eaten stuffed or in pastries or soaked in Armagnac. The population of the commune was 32,801 in 2023.
agent-orange: Agent Orange was one of a group of tactical-use herbicides known as the Rainbow Herbicides. Its active ingredient was an equal mixture of two phenoxy herbicides, 2,4-D and 2,4,5-T, and it contained traces of the dioxin TCDD, typically 2 to 3 parts per million. Several herbicides were developed by the United States and the United Kingdom as weapons during the Second World War. Agent Orange itself was produced in the United States from the late 1940s for industrial agriculture and for clearing undergrowth along railways and power lines. The British had experimented with defoliants in Malaya during the Malayan Emergency, which influenced its later use by the United States.
