In mid-1961 President Ngo Dinh Diem of South Vietnam asked the United States to help defoliate the jungle that gave cover to the North Vietnamese army and the Viet Cong. In August the South Vietnamese air force conducted herbicide operations with American help. Many American officials supported the idea, noting that the British had used herbicides in Malaya, and in November 1961 President Kennedy authorised Operation Ranch Hand, the code name for the United States Air Force's herbicide programme, which ran from 1962 to 1971 and was formally directed by the government of South Vietnam. The military procured over 20,000,000 United States gallons, and nine chemical companies produced it, among them Dow Chemical and Monsanto.

The spraying also aimed to destroy crops. A RAND Corporation memorandum argued that because the Viet Cong obtained most of their food from the rural population, an effective programme would have to destroy large parts of the rural economy. Crops were sprayed and areas bulldozed, which forced many rural civilians to move to cities. About 17.8 per cent of Vietnam's forested area, some 31,000 square kilometres, was sprayed.

The government of Vietnam states that 4 million of its citizens were exposed and that as many as 3 million have been ill because of it. The Vietnamese Red Cross estimates that up to 1 million people are disabled or have health problems. The United States government has called these figures unreliable. Exposure has been linked to birth defects, cancers, cardiovascular disease and diabetes, though the science on causation remains incomplete. Some lawyers, historians and academics, and the Swedish prime minister Olof Palme, have described the destruction of forest as ecocide.

In 1978 the veteran Paul Reutershan sued Dow Chemical, and his case became a class action for thousands of veterans. The Agent Orange Act of 1991 let the Department of Veterans Affairs declare certain conditions presumptive of exposure.
agesilaus-ii: Agesilaus was the son of King Archidamos II of the Eurypontid dynasty and his second wife Eupolia. His half-brother Agis was the son of Archidamos's first marriage, and his sister Kyniska was the first woman in ancient history to achieve an Olympic victory. The year of his birth is disputed, the majority putting it in 445/4 BCE and a minority about 442; the only secure fact is that he was 84 at his death. He was born with a limp.

Starting at seven he went through the Spartan education system, the agoge, which heirs-apparent were exempt from, and he completed it brilliantly, which added to his prestige as king. Little is known of his adult life before his reign, because Xenophon, his friend and main biographer, wrote only about his reign.

Agis II died between 400 and 398 BCE. Agesilaus then contested the claim of Agis's son Leotychidas, whom many Spartans believed to be the illegitimate son of the Athenian Alcibiades, and whom Agis had recognised only on his deathbed. Diopeithes cited an oracle that a Spartan king could not be lame. Lysander answered that it should be read figuratively, as a warning about Leotychidas's doubtful paternity, and the argument won. Historians debate Lysander's role, which Plutarch makes central and Xenophon plays down.

In the summer of 399 BCE came the Conspiracy of Cinadon, a plot by a hypomeion, a Spartan who had lost citizen status, probably because he could not pay for the common mess. Historians suggest the influx of wealth after the victory over Athens in 404 BCE caused inflation that impoverished such citizens. The plot was uncovered and its leaders executed, probably with Agesilaus taking an active part, but nothing was done about the underlying crisis, a failure modern historians criticise.

Our knowledge of his reign rests largely on Xenophon's Hellenica, which covers 411 to 362 BCE, and his admiring biography. A more hostile tradition survives in the Hellenica Oxyrhynchia and in Diodorus of Sicily, and Plutarch's biography includes matters Xenophon left out. Ancient writers praised his courage, endurance and kindness as father and friend; modern writers rate him an excellent soldier with a poor understanding of sea power and siege warfare.

Agesilaus lacked the diplomatic skills to keep Sparta's position against the rising power of Thebes, and some historians hold that his unremitting hatred of Thebes helped lead to the defeat at Leuctra in 371 BCE and the end of Spartan hegemony. J. B. Bury saw something melancholy in a career that began in the unquestioned continental power of Greece and ended with a Sparta reduced by defeat, falling population and a shortage of money, its soldiers more and more sent on campaigns for pay.
agha-mohammad-khan-qajar: Agha Mohammad Khan was born around 1742 at Astarabad, the eldest son of Mohammad Hasan Khan Qajar, chieftain of the Quwanlu branch of the Qajar tribe. The Qajars were one of the Turkoman Qizilbash tribes that had supplied power to the Safavids from the dynasty's earliest days. When Nader Shah died in 1747 and Afsharid rule fell apart, Mohammad Hasan seized Astarabad. Nader's nephew Adel Shah marched against him, failed to take him, but captured the boy Agha Mohammad, had him castrated and then freed him.
His father was killed in 1759. In 1763 Karim Khan Zand, Iran's new overlord, captured him, and he spent the next sixteen years as a hostage at Karim Khan's court in Shiraz.

After Karim Khan's death Agha Mohammad escaped to northern Iran. In Mazandaran he first had to assert himself over his own brothers, defeating Reza Qoli and Morteza Qoli on 2 April. Reza Qoli later captured him at Babol in the autumn of 1780, and Morteza Qoli freed him on 1 January 1781. He went on to seize Qumis, Semnan, Damghan, Shahrud and Bastam and made the ruler of Gilan his vassal. In 1786 he made Tehran his capital, and it has remained the capital since.

He was enthroned as shah in 1789, though not yet crowned. On 25 June 1789 he fought the Zand ruler Lotf Ali Khan near Shiraz and besieged the city until 7 September. He had his brother Jafar Qoli Khan executed for presenting himself as the best heir of the Qajars, judging it necessary after seeing how quickly the Zand dynasty had declined through disputes over the throne. In 1791 he moved into Azerbaijan, bringing the Talysh, Sarab and Ardabil khanates into submission. In 1794 he defeated Lotf Ali Khan for good and inflicted immense destruction on Kerman.

In 1796 Agha Mohammad campaigned north of the Aras River, forced the local khanates to submit and sacked the Georgian city of Tiflis, and was then crowned shahanshah. On 17 June 1797, during a second campaign in the South Caucasus, he was assassinated by two servants whom he had condemned to death. His nephew and designated heir Fath-Ali succeeded him, and Fath-Ali's descendants ruled Iran until 1925.

He is remembered for cruelty, though Gavin Hambly notes that before the killing of Jafar Qoli there was little in his career to show him more brutal than his contemporaries. John R. Perry reads many of his acts as calculated to terrorise or to secure obedience, while others were gratuitous. Contemporary accounts praise his army's discipline, and he is also described as a shrewd military and political leader. His bureaucracy stayed small, and his court was in practice his camp.
aghlabid-dynasty: The Aghlabids were an Arab dynasty from the tribe of Banu Tamim. In 800 the Abbasid caliph Harun al-Rashid appointed Ibrahim I ibn al-Aghlab, son of a Khurasani Arab commander, as hereditary emir of Ifriqiya, in response to the anarchy that had followed the fall of the Muhallabids. There were perhaps 100,000 Arabs in the province, where Berbers still formed the great majority. Though independent in all but name, the dynasty never ceased to recognise Abbasid overlordship, paying an annual tribute of 800,000 dirhams and naming the caliph in the Friday sermon. Ibrahim built a new capital, al-Abbasiyya, outside Kairouan between 801 and 810, partly to escape the Malikite jurists who condemned the luxury of the dynasty and its Mu'tazilite theology.

The army combined Arab troops, the jund, with slaves recruited to counterbalance them. The jund rose in revolt in 824 under Mansur ibn Nasr al-Tunbudhi, occupying Tunis and Kairouan, and the emir Ziyadat Allah I crushed the rising in 827. In that year the conquest of Sicily began, under the qadi Asad ibn al-Furat, after the Byzantine rebel Euphemios asked for help. Palermo fell in 831 and became the capital of Muslim Sicily, Messina in 842 or 843, Syracuse in 878 and Taormina in 902. The Aghlabids also raided the Italian mainland, held Taranto from 840 to 880, and conquered Malta in 870.

In 876 Ibrahim II ibn Ahmad moved to a new palace-city, Raqqada. The dynasty declined under him: a Berber revolt was put down with much loss of life, and from 893 the Isma'ili Fatimid movement grew among the Kutama Berbers under Abu Abdallah al-Shi'i. Ibrahim II died besieging Cosenza in October 902. After the Aghlabid army was routed near al-Aribus on 18 March 909, Ziyadat Allah III fled towards Egypt, and the Fatimid Caliphate was established that year.

The Aghlabids built many of the oldest Islamic-era monuments in present-day Tunisia, among them the Ribat of Sousse, the Ribat of Monastir, the Great Mosque of Sousse and the Aghlabid Reservoirs of Kairouan. Ziyadat Allah I completely rebuilt the Great Mosque of Kairouan in 836. Its minaret is the oldest surviving one in North Africa, and its minbar, of carved teakwood, is the oldest surviving in the world.
agila-i: Agila, sometimes called Achila I, was Visigothic king of Hispania and Septimania from 549 until March 554. He came to power after the assassination of Theudigisel, who had ruled for less than two years. Peter Heather notes that his reign fell in a period of civil war following the death of Amalaric, the last member of the old Visigothic dynasty, when ambitious Gothic nobles competed openly for the throne.

Opposition appeared early. The city of Corduba revolted, which Isidore of Seville attributes to local Roman Catholics objecting to Agila's Arianism. In his account Agila defiled the church of the local saint Acisclus by drenching the tomb with the blood of the enemy and of their pack-animals, and he attributes the death of Agila's son in the conflict, together with most of the army and the royal treasury, to the agency of the saints. Heather lists further rebels: a local dynast, Aspidius, who established a hegemony in one mountainous region; the landowners of Cantabria, who formed a senate to govern their affairs; and the Sappi and Suani named by John of Biclar.

The most important rebel was Athanagild, whose open revolt began in 551, after Agila's defeat at Cordoba. The two armies met at Seville, where Agila was defeated a second time. A Byzantine army then arrived in southern Spain in 552. Heather understands Isidore to say that Athanagild summoned the Byzantines, while Jordanes implies in his Getica that Agila had asked them for help.

Agila was killed in March 554. According to Isidore, his own people killed him, because they had come to see the destruction his wars to keep power had caused, and feared even more that Roman soldiers might invade Spain on the pretext of giving help. Athanagild was then accepted as king.
agilolfings: The family took its name from Agilulf, a prince of the Suebi known partly from legend, said to descend from Hermeric, the 5th-century Suevic king of Galicia; he may be the Agilulf who served as steward of the Visigothic king Theoderic II and was executed in 457. German historiography counts Garibald I as the first duke of the line, though modern scholarship has doubted that he belonged to it, making Tassilo I, who ruled from 591 to 610, the first certain member. Garibald I married Waldrada, widow of the Merovingian king Theudebald, after her marriage to Chlothar I was annulled.

The Agilolfings ruled Bavaria on behalf of their Merovingian overlords, with their residence at Regensburg, and the Lex Baiuvariorum of about 743 names them as the leading dynasty. Under Duke Theodo, who ruled from 680 to 716, the duchy was divided among his sons Theodbert at Salzburg, Theobald, Tassilo II at Passau and Grimoald at Freising, before Grimoald and then Hugbert ruled the whole. Odilo, a son of Gotfried of Allemania, ruled from 737 to 748, and his son Tassilo III was the last duke, deposed by Charlemagne in 788.

A cadet branch ruled the Kingdom of the Lombards at intervals from 616 to 712. Theodelinda, a daughter of Garibald I, became Queen of the Lombards, and her son Adaloald was king from 616 to 626. The line of her brother Gundoald, Duke of Asti, gave the Lombards Aripert I, Berthari, Cunincpert and finally Aripert II, who reigned from 701 to 712.

Bound up with the fortunes of the Merovingians, the Agilolfings opposed the rise of the Carolingian mayors of the palace, who in the end took their power from them. Members of the family also appear at the Austrasian court, among them Chrodoald, a nobleman of Dagobert I killed in 624. After the deposition of Tassilo III, his son Theodo became a monk.
agilulf: Agilulf was born around 555 and was also known as the Thuringian. He belonged to the Anawas clan and was of Thuringian origin, a relative of his predecessor Authari. He is sometimes called dux Turingorum de Taurinis, which suggests he was a prominent leader among the Thuringians who had joined the Lombards after their kingdom fell to the Franks in 531.

He was chosen as king on the advice of Theodelinda, the Christian queen and widow of Authari, and he later married her. He took the royal title in November 590, and his formal investiture, in which Lombard warriors raised him on a shield, took place at Milan in May 591.

Agilulf was baptised to please his wife, and the Lombards followed, at first adopting the Arian rather than the Catholic faith. In 603, under Theodelinda's influence, he converted to Catholicism and had his son Adaloald baptised in the same rite. Together they built and endowed the Cathedral of Monza, where the Iron Crown of Lombardy is still kept. His own crown, now lost, was kept there too and was inscribed rex totius Italiae, king of all Italy.

Hostilities with Francia ceased after the death of Guntram, King of Burgundy, in 592, because the Franks then fell into civil war. In 598 Agilulf made a truce with the Papacy, ending three decades of Lombard incursions into the Ducatus Romanus, and took Sutri, Perugia and other Umbrian cities from the Exarchate of Ravenna. He also made a truce that year with the Byzantine emperor Maurice, with the help of Pope Gregory the Great, but in 599 the Exarch Callinicus broke it by abducting Agilulf's daughter. In 602 the Lombards took Padua and then Mantua, and in 605 the Byzantine emperor Phocas recognised Agilulf, agreed to pay tribute and ceded Orvieto and other towns.

In 607 Witteric, king of the Visigoths, formed an alliance against Theuderic II of Burgundy that included Theudebert II of Austrasia, Clotaire II of Neustria and Agilulf, but it appears to have achieved little. In 610 the Avars invaded Friuli and killed its duke, Gisulf. The last years of the reign were largely peaceful, and Agilulf died in April 616 after ruling for over a quarter of a century. His son Adaloald succeeded him, still an adolescent. His daughter Gundeberga later married Arioald, a future king of the Lombards.
agis-iii: Agis was the eldest son of King Archidamus III and the grandson of Agesilaus II, and belonged to the Eurypontid dynasty, one of the two royal families of Sparta. Since its defeat by Thebes at Leuctra in 371 BCE, Sparta had lost its status as a great power and a number of territories. In 351 BCE Archidamus and Agis waged a war in the Peloponnese to recover them, notably against Megalopolis, a city the Thebans had founded on Sparta's north-western border. There were also operations against Argos. Despite the support of 3,000 mercenaries from Phocis, the campaign was fruitless.

At the beginning of 338 BCE Archidamus left Greece to serve as a mercenary commander for Taras, a city founded by Sparta in Magna Graecia, and he died fighting the Lucanians on 2 August 338 BCE, the day of the Battle of Chaeronea. Agis, who had been regent in his absence, became king once the news arrived, probably at the end of August.

After Chaeronea, Philip II of Macedon founded the League of Corinth. Agis is likely to have been behind the Spartan decision to refuse to join it, which brought Philip into Laconia in autumn 338 BCE. Philip gave Sparta's neighbours and enemies several of its territories: Denthaliates to Messene, Aygitis and Belminatis to Megalopolis, Skiritis to Tegea and Thyreatis to Argos. Agis chose to let Sparta recover rather than oppose Macedon directly, and the city stayed quiet for five years after Chaeronea. It did not join the revolt of Thebes against Alexander the Great in 335 BCE.

His first move came in 333 BCE, when Darius III launched a counter-offensive. A Spartan named Euthycles was sent to Darius at Susa, and Agis himself went with a single trireme to the Persian commanders in the Aegean, Pharnabazus III and Autophradates, to ask for money and arms. They could spare only 30 talents and 10 ships, and news of the Battle of Issus checked their plans. Agis sent his brother Agesilaus to Crete, where he largely secured the island for Sparta.

In 331 BCE the Greek states in league against Alexander took advantage of the failure of the Macedonian general Zopyrion's campaign against the Scythians and of the Thracian revolt. Agis took the command and, with his Spartan troops and 8,000 Greek mercenaries who had fought at Issus, defeated a Macedonian army under Coragus in the Peloponnese. Joined by Elis, Achaea and Arcadia, he besieged Megalopolis until Antipater came to its relief. At the Battle of Megalopolis the Greeks faced a larger force and lost. According to Diodorus, Agis fought on his knees to give his men time to retreat, and was killed by a javelin. His brother Eudamidas I succeeded him.
agis-iv: Agis IV was the elder son of Eudamidas II and the 25th king of the Eurypontid dynasty, one of the two royal families of Sparta. His mother was Agesistrata, and according to Plutarch the family was the richest in Sparta. He had a younger brother, Archidamus. He succeeded his father as king in 245 BCE, at around the age of 20, and reigned four years. The interest of his reign lay in the crisis of Sparta, where wealth and luxury had undermined the old simplicity, land had passed into very few hands, and fewer than 700 families of full Spartan stock remained, while the poor were heavily in debt.

Agis proposed to cancel debts, to redistribute land in 4,500 lots among Spartans, selected perioikoi and resident foreigners, and to restore the agoge and the common messes. He won over his uncle Agesilaus, Lysander, whom he had elected one of the six ephors, and Mandrocleides, and he offered to give up his own lands first. His Agiad co-king Leonidas II led the opposition and the senate rejected the measure by one vote.

Lysander then had Leonidas deposed, and his son-in-law Cleombrotus took the throne. The debts were cancelled, and the bonds were burned in the market place. Agesilaus, with his debts gone, delayed the division of the land. While Agis led an army to help the Achaean League against the Aetolian League, the poor lost patience, and Leonidas was brought back.

Cleombrotus was allowed to go into exile. In 241 BCE Agis was betrayed by friends and imprisoned, and the ephors held a mockery of a trial. He was accused of seeking tyranny and was strangled, and his mother Agesistrata and grandmother Archidameia were strangled on his body. He was the first Spartan king put to death by the ephors.

His widow Agiatis was forcibly married to Leonidas's son Cleomenes III, and he was succeeded by his son Eudamidas III. Many writers have thought him too weak and good-natured for his task, but also sincere and the most attractive figure in Spartan history. A lost biography by Phylarchus was heavily used by Plutarch for his own.
agnello-participazio: Agnello Participazio was the tenth traditional and eighth historical doge of the Duchy of Venetia. He was born to a rich merchant family from Heraclea and was one of the earliest settlers of the Rivoalto islands. His family had provided a number of tribuni militum of Rivoalto, and he was married to the dogaressa Elena. Some historians say he was elected doge, while others say he was appointed by a Byzantine envoy, Arsaphios.

When Pepin, king of Italy and son of Charlemagne, tried to invade the lagoon, the co-doges Obelerio, Beato and Valentino degli Antenori fled, and after Pepin withdrew Agnello was elected doge. He deposed Fortunato, the pro-Frankish patriarch of Grado, whose faction had contributed to the earlier instability, and moved the ducal seat from Malamocco to Rivoalto, where he built the first doge's palace near the church of San Teodoro. Pepin's attempt led the Carolingian and Byzantine empires to agree the Peace of Aachen in 812, ratified in 814, which kept Venetia under the Byzantines and defined its boundaries with the Kingdom of Italy.

He rebuilt Heraclea, which Pepin and his predecessor had destroyed, as Cittanova, and repopulated Chioggia and Albiola. He put Nicolò Ardisonio in charge of fortifying the lidi, Lorenzo Alimpato of land reclamation and Pietro Tradonico of new building, the beginning of the city of Venice. He founded monasteries on Barnaba and San Giuliano.

Agnello made his son Giovanni co-doge while his elder son Giustiniano was away in Constantinople. Giustiniano was enraged, but his father changed his mind, and Giustiniano and his young son Agnello were raised to the co-dogeship while Giovanni was demoted and exiled. The young Agnello was sent to Constantinople in 820 for the coronation of Emperor Michael II and died there. Agnello Participazio governed from 811 to 827, and the family supplied further doges, among them Giustiniano, Giovanni I, Orso I and Giovanni II.
agnes-bernauer: Nothing is known of Agnes Bernauer's childhood and youth, and the existence of the barber-surgeon Kaspar Bernauer, traditionally named as her father, has not been proved. Because Albert took part in a tournament at Augsburg in February 1428, it is generally assumed that he met her there and soon brought her to Munich; a Munich tax roll of 1428 lists a pernawin in his household, probably Agnes.

By the summer of 1432 at the latest she was an integral part of the Munich court. She took part in the capture of the robber baron Münnhauser, who had fled to the Old Court in Munich, and her self-assured manner annoyed Albert's sister, the Palatine Countess Beatrix. There is no concrete evidence of a marriage ceremony. From 1433 Albert often stayed at Blutenburg Castle, and the sale of two nearby properties to Agnes suggests that the couple lived there together; no descendants are known.

Duke Ernest, fearing for the succession of his only son, had Agnes arrested while Albert was at a hunt arranged by his relative Henry of Bavaria-Landshut, and she was drowned near Straubing on 12 October 1435. Albert went to Duke Louis VII at Ingolstadt, but after a few months was reconciled with his father and in November 1436 married Anna of Brunswick. The feared war between father and son never came; Emperor Sigismund may have restrained Albert.

In December 1435 Albert endowed a perpetual mass for Agnes in the Carmelite cloister at Straubing, and in 1436 his father built an Agnes Bernauer Chapel in the cemetery of St. Peter, probably to appease him. Its red marble tombstone shows her almost life-size, holding a rosary, with two small dogs at her feet; her grave has never been found. The love story became a staple of folk songs and inspired works from Joseph August Graf von Toerring's play of 1780 to Hebbel's tragedy of 1855 and Carl Orff's Die Bernauerin of 1944.
agnimitra: According to Kalidasa's Sanskrit play Mālavikāgnimitra, Agnimitra belonged to a Brahmin family of the Baimbika clan, while the Puranas mention him as a Shunga. The play states that during the reign of his father, Pushyamitra, he served as goptri, or viceroy, at Vidisha. It names three of his queens: Dharini, the mother of the fourth Shunga ruler, Vasumitra; Iravati; and Malavika, a princess of Vidarbha. The play is the source for these details of his family and his years as viceroy.

According to the play, a war broke out between the Shungas and the neighbouring kingdom of Vidarbha while Agnimitra was viceroy at Vidisha, between about 175 and 150 BCE. Vidarbha had become independent of the Mauryan Empire when a former Mauryan secretary placed his brother-in-law Yajnasena on the throne. Madhavasena, a cousin of Yajnasena, asked Agnimitra for help in overthrowing him, but was captured while crossing the border of Vidarbha and imprisoned.

Agnimitra demanded the release of Madhavasena. In return Yajnasena demanded the release of the former Mauryan secretary, whom Agnimitra had captured earlier. Instead of agreeing, Agnimitra sent his army into Vidarbha. Yajnasena was defeated and forced to divide the kingdom with Madhavasena, and both cousins recognised the suzerainty of the Shunga rulers. The passages that tell this war are Act I, verses 6 to 8, and Act V, verses 13 and 14, of the play.

Agnimitra succeeded his father Pushyamitra in 149 BCE. The Vayu Purana and the Brahmanda Purana assign his reign a length of eight years, and it ended in 141 BCE. His successor was his son, called Vasujyeshtha in the Matsya Purana and Sujyeshtha in the Vayu, Brahmanda, Vishnu and Bhagavata Puranas.
agoge: The word agōgē comes from the verb ἄγω, to lead, and was used of training, guidance or discipline. There is no evidence that it referred to the Spartiate education system until the 3rd century BCE. According to Xenophon the system was introduced by Lycurgus, while modern scholars date its beginning to the 7th or 6th century BCE, and its structure changed over time. Participants were the sons of Spartiates and Spartiate-class mothers. Girls, helots, the mothax and other freeborn boys without two Spartiate parents were excluded, and the firstborn sons of the ruling houses were exempt. A few trophimoi, well-connected outsiders, took part by special permission, among them, reportedly, the sons of the Athenian Xenophon.

The boys were divided into three groups, the paides, paidiskoi and hēbōntes, and into packs called agelai, with whom they slept, each led by an older boy, the eirēn. They answered to the paidonomos, an upper-class official who oversaw the whole system. The paides learned the basics of reading and writing, competed in running, wrestling and choral dance, and were taught Laconism, the art of speaking in brief, witty phrases. They went barefoot and, from the age of 12, were given only a cloak a year.

The agōgē deliberately deprived boys of food, sleep and shelter. The paides were expected to steal food and were probably underfed to encourage this, and Xenophon says those caught were beaten. It was intensely competitive and sometimes fatal. Plutarch's account includes sexual violence by the older against the younger, while Xenophon says the relationships were widely but wrongly considered sexual. The most promising hēbōntes could be chosen for the Crypteia, which controlled the helots through violence, or for the 300 hippeis, an elite infantry cohort.

Plutarch held that its main purpose was to prepare bodies for war, and Stephen Hodkinson believes it taught the boys to put the community before the individual. Plato and Aristotle praised it as part of an ideal city-state, while Plutarch, writing under Rome, was critical of its brutality. Cleomenes III revived it in 226 BCE, Philopoemen abolished it when Sparta joined the Achaean League in 188/9 BCE, and it was restored after Rome took Sparta in 146 BCE. In the Roman period it became a tourist attraction, and Cicero describes naked boys whipped at the altar of Artemis.
agoo: Agoo is a coastal municipality in La Union province, Philippines, with a population of 65,256 at the 2024 census. It lies on a narrow plain between the foothills of the Cordillera Central and the Lingayen Gulf, 34 kilometres from the provincial capital San Fernando and 232.97 kilometres from Manila. A long beach faces the gulf along its western shore, and the land rises eastward to Mount Katayagan. The name is believed to come from a tree called aroo in Ilocano and agoho in Tagalog, the whistling pine, which once grew abundantly along the riverbanks and the western coast.

Agoo was a trading port of northern pre-Hispanic Pangasinan. Its coastline gave foreign vessels entering the Lingayen Gulf an excellent harbour, and gold brought down the Aringay-Tonglo-Balatok gold trail from the Cordillera was traded there. The town was established within the same decade in which the Spanish reached Luzon. In June 1572 Juan de Salcedo, sent north by Miguel Lopez de Legazpi, saw three Japanese ships on the Angalakan River and attacked them. When they fled he followed them to a Japanese settlement, where, after paying tribute, they were allowed to stay. They left when the port was later closed, after teaching the local people fish culture, rice cultivation, deerskin tanning, duck breeding and weapon making.

In 1899 Agoo became a centre of resistance to American troops, with Guerrilla Unit No. 5 under Captain Fontanilla attacking supply lines. At the start of the Second World War Agoo, Caba and Bauang were the first places the Japanese invasion force sought to control at Lingayen Gulf, giving it a secure beachhead from which it advanced south towards Manila. In 1981 South Provincial High School, founded in 1945, became one of the schools combined as the Don Mariano Marcos Memorial State University.

Most people in Agoo are Ilocano, and Iloco is the main language. The town is predominantly Roman Catholic and has 49 barangays. Agriculture is the chief livelihood, with rice, tobacco, corn and sugarcane, mushroom growing, and the farming of tilapia and milkfish; basketry and woodcarving are traditional crafts. Its landmarks include the Basilica Minore of Our Lady of Charity, the Museo de Iloko in the former presidencia and the Agoo-Damortis Protected Landscape and Seascape.
agora: The Greek word agorá literally means gathering place or assembly. Early in Greek history, from the 10th to the 4th century BCE, free-born citizens gathered in the agora for military duty or to hear statements of the ruling king or council. Later the agora also became a marketplace, where merchants kept stalls or shops amid arcades, and this drew artisans who built workshops nearby. Two Greek verbs came from these twin functions, one political and one commercial: agoreúō, meaning I speak in public, and agorázō, meaning I shop.

The agora was usually placed in the middle of a city or near its harbour, and it was the centre of athletic, artistic, business, social, spiritual and political life. Agoras were built of colonnades, rows of long columns, and contained stoae, long open walkways beneath the colonnades. They were decorated with fountains, trees and statues. When the Athenian agora was rebuilt after the Greco-Persian Wars, however, colonnades and stoae were not incorporated.

The Ancient Agora of Athens, below the northern slope of the Acropolis, is the best example. It was the primary meeting ground of the Athenians, where citizens in a democracy gathered to deal with the affairs of the state, where business was conducted, and where people watched performers and listened to philosophers. Religion was central to it. The layout centred on the Panathenaic Way, a road running through the middle of Athens to the city's main gate, the Dipylon, and serving as the route of the Panathenaic festival, held every four years in honour of the goddess Athena.

The agora housed the Temple of Hephaestus, the god of metalworking and craftsmen, which survives in good condition. Other temples once stood there to Zeus, Athena, Apollo and Ares. The modern term agoraphobia, for anxiety in unfamiliar or open places where the sufferer feels little control, takes its name from the agora as a large, open gathering place.
agostino-depretis: Agostino Depretis was born on 31 January 1813 at Bressana Bottarone, near Stradella, then part of Napoleon's French Empire. He graduated in law, became a disciple of Giuseppe Mazzini and took part in Mazzinian conspiracies, nearly being captured by the Austrians while smuggling arms into Milan. Elected a deputy in 1848, he joined the Left and founded the newspaper Il Diritto. Although he opposed Camillo Benso di Cavour, Cavour made him governor of Brescia in 1859.

In 1860 he went to Sicily to reconcile Cavour's wish for immediate union with Garibaldi's plan to wait, and replaced Francesco Crispi as pro-dictator, but he failed to persuade Garibaldi and resigned in September. He later served as minister of public works in 1862 and of the navy in 1866, when Italy's defeat at Lissa made his tenure controversial. After the death of Urbano Rattazzi in 1873 he became leader of the Left.

The fall of Marco Minghetti's government in March 1876, called the parliamentary revolution, made Depretis prime minister on 25 March 1876 with the first cabinet composed only of the Left. In the November 1876 election the Left won 414 of 508 seats. The Coppino law of 15 July 1877 made primary education compulsory, secular and free for children aged six to nine. He resigned in December 1877 and again in March 1878, then served briefly in 1879, and returned as prime minister in 1881 after the French occupation of Tunis.

On 20 May 1882 he signed the Triple Alliance with Germany and Austria-Hungary. An electoral reform of 1882 lowered the voting age from 25 to 21 and raised the number of eligible voters from 621,896 to 2,017,829. From 1883 he moved to the right and brought in Minghetti's conservatives in the process known as Trasformismo, a flexible centrist coalition meant to isolate the extremes. His governments completed the railway system and began colonial policy with the occupation of Massawa.

Despite gout, Depretis remained prime minister until his death at Stradella on 29 July 1887, aged 74. Francesco Crispi replaced him. Critics held that Trasformismo sacrificed principle for short-term gain, bred corruption and widened the gap between parliamentary Italy and the real country, and that his rule raised indirect taxation and strained finances through extravagance in public works. His defenders point to the reforms of his governments, which widened suffrage and free education.
agra: Agra lies on the banks of the Yamuna river in Uttar Pradesh, about 230 kilometres south-east of Delhi, in the Braj region. The country around it is almost entirely a level plain, and millet, barley, wheat and cotton are grown there. The most accepted derivation of the name is the Hindi agar, a salt pan, from the region's brackish soil. Under the Mughals the city was also called Akbarabad, a name coined by Shah Jahan in honour of his grandfather Akbar.

An ancient city on the east bank of the Yamuna, lost in the legends of Krishna and the Mahabharata, was re-established by Sikandar Khan Lodi in 1504-1505. The golden age began with the Mughals in the early sixteenth century. Agra was the foremost city of the subcontinent and the capital under Babur, Humayun, Akbar, Jahangir and Shah Jahan until 1658, when Aurangzeb shifted the court to Delhi.

Akbar commissioned the Agra Fort in 1565, and it took about eight years to build. Shah Jahan built the Taj Mahal between 1632 and 1648 in remembrance of his wife Mumtaz Mahal. Nur Jahan commissioned the tomb of I'timad-ud-Daulah for her father, Jahangir's chief minister, and Akbar's tomb at Sikandra was completed by Jahangir in 1613.

As Mughal power declined, the city passed in the late eighteenth century to the Jats, the Marathas, the Mughals, the ruler of Gwalior and finally the East India Company, which took it in 1803. The Jats took it on 12 June 1761 after a month-long siege. Agra was one of the centres of the Indian rebellion of 1857.

Agra has about 1.6 million people. The Taj Mahal and the Agra Fort became UNESCO World Heritage Sites in 1983. Agra was the birthplace of Din-i-Ilahi, the faith founded by Akbar, now extinct, and of the Radhaswami Faith. Its crafts include pietra dura, marble inlay and carpets.
agri-decumates: The region belonged to the Roman provinces of Germania Superior and Raetia and took in the Black Forest, the Swabian Jura and the Franconian Jura, including the sites of present-day Frankfurt, Stuttgart, Freiburg im Breisgau and Weißenburg in Bayern. The only ancient reference to the name is in chapter 29 of Tacitus' Germania, though the geographer Claudius Ptolemy mentions a desert of the Helvetians in the area. The meaning of Decumates is lost: the classicist Michael Grant thought it probably referred to a Celtic division into ten cantons, while another theory links it to a tithe paid by the inhabitants.

According to Tacitus the region was first inhabited by the Celtic Helvetii, and settlers from Gaul, whom he calls reckless adventurers emboldened by want, then occupied land of questionable ownership. Under the Flavian and later emperors the Romans settled it, built roads for military movement and improved its protection against tribes who used it to penetrate into Roman Gaul. Frontier fortifications, the limes, ran from Rheinbrohl to Pförring. The larger Roman towns were Sumelocenna (Rottenburg am Neckar), Civitas Aurelia Aquensis (Baden-Baden), Lopodunum (Ladenburg) and Arae Flaviae (Rottweil).

The emperor Gallienus evacuated the region before the invading Alemanni, when much of the western empire seceded under Postumus. Aurelian may briefly have reoccupied it and Probus recaptured it during his invasion of Germania, but by the 290s or 300s the Roman army seems to have left for good. By about 310 the Alemanni were becoming the dominant population, though the Roman way of life continued well into the 5th century. J. G. F. Hind has suggested that the former Roman inhabitants moved west of the Rhine, to the Decem Pagi between Mainz and Metz.
agrigento: Akragas was founded on a plateau overlooking the sea, between two rivers, the Hypsas and the Acragas. According to Thucydides its colonists came from Gela, with others from Crete and Rhodes, and it was the last of the major Greek colonies in Sicily. Control of the overland route to Himera was a key to the prosperity of the 6th and 5th centuries BCE, which became proverbial, and the city began minting coins around 520 BCE. Around 570 BCE it came under Phalaris, a figure of uncertain history remembered as the archetypal tyrant.

Theron of the Emmenid family became tyrant around 488 BCE and, allied with Gelon of Syracuse, defeated the Carthaginians at the Battle of Himera in 480 BCE. Great temples were built in this period, and, according to Diodorus Siculus, prisoners of the war served as labour. In 406 BCE Carthaginian forces captured and sacked the city. The Romans besieged it in 262 BCE and sold its population into slavery after taking it. They finally captured it in 210 BCE, renamed it Agrigentum, and under Roman rule it became prosperous again.

After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the inhabitants largely abandoned the lower city for the old acropolis, and in 828 CE the Saracens captured it. The Norman Count Roger I set up a Latin bishopric there in 1087. In 1927 Benito Mussolini's decree replaced the name Girgenti with the current Italian form of the Latin name.

Agrigento is the capital of its province, with a population of 55,227. The Valle dei Templi, a ridge and not a valley, holds seven monumental Doric temples of the 6th and 5th centuries BCE. The Temple of Concordia is remarkably intact because it was converted into a Christian church in 597 CE. The area was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1997. Agrigento is the birthplace of the dramatist Luigi Pirandello, and the philosopher Empedocles was a citizen of ancient Akragas.
agrippa-ii: Herod Agrippa II, whose Roman name was Marcus Julius Agrippa, was the son of Herod Agrippa I and the brother of Berenice, Mariamne and Drusilla. He was raised and educated at the court of the Emperor Claudius. He was only 17 when his father died, so Claudius kept him in Rome and sent Cuspius Fadus to govern Judaea as procurator. In Rome Agrippa spoke up for the Jews to Claudius, against the Samaritans and the procurator Ventidius Cumanus, who was thought to have caused disturbances.

When Herod of Chalcis died his small Syrian realm of Chalcis was given to Agrippa, with the right to superintend the Temple in Jerusalem and appoint its high priest, but only as tetrarch. In 53 he gave up Chalcis and received the title of king over the territories previously governed by Philip, including Iturea, Trachonitis and Paneas, and over the kingdom of Lysanias in Abila. In 55 Nero added Tiberias and Taricheae in Galilee, and Livias in Peraea. According to the New Testament, Paul the Apostle pleaded his case before Agrippa and Berenice at Caesarea Maritima, probably in 59 or 60.

Agrippa spent large sums beautifying Jerusalem and other cities, especially Berytus, and his partiality for Berytus made him unpopular with his subjects. In 65 or 66 he tried to prevent war with Rome and urged the Jews to endure the abuses of the procurator Gessius Florus, but he failed, and the citizens of Jerusalem expelled him and Berenice in 66. In the First Jewish–Roman War he sent 2,000 archers and cavalry to Vespasian, accompanied Titus and was wounded at the siege of Gamla. After the capture of Jerusalem he went to Rome, where he was made a praetor and given more territory.

The historian Josephus was on intimate terms with Agrippa, who supplied information for his Antiquities of the Jews, and Josephus preserved two of Agrippa's letters. According to the patriarch Photius, Agrippa died childless at 70, in the third year of Trajan, which is 100, but Josephus's statements and contemporary inscriptions from his kingdom cast serious doubt on this, and the modern scholarly consensus holds that he died before 93 or 94. He was the last ruler of the House of Herod.
aguascalientes: Aguascalientes lies in the northern part of the Bajío region in north-central Mexico, about 480 km from Mexico City, at an average altitude of 1,950 m. It is bordered by Zacatecas to the north, east and west and by Jalisco to the south, and covers 5,471 km2. Its climate is predominantly semi-arid, with a temperate highland climate in the Sierra Fría range. The name means hot waters and comes from the abundance of hot springs found in the area.

Arrowheads and rock paintings show that people lived here for more than 20,000 years. Before the Spanish arrived the land was inhabited by Chichimecas, specifically the Guachichil. To protect the Camino de la Plata, the silver road between Zacatecas and Mexico City, the Spanish built presidios. The king ordered the judge Gerónimo de Orozco to find a rich man to settle the territory and expel the Chichimecas, and Juan de Montoro founded the town of Aguas Calientes on 22 October 1575.

In 1789 the sub-delegation of Aguascalientes became a dependency of Zacatecas. A decree of Santa Anna ordered its separation but was never made official, and Aguascalientes continued to belong to Zacatecas for some years. It was later included as a state in a draft constitution passed by the 79 deputies present, which established the state.

The state has 11 municipalities, and most of its people live in the metropolitan area of its capital, also called Aguascalientes. It was once a major silver miner and a centre of railroad transport, thanks to its position between Mexico City, Guadalajara and Monterrey. Its San Marcos Fair is regarded as the national fair of Mexico.
agum-ii: Agum II may have been the eighth or, more likely, the ninth king of the third Babylonian dynasty, the Kassite dynasty that ruled Babylon until 1155 BCE. The only historical source calls him the son of Urzigurumaš, sixth king of the dynasty, but the Synchronistic King List has gaps where the eighth and ninth kings stand before Burna-Buriaš I, the tenth; the ninth place may show traces of the name Kakrime, said to mean Sword of Mercy or Weapon of Thunder.

His reign falls after the Hittite king Mursilis I sacked Babylon, in 1595 BCE by the middle chronology. A later tradition, the Marduk Prophecy, says the statue returned to Babylon of its own accord 24 years after it was taken, which suggests a Kassite occupation beginning around 1507 BCE in the short chronology.

Everything known of him comes from the Agum-Kakrime Inscription, an Akkadian text in Neo-Assyrian cuneiform, written in very short lines in imitation of an antiquarian style. It survives in two copies, one from the library of Ashurbanipal and one found elsewhere at Kouyunjik, ancient Nineveh. It tells how Agum recovered the statues of Marduk and his consort Zarpanītum from the land of Ḫana and restored them in the refurbished temple of Ésagila, lists his gifts to the temple, and claims his rule over Padan, Alman and the Guteans.

He presents himself as the shepherd of both Kassites and Akkadians. Those who doubt the text see it as later propaganda for the cult of Marduk, stressing tax exemptions, and note that Kassite royal inscriptions were usually in Sumerian; those who accept it point to the demons described on the door of the cella, which reflect a Middle Babylonian theology. A more recent analysis tends to support the text and Agum's existence.
agustin-de-iturbide: Agustín Cosme Damián de Iturbide y Arámburu was born in Valladolid, now Morelia, in Michoacán on 27 September 1783, the fifth child of his parents and the only male to survive. His father, Joaquín de Iturbide, came from a Basque family of gentry and migrated to New Spain as a younger son to make his fortune. The family were part of the landed class of Valladolid. In 1805 Iturbide entered the royal Spanish army and married Ana María Josefa Ramona de Huarte y Muñiz, whose dowry of 100,000 pesos bought the Hacienda of San José de Apeo.

When the War of Independence broke out in 1810, Miguel Hidalgo offered Iturbide the rank of lieutenant general in the insurgent forces, and he refused. He compiled a record of victories, often against far larger numbers, and earned the name El Dragón de Hierro, the Iron Dragon, but contemporaries of all factions also knew him for cruelty towards insurgents and their families. He was dismissed from command in 1816 over accusations of corruption and cruelty, and was reinstated in 1820 to defeat Vicente Guerrero.

The restoration of Spain's liberal Cadiz Constitution in 1820 made many in Mexico fear that the monarchy would be forced to abandon Spain. Iturbide allied with the insurgents under the Plan of Iguala of 1821, which aimed at an independent monarchy with Roman Catholicism as its official religion and the abolition of the caste system and slavery. The Treaty of Córdoba, signed with the Spanish official O'Donojú, offered the throne to Ferdinand VII or another European prince; when Spain refused, Iturbide entered Mexico City on 27 September 1821 and became president of the Regency.

He took the crown as emperor in 1822. Conflict with Congress, which claimed all the powers of the state, led him to dissolve it on 31 October 1822. A military revolt by Antonio López de Santa Anna, Guadalupe Victoria and Guerrero followed in December, and he abdicated on 19 March 1823.

Iturbide went into exile in Europe in May 1823. He returned to Mexico on 14 July 1824, landing at Soto la Marina, and was arrested by General Felipe de la Garza. He was executed by a local legislature on 19 July 1824. Early in the independence period the date of independence depended on politics: conservatives favoured 27 September, when Iturbide entered Mexico City, and liberals 16 September, Hidalgo's call to rebellion. Writing about him in modern Mexico is often hostile. The historian Eric Van Young calls him an opportunist who showed moments of political brilliance clouded by bad judgment.
agustin-gamarra: Agustín Gamarra Messia was born on 27 August 1785. He was a mestizo, of mixed Spanish and Quechua descent, and had a military life from childhood, fighting the royalist forces. He joined the cause of independence as second in command after Andrés de Santa Cruz and took part in the Battle of Ayacucho. In 1825 he married Francisca Zubiaga y Bernales. After the invasion of Bolivia in 1828 he was named a mariscal, a highly esteemed military rank.

After the defeat of José de La Mar in Gran Colombia, Gamarra urged his overthrow and took the presidency in 1829. His government held views contrary to those of La Mar. He put aside the Constitution of 1828, which he opposed for the limits it placed on the executive, and he supported protectionism. A peace treaty with Gran Colombia was signed during his government. When he left Lima to put down rebellions, the presidency passed to his vice president Antonio Gutiérrez de la Fuente, who plotted against him. Gamarra also faced opposition from Congress, which he closed in 1832. The election of his successor, Luis José de Orbegoso, set off a civil war, and gamarrista forces held out in the highlands for several months.

Gamarra shared with Santa Cruz the idea of annexing Bolivia, but while Bolivian elites did not think of one single state, Gamarra believed in incorporating Bolivian territory into a single Peruvian nation. In 1835 Orbegoso and Santa Cruz signed the treaty that created the Peru-Bolivian Confederacy. Gamarra opposed it and joined a campaign against it with the help of Chile, which led to the Battle of Yungay and the overthrow of Santa Cruz. The Peruvian congress then named Gamarra president. Chilean troops under General Manuel Bulnes stayed in Lima from January to October 1839 to steady the new regime.

Taking the presidency again as Restaurador del Perú, Gamarra met new rebellions and political instability. He declared war on Bolivia for supporting insurgent leaders. He was defeated and killed by Bolivian forces at the Battle of Ingavi on 18 November 1841. His death began the period known as the Military Anarchy, in which several magistrates and dictators fought for power until 1845, when President Ramón Castilla restored order. The presidency was officially vacant in the meantime.
ahab: Ahab was the seventh king of Israel, son and successor of Omri and husband of Jezebel, daughter of Ithobaal I of Tyre. According to 1 Kings he became king in the thirty-eighth year of Asa of Judah and reigned twenty-two years. Scholars date the reign differently: William F. Albright to 869-850 BCE, Edwin R. Thiele to 874-853 BCE and, most recently, Michael Coogan to 871-852 BCE. The Hebrew Bible says that under Jezebel's influence he abandoned Yahweh and set up the cults of Baal and Asherah. Edward Lipiński argues that his Baal was the Yahweh of Samaria, which Judean priests opposed as heresy, while others disagree on the evidence about Jezebel's upbringing.

Ahab continued Omri's policy toward Moab, a tributary of Israel; the Mesha Stele says Omri and Ahab oppressed Moab for many days. He allied himself with Jehoshaphat of Judah by marriage. He made peace with Aram-Damascus after its king promised to withdraw from conquered territory. In 853 BCE an Assyrian inscription, the Kurkh Monolith, records him among the allies defeated by Shalmaneser III at Qarqar, with 2,000 chariots and 10,000 men, though excavations of stables suggest the number of chariots was nearer the hundreds. Shalmaneser's later campaigns in 849 and 846 BCE imply that his victory had no lasting effect. Jezreel was Ahab's fortified chariot and cavalry base.

The Bible tells of four encounters with prophets, among them Elijah, who foretold a drought and condemned the execution of Naboth, and Micaiah, who warned that Ahab would die in battle. Ahab was mortally wounded by a stray arrow when he and Jehoshaphat tried to retake Ramoth-Gilead from the Arameans, and dogs licked his corpse, as Elijah had foretold.

Yahwist tradition judged his reign worse than those before it, since he institutionalised Baalism, and it faulted his oppressive policies. It also credits him with fortifying many Israelite cities and building an ivory palace. Rabbinic literature counts him among the wicked kings excluded from the world to come, though some teachers saw him as a model of repentance.
ahaggar-mountains: The Hoggar Mountains lie in the central Sahara in southern Algeria, along the Tropic of Cancer, and cover about 550,000 square kilometres, roughly 1,500 kilometres south of Algiers. The area is largely rocky desert with an average elevation above 900 metres. The mountains are mainly metamorphic rock about 2 billion years old, with younger rock where volcanic activity has laid down new material. Several of the more dramatic peaks, such as Ilamen, are extinct volcano domes worn away by erosion, which left the more resistant rock that plugged the cones. The highest peak, Mount Tahat, is 2,908 metres high.

Summers are hot and winters cold, with temperatures below freezing on winter nights, and rain is rare and sporadic. Because the climate is less extreme than in most of the Sahara, the range is a major location of biodiversity, including a number of relict species. The highlands are believed to be one of the main sources of the Tamanrasset River, an ancient river that flowed during the African humid period.

Rock paintings show that people settled here in prehistory, with dates as early as 6000 BCE. The massif is the land of the Kel Ahaggar Tuareg. The tomb of Tin Hinan, the woman believed to be the matriarch of the Tuareg, is at Abalessa, an oasis near Tamanrasset. In 1911 Charles de Foucauld built a hermitage at Assekrem, on the plateau at the top of the range, which a few Catholic monks still inhabit. France conducted underground atomic tests in the mountains in the 1960s.

Some wildlife has gone from the region. A population of African wild dogs just west of the range survived into the 20th century, and West African crocodiles persisted in the mountains until the early 20th century.

The mountains are home to the Ahaggar Cultural Park, called the Ahaggar National Park from 1987 to 2011, which covers about 450,000 square kilometres and holds Mount Tahat. Its vegetation includes Vachellia tortilis, myrtle and Tamarix aphylla. Barbary sheep and Dorcas gazelles live there, and BirdLife International has designated the park an Important Bird Area.
ahaz: Ahaz was the twelfth king of Judah and the son and successor of Jotham. His name is an abbreviation of Jehoahaz, meaning Yahweh has held. According to the Second Book of Kings he was 20 when he became king and reigned 16 years. The dates are disputed: Edwin R. Thiele placed a co-regency with Jotham from 736/735 BCE and a sole reign from 732/731 to 716/715 BCE, while William F. Albright dated his reign to 744 to 728 BCE.

At his accession Ahaz faced a coalition of Pekah of Israel and Rezin of Damascus, who wished to compel him to join them in opposing the Assyrians under Tiglath-Pileser III. The Book of Isaiah relates that the prophet counselled him to trust in God rather than foreign allies; Ahaz refused to ask for a sign, and Isaiah foretold the birth of a child to be called Immanuel. Ahaz instead called in the Assyrians. Tiglath-Pileser sacked Damascus and annexed Aram, and then took Galilee and other territory of Israel, deporting its people, as his own inscription also records. The campaign lasted two years, 734 to 732 BCE.

Judah was relieved of its neighbours, but its protector claimed suzerainty over it. In 732 Ahaz went to Damascus to swear homage to Tiglath-Pileser, and having admired an altar there he had a copy made in Jerusalem and made it a permanent part of Temple worship, with changes to the Temple's furniture. The biblical writers also say he offered his son by fire, or made him pass through fire; the words may describe a purification or a sacrifice. The Deuteronomistic historian judged his rule disastrous for the country's religion.

Ahaz died at the age of 36 and was succeeded by his son Hezekiah, whose reforms were largely aimed at undoing what Ahaz had done. According to 2 Chronicles, he was not laid in the tombs of the kings. Two inscribed objects name him. A clay seal impression reads Belonging to Ahaz, son of Yehotam, king of Judah, and most scholars think it authentic; a carnelian seal of the 8th century BCE, now at Yale University, belonged to Ushna, servant of Ahaz. The annals of Tiglath-Pileser III also record tribute from Ahaz of Judah.
ahaziah-of-judah: Ahaziah, also called Jehoahaz in 2 Chronicles, was the sixth king of Judah. He was the son of Jehoram and Athaliah, the daughter or possibly the sister of King Ahab of Israel. This made him the first Judahite king descended from both the House of David and the House of Omri. He was the youngest son of Jehoram, since according to 2 Chronicles his older brothers had been carried off in a Philistine and Arab raid. Biblical sources disagree on his age at accession: 2 Kings gives 22 and 2 Chronicles 42.

Under the influence of his mother Athaliah, Ahaziah introduced forms of worship that offended the Yahwistic party. Members of her family became his advisers and encouraged him to join his uncle Jehoram, king of Israel, in an expedition against Hazael, king of the Arameans. Jehoram was wounded in the battle and went to recover at Jezreel. Ahaziah left the field in Gilead, visited Jerusalem, and then came to Jezreel for a conference with Jehoram, where he was caught up in the revolt of Jehu.

According to 2 Kings, Ahaziah and Jehoram both went out to meet the rebellious general. Ahaziah watched Jehoram shot by Jehu with a bow, and fled, but was wounded at the pass of Gur in Ibleam and reached only Megiddo, where he died. 2 Chronicles gives a different account, in which Ahaziah hid in Samaria after Jehu's coup and was found and killed by Jehu's men on their king's orders.

The Tel Dan Stele, whose fragments were found in 1993 and 1994, claims that its author killed both the king of the House of David, Ahaziah, and the king of Israel, Jehoram. Its most likely author is Hazael of the Arameans. The inscription may be a contemporary witness, but kings of that time often boasted and exaggerated, and it is not clear whether Jehu killed the two kings, as the Bible reports, or Hazael did, or whether Jehu acted in concert with Hazael.

The calendars of Judah and Israel were offset by six months, with the Judean year starting in Tishri and that of Israel in Nisan. For Ahaziah the biblical data narrow his accession to between Nisan 1 and the day before Tishri 1 of 841 BCE. William F. Albright dated his reign to 842 BCE, and E. R. Thiele to 841/840, a date later scholars moved one year earlier. Leslie McFall proposed a one-year coregency with his father Jehoram, who had fallen ill, to explain the differing synchronisms in 2 Kings.
ahilyabai-holkar: Ahilyabai was born on 31 May 1725 in the village of Chandi in Maharashtra, to Mankoji Shinde, the village Patil, and Sushila Shinde. She had five brothers and was first educated at home. Malhar Rao Holkar, a commander under the Peshwa Baji Rao I and ruler of Malwa, saw her at a temple service on his way to Pune and advised his son Khanderao to marry her. They were wed in 1733, when he was nine or ten and she seven or eight.

Her mother-in-law, Gautama Bai Holkar, trained her in administration, accounts and politics and in 1759 gave her a khasgi, or land grant. From 1754 Malhar Rao involved her in diplomacy and the kingdom's finances. In a letter of 1765 he ordered her to take heavy artillery to Gwalior and attack the fort at Gohad, and the attack succeeded.

Khanderao was killed by cannon fire in 1754 while inspecting his troops at the siege of the Kumher fort. Ahilyabai announced that she would commit sati on his pyre, but her father-in-law begged her to live, and she did. Malhar Rao died on 20 May 1766. Her only son, Male Rao Holkar, was invested by the Peshwa as ruler of Indore on 23 August 1766 and died on 5 April 1767. Malhar Rao's adopted son Tukoji Rao Holkar was then made Subahdar on payment of a large tribute, and Ahilyabai became the de facto ruler.

Groups from neighbouring states, particularly the Chundawat clan of Jaipur, rebelled during the transfer of power, taking advantage of the devastation that followed the Third Battle of Panipat. Ahilyabai led Maratha armies against them and, despite a lack of resources, won every battle. Her daughter Muktabai committed sati on the funeral pyre of Yeshwantrao Fanse in 1791. She died on 13 August 1795, aged 70, and Tukoji Rao, her commander, succeeded her.

She is credited with repairing and adding to several temples, among them the Kashi Vishwanath Temple at Varanasi, and with the Dashashwamedh Ghat at Banaras. Her charities, paid from personal funds estimated at sixteen crore rupees, included temples, ghats and almshouses at Dwarka, Ujjain, Mathura, Ayodhya, Haridwar, Badrinath and Puri. She also supported women weavers who made Maheshwari saris.

Jawaharlal Nehru wrote in 1946 that her reign of thirty years was remembered as a period of perfect order and good government, and John Malcolm, who collected oral memories of her in the 1820s, called her one of the purest rulers that ever existed. John Keay calls her the philosopher queen. Indore's airport and university carry her name, and India issued a stamp in her honour on 25 August 1996.
ahlat: Ahlat stands on an elevated plateau on the western shore of Lake Van, with small rivers and streams running down to the lake. Mount Nemrut and Mount Sipan bound its horizon to the southwest and northwest. In size it was second only to Van among the cities on the lake's shores, and it was considered the largest port on Lake Van, which was also called the Lake of Khlat. According to the 11th-century chronicler Ibn al-Athir, Arabs called the city Khlat, meaning mixed, because its inhabitants spoke three languages: Arabic, Persian and Armenian.

Ahlat is one of the oldest settlements in Armenia. It was the chief city of the province of Bznunik, held by the Bznuni noble house, and then passed to the Bagratunis of Taron. Arabs first captured it between 644 and 656, and for four centuries it was ruled in turn by Arab governors, Armenian princes and Arab emirs. About 983 it came under the Kurdish leader Bāḏ and then the Marwanid dynasty. In the tenth and eleventh centuries it grew into one of Armenia's largest cities, a hub of craft and trade. In 1000 Emperor Basil II granted it to the Artsrunis, and the Seljuks captured and destroyed it after the Battle of Manzikert in 1071.

The Seljuks gave the city to the Turkmen commander Sökmen el-Kutbî, whose line were the Shah-Armens or Ahlat-shahs, and in 1100 they made it their capital. In the 13th century it was disputed among the Ayyubids, the Kingdom of Georgia and the Sultanate of Rum. Jalal al-Din captured it in 1230 and destroyed much of it, the Mongols took it in 1245, and an earthquake in 1246 ruined most of its buildings. It later belonged to the Ak Koyunlu. The Ottomans under Selim I first took it, and Suleiman I made it a stable part of the empire.

Ahlat is a town in Bitlis Province in eastern Turkey, with a population of 27,563 in 2021. It is known for the many historical tombstones left by the Ahlatshah dynasty, and for the Seljuk cemetery, the Çifte Kümbet twin tombs and the tomb of Emir Bayındır. Local authorities have sought to include the tombstones and the Urartian and Ottoman citadel on UNESCO's World Heritage tentative list. Armenian scribes copied manuscripts at its monastery in the 15th century, and the chronicler and poet Grigor Khlatetsi, born there in 1349, was a prominent figure of Armenian culture.
ahmad-al-mansur: Ahmad al-Mansur, also called al-Dhahabi, the Golden, was the fifth son of Mohammed ash-Sheikh, the first Saadi sultan of Morocco, and of Lalla Masuda. After his father was murdered in 1557 he and his brother Abd al-Malik fled their elder brother Abdallah al-Ghalib and stayed abroad until 1576. They spent seventeen years among the Ottomans, between the Regency of Algiers and Constantinople. Ahmad received an extensive education in religious and secular sciences, among them theology, law, poetry, geometry, algebra and astronomy.

In 1578 his brother Abd al-Malik I died in battle against the Portuguese at Ksar el-Kebir, and Ahmad succeeded him with the prestige and the ransom money of the Portuguese captives. He used the ransom to fill the royal coffers and began the El Badi Palace in Marrakesh in December 1578; it was finished in 1593 or 1594. Eventually the treasury ran low under the cost of the army, spy services, building projects and a propaganda campaign for his claim to the caliphate. He sent an ambassador to Elizabeth I of England in 1600 to negotiate an alliance against Spain.

He recognised Ottoman suzerainty at the start of his reign but later had coins minted and Friday prayers said in his own name. Murad III prepared an attack, which was called off when al-Mansur sent an embassy with gifts and tribute. After 1587 he stopped his payments and proclaimed himself caliph. In 1583 and 1584 his forces annexed Saharan oases and Chinguetti. On 16 October 1590 he dispatched an army of 4,000 men under Judar Pasha across the Sahara. At Tondibi it met a Songhai force of 40,000 that lacked gunpowder weapons and quickly fled, and the army sacked Timbuktu, Djenné and Gao.

Al-Mansur died in 1603 and was buried in the Saadian Tombs in Marrakesh. His sons Zidan al-Nasir, in Marrakesh, and Abou Fares Abdallah, in Fez, succeeded him. Holding the Songhai lands across the Sahara proved too difficult, and the Saadians lost control of the cities not long after 1620. He balanced the Europeans and the Ottomans against each other to preserve Moroccan independence, though he spent far more than he collected. In 1602 he used fatwas to discourage the use of tobacco.
ahmad-ibn-fadlan: Contemporary sources call Ahmad ibn Fadlan an Arab of Baghdad, but nothing is certain about his origin, ethnicity, education or the dates of his birth and death. From his own writing it appears that he was a faqih, an expert in Islamic jurisprudence, and that he had served for some time at the court of the Abbasid caliph al-Muqtadir before his mission.

In 921 Ibn Fadlan was sent from Baghdad as secretary to an ambassador of al-Muqtadir to Almış, the iltäbär or vassal king under the Khazars of Volga Bulgaria. The party, led by the eunuch Susan al-Rassi, left on 21 June 921. Its purpose was to explain Islamic law to the recently converted Bulgars and to answer the Bulgar king's request for help against the Khazars. Ibn Fadlan served as religious adviser and counsellor on doctrine and law.

The party travelled by caravan routes toward Bukhara, then turned north from what is now north-eastern Iran. Leaving Gurgan near the Caspian Sea, it crossed the lands of the Oghuz Turks, the Pechenegs on the Ural River and the Bashkirs, covering some 4,000 kilometres in all. It reached the Bulgar capital on 12 May 922. Ibn Fadlan read the caliph's letter to the Bulgar ruler and presented the gifts, but was criticised for not bringing the money promised to build a fortress against the enemies of the Bulgars.

His risāla, an account of the journey, long survived only in quotations in Yaqut's geographical dictionary, published in 1823 by Christian Martin Frähn. In 1923 Zeki Velidi Togan found a fuller 13th-century manuscript at Mashhad, which breaks off while describing the Khazars. Neither source seems to hold the complete report.

Ibn Fadlan judged the peoples he met largely by their practice of Islam, and he was angered by what he took to be unsound practice among the Bulgars. His longest passage concerns the Rūs, generally taken to be Volga Vikings trading by the river. He describes their appearance, their weapons and the ship funeral of a chieftain, which involved human sacrifice, and calls their hygiene shameless. He also gives early first-hand descriptions of the Oghuz Turks, who lived in felt tents, and of the Bashkirs. His text later inspired Michael Crichton's novel Eaters of the Dead.
ahmad-ibn-hanbal: Ahmad ibn Hanbal was born in November 780, a date his son Abdullah recorded. His family came originally from Basra and belonged to the Arab Banu Dhuhl tribe, and his father was an officer in the Abbasid army in Khorasan who later settled in Baghdad. Historians differ about his birthplace. Some say Merv, where his father and grandfather had worked, while the most accepted view is that his mother came pregnant from Merv and that he was born in Baghdad. His father died at about thirty, and his mother raised him with the help of his father's family.

He inherited a house in Baghdad and a property that yielded a small income. Ibn Kathir gives its amount as seventeen dirhams a month. Ahmad lived in poverty and worked as a baker. He did not marry until he was forty, which is said to be because he was busy seeking knowledge and travelled widely. Having studied jurisprudence and hadith under many teachers in his youth, he became widely known for his part in the Mihna, in which the caliph al-Ma'mun gave state support to the Mu'tazili doctrine that the Quran was created.

Ibn Hanbal's principal doctrine is called traditionalist thought, which accepts only the Quran and hadith as the foundations of orthodox belief, though he held that only a select few were authorised to interpret the texts. He affirmed the attributes of God that the Quran gives, such as hearing, sight and speech, and read the apparently anthropomorphic ones, such as God's hand and face, literally. He rejected the allegorical interpretation of the Jahmiyya and also the anthropomorphism of the Mushabbiha, and he upheld the formula bi-la kayfa, believing in them without asking how.

He compiled al-Musnad, the largest hadith collection, which influenced the methods later used in the collections of Bukhari and Muslim. Ibn al-Nadim's Fihrist lists works such as Kitab al-Zuhd, Kitab al-Iman and a book on the rites of the Hajj. Al-Tabari is reported to have counted him only an expert in prophetic tradition, but most scholars recognise him as a jurist, and al-Shafi'i called him an imam in eight fields. Al-Khallal and al-Khiraqi made the first written compilations of his legal views. His school, the Hanbali school, is dominant in Saudi Arabia and Qatar.
ahmad-ibn-ibrahim-al-ghazi: Ahmad ibn Ibrahim was born around 1506 and came from the lowlands of Hubat in the Adal Sultanate. Historians disagree about his ethnicity, regarding him as a Somali, a Harla or Harari, or a Balaw. He was known in Amharic as Grañ Ahmed and in Somali as Gurey, both meaning the left-handed. As a follower of Garad Abun Adashe in his struggle against the ruling Walashma dynasty, he showed courage and military skill, and Abun arranged his marriage to Bati del Wambara, the youngest daughter of the late Imam Mahfuz.

After Sultan Abu Bakr ibn Muhammad defeated and killed Abun near Zeila in 1525, Ahmad defeated the sultan in the field and held Hubat as an independent governor. His victory over the Ethiopian general Degelhan at the Battle of Hubat spread his fame. A swarm of bees that settled on his head was taken as a miracle and earned him the title of Imam. He later defeated and killed Abu Bakr, placed Umar Din on the throne as a puppet, and obtained firearms through the port of Zeila.

In 1529 Ahmad defeated the much larger army of Emperor Dawit II at the Battle of Shimbra Kure, an outcome Richard Pankhurst attributes to his matchlockmen. From 1531 he began the occupation of Abyssinia, winning at Antukyah and taking Fatagar and Shewa. His forces destroyed many churches, among them Atronsa Maryam and the Church of Our Lady Mary of Zion at Aksum. Arab Faqih, an Adal chronicler, describes massacres of Christians who refused to convert or pay jizya, and estimates that over 10,000 were killed in Tigray. Dawit II was forced to live as an outlaw and sent João Bermudes to ask Portugal for help.

A Portuguese force of 400 musketeers under Cristóvão da Gama landed in 1541. Ahmad was wounded at the Battle of Jarte, but after he obtained 2,000 musketeers from Arabia and troops and artillery from the Ottomans, his army killed nearly all of da Gama's men and executed da Gama. The Portuguese survivors joined Emperor Gelawdewos, and on 21 February 1543 the allies met Ahmad at the Battle of Wayna Daga. Ahmad was killed while trying to rally his troops, though sources differ on how he died, and his army was routed.

Bati del Wambara led the remnants of the army back to Harar. Gelawdewos had Ahmad's head carried around Abyssinia on a spear. Muslim sources portray him as an ascetic who forbade wine, gambling and drum dances, patronised jurists and built mosques. In Ethiopia the destruction he caused is still remembered, and the historian Enrico Cerulli held that Adal never recovered from his death. By 1577 the sultanate had disintegrated under tribal infighting and pressure from the Oromo migrations.
ahmad-ibn-tulun: Ahmad ibn Tulun was born on 20 September 835 or slightly later, probably in Baghdad. His father, Tulun, was a Turk from a region that Arabic sources call Tagharghar, meaning the Uyghur confederation. Tulun was taken captive in 815/6 and sent, with other Turks, as part of the tribute of Nuh ibn Asad, the Samanid governor of Bukhara, to the Caliph al-Ma'mun. These slaves became a corps of slave soldiers under al-Mu'tasim, and Tulun rose to command the caliph's private guard. After his death in 854/5, Ahmad came under the care of Yalbakh, a companion of his father, and, according to al-Balawi, the general Bakbak treated him as a son.

In 868 the Caliph al-Mu'tazz gave Bakbak charge of Egypt, and Bakbak sent Ahmad as his lieutenant. Ahmad entered Egypt on 27 August 868 and the capital, Fustat, on 15 September. He oversaw the army and led the Friday prayer, but the land tax lay with the veteran administrator Ibn al-Mudabbir, who had doubled taxes and was widely hated. Ibn Tulun refused the 10,000 dinars that Ibn al-Mudabbir and the postmaster Shukayr offered him on arrival. After four years of intrigue at the court in Samarra, he had Ibn al-Mudabbir transferred to Syria in July 871, took over the tax himself and, by 872, controlled every branch of the administration.

The Abbasid regent al-Muwaffaq was occupied with the Saffarids and the Zanj Rebellion, which left Ibn Tulun room to consolidate his power. In 878, with the support of Caliph al-Mu'tamid, he took over Syria and the frontier districts with the Byzantine Empire, though his hold on Tarsus was uncertain. In 882 his general Lu'lu' defected to al-Muwaffaq and Tarsus refused to acknowledge him. He then convened an assembly of jurists at Damascus, which denounced al-Muwaffaq as a usurper and called for a jihad against him, although neither side moved against the other militarily.

His attempt to bring Tarsus to heel in the autumn of 883 failed and he fell sick. He returned to Egypt and died on 10 May 884, and his son Khumarawayh succeeded without opposition. The Tulunid state lasted until January 905, when the Abbasids retook Fustat; their troops pillaged and razed his capital, al-Qata'i, sparing only the great mosque.

Historians regard his rule as a turning point: Egypt, for the first time since the Pharaohs, ceased to be a passive province and became a political actor in its own right. The realm he built, taking in Egypt, Syria, the Jazira and Cilicia, formed a new political zone, and later Egypt-based regimes, the Ikhshidids and the Fatimids, followed his policies of restoring the economy and keeping an autonomous bureaucracy, army and navy.
ahmad-khani: Ehmedê Xanî, also written Ahmad-e Khani, was born in 1650 in the village of Khan in the Hakkari region, in present-day south-eastern Turkey. He was educated in religious schools and studied in different parts of Kurdistan. He wrote his first poem at the age of fourteen and at twenty became a clerical secretary at the princely court of Bayazid. He may also have visited Syria and Egypt, and his poetry suggests that he lived for a long time at Jazira, or Cizre, capital of the Kurdish principality of Bohtan. In his last years he taught in Bayazid, where most scholars agree he died in 1707.

Mem and Zin, a long romantic epic, is his chief work and the best-known work of Kurdish literature among Kurds and others alike. He also wrote Nûbihara Biçûkan, The Spring of Children, a versified Arabic-Kurdish vocabulary, the religious poems Eqîdeya Îmanê and Eqîdeya Îslamê, a book of astronomy and geography, and a collection of poems. His works were studied in Kurdish schools from his own time until about the 1930s. He admired the Kurmanji poets Melayê Cizîrî and Feqiyê Teyran, and Joyce Blau called him the spiritual son of Cizîrî, Teyran and Ali Hariri.

Instead of praising the rulers of his day, as the introductions of classical Oriental poems usually did, the opening chapters of Mem and Zin lament that the Kurds were subject to the Ottomans and the Safavids and had no state or king of their own. Xanî held that such a ruler could free the Kurds and that an independent Kurdistan could keep the Kurdish language fit for science and learning. His poetry also speaks ill of Arabs, Persians and Armenians.

According to Ferhad Shakely, later Kurdish poets such as Haji Qadir Koyi followed his example in praising the struggle of the Kurds for liberty, and in the 20th century Mem and Zin was hailed as the earliest expression of Kurdish nationalism. Some regard Xanî as the founder of that nationalism. Hakan Özoğlu thinks it highly unlikely that he sought a nation-state, and Martin van Bruinessen holds that Kurd in his day meant the tribes and part of the urban elite, not the peasantry, though his works played an important part in the national movement. Leonard Michael Koff argues that he wrote of moral and cultural independence.
ahmad-qavam: Ahmad Qavam was born on 2 January 1873 into the prominent Mostowfian Ashtiani family. His uncle, Amin al-Dowleh, was a prime minister of Iran, and his older brother, Hasan Vossug, served twice as prime minister. Qavam entered the court of Naser al-Din Shah Qajar early in his career and obtained the title os-Saltaneh during the Constitutional Revolution of 1909. As Dabir-e Hozoor, the private secretary, he wrote the letter signed by Mozaffar ad-Din Shah accepting the Constitutional Revolution.

Qavam was appointed governor of Khorasan in 1918, where he dealt with famine and the Spanish flu pandemic; he was a hardline administrator and banned some of the region's newspapers. In 1921, during the coup d'état in Tehran, he was among the opponents Colonel Pessian was ordered to arrest. When the government of Seyyed Zia'eddin Tabatabaee fell and others refused the premiership in an unstable situation, Qavam, just released from Ishratabad prison, was offered it and accepted. He later crushed the revolt of Colonel Pessian with the aid of Reza Pahlavi. His terms also included the invitation to Arthur Millspaugh to assist with the government's finances, the riots of 1942 over economic hardship and the Tripartite Treaty of 1942 between Iran, Russia and Britain.

On 26 January 1946 the Majlis voted him prime minister by 52 to 51, hoping that, as the largest property owner in Azerbaijan, he could best resolve the Soviet-inspired rebellion in the occupied province.
