In the region of Tado they met the Alu, the earliest known inhabitants, who seem to have been ironworkers: slag lies across the area, and a blast furnace was found at Tado in 1970. Around the start of the second millennium newcomers joined them, whom the researcher Roberto Pazzi traces to the Za kingdom of the Niger bend, and around the 13th century came Aja migrants from the east under a leader named Togbui-Anyi. The three communities, Alu, Azanu and Aja, merged to form the Aja people, and the town of Azamé took the name Tado.

The Kingdom of Tado became the strongest in what is now southern Togo. In its golden age, roughly the 15th to the 17th centuries, it was a confederation stretching from the Volta to the Kouffo and inland to Agbonou and Kambolé, ruled by the Anyigbãfio, the Kings of the Land; the Spanish Jesuit Alonso de Sandoval described it in 1627 as a powerful kingdom with a safe port. Oral tradition tells that about 1600 three brothers, Kokpon, Do-Aklin and Te-Agbanlin, divided the Aja lands between Great Ardra, Abomey and Little Ardra, later Porto-Novo. Land shortage, smallpox and quarrels over chieftaincy drove groups away: those who mingled with the Gedevi on the Abomey Plateau became the Fon, and others became the Ewe of Togo and Ghana.

Dahomey conquered the Aja kingdom of Allada in 1724, killing thousands of soldiers and civilians, and sold about 8,000 captives into slavery in the Americas, many of them landed in Haiti, among them the parents of Toussaint Louverture. Until the late 18th century the Aja, Fon, Ewe and Ga-Adangbe made up most of the people carried from this coast in the transatlantic slave trade.

About two million Aja live in an area on the border between Benin and Togo, and many have moved to Cotonou, Lomé, Lagos and Libreville in search of land or work. They speak Aja-Gbe in three dialects, Tàgóbé, Dògóbè and Hwègbè, and many also speak French and Fongbe. Most Gbe-speaking peoples, above all the Ewe and Fon, regard the Aja as their mother tribe, and one source holds that vodún originated among them.
ajaigarh: Ajaigarh, also spelt Ajaygarh, is a town and nagar panchayat in Panna district of Madhya Pradesh, central India, and the headquarters of its tehsil. The hill fortress that gave the town and the princely state their name stands on a steep hill above the town, more than 800 feet (240 metres) high, bordered by the Vindhya Hills with views of the Ken River. The fort is also known as Ajaypal Fort.

The princely state of Ajaigarh was founded by Guman Singh, a Bundela Rajput and nephew of Raja Pahar Singh of Jaitpur. The British captured Ajaigarh in 1809, and it became a princely state in the Bundelkhand Agency of the Central India Agency. In 1901 it had an area of 771 square miles (2,000 km2) and a population of 78,236. Its rulers bore the title sawai maharaja, with an estimated annual revenue of about £15,000 and a tribute of £460. The chief lived at Nowgong, at the foot of the fortress. The town was often afflicted by malaria and suffered severely from famine in 1868–69 and 1896–97.

The state acceded to the Government of India on 1 January 1950, and the ruling chief received a privy purse of Rs. 74,700, which the government revoked in 1971 along with those of all former princes. The state became part of Vindhya Pradesh, which merged into Madhya Pradesh on 1 November 1956, and most of its territory, with the town, passed to Panna district.

The fort was built by the Chandela kings. Its architecture dates to the Chandela dynasty, and it contains the ruins of several temples with elaborately carved sculptures. It has two gates, where there were once five, two temples and two rock-cut tanks near the northern gate, named Ganga and Jamuna. An old inscription at the main entrance has never been deciphered; it is believed to hold the secret of a hidden treasure. The town had 16,656 people at the 2011 census. It is easily reached from Khajuraho.
ajanta-caves: The caves were made in two phases. The first began around the 2nd century BCE and belongs to the 2nd century BCE to 1st century CE. Older accounts place the second phase between 400 and 650 CE, but later scholarship dates it to a brief period of 460 to 480. Walter Spink places the whole second phase in the 5th century. He holds that the earlier group, dated only approximately to between 100 BCE and 100 CE, was then abandoned for over three centuries. According to him the Vakataka emperor Harishena, who reigned from 460 until his death in 477, sponsored numerous new caves, and work stopped soon after his death, which left many caves unfinished.

The caves are carved from flood basalt of the Deccan Traps, layered horizontally and of variable quality. Excavation began with a narrow tunnel at roof level, which was widened downwards and outwards, as the unfinished Caves 21 to 24 and Cave 28 show. Flaws in the rock caused cracks and collapses, such as that of the portico of Cave 1.

The complex is carved into a 75-metre wall of rock and consists of monasteries (viharas) and worship halls (chaityas) of different Buddhist traditions. There are 36 identifiable foundations, and the numbering from 1 to 29 is a convenience that does not follow the order of construction. Cave 10 is a vast apsidal prayer hall of about the 1st century BCE, with 39 octagonal pillars and a stupa at the end with a path for walking round it. Textual records suggest that the caves served as a monsoon retreat for monks and as a resting place for merchants and pilgrims.

Most of the wall paintings come from the second phase and mainly narrate the Jataka tales, the legends of the Buddha's previous births as an animal or a human, including scenes from Aryasura's Jatakamala. Caves 1, 2, 16 and 17 hold the largest body of surviving ancient Indian wall painting. Spink holds that Cave 1, among the last excavated, was never dedicated for worship, and that its stress on royal imagery reflects Harishena's patronage. A fresco in Cave 2 shows children at a school.

Medieval Chinese Buddhist travellers mention the caves, which were later covered by jungle. They were brought to contemporary attention in 1819 when Colonel John Smith came upon them during a tiger-hunting expedition. The caves are in the northern wall of the U-shaped gorge of the Waghur river, in the Deccan Plateau, and form a UNESCO World Heritage Site. Ellora, about 100 kilometres away, has caves of a similar period, and the Ajanta style appears there and at other cave sites.
ajatashatru: Ajatashatru was a contemporary of both Mahavira and Gautama Buddha. The Buddhist and Jain traditions give him different mothers, Kosala Devi in the Buddhist account and Chellana in the Jain, though both queens were called Vaidehi. He took over Magadha by force from his father Bimbisara and imprisoned him. Datings of his reign differ widely between scholars, who have proposed two quite different spans of years. Kashi, given to Bimbisara as a dowry by the king of Kosala, was taken back by Prasenajit after Bimbisara's murder, which led to a war between Magadha and Kosala that ended with a treaty. Prasenajit married his daughter Vajira to Ajatashatru.

Ajatashatru followed policies of conquest. He occupied Kashi, defeated the king of Kosala and, after a long struggle, conquered Vaishali, the republic of the Vajjika League led by the Licchavis. In the Jain account his brothers Halla and Vihalla fled with a war elephant and a necklace to their grandfather Chetaka, king of Vaishali, and Ajatashatru went to war to get them. In the Buddhist account the quarrel began over the shares of a diamond mine on the Ganges, and his minister Vassakara split the Vajjis after the Buddha named seven reasons for their strength. He also turned the village of Pataliputra into a fortified city and moved his capital from Rajgriha to Champa after his father's death.

Accounts of his death differ widely between the Jain and Buddhist traditions. Both claim him as a follower. The Jain Uvavai Sutta says he held Mahavira in the highest esteem. In the Samaññaphala Sutta he met the Buddha, took refuge in the Buddha, the Dhamma and the Sangha, and admitted his guilt over plotting his father's death. Tradition says he built a stupa over the Buddha's remains and was present at the first Buddhist council at Rajgriha. In the Mahayana Mahaparinirvana Sutra he is the prototype of a sinful person who can be saved only by the Buddha's compassion.
ajax-the-great: In Greek myth Ajax is the son of Telamon, himself a son of Aeacus and grandson of Zeus, and of Telamon's first wife Periboea. He is the elder half-brother of the archer Teucer and, through his uncle Peleus, a cousin of Achilles. The Iliad describes him as huge and the strongest of the Achaeans, trained by the centaur Chiron, and he carries a great shield of seven cowhides covered with bronze. His name is of uncertain origin. One folk etymology links it to a Greek verb meaning to lament, and Hesiod gave another, from the eagle that Zeus sent in answer to a prayer of Heracles. Athenians such as Cimon, Miltiades, Alcibiades and Thucydides traced their descent from him.

In the Iliad Ajax is chiefly a defensive warrior who covers the retreat of the Greeks and protects their ships, and he is not wounded in any of its battles. In Book 7 he is chosen by lot to duel with the Trojan Hector, and the fight lasts most of a day until heralds acting on the will of Zeus call a draw. The two exchange gifts, Ajax giving Hector a purple war-belt and Hector giving Ajax a silver-studded sword. Later, as Hector attacks the ships, Ajax leaps from ship to ship with an enormous spear and holds off the Trojans almost single-handed, though Hector burns one vessel. He often fights beside Teucer, who shoots from behind his shield.

In Book 9 Agamemnon sends Ajax, Odysseus and Phoenix to Achilles' tent, but Ajax cannot persuade Achilles to return to the fighting. After the death of Patroclus he and Menelaus fight off the Trojans and bring the body back, and after Achilles dies he recovers Achilles' body for burial while Odysseus holds the Trojans back.

When the council awarded Achilles' armour to Odysseus, with the help of Athena, Ajax killed himself with his sword. In the Little Iliad he first slaughters the cattle of the Greek army in a fit of rage. In Sophocles' play Ajax, Athena clouds his mind so that he slaughters sheep, imagining them the Greek leaders, and he kills himself rather than live in shame, with the sword Hector gave him. Homer says only that he lost the dispute, and in the underworld his shade refuses to speak to Odysseus.

Ajax was the guardian hero of Salamis, where a festival, the Aianteia, honoured him, and, after Salamis came under Athenian control, he became an Attic hero with a statue at Athens and a tribe named Aiantis. Since 2001 Yannis Lolos has excavated a Mycenaean palace at Kanakia on Salamis, which he suggests was the home of Ajax's dynasty.
ajax-the-lesser: Ajax the Lesser, also called the Locrian Ajax, was a Greek mythological hero, called the lesser to tell him from Ajax the Great, son of Telamon. His mother was Eriopis, and according to Strabo he was born at Naryx in Locris. In the Iliad he led his Locrians against Troy in forty ships. He is described as brave and skilled in throwing the spear, and next to Achilles the swiftest of the Greeks. In the footrace at the funeral games of Patroclus, Athena, who was hostile to him and favoured Odysseus, made him stumble. In later traditions he was a suitor of Helen, and in Etruscan legend he was called Aivas Vilates.

After the capture of Troy, Ajax rushed into the temple of Athena, where Cassandra had taken refuge embracing the goddess's statue, and dragged her away with the other captives. According to some writers he raped her inside the temple. Odysseus called for his death by stoning, but Ajax saved himself by swearing an oath of innocence to Athena while clutching her statue. According to the Bibliotheca, the seer Calchas warned the Greeks that Athena was furious and would destroy their ships unless they killed him. Ajax hid at the altar of another deity, and the Greeks, fearing divine retribution, let him live.

Athena persuaded Zeus to send a storm that sank many Greek ships. As Ajax sailed home, she struck his ship with a thunderbolt and wrecked it on the Whirling Rocks. He clung to a rock with Poseidon's help but then boasted that he would escape the sea against the will of the gods, and Poseidon split the rock with his trident and he was swallowed by the sea. Thetis buried him when his body washed up on Mykonos.

Other accounts place his death on the Capharean Rocks off Euboea. His spirit was said to dwell on the island of Leuce. The Opuntian Locrians worshipped him as their national hero and, when they drew up for battle, left one place open for him, believing he fought among them unseen. His abduction of Cassandra was often represented in Greek art.
ajivika: Ajivika is an ancient heterodox Indian school, a Śramaṇa movement of organised renunciates who formed discrete communities. The name means follower of the way of life, from a Sanskrit word for livelihood. Its origins are unknown but generally placed in the 5th century BCE, and Buddhist and Jain texts connect it with Makkhali Gosala, a contemporary of the Buddha and Mahavira. Some scholars hold that Gosala only led a large congregation of ascetics, and that the tradition existed well before him.

The Jain Bhagavati Sutra says Gosala was born in a cowshed, which gave him his name, near the city of Savatthi, and was the son of the mendicant Mankhali. It makes him Mahavira's disciple for six years, after which they quarrelled and parted. No original scriptures survive. Everything known comes from the Buddhist and Jain texts of rival groups, which may have misrepresented the school, and some scholars doubt that they summarise it fairly.

The school's distinctive doctrine was niyati, fate: everything that has happened, is happening and will happen is preordained by cosmic principles, and there is no free will. The Buddhist and Jain sources describe the Ajivikas as strict fatalists who rejected karma and held that religious or ethical practice does not change one's future. They were mostly considered atheists, yet believed that every living being has an atman. They also held that everything is made of atoms, whose aggregation was predetermined, and that all beings pass through development and are destined for final salvation.

Some scholars qualify this picture. Johannes Bronkhorst argues that Gosala taught only that new karma could be stopped, and Paul Dundas suspects that Jains and Buddhists deliberately distorted the doctrine for their own polemical purposes, since a creed denying the efficacy of effort could hardly found a path of renunciation.

The Ajivikas were most prominent in the late 1st millennium BCE. The Maurya emperor Ashoka dedicated several rock-cut caves as the Barabar Caves to them, in the 12th and 19th years of his reign, and these are the oldest surviving cave temples of ancient India. The word Ajivikas was later chiselled out of several inscriptions, probably by religious rivals.

After the Maurya Empire declined in the 2nd century BCE the Ajivikas appear only occasionally in Sanskrit literature. They survived in southern India, where at least 17 inscriptions, from about 446 CE to 1346 CE, record a tax on Ajivikas or Acuvas, a term many scholars take as a Tamil form of the name, though some doubt it. A 14th-century compendium of Indian philosophical systems does not mention them, which indicates the decline of the sect.
ajmer: Ajmer lies in a valley of the Aravalli Range in the Indian state of Rajasthan, on the lower slopes of Taragarh Hill. Its name comes from Ajaya Meru, Sanskrit for invincible hill, given by a Chahamana ruler, either Ajayaraja I or Ajayaraja II, and referring to Taragarh Hill. To the northwest the Nagapathar Range protects it from the spread of the Thar Desert. Because of its central position in the state it is called the Heart of Rajasthan.

The sources disagree on the founding. A prashasti issued by Vigraharaja IV states that Ajayadeva, meaning Ajayaraja II, moved his residence to Ajmer, and the earliest mention of the city's name is in a text copied in 1113 CE, so Ajmer existed before then. A later text says an earlier king built the fort that became Taragarh, and a historian, R. B. Singh, finds this likely since inscriptions of the 8th century have been found there. Singh suggests that Ajayaraja II expanded the town, built palaces and moved the Chahamana capital there from Shakambhari. The Ghurids later annexed Ajmer, and it was later returned to Gaur Rajput rulers on condition of tribute. By the 15th century Mewar had captured it.

Akbar conquered Ajmer in 1556 and made it capital of the Ajmer Subah. The Mughals made frequent pilgrimages to the dargah of Moinuddin Chishti, and Jahanara Begum and Dara Shikoh, children of Shah Jahan, were born there in 1614 and 1615. Mughal patronage waned by the early 18th century. The Scindias conquered the city in 1752, and the British gained authority in 1818. Under British rule it was headquarters of the Ajmer-Merwara Province, and Mayo College was founded in 1875 for the sons of chiefs and nobles. After independence in 1947 Ajmer continued as a separate state until 1956, when it was merged into Rajasthan.

Ajmer is the administrative headquarters of its district and division, and had 542,321 inhabitants in the 2011 census. The Ajmer Sharif Dargah, the shrine of Khwaja Moinuddin Chishti at the foot of Taragarh Hill, has white marble buildings around two courtyards and draws many pilgrims. Other sights include Taragarh Fort, the mosque known as Adhai Din Ka Jhonpra, Akbar's fort, now a museum, and the Ana Sagar Lake. The temple town of Pushkar lies a few kilometres away.
akademgorodok: Akademgorodok, Russian for Academic Town, is part of the Sovetsky District of the city of Novosibirsk. It lies 30 km south of the city centre and about 10 km west of Koltsovo, in birch and pine forest on the shore of the Ob Sea, an artificial reservoir on the river Ob. Formally it belongs to Novosibirsk and has never been a closed city.

Besides Novosibirsk State University it holds research institutes in fields from nuclear physics, catalysis and mathematics to cytology, genetics, history and philology, a medical academy, housing and community amenities. The House of Scientists, its social centre, has a library of 100 thousand volumes, a picture gallery, lecture halls and a concert hall.

The town was founded in 1957 under the auspices of the Academy of Sciences of the USSR. Academician Mikhail Alexeyevich Lavrentyev, a mechanician and mathematician and the first chairman of the Siberian Branch of the Academy, played a prominent part in establishing it. At its peak it was home to 65,000 scientists and their families and was a privileged place to live. Residents had access to special food distribution outlets, scientists with a doctorate to a doctoral food delivery service, and full and corresponding members of the Academy to a still higher level of service and to single-family houses called cottages, which were considered luxurious by Soviet standards.

In the early years residents enjoyed great freedom from the rules of the Soviet Union. A modernist cultural centre exhibited works by banned Soviet artists, poetry evenings were held, and research in areas dismissed in Moscow as dangerous pseudoscience, such as cybernetics and genetics, flourished. These freedoms were severely curtailed in the 1970s, in the Brezhnev era.

After the collapse of the Soviet Union many scientists were reduced to penury. From the mid-1990s private investment began to arrive: the software company Novosoft, whose chief client was IBM, was founded in 1992, and CFT, which specialises in banking software, started about then. Private investment reached US$10 million by 1997, $150 million by 2006 and about $1 billion by 2015. Intel and Schlumberger also brought work to the town.

Akademgorodok is sometimes called the Silicon Forest or Silicon Taiga. By 2015, 300 companies had been set up there since 2011, employing about 9,000 people. Its Technopark, with a distinctive headquarters built in 2013 of two inclined towers joined by a passage on the 13th and 14th floors, is nicknamed the geese.
akal-takht: Originally called the Akal Bunga, the seat stands directly opposite the Harmandir Sahib on ground where Guru Hargobind, the sixth Sikh Guru, had played as a child. With Baba Buddha and Bhai Gurdas he raised a platform about 3.5 metres high, from which he sat in court to receive petitions and give justice, surrounded by royal insignia such as the parasol and the fly whisk. When he revealed it on 15 June 1606 he put on two swords, one for spiritual authority (piri) and one for temporal authority (miri); the historian Kanwarjit Singh Kang dates the platform later, to 1609.

A hall was later built at the site. In the 18th century Ahmed Shah Abdali and Massa Rangar led attacks on the Akal Takht and the Harmandir Sahib, and in 1774 the takht was rebuilt in brick under Jassa Singh Ahluwalia, leader of the Sikh Confederacy. In the first half of the 19th century Maharaja Ranjit Singh raised the building to five storeys, and his general Hari Singh Nalwa added gold decoration and the golden dome. Murals painted around the middle of that century decorated the first and second storeys.

In 1983 Jarnail Singh Bhindranwale took refuge in the Golden Temple complex and later in the Akal Takht. The Indian army's operation against him between 3 and 8 June 1984, ordered by Prime Minister Indira Gandhi, heavily damaged the building, and Bhindranwale was killed. Baba Santa Singh of the Budha Dal rebuilt it with government support within a month and a half, which many Sikhs condemned; in January 1986 Baba Thakur Singh of the Damdami Taksal had that structure demolished and rebuilt, and Santa Singh was excommunicated.

The Akal Takht is the most prominent of the five takhts and the official seat of the jathedar, the spokesperson of the Khalsa. According to the historians Teja Singh and Ganda Singh, it was built close to the Harmandir Sahib so that politics and spirituality would each recall the other. It flies two Nishan Sahibs, said to stand for the two swords of miri and piri. The demolition of 1986 removed most of the old wall paintings and inlay work, and conservators have criticised the synthetic colours and methods used in the present building.
akathist: The Akathist is also known by the first words of its opening verse, Tēi hypermáchōi stratēgōi, "To you, invincible champion", addressed to Mary. It is the akathist par excellence, written for the feast of the Annunciation on 25 March. It was traditionally attributed to Romanos the Melodist, but recent scholarship rejects this, as it does for many other kontakia of the core repertoire.

Tradition links the feast to 626, when Constantinople, under Heraclius, was attacked by the Persians and Avars and was said to be saved through the intervention of the Theotokos. Sophocles disputed this origin, since the hymn could not have been composed in a day and its twenty-four oikoi contain no allusion to such an event. Authorship has also been given to Patriarch Sergius I of Constantinople and to George Pisida, but no certain ascription can be made. Under the influence of Leena Peltomaa's work, many scholars now favour a date in the 5th century or the early 6th.

The Greek original consists of twenty-four oikoi, each beginning with the next letter of the alphabet, so that the hymn forms an acrostic. Twelve oikoi are long and twelve short. A long oikos has a seven-line stanza followed by six couplets that begin with the greeting Chaire, "Rejoice", and end with the refrain "Rejoice, Bride without bridegroom!". A short oikos ends with Alleluia. The series of greetings are called chairetismoi.

The hymn is divided into thirteen parts, each made up of a kontakion and an oikos. Its four sections correspond to the themes of the Annunciation, the Nativity, Christ and the Theotokos herself. The final kontakion addresses Mary as the saviour of Constantinople in the siege of 626.

Besides its dedication to the menaion, the Akathist had the political function of celebrating military victories and asking for divine protection in war. Since the 14th century it has belonged to the moveable cycle of the triodion, and the whole hymn is sung in four sections through Lent, in the service of the Salutations to the Theotokos on the first four Friday evenings of Great Lent. The entire hymn is sung on the fifth Friday, and the fifth Saturday, known as the Saturday of the Akathist, takes its name from it. In monasteries of the Athonite tradition it is often sung nightly at Compline.

Newer akathists to saints, mostly pastiches of the original, developed in the Slavic traditions. In the Greek, Arabic and Russian Old Rite traditions only the original may be used in formal liturgy. The Enchiridion Indulgentiarum of 2004 confirmed a plenary indulgence for reciting it piously. Three icons on Mount Athos, at Dionysiou, Hilandar and Zographou, bear the title Akathist.
akbar: Jalal ud-din Muhammad Akbar was born on 15 October 1542 at the Rajput fortress of Amarkot, in what is now Sindh, where his parents had been given refuge by the local Hindu ruler Rana Prasad. His father, Humayun, had been defeated by the forces of Sher Shah Suri at Chausa in 1539 and at Kannauj in 1540 and had fled westward. Akbar succeeded Humayun under a regent, Bairam Khan, who helped the young emperor expand and consolidate Mughal domains. In 1560, at the age of eighteen, Akbar dismissed Bairam Khan and ordered him to leave on the Hajj.

Mughal rule was still precarious when Akbar took the throne, as the Surs had reconquered Agra and Delhi. Having established Mughal rule over northern India, he turned to Rajputana, and from 1561 the Mughals engaged the Rajputs in warfare and diplomacy. Most Rajput states accepted his suzerainty, though Mewar and Marwar stayed outside it. He then conquered Gujarat and Bengal, and from 1593 he campaigned against the Deccan Sultans, taking Asirgarh Fort on 17 January 1601. At his death the empire stretched from the Bay of Bengal to Kandahar and Badakhshan.

Akbar organised his army and nobility through the mansabdari system, which assigned each officer a rank and a number of cavalry to supply, in 33 classes. In 1580 he replaced a system of annual assessment with the dahsala, which took one-third of the average produce of the previous ten years, paid in cash. He abolished the sectarian tax, appointed non-Muslims to high posts and married Rajput princesses, treating their families as equals, though some Rajputs saw marriage to Akbar as humiliation. Under him the economy of Mughal India tripled in size and wealth.

He built a new walled capital at Fatehpur Sikri from 1569, moved the capital to Lahore in 1585 and back to Agra in 1599. In 1575 he built the Ibadat Khana at Fatehpur Sikri, where discussions that began among Muslims were opened to people of all religions. Disillusioned with orthodox Islam, he promulgated Din-i Ilahi, a syncretic creed drawn mainly from Islam and Hinduism. His court historian Abul Fazl chronicled the reign in the Akbarnama.

Akbar fell ill with dysentery on 3 October 1605 and never recovered. He is buried in his mausoleum at Sikandra, Agra, next to the tomb of his favourite consort, Mariam-uz-Zamani. His son Prince Salim, later Jahangir, succeeded him. Akbar firmly entrenched the authority of the Mughal Empire after the Afghans had threatened it in his father's reign, and folk tales about him and his courtier Birbal remain popular in India.
akechi-mitsuhide: Akechi Mitsuhide is believed to have been born on 10 March 1528 at Tara Castle in Mino Province. Genealogies of the Edo period make his family a branch of the Toki clan and name his father as Akechi Mitsutsuna, but no primary sources support this, and historians such as Kuwata Tadachika suspect he came from a lower branch of the Akechi. He was reputedly raised as a general by Saitō Dōsan, and when Dōsan's son Saitō Yoshitatsu rebelled in 1556 Mitsuhide sided with Dōsan. He later served the wandering shōgun Ashikaga Yoshiaki, and when Yoshiaki's request to Asakura Yoshikage was declined, Mitsuhide suggested Oda Nobunaga.

In November 1568 Nobunaga, Yoshiaki and Mitsuhide entered Kyoto. In January 1569 Mitsuhide and Hosokawa Fujitaka defended the shōgun against an attack by the Miyoshi clan, and he was soon one of the magistrates managing Kyoto's government under Nobunaga. After Yoshiaki raised a coalition against Nobunaga in 1573, Mitsuhide fought for Nobunaga as a direct vassal. In 1575 Nobunaga sent him to take control of Tanba Province, where the Akai clan resisted him at Kuroi Castle, and in 1578 he defeated them and the Hatano clan. Nobunaga rewarded him with Kameyama Castle and Tanba, with revenue of 550,000 koku. In 1580 Mitsuhide replaced Sakuma Nobumori and came to command the largest force in the Kinki area.

In 1582 Nobunaga ordered him west to assist Hashiba Hideyoshi against the Mōri. Mitsuhide instead assembled an army of 13,000 and surrounded Nobunaga at Honnō-ji, which was set on fire. Nobunaga was killed either in the fighting or by his own hand, and his son Oda Nobutada was killed at Nijō Shin Gosho. The reasons for the rebellion are unknown. Neither body was found, and Hideyoshi spread word that Nobunaga had escaped, so most of Nobunaga's vassals and allies would not join Mitsuhide.

Hideyoshi made peace with the Mōri and marched back with, among others, Tokugawa Ieyasu to avenge Nobunaga. The two armies met at the Battle of Yamazaki on 2 July 1582, where Mitsuhide had about 10,000 men to Hideyoshi's 20,000. Hideyoshi took the heights of Tennōzan, and the Akechi army broke after two hours. The bandit leader Nakamura Chōbei killed Mitsuhide as he fled. His short rule gave rise to the set phrase mikkatenka, a short-lived reign. A legend in Yamagata says he survived, but the historian Watanabe Daimon says there is no evidence for it.
akershus-fortress: Akershus Fortress stands on the banks of the Oslofjord, and its closeness to the sea mattered because most Norwegian commerce of the period went by water. Its construction is thought to have followed an attack on Oslo in 1287 by the nobleman Earl Alv Erlingsson of Sarpsborg, which showed that the city's existing defences were weak. Building probably began in the late 1290s under King Haakon V, and the castle replaced Tønsberg as one of the two most important Norwegian castles of the time, the other being Båhus. It is first mentioned in a letter of 1300 from Haakon to a church in Oslo.

The fortress was first tested in 1308, when the Swedish duke Erik Magnusson besieged it and a local Norwegian army broke the siege. Later sieges came in 1449 to 1450 under King Karl Knutsson Bonde, in 1502 when Scottish soldiers serving the Danish-Norwegian king attacked Knut Alvsson, and in 1523 when the townspeople under Hans Mule burned their own houses to drive out Swedish troops. A siege by Christian II in 1531 to 1532 was lifted by forces from Denmark and Lübeck, after which the castle was strengthened. In 1567 Christen Munk burned the city to deny supplies to the Swedes, and Charles XII failed to take the fortress in 1716.

Haakon V gradually made the castle a residence, and it helped to shift the capital from Bergen to Oslo. Olaf II was born there in 1370. After the great fire of 1624 Christian IV ordered Oslo rebuilt nearer the fortress as Christiania, and the castle was remodelled as a Renaissance castle with Italian inspired bastions. It served mainly as a palace until the turn of the 19th century. A section called Slaveriet held prisoners who could be rented out for work in the city, among them the rebels of the 1852 Sámi revolt at Guovdageaidnu. In 1940 it surrendered to Germany without a fight, and was handed to the resistance on 11 May 1945. Vidkun Quisling was executed there after the war.

The fortress is still a military area but is open to the public daily. It holds the Armed Forces Museum, Norway's Resistance Museum and the Prison Museum, and the headquarters of the Ministry of Defence and the Defence Staff lie in its eastern part. The castle is used for official dinners for dignitaries and foreign heads of state. Its Royal Mausoleum holds the burials of Haakon V, Queen Euphemia, Haakon VII, Queen Maud, Olav V and Harald V among others.
akhaltsikhe: Akhaltsikhe lies in the Akhaltsikhe Basin at an elevation of about 1,000 metres, on both banks of the small river Potskhovi, a left tributary of the Kura, which divides the old city in the north from the new in the south. Its Georgian name means new fortress. Before the 12th century the settlement was called Lomsia, a name preserved into the medieval period by Armenians and Persians, and the change to Akhaltsikhe is associated with a new citadel built under the House of Jaqeli. Arabic sources give the name as Akhiskha, Persian ones as Akhesqeh and Turkish ones as Ahıska.

Human habitation in the area is attested from the Early Bronze Age. At Amiranis Gora, on the north-eastern outskirts, the earliest carbon date, 3790–3373 BCE, comes from a metallurgical workshop, and the site is one of the best with fixed stratigraphy for the Kura–Araxes culture. The town is mentioned among the places conquered by the general Habib ibn Maslama al-Fihri under the Umayyad caliph Mu'awiya I (661–680). During the Mongol domination of Georgia, the Jaqeli rulers of the principality of Samtskhe-Saatabago were given the title of atabeg and allowed autonomy.

The Ottomans took the town in 1579 during the Ottoman–Safavid War of 1578–1590 and spread Islam and Ottoman customs. In the early 17th century it became the centre of the Akhalzik Eyalet, known as Ahıska, with a resident pasha, and it became a leading hub of the Caucasian slave market. By the late 17th century it had 400 households of Turks, Armenians, Georgians, Greeks and Jews. Russian troops under General Ivan Paskevich captured it in 1828, and the Treaty of Adrianople of 1829 ceded it to the Russian Empire. Meskhetian Turks, who use the name Ahıska for their homeland, were deported by the Soviet authorities in November 1944.

Akhaltsikhe is the administrative centre of the Samtskhe–Javakheti region of southwestern Georgia. The 9th-century Akhaltsikhe Castle, called Rabati, stands in the old town and holds an Orthodox church, a mosque and a madrasa within a single walled enclosure. Jews have lived in the town since antiquity by local tradition; the community numbered over 3,500 at its largest in 1915, and most emigrated to Israel in the second half of the 20th century. Two historic synagogues remain.
akhenaten: Akhenaten was born Amenhotep IV, a younger son of the pharaoh Amenhotep III and his principal wife, Tiye. His elder brother, the crown prince Thutmose, was recognised as heir, but Thutmose's early death, perhaps around the 30th regnal year of Amenhotep III, left Amenhotep IV next in line. Little is known of his youth. Donald Redford dates his birth to c. 1363–1361 BCE, and the only certain servant of the prince is Parennefer, whose tomb mentions him.

He married Nefertiti, his Great Royal Wife, at a date that is not known. A secondary wife, Kiya, is also attested. He had seven attested daughters, six of them by Nefertiti, among them Meritaten and Ankhesenamun. Tutankhamun was his son-in-law and is considered likely to have been his son as well.

Amenhotep IV took the throne most likely in 1353 or 1351 BCE, at an age estimated anywhere from 10 to 23. Scholars disagree whether he shared power with his father for up to 12 years or not at all. Eric Cline, Nicholas Reeves and Peter Dorman argue for no coregency or one of at most two years, while Donald Redford and others reject any. In the fifth year of his reign he changed his name to Akhenaten, meaning 'Effective for the Aten'.

Worship of the sun had grown under the Eighteenth Dynasty, and Amenhotep III had given the Aten royal patronage, but he still devoted himself chiefly to Amun-Ra. Redford traced three stages in Atenism. In the first the disc still rested on the head of the falcon-headed Ra-Horakhty. In the second the Aten was raised above other gods and its name was placed in cartouches. In the last it was shown as a disc whose rays end in human hands. Egyptologists differ on whether the religion was monotheistic, monolatristic or henotheistic.

Amarna art, which flourished under Akhenaten and his immediate successors, is more naturalistic and shows more movement than traditional Egyptian art. Akhenaten himself is drawn with a sagging stomach, broad hips, thin legs and a long face. Some have argued that this reflects a medical condition, but Dominic Montserrat reports a broad consensus among Egyptologists that the forms are not to be read literally, and suggests they made the king a symbol of the androgyny of the Aten.

After his death his monuments were dismantled and hidden, his statues destroyed and his name left out of later lists of rulers, and traditional worship was gradually restored, notably under Tutankhamun. Later rulers called him 'the enemy' or 'that criminal'. He was almost lost to history until the late 19th-century discovery of Amarna, the city he built. A mummy found in tomb KV55 in 1907 may be his, although its identification has been questioned.
akhetaten: Amarna lies on the east bank of the Nile in the Egyptian province of Minya, about 58 kilometres south of al-Minya and 402 kilometres north of Luxor, the site of the previous capital, Thebes. The name Amarna comes from the Beni Amran, an Arab tribe that settled the area before the 18th century; the ancient name Akhetaten means the horizon of the Aten. The ruins are laid out north to south along a Royal Road. The royal residences lay mostly in the North City, the central city held the Great Temple of the Aten, the Great Royal Palace and the Bureau of Correspondence of Pharaoh, and the south held residential suburbs with the estates of nobles and the workshop of the sculptor Thutmose.

The city was built at the direction of the Pharaoh Akhenaten on a site that was effectively virgin, as a capital dedicated to the worship of the Aten. Construction began in or around Year 5 of his reign (1346 BCE) and was probably completed by Year 9, although it became the capital two years earlier. Most buildings were of whitewashed mudbrick, with the most important faced in local stone. Fourteen boundary stelae, thirteen of them known, ring the city and record Akhenaten's conditions for its foundation, including his wish to be buried there.

After Akhenaten's death in 1332 BCE the royal government of Tutankhamun left for Thebes, and the city was abandoned almost completely, though it seems to have remained active for a decade or so and a shrine to Horemheb shows partial occupation early in his reign. It stayed uninhabited until Roman settlement began along the Nile. Excavation has shown that gods such as Bes and Taweret were worshipped there despite the Aten cult. In 1887 a local woman digging for sebakh found over 300 cuneiform tablets, the Amarna Letters, mostly in Akkadian, the diplomatic language of the Late Bronze Age. The city's art broke with Egyptian convention, showing informal scenes of the royal family and more realistic figures.

Because the city was left almost intact, Amarna preserves great detail of its internal plan, though it is questionable how representative it is of ancient Egyptian cities. The French priest Claude Sicard first described it in 1714, and Napoleon's scholars made the first detailed map in 1798-1799. Flinders Petrie worked there in 1891-1892, and a German expedition under Ludwig Borchardt found the bust of Nefertiti in Thutmose's workshop in 1912; it is now in Berlin's Neues Museum. Excavation by the Amarna Project continues.
akhmat-khan: Ahmed was a son of Küchük Muhammad and descended from Genghis Khan through Jochi and Orda Khan. In the 1460s he ruled jointly with his brothers, and in 1465 he seized power in the Horde by rising against his brother Mahmud bin Küchük, who had ruled it since 1459. His wife was the Timurid princess Badi' al-Jamal, a sister of Sultan Husayn Bayqara of Khorasan.

Ahmed tried to bring the former subjects of the Golden Horde, the Russians and Uzbeks among them, back under his rule and so reunite the realm. When the Polish and Lithuanian ruler Casimir IV refused an alliance against the Ottomans, he had to negotiate with the Ottoman sultan Mehmet II. His nephew won the throne of Crimea in 1476 but lost it within two years to Meñli I Giray, an ally of the Ottomans.

Ivan III, grand prince of Moscow, had refused to pay tribute since the start of his reign in 1462 and was beginning to unify the Russian principalities. Ahmed led several expeditions against him, and when his tax collectors were again turned away in 1479 he prepared for war in concert with Casimir. From spring to autumn 1480 his army stood on the banks of the Ugra River, about 240 km south of Moscow, in what became known as the Great Stand on the Ugra, waiting for Lithuanian reinforcements that never came.

In November 1480 Ahmed withdrew on news that Russian princes had risen against Casimir and were moving towards Sarai, and he lost the support of his forces. The Shaybanid ruler of Siberia, Ibak Khan, took the chance to attack the Great Horde, and Ahmed was killed in battle in January 1481. He had two sons, Mahmud Khan and Bahadur Khan, and a daughter, Khanzada Khanum, with Badi' al-Jamal, who eventually left the Horde and took the children to her brother's court at Herat.
akhmet-baitursynov: Baitursynov was born into a Muslim Kazakh family in what is now the Kostanay Region of Kazakhstan. When he was 13, police officers led by a Colonel Yakovlev staged a pogrom in his village; his father, Baitursyn Shoshak-uly, and three of his brothers beat the colonel and were sent to Siberia for 15 years. He learned to read Kazakh, Persian, Ottoman Turkish and Arabic from village mullahs, studied Russian at the Turgai Russian-Kazakh School and graduated in 1895 from the teachers' school in Orenburg founded by Ibrahim Altynsarin.

He then taught in village schools in the Aktyubinsk, Kostanay and Karkaraly regions. In Kostanay he married Alexandra Ivanovna, the daughter of a Russian forester, who converted to Islam and took the name Badrisafa Muhammetsadikova Baitursynova.

In 1905 he helped form the Kazakh wing of the Constitutional Democrat Party and was one of the authors of the Karkaraly Petition, which asked for an end to the expropriation of Kazakh land and to the flow of settlers. He was imprisoned in 1907 for criticising the Tsarist administration and again in 1909, for eight months without trial, in Semipalatinsk, after which he moved to Orenburg.

There he published the political work Masa (Mosquito) in 1911, translated the fables of Ivan Krylov and in 1913 founded Qazaq with Alihan Bökeyhan and Mirjaqıp Dulatulı. In 1912 he reformed the Arabic script for Kazakh, dropping letters the language did not use and adding its own sounds; the result, Töte jazu, is still used by Kazakhs in China, Afghanistan and Iran. After the revolution of 1917 he was elected to the Constituent Assembly for Turgai. Amnestied on 4 April 1919, he joined the Bolshevik party and, as Commissioner of Enlightenment of the Kazakh Krai, helped reform education and found the first university of the Kazakh SSR.

The NKVD arrested him in June 1929 and sent him to prison in Kyzyl-Orda and then to the Arkhangelsk region; he was released in 1934 at the request of Yekaterina Peshkova of the Red Cross Commission. Arrested again in October 1937 for bourgeois nationalist sentiments, he was executed on 8 December. In Kazakhstan he is regarded as a national hero for his work for literacy; a home museum in Alma-Ata, statues in Kostanay and Astana and a monument and park in Ankara commemorate him, and UNESCO marked the 150th anniversary of his birth.
akhmim: Akhmim lies on the east bank of the Nile in Upper Egypt, 6 kilometres north-east of Sohag. The ancient Greeks called it Khemmis or Chemmis and Panopolis. In ancient Egypt it was known as Ipu, Apu or Khent-min, and it was the capital of the ninth nome of Upper Egypt. It is the largest town on the east side of the Nile in Sohag Governorate, and its climate is hot desert.

The god Min, whom the Greeks identified with Pan, was worshipped here as the strong Horus. Herodotus mentions a temple of Perseus at Chemmis and says that games were held there in his honour, though he may have confused the place with Coptos. Strabo names linen-weaving and stone-cutting as ancient industries, and the cemetery of Akhmim is one of the chief sources of the textiles of the Roman and Christian ages. The city is a suggested hometown of Yuya, an official of Tuthmosis IV and Amenhotep III, and the parents of Queen Tiye are associated with it.

Monasteries abounded in the region from an early date. Pachomius the Great founded a monastery known as Tkahshmin in the area, and Shenouda the Archimandrite was a monk at nearby Athribis. Nestorius, the exiled former patriarch of Constantinople, died in the neighbourhood. The Greek poet Nonnus was born at Panopolis at the end of the 4th century, and the alchemist Zosimos of Panopolis is placed in the 3rd or 4th century. Excavations have yielded Christian manuscripts, among them fragments of the Book of Henoch and of the Apocalypse of Peter. A grand temple still stood in the 13th century CE, but the temples were later dismantled and their stone reused.

Little of the ancient town survives. The destroyed corner of a Greco-Roman temple with colossal statues of Ramesses II and Meritamen was found in 1981, and the extensive cemeteries remain to be fully explored. Akhmim has several mosques and two Coptic churches, and the Monastery of the Martyrs lies about 6 kilometres north-east of the city. It keeps a weekly market and has long manufactured cotton goods.
akhnoor: Akhnoor is a town and municipal committee in the Jammu district of the union territory of Jammu and Kashmir, near the city of Jammu. It stands on the right bank of the Chenab River, just before the river enters the Pakistani Punjab, and its border location gives it strategic significance. The Shiwaliks, the Kali Dhar and the Trikuta range surround it on the north and east, and it lies on National Highway 144A between Jammu and Poonch. The average elevation is 301 metres.

Excavations by the Archaeological Survey of India established that Akhnoor was one of the last bastions of the Indus Valley civilisation and that Manda, at Akhnoor, is its northernmost site, where terracotta figures of the later Indus period were found. Some believe the place is the ancient Virat Nagar of the Mahabharata, though Bairat in Rajasthan is better established as that city.

Excavations at the Ambaran-Pamberwan sites showed that the area was a prominent centre of Buddhism in the Kushan and Gupta periods. They yielded an eight-spoke stupa of baked bricks with stone pathways and meditation cells, life-sized terracotta busts of the Buddha, coins and silver caskets. The stupas lie on the ancient routes from Pataliputra, now Patna, to Taxila. The Chumb-Jourian-Akhnoor sector was the setting of Operation Grand Slam.

Tradition says the Mughal emperor Jahangir named the town: his eyes were infected on his return from Kashmir, the fresh air blowing over the Chenab cured them, and he called it Aankho-ka-Noor, light of the eyes. The town's official site gives another account, in which an emperor's wife washed her eyes with the Chenab's water on a Hindu priest's advice and regained her sight. The 2011 census counted 11,225 people, and the town is governed by a municipal committee of 13 wards. Dogri is the main language, and Hinduism is the largest religion.
akim-oda: Akim Oda lies in the south of Ghana, surrounded by rain forest, in the basin of the Birim River, which flows through the town and is rich in gold and diamonds. The climate is semi-equatorial and wet. Rain falls heavily from April to June and again from September to November, and a dry season, with markedly lower temperatures, lasts from December to February. The town is the capital of the Birim Central Municipal District and had 60,604 residents as of 2013.

Cocoa is grown on formal and informal plantations, sometimes along the roads; the harvested beans are dried and kept in warehouses until they are shipped. North of the Birim there are palm oil plantations covering roughly 6,000 hectares, most of them small and independently owned, and bamboo is also cultivated. Local miners take gold and diamonds from the river bank by traditional methods, often with simple tools.

The forests near the town are cut for timber. Ghana's forest cover shrank from 8.2 million hectares in 1900 to 1.6 million in 2000, and forest plantations are being established near Akim Oda under the National Forest Plantation Development Program. Visitors are shown a tree described as the largest in West Africa, 12 metres in circumference and 66.5 metres high, and may see the mining from dug-out boats and ceremonies with Akan drumming.

The Akim Oda Government Hospital serves the Kotoku traditional area and takes referrals from nearby communities in the Akyem states; private hospitals in the town also serve Akyem Bosome and part of the Abuakwa traditional area. The public sector has more than fifteen primary and junior high schools and three senior high schools, and four radio stations broadcast from the town.
akita-prefecture: Akita Prefecture lies on the north-western side of Honshu, in the Tōhoku region, on the coast of the Sea of Japan. It borders Aomori Prefecture to the north, Iwate to the east, Miyagi to the southeast and Yamagata to the south. Its borders roughly form a rectangle 169 kilometres from north to south and 86 kilometres from west to east, covering 11,637 square kilometres. The Oga Peninsula is a prominent feature of the western edge, the Ōu Mountains, the longest range in Japan, mark the eastern border, and the higher Dewa Mountains run through the centre. Winters are cold, especially away from the sea.

The region was created from the ancient provinces of Dewa and Mutsu. Separated from the main centres of Japanese commerce, politics and population by several hundred kilometres and by mountain ranges, Akita remained largely isolated from Japanese society until after the year 600, and was a region of hunter-gatherers and principally nomadic tribes. The first historical record dates to 658, when Abe no Hirafu, governor of Koshi Province, conquered the native Ezo tribes at what are now the cities of Akita and Noshiro and built a fort on the Mogami River, which began Japanese settlement.

In 733 a new military settlement, later renamed Akita Castle, was built in what is now the Takashimizu area of Akita. The region served as a base from which the Japanese empire drove the Ezo people from northern Honshu. Under the Tokugawa shogunate it was given to the Satake clan, who ruled it for 260 years and developed the agriculture and mining that remain important. In 1871, during the Meiji Restoration, Dewa Province was reshaped and the old daimyō domains were abolished, which produced the modern borders of Akita.

The city of Akita is the capital and largest city, and Yokote, Daisen and Yurihonjō are other major cities. The economy has long rested on agriculture, fishing and forestry, and the prefecture is known for rice and sake. Population has declined since 1955. Kakunodate preserves many samurai houses, among them the former home of Odano Naotake, who illustrated Japan's first modern guide to human anatomy. The Namahage ritual in Oga on New Year's Eve and the Akita Kantō festival in August are among its best-known customs.
akitu: Akitu, Sumerian a-ki-ti and Akkadian akītu, was a spring festival held in the month of Nisan to celebrate the sowing of barley, and it grew out of the Sumerian spring New Year festival of Zagmuk. At Babylon the whole city took part: the awilu, the upper class, the muskena, the middle class, and the wardu, the lower class, along with the high priest and the king. Each day the priest of Ésagila, Marduk's house, went to the temple to beg the god's forgiveness and protection for Babylon in a prayer known as the Secret of Ésagila.

The early days were given to prayers of lament expressing humanity's fear of the unknown; on the second the high priest bathed in the Euphrates, and on the third craftsmen made two figures of wood, gold and precious stones, dressed in red, and the king brought a statue of Nabu, son of Marduk, into the temple. On the fourth day the priests recited creation stories while the people sang and danced. On the fifth the king was brought into the temple to show humility before the gods; the high priest struck him, and the king's tears were taken as a good omen for the year.

On the sixth day the figures were burned amid mock battles, a commotion signifying that without Marduk the city would fall into chaos. Marduk was said to vanish on the seventh day to fight the goddess Tiamat, and Nabu and other gods went out to free him from a prison in the mountains. On the eighth the gods gave their power to Marduk, on the ninth a great procession was held with the king and the gods, and on the tenth Marduk marked his victory and performed a ritual marriage for the fertility of the land. On the eleventh the gods met in the Hall of Destinies to decide the fate of the people, and on the last day they returned to the temple.

After the destruction of Babylon the festival was adopted in the Neo-Assyrian Empire: Sennacherib built an Akitu house outside the walls of Assur in 683 BCE, and another stood outside Nineveh. It continued through the Seleucid Empire and into the Roman period, and early in the 3rd century it was still held at Emessa in Syria for the god Elagabal, and the Roman emperor Elagabalus, who was of Syrian origin, introduced it in Italy. Assyrians revived it in the 1960s, and since the 1990s it has been observed openly on 1 April with parades, picnics and traditional dress, in Iraq and in the diaspora.
akkadian-empire: The Akkadian Empire takes its name from the city and region of Akkad, near the confluence of the Tigris and Euphrates. The city has not yet been identified on the ground, but it is known from textual sources, at least one of them older than Sargon's reign. The period is generally dated to 2334–2154 BCE by the middle chronology; the short-chronology dates of 2270–2083 BCE are now considered less likely. It followed the Early Dynastic Period and was succeeded by the Ur III Period, though both transitions are blurry.

Its founder, Sargon, was a usurper, and he is not known to have had a father or predecessor on the throne of Akkad, until then a marginal city. Later texts make it hard to separate legend from reality. Some historians, drawing on a late legend, suggest he rebelled against Ur-Zababa of Kish, but this is hypothetical. He then faced Lugal-zage-si of Uruk, the most powerful king in the south, and according to copies of his inscriptions defeated him around 2300 BCE. Lugal-zage-si was captured, made to wear a yoke and paraded at Nippur.

Sargon installed loyal governors in several Sumerian cities and so created a kingdom covering all of southern Mesopotamia, with Akkad as its capital. His influence is said to have stretched from the Mediterranean to Iran, and expeditions went as far as Dilmun and Magan. His sons Rimush and Manishtushu struggled to keep control, and both may have died violently. Sargon's grandson Naram-Sin called himself King of the Four Quarters and had himself called god of Akkad, with a cult in his honour, though whether he was considered a full deity is debated.

Naram-Sin's successors were weaker. The empire collapsed, probably through a combination of internal unrest, severe environmental and economic stress from a drought associated with the 4.2-kiloyear climate event, and threats from the Gutians, Amorites and Elamites.

The Akkadian language became the empire's lingua franca, while Sumerian stayed important in religion and literature. The kings had their exploits written in long inscriptions on stelae and statues, and their royal art, with a more naturalistic sculpture centred on the king, had a lasting influence on Mesopotamian art. Enheduanna, Sargon's daughter, served as high priestess and is often recognised as the first known named author in history. The kingdom of the Third Dynasty of Ur stood in the tradition of the first empire. Later, Sargon became the example to follow and Naram-Sin the example to avoid, and several rulers took the title King of Akkad.
akkadian-language: Akkadian is an East Semitic language attested in ancient Mesopotamia from the mid-third millennium BCE. It is the earliest documented Semitic language and is named after the city of Akkad, a major centre during the Akkadian Empire (c. 2334–2154 BCE). Akkadian names appear in Sumerian texts from the mid-3rd millennium BCE, and texts fully in Akkadian begin to appear from about the 24th century BCE.

It was written in cuneiform, adopted from the Sumerians. Sargon of Akkad's empire introduced Akkadian as a written language by adapting Sumerian cuneiform. In the Middle Bronze Age it virtually displaced Sumerian, assumed to have been extinct as a living language by the 18th century BCE. By the 20th century BCE two forms were in use, Assyrian and Babylonian.

Akkadian is a fusional language with grammatical case, and like other Semitic languages it builds words on consonantal roots, most of them of three consonants. It has three cases and three numbers, though the dual is vestigial. Unlike most Semitic languages it uses subject–object–verb word order. Sumerian influenced its phonology, vocabulary and syntax, and scholars describe the two languages as a sprachbund.

Cuneiform suited it poorly, since it could not represent the glottal stop, the pharyngeals and the emphatic consonants. Scribes used signs as Sumerian logograms, Sumerian syllables or Akkadian syllables. The sign AN, for example, can stand for ilum ('god'), for the god Anu or for the syllable -an-.

In its Assyrian and Babylonian forms Akkadian was the native language of the Mesopotamian empires through the later Bronze Age and became the lingua franca of much of the Ancient Near East by the time of the Bronze Age collapse c. 1150 BCE. It declined under the Neo-Assyrian Empire, by about the 8th century BCE, in favour of Old Aramaic. By the Hellenistic period only scholars and priests in the temples used it, and the last known Akkadian cuneiform document dates from the 1st century CE.

Hundreds of thousands of texts and fragments survive, including religious narrative, legal and scientific works and letters. Literary works include the Atrahasis Epic, the Enûma Elish, the Amarna letters and the Epic of Gilgamesh. The Chicago Assyrian Dictionary, in 21 volumes, was begun in 1921 and completed in 2011.
akkar: Akkar District is the only district of the Akkar Governorate in Lebanon, with which it is coextensive, and covers 788 square kilometres. Its capital is Halba, and the largest cities are Halba, Bire Akkar and Al-Qoubaiyat. It has a relatively large coastal plain with high mountains to the east, and is divided into seven parts: Qaitea, Jouma, Dreib, Jabal Akroum, Wadi Khaled, Cheft and As-Sahel. The plain is the region's agricultural wealth, and Akkar is strategically important as the northern gateway into Syria.

Akkar has many important Roman and Arabic archaeological sites. The Tell of Arqa near Miniara is the birthplace of the Roman emperor Severus Alexander, who died in 235, and several prehistoric sites in the foothills have been suggested as used by the Heavy Neolithic Qaraoun culture.

The Al Merehb family, of sharifian lineage, exercised political and military influence over the territory after its arrival in the early 18th century, until the end of the Ottoman Empire. In the 1970s the peasants of Akkar formed an alliance against the landowners, in a system where 3 per cent of the population held about 73 per cent of the land. They were led by Khalid Saghiya, a Syrian Baathist lawyer from Baynu. After Black September in Jordan firearms were available to all and the revolt escalated, and Syria's involvement and the diverse population produced many rivalries.

The UNHCR estimated the population of the district at 389,899 in 2015, including 106,935 registered Syrian refugees and 19,404 Palestinian refugees. The region is home to the second-largest population of Alawites in Lebanon, and Lebanese Turks form a majority in Kouachra and Aydamun.
akrotiri-prehistoric-city: Akrotiri is a Cycladic Bronze Age settlement on the volcanic Greek island of Santorini. It takes its name from the nearby village of Akrotiri, and the name by which it was known in antiquity is unknown. Although it was a Cycladic settlement, it is associated with the Minoan civilization because of inscriptions in Linear A and close similarities in artefacts and fresco styles.

The earliest evidence of habitation dates to the fifth millennium BCE, when Akrotiri was a small fishing and farming village. By the end of the third millennium BCE it had grown significantly, helped by trade with other Aegean cultures, shown by fragments of foreign pottery. It lay on the main sailing route between Cyprus and Minoan Crete, which made it a point in the copper trade and a centre for processing copper, as moulds and crucibles show. Paved streets, an extensive drainage system and high-quality pottery point to its sophistication.

The settlement was buried by the eruption of Thera, an event dated by radiocarbon most probably between 1620 and 1530 BCE, while similarities of material culture elsewhere in the Aegean suggest 1570 to 1500 BCE. Tree rings show unusual growth in 1597, 1560, 1546 and 1544 BCE. Only a single gold object has been found, hidden beneath flooring, and no unburied human remains, which indicates an orderly evacuation with little or no loss of life.

The French geologist F. Fouque carried out the first excavations on Santorini in 1867, after local people found old artefacts at a quarry. Spyridon Marinatos began the extensive modern excavation in 1967, and within hours the remains of the buried city appeared. Many buildings stood more than one storey high, and he abandoned an experiment with tunnelling into the pumice. Christos Doumas took over as head of excavations in 1975.

The frescoes are especially important for the study of Minoan art because they are far better preserved than the fragments from Knossos and other sites on Crete. The Blue Monkeys fresco was found in 1969, and the Spring Fresco in 1970, the first to be found perfectly preserved in its original position. The plaster-of-Paris casts made in cavities left by decayed wooden furniture preserved beds, tables and stools. A deposit of between 300 and 500 horns was found in the House of the Benches, and their purpose is unknown. A roof built to protect the site collapsed in 2005, killing one visitor, and the site stayed closed until April 2012. Excavations paused from 2005 to 2016 for lack of funding.
aksaray: Aksaray stands in the Central Anatolia region of Turkey, at an average elevation of 980 metres, with the Melendiz river running through it. Mount Hasan rises to 3,268 metres. The city was an important stopover on the Silk Road across Anatolia for centuries. Its name means white palace in Turkish. In antiquity the area was called Archelais Garsaura, which became Taksara under the Seljuks and then Aksaray.

Ancient Hittite texts first mention the place as Šinaḫuttum or Šinuhtu. The Aksaray Stela, written in Luwian hieroglyphs, was dedicated by a king named Kiyakiyas, who described his prosperity and the benevolence of the weather god Tarhunzas. He may be the king Kiyakki of Šinuḫtu who ruled before 718 BCE, when the Neo-Assyrian king Sargon II took the city and deported him.

The Hittite name Kurşaura became Garsaura, which Strabo mentions. Archelaus of Cappadocia, the last Cappadocian king, renamed the town Archelaïs, and in Roman times it was a colony and a bishopric. Its bishops attended councils from Nicaea in 325 to the Trullan Council of 692.

In Byzantine times, as Koloneia, it was an important military centre. Between 1081 and 1084 it formed part of the domain of Suleiman ibn Qutalmish, and later of the Sultanate of Rum, whose sultans left important landmarks in and around the town. Ibn Battuta, who visited in the 14th century, called it a beautiful city surrounded by waterways and gardens, with water brought to the houses, and noted its class of Muslim traders.

The Mongols raided it in 1277 and killed or enslaved 6,000 of its people. İshak Pasha incorporated it into the Ottoman Empire in 1470 after a long struggle against the Karamanids, and many inhabitants were moved to Constantinople, where a district also came to be named Aksaray. The nearby Lake Tuz, the main source of salt for Anatolia, helped the town to prosper.

Aksaray is the seat of Aksaray Province, with 247,147 inhabitants in 2021. The Red Minaret Mosque has a Seljuk minaret of 1236 from the reign of Aläettin Keykubat, and the Zincirye Medresesi, a Koranic school built by the bey of Karaman in 1345, now serves as the local library. The Aksaray Grand Mosque dates from 1408-09 and the Karamanoğlu dynasty, and the Hakiki Yusuf Baba complex holds the tombs of the 14th-century Somuncu Baba and the scholar Cemaleddin'i Aksaray.
aksehir: Philomelion was probably a Pergamene foundation on the great Graeco-Roman highway from Ephesus to the east. Cicero, on his way to Cilicia, dated some of his extant correspondence there. Saint Paul passed the city on his second and third missionary journeys in the first century, and numerous Christian inscriptions in the region trace his impact. The Smyrniotes wrote the letter describing the martyrdom of Polycarp to the townspeople of Philomelion. The town became a bishopric and remains a titular see of the Catholic Church.

After 1071 the city fell to the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum. Forces of the First Crusade retook it, and in 1098 Stephen of Blois met the emperor Alexios I Komnenos there and persuaded him not to continue his march to Antioch. Alexios conquered it in 1116 and returned with many Greek refugees to Byzantine lands. In 1146 the emperor Manuel I Komnenos took the town after defeating the forces of the Sultanate of Rum at Akroinon, burned it, released prisoners held there, and moved its population to Pylae. German members of the Third Crusade took it in 1190, and Kaykhusraw I rebuilt it in 1196 and resettled it with Greek captives from a raid on Caria.

It became an important Seljuk town and late in the 14th century passed into Ottoman hands. With Beyshehir it formed the border between the Ottomans and the Karamanid beylik, and the two towns changed hands several times until Mehmed II annexed the Karamanid state. According to Ali of Yezd, Sultan Bayezid I died there after his defeat at the Battle of Ankara at the hands of Timur.

Akşehir is a municipality and district of Konya Province, at the edge of a fertile plain on the north side of the Sultan Mountains, at an elevation of 1,025 metres. The name means white city. Its landmarks include the alleged tomb of Nasreddin Hodja and the tomb of Seydi Mahmut, along with old Turkish houses. A house used as headquarters by the Turkish Army in the last phase of the Greco-Turkish War of 1919–1922 also stands there. Commemorations of Nasreddin Hodja are held each year between 5 and 10 July. Akşehir is a member of the European Association of Historic Towns and Regions.
aksumite-empire: Before Aksum, Eritrea and the Tigray Plateau were home to a kingdom known as Dʿmt, which archaeological evidence suggests was influenced by Sheba, now Yemen. Scholars once held that the Sabaeans founded Semitic civilisation in Ethiopia, but that view is now refuted and their influence is considered minor; it included the Ancient South Arabian script, which developed into the Geʽez script. Excavations at Betä Giyorgis show a settlement near Aksum dating to about the seventh to fourth centuries BCE. The Aksumite polity itself arose between 150 BCE and 150 CE, and its early centuries remain largely obscure.

Stuart Munro-Hay concludes that the early kingdom was probably a confederacy led by a district-level king who commanded the allegiance of lesser kings, so that its ruler was a king of kings. There is no evidence of a single royal lineage, and a new king of kings may have been chosen from among all the kings.

Mani, the founder of Manichaeism, counted Aksum among the four great powers of the 3rd century, with Persia, Rome and China. Under Gedara (c. 200 to 230) it took much of western Yemen, until a Himyarite and Sabean alliance pushed it out. Under Endybis (270 to 310) it began minting coins. Ezana (320s to c. 360) adopted Christianity as the state religion in the mid 4th century and conquered Meroë in 330 for a short time. After they adopted Christianity the Aksumites stopped building steles.

Aksum reached its height under Kaleb (514 to 542), who at the request of Byzantine emperor Justin I invaded the Himyarite Kingdom to end the persecution of Christians by its Jewish king Dhu Nuwas. With Himyar annexed, the kingdom spanned about 2,500,000 square kilometres, but it lost the territory in the Aksumite–Persian wars. Decline began by the 7th century, when currency ceased to be minted; Persian and later Muslim power in the Red Sea and the weakening of Rome, a major trade partner, damaged its economy. The final three centuries are considered a dark age, and the kingdom collapsed in uncertain circumstances around 960.

The Aksumites left their own alphabet, the Geʽez script, later modified to include vowels, and giant obelisks marking tombs, the best known of which is the Obelisk of Aksum. Greek was the official and literary language of the state, used in administration, diplomacy and trade, and Ezana made Geʽez an official language beside it. After the Muslim conquests isolated Aksum from the Greco-Roman world, Geʽez replaced Greek entirely. Texts were translated into Geʽez from the early Christian period, the best known being the Garima Gospels, dated between the 4th and 6th centuries. The Aksumite church gave rise to the Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church.
al-adid: Al-Adid was the son of the Fatimid prince Yusuf, a younger son of the eleventh caliph al-Hafiz. According to the commonly accepted date he was born on 9 May 1151, though some authors give 1145 or 1149. In 1154 the vizier Abbas ibn Abi'l-Futuh had Yusuf executed after the assassination of the caliph al-Zafir. By then the caliphs had become virtual puppets of their chief ministers, whose names were mentioned beside theirs in the Friday sermon, and the dynasty's Isma'ili doctrine had lost much of its appeal. Al-Adid was raised to the throne on 23 July 1160, aged nine, by the vizier Tala'i ibn Ruzzik, who married him to one of his daughters.

Throughout his reign al-Adid was a figurehead while viziers fought for the spoils. Ibn Ruzzik was assassinated on 11 September 1161 and followed by his son Ruzzik ibn Tala'i. Shawar overthrew Ruzzik in December 1162, and was himself evicted by Dirgham in August 1163. The turmoil allowed the Crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem and the Zengid ruler Nur al-Din to intervene. Shawar returned with Nur al-Din's general Shirkuh and Shirkuh's nephew Saladin, then allied with the Crusaders against them. In 1167 a Crusader garrison was placed in Cairo, and in 1168 King Amalric besieged the city. Shirkuh arrived in January 1169, had Shawar executed and became vizier, and when Shirkuh died on 23 March 1169 Saladin was appointed in his place.

Saladin gradually dismantled the Fatimid regime. He purged Fatimid troops, defeating a revolt of the Black African troops on 21 August 1169, and in August 1170 he changed the call to prayer to the Sunni form. He placed Sunni jurists in office and suspended Isma'ili lectures at the al-Azhar Mosque. On 10 September 1171 the name of the Abbasid caliph al-Mustadi was proclaimed in the sermon in place of al-Adid's. Al-Adid died on 13 September 1171, aged twenty, probably of a severe illness; some medieval sources claim poison or murder, but the historian Heinz Halm finds no serious evidence for it. The Fatimid family was placed under house arrest, and Isma'ilism had been effectively purged from Egypt by the end of the thirteenth century.
al-adil: Al-Adil was born in June 1145, possibly in Damascus, a son of Najm ad-Din Ayyub and a member of the Kurdish Ayyubid family. He first won distinction as an officer in the army of Nur ad-Din Zengi during his uncle Shirkuh's last campaign in Egypt, in 1168 to 1169. After Nur ad-Din's death in 1174 he governed Egypt for Saladin and mobilised its resources for his brother's campaigns in Syria and the war against the Crusaders. He was governor of Aleppo from 1183 to 1186 and returned to administer Egypt during the Third Crusade. Crusaders knew him as Saphadin, from his title Sayf ad-Din.

After Saladin's death in March 1193, al-Adil was governor of Damascus. Saladin had made the emirs swear loyalty to his son al-Afdal Ali, but other sons refused to accept him. Al-Adil first mediated, then concluded that al-Afdal was unfit to rule and backed al-Aziz Uthman. When al-Aziz died after a riding accident in 1198, al-Afdal and his brother az-Zahir Ghazi besieged Damascus. Al-Adil played his nephews against each other, and his son al-Kamil arrived with reinforcements, ending the siege in December 1199. He defeated al-Afdal at Bilbeis and proclaimed himself sultan on 17 February 1200. By the spring of 1202 az-Zahir had admitted his suzerainty.

His reign was one of consolidation. He rebuilt a treasury emptied by wars, reformed the currency and taxation, and met the low Nile floods of 1199 to 1202 partly by sending soldiers to work the land. To avoid a new crusade he encouraged trade with European merchants, though Frankish fleets raided Rosetta in 1204 and Damietta in 1211. He married his daughter Dayfa Khatun to az-Zahir in 1212, ending the rivalry between two branches of the family, and rebuilt the citadel of Damascus. He took Ahlat in 1207, ending the Ahlatshahs.

In September 1217 a new crusader army landed at Acre. Al-Adil, aged seventy-two, took his forces into Palestine without notable success. In August 1218 news came that a second force had landed in Egypt and was attacking Damietta. He fell ill and died on campaign, on 31 August 1218, and al-Kamil succeeded him. Succession to the sultanate stayed in his eldest male line, and his descendants held Mayyafariqin. Saladin's descendants kept Aleppo, while Damascus changed hands among the branches of the family until Ayyubid rule ended. He had 16 sons and several daughters.
al-afdal-shahanshah: Al-Afdal Shahanshah was born Abu al-Qasim Shahanshah bin Badr al-Jamali in Acre, the son of Badr al-Jamali, an Armenian mamluk who became Muslim. Badr was vizier of the Fatimids in Cairo from 1074 until his death in 1094, when al-Afdal succeeded him.

The Caliph al-Mustansir Billah died soon after Badr, and al-Afdal appointed as caliph al-Musta'li, a child, in place of his much older brother Nizar ibn al-Mustansir. Nizar revolted and was defeated in 1095, which led to tension between al-Afdal and Nizar's supporters, chiefly Hassan-i Sabbah and his Nizari Isma'ili group, known as the Assassins. In 1097 al-Afdal captured Tyre from the Seljuk Turks, and in 1098 he took Jerusalem. He took the Crusaders for Byzantine mercenaries and hoped for an alliance against the Seljuks, but they took Jerusalem on 15 July 1099, and on 12 August 1099 Godfrey of Bouillon surprised and completely defeated him at the Battle of Ascalon.

When al-Musta'li died in December 1101 al-Afdal raised the five-year-old al-Amir bi-Ahkam Allah to the throne and married him to his own daughter. Under him the caliphs were confined to their palace and lost their ceremonial functions, and he built his own palace, the Dar al-Mulk, outside Cairo in 1106–1108. He was defeated at the Third Battle of Ramla in 1105 and lost Tripoli in 1109. He also introduced an iqta' tax reform that lasted until Saladin took over Egypt.

An assassin tried to kill al-Afdal in 1115, and another attack failed in 1118. He was assassinated in December 1121 during a procession on the last day of Ramadan. The deed was commonly attributed to the Nizari Assassins, and modern scholars commonly accept their responsibility, but the Syrian chronicler Ibn al-Qalanisi blamed the Caliph al-Amir and al-Afdal's chief of staff, al-Ma'mun al-Bata'ihi, who succeeded him as vizier. Al-Amir confiscated his enormous wealth. Little survives of his buildings: the only surviving work is the mihrab of the Mosque of Ibn Tulun.
al-afshin: Afshin was the hereditary title of the princes of Oshrusana in Transoxiana from before the Muslim conquest; the scholar Minorsky suggests it was of Sogdian origin. Khaydhar was of Sogdian descent. Two classical sources call him a Turk, but Arab writers of the time used the word loosely for the caliph's new troops. His father, Kawus ibn Kharakhuruh, withdrew his allegiance from the Arabs, and shortly after the caliph al-Ma'mun reached Baghdad from the east a power struggle broke out in the ruling family of Oshrusana.

In the service of al-Mu'tasim, al-Ma'mun's heir, who gave him exceptionally large salaries and allowances, Afshin put down uprisings in Egypt between 831 and 833, taking Bima on 2 June 832. Made governor of Adharbayjan in 835 to fight the Khurramites of Babak Khorramdin, he took Babak's castle of Bazz in August 837, freeing 7,600 Arab prisoners according to Ya'qubi. The Christian prince Sahl ibn-Sunbat handed Babak over to him, and the caliph added Sind to his governorships of Armenia and Adharbayjan.

In the campaign of 838 against Byzantium he led the northern army, estimated at 20,000 to 30,000 men with some 10,000 Turkish horse-archers, from the region of Melitene. Emperor Theophilos chose to attack him first, and at the Battle of Anzen in July Afshin's horse-archers checked the Byzantine advance; the army collapsed and the emperor barely escaped. Afshin then joined the caliph at Ancyra, commanded the rear guard on the march to Amorium, and took turns with Ashinas and Itakh in assaulting the breach until the city fell in mid-August.

Apparently jealous of Abdallah ibn Tahir, the governor of Khorasan, Afshin allegedly encouraged in secret the rebellion of Mazyar, the Karenid ispahbadh of Tabaristan, crushed in 839. Their correspondence was found, and Abdallah claimed to have intercepted wealth of Babak that Afshin was sending to Oshrusana. Arrested when Mazyar reached Samarra, he faced questions on the sincerity of his conversion from Zoroastrianism, answering that his Zoroastrian books were family heirlooms. Al-Mu'tasim held him in a minaret-shaped prison called The Pearl, where he died in May–June 841. His corpse was crucified at the place used for those of Babak and Mazyar.
al-ahsa-oasis: Al-Ahsa, also known as al-Hasa or Hajar, is an oasis and historical region in eastern Saudi Arabia about 60 kilometres inland from the Persian Gulf. The name is the plural of al-Hisa, a landscape of accumulated sand over an impermeable layer, which holds rainwater as an aquifer that wells can reach. Springs have drawn settlement and date-palm cultivation since prehistoric times.
