The name Hajar may be related to the ancient toponym Agarum, mentioned in Dilmunite inscriptions as the home of their chief deity Inzak, though this reading has been criticised and other sources place Agarum on the island of Failaka.

Eastern Arabia was conquered by the Rashidun Caliphate in the 7th century and later passed to the Umayyads and Abbasids. In 899 the Qarmatian leader Abu Tahir al-Jannabi took control and declared the region independent of the Abbasid caliphate, with a capital at al-Mu'miniya near modern Hofuf. The Uyunids overthrew the Qarmatian state in 1077, followed by the Usfurids and the Jabrids. In 1550 Al-Ahsa and nearby Qatif came under the Ottoman Empire under Suleiman I, usually as a vassal region, and the Ottomans were expelled in 1670, when the Banu Khalid Emirate took over.

Al-Ahsa was incorporated into the Wahhabist Emirate of Diriyah in 1795, returned to Ottoman control in 1818 through an invasion ordered by Muhammad Ali of Egypt, and was retaken by the Emirate of Nejd in 1830. Direct Ottoman rule was restored in 1871, first under Baghdad Vilayet and from 1875 under Basra Vilayet. In 1913 Ibn Saud, founder of modern Saudi Arabia, annexed Al-Ahsa and Qatif to Najd. Petroleum deposits found near Dammam in 1938 brought rapid modernisation.

The oasis has four main cities and 22 villages, among them Al-Mubarraz and Al-Hofuf, and more than 2.5 million palm trees, watered by an underground aquifer and over 280 artesian springs. The region is known for tailoring, especially the bisht cloak, and was one of the few parts of the Arabian Peninsula where rice was grown. It became a World Heritage Site in 2018 as the Cultural Landscape of Al-Ahsa Oasis, which comprises 12 locations, among them the Suq Al-Qaysariyah, the forts of Qasr Khuzam, Qasr Sahood and Qasr Ibrahim, and the Jawatha Mosque.
al-amin: Muhammad, the future al-Amin, was born in April 787, the son of Harun al-Rashid and Zubayda, who was descended from the caliph al-Mansur. His elder half-brother Abdallah, the future al-Ma'mun was the son of a Persian slave concubine, so Muhammad's pure Abbasid descent gave him seniority; he was the only Abbasid caliph to claim it. In 792 Harun had him receive the oath of allegiance under the name al-Amin, the Trustworthy, marking him as main heir, while al-Ma'mun was named second heir only in 799. In 802 the arrangements were proclaimed at Mecca: al-Amin would rule in Baghdad, and al-Ma'mun would succeed him and govern an enlarged Khurasan. Harun's third heir, al-Mu'tamin, was to hold the frontier with the Byzantine Empire.

Harun died on 24 March 809 at Tus, and al-Amin succeeded without difficulty. The first two years of his reign were generally peaceful. Al-Ma'mun mistrusted his brother, and al-Amin, urged on by ministers, especially al-Fadl ibn al-Rabi, had Harun's succession documents brought from Mecca and destroyed them. He asked al-Ma'mun to recognise al-Amin's son Musa as heir and return to Baghdad, and al-Ma'mun refused. In November 810 al-Amin dropped his brother's name from the Friday prayer, and later removed him and al-Mu'tamin from the succession in favour of his own sons. Al-Ma'mun answered by declaring himself imam.

In January 811 al-Amin appointed Ali ibn Isa governor of Khurasan and sent him against al-Ma'mun with 40,000 men. Al-Ma'mun's general Tahir ibn Husayn defeated and killed Ali near Rayy in 811. Tahir took Ahwaz, Basra and Kufa swore allegiance to al-Ma'mun, and Dawud ibn Isa in Mecca led worshippers in swearing allegiance to him.

In 812 Tahir camped near the Anbar Gate of Baghdad and besieged the city, and prisoners who broke out of jail added to the suffering. When Tahir pushed into the city, al-Amin sought safe passage on condition that he hand over his sceptre and seal. He tried to leave by boat, was thrown into the water, swam to shore, was captured and was executed, and his head was placed on the Anbar Gate. He died on 24 or 25 September 813. Al-Ma'mun refused to acknowledge al-Amin's son Musa as heir, and the throne went to him.
al-andalus: Al-Andalus refers to the territories of the Iberian Peninsula under Muslim rule between 711 and 1492, a name first attested on dinars minted in 716 with inscriptions in Latin and Arabic. At its widest extent under Umayyad rule it covered most of the peninsula and Septimania in southern France. It was first divided into five administrative units, corresponding roughly to Andalusia, Castile and León, Navarre, Aragon and Catalonia, Portugal and Galicia, and Languedoc-Roussillon. Its boundaries then shrank in a series of conquests that Western historiography has traditionally called the Reconquista, until only the Emirate of Granada remained.

In 711 Tariq ibn-Ziyad led an army of 7,000 that landed at Gibraltar on 30 April, ostensibly to intervene in a Visigothic civil war. After a victory over King Roderic at the Battle of Guadalete on 19 July 711, he and Musa ibn Nusayr brought most of the Visigothic Kingdom under Muslim rule in seven years. Al-Andalus was first a province of the Umayyad Caliphate, with Córdoba as its capital. It became the Emirate of Córdoba (c. 750–929) and then the Caliphate of Córdoba (929–1031), under which Córdoba became a leading cultural and economic centre. Resistant Visigoths took refuge in the Cantabrian highlands and formed the Kingdom of Asturias.

After 1031 al-Andalus split into taifa states. The Christian capture of Toledo in 1085 brought in the Almoravid Empire, and then the Almohad Caliphate, both based in Marrakesh. In the 13th century most of the south fell to Portuguese, Castilian and Aragonese conquests. The Emirate of Granada (1238–1492), a tributary of the Crown of Castile, surrendered to the Catholic Monarchs in 1492.

Society in al-Andalus consisted of Muslims, Christians and Jews, with Arabs at the top, followed by Berbers, Muladies, Mozarabs and Jews. Non-Muslims had the status of ahl al-dhimma and paid a tax, and scholars still debate their treatment. Andalusi scholars advanced trigonometry (Jabir ibn Aflah), astronomy (al-Zarqali), surgery (al-Zahrawi), pharmacology (Ibn Zuhr) and agronomy. Alfonso X of Castile and other Christian monarchs had Andalusi libraries translated into Latin.

Many Muslims were forced to convert in the later Reconquista, particularly after the decrees of 1502 and 1526, and these converts, the Moriscos, were expelled in the early 17th century. Among the surviving monuments are the Cathedral of Córdoba, the Alhambra and the Giralda.
al-aqsa-mosque: The mosque stands on the southern part of the Temple Mount, or Haram al-Sharif, an enclosure that King Herod the Great expanded from 20 BCE during his rebuilding of the Second Jewish Temple. In the late Second Temple period the site held the Royal Stoa, a basilica along the southern wall, which was destroyed with the Temple during the Roman siege of Jerusalem in 70 CE. The Nea Church of Justinian, consecrated in 543, was once thought to have stood here, but remains identified as its were found in the Jewish Quarter in 1973.

According to Islamic tradition, Umar, the second caliph (r. 634–644), built a small prayer hall on the compound. In the reign of Mu'awiya I (r. 661–680) a quadrangular mosque for 3,000 worshippers is recorded. The present mosque was built by the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik (r. 685–705), his successor al-Walid I, or both, on the same axis as the Dome of the Rock.

An earthquake destroyed the mosque in 746, and the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur rebuilt it in 758. Al-Mahdi expanded it in 780 to fifteen aisles and a central dome. Another earthquake destroyed it in 1033, and the Fatimid caliph al-Zahir rebuilt it with seven aisles, preserving the outline that survives. The Fatimid caliph al-Mustansir Billah had its facade built in 1065.

After the Crusaders captured Jerusalem in 1099 the mosque served as a palace and as the headquarters of the Knights Templar. Saladin conquered the area in 1187 and restored its use as a mosque. The Ayyubids, Mamluks, Ottomans, the Supreme Muslim Council of British Palestine and the Jordanian administration all later renovated or enlarged it. The dome was destroyed by fire in 1969 and its painted interior was reconstructed using the trateggio technique.

The name al-Masjid al-Aqṣā, 'the furthest mosque', occurs in the Quran's Surah 17 and was first applied to the whole compound, since no buildings stood there then. The building discussed here is the silver-domed congregational mosque, called Jāmiʿ al-Aqṣā or the Qibli Mosque for its place at the southern end of the compound. Medieval writers such as al-Muqaddasi called it al-Mughattâ, 'the covered part'.

The mosque is 83 metres long and 56 metres wide and can hold up to 5,000 worshippers. It has seven aisles. Its facade has fourteen stone arches, mostly Romanesque, some made from sculpted material taken from Crusader buildings, and the porch was ordered by al-Mu'azzam Isa in 1217. It has 121 stained glass windows from the Abbasid and Fatimid eras. Unlike the Dome of the Rock, which reflects classical Byzantine architecture, it is characteristic of early Islamic architecture.
al-ashraf-khalil: Al-Ashraf Khalil was the second son of Sultan Qalawun and a woman named Qutqutiya. His exact year of birth is not known, although the Mamluk historian al-Safadi says that he died in his thirties or less. In 1284 he married Ardukin, the daughter of Sayf ad-Din Nukih ibn Bayan, a Mongol emir of Qalawun, a match thought prestigious among the Mamluks. Qalawun had named his elder son as-Salih Ali heir in 1280, and when as-Salih Ali died in 1288 he appointed Khalil co-sultan, but he never signed Khalil's diploma of investiture.

Khalil succeeded after Qalawun died on 9 November 1290. He absorbed his father's roughly 6,000 Mansuriyya mamluks into his own mostly Circassian corps of 1,200, the Ashrafiyya. When the viceroy Turuntay attempted an assassination in the accession procession, Khalil had him imprisoned, tortured and put to death. Qalawun had already conquered the County of Tripoli in 1289, and Khalil resumed his father's offensive against Acre on 2 March 1291, calling on the emirs of Syria to bring their mangonels. The Mamluks assaulted the city in May and captured it by 17 June after heavy fighting with the Knights Templar. Khalil ordered the execution of the remaining defenders and inhabitants and had the fortifications destroyed.

Within weeks the Mamluks took Tyre, Sidon, Beirut, Haifa and Tartus, and in August the Templar fortress of Atlit. In 1292 he captured Qal'at ar-Rum, the seat of the Patriarch of Armenia, after thirty days. He also sent an army under Izz al-Din al-Afram to Makuria, which sacked Dongola after King Samamoun declared he could not pay the tribute due under the Baqt agreement. In 1293 he answered a threatening letter from the Mongol ruler Gaykhatu with a military parade and a defiant reply.

Many emirs disliked Khalil. He treated them roughly after his victories, signed documents with the letter KH alone, and favoured his vizier Ibn al-Sal'us. On 14 December 1293, on a hunting trip at Turug, he was attacked and killed by his commander in chief Baydara and other emirs, after he had insulted and threatened Baydara before them. Baydara was proclaimed sultan but was soon killed under the orders of Kitbugha, and the emirs installed Khalil's nine-year-old brother al-Nasir Muhammad. Khalil was buried in a mausoleum attached to a madrasa he had commissioned in 1288 in Cairo's Southern Cemetery. Muslim historians remembered him as an intelligent sultan fond of reading and learning.
al-azhar: Cairo was founded by the Fatimid general Jawhar al-Siqilli on behalf of the caliph al-Mu'izz after the conquest of Egypt in 969, and Jawhar had al-Azhar built as a base for spreading Isma'ili Shi'a Islam. Work began on 4 April 970, using limestone from the Mokattam Formation, and the first Friday prayers were held on 22 June 972. The name, meaning resplendent, is usually thought to come from az-Zahra, a title of Fatima, the daughter of Muhammad, though no Arabic source confirms this.

Under the Fatimids the secretive teachings of the Isma'ili school of law were opened to the public. Al-Nu'man ibn Muhammad, appointed qadi by al-Mu'izz, taught the doctrine in classes at the palace and at the mosque, with separate sessions for women. In 973 the caliph rededicated it as Cairo's official congregational mosque, and in 989 the mosque authorities hired 35 scholars.

The original mosque measured about 85 by 69 metres, with three arcades around a courtyard and a hypostyle prayer hall five aisles deep. Its marble columns were reused from Pharaonic, Roman and Coptic sites, their different heights levelled with bases of varying thickness. It had three domes, none of which survived the later renovations. Under the Mamluks the Madrasa al-Taybarsiyya was added in 1309, and the Bab al-Gindi of 1495 carries the minaret of Qaytbay.

In the Ottoman period Abd al-Rahman Katkhuda nearly doubled the mosque. He added three gates, among them the Bab al-Muzayinin of 1753, which became the main entrance, and a second prayer hall with its own mihrab.

Saladin overthrew the Fatimids in 1171 and distrusted the mosque for its Shi'ite past. His qadi banned congregational prayers there, a silver band naming the Fatimid caliphs was removed from the mihrab, the library was neglected and students lost their funding. Sultan Baibars restored congregational prayers on 16 January 1266, and stipends and repairs returned under the Mamluks. After the Ottoman annexation of 1517 the rulers showed deference but gave little money.

In 1798 Napoleon set up a diwan of nine al-Azhar sheikhs to govern Cairo. Muhammad Ali seized the mosque's tax-free lands in 1809 and promoted rival schools. After the revolution of 1952 the university was separated from the mosque, and it was officially designated a university in 1961 with secular faculties such as medicine and engineering.
al-bakri: Abū ʿUbayd ʿAbd Allāh al-Bakrī was an Arab Andalusian historian and geographer born in Huelva about 1040. His father was sovereign of a short-lived principality that the family set up there when the Caliphate of Córdoba fell in 1031. When al-Mu'tadid, the ruler of the Taifa of Seville, deposed his father, the family moved to Córdoba, where al-Bakri studied with the geographer al-Udri and the historian Ibn Hayyan. He spent his whole life in Al-Andalus, mostly in Seville and Almeria, and was in Seville when El Cid arrived to collect tribute from Alfonso VI. He died in Córdoba in 1094 without ever having travelled to the places he described.

Al-Bakri wrote about Europe, North Africa and the Arabian peninsula, but only two of his works survive. The Mu'jam mā ista'jam lists place names, mostly in the Arabian peninsula. His most important work is the Kitāb al-Masālik wa-al-Mamālik, the Book of Highways and of Kingdoms. It draws on earlier literature and on the reports of merchants and travellers, including Muhammad ibn Yūsuf al-Warrāq and Abraham ben Jacob. Some of al-Warraq's material dates from the 10th century, but al-Bakri also included recent events. For each area he describes the people, customs, geography, climate and main cities, and adds anecdotes. His works are noted for their relative objectivity. Parts of the main work are lost.

The book is one of the most important sources for the history of West Africa and gives crucial information on the Ghana Empire, the Almoravid dynasty and the trans-Saharan trade. Of Ghana he wrote that the city consisted of two towns on a plain, and that the one inhabited by Muslims was large and had twelve mosques, with salaried imams and muezzins, jurists and scholars.

Al-Bakri recorded that Gao was one of the few early centres in the trans-Saharan trade along the Niger to have native Muslim inhabitants, and that other centres, among them Takrur, Songhay, Kanem-Bornu and the Hausa territories, eventually followed. By the 11th century reports of such flourishing Islamic cities had reached Al-Andalus, which made his account possible. A crater on the Moon is named after him.
al-biruni: Al-Biruni's name comes from the Persian word bīrūn, meaning outskirts, since he was born in an outlying district of Kath, the capital of the Afrighid kingdom of Khwarazm. He spent his first twenty-five years in Khwarazm, studying Islamic jurisprudence, theology, grammar, mathematics, astronomy, medicine and philosophy. His mother tongue was Khwarezmian, an Eastern Iranian language. He was sympathetic to the Afrighids, who were overthrown by the rival Ma'munid dynasty in 995, and he then left for Bukhara, under the Samanid ruler Mansur II, where he corresponded with Avicenna.

In 998 he went to the court of the Ziyarid amir of Tabaristan, Qabus, and there wrote his first major work, al-Āthār al-bāqiya, on historical and scientific chronology, probably around 1000. He later made peace with the Ma'munids, whose court at Gurganj was gaining a reputation as a gathering place for scientists, and collaborated there with his former teacher Abu Nasr Mansur.

In July 1017 Mahmud of Ghazni invaded Khwarazm and took Kath. Al-Biruni and most other scholars left with him, possibly as prisoners, and were brought to Ghazni, where he spent much of the rest of his life. He was made court astrologer and from 1017 accompanied Mahmud on his campaigns in the Indian subcontinent, living there for several years. During those journeys he studied the Hindu faith and Indian culture, and wrote the Tārīkh al-Hind, which he finished around 1030. He died at Ghazni around 1050.

Of the 146 books attributed to him, 95 concern astronomy, mathematics and related subjects. In the Mas'ud Canon he observed, contrary to Ptolemy, that the Sun's apogee was mobile and not fixed. He wrote a treatise on the astrolabe, and a later work refuting astrology, which he distinguished from astronomy. He devised a method of finding the Earth's radius from the height of a mountain and the dip of the horizon, which he carried out at Nandana in present-day Pakistan. He also developed experimental methods for determining density with a hydrostatic balance, and classified gems by properties such as specific gravity and hardness rather than colour.

His Taḥqīq mā li-l-Hind explored nearly every aspect of Indian life, and he also translated the yoga sutras of Patanjali. He chose to record civilian and scholarly life rather than military and political history, and said he would set out the theories of the Hindus as they are, comparing them with similar Greek theories. He was conversant in Khwarezmian, Persian, Arabic and Sanskrit and also knew Greek, Hebrew and Syriac. He is widely considered an important Muslim authority on the history of religion, though he assumed the superiority of Islam. Some call him the first anthropologist, but others say he can hardly be considered one in the conventional sense.
al-bu-said-dynasty: The name Al Bu Said means house of Abu Said, the kunya of the ancestor Al Muhallab ibn Abi Suffrah, a general of the Umayyad period. The family traces its roots to the Azd tribes. Ahmad bin Said Al Busaidi was governor of Sohar during the Omani Civil War when a Persian fleet attacked the town. He held out for nine months and forced the commander of Nader Shah's army to come to terms and leave the country within a few years. He was elected imam on 20 November 1744, and the dynasty he founded is among the oldest surviving royal dynasties in Arabia. His descendants took the title Sayyid, not Imam, and so gave up spiritual authority.
Ahmad's son Said bin Ahmed was chosen by the ulema in 1778, and his own son Hamad bin Said moved the capital from Rustaq to the coastal city of Muscat in 1783 and took the title sultan.

Sultan bin Ahmed sought British help against rivals and in 1798 signed a Treaty of Commerce and Navigation with Britain, which opened Muscat to a British consul. Said bin Sultan took Oman to its height as a maritime power, with Mombasa, Zanzibar, Pemba, Mafia, Lamu and parts of the Persian coast under its rule. In 1832 he made Zanzibar a second capital and promoted the cultivation of cloves, for which he sought slaves as labour. In 1833 he signed a treaty of friendship and trade with the United States. He died at sea on 19 October 1856.

His sons quarrelled over the empire. Majid proclaimed himself sultan of Zanzibar on 28 October 1856, and his elder brother Thuwaini in Muscat refused to recognise him. Lord Canning, Governor-General of British India, arbitrated, dividing the empire between the sultanates of Zanzibar and of Muscat and Oman. The Zanzibar Guarantee Treaty, signed in Paris on 10 March 1862, bound Britain and France to respect the independence of both.

The Zanzibar line ended with the revolution of 1964, led by the island's black African citizens, which overthrew the last sultan, Jamshid bin Abdullah. In Oman, Imam Azzan bin Qais seized power in 1868, but Turki bin Said, backed by the British, defeated him in January 1871 and restored the sultanate. His great-grandson Qaboos bin Said took power in 1970 by a palace coup against his father Said bin Taimur. Qaboos died on 10 January 2020 and was succeeded by his cousin Haitham bin Tariq, named in a letter Qaboos himself had written.
al-burda: The poem takes its name from a story told of its author. Al-Busiri, afflicted by illness, is said to have praised Muhammad without ceasing until Muhammad appeared to him in a dream and wrapped him in a mantle; in the morning the poet found that God had cured him. The name had an older history. Bānat Suʿād, a poem by Ka'b ibn Zuhayr, was first called Al-Burda: Ka'b recited it before Muhammad after embracing Islam, and Muhammad, moved, took off his mantle and wrapped it round him. That earlier Burda is less widely known than al-Busiri's.

The Burda has 160 verses in ten chapters, all on one rhyme: every verse ends in the Arabic letter mīm, a form called mīmiyya. Between the verses runs a refrain asking God to send blessings and peace continuously and eternally on His Beloved, the Best of All Creation. The chapters treat, in turn, lyrical love and yearning, warnings about the caprices of the self, the praise of the Prophet, his birth, his miracles, the exalted stature of the Qur'an, the Ascension, the struggle of God's Messenger, seeking intercession through the Prophet, and finally the poet's own intimate petition.

Sufis have long venerated the poem. It is memorised and recited in congregations, above all on occasions such as the Mawlid, and its verses decorate public buildings and mosques; for centuries it adorned the Prophet's Mosque in Medina, where all but two lines were later erased. More than 90 commentaries have been written on it, among them works by Ibn Hajar al-Haytami, Nazifi and Qastallani, and the Shafi'i hadith scholar Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani studied it through a chain of transmission going back to al-Busiri himself.

It has been translated into Persian, Turkish, Urdu, Punjabi, Sindhi, Saraiki, Hausa, the Berber languages, French, German, Norwegian, Chinese and other languages, and into English by Timothy Winter. Not all scholars accepted it: Muhammad ibn Abd al-Wahhab considered it shirk, or idolatry. The poem gave its name to a whole family of later works, from Ahmad Shawqi's Nahj al-Burda to Tamim al-Barghouti's Burdat Tamim, written in November and December 2010 and first published in 2013.
al-farabi: Little is known of al-Farabi's life. The accounts of his origins vary and seem to rest on hearsay or guesses, and Arabic biographers of the 12th and 13th centuries had few facts and used invented stories. His full name was Abu Nasr Muhammad ibn Muhammad al-Farabi, sometimes with the family name al-Tarkhani. His birthplace could have been any of several places in Central Asia, then called Khurasan, since farab is a Persian term for land irrigated by springs or a nearby river. Candidates include Farab (Otrar) on the Syr Darya, a village near Türkmenabat and Faryab in present-day Afghanistan.

From incidental accounts it is known that he spent most of his scholarly life in Baghdad with Syriac Christian scholars, among them Yuhanna ibn Haylan, Yahya ibn Adi and Abu Ishaq Ibrahim al-Baghdadi. He later spent time in Damascus and in Egypt before returning to Damascus, where he died around the middle of the 10th century. His religious affiliation is disputed, and some scholars place him as Sunni and others as Shia or influenced by Shia thought.

Al-Farabi is credited with over one hundred works, among them prolegomena to philosophy and commentaries on Aristotle, including the Nicomachean Ethics. His main influence was the Aristotelian tradition of Alexandria, with elements of Neoplatonism and of Ptolemy's planetary model. In logic he was mainly an Aristotelian but discussed future contingents, the relation of logic to grammar and Stoic forms of inference, and he introduced the concept of the poetic syllogism in a commentary on Aristotle's Poetics. He also wrote on alchemy, in The Necessity of the Art of the Elixir, and was a practical musician and music theorist.

In metaphysics he held that the subject was being as such, related to God only as a principle of absolute being, and Avicenna remarked that he understood Aristotle's Metaphysics only after reading al-Farabi's prolegomenon. His cosmology had the First Cause, by contemplating itself, give rise to a cascade of ten intellects, each bringing a celestial sphere into being, beneath which lies the material world. The process was necessary rather than willed, a view that al-Ghazzali later criticised.

Later writers called al-Farabi the Second Master, with Aristotle the first. He is credited as the first Muslim to present philosophy as a coherent system, and he is called the founder of Islamic political philosophy. Among those he influenced are Avicenna, Averroes, Maimonides and Albertus Magnus. He helped to pass on Aristotle's thought to the Christian West, and he is the only philosopher named in Maimonides's Treatise on Logic.

In Kazakhstan a large university, KazNU, bears his name, and monuments to him stand in Alma-Ata, Shymkent and Turkestan. An anniversary of his birth was marked in 1975, and the asteroid 7057 Al-Fārābī is named after him.
al-hajjaj-ibn-yusuf: Al-Hajjaj came from Ta'if in the Hejaz, from the Abu Aqil family of the Thaqif tribe. The family was not distinguished: it was poor, and its members had worked as stone carriers and builders. He was a schoolmaster in his hometown, teaching pupils to copy and recite the Quran, which his enemies later mocked, as they did the boyhood nickname Kulayb, little dog. He and his father then took up military service under the caliph Yazid I. In the Second Fitna he fought at al-Harra in 682 and al-Rabadha in 684, without distinction, and at al-Harra he fled the field. His first public post, as governor of Tabala, he abandoned as beneath his ambition, which gave rise to an Arabic proverb.

Abd al-Malik promoted him to head of the caliph's select troops and to governor of the Hejaz in 692-694. In early 694 he was sent to govern Iraq, combining the governorships of Kufa and Basra. The post was a vice-royalty from Mesopotamia to Central Asia and the Indian subcontinent, comprising half the caliphate's territory and producing more than half its income, and in 697/8 he received Khurasan and Sistan as well. He kept it until his death under Abd al-Malik and his successor al-Walid I, whose decisions he strongly influenced. In 701, with Syrian reinforcements, he crushed the great rebellion of Ibn al-Ash'ath, and he then founded the city of Wasit to house the loyal Syrian troops on whom he relied.

He chose the generals of a wave of expansion: Muhammad ibn al-Qasim for Sindh, Qutayba ibn Muslim for Transoxiana and Mujja'a ibn Si'r for Oman. In 695 he began minting gold and silver coins bearing the name of Allah in place of Byzantine and Sasanian designs, and he had the tax registers of Iraq translated from Persian into Arabic. To restore agriculture he rebuilt the canals of lower Iraq, sent converts back to their villages and collected the poll tax from them.

Al-Hajjaj died at Wasit in May or June 714, reportedly of stomach cancer. The next caliph, Sulayman, allied with many of his opponents, dismissed his appointees, and had Muhammad ibn al-Qasim removed from Sindh and executed at Wasit. Later pro-Abbasid writers made him an object of deep enmity and ascribed to him persecutions and mass executions, among them a charge recorded by al-Tabari from an anonymous source of the killing of between 11,000 and 130,000 men in Basra. Julius Wellhausen judged him harsh and at times hard, but not cruel, petty or bigoted.
al-hakam-i: Abu al-As al-Hakam ibn Hisham ibn Abd al-Rahman was the second son of Hisham I, Emir of Córdoba, and a concubine named Zokhrouf; his older brother had died young. He was a complete contrast to his father. Chroniclers describe a tall, dark, slim man who led his troops into battle himself, enjoyed wine and women in quantity, cultivated his gifts as a poet and orator and promoted learning. The religious elite, who preferred the near-asceticism of his father, were not won over by him.

When he came to power in 796 he was challenged by his uncles Sulayman and Abdallah, sons of Abd ar-Rahman I. After a four-year struggle Sulayman was captured and executed, and his head was paraded on a pike through Córdoba. Abdallah took his sons to the court of Charlemagne at Aix-la-Chapelle to seek aid, without result, and was pardoned. Al-Hakam gave him lordship over Valencia and the east coast of al-Andalus with a rich pension, on condition that he stay there, and married two of his sisters to Abdallah's sons.

He spent much of his reign putting down rebellions in Toledo, Saragossa and Mérida, and the uprisings twice reached Córdoba. When a plot to replace him with his cousin Muhammad ibn al-Kasim was exposed, seventy-two nobles were executed and crucified along the banks of the Guadalquivir. He raised new taxes to pay for his campaigns, which the clerics decried as un-Islamic, and he tolerated the public sale of wine for revenue. He formed a bodyguard, the Al-Haras, led by the Christian count Rabi, and a troop of Frankish warriors.

In the spring of 818 the townsfolk of the suburb of Shaqunda, across the Roman bridge, rose after a palace guard killed a townsman, and stormed the city. His cousin Ubayd Allah ibn Abd Allah surprised the rebels from behind, and for three days the suburb was given over to the troops. The emir then had three hundred leading citizens crucified and gave the surviving inhabitants, thousands of Muslims, Christians and Jews, four days to leave al-Andalus. Some went to Fez, Egypt and Crete.

Al-Hakam I died in 822 after ruling for 26 years. By his wife Halawah he had five children, among them Abd ar-Rahman II, who succeeded him as emir. His concubine Ajab founded a leper colony in the suburbs of Córdoba, funded by the estate of Munyat Ajab, and another concubine, Mut'a, established a cemetery that still existed in the 10th century.
al-hakam-ii: Al-Hakam II was born on 13 January 915, the son of Abd al-Rahman III and Murjan, and succeeded his father in 961. He secured peace with the Catholic kingdoms of northern Iberia and used the stability to build irrigation works, widen streets and build markets. Internal administration passed increasingly to the vizier al-Mushafi, while the general Ghalib ibn Abd al-Rahman gained influence as leader of the army in North Africa. There he repulsed the last Norman attacks, about 970, and fought the Zirids and Fatimids in northern Morocco, where the Fatimids were defeated in 974. The caliphate kept its supremacy over Navarre, Castile and León.

From 961 al-Hakam enlarged the Great Mosque of Córdoba, extending the prayer hall 45 metres to the south. The addition brought a richly decorated mihrab, intersecting multifoil arches and four ribbed domes, which survive today. The palace-city of Madinat al-Zahra, begun by his father after 936, was also built up and renovated.

Al-Hakam was well versed in many sciences and had books bought from Damascus, Baghdad, Constantinople, Cairo, Mecca, Medina, Kufa and Basra. His patronage brought him such fame that even books written in Persia were dedicated to him. A large translation effort rendered Latin and Greek works into Arabic, carried out by a joint committee of Muwallad Muslims and Mozarab Catholics. He wrote a history of al-Andalus himself.

The mathematician Lubna of Córdoba served as his private secretary, and the physician and surgeon Abu al-Qasim al-Zahrawi was active at his court. After his death Almanzor had the books of ancient science destroyed.

Al-Hakam married Subh, a Basque concubine who held strong influence over the court, and they had two sons, Abd al-Rahman, who died young, and Hisham II. A stroke near the end of his life curtailed his activities and may explain why he did not prepare his son for leadership. Modern scholars think a second stroke, possibly brought on by cold weather, killed him in October 976. Hisham II was eleven years old at his accession, and the regency was held by Ghalib, al-Mushafi and Subh, with Almanzor as her secretary.
al-hira: Al-Hira was an ancient city in Mesopotamia, in what is now south-central Iraq, on the western bank of the Euphrates a few miles south of Kufa, near present-day Najaf. It lay on the northwestern edge of the Samarra Desert between the river and a seasonal lake known as the Najaf Sea. Its open connection to the Arabian Peninsula meant that Arab tribes could reach it freely, and canals from the Euphrates made the region one of the most fertile in Iraq. The name probably derives from a Syriac word meaning enclosure, referring to the first permanent encampment of Lakhmid leadership.

The city was sometimes called the White, because of the quantity of its buildings. Little is known of its society, since most histories come from early Abbasid times and have been substantially reworked into a narrative.

Under the Lakhmids, Al-Hira was capital of the major Arab client kingdom of the Sasanian Empire. Its kings ruled Arab populations from Mesopotamia deep into Eastern and Central Arabia through a divide-and-rule policy, appointing tribesmen as kings, military leaders and tax collectors. Al-Nu'man I ibn Imru al-Qays, who reigned from 403 to 431, abdicated to live as a monk, and is credited with building the palaces of Al-Khawarnaq and Al-Sadir. The court reached its height under Al-Nu'man III ibn al-Mundhir, from 580 to 602, attracting poets such as Al-Nabigha al-Dhubyani and Hassan ibn Thabit. After Al-Nu'man III converted to Christianity and defied Sasanian orders he was removed, and the kingdom was absorbed into the Sasanian Empire in 602.

Christianity came to the city in the fourth century, and by 410 it had a bishop. It became a base for missions to the Sasanian world and to the Arabs of the desert; the Chronicle of Seert records the work of the monastic founder Abraham of Kashkar there. Al-Hira was a multilingual crossroads, and its Hiri script, derived from the Aramaic alphabet, is considered a precursor of the Arabic script.

Al-Hira surrendered peacefully in 633, after a brief siege led by Khalid ibn al-Walid, commander of the Rashidun Caliphate's army, one of the first major cities of Iraq to fall to Muslim control. It lost political significance to the new city of Kufa but remained inhabited until the tenth century, and Abu al-Abbas al-Saffah and Harun al-Rashid stayed there. By the 13th century it had ceased to function as a city. Some inhabitants migrated to Nishapur in Khorasan, where a quarter bore the name of Al-Hira.
al-hoceima: Al Hoceima lies on the Mediterranean coast on the northern edge of the Rif Mountains, in the heart of the Central Rif, surrounded by the range's highest peaks, among them Mount Tidghin at 2,452 metres. It is the capital of Al Hoceima Province and remains a cultural centre for the Ayt Waryaghar tribe. Its name is an Arabised form of Alhucemas, the Spanish name of the nearby Spanish-owned Alhucemas Islands, meaning lavender islands, itself from the Andalusi Arabic al-Khuzāmā. Some, among them the author of the Spanish encyclopedia Espasa-Calpe, derive Alhucemas from al-Mazimma. The climate is a hot-summer Mediterranean one.

The Ait Ouriaghel Berber tribe, also called Beni Urriaguel, dominated the area. Abd el-Krim, whose father was a qadi of the Ait Youssef ou Ali clan, organised a guerrilla force against the Spanish during the Rif War and established the Republic of the Rif in 1921, which lasted until 1926. In September 1925 the Spanish general José Sanjurjo landed at Al Hoceima and claimed the territory for Spain. The Spanish developed the town and named it Villa Sanjurjo; its first mayor was Florian Gómez Aroca. The beach where Sanjurjo and his troops landed, Playa Quemado, is still one of its well-known beaches.

After Morocco became independent in 1956 the town grew quickly and the government gave it the name Al Hoceima, following the standard French spelling. The years from 1956 to 1959 were hard in the Rif. In October 1958 the Beni Urriaguel rebelled against the central administration, and two thirds of the Moroccan army, led by the crown prince, the future Hassan II, were sent to Al Hoceima; a significant number of people lost their lives in the Rif in this period.
Two earthquakes struck the city and its villages within ten years: one of magnitude 6.0 on 26 May 1994 and one of magnitude 6.4 on 24 February 2004, which killed more than 560 people.

Al Hoceima is a moderate-size city whose income comes from fishing and tourism, and it has the second-largest port of the Rif region after Nador. Many of its former inhabitants migrated to Europe between the 1960s and the 1980s, and large numbers of Moroccans in the Netherlands, France and Belgium come from the city; many return in summer. The first schools built by the Spanish, a college and an elementary school, and a Spanish Catholic church still exist. In the early 1950s and 1960s the small houses were mostly painted white and blue, colours that were regarded as the city's own, and in 2007 the mayor stated that new houses would be painted in them.
al-jazeera: Hamad bin Khalifa Al Thani first floated the idea of an international news channel in August 1994, while still crown prince of Qatar. The channel followed the closure of the first BBC Arabic television station, a joint venture with Orbit Communications Company, owned by a cousin of the Saudi King Fahd, that ended after a year and a half when the Saudi government tried to stop a documentary on executions of Saudi dissidents. Many of its journalists joined Al Jazeera. After a six-hour test broadcast screened in London, the emir dropped his plan to mix news with entertainment in favour of an all-news format.

The network was launched with about $137 million from the Qatari government, first as a loan and later as a grant. It gained credibility in the Arab world with coverage openly critical of autocratic leaders, a wide range of viewpoints and frontline reporting of the Second Intifada and the Iraq War. Its Arabic website's traffic rose sharply after the September 11 attacks of 2001 and the American strikes on Afghanistan. Al Jazeera English followed on 15 November 2006, and the coverage of the Arab Spring in 2011 won the network a Peabody Award.

The network grew into a group of channels: a children's channel in 2005, sports channels from 2004 that were spun off as beIN Sports in 2014, the online channel AJ+ in 2014, and Al Jazeera America, which began on 20 August 2013 after the purchase of Current TV. In 2011 it was legally restructured from a public institution to a private institution of public utility. The scholar Philip Seib coined the term Al Jazeera effect for Arab governments losing control of information.

Al Jazeera Media Network is headquartered in Wadi Al Sail in Doha and chartered under Qatari law as a private foundation for public benefit, funded mainly by the government of Qatar, with further income from advertising, subscriptions and the sale of footage and broadcast rights. It broadcasts in Arabic, English and Spanish. Its Arabic and English channels are editorially separate. Governments have often objected to its reporting: Bahrain banned its correspondents in 2002 and again in 2010, and during the Qatar diplomatic crisis several Arab states demanded its closure. Critics regard the Arabic channel as influenced by Qatari foreign policy, while Qatar maintains the network is independent.
al-kamil: Al-Malik al-Kamil Nasir ad-Din Muhammad was born around 1177 and was the fourth Ayyubid sultan of Egypt. He was the son of the Kurdish sultan al-Adil, known to the Crusaders as Saphadin, a brother of Saladin. In 1199 his father left him to command the siege of Mardin, and a combined force from Mosul, Sinjar and Jazirat ibn Umar drew him into a battle in which he was badly defeated.

Dissent among his opponents nevertheless let him secure Ayyubid rule in the Jazira by taking Harran. After al-Adil proclaimed himself sultan in 1200, he made al-Kamil his viceroy in Egypt. Al-Kamil oversaw much of the work on the Cairo Citadel and issued decrees in his own name until his father's death on 31 August 1218.

On al-Adil's death the Ayyubid lands were divided, with al-Kamil ruling Egypt, al-Muazzam Isa in Palestine and Transjordan, and al-Ashraf Musa in Syria and the Jazira. Al-Kamil took command of the defence of Damietta against the Fifth Crusade. In 1219 a conspiracy of the amir Imad ad-Din ibn al-Mashtub nearly overthrew him and he had to flee the camp, and the arrival of al-Muazzam with reinforcements ended it.

He offered to return Jerusalem and rebuild its walls, but the papal legate Pelagius had the offers rejected. He met Francis of Assisi, a meeting later painted by Giotto and others. Damietta fell in November 1219 after famine and disease, but in 1221 he opened the dams and let the Nile flood, and the Crusaders accepted an eight-year peace. He retook Damietta in September.

In February 1229 al-Kamil negotiated the Treaty of Jaffa with Frederick II, a ten-year peace. Jerusalem, Bethlehem and a corridor to the sea went to the Kingdom of Jerusalem, while the Muslims kept the Temple area, the Dome of the Rock and the Aqsa Mosque, and Muslim residents kept their homes and their own officials and courts. No other crusading treaty was reached by diplomacy alone in this way.

He then turned on Damascus, which surrendered on 25 June 1229 to his brother al-Ashraf and was given to him. Al-Kamil died on 6 March 1238 after contending with the Seljuks and the Khwarezmians. His sons as-Salih Ayyub and al-Adil II succeeded him in Syria and Egypt, and the Ayyubid empire descended into civil war. When the treaty expired in 1239, Jerusalem came under Ayyubid control.
al-khayzuran: Al-Khayzuran was kidnapped by a Bedouin and sold in a slave market near Mecca to al-Mahdi during his pilgrimage. Enslaving a Muslim was officially forbidden, but the sources all agree she was a slave, and such breaches were not unusual. Described as beautiful, intelligent and gifted, she took regular lessons in fiqh, Islamic law, from the most learned qadis. When al-Mahdi became caliph in 775 and married her, his first wife Rayta, daughter of the caliph al-Saffah, lost her privileges and her son his place as heir. Naming the sons of a slave as heirs went against custom.

Al-Khayzuran ran the caliph's harem and sat behind a curtain when he held court, touching his back unseen when she disagreed. Allied with the Barmakids, she helped decide military and state affairs, met foreign ambassadors and signed official papers. She ran estates, factories and foreign trade through her own agents, and her annual income is put at a third of the caliphate's. She made her brother Ghatrif governor of Yemen. When al-Mahdi died suddenly in August 785, she had the viziers pay the army's wages and swear allegiance to al-Hadi in his absence. She is said to have preferred her second son Harun and to have pressed al-Mahdi to exclude Musa.

Al-Hadi resented her audiences with generals and officials as improper mixing with men. When she pressed him publicly on behalf of a petitioner, Abdallah ibn Malik, he threatened to behead anyone of his entourage who brought her a petition and told her to keep to her spindle and her Koran. Accounts of the rumoured murder that followed differ: one says she learned he planned to kill Harun, another that he tried to poison her, and one that a concubine smothered him with cushions on her orders.

Harun al-Rashid openly trusted her advice and governed beside her, saying he had no reason to be ashamed of sharing power with a woman of her ability. Coins were struck in her name, palaces were named after her, and the cemetery where later Abbasid rulers were buried carries her name. When she died in 789 Harun broke custom by mourning her in public and taking part in her funeral. Many literary historians believe her strong personality influenced the figure of Scheherazade in One Thousand and One Nights.
al-khazneh: Al-Khazneh, also known as Khaznat el-Far'oun, the treasury of the pharaoh, is one of the most elaborate rock-cut tombs in Petra, a city of the Nabatean Kingdom inhabited by Arabs in ancient times. Like most of the buildings there, including the Monastery, Ad Deir, it was carved out of a sandstone rock face. It is thought to have been built as a mausoleum and crypt at the beginning of the 1st century CE, during the reign of Aretas IV Philopatris.

The name Al-Khazneh, Arabic for the Treasury, derives from legends about the decorative stone urn high on the second level, which is in reality solid sandstone. Bedouins began calling it Al-Khazneh in the early nineteenth century because they believed it held treasure. One legend says the Egyptian pharaoh, escaping the closing of the Red Sea while pursuing Moses, created it by magic as a safe place for his treasury. Significant bullet damage can be seen on the urn, which the Jordanian government attributes to Bedouins who believed the legend.

Many of the architectural details have eroded over two millennia. The sculptures are thought to represent mythological figures associated with the afterlife. On top are four eagles that would carry away souls, the figures on the upper level are dancing Amazons with double axes, and the entrance is flanked by the twins Castor and Pollux, who lived partly on Olympus and partly in the underworld. In contrast to the elaborate façade, the interior consists of a plain main chamber and three antechambers, with an interior volume of around 2,000 cubic metres.

The Swiss explorer Burckhardt noted Petra and Al-Khazneh in 1812. As exploration of the Middle East continued, tourism became more common, and by the 1920s a small hotel had opened near Petra. Humidity from crowds and stearic acid from hands resting on the walls have caused damage, and the surface of the Khazneh receded by 40 mm in less than ten years. The monument gained particular fame as the entrance to the Holy Grail's resting place in the 1989 film Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade. The Zamani Project documented it in 2012 by laser scanning, making a permanent record for research and conservation.
al-khwarizmi: Few details of al-Khwarizmi's life are known with certainty. Ibn al-Nadim gives his birthplace as Khwarazm, a region of Greater Iran now divided between Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan, and he is generally thought to have come from there; his name means from Khwarazm. He was of Persian descent, probably Khwarezmian, but wrote his scientific works entirely in Arabic. The historian al-Tabari gives him the further epithets al-Majusi and al-Qutrubbulli. Roshdi Rashed holds that these belong to a second person, whereas David A. King affirms that he was born just outside Baghdad, at Qutrubbul. The epithet al-Majusi may point to Zoroastrian forebears, but the pious preface to his algebra shows that he was an orthodox Muslim.

Most of al-Khwarizmi's work was done between 813 and 833. Baghdad had become the centre of scientific studies and trade, and around 820 he was appointed astronomer and head of the library of the House of Wisdom, which the Abbasid caliph al-Ma'mun had established. He studied the sciences and mathematics, including the translation of Greek and Sanskrit scientific manuscripts. He is said to have assisted a project to determine the circumference of the Earth and to have overseen 70 geographers in making a world map for al-Ma'mun. During the reign of al-Wathiq he is said to have taken part in the first of two embassies to the Khazars.

His treatise on algebra, compiled between 813 and 833, presented the first systematic solution of linear and quadratic equations by reducing them to six standard forms using the operations al-jabr, restoration, and al-muqabala, balancing, and it gave algebra its name. It was written with the encouragement of al-Ma'mun and is full of examples from trade, surveying and legal inheritance. Robert of Chester translated it into Latin in 1145, and it was used until the 16th century as the principal mathematical textbook of European universities. His book on Hindu numerals, written about 825, spread the Hindu-Arabic numeral system, and its Latin translation in the 12th century introduced the term algorithm, from the Latinized form of his name, to the Western world.

His Zij as-Sindhind, based on Indian astronomical methods, held 116 tables for the Sun, Moon and five planets, and marked a turning point in Islamic astronomy. His Geography, finished in 833, reworked Ptolemy's and listed 2,402 coordinates; it corrected Ptolemy's overestimate of the length of the Mediterranean, 63 degrees of longitude, to nearly 50. He also wrote on the astrolabe, the sundial and the Hebrew calendar, and produced a book of annals that does not survive.
al-kitab-al-mukhtasar-fi-hisab-al-jabr-w: Al-Jabr, also called Algebra, is an Arabic-language treatise on algebra written in Baghdad around 820 by al-Khwarizmi; its Latin title is Liber Algebræ et Almucabola. It gave an exhaustive account of solving for the positive roots of polynomial equations up to the second degree, and it was the first text to teach elementary algebra and the first to teach algebra for its own sake. The historian Victor J. Katz regards it as the first true algebra text that survives. The word algebra comes from the title's al-jabr, borrowed into Medieval Latin as algebrāica. Several later authors also published books under this title, among them Abu Kamil and Šarafaddīn al-Ṭūsī.

The book compiled and extended known rules for solving quadratic equations and some other problems. It introduced two operations. Al-jabr, meaning restoring or forcing, moves a deficient quantity to the other side of an equation, so that, in al-Khwarizmi's example, x² = 40x − 4x² becomes 5x² = 40x. Al-muqābala, balancing, subtracts the same positive quantity from both sides.

Together they eliminate negative quantities and leave squares, roots and numbers appearing at most once, which shows that there are only six basic solvable types when all coefficients and solutions are positive. Islamic mathematicians, unlike Indian ones, did not deal with negative numbers. As Carl Boyer notes, the algebra is thoroughly rhetorical: equations are described in words, and even numbers are written out in words rather than symbols.

A second chapter catalogues methods of finding area and volume, including three approximations of pi, one of them 3.1416, which had appeared earlier in the Indian Āryabhaṭīya of 499. The book also explains the Jewish calendar and its 19-year cycle, and about half of it deals with the complex Islamic rules of inheritance, which require skill in first-order equations.

Robert of Chester translated the work into Latin in 1145, and until the sixteenth century it was the principal mathematical textbook of European universities. Rashed and Angela Armstrong write that it differs from Babylonian tablets and from Diophantus' Arithmetica in treating the equation itself as the object of study, defining an infinite class of problems. O'Connor and Robertson call it a revolutionary move away from the Greek view of mathematics as essentially geometry. Algebra is now taught worldwide as part of school curricula.
al-mamun: Abdallah, the future al-Ma'mun, was born in Baghdad on the night of 13 to 14 September 786 to Harun al-Rashid and a concubine, Marajil. That night, later called the night of the three caliphs, his uncle al-Hadi died and Harun became caliph. His mother died soon after, and Harun's wife Zubayda raised him. Though the eldest son, he was named second heir in 799, after his half-brother al-Amin, who was born to Zubayda, a woman of Abbasid descent. He was educated in Arabic, adab, music, poetry, law and hadith, and a modern scholar calls him the most intellectual caliph of his family.

Al-Ma'mun reigned from 813 and spent the early years in Merv, while Iraq was disturbed. In Mecca a claimant, Muhammad ibn Ja'far, proclaimed himself caliph in November 815 and soon abdicated. In Baghdad, neighbourhood watch groups led by preachers such as Sahl ibn Salama al-Ansari held authority until military chiefs crushed Sahl in 817 to 818. In 817 al-Ma'mun named Ali al-Rida, the eighth Shia Imam, as his heir. This may have been meant to reconcile the Alid and Abbasid branches of the family, but the Hashimites in Baghdad deposed him and elected Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi. Al-Rida died in 818, and Shia sources hold the caliph responsible for poisoning him.

With Byzantium, border raiding gave way to a larger contest after Michael II took power in 820. Crete fell to Andalusian invaders in 824, and Arabs from Tunis invaded Sicily in 827 and took Palermo in 831. In 830 al-Ma'mun invaded Anatolia and took forts, sparing those who surrendered. Theophilos took Tarsus in 831. Al-Ma'mun offered him the shahada, tribute or war, and died near Tarsus on 9 August 833, on the way to a campaign, after eating dates by a river. In 833 he also began the mihna, an inquiry that required acceptance that the Quran was created, which led to the imprisonment of Ahmad ibn Hanbal.

Al-Ma'mun gathered scholars of many religions at Baghdad. He sent an emissary to the Byzantine Empire to collect manuscripts and had them translated into Arabic. His peace treaty with the Byzantine emperor entitled him to a number of Greek manuscripts each year, among them Ptolemy's Almagest. He built the first observatory in the Round City of Baghdad and others elsewhere, with scholars from the House of Wisdom. Around 830 astronomers and geographers measured the arc between Tadmur and Raqqa, found it to be one degree of latitude, and calculated the circumference of the Earth at 40,007 kilometres, close to the modern value. His reign saw the publication of al-Khwarizmi's book on algebra. Almanon, a lunar crater, is named after him.
al-maqrizi: Taqi al-Din Abu al-Abbas Ahmad ibn Ali al-Maqrizi was born in Cairo in 1364 to a family of Syrian origin that had recently moved from Damascus. His name refers to a quarter of Baalbek, from which his paternal grandparents came. He was a direct student of Ibn Khaldun. He was trained in the Hanafite school of law, later switched to the Shafi'ite and finally to the Zahirite school, and he studied theology under one of the leading figures of the Zahiri Revolt. His vocal sympathy with that revolt against the Mamluks likely cost him higher administrative and clerical positions.

He confessed to close friends that he believed he was related to the Fatimids through a son of al-Mu'izz li-Din Allah, and Ibn Hajar preserves an account in which his father told him, entering the al-Hakim Mosque, that he was entering the mosque of his ancestor. Walker concludes that his interest in the Fatimids was no more than antiquarian.

In 1385 al-Maqrizi went on the Hajj. He was for some time secretary in a government office, and in 1399 became inspector of markets for Cairo and northern Egypt. He soon gave that post up to become a preacher at the Mosque of Amr ibn al-As, president of the al-Hakim Mosque and a lecturer on tradition. In 1408 he went to Damascus as inspector of the Qalanisryya and lecturer, and later retired into private life in Cairo. In 1430 he made the Hajj again with his family and travelled for some five years. He died in 1442.

Most of his more than 200 works concern Egypt. The best known is al-Mawa'iz wa al-I'tibar bi Dhikr al-Khitat wa al-Athar, on the planning of Cairo and its monuments, translated into French by Urbain Bouriant. Kitab al-Suluk li-Ma'rifat Duwal al-Muluk treats Mamluk history in Egypt, and Itti'az al-Hunafa' deals with the Fatimid state. Other works cover the Arab tribes in Egypt, the famines that struck Egypt, coinage and weights and measures. The Muqaffa was a biographical encyclopedia of which the first sixteen volumes were written. He is recognised as the most influential historian of premodern Egypt. His learning was great, his observation accurate and his judgement good, but his books are largely compilations, and he does not always acknowledge his sources.
al-marj: Marj, in Arabic al-Marj, meaning The Meadows, is a city in northeastern Libya and the administrative seat of the Marj District. It lies in an upland valley separated from the Mediterranean Sea by a range of hills, part of the Jebel Akhdar Mountains. It had an estimated population of 85,315 in 2004. Under Italian rule it was linked to Benghazi by the Bengasi-Barce railroad, of which it was the eastern terminal, and today two roads join it to Benghazi, one through Tocra on the Libyan Coastal Highway and the other through Al Abyar.

Most archaeologists place the ancient city of Barca at Marj, although Alexander Graham located it at Tolmeita, ancient Ptolemais. The modern town grew around a Turkish fort built in 1842 and now restored. During the colonial dominance of Libya, from 1913 to 1941, it was called Barce and was developed as an administrative and market centre and a hill resort.

In the North African campaign of World War II, the 1st Field Regiment of the Royal Australian Artillery won a battle for the region of Barce on 5 February 1941, and the regiment commemorates it by naming its facilities at Enoggera Barce Lines. From 1942 to 1943 the town was the capital of British-occupied Cyrenaica. A 5.6 earthquake on 21 February 1963 destroyed most of it, killing some 300 people and injuring 500 more. Major rebuilding took place about 5 kilometres from the old site and was completed about 1970.
al-masudi: Little is known of al-Masudi apart from what he writes of himself. He was born in Baghdad and was descended from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, a companion of Muhammad. His travels occupied most of his life and took him to most of the Persian provinces, Armenia, Georgia, Azerbaijan and the Caspian region, where he recorded oil lands near Baku, as well as Arabia, Syria, Egypt, the Indus Valley and the western coast of India. He voyaged more than once to East Africa. How he funded these journeys is unknown, and it has been speculated that he traded.

He lived when books were cheap and Baghdad had large public libraries. He was a pupil or junior colleague of philologists such as al-Zajjaj and Ibn Duraid, read the philosophy of al-Kindi, al-Razi and al-Farabi, and knew Galen and Ptolemaic astronomy.

His major work, The Meadows of Gold (Murūj al-Dhahab), combines universal history with scientific geography, social commentary and biography. Only a draft survives, although he later wrote a revised edition. Shortly before his death he wrote the Kitāb al-Tanbīh wa'l-Ishrāf, an abridgement with new material on the Byzantines. Ahmad Shboul notes that he is distinguished among contemporaries by his coverage of non-Islamic lands: India, China, the Turkic peoples, the Khazars, Byzantium and even Britain. His account of the Rus is an important early source for Russian history; he describes them as a varied collection of peoples, pagan and without strong central authority.

He recounts that the Greeks called Constantinople simply the City, and from his writing the name Istanbul can be traced. Ernest Renan compared him to the Greek geographer Pausanias, and he is sometimes called the Herodotus of the Arabs. The Sunni scholar Ibn Hajar called his books imprecise because he was a Shi'a and a Mu'tazili.
al-mukhtar-al-thaqafi: Al-Mukhtar ibn Abi Ubayd al-Thaqafi was born in Ta'if around 622, the son of Abu Ubayd al-Thaqafi, a Muslim army commander of the Banu Thaqif. His father was killed at the Battle of the Bridge in November 634 on the Iraqi front, and Mukhtar, then thirteen, remained in Iraq and was raised by his uncle Sa'd ibn Mas'ud al-Thaqafi. Under Ali he held minor office in Kufa, and little else is known of his early life; he rose to prominence at about sixty. Husayn was killed at Karbala on 10 October 680 while Mukhtar was imprisoned. After his release he allied for a time with Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr in Mecca, but the alliance proved short-lived.

Returning to Kufa, Mukhtar declared Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiyya the Mahdi and Imam and called for vengeance for Husayn. A letter in Ibn al-Hanafiyya's name that won over the tribal chief Ibrahim ibn al-Ashtar was likely fabricated, and Ibn al-Hanafiyya seems to have had no part in the revolt. After the Tawwabin were defeated at Ayn al-Warda in January 685, most pro-Alid Kufans turned to Mukhtar, who took Kufa on 18 and 19 October 685 and expelled the Zubayrid governor. He ruled most of Iraq, for about eighteen months.

He freed slaves among the mawali who joined him and gave the mawali war booty, army salaries and the right to ride horses, which estranged the Arab nobility. After a Kufan noble revolt was put down, he executed most of those involved at Karbala, including Umar ibn Sa'd and Shimr ibn Dhi al-Jawshan, and about ten thousand Kufans fled to Basra. In early August 686 Ibn al-Ashtar defeated the Umayyad army at the Khazir River, where Ubayd Allah ibn Ziyad was killed.

In 687 Mus'ab ibn al-Zubayr, governor of Basra, attacked Kufa with an army that included Kufan nobles who had fled. Mukhtar's forces were beaten at Madhar and Harura, and Mus'ab besieged his palace for four months. On 3 April 687 Mukhtar came out with nineteen supporters and was killed fighting; about six thousand of his followers who surrendered were executed.

His followers became the Kaysanites, a Shia sect that taught the Occultation and Return of the Mahdi, and the mawali and Kaysanites later played a significant part in the Abbasid Revolution. Sunnis generally condemn him as a false prophet, though Julius Wellhausen holds that he did not explicitly call himself one; most Shia revere him as a sincere partisan of Ali's family.
al-mustali: Abū al-Qāsim Aḥmad ibn al-Mustanṣir was born in Cairo, most probably on 15 or 16 September 1074, to the eighth Fatimid caliph, al-Mustansir Billah. He was most likely the youngest of his father's sons. An older brother born in 1060 had the same name, and some later sources confuse the two. At the time the Fatimid Caliphate had lost most of Syria to the Seljuk Turks, and fighting between Turkish and black African troops had brought famine and anarchy to Egypt. In January 1074 the general Badr al-Jamali became vizier and restored order, at the price of taking over the government, army and religious and judicial administration from the caliph.

Al-Mustansir died on 29 December 1094. Nizar, the eldest son, was widely expected to succeed, though no formal designation of him is recorded. Shortly before the caliph's death Ahmad had married Sitt al-Mulk, the daughter of Badr al-Jamali, and Badr's son, the vizier al-Afdal Shahanshah, put his brother-in-law Ahmad on the throne as al-Mustaʿlī biʾllāh. Nizar fled to Alexandria, proclaimed himself caliph and held out against al-Afdal until the city fell. He was taken to Cairo and immured, and he died there. Modern historians such as Farhad Daftary regard the accession as a de facto coup by al-Afdal, who wanted a compliant figurehead.

The dispute split the Isma'ili movement for good. The Fatimid establishment and the Isma'ili communities in Egypt, Syria and Yemen accepted al-Musta'li, but most communities in Persia and Iraq, under Hassan-i Sabbah, recognised Nizar and formed the Nizari branch. Al-Musta'li remained subordinate to al-Afdal throughout his reign. The Egyptian historian Ibn Muyassar wrote that al-Afdal directed state affairs like a sultan, not a vizier. Egypt stayed prosperous under al-Afdal's administration.

Abroad, the Fatimids faced the Sunni Seljuks and the Abbasid caliph al-Mustazhir. They recovered Tyre in 1097 and, while the First Crusade was in Syria, took Jerusalem from its Artuqid rulers in July or August 1098. The Crusaders captured Jerusalem on 15 July 1099, and a Fatimid army under al-Afdal was defeated at the Battle of Ascalon on 12 August 1099. Many Syrians fled to Egypt, where a famine broke out in 1099 or 1100.

Al-Musta'li died on 11 or 12 December 1101, amid rumours that al-Afdal had poisoned him. He left three infant sons, and the eldest, al-Mansur, not yet five, was proclaimed caliph as al-Amir. The Musta'li branch of Isma'ilism takes its name from him.
al-mustarshid: Abu Mansur al-Fadl ibn Ahmad al-Mustazhir was born in 1092, the son of the Caliph al-Mustazhir and a Slavic concubine named Lubanah. He took the regnal name al-Mustarshid Billah and succeeded his father in 1118. His only wife was Amira Khatun, a daughter of the Seljuk sultan Ahmad Sanjar, whom he married in 1124.

Al-Mustarshid gained more independence while the Seljuk sultan Mahmud II was engaged in the east. In 1122 he deposed and imprisoned his vizier Amid al-dawla Jalal al-Din Hasan ibn Ali, and Mahmud then imposed Ahmad ibn Nizam al-Mulk as vizier. The caliph also installed Aqsunqur al-Bursuqi as commander-in-chief of Iraq and Baghdad. The Mazyadid chief Dubays ibn Sadaqa fought Seljuk forces in Iraq, and the Seljuk commander Zengi defeated him at the Battle of Mubarraqiyya in March 1123.

In 1125 the caliph himself rebelled. He sent an army to take Wasit but was defeated near Baghdad and confined to his palace the following year. The Seljuks pillaged his palace, and he had to pay a large ransom to make peace. After Mahmud II died, the Seljuk west fell into civil war. On 20 June 1132 Zengi and Dubays, invited by Sanjar, met the caliph's forces at Hisn al-Baramika, north of Baghdad. Al-Mustarshid prevailed despite their superior numbers, then pursued Zengi to Mosul and besieged him there for three months without success. The campaign was a milestone in reviving the military power of the caliphate.

Not long after Zengi's siege of Damascus in 1134, al-Mustarshid marched against the Seljuk sultan Mas'ud, who had received the title in Baghdad in January 1133 from the caliph himself. The armies met near Hamadan, where the caliph's troops deserted him and he was taken prisoner. He was pardoned on promising not to leave his palace, but was found murdered in the caliphal tent while reading the Quran. He died on 29 August 1135. The murder is supposed to have been the work of an emissary of the Assassins, and the Nizari Ismailis listed him among their victims. Modern historians have suspected that Mas'ud instigated it, although the chroniclers Ibn al-Athir and Ibn al-Jawzi did not speculate on the matter.
His son al-Rashid Billah succeeded him and was deposed on 17 August 1136, after the people of Baghdad rose against him. Al-Rashid's half-brother al-Muqtafi followed him on 17 September 1136.
al-mustasim: Abu Ahmad Abdallah was born around 1213, a son of the Abbasid caliph al-Mustansir and his Abyssinian concubine Hajir. After his father's death he succeeded to the throne in late 1242 as al-Musta'sim billah, and he imprisoned several members of the Abbasid family who might rival him, among them his uncle Ahmad ibn al-Zahir.

In 1249 the Ayyubid sultan of Egypt and Syria as-Salih Ayyub died during the Seventh Crusade, and Mamluk troops proclaimed his widow Shajar al-Durr sultan. Al-Musta'sim refused to recognise her because of her gender, reportedly sending the message that if the Mamluks had no men, he would send them some. Since an Ayyubid sultan gained legitimacy only through the caliph's recognition, this was a setback for the Mamluks, who installed their leader Aybak. Al-Musta'sim's mediation later helped bring an agreement giving the Mamluks southern Palestine.

The Mongol empire had meanwhile come to border his state. In 1255 Hulegu Khan forced him to lend troops for the Alamut campaign, and in 1258 the khagan Möngke ordered Hulegu to subjugate the caliphate. Al-Musta'sim refused the terms, largely on the advice of his grand vizier Ibn al-Alkami, who seems to have assured him that the Islamic world would come to Baghdad's aid. He raised 20,000 ill-equipped and poorly disciplined cavalry, but had lost the loyalty of the Mamluks.

By 11 January 1258 the Mongols held both banks of the Tigris. They breached its dikes on 29 January, trapped the caliph's cavalry and took much of the defences by 5 February with siege engines. Hulegu refused negotiation and about 3,000 notables sent to treat were murdered. The city surrendered on 10 February, and three days later the Mongols entered and began a week of massacre and destruction, looting mosques, palaces, libraries and hospitals. Al-Musta'sim was forced to watch and was executed on 20 February, according to most accounts wrapped in a rug and trampled by horses.

His death ended the caliphate as a political and religious entity in Baghdad. The Mamluk sultan Baybars later installed members of his family as caliphs in Cairo, a line of symbolic figures that lasted until the Ottoman conquest of Egypt in 1517. For almost a century Sultans of Delhi kept putting his name on their coins.
al-mutadid: Al-Mu'tadid was born Ahmad, son of Talha, a son of the caliph al-Mutawakkil, and a Greek slave named Dirar. Talha took the name al-Muwaffaq and became effective ruler of the caliphate during the reign of his brother al-Mu'tamid. Ahmad gained his first military experience against the Zanj, and when he was appointed to command in December 879 at the head of 10,000 troops, the war turned. He and his Turkish slave-soldiers played the major role in the long struggle, which included amphibious operations in the Mesopotamian Marshes, and in August 883 they stormed the Zanj capital of al-Mukhtara.

Relations with his father later worsened, and in 889 he was imprisoned until May 891. When al-Muwaffaq died on 2 June 891 he took power at once, removed his cousin from the succession on 30 April 892 and became caliph when al-Mu'tamid died on 14 October 892.

Al-Mu'tadid owed his power to the army and led it in person, so that he was the most militarily active of the Abbasid caliphs. He also made compromises with powers too strong to defeat. In 893 he confirmed Khumarawayh as autonomous emir of Egypt and Syria for an annual tribute of 300,000 dinars, and married Khumarawayh's daughter Qatr al-Nada himself, who brought a dowry of a million dinars. In the Jazira he took Mosul in 893, captured Hamdan ibn Hamdun in 895 and had the Kharijite leader Harun ibn Abdallah crucified at Baghdad, and in 899 he made his son al-Muktafi governor of the whole province.

He recognised the Saffarid Amr ibn al-Layth in Khurasan, eastern Persia and Fars, and deposed the Dulafids in 896. Over 80 per cent of recorded government spending went to the army, which gave him a reputation for avarice, and his punishment of criminals was known for its cruelty. The Qarmatians, a radical Isma'ili sect, seized Bahrayn in 899 and defeated a caliphal army the next year.

Al-Mu'tadid died at the Hasani Palace on 5 April 902. There were rumours of poison, but the strain of his campaigns more likely weakened his health. Three of his sons, al-Muktafi, al-Muqtadir and al-Qahir, became caliphs in turn, and he was the first Abbasid caliph buried within Baghdad. Hugh Kennedy judges that his reign was too short to reverse long-term trends or to re-establish Abbasid power lastingly, and the revival depended too much on capable men at the helm.
al-mutasim: Muhammad, the future al-Mu'tasim, was born in the Khuld Palace in Baghdad in 796, according to al-Tabari. His father was the caliph Harun al-Rashid, and his mother, Marida bint Shabib, was a slave concubine whose family came from Soghdia. As one of Harun's younger sons he was at first of little consequence. From about 814 he began to form a corps of Turkish troops, first buying domestic slaves in Baghdad and then receiving Turkish slaves from Central Asia under an agreement with the Samanid rulers. The force numbered perhaps three to four thousand men at his accession, but it was highly trained and disciplined, and it made him a man of power in his own right.

Al-Ma'mun made no official provision for his succession. According to al-Tabari, on his deathbed he dictated a letter naming his brother rather than his son al-Abbas, and Abu Ishaq was acclaimed caliph on 9 August 833. It cannot be known whether the letter was genuine. Al-Mu'tasim relied almost exclusively on his Turks, and the historian Tayeb El-Hibri describes his regime as militaristic and centred on the Turkish corps. In 836 he established a new capital at Samarra, to set the regime apart from the restive populace of Baghdad, where the Turkish troops had come into conflict with residents.

He continued al-Ma'mun's support for Mu'tazilism and its inquisition, the miḥna, with the chief qadi Ahmad ibn Abi Duwad as a dominant influence at court. His armies suppressed the Khurramite uprising of Babak Khorramdin and a revolt by Mazyar of Tabaristan. In 838 al-Mu'tasim himself led a campaign against the Byzantine Empire, defeated Emperor Theophilos and sacked Amorium, a victory that became a cornerstone of caliphal propaganda. A plot against him in 838 led to a large-scale purge of the army, and about seventy commanders and soldiers were executed, according to the Kitab al-'Uyun.

Al-Mu'tasim fell ill on 21 October 841 and died on 5 January 842. He was buried in the Jawsaq al-Khaqani palace at Samarra, and his son al-Wathiq succeeded without opposition. The dominance of the Turkic military elite eventually led to the Anarchy at Samarra and the collapse of Abbasid power in the mid-10th century. Yet the system of slave soldiers, the ghulām system, that he inaugurated was widely adopted throughout the Muslim world.
al-muti: Al-Muti was born in Baghdad in 913/14 as al-Fadl, a son of the Abbasid caliph al-Muqtadir and a Slavic concubine, Mash'ala. He was the brother of the caliphs al-Radi and al-Muttaqi and grew up in a time of crisis, as military strongmen took control of the provinces and then of Iraq itself. The commander-in-chief Tuzun deposed and blinded al-Muttaqi in September 944 and chose al-Mustakfi, from a rival line, as caliph. The two princes were said to hate each other, and al-Fadl, who like his father was known for his piety, went into hiding.

In December 945 the Daylamite troops of the Buyid ruler Mu'izz al-Dawla seized Baghdad. Al-Mustakfi was deposed on 29 January 946, or 9 March according to other accounts, and Mu'izz al-Dawla raised al-Fadl to the caliphate that day as al-Muti li-llah. The deposed caliph was blinded, apparently at al-Muti's instigation, and died a prisoner in September 949.

Al-Muti was in effect a puppet of the Buyids, first of Mu'izz al-Dawla and then of his son Izz al-Dawla. The Buyids still acted in the caliph's name and sought from him the honorific titles and diplomas that gave them legitimacy, while his own duties shrank to oversight of the judiciary, religious institutions and the Abbasid clan. A daily salary of 2,000 silver dirhams, later supplemented by estates at Basra, paid for gifts to the Kaaba, support for needy relatives and several pavilions in the palace grounds.

Outside Buyid lands his authority declined. The Samanids refused to recognise him until a peace in 955, and the Fatimids conquered Egypt in 969 and began to expand into the Levant. In 972, when Byzantine raids reached Nisibis, Amida and Edessa, refugees crowded into Baghdad, and Izz al-Dawla pressed al-Muti to sell his valuables and provide 400,000 dirhams. He protested in a much-quoted letter but complied.

On 1 August 974 the Turkic commander Sabuktakin seized Baghdad. Al-Muti, aged and paralysed on his right side after a stroke in 970, was induced to abdicate on 5 August in favour of his son Abd al-Karim, who became al-Ta'i. It was the first succession from father to son since 902. Al-Muti died on 12 October 974 at Dayr al-Aqul on a campaign against the Buyids. Medieval and modern writers regard his reign as the lowest point of Abbasid power, though it brought stability: it lasted 29 Hijri years and four months, far longer than those of his predecessors.
al-muwaffaq: Talha, known as Abu Ahmad, was a son of Caliph al-Mutawakkil and a Greek concubine, Ashar, called Umm Ishaq. According to the historian al-Tabari, he was drinking with his father on the night in 861 when Turkish soldiers murdered him at Samarra, and withdrew after a brief attempt to defend him. Hugh Kennedy suggests that his close later ties with the Turkish commanders may have been formed then or before. During the turmoil known as the Anarchy at Samarra he led the siege of Baghdad against Caliph al-Musta'in from February to December 865, but his brother al-Mu'tazz later imprisoned him as a rival. In 869 he declined the caliphate when the army and people called for him.

From 870 he and the Turkish commander Musa ibn Bugha took control of the government, leaving Caliph al-Mu'tamid little more than his title. After the Zanj sacked Basra in 871 he received a vast governorship and the name al-Muwaffaq Billah, Blessed of God, and in 875 he was placed in the succession after al-Mu'tamid's son. With his secretaries, among them Sa'id ibn Makhlad, he ruled from Baghdad and from 877 appointed the caliph's viziers himself.

When the Saffarid Ya'qub ibn al-Layth advanced on Baghdad, he and Musa routed him at the Battle of Dayr al-Aqul, saving Baghdad. Against the Zanj, whose slave rebellion in the marshes of southern Iraq had begun in 869, he joined his son Abu'l-Abbas in 880 and took their capital, Mukhtara, in August 883, earning the title al-Nasir li-Din Allah. He failed to unseat Ahmad ibn Tulun of Egypt, and in 882 had the caliph seized on his flight towards Ibn Tulun and held at Wasit; in 886 he recognised the Tulunids as hereditary governors of Egypt and Syria for 30 years. Campaigns against Amr ibn al-Layth in Fars won ground in 886 and 887, but settlements later restored Amr's position.

In 889 he had Abu'l-Abbas imprisoned, for reasons that are unclear. Crippled by gout, he returned to Baghdad in May 891 from two years in Jibal, and the troops' support for his son forced his release and recognition as heir. Al-Muwaffaq died on 2 June 891 and was buried in al-Rusafah near his mother. His defeat of the Saffarids and the Zanj began a recovery of caliphal power that culminated when Abu'l-Abbas became caliph as al-Mu'tadid in 892.
al-nasir-muhammad: Al-Nasir Muhammad ibn Qalawun was the third son of Sultan Qalawun and the brother of Sultan al-Ashraf Khalil. He was born in Cairo, in the Citadel. His father was of Turkic origin from a Kipchak tribe, and his mother, Ašlūn, was the daughter of a Mongol notable. He was raised and behaved in Mongol fashion until, after an illness in 1315, he and his followers shaved their heads and gave up their flowing locks. He married a Turkic woman, Khawand Toghay, who began as his slave and was freed by him.
