After the assassination of al-Ashraf Khalil in December 1293, al-Nasir Muhammad was installed as sultan at the age of eight or nine, but real power lay with the regent Kitbugha and the vizier Sanjar al-Shuja'i. Kitbugha deposed him and took the throne himself. He was recalled from al-Karak in 1299, aged about fourteen, and again ruled in name only, under the vice-sultan Salar and the ostadar Baibars al-Jashnakir. In 1303 he and the caliph marched to Syria, where a Mongol army of 50,000 under Qutlugh-Shah was met at Marj al-Saffar. By 1309, unwilling to be dominated, he went to al-Karak and stayed there, and Baibars took the sultanate.

After about ten months Baibars was forced to flee an angry mob, and al-Nasir Muhammad returned to Egypt in 1310, aged about twenty-four. He executed Baibars, arrested Salar, who died in prison, and increased his own power step by step. He annulled the exceptional taxes imposed on commoners, discharged the Oirat Mongols from royal service and appointed Ibn al-Waziri, known for his firmness against corruption, to head the Court of Justice. In 1314 he abolished the post of vice-sultan, and in 1315 he ordered a land survey to re-establish the taxes due from landowners.

His long reign marked the high point of Mamluk power. A canal linking Alexandria with the Nile was redug and opened in 1311, and in Cairo he built the Midan al-Nasiri, additions to the Citadel including the Qasr al-Ablaq, and madrasas, and renovated more than thirty mosques. He became ill on the day of Eid al-Fitr in 1341, named his son al-Mansur Abu Bakr crown prince and died that year.
al-qaeda: The name is a simplified transliteration of the Arabic al-qāʿidah, meaning the foundation or the base. The organisation was founded in a series of meetings held in Peshawar during 1988, attended by Abdullah Yusuf Azzam, Osama bin Laden, Mohammed Atef, Ayman Al-Zawahiri and other veterans of the Soviet–Afghan War. Building on the networks of Maktab Al-Khidamat, the founders decided to create a vanguard for jihad. The writings of the Egyptian Islamist ideologue Sayyid Qutb strongly inspired them. Qutb held that the Islamic world had reverted to the pre-Islamic ignorance known as jahiliyyah and that a vanguard of righteous Muslims was needed to restore Islam.

When Iraqi forces occupied Kuwait in 1990, bin Laden offered to support Saudi Arabia with his fighters. The Saudi government refused and sought the help of the United States instead. The stationing of American troops on the Arabian Peninsula led bin Laden to declare a jihad against the rulers of Saudi Arabia, whom he denounced as apostates, and against the United States. From 1992 the group had its headquarters in Sudan until it was expelled in 1996, and it then moved to Taliban-ruled Afghanistan. In 1996 and 1998 bin Laden issued two fatwas demanding the withdrawal of American troops from Saudi Arabia.

In 1998 the group carried out the bombings of the American embassies in Kenya and Tanzania, which killed 224 people. In 2001 it carried out the attacks of 11 September, which killed 2,996 people, including the 19 hijackers. Two airliners were flown into the Twin Towers of the World Trade Center, a third into the Pentagon, and a fourth crashed in a field in Pennsylvania after passengers revolted. The United States launched the war on terror and invaded Afghanistan to remove the Taliban. In 2004 the group launched an Iraqi branch, which later became the Islamic State of Iraq and then separated from it. American forces killed bin Laden in Pakistan in May 2011.

Al-Qaeda controlled its day-to-day operations only indirectly: decision making on strategy was centralised, while execution was left to mid-level groups, which had to consult the leadership before large attacks. The top leadership included a shura council and committees for military operations, finance and information. Its financing came partly from bin Laden's personal wealth, the heroin trade and donations from supporters in Kuwait, Saudi Arabia and other Gulf states. After the war on terror its leadership became isolated and the organisation regionalised into several groups, among them al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, in the Islamic Maghreb and in the Indian subcontinent, and al-Shabaab. Its long-term aim is a supra-national caliphate; its immediate objectives include the removal of American troops from the Arabian Peninsula.
al-qaeda-in-the-arabian-peninsula: Al-Qaeda in the Arabian Peninsula, or AQAP, is a Salafi-jihadist militant organisation that seeks to overthrow the Yemeni and Saudi governments and to establish an Islamic emirate across the Arabian Peninsula. In the 2000s, al-Qaeda's Saudi branch carried out several mass-casualty attacks on civilians in Saudi Arabia. After that bombing campaign failed and its cells were dismantled, several operatives fled to Yemen. AQAP was formed in January 2009 by a merger of Al-Qaeda in Yemen and Al-Qaeda in Saudi Arabia, and at the time it had no more than a few hundred members.

Its first notable attacks were suicide bombings in March 2009 that targeted South Korean nationals. On 25 December 2009 Umar Farouk Abdulmutallab tried to blow up Northwest Airlines Flight 253 as it approached Detroit, and AQAP claimed responsibility three days later. In October 2010 two printer cartridge bombs sent from Sana'a on cargo planes were found at East Midlands Airport and in Dubai, and AQAP claimed the plot on 5 November 2010.

During the Yemeni Revolution of 2011, AQAP created a local subsidiary, Ansar Al-Sharia, which seized towns in Abyan and Shabwah in the south and declared an Islamic Emirate of Waqar. A government offensive after Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi took power in February 2012 drove it out of most of this territory. After the Yemeni civil war began in 2014, AQAP reached its territorial peak in 2015, taking much of southern Hadhramaut, including its capital Mukalla, and fighting the Houthis in Al-Bayda, Aden and Taiz.

Its strength later waned through internal struggles and operations by several parties in the civil war. Attacks abroad claimed by or linked to the group included the Charlie Hebdo shooting in Paris on 7 January 2015, which AQAP claimed on 14 January, and the shooting at Naval Air Station Pensacola on 6 December 2019.

The group has an emir, who consults a Shura Council, and a general command of the emir and six to eight other leaders. A UN Security Council report of 2018 described doctrinal, propaganda, military, security and financial subdivisions. In July 2010 its Al-Malahem Media launched Inspire, an English-language magazine aimed at a Western audience. Its income came mainly from robberies, kidnappings and donations.

Since 2009 the United States has led a drone campaign against it. A strike on 30 September 2011 killed the preacher Anwar Al-Awlaki and the Inspire editor Samir Khan, and further strikes killed leaders including Nasser Al-Wuhayshi in June 2015 and Qasim Al-Raymi in January 2020. The United Nations, the United States, Saudi Arabia and the UAE, among others, have designated it a terrorist organisation.
al-rashid-of-morocco: Moulay al-Rashid was born in Sijilmasa in 1631, the year his father Moulay Sharif was crowned Emir of Tafilalt. Moulay Sharif abdicated in 1640 in favour of his eldest son Sidi Mohammed. In 1646 the Dilaite leader Mohammed al-Hajj defeated Sidi Mohammed, and al-Rashid, aged 15, saw Dilaite troops sack Sijilmasa, an event he later blamed on his brother's failures. After Moulay Sharif's death in 1659 al-Rashid refused to pledge allegiance to Sidi Mohammed, who imprisoned him. He escaped twice, lived as a fugitive and settled at Taza, where he stayed until 1664.

In 1664, with troops secured from Ali Soliman, al-Rashid seized the citadel of Dar Ibn Mich'al by pretending to make an official visit, and used its plunder to equip his army. At the battle of Angad on 2 August 1664 Sidi Mohammed was killed by a bullet in the neck and his leaderless army was routed. Al-Rashid washed his brother's body himself. After he took Fez its ulama and inhabitants gave him the Bay'ah, and he became sultan in 1666. He defeated Khadir Ghaïlan near Ksar el-Kebir, the Dilaites near Fez, and the al-Shabani rulers of Marrakesh, whose last ruler, Abu Bakr, he had executed.

He built the Oued Sebou Bridge in 1670 and Fez's Errecîf bridge in 1671, added a library to the Qarawiyyin Mosque and ordered the Cherratine Madrasa. In May 1669 he minted the Rechîdiya currency, ending a decade of currency shortage. Moroccan historians portray him as wise and politically astute, and he was known for respecting scholars.

Al-Rashid died in Marrakesh on 9 April 1672, aged 42, after a fall from his horse. His sons were infants and so ineligible to inherit by 'Alawi custom, and he was succeeded by Moulay Ismail, who had been his lieutenant, his regent during the campaign of 1669 and Khalifa of Meknes since 1666. Moulay Ismail married al-Rashid's widowed first wife and was guardian of his sons until 1680.
al-sabah: The Al Sabah family come from the Bani Utbah confederation. Before settling in Kuwait they were expelled from Umm Qasr in southern Iraq by the Ottomans for preying on caravans to Basra and ships in the Shatt al-Arab. According to one oral tradition they settled in southern Iran and Iraq before reaching Kuwait around the middle of the 1700s. Another, told to the British political agent by Shaikh Abdulla, says they fled drought in central Arabia in the early 1700s, tried Zubara on the west coast of Qatar and finally moved north to Kuwait, where they found water. That move north, atabu ila al-shimal, is one account of the name Bani Utub. Sabah I bin Jaber is counted as first ruler, from 1752 to 1762.

In 1892 Sheikh Mohammed came to power and fell out with his brother Mubarak. In 1896 Mubarak rode into Kuwait with his sons Jabir and Salim, entered Mohammed's house in secret and killed Mohammed and their brother Jarrah. Mubarak the Great reigned from 1896 to 1915 and forged the alliance between Kuwait and Britain, drawing Kuwait away from the Ottomans and the rising Al-Saud.

On 19 June 1961 Sheikh Abdullah Al-Salim Al-Sabah ended the British protectorate by treaty, and he introduced the Constitution of Kuwait in 1962 and the Parliament in 1963. During the Gulf War the emir, Sheikh Jaber Al-Ahmad Al-Sabah, and his government worked in exile from a hotel in Ta'if, Saudi Arabia, directing an underground resistance and providing services such as emergency care from oil funds saved earlier. The war ended on 28 February 1991, and the government returned on 15 March 1991 after three months of martial law.

After Abdullah Al-Salim, who ruled from 1950 to 1965, the emirs were Sabah Al-Salim, Jaber Al-Ahmad, Saad Al-Abdullah, who held office from 15 to 29 January 2006, Sabah Al-Ahmad, Nawaf Al-Ahmad, who ruled from 2020 to 2023, and Mishal Al-Ahmad Al-Jaber Al-Sabah. Sheikhs of the house have led Kuwait's military since its first defence infantry and cavalry forces. Since the first cabinet was formed on 17 January 1962, the defence, interior and foreign ministries have all been led by members of the house.
al-shafii: Al-Shafi'i was born in Gaza, near Ashkelon, in the later eighth century. The oldest surviving biography, by Ibn Abi Hatim al-Razi, who died in 938 or 939, is a collection of anecdotes, some fantastical, and the first full biography is filled with what a modern eye calls pious legends. His father died while he was a child, and his mother took him to Mecca at about the age of two, where he grew up in poverty. He had memorised the Quran by seven and Malik ibn Anas's Muwatta by ten, and was authorised to issue rulings at fifteen.

He then went to Medina and studied for many years under Malik ibn Anas, whom he always called the Teacher, though he later differed from some of his views. At thirty he was appointed Abbasid governor of Najran in Yemen. In 803 he was accused of aiding the Alids in a revolt and was brought in chains to the caliph Harun al-Rashid at Raqqa. His defence persuaded the caliph to dismiss the charge, and the incident brought him into contact with the Hanafi jurist Muhammad al-Shaybani.

In Baghdad al-Shafi'i studied with al-Shaybani and developed his first school, influenced by both Abu Hanifah and Malik and later called his old school. He left for Mecca in 804, where he lectured at the Sacred Mosque and impressed students including Ahmad ibn Hanbal, and he returned to Baghdad in 810. In 814 he left for Egypt. There he lectured in the mosque of Amr, composed the surviving version of his al-Risala and dictated most of the texts collected in Kitab al-Umm to his disciples, who read them back for correction. His Egyptian teaching is called his new doctrine.

Al-Shafi'i gave attention to the methods by which the Quran and the sunna were applied in law. He framed rules for analogical reasoning (qiyas) and used it to chart a middle course between conservative traditionalism and legal innovation. His al-Risala was among the earliest works devoted to legal theory and gave it a systematic form.

Al-Shafi'i died in al-Fustat on 20 January 820. One authority says he died of injuries from an attack by supporters of a Maliki named Fityan, but Ibn Hajar al-Asqalani doubts the story, and the cause is not known. He was buried in the vault of the Banu Abd al-Hakam in the City of the Dead near Mokattam, and the Ayyubid sultan al-Kamil built the dome in 1212. His mausoleum remains an important site, and in Egypt his school came to compete with the Maliki school for supremacy.
al-sharif-al-radi: His full name was Abu al-Hasan Muhammad bin al-Husayn bin Musa al-Abrash al-Musawi. He was born in 970 in Baghdad, the Abbasid capital, the third of four children, with two sisters and a brother. His father, Abu Ahmad al-Husayn ibn Musa, descended from Ibrahim al-Asghar, a son of the seventh Shia imam, Musa al-Kazim, although other claims trace the line to Ibrahim al-Mujab, a grandson of al-Kazim. In 965 the Buyid ruler Mu'izz al-Dawla appointed his father naqib al-ashraf, the dean of the Alids in Iraq.

His mother, Fatima, was a granddaughter of Hasan al-Utrush, a descendant of the fourth Shia imam, Ali Zayn al-Abidin. Because he traced his descent to the Ahl al-Bayt through both parents, he was called thil hasabayn, the possessor of two lineages. The family was wealthy: Fatima had inherited a fortune from her father, and she supported the household when the Buyid prince 'Adud al-Dawla confiscated her husband's property.

He studied under Abu Ali al-Farisi. After his father's death he took over his father's post at the head of the Alids. He founded a school called Dar ul'Ilm, the House of Knowledge, where he trained many students, and he wrote several books on Islamic questions and on the interpretation of the Quran. His son, the scholar Abu Ahmad Adnan, left no children. Al-Radi died in Baghdad in 1015 and was buried in Kadhimiya.

His best-known work, the Nahj al-Balagha, gathers sermons, precepts, prayers, epistles and aphorisms of Ali. Ali's sermons had already been compiled, read and taught before al-Radi was born, and his collection brought them together with Ali's other words. The collection covers Islam, theology and metaphysics, worship, wisdom and philosophy, and piety and the afterlife. Several of his contemporaries wrote commentaries on it. Critics of the Nahj al-Balagha have raised two objections: that his brother al-Sharif al-Murtada was one of its authors, and that most of its contents are not by Ali.
al-shaykh-al-mufid: Abu 'Abd Allah Muhammad ibn Muhammad ibn al-Nu'man was born in 'Ukbara, a small town north of Baghdad, in 336 AH according to one account and 338 AH according to Shaykh Tusi. His family belonged to the al-Harithi clan of the tribe of Madhhaj, and because his father was a teacher he was also called Ibn al-Mu'allim, son of the teacher. He moved with his father to Baghdad, where the Shia Buwayhids were ruling. There he studied hadith with Al-Shaykh al-Saduq and also learned from Ibn Qulawayh and from the Mutazilite scholars Abu Abdallah al-Basri and Ali ibn Isa al-Rummani.

Tradition explains his title in two ways. One story says al-Rummani gave him the name al-Mufid, the Instructor, after a dispute over the rebellion of Aisha, Talha and Zubayr against Ali; Ibn Shahr Ashub held that the twelfth Imam, Muhammad al-Mahdi, gave it to him.

Ibn al-Nadim, who knew him, called him the head of the Shia theologians, and al-Tawhidi described him as eloquent and skilful at dialectic. He defended the role of reason in theology. Macdermott places his theology closer to the old Baghdad school of Mutazilism than to the Basran system of his contemporary 'Abd al-Jabbar, though he parted from Mutazilism on the Imamate and on grave sin. He held that the Imams were superior to every prophet but Muhammad and could take the prophets' place in judging, enforcing the law and teaching mankind.

He disagreed at times with his teacher al-Saduq: his Tashih al-Itiqadat corrects al-Saduq's creed, and he rejected reliance on single traditions for legal rulings. Of some 200 works only about ten survive, among them the Amali, Awail al-Maqalat and al-Muqni'ah, whose commentary by Shaykh Tusi became one of the Shia Four Books.

His library and school were destroyed in attacks during his life. He died on the third day of Ramadan in 413 AH; Shaykh Tusi wrote that his funeral drew the largest crowd ever seen. After two years buried in his own house, his body was moved to the Kadhimiya shrine and laid beside Ibn Qulawayh, near the graves of the Imams Musa al-Kadhim and Muhammad al-Jawad. Iran's official calendar marks the ninth day of Azar in his memory.
al-walid-i: Al-Walid was born in Medina in about 674, the eldest son of Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan, a member of the Umayyad family's Hejaz line. His mother, Wallada bint al-Abbas ibn al-Jaz, descended from a 6th-century chief of the Banu Abs. In 684 the Umayyads of the Hejaz were expelled by the rival claimant Abd Allah ibn al-Zubayr and moved to Syria, where his grandfather Marwan I was recognised as caliph. As a prince, al-Walid led summer campaigns against the Byzantines in 696, 697, 698 and 699, and about 700 or 701 he patronised a fortified outpost, Qasr Burqu', on the desert route towards Mecca. He became heir apparent about 705, after the death of Abd al-Malik's brother Abd al-Aziz ibn Marwan.

Al-Walid acceded on 9 October 705 and continued his father's policies of centralisation and expansion. Unlike Abd al-Malik, he depended heavily on the viceroy al-Hajjaj ibn Yusuf, who ran the eastern half of the caliphate and influenced appointments and dismissals. In the east al-Hajjaj's lieutenant Qutayba ibn Muslim campaigned in Transoxiana between 705 and 715, winning the surrender of Bukhara, Khwarazm, Samarkand and Farghana, mostly through tributary alliances that left local rulers in place; after Qutayba's death in 716 local princes and the Turgesh nomads rolled back most of the gains. From 708 or 709 Muhammad ibn al-Qasim conquered Sind. In the west Musa ibn Nusayr conquered the Maghreb and Hispania, and the caliphate reached its largest territorial extent.

War spoils paid for building projects, among them the Great Mosque of Damascus, the al-Aqsa Mosque in Jerusalem, the Prophet's Mosque in Medina and the city of Anjar. He is described as the first caliph to set up programmes of social welfare, aiding poor and disabled Arabs in Syria. His reign was marked by domestic peace and prosperity, and he kept a balance between the Qays and Yaman army factions. The cost of the wars, and his grants to Umayyad princes, burdened his successors.

Al-Walid died of an illness at Dayr Murran, an Umayyad winter estate outside Damascus, on 23 February 715, about a year after al-Hajjaj. Umar ibn Abd al-Aziz led the funeral prayers. He had tried to nominate his son Abd al-Aziz in place of his brother Sulayman, whom his father had designated; Sulayman acceded and dismissed nearly all his governors, and expansion largely halted. Gerald Hawting calls the reigns of al-Walid and Abd al-Malik in some ways the high point of Umayyad power, and the historian Kennedy calls al-Walid's reign perhaps the zenith, though his own part in its successes is unclear. His Syrian contemporaries held him in high esteem.
al-walid-ii: Al-Walid ibn Yazid was the son of the Umayyad caliph Yazid II, who ruled until January 724, and of Zaynab bint Muhammad al-Thaqafi. Yazid had intended him to succeed at once but was persuaded by his brother Maslama to name his half-brother Hisham instead, with al-Walid second in the line of succession, a place he had been given at the age of eleven.

Hisham at first regarded his nephew with affection but grew disillusioned with his dissolute lifestyle, reduced his allowances and punished some of his associates. Al-Walid withdrew from the court to a remote desert residence, perhaps the ruined site now known as Qasr Tuba in the Jordanian desert. After the pilgrimage of 735 Hisham tried to persuade him to step down in favour of Hisham's own son Maslama, or to swear allegiance to Maslama as his successor, and al-Walid refused. Hisham secretly gathered support for Maslama, but the death of the general Maslama ibn Abd al-Malik in the late 730s was a major setback to the plan.

Al-Walid succeeded on the death of Hisham on 6 February 743. As heir he had been known for open-handedness, and as caliph he took special care of the crippled and blind, increasing their stipend. On 21 May 743 he named his two sons, al-Hakam and Uthman, to succeed him in that order. He ordered the arrest of Hisham's sons at Rusafa, but forbade any harm to Maslama and his household in memory of their old companionship. Al-Tabari quotes a number of his poems, and he was fond of versifying and of horse races.

His reputed drinking, singing and immorality aroused opposition, and he imprisoned Sulayman ibn Hisham. When Khalid ibn Abdallah al-Qasri, approached by plotters, declined to join and cautioned the caliph, al-Walid's anger was aroused; he imprisoned Khalid and handed him to Yusuf ibn Umar for fifty million dirhams, and Yusuf tortured and killed him, which intensely angered many of al-Walid's relatives. Yazid ibn al-Walid spoke against al-Walid's favour to the Qaysi Arabs over Yemenis and non-Arab Muslims, and drew support from the Qadariyyah and Murji'ah. Marwan ibn Muhammad wrote from Armenia urging prudence, but was disregarded.

Yazid slipped into Damascus and deposed the caliph in a coup, then distributed money from the treasury. Al-Walid was besieged in a castle outside the city. He fought well but in April 744, at Al-Aghdaf, in what is now Jordan, he was defeated and killed by the forces of Sulayman ibn Hisham. His cousin Yazid III succeeded him and imprisoned his two sons. According to Yazid's own account, al-Walid rejected an offer to set up a tribal assembly to decide the future of the realm and attacked.
al-zahrawi: Abu al-Qasim Khalaf ibn al-Abbas al-Zahrawi was born around 936 at Azahara, eight kilometres north-west of Córdoba, in the year the city was founded. His name's attribute al-Ansari suggests descent from the Ansar of Medina. He lived most of his life in Córdoba, where he studied, taught and practised medicine and surgery until shortly before his death about 1013, two years after the sacking of Azahara.

Few details of his life survive, since the destruction of the city in later conflicts. Ibn Hazm (993-1064) first lists him among the great physicians of Moorish Spain, and the first detailed biography, in al-Humaydi's Jadhwat al-Muqtabis, was completed some sixty years after his death. He served as court physician to the caliph al-Hakam II.

Al-Zahrawi specialised in curing disease by cauterisation, and he devised instruments to inspect the urethra and to examine, insert or remove foreign bodies in the throat, the ear and other organs. He described treating a slave girl who had cut her own throat, suturing the wound so that she recovered with only some hoarseness, and concluded that an incision in the larynx is not dangerous. He is also recorded as describing the drainage of fluid in children with hydrocephalus.

He wrote that before practising surgery a physician must know anatomy and the function of the organs, and he recalled a man who cut into a swelling of the neck thought to be an abscess, when it was an aneurysm, and the patient died on the spot. He stressed treating patients regardless of social status and spoke affectionately of his students as his children.

His Kitab al-Tasrif, a thirty-volume encyclopedia of medicine completed in the year 1000, draws on a career of almost fifty years. The first volume treats general principles, the second pathology, and most of the rest pharmacology; one chapter covers cosmetics. The last volume, On Surgery and Instruments, is the first illustrated surgical guide. He put surgery last because he held it the highest form of medicine, to be practised only after the other branches are mastered. It describes more than 200 instruments, the use of catgut for internal stitching, lithotrity with an instrument he called michaab, and dental work such as ligating loose teeth with gold or silver wire.

Gerard of Cremona translated the surgical volume into Latin in the 12th century, and it became a standard text at universities such as Salerno and Montpellier and the main surgical source in Europe for about five hundred years. Guy de Chauliac quoted the work over 200 times in the 14th century, and Pietro Argallata called its author the chief of all surgeons. The street where he lived in Córdoba is named Calle Albucasis.
al-zaytuna-mosque: Al-Zaytuna, the Mosque of the Olive, was the second mosque built in Ifriqiya and the Maghreb after the Mosque of Uqba in Kairouan. Its founder is disputed: the 11th-century writer al-Bakri credits both Hasan ibn al-Nu'man, who led the conquest of Carthage, and the Umayyad governor Ubayd Allah ibn al-Habhab. Ibn Abi Dinar reported a Byzantine church of Santa Olivia on the site, and excavations in 1969 and 1970 found an older Byzantine-era building with columns over a cemetery, perhaps a basilica, perhaps part of a fortification.

The work under the Aghlabids was completed in 864 to 865. Its inscriptions name the Abbasid caliph al-Musta'in Billah as patron, his mawla Nusayr as overseer and Fathallah as architect, but not the emir Abu Ibrahim Ahmad, and the plan closely follows the Mosque of Uqba. The Zirids added courtyard galleries and the Qubbat al-Bahu dome, dated 991. Under the Hafsids, when Tunis became the capital, the mosque overtook Kairouan in prestige and gained its first attested minaret in 1438 to 1439.

Spanish forces occupying Tunis in 1534 raided its libraries and destroyed or scattered many manuscripts. The Muradid and Husaynid dynasties later restored it, and from 1624 to 1812 the Bakri family held the post of imam. The present minaret, 43 metres high, imitates the Almohad minaret of the Kasbah Mosque.

Teaching was informal before the 14th century, given by ulama without set courses. From the 13th century the mosque became a major centre of Islamic learning, teaching exegesis of the Qur'an, fiqh, Arabic grammar, history, science and medicine; attendance was free, and a student able to teach a subject received an ijazah from his teacher. Reforms began under Ahmad Bey in 1842 and Khayr al-Din al-Tunisi in 1875, and physics, political economy and French were added in 1896. Under French rule it became a bastion of Arab and Islamic culture, where Algerian nationalists such as 'Abd al-Hamid ibn Badis studied. President Habib Bourguiba ended its status as an independent university in 1964 to 1965; it was declared independent again in 2012.
ala-ad-din-tekish: Tekish was the eldest son of Il-Arslan. When his father died in 1172, Tekish was governor of Jand, and his mother Terken Khatun backed his younger brother, Soltan-Shah, as Khwarazmshah. Tekish asked the Qara Khitai for help, received troops from Fuma, the consort of the reigning Qara Khitai monarch, and marched on Gurganj. Soltan-Shah and his mother fled to Khorasan, and Tekish became Khwarazmshah on 11 December 1172. On 11 July 1174 he routed his rivals at Suburni, and the struggle with his brother went on until his brother's death.

Tekish soon broke his tribute agreement with the Qara Khitai and turned back their invasion by flooding the Oxus. He married the daughter of the Kipchak khan, also called Terken Khatun, which gave him Kipchak and Kangly cavalry. In 1187 he took Nishapur, ending the Oghuz emirate there, and a coronation held at Radikat in 1188 affirmed his independence. Soltan-Shah died in September 1193, and Tekish took Merv that December.

Called in by Qutlugh Inanch, Tekish captured Ray in January 1193. The Seljuk prince Toghrul III retook it, but on 4 March 1194 he was defeated and killed at the Battle of Rayy, and by 25 June 1194 the Khwarazmians held all of Persian Iraq. This brought conflict with the caliph al-Nasir, whose army retook the region in 1195; Tekish won it back in July 1196 with a victory near Hamadan. When the Qara Khitai demanded compensation for a defeat by the Ghurids, he refused, declared his full independence and repelled their army at Gurganj. In 1199 he fought the Isma'ilis, failing to take Alamut, and the Bavandids.

Tekish fell ill in 1199. Back in Gurganj, he named his son Qutb ad-Din Muhammad, later Ala ad-Din Muhammad, as heir and built a mausoleum for himself there, where his remains still lie. He set out on a final campaign against the caliph but died on 3 July 1200 of a peritonsillar abscess. He left an organised army of Qipchaq, Qangli and Uran Turkic troops, and contemporaries reported content with his taxes and administration. His wife Terken Khatun then held much of the power under his successor.
alabama: Alabama covers 135,760 square kilometres and is bordered by Tennessee to the north, Georgia to the east, Florida to the south and Mississippi to the west, with a short coastline on the Gulf of Mexico. About three-fifths of the land belongs to the Gulf Coastal Plain, which slopes gently towards the Mississippi River and the Gulf. The north is mostly mountainous, with the Tennessee River cutting a large valley. The land rises from sea level at Mobile Bay to Mount Cheaha at 735 metres, and two thirds of it is forest.

The state takes its name from the Alabama people, a Muskogean-speaking tribe who lived just below the meeting of the Coosa and Tallapoosa rivers. The name first appears in accounts of Hernando de Soto's expedition of 1540. Its meaning is disputed: some scholars derive it from Choctaw words meaning 'clearers of the thicket' or 'herb gatherers', while the popular 'Here We Rest' has no support from experts in Muskogean languages.

Indigenous peoples lived in the area for thousands of years. The agrarian Mississippian culture covered most of the state from about 1000 to 1600 CE, and one of its major polities was centred on Moundville, the second-largest complex of the classic Middle Mississippian era after Cahokia. Finds there were the basis for scholars' definition of the Southeastern Ceremonial Complex. At the time of European contact the peoples of the region included the Cherokee and the Muskogean-speaking Alabama, Chickasaw, Choctaw, Creek and Koasati.

The Spanish expedition of Hernando de Soto passed through Mabila and other parts of the state in 1540. The French founded the first European settlement, Old Mobile, in 1702 and moved it to the present site of Mobile in 1711, claiming the region as part of Louisiana until 1763. The British held it from 1763 until the American Revolutionary War, and Spain held Mobile as part of Spanish West Florida until 1813.

Alabama was recognized as a state in December 1819. In the antebellum period it was a major cotton producer and made wide use of enslaved African American labour. In 1861 it seceded to join the Confederate States of America, with Montgomery as the first capital, and it rejoined the Union in 1868. Decades of economic hardship followed. The establishment of NASA's Marshall Space Flight Center at Huntsville in 1960 helped build a local aerospace industry.

Montgomery is the capital, Huntsville the largest city, and Mobile the oldest. The 2020 census counted about 5 million people. Moundville Archaeological Site preserves the Mississippian past, and the National Park Service administers the Tuskegee Airmen National Historic Site, the Selma to Montgomery National Historic Trail and the Trail of Tears National Historic Trail within the state.
alaeddin-mosque: The mosque stands on the hill known in antiquity as Kawania or Kaoania, near the artificial mound of the ancient acropolis, as part of the citadel complex that held the Seljuk Palace. It was probably built on the site of a Christian basilica, a view supported by 20th-century excavations and by the ancient spolia reused inside. Until the 1920s it shared the hill with the Eflatun Mescidi, the converted Byzantine church of Ayios Amphilochios. Both hill and mosque take their name from Sultan Alaaddin Keykubad I.

Sultan Mesud I began the work in 1155. An inscription dates the ebony minbar to that year, the first dated example of Seljuk art in Anatolia, and the polychrome ceramic frame of the mihrab and the dome above it may be as old. His son Kılıçarslan II continued the building. In 1219 Kaykaus I began a major rebuilding, moving the main entrance from the west to the north, opposite the mihrab, and adding a monumental façade facing the palace, but he died the same year.

His brother Keykubad I resumed the work, had several of Kaykaus's inscriptions altered and claimed the improvements for himself; an inscription over the main entrance credits him with completing the mosque in 617 AH, and another names the Syrian craftsman Muhammad ben Khaulan of Damascus. In 1235 Keykubad added a room of forty-two columns east of the mihrab, and he also built the Konya citadel around mosque and palace. The minaret, the marble mihrab of 1891 and the eastern door are Ottoman. The mosque was used to store army equipment in the Second World War, briefly became a museum and returned to worship in 1952; a full restoration began in 2014.

The eastern wing, its pillars made of reused Byzantine columns and capitals, is unusually open and spacious. In the courtyard a ten-sided tomb with a conical roof, commissioned by Kılıçarslan II, holds the sarcophagi of eight sultans, from Mesud I to Kayhusrew III. A second, octagonal marble tomb begun by Kaykaus I was left unfinished; it is known as the Nameless Mausoleum because the four people buried there are unknown.
alain-leroy-locke: Locke was born Arthur Leroy Locke on 13 September 1885, the only surviving child of Pliny Ishmael Locke, one of the first Black employees of the U.S. Postal Service, and Mary Hawkins Locke, a teacher; both descended from prominent families of free Black people. At sixteen he took the first name Alain. He graduated second in his class from Central High School in Philadelphia in 1902 and also attended the Philadelphia School of Pedagogy. At Harvard he joined Phi Beta Kappa and won the Bowdoin Prize. At Oxford several American Rhodes Scholars from the South refused to live in the same college as him; at Hertford College he studied literature, philosophy, Greek and Latin until 1910, and then philosophy at the University of Berlin.

Locke became assistant professor of English at Howard University in 1912 and wrote his Harvard dissertation, The Problem of Classification in the Theory of Value. Dismissed from Howard in 1925 after campaigning for equal pay for Black and white faculty, he was reinstated in 1928 under Mordecai W. Johnson, the university's first African American president, and taught there until he retired in 1953; the actor Ossie Davis was among his students.

In March 1925 he edited the Survey Graphic issue Harlem, Mecca of the New Negro, and for The New Negro he wrote five essays. His idea of the New Negro treated race as a matter of society and culture more than heredity. He urged Black artists to draw on Africa and on their own history, and he mentored writers such as Zora Neale Hurston. A pragmatist, he is counted an originator of cultural pluralism and a theorist of value. He declared his belief in Baháʼu'lláh in 1918 and remained a Baháʼí for the rest of his life. He was homosexual and, under discriminatory laws, not fully open about it.

After retiring Locke moved to New York, where he died of heart disease at Mount Sinai Hospital on 9 June 1954. His protégée Margaret Just Butcher used his notes to write The Negro in American Culture of 1956. His ashes passed through several hands and were found at Howard in 2007; former Rhodes Scholars paid for a plot, and he was buried at Congressional Cemetery in Washington on 13 September 2014. Howard's Alain Locke Hall bears his name, and Jeffrey Stewart's biography of him won the Pulitzer Prize in 2019.
alaknanda: The Alaknanda is one of the two headstreams of the Ganges, the major river of northern India and a river held holy in Hinduism. In hydrology it counts as the source stream of the Ganges because of its greater length and discharge and because it contributes a significantly larger share of the flow than the Bhagirathi, while in Hindu tradition the Bhagirathi is considered the source. It rises at the foot of the Satopanth and Bhagirath Kharak glaciers in Uttarakhand, and its system drains parts of the Chamoli, Tehri and Pauri districts.

From its source the river travels to the village of Mana and meets the Saraswati at Keshav Prayag. It runs through narrow valleys to the Badrinath valley and Hanumanchatti, where the Ghrit Ganga joins it. After Pandukeshwar it flows through wider valleys and steep terrain, and at Vishnuprayag the Dhauliganga joins it. It travels west to Joshimath, crosses the Main Central Thrust near Helang, and takes in the Birahi Ganga at Birahi. At Nandprayag it meets the Nandakini, at Karanprayag the Pindar, and at Rudraprayag the Mandakini. It then enters a wide valley near Srinagar in Garhwal. At Devprayag the Alaknanda meets the Bhagirathi and from there goes on as the Ganges.

In ancient Hindu texts the Alaknanda is used as a synonym for the Ganges, and in the Vishnu Purana the Ganges divides into four rivers, one of them called Alaknanda, which flows south to India. Five confluences along it, called prayags, are places of pilgrimage: Vishnuprayag, Nandaprayag, Karnaprayag, Rudraprayag and Devprayag, together the Panch Prayag. The river also passes the pilgrimage places of Badrinath and Joshimath. It is known for river rafting, and 37 hydroelectric dams on the river and its tributaries are in operation, under construction or planned.
alalakh: Alalakh, now Tell Atchana, lies in the Amik Valley about 20 kilometres northeast of Antakya in Turkey's Hatay Province, roughly 2 kilometres from the Syria–Turkey border. The mound covers about 22 hectares and stands on the flood plain of the Orontes River, where it enters the Amuq Plain, about 700 metres from Tell Tayinat. Settlements in the valley date back to the Neolithic period, as early as 6000 BCE.

Alalakh was founded by the Amorites in the late third millennium BCE, and its first palace was built around 2000 BCE. In the 18th century BCE it belonged to the kingdom of Yamhad, whose centre was modern Aleppo. Around 1750 BCE Abba-El I of Aleppo gave the city to his brother Yarim-Lim, and Alalakh became the capital of the city-state of Mukiš. It was destroyed in the second half of the 17th century BCE, possibly by the Hittite king Hattusili I.

After a gap of less than a century, written records resume. The statue inscription of Idrimi says that in the 15th century BCE he fled to Emar, lived seven years among the Hapiru, and took Alalakh by a sea attack. Scholars have long debated its historicity. In the mid-14th century BCE the Hittite Suppiluliuma I defeated Tushratta of Mitanni and took northern Syria, including Alalakh. According to Eric Cline the city was largely abandoned by 1300 BCE. The site was reoccupied in the Iron Age, but the port of Al Mina took its place.

Sir Leonard Woolley excavated Tell Atchana, assisted by the epigrapher Sidney Smith, and found palaces, temples, private houses and fortification walls in 17 levels. About 500 cuneiform tablets came from Level VII and Level IV. The Akkadian texts are mostly juridical tablets, recording the ruling family's control of land and income, and administrative records of goods passing in and out of the palace. The inscribed statue of Idrimi is now in the British Museum.

From 2003 a team directed by K. Aslihan Yener, first from the University of Chicago, has excavated the site. It found more than 70 wall-painting fragments in the Level VII palace. According to Manfred Hutter, the goddess Kubaba was first worshipped in the Amik Valley, especially at Alalakh, and her cult then spread to Carchemish and Anatolia.
alamgir-ii: Mirza Aziz-ud-Din Muhammad was born on 6 June 1699 at Burhanpur, the second son of Muizz-ud-Din, who as Jahandar Shah later became emperor, and a grandson of the emperor Bahadur Shah I. His mother was a Rajput princess, Anup Bai. He was seven when his great-grandfather Aurangzeb died in the Deccan. After Jahandar Shah was defeated by Farrukhsiyar, Aziz-ud-Din was imprisoned in 1714 and remained in captivity until 1754, so he had no experience of administration or warfare.

The vizier Imad-ul-Mulk, who had deposed Ahmad Shah Bahadur in 1754, released him and on 2 June 1754 gave him the title Alamgir II, hoping to follow Aurangzeb's centralised approach. He was 55, regarded as frail, and a weak ruler, with all power in the vizier's hands. Imad-ul-Mulk hired Maratha mercenaries, put the imperial revenues into his own pocket and starved the emperor's family. The empire nevertheless began to re-centralise, as many nawabs sought the emperor's help in resisting the Marathas, a development Imad-ul-Mulk did not welcome.

Ahmad Shah Durrani invaded India again and captured Delhi. In January 1757 Alamgir II and his courtiers went to meet him, and ties were strengthened when Durrani's son Timur Shah was chosen as the suitor of the emperor's daughter Zuhra Begum. In July 1757 the Marathas under Raghunathrao besieged Delhi. Najib-ul-Daula, the emperor's Mir Bakhshi, resisted for more than five months before withdrawing to Najibabad, and the Marathas looted the city. The emperor and his family fled to Bharatpur and returned with the help of a Jat regiment sent by Suraj Mal. In Bengal, Alamgir II refused to recognise Mir Jafar as nawab after Plassey in 1757.

Imad-ul-Mulk and Sadashivrao Bhau came to believe that the emperor was about to advance his son Ali Gauhar, who had escaped from Delhi in the summer of 1759, and they plotted his murder. Alamgir II was assassinated in November 1759, on 29 November, and Shah Jahan III was placed on the throne. His son-in-law Timur Shah Durrani's defeat by the Marathas in 1760 provoked Ahmad Shah Durrani to return, and Delhi was recaptured and placed under the nominal authority of Shah Alam II before the Third Battle of Panipat in 1761.
alamo-mission: In 1716 the Spanish government established several Roman Catholic missions in East Texas. Their isolation, with the nearest Spanish settlement, San Juan Bautista in Coahuila, over 400 miles away, made them hard to keep supplied. To help the missionaries, the new governor of Spanish Texas, Martín de Alarcón, wished to establish a waystation between the settlements on the Rio Grande and the new missions.

In April 1718 he led an expedition that erected a temporary structure of mud, brush and straw near the headwaters of the San Antonio River. It served as the mission of San Antonio de Valero, named after Saint Anthony of Padua and the viceroy of New Spain, the Marquess of Valero. On 1 May Alarcón entrusted it to Father Antonio de San Buenaventura y Olivares.

Within a year the mission moved to the western bank of the river, where it was less likely to flood, and in 1724, after the remnants of a Gulf Coast hurricane destroyed its structures, it moved to its present location. In 1803 the abandoned compound was occupied by the Second Flying Company of San Carlos de Parras, from Álamo de Parras in Coahuila, whom locals called the Alamo Company; the name may instead come from a grove of cottonwood trees, álamo in Spanish.

During the Mexican War of Independence parts of it served as a political prison, and from 1806 to 1812 it was San Antonio's first hospital. In December 1835 General Martín Perfecto de Cos surrendered it to Texian forces after the Siege of Béxar, and Colonel James C. Neill took command of the 100 soldiers who remained. The Battle of the Alamo followed in 1836.

In 1849 the United States Army began renting it as a depot, until 1876. The chapel was sold to the state of Texas in 1883 for $20,000, and the other buildings became a wholesale grocery business. The Daughters of the Republic of Texas, organized in 1892, worked to preserve the site, and Adina Emilia De Zavala and Clara Driscoll persuaded the legislature in 1905 to buy the remaining buildings and name the Daughters as permanent custodian.

The Alamo is a museum in the Alamo Plaza Historic District. Visitors tour the chapel and the Long Barracks, which holds paintings, weapons and artifacts from the era of the Texas Revolution, and a diorama recreates the compound as it stood in 1836. In 2015 the Texas Land Commissioner, George P. Bush, moved control of the Alamo from the Daughters to the Texas General Land Office. On 5 July 2015 the Alamo and the four missions of the San Antonio Missions National Historical Park were designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site.
alan-garcia: Alan Gabriel Ludwig García Pérez was born on 23 May 1949 in the Barranco District of Lima into a middle-class family. He first met his father at the age of five, because the father was imprisoned at El Sexto Prison for membership of the Peruvian Aprista Party. His mother founded the party's base in the Camaná Province of the Arequipa Region. He went to party meetings with his father from a very young age, and at fourteen gave a speech in honour of the party's founder Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre. Mentored by Haya de la Torre, he served in the Constituent Assembly of 1978 to 1979, was elected to Congress in 1980 and became General Secretary of the APRA in 1982.

García won the presidential election of 14 April 1985 with 45 per cent of the votes. His opponent Alfonso Barrantes of the United Left withdrew from the runoff, and García took office on 28 July. It was the first time the APRA had come to power in its 60-year history, and at 36 he was the youngest president in Latin America. His economic policy rested on APRA's early anti-imperialist values and distanced Peru from international markets. Hyperinflation reached 7,649 per cent in 1990, and foreign debt rose to 19 billion dollars by 1989. The currency, the inti, was replaced in 1991 by the nuevo sol.

After Alberto Fujimori's self-coup of 5 April 1992, García, who had been suspended as senator for life and was accused of illicit enrichment, went into exile for nine years in Colombia and France. He returned on 27 January 2001 and lost the second round of that year's election to Alejandro Toledo. In 2006 he defeated Ollanta Humala in a run-off on 4 June with about 53 per cent of the vote, and he governed from 28 July 2006 to 2011. During this term Peru signed free trade agreements with the United States and China, and poverty fell from 48 to 28 per cent. He placed fifth in the 2016 election.

On 17 April 2019 García shot himself while police were presenting him with an arrest warrant in a corruption investigation linked to the Odebrecht company, and died later that day. President Martín Vizcarra declared three days of mourning. Opinion on his career is divided: he was known as an immensely charismatic orator, and is considered one of Peru's most controversial politicians.
alan-lomax: Alan Lomax was born in Austin, Texas, on 31 January 1915, the third of four children of Bess Brown and the folklorist John A. Lomax. Two of his siblings, Bess Lomax Hawes and John Lomax Jr., also studied folklore. Because of childhood asthma, ear infections and frail health he was mostly homeschooled at first. He graduated from the Choate School in Connecticut at fifteen in 1930 and entered the University of Texas at Austin, where he read Nietzsche.

From 1937 to 1942 Lomax was Assistant in Charge of the Archive of Folk Song of the Library of Congress, to which he, his father and many collaborators contributed more than ten thousand field recordings. He also recorded long interviews with musicians such as Woody Guthrie, Lead Belly, Jelly Roll Morton and Big Bill Broonzy. In 1941 he went to Clarksdale, Mississippi, hoping to record Robert Johnson, but was told Johnson had died and was directed to Muddy Waters. In 1938 he drove through Michigan and Wisconsin with a disc recorder and a movie camera and returned with 250 discs and 8 reels of film.

In June 1950 the pamphlet Red Channels listed him as sympathetic to Communism, and in September he sailed for Europe, saying only that he was building a library of world folk music for Columbia Records. The FBI investigated him from 1942 to 1979 and found nothing incriminating. After returning to New York in 1959 he produced the concert Folksong '59 at Carnegie Hall, the first at which rock and roll and bluegrass were played on that stage. He was an organiser and board member of the Newport Folk Festival, founded in 1959.

Lomax died in Safety Harbor, Florida, on 19 July 2002, aged 87. He argued for what he called cultural equity, urging folklorists to help communities safeguard their own traditions against centralised commercial entertainment. His memoir The Land Where the Blues Began, published in 1993, linked the birth of the blues to debt peonage, segregation and forced labour in the American South. He received the National Medal of Arts in 1986 and a posthumous Grammy Trustees Award in 2003.

In March 2004 the Library of Congress acquired the material he gathered without its funding, and in 2012 about 17,400 recordings made from 1946 onwards were put online by the Association for Cultural Equity. He spent his last twenty years on the Global Jukebox, a multimedia project that drew on his Cantometrics research.
alan-turing: Alan Mathison Turing was born in Maida Vale, London, on 23 June 1912, while his father, Julius Mathison Turing, was on leave from the Indian Civil Service. His mother was Ethel Sara Turing, née Stoney, of an Anglo-Irish family. At Sherborne School in Dorset, which he entered in 1926, he formed a close friendship with Christopher Morcom, who has been described as his first love; Morcom died of complications of bovine tuberculosis in February 1930, shortly before graduation.

Turing sat the King's College, Cambridge scholarship examination in mathematics in 1930 and graduated from King's. He earned a doctorate from Princeton University in 1938. On returning to Cambridge he attended the 1939 lectures of Ludwig Wittgenstein on the foundations of mathematics, where the two disagreed, Turing defending formalism and Wittgenstein holding that mathematics invents its truths rather than discovering absolute ones.

From September 1938 Turing worked part-time with the Government Code and Cypher School and, with Dilly Knox, studied the Enigma cipher machine of Nazi Germany. At Bletchley Park he specified an electromechanical machine, the bombe, which could break Enigma more effectively than the Polish bomba kryptologiczna from which its name derived; with an enhancement by Gordon Welchman it became a main tool against Enigma messages. He took on the German naval Enigma as head of Hut 8, solving the essential part of its indicator system in December 1939 and devising Banburismus, a sequential statistical technique. In July 1942 he devised Turingery against the Lorenz cipher.

After the war he joined the National Physical Laboratory, and on 19 February 1946 presented the first detailed design of a stored-program computer, the Automatic Computing Engine. In 1948 he joined Max Newman's Computing Machine Laboratory at the University of Manchester. In 1951 he turned to mathematical biology and published The Chemical Basis of Morphogenesis in January 1952, proposing that chemicals reacting and diffusing together, a reaction-diffusion system, could account for the main phenomena of morphogenesis.

In 1952, after acknowledging a sexual relationship with another man, Turing was prosecuted for gross indecency. He received probation conditional on chemical castration and lost his security clearance. He died on 7 June 1954, aged 41, of cyanide poisoning, and the inquest ruled the death a suicide; his family and biographers have variously accepted, questioned or disputed that verdict.

His wartime work, covered by the Official Secrets Act, went unrecognised in his lifetime. Following a 2009 campaign, Prime Minister Gordon Brown apologised for the appalling way he was treated, and Queen Elizabeth II granted him a pardon in 2013. The Alan Turing law, part of a 2017 law, retroactively pardoned men cautioned or convicted under the criminalisation of homosexual acts.
alanya: Alanya lies on the southern coast of Turkey, in Antalya Province, 133 km east of the city of Antalya. It occupies a small peninsula on the Gulf of Antalya, in Pamphylia, between the Taurus Mountains to the north and the Mediterranean, along about 70 km of coastline. This natural strategic position made it a local stronghold for many Mediterranean-based empires, including the Ptolemaic, Seleucid, Roman, Byzantine and Ottoman empires.

Finds in the nearby Karain Cave indicate occupation as far back as the Paleolithic, and evidence shows a port at Syedra, south of the modern city, in the Bronze Age. The city appears in the 4th-century BCE periplus of Pseudo-Scylax, and the castle rock was probably inhabited under the Hittites and the Achaemenid Empire. After Alexander the Great's conquest it was first fortified in the Hellenistic period. Under Ptolemaic rule the port became a popular refuge for Mediterranean pirates. It resisted Antiochus III in 199 BCE but was loyal to the pirate Diodotus Tryphon, who seized the Seleucid crown from 142 to 138 BCE, and Antiochus VII Sidetes completed a new castle and port in 137 BCE.

Its names show its history. It was Korakesion in Greek, from a Luwian word for a protruding city, and Kalonoros under the Byzantine Empire. Its main political importance came in the Middle Ages under the Seljuk Sultanate of Rûm and Alaeddin Kayqubad I, from whom the city takes its name; it became Alaiye. His building campaign produced Alanya Castle, dating from 1226, the Kızıl Kule (Red Tower) and the Tersane (shipyard). In the 13th and 14th centuries Italian traders called the city Candelore or Cardelloro. Mustafa Kemal Atatürk finalised the form Alanya during a visit in 1935. It became a municipality in 1872. After the Treaty of Lausanne in 1923 many of its Christians were resettled in Nea Ionia in Greece.

Alanya is a district and resort city of Antalya Province, with a district population of 364,180 in 2022. Tourism has been the dominant industry since 1958. On the peninsula stands Alanya Castle, a Seljuk citadel built over earlier fortifications, with the Süleymaniye mosque and caravanserai built by the Ottoman ruler Suleiman inside it. Old walls surround much of the eastern peninsula, and within them stand historic villas, most built in the early 19th century. Akşebe Sultan, the castle's first commander under Kayqubad I, is buried in a mausoleum within the walls.
alaouite-dynasty: The Alawis were a family of sharifian religious notables who claimed descent from Muhammad through his grandson Hasan, the son of Ali and Fatimah. Like the Saadi dynasty before them, they came originally from Yanbu al-Nakhil in the Hejaz. According to the dynasty's official historians, the family moved to the Tafilalt, an oasis region in the Ziz Valley and the site of Sijilmasa, in the 12th or 13th century at the request of local people who hoped a sharifian family would benefit the region. Descent from the Prophet mattered because many communities in Morocco came to see sharifian status as the best claim to political legitimacy.

In the early to mid-17th century the Saadian sultans of Marrakesh were in serious decline and several factions contested the country, among them the Dala'iyya, a federation of Amazigh in the Middle Atlas. In 1631 the people of the Tafilalt chose the Alawi head, Mawlay al-Sharif, as sultan. After his sons took up the struggle, Al-Rashid was recognised as sultan in 1664 and his brother Sidi Mohammed was killed that year. Al-Rashid took Fez in June 1666, destroyed the Dala'iyya capital in 1668 and captured Marrakesh in July of that year. He reunited almost all of Morocco and died young in 1672.

His half-brother Mawlay Isma'il reigned for 55 years, from 1672 to 1727. He built a standing army of slaves, the Black Guard, retook coastal cities held by England and Spain, ended Ottoman attempts to gain influence and moved the capital from Fez to Meknes. After his death his sons fought over the succession from 1727 to 1757, until Mohammed ben Abdallah restored order. He founded Essaouira in 1764. European pressure grew in the 19th century. The Treaty of Fez of 30 March 1912 made Morocco a French protectorate, with a Spanish zone in the north, and the sultans kept only symbolic roles.

Mohammed V, acclaimed sultan in 1927 at eighteen, became increasingly associated with the nationalist cause. At the Anfa Conference of 1943 President Roosevelt expressed support for Moroccan independence after the war, and the sultan encouraged the formation of the Istiqlal Party. When Morocco regained independence in 1956 he resumed the role of independent head of state, and in 1957 he took the title of King. His successors Hassan II and Mohammed VI have ruled under the same title. The Kasbah of Moulay Ismail in Meknes, whose construction continued throughout Isma'il's reign, is among the dynasty's buildings.
alaric-i: According to Jordanes, a 6th-century Roman writer of Gothic origin, Alaric was born on Peuce Island in the Danube Delta and belonged to the noble Balti dynasty of the Thervingian Goths, but this cannot be verified. The historian Douglas Boin says only that he came from the Thervingi or the Greuthung. Alaric was probably a child when the Goths, pressed by the Huns, crossed the Danube and fought a war with Rome.

He grew up along Rome's frontier among veterans of the Battle of Adrianople of 378, in which the Goths killed Emperor Valens. A treaty of 382 required the Goths to supply troops to the Roman army in exchange for peace and land. Alaric began his career under the Gothic soldier Gainas and later joined the Roman army.

In 391 Alaric led a mixed band of Goths and allies into Thrace and was stopped by the Roman general Stilicho. By 392 he was in Roman service, and in 394 he led a Gothic force that helped Emperor Theodosius defeat the usurper Eugenius and his general Arbogast at the Battle of Frigidus. About 10,000 of his men died there.

He expected promotion to magister militum and command of regular Roman units, was refused, and mutinied. Theodosius died on 17 January 395, and modern writers regard Alaric as king of the Visigoths from that year. Jordanes records that he persuaded his people to seek a kingdom by their own exertions rather than serve others in idleness.

With the Empire divided between Theodosius's sons Arcadius and Honorius, Alaric exploited the rivalry between East and West, though he needed Roman authority to be supplied by Roman cities. In 396 he marched through Thermopylae and sacked Athens, and archaeology shows widespread damage there. Stilicho drove him into Epirus. Alaric invaded Italy in late 401 or 402. Stilicho met him at Pollentia on Easter Sunday, where he took Alaric's wife and children prisoner, and again at Verona, and each time allowed him to withdraw. Between 404 and 405 Alaric stayed in a Pannonian province, where he could play East against West.

Alaric marched into Italy again and died there, and his Goths sacked Rome in 410. His brother-in-law Ataulf succeeded him and married Honorius's sister Galla Placidia. According to Michael Kulikowski, Alaric had given his people a sense of community that outlived him. The Goths stayed together inside the empire and settled in Aquitaine, which Honorius granted them in 418 or 419, where they created the first autonomous barbarian kingdom inside the Roman frontiers.
alaric-ii: Alaric II succeeded his father Euric as king of the Visigoths on 28 December 484. He was the great-grandson of Alaric I, who sacked Rome in 410. His dominions included most of Hispania, Gallia Aquitania and the greater part of Gallia Narbonensis. His reign is poorly documented: the historian Herwig Wolfram notes that it gets no full treatment in the sources and is overshadowed by his death at Vouillé, and Isidore of Seville gives it a single paragraph, mostly about that battle.

The earliest recorded event concerns Syagrius, former ruler of the Domain of Soissons, who had been defeated by Clovis I of the Franks and took refuge with Alaric. According to Gregory of Tours, Clovis intimidated Alaric into surrendering him, and Clovis later had him executed. In 490 Alaric sent an army to raise Odoacer's siege of Pavia, where his fellow Gothic king Theodoric the Great was trapped. About 495 Visigothic rule in Hispania proved not deeply established, and Alaric took part in repressing the uprising of Burdunellus, which ended at Caesaraugusta in 496. By 502 he and Clovis had met near Amboise and made a peace treaty.

Alaric was an Arian, like the early Visigothic nobles, but he eased his father's persecution of Catholics and permitted them to hold the council of Agde in 506. He exiled Caesarius, bishop of Arles, to Bordeaux for a year on suspicion of conspiring with the Burgundians. He also appointed a commission under the referendary Anianus to prepare an abstract of Roman laws and imperial decrees as the authoritative code for his Roman subjects, known as the Breviary of Alaric.

Clovis broke the peace of 502 and invaded Visigothic territory, despite the diplomatic intervention of Theodoric, Alaric's father-in-law. Forced by his magnates to fight, Alaric met him at the Battle of Vouillé near Poitiers in 507. The Goths were defeated and, according to Gregory of Tours, Clovis himself killed Alaric. Clovis took the royal treasury at Toulouse, though with Ostrogothic help much of the Gallic territory was later recovered.

The gravest result was disarray in the kingdom. Alaric left an illegitimate elder son, Gesalec, and a legitimate younger son, Amalaric, still a child. Gesalec proved incompetent, and in 511 Theodoric took the throne ostensibly on Amalaric's behalf. The Montagne d'Alaric near Carcassonne is named after him, and local tradition says he buried a vast treasure there.
alasehir: Alaşehir lies in the valley of the Kuzuçay, called Cogamus in antiquity, at the foot of the Bozdağ Mountain, ancient Mount Tmolus. The town stands on high ground commanding the fertile plain of the Gediz River, the ancient Hermus. In antiquity it lay in Lydia, on the road between Sardis and Laodicea, and it was well known for its vulnerability to earthquakes. The Turkish name, meaning multicoloured town, is first attested in the memoir of the 13th-century historian Ibn Bibi.

The city was founded by the Attalid kings of Pergamon in the 2nd century BCE and named Philadelphia, meaning the city of him who loves his brother, for Attalus II Philadelphus. When the last Attalid king, Attalus III, died in 133 BCE, he bequeathed his kingdom to Rome. In 17 CE the city suffered badly in an earthquake, and Emperor Tiberius relieved it of taxes. Philadelphia is generally agreed to be the sixth of the seven churches addressed in the Book of Revelation, whose letter describes a community with little power and gives it no rebuke. Ignatius of Antioch wrote an epistle to its Christians in the early 2nd century.

In the 6th century Philadelphia was called little Athens for its festivals and temples. The Seljuk Turks took the city in 1074 and 1093-1094, and the Byzantine emperor Alexios I recovered it in 1098. In the 14th century the patriarch of Constantinople made it the metropolis of Lydia, because it had not capitulated to the Ottomans. It prospered in the 13th and 14th centuries, with a Genoese trading colony and a trade in leather goods and red-dyed silk.

Surrounded by Ottoman emirates but nominally loyal to the Byzantine emperor, it was the last Byzantine Greek stronghold in Asia Minor until Bayezid I took it in 1390. Timur captured it twelve years later. After the Greco-Turkish War much of the town was destroyed by fire, and refugees from it settled in the Athens suburb of Nea Filadelfia after the population exchange of 1923.

Alaşehir is a municipality and district of Manisa Province in Turkey, connected to İzmir by a 105-kilometre railway. Its name is associated with Sultana raisins. Remains of ancient Philadelphia include a theatre, a stadium, a temple, a necropolis, stretches of Byzantine wall and the Basilica of St John, built about 600.
alaska: Alaska lies at the northwest corner of North America, very near to Asia. It borders Canada's Yukon and British Columbia to the east, with the Pacific Ocean to the south, the Bering Sea, Bering Strait and Chukchi Sea to the west and the Arctic Ocean to the north. About 500 miles of Canadian territory separate it from Washington. In the Bering Strait the Russian Big Diomede Island and the Alaskan Little Diomede Island are only 3 miles apart. Its coastline is longer than that of all the other U.S. states combined. The name derives from an Aleut idiom, alaxsxaq, meaning 'the mainland'.

Indigenous peoples occupied Alaska for thousands of years before European contact, and linguistic and DNA studies support the settlement of North America by way of the Bering land bridge. At the Upward Sun River site the remains of a six-week-old infant belonged to a population genetically separate from other Native groups, which the archaeologist Ben Potter named Ancient Beringian. The Tlingit and Haida lived in the southeast, and all three of these peoples and others of the Pacific Northwest Coast suffered smallpox outbreaks from the late 18th century, the worst in the 1830s and 1860s.

The Russian Empire began to colonise the area in the 18th century, establishing Russian America. The expense and difficulty of holding it led to its sale to the United States in 1867 for US$7.2 million. Alaska became a territory on 11 May 1912 and the 49th state on 3 January 1959.

Alaska is a state of the United States, with Juneau as its capital and Anchorage as its most populous city. Juneau is on the mainland but has no road connection to the rest of the North American highway system. More than half the state is federally owned, in national forests, national parks and wildlife refuges. The Alaska Native Heritage Center celebrates the state's 11 cultural groups.
alatri: Alatri is a town and comune of the province of Frosinone in the region of Lazio, Italy. Its Latin name was Aletrium. The area of the modern town was settled as early as the 2nd millennium BCE, and the ancient town was a city of the Hernici. A hill in the centre of the city was adopted as its citadel.

Aletrium was a town of the Hernici which, together with Veroli, Anagni and Ferentino, formed a defensive league against the Volsci and the Samnites around 550 BCE. In 530 BCE the Hernici allied with the Rome of Tarquinius Superbus, which confirms the Etruscan influence in the area that archaeology also shows. Its relations with Rome in the 4th century BCE are told differently by different sources. In the time of Cicero it was a municipium and remained one throughout the imperial period.

After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the city decayed, and the Christian bishop was the only respected authority. In 543, during the Gothic Wars, Totila's troops sacked and destroyed Alatri. In the 12th century it became an important stronghold of the popes when Rome was unsafe for them. The following century it became a free commune under the authority of the bishops and the pope, governed by consuls until 1241, when a podestà was introduced. In the 15th century it began to lose its freedom, and after the short rule of Filippo Maria Visconti in 1434 it had to accept papal suzerainty. Spanish soldiers occupied it in 1556, and it became part of Italy in 1870.

Alatri has about 30,000 inhabitants and is known for its megalithic acropolis. Well-preserved polygonal fortifications of local limestone, probably up to about 9 m high, survive around the city, and on the citadel hill huge terrace walls over 15 m high enclose an area of 220 by 100 m. The Cathedral of San Paolo is documented since 930, and the Collegiata of Santa Maria Maggiore was largely rebuilt in the 13th century.
alauddin-khalji: Alauddin Khalji was born Ali Gurshasp, about 1266; the date rests on the chronicler Haji-ud-Dabir, who says he was 34 when he marched on Ranthambore. He was the eldest son of Shihabuddin Mas'ud, elder brother of the dynasty's founder Jalaluddin, and was brought up by Jalaluddin after his father's death. He married Jalaluddin's daughter Malika-i-Jahan, but the marriage was unhappy. When Jalaluddin became sultan, Alauddin was made master of ceremonies, and after helping to put down a revolt he became governor of Kara in 1291.

Alauddin financed a plan to depose Jalaluddin by raiding Hindu kingdoms. In 1293 he raided Bhilsa and learned of the wealth of the Yadava kingdom at Devagiri. He sent the loot to Jalaluddin and won the governorship of Awadh. After the raid on Devagiri in 1296 he had Jalaluddin killed and was proclaimed sultan at Kara in July 1296, then won support by grants and appointments and a year and a half's pay for every soldier. The chronicler Ziauddin Barani called his first year the happiest the people of Delhi had known.

Mongol armies of the Chagatai Khanate invaded repeatedly. Ulugh Khan defeated one on 6 February 1298, and other battles followed at Kili in 1299, Delhi in 1303 and Amroha in 1305. In 1306 his forces won a decisive victory near the Ravi. He took Ranthambore in 1301, Chittor in 1303 and Malwa in 1305, annexed Gujarat in 1304 and ended several Rajput and other Hindu dynasties. His slave-general Malik Kafur led campaigns south of the Vindhyas and made the Yadava, Kakatiya and Hoysala kings tributaries.

Alauddin undertook large-scale reforms, unlike earlier sultans who relied on the existing administration. According to Satish Chandra they rested on his conception of fear and control as the basis of good government and on his military ambitions. He took away the landed properties of his courtiers and nobles and cancelled their revenue assignments, and he sought to weaken the village headmen, whose resistance he saw as a main difficulty. Some land reforms were continued by his successors and formed a basis for those of Sher Shah Suri and Akbar, but his son Qutbuddin Mubarak Shah revoked others, including price control, a few months after Alauddin died on 4 January 1316.
alaungpaya: Alaungpaya was born Aung Zeya on 24 August 1714 at Moksobo, a village of a few hundred households in the Mu River Valley about 100 km north-west of Ava. He was the second son of a family of gentry that had administered the valley for generations. He grew up while the authority of the Taungoo dynasty declined and Manipuri raiders ransacked Upper Burma. He took over his father's duties as village chief in his early twenties and in 1736 was given a title at Ava and made deputy to his uncle, the lord of the valley.

In 1740 the Mon of Lower Burma founded the Restored Hanthawaddy Kingdom at Bago. By early 1752 its forces, aided by firearms supplied by the French East India Company and by Dutch and Portuguese mercenaries, had reached the gates of Ava. Aung Zeya refused to submit, persuaded 46 villages of the Mu Valley to join him, and on 29 February 1752 proclaimed himself king as Alaungpaya, founding the Konbaung dynasty. Ava fell to Hanthawaddy on 23 March 1752, and he stockaded his village, now renamed Shwebo. His forces retook Ava on 3 January 1754.

In January 1755 he invaded Lower Burma. By May his armies held the Irrawaddy Delta and he captured Dagon, which he renamed Yangon. The French-defended port of Thanlyin repelled several attacks and fell only after a siege of 14 months, in July 1756. Konbaung forces sacked Bago in May 1757, ending the Hanthawaddy kingdom. In 1758 he sent an expedition to the northern Shan states, and on 6 October 1759 a Konbaung force overran the fort of the East India Company at Cape Negrais.

Mon rebels found shelter in Siam, and in December 1759 Alaungpaya left Martaban with an army of 40,000 to invade it. The army reached Ayutthaya in April 1760, but five days into the siege he fell ill. Thai sources say he was wounded when a cannon exploded, while Burmese sources say he fell ill. The Burmese began their retreat on 17 April 1760, and he died on 11 May 1760 at Kinywa, near Martaban. His eldest son Naungdawgyi succeeded him. The Burmese historian Htin Aung describes him as leaving a people united and confident, though denied the time to calm the fever of nationalism he had roused.
alawites: The Alawites trace their faith to Muhammad ibn Nusayr, an Iraqi teacher of the ninth century who was a disciple of the Twelver imams Ali al-Hadi and Hasan al-Askari. After al-Askari died, a dispute over his succession arose in the Shia community, and Ibn Nusayr claimed to be the Bab (Door) and Ism (Name) of the dead imam and to have received his secret teachings. His teaching appears to be one of several early mystical ghulat movements.

The community was organised under Hamdanid rule in northern Syria (947–1008) by al-Khaṣībī, a follower of Ibn Nusayr who died in Aleppo about 969. His grandson and pupil Abu Sa'id Maymun al-Tabarani moved in 1032 to Latakia, then held by the Byzantine Empire, and died in 1034. The historian Stefan Winter calls him the last definitive scholar of Alawism, who founded its calendar and gave its teachings their final form.

Alawites have faced periods of subjugation or persecution under Muslim empires including the Abbasids, Mamluks and Ottomans. Until the 1920s the community usually called itself Nusayri, after Ibn Nusayr. Intellectuals within it then promoted the name Alawi, to stress a link with mainstream Islam and especially Shia Islam, and a name the French authorities also used.

The French Mandate of Syria, established in 1920, was a turning point. The French recruited many minority members into their armed forces and created areas reserved for minorities, among them the Alawite State. That state was later dismantled, but Alawites kept an important role in the Syrian army and later in the Ba'ath Party. After Hafez al-Assad took power in the 1970 coup, the state promoted a national ideology among Alawites to replace their traditional identity.

Alawite doctrine is secretive: some teachings are revealed only to a chosen few, and the community has practised taqiya, the concealment of belief, to avoid persecution. Its central belief is a divine Trinity of Ma'na (meaning), Ism (Name) and Bab (Door), which Alawites hold to have been incarnated seven times in human form. The seventh incarnation consists of Ali ibn Abi Talib, Muhammad and Salman al-Farisi. Alawites also believe in reincarnation, and the faith has been described as syncretic, drawing on Gnosticism, neo-Platonism and Christian practices such as a Mass with bread and wine.

Alawites have traditionally lived in the coastal mountains of western Syria, with Latakia and Tartus the main cities, and on the plains around Hama and Homs. They make up about 9 to 12 percent of Syria's population.
alba-iulia: Alba Iulia is the seat of Alba County in west-central Romania, on the river Mureș in the historical region of Transylvania. Its names reflect its layers of history. In Roman times the settlement was called Apulum, from the Dacian Apoulon mentioned by Ptolemy. From the 9th to the 11th centuries it bore the Slavic name Bălgrad, white castle. The Hungarian name Gyulafehérvár refers to Gyula II, a mid-10th-century Hungarian warlord baptised in Constantinople. The Saxons later called it Karlsburg, in honour of Charles VI.

Nearby stood the Dacian centre of Apulon. After Dacia became a Roman province the capital of Dacia Apulensis was established here, and Apulum, the largest urban centre in Roman Dacia, was the seat of the XIII Gemina Legion; its castrum, at 37.5 hectares, is the largest in Romania. According to the Gesta Hungarorum a regent named Jula or Geula, grandfather of Stephen I of Hungary, built his capital here in the 10th century and about 950 built the first church of Transylvania. After Stephen adopted Catholicism a Catholic bishopric was established, and the present cathedral dates from the 12th or 13th century. John Hunyadi used the citadel in 1442 to prepare against the Ottoman Turks and was entombed in the cathedral.

After the partition of the Kingdom of Hungary the city became in 1542 the capital of the autonomous Principality of Transylvania, until 1690. On 29 November 1599 Michael the Brave of Wallachia entered it and became Voivode of Transylvania, uniting Wallachia, Moldavia and Transylvania under his rule until he was murdered in 1601. Prince Gábor Bethlen founded an academy there. The city passed to the Habsburgs in 1690, and between 1716 and 1735 a seven-bastion baroque fortress, Alba Carolina, was built for Charles VI. On 1 December 1918 the National Assembly of Romanians of Transylvania and Hungary gathered there to proclaim the union of Transylvania with Romania, and in 1922 Ferdinand I was crowned king in the Orthodox cathedral.

The Upper Town, with the fortress, contains the Roman Catholic and Orthodox cathedrals, the Princely Palace, the Union Hall and the Batthyaneum Library, founded in 1780, which holds half of the 9th-century Codex Aureus of Lorsch. The Orthodox cathedral was built between 1921 and 1923. The city is historically important for Romanians, Hungarians and Transylvanian Saxons.
albaicin: The Albaicín is a neighbourhood of Granada centred on a hill on the north side of the Darro River. Its name comes from the Arabic al-Bayyāzīn, and there are several theories of its origin. One holds that it named the inhabitants of Baeza who settled here as refugees in the Nasrid period; another derives it from a phrase meaning the suburb of the falconers; a more likely one sees a local pronunciation of an Arabic word for the whiteners, those who whitewashed buildings.

The land around Granada has been settled since at least 5500 BCE. An Iberian oppidum, Ilturir, was founded by the Bastetani around 650 BCE and later became the Roman Iliberis, a colony in 44 BCE. Excavations on the Albaicín hill have shown a significant Roman town there. Under the Emirate and Caliphate of Cordoba the hill held a small fortress named Gharnāṭa, with a mainly Jewish population. After the caliphate collapsed in 1009, the Zirid leader Zawi ben Ziri founded the Taifa of Granada and built a citadel and palace on the hill, with walls enclosing about 75 hectares and a water system of cisterns and pipes. Part of the northern wall and the gate now called Puerta Monaita survive.

When the Nasrid dynasty rose in the 13th century, Ibn al-Ahmar moved the royal palace to the Sabika hill and began the Alhambra.
