Refugees from lands taken by Castile and Aragon swelled the population, and the Great Mosque of the Albaicín and a hospital, the Maristan of 1365–1367, were built. After Ferdinand and Isabella took Granada in 1492, forced conversion of the Muslims, who became known as Moriscos, set off a rebellion that began in the Albaicín in December 1499. Mosques were replaced by parish churches, often in a mix of Mudéjar and Renaissance styles. The Morisco rebellion of 1568 led to a mass expulsion and left much of the district abandoned, and its density stayed low until the 19th century.

The traditional house is the carmen, a freestanding whitewashed house with a small orchard or garden; the word derives from the Arabic karm, meaning vineyard. After 1568 Christian residents joined abandoned properties to their own and turned them into gardens. Among the oldest preserved houses are the Casa de Zafra and the Dar al-Horra, both from the Nasrid period, and at least twenty underground cisterns remain.

The district largely keeps its medieval street plan. Building of the Gran Vía de Colón between 1895 and 1908 pushed many residents into the Albaicín, where old houses were subdivided and crowded conditions lasted until the 1970s. UNESCO declared the Albaicín a World Heritage Site in 1994, as an extension of the Alhambra and the Generalife.
alban-berg: Alban Berg was born in Vienna on 9 February 1885, the third of four children of Johanna and Konrad Berg, whose father ran a successful export business. The family's finances declined after Konrad died in 1900. Berg cared more for literature than music as a child and several times considered becoming a writer. He began to compose at fifteen, teaching himself. In October 1904 he started to study counterpoint, theory and harmony with Arnold Schoenberg, and from 1907 composition, working with him for six years until 1911. He married the singer Helene Nahowski on 3 May 1911. The Piano Sonata, Op. 1, published in 1910, grew from his student sketches.

From Schoenberg Berg took the idea of developing variation, that every aspect of a work should grow from a single basic idea, and later the twelve-tone technique. His circle in Vienna included Alexander von Zemlinsky, Gustav Klimt, Karl Kraus and Adolf Loos. In 1913 two of his Altenberg songs, with a very large orchestra, were performed under Schoenberg at the Skandalkonzert, which caused a riot and had to be halted. Berg served in the Austro-Hungarian Army from 1915 to 1918 and worked on his first opera, Wozzeck, during leave in 1917. He completed it in 1922, and three excerpts performed in 1924 brought his first public success. The first performance was in Berlin on 14 December 1925.

Other works include the Chamber Concerto of 1923 to 1925 and the Lyric Suite of 1926, which was later shown to use elaborate cyphers to record a secret love affair. He began his second opera, Lulu, in 1928. In the 1930s the Nazis cancelled performances of his music in Germany and eventually proscribed it as degenerate, and Berlin rejected Lulu in the spring of 1934. He interrupted its orchestration to write a Violin Concerto, commissioned by Louis Krasner, in 1935.

Berg died in Vienna on Christmas Eve 1935, aged 50, of blood poisoning from a furuncle on his back, apparently caused by an insect sting in November, and was buried at Hietzing Cemetery. He had orchestrated only two of the three acts of Lulu, which were first performed in Zürich in 1937. His widow Helene banned any completion of the third act, and Friedrich Cerha's orchestration, made in secret, was first performed in Paris under Pierre Boulez in 1979. The Violin Concerto was dedicated to the memory of Manon Gropius, and it too was performed after his death. Berg is regarded as one of the most important composers of the 20th century and the most widely performed opera composer of the Second Viennese School.
alban-hills: The Alban Hills, in Italian the Colli Albani, are the caldera remains of a quiescent volcanic complex, 20 kilometres south-east of Rome and 24 kilometres north of Anzio. Monte Cavo, 950 metres high, forms a visible peak at the centre of the caldera, though the highest point is Maschio delle Faete, about 2 kilometres to the east and 6 metres higher. Subsidiary calderas on the rim hold Lake Albano and Lake Nemi. The hills are made of peperino, or lapis albanus, a tuff useful for construction that gives a mineral-rich ground for the nearby vineyards.

The hills, especially around the lakes, have been popular since prehistoric times. From the 9th to the 7th century BCE there were numerous villages, among them Alba Longa and Tusculum, and the Latini inhabited the area from the 5th to the 3rd century BCE. The Romans called Monte Cavo the Albanus Mons. On its summit stood the sanctuary of Jupiter Latiaris, where the consuls held the Feriae Latinae and several generals marked victories when they were not granted a regular triumph in Rome. The foundations and some fragments of the temple survived until 1777, when they were used to build a Passionist monastery for Cardinal York, but the Via Triumphalis leading up to it can still be seen.

Plutarch reports that in 406 BCE Lake Albano rose over the surrounding hills although no rain or tributary accounted for it, and the flood destroyed fields and vineyards before reaching the sea. It is thought to have been a limnic eruption, in which volcanic gases trapped in the lake sediment suddenly released. A document that may describe an eruption in 114 BCE is now thought to describe a forest fire. The Romans often used the area as an escape from the heat and crowds of Rome.

The four most recent eruptions have been dated to two peaks, around 36,000 and 39,000 years ago. The area has small earthquake swarms, uplift and a release of carbon dioxide and hydrogen sulfide, which have been interpreted as the effect of a slowly growing magma chamber 5 to 6 kilometres below the surface. The towns and villages of the hills are known as the Castelli Romani, and many villas and country houses stand there. Writers and artists including Goethe, Byron, Turner, Edward Lear and John Singer Sargent have produced work about the area.
albanian-fascist-party: On 25 March 1939 Benito Mussolini gave King Zog I of Albania an ultimatum demanding that he accept an Italian military protectorate. Zog refused, the Italians invaded on 7 April and deposed him, and he fled the country. Italy re-established the Albanian state as a protectorate of the Kingdom of Italy. On 11 April the Italian foreign minister Galeazzo Ciano arranged for a group of well-known Albanians to request the formation of the Albanian Fascist Party. On 23 April Achille Starace, the secretary of the National Fascist Party, arrived in Albania with two warships to announce the party officially.

The party, known in Albanian as Partia Fashiste e Shqipërisë or PFSh, received its constitution on 6 June 1939, but not an organised directorate and central council until March 1940. It was a fascist organisation active during World War II, and it held nominal power in Albania from 1939, the year Italy invaded the country, until Italy's capitulation to the Allies in 1943. Albania then fell under German occupation, and the Balli Kombëtar replaced the party. Its life therefore coincided with the period of Italian rule over Albania, and it did not outlast it.

The party existed as a branch of the National Fascist Party and was composed of ethnic Albanians and Italian colonists in Albania. Members swore an oath of loyalty to Mussolini. All Albanians serving the Italian occupiers had to join, and it became the only legal political party in the country. It enacted laws that barred Albanian Jews from joining and excluded them from professions such as education.
albanians: Albanians speak Albanian, an Indo-European language and the only surviving representative of the Albanoid branch of the Paleo-Balkan group. Most scholars hold that they descend at least partly from the Illyrians, but which other Paleo-Balkan groups contributed to their ethnogenesis is still debated. The name Albanoi first appears in the 2nd century CE in Ptolemy, who describes an Illyrian tribe around present-day central Albania. The first certain reference to Albanians as an ethnic group is by the 11th-century chronicler Michael Attaleiates, who places them in the theme of Dyrrhachium.

The Komani-Kruja culture, attested from late antiquity to the Middle Ages in central and northern Albania, is significant for the study of the transition from the classical population to the medieval Albanians. Their own name for themselves, Shqiptarë, is the most common native ethnonym, while Arnaut and Arbanasi are among the names used by neighbours.

Christianity in Albania was under the Bishop of Rome until the 8th century, when its dioceses passed to the patriarchate of Constantinople. After the schism of 1054 the north became identified with Roman Catholicism and the south with Eastern Orthodoxy. In 1190 Albanians established the Principality of Arbanon, with its capital at Krujë. When the Ottoman Empire overpowered the Balkans in the 15th century, the League of Lezhë, a union of Albanian principalities led by Gjergj Kastrioti Skanderbeg, resisted successfully.

By the 17th and 18th centuries many Albanians had converted to Islam, which offered equal opportunities in the Ottoman Empire. More than 40 Grand Viziers were of Albanian origin. The Albanian wālī Muhammad Ali founded a dynasty that ruled Egypt and Sudan until the middle of the 20th century. Albanians declared independence in 1912 during the Balkan Wars, and the borders set after the Treaty of Bucharest left about half the ethnic Albanian population outside them. Albania was governed by a communist government under Enver Hoxha from after the Second World War until 1991.

Albanian society was traditionally organised in tribes, the fiset, each a kin community usually tracing descent through the male line to one forebear. Tribal life depended on the Kanun, a code of oral customary law, and had chiefs, councils and blood feuds. It remained largely intact in the north until the communists took power in 1944, and is regarded as the only European tribal system of this kind to survive to the mid-20th century.

Albanians are traditionally both Christians and Muslims: Catholics, Orthodox, Sunnis and Bektashis. Albanian communities also settled outside the Balkans, such as the Arbëreshë in southern Italy and the Arvanites in southern Greece. Around five million Albanians live across the Balkan Peninsula, and a large diaspora lives in Europe and beyond.
albany-new-york: Albany lies on the west bank of the Hudson River, about ten miles (16 km) south of the river's confluence with the Mohawk River, and about 135 miles (217 km) north of New York City. It sits toward the north end of the navigable Hudson. The city is the economic and cultural core of New York State's Capital District, a metropolitan area that includes Schenectady, Saratoga Springs and Troy.

The Hudson River area was first inhabited by Algonquian-speaking Mohicans, who called it Pempotowwuthut-Muhhcanneuw, meaning the fireplace of the Mohican nation. The Iroquoian-speaking Mohawk, based to the west along the Mohawk River, called it skahnéhtati, through the pine woods, after the path they took there.

When the English captured New Netherland in 1664 the name Beverwijck was changed to Albany, in honour of Prince James, Duke of Albany, later King James VII and II. Duke of Albany was a Scottish title, given since 1398 generally to a younger son of the King of Scots. The Dutch briefly regained the town in August 1673 and called it Willemstadt; the English took permanent possession in 1674 under the Treaty of Westminster. Governor Thomas Dongan chartered Albany as a municipality on 22 July 1686, as a strip of land one mile wide and sixteen miles long, with about 500 people.

Albany was a centre of transportation for much of its history. By 1815 it was the turnpike centre of the state, and with canals and railroads it became the hub for pioneers travelling to Buffalo and the Michigan Territory. It was the original eastern terminus of the Erie Canal and was home to some of the earliest railroads in the world. Democratic Party politics dominated the city from the 1920s, when Daniel O'Connell's machine overcame the Republican one built in the 1890s by William Barnes Jr. Erastus Corning 2nd was mayor from 1942 until his death in 1983.

Albany is the capital of New York and the seat of Albany County. Its population was 99,224 at the 2020 census. It is governed by a mayor and a Common Council under the Dongan Charter of 1686, revised by referendum in 1998, which gives it the oldest active city charter in the United States.

The Empire State Plaza, built between 1965 and 1978 under Governor Nelson A. Rockefeller and the architect Wallace Harrison, dominates the view of the city. Beside it stands the 19th-century New York State Capitol, which houses the State Legislature and the governor's office. The New York State Museum, the New York State Library and the New York State Archives are in the Cultural Education Center at the south end of the plaza. The First Church in Albany, established in 1642, is the second-oldest Reformed Church in America.
albarracin: Albarracín lies in a meander of the Guadalaviar River, in the province of Teruel in Aragon, with the Sierra de Albarracín rising to the south and west. It is the capital of the mountainous comarca of that name. The town is surrounded by stony hills, red sandstone boulders and cliffs, which draw rock climbers, particularly boulderers. It stands near the ancient Roman city of Lobetum. In the Visigothic period it was called Santa María de Oriente, and the Arabs called the area Alcartam, probably from the earlier name Ercávida. Its present name is thought to come from the Banu Razin, so that it means the place of the sons of Razin; its official name until the 19th century was Ciudad de Santa María de Albarracín.

The Hawwara Berber dynasty of the Banu Razin made Albarracín its capital from the early 11th century until the Almoravids took it in 1104. From the later 12th century until 1300 it was an independent lordship, the Sinyoría d'Albarrazín, established after the partition of the Taifa of Albarracín under Pedro Ruiz de Azagra. Peter III of Aragon conquered it in 1284 and deposed the ruling House of Azagra. The last man to hold the title of Señor de Albarracín was Juan Núñez I de Lara; his son Juan Núñez II de Lara remained pretender until 1300, when the city and its lands were formally incorporated into the Kingdom of Aragon.

A Jewish community lived in the town from before the 12th century, according to the earliest written records. It suffered antisemitic incidents until the expulsion of the Jews in 1492. In the Spanish Civil War control of the town shifted several times between Republican and Nationalist forces. A Republican offensive in July 1937 took it on 8 July, except the town hall and cathedral, where soldiers and civilians were besieged; Nationalist reinforcements retook it on 13 July.

Albarracín has been a National Monument since 1961 and received the Gold Medal for Merit in the Fine Arts in 1996. It has been proposed to UNESCO for World Heritage status, and it has belonged to the association of the Most Beautiful Villages of Spain since its founding. The 2007 census recorded 1,075 inhabitants.
albert-camus: Albert Camus was born on 7 November 1913 in Mondovi, now Dréan, in French Algeria, into a working-class family. His mother, Catherine Hélène Camus, was of Balearic Spanish ancestry, deaf and illiterate. He never knew his father, Lucien Camus, a poor agricultural worker killed in action with a Zouave regiment in October 1914. Camus grew up in the Belcourt district of Algiers, without many material possessions. As a second-generation French inhabitant of Algeria he was a pied-noir, a French citizen with more rights than Arab and Berber Algerians under the indigénat.

His teacher Louis Germain gave him free lessons to prepare for a scholarship competition, and in 1924 Camus won a place at a lyceum near Algiers, although his grandmother had planned for him to become a manual worker. He later studied philosophy at the University of Algiers, and dedicated his Nobel Prize speech to Germain.

Camus was in Paris when the Germans invaded France in 1940. He tried to flee but finally joined the French Resistance, writing for and editing the outlawed newspaper Combat. He was a lifelong opponent of capital punishment. On the left he opposed Joseph Stalin and the Soviet Union as totalitarian, which brought him into conflict with others there, above all with Jean-Paul Sartre. During the Algerian War (1954–1962) he kept a neutral stance, advocating a multicultural and pluralistic Algeria, a position most parties rejected. In 1957 he received the Nobel Prize in Literature at the age of 44, the second-youngest recipient in history and the first laureate in literature born in Africa.

Camus wrote novels, plays, essays and short stories. His best-known works include The Stranger (1942), The Plague (1947), The Fall (1956), the essays The Myth of Sisyphus (1942) and The Rebel (1951), and the play Caligula, written in 1938 and performed in 1945. His thought is associated with absurdism: life is void of meaning, or man cannot know its meaning if it exists, and man should embrace this. In The Myth of Sisyphus he wrote that there is only one really serious philosophical question, and that is suicide.

Some count him an existentialist, but he rejected the term repeatedly. He said his philosophical origins lay in ancient Greek philosophy, Nietzsche and the 17th-century moralists, and his critique was aimed chiefly at the existentialism of Sartre. He is remembered for his sceptical humanism and his support for political tolerance, dialogue and civil rights. He died on 4 January 1960.
albert-duke-of-prussia: Albert was born on 17 May 1490 in Ansbach in Franconia, the third son of Frederick I, Margrave of Brandenburg-Ansbach. His mother, Sophia, was a daughter of Casimir IV Jagiellon, so he was a nephew of King Sigismund I of Poland and a great-grandson of Władysław II Jagiełło, who had defeated the Teutonic Knights at Grunwald in 1410. He was raised for a career in the Church, spent time at the court of the Elector of Cologne and became a canon of Cologne Cathedral. After the grand master Frederick of Saxony died in December 1510, Albert was chosen to succeed him early in 1511, in the hope that his kinship with Sigismund would help settle the dispute over eastern Prussia.

As grand master he refused to submit to the Polish crown, and a war that began in December 1519 devastated Prussia. A four-year truce followed in early 1521. At the Diet of Nuremberg in 1522 he met the reformer Andreas Osiander, who won him over to Protestantism. At Wittenberg Martin Luther advised him to abandon the rules of his order, to marry and to convert Prussia into a hereditary duchy. Sigismund agreed, with Prussia to be a Polish fief, and the arrangement was confirmed by a treaty at Kraków. On 10 February 1525 Albert swore a personal oath to Sigismund and was invested with the duchy for himself and his heirs.

In 1526 he joined the League of Torgau, and he took part in plotting against Emperor Charles V after the Augsburg Interim of 1548, though not prominently in the fighting. The lands and treasures of the church, which he confiscated, won over the nobles and paid for the court. He set up schools in every town and in 1544 founded the University of Königsberg, where he appointed Osiander in 1549.

Osiander's quarrel with Philip Melanchthon over justification by faith began the troubles of Albert's last years. With no church lands left to give, taxes rose and his rule became unpopular. After Osiander died in 1552 the duke favoured the preacher Johann Funck and the adventurer Paul Skalić. In 1566 the Estates appealed to King Sigismund II Augustus of Poland, whose commission had Funck executed, while Skalić fled. Albert, virtually deprived of power, died at Tapiau on 20 March 1568 of the plague, with his wife. His son Albert Frederick succeeded him. The University of Königsberg, the Albertina, was the second Lutheran university in the German states, after Marburg.
albert-einstein: Einstein was born in Ulm on 14 March 1879, a subject of the Kingdom of Württemberg in the German Empire. His parents, Hermann Einstein and Pauline Koch, were secular Ashkenazi Jews. The family moved to Munich in 1880, where his father and uncle Jakob founded a company making electrical equipment. His parents worried that he had a learning disability because he was slow to talk, and a compass his father gave him when he was five began a lifelong fascination with electromagnetism. He found the rote learning of the Luitpold Gymnasium harmful to creativity and left it to join his family in Italy.

He renounced his German citizenship on 28 January 1896, avoiding conscription, and enrolled that year at the Swiss federal polytechnic school in Zurich, graduating in 1900. He gained Swiss citizenship a year later and secured a permanent position at the Swiss Patent Office in Bern.

His first paper, on capillary attraction, appeared in 1901. In 1905, sometimes called his annus mirabilis, he published papers on the photoelectric effect, on Brownian motion, which showed that the movement could be taken as firm evidence that molecules exist, and on special relativity, and demonstrated that mass and energy are equivalent. The paper on the electrodynamics of moving bodies was received on 30 June 1905 and reconciled Maxwell's equations with Newtonian mechanics.

In 1915 he proposed a general theory of relativity that extended his mechanics to gravitation, and a paper of the following year introduced the cosmological constant and is regarded as the first step in modern theoretical cosmology. In 1917 he introduced spontaneous and stimulated emission, the latter the core mechanism behind the laser. In his last years he objected to the randomness of quantum theory and tried unsuccessfully to devise a unified field theory, which left him increasingly isolated from mainstream physics.

In 1914 Einstein moved to Berlin, and in 1917 he became director of the Kaiser Wilhelm Institute for Physics. He was visiting the United States in 1933 when Adolf Hitler came to power; horrified by the Nazi persecution of Jews, he stayed, and became an American citizen in 1940. He died on 18 April 1955.

The Nobel committee found that no nomination in 1921 met Alfred Nobel's criteria, so the prize in physics was carried forward and awarded to Einstein for his discovery of the law of the photoelectric effect. The element einsteinium was named after him in 1955, and Time named him Person of the Century in 1999.
albert-frederick-duke-of-prussia: Albert Frederick was born on 7 May 1553, the son of Albert of Prussia and Anna Marie of Brunswick-Lüneburg. He was the second and last Prussian duke of the Ansbach branch of the Hohenzollern family. He became duke after paying feudal homage to his cousin, King Sigismund Augustus of Poland, at Lublin on 19 July 1569. The Polish chronicler Jan Kochanowski described the homage in his work Proporzec.

As the great-grandson of the Polish king Casimir IV Jagiellon and a duke in Prussia who spoke fluent Polish, Albert Frederick was for a time seriously considered as a candidate for the Polish throne, with the support of Polish Lutherans. In 1573 he tried to gain acceptance to the Polish senate but was opposed by Jan Zamoyski, who feared the influence of Protestants in the legislature. He at first refused to recognise the election of Stefan Bathory and backed Maximilian of Austria, but gave Bathory his support at the Toruń sejm of October 1576. In 1573 he married Marie Eleonore of Cleves, daughter of Wilhelm, Duke of Jülich-Cleves-Berg.

From 1572 he showed signs of mental disorder. He twice tried to commit suicide, was prone to violent outbursts and held a great fear that Turks and Muscovites would overrun Germany. In early 1578 his cousin George Frederick of Brandenburg-Kulmbach took over as regent, and after his death in 1603 King Sigismund III Vasa appointed Joachim Frederick as regent in 1605.

Albert Frederick and Marie Eleonore had seven children, of whom two died in infancy. Their daughters married into the houses of Brandenburg, Courland and Saxony, among them Anna, who married John Sigismund, Elector of Brandenburg, and Eleanor, who married Joachim Frederick. Sigismund III allowed John Sigismund to succeed in 1611. Albert Frederick died on 27 August 1618, and the duchy passed to his son-in-law John Sigismund, uniting the two territories under one dynasty and forming Brandenburg-Prussia.
albert-i-duke-of-bavaria: Albert was born in Munich on 25 July 1336, the third son of Emperor Louis IV and his second wife Margaret II, Countess of Hainaut and Holland. As a younger son he could expect at best an appanage. He was ten when his father died, leaving most of his Bavarian inheritance to Albert's eldest half-brother Louis V, Duke of Bavaria, and some appanages to the younger sons.

His elder brother William had a long struggle with their mother, obtaining Holland and Zeeland from her in 1354 and Hainaut at her death in 1356. William was supported by the party of the burghers of the cities. They were opposed by the Hook faction, disaffected nobles who supported Margaret. The upheavals of these years gave rise to the two opposing parties.

William's insanity led to the appointment of the 22-year-old Albert as governor, or regent (ruwaard), of his brother's territories from 1358. During the regency affairs ran smoothly and trade improved, though the troubles between the Hoeks, or Hooks, and the Kabeljauws, or Cods, remained barely beneath the surface. William lived for another thirty years, and Albert did not formally succeed him until his death. By then Albert had arranged the marriage of his daughters to a number of imperial princes and other nobles. His daughter Margaret married John the Fearless, and her son Philip III, Duke of Burgundy, would ultimately inherit Albert's lands.

In Albert's own reign the two parties clashed because of a woman. Albert always had mistresses, but this time his attention fell on Aleid van Poelgeest, a member of the Kabeljauw party, who was considered very beautiful and gained a political influence that was resented. A plot was formed among the Hoeks and members of Albert's household, and on 22 September 1392 Aleid was murdered in The Hague by Hoek nobles. In his rage Albert persecuted the Hoeks by sword and fire, taking one castle after another, and his own son and heir William, no longer feeling safe, went to live in Hainaut. In his last years Albert fought the Frisians, who were beaten time and again but never completely conquered.

Albert died in The Hague on 13 December 1404, aged 68. His eldest son William succeeded him, and a younger son, John III, became Bishop of Liège. Albert had married Margaret of Brieg in Passau after 19 July 1353 and had seven children who lived to adulthood. After her death he married Margaret of Cleves in 1394, without children. When William died in 1417 a war of succession broke out between John and William's daughter Jacqueline of Hainaut. It was the last episode of the Hook and Cod wars and led to the counties passing into Burgundian hands.
albert-i-of-belgium: Albert was born in Brussels on 8 April 1875, the fifth child and second son of Prince Philippe, Count of Flanders, and Princess Marie of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen. He grew up in the Palace of the Count of Flanders, at first third in line to the throne. When his older brother Baudouin, who had been prepared for the crown, died young, he unexpectedly became second in line at the age of 16. Retiring and studious, he prepared strenuously for kingship, and in his youth he travelled incognito round working-class districts to observe living conditions.

On 2 October 1900 he married Elisabeth of Bavaria in Munich. They had three children: Leopold, later Leopold III, Charles, and Marie-José, last Queen of Italy. The couple cultivated friendships with scientists, artists and musicians and made their court at Laeken a kind of cultural salon.

Albert succeeded his uncle Leopold II on 23 December 1909 and took the accession oath in Dutch as well as French, an innovation. He and Elisabeth were popular for a simple lifestyle that contrasted with Leopold II's aloof, autocratic manner. Shortly before accession he had toured the Belgian Congo, annexed in 1908, found it in poor condition and recommended reforms to protect the native population.

During the First World War most of Belgium was under harsh German occupation. Albert worked through secret diplomatic channels for a negotiated peace without victors or vanquished, but neither Germany nor the Entente favoured it. At the end of the war he commanded Army Group Flanders of Belgian, British and French divisions in the final offensive that liberated Belgium. At the Paris Peace Conference in April 1919 he sought reparations and security, and advised against a harsh treaty with Germany, but his advice played a small role. In 1918 he formed a Government of National Union of Catholics, Liberals and Socialists and helped bring about universal male suffrage. In 1920 he changed the family name from Saxe-Coburg-Gotha to House of Belgium.

A passionate alpinist, Albert died on 17 February 1934 climbing alone on the Roche du Vieux Bon Dieu at Marche-les-Dames, near Namur. Official investigations gave two possible explanations: a boulder he leaned on came loose, or the pinnacle holding his rope broke, so that he fell about 18 metres. Rumours of murder were dismissed by most historians, and DNA testing of bloodstained leaves in 2016 concluded he had died at that spot. He was buried in the Royal Crypt at the Church of Our Lady of Laeken and succeeded by Leopold III. In 1925, influenced by Carl E. Akeley, he founded Africa's first national park, now Virunga National Park. Belgians call him the Knight King or Soldier King.
albert-ii-duke-of-austria: Albert II was born on 12 December 1298 at Habsburg Castle in Swabia, a younger son of King Albert I of Germany and Elisabeth of Carinthia, a member of the House of Gorizia. He first prepared for a career in the church and, while still a minor, was elected Bishop of Passau in 1313. He had to contend with a rival candidate and renounced the office in 1317. After the death of his elder brother Frederick the Fair in 1330, Albert and his brother Otto became joint rulers of the Habsburg lands in Austria and Styria. He married Joanna of Pfirt on 15 February 1324, and her inheritance, the Alsatian county of Pfirt and several cities, increased his possessions.

When his maternal uncle Duke Henry of Carinthia died in 1335, Albert established his claim to the Duchy of Carinthia and the March of Carniola, receiving the fief from Emperor Louis IV against the claims of the Luxembourg king John of Bohemia. His standing was high enough that Pope Benedict XII asked him in 1335 to mediate in the church's conflict with Louis, and Philip VI of France asked for his help against the emperor and Edward III of England two years later. Albert nonetheless stayed loyal to Louis until the emperor's death in 1347. After forces of Rudolf Brun demolished Rapperswil Castle in 1350, he marched against the Swiss Confederacy and laid siege to Zürich, to no avail.

In Austria he began the Gothic choir of St. Stephen's Cathedral in Vienna, known as the Albertinian Choir. He also issued the Albertinian House Rule, which set succession in the Habsburg lands by primogeniture. It was disregarded after his death but taken up again under Emperor Maximilian and adopted as part of the Pragmatic Sanction in 1713, remaining one of the basic laws of Austria until 1918. Styria and Carinthia owe their constitutions, the Mountain Book, to him.

Albert died in Vienna on 16 August 1358 and was buried at Gaming Charterhouse, a monastery he had founded. His nickname the Lame has been explained by a speculation that he suffered paralysis caused by polyarthritis, though he fathered numerous children, six of whom survived childhood. By his house rule his eldest son Rudolf IV succeeded him. After Rudolf's death in 1365 the Habsburg lands were divided between his younger sons Albert III and Leopold III in the Treaty of Neuberg of 1379.
albert-ii-duke-of-mecklenburg: Albert was born in Schwerin, the second but eldest surviving son of Henry II, Lord of Mecklenburg and Lord of Stargard, of the old princely clan of the Obotrites, and of his second wife, Princess Anna of Saxe-Wittenberg of the Ascanian house. On 10 April 1336 he married a kinswoman, Euphemia of Sweden and Norway, daughter of the Swedish duke Erik Magnusson and of Ingeborg, the only legitimate daughter of King Haakon V of Norway.

Albert followed his father as lord of Mecklenburg in 1329, and from the 1350s his princely seat was at Schwerin. Euphemia's estates and ancestry gave him standing in Sweden and a part in the politics of Scandinavia, where he sought fiefs and income; for his scheming and avarice the Swedes called him the Fox of Mecklenburg. Already in their lifetime her descent was seen as decisive for any future claim to the Scandinavian thrones.

He married his eldest son, the future Henry III of Mecklenburg, to Ingeborg, eldest daughter of King Valdemar IV of Denmark, around 1362, and their infant son was later put forward without success as heir to Denmark against Valdemar's youngest daughter, Margaret, the future ruler of the Kalmar Union. In Sweden, nobles opposed to Albert's brother-in-law King Magnus IV took his second son Albert as their claimant after the death of Magnus' son Eric. Duke Albert meant to be the real power behind the throne when the younger Albert deposed Magnus and became King Albert of Sweden.

After Euphemia's death Albert married Countess Adelheid of Hohenstein, daughter of Count Ulrich of Hohenstein, apparently without children. Five children of his first marriage survived: Henry, Albert and Magnus, Ingeborg, and Anna, who married Count Adolph IX of Holstein-Kiel. Albert died on 18 February 1379.
albert-ii-of-germany: Albert was born in Vienna on 10 August 1397, the son of Duke Albert IV of Austria and Joanna Sophia of Bavaria. He succeeded to the duchy at the age of seven on his father's death in 1404. His uncle Duke William of Inner Austria, of the rival Leopoldinian line, acted as regent, followed in 1406 by William's brothers Leopold IV and Ernest the Iron. Their quarrels and attempts to control the Albertinian territories produced near civil-war conditions. Albert, who had received a good education, took up the government of Austria proper in 1411, after Leopold's death, and with the help of his advisers cleared the duchy of the evils that had arisen during his minority.

In 1422 he married Elisabeth of Luxemburg, daughter and heiress of King Sigismund of Hungary, who later became Holy Roman Emperor and king of Bohemia. The marriage brought Albert claims to many realms of Central and Eastern Europe. He assisted Sigismund against the Hussites, which drew the Austrian duchy into the Hussite Wars; Sigismund designated him his successor and made him Margrave of Moravia in 1423. The Austrian lands were devastated several times, and Albert took part in the Battle of Domažlice in 1431, where the imperial troops were defeated.

When Sigismund died in 1437, Albert was crowned king of Hungary on 1 January 1438 and moved his court there. He was crowned king of Bohemia six months later but could not take possession of the country, and he was fighting the Bohemians and their Polish allies when he was elected King of the Romans at Frankfurt on 17 March 1438. He was never crowned emperor. His wars against heretics went with persecution of Jews in Austria. Taxes were laid on Jewish communities to fund his campaigns, and after Hussite raids Austrian Jews were accused of collaboration and arms trading. A charge of host desecration at Enns in 1420 gave him a pretext to destroy the community.

According to the chronicler Thomas Ebendorfer, on 23 May 1420 Albert ordered the Jews imprisoned and forcibly converted; those who would not convert were sent off in boats down the Danube, and wealthy Jews were held, some tortured and stripped of property. Pope Martin V intervened to stop the forced baptism of children. On 12 March 1421 Albert sentenced the remaining Jews to death, and ninety-two men and 120 women were burned at the stake outside Vienna's walls. He died at Neszmély on 27 October 1439 while defending Hungary against the Turks, and was buried at Székesfehérvár. His children included Ladislas V Posthumus, who was born after his death.
albert-iii-duke-of-bavaria: Albert was born on 27 March 1401, the son of Ernest, Duke of Bavaria, and Elisabetta Visconti, a daughter of Bernabò Visconti. In 1429 he was engaged to Elisabeth, the daughter of Eberhard III, Count of Württemberg, but she eloped with Count John IV of Werdenberg, who had been a page at her father's court.

In 1432, while Albert was administrator for his father in the former duchy of Bavaria-Straubing, he secretly married Agnes Bernauer, a maid from Augsburg. His father opposed the marriage. In 1435 Duke Ernest ordered her to be murdered: she was accused of witchcraft and thrown into the Danube while Albert was away hunting. Albert then stayed with Louis VII, Duke of Bavaria-Ingolstadt, at Ingolstadt, but he was reconciled with his father in November of that year.

After the reconciliation Albert married Anna of Brunswick-Grubenhagen-Einbeck, daughter of Duke Eric I of Brunswick-Grubenhagen, on 22 January 1437. They had ten children. In 1438 he succeeded his father as duke of Bavaria-Munich, and around 1438 to 1439 he turned Blutenburg Castle, set between two arms of the River Würm, into a hunting lodge. His third son Sigismund later extended it.

In 1440 Albert refused the offer of the Bohemian crown. In 1442 he expelled the Jews from all the Upper Bavarian territories, and Jewish settlement was not permitted there again for about 250 years. In 1444 and 1445 he led two campaigns against the robber barons. When the line of the dukes of Bavaria-Ingolstadt died out, he released that duchy in 1447 to his father's cousin Henry XVI of Bavaria-Landshut.

In 1455 Albert founded the Benedictine monastery at Andechs. He died in Munich on 29 February 1460 and was buried at Andechs. Of his children, John IV, Ernest and Albert died young or in early adulthood, while Albert IV, born in 1447, later became duke. Sigismund lived at Blutenburg, Margaret married Federico I Gonzaga in Mantua in 1463, and Elisabeth married Elector Ernst of Saxony in 1460. Albert also had at least three illegitimate children.
albert-iv-duke-of-bavaria: Albert IV was born in Munich on 15 December 1447, a son of Albert III, Duke of Bavaria, and Anna of Brunswick-Grubenhagen-Einbeck. He was intended for a spiritual career, but after the death of his older brother John IV, Duke of Bavaria, he gave it up and returned from Pavia to Munich. When his brothers Christoph and Wolfgang resigned, Albert became sole duke of Bavaria-Munich, although a new duchy of Bavaria-Dachau was created out of it for his brother Sigismund. It reverted to Bavaria-Munich after Sigismund's death in 1501.

Albert's marriage to Kunigunde of Austria, a daughter of Emperor Frederick III, came out of intrigue. He illegally took control of some imperial fiefs and then asked to marry Kunigunde, who lived in Innsbruck far from her father, offering the fiefs as her dowry. Frederick agreed at first but withdrew his consent after Albert seized another fief, Regensburg. The wedding took place in January 1487, before the change of heart could be communicated to her. Frederick's son Maximilian I mediated and a war was prevented. In 1491–1492 Albert fought the rebellious Löwlerbund, and in 1492 he returned his acquisitions in Swabia to avoid war with the Habsburg and the Swabian League.

After George, the last duke of Bavaria-Landshut, died in 1503, Albert reunited the whole of Bavaria in a war against George's heirs, the Palatinate line of the Wittelsbach family. As compensation for Maximilian's support he had to hand his brother-in-law the southernmost districts of Bavaria-Landshut: Kufstein, Kitzbühel and Rattenberg passed to Maximilian in 1506 and were united with Tyrol. For the Palatinate branch a new duchy of Palatinate-Neuburg was created.

To prevent any future division of Bavaria, Albert decreed in 1506 that the firstborn prince should always succeed. His oldest son and successor, William IV, nevertheless had to share power from 1516 with his younger brother Louis X, Duke of Bavaria, and the decree took effect only after Louis died in 1545. It remained in force until the end of the Bavarian monarchy in 1918. Albert and Kunigunde had eight children. He died on 18 March 1508 and is buried in the Frauenkirche in Munich.
albert-king-of-sweden: Albert, in German Albrecht, was the second son of Duke Albert II of Mecklenburg and Euphemia Eriksdotter, daughter of Duke Erik Magnusson and sister of King Magnus Eriksson of Sweden and Norway. He based his claim to the Swedish crown on these family ties: his mother's paternal grandfather was King Magnus Ladulås, which made him first in line after the dethronement or deaths of all of Magnus Eriksson's children. He also traced his descent through Princess Christina, a daughter of Sverker II, King of Sweden from 1196 to 1208.

In 1363 members of the Swedish Council of Aristocracy, led by Bo Jonsson Grip, came to the court of Mecklenburg. They had been banished after a revolt against Magnus Eriksson, who was unpopular with the nobility. At their request Albert invaded Sweden with the support of several German dukes and counts and Hanseatic cities, and Stockholm and Kalmar, with large Hanseatic populations, welcomed him. He was proclaimed king on 18 February 1364 at the Stones of Mora, and a fragment of the Three Crowns stone, one of the earliest uses of the three crowns as a Swedish symbol, commemorates the event.

His arrival began eight years of civil war between his supporters and Magnus's. At a battle near Enköping in 1365 his German forces defeated and captured Magnus. Valdemar IV of Denmark then intervened with Haakon VI of Norway on Magnus's behalf, joined by Swedish peasants. Albert was unpopular among Swedes because he appointed Germans as officials in every province. Haakon laid siege to Stockholm in 1371 but was beaten back, and a peace freed Magnus to return to Norway. Albert kept the crown but had to swear a belated oath conceding wide powers to the nobles' regency council. Bo Jonsson used them to seize 1,500 farms and became Sweden's largest landowner, controlling a third of the territory.

Most of western Sweden never supported him, and he lost Stockholm's support when he tried to reduce the nobles' large estates. In 1389 the regency council turned to Haakon's widow Margaret, whose troops defeated Albert at the Battle of Åsle in February. He was captured, deposed and held for six years at Lindholmen Castle in Scania. In 1395 he was released, agreeing to give up Stockholm within three years or pay large sums to Margaret. His son Erik had died by then, and Albert chose to give up Stockholm, which Margaret took in 1398.

Albert returned to Mecklenburg, married Agnes of Brunswick-Lüneburg, and had another son. He ruled there as Duke of Mecklenburg-Schwerin until his death, formally abdicating the Swedish throne in 1405, although until then he and his wife styled themselves king and queen. His tomb is in Doberan Minster.
albert-luthuli: Albert John Luthuli was born in about 1898 at the Solusi Mission Station, a Seventh-day Adventist mission near Bulawayo in Rhodesia, to John and Mtonya Luthuli. His father died when he was about six months old, and his mother, who had spent her childhood in the royal household of King Cetshwayo, raised him. In 1908 he moved to Groutville in Natal, where his family had lived, to attend school under the care of his uncle. After finishing his studies at Adams College in 1922 he stayed there as a teacher, one of its first African staff. His grandfather Ntaba had been elected chief in 1860 by the Christian community of the Umvoti Mission Station, and several relatives followed him in the office.

Luthuli became secretary of the Natal Native Teachers' Association in 1928 and its president in 1933. In the same year he was asked to succeed his uncle Martin as chief of the Umvoti River Reserve. He took two years to decide, since the post paid less than one-fifth of his teacher's salary. He was elected at the end of 1935 and held the chieftainship from January 1936. He joined the African National Congress in 1944. In 1946 he entered the Natives Representative Council, which adjourned that August in protest at the use of force against a mineworkers' strike.

He became president of the Natal branch of the ANC in 1951. In 1952 the government removed him as chief because he would not choose between the chieftainship and the ANC, and in December of that year he was elected President-General, with Nelson Mandela as his deputy. He received four banning orders, the first on 30 May 1953. After the Sharpeville massacre, in which sixty-nine Africans were killed, Mandela and others argued for armed resistance. Luthuli at first opposed violence and later gradually accepted it for the movement, while remaining committed to nonviolence himself.

Luthuli received the 1960 Nobel Peace Prize in 1961. Under his fourth ban, issued by the Minister of Justice John Vorster and effective from 31 May 1964, he was kept from travelling even to Stanger. United States Senator Robert F. Kennedy flew by helicopter to Groutville in 1966 to visit him. On 21 July 1967 Luthuli walked from his house toward his store and field near Gledhow station and died on the way back. The official account at the time was that a goods train struck him, but another account holds that he was murdered. The Luthuli Museum opened on 21 August 2004, and the ANC's headquarters in Johannesburg, Luthuli House, bears his name.
albert-of-brandenburg: Albert was born on 28 June 1490 at Cölln on the Spree, now part of Berlin, the younger son of John Cicero, Elector of Brandenburg, and Margaret of Thuringia. After his father died in 1499 his older brother Joachim I Nestor became elector, while Albert held only the title of margrave. In 1513 he became Archbishop of Magdeburg at the age of 23, and administrator of the diocese of Halberstadt.

In 1514 the Mainz cathedral chapter elected him Archbishop of Mainz, hoping for the support of the Elector of Brandenburg in defending Erfurt against the Saxon dukes. The choice broke the canonical ban on holding more than one bishopric, and Albert was also under age and without a degree, so he had received a study dispensation in 1513.

He borrowed 20,000 guilders from Jacob Fugger for the confirmation fee. In 1514 he proposed to Pope Leo X a special indulgence in his dioceses, half the income going to the new St. Peter's Basilica and half to himself. The bull was issued on 31 March 1515, and the indulgence was entrusted to him in 1517 for Saxony and Brandenburg. He employed Johann Tetzel to preach it. Martin Luther wrote to him in protest, sending the Ninety-five Theses on 31 October 1517, and Albert forwarded them to Rome, suspecting heresy.

He tried unsuccessfully in 1515 and 1516 to expel the Jews of Mainz, and became a cardinal in 1518. His correspondence with humanists, and his friendship with Ulrich von Hutten, raised hopes that he might turn Protestant, but after the Peasants' War of 1525 he joined the Catholic League of Dessau. He lived mostly at Halle, where he collected more than 8,100 relics. In 1541 the reformer Justus Jonas preached the Reformation into Halle, and Albert left for Aschaffenburg.

Albert was a patron of the arts and counted Erasmus among his friends. Matthias Grünewald and Lucas Cranach the Elder painted for him; Halle Cathedral received sixteen Passion altars with 140 pictures by Cranach and his workshop, the largest single commission in German art history. He took much of his collection to Aschaffenburg and sold part of the relics to settle claims of the chapters of Magdeburg and Halberstadt. He died at the Martinsburg in Mainz on 24 September 1545, and his tomb is in Mainz Cathedral.
albert-of-riga: Albert, also known as Albert of Livonia or of Buxhoeveden, was born about 1165 in Bexhövede, part of Loxstedt in Lower Saxony, into the powerful Buxhoeveden family; his brother was Hermann. He was a canon in Bremen when his uncle Hartwig, Archbishop of Bremen and Hamburg, named him Bishop of Livonia, on condition that he conquer and hold it and convince the pagan inhabitants to become Christians. The patent was granted on 28 March 1199, and in early spring 1200 he sailed for Livonia with a fleet of 23 vessels and more than 1,500 armed crusaders. He had the support of the German king Philip of Swabia and the implicit blessing of Pope Innocent III.

Albert arrived at Ikšķile (Üxküll) with a sizeable army and could send reinforcements without asking the pope's permission, which let him organize an annual summer expedition from Lübeck, the "perpetual crusade". Finding Üxküll too far from the Daugava to be effective, he founded a castle nearer the sea, where a small stream joined the river and made a natural harbour. In 1201, together with merchants from Gotland, he founded Riga, where a small community of Hanseatic traders from Lübeck already kept a tentative encampment. In 1204 he received a papal bull to enlist crusaders.

He converted many Livs under their leader Caupo, offering them protection against neighbouring Lithuanian and Estonian tribes, and later subjugated the Latvian principalities of Koknese, Jersika and Tālava. The conquest of Livonia occupied almost three decades of his life. In 1217 the Russians of Pskov and an Estonian force besieged Otepää, outraged that some Estonians accepted Latin rather than Orthodox Christianity; Albert's emissaries confirmed a peace in Novgorod, and a German withdrawal from the fortress followed. He created the Livonian Brothers of the Sword, and Philip made him a Prince of the Holy Roman Empire with Livonia as a fief, a title King Henry (VII) confirmed in 1225.

Albert declared his diocese independent of Bremen, and Riga was later raised to an archbishopric. He died in Riga on 17 January 1229 and, as a Catholic bishop, left no descendants. He was venerated as a Catholic saint until the Protestant Reformation. A first-hand account of him survives in the Livonian Chronicle of Henry by Henry of Latvia. Albert Street in Riga is named after him.
albert-sarraut: Albert-Pierre Sarraut was born on 28 July 1872 in Bordeaux. A Radical politician, he sat as Senator of Aude and served as Under-Secretary of State for the Interior. On 14 March 1907 Georges Clemenceau ridiculed him for pleading the case of his electorate during the revolt of the Languedoc winegrowers, saying that it would all end with a banquet. After massive demonstrations in June 1907, the south was occupied by 22 regiments of infantry and 12 of cavalry, and the gendarmerie was ordered to imprison the leaders. Sarraut refused to endorse this policy and resigned from the government.

Sarraut was Governor-General of French Indochina until 1914 and again from 1917 to 1919. He was noted for reform of native education, but the historian Hue Tam Ho Tai argues that his motive was paternalism: he believed the Vietnamese could not be civilised until their thinking, customs and institutions mirrored those of the French. He also supported the preservation of native arts, backing the scholar George Groslier in preserving Cambodian arts and funding the National Museum of Cambodia. On 18 January 1920 he replaced Henry Simon as Minister of the Colonies.

He was President of the Council twice: from 26 October to 26 November 1933 and from 24 January to 4 June 1936. As Minister of the Interior in the government of Édouard Daladier he grew concerned about Spanish refugees fleeing the Francoist regime, and in April 1938 called for prompt action to rid the country of the 'too numerous undesirable elements'.

On 10 July 1940 Sarraut voted to give the cabinet of Marshal Philippe Pétain authority to draw up a new constitution, which ended the Third Republic and established Vichy France. He then retired from politics and took over the family newspaper, La Dépêche de Toulouse, after the Milice killed its editor, his brother Maurice Sarraut, in 1943. Sarraut died in Paris on 26 November 1962. The Lycée Albert Sarraut in Hanoi was named after him.
albert-schweitzer: Ludwig Philipp Albert Schweitzer was born on 14 January 1875 in Kaysersberg, in Alsace, which had less than four years earlier become part of the German Empire. He later became a French citizen after the First World War. He grew up in Gunsbach, where his father was the Lutheran pastor and taught him to play music. The medieval parish church there was shared by two congregations, who prayed in different areas at different times on Sundays. Growing up in this setting, Schweitzer developed the belief that true Christianity should always work towards a unity of faith and purpose.

Schweitzer rapidly gained prominence as a musical scholar and organist. His study J. S. Bach: Le Musicien-Poète appeared in 1905, and he rewrote it in German in two volumes in 1908. He became a deacon at the church of Saint Nicholas in Strasbourg in 1899 and was ordained in 1900. In 1905, aged thirty, he answered a call from the Society of the Evangelist Missions of Paris, which sought a physician, though its committee considered his Lutheran theology incorrect. Despite protests from friends and family he resigned his post and began a three-year course in medicine. He planned to spread the Gospel by the example of healing rather than preaching, and founded the hospital at Lambaréné in French Equatorial Africa, now Gabon.

His Geschichte der Leben-Jesu-Forschung of 1906, published in English in 1910 as The Quest of the Historical Jesus, established his reputation. It criticised the liberal view of Jesus and maintained that his life must be read in the light of his own convictions, which reflected late Jewish eschatology. The keynote of his philosophy, which he considered his chief contribution to mankind, was Reverence for Life. He thought Western civilisation was decaying because it had abandoned affirmation of life as its ethical foundation. He was one of colonialism's harshest critics, yet was sometimes accused of paternalism, and he received the 1952 Nobel Peace Prize.
albert-speer: Albert Speer was born in Mannheim on 19 March 1905 into an upper-middle-class family, the second of three sons. He followed his father and grandfather into architecture, beginning at the University of Karlsruhe because the hyperinflation of 1923 limited his parents' income, then moving to Munich in 1924 and to the Technische Hochschule Berlin-Charlottenburg in 1925. There he studied under Heinrich Tessenow, whom he greatly admired, and after passing his exams in 1927 he became Tessenow's assistant at 22. He married Margarete Weber on 28 August 1928, and they had six children.

Speer applied for Nazi Party membership in January 1931. In 1932 Karl Hanke recommended him to Joseph Goebbels, and he renovated the Party's Berlin headquarters. The organisers of the 1933 Nuremberg Rally asked him for designs, which brought him into contact with Hitler for the first time and won him a national post for the presentation of Party rallies. Hitler had him manage the building site for Paul Troost's renovation of the chancellery, and Speer joined his inner circle. In 1937 he was appointed General Building Inspector for Berlin, and in that capacity was responsible for the Central Department for Resettlement, which evicted Jewish tenants from their homes.

On 8 February 1942 Fritz Todt, Reich Minister of Armaments and Munitions, died in a plane crash at Rastenburg, and Hitler appointed Speer in his place. Speer cancelled a seat on the plane the night before. He took over Todt's other posts and, by April 1942, had persuaded Hermann Göring to create a Central Planning Board that gave him authority over raw materials and production. Using misleading statistics, he promoted an armaments miracle that was widely credited with keeping Germany in the war. In 1944 a task force he set up to increase fighter production became instrumental in exploiting slave labour.

At the Nuremberg trial Speer was found guilty of war crimes and crimes against humanity, principally for the use of slave and forced labour, and was acquitted on the other two counts. On 1 October 1946 he was sentenced to 20 years. Three of eight judges favoured death, and the sentence was a compromise. He served the term in Spandau Prison and was released in 1966. He died of a stroke on 1 September 1981.

His memoirs, Inside the Third Reich and Spandau: The Secret Diaries, presented him as an apolitical technocrat who regretted not having discovered the regime's crimes. Historians call this image the Speer myth. It began to fall apart in the 1980s, and Adam Tooze later called the idea of an apolitical technocrat absurd. Martin Kitchen argues that much of the rise in arms production owed to systems set up by Todt and that Speer knew of the Final Solution.
albert-the-bear: Albert was the only son of Otto, Count of Ballenstedt, and Eilika, daughter of Magnus Billung, Duke of Saxony. He inherited his father's estates in northern Saxony in 1123, and on his mother's death in 1142 he succeeded to half of the lands of the house of Billung. About 1123 his relation Lothar I, Duke of Saxony, gave him the Margraviate of Lusatia. In 1126 he accompanied Lothar, by then King of the Germans, on a disastrous expedition against Soběslav I of Bohemia and was briefly imprisoned after the Battle of Kulm. In 1124 he married Sophie of Winzenburg, and they had many children.

When Henry II, Margrave of the Nordmark, died in 1128, Albert expected to receive the Northern March, but it passed to Udo V, Count of Stade. Albert attacked him and lost Lusatia as a result, and Udo was said to have been assassinated by servants of Albert in 1130. After serving the king in Italy, Albert received the Northern March in 1134. In 1138 King Conrad III deprived Henry the Proud of Saxony and awarded it to Albert if he could take it, but he was driven out. In 1142 Henry the Lion received the duchy, and Albert renounced his claim and received the counties of Weimar and Orlamünde.

He then turned to the thinly populated lands to the north and east and took part in the Wendish Crusade of 1147, in which his army besieged Demmin and recovered Havelberg. By an arrangement with Pribislav-Henry, the last Wendish prince of Brandenburg, he secured that district when the prince died in 1150. Taking the title Margrave in Brandenburg, he encouraged Dutch and German settlement in the Elbe-Havel region and established bishoprics under his protection, and he is regarded as founder of the Margraviate of Brandenburg in 1157.

Albert went on a pilgrimage to the Holy Land in 1158 and in 1162 accompanied Emperor Frederick Barbarossa to Italy, where he distinguished himself at the storming of Milan. In 1164 he joined a league of princes against Henry the Lion, and after peace in 1169 he divided his lands among his six sons. He died on 18 November 1170 and was buried at Ballenstedt. His heirs, the House of Ascania, held Brandenburg until the line died out in 1320. Thomas Carlyle explained his nickname as coming from the cognisance on his shield, and he was also called the Handsome.
albert-vii-archduke-of-austria: Albert was born on 13 November 1559, the fifth son of Emperor Maximilian II and Maria of Spain. At eleven he was sent to the Spanish court, where his uncle Philip II oversaw his education, and he was first meant for the church. On 3 March 1577 Pope Gregory XIII made him a cardinal, with a dispensation for his age. Philip planned to make him archbishop of Toledo, but the incumbent lived until 1594, and Albert took only lower orders; he resigned the see and the cardinalate in 1598.

In 1583 he became the first viceroy of Portugal after its union with Spain, helping to organise the Great Armada of 1588 and beating off an English counter-attack on Lisbon in 1589. Recalled to Madrid in 1593, he took a leading part in the government.

After the death of his brother Archduke Ernest, Albert entered Brussels on 11 February 1596 as Governor General of the Habsburg Netherlands. His first campaign took Calais, Ardres and Hulst, but Spain's third bankruptcy that year led to disasters and mutinies in 1597. The Peace of Vervins with France was concluded on 2 May 1598, and on 6 May Philip II announced that Albert would marry his daughter Isabella Clara Eugenia and that the two would hold sovereignty over the Netherlands. They married in Valencia on 18 April 1599.

Albert was beaten by Maurice of Nassau at Nieuwpoort on 2 July 1600 and, after the long Siege of Ostend, left command to Ambrogio Spínola, who took the town on 22 September 1604. Albert also made peace with England in the Treaty of London on 24 July 1604, and in 1609 he persuaded Philip III to ratify the Twelve Years' Truce, signed at Antwerp on 9 April 1609, which treated the United Provinces as a sovereign power.

During the Truce the archdukes encouraged land reclamation, including the Moeren, and the recovery of farming and luxury trades. They also secured the Counter-Reformation, tolerating remaining Protestants only if they did not worship in public, and supported the Jesuits, Capuchins and Discalced Carmelites. Peter Paul Rubens became their court painter in 1609, and they built a pilgrimage church in the planned town of Scherpenheuvel.

Albert succeeded his brother Matthias in 1619 as ruling Archduke of Austria but abdicated in favour of Ferdinand II the same year. He had no children, and died on 13 July 1621, just as the Truce was ending and war resumed. Sovereignty passed back to Spain, to Philip IV.
alberta: Alberta is bordered by British Columbia to the west, Saskatchewan to the east, the Northwest Territories to the north and the U.S. state of Montana to the south. Its southern border is the 49th parallel north and its northern border the 60th parallel, and its western boundary follows the Continental Divide in the Rocky Mountains. The eastern part of the province lies on the Great Plains, and the Rocky Mountains cast a rain shadow over much of it.

The province was named after Princess Louise Caroline Alberta (1848–1939), the fourth daughter of Queen Victoria and wife of John Campbell, Marquess of Lorne, Governor General of Canada (1878–83). Alberta has a rich diversity of Late Cretaceous dinosaur fossils, with at least 38 dinosaur type specimens collected there.

Paleo-Indians arrived in what is now Alberta at least 10,000 years ago, toward the end of the last ice age. Over time they differentiated into various First Nations. The Plains peoples of the south, such as those of the Blackfoot Confederacy and the Plains Cree, generally lived by hunting buffalo, while northerly peoples such as the Woodland Cree and Chipewyan hunted and trapped other animals and fished. The territory was also used by fur traders of the rival Hudson's Bay Company and North West Company.

The Dominion of Canada bought the lands that would become Alberta in 1870. From the late 1800s to the early 1900s many immigrants arrived, in an effort to prevent the prairies from being annexed by the United States, and growing wheat and cattle ranching became very profitable. The Alberta Act of 1905 created the province.

Until the 1930s politics was shared between the Liberals and the agrarian United Farmers of Alberta, and the Social Credit Party then held office continually from 1935 to 1971. Massive oil reserves were discovered in 1947, and the exploitation of the oil sands began in 1967. In 1950 Alberta became the second province, after Saskatchewan, to adopt a publicly funded health programme, a precursor of the modern medicare system.

Alberta is a province of Canada with Edmonton as its capital and Calgary as its largest city, and English is its official language. It is governed as a parliamentary democracy with a unicameral Legislative Assembly. Six UNESCO World Heritage Sites lie within it: the Canadian Rocky Mountain Parks, Dinosaur Provincial Park, Head-Smashed-In Buffalo Jump, Waterton-Glacier International Peace Park, Wood Buffalo National Park and Writing-on-Stone Provincial Park.
albertine-rift: The rift runs from the northern end of Lake Albert to the southern end of Lake Tanganyika, and the name covers both the valley and the mountains around it. It is the product of tectonic movements that are gradually splitting the Somali Plate away from the rest of Africa. The surrounding mountains are uplifted Pre-Cambrian basement rocks, overlaid in places by recent volcanic rocks.

Two ranges cross the northern part: the Rwenzori Mountains between Lake Albert and Lake Rutanzige, formerly Lake Edward, and the Virunga Mountains between Lake Rutanzige and Lake Kivu. The Rwenzori, about 120 km long and 65 km wide, have been identified with Ptolemy's Mountains of the Moon and rise to 5,119 m at Mount Stanley. The Virunga Massif on the border of Rwanda and the Democratic Republic of the Congo has eight volcanoes, of which Nyamuragira and Nyiragongo are still highly active. Further south stand the Itombwe Mountains, Mount Bururi, the Kungwe-Mahale Mountains, Mount Kabobo and the Marungu Mountains.

The Virungas divide the Nile Basin to the north and east from the Congo Basin to the west and south. Lake Rutanzige drains north through the Semliki River into Lake Albert, which receives the Victoria Nile and sends out the White Nile. Lake Kivu drains south through the Ruzizi River into Lake Tanganyika, which flows to the Congo through the Lukuga River. This system seems to be recent: eruptions of the Virunga volcanoes probably blocked Lake Kivu's northward outflow into Lake Edward and turned it south. Before then Lake Tanganyika may have lost water only by evaporation, and the later Lukuga let species of the Congo Basin into a lake that had had its own fauna.

The Albertine Rift montane forests are important eco-regions, with transitional forest from about 1,000 m, montane forest from about 1,600 m to 3,500 m, bamboo and elfin forest above 2,400 m, and heather and grasses higher still. Deforestation for farmland, illegal timber extraction and artisanal gold mining threaten them.
alberto-fujimori: Alberto Kenya Fujimori Inomoto was born on 26 July 1938 in the Miraflores district of Lima to Japanese parents, Naoichi Fujimori and Mutsue Inomoto, who came from Kumamoto Prefecture and had emigrated to Peru in 1934. Japanese was the language of the home, but his parents moved him in 1949 to a school taught only in Spanish so that their children could assimilate. He graduated first in his class in 1961 in agricultural engineering at the Universidad Nacional Agraria La Molina, studied physics in Strasbourg, and took a master's degree in mathematics at the University of Wisconsin–Milwaukee in 1969. He became rector of La Molina in 1984 and held the post until 1989.

Peru was in hyperinflation and political crisis under the first presidency of Alan García, with the internal conflict against the Shining Path under way. Fujimori entered the 1990 election as an outsider under the banner of Cambio 90 and defeated the novelist Mario Vargas Llosa. He became the country's first president of Japanese descent. His economic stabilisation programme, known as the Fujishock, used strict fiscal and monetary policy, deregulation and privatisation, and annual inflation fell from a peak approaching 7,500 per cent to single digits by 1994.

In 1992 he dissolved Congress and the Supreme Court in a self-coup carried out with the support of the National Intelligence Service and the armed forces. The coup was criticised by many politicians and governments but welcomed by the business sector and much of the public. A new constitution was approved by referendum in 1993, and he was re-elected in 1995 and, controversially, in 2000. During his rule the army repressed the Shining Path, halting its actions while also killing thousands of civilians. Vladimiro Montesinos, who headed the intelligence service, helped him to consolidate power.

Amid allegations of corruption and crimes against humanity, Fujimori went to Japan in 2000 and sent his resignation by fax. Congress refused it and voted to remove him, and Japan declined to extradite him as a Japanese citizen. He was arrested in Santiago in 2005, extradited in 2007 and sentenced to 25 years in prison. President Pedro Pablo Kuczynski pardoned him in 2017, and he was released in December 2023. He died on 11 September 2024 of complications of tongue cancer. He has been described as a dictator, while a poll of 2005 found his years in office rated favourably in Peru.
albertus-magnus: Albertus Magnus was probably born before 1200, since well-attested evidence shows he was over 80 when he died in 1280. Two later sources give his age as about 87, which led to 1193 being commonly given as his birth year, but that information cannot be confirmed. He was probably born in Lauingen, in what is now Bavaria, since he called himself Albert of Lauingen. He was probably educated chiefly at the University of Padua, where he was taught Aristotle's writings. In 1223 (or 1229) he joined the Dominican Order and studied theology at Bologna and elsewhere.

Albert taught for several years as lecturer at the Dominican house in Cologne, and also in Regensburg, Freiburg, Strasbourg and Hildesheim. In 1245 he became master of theology under Guerric of Saint-Quentin, the first German Dominican to do so, and taught at the University of Paris, where Thomas Aquinas began to study under him. He was the first to comment on virtually all of Aristotle's writings, which led him to the teachings of Avicenna and Averroes. In 1254 he became provincial of the Dominican Order. At the General Chapter at Valenciennes in 1259 he helped set up a program of studies that made philosophy part of Dominican training.

In 1260 Pope Alexander IV made him bishop of Regensburg, an office he resigned within a few years. Pope Urban IV then relieved him of his duties as bishop and asked him to preach the Eighth Crusade in German-speaking countries. He then became known as a mediator, and in 1258 his verdict, the Große Schied, ended a conflict between the citizens of Cologne and the archbishop.

Albert's writings, collected in 1899, filled thirty-eight volumes, on topics from logic and theology to botany, astronomy, mineralogy and zoology. He believed that Aristotle's approach to natural philosophy posed no obstacle to a Christian view of the natural order. His books on botany, zoology and minerals drew on ancient sources and on his own empirical investigations. In embryology it has been claimed that little of value was written after Aristotle until Albert, who identified organs within eggs. Many alchemical works were later falsely attributed to him, and there is scant evidence that he performed alchemical experiments himself.

Albert died on 15 November 1280 in the Dominican convent in Cologne. His relics are in a Roman sarcophagus in the crypt of St. Andrew's Church there. He was beatified in 1622, canonized and proclaimed a Doctor of the Church on 16 December 1931 by Pope Pius XI, and named patron saint of natural scientists in 1941. His feast day is 15 November.
albi: The first settlement at Albi dates to the Bronze Age. After the Roman conquest of Gaul in 51 BCE the town became the Civitas Albigensium, the territory of the Albigeois. Excavations have found no traces of Roman buildings, which suggests a modest settlement. In 584 Gregory of Tours reported that most of the townsfolk died of plague. In 1040 the town expanded and built the Pont Vieux, or Old Bridge, and its new quarters show considerable urban growth. It grew rich from trade and from the tolls charged to travellers on the bridge.

Early in the 13th century the Pope and the French king joined forces against the Cathars, who held their own version of ascetic Christian dualism, which the Catholic Church considered a dangerous heresy. Repression was severe, many Cathars were burnt at the stake, and the area, until then virtually independent, was afterwards annexed by the French Crown. Late in the 13th century the bishop Bernard de Castanet completed the Palais de la Berbie, a fortress-like episcopal palace, and ordered the building of Sainte-Cécile cathedral from 1282. Trade in woad then made the town prosperous, and the fine Renaissance houses show the fortunes of its woad merchants. A small medieval Jewish community was annihilated in the 1320s during the Shepherds' Crusade.

Albi is the prefecture of the Tarn department, on the river Tarn 85 km northeast of Toulouse, and the seat of an archbishop. Along with Toulouse and Montauban it is one of the main cities built in Languedoc red brick. Its episcopal city was added to the UNESCO World Heritage list in 2010.

Sainte-Cécile is a masterpiece of Southern Gothic, built between the 13th and 15th centuries, with an austere defensive exterior and a rich interior. Its rood screen is carved in the Flamboyant Gothic style and carries over 200 polychrome statues. The Pont Vieux, 151 metres long on eight arches, is still in use after almost a millennium. The Toulouse-Lautrec Museum in the Palais de la Berbie holds more than 1,000 works by the painter Henri de Toulouse-Lautrec, who was born in Albi in 1864.
albigensian-crusade: The Cathars held a dualist theology, in which the physical world was evil and created by a demiurge, Rex Mundi, while God was pure spirit. They rejected the Catholic priesthood, the real presence in the Eucharist and Purgatory, and replaced baptism with the consolamentum, given by the laying on of hands. Between 1022 and 1163 eight local church councils condemned them, and the Third Lateran Council repeated the condemnation in 1179. Many adherents lived around Albi, which gave the Albigensians their name.

They were most successful in the Languedoc, where political control was divided among many local lords. Its people spoke Occitan, not French, and did not consider themselves French. The County of Toulouse was a fief of the Angevin Empire, and the Crown of Aragon was in places more influential than the French king. After the murder of his legate Pierre de Castelnau in 1208, which he suspected Raymond VI, Count of Toulouse, of ordering, Pope Innocent III declared a crusade and offered the lands of the heretics to any French nobleman who would take up arms.

By mid-1209 some 20,000 to 30,000 Crusaders gathered, many staying only 40 days. The papal legate Arnaud Amalric, Abbot of Cîteaux, took command. On 18 June 1209 Raymond VI declared himself repentant, was scourged by the new legate Milo and took the Cross, so that his lands could not be attacked. The Crusaders turned instead to the lands of his nephew Raymond Roger Trencavel, viscount of Béziers and Carcassonne, who was not himself a Cathar but tolerated them. His request for peace was refused, and the Crusaders marched first on Béziers.

From 1209 to 1215 the Crusaders captured Cathar lands and crushed the movement. From 1215 to 1225 a series of revolts returned much of the land to the counts of Toulouse, but a renewed crusade retook it and by 1244 had driven Catharism underground. On 16 March 1244, after a siege of Montségur, over 200 Cathar perfects were burned there.

The crusade realigned the County of Toulouse with the French crown and diminished the distinct culture of Languedoc. The Inquisition was established under Pope Gregory IX in 1234 and, with the Dominicans preaching against heresy, had crushed Catharism as a popular movement by the 14th century; most penances were light and the majority of the accused escaped death. Historians differ on its character: Raphael Lemkin called it one of the most conclusive cases of genocide in religious history, while Robert E. Lerner argued that it was proclaimed against unbelievers, not a people. The troubadour tradition declined as the Occitan courts that supported it were destroyed.
alboin: Alboin was the son of Audoin, who had governed the Lombards in Pannonia for the young Walthari and then crowned himself. Alboin came to the throne between 560 and 565, elected by the tribe's freemen, who by custom chose the king from the dead sovereign's clan. Soon afterwards a new war broke out with the Gepids, now led by Cunimund. The sources disagree about the cause: Paul the Deacon blames the Gepids, while the Byzantine historian Menander Protector blames Alboin.

The Gepids won the support of the emperor, and a Byzantine army under Baduarius was sent against the Lombards, who were defeated. Alboin later gained the upper hand with the help of the Avars, but his success brought a stronger neighbour to his borders, and historians regard the Avar threat as the decisive reason for his decision to leave Pannonia.

The Lombard migration began on Easter Monday, 2 April 568. Alboin led a mixed host that included Heruli, Suebi, Gepids, Thuringi, Bulgars, Sarmatians and some Ostrogoths, along with 20,000 Saxon warriors and their families. He had recently adopted Arian Christianity, probably for political reasons, to bind the migrants together and set them apart from the Catholic Romans. Before leaving he ravaged Pannonia, creating a safety zone between the Lombards and the Avars.

The Lombards entered Italy without resistance from the border troops. Alboin made Forum Iulii (Cividale del Friuli) the capital of a duchy under his nephew Gisulf, then swept through Venetia, taking Treviso, Vicenza, Verona, Brescia and Bergamo, and took Milan in 569. Ticinum (Pavia) resisted from 569 and fell only in May or June 572, after a siege of three years. By 570 he held nearly all the Byzantine defences in the north apart from the coasts and a few isolated places. Historians disagree on how far he extended his rule into Tuscany.

Alboin made Verona his seat, in a palace built by Theodoric, and was killed there on 28 June 572. The earliest account, by Marius of Aventicum, says that Helmichis, a man close to the king, killed him with the queen's connivance. Paul the Deacon adds the story of a drinking cup made from the skull of Cunimund, Rosamund's father, and names Peredeo, the king's chamberlain, as the killer.

The coup failed because most Lombards opposed it, and they proclaimed Duke Cleph king. Helmichis and Rosamund fled to Ravenna, where they later killed each other. Alboin was the last of the hero-kings who had led the Lombards from the Elbe to Italy. His name survives in the Old English poem Widsith, and Saxon and Bavarian epic poetry long recounted his heroism.
alborz: The Alborz stretches from the border of Azerbaijan along the western and entire southern coast of the Caspian Sea, then runs north-east and merges into the smaller Aladagh Mountains, bordering the parallel ridge of the Kopet Dag in the northern parts of Khorasan. It is divided into the Western, Central and Eastern Alborz. The Western range, usually called the Talysh, runs south-south-eastward almost along the Caspian's western coast, while the Central Alborz, the range in the strictest sense, runs west to east along the whole southern shore.
