The range forms a barrier between the south Caspian and the Iranian plateau and is only 60 to 130 km wide. Its rocks are mostly sedimentary, chiefly Jurassic limestone over a granite core. The mountains were folded mainly during the Miocene, as the Arabian plate collided with the Iranian plate and the Eurasian plate pressed from the other side. Mount Damavand, in the Central Alborz, is the highest mountain in Iran at 5,610 m.

The name comes from Harā Barazaitī, a mountain named in the Avesta, the main text of Zoroastrianism; the Proto-Iranian form means Mountain Rampart. In Middle Persian it became Harborz. Many high peaks were given the name, including Mount Elbrus in the Caucasus, and the Persian poet Ferdowsi in the Shahnameh speaks of the mountains as though they lay in India. Zoroastrians seem to identify the range with the dwelling place of the Peshyotan, and the Ilm-e-Kshnoom sect identifies Damavand as the home of the Saheb-e-Dilan, the Masters of the Heart.

Archaeological evidence shows people in the region since at least the late Lower Paleolithic. Darband Cave in Gilan Province has evidence from that period, though its many bear bones and few stone artefacts suggest mainly a bear den. Neanderthals were probably present in the Middle Paleolithic, since their fossils were found at Azykh Cave in the north-west, and stone tools come from Buzeir Cave and Kiaram Cave. A riverside site at Garm Roud in Mazandaran Province dates to about 30,000 years ago and gives evidence for modern humans.

The southern slopes are usually semi-arid or arid, while the northern slopes are humid and covered by the lush Caspian Hyrcanian mixed forests, in zones of Hyrcanian forest, beech and oak. Animals include the Persian leopard, the Syrian brown bear and the bezoar ibex; the Caspian tiger, now extinct, also lived there. Because of its snowy winters the range has several ski resorts, among them Dizin, and its attractions include Alam Kuh, Tochal and Ovan lake.
albrecht-durer: Dürer was born on 21 May 1471, the third child and second son of Albrecht Dürer the Elder, a successful goldsmith who had moved to Nuremberg from Ajtós in Hungary by 1455, and Barbara Holper. Of the couple's eighteen children only three survived. After his apprenticeship Dürer took the customary Wanderjahre, about four years away from 1490. He may have hoped to work under the engraver Martin Schongauer, who died shortly before Dürer reached Colmar in 1492, and he stayed with Schongauer's brothers there and in Basel. In 1493 he went to Strasbourg, where he painted his first self-portrait, probably to send to his fiancée in Nuremberg.

Within three months of his marriage Dürer left alone for Italy, perhaps because of plague in Nuremberg, and studied in Venice, where he admired Giovanni Bellini and copied Andrea Mantegna. On his return in 1495 he opened his own workshop. His early woodcuts were larger, more finely cut and more complex in composition than most German woodcuts before them. It is now thought unlikely that he cut the blocks himself, a task for specialist craftsmen. On a second Italian journey, from 1505 to 1507, he returned to painting and made the altarpiece known as the Feast of the Rosary for the German community in Venice.

Back in Nuremberg from mid-1507 he painted Adam and Eve (1507) and the Assumption of the Virgin (1509) and completed the Great Passion and the Life of the Virgin woodcut series, both published in 1511. In July 1520, after the death of Emperor Maximilian I, he travelled to the Netherlands to renew the imperial pension and to win the favour of Charles V. His diary records to whom he gave, exchanged or sold prints, and shows that the trip was not profitable.

In his last years Dürer produced comparatively little as an artist, partly through declining health and partly because he was preparing treatises. His Four Books on Measurement dealt with geometry, from lines and regular polygons to architecture, typography and polyhedra. The Four Books on Human Proportion, of 1528, expressed the body's parts as fractions of its height, based in part on observation of two to three hundred living persons in his own words. In 1527 he published a book on the fortification of cities. He wrote in German, using craftsmen's language, rather than in Latin. His prints were the medium through which most contemporaries knew his art, and they influenced Raphael, Titian and Parmigianino to promote their own work through printmakers.
albrecht-von-haller: Haller was born on 16 October 1708 into an old Swiss family at Bern. Long ill-health kept him from boyish sports and gave his precocious mind more room. It is said that at four he read and expounded the Bible to his father's servants, and before he was ten he had sketched a Biblical Aramaic grammar. Before he was fifteen he had written metrical translations from Ovid, Horace and Virgil, lyrics, dramas and an epic of four thousand lines on the origin of the Swiss confederations, which he burned in 1729. He studied at Tübingen, then at Leiden under Herman Boerhaave, and graduated in May 1727.

In 1728 he went to Basel, where he studied higher mathematics under John Bernoulli and where his interest in botany was awakened. A tour through Savoy, Baden and Swiss cantons began the plant collection that became the basis of his work on the flora of Switzerland. In 1729 he returned to Bern to practise as a physician. His botanical and anatomical research gave him a European reputation, and in 1736 George II called him to the chair of medicine, anatomy, botany and surgery at the new University of Göttingen. He became a Fellow of the Royal Society in 1743 and was ennobled in 1749.

At Göttingen he organised a botanical garden and an anatomical theatre, and edited the monthly Göttingische gelehrte Anzeigen, to which he is said to have contributed twelve thousand articles. Never at home there, and elected to the great council of Bern in 1745, he resigned his chair in 1753 and returned to Switzerland. In his last years he held the minor post of Rathausmann and prepared his Bibliotheca medica. He withdrew from public business in about 1773 and relied on opium, whose excessive use is believed to have hastened his death on 12 December 1777.

In his thesis published at Göttingen in 1752 he distinguished sensibility from irritability: nerves were sensible because a person perceives contact, while muscle fibre was irritable because it measurably shortens when excited, whether or not the person perceives it. In 1757 he carried out experiments to distinguish nerve impulses from muscular contractions. In botany he was among the first to see the importance of herbaria for studying variation, and he resisted the binomial nomenclature Carl Linnaeus introduced in 1753.

His poem Die Alpen, of 490 hexameters, was finished in March 1729 and appeared in his Gedichte in 1732. It is one of the earliest signs of an appreciation of the mountains and contrasts the simple life of people of the Alps with the corrupt life of the plains.
albrecht-von-wallenstein: Albrecht von Wallenstein was born on 24 September 1583 at Heřmanice in Bohemia, into a poor Protestant branch of the old Czech House of Waldstein. His parents were Lutheran and Utraquist Hussite, and after their deaths he lived for two years with his uncle Heinrich Slavata, a member of the Unity of the Brethren, whose faith he adopted. He studied at the Protestant Latin school at Goldberg and then at the University of Altdorf, where brawls and sword fights landed him in the town prison. He later studied at Bologna and Padua and became fluent in German, Czech, Latin and Italian.

He served in the Long Turkish War from 1604 to 1606, converted to Catholicism in 1606, and in 1609 married a wealthy widow whose estates came to him when she died in 1614. Three years later he began a career as a mercenary by raising forces for the Emperor in the Uskok War against Venice.

In the Bohemian Revolt of 1618 he took the Catholic side, marching his regiment to Vienna with the Moravian treasury. After the Battle of White Mountain on 8 November 1620 he secured confiscated Protestant lands and formed them into the Duchy of Friedland in northern Bohemia. He became an imperial count palatine in 1622, a prince in 1623 and Duke of Friedland in 1625. That year he raised an army of 50,000 men, and a year later he defeated the Protestants at Dessau Bridge.

He became imperial generalissimo and, from April 1628, Admiral of the Baltic Sea. In 1630 Emperor Ferdinand II, wary of his ambition, released him from service. Protestant victories led Ferdinand to recall him, and he defeated the Swedish king Gustavus Adolphus at Alte Veste; Gustavus was later killed at Lützen. He relied on astrologers, among them Johannes Kepler, who drew a horoscope for him, and he suffered from painful joint illness from 1620.

In the summer of 1633 Wallenstein arranged armistices to negotiate peace, believing the war could last decades. Plotters accused him of treachery, and a secret court found him guilty. On 24 January 1634 the Emperor signed a secret patent removing him from command, and an open patent of 18 February charged him with high treason. Losing the support of his army, he travelled from Plzeň to Cheb on 23 February hoping to meet the Swedes.

On the night of 25 February Scottish and Irish officers in his force killed his loyal officers at a feast and then Wallenstein himself in his lodgings. The Emperor rewarded the assassins. Plays, poems and pamphlets about him appeared soon afterwards, and Schiller made his last period the subject of a play trilogy completed in 1788.
alcaeus: Alcaeus was born into the aristocratic warrior class of Mytilene, the strongest city-state on Lesbos and by the end of the 7th century BCE the most influential of the North Aegean Greek cities, with a strong navy and colonies guarding its trade routes in the Hellespont. The Penthilid clan had long ruled it as kings, but in his lifetime they were a spent force and rival aristocratic factions fought for supreme power. Alcaeus and his older brothers took passionate part in the struggle with little success. Melanchrus was overthrown between 612 and 609 BCE by a faction that included his brothers and Pittacus, but Alcaeus was then too young to take part.

Later verses show that the poet, his brothers and Pittacus plotted against the tyrant Myrsilus and that Pittacus betrayed them, after which Alcaeus and his brothers went into exile. Pittacus was voted supreme power by the assembly of Mytilene and governed from 590 to 580 BCE, apparently well, even allowing Alcaeus and his faction to return. Before 600 BCE Mytilene fought Athens for Sigeion, and according to Herodotus Alcaeus threw away his shield to escape and then marked it in a poem to his friend Melanippus. He probably travelled widely in exile, including at least once to Egypt.

Alexandrian scholars, Aristophanes of Byzantium and Aristarchus of Samothrace, collected his poems into ten books in the 3rd century BCE and counted him among the canonical nine lyric poets. His work survives only in fragments, in quotations by ancient scholars and in papyri from Oxyrhynchus and elsewhere in Egypt. Like Sappho and Anacreon he is counted a monodist, a solo singer, who wrote in his native Aeolic dialect, for friends, in short, metrically simple stanzas, among them the Alcaic stanza named after him.

Conventionally his works are grouped as political songs, drinking songs, hymns, love songs and miscellaneous pieces. His political songs treat the power struggles on Lesbos as a partisan, cursing opponents and rejoicing in their deaths. Dionysius of Halicarnassus said that without the metre they would be political rhetoric. He used few metaphors but liked the allegory of the storm-tossed ship of state. Almost all his love poetry is lost. The Roman poet Horace modelled odes on his forms and imagined meeting Alcaeus and Sappho in Hades, and Quintilian praised his attacks on tyrants while regretting his turn to love.

He and Sappho were contemporaries and countrymen who may have exchanged poems, and later Greek critics assumed they were lovers. The first modern printing of his verses was in Michael Neander's edition of the nine lyric poets, published at Basle in 1556.
alcantara-bridge: The Alcántara Bridge, also known as Trajan's Bridge at Alcántara, is a Roman stone arch bridge over the Tagus River at Alcántara in Extremadura, Spain. The name comes from the Arabic al-Qantarah, meaning the arch. It was built between 104 and 106 CE by order of the emperor Trajan, who had become emperor in 98. Its six arches have clear spans, from the right bank to the left, of 13.6, 23.4, 28.8, 27.4, 21.9 and 13.8 metres, and the bridge originally measured 190 metres in length, reduced today to 181.7 metres.

The bridge stood in the Roman province of Lusitania. In ancient Rome the costs of building and repairing bridges, known as opus pontis or bridge work, fell on several local municipalities, and their shared costs show that such bridges belonged to the region as a whole rather than to one town. The Alcántara Bridge was built at the expense of twelve local municipalities of Lusitania, whose names were recorded in an inscription on the archway over the central pier.

The bridge has suffered more damage from war than from the elements. The Moors destroyed one of the smallest arches in 1214, and it was rebuilt in 1543 with stone from the original quarries. The second arch on the northwest side was destroyed in 1760 by the Spanish to stop a Portuguese advance and was repaired in 1762 by Charles III, only to be blown up again in 1809 by Wellington's forces trying to stop the French.

Temporary repairs were made in 1819, but much of the bridge was destroyed again in 1836 by the Carlists. It was rebuilt in 1860 with mortared masonry. After the José María de Oriol Dam allowed the Tagus riverbed to be drained, its main pillars were completely repaired in 1969.
alcazaba-of-almeria: The word alcazaba comes from the Arabic al-qaṣabah and means a walled fortification within a city. In 955 the Caliph of Córdoba, Abd ar-Rahman III, gave Almería the title of medina, a city, and the building of a defensive citadel in the upper part of the town began. The citadel was provided not only with walls and towers but also with squares, houses and a mosque. It was meant to be the seat of local government and to command both the city and the nearby sea.

The complex was enlarged under the caliph Al-Mansur and again under Khayran as-Saqlabi, the first king of the independent taifa of Almería. The scholar Abul Walid Al-Baji is reported to have been buried within the grounds, according to the biographical work of Ibn Bashkawal, who wrote some fifty to sixty years afterwards.

The Alcazaba is arranged in three enclosures. The first is a wide area that corresponds to the earliest Muslim military camp, where the population could shelter in case of siege. For that purpose it had large cisterns. A wall called the Muro de la Vela, the Wall of the Sail, separates it from the second enclosure. The wall takes its name from a bell that warned the population of events such as the arrival of a ship in the port, danger or fire, and it was built by King Charles III of Spain.

The second enclosure held the residence of the governors, together with their soldiers and servants. It also included the mosque, baths, water tanks and tents. The third and outermost enclosure is the most recent part of the complex. After the Christian reconquest of Almería, the Catholic monarchs Isabella I of Castile and Ferdinand II of Aragon had a castle built in the highest part of the town, better able to resist the new gunpowder artillery.

Most of the objects found at the archaeological site are kept in the Museo de Almería, though some are in the Museo de la Alhambra. The Alcazaba has also served as a film location. Productions shot there include Conan the Barbarian, Indiana Jones and the Last Crusade, Never Say Never Again and Wonder Woman 1984, and the television series Queen of Swords used its inner courtyard and gardens. The sixth season of Game of Thrones used the fortress as the capital of Dorne.
alcazaba-of-malaga: Phoenicians occupied the hill from around 600 BCE, and remains of their fortification wall have been found there. In the Roman period it held a villa and industrial buildings, and a theatre was built into its western slope in the 1st century. After the Muslim conquest of Iberia, sources mention a fortress with a mosque on the hill, built by Abd ar-Rahman I. The present Alcazaba was begun by the Hammudid dynasty in the early 11th century, probably under Yahya I, who ruled from 1021 to 1036. After the Zirids of Granada took Málaga in 1056, Badis added to it, perhaps the double walls.

In the early 14th century the Nasrid emir Muhammad II largely rebuilt the fortifications and the palaces, and Yusuf I built the Castle of Gibralfaro and the walled corridor joining it to the citadel. Ferdinand and Isabella took the city after the Siege of Málaga, which ended with its surrender on 18 August 1487, and raised their standard on the Torre del Homenaje. From the 18th century the fortress lost its military role and became a poor quarter of the city, until from 1933 Leopoldo Torres Balbás moved the residents out and began restoration and excavation.

The Alcazaba has two walled enclosures, one inside the other, each with towers, and visitors had to pass five gates to reach the palaces on the summit. Torres Balbás saw it as the prototype of military architecture in the taifa period. The way up is a bent entrance through the Puerta de la Bóveda, the Puerta de las Columnas, built with two Roman columns from the theatre, and the Arco del Cristo, once a chapel. A well, the Pozo Airón, cuts 30 metres into the rock.

The inner enclosure is entered through the Puerta de los Cuartos de Granada, rebuilt in the 20th century. The southernmost palace, the only one of the 11th century, keeps an arcade of three horseshoe arches in a smaller form of the style of Madinat al-Zahra, and an annex with intersecting multifoil arches. North of it lies a Nasrid palace around the Patio de los Naranjos and the Patio de la Alberca, which keep their original pools and tile paving, and beyond it the Barrio Castrense, a quarter of eight houses for officials and servants, one of them with its own hammam.
alcazar-of-seville: Seville was conquered by the Umayyad Caliphate in 712. In 913–914, after a revolt against the government of Córdoba, Abd al-Rahman III built a fortified enclosure in place of a Visigothic Christian basilica. It was roughly square, about 100 metres on each side. In the 11th century the Abbadid ruler al-Mu'tamid extended it to the south and east and added a new palace called al-Mubarak, the Blessed.

Around 1150 the Almohad Caliphate began to develop Seville as its capital in al-Andalus, and its governor extended the complex westward, nearly doubling its size. In 1163 the caliph Abu Yaʿqub Yusuf made the Alcázar his main residence in the region, and in 1169 he added six enclosures. Apart from the walls, nearly every earlier building was demolished and about twelve palaces were built.

After Ferdinand III of Castile took Seville in 1248, the Castilian kings rebuilt most of the Islamic structure. A Gothic palace was built in 1258 for Alfonso X on the site of the Patio del Crucero, keeping the Almohad garden divided into quadrants. Alfonso XI added the Hall of Justice, a Mudéjar throne hall that commemorated his victory at the Battle of Río Salado in 1340. Much of the Gothic palace was destroyed in the 1755 Lisbon earthquake.

Pedro I rebuilt much of the complex in the 1360s. A Latin inscription on the façade gives the year 1364 and an Arabic inscription in the Hall of the Ambassadors gives 1366, which probably mark the start and end of construction. Its design resembles the Nasrid palaces of the Alhambra, and Muhammad V of Granada, Pedro's ally, probably sent craftsmen to help.

Later rulers continued to alter the palace. Under the Catholic Monarchs the upper floor was extended and became their main residence, and in 1526 Emperor Charles V and Isabella of Portugal were married in the Hall of the Ambassadors. Charles V added the Renaissance upper storey of the Patio de las Doncellas between 1540 and 1572.

The upper storeys are still occupied by the royal family when it visits Seville and are administered by the Patrimonio Nacional. Excavations between 2002 and 2005, led by Miguel Ángel Tabales, uncovered the Mudéjar garden of the Patio de las Doncellas, which had lain buried under a marble floor since 1581–1584. In 1987 UNESCO registered the Alcázar as a World Heritage Site together with Seville Cathedral and the General Archive of the Indies.
alchemy: Alchemy comprises a plurality of traditions extending across about four millennia and three continents. Three major strands appear mostly independent, at least in their earlier stages: Chinese alchemy, closely connected to Taoism; Indian alchemy, called Rasayana, tied to the Dharmic faiths; and Western alchemy around the Mediterranean, whose centre shifted from Greco-Roman Egypt to the Muslim world and finally to medieval Europe. Whether they share a common origin is still an open question. The word comes from the Arabic al-kīmiyā, itself borrowed from Late Greek khēmeía.

Western alchemy began in Hellenistic Egypt, where Alexandria was a centre, from the Egyptian goldsmith's art, Greek philosophy and various religious traditions. Its texts are pseudepigraphic. The earliest historically attested author is Zosimos of Panopolis, writing around 300, who drew on older authors such as Mary the Jewess and Pseudo-Democritus, whose Four Books were probably written in the first century.

Alchemists tried to purify, mature and perfect materials. Common aims were chrysopoeia, the transmutation of base metals such as lead into noble metals, particularly gold; an elixir of immortality; and panaceas that could cure any disease. The philosopher's stone was variously linked with all of these, and the perfection of body and soul was thought to follow from the Great Work. Islamic and European alchemists developed laboratory techniques, theories and terms, some still in use, kept to the Greek idea of four elements, and guarded their work in secrecy with cyphers and symbolism. Mary the Jewess is credited with improvements to equipment, including the water-bath known as the bain-marie.

After the fall of the Roman Empire alchemy's centre moved to the Islamic world, and the works attributed to Jābir ibn Hayyān, known in Latin as Geber, introduced a new approach in the late ninth and early tenth centuries. Alchemy entered Latin Europe on 11 February 1144 with Robert of Chester's translation of the Liber de compositione alchemiae, and translation flourished in 12th-century Toledo.

Alcohol, elixir and athanor entered European vocabulary this way. The tradition flourished for some two hundred years after the 17th century and perhaps peaked in the 18th, until the rise of quantitative experiment ended it. Robert Boyle (1627–1691) pioneered the scientific method in chemistry, which led to the modern chemistry of Lavoisier and John Dalton.
alcibiades: Alcibiades was born in Athens. The family of his father, Cleinias, had old connections with the Spartan aristocracy, and the name Alcibiades was of Spartan origin. His mother, Deinomache, was the daughter of Megacles, head of the powerful Alcmaeonid family, so that Pericles and his brother Ariphron were her cousins. After Cleinias died at the Battle of Coronea in 447 BCE, Pericles and Ariphron became the boy's guardians.

According to Plutarch, Alcibiades had several teachers, Socrates among them, and was well trained in rhetoric, though ancient writers often mention his unruly behaviour. He fought at the Battle of Potidaea in 432 BCE, where Socrates was said to have saved his life, and returned the favour by rescuing Socrates at the Battle of Delium in 424 BCE.

Alcibiades first rose to prominence by urging aggressive Athenian action after the Peace of Nicias, the uneasy truce with Sparta. After the charges of sacrilege he vanished at Thurii and contacted the Spartans, who gave him sanctuary. Athens condemned him to death in absentia and confiscated his property. At Sparta he warned the ephors that the Athenians hoped to conquer Sicily, Italy and even Carthage; Donald Kagan thinks he knowingly exaggerated.

Having made powerful enemies in Sparta as well, he went to the Persian satrap Tissaphernes, whom he advised to delay bringing in the Persian fleet, so that Athens and Sparta would wear each other out. Thucydides says his real aim was restoration to Athens. He finally returned to Athens in the spring of 407 BCE, sailing into Piraeus to a hero's welcome.

In antiquity he divided opinion. Thucydides holds that his habits gave offence to everyone and led the Athenians to commit affairs to other hands, to the city's ruin, while Plutarch calls him the least scrupulous of men. Diodorus describes him as brilliant in spirit and intent on great enterprises. Scholars have argued that the Sicilian expedition, had it been under his command rather than that of Nicias, might have avoided disaster.
alcide-de-gasperi: De Gasperi was born on 3 April 1881 in Pieve Tesino in Tyrol, then part of Austria-Hungary, the son of a local police officer of limited means. He was active in the Social Christian movement from 1896 and studied literature and philosophy in Vienna from 1900, inspired by Pope Leo XIII's encyclical Rerum novarum. In 1904 he was imprisoned briefly with other students after protesting for an Italian-language university. From 1906 he edited the newspaper Il Trentino, which defended Italian culture in Trentino against Germanisation; at that time he did not seek unification with Italy. He sat in the Austrian Reichsrat from 1911 for six years, and in the First World War he sided with Italy.

In 1919 he helped found the Italian People's Party with Luigi Sturzo and served in the Italian Parliament from 1921 to 1924. He first backed the party's participation in Benito Mussolini's government but diverged from the Fascists over the Acerbo Law and violence against the constitutional parties, culminating in the murder of Giacomo Matteotti. The party was dissolved in November 1926. He was arrested in March 1927 and sentenced to four years in prison; the Vatican negotiated his release. From 1929 until July 1943 he worked as a cataloguer in the Vatican Library. In 1943 he published Ideas for Reconstruction, a programme for the Christian Democracy party, of which he became general secretary in 1944.

He became prime minister in December 1945, leading eight successive governments until 1953, at first with the Communists and Socialists. He was provisional head of state from 12 June to 28 June 1946, after a referendum in which 54 per cent voted for a republic. Italy signed the peace treaty of 1947, which lost its eastern border area to Yugoslavia, and joined NATO in 1949 and the European Coal and Steel Community. The Gruber–De Gasperi Agreement of September 1946 made South Tyrol an autonomous region. In May 1947 he formed a government without the Communists and Socialists, and in April 1948 the Christian Democrats won 48.5 per cent.

The 1953 election followed a change in the electoral law that its opponents called the Scam Law; the governing coalition won 49.9 per cent, just short of the supermajority bonus, and De Gasperi was forced to resign on 2 August. He gave up the party leadership in June 1954 and died on 19 August 1954 at Sella di Valsugana in Trentino. He is buried in the Basilica di San Lorenzo fuori le Mura in Rome, and the process for his beatification was opened in 1993. His former secretary Giulio Andreotti said that he taught his followers to search for compromise and to mediate.
alcmaeon-of-croton: Alcmaeon was born in Croton in Magna Graecia and was the son of Peirithous. Some say he was a pupil of Pythagoras, though there are reasons to doubt that he was a Pythagorean at all: his name seems to have crept into the lists of Pythagoreans given by later writers, and since 1950 the scholarly consensus holds him to be a figure independent of them. Although he wrote mainly on medical topics, there is some suggestion that he was a philosopher of science rather than a physician. Nothing more is known of the events of his life.

Alcmaeon was considered by many an early advocate of anatomical dissection and was said to be the first to identify the Eustachian tubes. Whether he dissected animals or human bodies is disputed, since Calcidius, the authority for the claim, says only that he first dared to undertake exsectio, and some modern scholars doubt Calcidius altogether. He was the first to dwell on the internal causes of illness, suggesting that health is a state of equilibrium between opposing powers and that illness arises from problems of environment, nutrition and lifestyle.

Theophrastus's De Sensu summarises his study of the senses. Where Empedocles held that sensation arises from like acting on like and placed the mind in the heart, Alcmaeon held that it arises from unlike and placed the seat of the mind in the head. He distinguished sensation from thought, which separated animals from man. He also held that sleep occurs when blood withdraws from the surface of the body to the larger vessels, and that death follows if it withdraws entirely.

A book titled On Nature is attributed to him, but only titles and a few fragments of his writings survive, preserved by Stobaeus, Plutarch and Galen. He taught that the soul is immortal because, like the heavenly bodies, it contains a principle of motion. The extent to which he can be counted as a Presocratic cosmologist is controversial, since the evidence is slight.
alcmaeonidae: The Alcmaeonids were a wealthy and powerful noble family of ancient Athens, a branch of the Neleides who claimed descent from the mythological Alcmaeon, the great-grandson of Nestor. Unlike many aristocratic families, they were named after a historical figure, Alcmaeon, the father of Megacles. They reused the names of grandfathers, so that Megacles, Alcmaeon and Cleisthenes recur throughout the family. The first noteworthy member was Megacles, son of Alcmaeon, who was Archon Eponymous of Athens in the 7th century BCE. Their main aristocratic rivals in the 6th and 5th centuries BCE were the Peisistratids.

As chief archon at the time of the Cylonian affair, around 632 BCE, Megacles had the followers of Cylon killed after they left the sanctuary where they had sought refuge, having promised them safety. This broke the sacred law protecting suppliants, and a curse was believed to cling to Megacles and his descendants. The family was exiled, and buried Alcmaeonid bodies were dug up and removed from the city. Later, Alcmaeon served as an intermediary between Croesus of Lydia and the oracle at Delphi and was allowed to take as much gold as he could carry, which gave the family wealth and a path back to prominence.

Another Megacles married his daughter to the tyrant Pisistratus, but, according to the account, Pisistratus refused to have children with her and Megacles and his allies banished him. Megacles later married Agarista, daughter of Cleisthenes of Sicyon. Their sons were Hippocrates and a second Cleisthenes, the reformer, while Hippocrates' daughter Agariste was the mother of Pericles. In 508 BCE the reformer Cleisthenes overthrew Hippias, the son of Pisistratus, with Spartan help obtained from the oracle at Delphi. He was opposed because of the curse and briefly exiled, but the citizens called him back. His reforms replaced the four traditional tribes with ten based on residence, created a Boule of 500 members, introduced sortition and established ostracism.

Herodotus reports an accusation that the Alcmaeonids signalled to the Persians with a shield during the Persian Wars, a story he himself refused to believe and which scholars debate. During the Peloponnesian War the Spartans cited the family's curse to discredit Pericles, who led Athens from roughly 461 to 429 BCE and began the building programme that produced most surviving structures on the Acropolis, including the Parthenon. Alcibiades, an orator, general and statesman, also belonged to the family and changed sides several times in the war. He was the last notable Alcmaeonid, and the family disappeared from prominence after the defeat of Athens.
alcoa: In 1886 Charles Martin Hall, a graduate of Oberlin College, found that passing an electric current through a bath of cryolite and aluminium oxide produced aluminium; Paul Héroult in France made the same discovery almost at once. The Hall–Héroult process cut production costs at a time when aluminium sold for almost five dollars a pound, more than silver or gold, and fewer than ten sites in the United States and Europe produced it.

Hall left a smelting company in Lockport, New York, which did not use his process, and joined Alfred E. Hunt. Arthur Vining Davis joined in 1888, and their first commercial pour took place on Thanksgiving Day that year.

The Pittsburgh Reduction Company began with an experimental plant on Smallman Street in Pittsburgh, with Hunt as president and Hall as vice president. It began production at New Kensington, Pennsylvania in 1891 and opened a plant at Niagara Falls in 1895. Hunt left in 1898 to fight in the Spanish–American War, caught malaria in Puerto Rico and died of its complications at the age of 44.

By about 1903 the company was the only legal supplier of aluminium in the United States. It became the Aluminum Company of America on 1 January 1907, and the acronym Alcoa was coined when Davis became president in 1910. During the First World War it raised production by 40% and exported about ninety million pounds to the Western Allies.

In World War II, as in World War I, about 90% of United States aluminium went to military uses. In 1938 the Justice Department charged Alcoa with illegal monopolization and demanded that it be dissolved, and the case, United States v. Alcoa, was settled six years later. Davis was chairman of the board from 1928 for thirty years. Alcoa bought Alumax in 1998, Reynolds Metals in 2000 and Cordant Technologies in 2000. In 2014 it settled with United States authorities over charges of bribing Bahraini officials.

Alcoa gave its name to places where it built facilities, including a town in Tennessee. It sponsored television anthology series from 1955 to 1963, among them The Alcoa Hour on NBC. On 1 November 2016 Alcoa Inc. split into two companies. The new Alcoa Corporation kept the mining and manufacture of raw aluminium, and the old company was renamed Arconic Inc., which processes aluminium and other metals. Alcoa Corporation produces aluminium in ten countries.
alcoy: The first traces of human presence near Alcoy date to about 60,000 years ago, when Neanderthal hunters settled at a site now called El Salt. Rock paintings near la Sarga date to about 10,000 to 6,500 years ago. From about the middle of the third millennium BCE people moved from the caves to the plain, where cereals were grown, and mountain fortifications were built at places such as Mola Alta de Serelles and El Puig. After the Roman conquest of the Iberians, rural villas and a necropolis appeared in the area.

The town was established in 1256 by James I of Aragon, who built a castle over the Serpis river to secure the southern frontier of the Kingdom of Valencia during the Reconquista. In 1291 James II of Aragon gave it to the Sicilian admiral Roger of Lauria, and it returned to royal possession only in 1430. In the War of the Spanish Succession Alcoy backed Archduke Charles, was besieged and lost many privileges, which began a period of decline.

Alcoy, or Alcoi in Valencian, is a city in the province of Alicante and has industries in textiles, paper, food and metal. In 1821 about 1,200 peasants destroyed 17 newly introduced wool carding and spinning machines that threatened their livelihoods, the first large-scale Luddite action in Spain, and in 1873 its workers rose in the Petroleum Revolution. The city has several Art Nouveau buildings built between 1904 and 1911, including the Casa d'Escaló and the Cercle Industrial, and a cemetery on the European Cemeteries Route. Its Art Deco Pont de Sant Jordi is the most popular image of the city. The Moors and Christians festival in April is its main tourist celebration.
alcuin-of-york: Alcuin was born in Northumbria, presumably in the 730s, and nothing is known for certain of his parents or family. The Vita Alcuini calls him of noble English stock, which scholars have usually accepted. His own writings name relatives such as Wilgils of Ripon, the father of the missionary Willibrord, and Beornrad, abbot of Echternach. Donald A. Bullough suggests that the family was of free but subordinate status, and that Alcuin and his kin rose through connections with the aristocracy.

He came as a young man to the cathedral church of York in the time of Archbishop Ecgbert and his brother, the Northumbrian king Eadberht. Ecgbert, a disciple of Bede, oversaw a reform of the English church that stressed the clergy and the tradition of learning that Bede had begun, and he was devoted to Alcuin. The York school was a centre of the liberal arts, literature, science and religious learning. Alcuin became a teacher in the 750s and head of the school after Æthelbert became archbishop in 767. He became a deacon but was never ordained a priest.

At Charlemagne's invitation Alcuin became a leading scholar and teacher at the Carolingian court, where he was a figure in the 780s and 790s. Einhard's Life of Charlemagne calls him the most learned man anywhere to be found. He is considered one of the chief intellectual architects of the Carolingian Renaissance, and many dominant intellectuals of the era were his pupils. He drew on the York school as a model, reviving the trivium and quadrivium. In 796 he was made abbot of Marmoutier Abbey, at Tours, where he worked on perfecting the Carolingian minuscule script, and he stayed there until his death.

His output included theological and dogmatic treatises, a few grammatical works and a number of poems. His nine scriptural commentaries consist mostly of sentences taken from the Church Fathers, and he engaged in textual criticism of the Vulgate; four Bibles were prepared by him or under his direction at Tours, probably in 799–801. He also wrote lives of saints, among them Willibrord, and opposed the Spanish Adoptionism of bishops Felix of Urgell and Elipandus of Toledo. A collection of about 53 mathematical word problems, the Propositiones ad acuendos juvenes, is sometimes attributed to him, and more than 310 of his letters survive.

Alcuin died on 19 May 804. The Church of England and the Episcopal Church honour him on 20 May, and he is traditionally venerated as a Blessed in the Catholic Church. Alcuin College at the University of York is named after him.
aldfrith-of-northumbria: Aldfrith, known in Irish as Flann Fína mac Ossu, was a son of Oswiu of Northumbria, who grew up in exile in Dál Riata, and of Fín, probably a princess of the Uí Néill; his date of birth is unrecorded. Northumbrian churchmen did not regard his parents' union as a lawful marriage, and early sources call him the son of a concubine. Educated for the church, he was reportedly on Iona when Ecgfrith fell at Nechtansmere. No resistance to his accession is recorded, and the historian Herman Moisl argued that he must have been installed by the Pictish and Dál Riatan alliance.

Aldfrith seems to have given up his predecessors' attempts to dominate Northumbria's neighbours, and Bede wrote that he ably restored the shattered fortunes of the kingdom, though within smaller boundaries. He corresponded with Aldhelm, later Bishop of Sherborne, who sent him the Epistola ad Acircium, and he bought a cosmography from Abbot Ceolfrith of Monkwearmouth-Jarrow for an estate of eight hides. Adomnán, Abbot of Iona, came to him twice to free the captives of Ecgfrith's Irish raid of 684 and gave him his De Locis Sanctis, which Aldfrith circulated.

His one lasting quarrel was with Bishop Wilfrid, whom he allowed back in 686 but would not help recover authority over the whole northern church, and whom he banished by 691 or 692. At the council of Austerfield in 702 or 703 the bishops rejected Wilfrid's return, and Aldfrith refused to receive the letters Pope John VI sent ordering his restoration. Northumbrian coinage is thought to have begun under him: silver sceattas bearing the king's name in Irish uncial script, most with a lion.

Aldfrith was married to Cuthburh, sister of King Ine of Wessex, who separated from him and founded an abbey at Wimborne Minster. After an illness he died on 14 December at Driffield, according to the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle, and his young son Osred won the throne after a civil war against Eadwulf. His reign is seen as the beginning of Northumbria's golden age, which saw the Lindisfarne Gospels, perhaps begun in his time, the scholarship of Bede and the first Anglo-Saxon missions to the continent. A collection of wisdom sayings attributed to Flann Fína survives in a later Middle Irish text.
aldhelm: Aldhelm was born around 639 and is said to have been a son of Kenten, of the royal house of Wessex. He was not, as his early biographer Faritius claims, the brother of King Ine. He first studied under the Irish scholar Máeldub at Malmesbury, then with Hadrian, abbot of St Augustine's at Canterbury, whose arrival with Theodore of Tarsus in 668 began a revival of learning. His studies there covered Roman law, astronomy, astrology, reckoning and the calendar. Early lives claim that he learned Greek and Hebrew, which is doubtful. Ill health made him leave Canterbury, and he spent fourteen years as a monk under Máeldub.

In 675, according to a charter of doubtful authenticity, Aldhelm succeeded Máeldub as the first abbot of Malmesbury. He introduced the Benedictine rule, won the monks the right to elect their abbot, and founded monasteries at Frome and Bradford-on-Avon; Pope Sergius I gave leave in 701 to found the one at Frome.

A synod of the church in Wessex sent him to argue with the Britons of Dumnonia over the date of Easter, and he wrote a long letter to King Geraint of Dumnonia, finally winning agreement with Rome. Around 705 he became the first bishop of Sherborne, a see created when the diocese of Winchester was divided. He kept Malmesbury and built a cathedral church at Sherborne. He drew crowds by singing hymns and gospel passages in public places.

Aldhelm died in 709 at Doulting while on his rounds, and was buried in the church of St Michael at Malmesbury. Dunstan translated his relics in 980, and his feast day is 25 May. He wrote in an elaborate Latin known as the hermeneutic style, which dominated Latin writing in England for centuries. His best-known prose work is De Laude Virginitatis, and his letter to Acircius, understood to be King Aldfrith of Northumbria, includes his best-known works, riddles in Latin hexameters. Michael Lapidge calls him the first English man of letters, while Peter Hunter Blair compares him unfavourably to Bede.
aldus-manutius: Aldus Manutius was born at Bassiano, near Rome, between 1449 and 1452, into a wealthy family, and was sent to Rome to become a humanist scholar. He studied Latin there under Gaspare da Verona and attended lectures by Domizio Calderini in the early 1470s. From 1475 to 1478 he studied Greek at Ferrara under Battista Guarino. In 1482 he went to Mirandola with his friend Giovanni Pico della Mirandola, who recommended him as tutor to his nephews Alberto and Leonello Pio, princes of Carpi. The families of Pico and Alberto Pio paid the first costs of his press and gave him lands in Carpi. He decided that Venice was the best place for his work and settled there in 1490.

In Venice he met the printer Andrea Torresano, who became his lifelong partner and printed his Latin grammar, the Institutiones grammaticae, on 9 March 1493. The Aldine Press, established in 1494, issued its first book in March 1495, Constantine Lascaris's Erotemata. Its first great achievement was a five-volume folio Aristotle, begun in 1495 and completed in 1497 and 1498, and it printed nine comedies of Aristophanes in 1498. Manutius wanted to give readers Greek works in their original form. He commissioned Greek and Latin types resembling humanist handwriting, the first known precursor of italic type, and introduced small portable books, the enchiridia, a predecessor of the paperback.

Erasmus asked him to publish his Latin translations of Hecuba and Iphigenia in Aulis; Iphigenia in Aulis appeared in December 1507. Erasmus then went to Venice, spent ten months at the press and lived in the house of Manutius and Torresano, and there expanded his collection of proverbs from 819 to 3,260 entries, published as the Adagiorum Chiliades in 1508. Wars interrupted the press, but in 1513 Manutius issued a Plato dedicated to Pope Leo X. In 1505 he married Maria, Torresano's daughter, which combined the partners' shares.

Manutius wrote his will on 16 January 1515 and died on 6 February. Torresano and his two sons carried on the business, and Manutius's son Paulus, born in 1512, later took it over, leading it from 1539 with his brothers under the imprint Sons of Aldus until his death in 1574. A Greek Septuagint he had begun appeared in 1518, the first printed. Paul F. Grendler wrote that Manutius ensured the survival of a large number of ancient texts and greatly eased the spread of Italian Renaissance humanism to the rest of Europe.
aleijadinho: Antônio Francisco Lisboa, called Aleijadinho, was the son of a respected Portuguese master builder and architect, Manuel Francisco Lisboa, and his African slave Isabel. The baptismal certificate cited by his biographer Rodrigo José Ferreira Bretas says he was born a slave and baptized on 29 August 1730 in Vila Rica, now Ouro Preto, and manumitted on that occasion by his father; the date of birth is not given, and arguments now favour a later year.

Little is known with certainty about his life. Almost all the available data derive from Bretas's biography of 1858, written 44 years after his death, which recent criticism considers largely fanciful, part of a romanticized process that made him an icon of Brazilianness.

In 1756 he may have gone to Rio de Janeiro with Friar Lucas de Santa Clara, who transported gold and diamonds, and may have been influenced there by local artists. Two years later he would have made a soapstone fountain for the Terra Santa Hospice and then set up as a self-employed professional. Being a mulatto, he was often forced to accept contracts as a day labourer rather than as a master.

From the 1760s until close to his death he produced many works, but without supporting documentation many are only attributions based on stylistic similarity with documented pieces. His work was carried out entirely in Minas Gerais, especially in Ouro Preto, Sabará, São João del-Rei and Congonhas, notably the Church of Saint Francis of Assisi in Ouro Preto.

In 1796 he received a commission of great importance, the sculptures of the Via Sacra and the Prophets for the Sanctuary of Bom Jesus of Matosinhos in Congonhas, considered his masterpiece. Between 1807 and 1809, his illness at an advanced stage, he closed his workshop but still carried out some work, and from 1812 his health deteriorated further. He died on 18 November 1814.

Aleijadinho worked in the transition from Baroque to Rococo, and his work reflects both. Artists of the time did not sign their works, so identification relies on contracts and receipts between religious brotherhoods and artists, on other documents and oral tradition, and on stylistic comparison, which is always conjectural. More than four hundred creations are associated with his name, most attributed without documents.

His documented gilded woodcarving includes at least four large altarpieces, in which the crowning arch, without a pediment, is replaced by a statuary group, which suggests a primarily sculptural vocation. Brazilian critics almost by consensus consider him the foremost exponent of colonial art in Brazil, and some foreign scholars the leading name of the Baroque in the Americas.
aleksandar-stamboliyski: Aleksandar Stoimenov Stamboliyski was born on 1 March 1879 to a farmer in the village of Slavovitsa. Bulgaria was then mainly a land of small peasant farmers, about four fifths of the population. The Bulgarian Agrarian National Union, founded in 1899 in reaction to the peasants' low standard of living, made him its leader, and by 1911 he was a notorious anti-monarchist who led the opposition to Tsar Ferdinand. He believed in a Balkan federation that would supersede national identities.

He opposed Bulgaria's entry into the First World War on the side of the Central Powers and was sentenced to life imprisonment in 1915. The regime released him on 25 September 1918, hoping he would quiet a rebellious army. The Radomir Rebellion, from 28 September until 2 October, was crushed with an estimated 2,000 soldiers killed, and Stamboliyski, whose name had been put to its republican declaration without his knowledge, went into hiding. Ferdinand fled on 3 October 1918 and was succeeded by Boris III.

Stamboliyski became prime minister on 14 October 1919, and the Agrarian Union confirmed him after an election victory on 20 March 1920. His government faced pressure from left and right, an international occupation force, large debts, food shortages and a flu epidemic. He aimed at the rule of the peasant, passing land redistribution laws with maximum holdings, expanding vocational education in rural areas and building cooperative organisations known as the Zemedelski Druzhbi. He founded the BANU Orange Guard, a peasant militia.

In foreign policy he abided by the Treaty of Neuilly-sur-Seine of November 1919, rejected territorial expansion and sought a détente with Yugoslavia. Bulgaria joined the League of Nations in 1920, the first of the defeated states to do so. He kept the army below the treaty's limit, which angered the military, and he never settled the Macedonian question. He survived an assassination attempt by the Internal Macedonian Revolutionary Organization on 2 February 1923.

On 9 June 1923 a coup by the Military League, the IMRO, the National Alliance and the army, led by Aleksandar Tsankov, overthrew his government. The Communist Party refused to intervene. Stamboliyski withdrew to Slavovitsa and tried to organise resistance, large in number but weak in arms. On 14 June 1923 activists of the IMRO captured him, tortured and killed him, and cut off the hand that had signed the Treaty of Niš. Other Agrarian leaders were killed, among them the mayor of Sofia, Krum Popov.
Many remember him as a kind of strongman, in spite of his electoral successes. In 1979 the town of Novi Krichim was renamed Stamboliyski, and a boulevard in central Sofia bears his name.
aleksander-kakowski: Kakowski was born on 5 February 1862 in Dębiny near Przasnysz, the son of Franciszek Kakowski and Paulina Ossowska. Ordained a priest in Warsaw on 30 May 1886 by Cardinal Wincenty Chościak-Popiel, he became a professor at the Warsaw Theological Seminary the following year and in 1910 rector of the Saint Petersburg Roman Catholic Theological Academy. He was ordained a bishop by Stanisław Zdzitowiecki on 22 July 1913 and installed as archbishop in St. John's Cathedral on 14 September 1913, which made him titular primate of the Kingdom of Poland.

Kakowski stayed in Warsaw after the outbreak of World War I. In 1917 he became one of the three members of the Regency Council, the semi-independent and temporary highest authority of the Kingdom of Poland, which the Central Powers had recreated as part of their Mitteleuropa plan and which served as a provisional head of state. In 1925 he was awarded the Order of the White Eagle, Poland's highest decoration, for his part in freeing the country from foreign occupation.

On 28 November 1919 he was the main consecrator of Achille Ratti, the papal nuncio to Poland and later Pope Pius XI, and in December he was himself made a cardinal. As archbishop he promoted a strong Catholic press, contributing to the success of Rycerz Niepokalanej, one of the most popular newspapers of prewar Poland, and he was the main founder of the theological faculty at Warsaw University and of the Catholic Action movement.

He continued to style himself Primate of the Kingdom of Poland until his death on 30 December 1938; his successor, August Hlond, was to bring back the title of Primate of Poland after the Second World War. In 1930 he became a bailiff of honour and devotion of the Order of St John of Jerusalem, and in July 1938 he briefly appeared as head of the chapter of the Order of the White Eagle.
aleksandr-solzhenitsyn: Aleksandr Isayevich Solzhenitsyn was born in Kislovodsk on 11 December 1918. His father, Isaakiy Semyonovich Solzhenitsyn, was of Russian descent, and his mother, Taisiya Zakharovna, of Ukrainian descent. The family defied the Soviet anti-religious campaign of the 1920s and remained devout members of the Russian Orthodox Church, but at a young age he became an atheist and embraced Marxism–Leninism. In the Second World War he commanded a sound-ranging battery in the Red Army, was involved in major action at the front, and was twice decorated; he received the Order of the Red Star on 8 July 1944.

In February 1945, while serving in East Prussia, he was arrested by SMERSH over nineteen months of correspondence with a friend, Nikolai Vitkevich, in which they criticised Joseph Stalin and the conduct of the war.

After the Gulag and internal exile, Solzhenitsyn was freed and exonerated following Nikita Khrushchev's Secret Speech of 1956. He taught at a secondary school by day and wrote in secret by night. In his Nobel lecture he recalled that until 1961 he was convinced he would never see a line of his work in print. His first novel, One Day in the Life of Ivan Denisovich, appeared in 1962 with Khrushchev's approval, and Matryona's Place in 1963 was his last work published in the Soviet Union.

After Khrushchev's removal in 1964 publication stopped and he became a non-person; by 1965 the KGB had seized some of his papers, including the manuscript of In the First Circle. Cancer Ward appeared abroad in 1966, In the First Circle in 1968 and August 1914 in 1971.

He kept working in secret on The Gulag Archipelago, published in 1973. On 12 February 1974 he was arrested and deported the next day to Frankfurt, West Germany, and stripped of his Soviet citizenship; the KGB had found the manuscript of its first part. His citizenship was restored in 1990, and in 1994 he returned to Russia, living in a dacha at Troitse-Lykovo in west Moscow.

Solzhenitsyn was awarded the 1970 Nobel Prize in Literature for the ethical force with which he pursued the indispensable traditions of Russian literature. The Gulag Archipelago amounted to a head-on challenge to the Soviet state and sold tens of millions of copies. In later political writings such as Rebuilding Russia he opposed any nostalgia for Soviet communism and called for a strong presidential republic balanced by local self-government. He died of heart failure near Moscow on 3 August 2008, aged 89, and was buried at the Donskoy Monastery in a spot he had chosen. A bronze statue of him stands on the seafront in Vladivostok.
aleksandras-stulginskis: Aleksandras Stulginskis was born on 26 February 1885. He began theological studies in Kaunas and continued them in Innsbruck, but decided not to become a priest and moved to the Institute of Agricultural Sciences at the University of Halle. He graduated in 1913, returned to Lithuania and worked as a farmer, publishing many articles on agronomy. In 1918 he began to publish the journals Ūkininkas, meaning Farmer, and Ūkininko kalendorius, Farmer's Calendar.

During the World War I he moved to Vilnius. He was a founder of the Lithuanian Christian Democratic Party, head of its Central Committee in 1917, and a co-organiser of the Vilnius Conference. He signed a memorandum to President Woodrow Wilson on the recognition of Lithuanian statehood and, unlike Antanas Smetona, looked to the Entente. Elected to the Council of Lithuania, he signed the Act of Independence on 16 February 1918 and advocated a democratic republic, strongly opposing the idea of monarchy. In independent Lithuania he organised the national army against the Bolsheviks and the Poles.

He served as a minister many times and was Speaker of the Constituent Assembly from May 1920, acting as head of state, and later the second President of Lithuania until 1926. Smetona's coup that year overthrew Stulginskis's successor, Kazys Grinius, and Stulginskis held the presidency formally for a few hours before it returned to Smetona. He was Speaker of the Seimas from 1926 to 1927.

Stulginskis withdrew from politics in 1927 and worked on his farm. In 1941 the Soviet NKVD arrested him and his wife and deported him to a gulag in Krasnoyarsk Krai, while she went to the Komi Republic. In 1952 the Soviet authorities sentenced him to 25 years in prison for his anti-socialist and clerical policies in pre-war Lithuania. After Stalin's death he was released in 1956 and allowed to emigrate, but refused and returned to the Lithuanian SSR. He settled in Kaunas and died there on 22 September 1969, aged 84, the last of the signatories of the Act of Independence.
aleksey-yermolov: Aleksey Petrovich Yermolov was born in Moscow on 4 June 1777 (24 May, Old Style), into an old noble family from the Oryol Governorate. His father owned a small estate with 150 serfs. He attended the boarding school of Moscow University from 1784 to 1791, fought in the Polish campaign of 1794 and received the Order of St. George, fourth class, in 1795. In January 1799 he was arrested on suspicion of joining a conspiracy against Tsar Paul I and exiled to Kostroma for two years, where he taught himself Latin. Alexander I pardoned him after Paul's assassination in 1801.

In the Napoleonic Wars Yermolov served at Amstetten, Austerlitz, Eylau, Friedland and Smolensk. At Borodino he was lightly wounded leading the counterattack that recaptured the Great Redoubt. He commanded the artillery of the Russian armies in 1813 and 1814, was decorated after Kulm with the Prussian Iron Cross, and was prominent in the battle round Paris.

On 21 April 1816 he became commander in chief of Russian forces in Georgia. His tasks were to secure Russia's hold over Georgia and the khanates taken from Persia, and to subdue the Muslim tribes of the mountains. He fortified a ford on the Sunzha in 1817 and founded the fortress of Grozny the next year. He founded Pyatigorsk and Kislovodsk, began rebuilding Tiflis in the European style and improved roads such as the Georgian Military Road.

For ten years he was both commander in chief and ambassador to Persia. His campaign included atrocities against non-combatants, among them the hanging of women and children in public squares. He was dismissed on 7 December 1827 and replaced by Ivan Paskevich, for reasons that are unclear; Nicholas I disliked him and blamed him for not keeping the tribes in check.

For the last thirty years of his life Yermolov lived at his manor near Oryol. He died in Moscow on 23 April 1861 (11 April, Old Style) and was buried in Oryol, leaving memoirs of his service from 1796 to 1816. In Russia he was known for his courage and strategy, and Alexander Pushkin and Vasily Zhukovsky wrote of him.

In the Caucasus, except in Ossetia, he is remembered for atrocities. The historian Charles King calls him the first to use a comprehensive strategy for subduing the highlands, whose methods might today be called state-sponsored terrorism. Moshe Gammer writes that his activities deepened hatred of Russia and helped spread the Naqshbandi Sufi brotherhood.
aleppo: Aleppo lies about 120 km inland from the Mediterranean on a plateau 380 metres above sea level, with farmland to the north and west and the dry Syrian Desert to the east. It is one of the oldest continuously inhabited cities in the world, and its long history is attributed to its position as a trading centre between the Mediterranean and Mesopotamia, at one end of the Silk Road. The modern city occupies the ancient site, so archaeologists have scarcely touched it. The Amorites called the city Ḥalab in the second millennium BCE, and the Hittites Ḥalpa or Ḥalpu.

The first record of Aleppo comes from the third millennium BCE, in the Ebla tablets, where it is written Ha-lam. Excavations at Tell as-Sawda and Tell al-Ansari show that Amorites occupied the area by the late third millennium, and tablets from Ebla and Mesopotamia speak of it as part of the Amorite state of Yamhad. The main temple of the storm god Hadad stood on the citadel hill. Alexander the Great took the city in 333 BCE, and between 301 and 286 BCE Seleucus Nicator founded a Hellenic settlement there, calling it Beroea after the Macedonian city. Bishops of Beroea attended the councils of the 4th and 5th centuries.

The Sasanian king Khosrow I pillaged and burned the city in 540, and Rashidun forces under Abu Ubaidah ibn al-Jarrah took it in 637. In 944 it became the seat of an independent emirate under the Hamdanid prince Sayf al-Dawla, and was then home to the poet al-Mutanabbi and the philosopher al-Farabi. The Byzantine general Nikephoros Phokas sacked it in 962, the Fatimids took it in 1017, and the Mirdasid dynasty ruled it from 1024 to 1080, apart from two short intervals.

The Ottoman sultan Selim I took Aleppo in 1516, when it had about 50,000 inhabitants. For centuries it was the largest city of the Syrian region and the Ottoman Empire's third largest after Constantinople and Cairo. The opening of the Suez Canal in 1869 diverted much trade to the sea, and Aleppo began a slow decline. After the First World War it lost its northern hinterland and the Baghdad Railway to Turkey, and in 1939 its main access to the sea.

Aleppo is the capital of the Aleppo Governorate in northern Syria. Its covered souq, about 13 km long, is the largest in the world, and its architecture shows the work of Romans, Byzantines, Umayyads, Seljuks, Ayyubids, Mamluks and Ottomans. UNESCO declared the Old City a World Heritage Site in 1986.
alessandro-de-medici: Alessandro de' Medici was born in Florence on 22 July 1510 and nicknamed il Moro for his dark complexion. Most contemporaries took him for the only son of Lorenzo II de' Medici, Duke of Urbino, while a minority held that he was the illegitimate son of Giulio de' Medici, later Pope Clement VII. The historian Christopher Hibbert presents two rumours of a Moorish slave or a peasant woman of the Roman Campagna as his mother, but documents name her as Simonetta da Collevecchio, a servant of his grandmother Alfonsina Orsini, and Giorgio Spini calls the slave story unfounded.
He spent his early childhood in Rome and, after deaths in the senior line of the family, Cardinal Giulio moved him to Poggio a Caiano with his half-sister Catherine and his cousin Ippolito.

When Giulio became pope in 1523, Alessandro and Ippolito were left to lead Florence under the regency of Cardinal Silvio Passerini. During the Sack of Rome in 1527 the Florentines overthrew the Medici, and Alessandro lived in exile for three years. After a siege of nearly ten months backed by Spanish troops, he was named head of state in 1530, and arrived in Florence on 5 July 1531. Nine months later Charles V made him hereditary duke, ending the Florentine Republic and beginning over 200 years of Medici monarchy.

The Florentine Constitution of 1532 consolidated his power, and in 1534 he ordered the Fortezza da Basso. In 1536 he married Charles V's illegitimate daughter Margaret of Austria. His government drew both praise and criticism. Supporters said his sense of justice won affection and that he was a champion of the poor, and he commissioned works from Giorgio Vasari, Jacopo Pontormo and Benvenuto Cellini. The exile community judged his rule harsh and incompetent, an assessment historians debate. In 1535 Ippolito died, under questionable circumstances, on the way to denounce him to Charles V, and rumour said Alessandro had him poisoned.

On the night of Epiphany, 5 to 6 January 1537, his cousin Lorenzino de' Medici lured him with the promise of a meeting with a widow and stabbed him with a servant's help. Officials wrapped the body in a carpet and buried it secretly at San Lorenzo for fear of an uprising. Lorenzino said he had acted to preserve the republic, but the anti-Medici faction did not rise, and Charles V had him killed in Venice in 1548. Power passed to Cosimo I, of the junior branch.
alessandro-farnese-duke-of-parma: Alessandro Farnese was born on 27 August 1545, the son of Duke Ottavio Farnese of Parma and Margaret of Austria, an illegitimate daughter of Charles V. His twin brother Carlo died in 1549. When Margaret became Governor of the Netherlands, he went with her to Brussels in 1556 and was delivered to Philip II to ensure the loyalty of the Farnese. He was raised in Spain with his cousin Don Carlos and his half-uncle Don Juan. In 1565 he married Maria of Portugal, and in 1571 he commanded three galleys at the Battle of Lepanto.

Farnese joined Don Juan in the autumn of 1577, and his strategy decided the Battle of Gembloux in early 1578. The sack of Zichem that year, where the garrison was put to the sword, is considered the biggest stain on his career. After Don Juan died in October 1578 he insisted on holding both the posts of Captain-General and Governor-General. By the Treaty of Arras in January 1579 he won over the Catholic nobles of the south, and the northern provinces answered with the Union of Utrecht.

His troops took Maastricht after a siege that began on 12 March 1579 and sacked it for three days. In most later sieges he offered generous terms, with no massacres or looting and a gradual return to the Catholic Church.

The siege of Antwerp began in 1584, and he cut off the city from the sea by building a bridge of boats across the Scheldt from Kallo to Oordam. Protestants had to leave within four years. He was to lead the land invasion of England with the Spanish Armada in 1588, but his barges, blockaded by English ships, could not leave Nieuwpoort and Dunkirk. He then entered France twice, relieving Paris for the Catholic League in 1590 and marching on Rouen in 1592, where a musket shot wounded his forearm at Caudebec.

Spanish courtiers jealous of his success had worked to discredit him with Philip II, who drafted a letter recalling him from the Netherlands. He knew of his failing health and left Brussels on 11 November 1592 for a final expedition to France, but died at Arras at the age of 47. He was buried in the Capuchin church in Parma, and his remains were later moved to the crypt of the Basilica of the Madonna della Steccata. When they were exhumed in January 2020, his death was ascribed to pneumonia. Edward Shepherd Creasy and John Keegan praised his military skill, and his campaigns gave the Spanish crown lasting control of the southern provinces.
alessandro-manzoni: Alessandro Manzoni was born in Milan on 7 March 1785. His maternal grandfather was the philosopher Cesare Beccaria, and his biological father was probably Giovanni Verri rather than Pietro Manzoni. His parents separated in 1792, and from the age of six he was schooled in religious boarding schools run by the Somaschi and Barnabite fathers. He was drawn early to poetry and to ideals of liberty and reason, and his poem The Triumph of Liberty (1801) praised the French Revolution.

After his father's death in 1807 he joined his mother's household at Auteuil and met the Idéologues, including Claude Charles Fauriel. In 1808 he married Henriette Blondel, a Calvinist banker's daughter who became a Roman Catholic in 1810. That year Manzoni passed through a religious crisis that took him from agnosticism to an austere Catholicism. His Sacred Hymns appeared in 1815.

Manzoni began Fermo e Lucia on 24 April 1821, after reading the novels of Walter Scott in French translation, and finished the first manuscript in September 1823. The reshaped novel, The Betrothed (I promessi sposi), was published a volume a year in 1825–1827. It follows two ordinary fiancés, Renzo Tramaglino and Lucia Mondella, through famine, war and plague and through corruption in Church and State in 17th-century Lombardy under Spanish rule. Real figures appear, among them Cardinal Federico Borromeo and the outlaw called the Unnamed, historically identified with Francesco Bernardino Visconti.

The novel went through 68 editions and sold over 60,000 copies in fourteen years. Manzoni's tragedy Adelchi (1822), on Charlemagne's overthrow of the Lombard domination in Italy, carried veiled allusions to Austrian rule. Later he wrote mainly essays, above all on language. In 1868 he reported to the minister Emilio Broglio, proposing that Florentine be taught in schools. He supported Italian unification and became a senator in February 1860.

Manzoni outlived his first wife, who died on 25 December 1833, his second wife, Teresa Borri, six of his children and his closest friends. His eldest son, Pier Luigi, died on 28 April 1873. Manzoni had fallen on 6 January while leaving the San Fedele church, and he died of cerebral meningitis, a complication of the blow to his head, on 22 May 1873. His funeral was held in Milan Cathedral with almost royal pomp, and he was buried in the Monumental Cemetery of Milan.

He is counted with Ugo Foscolo and Giacomo Leopardi as one of the three crowns of Italian Romanticism. The Betrothed is a symbol of the Risorgimento for its patriotic message, and it was a milestone in the development of the modern and unified Italian language.
aleut: Archaeological evidence indicates that the Aleuts first occupied the Aleutian Islands about 9,000 years ago, beginning with the eastern islands, where sites on Unalaska and Anagula date to that period. They then spread westward, and the oldest sites on the western islands begin to appear about 2,500 years ago. Their technologies centred on food and resources from the sea and coast: fishing, gathering marine invertebrates and hunting sea mammals. Tools were made from local obsidian and chert, bird bones for needles and awls, and mammal bones for wedges, spoons and harpoon points. Before sustained European contact about 25,000 Aleuts lived in the archipelago.

In the 18th century Russian traders, the promyshlenniki, set up settlements on the islands, driven by demand for the furs the Aleuts hunted. They took Aleut women and children hostage to force the men to hunt foxes and sea otters, and often enslaved Aleut men as well. The Aleuts also suffered heavy deaths in the 19th and early 20th centuries from Eurasian infectious diseases to which they had no immunity, and their customary ways of life were disrupted. Russian Orthodox missionaries reached Kodiak in 1794 and many Aleuts became Christian; Saint Peter the Aleut is counted among the earliest Christian martyrs in North America.

In the 1820s the Russian-American Company, which administered much of the North Pacific, moved many Aleut families to the Commander Islands and to the Pribilof Islands, which still have majority-Aleut communities. The islands are now divided politically between Alaska and Russia's Kamchatka Krai.

The Aleuts call themselves Unangan in the eastern dialect and Unangas in the western, terms translated as 'original people'. Their language, Unangam Tunuu, belongs to the Eskaleut family and was written in Cyrillic from 1829 and in Latin script from 1870. An estimated 150 people in the United States and five in Russia speak it, and there are revitalisation efforts.

Aleuts traditionally lived in barabaras, partly underground houses roofed with driftwood, grass and earth, which sheltered several families from wind, rain and cold. They fish for salmon, cod, crabs and shellfish and hunt seals, walrus and whales, drying, smoking or roasting the catch, and many still eat locally sourced foods. The 2000 census counted 11,941 people who identified as Aleut and 17,000 more with partial Aleut ancestry.
aleutian-islands: The Aleutian Islands are a chain of 14 main volcanic islands and 55 smaller ones. They extend westward roughly 1,200 miles (1,900 km) from the Alaska Peninsula towards Kamchatka and separate the Bering Sea to the north from the Pacific Ocean to the south. The 57 volcanoes of the islands form the northernmost part of the Pacific Ring of Fire. Before 1867 the islands were known as the Catherine Archipelago. The climate is oceanic, with heavy rainfall and almost constant fog, and the vast majority of the chain has no native trees.

The first occupants probably arrived following Beringian migrations. The earliest archaeological sites, on Unalaska, date to about 9,000 years ago, those on Adak to about 6,000 years ago, and the western islands were settled last, about 2,500 years ago. The native people call themselves Unangan and are generally known as Aleut. They developed a culture tied to marine resources, with boat building, tools for fishing and sea-mammal hunting, and noted basketry and weaving.

In 1741 Vitus Bering and Aleksei Chirikov sailed from Russia on a voyage of discovery, and after a storm separated them Chirikov found several eastern islands and Bering several western ones. Bering was shipwrecked and died on the Commander Islands, and his survivors reported that the islands were rich in fur-bearing animals. Siberian fur hunters moved eastward across the chain, and the islands belonged to Russia until the Alaska Purchase of 1867. Grigory Shelikhov founded a company in the 1780s based on the systematic exploitation of the indigenous peoples, with sporadic conflict such as the Awa'uq Massacre. The first Orthodox missionaries arrived in 1793.

On 3 June 1942 Japanese forces invaded Attu and Kiska, the only invasions of the United States during the war. The United States moved over 800 civilians to camps in the Alaska Panhandle, and more than 90 Americans were taken to Japan as prisoners. American forces landed on Attu in May 1943 and on Kiska later that year, where 313 Allied men died from accidents. The United States tested nuclear weapons underground on Amchitka from 1965 to 1971.

Most of the islands belong to the U.S. state of Alaska, while the Commander Islands, farther west, belong to Kamchatka Krai in Russia. The 2020 census recorded 7,152 people on the islands, 4,254 of them in Unalaska, the main settlement. Fishing is the main economic activity, and nearly all the islands are protected within the Alaska Maritime National Wildlife Refuge. Large seabird colonies breed there, and sea otters help keep kelp forests along the coasts.
alexander-burnes: Alexander Burnes was born in Montrose, Scotland, on 16 May 1805, the fourth son of James Burnes, the local provost, who was a first cousin of the poet Robert Burns. At sixteen he joined the army of the East India Company, learned Urdu and Persian in India, and was made an interpreter at Surat in 1822. In 1826 he was moved to Kutch and was based at Bhuj for three years as assistant to the political agent, where he took an interest in the history and geography of north-western India and neighbouring countries.

The British government needed intelligence about Afghanistan, which lay between the rival British and Russian empires, and in 1831 Burnes, travelling in disguise, surveyed the route through Kabul to Bukhara. In the same year he took horses from King William IV to Maharaja Ranjit Singh at Lahore, and used the voyage up the Indus to survey the river in secret. He refused a military escort, fearing it would suggest an invasion, and his diplomacy opened areas of the Indus to him that Europeans had not entered. In October 1831 he arranged the meeting at Rupur between Ranjit Singh and the Governor General Lord William Bentinck. In Delhi he met Mohan Lal, who became his travelling companion.

His narrative Travels into Bokhara was one of the most popular books of its time. The Royal Geographical Society of London recognised him, he was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society and the Athenaeum Club admitted him without ballot. In 1836 he undertook a mission to Dost Mohammad Khan at Kabul. He advised Lord Auckland to support Dost Mohammad, but Auckland followed Sir William Hay Macnaghten and restored Shah Shuja, which led to the First Anglo-Afghan War. Burnes was knighted on 6 August 1838.

After Shah Shuja's restoration Burnes was political agent at Kabul. British numbers and taxation drove up prices, and many Afghans held Burnes responsible. On 1 November 1841 Mohan Lal warned him of a plot and urged him to leave for the cantonment, but he stayed. A mob gathered at his house in the old city, Major William Broadfoot was shot, and Burnes and his brother Charles were hacked to death. Help from the cantonment, half an hour's march away, was delayed by arguments among senior officers. In 1860 it emerged that some of his 1839 dispatches had been altered to convey opinions that were not his.
alexander-bustamante: Bustamante was born William Alexander Clarke in Blenheim, Hanover, to Mary Clarke, a woman of mixed race, and Robert Constantine Clarke, the son of an Irish Catholic planter. He said that he took the name Bustamante from a Spanish sea captain who adopted him, but he did not leave Jamaica until 1905, when he went to Cuba among Jamaican migrants seeking work in the sugar industry. He returned permanently in the 1930s and gained recognition by writing frequent letters on colonial issues to the Daily Gleaner. In 1937 he was elected treasurer of the Jamaica Workers' Union, which after the labour rebellion of 1938 became the Bustamante Industrial Trade Union.

During the rebellion he became the spokesman of the striking workers, who were mostly of African and mixed-race descent, and was known as The Chief. He was imprisoned in 1940 on charges of subversive activities, defended by his cousin Norman Manley, and released in 1943.

That year he founded the Jamaica Labour Party, having earlier belonged to the People's National Party that Manley founded in 1938. In the 1944 election, the first held under universal suffrage, the party won 22 of 32 seats. Bustamante became the unofficial government leader, though real power stayed with the governor, and in 1953 he became Jamaica's first chief minister, serving until the party lost the 1955 election.

Bustamante first supported the Federation of the West Indies but in the 1950s came to oppose it and to press for independence. In the 1961 referendum Jamaica voted 54 per cent to leave the federation, and his party won the election of 10 April 1962. He replaced Manley as premier and became the first prime minister when Jamaica became independent on 6 August 1962. In April 1963 he ordered the police and army to "Bring in all Rastas, dead or alive"; over 150 Rastafarians were detained and an unknown number killed. After a stroke in 1965 he withdrew from public life, and his deputy Donald Sangster held the real power. He retired two days after the 1967 election.

Bustamante died in 1977 and was buried in National Heroes Park in Kingston. In 1969 he was made a National Hero, alongside Norman Manley, Marcus Garvey, Paul Bogle and George William Gordon. He was made a member of the Privy Council of the United Kingdom in 1964 and a Knight Grand Cross of the Order of the British Empire on 9 June 1967.
