His portrait appears on the Jamaican one dollar coin and the thousand dollar note, and a coconut and ginger sweet, the Bustamante backbone, is named after him.
alexander-dubcek: Alexander Dubček was born in Uhrovec, Czechoslovakia, on 27 November 1921. When he was three his family moved to the Soviet Union in search of work and a better life, and he spent most of his childhood in Interhelpo, an Esperantist industrial cooperative in Kyrgyzstan. In 1933 the family moved to Gorky. In 1938 they chose to return to Czechoslovakia rather than renounce their citizenship. At 17 he joined the then-illegal Communist Party of Slovakia. He fought against the wartime pro-German Slovak state of Jozef Tiso and, in August 1944, joined the Jan Žižka partisan brigade during the Slovak National Uprising, in which his brother died.

After the Communist Party took power in 1948, Dubček rose through party posts in Trenčín, Bratislava and Banská Bystrica. He studied in the Soviet Union from 1955 to 1958 and was transferred to Prague in 1960. There he worked on the commissions that rehabilitated victims of repression in 1962–1963, and learning of the mechanisms of repression, he later said, was a watershed that dedicated him to reform. The Czechoslovak economy had begun to plateau in the early 1960s, and reformers concluded that the country had fallen behind the rest of the world.

Dubček was First Secretary of the party from January 1968 to April 1969 and became best known for the slogan Socialism with a human face. His reforms accelerated cultural and economic liberalisation, and culture changed most quickly. On the night of 20–21 August 1968 Soviet-led Warsaw Pact forces, reportedly about half a million troops, invaded Czechoslovakia. Albania, Romania and East Germany did not take part.

The invasion was meant to enable a coup by conservatives, but it could not succeed because of the lack of a viable pro-Soviet leadership and the popularity of Dubček. He was forced to resign in April 1969 and succeeded by Gustáv Husák, and was expelled from the party in 1970.

Dubček then lived as a nonperson whose very mention was banned, in Bratislava. In November 1989, during the Velvet Revolution, he spoke to a crowd at the trial of the Bratislava Five on 14 November, was briefly arrested on 17 November at the students' march in Prague, and appeared on 23 November in Bratislava.

He became Chairman of the federal parliament from 1989 to 1992, and the European Parliament awarded him the Sakharov Prize in 1989. He died on 7 November 1992 of injuries from a car crash on 1 September on the D1 motorway near Humpolec. A later investigation ruled the cause aquaplaning at excessive speed, though his son Pavol remained sceptical. Andrei Sakharov wrote that the breath of freedom under Dubček was a prologue to the peaceful revolutions in eastern Europe.
alexander-graham-bell: Alexander Bell was born in Edinburgh on 3 March 1847, the son of the phonetician Alexander Melville Bell and Eliza Grace Bell. For his eleventh birthday his father allowed him to adopt the middle name Graham. He left the Royal High School in Edinburgh at fifteen, having completed only four forms, and his interests lay in the sciences. His father, grandfather and brother were all associated with work on elocution and speech, and both his mother and his wife were deaf. With his brother Melville he built an automaton head that could say a few words. In 1870 Bell travelled with his parents to Ontario, where the family bought a farm near Brantford.

In April 1871 Bell went to Boston to train teachers of the deaf in his father's Visible Speech system. In 1872 he became professor of Vocal Physiology and Elocution at the Boston University School of Oratory, and in autumn 1873 he decided to concentrate on experiments in sound. His work on a harmonic telegraph, which would send several messages through one wire at different pitches, led towards the telephone.

On 14 February 1876 Bell's lawyer filed his application at the US Patent Office on the same day that Elisha Gray filed a caveat for a telephone design, and there is considerable debate about who arrived first. Bell received the first US patent for the telephone on 7 March 1876, and on 10 March he called his assistant Thomas Watson in another room. Over 18 years the Bell Telephone Company faced 587 court challenges, and none established priority over Bell's patent. He married Mabel Hubbard on 11 July 1877 and co-founded the American Telephone and Telegraph Company in 1885.

Bell held 18 patents in his own name and shared 12 more. With Charles Sumner Tainter he invented the photophone, which sent speech on a beam of light. He also built an early metal detector after the shooting of President James A. Garfield in 1881, and he began experiments on powered flight in 1891. He took an interest in heredity and bred sheep on his estate in Nova Scotia for more than 30 years. He served as the second president of the National Geographic Society from 1898 to 1903. Bell died at his estate in Cape Breton on 2 August 1922, aged 75.
alexander-hamilton: Hamilton was born on 11 January 1755 or 1757 in Charlestown, the capital of Nevis in the British Leeward Islands. He and his older brother, James Jr., were born out of wedlock to Rachel Lavien, a married woman of half-British and half-Huguenot descent, and James A. Hamilton, a Scotsman. He was orphaned as a child, taken in by a merchant, and given a scholarship to King's College (now Columbia University) in New York City.

In 1775, after the fighting at Lexington and Concord, he joined a New York volunteer company and was elected an officer. In 1776 he raised the New York Provincial Company of Artillery and was appointed captain. He served for four years as aide-de-camp to George Washington and fought at the Siege of Yorktown.

Hamilton resigned his commission in March 1782 and was appointed to the Congress of the Confederation, whose want of power he had criticised. He founded the Bank of New York, led the Annapolis Convention of 1786 and was a delegate to the Philadelphia Convention, which drafted the Constitution. He wrote 51 of the 85 installments of The Federalist Papers.

Washington appointed him first secretary of the treasury, and he was sworn in on 11 September 1789. He argued that the Constitution's implied powers allowed the First Bank of the United States, funded by a tariff on imports and a whiskey tax, to take on the states' war debts. His views became the basis of the Federalist Party, opposed by the Democratic-Republican Party under Thomas Jefferson. He resigned in 1795 and resumed his law practice.

Hamilton opposed Aaron Burr's candidacy for governor of New York in 1804. Letters published in the Albany Register alleged that he had expressed a despicable opinion of Burr, and Burr demanded an apology. Hamilton refused because he could not recall such an insult, and a duel was arranged. It took place at Weehawken, New Jersey, on 11 July 1804. Hamilton was mortally wounded and died the next day.

His interpretations in The Federalist Papers remain highly influential and are cited in scholarly studies and court decisions. His dispute with Jefferson over a national bank was addressed in McCulloch v. Maryland, which largely adopted Hamilton's view.
alexander-i-of-epirus: Alexander belonged to the Aeacid dynasty and was the son of Neoptolemus I and the brother of Olympias, which made him the uncle and brother-in-law of Alexander the Great. Neoptolemus ruled jointly with his brother Arybbas. When Neoptolemus died, about 357 BCE, his son was only a child and Arybbas became sole king. About 350 BCE Alexander was brought to the court of Philip II of Macedon for his protection, and in 343/2 BCE Philip dethroned Arybbas and made Alexander king of Epirus. Aeacides, the father of Pyrrhus of Epirus, was his first cousin.

When Philip repudiated Olympias in 337 BCE, she went to her brother and tried to induce him to make war on her husband. Alexander declined, and formed a second alliance with Philip by agreeing to marry Philip's daughter Cleopatra, his own niece. During the wedding in 336 BCE, Philip was assassinated by Pausanias of Orestis.

In 334 BCE, at the request of the Greek colony of Taras in Magna Graecia, Alexander crossed into Italy to help it against several Italic peoples, including the Lucanians and Bruttii. After a victory over the Samnites and Lucanians near Paestum in 332 BCE he made a treaty with the Romans. He then took Heraclea from the Lucanians, Terina from the Bruttii and Sipontum on the Adriatic coast.

Through the treachery of some Lucanian exiles Alexander was forced to fight under unfavourable circumstances in the Battle of Pandosia, and he was killed by a Lucanian in 331 BCE. He left a son, Neoptolemus, and a daughter, Cadmea. Livy, in his passage speculating on what a military showdown between Alexander the Great and the Roman Republic would have brought, reports that as Alexander of Epirus lay mortally wounded at Pandosia he compared his fortunes with those of his nephew, saying that the latter had waged war against women.
alexander-i-of-russia: Alexander was born in Saint Petersburg on 23 December 1777, the eldest son of Paul I of Russia, and he and his younger brother Constantine were raised by their grandmother, Catherine the Great. He took in the ideas of Jean-Jacques Rousseau from the free-thinking atmosphere of her court and from his Swiss tutor, Frédéric-César de La Harpe, and learned the traditions of Russian autocracy from his military governor, Nikolay Saltykov. He disliked his father as emperor even more than his grandmother, writing that Russia had become a plaything for the insane.

Alexander became emperor on 23 March 1801, when his father was assassinated, and was crowned in the Kremlin on 15 September. Historians still debate his role in the murder. The most common theory is that he knew of the conspiracy but insisted that his father should not be killed. He appointed a Private Committee of young friends to plan reforms leading to a constitutional monarchy. In practice he continued absolutist policies, though he introduced major educational reforms in 1803 and 1804, including more universities. Plans for a parliament and a constitution were never carried out.

In foreign policy he changed Russia's position towards France four times between 1804 and 1812. After defeats at Austerlitz and Friedland he formed an alliance with Napoleon in the Treaty of Tilsit in 1807, and in 1809 he took Finland from Sweden. The alliance collapsed by 1810, above all over Poland. Napoleon's invasion of Russia in 1812 was a catastrophe for the French. After the defeat of Napoleon at Leipzig in 1813, Alexander, as supreme commander of the coalition forces in Germany, ordered them to cross the Rhine, and allied forces occupied Paris in 1814. He formed the Holy Alliance to suppress revolutionary movements in Europe.

From the end of 1818 his liberal views began to change, and Metternich gained influence over him. In the second half of his reign he became increasingly arbitrary and fearful of plots, ended many earlier reforms and purged schools of foreign teachers. Speransky was replaced as adviser by Aleksey Arakcheyev, who oversaw the creation of military settlements.

In the autumn of 1825 Alexander travelled to the south of Russia because his wife was ill. He caught typhus and died at Taganrog on 19 November 1825 by the Old Style calendar. He left no legitimate children, since his two daughters had died in childhood, and neither of his brothers wished to become emperor. After a period of confusion his younger brother Nicholas I of Russia succeeded him. A popular legend holds that he faked his death and lived as a hermit under the name Feodor Kuzmich. Historians regard him as a complex and often contradictory ruler whose achievements in foreign policy were not matched by equally far-reaching domestic reforms.
alexander-ii-of-russia: Alexander Nikolayevich was born in Moscow, the eldest son of Nicholas I of Russia and Charlotte of Prussia. He became Tsesarevich in 1825, when his father took the throne. Under Nicholas the intellectual atmosphere of Saint Petersburg suppressed freedom of thought. The poet Vasily Zhukovsky supervised his education. In 1837 he toured twenty provinces of Russia and was the first Romanov heir to visit Siberia.
He met Princess Marie of Hesse in Darmstadt on a tour of Europe, and they married in Saint Petersburg on 16 April 1841. The marriage produced six sons and two daughters.

Alexander became emperor on 2 March 1855. On 15 January 1856 he took Russia out of the Crimean War on the unfavourable terms of the Treaty of Paris, which cost the Black Sea Fleet. This gave him room for domestic reform: the Edict of Emancipation of 1861, which abolished serfdom, and changes to the courts, local self-government, censorship, schools and the army. Many reforms met intense backlash and were cut back, and after an assassination attempt in 1866 he moved towards a more conservative stance.

In 1863 a Polish uprising led him to strip Poland of its separate constitution and incorporate the kingdom directly into the Russian Empire. In 1867 he sold Alaska to the United States. The Russo-Turkish War of 1877–1878 brought independence to Bulgaria, Montenegro, Romania and Serbia. He also approved military plans in the Caucasus that culminated in the Circassian genocide.

After a last attempt on his life in February 1880, Count Loris-Melikov was given extraordinary powers against the revolutionaries, and his proposals called for a form of parliamentary body. On 13 March 1881 (1 March in the old-style calendar) Alexander was assassinated in Saint Petersburg. A bomb thrown by Nikolai Rysakov of the Narodnaya Volya damaged his carriage but left him unhurt, and a second member, Ignacy Hryniewiecki, then threw something at his feet.

Alexander had approved Loris-Melikov's plans as the first step towards a constitution. His successor, Alexander III, on the advice of Konstantin Pobedonostsev, abandoned them. The assassination brought suppression of civil liberties, use of the Okhrana secret police, and anti-Jewish pogroms and the May Laws.
alexander-iii-of-scotland: Alexander was born at Roxburgh on 4 September 1241, the only son of Alexander II and his second wife, Marie de Coucy, and became king at the age of seven on his father's death on 6 July 1249. His minority was marked by a bitter struggle between two parties, one led by Walter Comyn, Earl of Menteith, the other by Alan Durward, Justiciar of Scotia. When he married Margaret of England, daughter of Henry III, on 26 December 1251, Henry demanded homage for the Scottish kingdom, but Alexander did not comply. Two years after the meeting at Kelso in 1255, Menteith's party seized the king and forced the creation of a regency representing both sides.

On reaching his majority in 1262 Alexander laid a formal claim to the Western Isles before King Haakon IV of Norway, who rejected it and in 1263 invaded. Alexander prolonged negotiations off the Isle of Arran until the autumn storms, which damaged Haakon's ships. The Battle of Largs on 2 October 1263 was indecisive, but Haakon turned for home and died in Orkney on 15 December. In 1266 his son Magnus the Lawmender concluded the Treaty of Perth, ceding the Isle of Man and the Western Isles to Scotland in return for payments. Norway kept Orkney and Shetland until 1469.

Queen Margaret died in 1275, and all three of their children were dead by 1284, so that year Alexander had the Estates recognise his granddaughter Margaret, Maid of Norway, as heir presumptive. He married Yolande of Dreux on 1 November 1285. On 19 March 1286, after an evening at Edinburgh Castle, he rode through the dark and a storm to visit the Queen at Kinghorn, ignoring warnings at Inverkeithing, and was found dead with a broken neck near the shore the next morning. He was buried in Dunfermline Abbey.

The Maid of Norway died uncrowned in 1290, and six years of government by the Guardians of Scotland ended with the inauguration of John Balliol on 30 November 1292. A Scots poem recorded by Andrew of Wyntoun mourns the plenty lost with Alexander's death, though Richard Oram points out that the climate was already worsening at the time. A monument was raised near the spot of his death in 1886.
alexander-iv-of-macedon: Alexander IV was the younger son of Alexander the Great and Roxana of Bactria, a Sogdian. An older full brother had died in infancy in 326 BCE. Alexander the Great also had a son named Heracles, born of an informal relationship with Barsine, and Heracles's illegitimacy made the younger boy the primary successor.

When Alexander the Great died on 11 June 323 BCE, Roxana was between six and eight months pregnant and the child's sex was unknown. The infantry supported Philip III, the dead king's half-brother, who had a cognitive disability. The chiliarch Perdiccas, commander of the Companion cavalry, persuaded them to wait. The factions compromised: Perdiccas would rule as regent, Philip would reign only as a figurehead, and a male child would also be king. Alexander IV was born in the second half of 323 BCE.

Perdiccas was assassinated by his officers in 321 or 320 BCE, and at the Partition of Triparadisus Antipater became regent. He took Roxana and the two kings to Macedon. When he died in 319 BCE he left Polyperchon as successor, passing over his own son Cassander, who allied himself with Ptolemy Soter, Antigonus and Philip's wife Eurydice and declared war on the regency.

Cassander took full control of Macedon after Antigonus destroyed Polyperchon's fleet in 318 BCE, and Roxana and the boy fled with Polyperchon to Epirus. Olympias, with Aeacides of Epirus, then invaded; Eurydice's army refused to fight the mother of Alexander the Great and defected. Philip and Eurydice were executed on 25 December 317 BCE, leaving Alexander IV king under Olympias as regent. Cassander returned in 316 BCE, executed Olympias and held the king and his mother in the citadel of Amphipolis under Glaucias.

The peace of 311 BCE that ended the Third Diadoch War recognised Alexander IV's rights and stated that he would succeed Cassander when of age. Supporters of the Argead dynasty then began to argue that, as a teenager, he should rule himself. Cassander then ordered Glaucias to kill the boy and his mother secretly, and according to Pausanias they were poisoned.

The year of death is disputed, within a range from 311 to 304 BCE. Hammond and Walbank place it soon after the death of Heracles, though Peter Green argues Heracles died later. Alexander IV was recognised as king in Egypt and Babylonia until 304 BCE, which some take as posthumous dating and Harry Tolley as a sign he lived that long. A tomb found by Manolis Andronikos at Vergina in 1977/8 is believed to be his, and the skeleton appears to be of a youth in his mid-to-late teens, which would support the later date.
alexander-jagiellon: Alexander was born on 5 August 1461, the fourth son of King Casimir IV Jagiellon and Elizabeth of Austria, a daughter of King Albert II of Germany. By his father's death in 1492 his eldest brother Vladislaus was already king of Bohemia and, from 1490, of Hungary and Croatia, and the next brother, Saint Casimir, had died in 1484 after an ascetic and pious life. On his deathbed Casimir IV recommended John Albert as his successor in Poland and Alexander as ruler of Lithuania.

The Lithuanians elected Alexander grand duke in July 1492 without consulting the Polish nobility, although the union required both sides to agree. John Albert was elected king of Poland on 27 August 1492 and claimed to be supreme duke over his brother, which Alexander recognised but the Lithuanian Council of Lords did not. Soon after his accession Grand Prince Ivan III of Russia and the Crimean Tatars attacked Lithuania. A peace of 1494 ceded extensive land to Ivan, and in 1495 Alexander married his daughter Helena in Vilnius. Ivan resumed the war in 1500. After the Battle of Vedrosha, a truce of 25 March 1503 cost Lithuania about a third of its territory and 19 cities.

John Albert died on 17 June 1501, and Alexander was elected king of Poland on 3 October and crowned on 12 December. Short of money, he fell under the Polish Senate and nobility, who took the mint from him and curtailed his powers. In 1505 the Sejm passed the Act of Nihil novi, which forbade the king to make laws without the consent of the nobility's two chambers, except for those governing royal cities, crown lands, mines, fiefdoms, royal peasants and Jews. Pope Julius II issued 29 bulls in Poland's favour and granted Peter's Pence, which helped Alexander restrain the Teutonic Order.

Alexander never felt at home in Poland and favoured his fellow Lithuanians, above all the magnate Michael Glinski, whose victory over the Tatars at Kletsk on 5 August 1506 was reported to Alexander on his deathbed in Vilnius. He died on 19 August 1506. Interwar Lithuanian historians held that he understood but did not speak Lithuanian, though sources for this are lacking; his charters contain Ruthenian explanations of legal terms, and in 1504 he addressed a Tatar envoy in Ruthenian through an interpreter. His forgotten sarcophagus was found in Vilnius Cathedral in 1931.
alexander-jannaeus: Alexander Jannaeus, born Jonathan, was the third son of John Hyrcanus by his second wife. His half-brother Aristobulus I imprisoned him for the sake of his own security, and when Aristobulus died after a reign of one year, his widow released Alexander and his brothers in 103 BCE. His wife was Salome Alexandra, who came from a Pharisaic family. Their sons were Hyrcanus II and Aristobulus II.

Like his father, Alexander served as high priest. The Pharisees objected to the union of the two offices, and said he was unfit to serve because his mother had been captured and raped at Modi'in. The king was enraged and persecuted them for the rest of his life. The main sources for his reign are the Antiquities of the Jews and The Jewish War by Josephus.

Alexander's early campaigns drew him into a war with Ptolemy IX Lathyros, who had a base on Cyprus. Ptolemy defeated him at Asophon, near the Jordan, and overran much of the kingdom, but Ptolemy's mother Cleopatra III intervened and the Judean king kept his throne. After her death he campaigned again, capturing Gadara, Raphia and Anthedon, and defeating Gaza around 96 BCE; he is said to have massacred those who had taken refuge in the Temple of Apollo there.

Against the Nabataean king Obodas I he suffered a severe defeat in the Golan, where camel-mounted troops ambushed him. At home, during the Feast of Tabernacles, he poured the water libation on his feet instead of the altar, and the crowd pelted him with citrons. He killed six thousand people. The civil war that followed drew in Demetrius III Eucaerus, who beat Alexander at Shechem, but Alexander won in the end and had eight hundred rebels, mainly Pharisees, crucified in Jerusalem.

In his last campaigns, from 83 to 80 BCE, Alexander took cities in Gaulanitis and Galaaditis, including Golan, Gamala, Pella, Dium and Gerasa. At its largest the kingdom covered most of the Mediterranean coast of the Land of Israel and the lands around the Jordan. He died around 76 BCE during the siege of Ragaba, after three years of illness brought on by heavy drinking and quartan ague. He named his wife Salome Alexandra as his successor.

Menahem Stern held that the weakness of the Seleucid Empire and Roman restraint made the expansion possible. Aryeh Kasher argues that Josephus relied on hostile sources and that the wars grew from long-standing hostility between the Jews and the Hellenistic cities. Jannaeus's coins are the most abundant Jewish coinage of the period; Kenneth Atkinson reads their low quality as a sign of economic instability.
alexander-kerensky: Alexander Kerensky was born in Simbirsk, now Ulyanovsk, on 4 May 1881, the eldest son of Fyodor Mikhailovich Kerensky, a teacher and director of the local gymnasium. His father had taught Vladimir Ulyanov, later known as Lenin, and the two families were friends. In 1889 the family moved to Tashkent. Kerensky studied history and philology and then law at St Petersburg University, and took his law degree in 1904.

He became known as a defence lawyer in political trials of revolutionaries and in 1912 published material on the Lena massacre, after visiting the goldfields on the Lena River. That year he was elected to the Fourth Duma for the Trudoviks, a non-Marxist socialist labour party, and joined a Freemason society of anti-monarchy forces. In November 1916 he used the opening of the Duma to denounce the imperial ministers as guided by Grigori Rasputin.

After the February Revolution of 1917 Kerensky became vice-chairman of the Petrograd Soviet and a member of the Provisional Government, the only man in both. He became Minister of War after the crisis over Pavel Milyukov's note of May and urged soldiers at the front to do their duty. Under Allied pressure he launched the Kerensky Offensive on 1 July 1917. It was at first successful but was driven back by a German counter-attack, and the army showed that it was no longer willing to attack. Officers, angry that he had handed control to soldier committees, called him the persuader-in-chief.

After the July Days and the suppression of the Bolsheviks, Kerensky succeeded Georgy Lvov as prime minister on 21 July 1917. Following the Kornilov Affair at the end of August he made himself Supreme Commander-in-Chief, and on 15 September proclaimed Russia a republic. He continued the war, which was unpopular, while Lenin promised peace, land and bread, and an estimated two million men had unofficially left the army by autumn. On 7 November 1917 the Bolsheviks seized government buildings and the Winter Palace. Kerensky fled to Pskov, tried to retake Petrograd, was beaten at Pulkovo and eventually reached France.

During the Russian Civil War he supported neither the Bolsheviks nor the White Movement. He lived mostly in Paris and New York City and worked for the Hoover Institution at Stanford University. He died in New York on 11 June 1970 at the age of 89. The Russian and Serbian Orthodox churches refused his body, because of his Freemasonry and because they saw him as largely responsible for the Bolshevik seizure of power, and he was buried in the non-sectarian Putney Vale Cemetery in London.
alexander-khatisian: Khatisian was born on 17 February 1874 in Tiflis, in the Tiflis Governorate of the Russian Empire, to a prominent Armenian family of noble origins. After a state school in Tiflis he trained as a doctor at universities in Moscow, Kharkov and Germany, and he also worked as a journalist. As mayor of Tiflis from 1910 to 1917 he was consulted in the summer of 1914 by Count Illarion Ivanovich Vorontsov-Dashkov on forming Armenian volunteer detachments, which he enthusiastically supported and organised.

Khatisian joined the Armenian Revolutionary Federation in 1917 and sat for the Armenian National Council of Tiflis on the Armenian National Council. After the First Republic of Armenia was declared he served as foreign minister and signed the Treaty of Batum with the Ottoman Empire. He was later interior minister after the death of Aram Manukian, and resigned as prime minister in the aftermath of the Bolshevik-led May Uprising of 1920.

Armenia's first prime minister, Hovhannes Kajaznuni, praised his inexhaustible energy and administrative experience but complained that he had no moral authority and did not inspire confidence. After resigning, Khatisian sought aid for the republic in European capitals. On 3 December 1920 a delegation he led signed the Treaty of Alexandropol with Kemalist Turkey, although power had already passed to the new Soviet authorities, so that the government it represented no longer existed.

After the Soviet takeover of Armenia Khatisian went into exile in Paris. There he wrote his memoirs, The Memoirs of a Mayor, and a History and Development of the Republic of Armenia, published in 1930 and revised in 1968. Arrested after the liberation of Paris on suspicion of collaborating with the Germans, he was soon released, and he died in the city on 10 March 1945 at the age of 71.
alexander-kolchak: Kolchak was born in Saint Petersburg on 4 November 1874 (16 November in the modern calendar). His family was of Moldavian origin and both parents came from Odessa. His father, a former major-general of the marine artillery and a veteran of the 1854 siege of Sevastopol, worked as an engineer at an ordnance works near the capital. Kolchak entered the Naval Cadet Corps in 1888, graduated with honours in 1894 and served in the Baltic and Pacific between 1895 and 1899, publishing articles on hydrology.

As a lieutenant he joined Baron Eduard von Toll's Russian Polar expedition on the ship Zarya as hydrologist and cartographer. In the winter of 1901 he and Toll rode dog sleds for 500 km to survey the Taymyr Peninsula, and in spring they studied the New Siberian Islands. Kolchak returned in December 1902; Toll and three other explorers went further north and were lost. Kolchak took part in two Arctic expeditions to look for them, without finding them. He became a recognised expert on naval mines and the author of 16 articles on Arctic research.

Hearing of the war with Japan in December 1903, Kolchak summoned his fiancée Sophia Omirova to Siberia for a hurried wedding and went to Port Arthur. He served on the cruiser Askold and later commanded the destroyer Serdity, laying mines by night; one sank the Japanese cruiser Takasago. He was wounded and captured at the siege, and on his return lobbied the State Duma for submarines and aircraft. He became the youngest vice admiral in the Imperial Navy and was Baltic Fleet Chief of Operations when the First World War began.

Early in the Civil War he served briefly as Minister of War and Navy in the Provisional All-Russian Government until a November 1918 coup installed him as Supreme Ruler, heading a military dictatorship from Omsk. He opposed democracy, which he tied to pacifism, internationalism and socialism. After initial successes in early 1919 his forces lost ground for lack of local support and failure to unite the anti-Bolshevik leaders.

Omsk fell to the Red Army in November 1919 during the Great Siberian Ice March, and Kolchak moved his headquarters to Irkutsk. He was betrayed and detained by the Allied mission's chief, Maurice Janin, and the Czechoslovak Legion, which gave him to local Socialist-Revolutionaries in January 1920. The Bolsheviks shot him on 7 February 1920. His government won diplomatic recognition from no country, and he alienated the Czechoslovak Legion; the American commander Graves refused him military aid.
alexander-nevsky: Alexander was born in Pereslavl-Zalessky on 13 May 1221, although an older tradition placed his birth on 30 May 1220. He was the second son of Yaroslav Vsevolodovich, who held Pereslavl-Zalessky and the throne of Novgorod during the Mongol conquest of 1237 to 1238 and inherited the Grand Principality of Vladimir in 1238 after the death of his elder brother Yury. There is no consensus on the identity of Alexander's mother, whom his vita names as Feodosiya.

Alexander is first mentioned directly in 1228, when his father left him and his elder brother to rule Novgorod. Fyodor died in the summer of 1233, aged 14, leaving Alexander the eldest surviving son. In 1239 he married Aleksandra, a daughter of the prince of Polotsk, Bryacheslav Vasilkovich, and they had five children, among them Dmitry of Pereslavl, Andrey of Gorodets and Daniel of Moscow.

In 1236 the Novgorod Republic appointed Alexander prince of Novgorod. His father chose him and the veche approved, since it needed his armies. He ruled there in 1236 to 1240, 1241 to 1256 and 1258 to 1259. Alexander continued his family's anti-Western views, which made him unpopular with the veche. After the Mongols won the Battle of the Sit River in 1238 and Yuri II of Vladimir was killed, Yaroslav received the khan's permission to become prince.

In 1240 the Swedes, led by Birger Jarl, launched what is called the Second Swedish Crusade. According to Russian sources, their army landed at the confluence of the Izhora and Neva, and Alexander attacked it on 15 July 1240 and won the Battle of the Neva. The title Nevsky is attested from the 15th century. He also fought German crusaders in the Battle on the Ice in 1242. He agreed to pay tribute to the Golden Horde, which allowed him to preserve the Eastern Orthodox Church, and from 1252 to 1263 he was Grand Prince of Vladimir.

In 1263 Alexander visited Berke of the Golden Horde on a diplomatic mission. He fell ill on the way back and died at Gorodets on 14 November 1263, and was buried in Vladimir on 23 November. Veneration began almost at once. His remains were found incorrupt in 1380 and Macarius, Metropolitan of Moscow, canonized him in 1547. Peter the Great had the relics moved to Saint Petersburg in 1724, and Catherine I founded the imperial Order of Saint Alexander Nevsky in 1725.

His image as defender of Russia was used later, in Sergei Eisenstein's 1938 film and by Soviet authorities during the Second World War, who introduced a Soviet Order of Alexander Nevsky in 1942. Critics argue that the size and importance of his victories were exaggerated for political purposes and that he helped ensure the Golden Horde's dominance over Russia.
alexander-obrenovic: Alexander was born on 14 August 1876 to King Milan and Queen Natalie of Serbia, and belonged to the Obrenović dynasty. In 1889 Milan unexpectedly abdicated and withdrew to private life, proclaiming his son king. As Alexander was only thirteen, three regents were appointed, with Jovan Ristich at their head, and his mother also became a regent. On 13 April 1893 Alexander ordered the regents arrested, declared himself of age and dissolved the national assembly. On 21 May he abolished his father's liberal constitution of 1889 and restored the earlier one.

In 1894 the young king brought Milan back to Serbia, and in 1898 he made him commander-in-chief of the army; Milan was regarded as the real ruler of the country in these years. In 1898 penalties fell on the Radical and Russophil parties, which the court sought to tie to an attempted assassination of the former king. In the summer of 1900 Alexander suddenly announced his engagement to Draga Mašin, a widow who had served as maid of honour to his mother. She was nine years older than the king and unpopular in Belgrade society, and many believed she could not bear children.

His father had been arranging a match with a German princess, and both Milan and the prime minister, Vladan Đorđević, resigned. Alexander's mother also opposed the marriage and was banished from the kingdom. Nicholas II of Russia agreed to act as principal witness, and the wedding took place in August 1900, but the marriage weakened the king's position with the army and the wider country.

In 1901 Alexander issued a moderately liberal constitution of his own initiative, which introduced for the first time in Serbia a parliament of two chambers, the skupština and a senate, and granted an amnesty to the persecuted Radicals. It reconciled the parties but not the army, which was alarmed by rumours that one of Draga's brothers would be named heir presumptive. The country's growing dependence on Austria-Hungary was also resented. In March 1903 the king suspended the constitution for half an hour, long enough to publish decrees replacing the senators and councillors of state.

In 1902 Peter Karađorđević had been proclaimed king by followers at Šabac, and conspiracies formed. A group of officers led by Captain Dragutin Dimitrijević, known as Apis, invaded the palace in Belgrade. They found the royal couple, murdered them in the early morning of 11 June 1903 and threw their bodies from a window. Both were buried in the crypt of St. Mark's Church, Belgrade.
alexander-of-battenberg: Alexander was the second son of Prince Alexander of Hesse and by Rhine and his morganatic wife, Countess Julia von Hauke. He was a nephew of Tsar Alexander II, who was much attached to him, and in boyhood he often visited Saint Petersburg. He accompanied the tsar during the Bulgarian campaign of 1877. His brothers married into Queen Victoria's family, and their descendants included Earl Mountbatten of Burma. When Bulgaria became an autonomous principality under Ottoman suzerainty by the Treaty of Berlin in 1878, the tsar recommended his nephew for the throne, and the Grand National Assembly elected him unanimously on 29 April 1879.

He had no experience of government and was caught between the Russians, who wanted a passive prince, and quarrelling Bulgarian politicians. With the tsar's consent he suspended the constitution in 1881, but real power passed to two Russian generals, and he restored it in 1883, which led to a serious breach with Russia. The revolution of Plovdiv on 18 September 1885 united Eastern Rumelia with Bulgaria with his consent. Russia withdrew its officers from the Bulgarian army, and Serbia invaded. Alexander rallied the army, and the Bulgarians won a decisive victory at Slivnitsa on 19 November and captured Pirot on 27 November. Austria's intervention protected Serbia from the consequences, but the union with Eastern Rumelia was sealed.

Discontented officers, encouraged by Tsar Alexander III, seized the prince in the palace at Sofia on the night of 20 August 1886 and forced him to sign his abdication. A counter-revolution led by Stefan Stambolov allowed him to return, but his cousin the tsar refused his return, and he resigned the throne and left Bulgaria on 8 September 1886.

Alexander afterwards lived privately and in 1889 married the actress Johanna Loisinger, taking the style Count von Hartenau. He held a local command in the Austrian army at Graz, where he died of a ruptured appendix on 17 November 1893. His body was brought to Sofia, given a public funeral and buried in a mausoleum built in his memory. Battenberg Hill on Livingston Island in Antarctica is named after him.
alexander-of-greece: Alexander was born on 1 August 1893 at Tatoi Palace near Athens, the second son of Crown Prince Constantine and Princess Sophia of Prussia. He was related to royalty across Europe: his mother was a daughter of Frederick III, German Emperor, and Wilhelm II was his uncle. He was mischievous and extroverted, unlike his serious elder brother George. Educated in Greece at the Hellenic Military Academy, he was known more for his mechanical skills than for intellect, and was among the first Greeks to own an automobile.

He distinguished himself in the Balkan Wars of 1912-13, serving on his father's staff during the capture of Thessaloniki. In 1915 he fell in love with Aspasia Manos, the daughter of his father's Master of the Horse, and the couple became secretly engaged.

Alexander swore the constitutional oath on 11 June 1917, after the Entente Powers and the followers of Eleftherios Venizelos forced Constantine into exile. Russia's provisional government protested and wanted him called only regent, but was brushed aside. Only the Archbishop of Athens, his father, his brother and the prime minister Alexandros Zaimis attended, and he was in tears.

His father told him to consider himself a regent. The family left for exile, though Alexander stayed, and the royal household was gradually replaced by enemies of his father. His new ministers openly called him the son of a traitor, and Venizelos ruled as prime minister with Entente support. In 1919 Alexander married Aspasia Manos, though his father had asked him to wait until the war ended.

Both Venizelists and royalists opposed a marriage to a commoner, and the scandal forced the couple to leave Greece for several months. Under his reign Greek territory grew considerably, following the Entente's victory and the early stages of the Greco-Turkish War of 1919-1922.

On 2 October 1920 Alexander tried to part his dog from a pet Barbary macaque in the Tatoi grounds and was bitten deeply on the leg and torso by another monkey. The wounds were dressed but not cauterised, and sepsis set in. The government refused to let his mother return from exile, and he died on 25 October 1920 at the age of 27, twelve hours before his grandmother, Queen Olga, arrived. His descendants were excluded from the succession because of the marriage.

His death raised questions about the monarchy. Prince Paul refused the throne while his father and brother lived. In elections on 14 November 1920 the monarchists won, Venizelos left Greece, and a referendum restored Constantine I. Greece then lost the Greco-Turkish War, and the gains on the Turkish mainland were lost. Winston Churchill wrote that perhaps a quarter of a million people died of this monkey's bite.
alexander-pushkin: Alexander Pushkin was born in Moscow on 6 June 1799 (26 May in the Old Style calendar). His father, Sergei Lvovich Pushkin, came from a noble family that traced its ancestry to the 12th century. His mother, Nadezhda Ossipovna Gannibal, was a granddaughter of Abram Petrovich Gannibal, an African page taken to Constantinople as a gift for the Ottoman Sultan and later sent to Peter the Great.

Entrusted to nursemaids and French tutors, Pushkin spoke mostly French until the age of ten and learned Russian from household serfs and his serf nanny, Arina Rodionovna. His first poem appeared in 1814, when he was 15, and in 1817 in the first graduating class of the Imperial Lyceum at Tsarskoye Selo, where he absorbed the thought of the French Enlightenment.

In 1820 Pushkin published his first long poem, Ruslan and Ludmila, to much controversy. His commitment to social reform angered the government, which transferred him from the capital in May 1820. In Chișinău, in Bessarabia, he wrote The Prisoner of the Caucasus and The Fountain of Bakhchisaray. After a further clash with the authorities in Odessa he was exiled to his mother's estate of Mikhailovskoye, near Pskov, from 1824 to 1826.

At Mikhailovskoye he worked on the verse novel Eugene Onegin, which was serialized between 1825 and 1832, and in 1825 wrote the drama Boris Godunov. He could not get permission to publish the play until five years later, and its uncensored original was not staged until 2007. His poem Ode to Liberty was found among the belongings of the Decembrist rebels of 1825, and he was summoned to Moscow; many of the Decembrists were his friends.

By the autumn of 1836 Pushkin was deeper in debt and faced rumours that his wife, Natalia Goncharova, was having an affair. On 4 November he challenged Georges d'Anthès to a duel, but the challenge was withdrawn after friends intervened. D'Anthès then married her sister Ekaterina, yet continued to pursue Natalia in public. After Pushkin sent him a highly insulting letter in late January 1837, a duel could not be avoided. He was fatally wounded and died on 10 February 1837 (29 January in the Old Style).

Pushkin's works supplied material for composers: Mikhail Glinka's Ruslan and Lyudmila, and Pyotr Tchaikovsky's Eugene Onegin (1879) and The Queen of Spades (1890). His short drama Mozart and Salieri became the libretto of an opera by Nikolai Rimsky-Korsakov. In 1937 the town of Tsarskoye Selo was renamed Pushkin in his honour.
alexander-romance: The Alexander Romance has been called antiquity's most successful novel. Its author is uncertain, though some manuscripts attribute it pseudonymously to Alexander's court historian Callisthenes, so the writer is commonly called Pseudo-Callisthenes. The original was composed in Koine Greek, and the oldest Greek version, the alpha recension, can be dated to the 3rd century CE and survives in a single manuscript. It was the source of a Latin version by Julius Valerius Alexander Polemius in the 4th century and of an Armenian version in the 5th. Because so many works derive from it, the Alexander romance is sometimes treated as a genre rather than a single text, and none of its recensions can be considered canonical.

The book follows Alexander from his birth to his accession in Macedon, his conquest of the Persian Empire and his death. Although built around a historical core, it is mostly fantastical. Nectanebo II, the last pharaoh of Egypt, flees to the Macedonian court as a magician, and Olympias, wife of Philip II, becomes pregnant by him. Alexander kills Nectanebo as a boy and is taught by Aristotle.

Later episodes drew wide notice in their own right. In the Gates of Alexander, Alexander prays and two mountains draw together; he builds gates of bronze that enclose twenty-two nations, among them Gog and Magog. In the story of the Fountain of Life, shaped by earlier legends of Gilgamesh, his cook Andreas washes a fish in a fountain, the fish springs to life, and Andreas drinks the water. Alexander punishes him and the daughter who shared it, turning them into spirits of the sea and the desert. The Land of Darkness grew from a few statements in the original, especially in versions from Islamic lands.

In premodern times the Romance underwent more than 100 translations, elaborations and derivations in dozens of languages, from Mali to Malaysia, among them Coptic, Ge'ez, Syriac, Arabic, Persian, Armenian and Hebrew. Alexander was assimilated into the cultures of his readers: a Christian in Christian legends, a Muslim in Islamic ones. The story of Dhu al-Qarnayn in the Quran is generally seen as an allusive summary of the tradition as the Syriac Alexander Legend gave it.

In Europe, Leo the Archpriest found a Greek copy in Constantinople and made a Latin version, on which the Historia de Proeliis was based. It went through three recensions between the twelfth and fifteenth centuries and was translated more often over the next three centuries than any text except the Gospels. Vernacular versions followed in French, Middle English, Irish and Old Church Slavonic. In Persian the story reached Ferdowsi's Shahnameh and Nizami's Iskandarnameh. The first modern English translation was by E. H. Haight in 1955, and Richard Stoneman's of 1991 is the major one.
alexander-suvorov: Alexander Suvorov was born in Moscow, in a mansion on the Arbat given as a dowry by his maternal grandfather, Fedosey Manukov. His family was a noble one originating from Novgorod. His father, Vasily Ivanovich Suvorov, was a general-in-chief and a senator, and is credited with translating the works of Vauban into Russian. Suvorov entered the army in 1745 and served nine years in the Semyonovsky Lifeguard Regiment while attending classes at the Cadet Corps of Land Forces. He spent most of his time in the barracks, where the troops loved him and others thought him eccentric.

He was among the best-educated Russians of his time. He knew mathematics, history and geography, spoke German, French, Italian, Polish, Turkish, Arabic and Finnish, and had studied military works from Plutarch to his contemporaries. His first battle experience came in the Seven Years' War, where he took part in the victory over Frederick the Great at the Battle of Kunersdorf in 1759.

In the War of the Bar Confederation Suvorov captured Kraków in 1768 and won victories at Orzechowo and Opatów. Stormings of the fortified positions at Lanckorona and near Tyniec Abbey failed in 1771, which were among the few tactical setbacks of his career. In the Russo-Turkish War of 1768 to 1774 he captured Turtukaya twice and won at Kozludzha. From 1777 he built more than 30 fortifications on the Kuban with about 12,000 men, after which attacks from across the river ceased.

In the Russo-Turkish War of 1787 to 1792 he fought at Kinburn and Focșani and won the Battle of Rymnik, followed by the storming of Izmail. In 1794 he put down the Polish uprising and defeated the Poles at Praga. He quarrelled with Catherine the Great's heir Paul I, who after becoming emperor in 1796 often disagreed with him. In February 1799, with France winning in Europe, Paul reinstated him as field marshal. Given command of the Austro-Russian army, he won at the Trebbia and captured Milan and Turin. He then led his exhausted, outnumbered army out of the Swiss Alps after being cut off by André Masséna, and was promoted generalissimo.

Suvorov died of illness in Saint Petersburg on 18 May 1800 (6 May Old Style) and was buried in the Alexander Nevsky Lavra, where his gravestone reads simply: Here lies Suvorov. After Paul I was murdered within a year, his son and successor Alexander I erected a statue to his memory in the Field of Mars. Suvorov wrote military works, the best known being The Science of Victory and the Suzdal Regulations, and he is remembered for sayings such as: Perish yourself but rescue your comrade. Poets including Gavrila Derzhavin, Alexander Pushkin and Mikhail Lermontov mentioned him, and he appears in Leo Tolstoy's War and Peace.
alexander-tamanian: Alexander Hovhannesi Tamanian was born on 4 March 1878 in Yekaterinodar, in a banker's family, and graduated from the St Petersburg Academy of Arts in 1904. His early works were neoclassical, among them the mansion of V. P. Kochubei at Tsarskoye Selo in 1911 to 1912, the house of Prince S. A. Scherbatov on Novinsky Boulevard in Moscow in 1911 to 1913, railway employees' housing and a tuberculosis sanatorium near Moscow, and the central workshops of the Kazan railway at Lyubertsy in 1916. He became an Academician of Architecture in 1914 and in 1917 was elected Vice-President of the Academy of Arts.

In 1923 he moved to Yerevan to head the new construction effort in the republic. He was chief engineer of the local Council of People's Commissars and a member of the CEC of the Armenian SSR from 1925 to 1936. He designed layouts for Leninakan, now Gyumri, in 1925, Stepanakert in 1926, Nor-Bayazet, now Gavar, and Ahta-ahpara in 1927, and Echmiadzin in 1927 to 1928. His first general plan of modern Yerevan was approved in 1924, and his style helped turn a small provincial city into the capital and a major industrial and cultural centre.

He worked mainly in a neoclassical style with a national flavour, such as red tuff linings and traditional carving in stone. His best-known buildings in Yerevan include the first hydroelectric station of 1926, the Opera and Ballet theatre, built from 1926 to 1953, and Republic Square, built from 1926 to 1941. He chaired the Committee for the Protection of Historic Monuments in Armenia and was prominent in restoring historical landmarks.

Tamanian married Camilla Edwards, a maternal granddaughter of the architect Nicholas Benois. Their sons Gevorg and Yulius also became noted architects and continued his work. He died in Yerevan on 20 February 1936 and is buried at the Komitas Pantheon in the city centre.
alexander-the-good: Alexander I, known as Alexander the Good (Alexandru cel Bun in Romanian), was the son of Roman I and succeeded Iuga as Voivode of Moldavia. He ruled between 1400 and 1432. Although Sigismund of Hungary had backed him to the throne, his policy was built on alliances with Wallachia and Poland, generally directed against Hungary, because his main concern was to defend the country in wars against superior armies.

At home Alexander expanded the bureaucratic system by creating the Council of the Voivode and the Chancellory. In 1403 he added the office of logofăt, the chancellor of the official chancellery. He granted commercial privileges to the traders of Lviv in 1408 and of Kraków in 1409, improved the trade route linking the port of Cetatea Albă to Poland, strengthened the forts by guarding them, and expanded the ports of Cetatea Albă and Chilia.

He had a part in ending the conflict between the Moldavian Orthodox Church and the Patriarch of Constantinople, built the Bistrița Monastery and continued work on the Neamț Monastery, begun in the previous century. A grant of 31 families to Bistrița, along with some cattle, is the first documented confirmation of the enslavement of Roma in Moldavia.

In 1402 he became the sworn vassal of Jogaila, King of Poland, and the treaty was renewed in 1404, 1407, 1411 and 1415. He won two major battles against the Teutonic Order, at Grunwald in 1410 and at Marienburg in 1422. In 1420 he defended Moldavia against the first Ottoman incursion, at Cetatea Albă. He also became involved in the power struggles of Wallachia, helping Radu II Prasnaglava in 1418 to 1419 and Alexandru I Aldea in 1429, mostly to prevent the capture of Chilia.

Because of a Polish territorial claim, and because the Polish king had failed to fulfil his part of the vassal treaty during the Ottoman attack of 1420, Alexander attacked Poland during the Lithuanian Civil War. The war ended with the Treaty of Suceava on 18 November 1431. Alexander married several times, and his wives included Margareta Bánffy de Losoncz, Ana Jagiellon of Podolsk and Rimgailė, who was divorced in 1421. His children included Iliaș, Petru III, Stephen II, Peter Aaron and Bogdan II. He died on 1 January 1432 and was buried in Bistrița Monastery.
alexander-the-great: Alexander was born in Pella, the capital of Macedon, probably on 20 July 356 BCE, the son of Philip II and his fourth wife, Olympias, daughter of King Neoptolemus I of Epirus. According to the biographer Plutarch, Olympias dreamed that a thunderbolt struck her womb, and Plutarch suggested that Zeus was Alexander's father. Alexander claimed descent from Heracles and Perseus through his father and from Achilles through his mother. Aristotle tutored him until he was 16, after which he governed as regent while Philip fought the Thracians.

Philip was assassinated by his chief bodyguard Pausanias, probably on 25 October 336 BCE, and the army proclaimed the 20-year-old Alexander king. He executed his cousin Amyntas IV and two Macedonian princes, destroyed the city of Thebes and took over the League of Corinth. In 334 BCE he launched a pan-Hellenic invasion of the Achaemenid Persian Empire. After conquering Asia Minor he won decisive battles at Issus and Gaugamela, overthrew Darius III and took the whole empire.

In 326 BCE he invaded India and defeated the king Porus at the Battle of the Hydaspes, but facing a mutiny he turned back at the Beas River. According to Curtius, he slaughtered the entire population of Massaga. At Opis his troops mutinied again, resenting his adoption of Persian customs and his promotion of Persian officers.

Alexander died in Babylon on 10 or 11 June 323 BCE, at age 32. Plutarch describes a fever that worsened until he could not speak, while Diodorus tells of pain after a large bowl of unmixed wine. Civil wars then broke out and the Diadochi broke up the empire, beginning the Hellenistic period. He founded more than twenty cities, the most prominent being Alexandria in Egypt. The works of those who knew him, including Ptolemy and Nearchus, are lost, and Arrian, who drew on Ptolemy and Aristobulus, is generally considered the most reliable of the later writers.
alexander-von-bach: Alexander, Baron von Bach, was born on 4 January 1813 in Loosdorf, Lower Austria, into a legal family, his father holding a judicial office. At the age of 24 he was made a doctor of laws and then entered the imperial service, where he remained for nine years. He was regarded as an up-and-coming young radical; Adolph Schwarzenberg recorded that his motto must have been 'to improvise is to change, to be perfect is to change often'. A well-known liberal lawyer, he was first called a 'minister of barricades' before serving as Minister of Justice in 1848 and 1849.

As Minister of the Interior from 1849 to 1859, Bach favoured a departure from the absolute system of Metternich but was not prepared to go as far as the revolutionaries of 1848. Described by contemporaries as 'quite wonderfully unprincipled', he changed position often and was driven into conservative ranks by popular opposition. In March 1849 he endorsed Prince Schwarzenberg's centralising constitutional programme, which further inflamed Hungarian sentiment. The effect of his reforms on Hungary has been much debated: some historians see the revolution as the greater creator of Hungarian national identity, others the systems Bach built as the main driver of Hungarian nationalism.

After Schwarzenberg's death in 1852 Bach largely dictated policy in Austria and Hungary. He centralised administrative authority across the empire but also endorsed reactionary measures that reduced freedom of the press and abandoned public trials. He represented the clerical-absolutist direction, which culminated in the concordat of August 1855 giving the Roman Catholic Church control over education and family life. The period became known as neo-absolutism, or Bach's absolutism. He was created baron in 1854 and was guardian of the Science Academy from 1849 to 1859.

Bach's fall in 1859 was caused largely by the failure of the Italian war against the Kingdom of Sardinia and Napoleon III. His military reforms had put the army ahead of industrialisation, with barracks taking the place of factories and infrastructure. After leaving office he served as ambassador to the Holy See from 1859 to 1867. He died in seclusion on 12 November 1893 at Schöngrabern in Austria.
alexander-von-humboldt: Friedrich Wilhelm Heinrich Alexander von Humboldt was born in Berlin on 14 September 1769 and baptised a Lutheran. He was the younger brother of the Prussian minister and linguist Wilhelm von Humboldt. He graduated from the Freiberg School of Mines in 1792 and became an inspector in the Prussian Department of Mines in Bayreuth and the Fichtel Mountains. His gold ore output in his first year exceeded that of the previous eight years combined. He also opened, at his own expense, a free school for miners and tried to set up an emergency relief fund for them.

In Madrid Humboldt obtained authorisation from the Spanish crown to travel in its American realms, after a planned French voyage was postponed. With the botanist Aimé Bonpland he sailed from La Coruña on 5 June 1799, climbed the volcano Teide on Tenerife, and landed at Cumaná, Venezuela, on 16 July.

Between 1799 and 1804 they travelled through Venezuela, Cuba, the Andes and New Spain. In Bogotá, José Celestino Mutis gave Humboldt access to his great pictorial record of plants. Humboldt identified the source of the Orinoco River, and in 1802 he climbed in Ecuador to 19,286 feet, a world record altitude for a Westerner at the time. In 1804 he made an unplanned visit to the United States at the invitation of President Thomas Jefferson.

Humboldt spent his personal fortune publishing the results, in nearly thirty volumes with Bonpland as co-author. The Political Essay on the Kingdom of New Spain and the Personal Narrative of Travels were widely read. He was elected to the Prussian Academy of Sciences in 1805 and, in his sixtieth year, made an expedition to Russia.

His quantitative work on botanical geography laid the foundation of biogeography, and his advocacy of long-term, systematic geophysical measurement pioneered modern geomagnetic and meteorological monitoring. His multivolume Kosmos, which took shape in lectures at the University of Berlin in 1827–1828, sought to unify diverse branches of scientific knowledge and presented the universe as one interacting whole. In 1800 and again in 1831 he described local effects of development on climate. He died on 6 May 1859. Scholars argue over whether his writing carries an imperial bias; Pratt contends that he portrayed the South American natural world as free of people.
alexandra-feodorovna-alix-of-hesse: Alix was born on 6 June 1872 at the New Palace in Darmstadt, the sixth child and fourth daughter of Louis IV, Grand Duke of Hesse, and Princess Alice of the United Kingdom, the second daughter of Queen Victoria. Her older brother Prince Friedrich, who had haemophilia, died after a fall in May 1873, when she was about a year old.

Queen Victoria wanted her to marry into the British royal house and in 1889 invited her to Balmoral to meet Prince Albert Victor, known as Eddy. He proposed, and in May 1890 Alix refused him, writing that she saw him only as a cousin. Her heart lay elsewhere. She had met the Russian heir, Nicholas, in 1884 at the wedding of her sister Elisabeth to Grand Duke Sergei Alexandrovich in Saint Petersburg, and her sister and brother-in-law favoured a match with him.

Nicholas proposed in April 1894 at Coburg. Alix at first declined, because marriage to the Russian heir required her to leave Lutheranism for Russian Orthodoxy, but she later accepted. After Alexander III died on 1 November 1894, she was received into the Orthodox Church the next day as Grand Duchess Alexandra Feodorovna. She and Nicholas married on 26 November 1894 in the Grand Church of the Winter Palace. They were crowned in the Dormition Cathedral in the Kremlin on 26 May 1896.

The couple had four daughters, Olga, Tatiana, Maria and Anastasia, and a son, Alexei, who had haemophilia. His illness shaped her relations with religious advisers and healers, among them Grigori Rasputin, whom she came to believe could help the boy. She supported the preservation of the autocracy and opposed some proposed reforms. Historians still debate how far she influenced Nicholas II and how far she was responsible for the decisions of his government.

Nicholas abdicated on 15 March 1917 (2 March in the old-style calendar). The family was held under house arrest at the Alexander Palace at Tsarskoye Selo and later moved to Yekaterinburg. On 17 July 1918 Alexandra, Nicholas and their five children were murdered by Bolshevik forces at the Ipatiev House, together with several members of their household.

The Russian Orthodox Church Outside Russia recognised the family as martyrs in 1981. Alexandra was reinterred with Nicholas and three of their children in the Peter and Paul Cathedral in Saint Petersburg in 1998, and the Russian Orthodox Church canonised her as a passion bearer in 2000.
alexandre-de-rhodes: Alexandre de Rhodes, called Đắc Lộ in Vietnamese, was born on 15 March 1593 in Avignon, then in the Papal States. According to some sources he was of Jewish origin, and his paternal side came from Aragón in Spain. He entered the novitiate of the Society of Jesus in Rome on 24 April 1612 to dedicate his life to missionary work.

In 1624 he arrived in Đàng Trong, which Europeans called Cochinchina, with the Jesuit Girolamo Maiorica. He studied Vietnamese under Francisco de Pina before returning to Portuguese Macau. After two Jesuits visited Đàng Ngoài, or Tonkin, in 1626, his superior André Palmeiro sent him and Pero Marques to evangelise it. They landed in Thanh Hoá on 19 March 1627 and reached the capital Thăng Long, now Hanoi, on 2 July. De Rhodes worked there until he was forced to leave in 1630, spending three years in and around the court of the lord Trịnh Tráng. There he composed the Ngắm Mùa Chay, a Catholic devotion in Vietnamese.

He spent ten years at Macau, then returned to Đàng Trong, mainly around Huế. After six years he displeased the lord Nguyễn Phúc Lan and was condemned to death, but the sentence was reduced to exile. By 1649 he was back in Rome, pleading for more funds for the Catholic missions to Vietnam and telling somewhat exaggerated stories of its natural riches. His plea helped to found the Paris Foreign Missions Society in 1659.

He developed an early Vietnamese alphabet on the work of earlier Portuguese missionaries including Gaspar do Amaral, António Barbosa and Francisco de Pina. He compiled a catechism and the Dictionarium Annamiticum Lusitanum et Latinum, a trilingual dictionary and grammar, both published in Rome in 1651. They show his preference for the new Latin-script alphabet over the Nôm script. Later refined as chữ Quốc ngữ, it became the de facto written form of Vietnamese in the 20th century, while Maiorica's catechism and devotional texts favoured chữ Nôm, the main script of Vietnamese Christian literature until then.

Sent to Persia instead of back to Vietnam, he died at Isfahan in 1660 and was buried in the New Julfa Armenian Cemetery. In 1943 French Indochina issued two stamps in recognition of his contribution to the script.
alexandre-petion: Pétion was born Anne Alexandre Sabès in Port-au-Prince, the son of a wealthy French father, Pascal Sabès, and Ursula, a free woman of mixed ancestry. Like other gens de couleur libres with wealthy fathers, he was sent to France in 1788 to study at the Military Academy in Paris. In Saint-Domingue the free people of colour formed a third caste between the whites and the enslaved Africans. After the French Revolution they rebelled to gain the voting and political rights they believed were due to them as French citizens.

He returned to take part in the Haitian Revolution and skirmished with British forces. In the War of the South, which began in June 1799, he allied with André Rigaud and Jean-Pierre Boyer against Toussaint Louverture and commanded the defence of Jacmel, which fell in March 1800. He then went into exile in France. In February 1802 he returned with General Charles Leclerc's fleet of 32,000 French troops, hoping to secure power in the colony, and in October 1802 joined the rebels, supporting Jean-Jacques Dessalines. The rebels took Port-au-Prince on 17 October 1803, and Dessalines proclaimed independence on 1 January 1804.

Pétion and Henri Christophe conspired against Dessalines, who had crowned himself emperor in 1804 and was assassinated on 17 October 1806. Pétion then championed democracy and clashed with Christophe, who wanted absolute rule. Christophe was elected president but went north and set up the State of Haiti, while Pétion was elected president of the southern Republic of Haiti in 1807. The struggle lasted until 1810, when a peace treaty split the country in two. In 1811 Christophe made himself king in the north.

On 2 June 1816 Pétion changed the constitution to make himself president for life, and in 1818 he suspended the legislature. He seized plantations and redistributed the land to his supporters and the peasantry, which earned him the nickname Papa Bon-Cœur. Exports and state revenue fell sharply, as most of the population became subsistence farmers. He founded the Lycée Pétion in Port-au-Prince, and in 1815 he gave sanctuary and material and infantry support to Simón Bolívar.

Pétion died on 29 March 1818. The official record attributes his death to yellow fever, and he was succeeded by Boyer, his chosen successor. The historian Thomas Madiou suggested that he fell into a deep depression and died of inanition, exhaustion for lack of nourishment. Rumours of poisoning circulated, but most historians, including Beaubrun Ardouin, dismissed them. After Christophe died in 1820, Boyer reunited the country under his rule.
alexandria: Alexandria lies at the western edge of the Nile Delta and extends about 40 km along Egypt's northern coast. In ancient times the very large Lake Mariout lay directly south of it. Just to the east, where Abu Qir Bay is now, there were marshland and several islands, and port cities such as Canopus and Heracleion existed there from the 7th century BCE; Heracleion has been rediscovered underwater. A small Egyptian fishing village, Rhakotis, had existed nearby since the 13th century BCE, and it grew into the Egyptian quarter of the new city.

Greek Alexandria was divided into regions: Rhakotis, occupied chiefly by Egyptians, Brucheum, the royal or Greek quarter, and a Jewish quarter in the northeast. The city was laid out as a grid of parallel streets, each with a subterranean canal. As capital of the Ptolemaic Kingdom it became the foremost commercial, intellectual and cultural centre of much of the Hellenistic age and late antiquity, and at one time was the most populous city in the ancient world. It was also a major centre of early Christianity and the seat of the Patriarchate of Alexandria.

The Royal Library is generally thought to have been founded at the beginning of the 3rd century BCE under Ptolemy II, after his father had built the temple of the Muses, the Museion, from which the word museum derives.

In 619 the city fell to the Sassanid Persians. The Byzantine emperor Heraclius recovered it in 629, and in 641 the Arabs under 'Amr ibn al-'As took it after a siege of fourteen months. Egypt's capital then moved to Fustat, now part of Cairo. The Mamluk Sultan Qa'it Bay built the Citadel of Qaitbay in 1477 on the site of the Lighthouse of Alexandria. From the late 18th century the city was one of the most important trading centres in the world, thanks to the overland link between the Mediterranean and the Red Sea and the trade in Egyptian cotton, and its rebirth in the early 19th century began under Muhammad Ali.

Alexandria is Egypt's principal seaport, its second city after Cairo and the largest city on the Mediterranean coast. Surviving monuments include Pompey's Pillar, a Roman triumphal column about 30 m high, and the Catacombs of Kom El Shoqafa, a multi-level labyrinth forgotten until it was found by accident in 1900.
alexandria-eschate: The city stood on the south bank of the Jaxartes, at the south-western end of the Fergana Valley. Cyrus the Great had founded a city in the region as his north-easternmost outpost, Cyropolis, and Persia later settled Greek exiles from rebellious parts of its empire in this distant corner. Alexandria Eschate was probably Cyropolis renamed and re-established. Its remains lie in the tell of the old citadel of Khojand, where Soviet and Tajik excavations have found medieval, Hellenistic and Achaemenid layers below the surface, with fortifications dating to around the 4th century BCE.

To secure Sogdiana, Alexander attacked Cyropolis and a half dozen other towns in 329 BCE. His troops entered Cyropolis through a dried-up water course under the wall; Alexander was struck by a stone on the head and neck, and Craterus was wounded by an arrow. Arrian puts the defenders at about 15,000 fighting men and the dead of the first phase at 8,000, although he also cites Ptolemy as saying the town surrendered from the start. Veterans of Alexander's army were settled in the new city alongside the Greek exiles already there.

Surrounded by Sogdian tribes and about 300 km north of the nearest Greek settlement, Alexandria on the Oxus, the settlers built a wall of 6.0 km, which ancient authors say took about 20 days. From 250 BCE the city likely had closer contact with Bactria under the Greco-Bactrian king Euthydemus I. Scholars have speculated that the capital of Dayuan, the Great Ionians of Han Chinese records, was Alexandria Eschate. Zhang Qian reached Dayuan around 130 BCE, and the Han conquered it after the War of the Heavenly Horses, which helped open the Silk Road. According to Curtius, the city kept its Greek culture as late as 30 BCE.

The site lies within the modern city of Khujand in Tajikistan, where the oldest surface remains of the walls date only to the 10th century. Household utensils, armaments and building materials from the excavations are exhibited in the Museum of Regional Studies in Khojand, and the site has also yielded numerous Hellenistic coins and pottery.
alexandros-mavrokordatos: In 1812 Alexandros Mavrokordatos went to the court of his uncle John Caradja, Hospodar of Wallachia, and in 1818 he went with him into exile in the Austrian Empire, where he studied at the University of Padua. He joined the Filiki Eteria. When the revolution began in 1821 he was living in Pisa with the poet Percy Bysshe Shelley and his wife Mary Shelley, and he travelled to Marseille to buy arms and a ship for the voyage home. He was very wealthy, fluent in seven languages, and preferred Western dress and Western political models.

His experience of ruling in Wallachia led many to look to him as a future leader. At the First National Assembly at Epidaurus in January 1822 he was elected President of the Executive, and he wrote the first Greek constitution. He was more interested in his power base in West Rumeli, going to Hydra for warships and then to Missolonghi, where he supervised the defensive works and built a network of patronage among the western clans. He suffered a serious defeat at Peta on 16 July 1822 but resisted the First Siege of Missolonghi from November 1822 to January 1823.

In 1823 he became general secretary of the Executive and backed the Senate against the Executive dominated by his rival Theodoros Kolokotronis. In 1824 he welcomed Lord Byron to Greece. His pro-English leanings set him against the Russian party of Demetrius Ypsilanti and Kolokotronis. After the fall of Missolonghi on 22 April 1826 he retired for a time. Under King Otto he was Minister of Finance and in 1833 Premier, then envoy at Munich, Berlin, London and Constantinople, and he headed governments again in 1841, in 1844 and in 1854–1855.

Mavrokordatos died in Aegina on 18 August 1865. The American philhellene Samuel Gridley Howe noted that his friends ascribed every action to disinterested patriotism, while his enemies said they served his party or private interest. He is described as the best politician the Greek struggle produced, and he dominated, directly or indirectly, the assemblies that tried to establish a government for Greece.
alexandros-papagos: Alexandros Papagos was born in Athens on 9 December 1883, the son of Major General Leonidas Papagos and Maria Averoff, and so into the Greek social elite with close ties to the royal palace. He briefly entered the Law School of the University of Athens, then took up a military career, studying at the Brussels Military Academy and the Cavalry Application School at Ypres. He was commissioned a cavalry second lieutenant on 15 July 1906 and served in the Balkan Wars. A confirmed monarchist, he was dismissed in 1917 during the National Schism and exiled to islands including Ios, Thira, Milos and Crete.

He was recalled in 1920 and served in the Asia Minor Campaign. In 1935 he joined the service chiefs in toppling the government of Panagis Tsaldaris, and as Chief of the Army General Staff from 1 August 1936 he used the army to support Ioannis Metaxas's declaration of dictatorship on 4 August. When the Greco-Italian War began on 28 October 1940 he became Commander-in-Chief. His army halted the Italian advance by 8 November and forced it deep into Albania between 18 November and 23 December. After the German invasion of 6 April 1941 he endorsed the surrender in Macedonia. He was arrested in July 1943, held at Königstein Fortress and liberated by the Fifth U.S. Army on 5 May 1945.

Appointed Commander-in-Chief again in January 1949, he led the government forces in the Grammos-Vitsi campaign, with American material aid, and was made Field Marshal on 28 October 1949. In May 1951 he resigned to found the Greek Rally, which won 49 percent of the vote and 239 of 300 seats in November 1952.

His government brought Greece into NATO, allowed American bases and devalued the drachma by half in 1953. It faced the Cyprus question, which he took to the UN General Assembly in August 1954, and the Istanbul Pogrom of September 1955. Papagos fell ill in January 1955 and died of a lung hemorrhage on 4 October 1955. The Athens suburb of Papagou is named after him.
alexandros-zaimis: Alexandros Zaimis was born in Athens on 28 October 1855, the son of Thrasyvoulos Zaimis, a former prime minister of Greece, and Eleni Mourouzi. His grandfather Andreas Zaimis had also been prime minister. On his father's side he was related to the great Kalavrytan family that took a notable part in the Greek War of Independence from 1821, and on his mother's he descended from the Fanariote family of the Mourozidon. He studied law at the University of Athens and at Heidelberg, and attended the universities of Leipzig, Paris and Berlin.

Zaimis entered politics after his father's death, when he took over his parliamentary seat for Kalavryta, and became a member of parliament in 1885. He was Minister of the Interior and Minister of Justice in the government of Theodoros Deligiannis from 1890 to 1892 and Speaker of the Hellenic Parliament from 1895 to 1897. He became prime minister for the first time in 1897 and held the office six times in all. In 1906 he was appointed High Commissioner of Crete and presided over a critical period in the island's history up to its de facto union with Greece in 1908.

King Constantine I appointed him prime minister in October 1915 to succeed Eleftherios Venizelos, but he resigned a month later when his government failed to win a vote of confidence. In 1917 he served again under Constantine while Venizelos led a rival government in northern Greece, and under Entente pressure he resigned in favour of Venizelos in June of that year. During the First World War he was generally supposed to favour Greek neutrality while being personally in favour of the Allies. A moderate conservative, he served as prime minister again from 1926 to 1928 in a coalition of supporters of Venizelos and moderate conservatives under the Second Hellenic Republic.

Although he led the monarchist faction, Zaimis was elected the third and last President of the Second Hellenic Republic in 1929 and was re-elected in 1934. A year into his second term Georgios Kondylis forced him out, abolished the Republic and proclaimed himself regent pending a referendum on restoring the monarchy. The referendum recalled George II to the throne with almost 98 per cent of the vote, a total reached because the vote had no secrecy.

Zaimis died in Vienna on 15 September 1936 and was buried in the First Cemetery of Athens. He was married and had no children, and the political legacy of his family was continued by his siblings and cousins.
alexandru-ioan-cuza: Alexandru Ioan Cuza was born at Bârlad on 20 March 1820 into the boyar class of Moldavia, the son of Ioan Cuza, a landowner in Fălciu County, and Sultana, of the Phanariote and Genovese Cozadini family. He was educated at Iași, Pavia, Bologna and Athens and, after a brief military service, in Paris from 1837 to 1840. In the revolutions of 1848 he played a part prominent enough to establish his liberal credentials, and was shipped to Vienna as a prisoner, from where he escaped with British support. In 1858 he became Moldavia's minister of war and a speaker in the ad hoc Divan at Iași, where he strongly advocated union with Wallachia.

The pro-unionist Partida Națională nominated Cuza in both principalities, using an ambiguity in the Treaty of Paris. He was elected Prince of Moldavia on 5 January 1859 (Julian calendar) and, after street pressure changed the vote in Bucharest, Prince of Wallachia on 24 January. The Ottoman sultan did not recognise his authority until 23 December 1861, and then only for the length of Cuza's rule. On 5 February 1862 the union was formally declared, under the name Romania, with Bucharest as its capital, one assembly and one government.

With his councilor Mihail Kogălniceanu, Cuza nationalised monastic estates in 1863; probably more than a quarter of the farmland was held by untaxed dedicated monasteries,. After conservatives defeated his land bill, he held a plebiscite that approved wider suffrage and rule by decree. The Agrarian Law gave peasants title to the land they worked, with landlords keeping one third. Further measures included a Criminal Code and a Civil Code based on the Napoleonic Code and tuition-free compulsory primary education in 1864.

Cuza's land reform and his reliance on a shrinking group of appointed officials drew growing opposition, and financial distress and a scandal over his mistress added to it.
