A coalition of Conservatives and Liberals, called the monstrous coalition, ended his rule: military conspirators broke into the palace one morning in February 1866 and made him sign his abdication, and the next day led him across the border. Prince Karl of Hohenzollern-Sigmaringen was proclaimed Domnitor as Carol I on 20 April 1866. Cuza lived in exile, chiefly in Paris, Vienna and Wiesbaden, and died at Heidelberg on 15 May 1873. He is often counted among the founders of the modern Romanian state.
alexei-brusilov: Aleksei Alekseyevich Brusilov was born on 31 August 1853 in Tiflis, into a family in which three generations had served as officers in the Imperial Russian Army. His father, a lieutenant general, died of tuberculosis in 1856, and his Polish mother died soon after; he was raised by relatives in Kutaisi. He entered the Imperial Corps of Pages in Saint Petersburg in 1867 and in 1872 was posted as an ensign to the 15th (Tver) Dragoon Regiment, stationed near Kutaisi. He served in the Russo-Turkish War of 1877-78 and was decorated for the assault on the fortress of Ardagan and for attacks around Kars.

From 1881 Brusilov was at the Cavalry Officer School in Saint Petersburg, which he commanded from 1902 and made a recognised centre for training cavalry staff officers. He then commanded the 14th Army Corps in the Warsaw Military District from 1908 and the 12th Army Corps in Kiev from 1913. In July 1914 he took command of the 8th Army in Galicia, which crushed the Austro-Hungarian Third Army and advanced nearly 150 kilometres before retreating with the rest of the front. In the Great Retreat of 1915 the 8th Army withdrew 180 kilometres.

On 29 March 1916 he was given the Southwest Front. Earlier Russian offensives had struck ever narrower sections of the line. Brusilov instead attacked along the whole front, using fire on command posts and roads rather than saturation bombardment. Over three months the front advanced an average of more than 30 kilometres along more than 400 kilometres and took 450,000 Austro-Hungarian prisoners, but the supporting attack from the West Front was not delivered and Germany moved 17 divisions from France and Belgium to halt it.

He was one of eight Russian commanders awarded the Sword of Saint George with Diamonds. After asking for the Tsar's abdication in 1917 under pressure from General Mikhail Alekseyev, he became Commander in Chief on 4 June 1917 and was replaced by Lavr Kornilov after the failure of the Kerensky Offensive.

Brusilov sided with the Bolsheviks in the Russian Civil War. In May 1920 he published an appeal in Pravda to former officers to join the Red Army, and he served on a commission on its size and structure before becoming Inspector of Cavalry. He retired in 1924 and died in Moscow on 17 March 1926 of congestive heart failure; he was buried in the Novodevichy Convent. His memoirs appeared in English in 1930 as A Soldier's Notebook, 1914-1918. Many pro-tsarist historians avoided praising him because of his service in the Red Army, and Anton Denikin portrayed him as having suffered a psychological breakdown during the 1916 offensive. Bernard Montgomery counted him among seven outstanding fighting commanders of the First World War.
alexey-kaledin: Alexey Maksimovich Kaledin attended the Mikhaylovskoye Artillery School and the General Staff Academy. Early in the First World War he served as a cavalry commander, then took over a cavalry corps and rose to the rank of General of the Cavalry. On 5 April 1916 (23 March in the old calendar) he became commander of the 8th Army, part of the Imperial Russian Army's Southwestern Front. He took part in the Brusilov Offensive from June to September 1916 and won the Battle of Lutsk in June of that year.

At the Moscow State Conference of August 1917 Kaledin declared that all soviets and committees must be abolished, both in the army and in the rear. After the Kornilov affair he withdrew to Novocherkassk and the protection of the Cossack host, to avoid arrest by the Provisional Government. On 1 July 1917 (18 June in the old calendar) the Great Military Assembly of the Don Cossack Host elected him ataman. According to the historian Peter Kenez, he thus became the first democratically chosen leader of the Cossacks since 1723.

On 9 November, on hearing of the revolution in Petrograd, Kaledin invited the members of the Provisional Government to Novocherkassk to join him in organising the anti-Bolshevik struggle. Mikhail Alekseyev arrived on 15 November and began forming a new army, and on 20 November the host declared its independence. Between 9 and 15 December Kaledin, aided by the Alekseyev Organization, suppressed Bolshevik resistance in Rostov-on-Don. Lavr Kornilov arrived on 19 December and by the end of the month had reorganised the Alekseyev Organization as the Volunteer Army.

By January 1918 Vladimir Antonov-Ovseenko was threatening Rostov and Taganrog with a force led by Sivers, who took Taganrog on 10 February (28 January in the old calendar). Kornilov decided to retreat from the Don. Kaledin concluded that the situation was hopeless, resigned his post and shot himself on 11 February 1918 (29 January in the old calendar). His honours included the Order of St. George, 4th class for the fighting near Hnyla Lypa in October 1914 and 3rd class for the Battle of Kalush in September 1915.
alexios-i-komnenos: Alexios was the son of John Komnenos and Anna Dalassene and the nephew of Isaac I Komnenos, emperor from 1057 to 1059. His father had declined the throne when Isaac abdicated, and died a monk in 1067. Alexios and his elder brother Manuel served with distinction against the Seljuk Turks under Romanos IV Diogenes. In 1074 western mercenaries under Roussel de Bailleul rebelled in Asia Minor, and Alexios subdued them by 1076.

In 1078 Nikephoros III made him commander of the field army in the West, and he defeated the rebellions of Nikephoros Bryennios the Elder at the Battle of Kalavrye and of Nikephoros Basilakes. While troops were assembling against the expected Norman invasion under Robert Guiscard, the Doukas faction convinced him to join a conspiracy against Nikephoros III. His mother Anna Dalassene and the empress Maria of Alania played prominent roles in the coup of 1081.

As emperor from 1081, Alexios faced a Norman invasion of the western Balkans under Robert Guiscard and his son Bohemond. After initial defeats he allied with the Holy Roman Emperor Henry IV and had recovered most of the losses by 1085. In 1091 he won a decisive victory over the Pechenegs at the Battle of Levounion in Thrace with help from Cuman allies. In the later 1090s he turned to Asia Minor, most of which had fallen to the Seljuk Turks. His envoys appealed to Pope Urban II at the Council of Piacenza in 1095, and Urban called the First Crusade at the Council of Clermont. It concluded with much of western Anatolia restored to Byzantine rule.

He faced more rebellions than any other Byzantine emperor, from pretenders such as the monk Raictor, the Seljuq Turkic emir Tzachas, who took the title of emperor in 1092, and an impostor claiming to be Leo Diogenes. In 1092 he replaced the debased gold solidus with a gold coin of higher fineness, the hyperpyron. In his last twenty years he lost popularity, persecuted followers of the Paulician and Bogomil heresies, and burned the Bogomil leader Basil at the stake.

Alexios died on 15 August 1118 and was succeeded by his son John II Komnenos, whom he had crowned co-emperor at five in 1092. His daughter Anna Komnene later wrote the Alexiad on his reign. By allying with powerful noble families, he co-opted most of the nobility into his extended family and government, which gave continuity: every later emperor was related to him by descent or marriage. This undermined bureaucratic effectiveness by placing family connections over merit.
alexios-i-of-trebizond: Alexios was the eldest son of Manuel Komnenos and a grandson of the Byzantine Emperor Andronikos I, who reigned from 1183 to 1185. Andronikos was dethroned and killed in 1185, and his son Manuel was blinded and may have died from the mutilation. Manuel left two children, Alexios and David. Their mother's name is not recorded in the primary sources, and the chronicler Michael Panaretos calls Queen Tamar of Georgia their paternal relative, a phrase scholars have explained in several ways.

Scholars disagree about how the brothers reached Tamar's court. One view holds that they were taken from Constantinople in 1185, when Alexios was about three; another holds that they were educated in the capital and left later. His life between 1185 and 1204 is otherwise a blank.

Alexios and David occupied Trebizond in April 1204 with Tamar's help, and Alexios was proclaimed emperor that month at the age of 22. David then took much of the Pontus and Paphlagonia, while Alexios held the east. On one reading of the Georgian chronicle, Alexios took Limnia, Samsun and Sinope; the Muslim historian Ali ibn al-Athir wrote that he closed the sea to the Seljuks. By 1207 the brothers ruled the largest of the three Byzantine successor states, and parts of the Crimea were governed as the tributary province of Perateia.

Alexios defended Trebizond against a siege by the Seljuk sultan Kaykhusraw I. Theodore I Laskaris of Nicaea pressed the western frontier, and in 1208 David asked the Latin emperor Henry of Flanders for help. David then vanishes from the record; a note in a manuscript from Mount Athos says he died as a monk of Vatopedi monastery on 13 December 1212, and why he took vows is not documented.

In 1214 Alexios was captured while hunting outside Sinope, which the Seljuk sultan Kaykaus I was besieging, according to the chronicler Ibn Bibi. The Sinopians refused to surrender, saying that Alexios had grown sons in Trebizond who could govern. Kaykaus had him tortured in sight of the walls until the city gave in on 1 November 1214. Alexios was freed after pledging loyalty and promising tribute.

The loss of Sinope cut Trebizond off from the Empire of Nicaea and the other Greek lands. Alexios died on 1 February 1222 after a reign of eighteen years. His eldest son John was passed over in favour of his son-in-law, Andronikos I Gidos. His descendants later called themselves Megas Komnenos, grand Komnenos.
alexios-ii-of-trebizond: Alexios II Megas Komnenos, son of John II and Eudokia Palaiologina, came to the throne young, after his father's death, and was cared for by his uncle, the Byzantine Emperor Andronikos II Palaiologos. Andronikos wanted him to marry a daughter of the court official Nikephoros Choumnos, but Alexios married the Iberian princess Djiadjak Jaqeli, daughter of Beka I Jaqeli, atabeg of Samtskhe, around 1300. The Patriarch refused to annul the marriage, since the wife was reported to be pregnant, and Eudokia, sent to dissuade her son, advised him to keep her.

In 1301 or 1302 he defeated a Turkoman invasion that had conquered the province of Chalybia and reached Kerasous (modern Giresun), taking their general prisoner and building a fort above the sea to secure the city. He also cultivated the arts and sciences, acting as patron to the astronomer Gregory Chioniades and the scholar Constantine Loukites.

The Genoese had held a near monopoly of Black Sea trade since the Treaty of Nymphaeum with Michael VIII Palaiologos in 1261. Their settlement outgrew Daphnous, the suburb east of Trebizond, and their merchants refused to let imperial customs officials inspect their wares. When Alexios rejected their demands in 1306 they threatened to leave, and when he demanded dues on goods they took with them he sent Georgian mercenaries against them.

His troops prevailed, but the Genoese burned the suburbs. Peace was confirmed in surviving treaties of 1314 and 1316. In 1319 Alexios granted the Venetians, Genoa's rivals, the same privileges as long as they paid their dues. The Byzantinist Donald Nicol observed that the emperors of Trebizond did better out of foreigners than those of Constantinople, since the Italian merchants were not allowed to trade tax-free.

Pirates from the Emirate of Sinope also threatened the city and set fire to it in 1319, and Alexios built sea walls for the harbour in 1324. Over a decade earlier he had organised a night police force.

Pope John XXII wrote in 1329 urging Alexios to convert to Catholicism, as the Pope had urged his father. Alexios died of bubonic plague on 3 May 1330, after a reign of 33 years, and was succeeded by his eldest son Andronikos III. Two works on his death survive: a funeral oration by Constantine Loukites and a later eulogy by Joseph, Metropolitan of Trebizond. Under him the silver content of the empire's aspers was reduced by 15 percent and the coins began to show the emperor and Saint Eugenios on horseback, a design kept until Trebizond fell in 1461.
alexios-iii-angelos: Alexios was the second son of Andronikos Angelos Doukas and Euphrosyne Kastamonitissa; his paternal grandmother was Theodora Komnene, a daughter of Emperor Alexios I Komnenos, so he belonged to the extended imperial family. Around 1183 he conspired with his father and brothers against Emperor Andronikos I Komnenos and spent several years in exile at Muslim courts, including Saladin's. In 1185 Andronikos ordered his younger brother Isaac II executed; Isaac killed the leader of the agents, took refuge in Hagia Sophia and roused the populace, and the riot that followed deposed Andronikos and made Isaac emperor. By 1190 Alexios had returned to court and received the title sebastokratōr.

In March 1195, while Isaac II was hunting in Thrace, the troops acclaimed Alexios emperor, with the covert support of his wife Euphrosyne Doukaina Kamatera. He captured Isaac at Stagira, blinded him and kept him a close prisoner. To secure his position he scattered money so freely that the treasury emptied, and he gave army officers such licence that the empire was left practically defenceless. In 1196 Emperor Henry VI demanded a tribute of gold, which Alexios raised by plundering imperial tombs. The Seljuk Turks overran the east, and the Kingdom of Hungary, the Bulgarians and the Vlachs raided the Balkan provinces. In 1197 Dobromir Chrysos made himself master of Vardar Macedonia.

In 1202 Alexios IV Angelos, Isaac's son, appealed to the Fourth Crusade assembled at Venice. The crusaders reached Constantinople in June 1203. Alexios III took no effective measures, and his son-in-law Theodore Laskaris was defeated at Scutari. In July the crusaders took part of the walls and set fires that left 20,000 homeless. On 17 July Alexios led out an army that outnumbered them but turned back without fighting, and that night he fled by boat with his daughter Irene and about 1,000 pounds of gold.

From Adrianople and Mosynopolis Alexios tried to rally support, and in 1204 he received Alexios V Doukas, who married his daughter Eudokia and was later blinded and deserted by him. He eventually surrendered to Boniface of Montferrat, escaped in 1205, was recaptured and was ransomed about 1209 by Michael I of Epirus, who sent him to Asia Minor. There he plotted against Theodore Laskaris, now emperor of Nicaea, with the support of Sultan Kaykhusraw I. The sultan was defeated and killed at the Battle of Antioch on the Meander in 1211, and Alexios was captured and confined to a monastery at Nicaea, where he died later that year.
alexios-iii-of-trebizond: Alexios III was born on 5 October 1338, the son of Emperor Basil of Trebizond and his second wife, Irene of Trebizond, and was first named John. After Basil died in 1340, his first wife Irene Palaiologina succeeded him and sent his children to Constantinople, where Alexios was raised at the Byzantine court. At eleven he was sent to Trebizond by Emperor John VI Kantakouzenos to replace his deposed great-uncle Michael. He arrived on 22 December 1349, was accepted by the nobility under the megas doux Niketas Scholares, took the name Alexios and was crowned on 21 January 1350.

The young emperor was at first overshadowed by squabbling aristocrats and withdrew to the coastal castle of Tripolis. With his mother and loyal courtiers, among them Michael Panaretos, whose chronicle is the main source for the empire's politics, he subdued the nobles one by one. Niketas fled to Kerasous in 1354 and sailed against Trebizond in 1355 but turned back; Alexios took Kerasous and Kenchrina and brought Niketas to Trebizond, where he died in 1360. In 1363 the Kabasites and other nobles tried to assassinate Alexios. He escaped, arrested them and deposed the Metropolitan Niphon for his part in the plot.

On the frontier Alexios was less successful and suffered a major defeat against the Turkmen in 1355. He relied on marriage alliances with neighbouring Muslim rulers: his sister Maria married Fahreddin Kutlubeg of Aq Qoyunlu in 1352, and four of his daughters married Muslim princes, one of them Tajeddin, emir of Limnia, in 1379. Another daughter, Anna Megale Komnene, became the second wife of King Bagrat V of Georgia. He failed to displace the Genoese and Venetians from the empire's commerce, and in 1373 the Venetians conspired with Dobrotitsa of Dobruja to put Michael Palaiologos on the throne, a plan abandoned after five days.

Alexios III died on 20 March 1390 and was succeeded by his son Manuel III. He had repaired the capital and endowed several monasteries, especially Soumela, and founded the Dionysiou monastery on Mount Athos. Anthony Bryer links this generosity to confiscations after the defeat of the nobles who opposed strong central government: as their estates reverted to the crown he could refound St. Phokas in Kordyle (1362), Soumela (1364), Dionysiou (1374) and Theoskepastos (1376). Alexios also granted charters confirming noble families in their lands.
alexis-de-tocqueville: Tocqueville came from an old Norman aristocratic family and was the great-grandson of the statesman Malesherbes, who was guillotined in 1793. He took a law degree at the University of Paris in 1826. In 1831 the July Monarchy gave him a mission to examine prisons in the United States, and he travelled there with his friend Gustave de Beaumont as far as Michigan and New Orleans. He returned within nine months and published a report, The Penitentiary System in the United States.

He sat in the lower house for the Manche department from 1839 to 1851, on the centre-left, and was regarded as parliament's foremost expert on Algeria, which France had invaded in 1830. In the Second Republic he joined the commission drafting the constitution and sided with the Party of Order against the socialists. He opposed Louis Napoléon Bonaparte's coup of 2 December 1851, was detained at Vincennes and released, and withdrew from politics.

Democracy in America, published in 1835 with a second volume in 1840, set out to help the French understand their position between a fading aristocratic order and an emerging democratic one. Tocqueville saw democracy as balancing liberty and equality. He believed that Americans overcame selfish individualism by associating for common purposes, and warned that radical equality could lead to materialism and to new forms of tyranny, a despotism more dangerous than that of the Roman emperors. The book is considered an early work of sociology and political science.
In The Old Regime and the Revolution, begun after he left politics, he argued that the Revolution continued the modernising and centralising of the French state begun under Louis XIV.

Tocqueville suffered from tuberculosis and died of it on 16 April 1859. He was buried in the Tocqueville cemetery in Normandy and survived by his English wife, Mary Mottley, whom he had married in 1836; they had no children. His liberalism has been read in contrasting ways across the political spectrum.
alexis-of-russia: Alexis was born in Moscow on 19 March 1629, the son of Tsar Michael and Eudoxia Streshneva. He came to the throne at sixteen, after his father died on 12 July 1645, and was crowned on 28 September in the Dormition Cathedral. He was placed in the care of his tutor Boris Morozov, a boyar open to Western ideas, who pursued a peaceful foreign policy and in January 1648 arranged the tsar's marriage to Maria Miloslavskaya, marrying her sister Anna himself ten days later.

Morozov's demand for two years of tax arrears, tripling the burden, and his reputation as corrupt led Muscovites to rise against his faction in the Salt Riot of May 1648. The young tsar had to dismiss them and exile Morozov to a monastery. The unrest was partly responsible for the new legal code, the Sobornoye Ulozheniye, issued in 1649.

From 1648 Alexis reformed the army, creating New Order Regiments of reiters, soldiers, dragoons and hussars, with European military specialists made available by the end of the Thirty Years' War. Rebellions followed in Pskov and Novgorod in 1650. By the 1660s the wars with Poland and Sweden strained public finances; copper coins minted from 1654 devalued the ruble and brought the violently suppressed Copper Riot of 1662. In 1669 the Don Cossacks rose under Stenka Razin, who seized towns along the Volga until his failed siege of Simbirsk in October 1670; he was captured in April 1671 and drawn and quartered in Moscow.

In 1653 Alexis took advantage of Poland's disorder after the Khmelnytsky Uprising to attempt to annex parts of White and Little Russia. The 1654 campaign took Smolensk, and the Treaty of Pereyaslav brought Russian dominance over the Cossack Hetmanate in left-bank Ukraine. A war with Sweden from 1656 achieved little, and the Peace of Kardis of 2 July 1661 returned Russia's conquests. The Truce of Andrusovo of 11 February 1667 left Smolensk, Kiev and the eastern bank of the Dnieper with Russia. In 1649 he had broken off relations with England after the execution of Charles I.

In 1653 Patriarch Nikon began reforms to bring Russian Orthodox practice into line with the Greek church, among them making the sign of the cross with three fingers instead of two. Alexis supported him until Nikon abandoned his post in 1658. The Great Moscow Synod of 1666 deposed Nikon and excommunicated those who opposed the reforms, who broke away as the Old Believers and were harshly persecuted. The siege of the Solovetsky Monastery, where some had fled, ended on 22 January 1676. Alexis died on 8 February 1676 and was remembered as Tishayshy, the most quiet. Peter I was his son by his second wife, Natalya Naryshkina.
alfonsine-tables: The Alfonsine Tables, in Spanish Tablas Alfonsíes and in Latin Tabulae Alphonsinae, gave the data needed to compute the positions of the Sun, Moon and planets relative to the fixed stars. They are named after Alfonso X of Castile, who sponsored them, and were compiled in Toledo; their data begin on 1 June 1252, the date of the king's coronation. They were made as an addition to the Toledan Tables, an eleventh-century work, to improve the computation of mean motion. Alfonso gathered a team of scholars, among them Jewish astronomers such as Yehuda ben Moshe and Isaac ibn Sid, who also drew on earlier Islamic astronomical works and on observations made in Toledo.

The tables kept the framework and the Ptolemaic methods of the Toledan Tables: the geocentric model, mathematical prediction of planetary motion and calculation from tables. The authors concentrated on more advanced computational procedures. They divided the year into 365 days, 5 hours, 49 minutes and 16 seconds, very close to the figure accepted today.

Copernicus's remark that his system explained the planetary motions with no more than 34 circles has been taken to imply that many epicycles had been added to the Ptolemaic system in an attempt to match observation, though modern computations using Ptolemy's unmodified theory have reproduced the published tables. A remark credited, probably wrongly, to Alfonso says that, had the Lord consulted him at the creation, he would have recommended something simpler.

The earliest documented reference to the tables in Paris is by Geoffrey of Meaux in 1320. John of Murs wrote in 1321 that he had the tables but not the canons, and John of Saxony composed new canons for the Parisian version in 1327, which were chosen for the first printed edition of 1483; a second followed in 1492. The instructions were first written in Castilian.

Georg Purbach used the tables for his Theoricae novae planetarum, and Copernicus bought a copy while at the University of Cracow. One use of such tables was to calculate ephemerides, which astrologers used to cast horoscopes. The Prutenic Tables of Erasmus Reinhold, published in 1551, applied the Copernican model but were not widely adopted outside German speaking countries, and ephemerides based on the Alfonsine tables continued to appear until Kepler's Rudolphine Tables of 1627.
alfonso-ii-deste: Alfonso was born on 22 November 1533, the elder son of Ercole II d'Este and Renée de France, daughter of Louis XII of France and Anne of Brittany. As a young man he fought in the service of Henry II of France against the Habsburgs. Soon after he succeeded his father in 1559, Pope Pius IV forced him to send his mother back to France because of her increasingly Calvinist beliefs.

The 1570 Ferrara earthquake struck during his reign, and Alfonso restored the Castello Estense, which it had damaged. In 1583 he allied with Emperor Rudolf II in the war against the Turks in Hungary. He married three times: in 1558 Lucrezia di Cosimo de' Medici, daughter of Cosimo I de' Medici, who died two years later at sixteen, probably of pulmonary tuberculosis, though poisoning by the duke has been suspected; in 1565 Barbara of Austria, daughter of Emperor Ferdinand I, who died of tuberculosis in 1572; and in 1579 Margherita Gonzaga, daughter of William I, Duke of Mantua, and a niece of Barbara.

Alfonso's court was a centre of secular music for Italy and for Europe at large. Luzzasco Luzzaschi was his court organist, and the concerto delle donne, a group of women singers who performed for the duke and his court, was copied all over Italy. Fluent in Italian, Latin and French, he was patron of Torquato Tasso, Giovanni Battista Guarini and the philosopher Cesare Cremonini, as the princes of his house had long favoured the arts and sciences. His spending, however, damaged the public treasury.

Alfonso died on 27 October 1597 with no known children, and the legitimate line of the House of Este ended with him. Emperor Rudolf II recognised his cousin Cesare d'Este, of a cadet branch, as heir, and Cesare went on ruling the imperial duchies, but the popes did not accept the succession. Pope Clement VIII therefore took Ferrara, on grounds of doubtful legitimacy, and handed its government to a cardinal legate; Cesare and his family had to leave the city. Robert Browning based the duke of his poem My Last Duchess on Alfonso, and he is a central character in Maggie O'Farrell's novel The Marriage Portrait.
alfonso-ii-of-aragon: Alfonso was born at Huesca and was known from birth as both Alfonso and Ramon. He took the name Alfonso on the united throne of Aragon and Barcelona in deference to the Aragonese, to honour Alfonso the Battler. For most of his reign he was allied with King Alfonso VIII of Castile, against Navarre and against the Moorish taifas of the south, although the Crown of Aragon also owed Castile a formal bond of vassalage. In 1171 he reached Teruel, an important stronghold on the road to Valencia, and captured Caspe in the same year.

The Treaty of Sangüesa of 1168 with Sancho VI of Navarre divided the territory of the Taifa of Murcia between them. The Treaty of Cazorla of 1179 with Castile marked out zones of conquest in the south along the watershed of the rivers Júcar and Segura and secured the south of Valencia, including Denia, for Aragon. On 18 January 1174 he married Sancha of Castile at Zaragoza.

Under Alfonso, Catalan-Aragonese influence north of the Pyrenees reached its height. His realms took in Provence, held from 1166 or just before, the county of Cerdanya in 1168 and Roussillon, inherited in 1172. Béarn and Bigorre paid homage to him in 1187. In 1186 he supported his cousin Agalbursa in placing her grandson Hugh on the throne of Arborea in Sardinia. His involvement in Languedoc, which would later cost the life of his successor Peter II of Aragon, strengthened Aragonese trade and encouraged migration from the north to the newly reconquered lands.

Alfonso gave the first land grant to Cistercian monks on the banks of the Ebro in Aragon, and the Monasterio de Piedra was founded in 1194 with thirteen monks from Poblet Monastery. He also patronised the Carthusians and founded the first chapterhouse of Scala Dei in 1196. He was a noted poet and a close friend of King Richard the Lionheart. A tensó attributed to him and Giraut de Bornelh debates whether a lady is dishonoured by taking a lover richer than herself, and many troubadours mention him. He died at Perpignan in 1196, and his son Peter II succeeded him.
alfonso-ii-of-asturias: Alfonso was born in Oviedo around 759 or 760, the son of King Fruela I and Munia, a Basque woman whom Fruela had captured on a campaign and brought back to Asturias. After his father's death he was placed under the guardianship of his aunt Adosinda, though one tradition has him sent to the monastery of San Xulián de Samos.

He was governor of the palace under Adosinda's husband Silo. When Silo died, Adosinda's allies elected Alfonso king, but the magnates raised his uncle Mauregatus to the throne, and Alfonso fled to Álava, where his maternal relatives sheltered him. Mauregatus was followed by Alfonso's cousin Bermudo I, who abdicated after defeat at the Battle of the Burbia River.

Alfonso was elected king on 14 September 791. He moved the capital from Pravia, where Silo had placed it, to Oviedo, the city his father had founded and where he was born, and there built churches and a palace, among them San Tirso, where he is buried, and San Julián de los Prados. Hisham I began campaigns on the eastern Pyrenees and in the north-west, and in 794 a raid led by Abd al-Karim dealt a major blow to Alfonso on the eastern edge of his kingdom, in Cantabria and Castile, after which the raiders pillaged deeper into Asturias.

Alfonso sent embassies to Charlemagne at Toulouse and Aix-la-Chapelle in 796, 797 and 798. The Royal Frankish Annals acknowledge him as a king and Asturias as a kingdom for the first time. Troops from Asturias captured and sacked Lisbon in 798.

Tradition says that in 814 the body of Saint James was found at Compostela and that Alfonso was the first pilgrim to the shrine at Libredón. In 825 he defeated Saracen forces at Narón, near Ferrol, and at Anceo, and these victories began the resettlement of parts of Galicia, León and Castile, confirmed by charters. He died in 842 after a reign of 51 years, and the Crónica Sebastianense praises his government as chaste, sober, immaculate, pious and glorious.

After his death Nepotian tried to take the crown in place of Ramiro I. Later poets invented a story of a secret marriage between Alfonso's sister Ximena and Sancho, count of Saldaña, and of the exploits of their son Bernardo del Carpio.
alfonso-iii-of-aragon: Alfonso III was born on 4 November 1265, the son of King Peter III of Aragon and Constance, daughter and heiress of King Manfred of Sicily. He was called the Liberal and also the Free, or the Frank. He ruled as king of Aragon and Valencia and, as Alfons II, count of Barcelona from 1285 until his death.

Soon after taking the throne, Alfonso set out to bring the Balearic Islands back into the Crown of Aragon. They had been lost through the division of the realm by his grandfather, James I of Aragon. In 1285 he declared war on his uncle, James II of Majorca, and conquered Majorca that year and Ibiza in 1286. On 17 January 1287 he conquered Menorca, until then an autonomous Muslim state within the Kingdom of Majorca. The anniversary of that day is now Menorca's national holiday.

In Sicily he at first supported the claims of his brother James II. Shortly before his death he withdrew that support and tried to make peace with the Papal States and with France. In 1289 he founded the Order of the Collar of Paternò, in support of the defence of Menorca; it later became a dynastic order of the royal house of Aragon.

His reign was marked by a constitutional struggle with the Aragonese nobles. It ended in the articles of the Union of Aragon, sometimes called the Magna Carta of Aragon, which passed several key royal powers to the lesser nobles. His inability to resist their demands left a heritage of disunity, and the nobility came to see little reason to respect the throne. The kingdom was brought close to anarchy.

A marriage had been arranged for Alfonso with Eleanor, daughter of King Edward I of England, but he died on 18 June 1291, aged 25, before meeting his bride. He was buried in the Franciscan convent in Barcelona, and since 1852 his remains have lain in Barcelona Cathedral. In the Divine Comedy, Dante Alighieri places Alfonso's spirit outside the gates of Purgatory with the other monarchs he blamed for the chaotic political state of Europe in the 13th century.
alfonso-iii-of-asturias: Alfonso, the son and successor of Ordoño I, came to the throne in 866. In his first year he had to deal with a usurper, Count Fruela of Galicia, and was forced to flee to Castile, but Fruela was assassinated a few months later and Alfonso returned to Oviedo. He put down a Basque rebellion in 867 and, much later, a Galician one. Around 869 he allied with the Kingdom of Pamplona, sealing the link by marrying Jimena and by marrying his sister Leodegundia to a prince of Pamplona. His reign was notable for success in consolidating the kingdom while the Umayyad princes of Córdoba were weak.

His father had begun resettling the border lands, and Alfonso continued the work. His forces moved the south-western frontier to the Mondego river, and Christian troops resettled Porto and Coimbra and other cities such as Braga, Viseo and Lamego with men taken from Galicia. Fighting with the Umayyad prince al-Mundir was almost constant between 875 and 883. Alfonso defeated one army at the battle of Polvoraria and then intercepted al-Mundir in the valley of Valdemora. Emir Mohammad I of Córdoba had to pay a ransom and sign a three-year truce, the first time Córdoba had asked for peace.

In 884 Alfonso and Mohammad I made peace, since both faced serious internal problems. Alfonso's brothers Fruela, Odoario and Bermudo rose against him from Astorga but were quickly defeated and executed. In 901 the rebel Ibn al-Qitt, proclaimed Mahdi, attacked Zamora and was defeated and killed there. In 909 Alfonso moved the seat of his government to Oviedo. According to the Chronicle of Sampiro, his sons conspired against him; he had García imprisoned, but García was freed and later agreed to join a campaign against the Moors. Alfonso died at Zamora in 910 of natural causes, after reigning for 44 years.

After his death the kingdom was divided: García received León, Ordoño Galicia, and Fruela Asturias with Oviedo as capital. The lands were reunited in turn, but Fruela's death the next year began internal struggles that left the succession unstable for over a century. Alfonso ordered three chronicles that presented the kingdom of Asturias as the heir of the Visigothic kingdom. He was a patron of the arts, built the church of Santo Adriano and held the second Oviedo Council in 893. Around 908 he ordered the Cross of Victory, made by goldsmiths from the Frankish kingdom for the Cathedral of San Salvador; it appears in the flag of Asturias.
alfonso-iv-of-aragon: Alfonso was born in Naples on 2 November 1299, the second son of James II and Blanche of Anjou. In 1314, aged fourteen, he married Teresa d'Entença, heiress of Urgell and the same age as him, in the Cathedral of Lleida. Teresa's granduncle Ermengol X of Urgell had died childless after agreeing to make Alfonso his heir, on condition that he marry Teresa. At the wedding the young bridegroom is reputed to have spent so freely that the local councils limited what he could spend. They had seven children. In December 1319 Alfonso became heir after his older brother James renounced his rights to become a monk, and during his father's reign he was procurator-general of the Crown.

Teresa died in childbirth on 20 October 1327, and James II died on 2 November 1327, whereupon Alfonso became king. He was also Count of Barcelona, as Alfons III. In 1329 he began a long war with the Republic of Genoa over the city of Sassari, which had surrendered to him in 1323 but rebelled three more times and was contested by Genoa. His reign saw the incorporation of the County of Urgell, the Duchy of Athens and the Duchy of Neopatria into the Crown of Aragon.

In February 1329 he married Eleanor of Castile, sister of Alfonso XI of Castile, who had earlier been briefly married to his brother James. She bore Ferdinand by December that year and John five years later. Eleanor sought to advance her sons over his stepson Peter, the heir-apparent, and Alfonso granted Ferdinand the Marquisate of Tortosa and many cities, and gave John several lordships. When he also granted Ferdinand cities in the Kingdom of Valencia, local subjects protested and he revoked the grants. The issue created resentment and divided the nobility into two camps.

Alfonso died on 24 January 1336, aged only 36, and was succeeded by Peter IV, his 16-year-old son by his first marriage. His grants to his second family diminished the territorial patrimony of the Crown. Of his sons by Eleanor, Ferdinand was later killed by order of his half-brother Peter IV, and John was killed by order of his cousin Pedro of Castile.
alfonso-ix-of-leon: Alfonso was born in Zamora, the only son of King Ferdinand II of León and Urraca of Portugal. His father was the younger son of Alfonso VII of León and Castile, who divided his kingdoms between his sons, setting the stage for conflict in the family until Alfonso IX's son Ferdinand III reunited them. Alfonso had great difficulty obtaining the throne his birth entitled him to. In July 1188 his cousin Alfonso VIII of Castile required him to recognise the elder as overlord in exchange for recognising his authority in León.

The difficult economic situation at the start of his reign led Alfonso to raise taxes on the poorer classes, which caused protests and a few town revolts. In response he summoned the Cortes of León in the cloisters of the Basilica of San Isidoro, an assembly of nobles, clergy and city representatives, which then demanded compensatory spending and closer oversight of royal expenditure. Many historians, including John Keane, regard it as instrumental in forming democratic parliaments in Europe. The session of 1188 predates the first session of the Parliament of England. He also founded the University of Salamanca in 1218.

His marriages brought conflict with the papacy. In 1191 he married his first cousin Theresa of Portugal, and the papal legate Cardinal Gregory declared the marriage null for consanguinity. After Alfonso VIII was defeated at the Battle of Alarcos, Alfonso IX invaded Castile with the aid of Muslim troops and was excommunicated by Pope Celestine III.

In 1197 he married Berengaria of Castile to cement peace, and the kingdom was placed under interdict. Innocent III declared that marriage invalid in 1198, though they stayed together until 1204, and treaties of 1205, 1207 and 1209 forced Alfonso to concede territory. The treaty of 1207 is the first existing public document in the Castilian dialect. He captured Mérida and Badajoz in 1230, which allowed the later conquest of Seville under his son.

Alfonso died on 24 September 1230. His son Ferdinand III, already king of Castile, inherited León and Galicia as well, thanks to the negotiations of his mother Berengaria, who persuaded her stepdaughters to renounce their claim. Hearing the news, Ferdinand abandoned a campaign against Jaén and travelled to León to be crowned. The union of the two kingdoms went on to dominate the Iberian Peninsula.

Alfonso had eight children from his two marriages, both of which were annulled for consanguinity, and fathered many more with women of lower rank, among them Teresa Gil de Soverosa, with whom he had a relationship from 1218 until his death.
alfonso-v-of-leon: Alfonso, called the Noble, was born around 994 and succeeded his father, Bermudo II, in 999. As a child he was raised in Galicia by Count Menendo González, and his mother, Elvira García, and the count acted as his co-regents. When the count died in 1008, Alfonso ruled on his own. Like other kings of León he used the title emperor, Imperator totius Hispaniae, to assert his standing among the Christian rulers of Spain.

Alfonso began the work of reorganising the Christian kingdom of the north-west of the Iberian Peninsula after a disastrous period of civil war and Arab inroads. Enough is known of him to justify the belief that he had some of the qualities of a soldier and a statesman. His name and that of his wife are associated with the grant of the first franchises of León in 1017.

He married Elvira Menéndez, daughter of his tutor Menendo González, in 1013. They had two children: Sancha, who married Ferdinand I of León and Castile, and Bermudo III of León. After Elvira died on 2 December 1022, Alfonso married Urraca Garcés, sister of King Sancho III of Pamplona. Bishop Oliba of Vic called the match incestuous in a letter of 11 May 1023, because of the kinship between the two, yet the wedding took place before 13 November 1023, when the couple first appear together in a charter in the Cathedral of León. They had one daughter, Jimena.

On 7 August 1028 Alfonso was killed by an arrow while besieging the Muslim-occupied town of Viseu. He was buried beside his first wife, Elvira, as he had wished, at the Church of Saint John the Baptist and San Pelayo, which later took the name of the Basilica of San Isidoro. His tomb's epitaph records that he repopulated León, gave good laws, built the church and had battles with Muslim forces.
alfonso-vi-of-castile: Alfonso was the second son of Ferdinand I, King of León and Count of Castile, and Queen Sancha, and so would not normally have inherited the throne. At the end of 1063, probably on 22 December, Ferdinand summoned a Curia Regia at León and announced how his lands would be divided. Alfonso received the Kingdom of León, with Asturias, Astorga, El Bierzo and Zamora, together with the tribute payments (parias) of the taifa of Toledo. His elder brother Sancho received the new Kingdom of Castile and the parias of Zaragoza, and his younger brother García received Galicia, raised to a kingdom, with the parias of Badajoz and Seville.

Alfonso was crowned at León in January 1066. After the death of their mother on 7 November 1067, he faced the ambitions of Sancho II, who considered himself the sole rightful heir, and seven years of war among the three brothers followed. At Llantada the brothers agreed to a trial by ordeal in which the winner would take the loser's kingdom; Sancho won, but Alfonso did not comply. Later the two joined forces to divide García's Galicia between themselves. Alfonso took the title king of Galicia in 1071 and of Castile in 1072.

The conquest of Toledo in 1085 led him to style himself most victorious king of Toledo, of Spain and of Galicia. It also provoked an Almoravid invasion that he spent the rest of his reign resisting. His armies suffered decisive defeats at Sagrajas in 1086, Consuegra in 1097 and Uclés in 1108. At Uclés his only son and heir, Sancho Alfónsez, the child of his concubine Zaida, was killed. Valencia was abandoned, but Toledo remained part of the expanded realm.

Alfonso had five wives and two concubines according to Bishop Pelagius of Oviedo. His daughter Urraca, by Constance of Burgundy, succeeded him. His illegitimate daughter Teresa married Count Henry of Portugal, and their son Afonso Henriques became the first king of Portugal. In May 1107 Alfonso had imposed recognition of Sancho Alfónsez as heir, and after Sancho's death the succession passed to Urraca.

Alfonso died in Toledo on 1 July 1109, where he had come to try to defend the city from an imminent Almoravid attack. He was buried at the Royal Monastery of San Benito in Sahagún. He encouraged the Cluniac reforms in the monasteries of Galicia, León and Castile, made the first grant of a Leonese monastery to Cluny in 1073, and replaced the Mozarabic rite with the Roman one.
alfonso-vii-of-leon-and-castile: Alfonso VII was born on 1 March 1105 and raised in Galicia as Alfonso Raimúndez, the son of Urraca of León and Raymond of Burgundy, and the first king from the House of Burgundy. In 1111 Diego Gelmírez, Bishop of Compostela, and Pedro Froilaz, count of Traba, crowned him King of Galicia in the cathedral of Santiago de Compostela, although he was a child and his mother wished to keep sole rule of the united throne. By 1119 he had inherited the former Muslim Kingdom of Toledo, where its Cluniac archbishop, Bernard of Sédirac, became his patron.

After Urraca died, Alfonso was crowned in León on 10 March 1126 and began recovering Castile, then dominated by Alfonso the Battler of Aragón and Navarre. By the Peace of Támara of 1127 the Battler recognised him. When the Battler died childless in 1134, Alfonso claimed Aragón, but the nobles chose his brother Ramiro II, and García Ramírez was elected in Navarre. Alfonso retook La Rioja and defeated the joint army of Navarre and Aragón in several skirmishes, yet could not hold the two kingdoms.

On 26 May 1135 he was crowned Emperor of Spain in the Cathedral of León, probably to assert authority over the whole peninsula and leadership of the Reconquista. The title had long been attached to the ruler of León but had been little more than rhetoric. His imperial aims were not realised: Portugal became de facto independent in 1128 and was recognised as independent by the Treaty of Zamora in 1143, and in 1137 Petronila of Aragon was betrothed to Ramon Berenguer IV, combining Aragón and Catalonia in the Crown of Aragon.

From 1138 Alfonso led campaigns against the Almoravids, besieging Coria that year and taking it in 1142, and capturing the fortress of Oreja after a seven-month siege. In 1144 he advanced as far as Córdoba. When the Almohads invaded two years later, he refortified his southern frontier. The Chronica Adefonsi Imperatoris records his campaigns. In October 1147 a mixed army of Catalans and Franks, with a Genoese and Pisan fleet, occupied Almería, Castile's first Mediterranean port; a third went to Genoa.

In 1151 the Treaty of Tudilén with Ramon Berenguer IV fixed the zones of conquest in Andalusia. Alfonso died on 21 August 1157 at Las Fresnedas, north of the Sierra Morena, while returning from an expedition against the Almohads. By dividing his realm between his sons, he ensured that Christian Iberia would not meet the Almohad threat with a united front. He also introduced the Cistercians to Iberia by founding a monastery at Fitero, and was a patron of poets, probably including the troubadour Marcabru.
alfonso-viii: Alfonso was born at Soria on 11 November 1155, the son of Sancho III of Castile and Blanche, and was named after his grandfather Alfonso VII of León and Castile, who had divided his kingdoms between his sons. His father died in 1158, and the two-year-old king was regarded as nominal by nobles to whom a minority was convenient. The houses of Lara and Castro both claimed the regency, as did his uncle Ferdinand II of León. The regency fell to Manrique Pérez de Lara, and at barely fifteen Alfonso began restoring order, recovering Toledo by surprise from the Laras.

His uncle Sancho VI of Navarre had seized border lands, including much of La Rioja. In 1170 Alfonso sent an embassy to Bordeaux to seek the hand of Eleanor, daughter of Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine, which gave him a powerful ally. In 1188 the Treaty of Seligenstadt made his eldest child Berengaria heiress of Castile after any sons, and at Carrión de los Condes that year Alfonso knighted Alfonso IX of León, who accepted the Castilian king as overlord. Berengaria's marriage to Alfonso IX in 1197 brought a lasting peace, though the pope annulled it.

He took Cuenca on 21 September 1177. The Treaty of Cazola of 1179 defined the zones of expansion of the Christian kingdoms against the Almohads. In 1195 he was roundly defeated at Alarcos by the caliph Abu Yusuf Yaqub al-Mansur, and for seventeen years the frontier stood in the hill country outside Toledo. In 1212, through the mediation of Pope Innocent III, a crusade was called. Aragonese under Peter II, Navarrese under Sancho VII and Franks joined the Castilians. On 16 July they routed the caliph Muhammad al-Nasir at Las Navas de Tolosa.

Alfonso died on 5 October 1214 and was succeeded by his surviving son, Henry I. He founded a studium generale at Palencia, the first Spanish university, though it did not survive him, and with Eleanor he was the first to make the Alcázar of Segovia a residence. Through his daughters Berengaria and Blanche he was the grandfather of two monarchs who became saints.
alfonso-x-of-castile: Alfonso was born on 23 November 1221 in Toledo, the eldest son of Ferdinand III and Elizabeth (Beatrice) of Swabia. His mother was a cousin of Emperor Frederick II, to whom he is often compared. For his first nine years he was heir only to Castile; then his father united the kingdoms of Castile and León. He began as a soldier under his father at sixteen, and in the 1240s he helped conquer Muslim strongholds in Al-Andalus, among them Murcia, Alicante and Cádiz. In 1249 he married Violante, daughter of King James I of Aragon.

Alfonso succeeded his father in 1252. He invaded Portugal in 1253 and took the Algarve, which he returned in 1263. In 1254 he allied with Henry III of England and renounced Castile's claim to Gascony when his half-sister Eleanor married Henry's son Edward. In 1256 his descent from the Hohenstaufen gave him a claim to the German crown, and a dissident faction elected him king of Germany in 1257. He never went to Germany, while his rival Richard of Cornwall was crowned at Aachen. To raise money he debased the coinage, then set an arbitrary tariff to hold prices down, which ruined what trade there was. His nobles rebelled in 1272, and in 1275 the Pope won his oral renunciation of the imperial claim.

His eldest son Ferdinand died in 1275 at the Battle of Écija, leaving two infant sons. Alfonso's second son Sancho claimed to be heir, with the nobles' support, and a civil war led Alfonso in 1282 to accept Sancho. Only Seville, Murcia and Badajoz stayed loyal to the king. He died at Seville in 1284, leaving a will that tried to exclude Sancho and a legacy of civil war. In 1273 he created the Mesta, an association of sheep owners, which later grew powerful.

Alfonso's court employed Jewish, Christian and Muslim scholars who translated works from Arabic and Hebrew into Latin and Castilian under his supervision, and Castilian came to replace Latin in the royal chancery. Their main work was in astronomy and astrology, including the Alfonsine tables based on the calculations of al-Zarqali. He sponsored the Crónica general, finished in 1264, and the General Estoria, a world history left incomplete at the birth of Christ. He began the Siete Partidas, one of the most comprehensive law codes of medieval Europe, though it was promulgated only by his great-grandson. His Cantigas de Santa Maria, in Galician–Portuguese, comprise 420 poems with musical notation, mostly on miracles attributed to the Virgin Mary.
alfonso-xi-of-castile: Alfonso XI was born in Salamanca, the son of King Ferdinand IV of Castile and Constance of Portugal. His father died when he was one year old, and his grandmother María de Molina, his mother, his great-uncle Infante John and his uncle Infante Peter took up the regency. His mother died on 18 November 1313, and the two infantes were killed during a campaign against Granada in 1319 at the Disaster of the Vega. María de Molina then remained sole regent until her death on 1 July 1321.

He inherited the throne at a time of instability, with population decline, a shrinking royal treasury and increasingly ambitious regents. After 1319 Philip, Juan Manuel and Juan the One-eyed split the kingdom among themselves according to their aspirations for the regency, while Moors and rebellious nobles looted it.

His effective reign began in August 1325, when he was declared to have reached the age of majority in the Cortes of Valladolid. He crowned himself in 1332 after a ritual that took him to Santiago de Compostela and the monastery of Las Huelgas in Burgos. He worked to strengthen royal power by dividing his enemies and executing possible opponents. In 1326 he had Juan the One-eyed assassinated at Toro, with two of his knights, after luring him with promises of reconciliation.

He extended his kingdom to the Strait of Gibraltar through the victory at Río Salado over the Marinid dynasty in 1340 and the conquest of Algeciras in 1344, then turned against the king of Granada. Municipal government changed during his reign, with regimientos replacing the open councils, and he encouraged cartas pueblas to strengthen the population of the borderlands. He was called the Avenger and the Implacable for the ferocity with which he put down the nobles' disorders, and He of Río Salado for his victory. He could be bloody and killed for reasons of state without any trial. He neglected his wife Maria of Portugal and openly kept Eleanor of Guzman, who bore him ten children.

Stricken with plague during the siege of Gibraltar in 1349–1350, Alfonso died in the night of 25–26 March 1350 and became one of the most prominent victims of the Black Death. The Castilian forces withdrew, and some of the defenders came out to watch. His rival Yusuf I of Granada ordered his army and border commanders not to attack the procession carrying the king's body to Seville. After his death his widow Maria had Eleanor of Guzman arrested and later killed. Peter of Castile, his son by Maria, succeeded him, and Henry II of Castile, his son by Eleanor, became king in 1369.
alfonso-xii: Alfonso was born in Madrid on 28 November 1857, the eldest son of Queen Isabella II. His official father, her husband Francisco de Asís, was generally viewed as effeminate, impotent or homosexual, which led writers to question Alfonso's paternity. When the Revolution of 1868 forced Isabella to leave Spain, he went with her to Paris and was sent to study at the Theresianum in Vienna. On 25 June 1870 his mother abdicated in his favour in Paris.

The Cortes chose Prince Amadeo of Savoy as king in November 1870, but he abdicated in early 1873 after attacks on his life and the outbreak of the Third Carlist War. The First Spanish Republic followed, facing war in Cuba, uprisings in Spanish Morocco and the Carlist rising. Antonio Cánovas del Castillo led a group favouring a Bourbon Restoration and took charge of Alfonso's education, sending him to the Royal Military College, Sandhurst.

On 1 December 1874 Alfonso issued the Sandhurst Manifesto, which set out the ideological basis of the Restoration and proclaimed him the sole representative of the Spanish monarchy. At the end of 1874 Brigadier Martínez Campos led battalions to Sagunto, rallied the troops sent against him and entered Valencia in the king's name. The republic's president resigned and power passed to Cánovas. Alfonso was proclaimed king on 29 December 1874. In 1876 a campaign against the Carlists, in which he took part, ended with the defeat of Don Carlos.

Cánovas was the real architect of the Restoration, which proved a civilian regime lasting until Primo de Rivera's coup in 1923. The Constitution of 1876 and the Pact of El Pardo of 1885 endorsed turnismo, the alternation of conservative and liberal prime ministers. In 1881 Alfonso refused to sanction a law fixing ministers' terms at 18 months, and when Cánovas resigned he called the Liberal leader Práxedes Mateo Sagasta to form a government.

Alfonso died on 25 November 1885, aged 27, at the Royal Palace of El Pardo near Madrid. He had tuberculosis, but the immediate cause of death was a recurrence of dysentery. His widow, pregnant, became regent, and their son Alfonso XIII was born in 1886. Alfonso had won popular affection by visiting districts struck by cholera and by the Andalusian earthquake of 1884. His reign is credited with ending the political instability of the previous decades, and a monument to him by José Grases Riera was completed in the Parque del Buen Retiro in Madrid in 1922.
alfonso-xiii: Alfonso XIII was born at the Royal Palace of Madrid on 17 May 1886, the posthumous son of Alfonso XII, who had died in November 1885, and so he became king at birth. His mother, Maria Christina of Austria, served as regent until his sixteenth birthday in 1902. During the regency, in 1898, Spain lost Cuba, Puerto Rico, Guam and the Philippines to the United States in the Spanish–American War.

He received largely a military education, which gave him a Spanish nationalism strengthened by a military vocation, and he often presented himself as a soldier-king. He took his oath to the constitution before the Cortes on 17 May 1902. In 1906 he married Princess Victoria Eugenie of Battenberg, and their wedding was marred by an attempt on the king's life, from which he emerged unharmed.

Like other European monarchs of his time Alfonso played a political role, which involved a controversial use of his constitutional powers. He helped to keep Spain neutral in the First World War, using his links with other royal families, and was nominated for the Nobel Peace Prize in 1917 for his work with the European War Office.

Several factors weakened his constitutional legitimacy: the breakdown of the turno system, the crisis of the Restoration system in the 1910s, a trio of crises in 1917, and the violence in Morocco. The dictatorship of Miguel Primo de Rivera was installed in 1923 through a military coup, and the king acquiesced.

When the dictatorship failed, Alfonso withdrew his support, Primo de Rivera resigned in 1930, and the king tried to return to the position before 1923, but he had lost most of his political capital. On 12 April 1931 a republican coalition won a sweeping majority in the major cities in the municipal elections, which were seen as a plebiscite on the monarchy. The Civil Guard's José Sanjurjo reportedly told ministers that the armed forces could not be relied on to sustain the monarchy. Alfonso left Spain, and the Second Spanish Republic was peacefully proclaimed on 14 April 1931.

In November 1931 the Constituent Cortes debated his responsibility as king, citing interference in state institutions, his use of the army, and his part in the operation that ended in the disaster at Annual. It passed an act declaring him guilty of high treason.

On 15 January 1941 Alfonso renounced his rights to the Spanish throne in favour of his son Juan, and he died in Rome on 28 February 1941 of angina pectoris. His remains were moved to El Escorial in January 1980. He promoted tourism, including state-run lodges called Paradores, and patronised football clubs that took the title Real, the first being Deportivo de La Coruña in 1907.
alfred-deakin: Alfred Deakin was born on 3 August 1856 in Fitzroy, Melbourne, the younger of two children of William and Sarah Deakin, who were of English and Welsh descent. They had emigrated from Britain in 1850 during an economic depression and moved from Adelaide to Melbourne because of the Victorian gold rush. His father worked in the carrying and coaching trade and later for Cobb and Co, earning enough to keep the family comfortably middle class. Deakin worked as a barrister and journalist and in February 1879, aged 23, stood for West Bourke in the Victorian Legislative Assembly, winning in a general election in July 1880 after a first result was voided.

Deakin held Victorian ministerial office from 1883 and in the 1890s became a leading figure in the federation of the Australian colonies. He was a delegate to the federal conventions, served on the committees that drafted the constitution, campaigned at the referendums and lobbied the British government for its adoption. After Federation in 1901 he was the first attorney-general under his friend Edmund Barton, and he became prime minister on 24 September 1903 when Barton left for the High Court.

He served three terms, 1903 to 1904, 1905 to 1908 and 1909 to 1910, leading a Liberal Protectionist party that held the middle ground between Free Traders and the Australian Labor Party. His second term, the longest, saw laws such as the Copyright Act 1905 and the Quarantine Act 1908 and the founding of the Commonwealth Bureau of Census and Statistics and Bureau of Meteorology. In 1909 he joined the Free Traders and Joseph Cook in the Fusion, forming Australia's first majority government; some, including Sir William Lyne, called it a betrayal. Labor won both houses in 1910, and Deakin led the opposition, campaigning against constitutional amendments in 1911, until he retired in 1913.

In 1914 he chaired a royal commission on wartime food supply and in 1915 led the Australian delegation to the Panama-Pacific International Exposition in San Francisco. A degenerative neurological condition led to his death on 7 October 1919, aged 63. Contemporaries called him Affable Alfred. He is regarded as the principal architect of the Australian settlement, which combined the White Australia policy, compulsory arbitration, protectionism, state paternalism and support for the British Empire. He refused a knighthood, appointment to the Privy Council and most honorary degrees.
alfred-dreyfus: Alfred Dreyfus was born in Mulhouse, Alsace, on 9 October 1859, the youngest of nine children of Raphaël and Jeannette Dreyfus. His family belonged to a long established Alsatian Jewish family, and his father became a prosperous industrialist who started a cotton mill. After the Franco-Prussian War of 1870 and the German annexation of Alsace-Lorraine, the family moved to Basel and later to Paris. Seeing his family uprooted by the war prompted him to choose a military career.

He entered the École Polytechnique in October 1877 and was commissioned a sub-lieutenant in 1880. He became a captain in 1889, married Lucie Eugénie Hadamard in 1891, and graduated ninth in his class from the École Supérieure de Guerre, afterwards joining the General Staff as its only Jewish officer.

A torn-up note, the bordereau, was found in a wastebasket at the German Embassy and passed to French intelligence. It showed that information on artillery was reaching the German military attaché Maximilian von Schwartzkoppen. Suspicion fell on Dreyfus, who was arrested for treason on 15 October 1894. A closed court martial convicted him on 22 December 1894 and sentenced him to life imprisonment on Devil's Island. On 5 January 1895 he was formally degraded in the courtyard of the École Militaire, crying out: I swear that I am innocent.

In August 1896 Lieutenant Colonel Georges Picquart found evidence that the traitor was Major Ferdinand Walsin Esterhazy, and was transferred to Tunisia. Esterhazy was acquitted by a secret court martial. Émile Zola's J'Accuse...! of 1898 brought new momentum to the campaign. A second trial in 1899 again found Dreyfus guilty, but President Émile Loubet pardoned him that year. A military commission exonerated him on 12 July 1906, and he was reinstated as a major.

Dreyfus returned as a reserve artillery major when the First World War began, was promoted to lieutenant colonel, and served mostly behind the lines, though in 1917 he was at Verdun and the Chemin des Dames. He died in Paris on 12 July 1935, aged 75, and was buried in the Montparnasse Cemetery. A statue of Dreyfus holding his broken sword stands on Boulevard Raspail, and his family gave over three thousand documents to the Museum of Jewish Art and History in Paris.
alfred-i-prince-of-windisch-gratz: Alfred Candidus Ferdinand, Prince of Windischgrätz, was born on 11 May 1787 in Brussels, then the capital of the Austrian Netherlands. He belonged to an old Austro-Bohemian house that came originally from Styria and had received rights of nobility from the Bohemian Crown in 1574. His parents were Count Joseph Nicholas of Windischgrätz and his second wife, Duchess Maria Leopoldine Franziska of Arenberg. With the help of his mother's rich dowry, the family settled at Tachau (Tachov), a lordship his father had bought in 1781.

He entered the Habsburg imperial army in 1804 and took part in every war against Napoleon. He fought with distinction at the Battle of Leipzig and in the campaign of 1814, and in 1833 he was named Field Marshal-Lieutenant. In 1840 he became military commander of the city of Prague.

In 1848 he was briefly given control of the army around Vienna during the first uprisings and favoured putting down the citizens by force. Government ministers who preferred compromise forced him to retire to Prague, which made him unpopular with the Austrian public. Back in Prague he increased the garrison and fortified strategic positions, which angered the population.

On 7 June a crowd petitioned for his dismissal, and on 10 June students asked him to withdraw the troops and supply the citizens with muskets and cartridges. He refused. By 12 June fights between soldiers and armed citizens behind barricades had spread across the city. That evening his wife, Princess Eleonore of Schwarzenberg, was shot dead in her house by a shot from the windows of a hotel opposite. A crowd then seized him and tried to hang him, but his soldiers saved him, and he declared martial law throughout Bohemia.

Placed in chief command against the Hungarian revolutionaries under Lajos Kossuth, Windischgrätz reoccupied Buda and Pest in January 1849. His slowness in pursuit allowed the enemy to rally in superior numbers and prevented an effective concentration of the Austrian forces. After his defeat by Artúr Görgei at the Battle of Isaszeg he was relieved of command in April 1849, and he rarely appeared in public life again. He had married Eleonore on 15 June 1817, and they had seven children. He is remembered for a remark about constitutionalists: they did not want to hear of the Grace of God, and would hear the grace of the cannon. He died on 21 March 1862.
alfred-milner: Alfred Milner was born on 23 March 1854 at Giessen in the Grand Duchy of Hesse, the son of a London physician. He was educated at Tübingen, at King's College School and, from 1872, at Balliol College, Oxford, where he studied under Benjamin Jowett and graduated with a first in classics in 1877. He was called to the bar in 1881 but became a journalist, and in 1885 he lost an election as a Liberal candidate. In 1886 he supported the breakaway Liberal Unionist Party in opposing Irish Home Rule, became private secretary to George Goschen, and from 1889 to 1892 served as under-secretary of finance in Egypt.

In April 1897 Joseph Chamberlain appointed Milner Governor of the Cape Colony and High Commissioner for Southern Africa, after the Jameson Raid. The Transvaal had been founded in 1852 by Boer farmers who left the Cape, and after the discovery of gold in 1884 thousands of newcomers, whom the Boers called Uitlanders, were refused the vote. After Kruger's landslide in the February 1898 election, Milner concluded that Pretoria would never redress their grievances on its own, and in a speech at Graaff Reinet on 3 March 1898 he set out his determination to secure equality for British subjects in the Transvaal.

When the Second Boer War ended, Milner became governor of the new Crown colonies of the Transvaal and the Orange River Colony. He imposed a tax of 10% on the annual net produce of the gold mines and turned to the return of the Boers to their farms, settlement by British colonists, education, justice, police and railways. A Labour Ordinance imported Chinese labourers for the mines. Broken in health, he left Pretoria on 2 April 1905 amid an economic crisis and widespread criticism. On 20 March 1906 the House of Commons considered a motion censuring him over the flogging of Chinese labourers; Winston Churchill's amendment condemned the flogging but declined to censure individuals.

In the First World War Milner headed the National Service League, which advocated conscription, adopted in July 1916. He joined David Lloyd George's war cabinet on 8 December 1916. During the crisis of March 1918 he coordinated the unification of Allied command under Ferdinand Foch, whom he had selected. He became Secretary of State for War, signed the Treaty of Versailles, and ended his career as Secretary of State for the Colonies.

Milner was a leading advocate of imperial unity. In an article of 1907 he proposed a permanent imperial council and preferential trade within the empire, and he later supported tariff reform and Imperial Preference. The historian Caroline Elkins writes that he firmly believed in racial hierarchy. He married Violet Cecil on 26 February 1921 and died on 13 May 1925.
alfred-nobel: Alfred Nobel was born in Stockholm on 21 October 1833, the third son of the inventor and engineer Immanuel Nobel and Andriette Nobel. The family was impoverished, and only Alfred and his three brothers survived childhood. After business failures Immanuel went bankrupt and moved to Saint Petersburg, where he grew successful as a manufacturer of machine tools and explosives. In 1842 the family joined him. Private tutors taught the boy, who excelled in chemistry and languages and became proficient in Swedish, French, Russian, English, German and Italian. His only schooling was eighteen months at the Jacobs Apologistic School in Stockholm, and he never attended university.

Nobel studied with the chemist Nikolai Zinin, and in 1850 he went to Paris, where he met Ascanio Sobrero, who had synthesized nitroglycerin three years before. Sobrero opposed its use because it was unpredictable, but Nobel set out to find a way to control it as a commercial explosive. He filed his first patent, for a gas meter, in 1857, and invented a detonator in 1863 and the blasting cap in 1865. On 3 September 1864 a shed used for preparing nitroglycerin exploded at the factory in Heleneborg, killing five people, including his younger brother Emil; he lost his licence to produce explosives and founded Nitroglycerin AB in Vinterviken, in a more isolated area.

In 1867 he patented dynamite, nitroglycerin absorbed in kieselguhr, which was safer to handle, and first demonstrated it at a quarry in Redhill, Surrey. He took the name from the Greek word for power. Gelignite followed in the 1870s and ballistite in 1887. His brothers Ludvig and Robert founded the oil company Branobel, which operated mainly in Baku, and Nobel invested in it. During his life he was issued 355 patents, and by his death his business had established more than 90 explosives and armament factories.

On 27 November 1895, at the Swedish-Norwegian Club in Paris, Nobel signed his last will, setting aside 94 per cent of his assets, 31,225,000 Swedish kronor, to establish the five Nobel Prizes, to be awarded without distinction of nationality. A well-known story that a premature French obituary, calling him the merchant of death, moved him to this has not been verified, and some historians dismiss it as a myth. He had developed angina pectoris by 1895, and he died on 10 December 1896 after a stroke, aged 63. He never married. In 1968 Sveriges Riksbank gave the Nobel Foundation funds for a prize in economics in his honour, which has been disputed as a true Nobel Prize.
alfred-the-great: Alfred was the youngest son of King Æthelwulf of Wessex and his first wife Osburh. His grandfather Ecgberht became king of Wessex in 802. Asser, writing in 893, says Alfred was born at Wantage in Berkshire, though the West Saxon genealogical lists imply a slightly earlier date, and historians differ over the exact year. His public life began in 865, at 16, when Æthelred came to the throne, and Asser gave him the title secundarius, perhaps marking him as a recognised successor.

Æthelred died in April 871, leaving two under-age sons, and Alfred became king in accordance with an agreement the brothers had made earlier that year at Swinbeorg. After his victory at Edington in 878 he made an agreement with the Vikings dividing England between Anglo-Saxon territory and the Danelaw, and oversaw the conversion of the Viking leader Guthrum to Christianity. In 886 he began styling himself King of the Anglo-Saxons after reoccupying London.

In the late 880s or early 890s he issued a law code, a domboc, combining his own laws with those of Ine of Wessex in 120 chapters. He said he kept the laws that pleased him and rejected others on the advice of his councillors. He also began a revival of learning, perhaps inspired by Charlemagne, recruiting scholars from Mercia, Wales and abroad and having Latin works the king thought most necessary for all men to know translated into English. A chronicle of the rise of his house gave the West Saxon kings a genealogy back to Adam.

Alfred married Ealhswith, daughter of a Mercian nobleman, in 868. Their children included Edward the Elder, who succeeded him, and Æthelflæd, who became lady of the Mercians. He died on 26 October 899 at 50 or 51; how he died is unknown, though Asser's description of a lifelong painful illness has led modern doctors to suggest Crohn's disease or haemorrhoids. His will is the oldest to survive of any English king. He has been called the Great since at least the 13th century, though the epithet was popularised only from the 16th, and he is the only native-born English monarch given it.
alfred-von-tirpitz: Alfred Peter Friedrich Tirpitz was born in Küstrin in the Prussian province of Brandenburg, the son of the lawyer and later judge Rudolf Tirpitz, and grew up in Frankfurt (Oder). He recorded in his memoirs that he was a mediocre pupil. He joined the Prussian Navy more by accident than design, after a friend announced that he was doing so, and became a naval cadet on 24 April 1865, at the age of 16. He spoke English fluently and sent his two daughters to Cheltenham Ladies' College. He was raised to the Prussian nobility on 12 June 1900.

In 1877 Tirpitz was chosen to visit the Whitehead Torpedo Works at Fiume and was put in charge of the German torpedo section. He then developed torpedo boats and later called these years the eleven best of his life. When the Kaiser asked how the navy should develop, he advised building battleships, and he was transferred to Berlin to work on a strategy for a high seas fleet. He concluded that the best fighting arrangement was a squadron of eight identical battleships, which brought him into conflict with the Navy State Secretary, Admiral Friedrich von Hollmann, who favoured a mixed fleet with cruisers.

As State Secretary of the Imperial Naval Office from 1897, Tirpitz presented a memorandum that named Great Britain as the principal enemy. It set a target of two squadrons of eight battleships, plus a flagship and two reserves, to be completed by 1905 at 408 million marks, and neither the Reichstag nor the navy was to change it. In the First World War the High Seas Fleet could not end Britain's command of the sea, and the Battle of Jutland was a narrow German tactical victory but a strategic failure. Tirpitz advocated unrestricted submarine warfare and was dismissed at the beginning of 1916.

In September 1917 Tirpitz co-founded the nationalist Fatherland Party and served as its chairman. It opposed a negotiated peace and had about 1,250,000 members at its peak in the summer of 1918. It had ceased operating by February 1919. After Germany's defeat he supported the German National People's Party and sat for it in the Reichstag from 1924 to 1928. He died in Ebenhausen, near Munich, on 6 March 1930. His memoirs appeared in 1919, and the German battleship Tirpitz was named after him.
alfredo-stroessner: Alfredo Stroessner Matiauda was born in Encarnación on 3 November 1912. His father, Hugo Stroessner, was an accountant from Hof in Bavaria who had emigrated to Paraguay in the late 1890s; his mother, Heriberta Matiauda, was of Guaraní and Spanish criollo descent. He joined the Paraguayan army at the age of 16 and, after attending military school in Asunción, fought in the Chaco War against Bolivia, reaching the rank of first lieutenant by its end.

In the 1947 Paraguayan Civil War he supported the Colorado Party and played an important role in its victory. Opposition parties had been banned from 1947. In 1951 he became commander-in-chief of the army.

Stroessner objected to President Federico Chaves's plan to arm the national police and removed him in a coup on 4 May 1954. The National Assembly appointed Tomás Romero Pereira president, and he called special elections. Stroessner was the Colorado Party's nominee and won on 11 July 1954 as the only candidate. He took office on 15 August 1954 and was re-elected seven times, in 1958, 1963, 1968, 1973, 1978, 1983 and 1988, nearly always by margins above 80 percent. The constitution of 1967 permitted his re-election, and changes in 1977 effectively allowed indefinite rule.

Soon after taking office he placed the country under a state of siege, which allowed indefinite detention without trial and banned public meetings. It was renewed every 90 days until 1987, apart from a brief period in 1959, and in practice it applied to Asunción only after 1970. He was a committed anti-communist who brought Paraguay into the World Anti-Communist League and justified repression as a defence of the country. He gave a free hand to the military and to the Minister of the Interior, Edgar Ynsfrán, and relied on Colorado Party militias to crush dissent.

Lieutenant General Andrés Rodríguez Pedotti, his confidant, seized power in a coup on 2 and 3 February 1989, and Stroessner went into exile in Brazil on 5 February. He died in Brasília on 16 August 2006, aged 93. Puerto Presidente Stroessner, named for him, became Ciudad del Este in 1989. In 1992 the so-called Archives of Terror were found, documents showing that his government took part in Operation Condor, the anti-communist agreement for persecuting exiles.

His government exiled 20,814 Paraguayans. Around 425 to 500 people were forcibly disappeared, and an estimated 18,000 to 20,000 were tortured or otherwise abused. His 35 years in office were the longest of any South American ruler. His supporters, known as Stronistas, still hold that his was a time of security and stability.
algarve: The Algarve lies in the southernmost area of continental Portugal and the southwesternmost area of mainland Europe, covering 4,997 km2. It borders the Alentejo region to the north and the Atlantic Ocean to the south and west, while the Guadiana River marks the border with Spain on the east. The highest point is Pico da Fóia, 902 m, in the Monchique mountains. The Ria Formosa Lagoon, a nature reserve of over 170 km2, is a stopping place for hundreds of bird species. The western part of the region is called Barlavento and the east Sotavento.

Human presence in southern Portugal dates back to the Paleolithic and Neolithic periods, attested by megalithic stones at Vila do Bispo, Lagos and Alcoutim. Around 1000 BCE the Phoenicians founded Cádiz and, subsequently, ports along the Algarve coast.
