By the sixth century BCE the Cynetes, called Conii in Latin, were established in the region, then called Cyneticum; their ethnic and linguistic origins remain widely disputed.

The region came under Roman control after Fabius Maximus Servilianus defeated the Lusitanians and the Turduli, and remained under Roman influence for around 600 years, from 200 BCE to 410 CE. The name Algarve comes from the Arabic al-ġarb, meaning the west, that is, Western Al-Andalus; the Portuguese used it for the lands to their south under Muslim control, and it narrowed to the southwesternmost region.

After victories over the Wattasids in 1471 won Asilah and Tangier, the Portuguese called their North African possessions the Algarve-Beyond-the-Sea. Portuguese monarchs held the title of King or Queen of the Algarves until the Portuguese Republic was established.

The Algarve is the southernmost NUTS II region of continental Portugal, with 16 municipalities and its administrative centre at Faro, where the University of Algarve is also located. Surviving traces of the past include the Roman ruins of Milreu at Estói, the Megalithic Monuments of Alcalar, the Ribat of Arrifana, and Vila Real de Santo António, an example of the Marquis of Pombal's urban planning after the 1755 earthquake.
algebra: Algebra began in attempts to solve problems involving arithmetic calculations and unknown quantities, in Babylonia, Egypt, Greece, China and India. One of the earliest documents is the Rhind Mathematical Papyrus from Egypt, written around 1650 BCE, which solves linear equations. Babylonian clay tablets of about the same time explain methods for linear and quadratic equations, including completing the square. The Greeks used algebraic methods to solve geometric problems, and in the 3rd century CE Diophantus treated equations in his Arithmetica and was the first to experiment with symbolic notation for polynomials.

Whether these early works are algebra or only precursors is disputed, since they treated specific cases. In 825 CE Muḥammad ibn Mūsā al-Khwārizmī published The Compendious Book on Calculation by Completion and Balancing. He classified equations into six standard forms and gave systematic step-by-step procedures, abstracted from particular geometric figures, which made algebra a self-contained discipline distinct from geometry. Thābit ibn Qurra in the 9th century and Omar Khayyam in the 11th and 12th also contributed.

The word comes from the Arabic al-jabr, which originally referred to the surgical treatment of bonesetting. Al-Khwārizmī used it in the 9th century to name a method of transforming equations, and his treatise was translated into Latin as Liber Algebrae et Almucabola. The word entered English in the 16th century and at first meant only the theory of equations. Equations were described in words and abbreviations until the 16th and 17th centuries, when a rigorous symbolic formalism developed.

In the mid-19th century the scope widened to cover many kinds of algebraic operations and structures and the laws, called axioms, that they follow. Elementary algebra, taught in schools, generalises arithmetic by using variables for unknown quantities; linear algebra studies systems of linear equations; abstract algebra studies structures such as groups, rings and fields. Its methods also serve geometry, topology, number theory, calculus and logic.
algeciras: Algeciras stands on the western shore of the Bay of Gibraltar, opposite the Rock of Gibraltar and near the Strait of Gibraltar, the narrowest crossing between Europe and Africa. The Arabic name al-Jazira al-Khadra means green island or green peninsula. The traditional explanation derives it from the small island of Isla Verde, but this has been questioned, since Arab sources called that island Umm Hakim. The site was also that of the Roman port of Portus Albus and of the town of Iulia Traducta, and the earliest remains are Neanderthal.

In 859 Viking ships under Hastein and Björn Ironside besieged the city for three days, laid waste to much of it and burnt its two main mosques, but the inhabitants regrouped and drove them out. In 914 the Cordobese emir Abd al-Rahman III took the city, which had supported rebels, and had shipbuilding docks built for the Umayyad navy. It was an independent taifa from 1035 to 1058. In 1274 Nasrid Granada ceded it to the Marinids, and after 1282 Abu Yusuf built a walled precinct, al-Bunayya, across the Río de la Miel. Alfonso X of Castile besieged the city in 1278 without success.

Ferdinand IV of Castile laid the first siege in 1309. Alfonso XI began a second in 1342, and the city surrendered in March 1344. He made it the seat of a diocese, whose bishops of Cadiz held the title Aliezira until 1851, and Genoese and Catalan traders settled there. The Nasrids of Granada seized the town in 1369 with a Marinid fleet and Muhammed V of Granada ordered it destroyed; some date this scorched-earth policy to 1375. Refugees from Gibraltar refounded it after the Anglo-Dutch capture of that town in 1704. In 1705 it was described as a heap of stones, and in 1760 Charles III rebuilt it on its present rectangular plan.

The Algeciras campaign between the French and Spanish navies and the Royal Navy took place off the city in July 1801. In 1906 the town hall hosted the Algeciras Conference on the future of Morocco, which confirmed Morocco's independence against German threats and gave France control of banking and police interests.

Algeciras is a municipality of the province of Cádiz in Andalusia, with a registered population of 123,078 in 2020, the largest in the Campo de Gibraltar. Its port is the main crossing point between Spain and Tangier and other ports in Morocco, the Canary Islands, Ceuta and Melilla. The city is also a fishing and industrial centre.
algeria: Algeria is the largest country in Africa and the Mediterranean basin, covering 2,381,741 square kilometres. The Sahara covers most of it. In the north, the Tell Atlas and the Saharan Atlas form two parallel sets of reliefs, and the area from the coast to the Tell Atlas is fertile; south of it lies steppe, then the desert. The highest point is Mount Tahat, at 3,003 metres, in the Hoggar Mountains of the central Sahara. About 90% of Algerians live in the northern coastal area, and Algiers, Oran, Constantine and Annaba are the main cities.

Early finds show that hominins lived on the Mediterranean fringe of northern Africa earlier than previously thought. Neolithic life, richly depicted in the Tassili n'Ajjer paintings, predominated until the classical period. The Carthaginians established settlements on the coast, and by 600 BCE a Phoenician presence existed at places such as Icosium, now Algiers, and Hippo Regius.

They avoided conquering the strong Berber tribes of the interior, collected tribute and traded, and the Berbers supplied them with goods, slaves and skilled cavalry. Amazigh societies, among them the Numidians, whose kingdom became one of the earliest major states in the region, were also shaped by Roman, Vandal and Byzantine influences.

From the 7th century the spread of Islam and the arrival of Arab tribes gradually transformed the region, and from the 8th to the 15th centuries local Islamic dynasties ruled. The Regency of Algiers, established in 1516, became a largely autonomous state owing nominal allegiance to the Ottoman Empire. France invaded in 1830 and formally annexed Algeria in 1848, though it was not fully conquered until 1903. French rule brought mass European settlement that displaced the local population, and by the mid-1870s indigenous Algerians had declined by up to a third through warfare, disease and starvation.

Resistance to French colonisation ran from the campaigns of Emir Abdelkader and the Mokrani Revolt to the nationalist movements of the 20th century. The Sétif and Guelma massacre in 1945 catalysed the resistance that led to the outbreak of the Algerian War in 1954, and Algeria gained independence in 1962. A civil war lasted from 1992 to 2002. The country is a semi-presidential republic with a population of about 47 million. Its official languages are Arabic and Amazigh, most people speak Algerian Arabic, and Sunni Islam is the official religion.
algerian-war: France captured Algiers in June 1830, on the pretext of a slight to its consul, after Charles X and his ministers decided in January of that year on an invasion. The conquest spread inland under Marshal Bugeaud, the first Governor-General, and was violent, marked by a scorched earth policy. Between 500,000 and 1,000,000 of about 3 million Algerians are estimated to have been killed in the first three decades. Algeria was declared an integral part of France by the Constitution of 1848, in three departments, and French and other Europeans settled there; they later became known as the pieds-noirs.

The war effectively began on 1 November 1954, the Toussaint Rouge, when guerrillas of the National Liberation Front (FLN) attacked military and civilian targets across Algeria. The FLN was weak at first, and its armed wing had only some 3,000 badly equipped men. According to the historian Natalya Vince, its leaders knew they could not win militarily and used guerrilla warfare and urban terrorism to erode France's political will and expose French repression.

They also worked to internationalise the conflict, which became entangled with the Cold War. French forces used torture, indiscriminate shootings and bombing of villages, destroyed over 8,000 villages and moved over 2 million Algerians into regroupment camps. More than 12,000 Algerians died in FLN purges. Reports of torture reaching France in 1956 and 1957 made it known there as la sale guerre, the dirty war.

The war brought down the Fourth Republic in 1958, replaced by the Fifth with a stronger presidency. Charles de Gaulle opened negotiations with the FLN, which ended in the Évian Accords of March 1962. French voters approved them on 8 April 1962 with 91 percent, and on 1 July 99.72 percent in Algeria voted for independence. The Organisation armée secrète, which opposed withdrawal, carried out bombings and murders and tried to assassinate de Gaulle.

Estimates of Algerian deaths range from 400,000 to 1.5 million, with 25,600 French soldiers and 6,000 Europeans also killed. In a few months of 1962, 900,000 pieds-noirs fled to France. Harkis, Algerians who had served as auxiliaries with the French army, were regarded as traitors and many were murdered; about 20,000 Harki families reached France.
alghero: The area has been settled since prehistoric times: the Ozieri culture was present in the 4th millennium BCE, and the Nuragic civilisation settled around 1,500 BCE. By the 8th century BCE Phoenicians had arrived, and the metalworking town of Sant'Imbenia, with a mixed Phoenician and Nuragic population, traded with the Etruscans. The medieval name derives from Aleguerium, a Latin word for a stagnation of algae. The Doria family of Genoa built the first historical nucleus on an empty stretch of coast between 1102 and 1112, and the Dorias ruled the fortified port for centuries, apart from a year under Pisa in 1283 and 1284.

The Crown of Aragon took the town in 1354 at the behest of Peter IV of Aragon, who promoted its colonisation with families from Valencia, Majorca, Catalonia and Aragon. They were granted privileges and replaced the original population, some of whom were sent to the Iberian Peninsula and Majorca as slaves. In the early 16th century Alghero received papal recognition as a bishopric and the status of King's City. Spanish Habsburg rule lasted until 1702. In 1720 Alghero, with the rest of Sardinia, passed to the House of Savoy, which began a policy of Italianization. A famine in 1821 led to a revolt that was bloodily suppressed, and the town was demilitarised at the end of that century.

In the Fascist era part of the surrounding marshes was reclaimed and the suburbs of Fertilia and Santa Maria La Palma were founded. Alghero was bombed in 1943 and its historic centre was heavily damaged. Malaria in the countryside was finally overcome in the 1950s, and the town has since become a tourist destination.

Alghero has a population of 41,765, which makes it the fifth-largest city in Sardinia. Algherese, the Catalan dialect introduced by the colonists, has been officially recognised as a minority language, and since 1997 national and regional laws have granted a right to use it in the city. Its speakers call the town Barceloneta, little Barcelona. The old town keeps Catalan medieval architecture, and a book of 1888 by Eduardo Toda y Güell on this Catalan population restarted the connection between Catalonia and Alghero.

Ramparts begun in the 13th century on the Genoese system were restored by the Catalans, and most of the present walls were built in the 16th century under Ferdinand the Catholic, with seven towers and three forts. The Torre del Portal was built in 1360 at the expense of the Jewish community, and Charles V stayed in the Palazzo D'Albis in October 1541. The cathedral was begun in 1570 and consecrated in 1730, with Catalan Gothic chapels beneath later Renaissance work. The local red coral gives the coast the name Riviera del Corallo.
algiers: Algiers lies on the Mediterranean Sea in the north-central part of Algeria, along the Bay of Algiers and surrounded by the Mitidja Plain and mountain ranges. The historical centre was founded on the coastal hills to the east of the bay, and the city later spread over them towards the plain. The Arabic name al-Jazāʾir means the Islands, referring to four main islands off the western cape where people settled, which were joined to the mainland in 1525 by a pier now named after Kheireddine.

The city's history is believed to go back to between 1200 and 250 BCE, but it was a small Phoenician trading settlement of no importance until about the third century BCE, when Ikosim became a small port town of Carthage. Numidia annexed the town around 202 BCE. It later passed to several powers, among them the Roman Empire and various Islamic caliphates. Buluggin ibn Ziri formally founded Algiers in 972 CE on the ruins of the Punic city of Icosium, calling it Jazāʾir Banī Mazghanna, the islands of the Banu Mazghanna.

In 1516 Algiers became the capital of the Ottoman Regency of Algiers, and it remained so until the French invasion of 1830. During Ottoman rule its name was extended to the whole country, giving the name Algeria. The main building of the Kasbah was begun in 1516 and was the palace of the deys until the French conquest. The Djamaa el Kebir, the oldest mosque in the city, existed by 1097 according to an inscription on its pulpit, and its minaret was built in 1324 by the sultan of Tlemcen.

In 1830 Algiers was a fortified Casbah. After the French conquest its walls were demolished and a European quarter was built, and the two were unified into one municipality in 1832. The city served as the administrative centre of Free France from 1942 to 1944, and it has been the capital of independent Algeria since 1962.

Algiers is the capital and largest city of Algeria. The Casbah, a citadel and medina combining Algerian, Ottoman and Andalusian architecture, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, and a larger French-built section beside it shows other architectural styles. Because of its whitewashed buildings the city is called al bidha, the white.
algirdas: Algirdas was one of the seven sons of Grand Duke Gediminas. Before his death in 1341, Gediminas divided his domain and left his youngest son Jaunutis in possession of the capital, Vilnius. With the help of his brother Kęstutis, Algirdas drove out Jaunutis and declared himself Grand Duke in 1345. The two appeared to rule jointly, Kęstutis defending the western border. Their division of the realm shows in the sources, since Algirdas appears almost exclusively in East Slavic ones and Kęstutis mainly in Western chronicles. The Livonian Chronicles gave Algirdas the Latin title rex Letwinorum.

Lithuania was surrounded by enemies: the Teutonic Order, the Golden Horde, Poland and the principality of Moscow. Algirdas extended the borders to the Black Sea, with his principal efforts directed at the East Slavic lands of the former Kievan Rus'. He had his son Andrius elected Prince of Pskov, occupied Smolensk and Bryansk, and besieged Moscow in 1368 and 1370, although his relations with Moscow's grand dukes were generally friendly and he married two Orthodox Russian princesses. His victory over the Tatars at Blue Waters in 1362 broke up the Kipchaks and compelled the khan to move his headquarters to Crimea. In 1371 he wrote to the Ecumenical Patriarch Philotheus Kokkinos demanding a separate metropolitan for Kyiv and other cities.

Algirdas died in May 1377. Byzantine and Western sources describe him as a pagan until his death, while later Orthodox chronicles claim he was baptised, a claim not backed by contemporary sources. He was burned on a ceremonial pyre with 18 horses and many of his possessions in a forest near Maišiagala.

His heir, first named as his son Fiodor, became Jogaila, a son of his second wife Uliana of Tver, who ruled from 1377. Fiodor probably tried to seize power in a coup in 1381, but Jogaila regained the title in 1382. Jogaila became King of Poland and founded the dynasty that ruled Lithuania and Poland for nearly 200 years. Algirdas's descendants include the Trubetzkoy, Czartoryski and Sanguszko families, and he is honoured in Belarus as a unifier of Belarusian lands.
algirdas-brazauskas: Algirdas Mykolas Brazauskas was born in Rokiškis, Lithuania, on 22 September 1932. He finished Kaišiadorys High School in 1952 and graduated from Kaunas Polytechnic Institute in 1956 with a degree in civil engineering. He served as a conscript sailor in the Soviet Navy until 1960, began work in the governmental planning committee in 1967 and received a doctorate in economics in 1974. From 1965 he held posts in the government of the Lithuanian SSR and the Communist Party of Lithuania, among them minister of construction materials industry, deputy chairman of the State Planning Committee and, from 1977 to 1987, secretary of the party's Central Committee.

In the 1980s Brazauskas turned from party apparatchik to moderate reformer. He first thought the USSR might become a looser federation of independent communist states, and in 1990 said of the party that it had a dirty history. As first secretary of the Communist Party of Lithuania from 1988, he led its majority to support the independence movement and break away from the Soviet party in 1989; no other local communist party in the Soviet Union took this step. He was head of state as Chairman of the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet from 15 January to 11 March 1990, and the party became the social-democratic Democratic Labour Party.

After the 1992 elections, the first since 1938, he became speaker of parliament and acting president on 25 November 1992. He won the presidency in one round with 60 per cent of the vote and took office on 25 February 1993. He supported Lithuania's accession to NATO and the European Union and a pragmatic relationship with Russia; after a phone call with Boris Yeltsin, talks on the withdrawal of Russian troops resumed in 1993 and the withdrawal was completed. In 1995 he apologised before the Knesset for the Lithuanian people's actions during the Holocaust. He did not seek re-election and handed power to Valdas Adamkus on 25 February 1998.

Brazauskas returned as Prime Minister on 3 July 2001, appointed by parliament, and served until his government resigned in 2006. He led the Social Democratic Party of Lithuania until 19 May 2007. He was diagnosed with lymphatic cancer in December 2008 and died on 26 June 2010, aged 77. He is remembered as the first democratically elected president of post-Soviet Lithuania.
algonquin-people: The Algonquin are closely related, culturally and linguistically, to the Odawa, Potawatomi, Ojibwe, Mississaugas and Nipissing, with whom they form the larger Anicinàpe (Anishinaabeg) group. They call themselves Omàmiwinini, meaning downstream men, and speak Algonquin, one of the Anishinaabe languages. In their oral history of the Great Anishinaabeg Migration they came from the Atlantic coast and reached a First Stopping Place near Montreal. While other Anicinàpe continued up the St. Lawrence, the Algonquins settled along the Ottawa River, called Kitcisìpi, an old highway of commerce and exchange. Scholars estimate from oral history, archaeology and linguistics that Algonquin identity took shape about 2,000 years ago, near present-day Detroit.

The Algonquin first met Europeans in the summer of 1603, when Samuel de Champlain came upon a party led by the Kitcisìpirini chief Tessouat at Tadoussac, celebrating a victory over the Iroquois. Some Algonquins allied with Champlain, gaining access to European firearms. At that time the bands probably numbered about 6,000 people in all. The Kitcisìpirini, based on Morrison Island, prospered on the trade route between the Great Lakes and the St. Lawrence, collecting beaver pelts and levying a toll on canoes.

The Haudenosaunee, armed by Dutch and later English traders, drove Algonquins from their lands. A winter raid in 1642 caused severe casualties, and on 6 March 1647 a Mohawk war party almost exterminated the Kitcisìpirini near Trois-Rivières. Some Algonquins joined the mission at Sillery, where an epidemic destroyed most of them by 1676. Algonquin warriors fought with France until the British conquest of Quebec in 1760, and the Algonquins signed the Royal Proclamation of 1763. From the 1820s lumbering and settlement pressed on their lands, and from the 1830s they were confined to small reserves. In Ontario an Algonquin land claim has run since 1983, and an agreement-in-principle was reached in 2015; many Algonquins dispute its validity.

Traditionally the Algonquins hunted and fished and stressed mobility, using birch-bark canoes, toboggans, snowshoes and cradleboards, and living in birch-bark or wooden mìkiwàms. They were united by a clan and totem system rather than a state, and each band had its own chief who depended on the approval of its clan leaders. Many practised Midewiwin and believed in manitòk, or spirits in the natural world; French missionaries converted many to Catholicism in the 17th and 18th centuries. Today they live in nine recognised communities in Quebec and one in Ontario, and many still speak the Algonquin language.
alhama-de-granada: Alhama de Granada is a town in the province of Granada, about 50 kilometres from the city of Granada. Its name comes from the thermal baths there, called al-hammah in Arabic. The town looks out on an uninterrupted view of the Sierra Nevada, and the Sierras of Tejeda, Almijara and Alhama Natural Park lie a few kilometres to the south. Its position between Málaga and Granada gave it strategic importance for the Moors.

There is clear evidence that the Romans used the hot springs near the town. The Arabs consolidated the town beside them, and it was long believed that they built the baths, though the local historian Salvador Raya Retamero argues that the earliest baths are Roman in origin. The bath house in the Almohade style of the 12th century that survives in the spa is a good example of Arab bath construction. Horseshoe arches stand over the Roman remains under a vaulted roof pierced by star-shaped openings, and the oldest spring rises beneath it.

In 1482 the fortress town was taken from the Moorish Sultanate and Kingdom of Granada by the Catholic Monarchs. The Moors were fond of the town and its waters, and the cry of sorrow attributed to Abu Al-Hacen (Abu l-Hasan Ali, Sultan of Granada) after the battle, "¡Ay de mi Alhama!", entered the Spanish language as an exclamation of regret. The fall of Alhama was vital for the conquest of the Kingdom of Granada. Eleno de Céspedes, born into slavery in the town in 1545 or 1546, became possibly the first female surgeon in Spain, and perhaps in Europe.

Alhama de Granada suffered more than any other community in the 1884 Andalusian earthquake. El Defensor de Granada reported 463 dead and 473 injured, though the real number seems considerably higher, and more than 70 per cent of the houses collapsed. The newest spring was discovered in 1884.

In 1975 the municipality absorbed that of Ventas de Zafarraya. The town keeps a yearly round of fiestas, among them a Candelaria festival on 2 February, in which small fires are lit through the town and wine and food are offered to travellers, a wine festival, Easter processions and two ferias, in June and September. The reservoir at Arenas del Rey, built between 1947 and 1954, lies about 14 kilometres away.
alhambra: The Alhambra stands on Sabika hill, an outcrop of the Sierra Nevada that had been the site of earlier fortresses and of the 11th-century palace of Samuel ibn Naghrillah. The first reference to the Qal'at al-Ḥamra comes from the rule of 'Abdallah ibn Muhammad (888-912), when the castle was small and its walls could not deter an army. The name means the red one, after the reddish colour of its walls of rammed earth, which owes its hue to iron oxide in the local clay. Building of the present complex began in 1238 under Muhammad I Ibn al-Ahmar.

In the Nasrid period the Alhambra was a self-contained city separate from Granada below, with a Friday mosque, hammams, roads, houses, workshops, a tannery and a sophisticated water supply. It had at least six major palaces, of which the Mexuar, the Comares Palace, the Palace of the Lions and the Partal Palace are the best preserved. The Alcazaba fortress stands at its western tip, and the Generalife, a former summer palace, lies outside the walls. The site is about 700 to 740 metres long.

The palaces are organised around rectangular courtyards with a pool, fountain or water channel at the centre. Decoration was concentrated inside, in tile mosaics on lower walls and carved stucco above, with geometric patterns, plant motifs, Arabic inscriptions and muqarnas vaulting. The main gate, the Puerta de la Justicia, was built in 1348 under Yusuf I.

After the Christian conquest of 1492 the site became the Royal Court of Ferdinand and Isabella, where Christopher Columbus received royal endorsement for his expedition. In 1526 Charles V commissioned a Renaissance palace beside the Nasrid ones. Napoleon's troops destroyed parts in 1812. Washington Irving's Tales of the Alhambra (1832) brought it international attention, and an Alhambra-inspired style called Alhambresque became popular in the West after Owen Jones published his plans of the Alhambra in London from 1842 to 1845. M. C. Escher visited in 1922, and his study of the symmetries of the tiles, which contain nearly all of the seventeen possible wallpaper groups, inspired his work on tessellation.
ali-abdullah-saleh: Ali Abdullah Saleh was born on 21 March 1947 to a poor Zaydi family in the village of Beit al-Ahmar, in the territory of the Sanhan clan some 20 kilometres south-east of Sanaa. His father died after divorcing his mother, who then married his late husband's brother Muhammad Saleh, who became Saleh's mentor and stepfather. Saleh joined the Royal Armed Forces of North Yemen as an infantry soldier in 1958 and entered the Royal Military Academy in 1960. He was commissioned a second lieutenant in the armoured corps in 1963, and took part in the military coup of 1962 that removed King Muhammad al-Badr and established the Yemen Arab Republic.

He reached the rank of major during the North Yemen Civil War, trained as a staff officer in Iraq between 1970 and 1971, and became a full colonel in 1976, commanding a mechanised brigade. In 1977 President Ahmad al-Ghashmi appointed him military governor of Taiz.

After al-Ghashmi was assassinated on 24 June 1978, Saleh joined a four-man provisional presidency council, and on 17 July 1978 parliament elected him president of the Yemen Arab Republic. On 10 August 1978 he ordered the execution of 30 officers charged with conspiring against him. He survived a serious coup attempt in late 1978, became secretary-general of the General People's Congress on 30 August 1982 and was re-elected in 1983. Under him Yemen began to produce oil.

In 1990, with the Soviet Union in decline and communist South Yemen weakened, North and South unified. The South accepted Saleh as president, with Ali Salem al-Beidh as vice president. After al-Beidh left the Presidential Council in 1993, a brief civil war ended in July 1994 with the defeat of southern forces. Parliament made Saleh a field marshal in 1997, and he won the presidential election of 1999 with 96.2 per cent of the vote.

In early 2011, after the Tunisian revolution, protests demanded an end to his three decades in power. On 2 February 2011 he said he would not seek re-election, and on 18 March at least 52 people were killed when government forces fired on demonstrators in Sanaa. He resigned in 2012, and Abdrabbuh Mansur Hadi succeeded him.

Saleh allied with the Houthis in 2015, and in July 2016 they formed a Supreme Political Council. In December 2017 he declared that he was leaving the alliance, and on 4 December 2017 he was killed in Sanaa in fighting with Houthi forces. In 2013 he had opened a museum of his 33 years in power in a wing of the Al Saleh Mosque in Sanaa.
ali-adil-shah-ii: Ali Adil Shah II was the eighth sultan of Bijapur. He came to the throne on the death of Mohammed Adil Shah on 4 November 1656, through the efforts of the prime minister Khan Muhammad and of the queen Badi Sahiba, a sister of the Qutb Shah of Golkonda. The Mughal emperor Shah Jahan, who wished to annex Bijapur, found a pretext in doubts about Ali's parentage and, at the plea of his son Aurangzeb, sanctioned an invasion, although Bijapur was an independent ally of the Mughals and not their vassal. Aurangzeb had to raise the siege and hurry north for the war of succession to the Mughal throne.

With the accession of a young ruler, disorder began in the Karnataka, where the Nayaks tried to recover their former lands; Bangalore was Bijapur's administrative headquarters for controlling these feudatories. At court the struggle of factions for supremacy reached its height, and Aurangzeb intrigued with the Bijapur nobles and won over most of them. Shivaji meanwhile took more and more Bijapur territory, and his diplomacy prevented any coalition of the Mughals and Bijapur against him.

Through the sixteen years of his reign Ali fought both the Mughals and the Marathas, and he three times repulsed Mughal invasions. The reign was also marked by developments in Persian and Deccani literature and the fine arts. Beside the poet laureate Nusrati, the historian Nurullah wrote under his patronage a history known as the Tarikh-i Ali Adil Shah.

Ali died on 24 November 1672. By then the kingdom had lost most of its important territories, shrinking as Shivaji's kingdom grew, and the reign is seen as marking the decline of Bijapur. He was buried in Ali Ka Rouza, the monument at Bijapur known as the Bara Kaman.
ali-al-rida: Ali ibn Musa was born in Medina. Sources give several years, from 148 AH (765/766 CE) to 153 AH, and the date often given by Shia authorities is 11 Dhu al-Qa'da 148 AH. His father, Musa al-Kazim, was the seventh Twelver Shia Imam, a descendant of Ali and Fatima, and his mother was a freed slave, probably of Berber origin, whose name appears as Najma or Tuktam. He lived with his father in Medina until 795/796 CE, and when Harun al-Rashid arrested Musa and took him to Iraq, he managed the family's property and the affairs of the Shias as his attorney.

Musa al-Kazim died in a Baghdad prison in 799/800, and Ali became his heir and successor under his father's will. He spent the next ten years in the reign of Harun. Like the fourth to seventh Imams, he kept aloof from politics and refused to approve the Alid uprisings, which led the Zaydis, who favoured armed struggle, to oppose him. Yet he called the rule of his time a false government and held that obeying oppressors was wrong. He issued legal rulings in the Prophet's Mosque in Medina while in his twenties.

Al-Ma'mun, in a sudden departure from the anti-Shia policy of the Abbasids, possibly meant to ease Shia revolts, invited him to Merv in Khorasan and named him heir apparent, though he accepted only on condition that he not interfere in government. Many Abbasids opposed this and installed Ibrahim ibn al-Mahdi as anti-caliph in Baghdad. Al-Ma'mun married his daughter Umm Habib to al-Rida, and the marriage produced no children. He also arranged debates between scholars of different sects and religions in which al-Rida took part.

When al-Ma'mun's party left Khorasan for Baghdad, al-Rida fell ill and died at Tus around September 818, probably poisoned according to Shia sources; other dates range from September 817 to May 819. His death followed the assassination of the vizier al-Fadl ibn Sahl. Madelung, Hugh Kennedy and others consider al-Ma'mun responsible, while the Sunni historians al-Tabari and al-Masudi do not consider murder, and al-Masudi says he died from eating too many grapes.

Tus was later replaced by Mashhad, which grew around his grave. Works are attributed to him, among them the Al-Risalah al-Dhahabiah, a medical treatise, and the Sahifah of al-Ridha, 240 hadiths; the authenticity of the treatise and of Fiqh al-Rida is doubted. In Sufi tradition he stands in the chain of authority through Ma'ruf al-Karkhi, though one scholar regards the accounts of their meeting as apocryphal. His son Muhammad al-Jawad continued the line of Imams.
ali-bey-al-kabir: Ali Bey was born in the Principality of Abkhazia, and his father is said to have been a priest. About the age of thirteen he was kidnapped, taken to Cairo in 1741 and sold into slavery. Two Jewish customs agents bought him and in 1743 gave him to Ibrahim Ketkhuda, himself of Georgian origin and head of the Qazdughli faction of mamluks. Ali rose through his master's household, became a kashif in 1749 and in 1753 or 1754 led the pilgrim caravan to Mecca as amir al-hajj. His raids on the Bedouin on that journey earned him the Turkish nickname Balut Kapan, he who catches clouds, and on his return he was made a bey.

In 1760 the faction leader Abd al-Rahman Ketkhuda had him chosen shaykh al-balad, the chief of the country, intending to rule through him. Ali Bey instead built up a household of 3,000 mamluks, may have had an incoming governor poisoned before he could take office, and exiled Abd al-Rahman to the Hejaz in 1765. The Ottoman government sent Hamza Pasha with orders to bring him down, and in 1766 he was forced from office and took refuge in Gaza, where he won the support of Daher al-Umar of Acre.

Allied with Salih Bey and the Hawwara of Upper Egypt, he cut Cairo's supplies and entered the city without a fight in October 1767. He then removed his rivals one by one: two leading mamluks were killed in November 1767, Husayn Bey was beheaded and Khalil Bey strangled in 1768, and Salih Bey himself was assassinated that September. By taking the office of qa'immiqam he gained the governor's powers, and in November 1768 he ousted the governor. In 1769 he stopped the tribute to Istanbul and struck coins in his own name, and in 1770 and 1771 his armies took the Hejaz and occupied Syria.

After a victory over the governor of Damascus on 6 June 1771, his commander Muhammad Bey Abu al-Dhahab, turned against him by an Ottoman agent, broke off the war and returned to Egypt. Ali Bey lost power, though historians disagree on when, and he died in Cairo in 1773. Historians also disagree on his policies: Cleveland and Bunton credit him with expanding trade with Britain and France and hiring European military advisers, while Bidwell says he made no effort to build a modern army. Thomas Hope told his rise and fall in the 1819 novel Anastasius.
ali-ibn-abi-talib: According to tradition Ali was born around 600 CE to Abu Talib ibn Abd al-Muttalib and Fatima bint Asad of the Banu Hashim, a clan of the Quraysh in Mecca, and he may have been born inside the Ka'ba. When he was about five he came under the guardianship of Muhammad and Khadija. In 622, when Muhammad escaped a plot to kill him and left for Medina, Ali stayed behind as his decoy. Muhammad gave him his daughter Fatima in marriage, and Ali served as his secretary and deputy. At Ghadir Khumm in 632 Muhammad declared, "He whose mawla I am, Ali is his mawla", a saying whose meaning Shia and Sunni Muslims interpret differently.

When Muhammad died in 632, a group of Muslims met at the Saqifa in Ali's absence and appointed Abu Bakr. Ali accepted this, probably for the sake of Muslim unity, though he considered himself the best qualified. He later withdrew from public life under the first three caliphs. After Egyptian rebels killed Uthman in 656, Ali was offered the caliphate by the Iraqis, most of the Ansar and most of the Muhajirun, and he accepted after some hesitation.

He dismissed nearly all of Uthman's governors as corrupt and distributed the treasury equally, policies praised as righteous and criticised as naive. Talha, Zubayr and Muhammad's widow Aisha rebelled, and Ali defeated them at the Battle of the Camel in 656. Mu'awiya, governor of Syria, refused to step down, and the two fought the inconclusive Battle of Siffin in 657. The arbitration that followed alienated a group of Ali's army known as the Kharijites, whom he crushed at the Battle of Nahrawan in 658.

Ali was struck with a poisoned sword during the morning prayer at the Great Mosque of Kufa on 28 January 661, by the Kharijite Abd al-Rahman ibn Muljam, in revenge for Nahrawan, and died about two days later. His son Hasan was acknowledged as caliph in Kufa but abdicated in August 661 to Mu'awiya, who founded the Umayyad Caliphate. Alids were persecuted under the Umayyads and later under the Abbasids. Ali's other son Husayn was killed by Umayyad forces at Karbala in 680.

Sunni Muslims regard Ali as the last of the rightly guided caliphs, while Shia Muslims venerate him as their first Imam and Muhammad's rightful successor. Nahj al-balagha, a collection of sermons, letters and sayings attributed to him, was compiled in the eleventh century by Sharif al-Radi, and recent research attributes most of it to Ali.
ali-ibn-hammud-al-nasir: Ali ibn Hammud claimed descent from Idris ibn Abdallah, the founder of the Idrisid dynasty. The Caliphate of Córdoba had fallen into civil war after the largely figurehead caliph Hisham II was usurped by his cousin Muhammad II. Power was then contested between Hisham II, Muhammad II and Sulayman, another great-grandson of Abd al-Rahman III. By 1013 Sulayman had captured Córdoba with his Berber army after a siege of two and a half years, and Hisham II disappeared, with many believing he had been murdered. Sulayman's Berber troops then carried out revenge killings and destruction against his enemies.

To placate the Berbers and assert his claim, Sulayman gave territories in southern al-Andalus and north Africa to his Berber generals: Ceuta went to Ali ibn Hammud, and Tangier, Arcila and Algeciras to his brother al-Qasim ibn Hammud. Ali first posed as loyal, but in late 1013 he declared himself independent and announced that he would free the legitimate caliph Hisham II. He also promoted a story that Hisham, uncertain of his fate during the siege, had named him heir-presumptive and wished his death avenged. In 1014 he crossed the Straits of Gibraltar and took Málaga as a base.

The Berber rulers of southern al-Andalus offered the brothers little resistance. In the summer of 1016 Ali marched on Córdoba and on 17 June defeated Sulayman's Berber troops in the city. An exhumed body found in the palace was declared to be Hisham II, and Sulayman was charged with the caliph's murder and beheaded. On 3 July 1016 Ali was proclaimed caliph with the title al-Nasir.

Ali first tried to reduce the abuses of the Berber militia against the citizens of Córdoba, but without success, and the Córdobans came to regard his regime as pro-Berber. After about eight months he reversed course and let the Berbers again make arrests and seize property and arms, earning a reputation as a scourge of the Córdobans. Khayran al-Amiri, the ruler of Almería, and others who wanted a legitimate Umayyad as caliph turned against him, and by early 1018 open rebellion had broken out. As Ali prepared to meet it, three of his household servants killed him in the palace baths on 22 March 1018. His brother al-Qasim al-Ma'mun succeeded him.
ali-ibn-yusuf: Ali ibn Yusuf was born in 1084 or 1085 at Ceuta, the son of Yusuf ibn Tashfin, the fourth Almoravid ruler. Sources differ on his mother. Some name her Zaynab an-Nafzawiyyah, others Qamar, a Christian captive from al-Andalus who became Yusuf's concubine. He was 23 when his father died in September 1106 and succeeded him on 2 September 1106. He ruled from Morocco and made his brother Tamim ibn Yusuf governor of al-Andalus.

Ali took the Taifa of Zaragoza in 1110, and the early part of his reign marks the peak of Almoravid power in al-Andalus. His armies besieged Toledo in 1114, Barcelona in 1115 and Coimbra in 1117 but failed at each, and their fortunes turned. Alfonso I of Aragon took Zaragoza between 1118 and 1120, and Córdoba briefly rebelled in 1121. In the 1120s many Almoravid troops were recalled across the straits to face the new movement of Ibn Tumart, the Almohads.

Ali's son Tashfin ibn Ali, governor of al-Andalus from 1126, won victories at Aceca in 1130 and at Fraga and Badajoz in 1134, but from 1138 the initiative lay with the Christians, who took Oreja in 1139 and Coria in 1142, helped by a renewed Almohad offensive in Morocco. In 1139 Ali lost the Battle of Ourique to Afonso Henriques, which allowed Afonso to proclaim himself king. Ali died on 28 January 1143 and was succeeded by Tashfin.

Ali ibn Yusuf commissioned a minbar from a workshop in Córdoba for his grand mosque in Marrakesh, now known as the Minbar of the Kutubiyya Mosque, and the Almoravid Qubba bears his name. At the advice of Abu Walid Ibn Rushd, grandfather of Averroes, he spent 70,000 gold dinars on walls for Marrakesh, which doubled the city's size. He also had an irrigation system built with qanawat, and the first bridge over the Tensift River. According to the cartographer al-Idrisi, adventurers sent by Ali under the admiral Ahmad ibn Umar reached a sea covered by seaweed, which some identify as the Sargasso Sea.
ali-pasha-of-yanina: Ali Pasha was born into the Albanian Meçohysaj clan, a family of Christian Albanians who had converted to Islam in the Ottoman period. The family traced its descent to a Mevlevi dervish named Nazif, a claim Ali repeated to support his title to landholdings, but the tradition is unfounded: the family was of local Albanian origin. He is accepted today as a follower of the Bektashi order.

In his early years he made a name as a bandit in the mountains. The Ottoman government authorised Ahmet Kurt Pasha of Berat to subdue him, and by 1775 he was in Kurt's service. In 1779 he challenged Kurt openly, marching 2,000 to 3,000 Albanians through Thessaly to show the Porte that his power base was the stronger.

Ali was appointed mutasarrif of Ioannina at the end of 1784 or the beginning of 1785, on condition that he lead 1,000 troops on campaign. He did not, and turned instead on the villages around Gjirokastër. At Hormovë he killed the men, sold the women and children into slavery and roasted the village leader alive. He was made pasha of Ioannina in 1788, and was appointed Beylerbey of Rumelia on 28 January 1803.

As pasha he built an almost independent state across much of Albania and mainland Greece. Ioannina became a centre of education, culture and trade. He used Greek for the business of his court, allied himself with all religious and ethnic groups and crushed opponents fiercely. His Albanian soldiers and mercenaries subdued the independent community of Souli, and he dealt with France and Britain, meeting William Martin Leake in November 1807.

After the Second Serbian Uprising produced a semi-independent state in 1817, the Ottoman minister Halet Efendi drew Sultan Mahmud II's attention to Ali's unchecked power. Declared a rebel in 1820, Ali was besieged in Ioannina, agreed to a truce and withdrew to the Monastery of St Panteleimon on an island in Lake Pamvotis. He was killed on 24 January 1822; the circumstances of his death are unclear.

Historians still disagree about his character, which contemporaries both admired and criticised. The French consul François Pouqueville argued that Ali's rebellion was a vital precondition of the Greek Revolution: he weakened Ottoman control of Greece, and his death left a vacuum that Greek revolutionaries promptly filled. His rule also helped foster a sense of ethnic belonging among Albanians.
ali-qapu: Ali Qapu, a name meaning Grand Gate, was originally designed as a vast portal entrance to the grand palace that stretched from Naqsh-e Jahan Square to the Chaharbagh Boulevard. The name combines the Arabic ʿālī, meaning superior or imperial, with the Old Turkic qāpū, meaning door. It stands on the western side of the square, opposite the Sheikh Lotfollah Mosque, and UNESCO has inscribed the palace and the square as a World Heritage Site. The building was raised by decree of Shah Abbas the Great in the early 17th century, and the Safavid monarchs used it to entertain noble visitors and foreign ambassadors.

It was built in stages over about seventy years. The first was a cubical two-storey entrance building measuring 20 by 19 metres and 13 metres high. Upper halls were then added above the vestibule, followed by a music hall, an eastern veranda advancing towards the square, and a wooden balcony ceiling on 18 columns. A stairway on the southern flank, called the Kingly Stairway, and a water tower for the copper pool of the columned balcony followed.

The palace is forty-eight metres high and has six floors, each reached by a difficult spiral staircase. The chancellery stood on the first floor. Royal receptions and banquets were held on the sixth floor, which holds the largest rooms and was popularly called the Music Hall, where ensembles played and sang. Deep circular niches in its walls have an acoustic as well as a decorative value, and its stucco decoration is full of vessels and cups. From the upper galleries the shahs watched polo, army manoeuvres and horse races in the square.

Shah Abbas II expanded and renovated the palace, and his main addition was the grand hall on the third floor, with 18 mirror-covered columns and a painted ceiling. The interior is decorated with naturalistic wall paintings of flowers, animals and birds by Reza Abbasi, the court painter of Shah Abbas I, and his pupils.

Shah Soltan Hoseyn, the last Safavid ruler, had the palace substantially restored, but it fell into disrepair again during the short reign of the invading Afghans. Most of its richly ornamented doors and windows were looted in times of disorder, and only one window on the third floor survives. Under Naser ad-Din Shah Qajar the Safavid cornices and floral tiles above the portal were replaced by tiles bearing inscriptions. The palace is regarded as the best example of Safavid architecture and appears on the reverse of the Iranian 20,000 rial banknote.
ali-shir-navai: Alisher Nava'i was born in Herat in 1441 to a family of well-read Turkic chancery scribes, of the Chaghatai mir class of the Timurid elite. His father, Ghiyath al-Din Kichkina, served as a high-ranking officer in the palace of the Timurid ruler Shahrukh Mirza. After his father died, another ruler of Khorasan, Abul-Qasim Babur Mirza, became the young man's guardian. Alisher was a schoolmate of Husayn Bayqara, later sultan of Khorasan. He studied in Mashhad, Herat and Samarkand, and when Husayn Bayqara seized power in Herat in 1469 he joined his service.

In 1472 Alisher was appointed emir of the supreme council, the dīvān-i aʿlā. This brought him into conflict with the Persian bureaucrat Majd al-Din Muhammad Khvafi, whose centralising reforms threatened the privileges of the Turkic military elite. He stayed in Bayqara's service until his death on 3 January 1501, and was buried in Herat. He never married. He is reported to have founded, restored or endowed some 370 mosques, madrasas, libraries, hospitals, caravanserais and other institutions in Khorasan, among them the mausoleum of the poet Farid al-Din Attar at Nishapur. He backed historians such as Mirkhvand and Khvandamir, the poet Jami and musicians such as Husayn Udi.

Under the pen name Nava'i, he wrote mainly in Chagatai Turkic, producing 30 works over 30 years, and also wrote in Persian as Fāni. His four diwans, about 50,000 verses, correspond to the stages of life, from Wonders of Childhood to Benefits of Old Age. His Khamsa, five epic poems, answers that of Nizami Ganjavi, and Majalis al-Nafais collects over 450 biographical sketches of mostly contemporary poets. In Muhakamat al-Lughatayn he argued that Chagatai was superior to Persian for literary purposes, an uncommon view then.

Bernard Lewis called him the Chaucer of the Turks. His influence reached the Mughal founder Babur, who wrote of his respect in his memoirs. Soviet and Uzbek sources regard him as an ethnic Uzbek and the founder of Uzbek literature, though applying modern ethnonyms to his time is anachronistic.
aliaga: Aliağa is a municipality and district of İzmir Province in Turkey, about 50 kilometres north of İzmir. The district covers 379 square kilometres and had a population of 104,828 in 2022. It lies in the heart of ancient Aeolia, and its large port handles mainly oil and bulk cargo. The district has 30 neighbourhoods, among them Atatürk, Barbaros Hayrettin Paşa, Mimar Sinan, Aşağışakran and Yenişakran.

The town was named after Karaosmanoğlu Ali Ağa, a member of the influential Karaosmanoğulları ayan family, who owned an estate there. Before the Greco-Turkish War of 1919 to 1922 the population was mainly Greek. In 1937 it was a township in Menemen district, it became a municipality in 1952, and on 21 January 1982 it separated from Menemen and became a district.

The remains of the ancient city of Myrina lie within the district, about fifteen kilometres north of the town centre. Another ancient site, Gryneion, near the township of Şakran about fifteen kilometres to the south, is still unexplored. Visitors also use the road from Aliağa to reach the remains of Aigai on Yuntdağı in Manisa Province. In 2021 an illegal excavation uncovered a monastery and a floor mosaic, which archaeologists believe was in use from the 4th century to the 14th century.

Its economy rests on tourism, shipbreaking and an oil refinery. Several facilities dismantle and scrap ships, and the process sped up in 2020, when owners of idled cruise ships sought to cut their losses during the COVID-19 pandemic. The D.550 road runs through the town between Muğla and Edirne and on to İzmir, and the İZBAN commuter railway links Aliağa Railway Station to Alsancak Terminal in İzmir, with 15 trains a day.
alicante: The area around Alicante has been inhabited for over 7,000 years, and some of the earliest settlements stood on the slopes of Mount Benacantil. By 1000 BCE Greek and Phoenician traders had begun to visit the coast, introducing the native Iberian tribes to the alphabet, iron and the potter's wheel. The Carthaginian general Hamilcar Barca founded the fortified settlement of Akra Leuké, meaning White Mountain or White Point, in the mid-230s BCE, generally presumed to have stood on the site of the modern city. Rome ruled Hispania Tarraconensis for over 700 years, and Visigothic rule followed from 400 to 700.

Alicante returned to the Crown of Aragon in 1296, under King James II of Aragon, and became a Royal Village with representation in the medieval Valencian Parliament. After decades as a battlefield between Castile and Aragon, it grew into a trading station exporting rice, wine, olive oil, oranges and wool. The local Jewish community was expelled in 1492, and between 1609 and 1614 King Felipe III expelled thousands of Moriscos, which cost the region skilled artisans and agricultural labourers. After the War of the Spanish Succession the city declined for a long period, until international trade and the growth of the harbour brought a sharp recovery at the end of the 19th century.

In the Spanish Civil War Alicante was the last city loyal to the Republican government to be occupied by General Franco's troops, on 1 April 1939, and its harbour saw the last Republican officials flee the country. On 28 March 1939 the British ship SS Stanbrook, under Captain Archibald Dickson, carried off thousands of Republican families. The city is now the second largest of the Valencian Community and forms a conurbation of nearly a million people with Elche. It is the seat of the European Union Intellectual Property Office, and the foot of its city hall's main staircase is the zero point from which heights above sea level are measured throughout Spain.

The Castle of Santa Bárbara stands on Mount Benacantil, its oldest part the tower called La Torreta. The Explanada de España is a palm-lined promenade paved with 6.5 million marble tiles in a wavy pattern, and the Basilica of Santa María, built between the 14th and 16th centuries, stands over the former main mosque. The Bonfires of Saint John are held at the summer solstice.
alice-munro: Alice Ann Laidlaw was born on 10 July 1931 in rural Wingham, Ontario, during the Great Depression. Her father, Robert Eric Laidlaw, farmed foxes and mink and later turkeys, and her mother, Anne Clarke Laidlaw, was a schoolteacher. She published her first story, The Dimensions of a Shadow, in 1950 while studying English and journalism at the University of Western Ontario on a two-year scholarship.

In 1951 she left university to marry a fellow student, James Munro, and they moved to West Vancouver. In 1963 the couple moved to Victoria, where they opened Munro's Books. They divorced in 1972, and she returned to Ontario as writer in residence at the University of Western Ontario. In 1976 she married Gerald Fremlin, a retired cartographer.

Her first collection, Dance of the Happy Shades (1968), won the Governor General's Award. It was followed by Lives of Girls and Women (1971), a collection of interlinked stories, and by Who Do You Think You Are? (1978), which earned a second Governor General's Award and was shortlisted for the Booker Prize in 1980 under the title The Beggar Maid. From the 1980s to 2012 she published a collection at least once every four years, and her collections have been translated into 13 languages.

Many of her stories are set in Huron County, Ontario, and she is associated with the Southern Ontario Gothic. Her work tends to move forward and backward in time. A frequent theme of the early stories is a girl coming of age and coming to terms with her family and small hometown. Later collections, such as Hateship, Friendship, Courtship, Loveship, Marriage (2001), turned to the troubles of middle age, of women alone and of the elderly.

Munro received the Man Booker International Prize in 2009 for her life's work, and in 2013 the Nobel Prize in Literature, cited as a master of the contemporary short story. She was the first Canadian and the 13th woman to receive it. She stopped writing around 2013 and died at her home in Port Hope, Ontario, on 13 May 2024, aged 92. In 2024 her daughter Andrea Skinner disclosed that Fremlin had sexually abused her as a child, which has led to some reevaluation of Munro's legacy.
alids: The Alids are the descendants of Ali, cousin and son-in-law of the Prophet Muhammad, the fourth Rashidun caliph of Sunni tradition and the first Imam in Shia Islam. Their two principal branches are the Hasanids and the Husaynids, descended from Hasan and Husayn, the sons of Ali and Fatima, the daughter of Muhammad. Sources report that Ali had seventeen daughters and eleven, fourteen or eighteen sons. The lineage also continued through Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiya, Abbas ibn Ali and Umar al-Atraf, whose descendants bore the title Alawi. The direct line beginning with Ali forms the Twelve Imams of Twelver Shia Islam, and as the family of Muhammad the Alids are revered by all Muslims.

After Ali was assassinated in 661 and Mu'awiya founded the Umayyad Caliphate, the Alids and their supporters were heavily persecuted. Husayn and a small caravan were massacred by the Umayyads at Karbala in 680, and al-Mukhtar rose in 685 on behalf of Muhammad ibn al-Hanafiya. Zayd ibn Ali led a failed uprising around 740, and his followers became the Zaydites. The Abbasids had rallied Shia support in the name of the family of Muhammad, but many were disillusioned when al-Saffah declared himself caliph, and the Abbasids soon turned on their former allies. Many Alids revolted, among them the Hasanid brothers Muhammad ibn Abd-Allah and Ibrahim.

Some Alids took refuge in remote regions and founded dynasties. After the revolt of Husayn ibn Ali al-Abid was suppressed in 786, his brother Idris escaped and founded the first Alid dynasty in Morocco; Zaydite rulers appeared in northern Persia and in Yemen. Several Imams died under Abbasid surveillance or in prison, and Musa al-Kazim, the seventh, died in prison in 799. In 817 Caliph al-Ma'mun named Ali al-Rida heir apparent, but the policy was reversed under opposition. Twelver Shia hold that the twelfth Imam has been in occultation since 874. After the death of Ja'far al-Sadiq in 765 the Isma'ilites separated from the Imamites, and their efforts culminated in the Fatimid Caliphate.

Several dynasties have claimed descent from Ali, often through Hasan. The Hasanid dynasties include the Idrisites and the Sharifs of the Maghreb and the Hammudids in Andalusia, while the Fatimid Caliphate claimed Husaynid descent, a claim some have questioned. The Alids remain central to the doctrine of the Shia, who limited leadership of the community to them after the Abbasid betrayal.
alikhan-bukeikhanov: Alikhan Nurmukhameduly Bukeikhanov was born on 5 March 1866 into a Kazakh Muslim family in Tokyrauyn Volost of the Russian Empire. His father was Nurmuhammed Bukeikhanov, and as a great-grandson of Barak Sultan, a former khan of the Orta zhuz, he was a direct descendant of Genghis Khan. He graduated from the Omsk Technical School in 1890 and from the economics faculty of the Saint Petersburg Forestry Institute in 1894, and is believed to have been influenced by socialists in his youth.

Back in Omsk he taught mathematics at the school for Kazakh children from 1895 to 1897 and took part in the Shcherbina Expedition of 1896, which surveyed the land, resources and peoples of the steppe; his study of sheep-breeding came out of such work. He was the first biographer of the poet Abay Kunanbayev, whose obituary he published in 1905, and in 1909 he published a collection of Abay's works.

Bukeikhanov joined the Constitutional Democratic Party in 1905, and after a failed attempt to found a Kazakh Democratic Party he was arrested and barred from the steppe provinces. Elected to the State Duma in 1906, he signed the Vyborg petition against its dissolution, and from 1908 he lived in exile in Samara until 1917. His essay Kirgizy of 1910, on the Kazakhs, appeared in the party's book on the nationalities, and he helped create Qazaq, a newspaper in the Kazakh language.

In 1917 the Provisional Government appointed him its commissioner for Turgay Oblast, and with Akhmet Baitursynov he called the All-Kazakh Congress at Orenburg, which demanded the return of confiscated lands and native control of schools. A second congress raised the idea of territorial autonomy and founded the Alash party. After the October Revolution he was elected president of the Alash Orda government, which he led until 1920.

Once Soviet rule was established Bukeikhanov returned to scholarly work, but he remained under suspicion. Arrested in 1926 for counter-revolutionary activity and held in Moscow's Butyrka prison, he was released for lack of evidence, and he was arrested again in 1928. Banished to Moscow in 1930, he was arrested a final time in 1937 and executed on 27 September that year. The Soviet authorities rehabilitated him only in 1989.
alise-sainte-reine: Alise-Sainte-Reine is a commune in the Côte-d'Or department of eastern France, some 17 km southeast of Montbard and 50 km northwest of Dijon. Apart from the village it consists of farmland and some forest. The Ozerain river forms most of its southern border. The village lies at the foot of Mont Auxois, where excavations attest a Gallic oppidum. A mineral and thermal spring there was well known from Celtic times, and a large sanctuary beside it was dedicated to Apollo Moritasgus, a god of healing waters. The saint in the name is Sainte Reine, a Christian martyr said to have been beheaded at this place in 252, who is the commune's patron.

The village's name recalls Alesia, the fortress defended by Vercingetorix in 52 BCE, and it is the oldest site identified with it; the identification was already made in the Carolingian period. The Gallic levels of the oppidum on Mont Auxois are contemporary with the Gallic Wars. A Gallic inscription of the first century CE gives the place's name as Alisiia. Excavations in the reign of Napoleon III found traces of Roman siege works, and excavations by a Franco-German team in the 1990s found them consistent with Caesar's text, and found a sling shot bearing the name of Caesar's lieutenant Labienus.

Professional historians and archaeologists in France and abroad have reached a consensus on the site, though some associations and individuals continue to propose others. After the siege the site was not abandoned: excavations have uncovered a Gallo-Roman town with a theatre that could seat about 5,000, a temple, a basilica and a forum.

A statue of Vercingetorix, commissioned by Napoleon III from the sculptor Aimé Millet, was installed on Mont Auxois in 1865 and is the town's common symbol. The commune also has the Sainte-Reine Hospital (1659), the Chapel and Fountain of Sainte-Reine (1498) and a church of Saint-Léger that partly dates from as early as the 7th century. The MuséoParc Alésia, built on the site of the battle, opened its interpretation centre on 26 March 2012. A Mystery of Sainte Reine is performed on weekends in August, a tradition that dates back to 866.
alivardi-khan: Alivardi Khan was originally named Mirza Bande or Mirza Muhammad Ali and was a native of the Deccan. His father, Mirza Muhammad Madani, was of Arab descent and the son of a foster-brother of the Mughal emperor Aurangzeb; his mother descended from the Iranian Turkmen Afshar tribe of Khorasan. Muhammad Ali and his elder brother Mirza Ahmad found favour under Azam Shah, and he was named superintendent of the elephant-stables. After Azam Shah died in 1707 the family fell into poverty and moved to Cuttack in Orissa, where their relative Shuja-ud-Din was deputy governor. The brothers served him and later helped him become Nawab of Bengal.

In 1728 Shuja-ud-Din made Muhammad Ali faujdar of Rajmahal with the title Alivardi Khan, and in 1733 deputy governor of Bihar. On 10 April 1740, at the Battle of Giria, he defeated and killed Shuja-ud-Din's successor, Sarfaraz Khan, and took control of Bengal and Bihar. On 3 March 1741 he defeated Rustam Jang, deputy governor of Orissa, at the Battle of Phulwari, and Orissa also came under his control. The Mughal emperor Muhammad Shah then confirmed his takeover, and Alivardi resumed the policies of Murshid Quli Khan.

From 1742 the Marathas raided Bengal repeatedly, and Alivardi had a long ditch, called the Maratha ditch, dug around Calcutta. In 1747 Raghoji I Bhonsle's forces were routed at the Battle of Burdwan, but Orissa was overrun and ultimately surrendered to the Marathas, and a peace treaty with Raghoji was settled in 1751. Alivardi also put down Afghan rebels in Bihar and in 1750 forgave his grandson Siraj ud-Daulah, who had revolted and seized Patna. He kept a neutral stance towards the European powers and forbade the British, French and Dutch to fight one another in his dominions.

Some historians say that most of his reign went to wars against the Marathas, with the last years given to rebuilding Bengal. He patronised the veena and khol drums and commissioned manuscripts of the Shahnameh. Alivardi had one wife, Sharfunnesa, and three daughters but no sons. He died at 5 am on 9 April 1756 and was buried at Khushbagh next to his mother. His maternal grandson Siraj ud-Daulah, then aged 23, succeeded him.
aljaferia: The Aljafería was built outside the Roman walls of Zaragoza, which has since grown around it. Its construction, mostly completed between 1065 and 1081, was ordered by Abu Ja'far Ahmad ibn Sulayman al-Muqtadir Billah, the second ruler of the Banu Hud dynasty, as a symbol of the power the Taifa of Zaragoza had reached. He called it Qasr al-Surur, the Palace of Joy, and its throne room Maylis al-Dahab, the Golden Hall. The name Aljafería comes from his pre-name Abu Ja'far. A text by al-Yazzar as-Saraqusti names the architect as the Slav al-Halifa Zuhayr.

The plan follows the desert castles of Syria and Jordan: a square enclosure with towers and a tripartite central space around a courtyard with pools. On the north side stand the Golden Hall, framed by a band of Kufic inscriptions quoting the Quran, and a small private mosque with a mihrab. It is the only large example of Spanish Islamic architecture from the era of the taifas to survive. Its interlaced mixtilinear arches appear here for the first time, and its arabesque plasterwork, painted in blue, red and gold, influenced Almoravid and Almohad art.

After Alfonso I of Aragon took Zaragoza in 1118 the Aljafería became a residence of the Christian kings of Aragon. Peter IV extended it in 1336, and the Catholic Monarchs had a new palace built on the north wing between 1488 and 1495. In 1486 the Inquisition received part of the complex. In 1591 the secretary of Philip II, Antonio Pérez, was held there by the Inquisition, and a popular uprising stormed the palace to free him. The royal army put it down, and Philip II had the engineer Tibúrcio Spannocchi turn the palace into a fortified citadel.

It was later used to quarter regiments and was damaged in the Sieges of Zaragoza of the Peninsular War before being restored in the 20th century. It now houses the Cortes, the parliament of Aragon, and in 2001 its original restored structures were included in the World Heritage Site Mudéjar Architecture of Aragon.
all-blacks: Rugby union was introduced to New Zealand by Charles Monro in 1870, who had discovered it while studying in Finchley, England. The first recorded game took place in May 1870 at Nelson, between the Nelson rugby club and Nelson College. The first provincial union, Canterbury, was formed in 1879. In 1884 the first New Zealand team to travel overseas toured New South Wales and won all eight games. The New Zealand Rugby Football Union was formed in 1892 by most of the provincial unions, and the first officially sanctioned New Zealand side toured New South Wales in 1893, winning nine of ten matches.

The team's first true test match was against Australia on 15 August 1903 at the Sydney Cricket Ground, before over 30,000 spectators, and ended in a 22–3 victory. The first home test, against a British Isles side, was played in Wellington in 1904. A 34-game tour of Europe and North America in 1905 included five tests and brought one defeat, the team's first test loss, against Wales. By then the side wore all black except for the silver fern, and the name All Blacks dates from this tour. International rugby was suspended during the First World War, and a New Zealand Services team played in the King's Cup.

For the 1960 tour of South Africa, South African authorities insisted that Maori players be excluded, and the controversy led the New Zealand Rugby Union to refuse any tour of the country for ten years, until 1970, when Maori players were accepted as honorary whites. New Zealand hosted and won the first Rugby World Cup in 1987, beating France 29–9 in the final. In 1996 under coach John Hart and captain Sean Fitzpatrick the team won a test series in South Africa for the first time.

The All Blacks compete with Argentina, Australia and South Africa in the Rugby Championship, which grew from the Tri-Nations when Argentina joined in 2012. They won the World Cup in 1987, 2011 and 2015, the first country to retain it, and completed Grand Slam tours of the four Home Nations in 1978, 2005, 2008 and 2010. The team performs a haka before every match, traditionally Te Rauparaha's Ka Mate, with Kapa o Pango also performed since 2005. The current jersey is entirely black except for sponsors' logos and the silver fern, but for the 1884 tour the team wore dark blue with a gold fern.
all-india-majlis-e-ittehadul-muslimeen: The Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen (MIM) was founded in 1927 by Nawab Bahadur Yar Jung and Nawab Mahmood Nawaz Khan Qiledar of Hyderabad State; its first meeting was held at Nawaz Khan's house on 12 November 1927. At first it had only a cultural and religious manifesto, but it soon took on a political character. Bahadur Yar Jung was elected its president in 1938 and died in 1944. After Hyderabad was merged into India by the police action known as Operation Polo, the Razakars and their leader Qasim Razvi were arrested.

Razvi was released in 1957 on condition that he go to Pakistan. In 1958, before leaving, he named Abdul Wahid Owaisi, a lawyer, as his successor, and Owaisi organised the party as the All India Majlis-e-Ittehadul Muslimeen. Under him it moved from a hardline policy of independence to a more pragmatic course. His son Sultan Salahuddin Owaisi took control in 1975 and was called Salar-e-Millat, commander of the community. The party's later president, Asaduddin Owaisi, has claimed that AIMIM is not the descendant of the Razakars.

The party's base was the old city of Hyderabad. It won the Mallepally ward of the Hyderabad Municipal Corporation in 1960, and Salahuddin Owaisi, elected to the state assembly from 1962, won the Hyderabad seat in the Lok Sabha in 1984 and held it until 2004; the party kept it after him. A split in 1993, when Amanullah Khan's faction formed the Majlis Bachao Tehreek, left AIMIM with a single assembly seat in Andhra Pradesh in 1994. It joined the Congress-led United Progressive Alliance in 2008 and left it in 2012. In the 2014 Telangana elections it won seven seats and was recognised as a state party.

In more recent years the party spread beyond Hyderabad. Imtiyaz Jaleel won the Aurangabad Lok Sabha seat in Maharashtra in 2019, the party's first outside Hyderabad, and lost it in 2024. In Bihar AIMIM won five assembly seats in the Seemanchal region in 2020; four of those members joined the RJD on 29 June 2022, and the party again won five seats in 2025. It also won municipal seats in Gujarat, Karnataka and Tamil Nadu. The party has at times fielded Hindu candidates, and three of Hyderabad's mayors elected from its ranks, among them K. Prakash Rao, were Hindus.
all-india-muslim-league: The League emerged from the Aligarh Movement. Syed Ahmad Khan founded the All-India Muhammadan Educational Conference in 1886 to promote British education, especially science and literature, among Indian Muslims, and the conference barred itself from discussing politics. The need for political representation grew during the Indian National Congress-led opposition to the 1905 partition of Bengal.

After the Simla Deputation of October 1906, the Nawab of Dacca, Khwaja Salimullah, proposed at the conference's 20th session in Dacca a party to protect Muslim interests, to be named the All-India Muslim League. The motion passed unanimously in December 1906. Aga Khan III became the first honorary president, though he did not attend, and the constitution of 1907, the Green Book, was written by Mohammad Ali Jauhar. Muhammad Ali Jinnah joined in 1913.

The League remained an organisation of the Muslim elite until 1937. After the Khilafat Movement ended in 1922 relations between Muslim and Hindu leaders cooled sharply: there were 91 riots between 1923 and 1927 in Uttar Pradesh alone, and the share of Muslims among Congress delegates fell from 11% in 1921 to under 4% in 1923. In 1930 Muhammad Iqbal gave the League's presidential address at Allahabad; some scholars hold that he proposed a province with a Muslim majority within an Indian federation, not partition. In 1933 Choudhry Rahmat Ali set out the name Pakistan in a pamphlet, Now or Never.

From 1937 the League under Jinnah began to mobilise the Muslim masses, and its membership rose above two million. At Lahore on 23 March 1940, on a motion by A. K. Fazlul Huq, it adopted a resolution for an autonomous and sovereign Muslim state taking in Sindh, Punjab, Baluchistan, the North West Frontier Province and Bengal. In the provincial elections of 1946 it won 425 of the 476 seats reserved for Muslims, about 89.2% of Muslim votes. Congress, led by Gandhi and Nehru, remained opposed to dividing India.

After the partition of 1947 the All-India Muslim League was formally disbanded. In Pakistan it continued as the Muslim League, led first by Jinnah and then by Prime Minister Liaquat Ali Khan; it was banned in 1958 and revived in 1962 as the Pakistan Muslim League, which later split into several parties. In India the Indian Union Muslim League succeeded it, with a base in Kerala. In East Bengal the League formed the first government, with Khawaja Nazimuddin as chief minister.
all-russian-central-executive-committee: The All-Russian Central Executive Committee was first formed in 1917 as the permanent body of the First All-Russian Congress of Soviets of Workers' and Soldiers' Deputies, held in Petrograd. The congress elected a committee of 320 deputies: 123 Mensheviks, 119 Social Revolutionaries, 58 Bolsheviks, 13 United Social Democrats and 7 others. Its chairman was the Menshevik Nikolay Chkheidze. This first committee was not a governing body, and Chkheidze was not head of the Russian state. After the July events it supported the Provisional Government, welcomed the appointment of the Social Revolutionary Aleksandr Kerensky as head of the government and decided to recognise its unlimited powers. It sat in the Tauride Palace until August 1917 and then moved to Smolny.

The committee tried to counteract the Bolshevization of the Soviets in the autumn of 1917. Its Social Revolutionary and Menshevik majority refused to recognise a congress of the Northern Region, held on 24–26 October in Petrograd, and declared the planned Second Congress of Soviets illegal, yet agreed to convene it, postponing the opening from 20 October to 25 October (7 November in the new style). The congress opened on 7 November at 10:40 pm, in the midst of the armed uprising in Petrograd. The Mensheviks and Social Revolutionaries condemned the Bolshevik actions as an illegal coup, and the old committee called the congress a private meeting of Bolshevik delegates.

On 8 November Lenin proposed dissolving the old committee and electing a new one. Of its 101 members, 62 were Bolsheviks and 29 Left Social Revolutionaries; moderate socialists boycotted it. Lev Kamenev became chairman. On 28 November it merged with the executive committee of 108 elected at the Extraordinary Peasants' Congress, after which the Left Social Revolutionaries joined the Council of People's Commissars in a coalition with the Bolsheviks.

The 1918 Constitution required the committee to convene the All-Russian Congress of Soviets at least twice a year. A full congress elected it, with no more than 200 members, and it was wholly subordinate to the congress. It gave general direction to the government's policies, reviewed and adopted draft decrees from the Council of People's Commissars, issued decrees of its own, and formed the Council and the People's Commissariats. State budgets were decided jointly with the congress.

Kamenev was chairman from 9 to 21 November 1917, Yakov Sverdlov from then until his death in office on 16 March 1919, and Mikhail Kalinin from 30 March 1919. After the Soviet Union was formed in December 1922, the chairmanship was mostly ceremonial. In 1937 the committee was replaced by the Presidium of the Supreme Soviet of the Russian SFSR.
allada: The present town of Allada corresponds to Great Ardra, also called Grand Ardra or Arda, the capital of an Adja-Eʋe kingdom that was also known as Allada. Its first inhabitants were ethnic Aja. According to oral tradition they migrated to southern Benin around the 12th or 13th century from Tado, on the Mono River in present-day Togo. The kingdom existed as a sovereign state from about the 13th or 14th century, the date of the first Aja settlements, which were reorganised as a kingdom around 1600, until 1724.

Oral tradition tells that around 1600 three brothers, Kokpon, Do-Aklin and Te-Agdanlin, divided the region among themselves. Kokpon took the capital, Great Ardra, and ruled the Allada kingdom. Do-Aklin founded Abomey, which became the capital of the Kingdom of Dahomey. Te-Agdanlin founded Little Ardra, also known as Ajatche or Little Adja, which Portuguese traders later called Porto-Novo, the present capital of Benin. In the middle of the sixteenth century Allada, then called Grand Ardra, had a population of about 30,000. In 1724 the kingdom fell to the armies of its neighbour, the Kingdom of Dahomey.

Allada is a town, arrondissement and commune in the Atlantique Department of Benin. The commune covers an area of 381 square kilometres, and its population at the 2013 census was 127,512. The Haitian revolutionary leader Toussaint Louverture was the grandson of the Allada prince Gaou Guinou, and a statue of him stands in the north of the town.
allah: The word Allah is thought to derive by contraction from al-ilāh, meaning the god, and is related to other Semitic words for God, among them the Aramaic Alāhā and the Hebrew Ĕlōah. Originally ilāh served as an epithet of the West Semitic creator god Ilu, the Ugaritic form of El, before it became the proper name of that god. Regional variants of the word occur in both pagan and Christian pre-Islamic Arabian inscriptions, and an inscription of a Christian martyrion dated to 512 opens with the phrase By the Help of al-ilah.

In pre-Islamic Mecca, according to Islamic sources, Allah was worshipped alongside a host of lesser gods, and goddesses were counted as his daughters. Ibn Kathir says the Arab idolaters regarded Allah as an unseen god who created and controlled the universe. Some scholars suggest he was a remote creator god gradually eclipsed by local deities, and there is disagreement over whether he played a major role in Meccan cult. No image of Allah is known.

In Islam the worship of Allah to the exclusion of all other deities is the fundamental tenet, expressed in the declaration La ilaha illa Allah. The Quran did not set out to prove that Allah exists but to purge belief in him of polytheistic additions. It presents the worship of Allah as the shared mission of all prophets, including Abraham, Moses and Jesus. Islamic theology stresses the absolute uniqueness of God in his essence, attributes and acts, and treats any comparison of God with created things as shirk, one of the gravest sins.

Most Quranic commentators regard Allah as a proper noun, while the 99 Names of Allah denote attributes, among them the Merciful and the Compassionate. In the Sufi practice of dhikr the name is chanted and contemplated.
