From the first centuries of Islam, Arabic-speaking commentators who were Jewish, Christian or Muslim used Allah as a generic term for the supreme being. Saadia Gaon used it interchangeably with Elohim, and Theodore Abu Qurrah rendered theos as Allah in his Bible. Arab Christians adopted the Muslim invocation bismillah and from as early as the 8th century made their own Trinitarian form.

Muslims leave many phrases containing the word untranslated, such as in shā'a llāh, meaning if God wills, and Allāhu Akbar. Through the Muslim presence in Iberia the word gave Spanish ojalá and Portuguese oxalá. Christians in Malaysia and Indonesia use Allah for God, a usage that goes back to Francis Xavier in the 16th century.
allat: The origin of the name al-Lat is uncertain. Medieval Arab lexicographers derived it from a verb meaning to mix or knead barley-meal, while another theory takes it as a feminine form akin to the name Allah. Herodotus, in the fifth century BCE, records the Arabian goddess as Alilat and equates her with Aphrodite Urania. Inscriptions in Safaitic, Hismaic, Nabataean and Palmyrene Aramaic give forms of the name, and scholars disagree over whether some of these forms are a proper name or a generic word for goddess.

Al-Lat was widely worshipped in north Arabia. In South Arabia she was not the object of an organised cult: two amulets inscribed Lat and Latan are the only sign. Safaitic inscriptions invoke her for mercy, well-being and prosperity, for good weather and protection on journeys, and for vengeance on anyone who defaces an inscription. The Nabataeans regarded her as the mother of the deities, sometimes the consort or mother of Dushara, and called her and al-'Uzza his brides. She was also venerated at Palmyra, where she was called the Lady of the temple, and at Hatra.

Under Greek and Roman influence she was identified with Athena, Tyche and Minerva, and in Palmyra from the second century CE she appears as Athena-Allāt, although the assimilation went no further than her iconography. At Ta'if, according to Islamic sources, she was the chief goddess of the Banu Thaqif and was worshipped as a cubic granite rock; the area around her shrine was sacred, and no tree could be felled, no animal hunted and no blood shed.

In Islamic tradition al-Lat, al-'Uzza and Manat were regarded as daughters of Allah, and the Quran names the three together in Quran 53:19–22. According to Islamic tradition, her shrine at Ta'if was demolished on the orders of Muhammad, around the time of the Battle of Tabuk in October 630 CE, as a condition for any reconciliation with the tribes of Ta'if. Medieval writers also told legends that linked her stone with a man who ground grain for pilgrims, al-latt, the grinder. The Lion of Al-Lat, a statue from her temple at Palmyra, was damaged in 2015 and later restored; it stands in the National Museum of Damascus.
allectus: Allectus served as treasurer to Carausius, a Menapian officer in the Roman navy who had seized power in Britain and northern Gaul in 286. In 293 Carausius became isolated when the western Caesar, Constantius Chlorus, retook some of his Gallic territories, above all the crucial port of Bononia, modern Boulogne, and defeated his Frankish allies in Batavia. Allectus assassinated Carausius and took command himself.

Allectus's reign has left little record. His coin issues are distributed much like those of Carausius, and they are found in north-western Gaul, which indicates that the recapture of Bononia did not end the rebel empire on that side of the Channel. Carausius had used his coinage as propaganda, and some of his slogans, such as a claim to have restored liberty, were designed to appeal to British sentiment.

In September 296 Constantius launched an invasion by sea in several divisions. He led one from Bononia but seems to have been delayed by bad weather. Another division, under the praetorian prefect Asclepiodotus, used fog to avoid Allectus's ships stationed at the Isle of Wight and landed near Southampton Water, where the troops burnt their ships. Allectus's forces retreated from the coast but were cut off by another of Constantius's divisions and defeated. Allectus was killed in the battle, having removed all his insignia in the hope that his body would not be identified. Archaeology suggests that his defeat took place at or near Calleva Atrebatum, modern Silchester.

A group of Roman troops separated from the main body by the fog caught up with the remnants of Allectus's men, mostly Franks, at Londinium and massacred them. Constantius seems not to have reached Britain until it was all over, and his panegyrist claims that the Britons welcomed him as a liberator. A medal struck after the victory calls him redditor lucis aeternae, restorer of the eternal light.

Geoffrey of Monmouth included Allectus in his History of the Kings of Britain, written around 1136, as an officer sent with three legions to depose Carausius, who is there a native British king. In that account his rule proves oppressive, and Asclepiodotus, here the Duke of Cornwall, deposes him. A coin showing his head, found in Dover in March 2019 by a metal detectorist, sold for £552,000 at auction. Rosemary Sutcliff's 1957 novel The Silver Branch is built around these events.
allied-invasion-of-sicily: The campaign in North Africa ended in May 1943, and the Allies had for the first time driven the Axis powers from a theatre of war. Led by the United States and the United Kingdom, they chose to attack Axis forces in Europe through Italy rather than Western Europe, citing wavering Italian morale, their control of Mediterranean sea lanes and the vulnerability of German supply lines along the Italian peninsula. Operation Mincemeat was the most successful of the deception operations.

Operation Husky planned two armies to land on the south-eastern and central southern coasts, supported by naval gunfire and by tactical bombing. General Dwight D. Eisenhower was overall commander, with General Sir Harold Alexander commanding the 15th Army Group. The Eastern Task Force was General Sir Bernard Montgomery's British Eighth Army, including the 1st Canadian Infantry Division, and the Western Task Force was Lieutenant General George S. Patton's American Seventh Army. The island was defended by the Italian 6th Army and the German XIV Panzer Corps.

The operation began on the night of 9/10 July 1943 with a large amphibious and airborne assault. Strong winds of up to 70 km/h blew the troop-carrying aircraft off course. The American paratroopers, making their first combat drop, were scattered widely between Gela and Syracuse, and only 12 of 147 British gliders landed on target, while 69 crashed into the sea and over 200 men drowned. Even so, scattered small units attacked vital points on their own initiative and caused confusion.

A platoon of the 2nd Battalion, South Staffordshire Regiment, under Lieutenant Louis Withers took the Ponte Grande bridge south of Syracuse and held it against counterattacks. By the time it surrendered, reduced to 18 men, the leading British 5th Division troops were 45 minutes away. The land campaign lasted six weeks and ended on 17 August.

The Allies drove Axis air, land and naval forces from the island, and the Mediterranean was open to Allied merchant ships for the first time since 1941. The invasion led to the ousting of Benito Mussolini and the fall of his regime, replaced by the first Badoglio government. German troops had to take over from Italian forces in Italy and, to a lesser extent, the Balkans, diverting one-fifth of the German army from the Eastern Front. The invasion opened the way to the invasion of mainland Italy.

Axis forces evacuated the island: the Italians some 62,182 men by one account, the Germans about 52,000. The U.S. Seventh Army lost 8,781 men and the British Eighth Army 11,843, and Canadian forces had 2,310 casualties. German losses are given as 27,940 in one study.
alm-s: Almış, whose title was iltäbär, was a son of Şilki and ruled the Volga Bulgars, probably from Bolghar, in about 895 to 925. The controversial History of Jaʿfar makes him a younger son who succeeded his older brother Bat Ugïr, and identifies him with Álmos, father of the Hungarian prince Árpád, an identification that is perhaps unlikely despite the likeness of the names and the rough match in time, although the Bulgars and Hungarians are believed to have shared some Hunnic or Onoghuric elements in their origins. The same text traces his descent back to Kubrat and Kotrag.

At first a vassal of the Khazars, Almış struggled to assert the independence and unity of the Bulgar tribes, and his turn to Islam may in part have served that aim. When the caliph's ambassador Aḥmad ibn Faḍlān met him at Bolghar in 922, the Abbasid caliphate became an ally of Volga Bulgaria. It is generally believed that under Almış the country became a united, strong and independent state, though little about his reign can be verified.

Ibn Faḍlān's account of his journey, which calls Almış the king of the Saqaliba, makes him the only ruler of Volga Bulgaria about whom a relative wealth of contemporary information survives. It mentions his brothers, wives and children: two of his daughters were married to the Khazar khaghan and to the ruler of the Esegel, and one of his sons was named Aḥmad in honour of the ambassador. According to the History of Jaʿfar he was succeeded in turn by two of his sons, Ḥasan, in about 925 to 930, and Mīkāˀīl, in about 930 to 943.
almagest: The work was originally called the Mathematical Syntaxis and consists of thirteen books. Book I outlines a cosmology in which the spherical Earth lies motionless at the centre of a spherical heaven, and introduces a table of chords and spherical trigonometry. Later books treat the length of the year and the motion of the Sun, the Moon and eclipses, the fixed stars, and the five planets that can be seen without a telescope, including their stations and retrograde motion. Ptolemy took over Hipparchus' model of the Sun and gave the Moon a further device, then built models for the other planets by adding a third device, the equant, where Hipparchus had failed.

Books VII and VIII hold a catalogue of 1022 stars in 48 constellations, each given an ecliptic longitude and latitude. It is the oldest star catalogue whose complete tables of coordinates and magnitudes survive. Its longitudes fit the middle of the first century CE better than the reign of Antoninus Pius, which Ptolemy gives as their date. Explanations offered include summation errors from Hipparchus' figure for precession, observations made earlier by Menelaus of Alexandria, and a miscalibrated instrument.

The first Arabic translations were made in the 9th century, in two separate efforts, one sponsored by the caliph al-Ma'mun, who received a copy as a condition of peace with the Byzantine emperor. The Arabic name, al-majisti, comes from the Greek megiste, a superlative of 'great'. No Latin translation existed before the 12th century. Gerard of Cremona finished his from the Arabic in 1175, working at the Toledo School of Translators, and it proved more influential than an earlier version made directly from Greek by Henry Aristippus.

In the 15th century a Greek text reached Western Europe. Regiomontanus made an abridged Latin version at the urging of Cardinal Bessarion, and George of Trebizond made a full translation with a commentary as long as the original, which drew criticism. The geocentric model of the work was accepted for more than 1,200 years, in the Byzantine and Islamic worlds and in Western Europe until the Scientific Revolution. Much of what is known of Hipparchus comes from it.

In 1977 Robert R. Newton argued in The Crime of Claudius Ptolemy that Ptolemy had invented or altered his observations. Bernard R. Goldstein and others rejected the charge of fraud, and Owen Gingerich, while noting some fishy numbers, did the same.
almanzor: Almanzor, born Muhammad ibn Abi Amir, was born around 938 or 939 in Torrox, a farm near the mouth of the Guadiaro river, to an Arab landowning family of Yemeni origin that had received lands there from Tariq ibn Ziyad. His father, Abd Allah, a pious man, died in Tripoli returning from the pilgrimage to Mecca.

As a youth he went to Córdoba and studied law and letters under his maternal uncle, since opportunities in the army were limited to Arabs and he meant to enter the administration. He joined the court administration and won the confidence of Subh, the mother of Caliph Al-Hakam II's children, whose patronage promoted him. He became director of the mint in 967 and quartermaster for General Ghalib ibn Abd al-Rahman's army in 973.

Al-Hakam II died on 1 October 976, leaving a son, Hisham, who was too young to rule. Ibn Abi Amir joined Ghalib and the chamberlain al-Mushafi in a triumvirate, then ruined al-Mushafi by gaining command of the capital's troops and promising to restore the army's prestige against Christian raids. In February 977 he led his first campaign, to Salamanca. After a clash in the spring of 980 over a campaign around Atienza he also eliminated Ghalib, his father-in-law. As chamberlain from 978 he held extraordinary power in al-Andalus and part of the Maghreb, while Hisham II was reduced to near-figurehead status.

He based his power on defending jihad, proclaimed in the caliph's name, and presented himself as a champion of Islam. He enlarged the mosque of Córdoba between 987 and 990 and purged works judged heretical from Al-Hakam's library. From 991 he made his son Abd al-Malik chamberlain beside himself. The faqihs, asked about replacing the caliph, refused, but he took the caliph's titles and powers and kept a parallel court at al-Zahira. He supervised Maghreb campaigns against the Fatimids and led about fifty-six against the Christian kingdoms, twenty of them between 977 and 985.

He died of illness at Medinaceli on 8 or 9 August 1002, aged about sixty-five, and commended the government to his son, who hurried to Córdoba to take his place. He was buried in the courtyard of his palace under the dust shaken from his servants' clothes after battles against the Christian kingdoms. Ibn Idhari gives an epitaph saying that no one like him would be given to the world again. His sons Abd al-Malik al-Muzaffar and Abd al-Rahman Sanchuelo governed after him until 1009.
almaty: Almaty lies in the foothills of the Trans-Ili Alatau mountains in southern Kazakhstan, near the border with Kyrgyzstan, at an elevation of 700 to 900 metres, with the Big Almaty and Small Almaty rivers running through it. The zone is seismically active, and three catastrophic earthquakes are recorded there before the late 19th century, in 1770, 1807 and 1865. The name comes from the medieval settlement Almatau, which stood near the present city, and a disputed theory derives it from the Kazakh word for apple.

In the Saka period, from 700 BCE to the beginning of the Christian era, the lands were held by the Saka and later the Wusun, who left burial mounds and settlements, among them the Issyk Kurgan, where the Golden Man was found. In the 12th century the region was ruled by the Qara Khitai until the Mongol invasion of 1218, and afterwards belonged to the Chagatai Khanate and Moghulistan. Russia absorbed the area in the 1850s.

Construction of Fort Zailiyskoe began on 4 February 1854, and before the year ended it was renamed Fort Vernoe, Loyal. Soviet power was established in Verny in 1918, and on 5 February 1921 the city was renamed Alma-Ata, one of its historical names. It was capital of the Kazakh ASSR from 1929 and of the Kazakh SSR from 1936 to 1991. Kazakhstan declared independence on 16 December 1991, and on 28 January 1993 the city took the Kazakh name Almaty. In 1997 the capital was moved to Akmola, renamed Astana in 1998.

Almaty is the most populous city in Kazakhstan, with more than two million residents, and is called the southern capital of the country. It is the second-largest city in Central Asia after Tashkent. It hosted the Alma-Ata Primary Healthcare Conference in 1978, and its landmarks include the Central State Museum of Kazakhstan, the Ascension Cathedral and the Green Bazaar.
almeria: Almería lies in south-eastern Iberia, between the eastern fringes of the Sierra de Gádor and the Andarax riverbed, along the Gulf of Almería on the Mediterranean. It has an exceptionally dry climate by European standards. The name comes from the Arabic Madīnat al-Mariyya, city of the watchtower. The settlement began as the port of Pechina and was first known as Mariyyat al-Bajjāna, Bajjāna being the Arabic name for Pechina.

The port became the base of the caliphal navy after 933 under Abd al-Rahman III, who after a devastating Fatimid naval attack in 955 decided to build the walls. A silk industry with hundreds of looms fed the economy, and Almería was also an important slave trade hub. After the Caliphate of Córdoba collapsed, it broke away around 1014 and was ruled as an independent taifa until it fell to Almoravid control in 1091. In the 11th and 12th centuries it was the third-largest city of Al-Andalus and its largest industrial centre, with over 800 workshops making tiraz textiles.

Alfonso VII led a crusade of Catalans, Genoese, Pisans and Franks against the city from 11 July 1147, and it was captured on 17 October 1147, ending its period of splendour. By 1157 it was in Almohad hands but did not recover its wealth. After Ibn Hud was assassinated in Almería in 1238 it passed to the Emirate of Granada, and it survived an Aragonese siege in 1309. It submitted to the Catholic Monarchs on 22 December 1489, and the Jewish community, dating to the 10th century, was expelled in 1492.

An earthquake devastated the city in 1522, and those who had remained Muslim were expelled after the War of Las Alpujarras in 1568. Barbary pirates raided the coast into the early 18th century, and mining in the hinterland later brought a revival. In the Spanish Civil War it was the last major Andalusian city to fall to Francoist forces, in 1939.

Almería is the capital of the province of the same name, and the municipality has 201,946 residents. Its Alcazaba, begun in the 10th century and damaged by the earthquake of 1522, is the second largest of the Muslim fortresses of Andalusia after the Alhambra. Greenhouse agriculture has dominated the local economy for about fifty years, and the arid Tabernas desert was the setting for many films.
almodovar-del-rio: Almodóvar del Río is a municipality in the province of Córdoba, in the Valle Medio del Guadalquivir, with the Sierra Morena to the north and open countryside to the south. The town stands 121 metres above sea level and the municipality covers about 173 square kilometres. A large part of its northern area is protected as part of the Sierra de Hornachuelos Natural Park.

The oldest settlements date to the Lower Paleolithic, and a cave on Cerro del Castillo held remains from the Chalcolithic. Iberian pottery shows continued settlement, and a stone frieze of 4th–3rd century BCE shows a deer hunted by horsemen, followed by a cart pulled by donkeys. In Roman times the main settlement lay around Cerro del Castillo and is generally, with some problems, identified with Carbula, a town named by Pliny, which was integrated into the territory of Colonia Patricia Corduba. The area was marked by olive cultivation and an extensive trade in olive oil exported in amphorae, and by underground aqueducts at Cortijo Nuevo and Fuenreal. Settlement continued in the Visigothic period.

After the Muslim conquest a fortress was established on the hill in 740 and the town was called al-Mudawwar al-Adna, the round one, from the shape of the hill. In the 11th century it belonged first to the taifa of Carmona and then to that of Seville; under the Almoravids it returned to Córdoba and in the 12th and part of the 13th century it depended on the Almohad court of Seville. In 1226 the Muslim king of Baeza was decapitated at Almodóvar del Río, accused by the Almohads of treason for his alliance with Ferdinand III of Castile and León. In 1240 the town was incorporated into the Crown of Castile by treaty, and in 1243 it joined the Council of Córdoba.

In 1394 Frederick of Castile, an illegitimate son of Henry II, died as a prisoner in the castle. In the 15th century the castle belonged to the House of Baena y Cabra and had been a residence of Peter I and Henry II, and a prison. The name Almodóvar del Río first appears around 1473.

The municipality had 8,093 inhabitants in 2022. Its castle remains the dominant feature on the hill above the Guadalquivir. In the 19th century the end of the manorial regime and the confiscations of church and municipal land strengthened the large estates, which led to social conflict that appeared during the Second Republic and the Spanish Civil War.
almohad-caliphate: The movement began with Ibn Tumart, a member of the Masmuda, an Amazigh tribal confederation of the Atlas Mountains of southern Morocco, at a time when the Almoravids, a Sanhaja Berber dynasty, ruled Morocco, Mauritania, western Algeria and parts of Spain and Portugal. His central principle was a strict tawhid, which denied that God's attributes exist independently, and he revolted against what he saw as anthropomorphism in Muslim orthodoxy. His followers were the al-Muwaḥḥidūn, those who affirm the unity of God. They recognised him as the Mahdi around 1121, and he made Tinmel in the Atlas his base.

Ibn Tumart died in August 1130, and his death was kept secret for three years, a period the Almohad chroniclers called ghayba or occultation. His successor Abd al-Mu'min, a Zenata Berber from Tagra in Algeria and so an outsider among the Masmuda, defeated his rivals, won back wavering tribes and was proclaimed caliph. He overthrew the Almoravids and captured Marrakesh in 1147. Rule extended across the Maghreb by 1159. Between 1146 and 1173 the Almohads took over the Muslim principalities of Iberia and moved the capital of Muslim Iberia from Córdoba to Seville, where the Giralda was erected in 1184.

Abu Ya'qub Yusuf I and Abu Yusuf Ya'qub al-Mansur were able rulers. Their government at first drove many Jewish and Christian subjects into the Christian states, and the Almohads rejected the status of dhimmi. Ya'qub al-Mansur earned his title by defeating Alfonso VIII of Castile at Alarcos in 1195. In 1212 his successor Muhammad al-Nasir was defeated at Las Navas de Tolosa by Castile, Aragon and Navarre. Córdoba fell in 1236 and Seville in 1248. In the Maghreb tribes and districts revolted piecemeal and the Marinids rose from 1215. The last ruler, Idris al-Wathiq, was reduced to Marrakesh and murdered by a slave in 1269.

The army was made up of Berber tribesmen in a hierarchy that reflected their standing in the movement, led by tribal shaykhs, with Arab auxiliaries, Christian mercenaries, black soldiers and the Ghuzz, who were paid more regularly than regular Almohad soldiers. The Friday sermon was given in Arabic and Berber. They worked to suppress the Maliki school of law, publicly burning copies of the Muwatta.

The period saw philosophers such as Ibn Tufayl, Ibn Rushd (Averroes) and Ibn ʿArabī. Almohad architecture, built mostly of rammed earth and brick, is considered a formative stage of Moroccan and Moorish building, with major sites at Fez, Marrakesh, Rabat and Seville. Their banners were white.
almora: Almora lies at about 1,604 m on a horse-saddle-shaped ridge at the southern edge of the Kumaon Hills of the Central Himalaya, in Uttarakhand, 365 km north-east of New Delhi. The eastern end of the ridge is called Talifat and the western end Selifat, and the market stands at the top, where the two meet. Pine, deodar and fir forests surround it, and the Koshi and Suyal rivers flow beside it. According to one account, the name comes from bhilmora, a sorrel used to clean the vessels of the sun temple at Katarmal; the people who brought it were called Bhilmori, later Almori. When Bhishm Chand laid the foundation of the town he named it Alamnagar, and earlier it was known as Rajapur.

The Mahabharata and the Vishnu Purana give early accounts of settlement in the region. The Katyuris are recorded as the dominant clans in copper and stone inscriptions before the Chand dynasty, whose rule is dated from 953 to the late 18th century. Almora was founded by Kalyan Chand, though the Chands are also said to have made it the seat of the strongest hill power in 1563. From then the Kumaon kingdom extended over the districts of Almora and Nainital. In 1688 King Udyot Chand built several temples at Almora, among them Tripur Sundari, Udyot Chandeshwer and Parbateshwer, to mark his victory over Garhwal and Doti.

Long wars with the rulers of Garhwal ended in the destruction of the Chand lands and the establishment of Gurkha rule. Francis Hamilton was told that Almora held around a thousand houses during Gorkha rule, and G. W. Traill counted 742 houses and 3,505 people in 1821. In 1871 Buddhiballav Pant founded a debating club in the town, which led to a press and to the Almora Akhbar, the region's first Hindi weekly.

Almora is a municipal corporation and cantonment town, the administrative headquarters of Almora district, and is considered the cultural heart of the Kumaon region. Its population was 35,513 at the 2011 census, and Kumaoni is the mother tongue of most of its people. Rabindranath Tagore spent time in the area, Swami Vivekananda visited three times, and Uday Shankar established a dance school there in the late 1930s.
almoravid-empire: The Almoravids came from Saharan Sanhaja nomads, a coalition of the Lamtuna, Gudala and Massufa, living between the Senegal and Draa rivers. The Lamtuna were the first and main founding tribe, around Awdaghust, and the Tuareg are believed to be their descendants. They had been converted to Islam in the 9th century. Around 1040 Yahya ibn Ibrahim, a Gudala chieftain, returned from pilgrimage to Mecca and met the Maliki jurist Abu Imran al-Fasi at Kairouan, where he voiced his disappointment at the lack of religious education among his people.

On Abu Imran's recommendation he went to the ribat of Waggag ibn Zallu in the Sous valley, which was called Dar al-Murabitin, and Waggag sent his student Abdallah ibn Yasin to preach Maliki Islam to the Sanhaja. The name Almoravid, al-Murabitun, is tied to the ribat, a frontier monastery-fortress. Medieval writers disagree on when and why it was adopted: Ibn Abi Zar says Ibn Yasin built a ribat on an offshore island, while Ibn Idhari says he chose it to raise morale after a costly battle in the Draa valley c. 1054.

Abdallah ibn Yasin sought to impose a rigorist, orthodox Maliki Sunni Islam, and he died in 1058 or 1059. The Almoravids founded Marrakesh as their capital c. 1070 and then divided into a northern branch under Yusuf ibn Tashfin and a southern branch in the Sahara under Abu Bakr ibn Umar. Yusuf ibn Tashfin crossed to Iberia six times between 1086 and 1102, and the Battle of Sagrajas in 1086 was among their signature victories. This united the Maghreb and al-Andalus politically for the first time. After Yusuf failed to take Ceuta in 1078 for lack of sea power he built a fleet and founded a shipyard at Ksar es-Seghir.

Their rulers took the title Amir al-Muslimin, Prince of the Muslims, while acknowledging the Abbasid caliphs, whose black colour they adopted for their banners. Almoravid power in al-Andalus declined after the loss of Zaragoza in 1118. The Almohad rebellion, begun by Ibn Tumart in the 1120s, brought them down: the last ruler, Ishaq ibn Ali, was killed when the Almohads captured Marrakesh in 1147.

Their period contributed to the Islamization of the Sahara and the urbanization of the western Maghreb, and contact between al-Andalus and Africa spurred cultural developments, creating a widespread Andalusi–Maghribi style. Marble tombstones with Kufic inscriptions survive from Almería, and the empire also produced minbars at Córdoba and textiles at Almería, Málaga and Seville. Christian chronicles after the death of El Cid told of a Turkish woman leading 300 black female archers; it has been suggested that the legend arose from the veiled warriors, whose robes were dyed with indigo.
almos: The Gesta Hungarorum, written around 1200 or 1210 by an anonymous notary of Béla III, says that Álmos descended from the line of Attila the Hun and was born to the Scythian leader Ügyek and Emese, a daughter of Prince Eunedubelian. The 14th-century Illuminated Chronicle names Előd, a son of Ügyek, as his father instead. Historian Gyula Kristó suggested that both names may be inventions of the chroniclers.

Both chronicles preserve a legend that his pregnant mother dreamed of a bird of prey, likened to a hawk, which made her pregnant. The notary connected the name with the Hungarian word álom, dream. Simon of Kéza, a chronicler of the late 13th century, called Álmos of the Turul kindred. Other scholars have argued for a Turkic origin of the name, while the linguist Bela Kalman held it to be a Hungarian formation from a Finno-Ugric word.

According to the uniform account of the Hungarian chronicles, Álmos was the first head of the loose federation of the Hungarian tribes from around 850. The Gesta Hungarorum says the heads of the seven tribes elected him and swore an oath sealed with their blood in a single vessel. Pál Engel judged this account of a treaty by blood to reflect its author's political thought rather than actual events. Whether Álmos was the sacred ruler (kende) or the military leader (gyula) is still debated.

Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus, writing around 950, tells a different story: the Khazar khagan sought a prince for the Hungarians, Levedi proposed Álmos or his son Árpád, and the Hungarians chose Árpád. Kristó and others reject the omission of Álmos. The Hungarians seem to have acted independently of the Khazars from about 860, and the Annals of St. Bertin record an incursion into the realm of Louis the German in 862.

The Hungarians left the Pontic steppes around 895 after a conflict between the First Bulgarian Empire and the Byzantine Empire brought a counter-invasion by the Bulgars and Pechenegs. The Gesta Hungarorum says Álmos appointed Árpád as leader at Ungvár and then drops out of the story. The Illuminated Chronicle says he could not enter Pannonia, because he was killed in Transylvania.

Kristó read this as the memory of a ritual sacrifice of a sacred leader after a catastrophic defeat. András Róna-Tas instead saw a political murder committed or initiated by his own son. Victor Spinei doubted that he died in Transylvania at all, since the Gesta says the Hungarians bypassed that region. No source names Álmos's wife, and Árpád is his only child known by name.
almos-duke-of-croatia: Álmos was the younger of the two surviving sons of the future King Géza I, probably by his first wife, Sophia; the historians Gyula Kristó and Márta Font place the births of both brothers around 1070. When Géza died on 25 April 1077 his sons were minors, and the throne passed to their uncle, Ladislaus I, who unusually chose the elder brother, Coloman, for a career in the Church. Álmos held Slavonia between 1084 and 1091 and Croatia between 1091 and 1095. In spring 1095, falling gravely ill on a campaign against Bohemia, Ladislaus named Álmos his heir, and Coloman fled to Poland.

After Ladislaus's death Coloman returned, and early in 1096 he was crowned at Székesfehérvár. The Illuminated Chronicle says Álmos yielded the crown and received the ducatus, one third of the kingdom, with full rights. While Coloman campaigned in Croatia in 1097, Álmos gathered troops, but in 1098 the two armies met at Tiszavárkony on opposite banks of the Tisza and their commanders refused to fight, forcing a peace.

When Coloman had his four-year-old son Stephen crowned in 1105, Álmos rebelled, sought help from Emperor Henry IV and then from his brother-in-law Boleslaw III of Poland, and took the fortress of Abaújvár. While he was on pilgrimage to the Holy Land, Coloman took over his duchy. Accused, falsely according to the Chronicle, of plotting the king's murder at the consecration of his monastery at Dömös, he fled to Passau, and Henry V besieged Pressburg on his behalf in September 1108 without success. After a further conspiracy Coloman had Álmos and his young son Béla blinded.

Álmos lived in seclusion at Dömös until, fearing King Stephen II, he fled to the Byzantine Empire, probably about 1125. Emperor John II Komnenos settled him and his followers in a town in Macedonia, gave him the name Constantine and refused Stephen's demand for his expulsion; a war between the two realms followed from 1127 to 1129. Álmos died in exile on 1 September 1127. His son became king as Béla II in 1131, and his remains were brought back to Hungary in 1137.
almunecar: The Phoenicians first settled at Almuñécar in about 800 BCE, and over six hundred years it grew into an important port named Ex or Sexi, with a large fish-salting and curing industry that was a major supplier of Greece and Rome. It also produced garum, a prized fish paste made by fermenting the intestines of small fish. Most archaeological evidence comes from Phoenician cemeteries, the earlier Laurita necropolis on the hillside of Cerro San Cristobal and the later necropolis at Punte de Noy.

The Romans came to southern Spain in 218 BCE during the Second Punic War, and in 49 BCE the town, one of twenty cities in Spain so honoured, was given the title Firmium Julium Sexi in recognition of its loyalty to Rome. During about 700 years of Roman rule the fish industry was rebuilt and modernised, as excavations in the Majuelo Botanical Gardens show. In the 1st century CE the Romans built four miles of water conduit in the valleys of the Rio Seco and Rio Verde, with five aqueducts. Four are still in use, adapted by the Moors for crop irrigation. The fish-curing industry declined rapidly under the Visigoths, who became the dominant power in Hispania by 456.

In 755 the Umayyad Abd ar-Rahman I, founder of the Emirate of Córdoba, arrived from North Africa. The castle remained the stronghold and seat of government, and under the Moors the town flourished as a fishing town called al-Munakkab, from which the present name derives. It surrendered and was annexed to the Kingdom of Castille in 1489. King Carlos I granted the town its coat of arms in 1526 for destroying a Berber raiding force. In 1563 the Ottoman corsair Turgut Reis captured the coastal settlements of the area, Almuñécar among them, with 4,000 prisoners. The castle was last defended by the French in the Napoleonic Wars, and on 27 May 1812 the crew of HMS Hyacinth and Spanish partisans forced the garrison to flee.

Almuñécar is a city and municipality on the Mediterranean coast in the Costa Granadina, in the province of Granada, and some inhabitants still call themselves Sexitanos. Its museum, in the Castle of San Miguel and the Cueva de Siete Palacios, which is in fact the largest remnant of a Roman palace found in the town, displays Phoenician grave goods and other finds. Since 1975 it has been one of the main tourist towns of the province.
alnwick: Alnwick is the traditional county town of Northumberland, standing on the south bank of the River Aln, 32 miles south of Berwick-upon-Tweed and the Scottish border, 5 miles inland from the North Sea at Alnmouth and 34 miles north of Newcastle upon Tyne. Its name comes from the Old English wic, meaning dairy farm or settlement, and the name of the river. The town dates to about 600 CE and thrived as an agricultural centre. It was a staging post on the Great North Road between Edinburgh and London, and its history is largely the history of the castle and its lords.

William the Conqueror's standard-bearer Gilbert Tyson received the estate. It then passed to the De Vesci family, who held it for over 200 years, and in 1309 to the House of Percy. Ivo de Vesci founded the castle as a timber structure about 1096, and David I of Scotland captured it in 1136, the first recorded capture. Alnwick Abbey, for Premonstratensian canons, was founded in 1147, and about then the castle was rebuilt in stone. Malcolm III of Scotland was killed in the first Battle of Alnwick in 1093, and in 1174 William the Lion was captured by about 400 mounted knights led by Ranulf de Glanvill.

Scottish raiders burnt much of the town in 1424 and again in 1448, after which the town was walled. Henry IV took the castle in 1403 after the Percys challenged him. In the Wars of the Roses it changed hands repeatedly, and finally fell to the Yorkists on 23 June 1463, which made it, according to the historian Dan Spencer, the most besieged place in the country in that war.

Both Alnwick Abbey and Hulne Priory, a Carmelite friary founded about 1240, were suppressed in 1539, and the Percys left the castle to decay until they resumed residence in the mid-18th century, since when they have remained there. The castle stands in grounds landscaped by Capability Brown and is one of the homes of the Duke of Northumberland. The Bondgate Tower is the only upstanding part of the medieval town wall. St Michael's Church on Bailiffgate dates from the 15th century with fragments of the 12th. Brizlee Tower, designed by Robert Adam in 1777 and erected in 1781, stands in Hulne Park. The population at the 2021 census was 8,430.
alodia: Alodia, also called Alwa, lay in what is now central Sudan, in a heartland called the Gezira, a fertile plain between the White and Blue Niles. The name may be of considerable antiquity: Alut on the stele of the Kushite king Nastasen, and Alwa in Pliny the Elder's list of Kushite towns. The Kingdom of Kush was in decline by the early 4th century, and Nubian speakers settled in the Nile valley. An Aksumite inscription describes an expedition that plundered several Kushite towns, Alwa among them. Alodia was founded sometime after Kush fell and is first mentioned in records in 569.

Alodia was the last of the three Nubian kingdoms to become Christian. According to John of Ephesus, its king knew of the conversion of Nobadia in 543 and asked for a bishop. In 580 Longinus was sent and baptised the king, his family and the nobility, and Alodia came under the Coptic Patriarchate of Alexandria. Christianity probably spread slowly among the rural population. Alodia possibly reached its peak in the 9th to 12th centuries, when records show it exceeded its northern neighbour Makuria in size, military power and wealth.

From the 12th century, and especially the 13th, Alodia declined, possibly because of invasions from the south, droughts and shifting trade routes. Ibn Sa'id al-Maghribi says a people called the Damadim attacked Nubia in 1220. By around 1500 Soba had fallen. It is unclear whether Arabs under Abdallah Jammah or the Funj under Amara Dunqas destroyed it, but most modern scholars favour the Arabs. In 1504-1505 the Funj founded their sultanate, incorporating Abdallah Jammah's domain. David Reubeni, who visited in 1523, found Soba in ruins, and oral traditions say Alodia survived as the Kingdom of Fazughli.

Alodia was a large, multicultural state, essentially Nubian, administered by a powerful king and provincial governors he appointed. According to al-Aswani the king reigned as an absolute monarch, and the throne passed to the king's sister's son. Soba prospered as a trading hub, with goods arriving from Makuria, the Middle East, western Africa, India and China. Literacy in both Nubian and Greek flourished, and Greek was the language of the liturgy. About 400 churches reportedly existed, though only seven have been identified.
alonso-de-ojeda: Alonso de Ojeda was born around 1466 in Torrejoncillo del Rey, New Castile. His father, Rodrigo de Huete, was a minor noble who fought for Isabel in the War of the Castilian Succession, and she took the son under her protection. In his youth he served the Duke of Medinaceli, Luis de la Cerda, and distinguished himself in the conquest of Granada. Bartolomé de las Casas described him as small but with every bodily perfection.

Ojeda captained a ship on Columbus's second voyage, which left in September 1493. On Hispaniola he led armed parties, one of which brought back gold from the Cibao in January 1494. At a river crossing he arrested a local cacique on a charge of stolen clothes and cut the ears off one captive, an act that turned the local people against the Spaniards. According to Las Casas, he persuaded the cacique Caonabo to wear polished brass manacles as a mark of royalty and brought him to Columbus. After a rebellion late in 1494, a force of 500 led by Ojeda defeated the rebels, and some 1,500 were taken as slaves.

He returned to Spain in 1496 and was commissioned by the Catholic Monarchs, without Columbus's permission, to sail again. With Juan de la Cosa and Amerigo Vespucci he left on 18 May 1499 with three caravels and explored the coast from the Gulf of Paria to the Guajira Peninsula. The name Venezuela, Little Venice, is said to come from stilt villages of the Wayuu people. A second voyage in 1502 founded Santa Cruz on the Guajira, the first Spanish settlement on the American mainland, but it lasted under three months, and Ojeda was imprisoned on Hispaniola until 1504.

In 1508 he was made governor of New Andalusia. Landing near Cartagena in 1509, his party raided villages for slaves and suffered a heavy defeat at Turbaco, where Juan de la Cosa died. On 20 January 1510 he founded San Sebastián de Urabá, a fort that soon ran short of food. Ojeda left Francisco Pizarro in charge and never returned; Pizarro abandoned the post.

Ojeda was shipwrecked on the south coast of Cuba and crossed it on foot, losing half his companions, before Pánfilo de Narváez rescued the survivors. He gave up his governorship and spent his last five years in Santo Domingo, dying around 1515 in the monastery of San Francisco, sick and poor. He asked to be buried beneath its door so that visitors would walk over his grave. Las Casas wrote that he had stolen much gold and pearls from the Indians. The city of Ciudad Ojeda, on Lake Maracaibo, is named after him.
alor-setar: Alor Setar lies in the north-west of Peninsular Malaysia, at the edge of the Strait of Malacca, in the district of Kota Setar. Several rivers run around it, among them the Kedah, Langgar and Tajar. Mount Keriang, a limestone hill of 217.9 metres, rises nearby and contains a network of caves. The climate is tropical monsoon, with average highs around 32 °C and about 2,300 millimetres of rain a year. The name joins two Malay words, alor, a small stream, and setar, a tree related to the mango, Bouea macrophylla. Rice growing was traditionally the basis of the local economy.

The city was established in the 18th century by a sultan of Kedah as the eighth administrative centre of the sultanate since its founding in 1136. The site was a small village, which the sultan found well placed at the point where the two estuaries of the Kedah River meet. With the agreement of several nobles it was founded as Kota Setar, the Town of Setar. The sultan lived in the Istana Kota Setar.

In 1770 a Bugis fleet under Raja Haji destroyed the palace and the Balai Besar, the Grand Hall. In 1771 Francis Light for the British and Sultan Abdullah Mukarram Shah made an agreement to halt Bugis influence in Kedah. On 17 March 1805, during the coronation of Ahmad Tajuddin Halim Shah II, Siamese forces occupied the capital, and the sultan withdrew to Penang and later Malacca. The town stood still for twenty years. He was restored in 1842, and the capital moved briefly to Kota Kuala Muda before returning to Kota Setar. The railway station opened in 1915 and the airport in 1929, among the early ones in Malaya.

Alor Setar is the state capital of Kedah and the seat of the Central State Administration Centre, and the sultan's official residence is at Anak Bukit. It is the second-largest city in the state, after Sungai Petani. Its census population was 374,051 in 2020. The name was changed to Alor Star at a ceremony proclaiming city status on 21 December 2003 and the old name was restored on 15 January 2009. Tunku Abdul Rahman, the first prime minister of Malaysia, and Mahathir Mohamad were born there.
aloysius-gonzaga: Aloysius, in Italian Luigi, was born on 9 March 1568 at his family's castle in Castiglione delle Stiviere, between Brescia and Mantua, the eldest of eight children of Ferrante Gonzaga, Marquess of Castiglione, and Marta Tana di Santena. His father expected him to become a soldier and sent him to a military camp at five. In 1576 he and his brother Rodolfo were sent to the court of the Grand Duke Francesco I de' Medici at Florence, where a kidney disease began that troubled him all his life. He read about the saints and prayed much.

He received his First Communion from Cardinal Charles Borromeo on 22 July 1580. After reading a book about Jesuit missionaries in India he wanted to become a missionary. In 1582 the family were at Madrid, where he and Rodolfo served as pages to the Infante Diego, and he decided to join the Jesuits. His father was furious and prevented him, and after the family's return to Italy in 1584 relatives tried to persuade him to become a secular priest.

In November 1585 Gonzaga gave up all rights of inheritance, which was confirmed by the emperor, and on 25 November 1585 he was accepted into the Society of Jesus in Rome. He was asked to moderate his asceticism. On 25 November 1587 he took the three vows of chastity, poverty and obedience, and in 1588 he began to study theology.

In 1591 a plague broke out in Rome. The Jesuits opened a hospital, and Gonzaga volunteered, begging alms and carrying the dying from the streets. He confessed privately to his spiritual director, Robert Bellarmine, that he had to work hard to overcome his physical repulsion. He was infected and was bedridden by 3 March 1591, a few days before his 23rd birthday.

He died just before midnight on 21 June 1591, after Bellarmine gave him the last rites. He was buried in the church that became Sant'Ignazio in Rome. Pope Paul V beatified him on 19 October 1605, and Pope Benedict XIII canonised him with the Jesuit novice Stanislaus Kostka on 31 December 1726. In 1729 Benedict XIII declared him patron of youth and students. His feast day is 21 June. Schools and colleges bear his name, and in art he is shown with a lily, a cross, a skull and a rosary.
alp-arslan: Alp Arslan was the son of Chaghri Beg, a co-founder of the Seljuk Empire, and the nephew of the Seljuk sultan Tughril I. Sources disagree on his birth; 20 January 1029, which Ibn al-Athir gives as an alternative, is generally accepted because the dates of 1032–1033 do not fit the known facts of his life. Following the Battle of Dandanaqan he entered Tughril's service at a young age, and in about three years he became a respected figure whose counsel was heeded on complex affairs of the empire.

He accompanied Tughril on campaigns in the south against the Fatimids, then worked in administration in Khorasan at his father's suggestion. There his father introduced him to Nizam al-Mulk, later his vizier. During a campaign against the Ghaznavids in 1043–44, Chaghri Beg fell ill and put his son in command; Alp Arslan defeated the Ghaznavids, and the Seljuks took Termez, Kunduz and other lands of Tokharistan. He was Seljuk malik of Khorasan from 1060 to 1063.

In 1063 Alp Arslan defeated his rivals and became sultan, ruling until 1072. His strength lay in the military sphere, while his able vizier Nizam al-Mulk founded the administrative organisation that marked the sultanate under Alp Arslan and his son Malik Shah. Military iqtas governed by Seljuk princes supported the soldiery and settled the nomadic Turks within the established agricultural society. This allowed him to keep a large standing army without relying on tribute from conquest, and taxes on merchants funded his continuous wars.

Muslim sources present him as deeply devout and just. He built mosques in conquered non-Muslim lands, was devoted to the Hanafi school and kept a qadi at his side, even in battle. He believed the survival of the Seljuk Empire depended on Sunni Islam and was strict towards Shia Islam.

After the victory at Manzikert the sultan's dominion covered much of western Asia, and he prepared to march against Turkestan. On the banks of the Oxus he had to subdue fortresses, one defended by the rebel Yusuf al-Kharezmi. When the captive was brought before him, Alp Arslan sentenced him to a slow death. Yusuf drew a dagger and rushed at the throne; the sultan, a skilled archer, stopped his guards and drew his bow, but his foot slipped and he was stabbed in the chest. He died four days later, on 24 November 1072, and was buried at Merv, having named his 18-year-old son Malik Shah as successor. His conquest of Anatolia from the Byzantines is seen as one of the precursors of the Crusades.
alp-tegin: Alp-Tegin came from the nomadic Turks of the Central Asian steppes. He was captured and brought through the Samanid slave trade to Bukhara, the Samanid capital, where he was raised at court. Although of Turkic origin he became highly Persianized. Under Nuh I, who reigned from 943 to 954, he was appointed head of the royal guard, and under Nuh's son Abd al-Malik I, who reigned from 954 to 961, he became governor of Balkh.

By 961 Alp-Tegin was commander in chief of the Samanid army in Khorasan, succeeding Abu Mansur Muhammad. He arrived in Nishapur on 10 February 961 with his vizier Abu Abdallah Muhammad ibn al-Shibli, and he helped appoint Muhammad Bal'ami as vizier, becoming his close ally. When Abd al-Malik I died in November 961, Alp-Tegin and Bal'ami tried to place the dead ruler's young son Nasr on the throne so as to rule for him.

Powerful figures such as Fa'iq Khassa favoured Abd al-Malik's brother Mansur I, who became ruler. Bal'ami went over to Fa'iq's side, leaving Alp-Tegin isolated, and Mansur dismissed him from the governorship of Khorasan.

Alp-Tegin took his guard of Turkic slave soldiers and a group of Iranian ghazis to Balkh, where in April 962 he defeated an army sent by Mansur I. He then went south over the Hindu Kush to Ghazna, a small town in Zabulistan between Kabul and Kandahar held by the local Lawik dynasty, defeating the forces of the rulers of Bamiyan and Kabul on the way. He seized Ghazna from Abu Bakr Lawik, a kinsman of the Kabulshah, and secured his position by receiving investiture from the Samanids as governor.

He died in September 963 and was succeeded by his son Abu Ishaq Ibrahim. In 977 the Turks of the town appointed Sabuktigin, a slave bought by Alp-Tegin who had accompanied him, as ruler. That marked the start of the Ghaznavid dynasty, which went on to conquer Transoxiana and Khurasan.
alpes-graiae: The province of the Alpes Graiae et Poeninae joined two Alpine districts, the Alpes Poeninae (also called Vallis Poenina) and the Alpes Graiae (also called Alpes Atrectianae). It comprised the modern Canton of Valais in Switzerland, the Tarantaise Valley, Beaufortain and Haut-Faucigny in France, and the Aosta Valley in Italy. It was one of three provinces straddling the Alps between modern France and Italy, together with the Alpes Maritimae and the Alpes Cottiae.

The names are of local origin. According to Livy, Poeninae comes from an indigenous deity, Poeninus, attested on inscriptions and in the cult title Jupiter Poeninus; the name survives in the Pennine Alps and Valais. Xavier Delamarre proposed a Celtic god *Graios as the source of Graiae, while Guy Barruol suggested that Atrectianae may come from an unattested local king, *Atrectius, by analogy with the Alpes Cottiae, though no direct evidence for such a ruler exists.

At the time of the Roman conquest the Valais was inhabited by Celtic tribes known as the Vallenses: the Nantuates, Veragri, Seduni and Uberi. After the Roman invasion led by Augustus in 16–15 BCE the area was placed under military control, under a praefectus Raetis, Vindolicis, vallis Poeninae, and incorporated into the province of Raetia et Vindelicia, which stretched between the central Alps and the Danube.

Under Claudius (41–54 CE) the Vallensian tribes received Latin rights and were grouped into a single civitas Vallensium. Most scholars place the start of the administrative reorganisation that linked the Vallis Poenina to the Alpes Graiae, the Ceutron territory west of the Little St Bernard Pass, in this period. An inscription of his reign still shows the valley under the procurator of Raetia, however, and some scholars date the definitive union to the reign of Septimius Severus (193–211) instead.

By the 2nd century the combined province had a procurator seated at Axima, which became Forum Claudii Ceutronum (modern Aime-la-Plagne), the chief town of the Graian division. He was assisted by a praefectus at Octodurus, which became Forum Claudii Vallensium (Martigny), the centre of the Poenine district. An inscription of 193–235 uses the variant Alpium Atrectianarum et Vallis Poeninae.

Under the reforms of Diocletian (284–305) the province was placed under a praeses in the Dioecesis Galliarum. The first bishop of the region, Theodul, is mentioned in 381. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire the region was invaded by the Burgundians and joined their kingdom. It passed to the Frankish Kingdom in 534 and was briefly invaded by the Lombards in 574.
alpheios: The Alpheios drains a valley system in the centre of the Peloponnesus. Like most Greek rivers it has no single source but begins where several springs and intermittent streams join, and its source has long been disputed. In limestone country such as the Peloponnesus, rivers can run underground for some distance, and some have tried to connect the Alpheios by underground channels to the high plateau of central Arcadia. Published lengths run from 110 to 113 km, most of them measured from a point about 4.2 km south of Megalopoli.

The catchment covers between 3,610 and 3,810 km2 by different studies, about a quarter of the Peloponnesus, with a maximum elevation of 2,253 m. About 60 per cent of it lies in Arcadia, 30 per cent in Elis and 10 per cent in Achaea. The river passes the tributary mouths of the Elissonas near Thoknia and the Lousios below Karytaina, flows north-west past Andritsaina, and is joined near Tripotamia by the Ladon and the Erymanthos. It then turns west at Olympia and empties into the Gulf of Kyparissia of the Ionian Sea south of Pyrgos. Near Megalopoli it runs through a steep gorge that served as a defence against enemies on foot.

The right bank of the valley formed a natural defensive zone. When Dorian highlanders from central Greece overran the coastal regions of the Peloponnesus from about 1000 BCE, expelling or subjugating the Mycenaean population, they could not climb the mountains of central Arcadia, whose people kept their culture and political independence. The Dorians kept the valley, which accounts for the predominance of Doric architecture at Olympia. In antiquity the road linking Patras and Kalamata ran along the river for most of its length east of Olympia.

In Greek mythology the Alpheus and the Peneus were the two rivers that Heracles redirected in his fifth labour to clean the Augean Stables in a single day. Virgil's Aeneid describes the Alpheus flowing under the sea to resurface at Ortygia in Sicily, and the nymph Arethusa, turned into a fountain, was called Alpheias because her stream was believed to be connected underground to the river. Samuel Taylor Coleridge's Kubla Khan refers to the river as Alph, though he set it in Mongolia.

The river is among the 45 permanently flowing rivers counted among the 765 recorded in Greece. It has been widened by damming, partly straightened by embankments and used for irrigation and municipal water, and the Flokas Dam, a hydroelectric facility, impounds it before it reaches the sea. Lignite is mined in the upper valley near Megalopoli, where a power company opened a lignite-burning plant in 1969. The gorge near Megalopoli is popular for rafting.
alphonse-count-of-poitiers: Alphonse was born at Poissy on 11 November 1220, a son of King Louis VIII of France and Blanche of Castile. He was the younger brother of King Louis IX and the older brother of Count Charles I of Anjou. By the terms of his father's will he received an appanage of Poitou and Auvergne, and Louis IX won the battle of Taillebourg in the Saintonge War together with him against a revolt allied with King Henry III of England. In 1229 Blanche, as regent, forced the Treaty of Paris on Count Raymond VII of Toulouse, which stipulated that a brother of the king would marry Raymond's daughter Joan; Alphonse married her in 1237.

Alphonse took part in two crusades with Louis IX, the Seventh Crusade in 1248 and the Eighth in 1270. For the first he raised a large sum and a substantial force and reached Damietta on 24 October 1249, after the town had already been captured. He sailed for home on 10 August 1250. His father-in-law had died while he was away, and Alphonse went directly to Toulouse to take possession; some resistance to his accession was suppressed with the help of Blanche, regent in Louis's absence.

Aside from the crusades, Alphonse stayed mainly in Paris, governing his estates through officials, inspectors who reviewed their work and a constant stream of messages. He repaired the effects of the Albigensian war and made a first attempt at administrative centralisation, preparing the way for union with the crown. On 8 October 1268 he had all Jews throughout his lands arrested and their property confiscated.

Alphonse accompanied his brother on the Eighth Crusade but did not return, dying at Savona in Italy on 21 August 1271 on his way home. His wife Joan died four days later. Their death without heirs raised questions about succession: Charles of Anjou claimed that the lands should be redistributed within the family, but in 1283 the Parlement decided that the County of Toulouse should revert to the crown if there were no male heirs. Joan's will, leaving her lands to her nearest female relative Philippa de Lomagne, was invalidated in 1274. A bequest in Alphonse's will giving his wife's lands in the Comtat Venaissin to the Holy See was allowed, and the territory remained papal until 1791.
alphonse-de-lamartine: Alphonse Marie Louis de Prat de Lamartine was born in Mâcon, Burgundy, on 21 October 1790, into a family of the French provincial nobility, and spent his youth at the family estate. His first collection of poems, Les Méditations Poétiques, appeared in 1820 and brought him instant fame. It included the partly autobiographical Le Lac, dedicated to Julie Charles, which describes a couple's fervent love from the point of view of the bereaved man. He was made a Chevalier of the Legion of Honour in 1825, worked for the French embassy in Italy from 1825 to 1828 and was elected to the Académie française in 1829.

Lamartine began as a moderate royalist, failed in his first run for Parliament in 1831 and was elected to the Chamber of Deputies in 1833. Asked which side of the chamber he would sit on, he answered on the ceiling. He sat in opposition, founded his own Social Party under Saint-Simonian influence and became a prominent critic of the July Monarchy of Louis-Philippe. His Histoire des Girondins (1847) was an instant success, and he styled himself the Minister of Public Opinion. On a journey to Lebanon, Syria and the Holy Land in 1832 and 1833, his daughter Julia died in Beirut, aged ten.

He was Minister of Foreign Affairs from 24 February to 11 May 1848, and the ageing chairman of the Provisional Government effectively delegated many of his duties to him. He declared the Republic from the balcony of the Hôtel de Ville and, on 25 February 1848, argued successfully for keeping the tricolour rather than the red flag. The Second Republic abolished slavery and the death penalty, recognised the right to work and set up the short-lived national workshops. His moderate stance cost him followers, and he won fewer than 19,000 votes in the presidential election of 1848, losing to Louis Napoléon Bonaparte.

After 1848 he retired from politics and wrote on many subjects. Under the Empire he was pursued by creditors and condemned himself, in his words, to literary hard-labour to pay his debts. He ended his life in poverty, publishing the Cours familier de littérature in monthly instalments, and he died in Paris on 28 February 1869. He is considered the first French romantic poet, and Paul Verlaine and the Symbolists acknowledged his influence. His praise of Frédéric Mistral's poem Mirèio helped make that writer's name.
alps: The Alps stretch across Monaco, France, Switzerland, Italy, Liechtenstein, Germany, Austria and Slovenia, from Nice on the Mediterranean to Trieste on the Adriatic and Vienna at the edge of the Pannonian Basin. Austria holds 28.7 per cent of the range, Italy 27.2 per cent, France 21.4 per cent and Switzerland 13.2 per cent. The highest peak is Mont Blanc, at 4,810 m, in the Western Alps, and 82 peaks exceed 4,000 m.

The mountains arose from the collision of the African and Eurasian tectonic plates, which began in the late Cretaceous. Marine sedimentary rocks were pushed up by thrusting and folding into peaks such as Mont Blanc and the Matterhorn. The name comes from the Latin Alpes, possibly from albus, white. In modern languages an alp is a high summer pasture below the glaciers, not a peak.

After the ice melted at the end of the Würm glaciation, Palaeolithic settlements arose along lake shores and in caves. The mummified man known as Ötzi, found on a glacier at the Austrian–Italian border in 1991, is about 5,000 years old. Celtic tribes settled in what is now Switzerland, the Celts mined salt near Salzburg, and by the 6th century BCE the La Tène culture was established.

In 218 BCE, during the Second Punic War, the general Hannibal crossed the Alps with a herd of elephants. The Romans, who expanded to control the Alpine trade routes, built roads over the passes that remained in use through the medieval period, and Roman road markers can still be found there. In 1800 Napoleon crossed one of the passes with an army of 40,000. Naturalists, writers and artists, among them the Romanticists, came in the 18th and 19th centuries, followed by the golden age of alpinism.

About 14 million people live in the Alps, across eight countries. The largest city in the range is Grenoble. The region is linguistically diverse, with dialects varying from valley to valley, and Romansh, spoken by two per cent of the population in south-eastern Switzerland, derives from Latin.

Farming, cheese making and woodworking remain part of Alpine culture. Cows are driven to the high pastures in mid-June and brought down in mid-September, a descent marked with garlands and large cowbells. Tourism expanded after the Second World War, and the Winter Olympic Games have been held in the Swiss, French, Italian, Austrian and German Alps.
alpujarras: The Alpujarra lies on the south slopes of the Sierra Nevada and the valley below, at an average height of 1,200 metres. Its name most probably comes from the Arabic al-basharāt, roughly sierra of pastures. The range runs about 80 km from west to east and includes the Mulhacén, at 3,479 metres the highest mountain of mainland Spain. Most of the snow melts in spring and summer, so the southern slopes stay green, fed by innumerable springs channelled to terraces and villages.

Olives grow on the lower slopes and in the valley of the Guadalfeo river from Órgiva to Cadiar, with grapes, citrus and almonds nearby. The eastern end, towards Ugijar in Almería, is much drier. The administrative centres are Órgiva in Granada and Alhama de Almería.

The Spanish Muslim people of al-Andalus, who lived here for centuries after the conquest of 711, built the terraces and irrigation of the upper Alpujarra and villages of narrow winding streets and small flat-roofed houses in the manner of the mountains of North Africa. The revolt of 1568 was a civil war fought with much cruelty on both sides, ending with the death of the last Muslim leader in March 1571. The entire Muslim population of the territory of Granada was then taken on forced marches to other parts of Spain; only a few judged true converts stayed to teach the silk industry.

Settlers came from all over Spain, many from Galicia, but resettlement went badly: a population estimated at 40,000 before the last revolt was about 7,000 by the end of the century. The region stayed poor and isolated until roads opened it in the 20th century. Nationalist and Republican forces fought over it in the Civil War of 1936 to 1939, and guerrillas held out in the mountains until their leader was captured in 1942.

The high villages have lost people to the cities, while tourism and foreign residents have brought income. Serrano ham cured in Trevélez and other high villages is a major product, the GR 7 / E4 footpath crosses the region, and the Sierra Nevada and most of the upper Alpujarra are protected.
alsace: Alsace is a plain on the west bank of the upper Rhine, between the river and the Vosges mountains, almost four times longer than it is wide. It covers 8,283 square kilometres and includes the departments of Haut-Rhin and Bas-Rhin, formerly Sundgau and Nordgau. Until 1871 it also included the area now called the Territoire de Belfort. The plain is a rift valley dating from the Oligocene, and the Vosges shelter it from rain; Colmar is the second driest city in France, a condition suited to the Alsatian wine. The name comes from Old High German Ali-saz, meaning foreign domain, or perhaps from Ell-sass, seated on the Ill.

Hominids lived in Alsace 600,000 years ago, and farming arrived with the Linear Pottery culture by 4000 BCE. In 58 BCE Julius Caesar routed the Suebi of Ariovistus at the foot of the Vosges, near what became Cernay. The region lay in the Roman province of Germania Superior. As Roman power declined it passed to the Alemanni, whose language forms the basis of the dialects of the Upper Rhine, and in the 5th century the Franks under Clovis defeated them. Alsace was then part of the Kingdom of Austrasia. Under the Treaty of Verdun of 843 it fell to Middle Francia, ruled by Lothar I, and later it prospered under the Hohenstaufen emperors in the 12th and 13th centuries.

Within the Holy Roman Empire, France took most of Alsace in the 17th century. The Habsburgs sold their Sundgau territory to France in 1646 for 1.2 million thalers, and the Treaty of Westphalia of 1648 recognised most of Alsace as French, though some towns stayed independent. The inhabitants kept their existing rights and customs, German remained the language of administration, schools and the Lutheran University of Strasbourg, and the Edict of Fontainebleau of 1685 was not applied there. Strasbourg Cathedral, Lutheran from 1524 to 1681, returned to the Catholic Church.

The French Revolution divided Alsace into the departments of Haut-Rhin and Bas-Rhin. In 1792 Rouget de Lisle composed La Marseillaise in Strasbourg for the Army of the Rhine. In 1871 Alsace became part of the German Empire as part of Alsace-Lorraine. It was returned to France after the First World War, reincorporated into Germany in 1940, and became French again after 1944.

Alsace has a population of 1,919,745 in 2021, and its capital and largest city is Strasbourg. The Alsatian language is an Alemannic dialect, though most people mainly speak French. Under the local law of Alsace-Moselle, the Napoleonic Concordat of 1801 still provides public support for the Catholic, Lutheran, Calvinist and Jewish faiths. The region is known for vineyards along the Route des Vins d'Alsace, timber-framed houses and historic towns such as Colmar and Sélestat.
alsace-lorraine: The Imperial Territory of Alsace-Lorraine had a land area of 14,496 square kilometres and its capital was Strasbourg. It was divided into three districts: Upper Alsace, with Colmar as its capital, corresponding to the present department of Haut-Rhin; Lower Alsace, with Strasbourg, corresponding to Bas-Rhin; and Lorraine, with Metz, corresponding to Moselle. At the 1910 census the largest towns were Strasbourg with 220,883 inhabitants, Mulhouse with 128,190 and Metz with 102,787. Most inhabitants spoke German dialects, while French was spoken mainly in parts of Lorraine; in 1900 about 86.8 per cent gave a German or Germanic dialect as their first language.

France had conquered Alsace progressively under Louis XIII and Louis XIV in the 17th century, taking Strasbourg in 1681, and incorporated Lorraine from the 16th century to the 18th, the Duchy of Lorraine passing to the French crown on the death of Stanisław I Leszczyński in 1766. German nationalism, which arose in the 19th century as a reaction to Napoleon's occupation, pointed to the German dialects spoken in Alsace and northern Lorraine to justify including them in a future German state.

In 1871 the new German Empire took the territory after its victory in the Franco-Prussian War. The annexation was controversial even in Germany: Chancellor Otto von Bismarck was at first opposed, thinking it would create permanent French hostility, and some German industrialists feared competition from Mulhouse's cloth makers. The territory was ruled directly by the imperial government rather than as a state. A Territorial Committee with a consultative role was set up by decree of Emperor Wilhelm I on 29 October 1874, and an imperial governor was introduced in 1879. The constitution of 31 May 1911 gave it an elected Landtag and three representatives in the Bundesrat. The French laws on religious bodies were kept, with public status for Catholic, Lutheran, Calvinist and Jewish bodies.

French resentment over the loss of the territory was one of the contributing factors to the First World War. After Germany's defeat in 1918 France took Alsace-Lorraine, and the cession was confirmed under the Treaty of Versailles. During the Second World War Alsace and Moselle were annexed by Nazi Germany before being restored to France in 1944-45. Some legal provisions specific to the territory remain in force as the local law of Alsace-Moselle, and since 2016 the area has formed part of the French administrative region of Grand Est.
alster: The Alster is a right tributary of the Elbe, 56 km long, falling from 31 m to 4 m above sea level, with a drainage basin of about 587 square kilometres. Its source is a small bog pool in the Timhagen Brook near Henstedt-Ulzburg, about 25 km north of Hamburg. The brook enters Hamburg territory at Duvenstedt and Wohldorf-Ohlstedt, and the river runs past Wellingsbüttel Manor. Hamburgers use its upper course for canoe and kayak trips. Below Fuhlsbüttel its course has been straightened in several places, and 42 bridges cross it between the city limits and the first lake, the Außenalster.

Hamburg was founded at the mouth of the Alster in the 9th century and used it as a port, and its water flooded the moats of the fortifications. The river has been dammed since 1190, originally to power a watermill. A further dam of 1235 for a second mill changed the river's shape into that of a lake, creating the Außenalster and the smaller Binnenalster in the centre of the city. The final section between the Kleine Alster and the mouth at the Binnenhafen is the Alsterfleet, part of a network of inner-city canals.

In the 15th and 16th centuries an Alster canal was built to connect Hamburg with Lübeck, running about 8 km from the Alster to the Beste, a tributary of the Trave, at Sülfeld. It had difficulty holding water, especially near the marshes, and the 91 km waterway was navigable only from 1529 to 1550. Hamburg expanded along the shores of the Alster, locks were built, and until the 19th century barges carrying building material, fuel and food went up to Kayhude.

The Alster is Hamburg's second most important river. Unlike the tidal Elbe, which is prone to flooding, it is non-tidal and slow-flowing, and is navigable about 9 km upstream from the mouth. Ferries run on it in the city, and rowing and paddle boats can be hired. Its swans have been cared for out of public funds since the 16th century. The Alster basin was an important model for the design of the Charles River basin in the early 20th century. In much of Germany an Alsterwasser is a shandy of equal parts beer and lemonade.
altai-mountains: The Altai Mountains cover about 845,000 square kilometres and stretch 2,525 kilometres from north-west to south-east, where Russia, China, Mongolia and Kazakhstan converge. They are the headwaters of the Irtysh and the Ob. The highest summit is the double-headed Belukha at 4,506 metres, and the second highest is Khüiten Peak, in the Mongolian part, at 4,374 metres. In the north-east the range merges with the Sayan Mountains, and in the south-east it falls to the plateau of the Gobi Desert. The name comes from a form meaning gold or golden, as in Old Turkic altun.

The Denisova Cave in the Altai is the only place known where Neanderthals, Denisova hominins and Homo sapiens all lived. The Denisova hominin, dated to 40,000 years ago, was found there in 2008, and knowledge of it comes mainly from DNA and artefacts, since no complete skeleton has been recovered. The Afanasievans, descended from people who migrated across the steppe about 3700 to 3300 BCE, are considered the earliest herders of East Asia. Eastern Scythian remains with skin and hair preserved have been found in the mountains.

The area was part of the Xiongnu Empire, the First Turkic Khaganate, the Uyghur Empire and the Yeniseian Kyrgyz, and in these centuries the local population became fully Turkic in culture and language. From the 18th century runaway Russian peasants, serfs and religious schismatics settled the Bukhtarma valley, then on Chinese territory, and created a free republic there; after its annexation to Russia in 1869 the valley was rapidly colonised.

The sparse population includes Turkic peoples, Mongols and Volga Germans, but is mostly made up of indigenous semi-nomadic minorities, and the local economy rests on herding, hunting, agriculture, forestry and mining. An area of 16,178 square kilometres, including Lake Teletskoye, Mount Belukha and the Ukok Plateau, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site named the Golden Mountains of Altai. The mountains shelter the snow leopard, the Altai argali and the Siberian ibex. The discredited Altaic language family takes its name from them.
altan-khan: Altan was the second son of Bars Bolud Jinong and a grandson of Dayan Khan. After Dayan Khan the Mongols formed six tümen divided into a Left Wing under the Great Khan and a Right Wing under Altan's father, who held the office of jinong, or vice-regent. Altan ruled the Tümed, whose pastures lay north of the border with Shanxi. When his elder brother Gün Bilig died in 1542, Altan became the effective leader of the Right Wing. After the death of Bodi Alagh Khan in 1547 he forced the new khagan, Darayisung Küdeng Khan, to flee eastward, and in 1551 Darayisung compromised by granting him the title Gegeen Khan.

Altan wanted to trade horses for Chinese farm produce and textiles, but the Ming court, suspicious of him, repeatedly refused and sometimes killed his envoys. He raided northern China in 1529, 1530 and 1542, and in 1550 crossed gaps in the Great Wall and besieged Beijing, setting its suburbs on fire. He strengthened his Tümed base by settling Chinese refugees there and kept a network of Ming conspirators led by Zhao Quan, a disciple of the White Lotus. In 1552 he gained control of the remains of Karakorum.

In 1570 his grandson Daičing Ejei Taiji defected to the Ming after a family quarrel. Ministers of the Longqing Emperor proposed that Altan accept a Ming title and hand over Zhao Quan in return for his grandson and trading rights. Altan agreed; Zhao and his fellow conspirators were executed, Altan was made Shunyi prince and his capital was renamed Guihua. The American Orientalist Owen Lattimore writes that the Mongols were nominally vassals, but that the Ming was eager to please them and the arrangement was more or less of benefit to both.

Altan first invited Sonam Gyatso in 1569; the lama accepted a second invitation in 1577, and Altan later had Thegchen Chonkhor, Mongolia's first monastery, built where they met. Sonam Gyatso declared Altan a reincarnation of Kublai Khan. One reason for adopting Buddhism was a fear among the Mongol elite that the peace of 1571 would spread Chinese cultural influence. Laws set out by Sonam Gyatso and instituted by Altan forbade blood sacrifices and the burning of widows. Altan died on 13 January 1582, aged 74 or 75, and his son Sengge Düüreng succeeded him as Shunyi prince. His great-grandson Yonten Gyatso was chosen as the 4th Dalai Lama in 1601.
altdorf-uri: Altdorf stands on the right bank of the Reuss, about 2 kilometres south of where the river flows into the Urnersee, an arm of Lake Lucerne. The town lies at 458 metres above sea level on a flat alluvial plain between the river and the steep hillside of the Rossstock, at the junction of two major Alpine passes, the Saint Gotthard to the south and the Klausen Pass to the east. Its name may come from the old town to which the inhabitants were driven back when the Reuss flooded the low-lying settlements.

The earliest evidence of settlement is La Tène bronze axe-heads and iron tools of the 3rd century BCE. After the collapse of the Roman Empire the local Gallo-Roman population began to mix with the Germanic Alamanni in the 7th century, and the earliest sign of this is the grave of an armed horseman of 670 to 680 in St Martin's Church. The town is first mentioned in 1223 as Alttorf. In the second half of the 13th century the territory around it had been cultivated to the banks of the Reuss, and hamlets such as Utzingen in 1277 are documented. Walser people migrated from Bosco/Gurin into the 17th century.

The medieval economy alternated grain cultivation with pasture, and cattle raising came to predominate. Around 1522 many villagers acquired exclusive rights to much of the communal land, while the Bannwald forest stayed in common use, protected from the 14th century by measures against landslides and avalanches. French occupation in the late 18th century caused a lasting demographic shock, and the population did not return to its 1799 level until the mid-19th century. The building of the Gotthard railway from 1872 to 1882 brought new immigrants, especially from Italy. In 1834 the town had 153 buildings, and by 1900 it had 351 houses.

Altdorf is the capital of the canton of Uri and retains historic town privileges. Its official language is Swiss Standard German, and the main spoken language is the local Alemannic dialect. According to legend, its marketplace is where William Tell shot the apple from his son's head. Richard Kissling's bronze statue of Tell was unveiled there in 1895, and a theatre opened near the centre in 1899 for performances of Schiller's play Wilhelm Tell. The Historisches Museum, opened in 1905, holds local antiquities and portraits of Uri citizens. The town is the last station on the Gotthard railway before it enters the Gotthard Base Tunnel.
alte-pinakothek: The Alte Pinakothek is part of the Bavarian State Painting Collections and stands in the Kunstareal area of Munich. Its name refers to the period covered, the fourteenth to the eighteenth century. The Neue Pinakothek covers nineteenth-century art and the Pinakothek der Moderne, opened in 2002, modern art.
