The Wittelsbach collection was begun by Duke Wilhelm IV, who ordered contemporary painters to create history paintings, among them Albrecht Altdorfer's The Battle of Alexander at Issus. Elector Maximilian I commissioned four hunt paintings from Rubens in 1616 and acquired many works by Albrecht Dürer, including The Four Apostles in 1627. Maximilian II Emanuel bought many Dutch and Flemish paintings, among them Rubens and Van Dyck in Antwerp in 1698. Johann Wilhelm, Elector Palatine, received Raphael's Canigiani Holy Family as a dowry for his wife. After Bavaria and the Palatinate were reunited in 1777, the galleries of Mannheim, Düsseldorf and Zweibrücken were moved to Munich, and in 1800 Napoleon's armies took 72 paintings to Paris, including Altdorfer's battle, mostly never returned.

Secularisation brought many paintings from churches and former monasteries into state hands. King Ludwig I of Bavaria collected especially early German and early Dutch paintings, and in 1827 acquired the Boisserée collection of 216 Old German and Old Dutch works and in 1828 the 219 pictures of Prince Wallerstein. In 1826 he ordered Leo von Klenze to build a new gallery, and Georg von Dillis, the gallery inspector, shaped the project. Construction lasted from 1826 to 1836. The building was 150 metres long and lit by skylights, and its Neo-Renaissance exterior stood apart from the castle-like museums of the time. It became a model for galleries including the Hermitage in Saint Petersburg and others in Rome, Brussels and Kassel.

The building was damaged by bombing in the Second World War, and in December 1944 an aerial mine tore a 45-metre gap through its middle. After long disagreement it was decided in February 1952 to keep it as a monument. Hans Döllgast rebuilt it without hiding the damage, using rubble bricks that stay visible beside the old masonry. It reopened on 7 June 1957 with President Theodor Heuss attending, though the interior was not complete until November 1963.

More than 800 paintings are shown in the building. The collection is the most comprehensive of German Old Masters, with Dürer's Four Apostles and Paumgartner Altar, and its early Netherlandish paintings include van Eyck, Rogier van der Weyden and Hieronymus Bosch. The Rubens collection, with 72 paintings, is the largest permanent collection of his work. The Italian holdings include Raphael's Madonna della tenda and Leonardo's Madonna of the Carnation, bought after 1875 with El Greco's Disrobing of Christ. In April 1988 a vandal threw acid on three Dürer paintings.
altenburg: Altenburg lies in the flat, fertile landscape of Osterland on the Pleiße river, in the far east of Thuringia next to Saxony, 40 km south of Leipzig. It is the capital of the Altenburger Land district. The city centre stands at about 200 m, on the Blaue Flut, a small tributary of the Pleiße that feeds the Großer Teich, an inner-city pond. Loess soil makes the surrounding land very fertile, and lignite is mined on the surface north of the town.

The town was first mentioned in 976 in a deed to the Bishop of Zeitz. Remains of a Slavic castle on the Schloßberg suggest a Slavic foundation, the capital of the shire of Plisni, taken over when Henry I conquered Meissen. Its position on the imperial road Via Imperii between Halle and Cheb gave it importance in the salt trade. The castle became an imperial palatinate and played an important part in the German settlement of the lands between the Harz and the Elbe. In the middle of the 12th century the Hohenstaufen emperors made Altenburg a Kaiserpfalz, and it became a market and a mint. Frederick Barbarossa built much there, visiting between 1165 and 1188; the parish church was finished in 1172.

During the Interregnum of 1254 to 1273 the Terra Plisnensis was impounded, then bought back by Rudolph I. After the Battle of Lucka in 1307 King Albert I lost Altenburg and the Pleiße lands to the Wettin margraves of Meissen, who held the city until 1918. Since the 17th century it was the residence of Ernestine duchies, among them Saxe-Altenburg, which lasted until the end of monarchy in Germany in 1918. Industrialization came early in the 19th century, and the town became known for sewing machines and playing cards.

The card game Skat is said to have originated in Altenburg in the 1810s, based on the Bavarian tarock, and the town is nicknamed the playing-card town. The Altenburger Spielkartenfabrik was founded in 1831. Friedrich Arnold Brockhaus, founder of the Brockhaus Enzyklopädie, lived and worked there from 1810 to 1817. The castle, with its 11th-century Mantelturm and a playing card museum, the Lindenau-Museum, founded in 1876, and the Gothic St. Bartholomew's Church, built between 1428 and 1443, are among the sights. The city has about 33,000 inhabitants and was left unscathed by the Second World War, so its historic buildings are preserved.
althing: The Althing was established as an outdoor assembly, or thing, on the plains of Þingvellir from about 930. At first it was the general assembly of the Icelandic Commonwealth, where the most powerful leaders, the goðar, met to decide legislation and dispense justice. All free men could attend, and it was usually the main social event of the year. The centre was the Lögberg, or Law Rock, where the Lawspeaker presided and recited the laws in effect.

The Gulathing Law was adopted at the first Althing in 930, introduced by Úlfljótr, who had spent three years in Norway studying its laws. According to Njáls saga, the Althing declared Christianity the official religion in 1000, after Thorgeir Ljosvetningagodi, a pagan chieftain, proposed one law and one religion for the whole of Iceland.

The legislative section, the Lögrétta, was the most powerful institution. It comprised the 39 district chieftains, nine additional members and the Lawspeaker. After the country was divided into four quarters around 965 a court of 36 judges was set up for each at the Althing. When the Icelanders submitted to the Norwegian king under the Old Covenant of 1262, the Commonwealth ended and the goðar ceased to rule. The Lögrétta, now of 36 members, shared legislative power with the king. When Denmark introduced absolute monarchy, Icelanders gave up the right to initiate and consent to legislation, and the Althing served almost only as a court.

A royal decree disbanded it in 1800, and a High Court in Reykjavík took over its functions. A decree of 1843 provided for a new Althing, which met in Reykjavík on 1 July 1845 as a consultative assembly of 26 members, elected by only about 5 percent of the population. The Constitution of 1874 gave it joint legislative power with the Crown, and it met from 1881 in the newly built Parliament House. A constitutional amendment confirmed on 3 October 1903 granted home rule. The Act of Union took effect on 1 December 1918, and the Althing declared the republic at a session at Þingvellir on 17 June 1944.

The Althing claims to be the longest-running parliament in the world. Its two chambers were merged into one in 1991. The unicameral parliament now has 63 members, elected every four years by party-list proportional representation, and sits in the Alþingishús, built of hewn Icelandic stone in 1881.
altmark: The Altmark lies west of the Elbe between Hamburg and Magdeburg and takes up the northern third of Saxony-Anhalt, mostly within the districts of Altmarkkreis Salzwedel and Stendal. The Drawehn hills and the Drömling depression divide it from the Lüneburg Heath to the west; the Wendland lies to the north, the Magdeburg Börde to the south and the Prignitz across the Elbe. It is a thinly peopled, rural part of the North European Plain, much of it forest and heath, drained by the Elbe, the Jeetzel and the Milde-Biese-Aland system, and its largest natural lake is the Arendsee.

The Lombards lived here before migrating south-east to Pannonia; afterwards the Saxon tribes took in the north-west and the Slavic Drevani the north-east along the Elbe. After the Saxon Wars the region became part of the Carolingian Empire, and by 822 the district of Arendsee counted as part of Eastphalia, bordering the Slavs. Otto I gave these frontier lands to Count Gero, whose northern march passed in 965 to Dietrich of Haldensleben. Dietrich lost everything east of the Elbe in the Slavic uprising of 983 but kept the lands west of the river; how far the later Altmark lay within his and Gero's marches is debated.

In 1134 Emperor Lothair of Supplinburg granted the Northern March to Albert the Bear, who in 1150 inherited the Hevelli prince Pribislav's lands around Brandenburg an der Havel. As the margraves pushed east, the original western territory became the Old March, in contrast to the Mittelmark and the Neumark, a name first recorded in 1304 as Antiqua Marchia. Bismarck, born at Schönhausen near Stendal, called it the cradle of Prussia. Held by the House of Hohenzollern from 1415, it passed by the Treaty of Tilsit to the Kingdom of Westphalia and returned to Prussia in 1815, but as part of the Province of Saxony rather than Brandenburg.

After World War II the region lay east of the inner German border, in Saxony-Anhalt and from 1952 to 1990 in Bezirk Magdeburg, and since reunification in 1990 it has again been part of Saxony-Anhalt. Its largest towns are Stendal, with about 39,000 people, and Salzwedel, with about 21,500; others include Tangermünde, Gardelegen, Havelberg and Osterburg.
aluksne: Alūksne lies on the shores of Lake Alūksne in the Vidzeme region, in the East Vidzeme Upland at 217 metres above sea level, which makes it the highest city in Latvia. It is the seat of the Alūksne municipality. The lake is the eleventh largest in Latvia and holds four islands: Cepurītes, Garā, Tīklu and Pilssala, or Castle Island. Its average depth is about 7 metres and its deepest point about 20 metres.

The region has been continually inhabited since around the turn of the first millennium CE, and stray flint and stone tools from the late Neolithic and Bronze Age have been found near the lake. The Pskov Chronicles mention the area in the 13th century, and a Latgalian hillfort on the Tempļakalns hill is thought to date from then. The region is believed to have belonged to the Latgalian state of Atzele. Parts of its territory passed to the Livonian Brothers of the Sword under a 1224 agreement with the Archbishop of Riga, and after the order's destruction in 1237 to the Teutonic Order.

In 1342 the Teutonic Order began a castle on the lake's largest island, which became the centre of the Gaujiena commandery. Its foundations were laid on the Feast of the Annunciation, so the castle and the town were named Marienburg, the official name until Latvian independence. Ivan IV of Russia's troops took the town in 1560 during the Livonian War. It joined the Polish–Lithuanian Commonwealth in 1582, changed hands in the Polish-Swedish wars, and became Swedish in 1629. Russian troops under Boris Sheremetyev conquered it in 1702.

The Lutheran clergyman Ernst Glück, the first translator of the Bible into Latvian, lived in the town in 1683, when he founded the first Latvian language schools in Vidzeme. In the 1780s Otto Hermann von Vietinghoff commissioned the neoclassical architect Christoph Haberland to build the Lutheran church, and the Tudor Revival New Palace was built for Alexander Joseph von Vietinghoff between 1859 and the early 1860s. Alūksne was liberated by the Latvian Army in May 1919 and received its town charter in 1920. It was under German occupation from 5 July 1941 until 19 August 1944; up to 300 Jews from the region were murdered near the village of Siseņi.
alula: AlUla lies in the Hejaz, 350 kilometres north-west of Medina, in a valley of vertical sandstone cliffs that contrast with the palm groves of its oasis. It was a market city on the incense trade route that linked India and the Persian Gulf to the Levant and Europe. The cliffs carry rock art: a survey of about 1,000 square kilometres around the valley recorded 19,802 identifiable panels, mostly engravings, spanning more than 12,000 years.

The earliest images show life-sized wild animals, including wild camels, equids and ibex. Later phases add cattle and hunting scenes, and from the Iron Age onward domesticated camels dominate, often with riders, alongside horsemen, battles and, in the latest periods, objects such as firearms and motor vehicles. The Jabal Ikmah inscriptions, nearly 300 texts from the second half of the first millennium BCE in Aramaic, Dadanitic, Thamudic and Minaic, were inscribed on the UNESCO Memory of the World register in 2023.

The oasis has been settled permanently since 5000 BCE. It stands on the site of the biblical Dedan, and the Dedanite kingdom is dated to the 7th and 6th centuries BCE. The Harran Stela tells how Nabonidus, last ruler of the Neo-Babylonian Empire, campaigned in northern Arabia in 552 BCE or somewhat later and took Tayma, Dedan and Yathrib. The kingdom of Lihyan then held the region for about four hundred years, until around 100 BCE. The Nabataeans were lords of the region until 106 CE, when the Roman Empire annexed it into its province of Arabia Petraea.

In the Islamic period al-Mabiyat, some 20 kilometres away, became the commercial centre from about 650 CE and declined before 1230. In the 13th century the old walled town of al-Dirah was built, reusing stones from the Dedanite and Lihyanite ruins; at its largest it held more than 1,000 houses joined to form a defensive wall. The Ottomans built the Hejaz railway between 1901 and 1908, with stations at Hegra and al-Ula. The last family is said to have left the old town in 1983.

Antonin Jaussen and Raphaël Savignac, French priests, visited three times in 1907, 1908 and 1910 and collected many Lihyanite, Minaean, Thamudic and Nabataean inscriptions; their work became the basis of later study. Charles Doughty described the town in 1876, and Charles Huber and Julius Euting followed.

Today AlUla is the capital of a governorate of Medina Province and had a population of 60,103 in 2022 for the municipality as a whole. Hegra, 22 kilometres to the north, is Saudi Arabia's first UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Royal Commission for al-Ula, set up in July 2017, directs conservation and tourism development.
alulim: Alulim was a mythological Mesopotamian ruler, regarded as the first king ever to rule. Assyriologists consider him a fictional figure, and he is absent from Early Dynastic sources. Mentions of him are largely limited to lists of mythical ancient rulers, which place his reign before the great flood. All known sources listing primordial kings consistently place him in Eridu, a city of particular symbolic importance, unless they name no city.

His name was written A2-lu-lim or A-lu-lim in cuneiform and can be translated from Sumerian as either horn of the red deer or seed of the red deer, depending on the first sign. Jeremiah Peterson suggests that it may reflect the Mesopotamian belief that humans at the dawn of history behaved like animals. Variant forms include Alulu and Ayalu, the latter probably shaped by the word ayyalu, deer or stag. The name was never used as an ordinary given name.

According to the Sumerian King List, Alulim held the kingship for 28,800 years before Alalngar succeeded him and reigned for 36,000 years. The Ballad of Early Rulers gives him 36,000 years, and other texts give figures such as 36,200 years (tablet BM 40565) and 67,200 years (tablet WB 62), according to Irving Finkel. The King List is assumed not to reflect historical reality and cannot be used to reconstruct early Mesopotamian chronology. His long reign became proverbial: the astrologer Ašarēdu wrote to a Babylonian king wishing him the years of Alulu.

A tablet of the Eridu Genesis from Ur, published in 2018 and dating to the Old Babylonian period, describes the gods An, Enlil and Enki choosing Alulim from among vast and many people to be shepherd of the entire population. It has been read as an explanation of how kingship began, with the first ruler chosen to guide still animal-like humans. Peterson notes that its grammar might not mark Alulim as a human at all.

In the Ballad of Early Rulers Alulim stands among ancient figures such as Etana, Gilgamesh, Ziusudra, Humbaba and Enkidu. Neo-Babylonian incantations against field pests call him a king from before the deluge and the creator of insects, able to expel them with a wand. In late tradition the sage Adapa became his vizier, who gave him wisdom on behalf of the god Ea.

The Greek form of his name, Aloros, appears in citations of Berossus preserved by Eusebius and Syncellus, where he reigns 36,000 years and is followed by Alaparos. In the Tabaqat-i Nasiri, written in 1259–1260, Minhaj-i Siraj Juzjani gives a derivative, Aylūrūs, as the first king of the people opposed to giants and equates him with Gayūmart.
alvar-aalto: Hugo Alvar Henrik Aalto was born on 3 February 1898 in Kuortane, Finland. His father, Johan Henrik Aalto, was a Finnish-speaking land surveyor, and his mother, Selma Matilda Hackstedt, was a Swedish-speaking postmistress. The family moved to Alajärvi and then to Jyväskylä. In 1916 he began to study architecture at the Helsinki University of Technology, interrupted by the Finnish Civil War, in which he fought on the White side. He graduated in 1921, opened an office in Jyväskylä in 1923 and on 6 October 1924 married the architect Aino Marsio.

His career ran from the 1920s to the 1970s. His style moved from the Nordic Classicism of his early houses and first public buildings, such as the Jyväskylä Workers' Club of 1925, to a rational International Style modernism in the 1930s and then to a more organic modernism from the 1940s. His first completed church, at Muurame, shows the transition to Functionalism. In 1949 Sigfried Giedion's Space, Time and Architecture gave him more attention than any other modernist architect, including Le Corbusier. He received the Royal Gold Medal of the Royal Institute of British Architects in 1957.

Aalto saw architecture as a total work of art, and with Aino he designed the building together with its interior surfaces, furniture, lamps and glassware. He regarded painting and sculpture as branches of the tree whose trunk is architecture. He invented a form of laminated bent-plywood furniture in 1932, patented in 1933, and was the first furniture designer to use the cantilever principle in wooden chairs. The ceiling of the Vyborg Library is an undulating wave of red-hearted pine, and the stairway at Villa Mairea evokes a forest with beech columns bound with withes.

His standing has been questioned. The historians Manfredo Tafuri and Francesco Dal Co argued that his historical significance had perhaps been exaggerated and that his architecture was unsuited to urban types, while in his last decade fellow Finnish architects found his work unfashionably individualistic beside rationalism and constructivism.
alvar-nunez-cabeza-de-vaca: Álvar Núñez Cabeza de Vaca was born around 1490 in the Andalusian town of Jerez de la Frontera. His father was an hidalgo, a rank of minor Spanish nobility, as was his mother's family. The main influence in his life was his paternal grandfather, Pedro de Vera y Mendoza, who completed the conquest of Gran Canaria in 1483 and as its military governor captured Guanches and sold them as slaves in Spain. Many years later Cabeza de Vaca named a province in South America, Vera, in his honour.

On 11 December 1526 Charles V commissioned Pánfilo de Narváez to explore, conquer and settle La Florida. Cabeza de Vaca was named treasurer by royal appointment, which made him second in command. The fleet sailed on 17 June 1527 with 600 soldiers and colonists. In Cuba a hurricane destroyed two ships, with the loss of sixty men and twenty horses.

After the party was wrecked on Galveston Island in November 1528, Cabeza de Vaca and his last three men were held for two years by the Han and Capoque, travelled through the American Southwest and reached Mexico City nearly eight years after the wreck. He returned to Spain in 1537. In 1540 he was appointed adelantado of the Río de la Plata and led 250 musketeers and 26 horses overland to Asunción. In 1544 he was charged with poor administration and arrested, and he was sent to Spain for trial in 1545. His sentence was eventually commuted, but he never returned to the Americas.

His account of the Narváez expedition appeared in 1542 as La relación and was later retitled Naufragios. The Comentarios, written from memory in 1555 on his time in South America, was later joined to it. It has been called the first European book devoted completely to North America. He described the Capoque, Han, Avavare, Arbadao and other peoples, and at times he and his companions served as slaves to survive. For many of these peoples his account is the only written record, and later reports and oral traditions have supported its accuracy. He wrote that he grieved at the destruction of villages and enslavement of their inhabitants by Spanish troops.
alvaro-arzu: Álvaro Enrique Arzú Irigoyen was born in Guatemala City on 14 March 1946 and studied Social and Legal Sciences at Rafael Landívar University. In 1978 he became director of the Guatemalan Institute of Tourism and held the post until 1981, when he was elected mayor of Guatemala City for the Guatemalan Christian Democracy party. The 1982 military coup annulled the elections, and he declined the military's offer of the post of municipal intendent. He won the mayoralty in 1986 under a civic committee that became the National Advancement Party in 1989. He finished fourth in the 1990 presidential election with 17.3 percent, and in 1991 he resigned as foreign minister in protest at President Jorge Serrano's decision to normalize relations with Belize.

Arzú won the first round of the 1995 elections in November and narrowly beat Alfonso Portillo of the Guatemalan Republican Front in January 1996, with 51.2 percent. The negotiations with the guerrilla group URNG had begun in 1990, and he gave them new impulse by meeting its leaders in Mexico on 26 February 1996. A ceasefire followed on 20 March, an accord legalizing the URNG was signed in Madrid on 12 December, Congress passed a partial amnesty on 18 December, and the final accord was signed on 29 December. His government proposed constitutional reforms to disband the Presidential Guard, reduce the armed forces and recognize indigenous rights, but a 1999 referendum rejected them.

His government improved roads and expanded electric and telephone coverage, and privatized the electric utility, the telephone company, the national airline and the railway, which drew criticism over alleged irregularities. Archbishop Juan José Gerardi was murdered in 1998, a crime later attributed to members of the Presidential Guard; Hurricane Mitch struck that year, and crime rose.

After his term Arzú sat in the Central American Parliament from 2000 to 2004 and was elected mayor of Guatemala City again in 2003, 2007, 2011 and 2015. As mayor he established the Transmetro bus rapid transit system and worked on restoring the historic centre. On 27 April 2018 he had a heart attack while playing golf and died in hospital that day. He received UNESCO's Félix Houphouët-Boigny Peace Prize in 1996.
alvaro-obregon: Álvaro Obregón was born on 19 February 1880 at Siquisiva, near Navojoa in Sonora, the eighteenth child of Francisco Obregón and Cenobia Salido. His father had once owned a large estate, but the Liberal government confiscated it in 1867 because his business partner had supported Emperor Maximilian, and he died in the year of Álvaro's birth. The boy grew up in straitened circumstances with his mother and sisters, a poor relation of a locally prominent family. Sonora's economy was tied closely to the United States, and Obregón made a living as a young man by farming garbanzos; in 1909 he invented a garbanzo harvester and founded a company to manufacture it.

Obregón took no part in Francisco Madero's rising of 1910. He volunteered in April 1912 to oppose Pascual Orozco's revolt, winning battles by traps and surprise assaults, and rose to colonel. After the coup of February 1913 that brought Victoriano Huerta to power he joined the Revolution under Venustiano Carranza and became the Constitutionalist Army's most prominent general along with Pancho Villa. In 1915 he defeated Villa, though he lost his right arm. Carranza made him Minister of War, and he founded a staff college, a school of military medicine and a department of aviation. In 1920 he, Plutarco Elías Calles and Adolfo de la Huerta ousted Carranza under the Plan of Agua Prieta.

As president from 1920 to 1924 he named José Vasconcelos Secretary of Public Education; about 1,000 rural schools and 2,000 public libraries were built, and Mexican muralism began. In August 1923 he signed the Bucareli Treaty on rights of U.S. oil interests, which brought U.S. diplomatic recognition. When he chose Calles as his successor, de la Huerta rebelled; Obregón took the field and defeated him with U.S. arms and aircraft.

After Calles took office in 1924 Obregón farmed in the Yaqui Valley, introducing modern irrigation. In October 1926 Congress repealed term limits, and he won the 1928 election, after two old allies who opposed his re-election, Francisco Serrano and Arnulfo R. Gómez, were killed. On 17 July 1928, before he could take office, José de León Toral, a Roman Catholic opposed to the government's anti-Catholic policies, shot him at La Bombilla Café in Mexico City, during the Cristero War. Toral was tried and executed by firing squad.

The assassination caused a political crisis, resolved when Calles founded the National Revolutionary Party, later the Institutional Revolutionary Party. The historian Linda B. Hall called Obregón the organiser, peacemaker and unifier. He is generally seen as one of the revolution's ultimate victors, but has no posthumous cult like those of Villa and Emiliano Zapata.
alvise-cadamosto: Alvise was born at the Ca' da Mosto, a palace on the Grand Canal of Venice from which his name derives. His father, Giovanni da Mosto, was a Venetian civil servant and merchant, and his mother, Elizabeth Querini, came from a leading patrician family. From 1442 to 1448 he made trips on Venetian galleys to the Barbary Coast and Crete as a commercial agent of his cousin Andrea Barbarigo. On his return from a voyage to Flanders he found his father banished from Venice after a bribery scandal and his Querini relatives in possession of the family property.

In August 1454 Alvise and his brother Antonio sailed on a galley bound for Flanders, which bad weather held near Cape St. Vincent. Agents of Prince Henry the Navigator told the stranded merchants of his discoveries in Africa, and Cadamosto applied to Henry to undertake an expedition for him. Henry hired him on the spot. He set out on 22 March 1455 in a 43-tonne caravel and reached the mouth of the Senegal River, for which he gave the first recorded use of that name.

At an anchorage on the Grande Côte he traded Iberian horses for slaves, at between 9 and 14 slaves a horse. The Damel of Cayor met him there, and he spent nearly a month inland observing the country and its customs.

In May 1456 he left Lagos with Antoniotto Usodimare and a second caravel. A storm off the Cape Vert peninsula drove them about 300 miles to sea, where they came upon uninhabited islands, the Cape Verde Islands, which Cadamosto claimed to have discovered, though Diogo Gomes disputed this. They then entered the Gambia River without opposition and sailed up it, and went on to the Geba River and the Bissagos Islands. The stretch of coast they discovered was the largest advance of the Portuguese discoveries since 1446.

Prince Henry died in November 1460, and Cadamosto returned to Venice in February 1463. In the mid-1460s he composed the Navigazioni from his notes and logs. It describes the Mali Empire and the trans-Saharan trade, including the carrying of salt from Teghaza to Timbuctu. It was first published in 1507 at Vicenza in Paesi novamente retrovati. Cadamosto recovered some of the family property and served Venice as proveditor at Cattaro and Corone and on missions to Dalmatia and Herzegovina. He died on 16 July 1483.
alyattes: Alyattes was the son of King Sadyattes of Lydia and Sadyattes's sister and queen, Lyde, both children of King Ardys. His great-grandfather Gyges had repelled attacks by the Cimmerians, nomads from the Eurasian Steppe, but in 644 BCE they defeated the Lydians, sacked Sardis and killed Gyges. The Thracian Treres, allied with the Cimmerians and the Lycians, sacked Sardis again, except for its citadel. Alyattes came to the throne in the midst of this turmoil. His name is Lydian in origin and meant the state of being a lion.

He began by continuing his father's war with the Ionian city of Miletus, a series of raids to seize the Milesians' grain. It ended in a treaty of friendship and alliance with the tyrant Thrasybulus, with Lydian metal exchanged for Milesian cereal. Herodotus tells that Alyattes fell ill after Lydian troops burned a temple of Athena and recovered only after rebuilding it, an account that appears not to be factual. He also dedicated a silver crater and an iron stand to Delphi. Relations with Ephesus, tied to the Mermnads by marriage, were always good.

With the Carians he kept the alliances begun under Gyges, and with the Scythians under Madyes he defeated the Cimmerians. He extended Lydian rule east into Phrygia. Around 600 BCE he turned on Smyrna, which gave Lydia a port; he then failed against Clazomenae, whose people were helped by the cavalry of Colophon. He later had the Colophonian cavalry massacred at Sardis and placed Colophon under direct Lydian rule. His war with the Median king Cyaxares began in 590 BCE over Scythian refugees at Sardis and lasted five years, until a solar eclipse in 585 BCE during a battle was taken by both sides as an omen to end it. Alyattes's daughter Aryenis married Astyages, son of Cyaxares, to seal the peace.

Alyattes died soon after the Battle of the Eclipse. His son Croesus, born of a Carian noblewoman, prevailed in a struggle for the throne against Pantaleon, whose mother was Greek. He is credited with the first coins, struck in electrum, and with standardising their weight. His tomb, a mound about sixty metres high and two hundred and fifty metres across at Bin Tepe near Sardis, covers a vault of marble blocks. Herodotus describes it as the work of market men, artisans and prostitutes. It was excavated in 1853 by Ludwig Peter Spiegelthal, by which time it had been looted.
alzey: Alzey lies in Rhenish Hesse, on the western edge of the northern Upper Rhine Plain, about 30 kilometres south-west of Mainz and 22 kilometres north-west of Worms. It is surrounded by the northern part of the Alzey Hills. The river Selz, a tributary of the Rhine, flows through the town, in places underground. The climate is oceanic, with low annual rainfall of about 535 millimetres. The town is also called Volkerstadt, because it is one of the Nibelungenstädte: the character Volker von Alzey appears in the Nibelungenlied.

Settlement in the area goes back to the Neolithic. Alzey was founded as a Roman vicus in the province of Germania Superior, and its name first appears on an altar stone dedicated to the nymphs on 22 November 223 by the Vicani Altiaienses, the villagers of Alzey. The village was destroyed about 350, and the fort Castra Alteium was built over it about 390. The Burgundians settled here as Roman confederates after 406 and 407, and their kingdom was destroyed in 436 by the Roman general Flavius Aëtius with Hunnish help, events worked into the Nibelungenlied. Alzey later passed to the Alamanni and the Franks, and in 897 it is first mentioned as an imperial fief.

By 1156 Alzey belonged to the Palatinate, and Konrad von Staufen became count palatine in the imperial castle, which was completed in 1118. Rudolf von Habsburg gave it the rank of town in 1277. Spanish forces under Ambrogio Spinola took it in 1620 in the Thirty Years' War, and in 1689 French troops burned the town and castle in the Nine Years' War. France annexed it in 1798, and it passed to the Grand Duchy of Hesse in 1816. A winemaking school founded in 1909 had Georg Scheu as its first head, and the Scheurebe grape is named after him.

Alzey is the fifth-largest town in Rhenish Hesse and the seat of the Alzey-Worms district. Since 1947 it has belonged to Rhineland-Palatinate. It is a centre of wine growing, with a well-kept old town of timber-frame houses within the ruins of the medieval town wall, and a winemakers' festival each September. The town has a history museum.

A Jewish community is recorded from the 14th century. Its members were murdered in 1349 during the Black Death, and it was renewed some years later. The synagogue built in 1791 was destroyed on 9 November 1938, and 76 Jews were deported from the town.
amadeo-i-of-spain: Amadeo was born in Turin on 30 May 1845, the second son of Victor Emmanuel II, later the first king of a unified Italy, and of Archduchess Adelaide of Austria. He bore the title Duke of Aosta from birth. He entered the Royal Sardinian Army as a captain in 1859 and fought in the Third Italian War of Independence in 1866 with the rank of major-general, leading his brigade at the Battle of Custoza and being wounded at Monte Croce. On 30 May 1867 he married Donna Maria Vittoria dal Pozzo, a Piedmontese noblewoman and sole heir to her father's large fortune. Victor Emmanuel had at first opposed the match.

After the Glorious Revolution deposed Isabella II in September 1868, the new Cortes looked for a liberal candidate from a new dynasty. The Duke of Aosta, descended on both sides from Spanish kings, was elected king on 16 November 1870. While he travelled to Spain, General Juan Prim, his chief supporter, was assassinated, and Amadeo swore to uphold the 1869 Constitution in Madrid on 2 January 1871 in the presence of Prim's corpse. The progressive faction later split between Prim's two successors, Práxedes Mateo Sagasta and Manuel Ruiz Zorrilla.

General Serrano headed the first government and organised the first elections under Amadeo, which returned a majority of 235 seats for the governing coalition. The opposition nonetheless included 52 Republicans, 51 Carlists and 18 Moderates, and the coalition was fragile. The reign met growing republicanism, Carlist rebellions in the north and the Cuban independence movement. After about three years Amadeo abdicated and returned to Italy in 1873, and the First Spanish Republic was declared.

Back in Italy, Amadeo resumed the title Duke of Aosta. The Republic lasted less than two years, and in November 1874 Alfonso XII, the son of Isabella II, was proclaimed king. Maria Vittoria died in 1876, leaving three sons, and in 1888 Amadeo married his niece Princess Maria Letizia Bonaparte. He remained in Turin until his death on 18 January 1890, and his friend Puccini composed the elegy Crisantemi for string quartet in his memory. The Philippine municipality of Amadeo in Cavite, established in 1872, and Lake Amadeus in central Australia, named by the explorer Ernest Giles, are named after him.
amadeus-v-count-of-savoy: Amadeus was the son of Thomas II of Savoy and Beatrice Fieschi, and through his mother a grandnephew of Pope Innocent IV. After his marriage to Sybille of Bâgé in 1272 he entered the service of his cousin, King Edward I of England, as a household knight. He served in the First Welsh War of 1277, and in the Second Welsh War of 1282 he commanded Edward's forces at Chester that relieved the siege of Rhuddlan Castle.

His childless uncle, Count Philip I of Savoy, died in 1285, and Amadeus's elder brother Thomas III of Piedmont had died by accident in 1282. Amadeus was awarded the County of Savoy. To lessen family rivalry, his younger brother Louis received the new Barony of Vaud. Through his wife, Countess of Bugey and Bresse, he added those Burgundian districts to his lands. On 1 October 1285 he was declared protector of Geneva after negotiations with its bishop. In 1287 he captured the castle of Ile, near Geneva, after a siege of fourteen weeks, and his victories over Amadeus II of Geneva and Humbert I, Dauphin of Viennois, led to the Treaty of Annemasse on 18 November 1287, by which both became his vassals.

In 1295 he acquired the fortress at Chambéry, and he brought Georges de Aquila, a student of Giotto, from Florence to decorate the castle. During the Gascon War of 1294 to 1303 he acted as an agent of Edward I in the talks that led to the Treaty of Montreuil in 1299 and the Treaty of Paris in 1303. In 1301 he settled a dispute over Valais with the diocese of Sion. His reign also saw friction between Savoy and the Duchy of Austria.

Alarmed by the recovery of Lyon by the kings of France, Amadeus sought a powerful ally in the German king Henry VII, who was married to the sister of Amadeus's second wife. He accompanied Henry on his Italian campaign of 1310 to 1313, which ended with Henry's coronation as Holy Roman Emperor on 29 June 1312. As a reward he became Imperial Count and imperial vicar of Lombardy and received the lordships of Asti and Ivrea. Henry also raised Aosta and Chablais to duchies, though they stayed part of Savoy.

In 1315 Amadeus helped the Knights Hospitaller defend Rhodes against the Turks. He died in Avignon on 16 October 1323. By his first wife he had eight children and by his second wife, Marie of Brabant, whom he married in 1297, four more. His son Edward succeeded him, then Edward's brother Aymon, and a daughter, Anna, married the Byzantine Emperor Andronikos III Palaiologos.
amadeus-vi-count-of-savoy: Amadeus VI, eldest son of Aymon, Count of Savoy and Yolande Palaeologina of Montferrat, inherited the county in 1343 at the age of nine. His father's will named two cousins, Amadeus III of Geneva and Louis II of Vaud, as co-regents; neither could make a significant decision without the other, and both were subject to review by a council of nobles. His cousin Joan of Savoy renewed a claim to the county, which Savoy's Semi-Salic tradition had already denied, and in 1345 Philip, Duke of Orléans, to whom she had left it, yielded the claim for 5000 livres annually.

He was taught to fight and ride and read classical works such as De Re Militari. The Black Death ravaged Savoy from 1348 to 1351, halving the population in some villages. Peasants blamed Jews for poisoning wells, and in Chambéry a mob broke into the castle where Jews had been locked for protection and killed several. Eleven more were executed and the rest fined 160 florins a month for six years.

In 1352 Amadeus put down a rising in the Valais, defeating the rebels on 3 November, tearing down part of the wall of Sion and fining its citizens. He took his nickname, the Green Count, in 1353, when he appeared at tournaments in green plumes and a green silk tabard, with eleven knights in green each led by a lady in green.

Fighting against Hugh of Geneva and the Dauphiné continued until April 1354. By the treaty of Paris in 1355 he gave up territory beyond the Rhone and Guiers in return for recognition as sovereign of Faucigny and Gex and suzerain over the Counts of Geneva. That year he married Bonne of Bourbon.

In 1366 he led a small crusade of 15 ships and 1,700 men against the Ottoman Sultan Murad I, to help his cousin John V Palaiologos, son of Anna of Savoy. With Francesco I of Lesbos and Louis I of Hungary he drove the Turks from Gallipoli, a gain lost a few years later. John V was held by the Bulgarians, so Amadeus took Mesembria and Sozopolis, besieged Varna and forced Tsar Ivan Alexander to release him.

In 1377 Amadeus ordered the region's first public mechanical clock and established a system of state-supported poor relief, one of the first of its kind in the late medieval world. In 1381 he mediated at Turin the peace ending the War of Chioggia between Genoa and Venice. In 1382 he joined Louis I, Duke of Anjou, on an expedition to Naples and shared in the conquest of Abruzzi and Apulia. He died near Castropignano in 1383 and was buried at Hautecombe Abbey. His son Amadeus VII succeeded him.
amadeus-vii-count-of-savoy: Amadeus was born in Chambéry on 24 February 1360, the son of Count Amadeus VI of Savoy and Bonne of Bourbon. In 1382, summoned by Charles VI of France, he led Savoyard troops to victory against Flemish rebels at the Battle of Roosebeke. After his father's death in 1383 his mother and grandmother fought over the regency.

In 1384 Amadeus led an army to suppress a revolt against his relative Edward of Savoy, Bishop of Sion, and the army attacked and pillaged Sion. In 1388 he acquired territories in eastern Provence and the port city of Nice, which gave the County of Savoy access to the Mediterranean and control of an important Alpine pass. Nice became part of the domains of the House of Savoy on 28 September 1388. Amadeus took advantage of internal struggles in Provence and negotiated the transfer of Nice and the Ubaye Valley with Giovanni Grimaldi, baron of Boglio and governor of Nice and Eastern Provence. The new lands were called the Terre Nuove di Provenza.

The pass, the Col de Largentière, now the Maddalena Pass on the border of France and Italy, was of great strategic and commercial importance because it linked Lyon with Italy. Amadeus was known for his hospitality, and never turned a person from his table without a meal.

On 1 November 1391 Amadeus died of tetanus after a hunting accident. His will caused controversy. He named his own mother, a sister of the Duke de Bourbon, as guardian of his son and heir Amadeus VIII, instead of following the tradition of appointing the child's mother, Bonne of Berry, a daughter of John, Duke of Berry. Because of the dispute between the two women, rumours that Amadeus had been poisoned soon emerged, and three months of negotiation were needed to restore peace in the family. His son Amadeus VIII was later known as Antipope Felix V.
amadeus-viii-duke-of-savoy: Amadeus was born in Chambéry on 4 September 1383, the son of Amadeus VII, Count of Savoy, and Bonne of Berry. He became count in 1391, when his father died on 2 November, a death attributed to poisoning or at least bad treatment by his physicians. His father's testament had named his own mother Bonne of Bourbon as regent rather than his wife, which set off a struggle at court between grandmother and mother that drew in the dukes of Berry, Bourbon and Orléans and King Charles VI of France. The grandmother acted as regent until 1397.

His early rule saw the centralisation of power and the territorial expansion of Savoy. In 1416 Sigismund, King of the Romans, raised him to Duke of Savoy, the first to hold the ducal title. In 1418 his cousin and brother-in-law Louis of Piedmont, the last male of the elder branch of the House of Savoy, died, leaving Amadeus as his heir-general and uniting the male lines of the house. From 1401 to 1422 he campaigned to recover the area around Geneva and Annecy, and he encouraged attempts to negotiate an end to the Hundred Years' War.

After his wife Mary of Burgundy died in 1428, he founded the Order of Saint Maurice with six other knights in 1434. They lived in a quasi-monastic state at the castle of Ripaille near Geneva, under a rule he drew up himself, while his son Louis acted as regent of the duchy. Amadeus was sympathetic to conciliarism, the movement to have the Church governed by councils, and had close relations with the Council of Basel. On 25 June 1439 the council deposed Pope Eugene IV, and on 5 November it elected Amadeus pope, with 26 votes in the ballot. He accepted on 5 February 1440 and took the name Felix V, naming his son Louis Duke of Savoy.

Felix V left Basel for Lausanne in 1442, and the council later moved its sessions to Lausanne. After Eugene IV died in 1447, both sides favoured a settlement. On 7 April 1449 Felix V accepted the authority of Pope Nicholas V and resigned; he was named a cardinal and Bishop of Sabina and papal legate in the territories of Savoy. He is the last historical antipope recognised by a significant part of the Catholic clergy. He died in Geneva on 7 January 1451 and was buried at Ripaille.
amadiya: Amedi, also written Amadiye, is a town in the Duhok Governorate of the Kurdistan Region of Iraq, built on a mesa in the broader valley of the Great Zab. According to Ibn al-Athir, its Arabic name, Amadiyya, comes from Imad al-Din Zengi, who built a citadel in 1142 on the site of an earlier fortification. Another theory derives it from Imad al-Dawla, though this is less likely, and Jeffrey Szuchman considers it of Hurrian or Urartian origin. It is the most northerly city in Iraq, with a hot-summer Mediterranean climate and occasional snow in winter.

From the Early Bronze Age until the 16th century BCE the region was part of Kurda and inhabited by Subartu, and under the Mitanni its people were known as Zubarians. Ashurnasirpal I of the Middle Assyrian Empire conquered it in the 11th century BCE. It later came under the Medes and the Achaemenid Empire, then the Parthian Empire, and then the Sasanian district of Adiabene until the Muslim conquest in the 640s. After that it was ruled for centuries by an amir of the Abbasid dynasty, reputed to be one of the richest families in the region.

Amedi was the birthplace of the messiah claimant David Alroy, active about 1160. In 1163, according to Joseph ha-Kohen, the town's Jewish population numbered about a thousand families who traded in gall-nuts. Alroy led a revolt against the city and was defeated and killed. From 1376 to 1843 Amedi was the seat of the semi-autonomous emirate of Bahdinan. The Qubahan School, for Islamic studies, was founded under Sultan Hussein Wali of Bahdinan (1534-1576), and the Great Mosque of Amedi dates from the 12th century.

The Dominican Leopoldo Soldini founded a mission for Kurdistan in Amedi in 1760. His colleague Maurizio Garzoni lived there for fourteen years and compiled an Italian-Kurdish dictionary and grammar, the first study of Kurdish grammar and language, for which he is often called the father of Kurdology. In 1907 the population was 6,000, of whom 2,500 were Kurds, 1,900 Jews and 1,600 Chaldean Catholic Assyrians. Ruins of a synagogue and of the Qubahan School survive, and the Sufi shaykh Ali Kurdi Maqtul, who died in 1519, is among the town's notable people.
amalasuntha: Amalasuintha was probably born in Ravenna in 495, the only child of Theodoric and his wife Audofleda, the sister of Clovis, King of the Franks. The marriage, made about 493, was political: Theodoric had defeated the various Gothic kingdoms and sought an alliance with the Franks. On her father's side she belonged to the Amali dynasty. She was married to Eutharic, an Amali prince, to ensure a legitimate heir, and they had two children, Athalaric and Matasuntha. Eutharic died in 522, which alarmed Theodoric, since his kingdom lacked an adult male heir.

Athalaric was ten years old when Theodoric died, and Amalasuintha took control of the kingdom as regent, although Cassiodorus and Procopius call Athalaric king. According to Procopius, the Gothic aristocracy wanted him raised in the Gothic manner, while she wanted him to resemble the Roman princes. She had close ties to the Byzantine emperor Justinian I, which made her adherence to Roman learning and customs the more objectionable to the Goths. Cassiodorus and Procopius both praised her wisdom and her command of Greek, Gothic and Latin.

Conscious of her unpopularity, she banished, and afterwards put to death, three Gothic nobles whom she suspected of plotting against her. Amory, Heather and Heydemann have suggested that one of them was Tuluin, a powerful Gothic noble and general. She also opened negotiations with Justinian, with the aim of removing herself and the Gothic treasure to Constantinople. Athalaric died in 534, most likely from heavy drinking combined with a disease, probably diabetes. She then ruled as queen and made her older cousin Theodahad co-ruler, hoping to win over her harshest critics, since he led the military aristocracy that opposed her pro-Roman stance.

Instead, Theodahad fostered the discontent of the Goths and had Amalasuintha imprisoned on the island of Martana in Lake Bolsena. There she was murdered while bathing, on 30 April 535 according to Agnellus, though Massimiliano Vitiello has suggested May. Procopius reports that she was considering handing Italy to Justinian around the time of her death. Some evidence suggests that the Byzantine empress Theodora arranged the killing through Justinian's ambassador Peter the Illyrian; modern scholarship holds that she acted on Justinian's behalf, since the murder gave him a clear justification to attack. He used it as a reason for the Gothic War. In 536 Witigis deposed Theodahad and had him put to death. Carlo Goldoni wrote a tragedy on her life, presented at Milan in 1733.
amalfi-coast: The Amalfi Coast is a stretch of coastline overlooking the Tyrrhenian Sea and the Gulf of Salerno, in the Province of Salerno in the Campania region. It lies south of the Sorrentine Peninsula and north of the Cilentan Coast, and takes its name from the town of Amalfi, which has historically been its main geographical and political hub. The climate is Mediterranean, with warm summers and mild winters. The relatively steep southern shore of the Sorrentine Peninsula leaves little room for rural and agricultural development, and the only land route is the 40-kilometre Amalfi Drive, which runs along the coast from Vietri sul Mare in the east to Positano in the west.

During the 10th and 11th centuries the Duchy of Amalfi existed on the territory of the coast, centred on the town of Amalfi. The coast was afterwards controlled by the Principality of Salerno, until Amalfi was sacked by the Republic of Pisa in 1137.

Thirteen municipalities lie on the coast, many centred on tourism, and it has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 1997. Terraced gardens along the whole coastline grow a lemon called the sfusato amalfitano, used for limoncello liqueur. Another local liqueur, concerto, a dark rosolio with spicy notes, is made in Tramonti. Amalfi is known for a hand-made thick paper called bambagina, historically used for private writings, legal acts and revenue stamps, and other products include anchovies from Cetara and the colourful handmade ceramics of Vietri. The Rulers of Amalfi are the central figures of John Webster's Jacobean tragedy The Duchess of Malfi, and the Dutch artist M. C. Escher made a number of artworks of the coast.
amalric-i-of-jerusalem: Amalric was the younger son of King Fulk and Queen Melisende. After Fulk died in 1143 following a horse-riding accident, Melisende was crowned again alongside her elder son, the 13-year-old Baldwin III, and later withheld power from him. In 1151 she gave Amalric the County of Jaffa, and he became her most important partisan besides the Church. In 1152 Baldwin besieged her and her loyal men, Amalric among them, in the Tower of David in Jerusalem and deposed her. Baldwin conquered Ascalon from Fatimid Egypt in 1153 and later granted both Ascalon and Jaffa to Amalric. In 1157 Amalric married Agnes of Courtenay, and they had a daughter, Sibylla, and a son, Baldwin.

Baldwin III died in Beirut on 10 February 1163 without children. The High Court refused to recognise Amalric as king unless he repudiated Agnes, and he accepted; the marriage was annulled on grounds of kinship, and the papal legate was present. The children's legitimacy was confirmed. The patriarch crowned him in the Church of the Holy Sepulchre on 18 February, the day of Baldwin's funeral. Early in his reign he passed the Assise sur la ligece, which let the vassals of powerful lords appeal directly to the king.

His chief aim was the conquest of Egypt, whose government was in disarray as the viziers Dirgham and Shawar fought for power. If Nur al-Din, who had united Damascus and Aleppo, took Egypt too, the crusader states would be encircled. After a first expedition in 1163, he supported Shawar against Dirgham and Nur al-Din's general Shirkuh in 1164. Amalric invaded again in 1167–68, but Egypt fell to Shirkuh instead. Shirkuh died in 1169, and Amalric launched a joint attack on Damietta with the Byzantine emperor Manuel I Komnenos, whose grandniece Maria became his second wife. It failed amid rain, shortage of food and poor cooperation, and Nur al-Din used Amalric's absences to plunder the kingdom.

Amalric's son Baldwin showed signs of leprosy in childhood, and William of Tyre, his tutor, found that the boy did not feel pain in his right arm. Amalric sought a capable son-in-law and invited Count Stephen I of Sancerre to marry Sibylla, but for unknown reasons Stephen refused and left. In 1174, while trying to profit from the confusion in Syria after Nur al-Din's death, Amalric caught dysentery and died on 11 July. His son succeeded him as Baldwin IV.

William of Tyre described him as serious and taciturn, intellectually gifted, daring in battle and fond of money. The Muslim chronicler Ibn al-Athir called him the bravest of the Crusader kings. One historian argues that acting without his Byzantine allies in 1168 may have allowed Egypt and Syria to be united under Saladin.
amami-oshima: Amami Ōshima is the largest island of the Amami archipelago, about 380 kilometres south of the southern tip of Kyūshū and 250 kilometres north of Okinawa. 35 square kilometres and is the seventh largest island of the Japanese archipelago after the four main islands, Okinawa Island and Sado Island. It is of volcanic origin, with Mount Yuwanda, at 605 metres, its highest peak, and a coral reef surrounds its coast.

The East China Sea lies to the west and the Pacific Ocean to the east. The climate is humid subtropical, with frequent typhoons. It is home to rare endemic animals, among them the Amami rabbit, sometimes called a living fossil, and Lidth's jay.

It is uncertain when the island was first settled. Stone tools point to the Japanese Paleolithic, and pottery and other artifacts show constant contact with Jōmon, Yayoi and Kofun period Japan. The Nihon Shoki mentions it under the year 657. In the Nara and early Heian periods it was a stopping place for envoys from Japan to the Tang court, and mother of pearl was an important export to Japan. It was briefly incorporated into the Ryukyu Kingdom as that kingdom expanded north along the archipelago.

Because Ryukyu was a tributary vassal of Ming China, this changed the island's status. Samurai of the Shimazu clan invaded in 1609 to counter Ming authority, and the Tokugawa shogunate recognised the island as the domain's holding in 1624. Shimazu rule was harsh: the inhabitants were reduced to serfdom and forced to raise sugar cane to meet high taxes, which often led to famine.

Saigō Takamori was exiled to the island in 1859 and stayed for two years, and his house is preserved as a memorial museum. After the Meiji Restoration it was incorporated into Ōsumi Province and later became part of Kagoshima Prefecture. After World War II the Amami Islands were occupied by the United States until 1953. The island has about 73,000 inhabitants, living in the city of Amami, the towns of Tatsugō and Setouchi and the villages of Uken and Yamato.

Much of it lies within Amami Guntō National Park, established in 2017, and in 2021 it was listed as part of a serial UNESCO World Heritage Site with Tokunoshima, the northern part of Okinawa Island and Iriomote. Two dialects of the Amami language are spoken there, and UNESCO classifies the language as endangered.
aman-andom: Aman Mikael Andom was born on 21 June 1924 in the village of Tsazega in Italian Eritrea, one of five children, and was a Lutheran. Educated in Sudan, he returned to Ethiopia with the British forces that defeated the Italians and restored Emperor Haile Selassie to the throne.

He commanded Ethiopian contingents in the Korean War and the Congo Crisis and was promoted to major general in 1962. During the Ethiopian–Somali Border War of 1964 he earned the nickname Desert Lion after a battle with Somali forces in the Ogaden. There is some evidence that he was in contact with the officers of the junta as early as February and March 1974, and by July he had been appointed its chief of staff.

On 15 September 1974, three days after the emperor was taken from his palace to imprisonment at the headquarters of the Fourth Division, the officers made Aman their chairman and acting head of state, while proclaiming Crown Prince Asfaw Wossen king-designate. According to the historians Ottaway, he was at odds with most of the Derg from the first day, even over whether he was its chairman or only its spokesman. He thought the council too large, wanted a negotiated settlement with the Eritrean Liberation Front where his opponents sought to crush it, and refused to approve the execution of former high officials, among them two former prime ministers and members of the royal family.

He visited Eritrea twice, from 25 August to 6 September and again in November, promising an end to old practices and an inquiry into the army's crimes against Eritreans. After Derg soldiers stormed the camp of the Corps of Engineers on 7 October, he sought support in the wider army, and on 15 November he sent all units a message highly critical of the Derg. Two days later Mengistu Haile Mariam demanded 5,000 men for Eritrea and the execution of six imprisoned officials.

Aman refused, resigned and retired to his house, appealing secretly to the Third Division, but Mengistu intercepted the appeals. He was killed in a gunfight with the troops sent to arrest him on 23 November 1974; the historian Bahru Zewde concludes that he had become an obstacle to the Derg's exercise of power.
amanirenas: Amanirenas, also spelled Amanirena, was queen regnant of the Kingdom of Kush in the mid to late 1st century BCE. Her full title was Amnirense qore li kdwe li, 'Amanirenas, qore and kandake'. Meroitic, the language of Kush, remains undeciphered, but inscriptions giving her both 'qore' and 'kandake' suggest that she ruled in her own right. Her name appears on stelae beside those of Teriteqas and Akinidad. Their relationship is not entirely clear, but scholars generally consider Akinidad her son and Teriteqas her husband, with kandake her title.

According to the geographer Strabo, whose account is the main source, Kushite forces attacked Thebais and Syene in 25 BCE while the prefect Aelius Gallus was away on his expedition to Arabia. They took Syene, Elephantine and Philae, enslaved inhabitants and destroyed statues of Augustus. Strabo calls the queen Candace, a Latinized form of her title, and describes her as blind in one eye. The war lasted three years, from 25 to 22 BCE.

Gaius Petronius, the new prefect of Egypt, marched against the Kushites at Syene with fewer than ten thousand infantry and eight hundred cavalry, according to Strabo, facing thirty thousand men armed with ox-hide shields, axes, pikes and swords. The Kushites were overwhelmed and fled, and their generals were captured and sent to Alexandria. Petronius then took Pselchis and Premnis. Amanirenas, at Napata with her son, offered to return the captives and the statues, but her envoys were ignored and the city was razed. She attacked Premnis a second time, but Petronius reached it first. Her ambassadors were then taken to Augustus at Samos, who imposed no further tribute.

The settlement moved the Roman frontier south of Egypt's former limit to Primis, now Qasr Ibrim. The Romans evacuated part of the Thirty-Mile Strip, the Meroites were exempt from tribute and the Romans kept the Dodekashoinos as a military border zone. The treaty remained in force until the end of the third century CE.

A bronze head of Augustus, larger than life, with eyes of calcite, metal rings and glass, was found by the archaeologist John Garstang in 1910 buried beneath the steps of a temple at Meroë and was given to the British Museum in 1911. The Hamadab Stela, found by Garstang in 1914, names Amanirenas and Akinidad and shows shackled prisoners beneath the ruling couple. It contains the Meroitic term Areme, which may mean Rome, and scholars think it may give a Kushite account of the campaign.
amanishakheto: Amanishakheto was a queen regnant, or kandake, of Kush. In Meroitic hieroglyphs her name is written Amanikasheto, and in Meroitic cursive she is called Amaniskheto qor kd(ke), meaning Amanishakheto, Qore and Kandake, that is, ruler and queen. Her mother is recorded as Ar(...)tḫwit. She is believed to have been the direct successor of the queen regnant Amanirenas, though how the two were related is unknown. The next Kushite ruler, and so her possible successor, was another queen regnant, Shanakdakhete.

Several monuments name her. She is mentioned in the Amun temple of Kawa, on a stela from Meroë, in the inscriptions of a palace building at Wad ban Naqa, on a stela from Qasr Ibrim, on another stela from Naqa and at her pyramid at Meroë (Beg. no. N6). A sandstone relief from the Temple of Amun at Naqa, now in the Khartoum National Museum, shows her beside two deities, identified as Amesemi and Apedemak. She wears the royal costume associated with the Nubian warrior and hunting gods, which marks her as protector of her kingdom, and is drawn taller than the two other figures.

A sandstone stele from the same temple shows her with the warrior goddess Amesemi. Both women wear fitted garments, a tasselled scarf, a collar and rounded wigs, and hieroglyphs on the back identify them. The temple at Naqa was built after her death.

She is best known for the jewellery found in her pyramid in 1834 by the Italian treasure hunter Giuseppe Ferlini, who destroyed the pyramid in search of burial goods. The find consisted of 10 bracelets, 9 shield rings, 67 signet rings, 2 collars or necklaces and many amulets, all made by craftsmen of the Kingdom of Meroë. The pieces are now in the Egyptian Museum of Berlin and the Egyptian Museum of Munich.
amanullah-khan: Amanullah Khan was born on 1 June 1892 at Paghman near Kabul, the third son of Emir Habibullah Khan by his second wife. He became governor of Kabul and held command of the army and the treasury. On 20 February 1919 Habibullah, on a hunting trip in Laghman Province, was shot in the head in his tent by an unknown assassin.

Habibullah's brother Nasrullah Khan was declared Emir at Jalalabad the next day. Amanullah, who had stayed in Kabul, seized the treasury and the central government. He proclaimed himself Emir within days and, despite an oath on the Quran that Nasrullah would come to no harm, had him arrested on 3 March. A court held on 13 April executed a colonel for the murder and, on manufactured evidence, judged Nasrullah complicit. Nasrullah received a life sentence and was killed in jail about a year later.

On 3 May 1919 Amanullah launched a surprise attack on British India, beginning the Third Anglo-Afghan War. After early successes the fighting settled into a stalemate, since Britain was still bearing the costs of the First World War. An armistice at the end of 1919 freed Afghanistan of British control over its foreign affairs.

With his father-in-law and foreign minister Mahmud Tarzi he drafted the country's first constitution, ratified on 11 April 1922 by 872 tribal elders and officials at a Loya Jirga in Jalalabad. More than 320 schools were founded, primary education was made compulsory, and strict dress codes for women were overturned, a policy in which his wife Queen Soraya Tarzi took part. A rebellion at Khost against these changes was put down in 1925. From late 1927 to 1928 he toured Europe, Turkey and other countries, where he met rulers including King George V and Mustafa Kemal Atatürk.

After his return, measures such as abolishing the veil, moving the weekly day of rest from Friday to Thursday and ordering Western clothes stirred conservative opposition. Habibullah Kalakani attacked Kabul on 14 December 1928 and took it on 7 January 1929. Amanullah abdicated on 14 January in favour of his half-brother Inayatullah Khan, who surrendered four days later. An attempt to retake the capital failed in April, and on 23 May 1929 he fled to India, never to return.

Mohammad Nadir Shah replaced Kalakani on 13 October 1929 and reversed most of the reforms, though his successor King Zahir later introduced a more gradual programme. Amanullah settled in Rome, where loyalists several times tried unsuccessfully to restore him. He died in Zürich on 26 April 1960 and was buried at Jalalabad near his father's tomb.
amapa: Amapá lies in the far north of Brazil and borders French Guiana for 730 kilometres, the Atlantic Ocean for 578 kilometres, Pará, and Suriname for 63 kilometres. Its capital and largest city is Macapá. About 90 per cent of its area is Amazon rainforest, and the mouth of the River Oiapoque marks the northern end of Brazil's coastline. Tumucumaque Mountains National Park, established in 2002, is the largest tropical forest national park in the world.

In the colonial period the region was called Portuguese Guiana and was part of Portugal's State of Brazil. From 1637 to 1654 it was merged into the Captaincy of Pará as the Captaincy of Cabo de Norte. It exported lumber, resins, annatto, vegetable oils and salted fish to Europe, and the French established sugarcane plantations. The discovery of mineral deposits drew British and Dutch invaders, whom the Portuguese repelled. The Treaty of Utrecht in 1713 set the boundary between Brazil and French Guiana, but the French did not respect it. A fort was built at São José de Macapá as a base of Portuguese power, and in the 18th century France retook control of the area.

The dispute with France continued until 1900. Gold and rubber raised the Portuguese population in the 19th century and brought it to a head, though French settlers had founded the Republic of Independent Guyana, which lasted from 1886 to 1891. Brazil took the claim to international arbitration at Geneva, which found for Brazil on 1 December 1900. The area was then incorporated into Pará as Araguari, and in 1943 became the federal territory of Amapá.

The discovery of rich manganese deposits at Serra do Navio in 1945 changed the local economy, and manganese remained its largest source of revenue. The decision to make Amapá a state was made on 5 October 1988, when Brazil's new constitution was promulgated, and the first state legislators took office on 1 January 1991. The state has 733,759 people at the 2022 census, most of them living in Macapá and Santana. Indigenous peoples such as the Galibi do Oiapoque, Karipuna, Palikur and Wayampi live in demarcated territories, and French is taught in schools because of the nearness of French Guiana.
amapala: Amapala is a municipality of the department of Valle, made up of El Tigre Island and its satellite islets and rocks in the Gulf of Fonseca, with an area of 75.2 square kilometres. A natural deep channel allowed it to serve for a long time as Honduras's main port on the Pacific despite its lack of modern infrastructure. The name is usually derived from Nahuatl, meaning close to amates, though another theory reads it as hill of corn in the Goajiquiro dialect. The climate is tropical savanna, with a pronounced dry season.

Local legend holds that the island was called Cerro de El Tigre because pirates under Francis Drake, seen by the inhabitants as wild beasts, operated there in the 16th century; Drake probably never stayed, though later pirates such as William Dampier did. The town was founded in 1838, and its port was opened and declared free in 1868. Through the 19th century it shipped large quantities of gold, silver and other ores, although the delay in building a transcontinental railway from Puerto Cortés held back its growth.

Mary Lester, writing as Mary Soltera, described the town in 1881 in A Lady's Ride Across Spanish Honduras. In 1895 El Salvador, Honduras and Nicaragua signed the Treaty of Amapala, which set up the short-lived Greater Republic of Central America. By the mid-1970s the port of San Lorenzo on the mainland had gradually taken its place.
The 2013 census counted 12,250 people in the municipality, most of them Mestizo. Most residents work as fishermen, and the community also depends on money sent by former residents living abroad.
amar-sonar-bangla: The Partition of Bengal took effect on 16 October 1905, after the Viceroy of India, Lord Curzon, announced it on 20 July. It split the Bengal Presidency into two parts along communal lines, East Bengal and Assam having a Muslim majority and West Bengal a Hindu one, a division claimed to have been politically motivated. Songs such as this one were meant to rekindle the unified spirit of Bengal and to raise public consciousness against it. Some sources claim the song was written in that context, but the original manuscript was never found, so the date of composition cannot be established with certainty.

Prashanta Kumar Paul, in his biography of Tagore, claimed that it was first sung on 25 August 1905 at an essay conference in Kolkata. Its lyrics appeared in September 1905 in the journals Bongodorshon and Baul, and the music in notation in the journal Shongeet Biggnan Praveshika. Tagore's niece Indira Devi wrote down the notation as she heard it from Tagore himself.

The words are an ode to Mother Bengal. Amar means my, and sonar, from sona, gold, is used as a term of endearment, so that Sonar Bangla can express both beloved and precious. The melody derives from Ami Kothay Pabo Tare, a song of the Baul singer Gagan Harkara, set to the rhythm cycle Dadra tala.

In Syed Ali Ahsan's English translation, the poem speaks of the air like a flute, the scent of mango orchards in Falgun, paddy fields in Ogrohayon, banyan trees along the riverbanks, and a childhood spent in the mother's playhouse with her soil smeared on the body. It closes with the speaker offering his head beneath her feet. Only the first ten lines are sung as the national anthem.

The Provisional Government of Bangladesh adopted the song in 1971, during the Bangladesh Liberation War, and Samar Das composed the orchestral version. When the Constitution of Bangladesh was drafted in 1972, two songs were proposed, this one and Dwijendra Lal Roy's Dhana Dhanya Pushpa Bhara, and Amar Sonar Bangla was selected.

According to Ziauddin Ahmed, the choice has drawn criticism since at least 1975. Some opponents point out that Bengali Muslims of East Bengal had welcomed the partition the song was written against. Others object that the word mother refers to a Hindu goddess. After the coup of 15 August 1975 a committee recommended replacements, including Kazi Nazrul Islam's Notuner Gaan, but the process halted when the president was removed. In 1979 Prime Minister Shah Azizur Rahman proposed Shahnaz Rahmatullah's Prothom Bangladesh instead, as Tagore was not Bangladeshi.
amarapura: The name Amarapura comes from the Pali for The Immortal City. King Bodawpaya of the Konbaung Dynasty founded the city as his new capital in May 1783, and it became a centre of Buddhist reforms and learning. In 1800 Buddhist clergy from Sri Lanka received higher ordination there and founded the Amarapura Nikaya, or Amarapura sect. In 1810 the town was estimated to hold 170,000 inhabitants, but a fire destroyed it that year. Bodawpaya's grandson, King Bagyidaw, moved the court back to Ava in November 1821, and by 1827 the population of Amarapura was estimated at only 30,000.

King Tharrawaddy brought the royal capital back to Amarapura in February 1842. In February 1857 King Mindon began to build Mandalay, 11 km to the north, as his new capital. The royal treasury had been depleted by the Second Anglo-Burmese War of 1852, so Mindon reused as much material from Amarapura as possible. The palace buildings were dismantled and carried to the new site by elephant, and the city walls were pulled down for roads and railways. Amarapura officially ceased to be the capital on 23 May 1859, when Mandalay took over that role.

The ruins of the city wall show that it formed a square with sides of about three-quarters of a mile, and at each corner stood a solid brick pagoda about 30 m high. The most notable building was a temple adorned with 250 lofty pillars of gilt wood, which held a colossal bronze statue of the Buddha.

Amarapura is now a township of Mandalay, bounded by the Irrawaddy River on the west and the old capital site of Ava to the south. It is known for the Burmese tradition of acheik textile weaving, which began there and became popular under the Konbaung dynasty, when sumptuary laws regulated who could wear acheik clothing. It is also known for silk and cotton weaving and bronze casting.

Its sights include the Pahtodawgyi, a stupa built by Bodawpaya in 1816 outside the city walls, and the ruins of the Amarapura Palace, with the tombs of Bodawpaya and Bagyidaw. The U Bein Bridge, a footbridge of about 1.2 km, was built by the mayor U Bein from teak columns salvaged from the old palace during the move to Mandalay.
amarna-letters: The Amarna letters, cited as EA for el-Amarna, are an archive on clay tablets, mainly diplomatic correspondence between the Egyptian administration and its representatives in Canaan and Amurru, or the leaders of neighbouring kingdoms. They span no more than 30 years in the middle of the 14th century BCE and were found at el-Amarna, the modern name of Akhetaten, the capital founded by Akhenaten. They are written in cuneiform, the writing system of ancient Mesopotamia, and not in Egyptian. Most are in a variety of Akkadian sometimes called Canaanite-Akkadian.

The known tablets total 382 with fragments, of which 350 are letters and the rest literary and school texts. Jørgen Knudtzon published 358 in Die El-Amarna-Tafeln (1907 and 1915), still the standard edition; the other 24 were excavated later.

The archive covers the reign of Akhenaten and that of his predecessor Amenhotep III. It sheds light on Egypt's relations with Babylonia, Assyria, Syria, Canaan and Alashiya, and with Mitanni and the Hittites. Letters of the Babylonian king Kadashman-Enlil I anchor Akhenaten's reign in the mid-14th century BCE. The letters contain the first mention of a group called the Habiru, whose possible connection with the Hebrews remains debated. Tushratta of Mitanni complains that Akhenaten sent him plated statues instead of solid gold ones. Rib-Hadda of Byblos pleads for Egyptian military help in more than 58 letters. Abdi-Heba of Jerusalem asks for archers against the Habiru and writes, in EA 287, that the king has placed his name in Jerusalem forever and cannot abandon it.

Local Egyptians digging in the ruins of Amarna found most of the tablets around 1887 and sold them on the antiquities market. Flinders Petrie recovered 21 fragments in 1891 and 1892, and only 26 tablets and fragments were found in their archaeological context. The first group is now scattered among museums, with 202 or 203 tablets in Berlin, 99 in the British Museum and 49 or 50 in Cairo. William L. Moran notes that the chronology presents problems that still elude definitive solution, and that the archive spans at most about thirty years, perhaps only fifteen. It closed when the city was deserted, commonly believed to be in the second year of Tutankhamun, about 1332 BCE.
amarna-period: The Amarna Period was the later part of the Eighteenth Dynasty, when the royal residence moved from Thebes to Akhetaten, meaning Horizon of the Aten, at the site of modern Amarna. The move took place under Amenhotep IV, who changed his name to Akhenaten to reflect a religious change in which the sun disc Aten was worshipped above all other gods. Four kings reigned in the period: Akhenaten, Smenkhkare, Neferneferuaten and Tutankhamun. A leading theory holds that Smenkhkare was co-regent towards the end of Akhenaten's reign. Neferneferuaten was a female ruler, perhaps Nefertiti or the wife of Smenkhkare, and the reigns of both are not confirmed.

Akhenaten's cult is the earliest verified expression of a form of monotheism, though scholars debate its nature: some say he restored monotheism, others that he suppressed one solar cult by asserting another and never abandoned other traditional deities. Its best-known text is the Great Hymn to the Aten. Royal portraiture changed too, showing Akhenaten in an androgynous, highly stylised manner, and builders used smaller blocks of stone set in strong mortar. Official inscriptions began to reflect the spoken language of the time. The royal women, among them Nefertiti, who bore six daughters, left more surviving text than any other women of ancient Egypt.

The Amarna Letters are the correspondence among the rulers of Babylon, Assyria, Mitanni and Hatti, which modern historians have called the Club of Great Powers. Their letters follow a consistent formula, opening with a greeting and good wishes, and the rulers addressed each other as brothers. The gifts they exchanged, especially gold, are a constant subject, and Akhenaten married a Mitanni princess to strengthen ties between the two states.

Tutankhamun came to the throne at about nine years old, and the traditional pantheon was swiftly restored. Much of the government moved to Memphis. He died before he was twenty without a surviving heir, and Ay succeeded him. Ay's three-year reign was followed by that of Horemheb, a general, who ordered Akhetaten torn down and cut the period from official histories and monuments, so that his monuments present him as the direct successor of Amenhotep III. Later Egyptians called the period the time of the enemy of Akhetaten, and Akhenaten suffered damnatio memoriae. Horemheb appointed Paramessu, who became Ramesses I in 1292 BCE, the first pharaoh of the Nineteenth Dynasty.
amasis-ii: Most information about Amasis comes from Herodotus and can be verified only imperfectly from monuments. According to the Greek historian he was of common origins, an officer in the Egyptian army born at Siuph near Saïs. He took part in a campaign of Pharaoh Psamtik II in Nubia in 592 BCE. His mother was a woman named Tashereniset, as a bust now in the British Museum shows, and a stone block from Mehallet el-Kubra names his maternal grandmother as Tjenmutetj.

Native Egyptian soldiers returning from a disastrous expedition to Cyrene in Libya suspected that they had been betrayed so that King Apries could rule more absolutely through his Greek mercenaries. Amasis was sent to quell the revolt but was proclaimed king by the rebels instead. Apries fled and was killed in a final attempt to regain power around 567 BCE, in the fourth year of Amasis, and an inscription records his honourable burial. Amasis married Khedebneithirbinet II, one of the daughters of Apries, to legitimise his kingship. In the same year the Babylonians under Nebuchadnezzar II invaded Egypt, and the evidence suggests they gained a foothold but were repelled.

Herodotus describes Amasis as a philhellene. He assigned the commercial colony of Naucratis on the Canopic branch of the Nile to the Greeks, contributed 1,000 talents to rebuild the temple at Delphi, and married Ladice, a Greek princess of Cyrene. He allied with Polycrates of Samos and Croesus of Lydia, added Cyprus to his kingdom, and adorned the temples of Lower Egypt with monolithic shrines. Herodotus writes that Egypt then reached its highest prosperity, with 20,000 inhabited cities. When Cyrus destroyed Lydia in 546 BCE and defeated the Babylonians in 538 BCE, Amasis was left without major allies and cultivated closer ties with the Greek states.
