Amasis died in 526 BCE and was buried at the royal necropolis of Sais, within the enclosure of the temple of Neith. His tomb has not been rediscovered. His son Psamtik III reigned about six months and was defeated by the Persians in 525 BCE at Pelusium. Herodotus relates that Cambyses had Amasis' mummy taken from its tomb, whipped and stabbed, and finally burned. In Herodotus' account the war began when Amasis sent Nitetis, a daughter of Apries, in place of his own daughter to Cambyses, who then learned of the trick.

Stories of Amasis circulated from the fifth century BCE in Egyptian and Greek sources, presenting him as an unconventional pharaoh of practical wisdom, a trickster on the throne. Herodotus tells how, when the Egyptians disrespected him as a commoner, he melted down a golden footbath into a statue that the people then worshipped. He then told them they now owed him the same respect.
amasra: Amasra lay in the ancient region of Paphlagonia, where the original city seems to have been called Sesamus. The name Amastris comes from Amastris, niece of the last Persian king Darius III, wife of Dionysius, tyrant of Heraclea, and later of Lysimachus. After separating from Lysimachus she combined four small Ionian colonies, Sesamus, Cytorus, Cromna and Tium, into a new community on a peninsula. Tium soon detached itself, and Sesamus served as the acropolis.

Its tyrant Eumenes presented the city to Ariobarzanes of Pontus in about 265–260 BCE, and it stayed in the Pontic kingdom until Lucius Lucullus captured it in 70 BCE in the second Mithridatic War. The younger Pliny, as governor of Bithynia and Pontus, described it to Trajan as a handsome city and obtained permission to cover an open drain. A coin of Trajan's time gives it the title Metropolis.

In the Byzantine era the acropolis became a fortress and a church was built that still survives. The Rus sacked the city during the First Russo-Byzantine War in the 830s. Historian Speros Vryonis states that in the 9th century local industry, trade and farming made it one of the more prosperous towns of the Black Sea, and the writer Niketas David Paphlagon called it the Eye of Paphlagonia.

Seljuk raids in the 12th century reduced it to a small town. In the 13th century it changed hands several times: a Georgian army led by David Komnenos seized it, making it a possession of the Empire of Trebizond in 1204, and it was later captured by the Seljuk Turks. In 1261 it passed to the Republic of Genoa. Genoese rule ended when the Ottoman Sultan Mehmed II conquered the Anatolian shores of the Black Sea.

Amasra is the seat of Amasra District in Bartın Province and had 6,098 inhabitants in 2021. It has two islands, Büyük ada and Tavşan adası. Amasra Castle was begun in the Roman period, its walls built by the Byzantines, and its front walls and gates by the Genoese in the 14th and 15th centuries. The Fatih Mosque was a Byzantine church of the 9th century, converted after 1460.

The archaeological museum holds a statue of the snake god Glykon, described as a fraudulent creation of a local entrepreneur in Roman imperial times. Early in its Christian history the see of Amastris had a bishop named Palmas, mentioned in a letter of Dionysius of Corinth, and it is now a Catholic titular see. Amasra belongs to the European Association of Historic Towns and Regions.
amasya: Amasya lies in the Black Sea Region of northern Turkey, in a narrow cleft of the Yeşilırmak (Iris) river. Almost vertical cliffs and the high peaks of the Canik and Pontus mountains bound the valley, and the town takes the shape of a letter V as it follows a sharp bend in the river. Although it is near the Black Sea, the valley is set apart from the coast and has an inland climate, well suited to apples.

Archaeological research shows that the site was settled in turn by Hittites, Phrygians, Cimmerians, Lydians, Greeks, Persians and Armenians. A Pontic kingdom under the Persian Mithridatic dynasty arose at the end of the 4th century BCE, and Amaseia was its capital until 26 BCE. In 70 BCE a Roman force under Lucullus took the city from Armenia, and Pompey made it a free city and administrative centre of the province of Bithynia and Pontus. Strabo described it as it was between 60 BCE and 19 CE. Around 112 Trajan made it part of Cappadocia.

Amaseia was the seat of a Christian metropolitan bishop from the 3rd century. Turkic migrations reduced the Christian population from the 12th century, and in 1317 the metropolitan Callistus could not enter his see during a violent Turkoman attack, so with the permission of Patriarch John XIII the metropolitanate was moved to Limnia in the Empire of Trebizond. The Ottoman sultans Murad II and Selim I were born in Amasya, and young princes were sent there to govern.

Before the First World War the town had 30,000 inhabitants, among them 13,788 Armenians. They were deported during the Armenian genocide, and afterwards the Armenian quarter, the bazaar, the Armenian church and the Greek church were burnt. In 1922 the Orthodox metropolis counted 40,000 Greek Orthodox Christians, half of them Greek, and all Greeks were forcibly removed in the population exchange of 1923.

Amasya is the seat of Amasya Province, with a population of 114,921 in 2021. Wooden Ottoman houses along the Yeşilırmak have been restored and now serve as cafes, restaurants and hotels, and the rock tombs of the Pontic kings are carved into the cliffs above them. Local folklore places the tale of Ferhat and Shirin here: for love of the princess Shirin, Ferhat tunnelled through a mountain, and the story has been retold as a play, a novel and an opera.
amaury-vi-of-montfort: Amaury was the son of Simon de Montfort, 5th Earl of Leicester, and Alix de Montmorency, and the older brother of Simon de Montfort, 6th Earl of Leicester. His father left for the Albigensian Crusade in 1209, and Amaury may have joined him in the spring of 1210, when his mother brought reinforcements to the south. He was knighted on 24 June 1213 at Castelnaudary in a particularly solemn ceremony and fought under his father until Simon's death at Toulouse on 25 June 1218.

As his father's heir Amaury received the County of Toulouse, taken from Raymond VI of Toulouse, and other lands in Languedoc. In 1224 he ceded them to King Louis VIII, who in exchange raised Montfort-l'Amaury to a county, and in 1230 he succeeded his uncle Mathieu II of Montmorency as Constable of France. He had also inherited the earldom of Leicester, but as a liegeman of the French king he could not be a vassal of the English king as well. By 1230 he and his brother Simon had agreed to divide the inheritance, though only on 11 April 1239 did Amaury formally renounce his English rights.

In 1239 he left for the Holy Land on the Barons' Crusade with Theobald I of Navarre and Hugh IV, Duke of Burgundy, carrying the fleur-de-lys by leave of King Louis IX. On 13 November 1239 he was taken prisoner at Gaza, in the disastrous battle in which Henry of Bar was killed, and led to Egypt with six hundred other captives.

Amaury spent 18 months in the dungeons of Cairo, treated more severely than the others because he would not tell the sultan who his fellow prisoners were. He was freed on 23 April 1241, after the crusaders under Richard of Cornwall made an alliance with the sultan of Egypt against the sultan of Damascus, but died at Otranto on the way home. He was buried in St. Peter's Basilica at the pope's order, and his heart was taken to the Abbey of Haute-Bruyère, near Montfort-l'Amaury. With his wife Beatrix, daughter of Guigues VI of Viennois, he had a son, Jean I, and four daughters.
amaziah-of-judah: Amaziah was the ninth king of Judah, the son and successor of Joash. His mother was Jehoaddan and his son was Uzziah. He took the throne at the age of 25, after the assassination of his father, and reigned for 29 years, according to 2 Kings and 2 Chronicles. Edwin R. Thiele dates his reign to 797/796 to 768/767 BCE, with Uzziah becoming co-regent in the fifth year of the reign. The books of Kings and Chronicles consider him a righteous king, but with some hesitation.

As soon as his kingdom was established, Amaziah executed his father's murderers but let their children live, in obedience to the Mosaic law that a person shall be put to death for his own sin. According to Chronicles he hired a mercenary army of 100,000 soldiers from Ephraim for 100 talents, to supplement 300,000 Judean soldiers, in an attempt to reconquer Edom, which had rebelled in the reign of his great-grandfather Jehoram. An unnamed prophet commanded him to send the mercenaries back, and he did so, followed by a decisive victory over the Edomites. The angry mercenaries attacked and looted several towns in Judah.

After the victory Chronicles says Amaziah brought the idol of the conquered Edomites to Jerusalem, and when a prophet rebuked him he threatened him with execution. His pride swollen, he challenged Jehoash, king of Israel and grandson of Jehu, to recognise his suzerainty or fight. Jehoash answered with the parable of the thistle and the cedar. Amaziah refused to be warned and rushed into a disastrous battle at Beth-shemesh. He was captured, 400 cubits of the wall of Jerusalem were broken down, the city, the Temple and the palace were looted, and hostages were taken to Samaria.

A conspiracy followed in which he was killed. Tradition holds that he was tortured to death by his own subjects at Lachish, where he had fled, and his body was brought to Jerusalem and buried in the royal sepulchre. Kings records the conspiracy simply, while Chronicles connects it with his turning away from the Lord.

The Books of Kings say he did what was right in the sight of the Lord but fell short of David's standard, because he did not remove the high places and centralise worship in Jerusalem. Chronicles says that he did right but not with a loyal heart. The rabbis of the Talmud held, on a tradition, that the prophet Amoz was his brother, which would make Isaiah a member of the royal family.
amazons: The Amazons were portrayed as female warriors and hunters, known for strength, archery and riding. Their society was closed to men and they raised only their daughters, returning their sons to their fathers, with whom they socialised briefly in order to reproduce. According to Apollonius of Rhodes they were the offspring of Ares and the nymph Harmonia. The origin of the word is uncertain. It may derive from an Iranian word for warriors, and the Greeks folk-etymologised it as breastless, which led to a tradition that they removed the right breast. Ancient art always shows them with both breasts, and the false etymology may have produced the myth.

Greek authors placed their homeland at the edge of the known world. Most often it was Pontus on the southern shore of the Black Sea, where the queen ruled from Themiscyra on the Thermodon river. In the Iliad they appear in the Trojan War, and in the lost Aethiopis the queen Penthesilea, of Thracian birth, brought an Amazon force to Troy after Hector's death. She was killed in single combat by Achilles. The hero Bellerophon fought them in Lycia, and Diodorus Siculus lists twelve Amazons who died fighting Heracles in his quest for the girdle of Hippolyta.

Herodotus wrote in the 5th century BCE that the Sauromatae, predecessors of the Sarmatians, arose from a union of Scythians and Amazons. He also saw the Lycians, who traced descent through the mother, as descendants of the Amazons. Many classical scholars regard the Amazons as wholly fictional, invented by Greek men as anti-women or to stand for Persians. Later authors, among them Stephanus of Byzantium and Jordanes, who made the Goths' women Amazons under Marpesia, gave them lists of names and further exploits.

From about 550 BCE Amazons appeared on vases as fighters and riders, and after the Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE the Amazonomachy became a popular subject on pottery, in sculpture and on buildings such as the Parthenon. The motif remained popular into Late Antiquity.

Archaeology has offered a possible historical basis. About 20 per cent of the warrior graves on the lower Don and lower Volga held women dressed for battle, and armed women make up as much as a quarter of Sarmatian military burials. Over a thousand nomad graves between the Black Sea and Mongolia show that women warriors existed in the steppe cultures, though it is not known for certain that these people inspired the Greek myth. Amazons also appear in Shakespeare's A Midsummer Night's Dream and in Heinrich von Kleist's drama Penthesilea of 1808.
amberg: The town was first mentioned in 1034 as Ammenberg and became an important trading centre in the Middle Ages, exporting mainly iron ore and iron products. In 1269 it passed to the Wittelsbach dynasty that ruled Bavaria, and in 1329 the town and the whole region fell to the Palatinate branch of the family, which gave the region the name Upper Palatinate. It was no longer politically part of the duchy of Bavaria. In the 16th century its rulers turned to Protestantism and the town to Lutheranism; later attempts to introduce the more radical Calvinism failed because citizens were reluctant. In 1628 Amberg and the Upper Palatinate became part of the electorate of Bavaria.

On 24 August 1796, in the French Revolutionary Wars, the Battle of Amberg was fought in and around the city: 35,000 French under Jean Baptiste Jourdan faced 40,000 Austrians under Archduke Charles, and the French lost significantly more men in an Austrian victory. Amberg was the regional capital of the Upper Palatinate until 1810, when power passed to the larger city of Regensburg.

Jews had settled in Amberg before 1294, when the first documentation appears. In 1298 thirteen of the town's Jews died in the Rindfleisch massacres. In 1347 six families received permission to settle, and in 1367 a yeshiva opened. The community was expelled in 1403 and the synagogue was annexed to the nearby church. Twelve Jews remained in the town in 1942. A displaced persons camp near the town housed mostly Jewish refugees and survivors after 1945.

Amberg lies in the Upper Palatinate, about halfway between Regensburg and Bayreuth. After World War II, when Bavaria fell into the American sector, it was home to a United States Army post, Pond Barracks, which closed in 1992 and was turned over to the local community, mostly for social housing.
ambhi: Taxiles is the name Greek chroniclers gave to the ruler of the tract between the Indus and the Hydaspes rivers in the Punjab at the time of Alexander the Great's expedition. His real name may have been Ambhi, which the Greeks rendered Omphis, and they appear to have called him Taxiles after his capital, Taxila, near the modern city of Attock in Pakistan. He is dated to 326 to 316 BCE as a ruler. He seems to have been on hostile terms with his neighbour Porus, who held the lands east of the Hydaspes, and probably sought to strengthen himself against Porus by sending an embassy to Alexander while Alexander was still in Sogdiana, with offers of assistance, perhaps in return for money.

The embassy brought gifts of 200 talents of silver, 3,000 fat oxen, 10,000 sheep or more and 700 horsemen, and offered surrender. When Alexander first came down into India he was wary of the sight of Ambhi's forces and ordered his own men to form up. Ambhi hurried to relieve his apprehension, met him with valuable presents and placed himself and all his forces at his disposal.

Alexander gave Ambhi back his title and his gifts and added Persian robes, gold and silver ornaments, 30 horses and 1,000 talents in gold. Ambhi helped Hephaestion and Perdiccas build a bridge over the Indus where it bends at Hund, supplied their troops with provisions, and received Alexander and his whole army at Taxila with every sign of friendship and generous hospitality. Alexander felt emboldened to divide his forces. When the king advanced, Taxiles accompanied him with 5,000 men and took part in the Battle of the Hydaspes. Afterwards Eudemus briefly took over Taxila, and by 317 BCE Chandragupta Maurya had conquered Alexander's satraps in the Indian subcontinent.
ambiorix: Ambiorix, together with Cativolcus, was prince of the Eburones, a Belgic tribe of north-eastern Gaul where modern Belgium lies. His name is generally accepted as Gaulish, formed from the prefix ambio- and rix, 'king'. Some scholars translate it as 'king of the surroundings' or 'king of the enclosure'; Fredrik Otto Lindeman instead renders it 'protector-king'.

Julius Caesar conquered parts of Gaul and Belgica in 57 BCE. In 54 BCE the harvest was poor and Caesar's troops urgently needed food, so the local tribes were forced to hand over part of their grain. The starving Eburones were reluctant, and Caesar had camps built near their villages, with each centurion made responsible for the deliveries. This created resentment, even though Caesar had earlier freed Ambiorix from paying tribute to the Atuatuci.

In the winter of 54 BCE Ambiorix joined Cativolcus in an uprising against the Roman forces of Quintus Titurius Sabinus and Lucius Aurunculeius Cotta. According to Caesar, Ambiorix deceived the Romans, claiming that the attack had been made without his consent and advising them to flee because a large Germanic force was about to cross the Rhine. Sabinus and Cotta's troops left the next morning and were ambushed and massacred a short distance from their camp.

Ambiorix then led a coalition of Belgic tribes that surrounded the camp of Quintus Tullius Cicero, brother of the orator Marcus, among the Nervii. A Roman messenger slipped through the lines and reached Caesar, who marched to the rescue. Caesar was heavily outnumbered, but he had his troops appear confused and frightened and so drew the Belgae into an attack on ground favourable to the Romans. His counterattack put them to flight.

Ambiorix had killed fifteen cohorts, and Caesar swore to destroy all the Belgic tribes. The campaigns took a few years; the tribes were slaughtered or driven out and their fields burned, and the Eburones disappeared from history. According to the writer Florus, Ambiorix and his men escaped across the Rhine and vanished from the record.

Ambiorix remained a relatively obscure figure until Belgian independence in 1830 prompted a search for national heroes and he was rediscovered in Caesar's Commentarii de Bello Gallico. In 1841 the poet Joannes Nolet de Brauwere Van Steeland wrote a lyrical epic about him, and on 5 September 1866 a statue of him was erected on the market square of Tongeren, which Caesar called Atuatuca. He now appears in Belgian comics and gives his name to many businesses.
ambohimanga: Ambohimanga is a hill and fortified royal settlement, called a rova, in the central highlands of Madagascar. The hill rises steeply on its eastern side, and the royal city at its peak looks over surrounding hills and valleys. Terraced rice paddies on the slopes were made in the 17th and 18th centuries. The crest is higher than the other hills among the twelve sacred hills of Imerina, which symbolises its political importance, and a forest on top escaped the deforestation of the highlands because it is sacred. The name joins ambohi, hill, and manga, which can mean sacred, blue, beautiful or good.

The highlands were first settled between 200 BCE and 300 CE by the Vazimba, and by the 15th century the Merina had migrated in from the south-east coast. In the mid-16th century the Merina principalities were united as the Kingdom of Imerina under King Andriamanelo, who fortified his hill town with earthen walls, stone gateways and deep trenches. This model of fortified town, the rova, spread among the nobility of Imerina until French colonisation.

Around 1700 a dethroned prince, Andriamborona, settled on the hilltop and renamed it Ambohitrakanga, hill of the guinea fowls. King Andriamasinavalona gave it its present name, and early in the 18th century divided Imerina into four quarters, giving the north-east to his son Andriantsimitoviaminiandriana, who ruled it from Ambohimanga. The division led to 77 years of civil war. Andrianampoinimerina ended it from Ambohimanga by negotiation and campaigns, reuniting Imerina under his rule by 1793.

After taking Antananarivo, Andrianampoinimerina moved the court and political functions back there, declaring the two cities of equal importance, with Ambohimanga the spiritual capital. He and his successors kept performing royal rituals at the site and lived in and remodelled it until the French colonised the kingdom and exiled the royal family in 1897.

The royal city is surrounded by ditches and stone walls and entered through 14 gateways, many of them once sealed by stone discs. Within it are three compounds, Bevato, Mahandrihono and Nanjakana. Mahandrihono, founded in the early 18th century, is the best preserved and holds the royal tombs, Andrianampoinimerina's house and a summer palace of Queen Ranavalona II. By custom the homes of the living were built of wood and plant material and the tombs of the dead of stone. The tombs of several Vazimba lie on and around the hill, and pilgrims still come. Ambohimanga was inscribed as a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001, covering 59 hectares with a buffer zone of 425 hectares.
ambon-island: Ambon Island has an area of 743 square kilometres and lies off the south-west coast of Seram, on the north side of the Banda Sea. It is 51 kilometres long and almost divided in two by Ambon Bay. The smaller south-eastern part, Leitimur, is joined by a narrow neck to the larger northern part, Leihitu, also called Hitoe. The highest mountains, Wawani and Salahutu, are volcanoes with hot springs. The island belongs to Wallacea, which deep water has always separated from the Asian and Australian continents, so it has few native mammals but many birds and insects. It gave its name to Amboyna, a prized figured wood first exported from it.

The Portuguese were the first Europeans to land, in 1512, and made Ambon a centre of their activity in Maluku. They set up a factory in 1521 but did not hold it peacefully until 1580, and were regularly attacked by the Muslims of Hitu on the north coast. The Dutch took the fort in 1605 under Steven van der Hagen without a shot. Ambon was the headquarters of the Dutch East India Company from 1610 to 1619, until Batavia was founded. An English settlement at Cambello, begun about 1615, was destroyed by the Dutch in 1623, with tortures of its inhabitants that became known as the Ambon Massacre.

The Company imposed a clove monopoly centred on Ambon, and until the nineteenth century the Dutch forbade clove trees on their other islands. Hitu resisted. Its leader Kakiali was murdered by a traitor in 1643, and Telukibesi's last stand at the fortress of Kapahaha ended in July 1646. A further revolt, the Great Ambon War, began in 1651 and was crushed by Arnold Vlaming van Oudshoorn in 1656 with great loss of life. The British held Ambon in 1796 to 1802 and in 1810 to 1814. Imperial Japanese forces captured the Dutch military base in 1942, and more than 300 Allied prisoners of war were then shot in the Laha massacre.

The island consists of the city of Ambon, the capital of Maluku province, in the south, and three districts of the Central Maluku Regency in the north. About 482,800 people lived there in mid 2023. The Ambonese are of mixed Malay and Papuan origin and are mostly Christians or Muslims. Ambonese Malay, which developed as the trade language of central Maluku, is the main language, and many families still carry Portuguese names such as Muskita and De Fretes. Cassava and sago are the chief crops, and cloves and nutmeg, once the main exports, are now grown in limited quantities.
ambracian-gulf: The Ambracian Gulf, also known as the Gulf of Arta, the Gulf of Actium or in some official documents the Amvrakikos Gulf, is about 40 kilometres long and 15 kilometres wide. It is one of the largest enclosed gulfs in Greece. It takes its name from the ancient city of Ambracia near its shores, and its alternative name from Arta, the medieval and modern city on the same site.

The entrance is a channel 700 metres wide between Aktio, the ancient Actium, on the south and Preveza on the north. The gulf is shallow, and marshes break its northern shore. The Louros and Arachthos rivers flow into it, so it is warmer and less salty than the Ionian Sea.

The gulf was the site of the Battle of Actium, in which the forces of Augustus defeated those of Mark Antony and Cleopatra. In 1538 the Ottoman admiral Hayreddin Barbarossa defeated the Holy League's admiral Andrea Doria at the Battle of Preveza, fought in the same gulf. From Greek independence, confirmed in the Treaty of Constantinople of 1832, until the Treaty of Bucharest of 1913 after the Second Balkan War, the gulf formed part of the border between the Kingdom of Greece and the Ottoman Empire. The remains of many ancient cities lie on its shores, among them Nicopolis, Limnaea and Olpae.

The towns of Preveza, Amphilochia and Vonitsa lie on the gulf, which is a national park of Greece because of its ecological importance. Its lagoons attract pelicans and flamingoes, and it is known for its large local shrimp. Since 2002 the Aktio-Preveza undersea tunnel has joined the two sides of the entrance; before that the crossing was possible only by ferry.
ambrogio-lorenzetti: Ambrogio Lorenzetti was born about 1290 and was active as a painter from about 1317 to 1348. His elder brother was the painter Pietro Lorenzetti. He was influenced by both Italo-Byzantine art and classical art forms, and his work shows the influence of Simone Martini while being more naturalistic. His earliest dated work is a Madonna and Child of 1319, now in the Museo Diocesano at San Casciano. He is documented in Florence until 1321 and returned there after spending a number of years again in his native Siena. He experimented with perspective and physiognomy and studied classical antiquity, interests often thought to have begun later in the Renaissance.

In his Madonna and Child the debt to Byzantine art is clear, especially in the frontality of the Virgin, but he conveys the monumentality of the figures without chiaroscuro, using colour and patterns. His Maestà, completed in 1335, adds an intense scene of maternal bonding that was unusual in Sienese art, and it contains allegorical elements that refer to Dante. Ghiberti mentions his interest in an antique statue found in an excavation at Siena, attributed to Lysippus.

His best-known work is the Allegory of Good and Bad Government, three fresco panels painted between February 1338 and May 1339 in the Sala dei Nove, the council hall of the nine executive magistrates of the Republic of Siena, in the Palazzo Pubblico. The Effects of Good Government on Town and Country is a pictorial encyclopedia of incidents in a peaceful medieval town and countryside. The landscape in the series is the first to appear as a subject in Western art after the Classical period. One of the frescoes, the Allegory of Bad Government and its Effects, holds the first evidence of the hourglass. His last work, the Annunciation of 1344, contains one of the first uses of clear linear perspective.

Both Ambrogio and Pietro are believed to have died of bubonic plague in 1348. Ambrogio's will is dated 9 August 1348. Giorgio Vasari included a biography of him in his Lives of the Most Excellent Painters, Sculptors, and Architects, describing his manners as more those of a gentleman and philosopher than those of an artist.
ambrogio-spinola: Ambrogio Spinola was born in Genoa in 1569, the eldest son of Filippo Spinola, one of the wealthiest of the Genoese nobility, and Polissena Grimaldi. Genoa was in practice a protected state of the Spanish Empire, and its people were the bankers of the Spanish monarchy. His younger brothers sought their fortunes in Spain, while he stayed home and in 1592 married Giovanna Bacciadonne. After losing a lawsuit against his family's rivals, the Doria, he decided to serve the Spanish monarchy in Flanders.

In 1602 Spinola and his brother Federico contracted with the Spanish government, risking the whole fortune of their house. Ambrogio raised 9,000 Lombard mercenaries at his own expense, while Federico formed a squadron of galleys and was killed in a fight with the Dutch in 1603. Spinola had no earlier experience as a soldier when he took over the Siege of Ostend as general on 29 September 1603. The ruins of the town fell to him on 22 September 1604, and he became a Knight of the Golden Fleece in 1605.

As commander-in-chief in Flanders he took Oldenzaal, Lingen, Wachtendonk, Groenlo and Rheinberg from Maurice of Nassau. The Spanish government pledged his entire fortune as security for the war's costs and never repaid him, so that by 1611 he was ruined, though he received the grandeeship he had sought. From 1620 to 1622 he led the Palatinate campaign in the Lower Palatinate and was made Captain-General. He suffered his worst setback at Bergen op Zoom in 1622, but captured Breda after a siege from 28 August 1624 to 5 June 1625. He let the Dutch garrison leave with its banners and arms, a gesture shown in Velázquez's painting Las Lanzas.

Hindered by the enmity of the royal favourite Olivares, Spinola left Flanders in January 1628 and did not return. In 1629 he went to Italy as plenipotentiary and general in the War of the Mantuan Succession, accompanied by Diego Velázquez, but Olivares had his powers taken away. He died on 25 September 1630 at the Siege of Casale, aged 61. He was a field commander whose daring often caught opponents off guard, and his family received only the title of Marquess of Los Balbases for the fortune it spent in the service of Philip III and Philip IV.
ambrose: Ambrose was born in 339 into a Roman Christian family of Greek descent, at Augusta Treverorum, modern Trier, then the capital of the province of Gallia Belgica. Scholars disagree on who his father was: some identify him with the praetorian prefect of Gaul Aurelius Ambrosius, others with an official named Uranius. A legend says that bees settled on his face in his cradle and left a drop of honey, taken as a sign of future eloquence. Trained in rhetoric and law, he served as Roman civil governor of Aemilia-Liguria at Milan before the people unexpectedly chose him as bishop by acclamation in 374.

As bishop Ambrose defended Nicene Christianity against Arianism, tried to mediate between the emperors Theodosius I and Magnus Maximus, and opposed the execution of Priscillianist heretics. After a massacre he excommunicated Theodosius, maintaining that an emperor is within the church, not over it. He advocated monasticism and asceticism, and his writing helped transmit Eastern Christian theology to the Latin West.

Despite heavy administrative duties he preached and presided at the Eucharist several times a week and dealt directly with the poor, widows, orphans and his clergy. He respected local customs, and advised Augustine of Hippo to follow the custom of the church where he found himself, since at Rome Ambrose fasted on a Saturday and at Milan did not. This gave rise to the saying When in Rome, do as the Romans do.

Ambrose wrote works of advocacy for Nicene Christianity, among them De Virginibus (377), the Exameron (386-390) and De officiis ministrorum (377-391), a practical guide for his clergy. De sacramentis contains the earliest witness to the present Roman Canon of the Mass, though its authorship is less certain than that of De mysteriis.

He was an important innovator in Christian hymnody. Hilary of Poitiers had written Latin hymns earlier, but only fragments survive, so Ambrose's are the earliest extant complete Latin hymns. Four, including Veni redemptor gentium, are universally accepted as his, each with eight four-line stanzas in iambic tetrameter. Ambrosian chant bears his name, but no melody in it can be attributed to him. With Augustine, Jerome and Gregory the Great he is one of the four Latin Doctors of the Church, formally declared in 1298.
ambrosius-aurelianus: Gildas, in his sermon De Excidio et Conquestu Britanniae, names Ambrosius Aurelianus as the only person from the 5th century he identifies. He describes a gentleman who perhaps alone of the Romans survived the Saxon assault, in which his parents, who had worn the purple, were slain. Gildas says his descendants in his own day had become greatly inferior to their grandfather's excellence. Under his leadership the survivors regained their strength and challenged the victors to battle. Gildas credits his victories to God's help, so he was very likely a Christian, and he adds that the Saxons and the Romano-British won in turn, so the victory was not decisive.

Scholars have debated what it meant that his family had worn the purple. It may refer to aristocratic rank, to a family of military tribunes, to the robes of a bishop or martyrdom, or to a provincial governor of consular rank. The Notitia Dignitatum lists two such governors in Roman Britain. Alex Woolf suggested a relation to the usurpers Marcus or Gratian, and N. J. Higham thinks he may have been distantly related to imperial families such as the Theodosian dynasty. Higham also argues that Gildas was not writing a biography but setting Ambrosius up as a model leader, in contrast to the rulers of his own time.

Bede follows Gildas closely in his Ecclesiastical History of the English People and dates the victory to the reign of the emperor Zeno, who ruled from 474 to 491. The Historia Brittonum, whose authorship and date remain open questions, says in its thirty-first chapter that Vortigern ruled in fear of Ambrosius. William of Malmesbury wrote that Ambrosius, the sole survivor of the Romans, ruled after Vortigern and that Arthur won the Battle of Badon on his behalf. It is not known whether Ambrosius or his successors took part in that battle, since Gildas names none of the combatants. Léon Fleuriot proposed that he was the same man as Riothamus, who fought the Goths in France around the year 470.

Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae calls him Aurelius Ambrosius, a son of King Constantine, who is exiled to Brittany as a child with his brother Uther. The brothers return, destroy Vortigern and defeat the Saxon leader Hengist. Ambrosius becomes king and is poisoned by his enemies, and Uther succeeds him. This does not fit Gildas, in which Ambrosius's family perished in the Saxon uprisings. In Welsh texts he is Emrys Wledig. As a young prophet who meets Vortigern, he was later transformed into the wizard Merlin. It has been suggested that the place-name Amesbury in Wiltshire preserves his name.
amdo: Amdo, also called Domey, is one of the three traditional regions of Tibet, with Ü-Tsang and Kham. It runs from the Machu, or Yellow River, to the Drichu, or Yangtze, and takes in the upper Yellow River and Lake Qinghai; the Bayan Har Mountains mark its southern edge. The land is wind-swept and treeless, with much grass, and it has long been known for the horses raised and running wild there. Wild yak and kiang live in the region, and herders keep yaks, dzo, goats, sheep and Mongolian horses. The name Amdo has become more common since the nineteenth century, when older sources used Domey. Its people call themselves Amdowa.

From the seventh to the ninth century the Tibetan Empire expanded into Amdo, and the Qiang, Sumpa, Tuyuhun and other peoples were gradually tibetanised. A treaty of 821 fixed the border between the empire and the Tang dynasty. The theocracy of Tsongkha ruled from 997 to 1104 and was often drawn into conflict with Western Xia, the Song, Liao and Jin.The Mongols had conquered eastern Amdo by 1240 and a priest and patron relationship began; the Yuan confirmed the division of Tibet into three commanderies. Mongols again took political control from the middle of the sixteenth century, and in 1642 Güshi Khan helped the fifth Dalai Lama reunify Tibet, though his own base in the Kokonor region stayed under Mongol control.

In the 1720s the Yongzheng Emperor of the Qing seized Qinghai from the Dzungars and fixed boundaries close to the modern ones, leaving monasteries and Tibetan chiefs near autonomy. After 1912 local chiefs, monasteries and Muslim warlords held power. Ma Qi fought the Labrang monastery in the name of the Republic of China, and his son Ma Bufang took the north-east corner in the 1930s. The 14th Dalai Lama was born in Amdo in 1935. The People's Liberation Army took much of the region from 1949, and the Communist Party assumed official control in 1958, when many nomads revolted and, according to reports, large numbers were killed, imprisoned or fled.

Amdo lies mostly within Qinghai province, with parts of Gansu and Sichuan, and Tibetans predominate in its western and southern parts, administered as autonomous prefectures. Han Chinese are the majority in the north and the east, around Xining and Haidong. It is the birthplace of Je Tsongkhapa, the Gelug reformer, and of the 14th Dalai Lama, and its monasteries include Kumbum near Xining, Rongwo in Rebgong, Labrang, the Kirti Gompas and Taktsang Lhamo. Traditionally Amdo Tibetans live as nomads or farmers, often keeping a summer base in the mountains and a winter one in the valleys.
amecameca: Amecameca lies in the eastern part of the State of Mexico, between Mexico City and the volcanoes Iztaccíhuatl and Popocatépetl of the Sierra Nevada. The town is the seat of a municipality of 181.72 square kilometres that governs more than 130 other named communities. The name comes from Nahuatl and has been interpreted as place where the papers signal or mark. The volcanoes give the area its soils and most of its fresh water, and the hill of Sacromonte stands wholly within the municipality.

Settlement began early in dispersed small villages. The Chichimeca Totolimpanecas arrived around 1268, and another dominion, Tlaylloltlacan Teohuacan, was formed in 1336. All these communities were known together as the Amaquemecans. In 1465 the Aztecs conquered the Valley of Chalco, replaced local leaders with military governors and made it a tributary province with Tlalmanalco as capital. Hernán Cortés reached the town in 1519 and noted well-built houses and about 20,000 inhabitants.

Franciscans took charge of conversion. In 1525 Martín de Valencia burned the houses of the local priests on the Sacromonte, and in 1527 work began on a Franciscan monastery. The cult of the Santo Entierro, or Señor del Sacromonte, replaced an earlier cult at the site. The church of La Asunción was begun in 1547 and finished in 1564. Commercial agriculture based on wheat and sheep became the basis of the economy by 1550, and by 1599 Amecameca headed a district of thirteen dependencies. Zapatistas made the area a stronghold by 1917, and agricultural land was redistributed in 1925.

The town was declared a cultural heritage of the State of Mexico in 1980. Sor Juana Inés de la Cruz came to live at the Panoaya hacienda in 1651 as a child of three and stayed until 1663, and its main building is now a museum named for her. The municipality is a major producer of walnuts in Mexico. The annual festival of the Señor del Sacromonte, held in the week containing Ash Wednesday, draws many visitors. At the end of the 19th century about 85% of the population spoke Nahuatl, and fewer than 200 speakers remain.
amel-marduk: Amel-Marduk, whose name means man of Marduk, was originally called Nabu-shum-ukin. He was probably not Nebuchadnezzar II's eldest son: Marduk-nadin-ahi is attested as an adult in charge of his own lands in 602/601 BCE and as living until 563 BCE. Amel-Marduk is attested as crown prince in 566 BCE, but why he was chosen is unclear.

Texts from the end of Nebuchadnezzar's reign point to trouble. One implicates father and son in a conspiracy and accuses one of them of neglecting temples and exploiting the people. Another is the prayer of an imprisoned son named Nabu-shum-ukin. The Assyriologist Irving Finkel argued in 1999 that this was the future king, who changed his name after release in reverence to Marduk, and other scholars have found the case convincing. A later Midrashic text says he was jailed with the Judean king Jeconiah after officials proclaimed him king while his father was away.

Very few cuneiform sources survive from his reign, and almost nothing is known of his achievements. The first tablet dated to him, from Sippar, bears the same day, 7 October, as the last of Nebuchadnezzar's reign, from Uruk. One of his inscriptions suggests he renovated the Esagila in Babylon and the Ezida in Borsippa, though no evidence confirms the work. Bricks and paving stones in Babylon bear his name, and he had at least one daughter, named Indû.

The only political act attributed to him in any source is the release of Jeconiah, king of Judah, after 37 years of imprisonment, told in 2 Kings 25:27–30, where he is called Evil-Merodach. Such acts of clemency are known from accession ceremonies, and the release may have been linked to the New Year festival. He also released Baalezer, the captured king of Tyre, and restored him to his throne. There is no sign that he tried to restore Judah.

The last document of his reign is a contract dated 7 August 560 BCE, from Babylon; four days later documents are dated to Neriglissar. Amel-Marduk was deposed and murdered by Neriglissar, his brother-in-law, who married one of Nebuchadnezzar's daughters, possibly Kashshaya. The quarrel may reflect rivalry between an older branch of the royal family, represented by Nebuchadnezzar's daughters, and a younger but more legitimate branch, represented by his sons.

Later Babylonian sources judged him harshly. Berossus wrote that he ruled capriciously and had no regard for the laws, and a cuneiform propaganda text says officials refused his orders and that he cared only for the worship of Marduk.
amelia-umbria: Amelia is a town and comune in the province of Terni, in central Italy, not far from the border with Lazio. It stands on the slope of a hill at about 406 metres above sea level, between the valley of the Tiber and that of the Nera, close to the point where the two rivers meet. It lies 24 kilometres from Terni and 13 kilometres from Narni.

According to Cato, the city was founded 964 years before the Third Macedonian War, which corresponds to 1135 BCE. The date cannot be given certain historical value, but it shows the great age attributed to the place. Another tradition, associated with Pliny the Younger, gives 1136 BCE and names either Amisio, said to be a king of the Aborigines, or a supposed princess of Veii as founder. The city later came under Etruscan influence. The opening of the Via Amerina in 240 BCE linked Rome and Umbria, and the town then began to take on an urban form.

Troops from Amelia fought against Hannibal's advance, and the town became a prosperous Roman municipium. Cicero described it as a flourishing municipality whose fertile land reached to the Tiber. Under Augustus its lands were divided among veterans, though it did not become a colony. Amelia is recorded as a bishop's seat from the 4th century, and the Goths later destroyed the city. In 731 the Lombard king Liutprand seized it, and in 1240 the troops of Frederick II sacked it. It remained tied to the Papal States until Piedmontese troops entered it on 21 September 1860.

Amelia is almost entirely encircled by polygonal walls of the 6th to 4th centuries BCE, among the most complete of their type. Their limestone blocks, sometimes more than 2 metres long, are fitted without mortar, and eighteenth-century travellers attributed them to the Pelasgians. The town also keeps Roman cisterns of the 2nd and 1st centuries BCE, ten barrel-vaulted chambers cut in the rock, and a bronze statue of Germanicus found outside the Porta Romana in 1963. Amelia is known for its dried figs, a product recorded since antiquity.
amenemhat-i: Amenemhat I was not of royal lineage. His parents were Senusret and Nefert, possibly related to the nomarchial family of Elephantine. Texts from the period place her in the Upper Egyptian nome of Ta-Seti, and many scholars in recent years have argued that she was of Nubian origin. He was probably the same man as the vizier Amenemhat who led an expedition to Wadi Hammamat under his predecessor Mentuhotep IV, and he possibly overthrew him. Scholars differ on whether he killed Mentuhotep IV, but there is no independent evidence of it, and there may even have been a period of co-regency between the two.

Amenemhat I was the first king of the Twelfth Dynasty of the Middle Kingdom. The relationship to his predecessors remains unclear. The inscriptions of a local governor, Nehri, suggest that his early reign was beset by political turmoil. He moved the capital from Thebes to Itjtawy. His Horus name, Wehemmesu, means 'renaissance' or 'rebirth' and alludes to the Old Kingdom, whose pyramid tombs and artistic motifs the kings of the Twelfth Dynasty emulated after the First Intermediate Period.

The composition of literary works such as the Prophecy of Neferti and the Instructions of Amenemhat, and the return to pyramid complexes like those of the 6th dynasty, are often seen as attempts to legitimise his rule. He built his pyramid at Lisht, with a core of roughly hewn limestone that contained relief blocks taken from Old Kingdom monuments, and it is now a ruined mound some 20 metres tall. A stele dated to year 30 of Amenemhat and year 10 of Senusret I shows that Senusret I became co-regent in year 20, the first known co-regency of a king and his son.

Both the Instructions of Amenemhat and the Story of Sinuhe suggest that Amenemhat was assassinated before he could celebrate his first Sed festival. In the Instructions the dead king tells his son how his own bodyguard attacked him at night. This was apparently while Senusret I was leading a campaign against the Libyans. Senusret hurried back to the palace without alerting his army, and a civil war broke out shortly afterwards, which he had to suppress. How he secured the throne is unknown.
amenemhat-ii: Amenemhat II was the son of Senusret I and of Neferu III, a daughter of Amenemhat I, who is named in the Story of Sinuhe as the wife of Senusret I. He had two sisters, Sebat and Itakayet, who were buried at Lisht near the pyramid of Senusret I. The identities of his spouses are unknown. An early mention may come from the tomb of the nomarch Amenemhat at Beni Hasan, who escorted the king's son Ameny on an expedition to Nubia; this prince is believed to be Amenemhat II in his youth. On taking the throne he took the prenomen Nubkaure, the name found mostly on private monuments.

A double-dated stela of an official named Wepwawet-aa, dated to Year 44 of Senusret I and Year 2 of Amenemhat II, has sometimes been read as evidence of a coregency, while other researchers regard that as unlikely. The most important record of his early reign is the so-called Annals of Amenemhat II, found as fragments at Memphis and later reused in the 19th Dynasty. It records donations to temples and some political events, among them a military expedition into Asia, the destruction of two cities, Iuai and Iasy, whose locations are unknown, and the coming of tribute-bearers from Asia and Kush.

Several mining expeditions are known: at least three in the Sinai, one in the Wadi Gasus in Year 28, and one for amethysts in the Wadi el-Hudi. He ordered building works at Heliopolis, Herakleopolis, Memphis and the Eastern Delta and rebuilt a ruined temple at Hermopolis. The Great Sphinx of Tanis, later usurped by many kings, is associated with him. A treasure of silver objects found under the temple of Montu at Tod bears his name, and many of its objects are Aegean rather than Egyptian, which shows contacts between Egypt and other civilisations. His highest dated attestation is Year 35, on the stela of Hapu at Konosso, which also shows that he shared a brief coregency with his successor Senusret II.

His mummy has not been recovered. He chose Dahshur for his pyramid, originally named Amenu-sekhem and now called the White Pyramid, a site not used as a royal cemetery since the reign of Sneferu. His two predecessors had built at Lisht. The pyramid is poorly preserved and only partly excavated.

Jacques Morgan discovered tombs in the complex in 1894 or 1895. They included the burials of three women titled king's daughters, Ita, Itaweret and Khenmet, found untouched with their jewels and weapons; examination of their remains shows that the women used the weapons regularly. His court is known from viziers such as Senusret and Ameny, from the treasurers Rehuerdjersen and Merykau, and from the provincial governor Khnumhotep II, whose decorated tomb is at Beni Hasan.
amenemhat-iii: Amenemhat III, also written Amenemhet III, was the sixth king of the Twelfth Dynasty and the son of Senusret III. No text states the relationship outright, but it is inferred from their coregency. His mother is unknown. Two of his wives, Aat and Khenemetneferhedjet III, were buried in his pyramid at Dahshur, and his one confirmed daughter, Neferuptah, appears to have been groomed as his successor, since her name is written in a cartouche. She seems to have died before him.

The regnal dates roll over from Year 19 of Senusret III, its highest dated attestation, to Year 1 of Amenemhat III, and the two are believed to have shared the throne for about twenty years, with Amenemhat III as the active king, though not all scholars accept a coregency.

The campaigns and domestic policy of Senusret III left Amenemhat III a stable Egypt, and there is little evidence of military expeditions in his reign: a small mission in Year 9 near the fortress of Kumma in Nubia is recorded in a rock inscription whose author says that nobody died on the return. A few expeditions went to Punt.

Mining of turquoise and copper in the Sinai reached its peak, with more than fifty texts at Serabit el-Khadim, Wadi Maghara and Wadi Nasb, and near-permanent settlements grew up round the workings. Quarries at Wadi Hammamat, Wadi el-Hudi, Tura, Hatnub and Aswan were also worked.

These resources paid for a large building programme, above all in the Faiyum, where he dedicated a temple to Sobek and a chapel to Renenutet, set up two colossal statues of himself at Biahmu and contributed to the excavation of Lake Moeris. He built at Bubastis and enlarged the temples of Hathor at Serabit el-Khadim and of Ptah at Memphis. In his Year 30 he held his Sed festival, the jubilee that renews royal authority.

He built two pyramids, at Dahshur and Hawara, the first king since Sneferu to build more than one, and was buried in the second, at Hawara, in his Year 46. Flinders Petrie found only burned fragments of bone and wood in the burial chamber, which suggests that robbers burned the coffins and mummy.

Late in his reign he made Amenemhat IV a junior coregent, and Sobekneferu later succeeded Amenemhat IV as the last ruler of the dynasty. Scholars link the lack of a recorded male heir to the decline of the Twelfth Dynasty. Amenemhat III was deified and worshipped in the Faiyum for centuries. His statues of his later years show heavy eyelids, sunken cheeks and deep lines, a departure from the idealised youth of earlier kings, according to the art historian Gay Robins.
amenemhat-iv: Amenemhat IV was the seventh and penultimate king of the late Twelfth Dynasty. His mother was a woman named Hetepti, whose only known attestation is an inscription in the temple of Renenutet at Medinet Madi, where she is called King's Mother but not King's Wife or King's Daughter. Manetho made him a son of Amenemhat III, but he is never called King's Son, so some historians think he was a grandson. Kim Ryholt has proposed that Hetepti was married to another man before Amenemhat III and that Amenemhat IV was Sobekneferu's stepbrother.

He first ruled as a junior coregent of Amenemhat III. Monuments with the two names side by side attest the coregency, which most scholars think lasted two years. The Turin Canon gives him a reign of 9 years, 3 months and 27 days, and Africanus's epitome of Manetho gives eight years. His rule seems to have been peaceful. Four expeditions to the turquoise mines of Serabit el-Khadim in the Sinai are dated to it, the last in his ninth year and possibly the last of the Middle Kingdom. In his second year the assistant treasurer Sahathor led an expedition for amethyst to the Wadi el-Hudi.

A stela of year 7 was found at Berenice on the Red Sea. An ostracon from Wadi Gawasis mentions an expedition to Punt in year 8 under the royal scribe Djedy. Nilometer records at Kumna in Nubia for years 5 to 7 show that Egypt kept its presence there. At Byblos an obsidian and gold chest and a jar lid bore his name. He completed the temple of Renenutet and Sobek at Medinet Madi that Amenemhat III had begun, which Zahi Hawass called the only intact temple surviving from the Middle Kingdom, and he finished a shrine at the temple of Hathor in the Sinai.

His tomb has not been identified. The ruined Southern Mazghuna pyramid is a possibility, as are a pyramid at Dahshur beside that of Amenemhat II and, less likely, Amenemhat III's first pyramid. Sobekneferu, daughter of Amenemhat III, succeeded him and ended the Twelfth Dynasty, which gave way to a much weaker Thirteenth Dynasty. Ryholt and Aidan Dodson see its first two kings, Sobekhotep I and Sonbef, as his sons, but Julien Siesse disputes this. Asiatic immigration into the Delta, begun under his predecessor, accelerated, and about 80 years after his reign the administration seems to have collapsed completely, beginning the Second Intermediate Period.
amenhotep-iii: Amenhotep III was the son of Thutmose IV and a minor wife, Mutemwiya, and was born about 1401 BCE. He probably became pharaoh at between 6 and 12 years of age. A regent would likely have ruled until he came of age, but none is attested in the surviving records. In his second regnal year he married Tiye, daughter of Yuya and Thuya, who remained Great Royal Wife throughout his reign. They had at least two sons, Thutmose and the future Amenhotep IV, and at least four daughters. He also married daughters of the rulers of Mitanni, Babylon and Arzawa, and, in his last decade, at least two of his own daughters, Sitamun and Iset.

The only military campaign in which he is known to have taken part was against a rebellion in Kush in his fifth year, commemorated on stelae near Aswan and Saï. His court is known mainly from officials' tombs at Thebes, among them the viziers Ramose and Ptahmose and the Viceroy of Kush, Merimose. He built the palace of Malkata, begun about his eleventh year, and moved there permanently around year 29. He held three Sed festivals, in years 30, 34 and 37, jubilees that affirmed the king's fitness to rule and his transition to divinity.

Diplomatic letters from Assyria, Mitanni, Babylon, Hatti and other states survive among the Amarna Letters, often asking for gold. In one, the Babylonian king Kadashman-Enlil I quotes the pharaoh refusing him an Egyptian princess: no daughter of the king of Egypt is given to anyone. Amenhotep did take foreign princesses as wives. In his thirty-sixth year the Mitannian king Tushratta sent the statue of Ishtar of Nineveh to Egypt, most likely to bless the pharaoh's marriage to Tadukhipa. Historians disagree whether he shared a coregency with Amenhotep IV; most now argue for none, or at most two years.

His latest attested date is year 38, and he may have died early in year 39. Reliefs show him weak, and scientists believe he suffered from arthritis and obesity, with painful, worn teeth. He was buried in tomb WV22 in the Western Valley, though his mummy was later moved to the cache in KV35, where Victor Loret found it in 1898. He left more surviving statues than any other pharaoh, over 250, and built at Karnak, Luxor and across Nubia. His mortuary temple fell into ruin within two hundred years, leaving the Colossi of Memnon, each 18 m high. His son Amenhotep IV, later Akhenaten, succeeded him and moved the capital from Thebes to Amarna.
amenirdis-i: Amenirdis I, whose throne name was Hatneferumut, was a God's Wife of Amun during the 25th Dynasty of ancient Egypt. She came from the Kingdom of Kush and was the daughter of Pharaoh Kashta and Queen Pebatjma. She is likely to have been the sister of the pharaohs Shabaka and Piye. Under the 25th and 26th Dynasties the office of Divine Wife took on new importance: its holders were princesses of royal lineage who never married an earthly king, since their spouse was the god Amun, and they were regarded as queens and bore the corresponding titles. Succession was by adoption, a daughter following her mother on the latter's death.

Kashta had Amenirdis adopted at Thebes by the Divine Adoratrice of Amun, Shepenupet I, as her successor. This shows that Kashta already controlled Upper Egypt before the reign of his successor Piye. Amenirdis ruled as high priestess approximately between 714 and 700 BCE, under Shabaka and Shabataka, and also held the titles Divine Adoratrice of Amun and God's Hand. In the Theban theocratic state the Divine Wife exercised royal or princely authority, acting to a degree as the king's successor, while her priestly functions grew in importance. She adopted Piye's daughter Shepenupet II as her successor, and the two were the nominal heads of the Theban theocracy for the duration of Nubian rule in Egypt.

Amenirdis was buried in a tomb in the grounds of Medinet Habu. Her funerary chapel stands within the temple enclosure there, south-east of the mortuary temple of Ramesses III, and was the second in a row of four chapels built for the God's Wives of Dynasties Twenty-three to Twenty-six. Only the two central ones, hers and Shepenupet II's, survive, and hers is the best preserved. She is depicted in the temple of Osiris-Hekadjet at Karnak and at Bab El-Gasus, and is named on offering tables, statues, a stela and small objects such as scarabs. A granitoid statue of her decorated with gold leaf is in the Nubian Museum at Aswan.
american-civil-war: The war grew from the desire of the Southern states to preserve slavery. Historians in the 21st century overwhelmingly agree on the centrality of slavery in the conflict, at least for the Southern states, though they disagree on the Union's reasons for refusing to let the South secede. Abraham Lincoln, a Republican who opposed slavery's expansion, won the presidential election of 1860, and Southern leaders feared he would put slavery on a course toward extinction.

South Carolina's convention voted unanimously to secede on 20 December 1860. Six more Deep South states followed in January and February 1861 and seized federal forts and arsenals. The war began on 12 April 1861, when Confederate forces opened fire on Fort Sumter in Charleston harbour. Four more states seceded afterwards, so that the Confederacy, led by President Jefferson Davis, comprised eleven states.

In the western theatre the Union captured New Orleans and, under Ulysses S. Grant, won at Fort Henry and Fort Donelson in February 1862, gaining control of the Tennessee and Cumberland rivers. On 1 January 1863 Lincoln issued the Emancipation Proclamation, which made abolition a Union war goal. The Union siege of Vicksburg split the Confederacy at the Mississippi, and General Robert E. Lee's incursion north failed at the Battle of Gettysburg. A naval blockade of Southern ports, announced in April 1861, cut the South's trade.

In 1864 Lincoln made Grant commander of all Union armies. General William Tecumseh Sherman took Atlanta on 2 September 1864 and marched to Savannah, seizing provisions and destroying railroads. Richmond fell on 2 and 3 April 1865, and Lee surrendered to Grant at Appomattox Court House on 9 April. Lincoln was shot on 14 April and died the next day.

The war left an estimated 700,000 soldiers dead, along with an undetermined number of civilians, and it remains the deadliest in United States history. About 190,000 African Americans served in the Union Army after the Emancipation Proclamation. The Thirteenth Amendment abolished slavery, freeing four million people. The war destroyed much of the South's wealth, including the value held in enslaved people.

Reconstruction, which lasted until 1877, rested on three amendments to the Constitution: the thirteenth outlawing slavery, the fourteenth guaranteeing birthright citizenship and equal protection, and the fifteenth prohibiting the denial of voting rights on account of race. The white South developed the myth of the Lost Cause, which the historian Alan T. Nolan calls a rationalisation to vindicate those in rebellion.
american-colonization-society: The society began in 1816, when Charles Fenton Mercer, a Federalist member of the Virginia General Assembly, found accounts of earlier legislative debates on Black colonization after Gabriel Prosser's rebellion. His contact John Caldwell approached his brother-in-law, the Presbyterian minister Robert Finley, who endorsed the plan. It was first called the Society for the Colonization of Free People of Color of America. Its members held that free people of color could not integrate into American society. The population of free Black Americans had grown from 60,000 in 1790 to 300,000 by 1830, and slave owners feared that they might help enslaved people escape or organise rebellions.

The society drew on the example of the Committee for the Relief of the Black Poor, which in 1786 began a colony in Sierra Leone, and of Paul Cuffe, a Quaker ship owner in Boston who took 38 Black Americans to Freetown in 1816. Its first president was Bushrod Washington, a Supreme Court justice, and Henry Clay of Kentucky, a slaveholder, led it from 1836 to 1849.

The society raised money by selling memberships and by lobbying Congress, which gave it $100,000 in 1819. On 6 February 1820 the Elizabeth sailed from New York with three white agents and 86 Black emigrants. In 1821 Lt. Robert Stockton pressed King Peter to sell Cape Montserrado, where Monrovia was founded, and in 1825 and 1826 Jehudi Ashmun leased, annexed or bought more coastal land. Of 4,571 emigrants who arrived in Liberia between 1820 and 1843, only 1,819 were alive in 1843, and the society knew of the death rate but kept sending people. From 1825 it published the African Repository.

Most Black Americans opposed the plan. James Forten wrote in 1817 that they had no wish to separate from their homes, and 3,000 people met in a Philadelphia church to denounce it. From the 1830s abolitionists led by William Lloyd Garrison, whose Thoughts on African Colonization appeared in 1832, called it a fraud that helped preserve slavery. By 1833 it had moved only 2,769 people, and some were pressured to go.

The society continued during the American Civil War, when it sent 168 Black people to Liberia, and 2,492 in the five years after. Abraham Lincoln tried repeatedly to arrange resettlement of this kind early in his presidency, and each attempt failed. It essentially ended after 1919 but was formally dissolved only in 1964, when it gave its papers to the Library of Congress. Historians have judged it differently: some have seen it as a proslavery body, others, more recently, as an antislavery one, while many examine its racist rhetoric. Marc Leepson called colonization a giant failure.
american-popular-revolutionary-alliance: Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre founded APRA in Mexico City on 7 May 1924, meaning it to become a continent-wide network of anti-imperialist movements; the party was founded nationally in Lima in 1930. He drew on what he had seen of fascist and communist parties in Europe. Its early programme combined anti-imperialism, Pan-Americanism, international solidarity and economic nationalism, and it drew middle-class Peruvians, left-wing intellectuals and the young labour movement. Members call one another compañeros. It influenced Bolivia's Revolutionary Nationalist Movement, the Dominican Revolutionary Party and Costa Rica's National Liberation Party.

Banned in the 1930s as communist, a charge the label did not fit, APRA came into near civil war with the government of Luis Miguel Sánchez Cerro. On 2 July 1932 APRA militants killed sixty soldiers in Trujillo; the government's response left about 1,500 Apristas dead and Haya de la Torre arrested, and in April 1933 an Aprista, Abelardo Mendoza Leyva, assassinated the president. Under United States pressure against communism, the party moved by the 1940s to an anti-communist, mildly right-wing populism, and in 1944 joined the National Democratic Front that elected José Luis Bustamante y Rivero.

Legal again in 1979, APRA won a majority in the Constituent Assembly, which Haya de la Torre chaired before his death; a split between Armando Villanueva and Andres Townsend then cost it the 1980 election. Alan García took office on 28 July 1985, the first time the party governed. His term saw hyperinflation of over 13,000 percent a year and corruption charges that the Supreme Court later declared null. García won again in 2006 with a centre-right, free-market programme. After his suicide in April 2019, during the Odebrecht investigation, the party fell below the threshold in 2020, ending 25 years in Congress.

Years of repression and clandestine work, and Haya de la Torre's personal dominance, gave the party sectarian and hierarchical traits, and its structure and the loyalty of members over several generations proved more lasting than its first programme. The founder kept the title of Chief; a party presidency was created in 1985 for García. APRA belongs to the Socialist International.
american-revolution: After the Glorious Revolution in England, Britain followed a trade policy of salutary neglect, and the Thirteen Colonies were largely left to govern themselves. Discontent began shortly after the French and Indian War ended in 1763. Parliament imposed new taxes on the colonists, ostensibly to compensate for the cost of the war, and in 1765 delegates from several colonies met at the Stamp Act Congress in New York City and argued that taxation without representation violated their rights as Englishmen.

Tension rose again after the Townshend Acts, and British troops sent to Massachusetts were involved in the Boston Massacre of 1770. In December 1773 a faction of the Sons of Liberty dumped chests of tea owned by the British East India Company into Boston Harbor. Parliament answered with the Intolerable Acts, meant to end self-government in Massachusetts, which instead increased American support for revolution.

The Battles of Lexington and Concord on 19 April 1775, fought when the British tried to seize the rebels' weapons, began the war. The Second Continental Congress created the Continental Army and appointed George Washington its commander-in-chief. The army besieged Boston and forced the British to withdraw by sea in March 1776. Congress passed the Lee Resolution for independence on 2 July 1776 and unanimously adopted the Declaration of Independence on 4 July.

The British returned in July, landed in New York and defeated Washington in August at the Battle of Brooklyn, the largest battle of the war. France and Spain later entered the war. On 28 September 1781 Washington commanded the capture of a British army under General Cornwallis at the Siege of Yorktown, after which opinion in Parliament shifted towards ending the war on American terms.

On 3 September 1783 the British signed the Treaty of Paris, recognising American independence and ceding nearly all the territory east of the Mississippi River and south of the Great Lakes. The British largely abandoned their Indigenous allies, who were not party to the treaty, and kept forts in American territory until the Jay Treaty of 1795.

The national government under the Articles of Confederation could not tax, and the Philadelphia Convention of 1787 produced a Constitution, ratified in 1788. The new government under President George Washington took office in March 1789, and the Bill of Rights was ratified in 1791. The first successful revolution against a European empire also gave other colonial peoples a model of self-government.
american-revolutionary-war: After the British victory over France in the Seven Years' War, which ended with the Peace of Paris of 1763, tensions grew between Britain and its Thirteen Colonies. The war's debt and demands from British taxpayers for cuts in spending meant that Parliament expected the colonies to pay for their own defence. The Sugar Act and Stamp Act brought new taxes, and the Rockingham ministry repealed the Stamp Act in 1765 but asserted Parliament's authority in the Declaratory Act. After the Boston Massacre of 5 March 1770 and the Intolerable Acts of 1774, twelve colonies sent delegates to the First Continental Congress, which passed the Continental Association in October 1774, a boycott of British goods.

The war began on 19 April 1775 with the Battles of Lexington and Concord, after which British troops lost around 300 men on their withdrawal to Boston. In June 1775 the Second Continental Congress created the Continental Army and unanimously appointed George Washington its commander. It adopted the Declaration of Independence on 4 July 1776, the text written almost exclusively by Thomas Jefferson. The British captured New York City in November 1776, but Washington crossed the Delaware on the night of 25 to 26 December and overwhelmed the Hessians at Trenton, taking 900 prisoners.

In October 1777 a British force under John Burgoyne surrendered at Saratoga, which convinced France and Spain that American independence was viable. France signed a Treaty of Alliance in February 1778, and Spain allied with France against Britain in 1779. The British then turned to the southern colonies, where they had wrongly assumed strong Loyalist support. In 1779 the Sullivan Expedition ravaged the lands of the Haudenosaunee allied with Britain. A Franco-American army besieged General Cornwallis at Yorktown, Virginia, in September and October 1781, and the French navy cut off his escape, so that he surrendered.

Fighting largely ceased in North America after Yorktown, though the British wars with France and Spain went on for two more years. In the Treaty of Paris, signed on 3 September 1783, Britain recognised the sovereignty and independence of the United States. The Treaties of Versailles settled its conflicts with France and Spain, and Britain gave Tobago, Senegal and small territories in India to France, and Menorca, West Florida and East Florida to Spain. Historian Terry M. Mays describes the war as three kinds of conflict: a colonial dispute over trade regulation as well as taxation, a civil war between Patriots, Loyalists and the neutral, and a wider war with France and Spain.
americas: The Americas are a landmass made up of North America and South America. Together with their islands they cover 8% of Earth's surface and 28.4% of its land area, and they make up most of the land in the Western Hemisphere. The mainland extends about 14,000 km from north to south, and its climate ranges from arctic tundra in northern Canada, Greenland and Alaska to tropical rainforest in Central America and South America. A long chain of mountains, the American Cordillera, runs along the west coast, while the flatter east is dominated by river basins such as the Amazon and the Mississippi. The two continents were joined by the Isthmus of Panama by about three million years ago.

Humans first settled the Americas from Asia between 20,000 and 16,000 years ago, though the dates and routes are subject to research. The pre-Columbian era saw urban settlement, agriculture and monumental architecture in Mesoamerica, among the Olmec, Zapotec, Aztec and Maya, and among the Andean civilizations. Norse settlements in Greenland, and perhaps on the mainland, were later abandoned.

The voyages of Christopher Columbus from 1492 to 1504 brought permanent contact with Europe and began a period of exploration, conquest and colonisation. Large numbers of Indigenous people were enslaved, and diseases from Europe and West Africa devastated them. Decolonisation began with the American Revolution in the 1770s and largely ended with the Spanish–American War in the late 1890s. The name America was first recorded in 1507, on a world map by Martin Waldseemüller, and is generally thought to derive from Amerigo Vespucci.

The Americas have more than a billion inhabitants and 35 sovereign states, together with dependent territories of Denmark, France, the Netherlands, the United Kingdom and the United States. The legacy of European settlement is a set of shared cultural traits, most notably Christianity and the use of West European languages, chiefly Spanish, English, Portuguese and French. The population descends from Indigenous peoples and from people of European, African and Asian ancestry, along with people of mixed ancestry.
amfissa: Amphissa lies on the northern edge of the olive forest of the Crissaean plain, between the mountains Giona to the west and Parnassus to the east, about 200 km north-west of Athens and 20 km from Delphi. It is the seat of the municipality of Delphi. The name is believed to derive from a Greek verb meaning to surround, since mountains surround the town. After the independent Greek state was established, the ancient name was restored in 1833.

Amphissa was the chief town of Ozolian Locris. A Mycenaean tomb was in use from the 13th to the 11th century BCE, and the town was organised as a polis in the 7th century BCE. It fought on Sparta's side in the Peloponnesian War and later sided with Thebes. In 338 BCE, in the Fourth Sacred War, Philip II of Macedon destroyed it and expelled much of its population. It was rebuilt, joined the Aetolian League in 250 BCE and was besieged by Roman forces in 190 BCE until a truce was reached. In the 2nd century CE it was prosperous, with a population of 70,000 in 180.

Visigoths under Alaric I and the Huns devastated it in the early Byzantine period, and Samuel of Bulgaria destroyed it in 996. After the Fourth Crusade, Boniface of Montferrat conquered central Greece in 1205 and Amphissa became the seat of the Lordship of Salona under Thomas I d'Autremencourt. Its new rulers built the Castle of Salona on the ancient acropolis, and the town took the name Salona. The Catalans conquered the region in 1311 and the Ottomans in 1394.

Salona was the first town of central Greece to revolt in the Greek War of Independence. On 10 April 1821 the Greeks took the Castle of Salona, the first fortress to fall into Greek hands. In November 1821 a council there drew up a proto-constitution, the Legal Order of Eastern Continental Greece, and set up a governing council of 71 notables. Salona was the capital of that regime until the Ottomans retook the region in 1825.

Landmarks include the Castle of Salona, the Archaeological Museum of Amphissa, the Annunciation Cathedral with murals by Spyros Papaloukas, the 11th-century Byzantine Savior Church and a Mycenaean tomb called Lykotrypa.
amharic: Amharic belongs to the Ethio-Semitic group, a subdivision of the Semitic branch of the Afroasiatic languages. Linguistic analysis suggests that Semitic languages were present in Ethiopia as early as 2000 BCE, and archaeology places Semitic speakers there before 500 BCE. One theory brings them from South Arabia; Messay Kebede and Daniel E. Alemu argue that movement across the Red Sea was a matter of reciprocal exchange, if it happened at all, and that Ethio-Semitic speakers were not foreign invaders.

Amharic has been the language of courts, trade and the military since the late 12th century. By one account Amhara nobles supported the Zagwe prince Lalibela, who made Amharic Lisane Negus, the tongue of the king; the title and the language's use at court are otherwise traced to the emperor Yekuno Amlak. The oldest surviving written Amharic dates from the reign of Amda Seyon I in the 14th century, whose poems known as Soldier songs praised him and his troops.

Amharic is written from left to right in an extended form of the Ge'ez script, called fidäl. It is an abugida: each character stands for a consonant plus a vowel. There are 34 basic characters, each in seven forms, and 49 further letters for sounds involving w, some 288 in all. Some consonants have more than one series of letters, because the letters once stood for distinct sounds that merged. Gemination, the lengthening of a consonant, distinguishes words, as in alä, he said, and allä, there is, but the script does not mark it. The dialects are mutually intelligible, and the Beta Israel speak Jewish Amharic, which replaced many Christian phrases with Jewish ones.

Amharic is the first language of the Amhara and a lingua franca among other peoples in Ethiopia's towns. It is the official working language of the federal government and of several regions, and until 2020 it was the sole official language of Ethiopia. The Bible was first translated into it by Abu Rumi in the early 19th century, and Haddis Alemayehu's novel Love to the Grave is regarded as the best known in the language.

The word Rastafari comes from Ras Täfäri, the title and name of Haile Selassie before his reign, and Rastafari treats Amharic as a holy language. After the emperor visited Jamaica in 1966, study circles in Amharic were organised there, and reggae artists of the 1970s such as Ras Michael and the Abyssinians sang in it.
amhran-na-bhfiann: Peadar Kearney wrote much of the text in the Swiss Café at the corner of O'Connell Street and North Earl Street in Dublin. Kearney and Patrick Heeney had collaborated on songs since 1903. Kearney's first draft, handwritten on copybook paper, sold at auction in Dublin in 2006 for 760,000 euros. After the magazine The United Irishman rejected the text, Irish Freedom published it in 1912. The Irish Volunteers used it as a marching song, and rebels sang it in the General Post Office during the Easter Rising of 1916. It grew more popular among rebels held in the Frongoch internment camp after the Rising.

The Free State adopted no official anthem at first, since the aftermath of the Civil War made the government wary of controversy, and former unionists still regarded God Save the King as the anthem. W. T. Cosgrave avoided naming the song the national anthem for fear of antagonising unionists in Northern Ireland, yet did not want to leave a potent symbol to republican opponents. Radio Éireann played it at closedown from 1926. In 1934 the Department of Finance bought the copyright for 1,200 pounds, and bought it again in 1965 for 2,500 pounds after copyright law changed. The 1937 Constitution created the office of President of Ireland, for whom the Presidential Salute, the first four bars followed by the last five, is played.

Liam Ó Rinn, later Chief Translator of the Oireachtas, wrote the Irish translation, which was published in An tÓglach on 3 November 1923. Several other translations existed by 1923, and Ó Rinn criticised them as unreadable, since they were in literary Classical Irish rather than the spoken language of the Gaeltacht. From the 1930s the Gaelic Athletic Association encouraged singing the anthem in Irish at its matches. The English version has been almost totally eclipsed, and many are unaware that the Irish words are a translation. Only the chorus is the anthem, though the song has three verses. Colm Ó Lochlainn said the tune sounded to him something between a Sousa march and a German regimental song.
amiens: The first known settlement on the site was Samarobriva, meaning Somme bridge, the central settlement of the Ambiani, one of the principal tribes of Gaul.
