The Romans named the town Ambianum, the settlement of the Ambiani. In the 4th century the name of the people replaced the old name of Samarobriva, and Amiens became an episcopal seat. It was part of Francia from the 5th century, and the Normans sacked the city in 859 and again in 882.

The town was fought over in both World Wars, was repeatedly occupied by both sides and suffered heavy damage. The Battle of Amiens in 1918 was the opening phase of the Hundred Days Offensive, which led directly to the Armistice with Germany. The Royal Air Force bombed the town heavily in the Second World War, and afterwards it was rebuilt to the plans of Pierre Dufau with wider streets, in brick, concrete and white stone with slate roofs. Auguste Perret designed the railway station and the nearby Tour Perret.

Amiens lies on the Somme, 120 km north of Paris and 100 km southwest of Lille, and is the prefecture of the Somme department in the Hauts-de-France region. It has 136,449 inhabitants (2023). Its landmark is Notre-Dame d'Amiens, the largest Gothic cathedral in France.

The writer Jules Verne lived in the city from 1871 until his death in 1905 and served on the city council for 15 years. The Musée de Picardie, opened in 1867 after a visit by Napoleon III, was the first building in France built to serve as a museum and was nicknamed the Little Louvre of the Province. The commune has 60 listed monuments, and local specialities include almond macarons and duck pâté in pastry.
amilcar-cabral: Amílcar Lopes Cabral was born on 12 September 1924 in Bafatá, Portuguese Guinea, to Cape Verdean parents from Santiago. He was educated at the Gil Eanes secondary school in Mindelo, Cape Verde, and then at the Instituto Superior de Agronomia in Lisbon. There he founded the Centro do Estudos Africanos, which used cultural activities as cover for dissident politics under the Estado Novo, which banned unions and associations.

From 1953 Cabral conducted an agricultural census in Portuguese Guinea, travelling more than 60,000 kilometres, which gave him close knowledge of the land and its people. In 1956 he founded the PAIGC, the African Party for the Independence of Guinea and Cape Verde, and in the same year was among the founders of the Popular Movement for the Liberation of Angola, together with Agostinho Neto.

From 1963 he led the PAIGC's guerrilla war against the Portuguese government, which became one of the most successful wars of independence in modern African history. He set up training camps in Ghana with the permission of Kwame Nkrumah. As an agronomist he had his soldiers teach farmers better methods and till the fields beside them, and the PAIGC ran a travelling bazaar selling staple goods below colonial prices, and a roving hospital supplied from the USSR and Sweden.

In his writings Cabral argued that the peasantry of Guinea was a great physical force but not by itself a revolutionary one. He held that the petty bourgeoisie would inherit state power and should commit suicide as a class by identifying with workers and peasants. He also held that liberation could not be complete without the full participation of women.

On 20 January 1973 Cabral was shot dead at a roadblock in Conakry by Inocêncio Kani, a former PAIGC rival, and another party member. Theories of Portuguese or Guinean involvement remain unproven, and about one hundred PAIGC officers and soldiers accused of the conspiracy were summarily executed. His half-brother Luís Cabral became leader of the Guinea-Bissau branch of the party and later President of Guinea-Bissau. Cabral died before the independence of Guinea-Bissau and Cape Verde. Cape Verde's main international airport at Sal and a university in Bissau bear his name.
amir-hamzah: Amir Hamzah was born in Tanjung Pura, Langkat, North Sumatra, the youngest son of Vice Sultan Tengku Muhammad Adil and his third wife Tengku Mahjiwa. Sources disagree on the day of his birth in February 1911. He was schooled in Islamic principles, studied at the Azizi Mosque, and remained a devout Muslim throughout his life.

He completed his schooling in Medan, Batavia and Surakarta, where he studied Javanese, Sanskrit and Arabic literature. In Surakarta he joined the nationalist movement and in 1930 became head of the local branch of Indonesia Muda, insisting on speaking Malay when most educated youth preferred Dutch.

The Dutch, concerned about his nationalism, persuaded the Sultan to send him back to Langkat in 1937. There he was married to the Sultan's eldest daughter, Tengku Puteri Kamiliah, whom he had barely met, and he became a prince and a court official handling administrative and legal matters. Their only child, a daughter, was born in 1939.

In 1932 Amir co-founded the literary magazine Poedjangga Baroe. He wrote fifty poems, eighteen pieces of lyrical prose and other works, including translations, and none of his creative works is dated. His first collection, Nyanyi Sunyi, appeared in the magazine in November 1937, and the collection Buah Rindu in June 1941. Buah Rindu is generally considered to have been written earlier, between 1928 and 1935, and is united by longing for his mother, his lovers and his homeland. Nyanyi Sunyi is more religious in tone. Scholars disagree over whether Islamic orthodoxy or Sufism shaped his view of God.

His diction mixes Malay with Javanese and Sundanese words and draws on old Malay terms. The critic H.B. Jassin notes that, unlike some contemporaries, he included no symbols of European modernity such as trains or telephones. His translations in Setanggi Timur, published in 1939, include poems by Omar Khayyám, Du Fu and Rabindranath Tagore, read from Dutch translations.

After Indonesia proclaimed independence on 17 August 1945, Amir was chosen on 29 October 1945 as the government representative in Langkat. On 7 March 1946, during a social revolution led by factions of the Communist Party of Indonesia, a group strongly against feudalism and the nobility, he was stripped of his power and arrested. He was held with other nobles at a plantation at Kuala Begumit, and on the morning of 20 March 1946 he was killed with 26 others and buried in a mass grave.

In 1948 his remains were identified by a missing false tooth, and in November 1949 he was reburied at the Azizi Mosque in Tanjung Pura. He was declared a National Hero of Indonesia in 1975. The scholar A. Teeuw considers him the only international-class Indonesian poet from before the Indonesian National Revolution.
amir-kabir: Amir Kabir was born on 9 January 1807 in Hazaveh, in the Arak district. His father, Karbalaʾi Mohammad Qorban, was a cook in the service of Mirza Bozorg Qa'em-Maqam of Farahan, who saw signs of unusual talent in the boy and had him study with his own children. He entered government service in Tabriz, rose to supervise the finances of the army of Azerbaijan, and spent almost four years in Erzurum as part of a commission to delineate the Ottoman-Iranian frontier, which taught him the methods of international diplomacy. In 1848 he became chief tutor to the crown prince Naser al-Din, then fifteen.

Mohammad Shah died in September 1848, and Naser al-Din's minister could not raise the money for the journey to Tehran, so Amir Kabir arranged it. The new shah made him head of the army and, in October 1848, chief minister with the titles amir-e kabir and atabak. The Queen Mother, Malek Jahan Khanom, and other princes resented the cuts he made in their allowances.

He tried to balance an empty treasury by cutting the salaries of civil servants, often by half, and by removing stipends of pensioners who did little work. He had Iranians vaccinated against smallpox. He founded the Dar ol-Fonun in Tehran, which taught medicine, mathematics and natural sciences, and whose Austrian instructors reached Tehran in November 1851, after his dismissal. He also founded the newspaper Vaqayeʿ-ye Ettefaqiyeh, sought to curb the power of the clergy, and followed a policy of granting concessions to neither Britain nor Russia.

He regarded the Bábís as a threat. He suppressed the Babi uprisings of 1848 to 1851, personally ordered the public beheading of seven prominent Bábís in February 1850, and in mid-1850 ordered the execution of the Báb at Tabriz. ʻAbdu'l-Bahá called him the worst oppressor of the religion but also acknowledged his reforms.

Those whose incomes he had cut, among them the Queen Mother, formed a coalition against him with Mirza Aqa Khan Nuri and Mirza Yusuf Khan Ashtiyani, backed by foreign powers whose influence had diminished. Amir Kabir was demoted to head of the army, with Nuri made premier, and was then arrested and sent to Kashan. Six weeks later the Queen Mother and his executioner convinced the shah that Russia would soon protect him, and he was murdered at Kashan on 10 January 1852. His services were generally unappreciated in the Qajar era, but modern Iranian historiography depicts him as one of the few capable and honest statesmen of the period.
amir-khusrau: Khusrau was born in 1253 at Patiyali, in what is now Uttar Pradesh, the son of Amir Saif ud-Din Mahmud, a Turkic officer, and Bibi Daulat Naz, a native Indian. His father belonged to the Turkic Hazara-yi Lachin clan of Transoxiana and came to India after the invasion of Central Asia by Genghis Khan, finding refuge at the court of Sultan Shams ud-Din Iltutmish of Delhi. His father died in 1260, when Khusrau was eight. He began to write poetry at nine, and his first divan, Tuhfat us-Sighr, was compiled in 1271.

Khusrau joined the army of Malik Chajju, a nephew of Sultan Ghiyas ud-Din Balban, and his poetry came to the notice of the royal court. He then served Balban's sons as patrons, including Khan Muhammad at Multan.Jalal ud-Din Firuz Khalji, who took the throne in 1290, gave him the title Amir. Under Ala ud-Din Khalji he wrote the Khaza'in ul-Futuh on the sultan's buildings, wars and administration, and by 1298 had completed his Khamsa, five masnavis modelled on the quintet of the earlier Persian poet Nizami Ganjavi. In 1310 he became a disciple of the Chishti Sufi Nizamuddin Auliya, and he died in October 1325, six months after his master, and was buried beside him in Delhi.

Khusrau wrote chiefly in Persian, but also in Hindavi and Punjabi, in verse forms such as the ghazal, masnavi, qata, rubai and do-baiti. He is regarded as the father of qawwali, which he is credited with creating by fusing Persian, Arabic, Turkic and Indian singing traditions, and with introducing the ghazal into India. Musicians credit him with six styles, among them qaul, qalbana and khyal, but the evidence for this is insufficient. Many Hindustani verses are attributed to him, although there is no evidence that they were composed before the 18th century. His riddles remain a popular form of Hindavi poetry.
amman: Amman lies on the East Bank Plateau, an upland crossed by three major wadis, at an elevation of 700 to 1,100 metres. The city was originally built on seven hills and now spans more than 19. Its areas take their names from the hills (jabal) or valleys (wadi) they occupy, as in Jabal al-Luweibdeh and Wadi Abdoun.

Settlement in the area dates to at least the 8th millennium BCE at 'Ain Ghazal, now on the city's outskirts. Around 7000 BCE this aceramic Neolithic village covered 15 hectares and had about 3,000 inhabitants, four to five times the population of contemporary Jericho. The site was found in 1974 by workers building a road.

The ancient city was the capital of the Ammonites, who called it Rabat ʿAmmān. After Alexander the Great conquered the Near East in 332 BCE, the region east of the Jordan became a disputed frontier between the Ptolemies and the Seleucids. Ptolemy II, who reigned from 283 to 246 BCE, founded a military colony on the site that grew into a Greek-type city, and renamed it Philadelphia after his own epithet. The Rashidun Caliphate conquered the region from the Byzantines in the 630s and restored the old name as Amman. The Umayyads built a large palace on the Citadel hill, but earthquakes, including a severe one in 749, later devastated the town.

Amman was resettled in 1878, when several hundred Muslim Circassians, expelled from the North Caucasus by the Russian Empire, were directed there by the Ottoman authorities. Their first houses were built with stones from the Roman theatre. A city council was established in 1909, and the town became a hub on the Hejaz Railway by 1914. Its population grew from roughly 1,000 in 1890 to around 1,000,000 in 1990, mainly through immigration, including Palestinians in 1948 and 1967 and Iraqis in 1990.

Amman is the capital and largest city of Jordan, which it became the capital of as Transjordan in 1921. It had about four million inhabitants in 2015, some 42 per cent of the country's population, and is governed as the Greater Amman Municipality. The Jordan Museum holds the Neolithic limestone statues of 'Ain Ghazal, and the Roman theatre and the Umayyad Palace remain among its monuments.
ammianus-marcellinus: Ammianus was born around 330 in the Roman Levant, possibly in Syria or Phoenicia, into a noble family of Greek origin. He called himself a former soldier and a Greek, and Greek was his native language, though he also knew Latin. His enrolment among the elite protectores domestici, the household guards, indicates a middle-class or higher birth. He entered the army young, under Constantius II, and was sent to serve under Ursicinus, governor of Nisibis in Mesopotamia and magister militum, with whom he campaigned twice in the East.

Ammianus travelled with Ursicinus to Italy against Silvanus, an officer who had proclaimed himself emperor in Gaul. Ursicinus had Silvanus assassinated and stayed to help install Julian as Caesar of Gaul, Spain and Britain. In 359 Constantius sent Ursicinus back east to meet a Persian invasion led by King Shapur II. Ammianus served again as a staff officer and was at Amida when the Persians besieged and sacked it; he barely escaped with his life.

After Constantius dismissed Ursicinus, Ammianus seems to have retired, though some modern scholars think he continued to serve. He accompanied Julian, whom he admired, against the Alamanni and the Sassanids, and went with the new emperor Jovian as far as Antioch. He was living at Antioch in 372, when he claims to have witnessed how Theodorus and others, suspected of divining Valens's successor, were tortured and punished. He later settled in Rome. The year of his death is unknown, but scholars place it between 392 and 400 at the latest.

In Rome in the 380s Ammianus wrote the Res gestae in Latin, a history from the accession of Nerva in 96 to the death of Valens at Adrianople in 378, in effect a continuation of Tacitus. It praises the Serapeum of Alexandria as the glory of the empire, so it was presumably finished before the building's destruction in 391. Of its thirty-one books the first thirteen are lost. The eighteen that survive, covering 353 to 378, are the foundation of modern understanding of the fourth-century empire. Its report of the earthquake and tsunami of 21 July 365 at Alexandria accurately describes the sequence of quake, retreating sea and sudden wave.

Scholars generally describe him as a pagan tolerant of Christians. He remarked that no wild beasts are so hostile to men as Christian sects are to one another, and he condemned Julian for his attachment to sacrifice and for his edict barring Christians from teaching posts. Edward Gibbon judged him an accurate and faithful guide, while Kimberly Kagan argues that his battle accounts stress the soldiers' experience at the cost of the larger picture. Almost every manuscript derives from a ninth-century text, Vatican lat. 1873, made at Fulda.
ammonius-saccas: Ammonius Saccas was a self-taught philosopher from Alexandria in Roman Egypt, generally regarded as a precursor or one of the founders of Neoplatonism. Most details of his life come from fragments of Porphyry's writings. The meaning of his cognomen is disputed. Many scholars take it to mean he was a porter in his youth, a view supported in antiquity by the Byzantine bishop Theodoret, while others have connected it with the Śākyas, an ancient ruling clan of India, and argued for Indian origin.

Scholars who reject an Indian origin point out that Ammonius came from the Brucheion quarter of Alexandria, the royal quarter inhabited mostly by Greeks, and that the name Ammonius was common among Greeks. His name is also theophoric, honouring the god Amun, which may indicate Egyptian origins. Porphyry says his parents were Christians and that he rejected their religion for paganism when he learned Greek philosophy. Jerome and Eusebius deny this and say he remained a Christian to the end.

According to Longinus, Ammonius wrote nothing, and little is known of his own philosophical views. Hierocles, writing in the 5th century, states that his fundamental doctrine was that Plato and Aristotle were in full agreement. According to Nemesius, a bishop and Neoplatonist around 400, he held that the soul is immaterial. Two of his pupils, Origen the Pagan and Longinus, seem to have held positions closer to Middle Platonism than to Neoplatonism, which may suggest that Ammonius' own doctrines were closer to Middle Platonism too.

Some scholars explain the confusion about his faith by supposing there were two men called Ammonius, Ammonius Saccas who taught Plotinus and an Ammonius the Christian who wrote biblical texts. Ammonius is also said to have had two pupils named Origen, one Christian and one pagan, and Herennius and Cassius Longinus were among his other students.

His best-known pupil was Plotinus, who according to Porphyry went to Alexandria in 232 at the age of 28 to study philosophy. Disappointed by the teachers recommended to him, he was sent to Ammonius and said to a friend, This is the man I was looking for. He stayed with Ammonius for eleven years, and Porphyry says he then became eager to learn the Persian and Indian disciplines of philosophy.

Ammonius was undoubtedly the most significant influence on Plotinus in his development of Neoplatonism, although his own role in its development is little known. Porphyry suggests Ammonius helped Plotinus think about philosophy in new ways, and Plotinus does not seem to have thought he departed in any significant way from his master's teaching.
amol: Amol is a city in the Central District of Amol County, Mazandaran province, Iran, and the capital of both the county and the district. It stands on the Haraz River, less than 20 kilometres south of the Caspian Sea and less than 10 kilometres north of the Alborz mountains, at an altitude of 76 metres. It lies 124 kilometres northeast of Tehran by one measure and 60 kilometres west of the provincial capital, Sari. Mount Damavand, the highest peak in Iran and the Middle East, rises to the south. The Haraz route is one of the oldest roads joining the north of Iran to the central plateau. Most Amoli people speak the Mazandarani language as their mother tongue, and Persian is the lingua franca.

Amol is one of the oldest cities in Iran. Its foundation goes back to the Amardi tribe, who inhabited the region in the Iron Age and are mentioned by the Roman historian Ammianus Marcellinus. A number of historians and geographers believe it was established in the 1st millennium BCE, and some attribute its birth to the reign of the mythological king Tahmuras. Excavation at Qaleh Kesh has found ancient jewellery dated to the 1st millennium BCE or the Bronze Age.

In the era of the Alid dynasties and the Marashi dynasty, Amol was the capital of northern Iran, and it was also the capital of the Bavand and Ziyarid dynasties. Its inhabitants embraced Islam during the reign of the Abbasid caliph Mahdi (775 to 785), after initially resisting the Arabs. In the ninth century it was one of the largest cities in Iran. During the Umayyad period Sa'id ibn al-As led an army of 4,000 against Tabaristan in the reign of Muawiyah I, and his war with Farrukhan the Great lasted two years. The city has suffered earthquake and flood damage several times and recovered each time. The historian Muhammad ibn Jarir al-Tabari, who lived from 839 to 923, came from Amol.

Amol is known as a centre of rice cultivation. The Rice Research Institute of Iran was established there in 1963. The old bazaar, whose origins date to before Islam, forms the core of the old city. Among its historic sites are the Mausoleum of Mir Bozorg, the Jameh Mosque and Malek Bahman Castle. The 2016 census counted 237,528 people.
amon-of-judah: According to the biblical account, Amon was the fifteenth king of Judah. He was the son of King Manasseh of Judah and Meshullemeth, a daughter of Haruz of Jotbah, and he married Jedidah, the daughter of Adaiah of Bozkath, on a date that is unknown. He began to reign at the age of 22 after Manasseh's death. Other kings seem to have been made co-regents at about the age of 12, but his reign allows no period of co-regency even though his father was very old. This, with Manasseh's age of 44 at his birth, suggests he may have been a younger son.

Amon reigned for two years. The Hebrew Bible records that he continued his father's idolatry and sacrificed to all the images Manasseh had made. Later Jewish tradition judged him harshly: the Talmud says he burnt the Torah and let spider webs cover the altar, and Josephus describes his reign in similar terms to the biblical accounts. Arnold J. Toynbee took a different view and thought Amon and Manasseh nearer to historical truth as pious conservatives defending the faith of their ancestors.

His reign fell at a time of transition in the Levant. The Neo-Assyrian Empire, to the east of Judah, was beginning to disintegrate, and the Neo-Babylonian Empire had not yet risen. Egypt under Psamtik I was recovering from the Assyrian occupation. In this power vacuum many smaller states, Judah among them, could govern themselves without interference from larger empires.

Amon was assassinated by his servants or officials, who conspired against him. The murderers were unpopular with the people of the land, who killed them and proclaimed Amon's son Josiah, then eight years old, as his successor. It is not clear what succession the officials had intended. Some scholars, such as Abraham Malamat, hold that he was killed because people disliked the heavy influence of the Neo-Assyrian Empire over him. Out of respect for Josiah, rabbinic tradition did not place Amon on the list of kings excluded from the world to come, and the Gospel of Matthew names him in the genealogy of Jesus.
amorbach: Amorbach lies on the small river Mud in the north-eastern part of the Odenwald, in the Miltenberg district of Lower Franconia, Bavaria. It has around 4,000 inhabitants. The town began as a Benedictine monastery, which bit by bit grew into a settlement.

Amorbach was raised to the status of a town in 1253. It belonged to the Bishopric of Würzburg until 1656, when it passed to the Archbishopric of Mainz. After the German Mediatisation of 1803 secularised the archbishopric, Amorbach became the residence town of the short-lived Principality of Leiningen. It became part of the Kingdom of Bavaria only in 1816.

Several members of the princely house were born or died there, among them Carl Friedrich Wilhelm, 1st Prince of Leiningen, who died in 1807, and Emich Carl, 2nd Prince, who was the first husband of Princess Victoria of Saxe-Coburg-Saalfeld, mother of Queen Victoria, and the father of Queen Victoria's elder half-siblings, Carl and Feodora. The printer Johann Amerbach, who lived from about 1440 to 1513, was a son of the town.

Amorbach is the family seat of the princely Haus zu Leiningen and was recognised as a climatic spa in 1965. Its Baroque buildings draw visitors. The Stumm organ of 1782 in the former abbey church, with 5,116 pipes, is played daily at 12:00 and 15:00. The late-Baroque parish church of St Gangolf, built in 1751–3 by the brothers Johann Franz Wolfgang Damian von Ostein and Johann Friedrich Karl von Ostein, Archbishop of Mainz, was inspired by St Peter's Church at Mainz and has ceiling frescoes by Johannes Zick. The tithe barn of 1488, built to store produce paid as tithes to the prince, now serves as a cabaret theatre. In 1992 the town received the Europa Nostra Medal.
amorgos: Amorgos is the easternmost island of the Cyclades and the nearest to the Dodecanese. With 16 neighbouring islets, the largest of which is Nikouria, it forms a municipality of 126 square kilometres. Its position near the ancient Ionian towns of Miletus, Halicarnassus and Ephesus made it one of the first places through which the Ionians passed to the Cycladic islands and on to the Greek mainland. It has also been known as Yperia, Platagy, Pagali, Psichia and Karkisia.

Burial tombs and other finds show an intense presence on Amorgos in the first period of Cycladic civilisation, from 3200 to 2000 BCE, with almost a dozen inhabited centres. The island is the origin of many Cycladic figurines. The Kapsala figurines, from about 2700 BCE, are the earliest of the canonical types, a reclining female with folded arms, and the Dokathismata type, of 2400 to 2100 BCE, has a more slender and sometimes angular outline than the common Spedos type.

In the Archaic period three independent city-states stood on the island, probably with their own constitutions but one currency: Arkesini, Minoa and Aigiali. Because one was called Minoa, it has been suspected that Cretans settled there early, but no archaeological evidence supports this. About 630 BCE the poet Semonides led a Samian colony to the island. Amorgos belonged to the Delian League and the Second Athenian League. The walls of Arkesini and the towers scattered across the island are remains of this age. In 322 BCE Athens and Macedonia fought the naval Battle of Amorgos.

After the Fourth Crusade the island became a dependency of the duchy of Naxos, later disputed by other Venetians. In 1312 a Hospitaller fleet defeated a fleet of Menteshe there. Under Ottoman rule, from 1537 to 1829, it was called Yamurgi, and it became part of Greece on independence in 1830. An earthquake on 9 July 1956 with its epicentre about 30 km south of the island, of magnitude 7.7, caused a local tsunami of up to 30 m, which killed 53 people.

The monastery of Panagia Hozoviotissa stands on a cliff north-east of Chora. It was built early in the second millennium to protect an icon dated to 812, which is displayed inside. A group of windmills stands on a hill above Chora. The island is reached only by boat, and its geography prevents mass tourism. The film The Big Blue of 1988 by Luc Besson, with its views of the island's marine life, brought it international attention.
amorites: The Amorites were a Northwest Semitic-speaking Bronze Age people who originated in western Mesopotamia and first appear in Sumerian records around 2500 BCE. The most common view places their homeland in central Syria, identified with Jebel Bishri or the Syrian steppe. In Sumerian and Akkadian texts the term Amurru, written mar.tu, refers to the Amorites, their principal deity and their kingdom. Tablets from Ebla show them as a rural group on the middle and upper Euphrates, and for the Akkadian emperors mar.tu was one of the four quarters around Akkad. Naram-Sin of Akkad records defeating a coalition of Sumerian cities and Amorites near Jebel Bishri around 2240 BCE.

By the last days of the Third Dynasty of Ur, immigrating Amorites were such a force that Shu-Sin built a wall of 270 kilometres from the Tigris to the Euphrates to hold them off. Mesopotamian texts describe them as nomadic tribes under chiefs, often with contempt. After Ur declined, Amorite rulers gained power in several city-states, a rise that peaked in the Old Babylonian period. Shamshi-Adad I of Ekallatum conquered Assur, and Babylon became the major power under Sumu-la-El and his successors, among them Hammurabi, who destroyed the Amorite kingdom of Mari.

An Amorite presence in Egypt is thought to date from the 19th century BCE; the Fourteenth Dynasty had rulers with names such as Yakbim, and the Hyksos seem to have included Amorites. The Amorite era in Mesopotamia ended in the 16th century BCE with the fall of Babylon, which the Kassites occupied around 1595 BCE. Syrian Amorites then came under the Hittites and the Middle Assyrian Empire, and from about 1200 BCE they disappear from the record, displaced or absorbed by other West Semitic peoples, among whom the Arameans rose to prominence.

The Amorite language is known only from personal names and loanwords in other languages' texts, and was closely related to Canaanite and Aramaic. Their chief god was Amurru, with a consort Ašratum, whose name is cognate with Asherah. Dagan was supreme in many cities of the Euphrates region. The Hebrew Bible uses the name for highlanders of Canaan, descendants of Canaan in Genesis, and for the kings Sihon and Og east of the Jordan.
amos-prophet: According to the Bible, Amos was a shepherd and a sycamore fig farmer from Teqoaʿ, and an older contemporary of Hosea and Isaiah. He was active about 760 to 755 BCE, in the reigns of Jeroboam II of Israel and Uzziah of Judah. His own words, I am not a prophet nor a son of a prophet (7:14), mark him as outside the schools of prophets, and later prophets also begin by telling the story of their calling. The book dates his prophecies to two years before an earthquake.

Jeroboam II, who ruled about 781 to 741 BCE, had conquered Syria, Moab and Ammon and extended his lands from the source of the Orontes River to the Dead Sea. The northern kingdom enjoyed a long peace and a revival of art and commerce, but social corruption and the oppression of the poor were widespread, and some mixed the worship of the Lord with that of pagan deities.

Amos felt called to preach at Bethel, where there was a royal sanctuary, and to announce the fall of the reigning dynasty and of the northern kingdom. The head priest Amaziah denounced him to Jeroboam II and advised him to leave. Many scholars see no reason to doubt that he was forced out and returned home. Prevented from delivering his message, he is held to have written it down.

Amos is widely recognised as the first prophet to write down all the messages he received, and no earlier literary prophet is known; most later prophets followed his example. Isaiah certainly knew his book and imitated it in his early speeches. What is known of Amos derives solely from the book, and in recent years scholars have grown more sceptical of its account of his life. The apocryphal Lives of the Prophets says Amos was killed by the son of Amaziah and buried in his homeland.

The Book of Amos is attributed to him and is counted among the Twelve Minor Prophets. Its central teaching is that God is ethical, so that religion consists not in ritual but in righteousness. Prayers and sacrifices do not make up for bad deeds, and behaving justly matters more than ceremony, as in Amos 5:21–24, which ends with the call to let justice roll on like a river. Amos held that economic justice was necessary to preserve the nation, and he is described as an uncompromising monotheist.

He presents the relationship between God and Israel as a moral contract: if the people fall below God's moral requirements, the relationship will be dissolved. Amos is commemorated with the other minor prophets in several churches, with a feast day on 15 June in the Eastern Orthodox calendar.
amphora: An amphora has two expansive handles joining the shoulder of the body to a long, narrow neck. Most were made with a pointed base, so that they could be stood upright by embedding them in soft ground such as sand. Two principal forms existed: the neck amphora, in which neck and body meet at a sharp angle, and the one-piece amphora, in which they form a continuous curve. Neck amphorae were common in early Greece and were gradually replaced by the one-piece type from around the 7th century BCE.

An amphora holds less than half a ton, typically under 50 kilograms, whereas the larger storage jar called the pithos holds between half a ton and two and a half tons. Most amphorae stood around 45 centimetres high, and the wine amphora held a standard measure of about 39 litres.

Amphorae carried wine, olive oil and garum, and also olives, grain, fish and other agricultural products. The pointed base suited shipping: the jars were packed upright or on their sides in as many as five staggered layers, with ropes through the handles and heather or reeds as packing. They were produced on an industrial scale until approximately the 7th century CE.

Stamps and painted inscriptions recorded the workshop, the weight and the contents, and historians use them to reconstruct ancient trade networks. Because amphorae were too cheap to return to their origin, empty ones were broken up at their destination. At Rome the fragments formed Monte Testaccio, a hill 45 metres high. In Greece, painted amphorae were made for ceremonial purposes: Panathenaic amphorae, filled with olive oil from a sacred grove, were prizes at the Panathenaic Festivals.

Amphorae are of great use to maritime archaeologists, since they often indicate the age of a shipwreck and the origin of its cargo. The largest known wreck of an amphora cargo ship, carrying 6,000 jars, was found off Kefalonia. The German scholar Heinrich Dressel made the first systematic classification of Roman types, and the Dressel table is still used for many of the about 66 distinct types identified.
amr-ibn-al-as: Amr ibn al-As was the son of al-As ibn Wa'il, a wealthy landowner of the Banu Sahm clan of the Quraysh of Mecca, and inherited from him an estate and vineyards near Ta'if. Reports conflict about when he became a Muslim; the most credible version places it in 629 or 630, not long before Muhammad conquered Mecca. In 633 the first caliph, Abu Bakr, sent him as one of four commanders to conquer Syria and appointed him governor of Palestine, where he won the Battle of Dathin on 4 February 634.

From southern Palestine Amr launched the conquest of Byzantine Egypt; most Muslim sources say with Caliph Umar's reluctant approval, though some accounts say he acted without authorisation. With about 4,000 cavalry and no siege engines he took Pelusium and Bilbeis after month-long sieges and halted before Babylon, at the head of the Nile Delta. In July 640 he defeated the Byzantines at Heliopolis, and Babylon yielded on 9 April 641. Alexandria surrendered in 641 or 642, and Amr then advanced west as far as Cyrenaica and Tripoli.

He guaranteed the security of Egypt's people in a treaty with the Byzantine governor Cyrus and imposed a poll tax on non-Muslim adult men. He kept the Coptic-dominated bureaucracy and founded Fustat, beside Babylon, as the garrison town, because Umar rejected Alexandria as the capital. Amr ruled with relative independence and amassed great wealth, and Caliph Uthman dismissed him in 646 after he and Abd Allah ibn Sa'd accused each other of incompetence.

Amr then criticised Uthman openly. In the First Fitna he sided with Mu'awiya ibn Abi Sufyan against Caliph Ali, in return for the promise of Egypt, and in July or August 658 he defeated Ali's troops at al-Musannah and took Fustat. Mu'awiya, once caliph, confirmed him in Egypt.

Amr died of natural causes, most credibly in 43 AH (663–664 CE), and was buried at the foot of the Muqattam hills east of Fustat; the grave is not identified. He left seventy sacks of gold dinars, which his sons refused to inherit and Mu'awiya confiscated.
amritsar: Amritsar lies in the Majha region of Punjab, 28 kilometres from the India-Pakistan border and 47 kilometres north-east of Lahore. It takes its name from Amṛta Sarovara, Sanskrit for Pool of Nectar, the pool that surrounds the Golden Temple, and it was formerly also called Rāmdāspur. Tradition links the area to the Ramayana: the Bhagwan Valmiki Tirath Sthal is believed to be the ashram of Maharishi Valmiki, where Sita gave birth to Lava and Kusha.

In the Sikh tradition Guru Ram Das, the fourth guru, founded the city in 1574. One account says that the land was bought with Sikh donations from the owners of the village of Tung, another that Guru Amar Das chose the site. Ram Das first completed the pool, built his centre next to it and invited merchants and artisans from other parts of India to settle. The town grew under Guru Arjan Dev, financed by donations and built by volunteers, and in 1604 he installed the scripture of Sikhism in the new Harmandir Sahib. Ahmad Shah of the Durrani Empire besieged Amritsar in 1762 and again in 1766 and 1767, massacred its people and destroyed the city.

Under the Sikh Empire Maharaja Ranjit Singh fortified the city in 1822, and Sher Singh later completed the walls with twelve gates. The British annexed Punjab in 1849 and built a thirteenth gate in 1866. They supported a textile industry, and Khalsa College made the city a centre of colonial education. On 13 April 1919, the day of Vaisakhi, Colonel Reginald Dyer ordered troops to fire into a crowd of thousands in the Jallianwala Bagh without warning, for about ten minutes. A British government inquiry put the death toll at 379, and the Indian National Congress estimated about 1,000.

After the partition of India many Hindu and Sikh refugees from the Lahore and Sialkot districts settled in Amritsar. In June 1984 the Indian army carried out Operation Blue Star to remove militants from the Golden Temple, an action that remains controversial. Official reports gave 83 army deaths and 493 civilians killed, while independent estimates run to more than 5,000. The city is the holiest in Sikhism and the Golden Temple its most-visited gurdwara. In 2011 the municipality had 1,159,227 inhabitants, with Hindus and Sikhs the two main communities, and the city is known for wooden chessboards and chess pieces.
amsterdam: Amsterdam lies in the province of North Holland, in the western Netherlands, at an elevation of about 2 metres below sea level. The river Amstel ends in the city centre and connects to a large number of canals that eventually terminate in the IJ. The surrounding land is flat and formed of large polders, and the city is connected to the North Sea by the North Sea Canal. More than 100 kilometres of canals run through it, most of them navigable. The three main ones are the Prinsengracht, the Herengracht and the Keizersgracht.

Farmers settled around the area of the later city about three millennia ago, along the prehistoric IJ and upstream on its tributary the Amstel. A permanent settlement was not possible until water issues were controlled, because the river mouth and banks were too wet. Amsterdam was founded at the mouth of the Amstel, which was dammed to control flooding, and it began as a small fishing village in the 12th century. Its population was around 1,000 in 1300. It grew in the 15th and 16th centuries, mainly through the Baltic grain trade after the Burgundian victory in the Dutch–Hanseatic War in 1441.

The population then rose sharply during the Dutch Revolt. Many people from the Southern Netherlands fled north, especially after Antwerp fell to Spanish forces in 1585, and Jews from Spain, Portugal and Eastern Europe, Germans and Scandinavians also settled there. The population more than doubled between 1585 and 1610, stood at about 50,000 in 1600 and reached 200,000 in the 1660s. It then stabilised around 240,000 for most of the 18th century. The Amsterdam Stock Exchange was founded in 1602. In the 19th and 20th centuries the city expanded, and new neighbourhoods and suburbs were built.

Amsterdam is the capital and largest city of the Netherlands, though it is not the seat of government, which is in The Hague. Its 17th-century canal belt, the grachten, is a UNESCO World Heritage Site and preserves narrow canal houses with gabled façades. The Rijksmuseum, opened in 1885, holds Dutch Golden Age art, and the Stedelijk Museum opened in 1895. The city has two universities, the University of Amsterdam and the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, and hosted the Summer Olympics in 1928.
amulius: In Roman mythology Amulius was king of Alba Longa, son of Procas and brother of Numitor. He ordered the death of his infant twin grandnephews Romulus and Remus, and was deposed and killed by them when they grew up. Tradition gave him a reign of 41 years. According to the historian Dionysius of Halicarnassus, who wrote in the first century BCE, Procas willed the throne to Numitor, but Amulius deposed him. Fearing a threat to his rule, he had Numitor's son Aegestus killed and blamed thieves, while Numitor, who knew the truth, feigned ignorance.

Amulius appointed Numitor's daughter Rhea Silvia a Vestal priestess, so that her vow of chastity would prevent her having sons who might overthrow him. She nevertheless became pregnant, and in most tellings the father was the god Mars. In one source Amulius himself, in full armour, committed the rape. He had her watched and placed under guard, and she was either put to death or kept in a hidden dungeon.

Dionysius, citing Fabius Pictor, Cincius, Cato and Piso, writes that the king ordered the twins thrown into the Tiber. Floodwater kept his servants from the stream, so they left the basket in standing water at the site of the ficus Ruminalis. A she-wolf found and nursed the twins at her lair, the Lupercal, and Amulius' servant Faustulus took them home to raise.

According to Fabius, when the twins were 18 they quarrelled with Numitor's herdsmen, and Remus was captured in an ambush. Faustulus told Romulus the truth of their birth, and Numitor, to whom Amulius had handed Remus for punishment, told Remus the same. When Faustulus was caught by Alban guards carrying the basket into the city, he gave a false account to Amulius.

The twins and their grandfather led their supporters to the palace, killed Amulius and took control of the city. Numitor was restored as king of Alba Longa, and the twins went on to found Rome. Amulius' story is told in several versions, and the ancient accounts differ on details such as the twins' discovery, Rhea Silvia's fate and who saved the basket.
amur-river: The Amur, called the Heilong River in Chinese, rises where its two main headstreams, the Shilka and the Argun, meet in the hills of north-eastern China. It flows east along the border between the Russian Far East and Northeast China, then turns north-east beyond Khabarovsk, where it is joined by the Ussuri and ceases to form the border.

Its largest tributary is the Songhua. Measured with the Argun, it is 4,444 km long and drains a basin of desert, steppe, tundra and taiga. Its mouth faces the northern end of Sakhalin, and the island's name derives from a Tungusic word for black, as in the Manchu name for the river, Sahaliyan Ula.

For many centuries the valley was home to Tungusic peoples such as the Evenki, Nanai and Ulch, to the Daur, to some Ainu and, near the mouth, to the Nivkhs. Fishing in the river and its tributaries was the main livelihood of many of them. The Chinese called them collectively the Wild Jurchens, and used a term meaning Fish-skin Tatars for the Nanai and related groups because of their clothes of fish skin.

The Mongols of the Yuan dynasty kept a tenuous military presence on the lower Amur in the 13th and 14th centuries. Under the Yongle and Xuande Emperors the Ming dynasty reached the river: expeditions led by the eunuch Yishiha reached Tyr several times between 1411 and the early 1430s and obtained at least the nominal allegiance of the lower Amur's peoples, but the Ming presence soon faded.

Russian Cossacks led by Vassili Poyarkov and Yerofey Khabarov explored the Amur in 1643-44 and 1649-51 and collected tribute from local peoples, building the fort of Albazin on the upper river. The Qing turned north once their conquest of China was secure, founded Aigun about 1683-84 and took Albazin in 1685. The Treaty of Nerchinsk of 1689 left the whole valley from the meeting of the Shilka and the Argun downstream in Chinese hands. The region then remained a backwater of the Qing Empire for about a century and a half.

Russians returned to the river in the mid-19th century, and the Manchus yielded all lands north of the river to the Russian Empire by the Treaty of Aigun in 1858. Lands east of the Ussuri and along the lower Amur passed to Russia by the Convention of Peking in 1860.

The river gives its name to China's province of Heilongjiang and to Russia's Amur Oblast. The Khabarovsk Bridge, finished in 1916, let Trans-Siberian trains cross the river all year without ferries or tracks on the ice. The basin shelters the Amur tiger and leopard, and the kaluga, a sturgeon that can reach 5.6 m.
amyntas-iii-of-macedon: Amyntas III belonged to the Argead dynasty through his father Arrhidaeus, a son of one of the sons of Alexander I. The death of Alexander I in 454 BCE had set his five sons against one another in a dynastic crisis, and the king's descendants later met violent ends. After Archelaus died in 400 or 399 BCE, five kings ruled in less than seven years, nearly all of them ending violently. Amyntas seized the throne in 393 or 392 BCE after assassinating the previous king, Pausanias, according to Diodorus.

Shortly after becoming king Amyntas was driven out by the Illyrians, but the following year he recovered his kingdom with the aid of the Thessalians. Medius, head of the house of the Aleuadae of Larissa, is believed to have helped him. To guard against the Illyrians he allied himself with the Chalcidian League led by Olynthus and granted it rights to Macedonian timber, which was sent to Athens to help fortify its fleet. The money that flowed into Olynthus increased its power, so Amyntas sought other allies. Around 386 BCE he adopted the Athenian general Iphicrates, who was married to a daughter of the Odrysian chief Kotys, in recognition of his military services.

When Olynthus grew to threaten him, Amyntas appealed to Sparta, which was anxious to re-establish itself in northern Greece after the King's Peace of 387 BCE and was glad to weaken a city backed by Athens and Thebes. The Spartans fought alongside him, suffering two defeats at first, and in 379 BCE destroyed Olynthus. Amyntas also entered a league with Jason of Pherae and cultivated the friendship of Athens, and in 371 BCE he voted with other Greeks to help Athens recover Amphipolis. With Olynthus gone, he could keep the timber revenues for himself.

Amyntas took two wives, Eurydice and Gygaea, as Macedonian kings used polygamy to secure alliances and provide enough heirs. Eurydice bore him three sons who all became king in turn, Alexander II, Perdiccas III and Philip II, and a daughter, Eurynoe. Gygaea's sons Archelaus, Arrhidaeus and Menelaus never ruled and were all killed by their half-brother Philip II.

Amyntas died aged 50 and left his throne to his eldest son, Alexander II. Friends of Ptolemy killed Alexander at a festival in 368 BCE. Perdiccas killed Ptolemy in 365 BCE and was himself killed in battle by the Illyrians in 359 BCE.
amyrtaeus: Amyrtaeus of Sais bore a Greek form of the Egyptian name Amenirdisu. He is thought to be related to the royal family of the Twenty-sixth Dynasty and was probably the grandson of the earlier Amyrtaeus of Sais, who with Inaros II led a rebellion against the satrap of Artaxerxes I between 465 and 463 BCE. He is known from Aramaic and Greek sources and from the Demotic Chronicle, a prophetic text of the 3rd or 2nd century BCE, which names him as the first ruler after the Persians. He left no known monuments, and no hieroglyphic writing of his names has been found; his Egyptian name is reconstructed from demotic notices.

Amyrtaeus revolted against the Persian king Darius II as early as 411 BCE, leading a guerrilla action in the western Nile Delta around his home city of Sais. After Darius died he declared himself king in 404 BCE. According to Isocrates, Artaxerxes II assembled an army in Phoenicia under Abrocomas to retake Egypt, but trouble with his brother Cyrus the Younger prevented it, which gave the Egyptians time to throw off Achaemenid rule.

The Aramaic papyri from Elephantine show that Artaxerxes II was still recognised there as late as 401 BCE, while a papyrus of September 400 BCE refers to year 5 of Amortis, and that between 404 and 400 BCE, or even 398, Upper Egypt remained under Persian control while his forces dominated the Delta. Diodorus Siculus writes that a king named Psamtik, who may be Amyrtaeus under a lost regnal name, murdered the Greek admiral Tamos, who had taken refuge in Egypt after the defeat of Cyrus. If so, he may have wished to win favour with Artaxerxes II. He probably made an alliance with Sparta under which Egypt received military aid in exchange for grain.

Amyrtaeus was defeated in open battle by his successor, Nepherites I of Mendes, and executed at Memphis. The Aramaic papyrus Brooklyn 13 implies that this happened in October 399 BCE. Nepherites I then moved the capital to Mendes in Lower Egypt and reigned until 393 BCE. Sextus Julius Africanus and Eusebius of Caesarea record a reign of six years for Amyrtaeus. His successful revolt began Egypt's last significant phase of independence under native kings, which lasted about 60 years until the Persians conquered the country again.
an-lushan: An Lushan was born in 703. His mother was a Göktürk of the Ashide clan who served as a sorceress. Sources conflict about the origin of his biological father; he took the surname An from his stepfather, the Turkic general An Yanyan, who fled to the Tang during a disturbance among the Göktürk tribe in the Kaiyuan era. He settled in Ying Prefecture, roughly modern Chaoyang, and is said to have known six non-Chinese languages and to have worked as an interpreter in the frontier markets where silk was traded for horses. In 732 the general Zhang Shougui spared him from caning for stealing sheep and took him into his service.

An rose under Zhang Shougui. In 736 he was defeated by the Khitan and Xi after disobeying orders, and Emperor Xuanzong spared him over the objection of the chancellor Zhang Jiuling, who thought he looked like a rebel. By 742 he was military governor of Pinglu, and in 744 he also received Fanyang; in 751 he was given Hedong as well. He won favour by visiting Chang'an and offering gifts, and he became an adoptive son of the consort Yang Guifei. Xuanzong awarded him an iron certificate in 748 and made him Prince of Dongping in 750. After the death of the chancellor Li Linfu in 753, he became a rival of Yang Guozhong, who repeatedly accused him of plotting revolt.

On 16 December 755 An Lushan rebelled, claiming a secret edict to remove Yang. He crossed the Yellow River on 8 January 756, took Luoyang, and on 5 February declared himself emperor of a new state of Yan. His forces captured Tong Pass, and Xuanzong fled Chang'an. At Mawei Station the imperial guards killed Yang Guozhong and demanded the death of Yang Guifei. Li Heng took the throne as Emperor Suzong. Yan forces entered Chang'an, but the advance was slow, and the Tang generals Guo Ziyi and Li Guangbi regrouped.

As emperor An stayed in the Luoyang palace. He was nearly blind, ill and extremely obese, and grew violent and paranoid. Fearing that his father favoured another son, An Qingxu joined the eunuch Li Zhu'er in a plot, and on the night of 29 January 757 Li Zhu'er stabbed An Lushan to death. In 759 Shi Siming killed An Qingxu and buried An Lushan with the rites of a prince, giving him the posthumous name La. The rebellion he began lasted until 17 February 763. It is thought to have caused about 13 million deaths, and a fall of 36 million in the Tang census, which many scholars attribute to the breakdown of tax and census gathering.
an-lushan-rebellion: An Lushan was a general of uncertain origins, thought to have been adopted by a Sogdian father and a Göktürk mother of the Ashina tribe. He became a favourite of Emperor Xuanzong, who built him a luxurious house in the capital Chang'an in 751. The rebellion began as a commandery revolt meant to replace the Tang government with a new Yan dynasty, and it spanned the reigns of three Tang emperors: Xuanzong, Suzong and Daizong.

On 16 December 755 An Lushan marched out of Fanyang, near modern Beijing, treating surrendered Tang officials with respect so that many joined him. He took the Eastern Capital, Luoyang, on 18 January 756 and declared himself emperor of the Great Yan on 5 February. Resistance at Yongqiu and later at Suiyang, under the Tang defender Zhang Xun, kept his armies from the rich lands south of the Yangzi. At Tong Pass the Tang court executed two capable generals and ordered the replacement commander to attack on open ground; the Tang were defeated on 7 July, and Xuanzong fled to Sichuan. The rebels took Chang'an in July 756.

Xuanzong's son Li Heng was proclaimed Emperor Suzong, and his generals Guo Ziyi and Li Guangbi borrowed troops from the Uyghur Khaganate, while the Abbasid caliph al-Mansur sent mercenaries. With Uyghur help the Tang retook both capitals in late 757. An Lushan was killed by his son An Qingxu on 29 January 757. Shi Siming killed An Qingxu in 759 and took over the rebel cause, and was in turn killed by his son Shi Chaoyi. After Luoyang fell again, Shi Chaoyi killed himself on 17 February 763, ending the war.

The Tang allowed surrendered rebel generals to keep their commands as military governors, the jiedushi, and in Hebei three of these regions stayed virtually independent for the rest of the dynasty. The Tibetan Empire briefly took Chang'an on 18 November 763, and Tang control of the Western Regions was lost; by 790 Chinese control of the Tarim Basin was gone. Mutinies and revolts followed from 781.

The census of 755 recorded 52,919,309 people, and that of 764 only 16,900,000, but scholars attribute much of the gap to a breakdown in taxation and census-taking. The Tang survived, but historians treat the rebellion as a turning point in the dynasty's decline. It also hastened the shift of the economic centre of China from the Guanzhong region towards the Jiangnan region.
anabaptism: Anabaptism traces its origins to the Radical Reformation of the 16th century. Historians classify medieval groups with a similar approach to the Bible as forerunners, among them the Waldensians, the Hussites and the Brethren of the Common Life, and the 15th-century Bohemian reformer Petr Chelčický taught most of the beliefs now held integral to it. In Switzerland it began as an offshoot of the reforms of Ulrich Zwingli. Some of his young followers thought he moved too slowly, and the division became plain at a disputation in Zürich in October 1523, when Conrad Grebel asked what should be done about the mass.

Scholars disagree about its roots. One theory holds that the movement began in Zürich and spread from there, another that it developed from several independent movements. Research has also been coloured by enemies who slandered the Anabaptists and by supporters who defended them. It was long popular to class all Anabaptists with the radicals of Münster, and those who sought to correct this error tended to over-correct and deny any link between the larger movement and its most radical elements.

Anabaptists hold that baptism is valid only when candidates freely confess their faith in Christ and ask for it, so they reject the baptism of infants. The name is an exonym meaning one who baptizes again; early members refused it, saying infant baptism was not in scripture and their baptism of believers was their first true one. Early Anabaptists set out their beliefs in the Schleitheim Confession of 1527, written by Michael Sattler, who was arrested and executed soon afterwards.

Most adhere to a literal reading of the Sermon on the Mount, which they take to teach against hatred, violence, oaths, military action and participation in civil government. They see themselves primarily as citizens of the kingdom of God. Practices often include the love feast with feet washing, the holy kiss, and sharing possessions.

Roman Catholics and Protestants alike persecuted Anabaptists with torture and execution. Under Zwingli's Protestants, Manz became the first Anabaptist martyr in 1527, and King Ferdinand declared drowning, called the third baptism, the best antidote to Anabaptism. Anabaptism was never established by any state. Many found refuge in Moravia, which was more tolerant and became a centre of the movement.

The Amish, Hutterites and Mennonites descend directly from the early movement. According to the figures given, there were over 2.03 million baptized Anabaptists in 87 countries in 2025, mostly in Africa and North America. Voluntary church membership, freedom of conscience and the priesthood of all believers are among the 16th-century ideas that have influenced Western society.
anacaona: Anacaona was born in Yaguana in Jaragua, present-day Léogâne in Haiti. Her name joins the Taíno words ana, flower, and caona, gold. She was trained in zemi interpretation, for which she was highly respected, and her compositions were performed at areítos; none of her writings survive. Amid Kalinago raids on Hispaniola, her brother Bohechío arranged her marriage to Caonabo, a cacique from the Lucayos who had conquered Maguana in 1470. Caonabo had many wives, and the couple had one daughter, Higuenamota. Anacaona spent most of her time in Jaragua with her brother.

After Columbus reached Hispaniola in 1492, the Spanish began enslaving Taínos. Caonabo fought them and was captured by Alonso de Ojeda in 1496, then banished. When Bartholomew Columbus came to Jaragua in 1496 and 1497, Anacaona and Bohechío received him, the tribute of cassava bread and cotton was handed over at a feast, and she gave him many finely worked goods from a hamlet of her own. Historian Maria Isabel Cabrera Bosch speculates that she held considerable authority in Jaragua's administration.

On Bohechío's death in 1500 she became cacica, ruling a territory that reached east to the Neyba and Ozama rivers. She kept his policy of cooperating with the Spanish even as enslaved Taínos fled to Jaragua, along with refugees from Francisco Roldán's rebellion of 1497. Governor Nicolás de Ovando came to Jaragua with 300 men, and after the massacre of between 40 and 80 caciques she was taken to Santo Domingo, imprisoned and tortured, and hanged. Las Casas said such massacres were meant to instil fear, Oviedo that Ovando was quashing a planned rebellion; some modern historians point to the caciques' avoidance of demands for food and mine labourers.

Writers and artists have used her memory to advance various positions. Alfred, Lord Tennyson wrote the poem Anacaona as a student, first reciting it in 1830. Salomé Ureña wrote a poem about her in 1880, and Manuel de Jesús Galván made her a character in his novel Enriquillo. The salsa song Anacaona by Tite Curet Alonso, popularised in the United States by Cheo Feliciano in 1971, began a series of musical tributes. Jean Métellus wrote a play about her in 1986, and Edwidge Danticat a young adult novel in 2005.
anacreon: Anacreon came from Teos on the coast of Ionia, a tradition attested as early as Herodotus. The year of his birth is not known. When Persia conquered Teos in the 540s BCE the Teians moved to Abdera in Thrace, and Anacreon was probably already an adult. He then spent time on Samos. According to Himerius he was invited there to educate Polycrates, the future tyrant, whom Strabo reports to have been one of the main subjects of his poetry. Herodotus places him still on Samos in 522 BCE, when Polycrates was murdered.

From Samos he went to Athens on the invitation of Hipparchus, presumably after Hipparchus came to power in 528/7 BCE. Ancient sources do not say whether or when he left. He may have gone after the assassination of Hipparchus in 514 BCE or the expulsion of Hippias in 510 BCE, though some evidence places him in the city later.

Anacreon wrote in the Ionic dialect, in metrical verse composed to be sung or recited to the lyre, mostly as monody rather than for a chorus. His themes were love, infatuation, disappointment, revelry, parties and festivals, and everyday life. Two short hymns, to Artemis and to Dionysus, of eight and eleven lines, stand first among his few undisputed remains. The Suda and Athenaeus mention five books of his lyrics, but only fragments survive, gathered from citations by later writers.

A collection of poems by anonymous imitators, the Anacreontea, was long believed to be his own work. It survives in a 10th-century manuscript, and its poems were composed between the 1st century BCE and the 6th century CE, not in his Ionic dialect.

Anacreon probably died at the beginning of the fifth century BCE; Gregory Hutchinson says around 500, Hans Bernsdorff suggests 495 and David Campbell says 485. Valerius Maximus reports that he choked on a grape seed, a story generally regarded as apocryphal. An epigram in the Greek Anthology places his tomb on Teos.

He was depicted on Athenian red-figure vases while still alive, and later Greeks included him among the Nine Lyric Poets. By the Hellenistic period a caricature of him as drunken and lustful was established, though Plato portrayed him as a wise man. He was an important influence on Horace. The edition of the Anacreontea by Henricus Stephanus in 1554 began a fashion for short, playful Anacreontic verse that peaked in the eighteenth century.
anagarika-dharmapala: Dharmapala was born Don David Hewavitarne in Colombo on 17 September 1864, to a family among the richest merchants of Ceylon. He attended several Christian and other schools in and around Colombo, including the Colombo Academy. When the Theosophists Helena Blavatsky and Henry Steel Olcott arrived in Ceylon in 1880 and declared themselves Buddhists, he helped Olcott as a translator and took the name Dharmapala, meaning protector of the dharma. As an anagarika, a homeless one midway between monk and layperson, he took the eight precepts for life, which was highly unusual. He eventually broke with the Theosophists over Olcott's universalism.

In 1891 Dharmapala made a pilgrimage to the Mahabodhi Temple at Bodh Gaya, where the Buddha attained enlightenment. He was shocked to find it in the hands of a Saivite priest, the Buddha image transformed into a Hindu icon and Buddhists barred from worship, and began an agitation. The Maha Bodhi Society was founded at Colombo in 1891 and moved to Calcutta in 1892; one of its chief aims was the return of the temple to Buddhist control. Dharmapala brought a lawsuit against the Brahmin priests who had held it for centuries. Success came only in 1949, sixteen years after his death, when the temple's management passed to a committee of equal numbers of Hindus and Buddhists.

In 1893 he represented Southern Buddhism at the World Parliament of Religions in Chicago, where he read The World's Debt to Buddha and met Swami Vivekananda. He travelled and lectured for the next forty years, founded schools and hospitals in Ceylon and built temples in India, among them one at Sarnath. Mary E. Foster, whom he met in Hawaii, gave him a donation of over one million rupees.

The scholar Gananath Obeyesekere coined the term Protestant Buddhism, often applied to Dharmapala's form of the religion. It stresses the laity and individual experience, and is itself a protest against Christian claims of superiority and missionary work. Dharmapala presented Buddhism as consistent with science, especially evolution, in works such as Evolution from the Standpoint of Buddhism (1926). He also contributed to Sinhalese Buddhist nationalism, with a rhetoric that praised Buddhism and Sinhalese culture and blamed British imperialists and Christians. He was ordained a monk in 1931, took higher ordination in 1933 and died at Sarnath on 29 April 1933.
anagni: Anagni is a hill town of about 424 metres above sea level in the province of Frosinone, in Lazio, east-southeast of Rome. It keeps the look of a small medieval town, with twisting streets and steep lanes inside Roman boundary walls. The first people known by name in the area were the Hernici, said to have come from the Aniene valley, and Anagni was an important city and spiritual centre of theirs, built on an acropolis and partly defended by walls of almost squared stone.

In 307 BCE the Hernici, except for Alatri, Veroli and Ferentino, declared war on Rome and, after setbacks, surrendered. In 306 BCE Anagni and the other states that had borne arms were admitted to citizenship without the vote, forbidden councils and intermarriage, and left only magistrates in charge of religious rites. Several emperors later spent their summers there, among them Marcus Aurelius, Septimius Severus, Commodus and Caracalla.

Anagni has been a bishop's seat since the 5th century. From the 10th and 11th centuries the popes regarded it as a safer and healthier place than Rome, and it became one of their favourite residences. In 1160 Pope Alexander III excommunicated Emperor Frederick Barbarossa in the cathedral, and on 29 September 1227 Pope Gregory IX excommunicated Emperor Frederick II there. The town produced four popes in a century, three of them of the Conti family, among them Innocent III.

In 1303 Guillaume de Nogaret, adviser to Philip IV of France, and Sciarra Colonna led about two thousand mercenaries against the palaces of Pope Boniface VIII. The pope was held for three days without food or drink until the townspeople rose and freed him. This is called the Outrage of Anagni, and a later legend says Colonna slapped the pope with his gauntlet. Boniface died in Rome on 11 October 1303. The move of the papal court to Avignon began a long decline, and Duke Werner von Urslingen sacked the town in 1348.

The Romanesque cathedral of Saint Mary, built in 1071–1105 with Gothic additions in the mid-13th century, has frescoes among the best preserved examples of Romanesque and Byzantine art in Italy, and an unrestored Cosmati floor. The Communal Palace was built in 1163 by the Brescian architect Jacopo da Iseo. Excavations since 2006 at the imperial Villa Magna, south of the town, have revealed a large, richly decorated building devoted to wine production.
anah: Anah lies on the right bank of the Euphrates, along a bend of the river just before it turns south towards Hīt, roughly midway between the Gulf of Alexandretta and the Persian Gulf. Cuneiform texts of the Old Babylonian period call it Ha-na-at, and the scribes of Assur-nasir-pal II wrote An-at in 879 BCE; the name has been connected with the war goddess Anat. Greek and Roman writers knew it as Anathō and Anatha. In the 19th century it marked the boundary between the olive-growing north and the date-growing south.

The earliest references are probably in letters from the time of Zimri-Lim of Mari, and under Hammurapi of Babylon the town belonged to the governorate of Sūḫu. Xenophon's Charmande, where the army of Cyrus the Younger resupplied in 401 BCE, was likely Anah. The Roman emperor Julian met his first opposition there in 363 CE and relocated its people. In 1058 the caliph Qaim was exiled to Anah, and in the 14th century it was the seat of the catholicos of the Persian Christians, a trade town known for its palm groves and wine.

From around 1535 it was the de facto capital of the Abu Rish bedouin emirs, whom the Ottomans appointed as governors. Pietro Della Valle called it the principal Arab town on the Euphrates. In 1835 Arabs, Christians and Jews lived in separate parts of the town, and in 1909 it had an estimated 15,000 people. British forces took Anah in 1918, and by 1921 it was part of the Kingdom of Iraq. The Islamic State of Iraq and the Levant captured it in 2014, and the Iraqi army retook it after two days of fighting from 19 September 2017.

When the valley was flooded by the Haditha Dam in 1984/85, the Iraqi State Board of Antiquities cut the old octagonal minaret of the island mosque into sections and moved it to the new Anah, where it was re-erected to a height of 28 metres at the end of the 1980s. The town has a hot desert climate, with about 127 mm of rain a year.
analects: According to Ban Gu, writing in the Book of Han, the Analects began as individual records kept by Confucius's disciples of their conversations with him, which they collected and jointly edited after his death in 479 BCE. During the Han dynasty the work was titled Lunyu, which may mean edited conversations or selected speeches. Scholars agree that large portions were composed in the Warring States period and that the work reached its final form in the mid-Han dynasty.

Liu Xiang records that two versions existed at the beginning of the Han: the Lu version of twenty chapters and the Qi version of twenty-two. A third Old Text version, written in characters not used since the Warring States period, was found hidden in a wall of a house believed to be Confucius's. The received text is mostly based on the Lu version.

The chapters are grouped by theme but do not form a continuous argument, and adjacent chapters are often unrelated. Confucius describes himself as a transmitter of the traditions of the early Zhou, not an originator. The central idea is ren, an all-encompassing state of virtue that, in the text, no living person had completely attained. Asked to define it, Confucius responds indirectly, with examples, and the basic step towards it is filial piety.

In politics the text holds that a good ruler is self-disciplined and governs by education and example rather than by punishment. Confucius blames social chaos on rulers who claim titles they do not deserve. Education is a fundamental theme, and he is traditionally credited with teaching three thousand students, seventy of whom mastered what he taught. The Analects is arguably the most reliable source for his biography.

During most of the Han period the Analects was not a principal text of Confucianism. Under Emperor Wu only the Five Classics were canonical, and the Analects was treated as a collection of Confucius's commentary on them. By the Eastern Han it was widely read by schoolchildren. In the late Song dynasty Zhu Xi promoted it as one of the Four Books, and it came to be regarded as more insightful than the older Five Classics.

He Yan's Collected Explanations, written in 248 CE, is the oldest complete commentary still extant and remained the standard guide for nearly a thousand years. The Analects has been among the most widely read books in China for more than two thousand years, and its ideas continue to influence East Asian thought and values.
analytical-engine: Charles Babbage's first mechanical computing device, the difference engine, was a special-purpose machine meant to tabulate logarithms and trigonometric functions. It was never completed: Babbage quarrelled with his chief engineer, Joseph Clement, and the British government withdrew its funding. During that project he realised that a much more general design was possible, and work on the analytical engine began around 1833. In 1842 Luigi Federico Menabrea published a description in French based on Babbage's lectures in Turin. Ada Lovelace translated it into English in 1843 and annotated it extensively, adding a method of calculating Bernoulli numbers on the machine, widely considered the first complete computer program.

Programs and data were to be supplied on punched cards of three kinds: arithmetical operations, numerical constants, and loading and storing numbers. Output would come from a printer, a curve plotter and a bell, and the machine could punch numbers onto cards to be read later. It used ordinary base-10 fixed-point arithmetic. The store, or memory, was to hold 1,000 numbers of 40 decimal digits each, and an arithmetic unit called the mill would perform all four operations, comparisons and optionally square roots.

The language was akin to modern assembly languages. Because loops and conditional branching were possible, it would have been Turing-complete as Alan Turing later defined the term. Babbage developed some two dozen programs between 1837 and 1840, treating polynomials, iterative formulas, Gaussian elimination and Bernoulli numbers.

Babbage never completed any of his machines. Late in life he sought a simplified version and assembled a small part before his death in 1871. In 1878 a committee of the British Association for the Advancement of Science called the engine a marvel of mechanical ingenuity but recommended against building it. His son Henry Prevost Babbage built part of the mill and the printing apparatus between 1880 and 1910, and in 1910 it produced a faulty list of multiples of pi. It is displayed at the Science Museum in London.

Many later builders of computers knew little of Babbage's work. Howard Aiken, who built the Harvard Mark I, knew nothing of the engine's architecture while building it, and J. Presper Eckert and John W. Mauchly were unaware of its details when they designed the ENIAC. Konrad Zuse built the general-purpose Z3 in 1941.
anambra-state: Anambra State is named after the Omambala River, which flows through it and is a tributary of the Niger; Anambra is the anglicised form of Omambala. The state is bordered by Delta and Edo States to the west across the Niger, by Imo and Rivers to the south, Abia to the southeast, Enugu to the east and Kogi to the north. Its climate is tropical wet and dry.

Archaeological excavations at Igbo-Ukwu and Ezira show that the area's history stretches to the 9th century, with great works of art in iron, bronze, copper and pottery. These revealed a sophisticated system of divine kingship that held sway in the area from about 948 until 1911. The area has been the site of numerous civilizations, including the ancient Kingdom of Nri, whose capital was the town of Igbo-Ukwu. Awka was the craft industrial centre of the Nri hegemony, and Onitsha developed as a river port and commercial city on the Niger in the pre-colonial era.

Britain recognised some traditional kings and leaders under indirect rule in the Protectorate of South Nigeria, and from the 19th century appointed some leaders as Warrant Chiefs, authorising them to collect taxes. The old Anambra State was formed in 1976 from the former East Central State. During the Nigerian Civil War of 1967 to 1970 the area was part of the secessionist Republic of Biafra, and it was severely affected by the war.

Anambra is a state in southeastern Nigeria, with Awka as its capital and Onitsha as its most populous city. Nnewi is the second largest commercial and industrial city. The population is primarily Igbo, and the Igbo language is a lingua franca throughout the state. It consists of 21 local government areas, and most people are Christian, chiefly Catholic, Anglican and Pentecostal. The Onitsha Ofala Festival, marking the climax of the New Yam, is held each October.
anand-district: Anand district is an administrative district of Gujarat state in western India, popularly nicknamed Charotar. It is bounded by Kheda District to the north, Vadodara District to the east, Ahmedabad District to the west and the Gulf of Khambhat to the south. Its major towns are Umreth, Khambhat, Tarapur, Petlad, Borsad and Sojitra, and it is divided into eight talukas: Anand, Anklav, Borsad, Khambhat, Petlad, Sojitra, Tarapur and Umreth.

The 2011 census counted 2,092,745 people, a density of 711 inhabitants per square kilometre, with a growth rate of 12.57 per cent over the decade 2001 to 2011. About 30 per cent lived in urban areas, and the literacy rate was 85.79 per cent. Gujarati was the first language of 96.66 per cent of the population, Hindi of 2.10 per cent and Urdu of 0.58 per cent.

Anand is the birthplace of Tribhuvandas Patel, founder of Anand Milk Union Limited and of the cooperative movement there, and the town is nicknamed Milk City. Amul is the origin of Operation Flood, the White Revolution of India, and the National Dairy Development Board has its headquarters in the district. Education is represented by the Institute of Rural Management Anand, Anand Agricultural University and Sardar Patel University at Vallabh Vidyanagar.

Karamsad is the native place of Sardar Patel. Khambhat is a historic and ancient port in the Gulf of Khambhat, known for its trade with foreign countries. Bhadran was called the Paris of Gaekwad state because of the prosperity and civil works carried out by Maharaja Sayajirao Gaekwad III about a century ago. Umreth is regarded as a heritage city for Jainism, and Vadtal is also listed among the district's places of interest.
ananda-mahidol: Ananda Mahidol was born on 20 September 1925 in Heidelberg, where his parents Prince Mahidol Adulyadej of Songkla and Mom Sangwan were studying. He was the first Thai king born outside the country. The family returned to Thailand in 1928, and Prince Mahidol died in 1929. After the revolution of 1932 ended the absolute monarchy, his mother took her children to Lausanne in 1933, officially for their health and education. When King Prajadhipok abdicated in 1935, the cabinet had to decide on the succession because Prince Chula Chakrabongse, whose father had married a foreigner, was also a candidate. Pridi Banomyong persuaded the cabinet to exclude him, and the National Assembly elected Ananda Mahidol on 2 March 1935, when he was nine.

The king stayed in Switzerland to study while regents acted for him. In 1938 he visited Siam for the first time as monarch, and Field Marshal Plaek Phibunsongkhram was prime minister during most of his reign. Japan invaded Thailand on 8 December 1941, and from 24 January 1942 Thailand was a formal ally of Japan. The regent Pridi Banomyong refused to sign the declaration of war on the Allies, so it was legally invalid. After Japan surrendered on 15 August 1945 the king returned in December 1945 with a law degree. He won the affection of the Thai people, and visited Sampheng Lane in Bangkok's Chinatown to ease post-war tensions.

On 9 June 1946 the king was found shot dead in his bedroom in the Boromphiman Throne Hall, four days before he was to return to Switzerland. An initial radio announcement spoke of an accident, but a commission of inquiry reported in October 1946 that the death could not have been accidental, and that neither suicide nor murder had been satisfactorily proved.

After Plaek Phibunsongkhram's coup of November 1947, the king's secretary Chaliao Pathumrot and two pages, But and Chit, were tried for conspiracy to murder. After a trial that ended in 1951 and two appeals, the Supreme Court convicted all three, who were executed on 17 February 1955. Theories have since pointed to an accident, suicide or murder. The pathologist Keith Simpson considered suicide highly unlikely, and Rayne Kruger concluded that it was most probably an accidental suicide. His brother Bhumibol Adulyadej succeeded him. Ananda Mahidol was cremated at Sanam Luang on 29 March 1950.
ananda-temple: The temple takes its name from Ananda, the first cousin, attendant and one of the principal disciples of the Buddha; the word means bliss in Pali and Sanskrit. A legend holds that eight monks who had meditated in the Nandamula Cave in the Himalayas described it to King Kyansittha, who asked them to build a temple like it on the Bagan plain, and then had them killed so that they could build no other. The scholar George Coedes recorded a different story, in which the architect and a child were buried alive to serve as guardian spirits.

Kyansittha had adopted Theravada Buddhism and used the temple to present its teachings to his people in stone images, numbered plaques and standing Buddhas.
