In 1155 he left Vyshgorod for Vladimir, a small town on the Klyazma, taking with him the Icon of the Blessed Mother of God, afterwards known as the Virgin of Vladimir, an action the Kievan Chronicle condemned as theft.

After Yuri's death in 1157, Andrey became Prince of Vladimir-Suzdal. In 1162 he ousted his younger brothers Mikhail and Vsevolod from Rostov and Suzdal, united his father's lands under his sole rule and expelled four brothers, with their mother, to the Byzantine Empire. He began fortifications at Vladimir in 1158, completed in 1164, and the Dormition Cathedral. He sent an embassy to Constantinople asking for a separate metropolitan see at Vladimir, but the patriarch refused. In 1164 he attacked the Volga Bolgars, and he built the castle of Bogolyubovo near Vladimir, which became his favourite residence.

In March 1169 his troops sacked Kiev, plundering religious art, books and valuables and devastating houses and churches. Andrey stayed in Vladimir-Suzdal. He claimed the title of Grand Prince, kept his residence at Vladimir and placed his brother Gleb on the Kievan throne, an overlordship that ended with Gleb's death on 20 January 1171. His siege of Novgorod in 1170 failed, though a later blockade won the princedom there for his son Yury in 1171. In 1173 a second coalition he assembled was defeated at Vyshgorod.

The defeat at Vyshgorod, the growth of his authority and his conflicts with the boyars led to a conspiracy, and on the night of 28-29 June 1174 twenty boyars burst into his chambers and killed him in his bed. The chronicles say his right hand was cut off, but a miniature in the Radziwiłł Chronicle shows the left arm, and an examination of his exhumed body in 1965 found many cut marks on the left humerus and forearm bones. His death set off a war of succession in Suzdalia from 1174 to 1177. The Orthodox Church canonised him in 1702. The icon Theotokos of Bogolyubovo was painted in the 12th century at his request.
andrei-ii-of-vladimir: Andrey Yaroslavich was the third son of Yaroslav II. According to the Novgorod First Chronicle, the Novgorodians expelled his brother Alexander Nevsky from the city in the winter of 1240 to 1241 and asked Yaroslav to send another commander, and Andrey was sent in Alexander's place. In 1241 he joined his Suzdalian forces with Alexander's, and they retook Pskov, raided the Estonian countryside and fought in the Battle on the Ice.

The chronicles give different versions of how Andrey became prince of Vladimir. In one, after their father's death in 1247 Andrey and Alexander travelled to Karakorum, where Andrey was appointed grand prince by a charter of the great khan Güyük; on their return in 1249 they found that their younger brother Mikhail Khorobrit had seized Vladimir, but he was killed fighting the Lithuanians within months. In another, Andrey took the throne from his uncle Sviatoslav in 1248. In the winter of 1250 to 1251 he married Ustynia, a daughter of Danylo of Halych, who by 1251 appears to have been forming an anti-Mongol coalition.

When the great khan Güyük died in 1251, Andrey was expected to go to Sarai and have his charter renewed by Batu Khan in the name of the new great khan Möngke. He refused, although Alexander Nevsky complied. The Mongols took this as a challenge: Batu's son Sartak ordered a punitive expedition, and Andrey was defeated near Pereslavl and fled by way of Novgorod to Sweden. Alexander then received the throne of Vladimir from the Mongols in 1252. Modern scholars read these events as a rivalry between the brothers, with Andrey seeking an anti-Mongol alliance.

In 1255 Andrey returned from exile and went to Sarai to ask pardon. He received Suzdal and, from Alexander, the easternmost lands of Vladimir, including Nizhny Novgorod and Gorodets on the Volga. After Alexander died in 1263 Andrey hoped to add Vladimir to his possessions, but his younger brother Yaroslav of Tver thwarted him. He died in 1264. His sons included Yury, Mikhail and Vasily of Suzdal, and the house of Nizhny Novgorod-Suzdal, known since the 14th century as the House of Shuysky, descends from him.
andrei-rublev: Little information survives about Rublev's life, and even his birthplace is unknown. He probably lived in the Trinity Lavra of St. Sergius, near Moscow, under Nikon of Radonezh, who became hegumen after the death of Sergius of Radonezh in 1392. The first mention of him is in 1405, when he decorated icons and frescoes for the Cathedral of the Annunciation in the Moscow Kremlin together with Theophanes the Greek and Prokhor of Gorodets. His name came last in the list of masters, as the junior in rank and age. Theophanes, an important Byzantine master who had moved to Russia, is considered to have trained him.

Chronicles record that with Daniel Chorny he painted the Dormition Cathedral in Vladimir in 1408 and the Trinity Cathedral in the Trinity Lavra of St. Sergius between 1425 and 1427. After Daniel's death he went to Moscow's Andronikov Monastery, where he painted his last work, the frescoes of the Saviour Cathedral. He is also believed to have painted at least one miniature in the Khitrovo Gospels.

The only work authenticated as entirely his is the icon of the Trinity, of about 1410. It is based on an earlier icon, the Hospitality of Abraham, which illustrates Genesis 18. Rublev removed the figures of Abraham and Sarah and, through composition and symbolism, turned the subject to the mystery of the Trinity. His art is said to combine two traditions, the highest asceticism and the classical harmony of Byzantine style, and his figures are peaceful and calm.

Rublev died at the Andronikov Monastery between 1427 and 1430. His work influenced many artists, among them Dionisy, and the Stoglavi Sobor of 1551 promulgated his icon style as a model for church painting. The Andrei Rublev Museum at the Andronikov Monastery has displayed his work and related art since 1959. The Russian Orthodox Church canonised him in 1988, and his feast day is 29 January. In 1966 Andrei Tarkovsky made the film Andrei Rublev, loosely based on his life. The historian Serge Aleksandrovich Zenkovsky counted him among the names that signify the Russian spiritual and cultural revival of the late 14th and early 15th centuries.
andrej-hlinka: Andrej Hlinka was born on 27 September 1864 in Černová, now part of Ružomberok, in Liptov County, then under the Kingdom of Hungary. He graduated in theology at Spišská Kapitula and was ordained a priest in 1889. He tried to improve his parishioners' social position, fought alcoholism, organised lectures and theatre performances, and founded credit and food associations, writing a manual on how to found more. A defender of Catholic ethics against the secularising tendencies of Hungarian liberalism, he joined the Hungarian Catholic People's Party, but left it when it disregarded Slovak demands, and with František Skyčák founded the Slovak People's Party.

In 1905 he was elected parson of Ružomberok against the wishes of his Hungarian bishop Sándor Párvy. In 1906 he backed the Slovak candidate Vavro Šrobár, and the church hierarchy suspended him. On 27 June 1906 he was imprisoned and later convicted of sedition. The bishop ordered Hungarian-speaking priests to consecrate the church at Černová that Hlinka had helped build; local resistance led to the Černová massacre, which drew international attention to the Slovaks.

In prison Hlinka led a translation of the Old Testament into Slovak, and he later won his case against the bishop. He founded the Ľudová banka in 1907, and in 1913 became chairman of the Slovak People's Party, which had separated from the Slovak National Party, holding the post for life.

In 1918 he joined the Slovak National Council and signed the Martin Declaration, favouring union with the Czechs. Soon disappointed by Šrobár's methods and by the unequal position of Slovakia, he travelled to Paris in August 1918 on a passport issued by Poland in the name of Josef Berger, was arrested and expelled, and was then imprisoned. Elected to the Czechoslovak Parliament in April 1920, he was released.

For almost twenty years Hlinka led the struggle for Slovak autonomy, rejecting centralism and ethnic Czechoslovakism while accepting a common state. His party became the most popular in Slovakia. He died on 16 August 1938, and his party declared autonomy on 6 October 1938 after the Munich Agreement.

His party later produced the Hlinka Guard, a militia that took part in the Holocaust in Slovakia, and the first Slovak Republic, a client state of Nazi Germany, treated him as a national hero. Communist Czechoslovakia portrayed him as a clerofascist. After the fall of communism he reappeared as a respected figure, and his image was on the 1000-crown banknote. His mausoleum in Ružomberok was reopened in 1990.
andres-avelino-caceres: Andrés Avelino Cáceres Dorregaray was born on 10 November in the city of Ayacucho. His father, Domingo Cáceres y Ore, was a landowner, and his mother, Justa Dorregaray Cueva, was the daughter of a Spanish colonel. He was mestizo and counted the Inka-Wanka princess Catalina Huanca among his maternal ancestors. In 1854 he left his studies to join the Ayacucho Battalion as a cadet, and he fought in the rebellion of General Ramón Castilla at the Battle of La Palma on 5 January 1855.

He was exiled to Chile for criticising President Juan Antonio Pezet, who had allowed the Spanish occupation of the Chincha Islands, and he fought at the Battle of Callao on 2 May 1866. In the War of the Pacific, which began on 5 April 1879, Cáceres fought at San Francisco and Tarapacá, where his intervention was decisive in a Peruvian victory. He was at the defeat at Tacna on 26 May 1880 and was wounded at Miraflores in the defence of Lima. When Lima fell in January 1881 he escaped to Jauja.

Named political and military chief of the central departments on 26 April 1881, he organised a guerrilla war that mobilised the peasant population. He defeated several Chilean expeditions, at Pucará, Marcavalle and La Concepción, and was nicknamed the Brujo de los Andes. The better armed Chilean forces defeated him at Huamachuco on 10 July 1883, and the Treaty of Ancón of 10 October 1883 ended the war.

Cáceres refused to recognise President Miguel Iglesias, and in the civil war that followed he attacked Lima on 28 November 1885 and forced Iglesias to resign on 12 December. Elected as the sole candidate, he took office on 3 June 1886. His government signed the Grace Contract on 28 October 1888, which handed the railways, a guano concession and annual payments over 33 years to Peru's creditors in exchange for paying the debt and expanding the railways. Critics accused his administration of selling the country's main assets cheaply.

He handed power to Remigio Morales on 10 August 1890, and began a second term on 10 August 1894 amid accusations of fraud. Rebellions united under Nicolás de Piérola attacked Lima on 17 March 1895, and Cáceres resigned after an armistice. He later served as ambassador in Italy, became a Marshal on 10 November 1919, and died at Ancón on 10 October 1923, aged 86.
andres-bello: Andrés Bello was born in Caracas on 29 November 1781, the first son of the lawyer Bartolomé Bello and Ana Antonia López. He studied Latin with Father Cristobal de Quesada at the Convent of las Mercedes and, after the monk's death in 1796, translated Book V of the Aeneid. He studied liberal arts, law and medicine at the University of Caracas, graduating as a Bachelor of Arts on 9 May 1800, and taught himself English and French. Simón Bolívar was briefly his pupil, and Bello accompanied Alexander von Humboldt on part of his expedition. In 1802 he won by contest a post as second secretary of the colonial government and edited the Gazeta de Caracas.

After events of 19 April 1810 that led to the dismissal of Captain General Vicente Emparan, the Supreme Junta of Caracas named Bello first officer of its foreign ministry. He sailed to London that June with Bolívar and Luis López Méndez to seek British support for independence, and he stayed for nineteen years. He lived in hardship, teaching Spanish and tutoring the children of Lord Hamilton, and acted as secretary to legations for Chile and Colombia. With Juan García del Río he published the Biblioteca América in 1823, and in 1826 the Repertorio Americano. His poem La agricultura de la zona tórrida was published there. His friendship with Bolívar ended when Bolívar gave Bello's post to someone else.

In 1829 he moved to Chile to work in the Ministry of Foreign Affairs under Diego Portales, and was later a senator for Santiago. He became the first rector of the University of Chile and held the post for more than two decades. The Chilean Congress gave him citizenship on 17 October 1832.

Bello worked for twenty years on the Civil Code of Chile, drawn up in 1852 and passed by Congress in 1855, an innovative code compared with Europe's Napoleonic Code, which Colombia and Ecuador later adopted. His Gramática de la lengua castellana destinada al uso de los americanos, finished in 1847, was the first Spanish-American grammar and was republished with revisions, the most significant by Rufino José Cuervo. His Spanish spelling reform, worked out with García del Río, became official in several Spanish American countries, most lastingly in Chile. He died in Santiago on 15 October 1865, aged eighty-three. He appears on Chilean 20,000 peso notes, and universities and a diplomatic academy bear his name.
andres-bonifacio: Andrés Bonifacio y de Castro was born on 30 November 1863 in Tondo, Manila, the first of six children of Catalina de Castro and Santiago Bonifacio. He was named for Saint Andrew, on whose feast day he was born. He attended private and municipal schools and reached the third year of a private secondary school. To support his family he made walking canes and paper fans and posters for business firms, and he and his brothers later worked for private and government companies. Some sources say he was orphaned young, but an 1881 record listing his parents as living in Tondo leaves this disputed.

In 1892 Bonifacio was among the founding members of José Rizal's La Liga Filipina, which called for reform in the colonial government. It disbanded after one meeting because Rizal was arrested and deported to Dapitan, and Bonifacio, Apolinario Mabini and others revived it. On the night of 7 July 1892, the day after Rizal's deportation was announced, Bonifacio and others founded the Katipunan, a secret society that sought independence from Spain by armed revolt. Its rituals and organisation drew on Freemasonry, and Bonifacio was himself a Freemason.

Spanish authorities confirmed the existence of the Katipunan on 19 August 1896 and arrested hundreds of suspects. Bonifacio tried to persuade Rizal to escape from his ship in Manila Bay and join the revolt, but Rizal refused. In the last days of August the Katipunan decided to rise, in what was later called the Cry of Balintawak or the Cry of Pugad Lawin, whose place and date are disputed. Bonifacio organised the society into a revolutionary government, the Haring Bayang Katagalugan, with himself as president, and directed guerrilla warfare around Manila from Morong.

In late 1896 rebel leaders invited him to Cavite to mediate between two rival Katipunan councils there, the Magdalo and the Magdiwang. At the Tejeros Convention of 22 March 1897 an election was held to settle the governance of the movement, and Emilio Aguinaldo took office as president the next day. Bonifacio repudiated the result.

Aguinaldo's government ordered Bonifacio's arrest. He and his brother were tried before a jury composed entirely of Aguinaldo's men, and historians have condemned the trial as unjust. Bonifacio was executed at Maragondon on 10 May 1897 on a charge of sedition and treason, by an execution party under Major Lázaro Macapagal. Accounts of the shooting differ.

Historians still dispute whether his death was a justified execution or a political murder. Some argue that he, not Aguinaldo, should count as the first President of the Philippines, and some that he should share or replace Rizal as the foremost national hero. Bones said to be his were found in 1918 and were lost during the Second World War.
andres-de-santa-cruz: Andrés de Santa Cruz y Calahumana was born on 30 November 1792 at Huarina, near Lake Titicaca. His father, José de Santa Cruz y Villavicencio, came from a colonial noble family of Huamanga, and his mother, Juana Basilia Calahumana, was an heiress of Aymara descent who held the curacazgo of Huarina. He later claimed descent from Inca rulers through her.

He studied at the San Francisco Convent and the San Antonio Abad Seminary in Cuzco. He then joined the Spanish Army and fought for the Crown at Guaqui, Vilcapugio and Ayohuma, and against the rising of Mateo Pumacahua. He was captured at La Tablada in 1817 and escaped to Rio de Janeiro and Lima.

Captured by the patriots at the Battle of Pasco on 6 December 1820, Santa Cruz joined San Martín's army on 8 January 1821 and was a brigade general by 1822, after Pichincha. He fought at Zepita in 1823 and at Junín in 1824 under Simón Bolívar, became prefect of Chuquisaca, and was in charge of the Peruvian executive after Bolívar left in September 1826. He was interim president of Peru in 1827 until José La Mar was elected.

Sworn in as president of Bolivia on 24 May 1829, he found a country near bankruptcy and disorder. He reformed the army, bureaucracy and finances, issued new currency, a constitution and a civil code based on the Napoleonic Code, and made Cobija a free port. His regime brought stability at a time of unrest in Latin America.

In 1835 President Luis José de Orbegoso of Peru asked for help against Felipe Santiago Salaverry. Santa Cruz defeated Agustín Gamarra at Yanacocha and Salaverry at Uchumayo, and had Salaverry executed. Assemblies of southern and northern Peru founded the Republic of South Peru and the Republic of North Peru in 1836, and the Peru-Bolivian Confederation was created on 28 October 1836, with Santa Cruz as Supreme Protector.

A pact of 1 May 1837 named him protector for ten years. Many Peruvian politicians opposed it and fled to Chile, where they found support. The first Chilean expedition surrendered by the Treaty of Paucarpata on 17 November 1837, but a second defeated him at Yungay on 20 January 1839, and the Confederation was dissolved.

Santa Cruz resigned on 20 February 1839 and fled to Ecuador. After a failed landing in 1843 he was held in Chile at Chillán until 1846. He later lived in France at Versailles and died near Nantes on 25 September 1865. His remains were returned to La Paz in 1965.
andres-de-urdaneta: Andrés de Urdaneta was born in 1508 near Ordizia, a Basque town then called Villafranca, in the Crown of Castile. His father, Juan Ochoa de Urdaneta, served as its mayor. At seventeen he joined the Loaísa expedition to the Spice Islands as a page to Juan Sebastián Elcano. Seven ships left A Coruña on 24 July 1525; storms and desertions reduced the fleet, and both Loaísa and Elcano died. The last ship reached the Spice Islands in October 1526 with 105 of the original 450 men.

Urdaneta stayed there for more than eight years, acting as an emissary to local leaders, scouting and leading sorties against the Portuguese. A powder explosion burned and disfigured him. He left on 15 February 1535 and reached Lisbon on 26 June 1536, where the Portuguese confiscated his maps and journals. In Valladolid he wrote a report for the Council of the Indies and received 60 gold ducats.

He sailed for New Spain on 16 October 1538 as chief navigator for Pedro de Alvarado, who was killed in a native rebellion in New Galicia in 1540. Urdaneta then worked for Viceroy Antonio de Mendoza and in 1543 became corregidor of a district in Michoacán and visitador. In 1552 he joined the Augustinians, professing his vows in 1553 and being ordained a priest in 1557.

In 1559 Philip II ordered the viceroy to secure his services for an expedition to the Philippines. Urdaneta declined to lead it and recommended Miguel López de Legazpi, serving as adviser and head of the Augustinian missionaries. The fleet left La Navidad on 21 November 1564, reached Guam on 23 January 1565 and Samar on 13 February, and settled on Cebu. Urdaneta founded the first churches in the Philippines.

The San Pedro, commanded by Legazpi's grandson Felipe de Salcedo, left Cebu on 1 June 1565 with Urdaneta advising. It sailed northeast to the 38th parallel, where westerly winds carried it across the Pacific, sighted Catalina Island on 18 September and reached Acapulco on 8 October after four months and eight days. Only 18 men could still sail the ship. Another ship under Alonso de Arellano had reached New Spain first, but he was suspected of mutiny and desertion and his account was vague, so Urdaneta was recognised as the pioneer of the route. Spanish ships, above all the Manila galleon, used it for more than 200 years. He died at the friary in Mexico City on 3 June 1568.
andrew-duke-of-calabria: Andrew was born on 30 October 1327, the second of the three surviving sons of King Charles I of Hungary and his third wife, Elizabeth of Poland. His betrothal in 1334 to his cousin Joanna, granddaughter and heir presumptive of King Robert of Naples, joined two members of the Capetian House of Anjou, for Andrew's father was a nephew of Robert.

Andrew's grandfather, Charles Martel of Anjou, had died young, so by primogeniture the throne of Naples should have passed to Andrew's father. Fearing an invasion from Sicily, Charles II of Naples judged a seven-year-old heir too risky; his next son, Louis, refused the crown on religious grounds, and it passed to Robert, while Andrew's father received the claim to Hungary instead.

When Robert died in 1343, his will left the kingdom to Joanna and made no mention of Andrew. With the approval of Pope Clement VI, Joanna was crowned sole monarch in August 1344. Fearing for his life, Andrew wrote to his mother that he would flee; she came on a state visit and, it was alleged, bribed the pope to permit his coronation, and gave him a ring meant to guard him against blade and poison. While Joanna was ill that summer, Andrew released the Pipini brothers, imprisoned by Robert for murder, rape, pillage and treason, and the nobles who had received their lands turned against him.

Hearing that the pope had reversed himself, a group of noble conspirators resolved to prevent the coronation; Joanna's involvement has never been proven. On 18 September 1345, at Aversa, Andrew left his room at night, a servant barred the door behind him, and after a fierce struggle he was strangled with a cord and thrown from a window. His Hungarian nurse, Isolde, kept watch over the body and told the Hungarian knights what had happened, and they carried the news to King Louis I of Hungary.

Joanna was twice acquitted at the trials that followed, but the deed tainted her reign. Louis invaded Naples several times. Andrew's posthumous son, Charles Martel, born on 25 December 1345, died young in Hungary.
andrew-i-of-hungary: Andrew belonged to a younger branch of the Árpád dynasty. Medieval sources give contradictory accounts of his parents, but modern historians agree that he and his brothers Levente and Béla were sons of Vazul and a concubine from the Tátony clan. According to the chronicles, King Stephen I had Vazul blinded in 1031, after the death of his own son Emeric, and the sons left Hungary. The contemporary Annals of Altaich says that Stephen did this to secure the succession of his sister's son Peter Orseolo.

The brothers went first to Bohemia, then to Poland, where Béla married a daughter of Mieszko II. Andrew and Levente moved on, and in the late 1030s they reached the court of Yaroslav the Wise in Kiev, whose daughter Anastasia Andrew married.

Peter Orseolo had alienated many lords and prelates, above all by recognising the suzerainty of Emperor Henry III in 1045. Discontented lords sent envoys to Andrew and Levente, but by the time they returned a revolt dominated by pagans had broken out. According to the Illuminated Chronicle the brothers gave in to the rebels' demands, and the pagans killed several prelates, among them Bishop Gerard of Csanád. Peter fled but was tricked into returning, captured and blinded.

Three surviving bishops crowned Andrew at Székesfehérvár in late 1046 or in 1047. He soon broke with his pagan supporters, restored Christianity and declared pagan rites illegal, and his epithets the White and the Catholic are connected with these events.

Henry III invaded Hungary in August 1051, but Andrew and Béla used scorched earth tactics and forced the imperial troops to withdraw. The emperor returned the next summer and besieged Pressburg, and after Pope Leo IX mediated a peace he lifted the siege. Andrew had granted Béla a third of the kingdom as a duchy in 1048.

Andrew's son Solomon was born in 1053, and Andrew tried to secure his succession against Béla, who had a strong claim by the principle of agnatic seniority. Struck by a stroke, he had the four-year-old Solomon crowned from the autumn of 1057. Béla fled to Poland and returned with Polish troops, while Bavarian, Bohemian and Saxon troops came to Andrew's aid. Andrew lost the decisive battle east of the Tisza, was badly wounded and died before Béla was crowned on 6 December 1060. He was buried in the crypt of Tihany Abbey, which he had founded in 1055.
andrew-ii-of-hungary: Andrew was the younger son of King Béla III of Hungary and Agnes of Antioch. The year of his birth is not known, but historians place it around 1177. In 1188 his father invaded the Principality of Galicia and granted it to him. His rule there was unpopular, since Hungarian soldiers insulted local women and did not respect Orthodox churches, and the boyars expelled him in August 1189 or 1190. In December 1197 he allied with Duke Leopold VI of Austria and defeated the royal army of his brother King Emeric at Mački. Emeric then gave him Croatia and Dalmatia, which he governed almost as an independent ruler.

After Emeric's death on 30 November 1204, Andrew acted as regent for his nephew Ladislaus III, who died in Vienna on 7 May 1205. Andrew was crowned at Székesfehérvár on 29 May. He gave away royal castles and estates as inheritable grants, a policy he called the new institutions. The historian László Kontler holds that the turmoil of his reign began to break up the social order that had arisen under Stephen I. Andrew also took the title King of Galicia and Lodomeria and fought at least a dozen wars for the two principalities, but local boyars and neighbouring princes repelled him.

In July 1217 he set out on the Fifth Crusade and reached Acre in October, but the crusade failed. He returned to a kingdom he called destroyed and deprived of its revenues. The royal servants, the servientes regis, rose up, and in 1222 he issued the Golden Bull, confirming their privileges. His Diploma Andreanum of 1224 confirmed the privileges of the Transylvanian Saxons.

Andrew died on 21 September 1235 and was buried in Egres Abbey. His first wife, Gertrude of Merania, was murdered in 1213, and their daughter Elizabeth was canonised during his lifetime. Their son Béla IV succeeded him. His third wife, Beatrice d'Este, bore a son, Stephen, after his death, and Béla and his brother Coloman did not accept the child as legitimate. Andrew's grandson, also named Andrew, became the last monarch of the House of Árpád.
andrew-iii-of-hungary: Andrew was the son of Stephen the Posthumous, the self-styled Duke of Slavonia, and his second wife Tomasina Morosini, the daughter of a wealthy Venetian patrician. Stephen was the posthumous son of Andrew II of Hungary, but Andrew II's elder sons Béla IV of Hungary and Coloman of Halych accused their stepmother of adultery and refused to acknowledge him. Andrew was born about 1265 and grew up in Venice, under guardians his father had named before dying in 1272. In 1278 the rebellious baron Ivan Kőszegi invited him to Hungary, but the plot against Ladislaus IV of Hungary collapsed and he went back to Venice.

Andrew returned in 1290 but was captured and held in Vienna by Albert I, Duke of Austria. When Ladislaus IV was murdered on 10 July 1290, two monks sent by Archbishop Lodomer helped him escape in disguise, and Lodomer crowned him at Székesfehérvár on 23 July. The lords swore loyalty only after he issued a charter promising peace and respect for the privileges of nobles and clergy. He faced several rivals, among them Albert of Austria and Mary, sister of Ladislaus IV and wife of Charles II of Naples. He forced Albert to the Peace of Hainburg in August 1291.

Powerful families such as the Kőszegis and the Csáks governed their domains on their own and rebelled almost yearly. The Kőszegis captured Andrew in 1292 and freed him only after his supporters sent relatives as hostages. A diet of 1298 even threatened him with excommunication if he did not enforce its decrees. In August 1300 the twelve-year-old Charles Robert landed at Split at the urging of several lords, and most Croatian and Slavonian lords recognised him, but the Kőszegis and Matthew Csák soon reconciled with Andrew.

Andrew died in Buda Castle on 14 January 1301 after a period of poor health. Contemporary gossip that he was poisoned cannot be proved, according to the historians Attila Zsoldos and Gyula Kristó. He was buried in the Franciscan church in Buda. Years later Palatine Stephen Ákos called him the last golden branch of the tree of King Saint Stephen's family. A civil war between Charles Robert, Wenceslaus of Bohemia and Otto of Bavaria lasted seven years and ended with Charles Robert's victory, though he went on fighting powerful lords until the early 1320s.
andrew-jackson: Andrew Jackson was born on 15 March 1767 in the Waxhaws region of the Carolinas to Scots-Irish Presbyterian parents who had emigrated from Ulster in 1765. During the American Revolutionary War he and his older brothers served on the Patriot side. After the war he worked as a saddler and a teacher, studied law in Salisbury, North Carolina, and was admitted to the bar in September 1787, then was appointed a prosecuting attorney in the Western District of North Carolina, the later Tennessee.

Jackson was elected Tennessee's first U.S. representative in 1796, was a senator in 1797 and served as a Tennessee Superior Court justice from 1798 to 1804. He bought the plantation called the Hermitage near Nashville, which grew to 1,000 acres and was one of the largest cotton-growing plantations in the state. As commander of the Tennessee militia he led troops in the Creek War of 1813–1814, and the Treaty of Fort Jackson forced the Creek to cede large areas of what are now Alabama and Georgia. His victory over the British at the Battle of New Orleans in 1815 made him a national hero. He later commanded American forces in the First Seminole War, which helped lead Spain to negotiate the cession of Florida.

In 1824 Jackson won a plurality of the vote, but the House of Representatives elected John Quincy Adams. His supporters alleged a corrupt bargain and formed a coalition that became the Democratic Party. Jackson defeated Adams in a landslide in 1828 and was inaugurated on 4 March 1829.

In 1830 he signed the Indian Removal Act, which displaced tens of thousands of Native Americans from east of the Mississippi River and caused thousands of deaths in what became known as the Trail of Tears. In 1832 he vetoed the renewal of the Second Bank of the United States, which he saw as a fourth branch of government run by an elite.

Jackson's presidency ended on 4 March 1837, and he retired to the Hermitage, where he remained influential in national and state politics. He died on 8 June 1845. His legacy is controversial: supporters call him a defender of democracy and the Constitution, while critics describe an autocratic demagogue and condemn his policies toward Native Americans and his enslavement of hundreds of people at the Hermitage.
andrew-the-apostle: The name Andrew, from the Greek andreía, meaning manhood or valour, appears to have been common among Jews and other Hellenised people since the second or third century BCE, and no Hebrew or Aramaic name is recorded for him. He was born to a Jewish family in Bethsaida, in Galilee, possibly between 5 and 10 CE. The New Testament says he was the brother of Simon Peter and, like him, a son of Jonah. His Greek name has been read as pointing to a cultural openness in his family, in a Galilee where Greek language and culture were quite present.

Andrew and Peter were fishermen by trade, which is why tradition says Jesus called them to be fishers of men. According to Mark 1:29 they shared a house at Capernaum. In Matthew and Mark, Jesus sees the two brothers fishing on the Sea of Galilee and calls them together. In the Gospel of John, Andrew is first a disciple of John the Baptist; he follows Jesus, recognises him as the Messiah and introduces Peter, which is the source of the title First-Called used by the Eastern Orthodox Church.

The apocryphal Acts of Andrew, mentioned by Eusebius and Epiphanius of Salamis, shows signs of a mid-2nd-century origin. It describes his supposed travels, his miracles and his martyrdom. Eusebius dismissed it as the work of a heretic and absurd, and it appears among rejected books in the Decretum Gelasianum. Georgian church tradition regards Andrew as the first preacher of Christianity in Georgia. It derives from Byzantine sources, notably Niketas David Paphlagon, who died about 890 and wrote that Andrew preached to the Iberians, Sauromatians, Taurians and Scythians. Georgian ecclesiastics of the 10th and 11th centuries used the story to give their church an apostolic origin.

Relics said to be Andrew's were kept at Patras, and according to one account Constantius II had most of them moved to Constantinople around 357. In 1208, after the sack of Constantinople, Cardinal Peter of Capua took relics of Andrew to Amalfi, where most remain in the cathedral crypt. In 1461 Thomas Palaiologos fled Patras before the Ottomans with what was said to be Andrew's skull and gave it to Pope Pius II. A legend says the monk Regulus carried some bones to Fife in Scotland, though the relics probably reached Britain in 597 and Fife in 732, with Bishop Acca of Hexham.

Andrew is the patron saint of Scotland, Romania, Russia, Ukraine and Patras, among other places, and his saltire cross appears on the flag of Scotland. His feast is on 30 November in the Eastern and Western churches.
andrianampoinimerina: Andrianampoinimerina was born around 1745 as Ramboasalamarazaka, the son of Princess Ranavalonandriambelomasina, a daughter of King Andriambelomasina of Imerina, and Andriamiaramanjaka, a noble of the Zafimamy royal family. His parents' marriage was a political alliance, and it was agreed that the throne would pass after his uncle Andrianjafy to the son of Andriambelomasina's daughter. He was born when conflict and famine afflicted Imerina, after King Andriamasinavalona divided the kingdom among four sons and brought on 77 years of civil war. As a young man he worked as a merchant and may also have traded in slaves, and he won a reputation among commoners as a defender against Sakalava raids and corruption.

Andrianjafy, who ruled the northern quarter of Imerina from 1770, feared him and made several attempts on his life. In 1787 an elder advised him to sacrifice a ram to invoke ancestral protection and gathered twelve respected men of Ambohimanga and thirty soldiers, who deposed Andrianjafy. The new king took the name Andrianampoinimerina, meaning the king in the heart of Imerina.

He made Ambohimanga his capital and defeated Andrianjafy's followers from Ilafy. He conquered Antananarivo in 1793, moved the political capital there in 1794, and by 1795 had gained the submission of all the territories that had formed Imerina under Andriamasinavalona. Around 1800 he began to unite the island's ethnic groups, sending messengers with invitations to become vassals or face conquest. He absorbed Betsileo, Sihanaka and Bezanozano territories, though the Sakalava resisted, mounted slave raids into Imerina and nearly reached the capital more than once.

He created formal civil and penal codes, declared twelve crimes capital offences and set up official markets with standard weights and measures, including the Friday market at Analakely. He expanded irrigated paddy fields on the Betsimitatatra plains with fanompoana, labour owed as a tax, and organised a citizen army, the foloalindahy. His regulation of the slave trade, which is estimated at about 1,800 slaves a year, mainly sold to French merchants in exchange for firearms, enriched the crown.

Andrianampoinimerina died in the Rova of Antananarivo on 6 July 1810, aged 65, and was succeeded by his 18-year-old son Radama I. To keep an oath that Radama's child would inherit, he had his oldest son Ramavolahy killed. Radama carried on the conquests, and the king is said to have told him that the sea was the embankment of his rice fields. The French destroyed his tomb at Ambohimanga in March 1897 and moved his remains to Antananarivo, in an effort to desanctify the city and break the Menalamba resistance. Ambohimanga became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 2001, and Malagasy textbooks present him as the originator of a unified national identity.
andries-pretorius: Andries Wilhelmus Jacobus Pretorius was born on 27 November 1798 in the eastern frontier country of the Cape Colony. He was educated at home and was literate enough to read the Bible and write down his thoughts. He descended from the earliest Dutch settlers of the Cape, belonging to the fifth generation of Johannes Pretorius, son of Reverend Wessel Schulte, who had changed his name to the Latin form Wesselius Praetorius while studying theology at Leiden.

Details of his early life are scant, but he most likely grew up on his father's farm Driekoppen, about 40 kilometres north-east of Graaff-Reinet. His eldest son, Marthinus Wessel Pretorius, later became the first president of the South African Republic (Transvaal).

Pretorius left the Cape Colony permanently and hurried to the Klein-Tugela River in Natal when the Voortrekkers there were left leaderless, Gerrit Maritz having died of illness and Andries Potgieter having moved inland. Dingane had ordered the murder of Piet Retief and his men in February 1838. Pretorius reached the Trekkers' main camp on 22 November 1838 and was appointed chief commander of the punitive commando.

On 16 December 1838, beside the Ncome River, his 470 men and 64 wagons defeated an attacking Zulu army of 10,000 to 15,000. The Voortrekkers had muzzle-loading muskets and two small cannons; an estimated 3,000 Zulu died, and the Boers had no deaths, only three wounded. In January 1840 he helped Mpande in his revolt against Dingane at the Battle of Maqongqo.

In 1842 Pretorius besieged the British garrison at Durban but withdrew on the arrival of reinforcements under Colonel Josias Cloete. Governor Sir Henry Pottinger refused to receive his grievances in 1847, and in 1848 Pretorius moved north of the Vaal. He took Bloemfontein on 20 July 1848 but was defeated by Sir Harry Smith at Boomplaats in August. On 17 January 1852 he met British commissioners near the Sand River and concluded the convention by which Britain recognised the independence of the Transvaal Boers.

Pretorius died at his home at Magaliesberg in July 1853. The historian Theal called him the ablest leader and most perfect representative of the Emigrant Farmers. In 1855 his son Marthinus Wessel Pretorius named a new town and district Pretoria in his honour. The Boers hold that God granted them victory at Blood River in answer to a vow, and the day was kept as a day of rest: called Dingane's Day until 1910, then the Day of the Vow and Day of the Covenant, it became a public holiday of the Union of South Africa. After 1994 the democratic government kept it as the Day of Reconciliation.
andriscus: Ancient sources agree that Andriscus was a fuller from Adramyttium in Aeolis, in western Anatolia, and are unanimous in calling him an impostor; his chief asset was a close resemblance to Perseus. By his own story he was raised by a Cretan, and on reaching maturity was given a sealed parchment said to be written by Perseus, with the places of two hidden treasures at Amphipolis and Thessalonica. Around 154/153 BCE he went to Syria to ask his claimed uncle, the Seleucid king Demetrius I Soter, for help; Diodorus Siculus says he was already a mercenary in Demetrius's army.

His claim caused riots in Antioch, and Demetrius sent him to Rome, where the Senate, knowing the real Philip had died at Alba Fucens, judged him harmless and exiled him to an Italian city. He escaped to Miletus and through Ionia, where Kallipa, a former concubine of Perseus, gave him money and slaves. In Thrace, Teres III, married to a granddaughter of Perseus, crowned him and lent him a few hundred troops. After an early failure he defeated Rome's Macedonian client republics in Odomantice and on the Strymon and crowned himself king at Pella.

He enlarged his army and invaded Thessaly. The praetor Publius Juventius Thalna, sent with a legion, was killed and his force almost destroyed, the worst defeat Rome suffered at Macedonian hands. Carthage, at war with Rome, promised him money and ships, though none arrived, while the Achaean League and Attalus II of Pergamon stayed loyal to Rome. His persecution of pro-Roman republicans grew harsher after the victory and cost him support; only three of his coins are known.

Rome sent two legions under Quintus Caecilius Metellus, who advanced along the Thessalian coast with a Pergamene fleet. Beaten at Pydna, Andriscus lost Macedon at once, fled to Thrace and was routed again; the Thracian prince Byzes handed him over. After two years as a prisoner he was paraded in Metellus's triumph in 146 BCE and executed. Recognising the strength of anti-Roman feeling, the Senate made Macedonia a province with Metellus as its first governor.
andromeda-galaxy: The Andromeda Galaxy is a barred spiral galaxy, also catalogued as Messier 31, M31 and NGC 224, and originally called the Andromeda Nebula. Its name comes from the constellation of Andromeda, named after the princess who was the wife of Perseus in Greek mythology. 56 kiloparsecs (152,000 light-years), which makes it the largest member of the Local Group in extent. Estimates of its total mass lie between about 8 and 11 hundred billion solar masses, of the same order as the Milky Way, and the relative masses of the two have been revised several times.

A merger with another galaxy 2 to 3 billion years ago is thought to have formed much of its halo. At its centre lies a dense star cluster and a supermassive black hole, and some 460 globular clusters are associated with the galaxy.

Around 964 the Persian astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi described it in his Book of Fixed Stars as a nebulous smear or small cloud, the first historical reference to it and the earliest known reference to a galaxy other than the Milky Way. In 1612 the German astronomer Simon Marius described it from telescopic observations. Pierre Louis Maupertuis conjectured in 1745 that the blurry spot was an island universe.

Charles Messier catalogued it as M31 in 1764 and wrongly credited Marius as its discoverer, although it is visible to the naked eye. In 1785 William Herschel took it for the nearest of the great nebulae, and guessed its distance at no more than 2,000 times that of Sirius. In 1850 William Parsons, 3rd Earl of Rosse, drew its spiral structure.

Immanuel Kant had proposed in 1755 that the Milky Way is only one of many galaxies, and had argued that elliptical nebulae such as Andromeda were galaxies like it. In 1917 Heber Curtis observed a nova in Andromeda and found 11 more in the photographic record. They were on average 10 magnitudes fainter than novae elsewhere in the sky, which gave him a distance estimate of 500,000 light-years, the first within a factor of ten of the modern value. Curtis became a proponent of the island universes hypothesis. The estimated distance was doubled in 1953, when a second, dimmer type of Cepheid variable star was discovered.

The galaxy lies about 2.5 million light-years from Earth. It is visible to the naked eye in dark skies, and best seen from the Northern Hemisphere on autumn nights, when it passes high overhead. It is approaching the Milky Way at about 110 kilometres per second. Earlier calculations predicted a collision in about 4 billion years, but later ones, using a higher sideways velocity measured by the Gaia spacecraft, found a much lower probability of a merger.
andronikos-ii-palaiologos: Andronikos was born on 25 March 1259 at Nicaea, the eldest surviving son of Michael VIII Palaiologos. He was acclaimed co-emperor after his father recovered Constantinople from the Latin Empire in 1261 but was not crowned until 8 November 1272. He was compelled to support his father's unpopular Church union with the Papacy, and when Michael's death in 1282 made him sole emperor he at once repudiated it. He could not resolve the related schism among the Orthodox clergy until 1310.

Andronikos faced an empty treasury and was forced in 1285 to dismantle the imperial fleet, which left the empire dependent on Genoa. He devalued the hyperpyron and raised taxes. His campaigns brought little: an attack on Thessaly in 1283 ended when an epidemic killed its commander, an expedition to Epirus in 1292 failed, and a war with Venice from 1296 to 1302 changed almost nothing. By diplomacy he married Yolanda of Montferrat, ending the Montferrat claim to the Kingdom of Thessalonica, and in 1298 married his five-year-old daughter Simonis to King Stefan Milutin of Serbia.

The Anatolian frontier was his chief concern. Alexios Philanthropenos won victories there in 1294 and 1295 but then rebelled, and was blinded and captured by his own Cretan soldiers. After the disastrous Battle of Bapheus in 1302 the government hired the Catalan Company under Roger de Flor. After Roger's murder in 1305 the Catalans turned on their employers and devastated Thrace, Macedonia and Thessaly before conquering the Duchy of Athens. Meanwhile the Turkish beyliks advanced: the Aydinids took Smyrna in 1310, and Prusa fell to the Ottoman Turks in 1326.

Andronikos disowned his grandson Andronikos III Palaiologos after the death of his son Michael IX in 1320, and the First Palaiologan Civil War followed, lasting with interruptions until 1328. In 1328 Andronikos III entered Constantinople and the old emperor was forced to abdicate. He died as a monk in Constantinople in 1332 and was buried in the Lips Monastery. His reign marked the beginning of the restored empire's final decline.
andronikos-iii-palaiologos: Andronikos was born in Constantinople on 25 March 1297, the son of the co-emperor Michael IX Palaiologos and Rita of Armenia. In 1320 he accidentally caused the death of his brother Manuel, and his father died in grief soon afterwards. His behaviour and that of his circle of young aristocrats opened a rift with his grandfather, Andronikos II Palaiologos, who disowned him. Andronikos fled, rallied supporters in Thrace and began to reign as a rival emperor in 1321. Intermittent civil war followed until 1328, when he became sole emperor on 24 May and his grandfather retired to a monastery.

His reign saw the last failed attempts to hold back the Ottoman Turks in Bithynia. Sultan Orhan defeated a relief attempt for besieged Nicaea at the Battle of Pelekanon in June 1329, took Nicaea in 1331 and Nicomedia in 1337, and only Philadelphia and a few ports remained Byzantine in Anatolia. In the Balkans Tsar Ivan Alexander of Bulgaria defeated the Byzantines at Rusokastro on 18 July 1332, and Serbia gained Ohrid, Prilep and Strumitsa by the peace of 26 August 1334.

There were also successes. A fleet deposed the Genoese ruler Martino Zaccaria and regained Chios in 1329, Phocaea returned in 1334, and Byzantine control was extended over Thessaly and, from 1337, Epirus. John Kantakouzenos, as megas domestikos, held effective administrative authority, while the emperor enjoyed hunting and war. Andronikos also created a panel of four judges, the Universal Justices of the Romans.

Andronikos III died at Constantinople on 15 June 1341, aged 44, possibly of chronic malaria. His son John V Palaiologos was only nine and needed a regent. Within months a dispute over the regency and the position of John Kantakouzenos led to a destructive civil war, which left the empire unable to prevent the rise of the Serbian Empire or the Ottoman entry into Europe. Historians generally do not blame his leadership for the later decline, and hold that under him the empire came closest to regaining power in the Balkans after the Fourth Crusade.
andronovo-culture: The name comes from the village of Andronovo in the Uzhursky District of Krasnoyarsk Krai, where the zoologist Arkadi Tugarinov found the first remains in 1914. They were crouched skeletons in graves with richly decorated pottery. The archaeologist Sergei Teploukhov identified the culture in the 1920s. Some researchers prefer to call it an archaeological complex or horizon, since it is a collection of similar local cultures. Its main subcultures are the Alakul and the Fëdorovo, and some authors add the Alekseyevka-Sargary. The slightly older Sintashta culture, once included in it, is now thought to be distinct.

Andronovo sites run from the southern Urals to the upper Yenisei and western Xinjiang, and south to Tajikistan and Uzbekistan. On the west it overlapped with the Srubna culture, with which its interaction was the most intense, and in southern Siberia and Kazakhstan it was succeeded by the Karasuk culture. Genetic studies of 2015 and 2019 found its people closely related to those of Sintashta and to the Corded Ware culture, which suggests an eastward spread of people with steppe ancestry. Most researchers associate the Andronovo horizon with early Indo-Iranian languages, though scholars such as Mallory acknowledge the difficulty of tracing expansions from it into South Asia.

Andronovo communities included both highly mobile groups and settled villages, usually of two to twenty houses, though some had as many as a hundred. Houses were built of pine, cedar or birch beside rivers, and about twenty fortified sites with ditches, banks or palisades are known. The people kept cattle, horses, sheep, goats and camels but no domestic pigs, and agriculture played a small part. They mined copper ore in the Altai Mountains from about the 14th century BCE and made many bronze objects. The dead were buried in timber or stone chambers under kurgans, with livestock, wheeled vehicles, horse cheek-pieces and weapons. Chariot burials date from around 2000 BCE, some with a ritual burial of the horse's head and hooves.
andujar: Andújar is a municipality in the province of Jaén, in Andalusia, divided by the Guadalquivir River. The northern part holds the Natural Park of the Sierra de Andújar, and to the south lie agricultural fields. The city itself stands on the right bank of the river, on the Madrid-Córdoba railway. It was long known for its porous earthenware jars, the alcarrazas or botijos, which keep water cool in the hottest weather and were made from a whitish clay found nearby.

The first known inhabitants were the Oretani, an Iberian people, who founded the town of Isturgi on the site now occupied by the hamlet of Los Villares de Andújar. In Roman times the Municipium Isturgi Triumphale flourished through its production of terra sigillata and its position on the Guadalquivir, and after the empire it survived as the Visigothic town of Sturgi. When the Moors invaded in the 8th century the population moved to the present site. After the Battle of Guadalete in 711 the region became part of Al-Andalus, and the town was first called Anduyar under Muhammad I of Córdoba, in 853. The Almohads fortified it in the 12th century.

In 1225 the Muslim king of Baeza handed the castles of Jaén, Andújar and Martos to Ferdinand III of Castile, though some scholars believe the transfer happened at another time. Troops of the military orders of Santiago and Calatrava occupied the area, and Andújar became a rendezvous for the Christian armies fighting south of the Sierra Morena. Its Muslim inhabitants left at the end of 1226, and the first Christian settlers arrived in 1227 or 1228. Henry IV of Castile granted it the title of city in 1467.

In 1808 French troops occupied the city, and General Pierre Dupont de l'Étang made it his headquarters; after he lost the battle at Bailén, the capitulations were signed at Andújar in the Palace of Gracia Real. In 1835 the first Junta of Central Sovereignty of Andalusia met there, regarded as a pioneer of the autonomist movement in Andalusia. During the Spanish Civil War Republican forces besieged a Nationalist force sheltering in the sanctuary of Our Lady of the Cabeza for eight months.

The municipality has 35,619 people (2024). Its best-known festival is the Pilgrimage of the Virgen de la Cabeza, held on the last Sunday of April. According to local legend, on the night of 12 August 1227 a shepherd named Juan Alonso de Rivas found the image of the Virgen de la Cabeza on a hill after seeing strange lights and hearing a bell.
anegada: Anegada lies about 24 kilometres north of Virgin Gorda. It is the only inhabited British Virgin Island formed from coral and limestone rather than volcanic rock, and while the other islands are mountainous it is flat and low, its highest point only about 8.5 metres above sea level. Its name comes from the Spanish tierra anegada, flooded land. It covers about 38 square kilometres, making it the second-largest of the British Virgin Islands, and most of its people live in the only village, The Settlement; the census of 2024 counted 450 residents.

Large salt ponds cover much of the west end and were designated a Ramsar Site on 11 May 1999. Thousands of Caribbean flamingos lived in them in the 1830s, but hunting for food and feathers in the 19th and early 20th centuries removed them by 1950, and they have since been re-established. The island is also home to the Anegada rock iguana, which a zoo-run headstart programme in The Settlement has raised for release.

The Horseshoe Reef, 29 kilometres long, is one of the largest barrier coral reefs in the Caribbean. It makes navigation to the island difficult and has caused hundreds of shipwrecks, among them HMS Astraea in 1808, the Donna Paula in 1819 and the MS Rocus in 1929. The government has made anchoring on the reef illegal.

On the south side the reef flats hold many bonefish. The reef beside The Settlement was once among the more fertile conch grounds of the Caribbean, but overfishing wiped out its conchs, and heaps of empty shells lie along the shore.

Tourism is the island's main business, with fishing second; local fishermen supply most of the fresh fish and lobster of the British Virgin Islands. Anegada is reached by the small Auguste George Airport, by ferry and by private boat. Residents traditionally rode out hurricanes by tying their dories to mangrove trunks. In 2010 the eye of Hurricane Earl passed north of the island, flooding its south side, and on 6 September 2017 the northern eyewall of Hurricane Irma passed directly over it and caused major damage; no serious injuries were reported on either occasion.
aneirin: Aneirin, also written Aneurin or Neirin, is believed to have been a bard or court poet in one of the Cumbric kingdoms of the Old North, probably Gododdin at Edinburgh. Some records make him the son of Caunus, or Caw, and a brother of Gildas, born at Dumbarton on the River Clyde, but some scholars hold these records to be later and erroneous inventions. His mother, Dwywei, is named in Y Gododdin; she may be the lady who, according to Old Welsh pedigrees, married King Dunod.

His poems survive in the Book of Aneirin, a manuscript of the late 13th century. Its language has been partly modernised into Middle Welsh, but passages in Old Welsh suggest that at least some of the poetry dates from about Aneirin's time, so the attribution may well be genuine. The verses probably lived in oral tradition until they were first written down, perhaps in the 9th century. Y Gododdin mourns the warriors who, in about 600, fell against the Angles of Deira and Bernicia at Catraeth, probably Catterick in North Yorkshire.

The poem is full of textual difficulties, and readings of it vary. One stanza compares a fallen warrior with Arthur, which may be the earliest reference to King Arthur, though the identification is conjectural. The poem says that Aneirin himself was at the battle, was taken prisoner as one of only two or four Brittonic survivors, and stayed a captive until Ceneu ap Llywarch Hen paid his ransom.

The Welsh Triads call Aneirin prince of bards and of flowing verse, and Nennius names him among the Cynfeirdd, the earliest Welsh poets, with Talhaearn, Taliesin, Bluchbardd and Cian. The Poets of the Princes refer to him, but his fame declined in the later Middle Ages until antiquarian writers of the Tudor period reasserted Welsh identity. From the 17th century he was usually called Aneurin. His poetry is still highly regarded, although who exactly wrote it is debated.
anfal-campaign: After Iraq invaded Iran in 1980, the Kurdish opposition parties in Iraq, the Patriotic Union of Kurdistan and the Kurdistan Democratic Party, regained strength. Kurdish fighters, the peshmerga, waged a guerrilla war and took effective control of the mountainous Kurdish areas of northern Iraq. In 1983, after the capture of Haj Omran, the Iraqi government arrested 8,000 Barzani men and executed them, and it used gas weapons for the first time. In March 1987 Ali Hassan al-Majid, a cousin of President Saddam Hussein, became secretary-general of the Ba'ath Party's Northern Bureau, which covered Iraqi Kurdistan.

The name comes from the eighth chapter of the Qur'an, al-Anfal, meaning the spoils of war. The main operations were fought from February to August or September 1988. They combined ground offensives, aerial bombing, chemical weapons, the systematic destruction of settlements, mass deportation and firing squads. Eight phases followed one another: seven targeted areas held by the Patriotic Union, and the last, from 25 August to 6 September, the Badinan region held by the Kurdistan Democratic Party. Villages were attacked with poison gas in most phases, and a gas attack at Halabja on 16 March 1988 killed several thousand people, most of them civilians.

Kurdish collaborators armed by the government, called Jash, led troops to villages and hideouts, and amnesties announced during several phases proved to be traps. Men were separated from women, children and the elderly. The men were not seen again, and the others were sent to camps such as Dibs and Nugra Salman. About 1,200 Kurdish villages were destroyed. A census in October 1987 and the resettlement of Arabs in Kirkuk formed part of a policy of Arabisation of areas rich in oil.

Precise figures of the dead do not exist. Human Rights Watch wrote in 1993 that the toll could not be fewer than 50,000 and might be twice that. Kurdish figures run higher, including 182,000, which Human Rights Watch says rests on extrapolation. Survivors were held in camps under military rule until Iraqi Kurdistan gained autonomy in 1991, and most then returned and rebuilt the villages.

On 23 June 2007 an Iraqi tribunal convicted al-Majid and two co-defendants of genocide and related charges. The Iraqi courts and the International Association of Genocide Scholars call the campaign a genocide. A Dutch appeal court in 2007 found that the documents were not enough to establish genocide, while convicting a Dutch businessman of complicity in war crimes. Many Iraqi Arabs deny that mass killings occurred. The Kurdistan Regional Government marks 14 April as a day of remembrance.
ang-duong: Ang Duong was born on 12 June 1796, the son of King Ang Eng, who ruled from the capital Oudong, and of Ros, a royal consort later known as Queen Vara. Siam had long kept Cambodian royals at its court as hostages, and so controlled the kingdom's policies and succession. Ang Duong spent 27 years in Bangkok, from the age of 16 until he was 43, and in 1834 he was appointed governor of the Siamese district of Mongkol Borey.

In Bangkok he wrote poetry and works of classical Cambodian literature, among them Neang Kakey, as well as historical works, and he took part in the development of Khmer classical dance. He translated the Cambodian folktale Vorvong and Sorvong into Thai as a birthday present for the Siamese crown prince Mongkut.

Siam and Vietnam, united since 1802 under Emperor Gia Long, fought for control of the Mekong basin, the Cambodian heartland. After Vietnam drove back the Siamese in the Siamese–Vietnamese War of 1833–1834, it restored King Ang Chan II and, after his death in 1835, installed Princess Ang Mey under Vietnamese supervision. Cambodian opposition to that rule helped bring a renewed Siamese intervention in 1841, and the settlement of 1845 left Cambodia under joint Siamese and Vietnamese suzerainty and opened the way for Ang Duong's recognition as king.

Crowned in Bangkok, he returned to Oudong. He issued the first substantial revision of the legal code in centuries and supervised religious and cultural reforms, though limited power, poverty and internal dissension kept his work from lasting success. Seeking to free Cambodia from both neighbours, he first sought help from the British in Singapore and then opened secret negotiations with France in a letter to Napoleon III.

Ang Duong died on 19 October 1860, three years before the negotiations ended. His son Norodom signed the French protectorate on 11 August 1863, and it lasted 90 years. Historians have debated the wisdom of his policy; against some 19th-century French writers, it has been argued that he did not seek a protectorate but an ill-defined, unequal relationship with France. He had 18 legitimate children and was the ancestor of the royal Houses of Norodom and Sisowath, and he is venerated in Cambodia for his efforts to revive the kingdom.
angaur: Angaur, called Ngeaur in Palauan, is an island and state of Palau. It is a coralline raised platform island about 10 kilometres south-west of Beliliou at the southern tip of the main group, outside the lagoon and enclosing reef of that group. It covers 8 square kilometres. The highest point, a small hill north-west of Rois, is only 40 metres above sea level, though the ground is rugged, with jagged outcrops of ancient reef and marshy swamps in the south-east.

Settlement is concentrated on the west coast, in the villages of Rois and Ngaramasch, and the state capital is Ngeremasch. A large area of taro swamp gardens, Ngetkebui, lies in the south. Ucherbelau is the title of the traditional high chief. The island has its own constitution, adopted in 1982, which names Palauan, English and Japanese as official languages.

Angaur was traditionally divided among some eight clans, whose areas are marked by stone platforms and cemeteries. Shell found at archaeological sites shows intensive use of the lagoon and fishing outside the reef. The first recorded sighting by Westerners of Angaur, Babeldaob, Koror and Peleliu was by the Spanish expedition of Ruy López de Villalobos at the end of January 1543, which charted them as Los Arrecifes. Spanish expeditions under Francisco Padilla in 1710 and Bernardo de Egoy two years later explored them further.

Phosphate mining ran from 1909 until 1954, first under the Germans, then the Japanese and finally the Americans, in mines in the north-west and along the east coast. Angaur was the site of a major battle of the Second World War, part of Operation Forager, which ran from June to November 1944. The Americans took the island partly for the airstrip built by the Japanese, and it received much less shelling beforehand than Peleliu, so the battle did not bring the same loss of life. Macaques that escaped under German occupation left feral monkeys, giving the island the name Monkey Island.

Angaur had a population of 130 in the 2012 mini census and 119 in the 2015 census. From 1945 to 1978 an American Coast Guard unit ran a LORAN station there. Remains of American and Japanese weapons are scattered across the island, and visitors can see a cemetery of wrecked planes and ships, a Buddhist memorial to the Japanese dead and a small Shinto shrine.
angelos-dynasty: The Angeloi were a Byzantine Greek family of little standing until the first half of the 12th century. Their founder was Constantine Angelos, a minor noble from Philadelphia in the Thracesian Theme in Asia Minor, whom the historian John Zonaras described as brave, skilled and handsome but of lowly origin. Around 1122 he married Theodora Komnene, a daughter of Emperor Alexios I Komnenos, and as an imperial in-law received the title sebastohypertatos, though he was not considered the equal of Alexios's other sons-in-law. The couple had seven children. The surname is commonly held to come from the Greek word for angel or messenger, although another theory derives it from a district near Amida.

Constantine's third son, Andronikos Doukas Angelos, founded the imperial line. His son Isaac II Angelos gained popular support in a coup against Andronikos I Komnenos in 1185 and made himself emperor. He could not repair the weaknesses he inherited and in 1187 was forced to recognise the Bulgarian empire. In 1195 his brother Alexios III Angelos deposed him, and his reign saw abuses in provincial administration and growing autonomy of regional magnates.

In 1201 Isaac's son Alexios IV Angelos went west and brought about the diversion of the Fourth Crusade to Constantinople to restore his father. On 1 August 1203 the blinded Isaac II, after eight years of imprisonment, was crowned co-emperor with Alexios IV. Friction with the Crusaders over their demands led to their deposition in January 1204 by Alexios V Doukas, and both were killed soon afterwards. The Crusaders sacked Constantinople and set up the Latin Empire, ending Byzantine rule there for nearly half a century.

The line of Constantine's eldest son John Doukas is known as the Komnenodoukai, since most of its members used Doukas or Komnenos Doukas rather than Angelos. In 1205 John's son Michael I Komnenos Doukas founded the Despotate of Epirus, with its capital at Arta. In about 1224 his half-brother Theodore Komnenos Doukas took Thessalonica and claimed the imperial title, but he was defeated and captured at the Battle of Klokotnitsa in 1230. Nicaea took Thessalonica in 1246, and the family lost Epirus and Thessaly in 1318.

The Angeloi's period of rule saw the decline and fragmentation of the empire. Later members of the family held Epirus and Thessaly under Byzantine and Serbian rule. After the Ottoman conquest of Thessaly in 1394 the Angeloi Philanthropenoi took refuge in Serbia. One of their descendants, Mahmud Anđelović, was captured as an infant, converted to Islam and rose to become Grand Vizier of the Ottoman Empire in 1455.
angers: Angers lies about 300 km south-west of Paris and is the prefecture of the Maine-et-Loire department. It stands just south of the confluence of the Loir, the Mayenne and the Sarthe, which together form the short, wide river Maine, and the Maine runs south through the city to the Loire a few kilometres away. The meeting of three rivers and the nearness of the Loire make a natural crossroads, which favoured the founding of the ancient Juliomagus. The oldest streets and buildings stand on the promontory where the castle rises, and their structure dates from the 13th, 14th and 15th centuries.

The first sign of human presence dates to around 400,000 BCE, and burials of about 4500 to 3500 BCE were found on the castle grounds. In the 5th century BCE the Andecavi, a Celtic people, settled north of the Loire, and by the end of the Iron Age Angers was a fairly densely populated hillfort. Ptolemy mentions it around 150 CE as Juliomagus, a name that joins Julius, probably Julius Caesar, to the Celtic magos, meaning market. The Roman town had villas, baths, an amphitheatre and a Mithraeum.

Angers received its first bishop in 372, at the election of Martin of Tours. The abbey of Saint-Aubin was built in the 7th century to house the sarcophagus of Saint Albinius, and Saint-Serge Abbey was founded a century later by the Merovingian kings Clovis II and Theuderic III. The castle was built between 1230 and 1240 by Louis IX of France, with walls about a kilometre long and 17 towers.

After the Black Death and the Hundred Years War had weakened the city, King René of Anjou revived it, making Angers a cultural and political centre. The city received its communal charter from Louis XI in February 1475. In 1619 Louis XIII gave the governance of Anjou to his mother, Marie de' Medici, who settled in Angers with her chaplain, Cardinal Richelieu. The French Revolution abolished Anjou as a political entity in 1790, and in March 1793 the royalist army of the War of Vendée had to attack Angers to cross the Loire again.

Angers has 157,555 inhabitants within its 42.70 square kilometres. It remains the prefecture of Maine-et-Loire. The Château d'Angers houses the Apocalypse Tapestry, the largest ensemble of medieval tapestry in the world. The city lies at the edge of the Val de Loire World Heritage Site.
angkor: The ruins of Angkor lie among forests and farmland north of the Great Lake, Tonlé Sap, and south of the Kulen Hills, near the modern city of Siem Reap. The name comes from the Khmer nokor, meaning kingdom, itself derived from the Sanskrit nagara, city. In Angkorian times non-religious buildings, including the king's residence, were built of perishable materials such as wood, because only the gods had a right to residences of stone, so the surviving monuments are almost all religious. A 2007 study using satellite photographs concluded that Angkor was the largest pre-industrial city in the world by area, with a water network of canals and reservoirs that offset the unpredictable monsoon.

The Angkorian period began shortly after 800, when Jayavarman II declared the independence of Kambujadesa from Java and took the title devaraja, god-king. King Suryavarman II built Angkor Wat between 1113 and 1150. In 1177 the Cham launched a water-borne invasion, sacked the capital Yasodharapura and killed the king. A Khmer prince rallied his people, defeated them, and in 1181 took the throne as Jayavarman VII. He built the walled city of Angkor Thom with the Bayon at its centre, and the temples of Ta Prohm and Preah Khan, and made Mahayana Buddhism the state religion. His successor Jayavarman VIII, a Shaivite iconoclast, began a Hindu restoration around 1243.

In 1296 the Chinese diplomat Zhou Daguan spent a year at Angkor under King Indravarman III, and his account The Customs of Cambodia describes religion, kingship, agriculture, slavery and commerce. Angkor fell under Ayutthayan suzerainty in 1351. The end of the Angkorian period is generally placed around 1431, when Ayutthaya sacked it, though the main cause of its decline is unknown. Through the 15th century nearly all of it was abandoned except Angkor Wat, which remained a Buddhist shrine.

Angkor, in Siem Reap Province, contains over a thousand temples, among them Angkor Wat, the Bayon and Ta Prohm, and was declared a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1992. The Portuguese friar António da Madalena is the first recorded European visitor to Angkor Wat, in 1586. From 1907 to 1970 the École française d'Extrême-Orient cleared the forest, repaired foundations and installed drains, and scholars of the school, among them George Coedès, laid the foundations of present understanding of the site.
angkor-thom: Angkor Thom, from the Khmer for Great City, was the last and most enduring capital of the Khmer Empire. King Jayavarman VII established it as the centre of his massive building programme, and one inscription found in the city calls the king the groom and the city his bride. It was not the first Khmer capital on the site. Yasodharapura, dating from about three centuries earlier, lay slightly further northwest, and Angkor Thom overlapped parts of it. The Baphuon, a former state temple, and Phimeanakas, which was incorporated into the Royal Palace, stand within its walls. The name Angkor Thom came into use from the 16th century.

The city covers 9 square kilometres on the west bank of the Siem Reap River. Its laterite walls, 8 metres high and flanked by a moat, are each 3 kilometres long. A gate stands at each cardinal point, with roads leading to the Bayon, Jayavarman's state temple, at the centre. Archaeologists interpret the walls and moat as the mountains and oceans around the Bayon's Mount Meru.

The gate towers, 23 metres high, carry faces like those of the Bayon, which may represent the king, the bodhisattva Avalokiteshvara, guardians of the cardinal points, or some combination. Each causeway across the moat has devas on one side and asuras on the other, holding a naga in a tug-of-war that appears to refer to the Churning of the Sea of Milk. Most of the enclosed land held secular buildings, of which nothing remains.

The last temple known to have been built there, Mangalartha, was dedicated in 1295. The city is believed to have supported 80,000 to 150,000 people. The Ayutthaya Kingdom sacked it, and the Khmers under Ponhea Yat moved their capital southeast to Phnom Penh. Angkor Thom was abandoned before 1609, when an early western visitor described an uninhabited city. The Poem of Angkor Wat, composed in Khmer verse in 1622, describes its beauty.
angkor-wat: Angkor Wat was commissioned by the Khmer king Suryavarman II in Yaśodharapura, the capital of the Khmer Empire, as his state temple, and is generally considered to have been intended as his mausoleum. No contemporary inscription naming the temple has been found, so its original name is unknown; it may have been Vrah Viṣṇuloka. Work stopped after the king's death, leaving some bas-reliefs unfinished. In 1178 the Chams sacked Angkor. The Khmer empire was then restored by Jayavarman VII, who founded a new capital at Angkor Thom, with the Bayon as its state temple, and Angkor Wat was gradually converted into a Buddhist site.

The temple stands on a site of 162.6 hectares. It combines the temple mountain with the later plan of concentric galleries. The outer wall measures 1,024 m by 802 m, and a moat 190 m wide surrounds it. The layout is generally read as a representation of Mount Meru: the central quincunx of towers stands for its five peaks, and the walls and moat for the surrounding ranges and ocean. Lay people were admitted only to the lowest level. Unlike most Angkorian temples it faces west.

Most of the visible blocks are Kulen sandstone, quarried about 40 km to the northeast, with laterite for the outer wall. The monument contains five to ten million blocks, none heavier than 1.5 tons. At the equinoxes the rising sun aligns with the central tower when seen from the western causeway, an alignment generally regarded as intentional.

Portuguese traders and missionaries in the 16th century found a stone city in the forests that had seemed abandoned for over 150 years, and the Capuchin friar António da Madalena explored the ruins in 1586. In 1860 the French naturalist Henri Mouhot brought the temple to wider notice in the West. The École française d'Extrême-Orient founded the Conservation d'Angkor in 1908, and major restoration followed in the 1960s. The work was abandoned under the Khmer Rouge. The Angkor area became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1992. Angkor Wat has remained a Buddhist monastery and appears on the Cambodian national flag.
anglesey: Anglesey lies off the north-west coast of Wales. At 676 square kilometres it is the largest island in Wales and the Irish Sea and the seventh largest in Britain. The Menai Strait, about 250 metres wide at its narrowest, separates it from the mainland. It is low-lying, with low hills across the north, of which Holyhead Mountain, at 220 metres, is the highest. Holy Island lies to its west and belongs to the same county. Large parts of the coast are an Area of Outstanding Natural Beauty, and cliffs such as South Stack hold seabird colonies.

Settlement began in the Mesolithic period. One of the first villages in Wales was built at Llanfaethlu from about 4000 BCE, and the burial chamber of Bryn Celli Ddu began as a henge enclosure around 3000 BCE. Anglesey has long been associated with the druids. In 60 CE the Roman general Gaius Suetonius Paulinus, determined to break their power, attacked the island with an amphibious Batavian vanguard and destroyed the shrine and the sacred groves, but news of Boudica's revolt made him withdraw before he had consolidated the conquest. Gnaeus Julius Agricola finally brought the island into the Roman Empire, and in the Roman period it was notable for copper mining.

The medieval House of Aberffraw, which ruled the Kingdom of Gwynedd until 1283, originated on Anglesey and kept courts at Aberffraw and Rhosyr. After Edward I conquered Wales, Beaumaris Castle was built at the island's south-eastern corner. In the nineteenth century the Menai Strait was bridged by Thomas Telford's Menai Suspension Bridge of 1826 and by the Britannia Bridge, originally designed by Robert Stephenson in 1850.

Holyhead, on Holy Island, is the largest town and a ferry port for Dublin, and Llangefni is the administrative centre. Anglesey is regarded as a heartland of the Welsh language. Beaumaris Castle is part of the Castles and Town Walls of King Edward in Gwynedd World Heritage Site. The English name may derive from the Old Norse Ǫngullsey, Hook Island, or Ǫnglisey, Ǫngli's Island; the reading Island of the Angles has no merit.
anglicanism: Anglicanism declared its independence from the Holy See through the Act of Supremacy in 1534, a separation consolidated by the Elizabethan Settlement of 1559. The Church of England kept the apostolic succession of its bishops, while its formularies of the mid-sixteenth century correspond closely to those of historical Protestantism. The Settlement joined the radical 1552 prayer book to the conservative 1549 one in the Book of Common Prayer of 1559. In the first half of the seventeenth century some Anglican divines presented the church as a middle way, a via media, between Lutheranism and Calvinism.

After the American Revolution, Anglican congregations in the United States and British North America became autonomous churches with their own bishops. Through the British Empire and Christian missions this model was adopted for many new churches, especially in Africa, Australasia and the Asia-Pacific. The term Anglicanism was coined in the late nineteenth century for the tradition common to these churches and the Scottish Episcopal Church.

Anglicans base their faith on the Bible, the traditions of the apostolic church, the Church Fathers and, historically, the Thirty-nine Articles. Doctrine is not set by a central authority or a founder, and high-church Anglicans look to the prayer books as its main expression, by the principle lex orandi, lex credendi, "the law of prayer is the law of belief". The Book of Common Prayer, first issued in 1549, replaced the various Latin rites with one volume in English. Its 1662 version was mandatory in England and Wales and in standard use until the mid-twentieth century.
