The ministry is threefold: deacons, priests and bishops. The Anglican Communion has no international juridical body. Its provinces have historically been in full communion with the see of Canterbury, whose archbishop is first among equals with no direct authority outside England. He invites the bishops to the Lambeth Conference, first convened in 1867 by Archbishop Charles Longley.

The Oxford Movement of the mid-nineteenth century revived practices close to Roman Catholicism, and the Tractarians, especially John Henry Newman, saw the English church as a via media between Protestant and Catholic traditions; Newman later rejected the theory. Anglicans have been active in social causes: William Wilberforce against slavery, Lord Shaftesbury for factory and mine reform, Frederick Denison Maurice in Christian socialism, and Desmond Tutu and Ted Scott against apartheid. By 2020 the centre of Anglicanism had shifted to the Global South, with 63,556,000 adherents in Africa and 24,400,000 in Europe.
anglo-burmese-wars: The Anglo-Burmese Wars, also called the Indo-Burmese Wars, were an armed conflict between two expanding empires, the British Empire and the Konbaung dynasty. The expansion of Burma, present-day Myanmar, under the Konbaung dynasty had consequences along its frontiers. As those frontiers moved ever closer to the British East India Company and later British India, there were problems both with refugees and with military operations spilling over ill-defined borders. Three wars were fought between 1824 and 1885.

The First Anglo-Burmese War (1824–1826) ended in a victory for the British East India Company. By the Treaty of Yandabo, Burma lost territory it had conquered in Assam, Manipur and Arakan. The British also took possession of Tenasserim, intending to use it as a bargaining chip in future negotiations with Burma or Siam. As the century wore on, the Company began to covet the resources and main part of Burma during an era of great territorial expansion.

In 1852 Lord Dalhousie sent Commodore Lambert to Burma over a number of minor issues arising from the earlier treaty. The Burmese at once made concessions, including the removal of a governor whom the British had made their casus belli. Lambert eventually provoked a naval confrontation in extremely questionable circumstances, which began the Second Anglo-Burmese War in 1852. It ended with the British annexation of Pegu province, renamed Lower Burma, and led to a palace revolution in which King Pagan Min (1846–1853) was replaced by his half-brother Mindon Min (1853–1878).

King Mindon tried to modernise the Burmese state and economy to secure its independence and established a new capital at Mandalay, which he fortified. The efforts proved unsuccessful. The British claimed that Mindon's son Thibaw Min, who ruled from 1878 to 1885, was a tyrant intending to side with the French, that he had lost control of the country and so allowed disorder on the frontiers, and that he was reneging on a treaty signed by his father.

They declared war again in 1885 and conquered the rest of the country in the Third Anglo-Burmese War, which ended in the total annexation of Burma. The wars became the longest and most expensive of British India's wars, costing between 5 and 13 million pounds sterling over more than 60 years.
anglo-dutch-treaty-of-1824: The treaty, also called the Treaty of London, was meant to settle disputes left by the Anglo-Dutch Treaty of 1814, which had dealt with the British occupation of Dutch colonies during the Napoleonic Wars and with old trading rights in the Spice Islands but had not set limits to either side's expansion. Sir Stamford Raffles's founding of Singapore in 1819 sharpened the quarrel: the Dutch held that his treaty with the Sultan of Johor was invalid and that Johor lay in their sphere.

Under pressure from British merchants, Lord Castlereagh and Hendrik Fagel opened talks on 20 July 1820, agreeing only on free navigation and the suppression of piracy before breaking off on 5 August. Talks resumed in December 1823, when the British had understood Singapore's commercial value; the Dutch, seeing that its growth could not be stopped, offered to give up their claims north of the Strait of Malacca and their Indian colonies in return for a free hand to the south.

Fagel and Anton Reinhard Falck signed for the Netherlands and George Canning and Charles Williams-Wynn for the British on 17 March 1824. The Netherlands ceded its establishments in India and the city and fort of Malacca, dropped its objection to the British in Singapore and undertook to open no office on the Malay Peninsula. The United Kingdom ceded Fort Marlborough at Bencoolen and its other possessions on Sumatra, accepted Dutch occupation of Billiton and agreed to stay off the islands south of the Strait of Singapore, among them Batam and Bintan.

Each side's subjects could trade in the other's territories as a most favoured nation, piracy was to be opposed, and British traders gained access to Ambon, Banda and Ternate. Transfers were set for 1 March 1825, with the Netherlands paying 100,000 pounds sterling.

The United Kingdom ratified the treaty on 30 April 1824 and the Netherlands on 2 June. It divided British Malaya from the Dutch East Indies, whose successors are Malaysia and Singapore on one side and Indonesia on the other, and its line became most of the border between Indonesia and Malaysia. The division also helped the shared Malay language diverge into Malaysian and Indonesian forms.
anglo-dutch-wars: The English and the Dutch both sought profits overseas as the Age of Exploration began, and by the middle of the 17th century the Dutch had one of Europe's largest merchant fleets, with more merchant ships than all other nations combined. After the execution of King Charles I in 1649, Oliver Cromwell united Great Britain in the Commonwealth of England and expanded the navy, promoting officers on merit. In 1651 Parliament passed the first of the Navigation Acts, which required that goods imported into England be carried by English ships or ships of the exporting countries, which excluded Dutch middlemen.

The first war began after a skirmish off Dover on 29 May 1652, when Maarten Tromp refused to lower his colours to an English fleet under Robert Blake. England declared war on 10 July. After defeating the Dutch at the Kentish Knock, the English were routed at Dungeness in December, but later used the line of battle to drive the Dutch from the Channel and the North Sea. Tromp was killed at Scheveningen in August 1653, and the Treaty of Westminster ended the war on 5 April 1654.

The second war (1665–1667) followed a renewed deterioration in relations after the Restoration. The English took New Netherland and New Amsterdam, and the Dutch captured the Royal Navy flagship Prince Royal in the Four Days' Battle in June 1666. In June 1667 the Dutch raid on the Medway, led by Michiel de Ruyter, burned warships and towed away the Royal Charles.

In the third war (1672–1674) Charles II, bound by the secret Treaty of Dover, was obliged to help Louis XIV attack the Dutch Republic. De Ruyter won a series of victories over the Anglo-French fleet and prevented an invasion, and Parliament forced Charles to make peace. The fourth war, fought from 1780 to 1784, followed Dutch support for the American rebels and was a British victory.

England was successful in the first war and the Dutch in the second and third. In 1688 William of Orange invaded England and became king, which ended further Anglo-Dutch conflict for a time. In the following century the Royal Navy became the most powerful maritime force in the world, while the Dutch States Navy fell to fourth place, and the fourth war was a profound humiliation for the Dutch. In the French Revolutionary and Napoleonic Wars Britain captured most of the Dutch colonial empire.
anglo-egyptian-condominium: The condominium followed the Anglo-Egyptian reconquest of Sudan, which overthrew the Mahdist State in 1898. Britain and Egypt acted together, but the reconquest was also driven by colonial competition, above all with France, whose expansion towards the Upper Nile threatened British interests. Kitchener's campaigns culminated in the Battle of Atbara and the Battle of Omdurman on 2 September 1898, which caused heavy Mahdist casualties. Reports of troops killing wounded fighters led to controversy in Britain, and Muhammad Ahmad's tomb was destroyed and his body exhumed.

In September 1898 Herbert Kitchener confronted a French expedition under Jean-Baptiste Marchand at Fashoda, and France ordered its forces to withdraw in November. Britain then forced the Egyptian khedive Abbas II to accept British control. Whereas British influence in Egypt was officially advisory, the British insisted that their role in Sudan be formalised. Under the agreement of January 1899 the khedive appointed the governor-general on British recommendation and could dismiss him only with British consent.

Kitchener was the first governor-general; Reginald Wingate succeeded him in December 1899 and oversaw most of the administrative development. Sudan was divided into provinces governed largely by British officers, assisted by inspectors and district commissioners. From 1901 British civilian officials formed the Sudan Political Service, while Egyptians generally held middle-ranking posts and Sudanese the lower ones. District commissioners increasingly governed through local chiefs under native administration, and the three southern provinces were administered separately.

The economy was agrarian. Cotton became the main export, grown under the Gezira Scheme and helped by the Sennar Dam of 1925, and railways reached the Red Sea in 1905 and Port Sudan in 1906. Gordon Memorial College, opened in 1902, trained teachers, engineers and surveyors, and in the south education depended largely on missions. The first nationwide census, of 1955 to 1956, counted 10,262,536 people.

During the First World War the administration annexed Darfur after the defeat of Ali Dinar in 1916. After the assassination of Governor-General Lee Stack in Cairo in 1924, Britain ordered Egyptian troops and officials out of Sudan, and the Sudan Defence Force replaced Egyptian-controlled units. The Anglo-Egyptian treaty of 1936 allowed Egyptian soldiers to return. In 1946 Britain reversed its separate southern policy and began to integrate the northern and southern administrations, a decision taken without consulting southern leaders.

Sudanese nationalists disagreed over independence or union with Egypt. After the Egyptian revolution of 1952 Egypt accepted Sudanese self-determination, and on 12 February 1953 Britain and Egypt agreed on self-government followed by a decision on Sudan's future. Ismail al-Azhari headed the government from 1954. Southern resistance to northern control contributed to the Torit mutiny in August 1955. Parliament declared independence on 19 December 1955, and Sudan became an independent republic on 1 January 1956.
anglo-egyptian-treaty-of-1936: In November 1918 Sa'd Zaghlul and six other Egyptians formed a delegation, the Wafd, to seek complete independence, and when the British High Commissioner refused to let them attend the Paris Peace Conference they took their case to the people, founding what became one of Egypt's most popular parties. In 1922 Britain declared Egypt independent on its own terms, reserving four key areas to itself. Under the constitution of 1923 the king could dissolve parliament, and politics became a struggle between the British-backed King Fuad I and the Wafd.

Italy's invasion of Ethiopia in 1935 led Britain to agree to renegotiate the 1922 declaration, and King Farouk feared that the Italians might invade Egypt or draw it into the war. The treaty was negotiated at the Zaafarana palace and signed in the Locarno Room of the Foreign Office in London in August 1936 by the Egyptian premier Nahas Pasha and the Foreign Secretary Anthony Eden. It was ratified on 22 December and was to last twenty years.

British forces were to leave the Egyptian cities for the Suez Canal area, limited in peacetime to 10,000 soldiers and 400 pilots with their support staff, though Britain could add more in war, and were to stay in Alexandria for eight years. Britain would supply and train the Egyptian army, and in war Egypt was to give British forces the use of its ports, airports and roads. Egypt gained the right to make treaties not in conflict with this one, to exchange ambassadors with Britain and to seek the abolition of foreign privileges, and its army returned to Sudan under joint administration. The question of Sudan itself was left unresolved.

Nationalists such as Young Egypt, who wanted full independence, rejected the treaty, and its signing set off demonstrations against the British and the Wafd. After the Second World War, on 23 September 1945, Egypt demanded an end to the British military presence and the annexation of Sudan, and by 1947 British troops had left every base outside the Canal Zone. After winning the election of 1950, the Wafd government abrogated the treaty on 15 October 1951. Under the Anglo-Egyptian Agreement of 1954 Britain agreed to withdraw from the Canal Zone, completing the withdrawal in June 1956, the date often taken as that of Egypt's full independence. Egypt nationalised the Suez Canal on 26 July 1956, and the Suez Crisis followed.
anglo-german-naval-agreement: Part V of the Treaty of Versailles of 1919 had allowed Germany no submarines and no naval aviation, and only a small force of obsolete battleships, light cruisers, destroyers and torpedo boats. Many in Britain felt these terms were too harsh, and British policy favoured revising them in Germany's favour as the best way to keep the peace. Deep cuts after the Washington Naval Conference of 1921–1922 and the London Naval Conference of 1930 had also led the Admiralty to value treaties that limited potential enemies.

Hitler had written in Mein Kampf of seeking a sea pact with Britain, a renunciation of naval rivalry in return for an alliance against France and the Soviet Union. Germany began building U-boats again in 1933, and on 25 April 1935 the British naval attaché was told that twelve had been laid down at Kiel. In his peace speech of 21 May 1935 Hitler offered a German navy fixed for ever at a 35:100 ratio, and the British Cabinet voted the next day to take up the offer.

The agreement fixed the tonnage of the Kriegsmarine permanently in proportion to that of the Royal Navy and required Germany to divide its tonnage by categories of warship. It was registered in the League of Nations Treaty Series on 12 July 1935. For Germany it was meant to open an Anglo-German alliance; for Britain it was to be the first of a series of arms limitation agreements, and a step towards an air pact outlawing bombing. The French government regarded it as treachery, and it was signed on the 120th anniversary of the Battle of Waterloo.

Its effect on the size of the German navy was limited. German and British experts reckoned that Germany could not reach the limit before 1942, and shortages of shipyards, skilled workers, steel and foreign exchange kept the navy far below it. The rule of building by categories forced Germany into a balanced fleet that reflected British priorities, which the Royal Navy's leaders thought the easiest kind to defeat.

At Munich in September 1938 Hitler told Neville Chamberlain that Germany would denounce the agreement if Britain signalled it might intervene in a European war. In January 1939 he gave the navy first priority and launched Plan Z, a fleet of 10 battleships, 8 aircraft carriers and 249 U-boats by 1944, far beyond the agreed ratio.
anglo-iraqi-war: Britain governed Iraq under a League of Nations mandate until 1932, when it became nominally independent. Before that, the Anglo-Iraqi Treaty of 1930 allowed British military bases and the unrestricted movement of British forces through the country. Many Iraqis resented these terms, which Britain imposed to secure Iraqi petroleum. After 1937 no British troops remained in Iraq, but the Royal Air Force kept two bases, RAF Shaibah near Basra and RAF Habbaniya, between Ramadi and Fallujah, on the air route between Egypt and India.

On 1 April 1941 Rashid Ali al-Gaylani and the Golden Square, four senior army commanders, seized power in a coup. The Regent, Prince 'Abd al-Ilah, had fled Baghdad the day before. The new government intended to retain links with Italy and to resist further concessions to Britain, and on 17 April Rashid Ali asked Germany for military help in the event of war. Winston Churchill refused to recognise the government.

Between 18 and 29 April the 20th Indian Infantry Brigade landed at Basra. On 30 April an Iraqi force of between 6,000 and 9,000 men with artillery left Baghdad and occupied the plateau south of Habbaniya, and by 1 May it had grown to about 9,000 regular troops and some 50 field guns. The base held training aircraft and was protected by an RAF armoured-car company and Assyrian levies.

Air Vice-Marshal Harry Smart decided to strike first. At 05:00 on 2 May, 33 aircraft from Habbaniya and eight Wellington bombers from Shaibah attacked the Iraqi positions, and attacks on airfields near Baghdad destroyed 22 aircraft on the ground. The base's pilots flew 193 sorties that day. Thirteen people on the base were killed. The Iraqi force withdrew, and a column from Palestine, known as Habforce, arrived to take the offensive. Colonel Roberts left Ramadi isolated and secured the bridge over the Euphrates at Fallujah. Major-General Clark, with about 1,450 men against at least 20,000 Iraqi defenders, pressed on to Baghdad and the government collapsed.

Rashid Ali's government fell, the Regent returned to power and British influence grew across the Middle East. Germany had been willing to help and sent Fritz Grobba to Iraq to lead a diplomatic mission, with Axis access to be arranged through Vichy French Syria. Wavell wrote that the resistance of British troops in Crete and their heavy losses prevented the Germans from sending more reinforcements.

After the armistice, Baghdad was torn by rioting and looting. Much of the violence was directed at the Jewish Quarter, where over 180 Jewish residents were killed and about 850 injured before police were ordered to use live ammunition. The British and Commonwealth forces awarded the battle honour Iraq 1941 to 16 units, with separate honours for the defence of Habbaniya, Falluja and Baghdad.
anglo-irish-treaty: The Irish War of Independence ended in a truce in July 1921, and Éamon de Valera met David Lloyd George in London four times in the week from 14 July. De Valera argued that Britain was negotiating with a sovereign state, which Lloyd George continually denied, and in August he became President of the Republic mainly so that he could accredit plenipotentiaries. The Irish team, led by Arthur Griffith and Michael Collins, went to London with draft treaties and instructions to refer the full text of any draft back to the cabinet before signing. De Valera himself did not attend. Both sides knew that failure would end the truce and bring a war neither wanted.

Formal sessions began in October, with the Irish delegation based at 22 Hans Place in Knightsbridge, and informal talks followed in which only Griffith and Collins and two British negotiators took part. It was clear that a 32-county Irish Republic was not on offer, and the main outstanding point was the form of an oath to the monarch. Collins and Griffith won concessions on the oath and on defence and trade, together with a boundary commission and a clause upholding Irish unity. The treaty was signed soon after two in the morning on 6 December 1921. Collins later said that Lloyd George had threatened immediate and terrible war if it was not signed at once, and no message was sent to Dublin beforehand.

Crown forces were to withdraw from most of Ireland, which became a self-governing dominion of the British Empire, like Canada and Australia, with the King as head of state, represented by a Governor General. Members of the new parliament were to swear an oath of allegiance to the Irish Free State and to be faithful to King George V in virtue of common citizenship. Northern Ireland could withdraw within a month, in which case a Boundary Commission would draw the border. Britain kept control of the Treaty Ports for the Royal Navy, and the Free State was to take a share of the United Kingdom's debt.

De Valera came out against the treaty on 8 December, but the cabinet voted four to three to recommend it to the Dáil. The British Commons approved it on 16 December by 401 to 58 and the Lords by 166 to 47. The Dáil approved it on 7 January 1922 by 64 to 57, and the meeting the treaty required confirmed it on 14 January. The main dispute was dominion status as against an independent republic, and partition was a significant matter of dissent. The split led to the Irish Civil War, which the pro-treaty side won. The Irish Free State came into being on 6 December 1922.
anglo-mysore-wars: The Anglo-Mysore wars were four wars fought in the last three decades of the 18th century between the Sultanate of Mysore and the British East India Company, represented chiefly by the neighbouring Madras Presidency, together with the Maratha Empire, the Kingdom of Travancore and the Kingdom of Hyderabad. Hyder Ali and his son and successor Tipu Sultan fought on four fronts, with the British attacking from the west, south and east and the Nizam's forces from the north.

In the First Anglo-Mysore War, from 1767 to 1769, Hyder Ali almost captured Madras. The British persuaded the Nizam to attack him, but the Nizam signed a new treaty with the British in February 1768. Hyder Ali faced a Bombay Army from the west and a Madras Army from the north-east, yet his attack towards Madras led the Madras government to sue for peace and the Treaty of Madras.

The Second War, from 1780 to 1784, saw bloodier battles. Tipu defeated William Baillie at Pollilur in September 1780 and John Braithwaite at Kumbakonam in February 1782, taking both prisoner. Sir Eyre Coote defeated Hyder Ali at Porto Novo and Arni. Tipu continued after his father's death, and the Treaty of Mangalore of 11 March 1784 restored the earlier position. In the Third War, from 1790 to 1792, Tipu, now an ally of France, invaded Travancore, a British ally, in 1789. Charles Cornwallis commanded the British forces, and the siege of Srirangapatana in 1792 ended in the Treaty of Srirangapatana, by which Tipu gave up part of his kingdom.

In the Fourth War, from 1798 to 1799, Mysore's alliance with the French was seen as a threat to the Company. Mysore had 35,000 soldiers against 60,000 British troops, and the Nizam and the Marathas invaded from the north. The British won a decisive victory at the siege of Seringapatam in 1799, where Tipu Sultan was killed defending the city. Much of Mysore was annexed by the British, the Nizam and the Marathas, and the core around Mysore and Seringapatam was restored to Yuvaraja Krishnaraja Wadiyar III under his grandmother's regency. The Wodeyar dynasty ruled the remnant kingdom until 1947, when it joined the Dominion of India.

Tipu's rockets at Pollilur, with iron tubes holding the propellant, had a longer range, up to 2 kilometres. Captured rockets influenced British rocket development and inspired the Congreve rocket, used in the Napoleonic Wars.
anglo-nepalese-war: The Gorkhas conquered the Kathmandu Valley in 1768, and the East India Company established a Residency in Kathmandu in 1801. Two expanding powers met along an ill-defined frontier of some 1,500 kilometres. Nepal had extended its rule from the Teesta River in the east to the Sutlej in the west, while the Company consolidated its position from Calcutta, Madras and Bombay. The causes were a dispute over the border districts of Butwal and Sheoraj in the Tarai, the Company's interest in trade routes into Tibet, and fears that Nepal might join an anti-British alliance. In May 1814 a small Nepalese force attacked Company police outposts in Butwal and killed 18 officials, and the Governor-General formally declared war on 1 November 1814.

Nepal fought alone, since Bhimsen Thapa's attempts to win allies among the Marathas, the Sikhs and Qing China failed. The Company drew on the wealth of the Nawab of Awadh, who was asked for two crore rupees, and backed deposed rulers in Kumaon, Garhwal and Sikkim. The British attacked on two fronts, with columns led by Major-General Bennet Marley and Major-General John Sullivan Wood in the east and by Major-General Rollo Gillespie and Colonel David Ochterlony in the west, against the army of Amar Singh Thapa.

The first campaign went badly. At Nalapani a garrison of about 600 under Captain Balbhadra Kunwar held out against more than 5,000 men from 31 October to 30 November 1814, and Gillespie was killed on the first day. At Jaithak two assaults failed.

Ochterlony then brought up heavy guns and over 10,000 men to Malaun, cut Nepalese communications with the far west, and sealed the fate of Amar Singh Thapa at Malaun and his son Ranajor Singh Thapa at Jaithak. He led the second offensive of 1816 with about 17,000 men, most of them Indian sepoys.

The Treaty of Sugauli was ratified on 4 March 1816. Nepal lost Sikkim, Kumaon, Garhwal and the western Tarai, the Mechi River became its eastern border and the Mahakali its western one, and the Company agreed to pay 200,000 rupees a year for the lost Tarai revenue. A British Resident was set up in Kathmandu, though Nepal's rulers isolated him almost to house arrest. Nepal kept its independence. The war cost the Company more than its campaigns against the Marathas and Pindaris, and the Company recruited Gorkha defectors into battalions such as the Nasiri regiment and the Sirmoor battalion.
anglo-norman-invasion-of-ireland: Twelfth-century Gaelic Ireland was made up of over-kingdoms under a High King who took tribute but did not rule a unitary state, while the Norse-Irish held the port towns of Dublin, Wexford, Waterford, Cork and Limerick. Norman lords had already conquered much of south Wales. In 1155 Henry II of England discussed invading Ireland at a council in Winchester, and Anglo-Norman churchmen, wanting control of the Irish church and full Gregorian reform, backed intervention; the papal bull Laudabiliter, or an equivalent, was said to authorise it.

In 1166 most Irish kings acknowledged Ruaidrí Ua Conchobair of Connacht as High King, and his coalition ousted Diarmait mac Murchada from Leinster. Diarmait sailed to Bristol, swore loyalty to Henry and won leave to recruit Marcher lords, among them Richard de Clare, called Strongbow, Robert FitzStephen and Maurice FitzGerald, promising Strongbow his daughter Aoífe and the succession to Leinster.

In May 1170 Raymond FitzGerald landed at Bannow Bay, routed a larger force at Baginbun and executed 70 captives. Strongbow landed at Passage on 23 August with at least 200 knights and 1,000 soldiers, stormed Waterford, married Aoífe and, crossing the Wicklow Mountains to avoid Ruaidrí's army, took Dublin. After Diarmait died in May 1171 most of the Irish kingdoms besieged Dublin for two months, but the Normans held most of their territory.

Fearing that Strongbow might found an independent kingdom, Henry landed with a large army in October 1171. He granted Strongbow Leinster as a fief, took the Norse-Irish towns as crown land, called the Synod of Cashel to reform the church and received the submission of many Irish kings, while granting Meath to Hugh de Lacy.

Fighting went on after Henry left in 1172. Domnall Ua Briain's forces defeated part of Strongbow's army at the Battle of Thurles in 1174. The Treaty of Windsor of 6 October 1175 made Henry overlord of the conquered land and Ruaidrí of the rest, but it soon collapsed, and in 1177 Henry made his son John Lord of Ireland and allowed further conquest. The Normans brought castles, charters, coinage and new crops and animals. Contemporaries called the invaders English, and historians still differ over whether to call them Normans or English.
anglo-normans: The Anglo-Normans were not Normans alone but a mix of Normans, Bretons, Frenchmen, Flemings, Anglo-Saxons and Celtic Britons. A few Normans had settled in England before the conquest, having befriended Edward the Confessor during his exile in Normandy. After Duke William the Conqueror defeated Harold Godwinson at the Battle of Hastings, many Anglo-Saxon nobles and lesser thegns lost their lands and titles to Norman and northern French magnates, and some free geburs sank into the unfree status of villeins. Over time the conquerors' Old Norman became the distinct Anglo-Norman language.

The conquest changed the way war was waged. Many of the younger Anglo-Saxon military elite emigrated, some going on to the Varangian Guard in Constantinople, while William had Saxon infantry trained by Norman cavalry, forming a mixed Anglo-Norman army. Historians dispute how deep the hostility between Normans and English ran. The chronicler Orderic Vitalis praised English resistance, and the murdrum fine was revived for the secret killing of a Norman.

Beyond England the Normans built fortifications in Wales and set up the Marches along the border. After 1130 parts of southern and eastern Scotland came under Anglo-Norman rule: David I, king of Scotland from 1124, brought Anglo-Norman nobles into the Scottish aristocracy, introduced feudal tenure, sheriffs and the first royal burghs. In Ireland Richard de Clare, 2nd Earl of Pembroke, known as Strongbow, led the knights whom Diarmuid Mac Murchadha had sought from Henry II. Most of them came from Wales, so historians such as Seán Duffy call them Cambro-Normans.

The two peoples intermarried from soon after the conquest, and by the 1170s and 1180s nobles living in England, whatever their origin, called themselves English and set themselves apart from foreign-born royal ministers. The distinction between Norman and English seems to have faded towards the end of the 12th century. In Ireland the settlers married into the Celtic nobility and took up parts of its culture, above all outside the Pale around Dublin; they came to be called the Old English, a term first used in 1580. The House of Beauchamp, the House of Percy, the House of Neville and the House of Mortimer are among the families counted as Anglo-Norman.
anglo-persian-war: In the Great Game, the Anglo-Russian contest for influence in Central Asia, the British wanted Afghanistan to remain independent as a buffer state against Russian expansion towards India. They opposed Iranian influence there because they thought Iran unduly influenced by Russia. Iran, ruled by the Qajar dynasty, took Herat on 25 October 1856, in violation of an existing Anglo-Persian treaty.

Herat had declared itself independent under its own rebellious emir and placed itself under British protection. The British governor-general in India, acting on orders from London, declared war on 1 November. The Qajar army listed 86,700 men on paper, but Tehran could mobilise no more than 20,000, and morale was low in all but a few Imperial Guard regiments.

The first division of the expedition landed near Bushehr on 5 December 1856, stormed the old fort at Reshire and, after a naval bombardment, took the city. Since 4,000 Iranian troops were at Shiraz, the division was too weak to go inland, and a second division came from India in late January 1857 under Sir James Outram of the Bombay army. On 8 February 1857 Outram defeated the Iranian army of 7,000 to 8,000 under Shoja ol-Molk at Khushab, where the 3rd Bombay Light Cavalry broke into the enemy infantry.

The British then moved up the Shatt al-Arab with 1,500 British and 2,400 Indian soldiers to Mohammerah, at the junction with the Karun River. The Royal Navy and the 64th Foot and 78th Highlanders took Ahvaz on 1 April 1857.

A peace treaty was signed in Paris on 4 March 1857, though news reached the force only on 4 April, when Outram was planning an invasion of the interior. The Shah agreed to withdraw from Herat, refrain from interfering in Afghanistan, apologise to the British ambassador, sign a commercial treaty and cooperate in suppressing the slave trade in the Persian Gulf. The British dropped their demand that the Iranians replace their prime minister and agreed not to shelter the Shah's opponents in their embassy.

The British left Bushehr in October, and the troops were soon needed in central India for the Indian Rebellion of 1857. Three Victoria Crosses were awarded for the expedition. Herat returned to more direct Afghan control when Dost Mohammed Khan retook it in 1863.
anglo-saxon-chronicle: The first version of the Chronicle is lost. Known as the Common Stock, it was created in the late ninth century, probably in Wessex, in the reign of King Alfred the Great (r. 871–899), and dates to around 893, since it covers the return of the Vikings from the Continent in that year and a version was available to Bishop Asser for his Life of King Alfred of 893. It drew on annals relating to Kent, the South Saxons, Mercia and, above all, Wessex, and on sources now otherwise lost, some as early as the seventh century. Its earliest annal, for 60 BCE, records Julius Caesar's invasions of Britain.

The Common Stock was intended chiefly to legitimise the House of Wessex and the reign of Alfred. Copies were made and sent to monasteries across England, where they were updated, partly independently.

Almost all the material is in annals, year by year. Nine manuscripts survive in whole or in part, labelled A to I; none is the original. The oldest, the Winchester or Parker Chronicle, was begun at Old Minster, Winchester, towards the end of Alfred's reign and carries entries in the hands of several scribes through the tenth century. The Peterborough Chronicle was copied after a fire at that monastery in 1116 and continued to 1131, and in one manuscript the annals were still being added in 1154.

The manuscripts reflect the places and aims of their compilers. One includes the Mercian Register, covering 902 to 924 with a focus on Æthelflæd. Most copies include a poem on the Battle of Brunanburh in 937. The annal for 829 says the Northumbrians offered Egbert submission and peace, whereas the Northumbrian chronicles used by Roger of Wendover say he laid waste the province and made King Eanred pay tribute. Copying also introduced errors: the whole Common Stock is out by two years for the period 756 to 845.

Much of what the Chronicle records appears nowhere else, and it provides a relatively clear chronological framework, so it is among the most influential sources for England between the end of Roman authority and the decades after the Norman Conquest. Nicholas Howe called it and Bede's Ecclesiastical History of the English People the two great Anglo-Saxon works of history. Its annals from 1131 onwards in the Peterborough text give key evidence for the change from Old English to early Middle English.

John of Worcester, William of Malmesbury and Henry of Huntingdon each had a copy and adapted it. Benjamin Thorpe's edition of 1861 gave the manuscripts the letters used today, and the standard modern English translations are by Dorothy Whitelock, David Douglas and Susie Tucker, and by Michael Swanton.
anglo-saxons: The Anglo-Saxon period in Britain is considered to have begun by about 450 and ended in 1066. Although the settlers came from continental Europe, their culture developed in Britain, and by the 8th century an identity called Englisc had grown out of their interaction with Romano-British culture.

Bede gave the earliest detailed account of their origins in the early 8th century: he believed the first settlers came from several tribes of northern Europe, among them the people of Old Saxony, the Jutes of Jutland and the Angles, whose homeland he placed between the two. Roman writers describe the earliest Saxons as North Sea raiders, and the Romans placed a commander over a chain of coastal forts, the Saxon shore. The compound term Anglo-Saxon first appears in the mid-8th century.

At the end of the 6th century the missionary Augustine landed on the Isle of Thanet and went to King Æthelberht's town of Canterbury, sent by Pope Gregory the Great to Christianise Kent. From the conversions the first well-attested English kings and kingdoms appear in the written record. The period of competing kingdoms is traditionally called the Heptarchy, a term scholars have not used since the early 20th century because there were more than seven kingdoms. By 660 smaller territories had coalesced into kingdoms, and larger ones dominated the smaller.

After the Norman Conquest many nobles were exiled or joined the peasantry, and it has been estimated that only about 8% of the land was under Anglo-Saxon control by 1087. Some nobles went to Scotland, Ireland and Scandinavia, and others to the Byzantine Empire, where Anglo-Saxons became the predominant element in the Varangian Guard. For most of the population little changed at once, except that a Norman lord replaced an Anglo-Saxon one.

Royal dynasties often claimed descent from Woden, but the true basis of kingly power was war-leadership. Kings were buried as warriors, and war helmets rather than crowns were used in coronations until the 10th century. Warriors fought for the king in return for food, shelter and gifts such as weapons, and loyalty was owed to the person of a lord, so a kingdom was only as strong as its king.

Kings issued written law codes, one of the earliest attributed to Æthelberht of Kent. Women enjoyed considerable independence, as abbesses of double monasteries, as landholders and as legal principals. Buildings were mainly timber with thatch roofs, and Old English was spoken until the mid-12th century, when it had evolved into Middle English.
anglo-soviet-invasion-of-iran: Reza Khan Pahlavi carried out a coup against the Qajar dynasty in 1921, overthrew it in 1925 and crowned himself Reza Shah that year. He began a programme of economic, cultural and military modernisation and pursued neutrality in foreign policy. Although he declared Iran neutral in the Second World War, he tilted towards Germany and allowed hundreds of German agents to operate in the country. The British feared that the Abadan Refinery of the Anglo-Iranian Oil Company, which refined eight million tons of oil in 1940, might fall into German hands. Relations had been strained since 1931, when the Shah cancelled the D'Arcy Concession.
After the German invasion of the Soviet Union in June 1941, Britain and the Soviet Union became allies, and two notes of 19 July and 17 August demanded the expulsion of German nationals.

The invasion, code named Operation Countenance, began on 25 August 1941. A British naval force attacked from the Persian Gulf to seize Bandar Shahpur, Abadan and Khorramshahr, and British Commonwealth forces came by land and air from Iraq. The Soviet Union invaded from the north with three armies, including about 1,000 tanks, occupying the northern provinces. Iran fielded nine infantry divisions but lacked the training, armour and air power to fight on several fronts. By 28 and 29 August the military situation was in chaos, the Allies controlled the air, and Soviet aircraft dropped leaflets over Tehran. The Shah ordered resistance to end, a ceasefire was agreed on 30 August, and the government formally surrendered on 31 August.

On 16 September 1941 Reza Shah was forced to abdicate and went into exile, and his young son Mohammad Reza Pahlavi succeeded him. The Persian Corridor carried over 5 million tons of matériel to the Soviet Union and to the British in the Middle East. Under the Tripartite Treaty of 29 January 1942 the Allies promised to leave Iran not more than six months after the end of hostilities. The occupation brought food shortages, bread riots in Tehran in 1942 and sharp inflation.

In late 1945 Soviet-backed separatist republics were founded, including a People's Republic of Azerbaijan. Britain began to withdraw on 2 March 1946, but the Soviets stayed until May, after Iran lodged a complaint with the new United Nations Security Council.
anglo-spanish-war-1585-1604: Protestant refugees from the Netherlands settled in England, and some raided Spanish shipping from English ports. English sailors led by Sir John Hawkins traded with Spanish colonies in the West Indies from 1562, which Spain called smuggling. A slaving expedition led by Hawkins and Sir Francis Drake was surprised by the Spanish in September 1568 and lost several ships at the Battle of San Juan de Ulúa. Drake's privateering voyage of 1577 to 1580 circumnavigated the globe and plundered Spanish ports. After the Portuguese succession crisis of 1580, England backed António, Prior of Crato, against Philip II, while Philip supported the Catholic rebellion in Ireland.

The war broke out in 1585 after the seizure of English merchant ships in Spanish harbours. In August England joined the Dutch against Spain, and Robert Dudley, Earl of Leicester, took the governorship of the United Provinces, which angered Elizabeth I. His campaign lost Grave, Zutphen and Deventer and ended with the fall of Sluis in June 1587. Drake sacked Santo Domingo and Cartagena de Indias in 1586, and in April 1587 burned 37 Spanish ships at Cádiz. After the execution of Mary, Queen of Scots on 8 February 1587, Philip prepared the Armada of 1588 of about 130 ships.

Drake and Sir John Norris led the English counter-armada of 1589, which plundered the lower town of Coruña but was repulsed at its citadel with heavy losses. In the 1590s Spain's convoy system protected its treasure fleets, and in 1591 the Spanish captured the English flagship Revenge near the Azores. The Spanish landed in Brittany in 1590, and a second Armada sent towards Ireland in October 1596 lost about forty ships and 5,000 men to a storm. In 1600 the Anglo-Dutch army beat the Spanish at the Battle of Nieuwpoort, and in 1602 an English squadron under Richard Leveson blockaded Spain.

The Treaty of London of August 1604, between Philip III of Spain and James I of England, restored the situation before the war. England ended its high-seas privateering, both sides agreed to stop intervening in the Netherlands and Ireland, trade resumed, and Spain recognised James as king. English-held cautionary towns in Holland were not surrendered. The treaty was unpopular in England, where many saw it as a humiliating peace that abandoned the Dutch. Spain and the Dutch Republic agreed the Twelve Years' Truce in 1609, and Spain formally recognised Dutch independence in the Peace of Münster in 1648.
anglo-zanzibar-war: Britain recognised Zanzibar's sovereignty in 1886, and Britain and Germany competed for trade rights and territory in East Africa. The agreement of 14 June 1890 made Zanzibar a British protectorate and required any candidate for the sultanate to obtain the permission of the British consul. Sultan Hamad bin Thuwaini, who came to the throne in 1893, kept close ties with Britain, though his subjects disliked the growing British control and the abolition of the valuable slave trade.

Hamad died suddenly on 25 August 1896, and some suspected his nephew Khalid bin Barghash of having killed him. Khalid moved into the palace without British approval, though they preferred Hamoud bin Mohammed. He ignored warnings from the consul Basil Cave and General Lloyd Mathews and mustered about 2,800 men, mostly civilians but including 700 askaris, with artillery and machine guns aimed at the British ships in the harbour.

On 26 August the government of Lord Salisbury authorised Cave and Rear-Admiral Harry Rawson to use whatever means they thought necessary, and Rawson sent an ultimatum requiring Khalid to haul down his flag and leave the palace by 09:00 on 27 August. Khalid replied that he did not believe the British would open fire. At 09:02 the ships Racoon, Thrush and Sparrow began a bombardment, and the wooden palace caught fire.

In a small naval action the old royal yacht Glasgow fired on St George and sank in the shallow harbour. The shelling ceased at around 09:40, with the sultan's artillery silenced and his flag shot down. Sources give the length of the war as 38, 40 or 45 minutes, depending on where its start and end are placed, and 38 minutes is the most often quoted.

About 500 Zanzibaris were killed or wounded, most of the dead from the fire, and the only British casualty was a petty officer who recovered. Khalid took refuge in the German consulate, whose consul refused extradition because the treaty excluded political prisoners, and on 2 October a German ship took him to Dar es Salaam. British forces captured him in 1916, and he died at Mombasa in 1927.

Hamoud was installed as sultan with much reduced powers, at the head of an essentially British-run government. The war ended Zanzibar's sovereignty and began a period of heavy British influence, and there were no further rebellions during the 67 years of the protectorate. Several months later Hamoud, prompted by the British, abolished slavery in all its forms.
anglo-zulu-war: The Zulu Kingdom grew from a small tribe to a large regional power under Shaka in the 1810s, and under his successors Dingane and Mpande it acquired two powerful new neighbours, the Boers and the British Empire. After a civil war in the 1850s Mpande's son Cetshwayo became heir and de facto ruler, and he was acclaimed king in 1873 after his father died. Lord Carnarvon thought a federation in South Africa, as in Canada, might yield a ruling white minority and a large pool of cheap labour.

In 1877 Sir Bartle Frere was appointed British High Commissioner for Southern Africa to carry out such plans. A border dispute between the Zulu and the Boers of the Transvaal was one obstacle. Sir Theophilus Shepstone, whom Cetshwayo regarded as a friend, first supported him, but after taking over the Transvaal as administrator he saw the matter from the Boer side and began to paint the Zulu as an aggressive threat.

Frere seized on three border incidents in 1878, including the seizure and execution of two wives of Sihayo kaXongo who had fled into Natal, and on 11 December 1878 sent Cetshwayo an ultimatum. It demanded that the Zulu army be disbanded and its military system ended, and that a British Resident be admitted. Frere delayed telling the Colonial Office until the full text reached London on 2 January 1879, by which time Lord Chelmsford had assembled more than 17,000 men on the border. The British invaded on 11 January 1879, crossing the Buffalo River at Rorke's Drift, and the war began with the Zulu victory at Isandlwana, followed by the defence of Rorke's Drift by a small garrison.

Chelmsford's second, heavily reinforced invasion advanced with extreme caution in June, building fortified camps. Victories at Kambula, Gingindlovu and Eshowe had already restored the British position. Cetshwayo tried to negotiate, but Chelmsford wished to restore his reputation before Sir Garnet Wolseley replaced him, and on 4 July he defeated the main Zulu army at Ulundi.

After Ulundi the Zulu army dispersed and most leading chiefs submitted. Wolseley captured Cetshwayo on 28 August and deposed him, discarded Frere's confederation scheme, and divided Zululand into thirteen chiefdoms under compliant chiefs, so that the Zulu would not again unite under one king. This made internal divisions and civil wars inevitable. Chelmsford received a Knight Grand Cross of the Bath but was criticised by an investigation and never again served in the field, and Frere was moved to a minor post in Cape Town. The British made the Zulu Kingdom a protectorate and annexed it in 1887.
angola: Angola covers 1,246,700 square kilometres on the western coast of Southern Africa, making it the seventh-largest country in Africa. It borders Namibia, Zambia and the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and its province of Cabinda is an exclave on the Atlantic coast. Luanda, the capital, lies on the coast in the north-west. Angola has four natural harbours: Luanda, Lobito, Moçâmedes and Tômbua. Like the rest of tropical Africa it has alternating rainy and dry seasons, and the dry season is known as the cacimbo.

Before the Bantu migrations the region was populated by nomadic Khoi and San hunter-gatherers. In the first millennium BCE Bantu peoples arriving from the north displaced them and introduced bananas, taro and large cattle herds. States were formed by the 13th century, and the Kingdom of Kongo achieved hegemony from the 14th century. To its south lay Ndongo and Matamba, and the title ngola, held by the kings of Ndongo and Matamba, gave the Portuguese the name Angola. The Portuguese established relations with Kongo in 1483, and Diogo Cão reached the area in 1484.

Paulo Dias de Novais founded São Paulo de Loanda in 1575 with a hundred families of settlers and four hundred soldiers, and Benguela was fortified in 1587. Kongo fought three wars against the Portuguese, ending in the Portuguese conquest of Ndongo. The colony did not reach its present borders until the early 20th century, and met strong resistance from groups such as the Cuamato, the Kwanyama and the Mbunda.

After an anti-colonial struggle from 1961 to 1974, Angola became independent in 1975 as a one-party republic and at once fell into a civil war. The ruling MPLA, backed by the Soviet Union and Cuba, fought the National Union for the Total Independence of Angola, supported by the United States and South Africa, and the National Liberation Front of Angola, backed by Zaire. The civil war ended in 2002, and the peace allowed the resettlement of 4 million displaced persons.

The 2010 constitution made the leader of the winning party in parliamentary elections president, so that there are no separate presidential elections. Oil and diamonds have been the most important resources since independence. Angola had 36,604,681 inhabitants at the 2024 census. Portuguese is the official language and is spoken natively by 45.5 per cent, and Umbundu, Kimbundu and Kikongo are the most widely spoken indigenous languages.
angolan-war-of-independence: Portuguese ships under Diogo Cão reached the Kingdom of Kongo in 1482, and Paulo Dias de Novais founded Luanda in 1575. The conquest of the interior of present-day Angola began only in the 19th century and was not concluded before the 1920s. The Colonial Act of 1933 turned the overseas provinces into colonies and, while it allowed natives to study, it left them at a clear disadvantage. The Union of the Peoples of Northern Angola, led by Holden Roberto, was founded in 1954, and it became the National Liberation Front of Angola (FNLA) in 1962. The Baixa de Cassanje revolt, a labour conflict in a cotton region, is sometimes counted as the first event of the war.

On 15 March 1961 the Union of Peoples of Angola (UPA), under Holden Roberto, crossed from the Congo into northern Angola with 4,000 to 5,000 militants. They took farms, outposts and trading centres, killing officials and civilians, many of them Ovimbundu contract workers. The dead are put at about 1,000 white and 6,000 Black people, including women and children. Settlers who survived mostly stayed and held out in towns such as Carmona and Negage. Portugal answered with a counter-insurgency campaign, and atrocities were committed by all forces.

The MPLA opened an Eastern Front in May 1966 under Daniel Chipenda. UNITA made its first attack on 25 December 1966 on the Benguela railway, and it was expelled from Zambia in 1967 after derailing trains. The United States first supplied the UPA, and the Soviet Union backed the MPLA, which agreed in 1969 to grant it bases after independence. Rhodesia and South Africa aided Portugal, and oil found off Cabinda in 1966 helped to fund the war. From 1972 the Portuguese pacified the east, helped by intelligence from UNITA, and the MPLA leader Neto retreated with 800 militants to the Republic of the Congo.

A coup in Lisbon in April 1974 overthrew the Estado Novo, and the new government stopped military action in the colonies and declared its intention to grant independence. The MPLA, UNITA and the FNLA met at Mombasa on 5 January 1975 and signed the Alvor Agreement on 15 January, setting independence for 11 November and a transitional government. FLEC and the Eastern Revolt were excluded. The coalition soon failed, and civil war resumed by May 1975. More than 300,000 people left Angola by November, most evacuated by air, and the civil war that followed lasted decades and claimed a million lives and refugees.
angouleme: Angoulême stands on a plateau overlooking a meander of the river Charente, and is nicknamed the balcony of the southwest. The old city is built on a rocky outcrop at an altitude of 102 m, above a cliff 80 m high. Ramparts have surrounded the plateau since Roman times and were repeatedly destroyed and rebuilt until reconstruction stopped in the 19th century. The city's position at the crossroads of key routes exposed it to many sieges.

Little is known of the city before the Roman period, except that the plateau held an oppidum called Iculisma. Held by the Visigoths, who followed the Arian form of Christianity, the city was first besieged by Clovis in 507 and taken in 508, miraculously according to Gregory of Tours. On 18 May 1204 King John of England signed a charter creating the commune of Angoulême. Under the Treaty of Brétigny the city passed in 1360 to the English, and John Chandos took possession of it for Edward III in October 1361.

Angoulême was the seat of the County of Angoumois, which came to a branch of the Valois family from which came François I, born in Cognac in 1494. In 1524 the navigator Giovanni da Verrazzano told François I that he had discovered a new territory, which he named New Angoulême in the king's honour; the area later became New Amsterdam and then New York. In the Revolution the city was called Mountagne-Charente. German troops arrived on 24 June 1940 and neutralised between 10 and 20 thousand French soldiers.

Angoulême is the prefecture of the department of Charente, with a population a little under 42,000. Papermaking and printing have been connected with the town since the 14th century, helped by the steady temperature and volume of the water of the river Touvre. The cathedral of Saint-Pierre, a Romanesque church of the 12th century, was partly rebuilt in the later 19th century by Paul Abadie. The town hall, also by Abadie, keeps two 13th-century towers, Lusignan and Valois, from the castle of the counts. Since 1983 the city has had a school of fine arts with France's first cartoon section.
anguilla: Anguilla lies east of Puerto Rico and the Virgin Islands and directly north of Saint Martin, from which it is separated by the Anguilla Channel. The main island is about 16 miles (26 km) long and no more than about 3 miles (5 km) wide at its widest point, and the territory also includes smaller islands and cays with no permanent population, among them Dog Island, Scrub Island and Sombrero. It is flat and low-lying, built of coral and limestone, with thin, poor soil. The Italian word anguilla, meaning eel, gave the island its name, in reference to its shape. The Indigenous Arawakan name was Malliouhana.

Indigenous peoples who migrated from South America first settled Anguilla, and the earliest artefacts found there date from around 1300 BCE. Settlement remains date from 600 CE, and the rock ledges of Big Spring hold more than 100 petroglyphs from between 600 and 1200 CE. It is uncertain when Europeans first saw the island. The Dutch West India Company built a fort in 1631, which the Spanish destroyed in 1633.

According to traditional accounts, English settlers from Saint Kitts colonised the island from 1650, planting tobacco and some cotton. The French took it temporarily in 1666 and returned it the next year under the Treaty of Breda. Enslaved Africans were probably brought by the early settlers, and archival evidence shows at least 100 enslaved people there by 1683. They worked on sugar plantations, and in time they and their descendants vastly outnumbered the white settlers. The British Empire ended the slave trade in 1807 and outlawed slavery in 1834.

Anguilla was placed under the administrative control of Saint Kitts in 1825 and federated with Saint Kitts and Nevis in 1882, against the wishes of many Anguillans. Full adult suffrage came in 1952. In 1967 the associated state of Saint Kitts-Nevis-Anguilla gained internal autonomy, and on 30 May 1967 Anguillans forcibly ejected the Saint Kitts police and declared independence from Saint Kitts. The revolution, led by Atlin Harrigan and Ronald Webster among others, aimed at separation and a return to British colonial status. Britain sent 300 troops in March 1969, and the Anguilla Act 1971 confirmed British authority. Anguilla formally seceded from Saint Kitts and Nevis in 1980.

Anguilla is a British Overseas Territory with The Valley as its capital. It is internally self-governing, with a governor appointed by the British government. Its people are mostly descended from enslaved Africans. English is the main language, alongside an English-lexifier Creole called Anguillian. Boat racing is the national sport.
angul-district: Angul district, also spelt Anugul, lies in the centre of Odisha between latitudes 20°31′N and 21°40′N and longitudes 84°15′E and 85°23′E. It covers 6,232 square kilometres at altitudes of 564 to 1,187 metres. Dhenkanal and Cuttack lie to the east, Deogarh, Kendujhar and Sundargarh to the north, Sambalpur and Sonepur to the west, and Boudh and Nayagarh to the south. The town of Angul, the district headquarters, is about 150 kilometres from the state capital Bhubaneswar. The district has extensive forests, including the Satkosia Tiger Reserve.

The district takes its name from its headquarters. According to L. S. S. O'Malley the name is believed to come from Anugol, with a legend attached: the region was held by Khonds, Savaras and Gonds, with the Khonds predominant, under chiefs who paid tribute once the Odisha king had established rule. The last Khond chief, Anu, rebelled and was deposed through a struggle called gol, and the conquerors named the land Anugol.

The district is a conglomeration of parts with different histories. The Angul area was a feudatory state under the East India Company after a treaty made when Maratha authority lapsed around 1803. In 1847 its raja, Somanath Singh, revolted against the Company and was deposed and exiled, and the state became a Government Estate. In 1891 the Bengal Presidency constituted Angul a separate district, adding the Phulbani subdivision, and in 1936 the new province of Orissa abolished it and merged the Angul portion with Cuttack district.

The Pallahara, Athamallik and Talcher areas were separate feudatory states, called Garhjats, each ruled by a raja under a Superintendent at Sambalpur. After 1949 all four became part of Dhenkanal district. On 1 April 1993 they were combined into the present district.

The 2011 census counted 1,273,821 people, of whom 95.50% gave Odia as their first language. The district is divided into four subdivisions (Angul, Athmallik, Talcher and Pallahara) and eight blocks. It is a major industrial area of Odisha, with industries relating to coal, bauxite and steel. The Radhikapur West coal block is known for good quality coal, and in December 2020 coal mines were auctioned to supply an aluminium smelter at Jharsuguda.
ani: Ani stands on a triangular, naturally defensive site about 1,340 metres above sea level, protected on the east by the ravine of the Akhurian River and on the west by the Bostanlar valley. It lies in the Turkish province of Kars, about 400 metres from the border with Armenia. The city stood on various trade routes, and its buildings are of local volcanic basalt, a tufa that is easily carved and comes in colours from creamy yellow to rose-red and black. Walls encircled the city, with a double line on the northern side, the only part not guarded by rivers or ravines; chroniclers credit King Smbat (977–989) with building them.

Armenian chroniclers first mention Ani in the 5th century as a hilltop fortress of the Kamsarakan dynasty. By the early 9th century it had passed to the Bagratuni dynasty, and between 961 and 1045 it was the capital of their kingdom. Byzantium held it from 1045. In 1064 a Seljuk army under Alp Arslan took it after a siege of 25 days and, according to an eyewitness quoted by Sibt ibn al-Jawzi, massacred its people and took some 50,000 prisoners.

In 1199 Queen Tamar of Georgia captured the city and in 1201 gave its governorship to the generals Zakare and Ivane, whose Zakarian dynasty regarded itself as successor to the Bagratunis. Prosperity returned: defences were strengthened and many churches built. The Mongols besieged Ani unsuccessfully in 1226 but captured and sacked it in 1236, massacring many of its people. A devastating earthquake in 1319 and the shifting of regional trade routes completed its decline.

The Cathedral, begun in 989 under Smbat II and finished in 1001 to the design of the architect Trdat, has pointed arches and clustered piers that give it the look of Gothic architecture, which it predates by several centuries; its dome collapsed in 1319. The Church of St Gregory of Tigran Honents, finished in 1215, is the best preserved monument and holds an extensive fresco cycle. The minaret of the Mosque of Manuchihr, named for the first of the Shaddadids, also survives.

The city was called the City of 1,001 Churches, though the real number was far smaller: archaeologists have excavated 50 churches, 33 cave chapels and 20 chapels. Its population is put at perhaps 100,000, though some historians doubt this. The archaeological site was inscribed on the UNESCO World Heritage List in 2016.
ani-cathedral: Armenia regained independence under the Bagratid dynasty around 885, and King Ashot III made Ani its capital in 961; at its height the city had 100,000 residents. King Smbat II commissioned the architect Trdat to build a cathedral there, but work stopped when Smbat died, according to an inscription on the south wall. Meanwhile Trdat was called to Constantinople to direct repairs to the dome of the Hagia Sophia, returning in 993. The building was finished by Queen Katranide, wife of King Gagik I, and it served as the seat of the Catholicos of the Armenian Apostolic Church until the mid-11th century.

The cathedral is a domed basilica on a rectangular plan, 34.3 metres long and 21.9 metres wide, which once stood about 38 metres high and was the tallest building in Ani. It is built mainly of polished yellow tuff, with black and red stone, and has three entrances, the main one on the west. Inside, freestanding piers divide the space into three aisles, and the nave ends in an eastern apse. The scholar Josef Strzygowski did most to popularise the view that its pointed arches and clustered piers anticipated the Gothic; Sirarpie Der Nersessian rejected it, arguing that the arches do not serve the same function in supporting the vault.

After the Seljuks under Sultan Alp Arslan took Ani in 1064 the cathedral became a mosque, the Fethiye Mosque, and according to Matthew of Edessa its silver cross was carried off to Nakhchivan. It returned to Christian use when King David IV of Georgia took the city in 1124 and prospered under the Zakarid princes after 1198. Ani declined after the Mongol sack of 1239 and was deserted by the 18th century.

An earthquake in 1988 tore a hole in the north-western corner. The World Monuments Fund and the Turkish Ministry of Culture began a conservation project in May 2011, and the site of Ani was inscribed as a World Heritage Site on 15 July 2016. The cathedral's design was echoed in the church of Marmashen monastery and in Sourp Nshan Cathedral in Beirut, completed in 1938.
aniene: The Aniene, known to the Romans as Aniō, is a river of Lazio, 99 kilometres (62 miles) long. It flows westward past Subiaco, Vicovaro and Tivoli to join the Tiber in northern Rome. It formed the principal valley east of ancient Rome and became an important water source as the city's population grew. The falls at Tivoli were noted for their beauty. Its historic bridges include the Ponte Nomentano, Ponte Mammolo, Ponte Salario and Ponte di San Francesco, all of which were originally fortified with towers. The Roman name has no known etymology, though Plutarch derived it from a mythical Etruscan king Anius who drowned in the river.

The confluence of the Aniene and the Tiber was controlled by Antemnae, a Latin settlement on a hill just to the south. In antiquity three of Rome's principal aqueducts, the Aqua Anio Vetus, the Aqua Anio Novus and the Aqua Claudia, had their sources in the valley. Together with the Aqua Marcia they were regarded as the four great aqueducts of Rome. The Anio Vetus was built around 270 BCE, and the Anio Novus was begun under Caligula around 38 CE and completed under Claudius in 48.

The emperor Nero created three lakes on the river for his villa at Subiaco. The largest of these dams was the highest in classical antiquity and remained in use until a flood destroyed it in 1305. Trajan later connected the Anio Novus to one of the lakes. A series of floods in the early nineteenth century, above all the one of 1826, led Popes Leo XII and Gregory XVI, as sovereigns of the Papal States, to control the water by canalising the river upstream from Tivoli, cutting a tunnel through Monte Catillo and diverting the river round Tivoli.
anita-garibaldi: Ana Maria de Jesus Ribeiro was born on 30 August 1821 in Laguna, then part of the Kingdom of Brazil, a year before the country's independence. Her family was poor and of Azorean Portuguese descent. She was the third of ten children of Maria Antônia de Jesus Antunes and Bento Ribeiro da Silva, a tropeiro. In 1835, at fourteen, she was forced to marry Manuel Duarte Aguiar, who abandoned her to join the Imperial Army.

Giuseppe Garibaldi, a Niçois sailor of Ligurian descent, had fled Europe in 1836 and was fighting for the separatist Riograndense Republic in the Ragamuffin War. Anita joined him on his ship, the Rio Pardo, in October 1839, and a month later first saw action in battles at Imbituba and Laguna. A skilled horsewoman, she is said to have taught him about the gaúcho culture of the Pampas.

At the Battle of Curitibanos Garibaldi became separated from the front and Anita was captured. Her guards told her that he was dead, and she was allowed to search among the dead but did not find him. She then escaped on a horse, was pursued, and had her horse shot, and she waded the river Canoas. She spent four days in the woods without food or drink before reaching the rebels and was reunited with Garibaldi at Vacaria. Their first child, Menotti, was born a few months later. They married on 26 March 1842 in Montevideo.

Anita went with Garibaldi and his red-shirted legionnaires to Italy to join the revolutions of 1848. In February 1849 he joined the defence of the newly proclaimed Roman Republic against Neapolitan and French intervention, and she joined him there. Rome fell to a French siege on 30 June, and she fled with the Garibaldian Legion. Pregnant and sick with malaria, she died on 4 August 1849 in her husband's arms at Guiccioli Farm in Mandriole, near Ravenna. Her body had to be hurriedly buried.

In 1860 Garibaldi rode out to Teano to hail Victor Emanuel II as king of a united Italy wearing Anita's striped scarf. She is a symbol of Brazilian republicanism and was recognised as a national heroine after the fall of the Brazilian Empire. Laguna has a museum dedicated to her. In 1932 Mussolini had a monument to her raised on the Janiculum in Rome, near the equestrian statue of her husband.
ankara: Ankara lies on the central Anatolian plateau between the Kızılırmak and Sakarya rivers, in one of the driest regions of Turkey, surrounded mostly by steppe. Its historical centre is a rocky hill rising 150 metres over the left bank of the Ankara River, a tributary of the Sakarya, and the hill is still crowned by the ruins of Ankara Castle. The Galatians laid the castle's foundations on a lava outcrop and the Romans completed it; the Byzantines and Seljuks later restored it.

In antiquity the city was Ánkyra in Greek and Ancyra in Latin, from a Greek word meaning 'anchor'; it has been linked with the Hittite cult centre Ankuwaš, though this is debated. After the Seljuk Turks annexed it in 1073 it became known in many European languages as Angora, a form preserved in the names of the Angora goat, rabbit and cat, whose hair and wool were exported for centuries.

The oldest settlements around the city centre belonged to the Bronze Age Hattic civilization, which the Indo-European Hittites gradually absorbed between about 2000 and 1700 BCE. The city grew greatly under the Phrygians from around 1000 BCE, helped by a mass migration from Gordion after an earthquake damaged that capital. Phrygian tradition venerated King Midas as founder of Ancyra, but Pausanias noted that the city was far older, which agrees with archaeology. Lydians, Persians and Greeks followed. Ancyra was the capital of the Celtic state of Galatia from 280 to 64 BCE and then of the Roman province of Galatia, from 25 BCE to the 7th century CE.

The Ottomans made the city capital of the Anatolia Eyalet from 1393 to the late 15th century, of the Angora Eyalet from 1827 to 1864 and of the Angora Vilayet from 1867 to 1922. On 23 April 1920 the Grand National Assembly of Turkey was established there, and Ankara became the headquarters of the national movement in the Turkish War of Independence. It became the capital of the Republic on 29 October 1923, succeeding Istanbul. Planned for 500,000 inhabitants, it had about 75,000 in 1927. From the 1950s it grew faster than planned as people migrated from the countryside, building many unplanned houses called gecekondu.

Ankara is the capital of Turkey and the centre of its road and railway networks, with 5,782,285 people in the province in 2022. The citadel and the remains of a Roman theatre survive in the oldest quarter, and the Roman statues found at the theatre are shown in the Museum of Anatolian Civilizations. The region is also known for its pears, honey and Muscat grapes.
anklam: Anklam, formerly known as Tanglim and Wendenburg, lies on the banks of the Peene river, 8 kilometres from its mouth in the Kleines Haff, the western part of the Szczecin Lagoon. It is the head of navigation on the Peene. It was the capital of the former district of Ostvorpommern and, since September 2011, belongs to the district of Vorpommern-Greifswald. It had 12,177 inhabitants in 2021.

In the early Middle Ages an important Scandinavian and Wendish settlement stood nearby, at the place now called Altes Lager Menzlin, and Anklam began as an associated Wendish fortress. Part of the Duchy of Pomerania, the abandoned fortress became a settlement named Tanglim after its new founder during the German expansion eastwards. It received town status in 1244 and joined the Hanseatic League, a membership that brought it a measure of wealth, though it stayed small.

Because of its military importance Anklam suffered greatly in the Thirty Years' War, when Swedish and Imperial troops fought over it for twenty years; Imperial forces held it from 1627 to 1630 and Swedish forces afterwards. It became part of Swedish Pomerania in 1648 and was captured by Frederick William of Brandenburg in 1676. In 1713 Russian soldiers looted it; the town was not burned, as Peter the Great had ordered, largely through the resistance of Christian Thomesen Carl. The Treaty of Stockholm in 1720 gave the southern parts of Swedish Pomerania to Prussia. In the 19th century railways joined it to Berlin and Stettin, and linen, leather, beer and soap were made there.

Several bombing raids by the U.S. Air Force in 1943 and 1944, and the burning and levelling of most of the town by the advancing Soviets in the last days of the war, nearly destroyed it. In February 1945 a death march of Allied prisoners of war from Stalag XX-B passed through. After the war it was rebuilt in a rather uniform socialist style and, from 1952 to 1990, formed part of Bezirk Neubrandenburg.

Among its remaining buildings is the church of St Mary, of the 12th century, rebuilt in the 15th century, given a modern spire in the 19th and repaired in 1947. The Otto-Lilienthal-Museum commemorates the aviation pioneer, born there in 1848, and the Museum im Steintor covers local history. Others born in Anklam include the architect Gustav Lilienthal, the diplomat Ulrich von Hassell and the opera singer Johanna Gadski.
anna-amalia-of-brunswick-wolfenbuttel: Anna Amalia was born on 24 October 1739 at Schloss Wolfenbüttel, the fifth of the thirteen children of Karl I, Duke of Brunswick-Wolfenbüttel, and Princess Philippine Charlotte of Prussia, herself a composer. Her maternal grandparents were Frederick William I of Prussia and Sophia Dorothea of Hanover.

She was educated as a princess of the high nobility, chiefly by the theologians Johann Friedrich Wilhelm Jerusalem and Matthias Theodor Christoph Mittelstädt. Religious instruction came first, in German and French, within the Protestant tradition of the House of Brunswick but with rational principles of knowledge. She also learned history, geography, the fine arts, dancing and the piano, and studied music with Friedrich Gottlob Fleischer and Ernst Wilhelm Wolf.

On 16 March 1756 she married Ernst August II Konstantin, Duke of Saxe-Weimar-Eisenach, who was eighteen; she was sixteen. They had two sons. Ernst August died on 28 May 1758, leaving her regent for their infant son Karl August, then nine months old. She was pregnant with their second son, Prince Constantine, who was born three months later.

She administered the duchy with prudence during the troubles of the Seven Years' War, strengthening its resources. Karl August's governor was Count Eustach von Görz, but in 1771 Christoph Martin Wieland was appointed his tutor, and in 1774 the poet Karl Ludwig von Knebel came as tutor to Constantine. Karl August reached his majority on 3 September 1775, and she retired.

Anna Amalia gathered scholars, poets and musicians at the Wittum palace, a circle Wilhelm von Bode called a court of the muses; Johann Gottfried Herder, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe and Friedrich Schiller belonged to it. In 1771 she engaged Abel Seyler's theatre company, regarded as the best in Germany, and this marked the start of Weimar Classicism. In summer she received her circle at Ettersburg Castle. She also founded the Duchess Anna Amalia Library, which now holds some 1,000,000 volumes.

She was herself a composer, in the Empfindsamkeit style of Johann Adam Hiller and Anton Schweitzer. Her works include the Goethe settings Erwin und Elmire (1776) and Das Jahrmarktsfest zu Plundersweilern, a symphony of 1765, an oratorio of 1768 and harpsichord sonatas. From 1788 to 1790 she lived in Rome and Naples, an unusual journey for a widowed Protestant princess, with her travel arranged by Goethe and Johann Friedrich Reiffenstein. She died at the Wittum palace on 10 April 1807, and Goethe wrote her obituary. At her own request she was buried in the city church of Weimar.
anna-komnene: Anna was born on 1 December 1083 to Alexios I Komnenos and Irene Doukaina, the eldest of seven children. Alexios had become emperor in 1081 by usurping Nikephoros Botaneiates. She was born in the Porphyra Chamber of the imperial palace, which made her a porphyrogenita. At birth she was betrothed to Constantine Doukas, son of Emperor Michael VII, probably as a political match to support the legitimacy of her father, and from about 1090 she was raised in the household of his mother, Maria of Alania.

Her education covered Greek literature, philosophy, theology, mathematics and medicine. Georgios Tornikes said in a funeral oration that she read the Odyssey in secret from her parents. She gained expertise in medicine, helped treat her father in his last illness and administered a large hospital in Constantinople.

Anna and Constantine were heirs until her brother John II Komnenos was designated emperor in 1092. Constantine died around 1094, and about 1097 she married Nikephoros Bryennios, a soldier and historian whose family had held the throne before her father. When Alexios died in 1118, John was acclaimed emperor in Hagia Sophia.

Niketas Choniates, writing after 1204, says Anna was driven by ambition and revenge to plot against John, that Bryennios refused to join her, and that she forfeited her estates. Leonora Neville argues she was probably not involved, since only Choniates portrays her as a rebel. After her husband's death she entered the Kecharitomene convent, founded by her mother, and stayed there for the rest of her life.

In the convent Anna studied philosophy and history and held scholarly gatherings, including those on Aristotelian studies. She wrote the Alexiad in the mid-1140s or the 1150s, citing her husband's unfinished history as a reason. She drew on old soldiers, accounts from her father and uncles, and the imperial archives. It is written in Attic Greek modelled on Thucydides, Polybius and Xenophon.

The Alexiad describes weapons, tactics and battles and relations between Alexios and the West. She wrote of events of her childhood, and wrote to praise her father and denigrate his successors. Still, it is the only Byzantine eyewitness account of the First Crusade, giving the alarm felt in Constantinople at the western armies, whom she calls Celts.
anna-maria-luisa-de-medici: Anna Maria Luisa was born in Florence on 11 August 1667, the only daughter of Cosimo III de' Medici and Marguerite Louise d'Orléans. Her parents' relationship was quarrelsome, and on 26 December 1674 Cosimo consented to his wife's departure for the Convent of Montmartre in France. She left Tuscany in June 1675, and her daughter, not yet eight, never saw her again. Anna Maria Luisa was raised by her paternal grandmother, Vittoria della Rovere.

Several marriages were considered. Peter II of Portugal's ministers declined, fearing she had inherited her mother's temperament, and the Princess thought the Duke of Modena too lowly in protocol. Leopold I, Holy Roman Emperor, suggested Johann Wilhelm, Elector Palatine, who obtained the style Royal Highness for Cosimo in February 1691. They were married by proxy on 29 April 1691.

The Palatinate she arrived in was ravaged by the Nine Years' War. After a miscarriage in 1692 the marriage remained childless, but it was harmonious. Johann Wilhelm commissioned a theatre for her where Molière's comedies were performed, and by patronising many musicians she gave the Palatine court a reputation as an international centre of music. She invited Fortunato Chelleri as maestro di cappella and sponsored Agostino Steffani from 1703.

Because her siblings were also childless, the Medici were close to extinction. In 1713 Cosimo III deposited a bill in the Senate by which she would ascend the throne after her brother Gian Gastone, but Charles VI, Holy Roman Emperor, was furious, replying that Tuscany was an imperial fief. In 1718 Great Britain, France and the Dutch Republic chose Infante Charles of Spain as heir, without mention of her. The Elector Palatine died in June 1716, and she returned to Florence in October 1717.

Gian Gastone died on 9 July 1737. The envoy of Francis III of Lorraine, who was now heir, offered Anna Maria Luisa a nominal regency, which she declined.
