All the Medici's allodial possessions passed to her, and on 31 October 1737 she signed the Family Pact, willing the personal property of the Medici to the Tuscan state on condition that nothing was ever removed from Florence.

She lived in seclusion in the Palazzo Pitti, financed the building of the Cappella dei Principi, and gave much of her fortune to charity. She died on 18 February 1743, and the grand ducal line of the House of Medici ended with her. The Uffizi Gallery was opened to public viewing sixteen years later. When her bones were examined in 2012, they showed no trace of syphilis, from which she had long been thought to have died.
anna-of-bohemia-and-hungary: Anna was born in Buda on 23 July 1503, the eldest child of King Vladislaus II of Bohemia and Hungary and his third wife, Anne of Foix. Her paternal grandparents were King Casimir IV of Poland, of the Jagiellon dynasty, and Elisabeth of Austria. When Vladislaus died on 13 March 1516, Anna and her brother Louis were left in the care of the Holy Roman Emperor Maximilian I.

In 1515 Louis was married to Maximilian's granddaughter Mary of Austria, and Anna was betrothed to one of Mary's brothers, with Maximilian acting as proxy. She and Mary were educated together, first in Vienna and from 1516 in Innsbruck. Their humanist schooling stressed problem-solving, hunting, handling weapons, dancing and music, and they met humanists who visited the imperial library.

Anna married Archduke Ferdinand, second son of Joanna of Castile and Philip I of Castile, on 26 May 1521 in Linz. Ferdinand was then governing the Habsburg hereditary lands for his brother Charles V, and it was stipulated that he should succeed Louis if Louis died without legitimate male heirs. More than five years passed before Anna became pregnant; their first child, Elisabeth, was born in 1526.

Louis died after the Battle of Mohács against Suleiman of the Ottoman Empire on 29 August 1526, thrown from his horse. Ferdinand was elected king of Bohemia on 24 October with Anna as queen. In Hungary a group of nobles proclaimed him king, but another faction elected John Zápolya. The conflict lasted until 1570, when John Sigismund gave up the title in the Treaty of Speyer in favour of Ferdinand's son Maximilian. Ferdinand entrusted Anna with many responsibilities: she served as regent while he was in Brussels, chaired his Hofrat with the Bishop of Trieste, and presided over many diets in his name.

Anna and Ferdinand had fifteen children, all born in Bohemia or Austria, among them the next Holy Roman Emperor, two queens of Poland and a grand duchess of Tuscany. Her fertility resolved a shortage of heirs that had troubled both kingdoms for centuries. She died in Prague on 27 January 1547, days after the birth of her last daughter, Joanna.

Ferdinand never remarried, though advised to, and became emperor in 1556, nine years after her death. The Belvedere, called Queen Anne's Summer Palace, was begun for her on the grounds of Prague Castle in 1538 and was not completed in its present form until 1565. She was remembered for her charity and wisdom.
anna-of-kiev: Anne was a daughter of Yaroslav the Wise, Grand Prince of Kiev, and his second wife Ingegerd Olofsdotter of Sweden. Her birth date is unknown: Philippe Delorme has suggested 1027, and Andrew Gregorovich 1032. She was almost certainly the youngest daughter. A Cyrillic signature on a document of 1061 suggests that she could write her name. Yaroslav had married several of his children to Western rulers in an attempt to avoid Byzantine influence.

Negotiations for her marriage to King Henry I of France began in the late 1040s, after the death of his first wife and their only child. Henry needed an heir, and the Church increasingly disapproved of marriages between relatives, so he sought an unrelated bride. He sent Bishop Gauthier of Meaux and others to Yaroslav's court, and no record of the dowry survives. Anne travelled to Reims in 1050.

Anne married Henry, who was nearly twenty years older, on 19 May 1051, and was crowned immediately afterwards, the first French queen to celebrate her coronation at Reims Cathedral. They had three sons, Philip, Robert, who died young, and Hugh. Anne is often credited with introducing the Greek name Philip into the royal houses of Western Europe. Few records show her taking part in the royal council, but a charter of 1058 grants a privilege with her approval and that of her children.

Henry died on 4 August 1060 and Philip succeeded him. Count Baldwin V of Flanders became his guardian, but Anne's name appears in four times as many charters as Baldwin's. Her only surviving signature, in Cyrillic, probably reading Ana Reina, dates from this time.

Evidence of Anne's role in government disappears in 1061, around the time she married Count Ralph IV of Valois. The marriage was controversial because Ralph was Henry's cousin and was still technically married to his second wife, and he was excommunicated. Ralph died in 1074. In 1062 Anne paid for the restoration of a chapel at Senlis, which became the Abbey of St. Vincent. The date of her death is unknown: Delorme believes it was 5 September 1075, and others propose 1080.
anna-of-russia: Anna was born in Moscow on 7 February 1693, the daughter of Tsar Ivan V and Praskovia Saltykova. Ivan V, who was co-ruler with his younger half-brother Peter the Great but was mentally disabled, died in 1696, and Peter ruled alone. Her widowed mother raised Anna and her two sisters strictly. In 1708 Peter brought the family to St Petersburg, and Anna greatly enjoyed the splendour of the court. To increase his influence in Courland, Peter arranged her marriage to Frederick William, Duke of Courland, on 11 November 1710. The duke died on 21 January 1711, and Anna then ruled the duchy from Mitau for almost twenty years.

When Peter II died childless in 1730 the male line of the Romanov dynasty was extinct. The Supreme Privy Council chose Anna, a childless widow with some experience of government, in preference to her elder sister Catherine. It hoped she would be a figurehead, and made her sign Conditions under which she could not declare war, impose taxes or spend state revenue without its consent. On 7 March 1730 a faction opposed to the Dolgorouki and Galitzin families petitioned her, and she repudiated the Conditions. Some of their framers were hanged and many exiled to Siberia, and she ruled as an absolute monarch.

Her reign is often called the Age of Biron, after her favourite Ernst Johann von Biron, a Baltic German. Baltic Germans were favoured with offices, though the historian Walter Moss cautions that the picture of total German domination is exaggerated. Her Secret Office of Investigation punished political crimes, and Russian authorities listed around 20,000 victims. Russia fought a war with the Ottoman Empire from 1735 to 1739, which gained only Azov and its environs. The first ballet school in Russia was founded in 1738.

As her health failed Anna named her grandnephew Ivan VI as successor and Biron as regent. She died on 28 October 1740, aged 47, of a kidney stone. Ivan VI was a baby of two months, and Elizabeth Petrovna, Peter's daughter, soon won the favour of the people, imprisoned Ivan and exiled his mother. In the West Anna's reign was traditionally seen as a continuation of the transition from old Muscovy to the European court Peter had envisioned, while in Russia it is often called a dark era.
anna-of-savoy: Anna of Savoy, born Giovanna, was a daughter of Amadeus V, Count of Savoy, and his second wife Maria of Brabant. She was betrothed in September 1325 to Andronikos III Palaiologos, who was then involved in a civil war with his paternal grandfather Andronikos II Palaiologos. They married in October 1326. She joined the Eastern Orthodox Church and took the name Anna, and in Byzantium she was known as Anna Palaiologina. In 1328 Andronikos III entered Constantinople and finally deposed his grandfather.

Andronikos III died on 14 or 15 June 1341 and was succeeded by their son John V, three days short of his ninth birthday. Anna became regent with the titles augusta and autokratorissa. Andronikos had entrusted the administration to his adviser John Kantakouzenos, whom she distrusted. While Kantakouzenos was away dealing with Stefan Uroš IV Dušan of Serbia's invasion of northern Thrace, Patriarch John XIV and the courtier Alexios Apokaukos convinced her he was an enemy, and she declared him an enemy of the state. On 26 October 1341 Kantakouzenos proclaimed himself emperor at Didymoteicho, beginning a civil war that lasted until 1347.

Ivan Alexander of Bulgaria allied with Anna's side, while Stefan Dušan took the side of John VI Kantakouzenos, who later allied with Orhan I of the Ottoman emirate. Both rulers used the war for their own gain. Anna sought support in the West, and in summer 1343 an emissary declared her loyalty to Pope Clement VI in Avignon. In August 1343 she pawned the Byzantine crown jewels to Venice for 30,000 ducats, but the jewels disappeared and no help came. She lost the war, and her supporters deserted her.

On 3 February 1347 the two sides agreed that John VI would be senior emperor with John V as junior co-ruler, and John V would marry Helena Kantakouzene. John VI entered Constantinople and took effective control. In 1351 Anna went to Thessaloniki, where she held her own court, issued decrees in her name and controlled a mint, keeping the titles Augusta and Empress for some fourteen years. Her last official act was the donation of a convent to the Agioi Anargyroi. She became a nun, took the name Anastasia and died about 1365.
anna-walentynowicz: Anna Walentynowicz was born Anna Lubczyk in 1929 in the village of Sinne, in what is now Sadove in Ukraine, to a family of Ukrainian Shtundists. At the age of ten, during the Second World War, she began work as a maid, and after the war she moved into Poland. She began work at the Lenin Shipyard in Gdańsk in 1950, first as a welder and later as a crane operator. Recognised as an exemplary worker, she became disillusioned with the communist system, especially after the bloody events of December 1970 on the Baltic coast. She was never formally a member of the communist party, and she was a devout Catholic.

In 1978 Walentynowicz joined the newly formed Free Trade Unions of the Coast, and she edited the underground newssheet Robotnik Wybrzeża (The Coastal Worker), which she distributed at the shipyard. She was fired on 7 August 1980, five months before she planned to retire, for taking part in the illegal union. Workers struck on 14 August to demand her return. On 16 August management granted the shipyard's workers their demands, but Walentynowicz and Alina Pienkowska are credited in most eyewitness accounts with turning a strike over pay into one in solidarity with other striking workplaces, closing the gates to keep workers inside.

The Gdańsk Agreement of 31 August 1980 recognised the right to form free trade unions independent of the Party, and Solidarity registered soon afterwards with nearly ten million members. She sat on the presidium of the Interfactory Strike Committee. In October 1981 two security police officers tried to poison her at Radom, and a trial over the attempt began in 2015. After martial law was declared in December 1981 she helped organise a strike at the shipyard, was interned and was jailed on and off, in all for 19 months. She later criticised Lech Wałęsa for taking too much personal credit and for the distance between Solidarity's leaders and its workers.

Walentynowicz was awarded the Order of the White Eagle in 2006. She died on 10 April 2010 in the plane crash near Smolensk that also killed President Lech Kaczyński and many other Polish leaders on their way to commemorate the Katyn massacre. An exhumation in 2012 showed that another woman had been buried in her grave, and the bodies were reburied correctly. A square in Wrocław, a street in Szczecin and a monument in Kyiv bear her name, and the Sejm named 2019 the Year of Anna Walentynowicz. Time magazine chose her for its cover for 1980 in a series of women of the year.
annaba: Annaba lies in the north-eastern corner of Algeria, close to the Tunisian border and near the small Seybouse River. The present city grew up on the site of Aphrodisium, the seaport of the Roman city of Hippo Regius, and has since spread south over Hippo's ruins. Its former names Bône and Bona derive from Ubbo, a local form of Hippo. The Arabic name means "place of the jujubes", after the abundance of that fruit in the region.

Hippo Regius entered the record at the end of the 3rd century BCE as a possession of Massinissa's Numidian kingdom. Augustine of Hippo was its bishop from 396 until his death in 430. The Vandals destroyed the city in the 5th century and ruled it for about a century; in 534 their king Gelimer surrendered at Bône to Belisarius, general of the emperor Justinian I. After the Muslim conquest of the Maghreb in 699 Abbasids, Aghlabids, Fatimids and Zirids ruled it in turn. Flooding and the ravages of the Banu Hilal in 1033 led to its relocation to its present site.
The Kingdom of Sicily conquered it in 1153 and the Almohads took it in 1160. Hafsid rule began in 1250, and Ottoman rule in 1533, apart from Spanish rule from 1535 to 1540.

Under French rule from 1832, as Bône, it was a main French settlement with a sizeable pied-noir minority. A sheltered port of 80 hectares was built between 1856 and 1869 for iron ore from the Mokta el Hadid mine, and the railway from the mine, opened in 1864, was the first in Algeria. The mine produced 22,000 tonnes in 1865 and 255,000 in 1869. Bône had 10,000 inhabitants before the mine and 41,000 by 1924. In 1943 it was a crucial road and sea base for the Allied invasion of Tunisia in Operation Torch. It remained part of French Algeria until independence in 1962.

Annaba is a leading industrial centre of Algeria, with a large steel complex at El Hadjar south of the city. The Basilica of Saint Augustine recalls the ancient diocese of Hippo. The Bône War Cemetery, 5 kilometres from the city, holds 868 Commonwealth burials of the Second World War.
annaberg-buchholz: Annaberg-Buchholz lies in the Ore Mountains of Saxony, beside the Pöhlberg, which rises to 832 metres above sea level, and is the capital of the district of Erzgebirgskreis. The upper Ore Mountains were heavily forested until Franconian farmers settled them in the 12th and 13th centuries. Frohnau, Geyersdorf and Kleinrückerswalde, now part of the town, have been attested since 1397.

Silver deposits were discovered in the area in 1491, and Annaberg developed under the patronage of George, Duke of Saxony, and Barbara Jagiellon. They founded St. Anne's Church and a Franciscan monastery, dissolved in 1539, and Barbara gave the church a relic of Saint Anne, which made it a regional pilgrimage destination. The church, built between 1499 and 1525, is the largest of its kind in Saxony. The mines produced silver, tin and cobalt until before the First World War.

Barbara Uthmann introduced braid and lace-making in 1561, and Belgian refugees fleeing the Duke of Alba developed the craft in the 1590s. Annaberg and Buchholz were joined by rail to Chemnitz in the 19th century and each had a school for lace-making. In 1945 the two towns merged. From 1952 to 1990 the town was part of the Bezirk Karl-Marx-Stadt of East Germany.

The old town and market square are well known, and the Ore Mountains are called the Land of Christmas for their markets and carved figures. Annaberg's Christmas market ends with a miners' parade, the Bergparade. The town has monuments to Luther, to the mathematician Adam Ries and to Barbara Uthmann, and an Adam Ries Museum. After reunification in 1990 some old mines were restored for visitors. The Frohnauer Hammer, a working hammer mill at Frohnau, was declared a technical monument in 1907 and is open to the public.
annales-cambriae: The Annales Cambriae, Latin for Annals of Wales, is the title given to a complex of Latin chronicles compiled or derived from diverse sources at St David's in Dyfed, Wales. The earliest surviving text is a 12th-century presumed copy of an original of the middle of the 10th century, and later editions were compiled in the 13th century. Despite the name, the chronicles record not only events in Wales but also events in Ireland, Cornwall, England and Scotland, and sometimes further afield, although in the later two thirds of the text the focus is especially on Wales.

The chronicles are best known for their entries on King Arthur, Medraut (Mordred) and Merlin. In the A Text, year 72 (c. 516) records the Battle of Badon, in which Arthur carried the cross of Jesus Christ on his shoulders for three days and three nights and the Britons were victors. Year 93 (c. 537) records the Strife of Camlann, in which Arthur and Medraut fell and there was death in Britain and in Ireland. Merlin is not mentioned in the A Text, but year 129 (c. 573) records the Battle of Armterid, the Arfderydd that Welsh medieval literature associates with him.

Texts B and C omit the second half of the record for year 93. In the B Text the record for year 129 continues that the battle was fought between the sons of Elifer and Guendoleu son of Keidau, and that Guendoleu fell and Merlin went mad. Both texts show the influence of Geoffrey of Monmouth's Historia Regum Britanniae, as the form Merlinus, first found in Geoffrey, shows.

The Arthurian entries were once presented as proof that Arthur and Merlin existed, but that view is no longer widely held, since they could have been added as late as 970, long after the early Arthurian myth had developed. The cross at Badon is mirrored by a passage in Nennius, in which Arthur bears the image of the Virgin Mary on his shoulders, and the Old Welsh words for shoulder and shield were easily confused.
annals-of-the-joseon-dynasty: The Annals of the Joseon Dynasty, called the Veritable Records or sillok, are state-compiled records of the reigns of the Joseon kings in Korea, kept from 1392. They run to 1,893 volumes and are thought to be the longest continual documentation of a single dynasty in the world. They are written in Classical Chinese. The records of the first three kings, Taejo, Jeongjong and Taejong, were handwritten; those of Sejong, who reigned from 1418 to 1450, and later kings were printed with movable type, wooden and metal, making Korea the first nation in East Asia to print its royal records this way. The sillok is designated the 151st national treasure of South Korea and is listed in UNESCO's Memory of the World register.

Eight historians of the seventh, eighth and ninth ranks in the Office of Royal Decrees kept daily records of court activities. They accompanied the king at all times, and the Joseon kings did not conduct official business without a historian present. These daily records, the sacho, were the basis of the annals, which a special committee of high-ranking officials and scholars compiled after a king's death. Three drafts were made, and the drafts, the sacho and the historians' private memoranda were then pulped in water to prevent leaks. Historians were guaranteed legal protection and editorial independence, and only they were allowed to read the sacho.

A story in the records of Taejong shows the principle. In the fourth year of his reign, equivalent to 18 March 1404 in the Julian calendar, the king fell from his horse while shooting at a deer and said, 'Do not let the historians know about this.' The historian present recorded both the fall and the order.

From 1445 three additional copies were made and stored in Chungju, Jeonju and Seongju as well as in Seoul. During the Japanese invasions of 1592 to 1598 all but the Jeonju copy were destroyed, and the Jeonju records escaped fire only because scholars acted on their own initiative. Afterwards five repositories were kept, at the Ch'unch'ugwan, Mount Myohyang, Taebaeksan, Odaesan and Manisan. The Ch'unch'ugwan repository was destroyed in Yi Kwal's rebellion of 1624, and part of the Manisan collection was lost in the Qing invasion of 1636.

During the colonial period from 1910 to 1945 the Odaesan copies were taken to Tokyo Imperial University and mostly destroyed in the Great Kantō earthquake of 1923. The remaining 46 volumes were returned to Korea in 2006, the year the National Institute of Korean History digitised the annals and put them online.
annals-of-ulster: The entries run from 431 to 1540. Those up to 1489 were written by the scribe Ruaidhrí Ó Luinín for his patron Cathal Óg Mac Maghnusa on the island of Senadh-Mic-Maghnusa, now Belle Isle, near Lisbellaw on Lough Erne in the kingdom of Fir Manach, and later hands carried them on to 1540. Entries to the mid-6th century are retrospective, taken from earlier annals and histories; later ones were contemporary. T. M. Charles-Edwards holds that the main source for the first millennium was a lost Armagh continuation of the Chronicle of Ireland. Trinity College, Dublin, keeps the original manuscript, and a contemporary copy in the Bodleian Library in Oxford fills some of its gaps.

The annals are written in Irish with some entries in Latin, and because their sources were copied word for word they are also valuable for the history of the Irish language. They follow the lives of kings, their battles, raids and deaths: Máel Sechnaill mac Máele Ruanaid, king of the southern Uí Néill, appears from 839 until his death in 862, described as king of all Ireland, and Aed mac Neill's death in 879 is marked with a poem. Viking kings of Dublin such as Amlaíb Conung are followed in the same way, and Dublin, as Áth Cliath or Duiblinn, appears 66 times.

The first notice of the Vikings, in 794, reports the devastation of all the islands of Britain by heathens. Later entries record their raids for plunder and captives, such as the women carried off from Étar in 821, and by 841 their naval camp at Duiblinn. The annals call them foreigners, heathens, Norsemen and Danes, and often show them allied with one Irish faction against another, while some Irishmen are accused of raiding in the manner of the heathens. The battles of Brunanburh, Tara and Clontarf are noted briefly.

A century after they were compiled, the Annals of Ulster became an important source for the Annals of the Four Masters, and they also inform the Irish text Cogad Gáedel re Gallaib. There are two main modern English translations, by B. MacCarthy and by Seán Mac Airt and Gearóid Mac Niocaill in 1983.
annapolis-maryland: Annapolis lies on Chesapeake Bay at the mouth of the Severn River, 25 miles south of Baltimore and about 30 miles east of Washington, D.C. The city is part of the Atlantic Coastal Plain and is relatively flat, its highest point only 50 feet above sea level. It is the closest state capital to the national capital and, in land area, the smallest of the capital cities of the United States. It has a strong maritime culture and is known as America's Sailing Capital.

In 1649 Puritan exiles from Virginia, led by the third proprietary governor of Maryland, William Stone, founded a settlement called Providence on the north shore of the Severn. The settlers later moved to a better-protected harbour on the south shore. The settlement there was known from 1683 as the Town at Proctor's, then as the Town at the Severn, and in 1694 it received the name Anne Arundel's Towne. In 1696 St. John's College was founded in the city.

In 1783–1784 Annapolis was the seat of the Confederation Congress, the former Second Continental Congress, and the temporary national capital. On 23 December 1783 General George Washington resigned his commission as commander of the Continental Army before the Congress in the new Maryland State House. The Congress ratified the Treaty of Paris, which ended the American Revolutionary War, there on 14 January 1784, so that Annapolis became the first peacetime capital of the United States. It was also the site of the 1786 Annapolis Convention, which called on the states to send delegates to the Constitutional Convention held at Philadelphia the next year.

The Maryland State House, begun in 1772, with the legislature first meeting there in 1779, is the oldest in continuous legislative use in the United States. It is topped by the largest wooden dome built without nails in the country. In 1861 the midshipmen of the Naval Academy, established in 1845, were moved to Newport, Rhode Island, until 1865, and Camp Parole, a camp for paroled soldiers, was set up on the grounds of St. John's College; the Annapolis National Cemetery holds those who died. In July 1940 Grand Duchess Charlotte of Luxembourg arrived in Annapolis in exile.

Annapolis is the capital of Maryland and the county seat of Anne Arundel County, with a population of 40,812 at the 2020 census. The state legislature, the governor's office and the appellate courts are located there. The United States Naval Academy stands adjacent to the city limits, and the city hosts each year the largest in-water sailboat show in the world.
annapolis-royal: Annapolis Royal is a town in western Nova Scotia and the county seat of Annapolis County, on the Annapolis Basin. Its site, where the Annapolis and Allain rivers meet, is called Nme'juaqnek, 'the place of bountiful fish', by the Mi'kmaq, for whom it was for generations a gathering place for chiefs and leaders and a hub on the canoe routes between the Bay of Fundy and the South Shore. 'Port Royal' originally referred to the basin and was named by Samuel de Champlain in 1604.

The French settlement of Port Royal was founded in 1605 by Pierre Dugua, François Gravé Du Pont and Champlain, at a habitation about ten kilometres west of the present town, and it was the first year-round European settlement in Canada. Attackers from Virginia destroyed it in 1613. In August 1629 Scottish settlers under Sir William Alexander founded Charles Fort on the site of present-day Fort Anne, and the Treaty of Saint-Germain-en-Laye returned it to France in 1632. Under French rule it grew modestly, with about 400 people by 1671, and was often attacked and captured, only to be restored by treaty or recapture.

In 1710, during Queen Anne's War, it was captured for the last time and renamed for the queen. The Treaty of Utrecht gave Acadia to Britain in 1713, and from 1710 to 1749 the governor of Nova Scotia sat there; the Nova Scotia Council was formed there in 1720. French, Acadian and Mi'kmaq forces failed to retake it in 1711 and in four attempts during King George's War between 1744 and 1746. In December 1755, 251 men, 263 women and 1,150 children were loaded onto seven ships at Fort Anne and deported. From 1759 to 1768 some 8,000 New Englanders settled in the valley, and Loyalists arrived after the American Revolution. The fort ceased to be a military post in 1854.

Annapolis Royal was incorporated as a town in 1893. Its core is the Annapolis Royal Historic District National Historic Site, designated in 1994, which includes Fort Anne, Canada's oldest National Historic Site. The town lies within the Southwest Nova Biosphere Reserve, and its economy centres on tourism, heritage and services. The Annapolis Royal Generating Station, a tidal power station, operated from 1984 until 2019, and in 1984 the town elected Daurene Lewis, the first Black woman mayor in Canada.
anne-frank: Annelies Marie Frank was born on 12 June 1929 in Frankfurt, the younger daughter of Edith Frank, née Holländer, and Otto Heinrich Frank. Her sister was Margot. The family were Reform Jews who lived among a mixed community of Jewish and non-Jewish citizens, and her parents, who encouraged reading, kept an extensive library. In 1934, after Adolf Hitler had been appointed to govern Germany, the family moved to Amsterdam, among about 300,000 Jews who left Germany between 1933 and 1939. Anne joined the 6th Montessori School there. German occupation trapped the family in May 1940, and in 1941 she lost her German citizenship and became stateless.

For her thirteenth birthday on 12 June 1942 Anne received an autograph book with a small lock, which she decided to use as a diary and named Kitty. On 6 July 1942, as persecution of Jews increased, the Franks moved into a hiding place, the Achterhuis or Secret Annex, a three-storey space entered from a landing above the Opekta offices on the Prinsengracht, where Otto Frank's trusted employees acted as their helpers. A bookcase later covered the door. In the diary she wrote about the restrictions on Dutch Jews and about the strongly differing personalities of the people sharing the annex, and about her relationships with her family. She grew closer to Margot as she matured, and was closest emotionally to her father.

On 4 August 1944 German police led by SS-Oberscharführer Karl Silberbauer raided the annex. How it was found is uncertain: a biography of 2015 suggested a betrayal, and research published by the Anne Frank House in 2016 pointed to an investigation of ration-card fraud as a possible cause, without ruling out betrayal. The Franks were taken to Westerbork and, on the last transport from there, to Auschwitz on 3 September 1944. On 1 November 1944 Anne and Margot were moved to Bergen-Belsen, where they died, probably of typhus, in February or March 1945.

Otto Frank was the only member of the family to survive. Miep Gies and Bep Voskuijl had saved Anne's notebooks, and in July 1945 Gies gave them to him. He published the diary in 1947, and it appeared in English in 1952 as The Diary of a Young Girl. It has been translated into more than 70 languages and is the basis of several plays and films. Later editions restored passages cut from the first, including pages removed by Otto Frank himself. The Anne Frank House, opened on 3 May 1960, preserves the Prinsengracht building.
anne-hutchinson: Anne Marbury was baptised at Alford, Lincolnshire, on 20 July 1591, the daughter of the Anglican cleric Francis Marbury and Bridget Dryden. Her father had Puritan leanings, believed that clergy should be well educated, and had been censured and imprisoned for challenging his superiors. He gave her a far better education than most girls received. On 9 August 1612 she married William Hutchinson, a fabric merchant from Alford, at St Mary Woolnoth in London, and the couple returned to Alford, where they followed the preacher John Cotton in Boston, Lincolnshire. Cotton was compelled to emigrate in 1633, and the Hutchinsons followed a year later with their children; they had 15 in all.

The family arrived in Boston, Massachusetts, in the late summer of 1634 and built one of the largest houses on the peninsula. Anne worked as a midwife and gave spiritual advice to women in childbirth. She began hosting weekly meetings at which women discussed Cotton's sermons and heard her explanations, and the gatherings grew so popular that she held meetings for men too, sometimes for 60 people or more a week. She accused the colony's ministers, except Cotton and her brother-in-law John Wheelwright, of preaching a covenant of works rather than a covenant of grace. The dispute became known as the Antinomian Controversy, more recently called the Free Grace Controversy, and it shook the colony from 1636 to 1638.

She was tried for heresy, convicted and banished. During her imprisonment, supporters including her husband signed the Portsmouth Compact on 7 March 1638, and with the encouragement of Roger Williams they settled on Aquidneck Island in Narragansett Bay; she followed in April. After her husband's death, threats from Massachusetts to annex Rhode Island led her, some time after the summer of 1642, to move into Dutch New Netherland, near what became the Hutchinson River. In August 1643, during Kieft's War, Hutchinson, six of her children and others of her household were killed by Siwanoy people. Only her nine-year-old daughter Susanna was spared and taken captive.

Hutchinson claimed to be a prophetess who received direct revelation, and she taught that such revelation was as authoritative as the Bible, which Puritan clergy held to be antithetical to their theology. Cotton, John Winthrop and other former friends came to see her as an antinomian heretic. She is a key figure in the history of religious freedom in the English colonies and of women in ministry, and a monument at the Massachusetts State House honours her as a courageous exponent of civil liberty and religious toleration. In 1987 Governor Michael Dukakis pardoned her, revoking the banishment ordered 350 years earlier.
anne-marie-louise-dorleans-duchess-of-mo: Anne Marie Louise d'Orléans was born at the Louvre in Paris on 29 May 1627, the daughter of Gaston, Duke of Orléans, brother of Louis XIII, and his first wife Marie, Duchess of Montpensier. Her mother died five days after the birth and left her heiress to an immense fortune that included five duchies, the Dauphinate of Auvergne and the sovereign Principality of Dombes. She was known from birth as Mademoiselle, and her uncle Louis XIII gave her the new title Petite-Fille de France.

Her father was involved in conspiracies against Louis XIII and Cardinal Richelieu, and for two years after his secret marriage of 1632 she did not see him. When Louis XIV was born in 1638 she declared that she would marry him, calling him her little husband.

Mademoiselle played a prominent part in the Fronde. In 1650 she helped bring about the peace that ended the siege of Bordeaux, which made Queen Anne regard her as a frondeuse. In 1652 she went to Orléans on her father's behalf, entered the city through a gate on the river after the town's gates stayed shut, and stayed five weeks. On 2 July 1652, to let the Prince of Condé into Paris, she fired the cannon of the Bastille on the army of Turenne. Cardinal Mazarin remarked that with that cannon she had shot her husband, and she fled to Saint-Fargeau, where she stayed in exile until 1657.

Her plans to marry came to nothing. Proposals included Holy Roman Emperor Ferdinand III, Alfonso VI of Portugal and Charles Emmanuel II of Savoy. In 1670 she asked Louis XIV for permission to marry Antoine Nompar de Caumont, later Duke of Lauzun, and he first consented. Under pressure from the court he withdrew his consent on 18 December 1670, and in 1671 Lauzun was arrested and held at Pignerol until 1681. She secured his release on 2 February 1681 by selling the principality of Dombes and the County of Eu to the king's son, the Duke of Maine.

Mademoiselle fell ill on 15 March 1693 and refused to admit Lauzun. She died at the Palais du Luxembourg on 5 April 1693, unmarried and childless, and left her fortune to her cousin Philippe, Duke of Orléans. She was buried at the Royal Basilica of Saint Denis on 19 April. She is remembered for her part in the Fronde and for her Mémoires, which she began writing during an exile in the 1660s. She is also credited with bringing the composer Jean-Baptiste Lully to the king's court.
anne-of-brittany: Anne was born on 25 or 26 January 1477 in the Castle of the Dukes of Brittany in Nantes, the eldest child of Duke Francis II of Brittany and his second wife Margaret of Foix. She was raised by a governess, Françoise de Dinan, and probably learned to read and write in French and perhaps a little Latin. Because Francis II had no son, the Estates of Brittany recognised her as his heiress on 10 February 1486, and he promised her in marriage to various princes to obtain aid against the King of France.

Francis II died on 9 September 1488, after being defeated at Saint-Aubin-du-Cormier, and Anne became Duchess of Brittany at eleven. On his deathbed he made her promise never to consent to the subjugation of the duchy to France. She married Charles VIII of France in 1491 and was crowned queen at St. Denis on 8 February 1492, although the king forbade her to use the title of duchess. None of their children survived early childhood.

When Charles VIII died on 4 April 1498 she took charge of the administration of Brittany. She agreed to marry the new king, Louis XII, if he obtained an annulment from his wife Joan, and they married at Nantes on 7 January 1499. The contract recognised her right to the title Duchess of Brittany and made the couple's second child her heir, though this clause was not respected. She was crowned again on 18 November 1504, and was a patron of poets, musicians and artists.

Anne died of a kidney-stone attack at the Château de Blois on 9 January 1514. Her will left Brittany to her second daughter Renée, but Louis XII ignored it, confirmed the elder daughter Claude as duchess and married her to Francis, son of Louise of Savoy, who became King Francis I in 1515. This marriage later led to the formal union of France and Brittany.

Royal propaganda presented Anne as a perfect queen, a symbol of union between France and Brittany, and Breton regionalists chose her as a figure of patriotism in the mid-19th century. Historians disagree about her character: Georges Minois called her limited, petty and vindictive, while Philippe Tourault described a favourable personality attached to her country. With her husbands she built at the châteaux of Blois and Amboise.
anne-of-cleves: Anne was born in Düsseldorf in 1515, on either 22 September or 28 June, the second daughter of John III, Duke of Cleves, and Maria, Duchess of Jülich-Berg. She grew up in Schloss Burg near Solingen. Her father was influenced by Erasmus and followed a moderate course in the Reformation, siding with the Schmalkaldic League against Emperor Charles V. In 1527 she was betrothed to Francis, son of Antoine, Duke of Lorraine, but the betrothal was cancelled in 1535. Her brother William became Duke of Jülich-Cleves-Berg after their father's death in 1538. She had received no formal education and could read and write only in German.

Thomas Cromwell urged the match on Henry VIII, who sought an alliance with the German Protestants against France and the Holy Roman Empire. Hans Holbein the Younger painted Anne and her sister Amalia at Düren, and the king, finding the portrait flattering, agreed to the marriage. The treaty was signed on 4 October 1539. Henry first met Anne privately at Rochester on New Year's Day 1540, disguised, and was disappointed; he is reported to have said she was nothing so fair as she had been reported. The wedding took place on 6 January 1540 at Greenwich, performed by Archbishop Thomas Cranmer.

The marriage was never consummated. Anne was told to leave court on 24 June, and she consented to an annulment, granted on 12 July 1540 on grounds of non-consummation and her earlier pre-contract to Francis of Lorraine. Cromwell, the moving force behind the match, was attainted for treason. Anne received a generous settlement, including Richmond Palace and Hever Castle, and became known as the King's Beloved Sister, with precedence over all women in England except the king's wife and daughters.

Anne stayed in England for the rest of her life and never returned to Germany. She changed religion with the monarch, conforming to Catholic worship in 1540 and again under Mary I, whose coronation procession she joined in 1553. She lost royal favour in 1554 after Wyatt's rebellion, when the imperial ambassador Simon Renard suspected her of involvement in a plot linked to Elizabeth. She dictated her will in July 1557 at Chelsea Old Manor, where she died on 16 July, probably of cancer. She was buried in Westminster Abbey on 3 August, and she was the last of Henry VIII's wives to die.
anne-of-france: Anne was born at the Chateau of Genappe in Brabant on 3 April 1461, the eldest surviving daughter of King Louis XI by Charlotte of Savoy. She was betrothed to Nicholas, Duke of Lorraine, and was made Viscountess of Thouars in 1468, but Nicholas broke the engagement to pursue Mary of Burgundy and died in 1473. On 3 November 1473, when she was twelve, she married Peter of Bourbon, who had been ceded the title Lord of Beaujeu, and she took up rule of the Beaujolais. Her father called her the least foolish woman in France.

During the minority of Charles VIII, Anne and Peter held the regency from 1483 to 1491. They kept royal authority and the kingdom's unity against the Orléans party, which was in open revolt in the Mad War of 1483 to 1488. Concessions were made and land was restored to hostile nobles, including the future Louis XII, then Duke of Orléans, who tried to obtain the regency but was opposed by the Estates General. She supplied Henry Tudor with French troops for his 1485 invasion, which ended at the Battle of Bosworth on 22 August. She made the Treaty of Etaples and in 1491 arranged the marriage of Charles to Anne, Duchess of Brittany, to annex Brittany to the crown.

Her regency faded during 1491 and 1492, ending with an oath of mutual protection on 5 July 1492, and she left for the Duchy of Bourbon. She had Peter's nephew declared illegitimate so that he inherited the duchy. Anne raised many children of the aristocracy, among them Diane de Poitiers and Louise of Savoy, and oversaw the education of Margaret of Austria. Her daughter Suzanne was born on 10 May 1491 and succeeded Peter as Duchess of Bourbon on his death in 1503. Anne then administered the Bourbon lands with her own court at Chantelle, and in 1505 she married Suzanne to Charles of Montpensier.

Anne wrote an instruction book for her daughter, Lessons for My Daughter. In it she advises Suzanne to surround herself with frugal people and holds that true nobility comes from being humble, benign and courteous, and that without these other virtues are worth nothing. She died in 1522; Suzanne had died before her without surviving children, and Anne's line and that of her father became extinct.
anne-robert-jacques-turgot: Turgot was born in Paris on 10 May 1727, the youngest son of Michel-Étienne Turgot, provost of the merchants of Paris, from an old Norman family. He was educated for the Church and admitted to the Sorbonne in 1749, but in 1750 decided not to take holy orders, saying that he could not bear to wear a mask all his life. That year he wrote a work on the Idea of Progress, which covers the whole of culture, including institutions, legal codes and economy. He met the physiocrats Quesnay and Vincent de Gournay and wrote articles for the Encyclopédie.

In August 1761 Turgot became intendant of the generalité of Limoges, among the poorest and most over-taxed parts of France, and remained thirteen years. He surveyed the land to assess the taille more justly and replaced the corvée with a money tax, which let him leave a good system of highways.

Louis XVI made him minister of the navy in July 1774 and Controller-General of Finances on 24 August. His principles were no bankruptcy, no increase of taxation and no borrowing. His edict of 13 September 1774 freed the grain trade, and after the poor harvest of 1774 he firmly repressed the bread riots known as the guerre des farines. In January 1776 he presented the Six Edicts, of which the two most opposed suppressed the corvées and the craft guilds' privileges. He had nearly everyone against him, the queen included, and on 12 May 1776 he was ordered to resign. He spent his last years in scientific and literary study and died on 18 March 1781.

His best-known work, Reflections on the Formation and Distribution of Wealth, was written in 1766 and published separately in 1776. It divides society into three classes, develops Quesnay's theory that land is the only source of wealth, proposes a single tax on the land's net product and demands complete freedom of commerce and industry. He is thought to have been the first political economist to postulate something like the law of diminishing marginal returns in agriculture.
anscarids: The family's fortunes began with Anscar, a petty Burgundian count. With the support of Fulk the Venerable, archbishop of Rheims, he brought Guy III of Spoleto to Langres to be crowned King of France in 887. When the plot failed, Anscar and his brother went back to Italy with Guy and 500 Burgundian troops to seek the throne of Berengar I, and Guy rewarded him with the March of Ivrea. Anscar's descendants held the march until 1030.

Anscar's grandson Berengar seized the Italian throne in 950 after the death of Lothair II and imprisoned Lothair's widow Adelaide when she refused to marry his son Adalbert II. Emperor Otto I forced him to do homage in 952 and formally deposed father and son in 963. From 1002 to 1014 Arduin of Italy held the Italian throne in opposition to the German Henry II. Adalbert fled to Burgundy, and his son Otto William, adopted by Otto-Henry, Duke of Burgundy, became the first count of the County of Burgundy, created in 982.

Renaud III used the title franc-comte from 1127 to mark his independence of the emperor, though he had to submit to Conrad III. His heiress Beatrice married Frederick Barbarossa, and the county passed to the Hohenstaufen, returning to the house when Hugh of Chalon married Adelaide, countess of Burgundy. The main line ended with Otto IV in 1303. A younger line, Chalon-Arlay, acquired the principality of Orange and ended with Philibert of Chalon in 1530.

Raymond, fourth son of Count William I of Burgundy, travelled to Castile-León in the late 11th century and married the future queen Urraca. Their son Alfonso VII succeeded her, and the cadet Castilian branch ruled the Kingdom of Galicia from 1111 and Castile and León until 1369. The monarchs of Castile and León remained their male-line descendants until the 16th century, for the House of Trastámara, which took the crown in the late 14th century and ruled at times in Castile, Aragon, Naples and Navarre, was an illegitimate cadet branch of the family.
anschluss: The idea of an Anschluss, a union of Austria and Germany in a Greater Germany, arose after the unification of Germany in 1871 excluded Austria, and gained support after the Austro-Hungarian Empire fell in 1918. The Treaty of Versailles and the 1919 treaty of Saint Germain forbade the union. Support was strong in the 1920s, particularly on the Austrian left and centre, because many believed Austria, stripped of its imperial lands, was not viable economically. After Adolf Hitler became German chancellor on 30 January 1933 the aim was identified with the Nazi regime. Austrian Nazis assassinated the Austrian chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss during an attempted coup in July 1934.

On 12 February 1938, at Berchtesgaden, under threat of invasion, Chancellor Kurt Schuschnigg accepted an ultimatum to appoint the Austrian Nazi Arthur Seyss-Inquart as minister of the interior. On 9 March he announced a referendum on independence for 13 March. On 11 March Hitler demanded its cancellation and Schuschnigg's resignation, and President Wilhelm Miklas reluctantly appointed Seyss-Inquart in his place. Seyss-Inquart invited the German army to cross the border to restore order.

The 8th Army crossed on the morning of 12 March, and the Austrian army had been ordered not to resist. Many Austrians cheered the troops, though one anti-Nazi German observer suspected the welcome was staged. Within days 70,000 people had been arrested. A referendum on 10 April officially recorded 99.7 per cent approval. Historians agree the votes were accurately counted, but the vote was neither free nor secret, and about 360,000 people, 8 per cent of the eligible voters, had lost the right to vote.

The campaign against Austria's Jews began at once. They were driven through the streets of Vienna and their homes and shops were plundered, and over 6,000 Jews were arrested during the Kristallnacht pogrom of 9 and 10 November. The Anschluss was among the first steps towards the Greater German Reich, followed by the Munich Agreement of September 1938 and the dismantling of Czechoslovakia in March 1939. The Moscow Declaration of 1943 declared the annexation null and void, and a provisional government did the same on 27 April 1945. Austria stayed under Allied control until the Austrian State Treaty of 1955 restored its sovereignty.
anselm-of-canterbury: Anselm was born in or around Aosta between April 1033 and April 1034. At fifteen he wished to enter a monastery but could not obtain his father's consent. At 23 he left home and wandered for three years through Burgundy and France, and in 1059 he reached the Benedictine abbey of Bec in Normandy, where his countryman Lanfranc of Pavia was prior. On the advice of Maurilius, Archbishop of Rouen, he entered Bec as a novice at 27, was elected prior in 1063 and, after the death of the founder Herluin, abbot in 1078.

Anselm became Archbishop of Canterbury in 1093. He asserted the primacy of Canterbury over York and the Welsh bishops, and historians have traditionally seen his term as the English part of the Investiture Controversy. His resistance to royal control of the Church led to exile twice, from 1097 to 1100 and from 1105 to 1107, and in exile he took part in the Council of Bari.

The Monologion, written in 1075 and 1076, gives reasons for belief in God without appeal to scripture, at the request of his fellow monks. The Proslogion, of 1077 and 1078, seeks a single argument that proves God's existence: the being than which none greater can be conceived must exist, since one lacking existence could be surpassed. The monk Gaunilo answered with a parody about a perfect island, and Anselm replied that he had misunderstood. Kant's treatment gave it the name ontological argument.

Cur Deus Homo, written from 1095 to 1098 as a dialogue with his student Boso, argues that humanity's offence against God could be repaid only by one both divine and human, whose death has infinite worth. It largely replaced the earlier theory centred on Satan's power over fallen man, though critics have found its argument legalist.

Anselm died on 21 April 1109, now his feast day. His chaplain Eadmer wrote a biography soon after, and his students included Gilbert Crispin and Anselm of Laon. His works influenced Thomas Aquinas, Duns Scotus and William of Ockham, and he is often called the father of scholasticism. Thomas Becket asked for his canonization in 1163, and he was proclaimed a Doctor of the Church in 1720. Modern scholars remain divided: Southern upholds Eadmer's picture of a reluctant churchman, while Vaughn sees a skilled political operator.
ansgar: Ansgar was born on 8 September 801 into a noble Frankish family near Amiens. After his mother's early death he was brought up in the Benedictine monastery of Corbie in Picardy. According to the Vita Ansgarii, written by his pupil and successor Rimbert, a vision of his mother in the company of Mary, mother of Jesus, changed his careless attitude toward spiritual matters to seriousness. In 822 he was one of the missionaries sent to found the abbey of Corvey in Westphalia, where he became a teacher and preacher.

Ansgar went north to Jutland with King Harald Klak, who had been baptised in exile, but Harald's fall in 827 closed their school for the sons of courtiers. In 829 the Swedish king Björn at Hauge requested missionaries, and Louis the Pious sent Ansgar. He spent six months at Birka on Lake Mälaren and organised a small congregation. In 831 Louis appointed him to the new archbishopric of Hamburg-Bremen, with the right to send missions to all the northern lands, and he received the pallium in Rome.

In 845 the Danes raided Hamburg and destroyed all the church's treasures and books, leaving him with neither see nor revenue. In 847 Louis the German named him to the vacant diocese of Bremen, where he moved in 848. Pope Nicholas I approved the union of the two sees only in 864. Ansgar kept on good terms with the Danish kings Horik the Elder and his son Horik II and obtained permission to build a church at Sleswick. He also spent two years in Sweden, from 848 to 850.

Ansgar was buried in Bremen in 865. Rimbert wrote that he wore a rough hair shirt, lived on bread and water and showed great charity to the poor. Pope Nicholas I declared him a saint shortly after his death, and he was later called Patron of Scandinavia. A collection of brief prayers, Pigmenta, is reputedly his.
Statues of him stand in Hamburg, Copenhagen and Ribe, and a stone cross stands at Birka. His feast day is 3 February, and the lunar crater Ansgarius is named after him.
antaeus: Antaeus, whose Greek name means opponent, was known to the Berbers as Anti and appears in both Berber and Greek mythology. In Greek sources he lived in the interior desert of Libya. According to the Roman geographer Pomponius Mela his wife was the goddess Tinjis, for whom the city of Tangier in Morocco was said to be named, though it could be the other way round. His daughter Iphinoe consorted with Heracles. He was probably incorporated into Greek mythology after the Greek colonisation of Cyrenaica in the mid-seventh century BCE.

Antaeus challenged all passers-by to wrestling matches and remained invincible as long as he stayed in contact with his mother, the earth. Because Greek wrestling, like modern wrestling, aimed to force opponents to the ground, he always won and killed his opponents. He built a temple to his father with their skulls. Heracles met him on his way to the Garden of the Hesperides, as part of his eleventh labour. Heracles found that he could not beat Antaeus by throwing or pinning him, so he held him aloft and crushed him to death in a bear hug.

Ancient Greek art shows the myth from the 6th century BCE, mostly from Attica. Antaeus is bearded and hairy, sometimes shown large and often shrunk for lack of space, and figures such as Athena or Hermes may be present. Scenes where Heracles lifts Antaeus do not appear at first and may date from the later 5th century BCE, becoming popular in the following century. The contest was a favoured subject of Renaissance sculpture.

The location of the home of Antaeus was flexible. When the Roman commander Quintus Sertorius crossed from Hispania to North Africa, the people of Tingis told him that the giant remains of Antaeus lay in a tumulus. His men dug it open and found giant bones, and Sertorius closed it and made offerings. It has been proposed that this monument is the Msoura stone circle, 50 kilometres from Tangier.

The client king Juba II claimed descent from a union of Heracles and Tinga, the consort of Antaeus. Plutarch recounts a local story in which Heracles had a son, Sophax, by Tinge, who named Tingis after his mother, and Sophax was the father of Diodorus. Some said Heracles also had a son, Palaemon, by Iphinoe. The ancient city of Barca was also called Antapolis after Antaeus, and Antaeopolis was the Graeco-Roman name of the Egyptian city of Tjebu, whose tutelary god Nemty was identified with him, although that god may be different from the Libyan Antaeus.
antananarivo: Antananarivo stands about 1,280 metres above sea level in the Central Highlands of Madagascar, 160 kilometres from the east coast and 330 kilometres from the west coast. The city occupies the summit and slopes of a long, narrow, rocky ridge about 4 kilometres in length, rising some 200 metres above the rice fields to the west. It was originally a town called Analamanga, "Blue Forest", established by the Vazimba, considered the island's first occupants.

According to oral history, the Merina King Andrianjaka, who had migrated from the south-east coast, took the site with a garrison of 1,000 soldiers, and the city later took its name, Antananarivo, "City of the Thousand", from them under King Andriamasinavalona. Andrianjaka built a rova, a fortified royal compound, that grew to enclose the royal palaces and the tombs of Merina royalty. Accounts date the founding to around 1610 or 1625. Early Merina kings used statute labour to build a system of irrigated paddy fields and dikes around the city, of which the largest, the Betsimitatatra, still produces rice.

By 1810, when Radama I came to the throne, Antananarivo was the largest and most economically important city on the island, with over 80,000 inhabitants. Radama admitted the first European settlers, artisan missionaries of the London Missionary Society, who arrived in 1820 and opened the city's first public schools. His conquests brought nearly two-thirds of the island under his control, and the Merina sovereigns declared Antananarivo the capital of the whole island. Between 1829 and 1842, through war, forced labour, disease and harsh justice, the population of Imerina fell from 750,000 to 130,000. In the last years of the kingdom, most of the city's 50,000 to 75,000 people were slaves, largely captured in provincial campaigns.

The French military invaded Antananarivo in September 1894, and the queen surrendered after a cannon shell blasted a hole through a building at the Rova. The French made it the capital of their colony, writing the name as Tananarive. They built the Governor General's Residency at Antaninarenina, later the presidential offices, cut tunnels through two of the largest hills, and brought in water from the Ikopa River, sewers and electricity.

Antananarivo is the capital and largest city of Madagascar, with 1,274,225 inhabitants at the 2018 census and an urban area of almost 2.3 million. It is home to the Presidency, National Assembly, Senate and Supreme Court. The royal compound's largest building, the Manjakamiadana palace, stands at the summit of the hills; a fire in 1995 left only its stone casing, which was restored by 2009. Before the mid-19th century houses were built of wood, grasses and reeds, and only family tombs were of stone, a material thought fitting for the dead.
antanas-smetona: Antanas Smetona was born on 10 August 1874 in the village of Užulėnis in the Kovno Governorate of the Russian Empire, the eighth of nine children of a farming family of former serfs. His father died when he was eleven. He attended the Palanga Progymnasium, where Lithuanian books banned by the Tsarist authorities were easier to obtain, and the Jelgava Gymnasium, and in 1897 entered the law faculty of the University of Saint Petersburg. He joined Lithuanian student societies, rejected the socialist ideas he met, and was briefly imprisoned and deported to Vilnius for taking part in the student protests of February 1899. He graduated in 1902.

Smetona moved to Vilnius, worked at the Vilnius Land Bank until 1915 and devoted much of his time to the Lithuanian press, editing papers and founding the newspaper Viltis in 1907. In September 1917 he was elected chairman of the Council of Lithuania, and on 16 February 1918 he signed the Act of Independence. On 4 April 1919 the State Council elected him the first president of the Republic of Lithuania, and on 19 April 1920 the Constituent Assembly elected Aleksandras Stulginskis in his place.

Smetona led the coup of December 1926 that deposed President Kazys Grinius, and he became president again on 19 December. He dissolved parliament a year later and on 15 May 1928 promulgated a constitution with wider presidential powers. In 1929 he removed his prime minister Augustinas Voldemaras and took dictatorial powers. He was re-elected in 1931 and 1938 as the only candidate, and a third constitution of 1938 kept the authoritarian character of the second. His regime repeatedly arrested members of the banned Communist Party. It also put Nazis in the Memel region on trial in 1934–1935, and Memel was surrendered to Hitler in 1939. According to the account followed here, no anti-Jewish law was passed under his rule.

After the Soviet ultimatum of June 1940 Smetona proposed armed resistance, but the government and army commanders thought it hopeless. On 15 June he handed his duties to Prime Minister Antanas Merkys and crossed into Germany, then went on through Switzerland, Lisbon and Brazil to the United States, arriving in March 1941. He settled in Cleveland, where he worked on a history of Lithuania and his memoirs. He died on 9 January 1944 in a fire at his son's house; the official record blamed an overheated furnace, and a Soviet cause is considered doubtful. Lithuania has held since 1990 that Merkys's takeover of the presidency was illegal, since Smetona never formally resigned. Historians still debate his legacy.
antanas-snieckus: Antanas Sniečkus was born on 7 January 1903 in the village of Būbleliai, near Šakiai. During the First World War his family fled to Russia, where he saw the revolution of 1917, and by 1920, after their return to Lithuania, he had joined the Bolshevik Party. Arrested that year, he fled on bail to Moscow, became an agent of the Comintern and won the trust of Zigmas Angarietis and Vincas Mickevičius-Kapsukas.

In 1926 the Comintern sent him back to lead the banned Communist Party of Lithuania in place of the executed Karolis Požėla. He was imprisoned in Kaunas Prison in 1930, released in 1933 in an exchange for Lithuanian political prisoners held in the Soviet Union, and arrested again in 1939 and sentenced to eight years.

After the Soviet ultimatum and occupation of 1940 he was freed on 18 June and made head of the Department of National Security. He issued in the party's name the orders of Vladimir Dekanozov, sent to organise Lithuania's incorporation, and helped create an atmosphere of terror before the elections of 14 July to the People's Seimas, whose results were falsified. On 3 August the Supreme Soviet of the USSR annexed Lithuania.

Sniečkus initiated the first mass deportations, on 14–19 June 1941; his own brother was deported to Siberia and died there. He retreated with the Red Army to Moscow, where the Lithuanian Partisan Movement was created under his command on 26 November 1942, and returned in 1944. His mother, two brothers and three sisters fled to the West, and his mother disowned him. Under Nikita Khrushchev's amnesty he refused to let freed deportees return to Lithuania.

In his later decades his policies took on a nationalist colour, with some of Moscow's orders sabotaged and privileges sought for Lithuania. In 1949–1950 he shielded old communist comrades, and Lithuania was the only Soviet republic where no communist of the pre-Soviet years was arrested. He died on 22 January 1974 and was buried at Antakalnis Cemetery. A town for the workers of the Ignalina Nuclear Power Plant, founded in 1975, bore his name until it was renamed Visaginas in 1992.
ante-pavelic: Ante Pavelić was born on 14 July 1889 in the village of Bradina in Herzegovina, then Ottoman territory occupied by the Austro-Hungarian Empire. His parents had moved there from Lika to work on the Sarajevo-Metković railway line. He grew up near Jajce and in Travnik, where he became an adherent of the nationalist ideas of Ante Starčević and Josip Frank. A lawyer, he joined the Croatian Party of Rights, entered its leadership in 1918, and was elected to the Zagreb city assembly in 1921.

After King Alexander declared his 6 January Dictatorship in 1929, Pavelić left Yugoslavia. The Ustaša movement, founded on principles of racialism and intolerance, has 7 January 1929 as its official foundation date. In March 1929 it began a campaign of terror within Yugoslavia, and on 29 April Pavelić and Ivan Mihailov of the Internal Macedonian Revolutionary Organization signed the Sofia Declaration to separate Croatia and Macedonia from Yugoslavia. He was sentenced to death in absentia that August. Benito Mussolini allowed him to live in Rome and train paramilitaries, and in 1934 the Ustaše carried out the assassination of King Alexander in Marseille.

Slavko Kvaternik declared the Independent State of Croatia on 10 April 1941 in Pavelić's name, and Pavelić, calling himself the Poglavnik, took control of the puppet government. The Ustaše imposed anti-Serbian, antisemitic and anti-Roma policies that resulted in the deaths of hundreds of thousands of Serbs and tens of thousands of Jews and Roma, many in concentration and extermination camps run by the Ustaše. Hundreds of thousands of Orthodox Christians were forcibly converted to Catholicism or expelled to German-occupied Serbia. By November 1943 his regime controlled little of the state's territory.

Pavelić left Croatia on 6 May 1945 and fled to Austria. He reached Rome in 1946 disguised as a priest and arrived in Buenos Aires on 6 November 1948, where he served as a security adviser to Juan Perón. He was shot in an assassination attempt on 10 April 1957 and then went to Madrid, where Spain granted him asylum. He died there on 28 December 1959, aged 70, of his wounds, and was buried in San Isidro Cemetery. The mass killings and persecutions of the Independent State of Croatia have been described as the single most disastrous episode in Yugoslav history.
ante-trumbic: Trumbić was born on 17 May 1864 in Split, in the Austrian crownland of Dalmatia, and studied law at Zagreb, Vienna and Graz, taking his doctorate in 1890. He practised as a lawyer and from 1905 was mayor of Split. He favoured moderate reform in the Slavic provinces of Austria-Hungary, including the union of Dalmatia with Croatia-Slavonia demanded by the New Course Policy he helped draw up.

After the assassination of Archduke Franz Ferdinand and the invasion of Serbia, he became the leading Yugoslav nationalist abroad, heading the Yugoslav Committee that lobbied the Allies for an independent South Slav state. His talks with the Serbian prime minister Nikola Pašić produced the Corfu Declaration of 20 July 1917, which called for a united state of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes under the Serbian House of Karađorđević, and in 1918 he led the committee's delegation at the conference that issued the Geneva Declaration. As the first foreign minister of the new kingdom he defended its interests at the Versailles conference against Italian claims in Dalmatia.

He came to see the state as Serb-dominated. He opposed the constitution of 1921 as too centralised and was one of 35 representatives who voted against it while much of the opposition boycotted the assembly. In 1927 he was elected for the last time, for Zagreb on the list of the Croatian Bloc with Ante Pavelić.

When King Alexander of Yugoslavia abolished the parties and the constitution in 1929 and redrew Croatia-Slavonia and Dalmatia into banovinas, Trumbić was living in retirement in Zagreb. In a September 1932 interview with The Manchester Guardian he wondered whether Croatia should leave Yugoslavia and seek union with Austria, and in November he edited the Zagreb Points of the Peasant-Democratic coalition. After Vladko Maček's arrest in April 1933 he and Josip Predavec led the Croatian Peasant Party, and after Predavec's assassination on 14 July he acted as its head. He died on 17 November 1938; according to Henri Pozzi, he came to regret the end of Austria-Hungary.
antequera: Antequera lies at 575 metres above sea level, at the foot of the mountain ranges of El Torcal and the Sierra de la Chimenea, in a fertile valley bounded to the north by the Guadalhorce River. It is called the heart of Andalusia because of its central position among Málaga, Granada, Córdoba and Seville. The surrounding vega has long produced cereals, olive oil and vegetables.

Two Bronze Age burial mounds on the northern outskirts, the dolmens of Menga and Viera, date from the third millennium BCE and are the largest such structures in Europe. Menga was built with thirty-two megaliths, the largest weighing about 180 tonnes. The Romans knew the city as Anticaria, part of Hispania Baetica, and it was known for its olive oil. The present street plan largely follows that of the Roman town.

Anticaria was conquered around 716 and became Medina Antaquira under the Umayyad Caliphate. After the Christian victory at Las Navas de Tolosa in 1212 it became an important border town of the Nasrid Emirate of Granada and was attacked repeatedly for about two hundred years. On 16 September 1410, after a siege of nearly four months, it capitulated to a Castilian army led by the infante Ferdinand of Trastámara. The Muslim population was forced to leave for Archidona and Granada; 895 men, 770 women and 863 children departed.

The city grew after the conquest of Málaga in 1487 and became a centre of grain production and commerce in the sixteenth century. A humanist university, the Real Colegiata de Santa María la Mayor, was founded in 1504, and a school of poets arose, including Pedro Espinosa. Antequera was the site of the drafting of the Federal Constitution of Antequera in 1883 and of the Pact of Antequera in 1978, which led to autonomy for Andalusia.

Antequera is a city and municipality in the province of Málaga, in the autonomous community of Andalusia, and the largest municipality in the province by area. The Antequera Dolmens Site, which includes Menga, Viera, El Romeral, the Peña de los Enamorados and El Torcal, was inscribed as a World Heritage Site in 2016. There are 32 churches and convents in the city.
anthony-ashley-cooper-1st-earl-of-shafte: Anthony Ashley-Cooper was born on 22 July 1621 at Wimborne St Giles, Dorset, the home of his maternal grandfather, Sir Anthony Ashley. He was the eldest son of Sir John Cooper, 1st Baronet, of Rockbourne in Hampshire, and Anne Ashley. His mother died in 1628 and his father in 1630, which left him, at nine, a wealthy orphan and a baronet. In March 1640, still a minor, he was elected member of parliament for Tewkesbury. When the Civil War began in 1642 he first supported the King. In 1643 he raised a regiment of foot and a troop of horse at his own expense and became governor of Weymouth and Portland. In 1644 he joined the Parliamentarians.

Under the Commonwealth he sat on the committee on law reform chaired by Sir Matthew Hale and, after Oliver Cromwell nominated him to Barebone's Parliament as member for Wiltshire, on the English Council of State. In the elections of 1654 he led a slate of ten candidates in Wiltshire against republicans headed by Edmund Ludlow. He feared that Cromwell would rule through the Army rather than Parliament, and in January 1655 he stopped attending Council.

He returned to England with Charles II in late May 1660 and was appointed to the Privy Council on 27 May. He sat on the commission that tried the regicides. He was Chancellor of the Exchequer from 1661 to 1672 and Lord Chancellor from 1672 to 1673, and one of five members of the Cabal ministry after the fall of the Earl of Clarendon. Charles created him Earl of Shaftesbury in 1672. He invested in the Company of Royal Adventurers and the Royal African Company, serving as the latter's Sub-Governor in 1672 and 1673, and the two companies sent about 120 slaving voyages between 1663 and 1677 while he was associated with them. He also helped enshrine slavery in the Fundamental Constitutions of Carolina.

When it became widely known in 1673 that the King's brother and heir James had secretly become a Catholic, Shaftesbury, like many English Protestants, saw Catholicism as linked to arbitrary government. His sponsorship of the Exclusion Bill in 1679 led to two years of struggle and ended in defeat. In 1681 he was arrested for high treason, though the prosecution was dropped months later. Fearing re-arrest, he went into exile in Amsterdam in 1682 and died there on 21 January 1683. John Locke called him a vigorous and indefatigable champion for civil and ecclesiastical liberty. The Ashley and Cooper rivers in Charleston, South Carolina, are named in his honour.
anthony-eden: Robert Anthony Eden was born on 12 June 1897 at Windlestone Hall, County Durham, the third of four sons of Sir William Eden and Sybil Frances Grey, into a conservative family of landed gentry. He attended Sandroyd School in Surrey and, from January 1911, Eton College. His elder brother John was killed in action on 17 October 1914, aged 26. After the First World War Eden studied Oriental Languages, with Persian as his main language and Arabic as his second, at Christ Church, Oxford, from October 1919. He learned French and German on continental holidays, and in February 1934 conversed with Adolf Hitler in German.

Eden contested Spennymoor as a Conservative in 1922 without success and later sat for Warwick. In August 1931 he held his first ministerial office as Under-Secretary for Foreign Affairs. He became Foreign Secretary at 38, after Samuel Hoare resigned over the collapse of the Hoare-Laval Pact, and supported non-interference in the Spanish Civil War, but he resigned over Neville Chamberlain's policy of appeasement towards Benito Mussolini's Italy. In 1939 he returned to government as Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs, and Winston Churchill, on becoming prime minister in 1940, appointed him Secretary of State for War. He again served as Foreign Secretary from 1951, having been regarded as Churchill's crown prince since 1942.

Eden succeeded Churchill as prime minister in April 1955. In July 1956 Gamal Abdel Nasser nationalised the Suez Canal after Anglo-American funding for the Aswan Dam was withdrawn. Eden believed this violated the Anglo-Egyptian treaty of October 1954 and feared that Nasser meant to form an Arab alliance able to cut Europe's oil supplies; with France he decided Nasser should be removed from power. The United States refused to support the Anglo-French military response. Two months after ordering an end to the operation Eden resigned, on grounds of ill health and because he was widely suspected of having misled the House of Commons about collusion with France and Israel.

Eden left the Commons after 33 years and entered the House of Lords as the Earl of Avon in 1961. He died of metastatic prostate cancer at Alvediston Manor, Wiltshire, on 14 January 1977, aged 79. He was twice married; his son Simon was killed in action with the RAF in Burma in 1945.

He is generally considered among the least successful British prime ministers of the 20th century, though two broadly sympathetic biographies have shifted opinion somewhat, and most historians argue that he made a series of blunders at Suez, especially in not realising the depth of American opposition. Contemporaries judged him differently: Dick Crossman called him the idealist without conviction, while Nikita Khrushchev said that until Suez Eden had been in the top world class.
anthony-the-great: Most of what is known about Anthony comes from the Life of Anthony, written in Greek about 360 by Athanasius of Alexandria, which presents him as an illiterate holy man. He was born in Koma in Lower Egypt to wealthy landowning parents. When he was about 20 his parents died and left him responsible for his unmarried sister. Soon after, he took to heart the words of Matthew 19:21, gave away part of the family land to his neighbours, sold the rest and gave the money to the poor. He placed his sister with a group of Christian virgins and began an ascetic life. He probably spoke only Coptic, and seven letters dictated in that language survive.

For about fifteen years Anthony stayed near his village, first as the disciple of another local hermit. Ascetics already existed before him, but he went out into the desert proper, to the Nitrian Desert about 95 kilometres west of Alexandria, where he stayed 13 years. He ate only bread, salt and water, and at most once a day. According to Athanasius the devil attacked him with boredom, laziness and the phantoms of women. Around the age of 35 he withdrew to an abandoned Roman fort at Pispir, where he stayed some 20 years while food was thrown over the wall. Disciples settled in caves around the mountain, and about 305 he emerged to guide them.

He later withdrew to Mount Colzim, between the Nile and the Red Sea, where the monastery of Deir Mar Antonios still stands. About 311, during the Diocletianic persecutions, he went to Alexandria to visit the imprisoned, and in 338 he went there again to help refute the teachings of Arius. The emperor Constantine wrote to ask for his prayers.

Anthony died on about 17 January 356 and was buried in a secret grave on the mountain. His remains were reportedly discovered in 361 and moved to Alexandria, later to Constantinople, and in the 11th century were given to the French Count Jocelin. A church to house them, Saint-Antoine-l'Abbaye, was completed in 1297. Skin diseases such as ergotism were called Saint Anthony's fire. His temptations were depicted by Hieronymus Bosch and Matthias Grünewald, among many artists, and retold by Gustave Flaubert. He is called the Father of All Monks, though he was not the first monk and did not himself create a monastery.
anthony-wayne: Wayne was born on 1 January 1745 on his family's Waynesborough estate in Chester County, Pennsylvania, one of four children of Isaac Wayne, an Anglo-Irish Protestant immigrant, and Elizabeth Iddings Wayne. Against his father's wish that he farm, he trained as a surveyor at his uncle's academy and for two years at the College of Philadelphia. In 1765 Benjamin Franklin sent him to survey land granted in Nova Scotia, and he helped found a settlement at the Township of Monckton. He later worked as a tanner and was elected to the Pennsylvania General Assembly.

On 3 January 1776 Wayne became colonel of the 4th Pennsylvania Regiment. He served in the invasion of Quebec, covered the retreat at the Battle of Trois-Rivières and was made brigadier general on 21 February 1777. His defeat at the Battle of Paoli in 1777 damaged his name, but his leadership at Stony Point earned him the Congressional Gold Medal. Historians differ on whether his nickname came from a bayonet charge at Green Spring or from his temper. After the war he was a Federalist in Pennsylvania politics and acquired plantations in Georgia with 47 enslaved people; his election to Congress from Georgia in 1790 was, in Paul David Nelson's words, marred by horrendous corruption.

After St. Clair's defeat in 1791, President Washington recalled him to lead the Legion of the United States in the Northwest Indian War. Wayne recruited and trained the force from 1792, an effort later seen as the army's first formal basic training. He died of a stomach ulcer on 15 December 1796, returning from Detroit, while trying to court-martial his second in command, James Wilkinson, a Spanish spy who had worked against him; rumours that Wilkinson poisoned him have never been proven.

Wayne was buried at Fort Presque Isle; in 1809 his son Isaac had the body boiled and carried the bones to St. David's Episcopal Church in Pennsylvania, so he has two graves. Theodore Roosevelt called him America's best fighting general, while others see him as a reckless tactician rather than a strategist, and Mary Stockwell's biography records his heavy drinking and spending. More recently his slaveholding and his part in driving Native Americans from the Ohio Valley, which some historians call ethnic cleansing, have made him controversial; the Miami people objected when Fort Wayne, Indiana, created an Anthony Wayne Day in 2019.
anti-atlas: The Anti-Atlas, also called the Lesser or Little Atlas, is part of the Atlas Mountains in Morocco. It runs for about 500 km from the Atlantic Ocean in the southwest to the heights of Ouarzazate and on to Tafilalt, and it borders on the Sahara to the south. Its summits average 2,500 to 2,700 m. A plateau at 1,700 to 1,800 m lies to the north, and the Saharan highlands, at about 700 m, lie to the south. At Ouarzazate the Draa valley cuts through the massif and opens southward. The Jbel Saghro forms its eastern prolongation, the volcanic Jbel Sirwa, which reaches 3,304 m, its northern one, and the much lower Jebel Bani runs along its southern side.

The range is a remnant of the Paleozoic, formed about 300 million years ago when Gondwana and Euramerica collided in the same Alleghenian orogeny that raised the Appalachians. Indications suggest the mountains were once far higher than the Himalayas are today.
