Later uplift in the Paleogene and Neogene, as Europe and Africa met at the southern end of the Iberian Peninsula, and long erosion left them less massive than the High Atlas to the north.

The Anti-Atlas is a traditionally Berber region inhabited by the Chleuh group. It is sparsely populated and has no large cities; its main town, Tafraoute, has been described as Morocco's Berber heartland. Neolithic cave paintings survive in parts of the range.

The High Atlas shields it from the Mediterranean, so it belongs to the Saharan climate zone, with under 200 mm of rain a year in most places. The north and west slopes are wetter and carry thyme, rosemary and argan, while thorn shrubs are nearly all that remain in the south. The Moroccan citron grown there is used as the etrog in Jewish rituals.

Picturesque kasbahs, once places of shelter and supply depots for kinsmen, stand throughout the region, and terraced fields held by dry-stone walls cover the slopes nearby. With continued migration from the land, houses are being vacated and the irrigation systems that agriculture depends on are decaying.
anti-fascist-council-for-the-national-li: The Axis powers invaded Yugoslavia on 6 April 1941, and the Communist Party of Yugoslavia organised the Yugoslav Partisans under Josip Broz Tito. King Peter II and the government fled, and the government-in-exile was weak and divided. In November 1942 the Partisans captured Bihać and held much of western Bosnia, Dalmatia and Lika. On 26 and 27 November the council was established there at the initiative of Tito and the Communist Party.

At its founding session it adopted the principle of a multi-ethnic federal state, without deciding what system of government would follow the war. Shortly before the session Tito added the word Anti-Fascist to the name, to stress its temporary and anti-Axis nature, after the Comintern had urged him to set up a body solely to liberate the country and not to oppose the monarchy. Ivan Ribar was elected its president.

The council met again at Jajce on 29 and 30 November 1943. It declared itself the supreme legislative body, recognised the equal standing of Bosnia and Herzegovina, Croatia, Macedonia, Montenegro, Serbia and Slovenia in a future federation, denied the legitimacy of the government-in-exile, and forbade the return of King Peter II until the people could decide on the monarchy. Tito was given the rank of Marshal of Yugoslavia and became president of a National Committee that acted as an interim government. Stalin was enraged because he had received no prior notice, but the Western Allies recognised the Partisans as an Allied force at the Tehran Conference. In the Treaty of Vis of 16 June 1944 the government-in-exile recognised the council.

On 21 November 1944 its presidency declared the Germans of Yugoslavia collectively guilty for the war. About half a million Germans had lived in the country before 1944. About 240,000 were evacuated, 150,000 were deported to the USSR as forced labour, 50,000 died in Yugoslav-run camps and 15,000 were killed by the Partisans, and fewer than 56,000 remained by the 1948 census. The third session met in Belgrade in August 1945, and the Constituent Assembly that convened on 29 November 1945 ratified the council's decisions.

The council's decisions fixed the six units of the federation and defined their borders, known as the AVNOJ borders, which separated Serbs living in Bosnia and Herzegovina and Croatia from Serbia. They were drawn as administrative boundaries but gained importance with later decentralisation and the breakup of Yugoslavia. In post-war Yugoslavia the second session was commemorated on 29 and 30 November as a national holiday. Museums have been established in the buildings that hosted the first and second sessions.
anti-revolutionary-party: In the mid-19th century the historian Guillaume Groen van Prinsterer laid the foundations of an Orthodox Reformed body of political thought that opposed popular sovereignty, liberalism and rationalism, and his followers took the label antirevolutionary. In parliament they were a small group, often three or four members. After Groen withdrew, the theologian Abraham Kuyper took up the leadership, founding the newspaper De Standaard in 1872. An 1878 petition for equal payment for religious schools helped bring about the party's formal founding on 3 April 1879.

To win funding for religious schools Kuyper allied with the Catholics, a strategy justified by the idea of the Antithesis, which held that the divide between secular and confessional parties outweighed the rivalry between Protestants and Catholics. In 1888 the party won 27 seats and Aeneas Mackay Jr. led a confessional cabinet. A dispute over the extension of suffrage split the party: Alexander de Savornin Lohman and many aristocratic members left, and their group became the Christian Historical Union in 1904. Kuyper himself led the cabinet from 1901 to 1905, when he pushed harsh anti-strike laws through parliament after the railway strike of 1903.

Hendrikus Colijn, leader from 1922, stressed defence and fiscal conservatism and led several cabinets between 1933 and 1939. During the Second World War members of the party served in the government-in-exile under Pieter Sjoerds Gerbrandy and in the resistance, where they founded the paper Trouw. Its opposition to the decolonisation of the Dutch East Indies kept it out of government from 1946 until 1952. Under Willem Aantjes in the 1970s it took on a left-leaning radical evangelical image, and in 1974 it formed a federation with the KVP and CHU that campaigned as the Christian Democratic Appeal in 1977.

The party's thought rested on sphere sovereignty: Protestants were to build a society of their own within the Netherlands, with their own schools, papers and hospitals, funded equally by the state. Its motto was God, the Netherlands and the House of Orange. It drew first on the kleine luyden, the small folk of the middle class, farmers and workers, and later chiefly on members of the Reformed Churches in the Netherlands. It was strongest in Friesland, Overijssel, Zeeland and the Veluwe, and stood within a Protestant pillar that included the broadcaster NCRV and the Vrije Universiteit Amsterdam, founded in 1880.
anti-rightist-campaign: Both the Hundred Flowers Campaign and the purge that followed it were directed by Mao Zedong, and Deng Xiaoping and Peng Zhen also played important parts. Khrushchev's speech On the Cult of Personality and Its Consequences in 1956 and the unrest that followed in Poland and Hungary had a large effect in China, where similar unrest began. Critics during the Hundred Flowers asked for more: Chu Anping called on 2 June 1957 for greater representation of non-CCP members in the national government. Mao came to see such criticism as a threat to the party's rule, and on 8 June 1957 he drafted the inner-party directive Muster Our Forces to Repulse the Rightists' Wild Attacks, while the People's Daily published the editorial Why is This So?

By the end of 1957 some 300,000 people had been labelled rightists, among them the writer Ding Ling, and the future premier Zhu Rongji was purged in 1958. Rightists were officially intellectuals who seemed to favour capitalism or opposed one-party rule and forced collectivisation, but the label also reached teachers, employees and cadres, and was used to settle grudges and factional quarrels. Zhang Bojun and Luo Longji were called China's number one and number two rightists. The official count was 552,877, excluding other categories and the victims' families; estimates of all those persecuted range from 1 million to 3 million or more.

Punishments ran from criticism and salary cuts to labour camps and banishment to the countryside, and some people were executed. At the Jiabiangou camp in Gansu about 2,500 of some 3,000 political prisoners held from 1957 to 1961 died, mostly of starvation. The independent legal system was a main target: legal professionals were moved to other jobs and judicial power passed to cadres and the police. A second wave followed the Lushan Conference of 1959, which condemned the defence minister Peng Dehuai, a critic of the Great Leap Forward.

The campaign consolidated the People's Republic as a one-party state, halted early efforts to professionalise the judiciary, and laid ground for the targeting of intellectuals in the Cultural Revolution. After Mao's death in 1976, during the Boluan Fanzheng period, many verdicts were overturned, and the party's 1981 Resolution called the campaign correct and necessary but too broad in scope. A 2018 study by Zhaojin Zeng and Joshua Eisenman found that counties in Anhui, Henan and Jiangsu with more rightists still had worse economic and educational outcomes in 2000.
anti-socialist-laws: Two social democratic parties, the General German Workers' Association founded by Ferdinand Lassalle in 1863 and the Social Democratic Workers' Party of August Bebel and Wilhelm Liebknecht, merged in 1875 as the Socialist Workers' Party of Germany. Chancellor Otto von Bismarck feared a revolution like the one that created the Paris Commune. When Max Hödel on 11 May 1878 and Karl Eduard Nobiling on 2 June shot at Emperor Wilhelm I, Bismarck let it be said that social democrats were behind the attacks, although Hödel had been expelled from the party and Nobiling acted from personal delusions.

The Reichstag rejected a first draft by 251 votes to 57. Bismarck then dissolved it, and the new chamber was more conservative. The bill passed by 221 votes to 149, the National Liberals and both conservative parties voting for it, after Eduard Lasker had a clause added requiring renewal every two and a half years.

The law banned societies, meetings, publications, festivities and processions aiming at the overthrow of the existing political or social order through social democratic, socialist or communist endeavours, as well as collections of money for them. Members or those attending a banned meeting could be fined up to 500 marks or imprisoned for three months, and those who distributed a banned publication fined up to 1,000 marks. Convicts could be denied residence in a district, and foreigners expelled.

Some 330 workers' organisations, many of them trade unions, were banned, and 797 social democrats were expelled from cities under a minor state of siege, among them 67 from Berlin in November 1878 and 350 from Hamburg in 1880. Many went into exile in France, Switzerland, England and the United States.

Members met in outwardly non-political singing clubs and relief groups, and the newspaper Der Sozialdemokrat, printed in Zurich from 1879 and later in London, was smuggled into Germany. Union membership grew from 50,000 to 250,000, and the social democratic vote rose from 312,000 in 1881 to 1,427,000 in 1890, the most of any party. Bismarck's bid for a permanent and harsher law failed on 25 January 1890 by 169 votes to 98, which played a decisive part in his dismissal by Wilhelm II.
antibes: Antibes lies on the French Riviera in the Alpes-Maritimes, between Cannes and Nice. Its cape, the Cap d'Antibes, is one of the area's two major landforms, with Cap Ferrat to the northeast. The resort of Juan-les-Pins is within the commune, and the Sophia Antipolis technology park lies northwest of it. There are 48 beaches along 25 km of coastline around Antibes and Juan-les-Pins. Port Vauban, with more than 2,000 moorings, is the largest yachting harbour in Europe, and its old port was the heart of the ancient Greek city.

Traces of early Iron Age occupation have been found in the area of the castle and cathedral. An indigenous community had ties with Mediterranean peoples, including the Etruscans, as the underwater amphorae and wrecks off Antibes show, though most trade was with the Greek world through the Phocaeans of Marseille. Antibes was founded as a Greek colony by Phocaeans from Massalia, probably in the 4th century BCE, and named Antipolis, Opposite-City, from its position across the Var estuary from Nice.

The Bishopric of Antibes was established c. 450 by Pope Leo I. In the 10th century raiders from Muslim Spain menaced the coast until Count William I of Provence captured their stronghold at Fraxinetum in 975. He gave the liberated lands to his knights, and one of them, Rodoald, became Lord of Antibes.

Saracen pirates burned the cathedral in 1124 and kept preying on the town, and in 1244 the bishops moved to Grasse, where they stayed for five centuries. In 1383 Marie de Blois confiscated the lordship from the bishops of Grasse and awarded it two years later to the Genoese brothers Marc and Luc Grimaldi, who built the Château Grimaldi. Provence passed to King Louis XI and to France in 1481, which made Antibes a border town facing the County of Nice, then part of the Savoyard state. Andrea Doria sacked it in 1536, and Henry II ordered the building of Fort Carré in 1550, later reinforced by Vauban.

From December 1746 an Austro-Savoyard army under Maximilian Ulysses Browne besieged Antibes. It lifted the siege on 1 February 1747, but its guns had levelled 350 houses and destroyed the cathedral again, which Louis XV later rebuilt. On 1 March 1815 Napoléon Bonaparte landed at Golfe-Juan, 5 km to the southwest, on his return from Elba. He hoped for a warm welcome at Antibes, but the townspeople closed their gates to him. Antibes was transferred from Var to Alpes-Maritimes in 1860. In 1926 the municipality bought the Château Grimaldi, where Pablo Picasso lived for six months in 1946; it now houses the Musée Picasso.
antigonid-dynasty: The Antigonid dynasty was a Macedonian Greek royal house of the Hellenistic period, founded by Antigonus I Monophthalmus, a general and successor of Alexander the Great who first came to power in the wars of the Diadochi. It was one of four dynasties established by Alexander's successors, the others being the Seleucid, Ptolemaic and Antipatrid dynasties. The Argead dynasty of Macedon had become extinct when Cassander ordered the assassination, in 310 or 309 BCE, of the 14-year-old Alexander IV, son of Alexander the Great, and his mother Roxane, and the Antigonid and Antipatrid dynasties, the latter led by Cassander, son of Antipater, sought to fill the vacuum.

In 307 BCE Demetrius, son of Antigonus, ousted Cassander's governor of Athens, Demetrius of Phalerum, and after defeating Ptolemy I at the Battle of Salamis in 306 BCE he conquered Cyprus. Antigonus then took the title basileus, king, from the assembled armies, and ruled territory from the Aegean to the Middle East, sometimes called the Antigonid Empire. A revived coalition of Cassander, Ptolemy I Soter, Seleucus I Nicator and Lysimachus decisively defeated the Antigonids at the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE, where Antigonus was killed.

Demetrius, who is known as Poliorcetes, survived, took Athens and in 294 BCE made himself king of Macedon. In 288 BCE Pyrrhus and Lysimachus drove him out, and he died a prisoner of Seleucus I Nicator. After a long period of instability his son Antigonus II Gonatas established the family's control over Macedon and over most of the Greek city-states by 276 BCE, despite the loss of the Asian territory. Antigonus III Doson extended Macedonian influence in southern Greece and re-established the Hellenic Alliance with himself as leader. Under Philip V, Macedon first came into conflict with Rome, already a decisive power in the Mediterranean.

The last Antigonid king, Perseus, who reigned from 179 to 168 BCE, became known as the champion of Greek resistance to Rome, but he could not stop the Roman legions. His defeat at the Battle of Pydna in 168 BCE, in the Third Macedonian War, ended the dynasty, and Macedon came under the control of the Roman Republic. A rebel against Rome, Andriscus, claimed to be a son of Perseus.
antigonus-i-monophthalmus: Antigonus was born in Macedonia around 382 BCE to a nobleman named Philip. Ancient sources disagree about his family, some calling it peasant stock and others linking it to the royal house, but the family was in all probability socially prominent. When he first appears in the sources he commands a large part of Alexander's army, including about 7,000 allied Greek infantry. Plutarch records that an Antigonus lost an eye to a catapult bolt at the Siege of Perinthus in 340 BCE. He was an exceptionally large man, made more formidable by the missing eye.

In 334 BCE he commanded the allied Greek infantry in Alexander's invasion of Persia, and when Alexander marched east he appointed him satrap of Phrygia. He took a garrison of mercenaries into his own service and sent 1,500 of his mercenaries to reinforce Alexander before Issus.

After Alexander's death in 323 BCE the Partition of Babylon confirmed Antigonus in Phrygia, Lycaonia, Pamphylia, Lycia and western Pisidia. He incurred the enmity of the regent Perdiccas by refusing to help Eumenes take Cappadocia, and fled to Greece with his son Demetrius. After Perdiccas was murdered in 321 BCE, Antigonus became Strategos of Asia at Triparadisus and defeated the remnants of the Perdiccan faction at Orkynia and Cretopolis. After Antipater's death in 319 BCE he defeated Eumenes, entered Babylon and seized the treasury at Susa. Seleucus fled to Ptolemy, and Ptolemy, Cassander and Lysimachus joined a league against Antigonus.

In the Third Diadochi War he took Tyre after a year's siege. Seleucus regained Babylonia, and a peace followed in 309 BCE in which Antigonus held Greece, Asia Minor, Syria, Phoenicia and northern Mesopotamia, the height of his power. After his son Demetrius defeated Ptolemy at sea at Salamis in 306 BCE and conquered Cyprus, Antigonus took the title of king, which the other dynasts soon did as well. His invasion of Egypt failed, and Demetrius's siege of Rhodes in 305 and 304 BCE ended in a treaty.

Cassander, Seleucus, Ptolemy and Lysimachus allied against Antigonus, and the forces of Seleucus, Lysimachus and Cassander's general Prepelaos defeated him and Demetrius at the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE. He died there, struck by a javelin, in his eighty-first year; he had never lost a battle before. With his death plans to reunite Alexander's empire ended, and his kingdom was divided mostly between Lysimachus and Seleucus. Demetrius took control of Macedonia in 294 BCE, and Antigonus's descendants, the Antigonid dynasty, held it until the Roman conquest after the Battle of Pydna in 168 BCE.
antigonus-ii-gonatas: Antigonus Gonatas was born around 320 BCE; the origin of his nickname is unknown. His father was Demetrius Poliorcetes, son of Antigonus I Monophthalmus, and his mother was Phila, daughter of the regent Antipater. His grandfather came closer than anyone to reuniting Alexander's empire but was killed at the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE. Antigonus served his father as a general, and when the Boeotians rebelled in 292 BCE he defeated them and shut them up in Thebes. After Demetrius surrendered to Seleucus in 285 BCE, Antigonus offered to hand over his territory and to become a hostage for his father, but without result.

Demetrius died in captivity in 283 BCE. Antigonus brought his remains to Corinth by sea and had them buried at Demetrias in Thessaly. His attempt to retake Macedon was beaten by Ptolemy Keraunos, who was killed in the winter of 279 BCE when Gauls under Brennus invaded Macedonia, beginning two years of anarchy. After he defeated the Gauls at Lysimachia, Antigonus had a claim to the throne as a son of Demetrius and was seen as a saviour. He fought off rivals including Antipater Etesias and Ptolemy Epigonos, and took Cassandreia from the tyrant Apollodorus by a ruse after a siege of ten months. By the end of 276 BCE he held most of Macedon.

He kept garrisons in Corinth and other cities and controlled the Greeks through tyrants and intermediaries. In 267 BCE the Athenian Chremonides persuaded Athens to join Sparta in declaring war on him in the Chremonidean War. In 251 BCE Aratus expelled the tyrant Nicocles from Sicyon, and Antigonus tried to win him over with a gift of 25 talents, which Aratus gave away to his fellow citizens. At court he gathered philosophers, poets and historians, and Zeno of Citium sent his students Persaeus and Philonides the Theban in his place.

Antigonus died in 239 BCE, aged 80, and left the kingdom to his son Demetrius II. Apart from his victory over the Gauls he was not a notable military leader; his skills were political, and he relied on cunning, patience and persistence. More brilliant leaders, such as his father and Pyrrhus, aimed higher and fell lower, while Antigonus achieved a measure of security. He is also said to have won his subjects' affection through his honesty and his support for the arts. A tomb at Vergina has been suggested to be his own.
antigonus-iii-doson: Antigonus III Doson belonged to the Antigonid dynasty through his father, Demetrius the Fair, a son of Demetrius Poliorcetes who was briefly king of Cyrene. He was a half-cousin of his predecessor, Demetrius II Aetolicus. According to Eusebius his mother was a Thessalian noblewoman, Olympias, daughter of Pauliclitus of Larissa. Demetrius the Fair died around 250 BCE, assassinated at the instigation of his young bride Berenice II after he became the lover of her mother, Apama II. The by-name Doson means "going to give"; according to Plutarch it implied a man given to promising but not performing, though its exact meaning is unclear.

When Demetrius II died in battle in 229 BCE his son, the later Philip V, was nine years old. According to Plutarch the Macedonian army and nobility thought the situation too unstable to wait for him, and turned to Doson, who became regent and married Demetrius's widow Chryseis, Philip's mother. Only after he defeated the Dardanii invaders and put down a rebellion by the Thessalians, and showed a moderate rule, was he given the title of king. Even as king he apparently saw himself as a caretaker for Philip.

In under a decade he secured Macedon's borders and restored its position as the dominant power in the region. He formed alliances with Epirus and the Achaean League rather than seeking direct rule over his neighbours. When Cleomenes III of Sparta tried to establish control over the Peloponnese, Aratus of Sicyon invited Antigonus to intervene in 226 BCE. He based himself on the heights above Corinth and revived the Hellenic League of Philip II under his own leadership, probably in 224 BCE, calling it the League of Leagues. In the Battle of Sellasia in 222 BCE the Spartan forces were overwhelmed, and Cleomenes escaped with a few horsemen and took refuge in Egypt. Antigonus kept his soldiers from plundering Sparta, saying his enemy was Cleomenes.

While Antigonus was campaigning in the southern Peloponnese, Illyrians invaded Macedonia from the north. On his way back he passed through Tegea and Argos, where he was honoured by the Achaean League and other cities at the opening of the Nemean Games. He then fought the Illyrians and won, but fell ill during the battle, possibly from a ruptured blood vessel, and died in 221 BCE, soon after returning to Macedon.
antigua-guatemala: Antigua Guatemala lies in the Panchoy Valley of the central highlands, and three large volcanoes dominate its horizon. The Volcán de Agua, about 3,766 metres high, rises to the south; it took its Spanish name after a lahar from it buried the second site of the capital in 1541. To the west are Acatenango and the Volcán de Fuego, which is almost constantly active at a low level.

The first capital was founded on 25 July 1524 at the Kaqchikel Maya city of Iximche and named Ciudad de Santiago de los Caballeros de Guatemala. After Kaqchikel uprisings it was moved in 1527 to the Valley of Almolonga, where a lahar destroyed it on 11 September 1541. The authorities moved the capital eight kilometres north, and on 10 March 1543 Spanish conquistadors founded the present city, again named Santiago de los Caballeros. For 230 years it was the seat of the Captaincy General of Guatemala, which covered the present Guatemala, Belize, El Salvador, Honduras, Nicaragua and Costa Rica and the state of Chiapas in Mexico. It was laid out in a grid around a central square.

Franciscans, Jesuits and the Brothers of San Juan de Dios founded convents, schools and hospitals, and the Royal University of San Carlos Borromeo began classes on 7 January 1681. Earthquakes damaged the city repeatedly, notably in 1717 and 1751. After the Santa Marta earthquakes of 1773 the Crown ordered the capital moved in 1776 to the Valley of the Shrine, the site of the present Guatemala City. The abandoned city was called la Antigua Guatemala. Its population, at a peak of about 65,000 in the 1770s, fell as most residents left.

Antigua is the capital of Sacatepéquez Department. It was declared a National Monument on 30 March 1944 and a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1979, for its Spanish Baroque-influenced architecture, layout, churches and ruins. The Arco de Santa Catalina and the Palace of the Captaincy General, which houses the National Museum of Guatemalan Art, survive among the ruins. The city is known for its Holy Week processions over carpets of dyed sawdust and flowers.
antikythera-mechanism: The device is believed to have been made by Hellenistic scientists. Proposed dates range from 205 BCE through 150 to 100 BCE to about 87 BCE. It must predate the shipwreck that carried it, dated by several lines of evidence to about 70 to 60 BCE. Researchers in 2022 proposed 23 December 178 BCE as its initial calibration date, while others favour 204 BCE. Machines of similar complexity did not appear again until the 14th century in western Europe.

How it came to be on a Roman cargo ship is unknown. Its design drew on the astronomy of the 2nd century BCE, and Hipparchus of Rhodes, who studied the Moon's irregular motion, may have been consulted. Researchers in 2008 traced the calendar on the Metonic Spiral to Corinth or one of its colonies.

The mechanism was housed in a wooden case of about 34 by 18 by 9 centimetres. The front dial has a fixed ring of the twelve zodiac signs and, outside it, a movable ring. Scans in 2005 suggested 35 meshing bronze gears, 30 still visible, which followed the Sun and Moon through the zodiac, predicted eclipses and modelled the Moon's changing speed. The largest gear is about 13 centimetres across and had 223 teeth.

Inscriptions on the back door act as a manual and name the 76-year Callippic cycle, the 19-year Metonic cycle and the Saros cycle of 223. Whether it also showed the five classical planets is debated, since no planetary gearing survives. Freeth and Jones found that a simulation with planetary pointers is inaccurate, with the Mars pointer up to 38 degrees wrong at times, because of limits in Greek planetary theory rather than in the gearing.

Sponge divers from Symi under Captain Dimitrios Kontos found the wreck off Point Glyphadia on Antikythera in early 1900, at a depth of 45 metres. The mechanism was recovered in 1901 and went unnoticed for two years among statues and other finds. In 1902 the politician Spyridon Stais saw a gear in it, and the museum director Valerios Stais made the first study. The lump is now 82 fragments in the National Archaeological Museum in Athens. In 2005 a Cardiff University team led by Mike Edmunds used X-ray tomography to read faint inscriptions. Cicero describes two machines of Archimedes brought to Rome by Marcus Claudius Marcellus, suggesting the device was not unique.
antinoopolis: Antinoöpolis stood on the east bank of the Nile, nearly opposite Hermopolis Magna, at the foot of the hill on which the village of Besa, named after the god and oracle Bes, was seated. The Via Hadriana joined it to Berenice Troglodytica. In the New Kingdom the older city on the site, Hir-we, held the great temple of Ramesses II, dedicated to the gods of Khmun and Heliopolis.

The emperor Hadrian built the city in 130 CE on the site of Hir-we as the cult centre of Antinoüs, his deified young beloved. Earlier buildings, including a necropolis, were razed, except the Temple of Ramesses II. Hadrian intended it as the first Hellenic city in the Middle Nile region, a bastion of Greek culture, and encouraged Greeks to settle there with incentives. To bring Egyptians into the new culture he let Bes keep his worship beside the new chief deity, Osiris-Antinoüs. The city was laid out on a grid and adorned with columns and statues of Antinoüs. Games, the Antinoeia, were held there from spring 131, with athletic, chariot and musical contests, and were the most important in Egypt for several centuries.

A senate and a president governed the city, under the prefect of the Thebaid, and in 286 Diocletian made it the capital of the nome of the Thebaid. It was the seat of a Christian bishop by the 4th century and a metropolitan see in the 5th. The mathematician Serenus of Antinoöpolis was born there, and in a divorce decree of 569 it was still called most illustrious. The city was abandoned around the 10th century.

Travellers such as Claude Sicard in 1715 and Edme-François Jomard around 1800 still saw its theatre, temples, a triumphal arch, colonnaded streets and a hippodrome, but in the 19th century the stone was burned for lime or used for a dam and a sugar factory, and the large temple was destroyed for a cement works. The site is now the village of El Sheikh Ibada. Albert Gayet's excavations uncovered a large Coptic cemetery with mummies, grave goods and thousands of textiles, and the University of Rome dug there in the years 1965 to 68.
antinous: Antinous was born to a Greek family in Mantineion, a rural locality east of the city of Claudiopolis in the Roman province of Bithynia, in what is now north-west Turkey. His birth is estimated between 110 and 112 CE, and early sources place his birthday in November. His family background is not attested. Many writers from the Renaissance onward asserted that he had been a slave, but only one of about fifty early sources says so, and the deification of a former slave would have been highly controversial. His biographer Royston Lambert thought his family most likely peasant farmers or small business owners.

The Emperor Hadrian reached Claudiopolis in June 123, probably when he first met Antinous. The boy was probably sent to Italy and schooled at the imperial paedagogium on the Caelian Hill. Hadrian returned to Italy in September 125 and settled at his villa at Tibur, and at some point over the next three years Antinous became his personal favourite. When Hadrian left for Greece, Antinous travelled in his retinue. He attended the Eleusinian Mysteries at Athens with the emperor and was present in Libya when Hadrian killed the Marousian lion, an event the emperor publicised widely.

In late September or early October 130 the imperial party gathered at Heliopolis to sail up the Nile, and stopped at Hermopolis Magna, the main shrine of the god Thoth. Shortly afterwards, around the time of the festival of Osiris, Antinous fell into the river and died, probably by drowning. Gossip spread that he had been killed deliberately. Proposed explanations include a court conspiracy, killing by Hadrian himself, sacrifice or suicide, but no source settles the question.

Hadrian wept openly and, in October 130, proclaimed Antinous a god. The Egyptian priesthood identified him with Osiris. Hadrian ordered a city, Antinoöpolis, to be built on the site of Hir-we, designed on a Hippodamian grid as a Greek centre in the Middle Nile region, and founded games there, the Antinoeia, held annually for several centuries. He promoted the cult in Greece, linking Antinous with Hermes and, more widely, with Dionysus. Traces of the cult survive in at least 70 cities, from Britain to the Danube.

Pausanias, Lucian, Celsus and later Christian writers such as Tertullian, Origen and Jerome criticised the cult. Statues showing a youth with downcast eyes and tousled curls were produced across the empire, and many remained in public places until pagan worship was prohibited under Theodosius in 391. From the 18th century Antinous became a figure of interest to the homosexual subculture of Europe.
antioch: Antioch stood in northern Syria at the site of modern Antakya, in Hatay Province, Turkey. It lay in the southwest of the Amuq plain, a fertile lowland watered by three rivers. The Orontes skirted the plain's southern edge and cut westward through the mountains to the Mediterranean. Wheat, barley, olives and wine were grown there, and cypress wood and building stone were abundant. The plain had been inhabited for thousands of years, with Bronze Age powers at Tell Atchana and Tell Tayinat, and it stayed under Achaemenid rule until Alexander the Great invaded in 333 BCE.

After Seleucus I Nicator won the Battle of Ipsus in 301 BCE he ordered four settlements to secure northern Syria: Seleucia Pieria and Laodicea on the coast, and Antioch and Apamea inland. Antioch was founded in 300 BCE on a grid plan modelled on Alexandria, with the citadel on Mount Silpius. Later rulers added walled quarters, and it became known as Tetrapolis. It was the Seleucid capital from 240 BCE until the Romans took control in 63 BCE, then capital of Roman Syria, and may have had more than 500,000 inhabitants at its peak, the third largest city of the empire.

Antioch was a chief centre of early Christianity, and the New Testament asserts that the name Christian first arose there. When the emperor Julian visited in 362 he ordered the bones of the martyred bishop Babylas moved from the temple of Apollo at Daphne, which provoked a large Christian procession. A tax sedition in 387 cost the city its metropolitan status. Abu Ubayda ibn al-Jarrah took it for the Rashidun Caliphate in 637.

The Crusaders captured Antioch in June 1098 after a siege of eight months, and it became the centre of the Principality of Antioch. On 18 May 1268 Baibars took the city; he promised to spare its people but broke his promise and razed it, killing or enslaving nearly the whole population. By 1432 only about 300 houses within its walls were inhabited.

Little of the Roman city is visible beyond the fortification walls climbing the mountains east of Antakya, several aqueducts and the Church of St Peter. Most of it lies beneath alluvial deposits of the Orontes. Excavations between 1932 and 1939 did not find Constantine's Great Octagonal Church or the imperial palace, but recovered Roman mosaics from villas and baths. The Greek Orthodox Patriarchate of Antioch still bears the city's name.
antiochus-i-theos-of-commagene: Antiochus I was the son of King Mithridates I Callinicus and Queen Laodice VII Thea of Commagene. His mother was a Seleucid princess, daughter of Antiochus VIII Grypus and the Ptolemaic princess Tryphaena, which made him a descendant of several of the Diadochi, the generals who succeeded Alexander the Great. His father was possibly related to the kings of Parthia and claimed descent from Orontes and, through Orontes' marriage to Rhodogune, daughter of Artaxerxes II, from Darius I of Persia.

Little is known of his early life apart from its philhellenic character; he seems to have succeeded his father in 70 BCE. He married Isias, daughter of Ariobarzanes I of Cappadocia, and they had at least four children, among them Mithridates II, who succeeded him, and Laodice, who married Orodes II of Parthia.

Commagene was a small kingdom in the highlands of northern Syria, bordering Cappadocia to the north and Osroene to the south. It had been a vassal of the Seleucids and was considerably Hellenized, but in the 1st century BCE Iranian culture revived there, supported to stress the kingdom's ancient ancestry against Seleucid, Parthian and Roman claims. Antiochus suffered in the Roman war with Pontus and Armenia. Armenia at first extended its influence over Commagene, but he was forced to side with the Romans when Pompey declared war against him. His inscription at Mount Nemrut calls him a friend of the Romans, though some of Cicero's informants distrusted him.

He allied with the Parthian king Orodes II, and in 51 BCE nevertheless gave Cicero intelligence on a Parthian force under Prince Pacorus I. In 38 BCE the Romans defeated and killed Pacorus, and the remnants of his army took refuge in Commagene. Publius Ventidius besieged the capital Samosata to punish Antiochus. He offered 1,000 talents and a renewed alliance, which Mark Antony refused; Antony then took over the siege, could not take the city, and accepted a new offer of 300 talents. Antiochus's later life is obscure, and according to Cassius Dio he was killed by the Parthian king Phraates IV.

Antiochus built the sanctuary on Mount Nemrut, creating a royal cult in which he expected to be worshipped after death. His inscriptions say his tomb should stand on a high and holy place close to the gods. The gods were a blend of Greek and Iranian figures, such as Zeus-Oromasdes and Apollo-Mithras-Helios-Hermes, with Persian dress and Greek faces. Feasts on the 10th and 16th of each month marked his coronation and birthday, and families of priests were endowed to serve in perpetuity. German archaeologists excavated the tomb in 1883, and UNESCO listed it in 1987. Reliefs there include some of the oldest known images of two figures shaking hands.
antiochus-ii-theos: Antiochus II was the younger son of King Antiochus I Soter and Queen Stratonice, a daughter of Demetrius Poliorcetes. He was not at first expected to inherit the throne. In 267 BCE his father had his elder brother Seleucus executed on a charge of rebellion, and Antiochus II succeeded in the winter of 262 to 261 BCE.

Antiochus II inherited lasting tension with Ptolemaic Egypt and soon began the Second Syrian War in alliance with Antigonus II of the Antigonid dynasty. The fighting ran mostly along the coasts of Asia Minor and mixed with the intrigues of petty despots and restless cities. Antiochus gained direct access to the Aegean by capturing Miletus and Ephesus. He took the title Theos after killing the tyrant Timarchus on behalf of the Milesians. The war left the balance of power little changed, and Coele-Syria, the main disputed territory, stayed with the Ptolemies.

In 253 BCE, with his Antigonid allies knocked out of the war by rebellions, Antiochus made peace with Ptolemy II. He divorced his first wife Laodice and married Ptolemy's daughter Berenice, on the understanding that their children would inherit the throne. Laodice was well provided for, with estates in the Hellespont, near Cyzicus and Ilion, and in Caria, known from inscriptions. In the east he appears to have relied on independent-minded satraps such as Diodotus and Andragoras, whose appointments eventually led to the Greco-Bactrian Kingdom and the Parthian Empire. Little else is known of his eastern policy.

By 246 BCE, possibly on news of Ptolemy II's death, Antiochus left Berenice and their infant son in Antioch and went to live again with Laodice in Asia Minor. He soon died suddenly, and Laodice was widely accused of poisoning him. He was buried in the Belevi Mausoleum.

A struggle for the throne followed at once. Berenice held Antioch, but her son was an infant. Laodice proclaimed her eldest son as Seleucus II, claiming that Antiochus had named him on his deathbed. Ptolemy III marched from Egypt to support his sister Berenice and found her and her son murdered by Laodice's partisans. The Third Syrian War that followed proved a disaster for the Seleucid empire.
antiochus-iii-the-great: Antiochus III was the son of Seleucus II Callinicus and Laodice II, born about 242 BCE near Susa in Persia. He succeeded his brother Seleucus III Ceraunus, who was murdered in Anatolia, while he himself was in Babylon. He was about eighteen and inherited a disorganised state. Asia Minor had become detached, and Bactria and Parthia had broken away. Soon after his accession Media and Persis revolted under their governors, the brothers Molon and Alexander. An attack on Ptolemaic Syria, made under the influence of his minister Hermeias, ended in failure. Only in 221 BCE, advised by Zeuxis, did Antiochus go east in person, and the rebellion collapsed.

After his defeat by Ptolemy IV at the Battle of Raphia in 217 BCE, Antiochus turned to Asia Minor and by 214 BCE had driven his cousin Achaeus, who had taken the royal title, into Sardis. He had Achaeus executed. In 209 BCE he invaded Parthia, and in Bactria defeated Euthydemus I at the Battle of the Arius; after the Siege of Bactra he allowed Euthydemus to keep his royal title. He crossed into the Kabul valley and renewed his friendship with the Indian king Sophagasenus, receiving elephants, and returned by Seistan and Kerman in 206 or 205 BCE. These campaigns earned him the name the Great, and he took the title Basileus Megas, Great King.

Returning west, he renewed the war against the Ptolemies, and his victory over Scopas at the Battle of Panium in 198 BCE marked the end of Ptolemaic rule in Judea. His expansion in Asia Minor and Thrace earned the antagonism of Rome. In 192 BCE he invaded Greece with 10,000 men, advised by the exiled Hannibal and elected commander of the Aetolian League. The Romans under Manius Acilius Glabrio routed him at Thermopylae in 191 BCE, and Scipio Asiaticus defeated him at Magnesia ad Sipylum in 190 BCE. By the Treaty of Apamea in 188 BCE he gave up all lands north and west of the Taurus Mountains, which Rome gave mostly to Rhodes and Eumenes II of Pergamon.

The outlying provinces he had recovered reasserted their independence after Apamea. Antiochus mounted a new expedition to the east and was killed in 187 BCE while pillaging a temple of Bel at Elymaïs. His son Seleucus IV Philopator succeeded him, and later another son became Antiochus IV Epiphanes. Josephus portrays Antiochus III as friendly to the Jews of Jerusalem: he lowered taxes, granted subventions to the Temple and let the Jews live by the law of their forefathers, and he resettled 2,000 Jewish families from Babylonia in Lydia and Phrygia. The First Book of Maccabees recalls his defeat by the Romans.
antiochus-iv-epiphanes: Antiochus was a son of the Seleucid king Antiochus III the Great. Under the Treaty of Apamea of 188 BCE he became a political hostage of the Roman Republic, and when his elder brother Seleucus IV Philopator took the throne in 187 BCE he was exchanged for Seleucus's son Demetrius. He then lived in Athens, where he was when Seleucus was assassinated in 175 BCE by the minister Heliodorus. With the help of Eumenes II of Pergamum he reached Syria by November 175 BCE and took the throne as co-regent with Seleucus's infant son, who died in 170 BCE, possibly murdered by Antiochus.

Antiochus cultivated a reputation for extravagance. He scattered money in the streets of Antioch and held a great parade at Daphne, and his unexpected behaviour, such as appearing in the public baths, led detractors to call him Epimanes, the Mad, a play on his title Epiphanes, God Manifest. In 170 BCE the guardians of Ptolemy VI Philometor declared war to recover Coele-Syria. Antiochus defeated the Egyptian army, advanced into Egypt and captured Ptolemy. In 168 BCE he attacked again, but before he reached Alexandria the Roman envoy Gaius Popillius Laenas delivered a Senate order to withdraw, drew a circle in the sand round him, and demanded an answer before he left it. Antiochus withdrew.

In 171 BCE Antiochus had replaced the High Priest Jason with Menelaus, who offered a bribe. In 168 BCE a rumour that the king had died led Jason to attack Jerusalem, and Antiochus, returning, restored Menelaus and killed many Jews. According to 1 Maccabees he then outlawed Jewish rites, made the Temple a cult that included the worship of Zeus, and built a Greek citadel, the Acra. The Maccabean Revolt followed. Traditionally it is seen as resistance to foreign oppression, but some modern scholars see Antiochus as intervening in a civil war between traditionalist and Hellenized Jews.

Antiochus led the main army east against the Parthians, retook Armenia, but was driven from Persepolis, and died at Isfahan in 164 BCE. Polybius and the books of the Maccabees judge him harshly, but some historians doubt Polybius, who was a friend of Antiochus's rival Demetrius I. Jewish tradition remembers him as the persecutor of the story of Hanukkah.
antiochus-vii-sidetes: Antiochus VII Euergetes, nicknamed Sidetes after the city of Side in Asia Minor and also known as Antiochus the Pious, was born around 164 to 160 BCE. He was a son of Demetrius I Soter and the brother of Demetrius II Nicator; his mother may have been Laodice V. He was raised to the throne after Demetrius II was captured by the Parthians, and he married Cleopatra Thea, who had been Demetrius's wife. Their son became Antiochus IX.

Antiochus ruled the Seleucid Empire from July or August 138 to 129 BCE and spent his nine years trying to undo the heavy territorial and authority losses of recent decades. He defeated the usurper Diodotus Tryphon at Dora and in 134 BCE laid siege to Jerusalem. During the siege he allowed a seven-day truce so that the Jews could celebrate a religious festival, which impressed their leaders.

According to Josephus, the Hasmonean leader John Hyrcanus opened the tomb of King David, removed three thousand talents and paid Antiochus to spare the city. His respectful treatment of the Jews earned him their gratitude and the added name Euergetes, the Benefactor. Because no Jewish sources of the time survive, it is unclear whether the siege ended in a decisive Seleucid victory or a peace treaty. Jewish forces later assisted his wars, and for nearly twenty years after his death John Hyrcanus refrained from attacking Seleucid territory.

In his last years Antiochus tried to reclaim the eastern territories overrun by the Parthians under Mithridates I. He marched east with what proved to be the last great Seleucid royal army, including a unit of Judean troops under John Hyrcanus, and won three battles. He restored Mesopotamia, Babylonia and Media before dispersing his army into winter quarters.

Tension grew between the local population and the troops quartered upon them. The new Parthian ruler, Phraates II, released his prisoner Demetrius II, who returned to Syria to reclaim the throne. In the winter of 130–129 BCE several towns rose against their Seleucid garrisons, and Antiochus marched to relieve them. In the Zagros mountains he was ambushed and killed by Phraates II and a large Parthian force. Afterwards the Seleucid realm was restricted to Syria. His confirmed heir was Antiochus IX Cyzicenus.
antioquia-department: Antioquia covers 63,612 square kilometres in the central north-west of Colombia, with a narrow section on the Caribbean Sea in the Urabá region. About 80 per cent of its territory is mountainous, crossed by the Cordillera Central and the Cordillera Occidental of the Andes. The Cordillera Central divides to form the Aburrá valley, where the capital, Medellín, lies. The basis for the name is uncertain. A common explanation is that it was named after the Hellenistic city of Antioch on the Orontes.

Before Spanish colonisation the region was populated mainly by the Kalina, or Mainland Caribs, whose best-known groups in central Antioquia were the Catía, Nutabe and Tahamí, while the Quimbaya lived in the south. The Spaniards dominated or exterminated the Carib, and many Indigenous people died in epidemics of diseases from Europe and Asia. Rodrigo de Bastidas was the first known Spaniard in the area, in 1500. The first military incursion was an expedition under Francisco César in 1537, which reached the Cauca River; the warriors of the chief Nutibara harassed it until it returned to Urabá.

In 1541 the conquistador Jorge Robledo led an expedition north along the Cauca and founded Santa Fe de Antioquia. In 1813 it was declared the capital of the sovereign state of Antioquia, and it remained the seat of government until 1826, when Medellín became the capital. Antioquia kept a sovereign government until the Colombian Constitution of 1886. Its mountains left it isolated and short of farmland, so it depended on trade, especially in gold, after reforms that followed a visit in 1785 by the Crown inspector Juan Antonio Mon y Velarde.

Antioquia is one of the 32 departments of Colombia, and more than half of its population lives in the metropolitan area of Medellín, the second-largest city in the country. Other important towns are Rionegro, Apartadó, Puerto Berrío and Santa Fe de Antioquia, the old capital. The department is divided into nine subregions and 125 municipalities.
antipater: Antipater belonged to the Macedonian noble house of Iolaos, which may have served the Argead kings of Macedon since as early as 432 BCE. He came from the Macedonian city of Paliura and was the son of a nobleman named Iolaos. He had eleven children, among them Cassander, later king of Macedonia, and daughters who married Craterus, Ptolemy I Soter, Perdiccas and Lysimachus. Under Philip II of Macedon he became, with Parmenion, a trusted adviser and one of Philip's prominent Hetairoi. In 342 BCE Philip appointed him regent of Macedon during three years of campaigning in Thrace, and after the Battle of Chaeronea in 338 BCE he went to Athens as ambassador to negotiate peace.

When Alexander the Great left for Asia in 334 BCE, Antipater remained as regent of Macedonia and general of Europe. Thracian tribes rebelled in 332 BCE, and Agis III of Sparta, funded by the Persians, raised an army of 20,000 and besieged Megalopolis. Antipater pardoned the Thracian governor Memnon to avoid fighting two enemies, led a force of roughly twice Agis's size south, and defeated and killed him at the Battle of Megalopolis in 330 BCE. Plutarch reports Alexander calling the clash a battle of mice. His relations with Olympias deteriorated, and in 324 BCE Alexander ordered him to bring fresh troops to Asia while Craterus took over the regency. Alexander died before the change took effect.

In the Lamian War Antipater, with about 13,000 men against some 25,000 Greeks, was defeated near Thermopylae when his Thessalian cavalry defected, and was besieged at Lamia in 322 BCE. Relieved with the help of Leonnatus, he joined Craterus and defeated the Greeks at the Battle of Crannon. He imposed oligarchy on Athens and demanded the surrender of Demosthenes and Hypereides. Demosthenes took his own life; Hypereides was executed. Antipater then allied with Ptolemy and Antigonus against Perdiccas in the First War of the Diadochi.

At the Partition of Triparadisus in 321 BCE Antipater became regent of the whole empire and took the kings Philip III Arrhidaeus and Alexander IV back to Macedon. He died of old age in 319 BCE, aged 81. He passed over his son Cassander and named the officer Polyperchon regent, which began the Second War of the Diadochi. Cassander defeated Polyperchon and ruled Macedonia for nineteen years, founding the Antipatrid dynasty.

Historians generally see Antipater as a loyal supporter of the Argeads with little interest in Asia or supreme power. Some later writers, such as Justin, accused him of poisoning Alexander, a view most historians dispute.
antipope-anacletus-ii: Pietro Pierleoni was born into the powerful Roman family of the Pierleoni, the son of the consul Pier Leoni. One of his great-great-grandparents, Benedictus, was a Jewish banker who converted to Christianity. As a second son with ambitions, Pietro was destined for an ecclesiastical career. He studied in Paris and entered the Benedictine Abbey of Cluny, and later went to Rome, where he held several important positions.

In 1130 Pope Honorius II lay dying, and the cardinals entrusted the election to a commission of eight men led by the papal chancellor Haimeric. The commission hastily elected Cardinal Gregorio Papareschi as Innocent II, who was consecrated on 14 February, the day after Honorius died. On the same day the other cardinals, led by the senior cardinal bishop, Pietro of Porto, met with the leaders of Rome in the Basilica of S. Marco and announced that Innocent had not been canonically elected. They chose Pierleoni, who was elected by the cardinals, clergy, nobility and people of Rome.

Anacletus had the support of the entire Roman aristocracy except the Frangipani, rivals of the Pierleoni, and of the majority of the cardinals. The Pierleoni were powerful enough to take control of Rome, and Innocent fled north of the Alps. There he won the support of Bernard of Clairvaux, Peter the Venerable, abbot of Cluny, and Norbert of Xanten, and through them recognition from rulers such as Emperor Lothair. Rumours about Anacletus' descent from a Jewish convert were spread to damage him; Bernard wrote that it was a disgrace for Christ that a Jew sat on the throne of St. Peter's.

Among Anacletus' supporters were Duke William X of Aquitaine, who decided for him against the will of his own bishops, and Roger II of Sicily, whose title of King of Sicily Anacletus approved by papal bull. By 1135 his position was weak, and the schism ended only with his death on 25 January 1138. Gregorio Conti was then elected as Victor IV but submitted to Innocent within a month. Innocent returned to Rome and convened the Second Lateran Council in 1139, which ended the schism, though opinion remained divided. Anacletus' brother Giordano, leader of the Commune of Rome, opposed Innocent's successors in the following decade.
antofagasta: Antofagasta lies about 1,100 kilometres north of Santiago on a coastal plain, south of the Mejillones Peninsula and north of Cerro Coloso, at an average elevation of 40 metres. The urban area begins abruptly, breaking the monotony of the desert. The Tropic of Capricorn passes north of the city, near the Cerro Moreno International Airport, and a monument opened on 21 December 2000 marks it and works as a solar calendar. The name is presumed to derive from that of Antofagasta de la Sierra in Catamarca Province, Argentina.

In the 18th century the territory appeared on maps of the Captaincy General of Chile, depending on Copiapó, and it was disputed between Chile and Bolivia until the Boundary Treaty of 1866. On 18 September 1866 José Santos Ossa and Francisco Puelma obtained a Bolivian concession over nitrate lands after finding rich saltpeter deposits at the Salar del Carmen, and formed the Sociedad Exploradora del Desierto de Atacama. On 8 May 1872 the Bolivian government designated Antofagasta a Puerto Mayor, opening it to world trade.

In 1873 Bolivia signed a secret defensive alliance with Peru, and a contract with a Chilean company, the Compañía de Salitres y Ferrocarril de Antofagasta, which Bolivia's congress never ratified. In 1874 Chile and Bolivia signed a border treaty that barred new taxes on Chilean capital for 25 years. In the Bolivian version of events, congress imposed a tax of 10 cents because the contract was not in force; when Bolivia reactivated the tax after a Chilean note, it cancelled the company's concession. Chile occupied Antofagasta on 14 February 1879, which triggered the War of the Pacific (1879–83). The Treaty of Peace and Friendship, signed on 20 October 1904 and promulgated on 21 March 1905, fixed the border permanently.

A British community erected a clock tower in 1912 that replicates Big Ben, in the Plaza Colón. A mudslide on 18 June 1991 killed 92 people, left 16 missing and about 20,000 homeless, and destroyed 493 buildings; an earthquake of magnitude 7.3 struck on 30 July 1995.

Antofagasta is the capital of Antofagasta Province and Antofagasta Region, with a population of 401,096 at the 2024 census. It is a port and the chief service hub of one of Chile's major mining areas, where silver and saltpeter were historically important and copper has been by far the most important mineral since the mid-19th century. It is also a university city, home to the Catholic University of the North and the University of Antofagasta.
antoine-de-lamothe-cadillac: Cadillac was born Antoine Laumet on 5 March 1658 at Saint-Nicolas-de-la-Grave in Gascony. His father, Jean Laumet, was a lawyer in the Parlement of Toulouse, and the boy studied at a Jesuit institution. At 25 he left France for North America and arrived at Port Royal, the capital of Acadia, in 1683. On 25 June 1687 he married Marie-Thérèse, daughter of the Quebec merchant Denis Guyon. The marriage certificate is the first document to record his new identity, "Antoine de Lamothe, écuyer, sieur de Cadillac", with titles and arms modelled on those of a baron of Lamothe-Bardigues from villages near his birthplace.

Appointed an officer of marine troops in 1690, Cadillac was sent in 1692, as a lieutenant, with the cartographer Jean-Baptiste-Louis Franquelin to chart the New England coast. In 1694 he took command of Fort de Buade at Michilimackinac, where he clashed with Jesuits such as Étienne de Carheil, who accused him of supplying alcohol to Native Americans. After the king ordered trading posts closed in 1696, he proposed a new fort on the strait between Lakes Erie and Huron, which was approved in 1700.

On 24 July 1701 he led the founding of Fort Pontchartrain du Détroit, with Alphonse de Tonti as second in command. He called the settlement the Paris of New France. Charged with trafficking in alcohol and furs, he was imprisoned for a few months in 1704 and cleared in 1705.

In 1710 the king named him governor of Louisiana. He did not obey at once, but sailed for France in 1711 and persuaded the financier Antoine Crozat to invest there. The Cadillac family reached Fort Louis, now Mobile, in June 1713. In 1715 he and his son Joseph prospected in the Illinois Country and claimed to have found a copper mine, although there is no copper ore there, and he directed the first mining of lead at what is now Mine La Motte, using enslaved workers. After many arguments Crozat withdrew his authority and had him removed from colonial office.

Cadillac returned to France, and he and Joseph were imprisoned in the Bastille for five months. Released in 1718, he was decorated with the Order of Saint Louis, and in 1722 his rights to the concession on the strait were recognised. He became governor and mayor of Castelsarrasin, where he died on 16 October 1730. No authentic portrait of him survives, which historians suggest may reflect a damnatio memoriae started by his many enemies. Detroit grew from his fort, and an automobile company founded in 1902 took his name.
antoine-duke-of-brabant: Anthony was born on 21 August 1384, a son of Philip the Bold, Duke of Burgundy, and Margaret III, Countess of Flanders, and a brother of John the Fearless. Before he came into Brabant he was Count of Rethel, from 1402 to 1406. On the death of his childless great-aunt Joanna in 1406 he inherited the duchies of Brabant, Lothier and Limburg, and from 1411 he was also co-duke of Luxemburg.

At Arras on 21 February 1402 he married Jeanne of Saint-Pol, daughter of Waleran III of Luxembourg, Count of Ligny and Saint-Pol, who died in 1407. Their sons were John IV, Duke of Brabant, born in 1403, and Philip of Saint-Pol, born in 1404, who held the duchy from 1427 to 1430. At Brussels on 16 July 1409 he married Elisabeth of Görlitz, Duchess of Luxembourg, daughter of John, Duke of Görlitz; they had no children. He also had a daughter, Anna of Brabant, who married Pedro de Peralta y Ezpeleta.

Anthony reached the field of Agincourt late on 25 October 1415. In his haste he put on the improvised armour of his chamberlain and a surcoat made from a trumpeter's flag, and charged with a few retainers, crying Brabant! Brabant! At the English lines he was knocked down and captured by archers. He was then killed by a cut to the throat with the other prisoners whose execution King Henry V of England ordered; the English did not know his rank or ransom value because of his makeshift surcoat.

The order came while the smaller English army was stretched to its limits guarding prisoners with the battle not yet won. An attack on the king's baggage train led by Ysembart d'Azincourt is thought to have driven Henry to the decision, and some chroniclers gave Anthony's late charge as its cause. The killing stopped once the attack was seen to falter.
antoine-watteau: Jean-Antoine Watteau was born in October 1684 in Valenciennes, once an important town of the County of Hainaut that passed to France after the Franco-Dutch War. He was the second of four sons of Jean-Philippe Watteau, a roofer, and Michelle Lardenois. He left for Paris in 1702 and, after working as a scene-painter, found employment copying Flemish and Dutch genre paintings, where he developed his sketchlike technique. By 1705 he was assistant to Claude Gillot, in whose studio he came to know the characters of the commedia dell'arte, a lifelong passion. He then moved to the workshop of Claude Audran III, curator of the Palais du Luxembourg, where he saw the canvases of Peter Paul Rubens for Marie de Medici, a major influence.

Watteau failed to win the Prix de Rome in 1709 and 1712. He was accepted as an associate member of the Academy in 1712 and a full member in 1717, taking five years to deliver his reception piece, the Pilgrimage to Cythera. He then lived with the collector Pierre Crozat, whose collection let him study Rubens and the Venetian masters. He lacked aristocratic patrons, and his buyers were bourgeois, bankers and dealers.

His best-known works include Pierrot, long identified as Gilles, and Fêtes venitiennes. His last major work, the Shop-sign of Gersaint, was painted for the Paris dealer Edme François Gersaint in eight days, working only in the mornings, and has been compared with Las Meninas as a meditation on art and illusion. Sickly from childhood, he went to London in 1720 to consult Dr. Richard Mead, then returned to France and died in 1721, perhaps of tuberculous laryngitis, aged 36.

Watteau was little known in his lifetime beyond a small circle. His fêtes galantes are tinged with wistfulness at the transience of love, in contrast to the whimsy of Boucher and Fragonard later. Jean de Jullienne published etchings after his drawings in 1726 and 1728 and engravings after his paintings in 1735, which spread his influence across Europe. The Watteau dress, with loose pleats hanging from the shoulder at the back, is named after him. J. M. W. Turner was among his admirers in England, and Edmond de Goncourt published a catalogue raisonné in 1875.
anton-bruckner: Bruckner was born in Ansfelden on 4 September 1824, the eldest of the five children who survived of eleven born to the village schoolmaster Anton Bruckner Sr. His father was his first music teacher, and he learned the organ as a child, sometimes practising twelve hours a day. After his father died in 1837 he became a choirboy at the Augustinian monastery of Sankt Florian. He worked as an assistant teacher at Windhaag, where pay was appalling and his superior constantly humiliated him, and a belief in his own inferiority stayed with him all his life. From 1845 he spent ten years at Sankt Florian as teacher and organist, and in 1855 he was accepted as a pupil by the Vienna theorist Simon Sechter.

In 1868 he hesitantly took over Sechter's post at the Vienna Conservatory and concentrated on symphonies, which were poorly received and at times called wild and nonsensical. He was unhappy in Vienna, where the critic Eduard Hanslick dominated musical life; by aligning himself with Wagner in the feud between the followers of Wagner and of Johannes Brahms, he made an unintentional enemy of him. Supporters such as the conductors Arthur Nikisch and Franz Schalk brought his music to the public.

Bruckner composed eleven symphonies, from the Study Symphony in F minor of 1863 to the unfinished Symphony No. 9 in D minor, written between 1887 and 1896. Only the Fourth, the Romantic, had a subtitle from the composer. By the mid-twentieth century musicologists recognised that his orchestration followed the sound of the pipe organ, alternating between groups of instruments as an organist changes manual. His sacred music includes a Te Deum, a Magnificat, about forty motets and at least seven Masses. Helgoland of 1893 was his last completed composition, and his String Quintet in F major dates from 1879.

Bruckner died on 11 October 1896 and is buried at Sankt Florian. His admirers included Gustav Mahler. The leaders of Nazi Germany approved of his music, and Adolf Hitler consecrated a bust of him at the Walhalla in Regensburg in 1937. The Brucknerhaus in Linz, which opened in 1974, is named after him.
anton-denikin: Anton Denikin was born on 4 December 1872 in Włocławek in the Russian Empire. His father, Ivan, was born a serf and served 25 years in the army, retiring as a major, and his mother Elżbieta was a Polish Catholic. The family lived in poverty and Anton was raised in the Orthodox faith. He entered the army in 1889 and the Academy of the General Staff in 1895, and in the Russo-Japanese War a hill was named Denikin's sopka in his honour.

In the First World War Denikin commanded the 4th Rifle Brigade, the Iron Brigade, one of the most decorated units in the army, and was promoted to lieutenant general in 1915. After the February Revolution he became chief of staff to the Supreme Commander and criticised the Provisional Government's army reforms, and in August 1917 he was arrested for supporting General Lavr Kornilov. After the October Revolution he reached Novocherkassk, helped found the Volunteer Army and took command in April 1918, after Kornilov was killed.

In January 1919 he became Commander-in-Chief of the Armed Forces of South Russia. His Moscow Directive of 20 June 1919 began an offensive that took Kharkov, Kiev and Orel and came within 350 kilometres of Moscow. His supply lines were overstretched and peasant uprisings troubled his rear. His advance in Ukraine was accompanied by antisemitic pogroms, mostly by Cossack units, which killed tens of thousands; he forbade them, but his orders were not enforced. A Red Army counter-offensive defeated the Whites at Orel and Voronezh in late October. Denikin resigned in favour of General Pyotr Wrangel on 4 April 1920.

In exile Denikin wrote a five-volume history of the Civil War, The Russian Turmoil. When Germany invaded the Soviet Union in 1941 he urged émigrés to support the Red Army. He moved to the United States in December 1945 and died of a heart attack on 7 August 1947. His remains were reburied at the Donskoy Monastery in Moscow in 2005.

His reputation is disputed: Soviet writers portrayed him as an enemy of the people, while admirers saw a patriot. Historian Peter Kenez judged him a decent man but an ineffective leader, whose government failed to carry out an effective land reform and whose slogan of a great, united and indivisible Russia alienated the Cossacks and national minorities.
anton-florian-prince-of-liechtenstein: Anton Florian was born on 28 May 1656 at Wilfersdorf, in what is now Lower Austria. On 15 October 1679 he married Countess Eleonore Barbara Catharina von Thun und Hohenstein. They had eleven children, most of whom died in early childhood. During the War of the Spanish Succession he went to Spain, where he served as Chief Intendant and Prime Minister of the Archduke Karl. Karl became Emperor Charles VI after the sudden death of his brother in 1711, and Anton Florian returned to Vienna for the coronation.

At the imperial court he was Obersthofmeister, the Imperial Chief Intendant, and Chairman of the Secret Council, and he held both posts until his death in 1721. He was the 591st Knight of the Order of the Golden Fleece in Austria.

On 23 January 1719 Charles VI created the new principality of Liechtenstein from the Seigneury of Schellenberg and the County of Vaduz, both of which were held by the Liechtenstein family. The reason was that Anton Florian could be admitted to the Reichstag only if he held land subordinate to the Emperor alone, rather than land held in fief from higher nobles. In this way he became the first Prince of Liechtenstein.

Anton Florian died in Vienna on 11 October 1721. His son Joseph Johann Adam, born on 27 May 1690, was the surviving son who succeeded him as prince. Of the daughters, Anna Maria Antonie, born in 1699, married her cousin Joseph Wenzel I, Prince of Liechtenstein, and Maria Eleonore, born in 1703, married Count Friedrich August von Harrach-Rohrau and had sixteen children.
anton-korosec: Anton Korošec was born on 12 May 1872 in Biserjane, then in the Duchy of Styria in Austria-Hungary and now in Slovenia, and went to school in Ptuj and Maribor. He studied theology and was ordained a priest in 1895, then took a doctorate in theology at the University of Graz in 1905. A friend of Janez Evangelist Krek, he adopted Krek's political views. He became known as an orator.

In 1907 Korošec was elected to the Reichsrat for the Slovenian People's Party and, as president of the Yugoslav Club, read out the May Declaration, which called for all South Slavs to be united in one state unit within the Austro-Hungarian monarchy. After the break-up of Austria-Hungary, the National Council of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs, which he presided over, declared the State of Slovenes, Croats and Serbs on 29 October 1918.

Earlier he and Nikola Pašić had agreed the Geneva Declaration, in which Serbia recognised the equal rights of the components of such a state. The Kingdom of Serbs, Croats and Slovenes that followed was nonetheless a unitary monarchy. He was vice-president in its first government and again from 1924, and minister of the interior in 1924 and 1927. He opposed the Vidovdan Constitution and campaigned for Slovene autonomy.

After the assassination of Stjepan Radić in 1928 the king called Korošec to lead the first Yugoslav government without a Serbian prime minister, but dismissed him when the January 6th Dictatorship was proclaimed. He served in Petar Živković's government in 1929, which fell in 1930. In opposition he drew up the Slovenian Declaration, calling for a new multinational union, and was exiled to the island of Hvar in 1933.

In 1935 Korošec became minister of the interior under Milan Stojadinović and urged close relations with Nazi Germany. He later served as minister of education in the government of Dragiša Cvetković and Vladko Maček. In October 1940 he introduced two antisemitic laws, one limiting the participation of Jews in the wholesale food industry and the other limiting the number of Jewish students in secondary schools and universities.

When other ministers objected, he insisted that refusing would endanger relations with Germany. As interior minister he declared all Jews, Communists and Freemasons traitors, conspirators and enemies of the state, and he organised the anti-Communist Sentinel in the Tempest. He died in Belgrade on 14 December 1940, aged 68.
anton-webern: Anton Webern was born on 3 December 1883 in Vienna, the only surviving son of Carl von Webern, a civil servant and mining engineer. He grew up mainly in Graz and Klagenfurt. His mother Amalie was a trained pianist and singer, and he learned piano, cello and probably counterpoint from the local musician Edwin Komauer. He studied the Franco-Flemish School under Guido Adler, and Arnold Schoenberg taught him to compose from the music of Bach, the First Viennese School and Brahms. In 1911 he married his cousin Wilhelmine Mörtl, and the Catholic Church solemnised their union in 1915, after three children had been born.

Early in his career Webern was an unhappily peripatetic conductor, often assigned light music or operetta. From 1918 to 1921 he worked with Schoenberg, Alban Berg and Erwin Stein at the Society for Private Musical Performances in Vienna. He rose as a choirmaster and conductor and championed the music of Gustav Mahler. After the Austrofascists crushed the Social Democrats in the 1934 Austrian Civil War, his long association with them cost him a promising domestic conducting career, and he relied on teaching and editing for income.

He was marginalised as a cultural Bolshevist in Austria and Nazi Germany, and little of his mature music was performed in the Reich. He opposed fascist cultural positions but espoused pan-Germanism, and his hope for stable governance of Austria within Nazi Germany proved misplaced. He helped Jewish friends emigrate and hide while repeatedly considering emigrating himself. A soldier accidentally killed him after the end of the Second World War, on 15 September 1945.

Webern's music was concise, organic and sparing, built on very small motifs and palindromes. After his Op. 2 his music and Schoenberg's was freely atonal, and he later adopted twelve-tone technique. His earliest works were mostly Lieder, and the German Romantic Lied left a lasting influence on his lyricism and intimacy, even as his music became more abstract. About 1913 to 1926 he worked on almost sixty songs. His String Trio, Op. 20 (1926 to 1927) was his first large-scale non-vocal work in more than a decade.

His music was long considered difficult by performers and inaccessible by listeners. After the Second World War composers including René Leibowitz and Pierre Boulez championed it, and it became central to the postwar avant-garde at the Darmstädter Ferienkurse and to the tradition known as post-Webernism. Igor Stravinsky assimilated it, and choreographers have set it to dance. Scholars have contested his legacy in the serial wars.
antoni-radziwill: Antoni Henryk Radziwiłł was born in Vilnius on 13 June 1775, the son of Michał Hieronim Radziwiłł and Helena Przeździecka, and studied at the University of Göttingen with his brothers. As a scion of the Radziwiłł family he was hereditary Duke of Nieśwież and Ołyka and a prince of the Holy Roman Empire. The Hohenzollern court offered him the hand of Princess Louise of Prussia, a niece of Frederick the Great; the marriage took place in 1796, after the Kościuszko Uprising and the Third Partition had ended the Polish state.

His new family persuaded him to act as a go-between for the Poles of the Prussian partition and the authorities in Berlin. Moving between Berlin, Warsaw and Saint Petersburg, he proposed making South Prussia the core of a renewed Polish kingdom under the Prussian king in personal union. In 1806 he tried and failed to win Prince Józef Poniatowski away from Napoleon; the Greater Poland Uprising instead led to the Duchy of Warsaw.

After the Congress of Vienna King Frederick William III sent him to Poznań as Duke-Governor of the Grand Duchy of Posen. He had little real power, which lay with the Oberpräsident Joseph Zerboni di Sposetti and the district governors, and in 1824 his daughter Eliza's engagement to Prince William of Prussia, the future German Emperor William I, was broken off. When his brother Michał Gedeon Radziwiłł led the November Uprising of 1830 in Congress Poland, he was stripped of his powers, and the office was abolished the next year.

Radziwiłł is remembered more as a patron of the arts. In his palaces in Berlin, Poznań and Antonin he himself performed guitar, cello and opera concerts, and his guests included Niccolò Paganini, Johann Wolfgang von Goethe, Frédéric Chopin and Ludwig van Beethoven. Chopin wrote his Introduction and Polonaise Op. 3 for him and dedicated his Piano Trio Op. 8 to him, and Beethoven dedicated the overture Zur Namensfeier, Op. 115. He died in Berlin on 7 April 1833 and was buried in Poznań Cathedral.
antonie-van-leeuwenhoek: Antonie van Leeuwenhoek was born in Delft on 24 October 1632. His father, a basket maker, died when Antonie was five, and his mother came from a well-to-do brewer's family. At sixteen he became a bookkeeper's apprentice at a linen-draper's shop in Amsterdam. In July 1654 he married Barbara de Mey in Delft and opened a draper's shop. In 1660 he became chamberlain for the sheriffs in the city hall, a post he held for almost 40 years, and in 1669 he was appointed land surveyor by the court of Holland. He knew the painter Johannes Vermeer, whose will he executed in 1675. He was Dutch Reformed and Calvinist, and believed his discoveries were further proof of the wonder of creation.

Wanting to see the thread of his cloth better than the magnifying lenses of the time allowed, Van Leeuwenhoek took up lensmaking. A small glass rod pulled apart in a flame yields two whiskers of glass, and putting the end of one back in the flame forms a very small, high-quality lens. He kept his methods secret. He made more than 500 lenses and at least 25 single-lens microscopes, of which nine survive and magnify up to 275 times.

His friend, the physician Reinier de Graaf, introduced his work to the Royal Society in London, which in 1673 published a letter from him on mold, bees and lice. In 1674 he concluded that the moving objects under his microscope were little animals. His report of single-celled organisms, dated 9 October 1676, was met with scepticism until observers sent by the Royal Society confirmed his observations in 1677. He was elected to the Society in February 1680 but never attended a meeting, and he wrote only in colloquial Dutch. Visitors included Leibniz, John Locke and Peter the Great, though he refused to show them his best microscopes.

He was the first to recognize that the structures Marcello Malpighi and Jan Swammerdam had seen in blood were red blood cells. His records include protists in 1674, spermatozoa in 1677, the banded pattern of muscle fibres in 1682 and bacteria in 1683. He also experimented on himself, examining blood drawn from his finger and his own skin. He died on 26 August 1723, aged 90, and was buried in the Oude Kerk in Delft.
antonin-dvorak: Dvořák was born on 8 September 1841 in Nelahozeves, near Prague, then in the Austrian Empire. He was the eldest of 14 children, eight of whom survived infancy. His father František worked as an innkeeper, a professional zither player and a butcher. In 1847 he entered primary school and learned the violin from his teacher Joseph Spitz, playing in a village band and in church. In 1873 he married Anna Čermáková, the sister of Josefína Čermáková, with whom he had first fallen in love. They had nine children, several of whom died in infancy.

After public successes in Prague in 1872 and 1873, he won the Austrian State Competition in 1874, and again in 1877, when the critic Eduard Hanslick and Johannes Brahms were on the jury. Their offer of help led to his publication by Simrock. A London performance of the Stabat Mater at the Royal Albert Hall on 10 March 1883 began a run of performances in England and the United States, and he visited Britain at least eight times. His Seventh Symphony was written for the London Philharmonic Society and premiered on 22 April 1885.

From 1892 to 1895 Dvořák directed the National Conservatory of Music in New York, whose president, Jeannette Thurber, offered him $15,000 a year, twenty-five times his Prague pay, and admitted women and black students. On holiday in Spillville, Iowa, in 1893 he wrote the String Quartet in F major, Op. 96, known as the American. He returned to Bohemia on 27 April 1895 and died on 1 May 1904.

Dvořák drew on Slavic folk dance forms, among them the Bohemian furiant and sousedská, the Polish polonaise and mazurka and the Ukrainian dumka, which gave its name to his Dumky Trio. His nine symphonies generally follow classical models, and the Symphony From the New World has been numbered in turn the 5th, 8th and 9th, because four symphonies were only published after his death. In 1896–1897 he wrote five symphonic poems, four of them based on ballads from the collection Kytice by the folklorist Karel Jaromír Erben.

The Stabat Mater, the longest extant setting of that text, was inspired by the death of his daughter Josefa.
