His opus numbers do not always follow the order of writing: publishers gave early works high numbers to make a composer seem established, and Dvořák sometimes gave a work a lower number so that he could sell it outside his contract.
antonine-wall: Construction began around 142 on the orders of Emperor Antoninus Pius, who never visited Britain. Quintus Lollius Urbicus, governor of Roman Britain at the time, first supervised the work. Estimates of how long it took vary widely, with six and twelve years most commonly proposed. Pressure from the Caledonians probably led Antoninus to send the empire's troops farther north. The wall was meant to extend Roman territory and replace Hadrian's Wall, 160 km to the south, as the frontier of Britannia, but the Romans never conquered the Caledonians and the wall suffered many attacks.

The wall ran for about 63 km from Old Kilpatrick on the Firth of Clyde to Carriden, near Bo'ness, on the Firth of Forth. It was a bank about 3 metres high and 5 metres wide, of layered turves on a stone foundation, with a wide ditch on the north side and a military road to the south. It is thought a wooden palisade stood on top. Unlike Hadrian's Wall it had no ditch system behind it. The stone foundations and wing walls of the first forts show that a stone wall like Hadrian's was planned at first, but this was quickly changed.

The Romans first planned forts every 10 km, then revised this to every 3.3 km, with at least nine smaller fortlets between them, and a road called the Military Way linked all the sites. Rough Castle Fort is the best preserved, and Kinneil is the most visible fortlet. Coastal forts such as Inveresk served as outposts or supply bases, and forts further north, among them Ardoch and Strageath, were brought back into service. The soldiers who built the wall set up decorated distance slabs naming the length each legion built, and twenty survive. Research at Glasgow University has shown that they were once brightly painted.

The wall was abandoned within two decades of its completion, when the legions withdrew to Hadrian's Wall in 162. When Septimius Severus campaigned in Scotland in 208 to 210, there is no evidence that he paid any attention to it. Writing in 730, Bede, following Gildas, mistakenly ascribed it to the Britons. Medieval chronicles called it Gryme's dyke, which became Graham's dyke, a name still found at Bo'ness.

William Roy mapped it systematically in 1764, and where later development has destroyed it his drawings are the only reliable record. Sir George Macdonald published his survey in 1911. In the 16th century George Keith, 5th Earl Marischal, set a stone from the wall in the walls of Dunnotar Castle. The Antonine Wall was listed on 7 July 2008 as an extension to the World Heritage Site Frontiers of the Roman Empire, and several sites along it are in the care of Historic Environment Scotland.
antoninus-pius: Antoninus was born Titus Aurelius Fulvus Boionius Antoninus in 86, near Lanuvium, the son of Titus Aurelius Fulvus, consul in 89, and Arria Fadilla. His family was a relatively new senatorial house from Gallia Narbonensis, supported by the Flavians. After his father's early death he was raised by his maternal grandfather Gnaeus Arrius Antoninus, a friend of Pliny the Younger.

Between 110 and 115 he married Annia Galeria Faustina the Elder. He became consul in 120, administered part of Italy as one of four proconsuls, and was proconsul of Asia, probably in 134 and 135. On 25 February 138 Hadrian adopted him, on condition that he adopt Marcus Annius Verus and Lucius, son of Lucius Aelius, later the emperors Marcus Aurelius and Lucius Verus.

Antoninus made few changes at first, and his ruling team centred on a group of conservative senatorial families. He persuaded the Senate to grant divine honours to Hadrian, which is the most likely reason for the title Pius. J. J. Wilkes notes that he probably never commanded a Roman army and was never within five hundred miles of a legion in his twenty-three years. In Britain the governor Quintus Lollius Urbicus invaded southern Scotland and built the Antonine Wall from the Firth of Forth to the Firth of Clyde; it was decommissioned from the mid-150s and abandoned in the early 160s, for reasons that remain unclear.

He left a treasury of about 2.7 billion sesterces, suspended taxes in cities hit by fire and earthquake, and gave grants to rebuild Greek cities after earthquakes in about 140 and in 152. He is also credited with dividing imperial property into the patrimonium and the res privata.

Marcus Aurelius, consul with Antoninus in 140, took on more duties as the emperor aged. Antoninus died in 161, probably on 7 March, shortly after Marcus and Lucius were designated joint consuls. The Antonine Plague, brought back by soldiers after the Parthian victory, soon depleted the treasury. The only complete ancient account of his life, the Historia Augusta, is unreliable and largely fabricated, though it is the sole source to mention the Antonine Wall. Edward Gibbon and others praised him as an ideal landed gentleman, while some historians take a less favourable view. Only one of his four children reached adulthood, but he was ancestor of four generations of prominent Romans, including the emperor Commodus.
antonio-canovas-del-castillo: Antonio Cánovas del Castillo was born in Málaga and moved to Madrid after his father's death, living with his mother's cousin, the writer Serafín Estébanez Calderón. He studied law at the University of Madrid but showed an early interest in politics and Spanish history. His active political career began with the revolution of 1854 led by General Leopoldo O'Donnell, when he drafted the Manifesto of Manzanares. In the last years of Isabel II he held the interior portfolio in 1864 and the overseas territories portfolio in 1865–66. During the First Spanish Republic he supported a Bourbon restoration and drafted the Manifesto of Sandhurst for Alfonso XII.

After General Martínez Campos overthrew the Republic in 1874, Cánovas served as prime minister for six years, though he was twice briefly replaced, in 1875 and 1879. He was a principal author of the Constitution of 1876, which formalised the constitutional monarchy and limited suffrage. He helped end the last Carlist threat in 1876 by merging dissident Carlist deputies with his Conservative party. His term also saw the decree of July 1876 that ended the Basque provinces' specific status.

After 1881 he alternated in office with the progressive Práxedes Mateo Sagasta in the turno pacífico, an arrangement designed to reconcile the competing militarist, Catholic and Carlist power bases. After Alfonso XII died in 1885 he assumed the functions of head of state during the regency of María Cristina. He was also a historian, elected to the Real Academia de la Historia at 32 for his History of the Decline of Spain.

His repression of Cuban nationalists failed to prevent the rebellion of 1895 led by José Martí, and conflict over Cuba with the United States led to the Spanish–American War of 1898. After a bomb was thrown at a procession in Barcelona in 1896, three hundred people were arrested and held at Montjuïc; reputedly Cánovas ordered their torture.

Cánovas was shot dead in 1897 at the spa of Santa Águeda in Mondragón by the Italian anarchist Michele Angiolillo, who invoked vengeance for the execution of José Rizal and Barcelona anarchists. His peers nicknamed him el Monstruo. His restoration system gave way after the war to long political instability, which ended in the collapse of the monarchy and the constitution he had written.
antonio-da-correggio: Antonio Allegri was born in the small town of Correggio, near Reggio Emilia, around 1489. His father was a merchant, and little else is known of his youth. It is often assumed that his first artistic education came from his father's brother, the painter Lorenzo Allegri. In 1503–1505 he was apprenticed to Francesco Bianchi Ferrara in Modena, where he probably became familiar with the classicism of Lorenzo Costa and Francesco Francia. After a trip to Mantua in 1506 he stayed in Correggio until 1510, and by 1514 he was an independent and increasingly well-known artist there.

By 1516 Correggio was in Parma, where he spent most of the rest of his career. His first major commission, in 1519, was the ceiling of a private chamber of the abbess Giovanna Piacenza in the convent of St Paul, painted as an arbour pierced by oculi with playful cherubs. He then painted the Vision of St John on Patmos in the dome of San Giovanni Evangelista, and about three years later an Assumption of the Virgin in the dome of Parma Cathedral, crowded with layers of figures seen from below (sotto in su). Their illusionistic treatment of the dome influenced later fresco painters, from Pordenone to the Baroque artists Lanfranco and Baciccio.

He also painted a series of the loves of Jupiter from Ovid's Metamorphoses, commissioned by Federico II Gonzaga of Mantua and given to the visiting Holy Roman Emperor Charles V. It includes Leda and the Swan, Danaë, Ganymede Abducted by the Eagle and Jupiter and Io. Among his religious works are the Lamentation and the Martyrdom of Four Saints, both in the Galleria Nazionale of Parma.

Correggio died suddenly in his home town on 5 March 1534 and was buried the next day in San Francesco, near his early Madonna of St Francis, now in Dresden. Contemporaries remembered him as a shadowy, melancholic and introverted man. He left few direct followers outside Parma, but Vasari knew his work half a century later, and visitors' diaries of the eighteenth and nineteenth centuries led to a reassessment of him in the Romantic period. His illusionistic experiments, in which imagined space replaces the natural, seem to prefigure Mannerist, Baroque and Rococo approaches.
antonio-da-sangallo-the-younger: Sangallo was born Antonio Cordiani in Florence, the son of Bartolomeo Piccioni. His grandfather Francesco Giamberti was a woodworker, and his uncles Giuliano and Antonio da Sangallo were noted architects. He grew up in poverty, and about 1503 he followed his uncles to Rome and took the name Sangallo. His apprenticeship consisted of carpentry. After about three years he began working with Donato Bramante in 1506, preparing sketches for him because of the master's disability, and was eventually put in charge of the Passetto di Borgo between the papal apartments and the Castel Sant'Angelo, which was left unfinished.

In 1507 Sangallo received a major commission for the church of Santa Maria di Loreto in Rome. His main encouragement came from Cardinal Alessandro Farnese. His likely first independent commission was the fortress of Capodimonte on Lake Bolsena, and it was followed by the renovation of a house on the Campo dei Fiori in Rome, later the Palazzo Farnese. The palace was not completed until after his death but established him as a mature architect. When Bramante died in 1514, Pope Leo X appointed Sangallo, with Raphael and Giovanni Giocondo, to oversee the construction of St. Peter's Basilica.

He was also an engineer. He built the foundation of the church of San Giovanni dei Fiorentini on the unstable bank of the Tiber, at such expense that no money remained to build the church. For Pope Clement VII he built Saint Patrick's Well at Orvieto, whose two helical ramps around a central shaft allowed oxen carrying water to go down by one and up by the other. He designed the Fortezza da Basso in Florence in 1534 for Alessandro de' Medici, nearly finishing it in two years, and fortifications at Parma, Piacenza, Ancona and Orvieto. He kept control of his circle of assistants by visiting and surveying every site, and worked in six stages, from measuring the site to working drawings at full scale.

Sangallo's last project, commissioned by Pope Paul III, was in the Rieti Valley. He contracted malaria in the marshy ground and died at Terni on 3 August 1546 before finishing it. He was buried in St. Peter's Basilica, and Michelangelo became chief architect after him. Giorgio Vasari wrote that Antonio deserves to be praised no less than any other architect, ancient or modern.
antonio-de-andrade: António de Andrade was born in Oleiros, Portugal, and entered the Society of Jesus in 1596. In 1600 he went to Goa, the capital of Portuguese India, where he completed his studies and was ordained a priest. He became one of the Jesuits attached to the court of the Mughal emperor Jahangir and headed the Jesuit mission in Agra.

In 1624 he left Agra for Delhi, where he and the Jesuit brother Manuel Marques joined a party of Hindu pilgrims bound for the temple of Badrinath, in what is now Uttarakhand. After a hard journey they crossed the Mana Pass into Tibet. The ruler of the western Tibetan kingdom of Guge received them in his capital, Tsaparang, and within a month Andrade left again to seek formal permission, funds and companions from the Father-Provincial in Goa.

He returned in 1625 with other Jesuits. With the support of the king and members of the royal family they built a church and made many converts. Andrade went back to Goa in 1629. The mission foundered soon after, when Ladakh invaded Guge, the king who had favoured it died and a hostile government under Ladakhi control took over in Tsaparang; the missionaries were persecuted or expelled and the Tibetan Christians sent to Ladakh.

Andrade was Father-Superior of the Jesuit province of Goa from 1630 to 1633, then rector of the College of St. Paul, and a deputy of the Goa Inquisition. He was poisoned on 4 March 1634 and died on 19 March. An inquiry of the Inquisition found that he had been murdered by discontented Jesuits of the college, possibly backed by powerful enemies among the authorities and merchants of Goa, but the matter was hushed up and no one was prosecuted. His two accounts of Tibet, written in 1624 and 1626, were printed in Lisbon in 1626 and translated into the major European languages, shaping European knowledge of Tibet.
antonio-de-mendoza: Antonio de Mendoza was born in Alcalá la Real, the second son of Íñigo López de Mendoza y Quiñones, 2nd Count of Tendilla, and his second wife Francisca Pacheco Portocarrero, of the House of Mendoza, one of the leading noble families of Castile. He was a Knight of Santiago and represented Granada at the Cortes of Valladolid in 1518. During the Revolt of the Comuneros he supported the Crown, then entered the diplomatic service of Charles V, serving in Hungary, Italy and Germany.

Selected in 1529 as the first viceroy of New Spain, Mendoza was named in Barcelona on 17 April 1535 and governed for fifteen years, longer than any later viceroy. He found a recently conquered land beset by Indigenous unrest and rivalry among the Spaniards, and had to govern in the king's name without making an enemy of Hernán Cortés. With Bishop Juan de Zumárraga he helped found the Colegio de Santa Cruz at Tlatelolco in 1536 and the Royal and Pontifical University of Mexico in 1552. In 1536 he began the minting of silver and copper coins, and in 1539 the first printing press in the New World reached Mexico under his instructions.

When the crown issued the New Laws restricting the grants of labour to conquerors, he declined to enforce their harshest parts, with the policy of obedezco pero no cumplo, "I obey but do not comply". In 1542 he took the field against the Mixtón Rebellion, after which men, women and children were seized and executed, some by cannon fire or by dogs. He commissioned Francisco Vásquez de Coronado's expedition to the northern lands in 1540 to 1542, and the Codex Mendoza was made at his order.

Named viceroy of Peru in Brussels on 4 July 1549, Mendoza travelled overland from Mexico to Panama and then by boat to Peru, but soon fell ill and died on 21 July 1552. His tomb is in the Cathedral of Lima, beside that of Francisco Pizarro. He is credited with consolidating the Crown's sovereignty in New Spain and limiting the power of the first conquistadors, and many of his policies lasted through the colonial period. Cape Mendocino in California was named for him in 1565.
antonio-de-nebrija: Nebrija was baptized Antonio Martínez de Cala and Latinized his name as Aelius Antonius Nebrissensis, taking Aelius from the Roman inscriptions of his native Lebrija, called Nebrissa Veneria in Roman times. He was born into an hidalgo family in the province of Seville, and 1444 is the traditionally accepted year. At fourteen he enrolled at the University of Salamanca. A scholarship from the bishopric of Seville took him to the Royal College of Spain in Bologna, where he was inspired by Italian humanists, especially Lorenzo Valla. After ten years in Italy he returned to Spain.

He served the archbishop of Seville, Alonso de Fonseca y Ulloa, for three years, and after Fonseca died in 1473 he returned to Salamanca as a lecturer. In 1476 he was appointed to the First Chair of Grammar, and in 1481 he published the Introductiones latinae, a Latin textbook whose first printing of 1,000 copies sold out and which was reprinted dozens of times. After his marriage in 1487 he moved to Badajoz under the patronage of Juan de Zúñiga, master of the Order of Alcántara, and lived there for twelve years.

In 1492 he published the Gramática de la lengua castellana, dedicated to Queen Isabella I of Castile, one of the first books to codify a European vernacular. In the dedication he called language the instrument of empire and suggested the grammar would serve when the Catholic monarchs ruled peoples speaking other languages. In 1492 he also published a Latin-Spanish dictionary and about 1495 reversed it into the Vocabulario español-latino, which became the basis for later dictionaries, including Spanish-Arabic (1505), Spanish-Nahuatl (1547) and Spanish-Tagalog (1613).

Nebrija then turned to biblical scholarship, applying the critical methods Italian humanists used on classical texts. Around 1504 Diego de Deza, the Grand Inquisitor, confiscated and destroyed his work, but Cardinal Jiménez de Cisneros, who succeeded Deza in 1507, let him resume. He briefly served on the committee preparing the Complutensian Polyglot Bible and clashed with its conservative editors, and his input was largely ignored when it appeared in 1517. He also wrote on theology, law, archaeology, pedagogy and rhetoric. He died on 5 July 1522 in Alcalá de Henares.
antonio-de-oliveira-salazar: Salazar was born on 28 April 1889 in Vimieiro, near Santa Comba Dão, to a family of modest income. His father, a small landowner, had begun as an agricultural labourer and become manager for the Perestrelos, a wealthy landowning family. At eleven Salazar won a free place at the seminary in Viseu, where he studied from 1900 to 1908; he considered the priesthood but decided against it after receiving holy orders.

He studied law at the University of Coimbra from 1910, graduated in 1914 with 19 points out of 20, and specialised in finance. He took the chairs of economic policy and finance in 1917 and received his doctorate the next year. His politics grew from Catholic views aroused by the First Republic's anti-clerical stance.

After the coup of 28 May 1926 Salazar entered government as finance minister with the support of President Óscar Carmona and balanced the budget within a year. He became Prime Minister in 1932 and recast the Ditadura Nacional as the corporatist Estado Novo, whose constitution of 1933 was co-written by Marcelo Caetano. Its stated basis was Catholic social doctrine, but in practice its stability rested on suppressing dissent.

A secret police, founded in 1933 and reorganised in 1945 as the PIDE, monitored the population, applied censorship and suppressed opponents. Humberto Delgado, who challenged the regime in the 1958 presidential election, was assassinated by the PIDE in 1965. Salazar supported Francisco Franco in the Spanish Civil War and kept Portugal neutral in the Second World War. Portugal was a founding member of NATO in 1949 and joined the United Nations in 1955. Colonial war broke out in 1961, the year India annexed Goa.

In August 1968 Salazar suffered a cerebral haemorrhage, which most sources attribute to a fall from a chair. On 25 September President Américo Tomás dismissed him and appointed Marcelo Caetano. Those around him did not tell him he had been removed, and he died on 27 July 1970. He never married and had no known descendants.

The Estado Novo outlived him by four years and fell to a military coup in 1974, leading to a liberal-democratic constitution in 1976. Historians find a detached judgement difficult: his rule brought more stability and prosperity than most Portuguese then living had known, but at the expense of democracy and civil liberties.
antonio-de-ulloa: Antonio de Ulloa was born in Seville on 12 January 1716 into a socially prominent family. His father, Bernardo de Ulloa y Sousa, wrote on economics. At thirteen he sailed from Cádiz to Cartagena de Indias, and in 1733 he entered the Spanish naval academy. At nineteen he was chosen to replace another officer on the French Geodesic Mission to Quito, together with Jorge Juan. The mission measured the length of a degree of meridian arc near the equator to decide whether the Earth is flattened at the poles, as Newtonian theory predicted, or at the equator, as the Cartesians claimed. Its results, published by La Condamine in 1745, vindicated Newton.

Ulloa travelled through the Viceroyalty of Peru from 1736 to 1744. In one report he described for the first time in European scientific literature a metal he called platina, which he met in the gold panning of the Chocó region. On the voyage home in 1745 his ship was captured by the Royal Navy, but he was befriended by British scientists, elected a fellow of the Royal Society in December 1746 and released. His Relación histórica del viaje a la América Meridional appeared in 1748. From 1758 to 1764 he governed Huancavelica and managed its mercury mine, where his reforms were resisted by local authorities and the viceroy, Manuel de Amat y Junyent.

France ceded Louisiana to Spain in 1762, and in May 1765 Ulloa was appointed its first Spanish governor. He reached New Orleans on 5 March 1766, but his relations with the French Creole elite were strained. He delayed formal possession while awaiting troops, and lived at the fort of La Balize. On 28 October 1768 riots broke out over a decree of Charles III opening nine Spanish ports to direct trade with Louisiana. The Superior Council demanded that he leave within three days, and he sailed for Cuba on 1 November. Alejandro O'Reilly crushed the revolt in 1769.

In 1778 Ulloa commanded the last great treasure fleet between Cádiz and Veracruz and observed the solar eclipse of that year. He was charged with dereliction of duty after a mission to the Azores in 1779, but was acquitted in February 1782. He ended his career as chief of operations of the Navy and died on 3 July 1795. With Jorge Juan he wrote a confidential report on corruption in Spanish America, published only in 1826 as Noticias secretas, which historians still debate.
antonio-gramsci: Gramsci was born in Ales, in the province of Oristano, the fourth of seven sons of Francesco Gramsci and Giuseppina Marcias. His father was a low-level official of Arbëreshë (Italo-Albanian) descent, and the family moved through several Sardinian villages before settling in Ghilarza. In 1898 Francesco was convicted of embezzlement and imprisoned, which left the family destitute. The young Gramsci had to leave school and take casual jobs until his father's release in 1904.

In 1911 he won a scholarship to the University of Turin, sitting the examination at the same time as Palmiro Togliatti. He studied literature and linguistics under Matteo Bartoli and joined the Italian Socialist Party in late 1913. Poor health, money problems and political commitment led him to give up his studies in early 1915.

The failure of the workers' councils to grow into a national movement convinced Gramsci that a Communist party in the Leninist sense was needed. The group around L'Ordine Nuovo allied with Bordiga's far larger abstentionist faction, and on 21 January 1921 the Communist Party of Italy was founded at Livorno. Gramsci was a leader from the start but subordinate to Bordiga until 1924. In 1922 he went to Russia as the party's representative, where he met the violinist Julia Schucht; they married in 1923.

On 9 November 1926 the Fascist government passed emergency laws after an alleged attempt on Mussolini's life, and police arrested Gramsci despite his parliamentary immunity. His prosecutor said: "For twenty years we must stop this brain from functioning." He was sentenced to five years on the island of Ustica and then, the following year, to twenty years in Turi. His health failed in prison, and a campaign organised by Piero Sraffa at Cambridge demanded his release. He was moved to a clinic at Formia in 1933 and to one in Rome two years later, and was too ill to travel when his sentence ended in April 1937.

Gramsci filled more than 30 notebooks in prison, covering Italian history, fascism, Taylorism and Fordism, the state, religion and popular culture. His best-known concept, cultural hegemony, holds that the capitalist class maintains power not only by force but by spreading its own values until they pass for common sense. He divided the state into political society, which rules by force, and civil society, where leadership rests on consent. He also rejected economic determinism and the idea that revolution follows automatically from historical laws, and argued that each class produces its own organic intellectuals. Critics charge that his approach treats ideas as a struggle for power.
antonio-guzman-blanco: Antonio Leocadio Guzmán Blanco was born in Caracas on 28 February 1829, the son of Antonio Leocadio Guzmán, a journalist and politician who founded the Liberal Party, and Carlota Blanco Jerez de Aristeguieta. Banished under General Julián Castro, he joined General Juan Crisóstomo Falcón's invasion of Venezuela as his general secretary. After Falcón's defeat at the Battle of Coplé in September 1860 he was sent to the West Indies to seek help, and landed again with Falcón on the coast of Coro late in 1861.

On 22 May 1863 Guzmán signed the Treaty of Coche, which ended the fighting; an assembly at La Victoria then elected Falcón president and Guzmán vice president. He also served as Minister of Finance, negotiating a loan in London, and as Minister of Foreign Affairs, and was ambassador to Spain from 1863 to 1866. After Falcón was overthrown in 1868 he left the country, led a revolution in 1869 and in 1870 became provisional president with extraordinary powers.

He held the presidency from 1870 to 1877, from 1879 to 1884 and again from 1886. Between his terms allies held office, among them General Joaquín Crespo, while Guzmán lived in Paris as ambassador to France. A decree of 27 June 1880 made schooling free and compulsory for children aged 7 to 14, and the Ministry of Public Instruction followed in 1881. In 15 years from 1870 the number of primary schools quadrupled to nearly 2,000. He founded the Order of the Liberator in 1880 and adopted Gloria al Bravo Pueblo as the national anthem on 25 May 1881.

His governments built the Capitol, the National Pantheon and the Municipal Theater in Caracas, the La Guaira and Caracas Railway and a telephone line between the two cities, and founded the Venezuelan Academy of the Language. Historians describe his rule as autocratic and allegedly rife with corruption; he reportedly took money from the treasury, and after a dispute with a bishop he expelled clergy who opposed him and seized Church property. He had Simón Bolívar's remains moved to the National Pantheon. Guzmán died on 28 July 1899 and was buried in Passy Cemetery in France; his remains were later brought to the National Pantheon.
antonio-guzman-fernandez: Antonio Guzmán was born on 12 February 1911 in La Vega, in a family of Criollo Spanish descent, and studied at the primary and secondary schools of the town. He worked in the fruit export business and became a wealthy rancher. An early member of Juan Bosch's Dominican Revolutionary Party, he served as secretary of agriculture in Bosch's brief administration of 1963. In May 1966 he was the party's vice-presidential candidate with Bosch, but the election was won by Joaquín Balaguer. In 1974 he ran for president on a united opposition ticket, though he withdrew after Balaguer changed the rules in a way the opposition thought unfair and undemocratic.

Guzmán ran again in 1978 for the Dominican Revolutionary Party, with Jacobo Majluta as his running mate. When returns showed a clear trend in his favour the military stopped the count, but after vigorous protests at home and strong pressure abroad it resumed, and Guzmán handed Balaguer the first loss of his electoral career. It was the first time in the country's history that an incumbent president peacefully surrendered power to an elected member of the opposition.

Guzmán planned to reform the social and economic order slowly, and to deal with the armed forces by reassigning or removing officers sceptical of his plans, promoting younger officers loyal to him and creating an institution for more formal training. Congress was mostly held by Balaguer's Reformist Party, which could veto his reforms. He improved public transport and raised the minimum wage, but was criticised for not responding to the economic decline, which Hurricane David in 1979 deepened.

In June 1982 Hipólito Mejía, the secretary of agriculture, found the president crying on a beach and uncertain about the country's future, and warned Guzmán's wife of concern about his state of mind. Guzmán was found dead of a gunshot wound on 4 July 1982, and the government ruled the death a possible suicide. Vice President Jacobo Majluta took over for the 43 days left of the four-year term, and Salvador Jorge Blanco was then inaugurated. Guzmán is remembered as having helped bring the alternation of parties in power through elections, and for a period marked by respect for civil liberties.
antonio-jose-de-sucre: Antonio José de Sucre y Alcalá was born on 3 February 1795 in Cumaná into an aristocratic family that traced its roots to Flanders. In 1814 he joined the struggle for South American independence from Spain and quickly became a capable military leader. He became known as the Gran Mariscal de Ayacucho, the Grand Marshal of Ayacucho.

On 24 May 1822 Sucre led a Patriot army against a Royalist army under Field Marshal Melchor Aymerich on the slopes of the Pichincha volcano near Quito. The Royalist defeat brought the liberation of Quito and secured the independence of the provinces of the Real Audiencia de Quito, from which Ecuador would emerge. On 9 December 1824, as Simón Bolívar's lieutenant, he led the Patriot forces to victory over Viceroy José de la Serna at Ayacucho, at Pampa de La Quinua. Afterwards José de Canterac signed the capitulation of the Royalist army. The Peruvian Congress promoted Sucre to Marshal and the Colombian legislature to General in Chief.

On Bolívar's orders Sucre entered Upper Peru on 25 February 1825. Most Royalist troops there refused to fight on, and Pedro Antonio Olañeta died at the Battle of Tumusla on 2 April. Sucre reconvened the Constituent Assembly in Chuquisaca, which declared independence on 6 August 1825 and named the new state after Bolívar. Bolívar declined the presidency and passed it to Sucre, who became the first president of Bolivia and gave it its first Constitution in 1828.

A strong movement arose against Bolívar, his followers and the Bolivian constitution, and Sucre resigned in 1828. On 27 February 1829, heavily outnumbered, he defeated a Peruvian invasion force led by José de La Mar at the Battle of Tarqui.

Sucre was killed on 4 June 1830 in an ambush at Berruecos while travelling to Quito. The plot is attributed to José María Obando and carried out by men who later confessed, among them Apolinar Morillo and Juan Gregorio Sarria, and the identity of the conspirators remains a subject of historical speculation. Some have argued that his death left Bolívar with no clear successor. Sucre is buried in the Cathedral of Quito, as he had wished, where his wife Mariana Carcelén came from. Sucre, the capital of Bolivia, and Sucre State in Venezuela are named after him.
antonio-lopez-de-santa-anna: Santa Anna was born in Xalapa, Veracruz, on 21 February 1794 into a respected criollo family. His father was a lawyer, and his mother supported his wish for a military career against his father's wish that he be a shopkeeper. Through her friendship with the intendant of Veracruz he received a military appointment on 6 July 1810, though under age. He fought for the Spanish crown against the insurgency for over a decade, switching to the insurgents in 1821. His origins on the coast gave him immunity to yellow fever, an advantage over officers from elsewhere.

Agustín de Iturbide, ruler of the new Mexican Empire, gave him command of Veracruz and then removed him; in December 1822 Santa Anna rebelled with Guadalupe Victoria and Guerrero, and the Plan of Casa Mata of 1 February 1823 called for a republic. At Tampico he forced the Spanish general Isidro Barradas to surrender on 11 September 1829, ending Spain's last attempt to retake Mexico, and styled himself the Victor of Tampico.

He was elected president on 1 April 1833 but left government to Vice President Valentín Gómez Farías, whose anticlerical reforms he ended by dissolving Congress on 12 June 1834. In 1835 he repealed the liberal Constitution of 1824; Texas declared independence on 2 March 1836, and his expedition to recover it ended in disaster.

He lost part of a leg in the Pastry War of 1838 and used this to re-enter politics. In the Mexican–American War he took the presidency in 1846 and fought on to the end; one historian says that more than any other single person it was Santa Anna who denied Polk's dream of a short war. Invited back by conservatives, he was elected president on 17 March 1853 and declared himself dictator for life as His Most Serene Highness. He ceded territory to the United States in the Gadsden Purchase in 1854, and the Plan of Ayutla removed him in 1855.

From 1855 to 1874 Santa Anna lived in exile in Cuba, the United States, Colombia and Saint Thomas. In New York he tried unsuccessfully to sell chicle for carriage wheels, though he introduced chewing gum to the United States. President Sebastián Lerdo de Tejada allowed him to return to Mexico in 1874, and he died in Mexico City on 21 June 1876. Historians call the thirty years after independence the Age of Santa Anna and have called him an uncrowned monarch. He is often remembered in Mexico as a vendepatria, a traitor to the fatherland, because of the territory lost to the United States during his rule.
antonio-maceo: José Antonio de la Caridad Maceo y Grajales was born on 14 June 1845 on a farm called Jobabo near San Luis, in Oriente Province outside Santiago de Cuba. His father, Marcos Maceo, was a Venezuelan farmer and trader who had fought for Spain against Simón Bolívar and moved to Santiago de Cuba in 1823; his mother, Mariana Grajales y Cuello, was a Cuban woman of Dominican descent. At sixteen he began delivering goods by mule for his father, became a farmer and trader himself, and was initiated into Freemasonry.

About two weeks after the Cry of Yara of 10 October 1868, Maceo joined the Ten Years' War with his father and brothers, enlisting as a private. He rose quickly to lieutenant colonel and later brigadier general, fighting in more than 500 battles and recovering from more than 25 wounds, but his humble origin and the colour of his skin delayed his promotion to major general. He learned from the Dominican Máximo Gómez and took up the machete as a weapon. After the Protest of Baraguá he went abroad to raise men and arms, and from New York in 1879 he planned with Calixto García the short-lived Little War.

He settled in Guanacaste in Costa Rica, where he survived an assassination attempt by Spanish agents. José Martí persuaded him to join the war of 1895, which Maceo accepted on condition that Gómez hold the highest command. Landing near Baracoa in 1895, he became Lieutenant General, second in command, and with Gómez led two columns more than 1000 miles in 96 days, reaching Mantua at the western end of the island in October 1896. Valeriano Weyler answered the rebels' rural support with the reconcentration, in whose camps almost a third of the rural population died.

On 7 December 1896, near Punta Brava, Maceo was cutting a fence at the farm of San Pedro with a small escort when a Spanish column opened fire. He was hit in the chest and in the head. Francisco Gómez Toro, son of Máximo Gómez, stayed to guard his body and was killed. The two were buried in secret, and their remains now lie at the Monumento El Cacahual south of Havana, a place of pilgrimage. Monuments to Maceo stand in Santiago de Cuba and Havana.
antonio-pigafetta: Pigafetta was born to a prominent noble family in Vicenza in north-eastern Italy. Archival research indicates that his father was Giovanni Pigafetta and his mother a noblewoman named Lucia, daughter of Marco Muzan. They married in March 1492, so Antonio was born after that date. Details of his education are unknown, though he later boasted of having read many books. A tradition says he sailed the Mediterranean with the Knights of Rhodes as a youth, but there is no record of it. He entered the service of the papal ambassador Francesco Chiericati, also from Vicenza, whom Pope Leo X sent to the Spanish court in 1518, and he travelled with the ambassador's retinue to Zaragoza and Barcelona.

In Spain Pigafetta heard of Ferdinand Magellan's plan to find a western route to the Spice Islands and persuaded Chiericati that taking part would benefit the Vatican. Provided with letters of introduction, he set out for Seville in May 1519. Magellan hired him for 1,000 maravedís a month, enrolled under the name Antonio Lombardo as one of the servants of the captain and supernumeraries.

When the fleet sailed in August 1519 he was assigned to the flagship Trinidad, served Magellan and became his great admirer. He had no set duty except to keep a daily record, which he did diligently, noting geography, climate, natural history and above all the appearance, customs and languages of the peoples met. His own observations were accurate, but he tended to accept the most outrageous tales told to him. He was wounded on Mactan in April 1521, where Magellan was killed, recovered, and was one of the 18 men who returned on the Victoria under Juan Sebastián Elcano, reaching Sanlúcar de Barrameda in September 1522 out of about 240 who set out.

Pigafetta wrote his Relazione del primo viaggio intorno al mondo in Vicenza between late 1523 and January 1524. It is a collection of descriptions, events, translations, thoughts and illustrations, and it includes the first known use of the name Pacific Ocean on a map. His record of Cebuano is the first recorded document concerning that language. He presented lavish manuscripts to Charles V, John III of Portugal, Francis I of France and the Grand Master of the Knights Hospitaller, but all those copies are lost. Having returned with little wealth, he could not pay his share of the printing costs, and the work was not printed in his lifetime; Giovanni Battista Ramusio first published it in 1550.

Only four manuscripts survive, three in French and one in Italian, the last in the Biblioteca Ambrosiana in Milan. Carlo Amoretti published it there in 1800, though he altered many words. After the voyage Pigafetta also gained membership of the Knights of Rhodes.
antonio-prior-of-crato: António was born in Lisbon, the illegitimate son of Prince Luis, Duke of Beja, and Violante Gomes. Some sources argue that his parents later married. His mother may have been of Sephardic Jewish or new Christian extraction. António was educated in Coimbra, placed in the Order of St. John, and given the wealthy priory of Crato as a benefice. In 1571 he was named governor of the Portuguese fortification at Tangiers. In 1578 he accompanied King Sebastian of Portugal to Morocco and was taken prisoner at the Battle of Alcácer Quibir, where Sebastian was killed.

Sebastian's death left his old uncle Cardinal Henry as king, unable to have legitimate children. Philip II of Spain had the strongest claim, as the eldest grandson of King Manuel I by his eldest daughter Isabella; Catherine, Duchess of Braganza, was also a granddaughter of Manuel. António, as an illegitimate son, had no legal claim. He tried to prove that his parents had married after his birth, but no evidence was ever presented. Henry died in 1580 without having designated a successor.

The nobility and the church did not back António; his support came from the lower clergy, the peasantry and artisans. On 19 July 1580 he was acclaimed King of Portugal in Santarém and then in Lisbon and other towns, but never formally by the Cortes. The Duke of Alba's army defeated him at the Battle of Alcântara on 25 August. He then set up an opposition government on the island of Terceira in the Azores, which lasted until 1583 and minted its own coin. Philip II was recognised in the Cortes of Tomar.

In early 1581 António fled to France with the Portuguese Crown Jewels and was received by Catherine de' Medici. Promising to cede Brazil to her, he obtained a fleet, but Álvaro de Bazán, Marquis of Santa Cruz, defeated it at the Battle of Ponta Delgada on 25 and 26 July 1582. Elizabeth I of England also favoured him, and in 1589 he joined an English expedition under Francis Drake and John Norreys, which failed to provoke the rising he expected. He fell into poverty and lived on a small pension from King Henry IV of France. He died in Paris on 26 August 1595, leaving nine illegitimate sons by three women.
antonio-vieira: António Vieira was born in Lisbon on 6 February 1608, the son of Cristóvão Vieira Ravasco, whose mother Maria de Azevedo was a mulatto woman. In 1614 he went with his parents to Brazil, where his father was posted as a registrar, and was educated at the Jesuit college in Bahia. He entered the Jesuit novitiate in 1625 and pronounced his first vows two years later. At eighteen he was teaching rhetoric, and later dogmatic theology, at the college of Olinda. He was ordained a priest in 1635, and his three patriotic sermons at Bahia from 1638 to 1640 gave him a name as an orator.

After the revolution of 1640 placed John IV on the throne, Vieira went to Lisbon to congratulate the new king, who made him tutor to the Infante Dom Pedro, royal preacher and a member of the Royal Council. He worked for commerce and a national bank, and in pamphlets denounced a society that discriminated against New Christians and called for reform of the Inquisition. From 1647 he was a diplomat in England, France, the Netherlands and Italy, urging in his Papel Forte that Pernambuco be ceded to the Dutch as the price of peace.

Returning to Maranhão in early 1653, he fulfilled a youthful vow to work for the conversion of African slaves and native Indians. In April 1655 he obtained royal decrees that put the missions under the Jesuits, with himself as superior, and forbade the enslavement of natives except in specified cases. In August 1659 he signed the Treaty of the Mapuá with indigenous groups on the Marajó Archipelago.

Colonists and rival clergy opposed him, and in 1661, after a popular revolt, he and thirty-one other Jesuits were sent back to Portugal. His belief in the prophecies of the shoemaker poet Bandarra, and in a coming Fifth Empire, led the Inquisition to imprison him in Coimbra from October 1665 to December 1667 and forbid him to teach, write or preach.

Vieira regained his freedom on the accession of Pedro II and spent six years in Rome, where Pope Clement X invited him to preach before the cardinals and he became confessor to Queen Christina of Sweden. His report on the Inquisition led Pope Innocent XI to suspend it in Portugal for seven years, from 1674 to 1681. He returned to Brazil in January 1681, became superior of the province in 1687, and died in Salvador, Bahia, on 18 July 1697. His works include fifteen volumes of Sermões and the Cartas, and the Complete Works began publication in 2013.
antonio-vivaldi: Antonio Lucio Vivaldi was born on 4 March 1678 in Venice, the son of Giovanni Battista Vivaldi and Camilla Calicchio. He suffered from tightness of the chest, interpreted as a form of asthma, which kept him from playing wind instruments. His father, a barber before he became a professional violinist, taught him the violin. In 1693 he began studying for the priesthood and was ordained in 1703, and he was soon nicknamed il Prete Rosso, the Red Priest, after the colour of his hair.

In September 1703 Vivaldi became maestro di violino at the Ospedale della Pietà, an orphanage in Venice that gave the most talented girls a musical education and a place in its orchestra and choir. He composed most of his major works there over the next thirty years, including concertos, cantatas and more than sixty sacred works. His first opera, Ottone in villa, was performed in Vicenza in 1713, and he then became impresario of the Teatro San Angelo in Venice. His oratorio Juditha triumphans, composed in 1716 to celebrate the Republic of Venice's victory over the Turks, was sung entirely by the girls of the Pietà.

In 1717 or 1718 he was offered the post of Maestro di Cappella at the court of Prince Philip of Hesse-Darmstadt in Mantua, and he spent three years there. The Four Seasons, four violin concertos giving musical expression to the seasons, was published in Amsterdam in 1725 as the first four of the twelve concertos of Il cimento dell'armonia e dell'inventione. In 1728 he met the Emperor Charles VI at Trieste, who gave him the title of knight, a gold medal and an invitation to Vienna. Vivaldi composed more than 500 concertos, over 50 operas and a large body of sacred choral music.

Vivaldi went to Vienna, probably to stage operas, but Charles VI died soon after his arrival and left him without patronage or steady income. He became impoverished and died during the night of 27 to 28 July 1741, aged 63, of an internal infection. He was buried in a simple grave in the Bürgerspital-Gottesacker cemetery.

After almost two centuries of decline, his reputation revived in the early 20th century. In 1926 researchers found fifteen bound volumes of his music in a monastery in Piedmont, containing 300 concertos, 19 operas and over 100 vocal-instrumental works. Johann Sebastian Bach was deeply influenced by his concertos and arias, and transcribed six of them for solo keyboard and three for organ.
antsiranana: Antsiranana, named Diego-Suarez before 1975, is a city in the far north of Madagascar and the capital of Diana Region. It stands on Antsiranana Bay, one of the largest deep-water harbours in the Indian Ocean, though its remote location long made it unimportant for freight traffic. The first European to sight the island, the Portuguese captain Diogo Dias, did so on 10 August 1500 and named it the Isle of Saint Lawrence. The place took its name Diego Suarez from the first name of Dias, in Portuguese Diogo, and the surname of Admiral Fernão Soares, who recognised it in February 1506.

In the 1880s France coveted the bay as a coaling station for steamships. After the first Franco-Hova War, Queen Ranavalona III signed a treaty on 17 December 1885 granting France a protectorate over the bay and its surroundings. The French set up the French Establishment of Diego-Suarez under Frigate Captain Caillet, regarded as the founder of the city. The first inhabitants were Creoles from Réunion and Mauritius and from other French possessions, with runaway slaves, Antankarana and Sakalava making up much of the rest. The colony had 2,500 people in 1886, a civil governor from 1887 and a Decauville railway from 1900. In 1905 the Second Pacific Squadron of Imperial Russia anchored there and was resupplied on its way to the Battle of Tsushima.

In 1942 Diego-Suarez was the primary objective of Operation Ironclad, the start of the Allied invasion of Madagascar. The Allies feared that Japan would pressure Vichy France into granting use of the island, as it had with French Indo-China the year before. Japanese midget submarines attacked the British ships in the harbour, damaging the battleship HMS Ramillies and sinking the tanker British Loyalty. France kept a military base in the city after Malagasy independence in 1960 and withdrew its forces between 1973 and 1975.

The city had an estimated population of 115,015 in 2013. It has a cruise port that receives periodic visits, and Arrachart Airport links it mainly with other parts of Madagascar. The University of Antsiranana was founded in 1976. Its churches include the Roman Catholic Cathedral of St. Matthew, and there are also mosques.
antwerp: Antwerp lies on the river Scheldt, which links it to the North Sea through the Westerschelde estuary, about 40 kilometres north of Brussels and 15 kilometres south of the Dutch border. The city allegedly began as a Gallo-Roman vicus, and excavations near the Scheldt in 1952 to 1961 found pottery and glass from the mid-2nd to the end of the 3rd century. It was first named in the 4th century, when it was settled by the Germanic Franks.

After the silting-up of the Zwin and the decline of Bruges, Antwerp, then part of the Duchy of Brabant, grew in importance, and its population doubled between 1500 and 1569. At the end of the 15th century the foreign trading houses were moved from Bruges to Antwerp. The old Mediterranean trade routes were losing importance, and the new sea routes round Africa to Asia and across the Atlantic to America helped to push the city into prominence. Its stock exchange, first built in 1531, was the first purpose-built commodity exchange in the world.

The Treaty of Münster of 1648, which recognised the independence of the United Provinces, stipulated that the Scheldt be closed to navigation, which destroyed Antwerp's trade. The closure lasted until 1863, though it was relaxed under French rule from 1795 to 1814. By 1800 the population had fallen below 40,000. Napoleon funded a new dock, still named the Bonaparte Dock, and the deepening of the Scheldt, hoping to counter the Port of London, but he was defeated at Waterloo before the plan was complete. Belgian insurgents captured the city in 1830, while a Dutch garrison under General David Hendrik Chassé held the citadel, until he surrendered to a French army in December 1832.

Antwerp is the capital of Antwerp Province and the most populous municipality in Belgium, with 565,039 inhabitants. Its port is one of the largest in Europe, and the city is a centre of the diamond trade. It hosted the Summer Olympics in 1920. In the 17th century it had a school of painting that included Rubens, Van Dyck and Jordaens, and Rubens's former home and studio is now a museum.
anuradhapura: Anuradhapura lies in the north central plain of Sri Lanka, on the banks of the Malwathu Oya, 205 kilometres north of Colombo. According to the Mahāvaṃsa, a minister of Prince Vijaya named Anuradha founded a village, Anuradhagama, near the river, then called the Kadamba. In 377 BCE, in the reign of King Pandukabhaya, the village was formally established as the capital of the Sinhalese kingdom.

The Mahāvaṃsa places the city's founding in 437 BCE, but excavation of the citadel area puts human settlement as far back as the 10th century BCE. The protohistoric Iron Age there, from 900 to 600 BCE, shows iron technology, pottery, the horse, domestic cattle and paddy cultivation, and by 700 to 600 BCE the settlement covered at least 50 hectares. In the 2nd century CE Ptolemy named a place, Anourogrammoi, that scholars read as Anuradhapura.

The chronicles say King Pandukabhaya planned the city with gates and quarters for traders, and that it covered a square kilometre, one of the largest cities in Asia. It was the first capital of the Sinhala kingdom of Rajarata and the longest-serving ancient capital of Sri Lanka. It was a centre of Theravada Buddhism and a pilgrimage site, with temples and monasteries that cover over 100 square kilometres. Under King Dhatusena (455 to 473) the Theravada canon was redacted and 18 new viharas were built. The Jaya Sri Maha Bodhi is regarded as the oldest documented planted tree in the world, believed to descend from the Bodhi tree at Bodh Gaya.

The city was largely deserted after invasions by the Chola king Rajaraja I in 993 and by his son Rajendra I in 1014. The Culavamsa says the Chola army destroyed it utterly. Several later Sinhalese kings tried to return the capital to Anuradhapura, but the political centre had shifted to Polonnaruwa. Anuradhapura remained a pilgrimage site. In 1821 John Davy described it as a small mean village in the midst of a desert, with a large tank, stone pillars and mounds as its remains. British colonial authorities began surveys and restoration in the late 19th century.

Much of the modern city was moved in the mid-20th century, under the Anuradhapura Preservation Plan of 1949, to a planned New Town to the east so as to preserve the ancient capital. The ancient city was designated a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1982. Among its monuments are the Ruwanwelisaya, Thuparamaya, Abhayagiri Dagaba and Jetavanarama.
anwar-sadat: Sadat was born on 25 December 1918 in Mit Abu El Kom, in Monufia Governorate, to a poor family with 14 children. His Upper Egyptian father was a medical officer who had met his mother while posted in Sudan. He graduated from the Royal Military Academy in Cairo in 1938, joined the Signal Corps and was posted to Sudan, where he met Gamal Abdel Nasser. Together with other junior officers they formed the Free Officers, a group committed to ending British rule and state corruption.

During the Second World War Sadat belonged to the Young Egypt Party and collaborated with Nazi Germany in Egypt. He was arrested and imprisoned for much of the war, and was jailed again after the assassination of the finance minister Amin Osman in January 1946. He took part in the coup of 23 July 1952 that overthrew King Farouk I and read the revolution's first statement over the radio.

Under Nasser, Sadat was minister of State from 1954, edited the daily Al Gomhuria, presided over the National Assembly from 1960 to 1968 and was vice president from 1964. Nasser's supporters expected his successor to be short-lived and easy to manipulate. On 15 May 1971 Sadat announced a Corrective Revolution, dismissing and imprisoning Vice President Ali Sabri and Interior Minister Sharawi Gomaa and purging committed Nasserists.

After the October War, which began on 6 October 1973 with a crossing of the Suez Canal, a ceasefire followed under United Nations Security Council Resolution 338. Disengagement agreements with Israel were signed on 18 January 1974 and 4 September 1975. In 1977 Sadat visited Jerusalem and spoke before the Knesset. The peace treaty with Menachem Begin was signed in Washington on 26 March 1979 after the Camp David talks mediated by Jimmy Carter. It provided for mutual recognition and Israeli withdrawal from Sinai. Most Arab states rejected it, and the Arab League suspended Egypt from 1979 to 1989.

In September 1981 Sadat ordered the arrest of more than 1,500 people, among them Islamist militants, Coptic clergy and intellectuals. On 6 October 1981, at the annual parade in Cairo, Lieutenant Khalid Al-Islambuli and others fired on the grandstand. Sadat and eleven others died. Vice President Hosni Mubarak succeeded him. Five men, including Al-Islambuli, were executed on 15 April 1982, and Israel completed its withdrawal from Sinai, except Taba, by 25 April 1982.
anyang: Settlement near Anyang is very old. At Xiaonanhai, on the western edge of the present city, more than 7,000 artefacts, including stone tools and fossil animal bones, have been unearthed from the Stone Age occupation, which has been called the Xiaonanhai culture. Later tradition places the capitals of the sage-kings Zhuanxu and Emperor Ku in the area around 2000 BCE, and their mausoleums are shown today in Sanyang village, south of Neihuang County.

At the beginning of the 14th century BCE King Pangeng of the Shang dynasty established his capital about 2 kilometres north of the modern city, on the banks of the Huan River. This city, Yin, was the first stable capital in Chinese history, and the dynasty founded there also came to be called the Yin dynasty. The capital served 12 kings in 8 generations, among them Wu Ding, under whom the dynasty reached the height of its power. It ended when King Wu of the Zhou destroyed the dynasty in 1046 BCE.

Anyang itself became the seat of Anyang County around 607 CE and has remained so since. Its Tangyin County contains Yue Village, the birthplace of the Song dynasty general Yue Fei. Until 1912 the town was called Zhangde; it received its present name after the founding of the Republic of China. In 1949 the prefecture was briefly detached from Henan and placed in the experimental province of Pingyuan, and it returned to Henan in November 1953.

Anyang is a prefecture-level city and the northernmost city of Henan, bordering Hebei and Shanxi. Its population was 5,477,614 at the 2020 census, and the great majority are Han Chinese. The ground rises in the west into the foothills of the Taihang Mountains and falls in the east to the North China Plain. Industry, notably iron and steel and coal coking, is its main economic base.

Among its monuments are the Wenfeng Pagoda, believed to have been built in 925 and rebuilt under the Ming, which is the symbol of the city, and the Tianning Temple, founded under the Tang dynasty. The Yin ruins, with the tomb of Fu Hao, lie about 2 kilometres north-west of the city; the Yinxu museum opened there in 2005, and UNESCO named the site a World Heritage Site in 2006.
anzac-day: In 1915 Australian and New Zealand soldiers formed part of an Allied expedition that set out to capture the Gallipoli Peninsula in the Ottoman Empire and open the way to the Black Sea. The Australian and New Zealand Army Corps landed on 25 April and met fierce resistance from the Ottoman Army commanded by Mustafa Kemal, later known as Atatürk.

The campaign became a stalemate and dragged on for eight months. At the end of 1915 the Allied forces were evacuated after heavy casualties on both sides. Allied deaths totalled over 56,000, including 8,709 from Australia and 2,721 from New Zealand. News of the landing made a profound impact at home. The first Anzac Day marches were held in London and Australia in 1916; the historian Martin Crotty has argued that they served political purposes, chiefly recruiting.

Anzac Day is a national day of remembrance in Australia and New Zealand, observed on 25 April, and a public holiday in both and in Tonga. After the Second World War it came to commemorate those lost in that war and in later conflicts, and its meaning has since broadened to all who served and died in military operations. It was first marked at the Australian War Memorial in 1942 and has been observed there every year since.

The dawn service is timed to 4:28 am, when the landing began at Gallipoli. An Australian battalion held one on the Western Front on 25 April 1916, and services sprang up spontaneously in Australia in later years. The service at the Sydney Cenotaph in 1928 can claim to be the start of a continuous tradition.

Interest has varied. By the 1950s many New Zealanders were antagonistic or indifferent, partly because of the legal ban on commerce and on sport and entertainment; a new Anzac Day Act in 1966 allowed sport and entertainment in the afternoon.

Services are also held abroad, among them at Villers-Bretonneux in France, Ypres in Belgium and Hellfire Pass in Thailand. The name ANZAC Cove was officially recognised by the Turkish government in 1985, and in Australia the word Anzac is protected by the Protection of Word Anzac Act 1920. The day has met criticism too: from the labour movement at its inception, and in Alan Seymour's 1960 play The One Day of the Year, which questioned old values and drunken celebration.
anzus: After the fall of Singapore and the decline of British power in Asia, Australia sought other partners for its security. Australia and New Zealand also feared a resurgent Japan and the spread of communism to their north. In 1950 Percy Spender, Australia's minister for external affairs, sought a broad Pacific security agreement and said it would be meaningless without the United States. The outbreak of the Korean War in mid-1950 changed American views. The treaty eased antipodean fears that Japan might again become a threat, though the United States was at first reluctant and the president offered an informal guarantee instead.

The treaty was concluded at San Francisco on 1 September 1951 and entered into force on 29 April 1952. It recommits the parties to the purposes of the United Nations, and each declares that an armed attack on any of them would be dangerous to its own peace and safety and that it would act to meet the common danger in accordance with its constitutional processes. Unlike NATO, it has no automatic commitment to armed assistance, since Spender expected the United States Senate to wish to keep the power to declare war. It also has no integrated defence structure or dedicated forces.

New Zealand took part in the Vietnam War directly as an ANZUS member. After the Labour Party won the New Zealand election in 1984, Prime Minister David Lange barred nuclear-powered and nuclear-armed ships from New Zealand ports. In February 1985 New Zealand refused a visit by the destroyer USS Buchanan, because the United States would neither confirm nor deny whether its ships carried nuclear weapons.

After talks broke down, the United States announced in 1986 that it was suspending its obligations to New Zealand, calling it a friend but not an ally. Lange did not withdraw from the treaty, and New Zealand's policy became law in 1987. Australia did not support the ban and continued to allow American ship visits. The treaty remains in force between Australia and the United States, whose officials meet annually in the AUSMIN talks.
aomori-prefecture: Aomori is the northernmost prefecture of the Tōhoku region, on the northern end of Honshu. The Pacific Ocean flanks it to the east and the Sea of Japan to the west, with the Tsugaru Strait linking the two to the north, across which lies Hokkaido. The Shimokita and Tsugaru Peninsulas enclose Mutsu Bay, and between them lies the smaller Natsudomari Peninsula. The highest point is Mount Iwaki, an active stratovolcano of almost 1,625 m.

The name Aomori means green forest. It was first given to a port settlement established by the Hirosaki Domain in 1624, and most likely comes from a small forest on a hill nearby that fishermen used as a landmark.

Humans have lived in the prefecture for at least 15,000 years. The oldest evidence of pottery in Japan was found at the Ōdai Yamamoto I Site, and suggests that the Jōmon period began about 15,000 years ago. By 7,000 BCE fishing cultures had developed along the shores. Settlement at the Sannai-Maruyama Site, in the present-day city of Aomori, began around 3,900 BCE and shows wide interaction with people across Jōmon Japan, including Hokkaido and Kyushu. It ended around 2,300 BCE for unknown reasons, likely because its subsistence economy could not sustain growth during a neoglaciation. At the Kamegaoka site the Jōmon period continued up to 300 BCE, and small statuettes called Shakōkidogū have been found.

After centuries of rule by the Nanbu and Tsugaru clans, the prefecture was formed out of the northern part of Mutsu Province during the Meiji Restoration. Its population grew until the late 20th century, peaked at 1.52 million in 1985 and has declined since.

Aomori's economy is dominated by farming, forestry and fishing, especially apple orchards. Tsugaru-jamisen, a style of music played on the shamisen, was born in the Tsugaru region. The embroidery styles kogin-zashi and Nanbu hishizashi began in the Edo period, when peasant women used them to make linen clothing sturdier and warmer in the winters, since cotton was unavailable to the lower class. The Jōmon Prehistoric Sites in Northern Japan and Shirakami-Sanchi are World Heritage Sites, and the most noted festival is the Aomori Nebuta Matsuri.
aorsi: The Aorsi, called Aorsoi in Greek sources, were an Iranic people of the Sarmatian group. Their name is generally linked to the Avestan auruša- and the Ossetic ūrs or ors, meaning white. Together with an associated tribe, the Siraces, they are believed to have migrated from Central Asia to the lands north and west of the Caspian Sea, and their territory may have reached east as far as the Aral Sea. The Greek geographer Strabo is the main source for them.

Strabo places the Aorsi north-east of the Siraces, who lived between Lake Maeotis, the Sea of Azov, and the Caspian. Furthest east lived the Upper Aorsi, the largest and most numerous group, who held the Caspian coast and controlled the northern part of the Silk Route; the Aorsi were known for wearing golden ornaments. Strabo dates the strength of king Spadines to the reign of Pharnaces II of the Bosporan Kingdom, and says the Upper Aorsi could field even more horsemen than he.

Tacitus tells how in the Bosporan War of 49 CE the Aorsi, alongside Roman cohorts, besieged a town of the Siraces, massacred its people and forced king Zorsines of the Siraces to give hostages and bow before the image of Emperor Claudius. The defeated Tiberius Julius Mithridates threw himself at the feet of Eunones, who asked Claudius to spare him a triumph and execution; Mithridates was exiled instead. After the war the Siraces were much weakened and the Aorsi grew stronger.

Many scholars link the Aorsi and the Alans to Yancai, a steppe state of Chinese records. The diplomat Zhang Qian reported that Yancai lay 2,000 li north-west of Kangju and could raise 100,000 mounted archers, and the Hou Hanshu later says it had become a vassal of Kangju, renamed Alanliao. Y. A. Zadneprovskiy places that subjugation in the 1st century BCE, which pushed many Aorsi westwards. In the 1st century CE the closely related Alans absorbed or conquered them; some Aorsi survived north of Crimea, and Ptolemy names the Alanorsi.
aosta: Aosta is in the Alps, 110 km north-northwest of Turin, at the confluence of the Buthier and the Dora Baltea. It stands at the junction of the Great and Little St Bernard Pass routes, and near the Italian entrance of the Mont Blanc Tunnel and the Great St Bernard Tunnel. This position gave the city considerable military importance in antiquity. Its location in the rain shadow of the Mont Blanc massif leaves it with cool to very cold winters, hot summers and relatively dry conditions throughout the year.

Aosta was settled in proto-historic times and became a centre of the Salassi, many of whom the Romans killed or sold into slavery in 25 BCE. The campaign was led by Terentius Varro, who founded the Roman colony of Augusta Praetoria Salassorum, housing 3,000 retired veterans. After 11 BCE Aosta became the capital of the province of Alpes Graies. Its layout was that of a Roman military camp.

After the fall of the Western Empire the city was conquered in turn by the Burgundians, the Ostrogoths and the Byzantines. The Lombards, who had annexed it to their Italian kingdom, were expelled by the Frankish Empire under Pepin the Short. Under Charlemagne it gained importance as a post on the Via Francigena, which led from Aachen to Italy.

In the 10th century Aosta became part of the Kingdom of Burgundy, and after its fall in 1032 it passed to the lands of Count Humbert I of Savoy. The inhabitants were granted the privilege of holding an assembly of the states-general in 1189, and an executive council was nominated from it in 1536, which lasted until 1802. After the Congress of Vienna restored Savoy rule, the council was reconstituted and recognized by Charles Albert of Sardinia, at the birth of his grandson Prince Amedeo, who was created duke of Aosta.

Aosta is the capital of the bilingual Aosta Valley. The Roman town walls are preserved almost in their entirety, enclosing a rectangle of 724 by 572 metres, with twenty towers in all. The Porta Praetoria, the eastern gate dating to the 1st century, keeps its original form apart from the marble covering. The Roman theatre, built in the late reign of Augustus, held up to 4,000 spectators and its southern façade, 22 metres tall, remains. Outside the walls stands the Arch of Augustus, built to celebrate the victory over the Salassi. Anselm of Aosta, Archbishop of Canterbury from 1093 to 1109, was born in the city.
aosta-valley: The Aosta Valley is an Alpine valley which, with its tributary valleys, includes the Italian slopes of Mont Blanc, Monte Rosa, Gran Paradiso and the Matterhorn. Mont Blanc, at 4,810 m, makes it the highest region of Italy by its highest point. It is bordered by Auvergne-Rhône-Alpes in France, by Valais in Switzerland and by Piedmont. The region covers 3,260.90 km2 and is the smallest, least populous and least densely populated region of Italy.

The early inhabitants were Celts and Ligures. Rome conquered the region from the Salassi around 25 BCE and founded Augusta Prætoria Salassorum, now Aosta, to secure the mountain passes. In 1031–1032 Humbert I of Savoy received the title Count of Aosta from Emperor Conrad II and built a fortification at Bard. Saint Anselm of Canterbury was born in Aosta in 1033 or 1034. In 1191 Thomas I of Savoy granted the communes a charter of liberties, whose rights were defended until 1770. In the mid-13th century Emperor Frederick II made the county a duchy.

The region stayed in Savoy lands apart from French occupations in 1539–1563, 1691 and 1704–1706, and rule by the First French Empire from 1800 to 1814. As part of the Kingdom of Sardinia it joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1861. The Fascist government established a province of Aosta in 1927; it ceased to exist in 1945, and the region gained special autonomous status in 1948.

The Aosta Valley is the Autonomous Region of Aosta Valley, with Aosta as its capital. Italian and French are the official languages, and the Valdôtain dialect of Franco-Provençal is also recognised. It was the first government authority to adopt modern French as its sole official language, in 1536, three years before France itself. Its medieval castles include Fénis, Issogne, Sarre and Bard Fort.
apache: The Apache are several Southern Athabaskan-speaking peoples of the Southwest, the Southern Plains and northern Mexico, linguistically related to the Navajo. The six major groups are the Chiricahua, Jicarilla, Lipan, Mescalero, Plains and Western Apache. Anthropological evidence suggests that the Apache and Navajo lived in the north, where other Athabaskan speakers still live, before migrating to the Southwest sometime between 1200 and 1500 CE. Their homelands, known collectively as Apacheria, include high mountains, canyons, deserts and the southern Great Plains. The word Apache is Spanish; the first known written record is by Juan de Oñate in 1598, and the most widely accepted theory is that it comes from the Zuni word meaning Navajos.

The Apache fought the invading Spanish and Mexican peoples for centuries, though Spanish colonists and Apache bands also traded with each other; a band might be friendly with one village and raid another. The first Apache raids on Sonora seem to date from the late 17th century. As tensions grew, the Mexican government passed laws offering cash rewards for Apache scalps. In the 19th-century American Indian Wars the United States Army found the Apache to be fierce warriors and skilful strategists.

In 1875 the United States military forced the removal of about 1,500 Yavapai and Tonto Apache from the Rio Verde reserve to San Carlos, 180 miles away, on a march through flooded rivers and mountain passes that killed several hundred people. They were interned there for 25 years while settlers took their land. Most United States accounts place the final defeat of an Apache band on 4 September 1886, when 5,000 troops forced Geronimo's group of 30 to 50 men, women and children to surrender at Skeleton Canyon, Arizona. The army sent them and the Chiricahua scouts who had tracked them to confinement in Florida and then Fort Sill, Oklahoma.

Before the reservations Apache lived in extended family units, usually of a couple, their unmarried children, their married daughters and those daughters' husbands and children, living near one another. Housing varied: tipis on the plains, wickiups of wood and brush in the highlands, and earthen hogans in northern Mexico. Food came from hunting, gathering, trade, raiding and, among some groups, cultivation. The Apache distinguished raiding, done by small parties for a specific economic purpose, from war, waged by large parties usually for retribution.

Each Apache tribe is today politically autonomous, with tribes and reservations in Arizona, New Mexico, Texas and Oklahoma, and Apache settled in Sonora, Chihuahua and Coahuila in Mexico. Their languages are endangered, and Lipan is reported extinct.
apadana: Apadana is the Old Persian word for a hypostyle hall, a palace or audience hall of stone construction with columns. The word appears in Elamite as ha-ha-da-na and in Babylonian as ap-pa-da-an, and its etymology is ambiguous. It survived in later Parthian as a word for palace and passed into Arabic as fadan and Armenian as aparan-kʿ. The term is also used by modern scholars for the Urartian hypostyle halls excavated at Altintepe and Erebuni. These halls are older than the Persian ones, and it has been proposed that Urartu was the stylistic origin of the later Persian audience halls.

The Apadana at Persepolis belongs to the oldest building phase of the city, as part of the original design by Darius the Great, and its construction was completed by Xerxes I. It was the largest building on the Terrace. Its roof was supported by 72 columns, and modern scholarship holds that the reliefs on it show idealised social orders and are metaphorical in nature.

A second Apadana Palace stood at Susa. Work began there under Darius after the overall plan was chosen in 515 BCE and was finished under Xerxes I. Its walls were of clay with a brick facade and stone columns, and its inner walls carried glazed brick reliefs of soldiers of the Eternal Guard, a winged lion and a lotus flower. Parts of it burned under Artaxerxes I in 461 BCE and were rebuilt under Artaxerxes II in 359 BCE.

The Persepolis hall was destroyed in 331 BCE by the army of Alexander the Great, and stones from its columns were reused as building material in nearby settlements. By the start of the 20th century only 13 of the great columns were still standing. The German archaeologist Ernst Herzfeld, his assistant Friedrich Krefter and Erich Schmidt excavated it between 1931 and 1939, and material from the excavations is held in the archives of the Freer Gallery of Art in Washington, DC. A fallen column was re-erected in the 1970s as the fourteenth standing one. The Susa Apadana was largely abandoned and pillaged for building material. The form of the hall influenced Umayyad architecture, and early mosques in Persia and Iraq imitate its structure.
apalachicola-river: The Apalachicola River is about 106 miles (171 km) long and lies wholly in Florida. It forms near the town of Chattahoochee, on the Florida–Georgia state line, about 60 miles northeast of Panama City, where the Flint and Chattahoochee rivers meet. The confluence lies within the Lake Seminole reservoir formed by the Jim Woodruff Dam. The river flows south through the forests of the Florida Panhandle, past Bristol, receives the Chipola River from the west in northern Gulf County, and enters Apalachicola Bay, an inlet of the Gulf of Mexico, at Apalachicola. Its lower 30 miles run through extensive swamps and wetlands.

Its watershed, the Apalachicola, Chattahoochee and Flint (ACF) River Basin, drains about 19,500 square miles. The farthest headwaters, on the Chattahoochee in northeast Georgia, lie about 500 miles away, and the highest point of the watershed is Blood Mountain at 4,458 feet.

The name comes from Apalachicola Province, an association of Native American towns on what is now the Chattahoochee River. The Spanish treated the whole course from the southern Appalachian foothills to the Gulf of Mexico as one river and called all of it the Apalachicola. During Florida's British colonial period the river formed the boundary between East Florida and West Florida. Geologically it links the coastal plain and Gulf Coast with the Appalachian Mountains. Forests of the watershed were devastated by logging between 1880 and 1920, yet the Apalachicola still holds some of the finest remaining old growth forest in the southeast.

The watershed contains forests of high biological diversity, with temperate deciduous forest, longleaf pine landscapes and floodplain forest. The endangered tree Florida torreya grows on slopes and bluffs in Torreya State Park, on the east bank. Over 230,000 acres of the delta wetlands, including tidal marshes and seagrass meadows, lie in the Apalachicola National Estuarine Research Reserve. Other protected areas include Apalachicola National Forest, Tates Hell State Forest and the Nature Conservancy's Apalachicola Bluffs and Ravines Preserve. The basin is also known for tupelo honey, and the river forms part of the boundary between the Eastern and Central time zones in Florida.
apamea-syria: Apamea stands on the right bank of the Orontes River in north-western Syria, on the edge of the modern town of Qalaat al-Madiq, about 55 km north-west of Hama and overlooking the Ghab valley. The site was enclosed in a loop of the Orontes which, with a lake and marshes, gave it a peninsular form, hence its other name Cherronêsos. It lay at a strategic crossroads for eastern commerce and became one of the four cities of the Syrian tetrapolis.

The city began as Pella, a Macedonian military settlement founded after the Wars of the Diadochi. Seleucus I Nicator gave it the status of a polis around 300 BCE, fortified it and named it after his Bactrian wife Apama, daughter of the Sogdian warlord Spitamenes. Seleucus made it a military base with 500 elephants and a stud of 30,000 mares and 300 stallions. A census under Quintus Aemilius Secundus in 6 CE counted 117,000 citizens. Pompey razed its fortress in 64 BCE when the city was annexed to Rome, and it held out against Julius Caesar for three years in the revolt under Quintus Caecilius Bassus, until Cassius arrived in 46 BCE.

Much of the city was destroyed in the earthquake of 115 CE and rebuilt through the second century. From 218 to 234 the legion II Parthica was stationed there. In the early fifth century Apamea became capital of the province of Syria Secunda. Khosrow I destroyed it in the sixth century, and Shahrbaraz took it in 613 during the Byzantine–Sasanian War. After the Muslim conquest it was partly resettled as Afāmiya, regained importance under the Hamdanid dynasty and was taken by Tancred after the murder of its ruler Khalaf ibn Mula'ib. An earthquake destroyed it in 1152.

The Great Colonnade, the city's main avenue running nearly 2 km, was among the longest in the Roman world.
