The sea has a monsoonal climate. Historically, trade across it was restricted by the monsoon winds and the currents they produce. Intense upwelling in the summer monsoon makes it one of the most productive marine regions in the world. Geologically, the sea descends from the Tethys Ocean, whose connection between the Atlantic and Indian Oceans closed in two steps, around 20 and 14 million years ago, a closure thought to have allowed the upwelling and the modern South Asian monsoon to be established.

The Arabian Sea has been a route of maritime trade since the development of early coastal sailing vessels in the northern Indian Ocean and southern Arabia in the 4th and 3rd millennia BCE. The straits of Hormuz and Bab-el-Mandeb served as gateways linking the polities of the eastern and western Old World from the first international trade networks of the 3rd millennium BCE. From the 2nd century BCE the sea and its surrounding lands formed the central nexus of the Maritime Silk Road.

The trade carried peoples, ideas, technologies, crops and diseases. Millet and sorghum, for instance, reached the Indus Valley Civilization through sea trade with East Africa. The maritime trade also helped Islam spread from the Arabian Peninsula across the Indian Ocean to East Africa, South Asia, Southeast Asia and the Malay Archipelago.

The countries with coastlines on the Arabian Sea are Yemen, Oman, Pakistan, Iran and India, together with the westernmost islands of the Maldives and Lakshadweep. Its ports include Mumbai, Karachi, Gwadar and Salalah. The island of Socotra is a UNESCO World Heritage Site because of its biodiversity.
arabic-language: Arabic is classified as a Central Semitic language of the Afroasiatic family. Arabia had a wide variety of Semitic languages in antiquity, among them Ancient South Arabian languages in the southwest, Dadanitic and Taymanitic in the oases of northern Hejaz and Hasaitic in the east. Safaitic and Hismaic, attested on the northwestern frontier, share important features with later forms of Arabic, and scholars theorise that they are early forms of it, to be counted as Old Arabic. Linguists generally believe that Old Arabic, a collection of related dialects, first emerged during the Iron Age.

Classical Arabic, the modern Arabic varieties and the Safaitic and Hismaic inscriptions share features found in no other Central Semitic language, evidence of descent from a hypothetical ancestor, Proto-Arabic. Because several Arabic varieties keep features that Classical Arabic lacks, the vernaculars cannot descend from Classical Arabic, which is a sister language rather than their direct ancestor.

Arabic usually means Standard Arabic, which Western linguists divide into Classical Arabic and Modern Standard Arabic. Classical Arabic is the language of the Quran, used from Pre-Islamic Arabia to the Abbasid Caliphate, and follows the norms set by classical grammarians such as Sibawayh and the vocabulary of classical dictionaries such as the Lisān al-ʻArab. Modern Standard Arabic largely follows its grammar and vocabulary but has taken new vocabulary for concepts of the industrial and post-industrial era. Alongside it stand regional vernacular dialects, usually acquired in families, which are not necessarily mutually intelligible. Educated Arabs speak both, a situation called diglossia.

Arabic has a root-and-pattern morphology. A root of usually three bare consonants is fitted into a pattern to form words: from k-t-b, meaning write, come katabtu, I wrote, kitābun, book, and kātibun, writer. It is written with the Arabic alphabet, an abjad that runs from right to left and derives from the Aramaic through Nabatean.

During the Middle Ages Arabic was a major vehicle of culture and learning, especially in science, mathematics and philosophy, and many European languages borrowed words from it. The influence is seen mainly in Spanish, and less in Portuguese, Catalan and Sicilian, owing to the long Arabic cultural and linguistic presence in southern Iberia in the Al-Andalus era. Maltese is a Semitic language that developed from a dialect of Arabic and is written in the Latin alphabet.

Persian, Turkish, Hindustani, Malay, Hausa and Swahili are among the languages most markedly influenced. The lexicographic tradition lasted about a millennium before the modern period: the Kitāb al-ʿAyn of the 8th century is considered the first lexicon to include all Arabic roots, and Ibn Manzur's Lisān al-ʿArab of 1290 gives 9,273 roots. Arabic is one of the official languages of the United Nations and the liturgical language of Islam.
arachosia: Arachosia, in Old Persian Harauvatiš, was a satrapy of the Achaemenid Empire, centred mainly on the Arghandab River, a tributary of the Helmand, and reaching east as far as the Indus. The Greek name comes from Arachōtós, the Greek name of that river, and the Old Persian form is the etymological equivalent of Sarasvatī in Vedic Sanskrit. The region bordered Drangiana to the west, the Paropamisadae to the north, Hindush to the east and Gedrosia to the south.

Ancient writers list several cities. Isidore of Charax, Strabo and Pliny call Alexandria on the river Arachotus the metropolis of Arachosia; it is often wrongly identified with Kandahar, but a clay tablet inscription has shown that Kandahar traded with Persia well before Alexander. Ptolemy names an earlier capital, Arachotus, said to have been originally called Cophen and identified today with Arghandab, north-west of Kandahar.

The region first appears in the Elamite Persepolis fortification tablets and later in inscriptions of Darius I and Xerxes I, and it supplied ivory for Darius's palace at Susa. In the Behistun inscription Darius recounts that its governor Vivana defeated a rebel Persian three times and kept the province in his hands. Around 330 BCE Alexander the Great commissioned Alexandria Arachosia as its new capital, on the site of an earlier Persian fortress, and appointed his generals as governors. In 316 BCE Antigonus I sent most of the veteran Argyraspides to the satrap Sibyrtius to guard the frontier with India, with orders to send them out in small groups on dangerous missions so that their numbers dwindled.

After the Wars of the Diadochi the region passed to the Seleucid Empire, which ceded it to the Mauryan Empire in return for an alliance. Later it fell in turn to the Greco-Bactrian and Indo-Greek kingdoms, the Indo-Scythians, the Arsacids and Indo-Parthians, and the Kushans, who held it until about 230 CE, when the second Persian Empire defeated them.

Arachosia then came under vassals of that empire, the Kushanshas, who were driven out in 420 by the Chionites, founders of the Kidarite Kingdom. The Hephthalites replaced the Kidarites in the 460s and were defeated in 565 by a coalition of Persian and Turkish armies. Around 870 the Kushano-Hephthalites were replaced by the Saffarids, then by the Samanid Empire and the Ghaznavids in the early 11th century. Arab geographers called the region Rokhaj.

Its inhabitants were Iranian peoples, called Arachosians or Arachoti and also Pactyans, a name that may refer to the Pashtuns, though Frye calls the identification a guess that remains unproven. Isidore described its metropolis as Greek even in the 1st century CE, and said the Parthians called the region White India.
arad-romania: Settlement on the northern bank of the Mureș began in the 5th millennium BCE. Roman troops conquered the Dacian settlement in what is now the Micălaca district between 101 and 102, and in the Second Dacian War Trajan took the land north of the Mureș. The name of the city comes from its first ispán, or count, Arad. The area became part of the Principality of Hungary at the end of the 9th century, and the town is first mentioned in the 11th century.

An assembly of the realm in 1131 was followed by the massacre of 68 magnates blamed for the blinding of King Béla II. The Ottomans took the region in 1551 and held it until the Peace of Karlowitz of 1699, and Austrian forces captured the town in 1687. A new fortress was built between 1763 and 1783, and in 1834 Emperor Francis I declared Arad a free royal town. In the Revolution of 1848 it became a Hungarian headquarters, and from Arad Lajos Kossuth issued his proclamation of 11 August 1849 and handed supreme power to Artúr Görgey.

After Görgey's surrender at Világos, the fortress was recaptured, and on 6 October 1849 Julius Jacob von Haynau had thirteen rebel generals executed there. Arad has since been called the Hungarian Golgotha. In 1910 its 63,166 inhabitants were 73 per cent Hungarians and 16.2 per cent Romanians. In 1920 the Treaty of Trianon ceded it to Romania.

Arad is the capital of Arad County, on the Mureș, and a transport hub. Its growth in the later 19th and early 20th centuries produced its main buildings, among them the neoclassical Ioan Slavici Theatre of 1874 and the Neo-Gothic Red Church of 1906. The city had one of the first music conservatories in Europe, set up in 1833, and the first car factory in Hungary and present-day Romania. Preparandia, founded in 1812, was the first Romanian teacher-training school in Transylvania, and the Hirschl Theatre of 1817 is the oldest stone theatre in Romania. A monument to the thirteen martyrs stands in one of the public squares.
arado-flugzeugwerke: Arado began as the Warnemünde factory of the Flugzeugbau Friedrichshafen firm, which produced land-based military aircraft and seaplanes during the First World War. With its parent company it ceased operations after the war, when the Treaty of Versailles restricted German aviation. In 1921 Heinrich Lübbe bought the factory and began building aircraft again for export, with Walter Rethel, previously of Kondor and Fokker, as head designer. In 1925 the company joined the Arado Handelsgesellschaft, a trading firm founded by the industrialist Hugo Stinnes Jr. to cover illegal trade in military equipment.

When the Nazi government came to power in 1933, Lübbe took control of the company; just before, Walter Blume, formerly of Albatros, had replaced Rethel as designer. Arado became a supplier to the Luftwaffe with the Arado Ar 66, which remained one of its standard trainers into the Second World War, and with some of its first fighters, the Ar 65 and Ar 68. In 1936 the Reich Aviation Ministry insisted that Lübbe join the Nazi party as a show of loyalty. He refused, was arrested and was forced to sell the company to the state. It was renamed Arado Flugzeugwerke GmbH and placed under Erich Serno and Felix Wagenführ.

In the Second World War the Ar 96 became the Luftwaffe's most used trainer, and the Ar 196 became standard equipment on all larger German warships as a reconnaissance seaplane. Most of Arado's other designs were passed over in favour of competitors' products. Arado was the primary subcontractor for the Heinkel He 177 and built the Focke-Wulf Fw 190 and its components under licence. Its Ar 234 was the first jet-powered bomber. From August 1944 until their liberation by the Soviet army in April 1945, 1,012 slave labourers from Freiberg, a sub-camp of the Flossenbürg concentration camp, worked at the Arado factory, mostly Polish Jewish women and girls sent from Auschwitz.

Arado was liquidated and broken up in 1945. The Ar 234 came too late to affect the outcome of the war, but it was a sign of things to come. The Ar 96 trainer continued to be built in Czechoslovakia by Zlin after the war, as the C.2B.
aragonese-crusade: The Aragonese Crusade was fought as an extension of the War of the Sicilian Vespers, which lasted from 1282 to 1302. Pope Martin IV called it in retribution for the intervention of Peter III of Aragon in Sicily, which had damaged the political ambitions of the papacy and of France. Martin declared the crusade in 1284 and 1285 and formally deposed Peter, on the ground that Aragon was a papal fief: Peter's grandfather and namesake, Peter II, had surrendered the kingdom to the Holy See as a fief. Martin gave Aragon to Count Charles of Valois, a son of King Philip III of France.

The crusade split Aragon. Peter's brother James II of Majorca, who had inherited the County of Roussillon and so stood between the French and Aragonese dominions, joined the French; Peter had opposed his inheritance as a younger son. In 1284 the first French armies entered Roussillon, numbering 16,000 cavalry, 17,000 crossbowmen and 100,000 infantry, with 100 ships in southern French ports. The local people rose against them. The Bastard of Roussillon defended Elne, but the city was overcome and its cathedral burned, and the population was massacred except for him.

In 1285 Philip III entrenched himself before Girona and took it. On 28 April Cardinal Jean Cholet placed his own hat on Charles's head, and Charles was nicknamed the king of the hat. The French then suffered reverses. Peter's admiral Roger de Lauria destroyed their fleet at the Battle of Les Formigues, near Palamós, and dysentery struck the camp, afflicting Philip himself. The heir, Philip of Navarre, negotiated free passage for the royal family, but the troops were refused it and were decimated at the Battle of the Col de Panissars. The king of France died at Perpignan and was buried in Narbonne. Peter did not long survive him.

The defeat of 1285 effectively ended the fighting. The Treaty of Tarascon of 1291 restored Aragon to Alfonso III and lifted the Church's ban. The historian H. J. Chaytor judged the crusade perhaps the most unjust, unnecessary and calamitous enterprise ever undertaken by the Capetian monarchy, and W. C. Jordan has blamed it for the young Philip IV's later opposition to papal interference in French foreign policy. Its legacy to France was slight, but Majorca was devastated as an independent polity: Alfonso annexed Majorca, Ibiza and Menorca, and the Treaty of Anagni of 1295 returned the islands to James.
arakan-rohingya-salvation-army: According to a spokesman, the group was founded in 2013 as Harakah al-Yaqin, the Faith Movement, after the 2012 Rakhine State riots. A December 2016 report by the International Crisis Group said it was led by Ataullah abu Ammar Jununi, a Rohingya born in Karachi, Pakistan, and raised in Saudi Arabia, with a committee of émigrés in Saudi Arabia. Before 2016 its members patrolled villages with bamboo sticks; some months before its first attack it began recruiting men to train across the border in Bangladesh. It took its present name in a statement of 29 March 2017.

Its attacks of October 2016 on posts along the Bangladesh–Myanmar border left nine border officers and four soldiers dead. On 25 August 2017 it struck at least two dozen police posts; the government counted 77 insurgents and 12 members of the security forces killed. Myanmar's army blamed it for the killing of 99 Hindus at Kha Maung Seik that day, and Amnesty International reported in May 2018 that it had evidence of the massacre. ARSA denied such charges. It declared a one-month ceasefire on 9 September 2017, which the government rejected.

In the Bangladeshi refugee camps the group was accused of killing critics and community leaders, among them Mohammed Mohib Ullah, killed on 29 September 2021; Bangladesh Police named ARSA as responsible, which it denied. From 2024 it cooperated with the Tatmadaw against the Arakan Army, and was accused of forcing young men and boys to fight. Bangladesh's Rapid Action Battalion arrested Ataullah in Narayanganj on 18 March 2025.

ARSA calls itself an ethno-nationalist and secular group with no links to foreign Islamists, though it seeks fatwas from foreign Muslim clerics. Unlike other insurgent groups in Myanmar it has no ranks or uniforms, and in August 2017 most of its fighters carried machetes and bamboo sticks. Analysts have compared its tactics to those of insurgents in southern Thailand: small raids across a border, then retreat to a community of the same background. Most of its written statements are in English.
aral-sea: The Aral Sea was an endorheic salt lake between Kazakhstan to the north and Uzbekistan to the south. Its name roughly translates from Mongolic and Turkic languages as Sea of Islands, after the more than 1,100 islands that once dotted it. Formerly the fourth-largest lake in the world, with an area of 68,000 square kilometres, it had low native biodiversity but exceptional endemic fish, including three endemic sturgeon species. The Amu Darya flowed into the Caspian Sea until the Holocene, when its course changed to feed the Aral Sea from the south.

Climate shifts drove several phases of rising and falling water. Inflow from the Amu Darya and Syr Darya depends on glacial melt and rainfall, and shifts in the Amu Darya's course also changed the level. Artificial irrigation began in ancient times. Around 660-665 the sea was part of the western frontier of the Chinese Empire under the Tang dynasty. A Russian naval presence began in 1847 with the founding of Raimsk, soon renamed Fort Aralsk. Ships were taken apart at Orenburg and carried overland to be rebuilt, and a survey of the whole sea followed. The exiled Ukrainian poet and painter Taras Shevchenko took part and made sketches.

In the early 1960s the Soviet government planned for cotton, called white gold, to become a major export. The Amu Darya and the Syr Darya were diverted from the sea to irrigate the desert for cotton, melons, rice and cereals. By 1988 Uzbekistan was the world's largest exporter of cotton, but the farms relied heavily on agrochemicals and the soil degraded. The sea began shrinking in the 1960s and by 2007 had fallen to 10% of its original size, split into the North Aral Sea, the eastern and western basins of the South Aral Sea and the small Barsakelmes Lake.

The fishing industry, which at its peak employed about 40,000 people and reportedly produced one-sixth of the Soviet Union's fish catch, ended; commercial harvests were nonexistent by 1987. Moynaq, a harbour town that employed about 30,000 people, now lies 30 to 90 kilometres from the shore. The former eastern basin is called the Aralkum Desert. Kazakhstan completed the Dike Kokaral dam in 2005 to save the North Aral Sea, and by 2008 the water there had risen 12 metres above its 2003 level.
aramaic: Aramaic is a Northwest Semitic language that originated in the ancient region of Syria and spread to Mesopotamia, the southern Levant, Sinai, south-eastern Anatolia, the Caucasus and eastern Arabia. It belongs to the same group as the Canaanite languages, such as Hebrew and Phoenician, and as Amorite and Ugaritic. Early Aramaic inscriptions date from the 11th century BCE, which places it among the earliest languages to be written down, although its history before the first texts of the 9th century BCE is unknown.

By around 1000 BCE the Arameans had a string of kingdoms in what is now part of Syria, Lebanon, Jordan, Turkey and the fringes of southern Mesopotamia. Aramaic rose to prominence under the Neo-Assyrian Empire, whose kings adopted it as a lingua franca after Arameans had settled in greater numbers in Babylonia and in the Assyrian heartland. Written sources of the Neo-Assyrian and Neo-Babylonian empires were bilingual, with Aramaic used beside Akkadian.

The Achaemenid Empire continued the practice, and Aramaic gradually became the lingua franca of most of western Asia, Anatolia, the Caucasus and Egypt, replacing several related Semitic languages. Alexander the Great and his successors ended the Achaemenid order, and by 300 BCE all the main Aramaic-speaking regions were under the Seleucid Empire, which favoured Greek. During the 3rd century BCE Greek overtook Aramaic in many spheres of public life, especially in the Hellenized cities, but Aramaic went on among the literate classes of native communities and with local authorities.

Classical Syriac, the language of Syriac Christianity, arose in the 1st century CE in Osroene around Edessa. Its golden age was the 4th to 8th centuries, beginning with the translation of the Bible known as the Peshitta and including the prose and poetry of Ephrem the Syrian. Missionary activity spread Syriac from Mesopotamia and Persia into Central Asia, India and China.

Aramaic is written in the Aramaic alphabet, a descendant of the Phoenician alphabet. Its square style was adopted for the Hebrew alphabet, and the Syriac alphabet, a cursive form, grew up among Christian communities.

From the late 7th century Arabic gradually replaced Aramaic as the lingua franca of the Near East after the early Muslim conquests. Aramaic nevertheless remains a spoken, literary and liturgical language. Modern eastern varieties are spoken by Assyrians, Mandaeans and some Mizrahi Jews, and Western Aramaic survives in a few villages of western Syria, including Maaloula. Classical varieties are liturgical languages of several West Asian churches.
arame-of-urartu: Arame, also written Aramu, was the first known king of the state of Urartu. He lived in the time of King Shalmaneser III of Assyria and fought unsuccessfully against him. Nothing is recorded of his birth or family, and later Urartian rulers probably came from a different dynasty than his.

It has been hypothesised that Aramu was a military leader of Aramean origin, since the name Aram is first recorded in the 13th century BCE as that of the Aramean people of the Levant and southern Anatolia. He is not to be confused with another king Aramu, also called Adramu and Atarsamek, an Aramean ruler of Bit Agusi who lived at the same time and also fought Shalmaneser III.

Shalmaneser captured Arame's capital at Arzashkun. Sagunia, a previous capital that Shalmaneser also captured, seems to have lain near Lake Van or Lake Urmia. The Assyrian account is the source of what is known of him, and the outcome of his resistance was the loss of his royal cities.

Arame has been suggested as the prototype of both Aram, from which the popular given name Aram derives, and Ara the Beautiful, two forefathers of tradition of the Armenian people who are not historically attested. 5) places them six and seven generations after Hayk. The philologist Armen Petrosyan identifies Aramu with the Armenian Aram of tradition and proposes that he was named after an Armenian or related deity *Aram-.

Noting what he takes to be Armenian etymologies for both Aramu and his city Arṣašku, Petrosyan concludes that the first king of Urartu was an Armenian ruler and that Armenians lived in Arṣašku. This is one scholar's argument, set against the hypothesis of an Aramean origin.
aranuka: Aranuka is an atoll of Kiribati, just north of the equator in the Gilbert Islands. 6 square kilometres and had a population of 1,057 in 2010. It is triangular and mostly formed by two large islands, Buariki and Takaeang, both unusually large for an atoll of this size. 36 kilometres west of the main island.

Long sandbanks join the islands on the northern side and an underwater reef crest on the southern side, which also has a wide pass into the central lagoon. Boats can use the pass in moderate weather, though tidal streams are strong at several points. The lagoon is not rich in shellfish.

One road runs along the lagoon side of the island, where all the villages stand. Aranuka had only three villages from its first settlement until 1978, when a small fourth, Baurua, was founded. It is known for an old stand of Rhizophora stylosa mangroves that have grown as tall as coconut trees and are a breeding site for birds.

By local tradition Aranuka is the central island of Kiribati and the place where the God of the ancestors, Nareau, began the formation and separation of all the islands. For this reason it was formerly called Ananuka, meaning the middle of it. The first Europeans recorded as visiting were Thomas Gilbert and John Marshall, sailing the First Fleet vessels Charlotte and Scarborough, in June 1788. The US Exploring Expedition surveyed the island in 1841.

At some point between 1860 and the late 1880s, Aranuka and Kuria were conquered by the paramount chief of Abemama. A former ruler of the two islands, Ten Temea, gave them up and left for Maiana, another island of the group. They were afterwards ruled by Tem Binoka. A post office opened on Aranuka around 1924.

Aranuka Airport lies near the northern tip of Buariki and has two flights a week from South Tarawa, which also link to Kuria. Charter boats also serve the island. Visitors come for its beaches and for swimming and snorkelling at the uninhabited islets, and the island council runs a guesthouse.
aras-river: The Aras is a transboundary river of the Caucasus. It rises in eastern Turkey and flows along the borders between Turkey and Armenia, between Turkey and the Nakhchivan exclave of Azerbaijan, and between Iran and both Azerbaijan and Armenia, before it flows through Azerbaijan into the Kura as a right tributary. It drains the south side of the Lesser Caucasus, while the Kura drains the north side. Its total length is 1,072 kilometres and its watershed covers 102,000 square kilometres, which makes it one of the longest rivers in the Caucasus.

Its major tributaries include the Arpa Çayı, also called the Akhuryan, which gathers the waters of the Kars River and Lake Çıldır, the Hrazdan, which empties into Lake Sevan, and the Qareh Sū from the Sabalān Mountains. The lowest point in Armenia lies along the Aras, at 380 metres.

The Greeks of classical antiquity knew the river as the Araxes. Armenians called it Eraskh, and its modern Armenian name is Arax or Araks; in Old Georgian it was Rakhsi, and in Azerbaijani it is Araz. In Armenian tradition it is named for Arast, a great-grandson of the patriarch Haik. The Hellenized name Araxes was applied to the Kura–Araxes culture, a prehistoric people of the valleys of the Kura and Aras. Virgil's Aeneid calls the river angry at the bridge, since the Romans built a bridge over it.

Strabo cites a legend that in ancient times the Araxes in Armenia had no outflow to the Caspian Sea and spread across the plains to form a lake. Robert H. Hewsen described it as the only true river of Armenia, and as Mother Araxes, a symbol of pride to Armenians.

In 589, in the Sasanian era, a battle between Persians and Byzantines was fought on the river. In Islamic times it was known in Arabic as al-Rass and in Perso-Turkish contexts as Aras. By the Treaty of Gulistan and the Treaty of Turkmenchay the river was chosen as the border between the Russian Empire and Qajar Iran, which was forced to cede its Caucasian territories to Russia. Because of these 19th-century changes, one scheme that is not widely accepted draws the Aras as the line between Europe and Asia.

Iran and the Soviet Union built the Aras Dam near Nakhchivan between 1963 and 1970, creating the Aras Reservoir. Iran later built the Khoda Afarin Dam near the historic Khudafarin Bridges, and the Giz Galasi Dam 12 kilometres downstream, between 1999 and 2008. The valley in Iğdır Province, Turkey, is a wetland rich in bird species, and a bird research and education centre was founded there in 2006.
aratta: Aratta appears in the Sumerian tales of Enmerkar and Lugalbanda, two early and possibly mythical kings of Uruk who are also named in the Sumerian King List. The poems describe it as fabulously rich in gold, silver and lapis lazuli and in the artisans who worked them, remote and hard to reach, and the home of the goddess Inanna until she transferred her favour to Uruk. In Enmerkar and the Lord of Aratta a messenger crosses the Zubi mountains, Susa, Anshan and five, six, seven mountains before reaching it, and Aratta asks for grain in return for its treasures.

In Enmerkar and En-suhgir-ana the lord of Aratta challenges Enmerkar for Inanna's affection and sends a sorcerer from Hamazi to bewitch Uruk's livestock at Eresh, but a wise woman defeats him and casts him into the Euphrates, and the lord submits. In the Lugalbanda poems Enmerkar's army marches through the mountains against a rebellious Aratta, and Inanna advises him to carry off its metalsmiths, stonemasons and moulds; the city is given battlements of green lapis lazuli. Later hymns, proverbs and the Gudea cylinder name Aratta as a byword for treasure and remoteness.

Early 20th-century scholars took Aratta for an epithet of Shuruppak, a view since abandoned. In 1963 Samuel Noah Kramer placed it near Lake Urmia, reading a Mount Hurum in a Lugalbanda poem as a reference to the Hurrians, but the phrase is now read as mountain cave. Others looked to the Great Khorasan Road through northern Iran. When Anshan was identified with Tall-i Malyan in 1973, it lay 600 km south-east of Uruk, far from those routes. Yousef Majidzadeh has proposed the Jiroft culture of eastern Iran. No archaeological trace of Aratta has been found, and Hansman warned in 1978 against over-speculation.
aratus-of-sicyon: Aratus was born in 271 BCE in Sicyon in the northern Peloponnese. His father Cleinias had become head magistrate of the city after the murder of the previous tyrant. In 264 BCE Abantidas murdered Cleinias and made himself tyrant, and the seven-year-old Aratus escaped with the help of his aunt, who hid him until nightfall and smuggled him to Argos. He was raised there by friends of his father and won a prize in the pentathlon, but remained set on freeing Sicyon, and became leader of the exiles' party. He sought support from the kings of Macedon and Egypt.

In 251 BCE, acting on a prisoner's tip that the escape route out of Sicyon could be used to scale its walls, Aratus led a band of exiles in with ladders at night. The tyrant Nicocles escaped through a tunnel, and some citizens burned his house. Aratus recalled the exiles and, according to Plutarch, brought Sicyon into the Achaean League, the first non-Achaean city admitted.

He travelled to Alexandria and returned with 40 talents and a promise of 110 more from Ptolemy II Philadelphos, which helped settle disputes over confiscated property. Elected strategos of the League in 245 BCE, he held the office every two years with few interruptions, seventeen times in all.

In 243 BCE he took the Acrocorinth from its Macedonian garrison under Persaeus, using a less steep approach learned from Syrian mercenaries. Corinth, Megara, Troezen and Epidaurus then joined the League. After the Spartan king Cleomenes III conquered Argos and Corinth, Aratus secured an alliance with his former enemy Antigonus III Doson of Macedon, and their forces defeated Cleomenes at the Battle of Sellasia.

In the Social War against the Aetolian League he became a chief adviser to Philip V of Macedon. He was weaker as a battlefield commander: at the river Xerias near Argos in 235 BCE he retreated while the other wing was winning, and in 220 BCE a cavalry action he ordered against the Aetolians ended in a rout.

Aratus quarrelled with Philip V over his conduct at Messene, and he died in 213 BCE. Plutarch reports that Philip had him poisoned, but modern scholarship finds this unlikely, since Philip had no interest in an unstable Achaea. By special permission of the Oracle of Delphi he was the first person buried within the walls of Sicyon, as founder and saviour of the city. Plutarch judged him a great politician whose abilities did not extend to the battlefield. He was skilled at compromise, as when he handed the Acrocorinth to Macedon in return for help against Sparta, and under him the League became a major power in Greece.
aratus-of-soli: Accounts of Aratus's life by anonymous Greek writers, together with the Suda and Eudocia, make him a native of Soli in Cilicia, although one authority names Tarsus. He was the son of Athenodoros and had a brother of the same name. He studied with Menecrates at Ephesus and Philitas on Cos. As a disciple of the Peripatetic philosopher Praxiphanes in Athens, he met the Stoic philosopher Zeno, Callimachus of Cyrene and Menedemus, founder of the Eretrian school. His chief pursuits were medicine, which is also said to have been his profession, grammar and philosophy.

About 276 BCE Aratus was invited to the court of the Macedonian king Antigonus II Gonatas, whose victory over the Gauls in 277 BCE he set to verse. There he wrote his best-known poem, the Phenomena, which biographers say Antigonus wished to have made from the prose works of Eudoxus of Cnidus. He then spent some time at the court of Antiochus I Soter of Syria, but returned to Pella in Macedon, where he died before 240 or 239 BCE.

Several poems on other subjects and a number of prose letters are attributed to him, and the Suda lists works such as Hymns to Pan and a Correction of the Odyssey, but only the two astronomical poems survive.

The Phenomena has 732 verses and introduces the constellations, with rules for their risings and settings, and the circles of the sphere, the Milky Way among them. It describes the northern constellations by reference to groups around the pole and uses Orion as a starting point for those in the south. It holds that the Earth is motionless and the sky turns about a fixed axis, and it opens by asserting the dependence of all things upon Zeus. Its descriptions lack precision, and it contains errors that are partly Eudoxus's and partly due to how Aratus used him. Hipparchus, about a century later, wrote a commentary noting where his own observations differed.

The Diosemeia, of 422 verses, forecasts the weather from celestial signs and describes its effects on animals. It appears to imitate Hesiod and was in turn imitated by Virgil in the Georgics, drawing largely on Aristotle's Meteorologica and Theophrastus's work On Weather Signs.

The poems were very popular in the Greek and Roman world. Theocritus and Callimachus admired him, and Latin versions were made by Cicero, Ovid, Germanicus and Avienius. Twenty-seven commentators are known. Acts 17:28 quotes the fifth line of the Phenomena in Paul's address on the Areopagus, and the Caliph al-Ma'mun commissioned an Arabic translation in the ninth century.
arauco-war: The Arauco War, mostly fought in the Araucanía region of Chile, began as a reaction by the Mapuche to Spanish conquerors who tried to found cities and force the native people into servitude. South of the Bío Bío river the Spanish first sought to secure the valleys around the Cordillera de Nahuelbuta, intending to exploit placer deposits of gold with Mapuche labour from the densely populated valleys nearby. Gold mining killed many Mapuche, and because they had no tradition of forced labour like the Andean mita, they largely refused to serve.

An antecedent was the Battle of Reynogüelén in 1536, between a detachment of Diego de Almagro's expedition and a large group of Mapuche. The war itself began with the campaigns of Pedro de Valdivia, from 1540.

Valdivia fought a nine-year campaign to secure central Chile. His third expedition founded forts at Tucapel, Purén, Confines and Arauco, and in October 1553 the Quilacoya gold mine opened, with many Mapuche forced to work in it. That year the Mapuche held a council and resolved on war. They chose Caupolicán as toqui and as vice toqui Lautaro, who had served the Spanish cavalry and created the first Mapuche cavalry corps. In February 1554 Lautaro gathered an army of 8,000 men and met a punitive expedition under Francisco de Villagra at the Battle of Marihueñu; Concepción was found abandoned and he burned it.

In 1557 García Hurtado de Mendoza arrived with 600 soldiers, six pieces of artillery and 1,000 horses, and defeated the Mapuche at Lagunillas. A second rebellion began in July 1561 with the killing of the hated encomendero Pedro de Avendaño in the valley of Purén. In 1563 the governor Pedro de Villagra ordered Arauco abandoned, and the Mapuche regarded it as a victory.

On 21 December 1598 the governor Martín García Óñez de Loyola was surprised by Pelantaro in the Disaster of Curalaba and killed. A general uprising followed, the Destruction of the Seven Cities, which in six years eliminated every Spanish settlement south of the Bío Bío except those in the Chiloé Archipelago. The two sides then established a clear frontier, and from the 17th to the late 18th century Mapuche lonkos and Spanish governors held a series of parliaments.

A last major uprising began on 14 February 1655 under Clentaru, in reaction to the enslavement of the indigenous, and caused Spanish settlers to leave the lands south of the Maule. Philip II said that the war cost the largest number of Spanish lives in the New World, and it was called the Flandes indiano. Abduction of women and war rape were common on both sides.
arawakan-languages: Arawakan, also called Maipurean, is a language family of Indigenous peoples of South America, whose branches spread to Central America and to the Greater and Lesser Antilles, including the Bahamas. The Italian priest Filippo Salvatore Gilii recognised its unity in 1783 and named it Maipure, after a language of the Orinoco in Venezuela. A century later it was renamed after the culturally more important Arawak language of the Guianas.

Its dispersal is debated. One hypothesis holds that the family's diversity comes from a trade language spoken across much of tropical lowland South America. Michael thinks a break-up after 600 CE unlikely, since Arawakan internal diversity is greater than that of the Romance languages. Blench suggests a demographic expansion over a few thousand years. Arawak-speaking peoples are thought to have migrated to the Caribbean about 2,500 years ago.

The Maipurean family has about 64 languages, 29 of them now extinct, among them Taíno. Classification is difficult because many members are extinct and poorly documented, and several scholars, including Kaufman, Aikhenvald and Ramirez, have proposed internal trees. Almost all the languages share a first-person singular prefix nu-, but Arawak proper has ta-, an innovation of one branch. The languages are polysynthetic, mostly head-marking and mostly suffixing, with complex verb morphology. A word for maize, marisi in Lokono, recurs in related forms in Taíno, Wayuu and other languages of the family.

Arawak is the largest family in the Americas by number of languages. Its speakers occupy a large area from the eastern slopes of the central Andes in Peru and Bolivia, across the Amazon basin, northward to Suriname, Guyana, Venezuela and Colombia, and as far as Nicaragua, Honduras, Belize and Guatemala. Taíno was spoken on Cuba, Puerto Rico, Jamaica, the Bahamas and other islands, and a few of its words are still used by English, Spanish and Haitian Creole speakers there. Garifuna developed through the forced migration of people of mixed Arawak, Carib and African descent.
arcadius: Arcadius was born in 377 in Hispania, the eldest son of Theodosius I and Aelia Flaccilla. On 19 January 383 his father declared the five-year-old an Augustus and co-ruler for the eastern half of the empire, and ten years later Honorius was made Augustus of the west. After Theodosius died on 17 January 395, Arcadius, aged 17, fell under the influence of the praetorian prefect of the East, Rufinus, while the ten-year-old Honorius was placed under the guardianship of the general Stilicho.

The eunuch Eutropius arranged for Arcadius to meet Aelia Eudoxia, daughter of the Frankish general Bauto, and the two married on 27 April 395, though Rufinus had hoped to marry his own daughter to the emperor. In 395 Alaric I led a Gothic revolt, and the eastern court, whose army had gone west, could not respond. Rufinus was assassinated by Goths on 27 November 395 on the orders of Stilicho, and Eutropius and Eudoxia became the emperor's advisers. After the Ostrogoth Tribigild revolted, Arcadius dismissed Eutropius on 17 August 399 and later had him executed. Gainas then forced himself on the emperor as magister militum, until riots in Constantinople in July 400 killed as many as 7,000 Goths.

Eudoxia clashed with John Chrysostom, the Archbishop of Constantinople, who in 401 called her Jezebel. Arcadius banished him after the Synod of the Oak in 403 but recalled him when the people rioted. A new synod condemned him in early 404, and on 20 June 404 he was taken away to Abkhazia. On 13 July 399 Arcadius issued an edict ordering the demolition of all remaining non-Christian temples.

In his later reign Arcadius left much to the praetorian prefect Anthemius. He died on 1 May 408 and was succeeded by his young son Theodosius, and was buried in the Church of the Holy Apostles in a porphyry sarcophagus. J. B. Bury described him as thin and inactive, ruled by the strong personalities of his court. Older interpretations saw the court split between pro-Gothic and anti-Gothic factions, but Thomas S. Burns concludes that there were no such parties. Warren Treadgold judged that by continuing to reign so harmlessly, Arcadius maintained legal continuity during a troubled time.
arcelor: In 2004 Arcelor had a turnover of €30.2 billion and shipped 45 million metric tons of steel, which made it the second largest producer by output. At its height it employed 310,000 people in more than 60 countries and supplied the automotive, construction, metal processing, household appliance and packaging industries. It made flat steel at sites such as Ghent, Dunkirk, Avilés, Fos-sur-Mer, Liège and Bremen, as well as long steel products and stainless steel.

In January 2006 Arcelor announced that it would acquire Dofasco, Canada's largest steel producer, with an annual output of 4.4 million tons, after a bidding war with the German ThyssenKrupp that ended with a bid of 5.6 billion Canadian dollars. On 27 January 2006 Mittal Steel launched a hostile takeover bid for Arcelor. Arcelor's directors opposed it, as did the governments of France, Luxembourg and Spain, while Belgium declared itself neutral. Indian commentators called the French opposition economic nationalism, and the Indian commerce minister Kamal Nath warned of a trade war between India and France.

On 26 May 2006 Arcelor announced a merger with the steelmaker Severstal instead, a move that drew questions over its lack of transparency. On 25 June the board decided to go ahead with Mittal Steel, which had raised its offer to €40.37 a share, double the original; Arcelor paid Severstal €140 million for the failed merger. Lakshmi Mittal became president of the new company, and the Arcelor chairman Joseph Kinsch its chairman until his retirement.
arcelormittal: ArcelorMittal has its headquarters in Luxembourg City and is a multinational steel manufacturer with operations in iron ore and coke mining and in scrap recycling. It was created when Mittal Steel Company acquired Arcelor, in a purchase worth 33 billion dollars. The merger was completed after Mittal Steel raised its bid and the Mittal family agreed to give up a controlling stake and signed a standstill agreement not to take a controlling interest without the approval of independent directors. The resulting firm produced about 10 per cent of the world's steel and was then the largest steel company in the world.

In 2007 the company bought Sicartsa, which runs a plant in Mexico, from Grupo Villacero for 1.44 billion dollars and 90 per cent of the Chinese steel wire company Rongcheng Chengshan Steelcord. It raised its stake in China Oriental Group to over 73 per cent, becoming the first foreign company to control a steel mill in China. To satisfy the conditions for regulatory approval of the merger it sold the Bethlehem Steel plant at Lackawanna, New York, and the Sparrows Point Mill to Severstal in December 2008. In the same month, in the Great Recession, it closed its steel mill at Hennepin, Illinois.

In January 2011 the company spun off its stainless steel division as Aperam. In 2012, because of overcapacity and weaker demand in Europe, it idled 9 of its 25 blast furnaces and shut down two furnaces at Florange, France, but revived them two months later after agreeing a substantial investment with the French government. In 2013 it sold a 15 per cent interest in its Labrador Trough iron ore assets to Posco and China Steel for 1.1 billion dollars.

In 2014 an International Chamber of Commerce court awarded Senegal 150 million dollars and allowed it to cancel a 2.2 billion dollar contract to develop an iron ore deposit and a 750 km railway after the company stalled on construction. A consortium led by the company bought Ilva, owner of the Taranto steelworks in southern Italy, in November 2018 for 1.8 billion euros.

The company has steel-making operations in 14 countries and iron ore mining in Brazil, Canada, Liberia, Mexico, Ukraine and South Africa. It is vertically integrated, producing much of its own iron ore and coke. The European Commission fined it 45.7 million euros in April 2011, the largest of the fines on 17 producers, for taking part in a steel cartel between 1984 and 2002, and in 2016 the South African Competition Commission fined it for price fixing between 1984 and 2002.
archdiocese-of-freiburg: The Archdiocese of Freiburg im Breisgau comprises the former states of Baden and Hohenzollern, and its seat is Freiburg Minster. It and the Upper Rhenish ecclesiastical province were both set up in 1821, in the wake of the 1801 Concordat and the 1815 Congress of Vienna. The archdiocese was formed from the Diocese of Constance and parts of the dioceses of Mainz, Straßburg, Worms and Würzburg. Bernhard Boll became its first bishop in 1827, and well-known successors include Conrad Gröber and Hermann Schäufele.

The archbishop is also the metropolitan of the Upper-Rhine province, whose suffragan dioceses are Mainz and Rottenburg-Stuttgart; the province covers large areas of Baden-Württemberg and Hesse and small parts of Rhineland-Palatinate. The archdiocese is organised into seven regions, each divided into deaneries: Odenwald and Tauber, Rhine and Neckar, Middle Oberrhein and Pforzheim, Ortenau, Breisgau, Schwarzwald and Baar, Hochrhein, and Lake Constance and Hohenzollern. Its northernmost parish is St. Laurentius in Freudenberg. Its patron saints are the Virgin Mary and the bishops of Constance Conrad and Gebhard.

Through its scholarly foundation the archdiocese runs 17 comprehensive secondary schools, six Realschulen, one primary school, one technical school for elderly care, one vocational college and two boarding schools. It keeps a priestly seminary in Freiburg, the Collegium Borromaeum, where candidates live during their theological studies at the Albert-Ludwigs University, and pastoral training takes place at a seminary in St. Peter. In 2005 the archbishop issued Pastoral Guidelines for the first time in its history, under the title Shaping the awakening, and the archdiocese uses unions of pastoral guidance in place of parish consolidation.
archduke-franz-ferdinand-of-austria: Franz Ferdinand was born in Graz on 18 December 1863, the eldest son of Archduke Karl Ludwig, the younger brother of Emperor Franz Joseph I, and of his second wife, Princess Maria Annunziata of Bourbon-Two Sicilies. In 1875, when he was eleven, his cousin Francis V, Duke of Modena, died and named him his heir on condition that he add the name Este to his own. The inheritance made him one of the wealthiest men in Austria.

In 1889 Crown Prince Rudolf committed suicide at Mayerling, which left Karl Ludwig first in line to the throne. When Karl Ludwig died of typhoid fever in 1896, Franz Ferdinand became heir presumptive. Between 1892 and 1893 he travelled round the world, visiting India, Australia, Japan and the United States. He was an excessive trophy hunter, even by the standards of European nobility; his diaries record 272,511 game kills, and about 100,000 trophies were displayed at his Bohemian castle at Konopiště.

Like most males in the ruling Habsburg line, he entered the army young, and was promoted rapidly: lieutenant at fourteen, captain at twenty-two, colonel at twenty-seven and major general at thirty-one. He never received formal staff training but briefly led the largely Hungarian 9th Hussar Regiment. In 1898 he was commissioned to inquire into all aspects of the military services, and in 1913 he was appointed inspector general of the Austro-Hungarian Armed Forces. He received the rank of admiral in 1902. His relations with Franz Joseph were tense. His courtship of Sophie Chotek, a lady-in-waiting, caused conflict in the imperial household, and their morganatic marriage in 1900 was allowed only after he renounced his descendants' rights to the throne.

Historians disagree on how to characterize his politics: some attribute generally liberal views on the empire's nationalities, others stress his dynastic centralism and Catholic conservatism. He advocated greater autonomy for the Czechs in Bohemia and the south Slavic peoples in Croatia and Bosnia, who had been left out of the Compromise of 1867, but felt antipathy towards the Hungarians, whose nationalism he saw as a threat to the dynasty. He urged caution towards Serbia and clashed with Franz Conrad von Hötzendorf, the Chief of the General Staff, warning that harsh treatment of Serbia would bring conflict with Russia and ruin both empires.

On 28 June 1914 Franz Ferdinand and his wife were assassinated in Sarajevo by Gavrilo Princip, aged nineteen, a member of Young Bosnia. The killing led to the July Crisis and to Austria-Hungary's declaration of war against Serbia. Four weeks after his death the allies of Austria-Hungary and the allies of Serbia declared war on each other, which began the First World War. His assassination is regarded as the most immediate cause of the war.
archduke-john-of-austria: John was born at Florence on 20 January 1782, the thirteenth child of Grand Duke Leopold I of Tuscany and Maria Luisa of Spain. In 1790 Leopold succeeded his brother Joseph II as Holy Roman Emperor and the family moved to the imperial court in Vienna; two years later John's elder brother Francis II took the throne. The Swiss historian Johannes von Müller educated him, and he developed wide interests, above all in the history and geography of the Alpine countries.

John was given command of the Austrian army in September 1800, at 18 and reluctantly. His troops were crushed at the Battle of Hohenlinden on 3 December, and an armistice on 22 December stopped a retreat in which the army nearly disintegrated.

In 1809 he commanded the Army of Inner Austria in Italy, won at Sacile on 16 April, but was forced back after the Austrian defeat at Eckmühl, was beaten at the Piave on 8 May and at Raab on 14 June, and reached Wagram too late. His brother Archduke Charles criticised his tardiness.

He then retired to his estates and turned to nature, technology and agriculture. In Styria he founded the Joanneum Museum in Graz in 1811, the Styrian State Archive in 1817 and the Styrian Society for Agriculture in 1819, and he is remembered there as a modernizer who wore the local Steireranzug. In 1829 he married Anna Plochl, daughter of the postmaster of Aussee; the marriage was morganatic and excluded him from the succession.

On 16 June 1848, after riots in Vienna drove the imperial household to Innsbruck, John was appointed effective viceroy in the emperor's absence. On 29 June 1848 the Frankfurt Parliament elected him regent of the realm (Reichsverweser), and he accepted on 5 July. Reputed to favour German unity from a toast at Brühl in 1842, whose wording newspapers had altered, he was widely acceptable, although he did not consider himself a liberal.

His office gave him little scope, and he was forbidden to take part in drafting the Frankfurt Constitution, adopted on 28 March 1849. When Frederick William IV of Prussia rejected it in April 1849, John remained passive. The assembly shrank to a rump, and he was allowed to resign on 20 December 1849. He was elected the first mayor of Stainz on 23 July 1850 and held the post until 1858. He died at Graz on 11 May 1859 and is buried at Schenna near Meran.
archelaus-i-of-macedon: Archelaus was the son of Perdiccas II and his wife Simache, who is thought to have been once enslaved by Archelaus' uncle, Alcetas. Plato, through his interlocutors in the Gorgias, wrote that Archelaus murdered both his uncle Alcetas and his unnamed seven-year-old half-brother to gain the throne, but this cannot be confirmed. Aristotle reports that he gave his eldest daughter to the king of Elimea during a war against the Lyncestae. His son Orestes later became king.

Soon after taking power Archelaus was able to reverse Macedon's relationship with Athens, which had been a major threat for half a century. After the Athenian defeat at Syracuse in late 413 BCE destroyed most of their ships, Athens needed a large amount of timber, and Archelaus, in a position to set the price, supplied it generously. The Athenians honoured him and his children with the titles of proxenos and euergetes.

He issued an abundance of good quality coinage, built strongholds, cut straight roads, important for moving the army, and improved the organisation of the cavalry and the hoplite infantry. Thucydides credited him with doing more for his kingdom's military infrastructure than all his predecessors together.

In his new palace at Pella, to which he moved the capital from Aegae, he hosted poets and tragedians, among them Agathon and Euripides, who wrote Archelaus and The Bacchae while in Macedon, and the painter Zeuxis. He reorganised the Olympia at Dion, a festival of musical and athletic competitions honouring Olympian Zeus and the Muses.

According to Aelian, Archelaus was killed in 399 BCE during a hunt by one of the royal pages, Crateuas. Constantine Paparrigopoulos names three accomplices, among them Decamnichos, who had insulted Euripides in front of the king, was flogged in punishment with Archelaus' permission, and remained at court. Other sources give other versions of the king's death.
archelaus-of-cappadocia: Archelaus, whose full name was Archelaus Sisines, was a Cappadocian Greek nobleman. He was the first-born son of the Roman client ruler and high priest Archelaus of Comana, who served the goddess Bellona, and of Glaphyra, a hetaera who was famed in antiquity for her beauty. His grandfather, also named Archelaus, was the first of the family to hold the priesthood and rule at Comana and claimed descent from King Mithridates VI of Pontus. In 47 BCE Julius Caesar deposed his father and replaced him with Lycomedes. Glaphyra later became a mistress of Mark Antony.

Antony deposed and then executed the reigning king, Ariarathes X, in 36 BCE and installed Archelaus. Glaphyra had induced Antony to do so through their affair, and she appeared to hold great power at the royal court. Archelaus supported Antony until Actium in 31 BCE, where he went over to Octavian, and by making peace he kept his crown. Augustus regarded him as loyal. In 25 BCE Augustus gave him Cilicia Trachea, including the harbour city of Elaiussa Sebaste, parts of the Cilician coast and Armenia Minor, which helped suppress piracy and strengthened the border against Parthia.

Archelaus moved his palace to Elaiussa Sebaste, built a royal residence and a palace on the island in the harbour, and renamed the city Sebaste in honour of Augustus. He also renamed the village of Garsaura as Archelaïs and made it an administrative centre.

He wrote a geographical work and a treatise, On Stones and Rivers. He had two children by his first wife, an Armenian princess who died by 8 BCE: a daughter, Glaphyra, who married Prince Alexander of Judea in 18 or 17 BCE, and a son, Archelaus of Cilicia. He acted as a mediator in the Herodian family. In 8 BCE he married Pythodorida of Pontus, a union that doubtless Augustus arranged to bind together the royal houses of Anatolia. They had no children.

The Romans liked Archelaus, but he had less success with his subjects. Some citizens of Cappadocia accused him in Rome during Augustus's reign, and Tiberius, then at the start of his civil career, successfully defended him. Archelaus later paid more attention to Gaius Caesar, which aroused Tiberius's jealousy. When Tiberius became emperor in 14 CE, Archelaus's health had failed. By 17 CE he had reigned for fifty years.

That year there was a shortage of funds for military pay, and Tiberius wanted to turn Cappadocia into a province. He enticed Archelaus to Rome, where the Senate accused him of plotting a revolution. Archelaus died of natural causes before he could be condemned, though Tacitus leaves open that it may have been suicide. Cappadocia became a Roman province, and Armenia Minor went to his stepson Artaxias III.
archilochus: Archilochus was an iambic poet of the Archaic period from the island of Paros, dated by modern scholars to about 680 to 640 BCE. The biographical tradition is generally unreliable, and the fragmentary poems do not support firm inferences about his life. Aristotle records that Archilochus sometimes spoke in the voice of other people, as in a fragment in which a carpenter named Charon expresses indifference to the wealth of Gyges, king of Lydia. Such fragments help to date him, since Gyges reigned 687 to 652 BCE.

According to tradition he was born to a notable family on Paros. His father Telesicles founded a Parian colony on Thasos, and some modern scholars infer that the poet was born into a priestly family devoted to Demeter. There is no evidence for isolated reports that his mother was a slave or that he fought as a mercenary.

The ancient tradition names a Parian, Lycambes, and his daughters as the main targets of his anger. Lycambes is said to have betrothed his daughter Neobule to Archilochus and then reneged, whereupon the poet's abuse drove them to suicide. Some modern scholars believe they were fictional characters in a traditional entertainment.

Archilochus joined the Parian colony on Thasos and fought the indigenous Thracians. Later he returned to Paros and joined the fight against the neighbouring island of Naxos, where a Naxian warrior named Calondas killed him. A sanctuary to the poet, the Archilocheion, was established on Paros in the third century BCE, and his hero cult lasted there over 800 years.

Ancient scholars credited him with the invention of elegy and iambic poetry, though he probably built on a popular song tradition that predated Homer. He wrote in a wide range of metres and subjects. He is the earliest known Greek author to compose almost entirely on the theme of his own emotions and experiences. His works include a hymn to Heracles with which victors were hailed at the Olympic Games, and an elegy in which he says he threw away his shield to save himself.

Ancient opinion was divided. Critics condemned his abusive and obscene verse, and according to Valerius Maximus the Spartans banished his works for the sake of their children's morals. About three hundred fragments survive, half of them too short or damaged to show their context. His line that a fox knows many things but a hedgehog one big thing inspired Isaiah Berlin's essay The Hedgehog and the Fox.
archimedes: The details of Archimedes's life are obscure. Because John Tzetzes states that he lived 75 years before his death in 212 BCE, he is estimated to have been born around 287 BCE in the seaport of Syracuse, Sicily. In the Sand-Reckoner he gives his father's name as Phidias, an astronomer. Plutarch wrote that he was related to King Hiero II of Syracuse, while Cicero and Silius Italicus suggest humble origins. His works, addressed to Dositheus of Pelusium and to Eratosthenes of Cyrene, suggest that he kept up relations with scholars in Alexandria.

In Measurement of a Circle he used the method of exhaustion to show that a circle has the same area as a right triangle whose base and height equal its radius and circumference, and he bounded pi by polygons of 96 sides, finding it between 3 10/71 and 3 1/7. In Quadrature of the Parabola he proved that the area enclosed by a parabola and a straight line is 4/3 of that of a corresponding inscribed triangle. In On the Equilibrium of Planes he proves the law of the lever.

Archimedes died during the siege of Syracuse, killed by a Roman soldier despite orders that he should not be harmed. Cicero describes visiting his tomb, surmounted by a sphere and a cylinder that he had asked to have placed there. His mathematical writings were little known in antiquity. The first comprehensive compilation was made around 530 CE by Isidore of Miletus in Constantinople, and his work was later translated into Arabic and then into Latin. The first printed edition appeared at Basel in 1544.
archytas: Archytas was born in Tarentum, a Greek city in southern Italy that was part of Magna Graecia, the son of Hestiaeus. He was presumably taught by Philolaus and was affiliated with the Pythagorean school. He taught mathematics to Eudoxus of Cnidus and to Eudoxus's student Menaechmus. As a Pythagorean he believed that arithmetic, rather than geometry, provided the basis for satisfactory proofs, and he developed what was the best-known argument for the infinity of the universe in antiquity.

Archytas appears to have been the dominant political and military figure in Tarentum in his generation, somewhat comparable to Pericles in Athens half a century earlier. The Tarentines elected him strategos, or general, seven years in a row, which meant breaking their own rule against successive appointments. He was allegedly undefeated as a general. The Seventh Letter, traditionally attributed to Plato, asserts that Archytas tried to rescue Plato during his difficulties with Dionysius II of Syracuse, and some scholars argue that he was one model for Plato's philosopher king.

Archytas is said to be the first Greek to speak of arithmetic, geometry, astronomy and harmonics as kindred sciences, a grouping that became the medieval quadrivium. Only four fragments of his many works are generally believed authentic. According to Eutocius, he was the first to solve the problem of doubling the cube, with a geometric construction that used lines generated by moving figures. In music theory he named the harmonic mean, and Ptolemy considered him the most sophisticated Pythagorean music theorist.

Later tradition regarded him as the founder of mathematical mechanics and credited him with inventing the baby rattle, the ratchet, the screw and the pulley. A story that he built a wooden flying dove is recorded only five centuries later, by Aulus Gellius, who reports it with scepticism. A lunar crater and an asteroid are named after him.
arcos-de-la-frontera: Arcos de la Frontera lies about 64 kilometres north-east of Cádiz and 35 kilometres east-north-east of Jerez de la Frontera, on the right bank of the Guadalete. Part of the old town sits inside a sharp loop of the river, which runs at the foot of high vertical cliffs. The town stands on a sandstone ridge on the last western spurs of the Subbetic chain, a position that gave it a commanding view of the Guadalete valley and made it a strong point for defence. The name goes back to the Roman Arx-Arcis, a fortress on high ground, which became Medina Arkos under Muslim rule.

A hoard of 28 gold solidi found in 1969 on a farmstead in the municipality, none later than 408 CE, was probably hidden after the Suebes, Vandals and Alans crossed the Pyrenees in 409. A Visigothic necropolis of the 6th century lies at Sanlucareño. Under Muslim rule the town sided with the emir Abd al-Rahman I in the 8th century, and at the end of the 9th century its rebel castle was among those assaulted by the troops of the emir Abd Allah.

Arcos became an independent taifa in 1011, during the collapse of the Caliphate of Córdoba, under a Berber family of the Zenata who had been brought to al-Andalus by Almanzor. They moved their capital there from Calcena because the fortress was a firmer defensive position. In 1053 Emir al-Mutadid of Seville took the town and its taifa from a Berber chief. The Almoravid dynasty overtook the region in 1091, and in 1190 the Almohad caliph Yaʿḳūb al-Manṣūr gathered his troops at Arcos for his campaign against Portugal.

Ferdinand III of Castile took possession of Arcos in 1250. Its Muslim inhabitants rose in revolt the next year and were brought to submission in 1264 by Alfonso X. Afterwards the town lay on the border with the Emirate of Granada: in 1339 Abu Malik, son of the Marinid emir Abu al-Hasan, was ambushed and killed near Arcos, and Granada's raiders pressed on its lands until 1452. The constant state of war gave the town the second part of its name.

Arcos is a town and municipality in the Sierra de Cádiz, in the province of Cádiz in Andalusia. Its historic centre was declared a Historic-Artistic Monument in 1962. Among its buildings are a castle of Moorish origin rebuilt in the 15th century and the Basilica of Santa María de la Asunción, raised after the Christian conquest on a Visigothic temple and the remains of a mosque, with Gothic, Renaissance and Baroque features.
arctic-ocean: The Arctic Ocean is the smallest and shallowest of the world's five oceanic divisions, with an area of approximately 14,060,000 km2, and the coldest of them. The International Hydrographic Organization recognizes it as an ocean, although some oceanographers call it the Arctic Mediterranean Sea or North Polar Sea. It includes the North Pole region and extends south to about 60°N, surrounded by Eurasia and North America. Its borders follow topographic features: the Bering Strait on the Pacific side and the Greenland Scotland Ridge on the Atlantic side.

The ocean occupies a roughly circular basin, almost the size of Antarctica, with a coastline 45,390 km long. It is partially covered by sea ice throughout the year and almost completely in winter. Its salinity is the lowest on average of the five oceans, owing to low evaporation, heavy fresh water inflow from rivers and limited connection to saltier waters. It joins the Pacific through the Bering Strait and the Atlantic through the Greenland Sea and Labrador Sea. Its largest seas include the Barents Sea at 1.4 million km2, the Greenland Sea, the East Siberian Sea and the Kara Sea.

Human habitation in the North American polar region goes back at least 17,000 to 50,000 years, to the Wisconsin glaciation, when falling sea levels let people cross the Bering land bridge from Siberia to Alaska. Early Paleo-Eskimo groups included the Pre-Dorset (c. 3200-850 BCE), the Saqqaq culture of Greenland (2500-800 BCE) and the Independence I and II cultures. The Dorset culture spread across Arctic North America between 500 BCE and 1500 CE. The Thule people, who arose around the Bering Strait from about 200 BCE and spread across almost the whole North American Arctic, were the ancestors of the Inuit.

For much of European history the north polar regions remained largely unexplored and their geography conjectural. Pytheas of Massilia recorded a journey northward in 325 BCE to a land he called Eschate Thule, where the Sun set for only three hours a day and the water was replaced by a congealed substance. He was probably describing loose sea ice. Early cartographers were unsure how to draw the pole: Johannes Ruysch's map of 1507 and Gerardus Mercator's of 1595 included land, while Martin Waldseemüller's world map of 1507 showed only water. Expeditions added small islands such as Novaya Zemlya and Spitzbergen, and from the late 16th to the early 20th century they became more common, often in search of trade routes from Europe to the Pacific.
ardabil: Ardabil lies on the Baliqly Chay River at an average altitude of 1,263 metres, about 70 kilometres from the Caspian Sea and 210 kilometres from Tabriz, on an open plain just east of Mount Sabalan, where cold spells last until late spring. According to one source the name comes from the Avestan artavil, "holy place"; Vladimir Minorsky derives it from arta, "sacred law", and vēt, "willow". The city is known for silk and carpets, and the ancient Ardabil carpets are counted among the best of classical Persian carpets.

Its pre-Islamic history is vague. Muslim historians credit the Sasanian king Peroz I, who reigned from 459 to 484, with its foundation. During the Arab conquest the local marzban agreed to surrender on condition that the people keep their observances at the fire temple of Shiz. Near the Caucasus, the town was open to attack. In 730 to 731 the Khazars defeated and killed the Arab governor of Armenia on the plain outside it and captured it. In 1209 forces from Georgia plundered it, reportedly killing 12,000 residents, and in 1220 the Mongols sacked it, though it recovered. Ismail I, born in Ardabil, began his campaign to unify Iran there, but in 1501 named Tabriz his capital.

Near the frontier, Ardabil was often sacked by the Ottomans between 1514 and 1722. In the early Qajar period the Napoleonic general Gardane fortified it on the order of Abbas Mirza, and Russian troops stormed the ramparts in 1826 to 1828. The town's noted library was taken to St Petersburg by General Ivan Paskevich with a promise of return that was never kept. After the Treaty of Turkmenchay in 1828 the town lay only 40 kilometres from the new border and became a stop on a major caravan route for European goods entering Iran.

Ardabil is the capital of its province. The shrine of Shaykh Safi al-Din, who died in 1334, stands there with the tomb of Ismail I, and the shrine ensemble is a UNESCO World Heritage Site. The Safavids promoted it as a place of pilgrimage. In the late 1530s Shah Tahmasp enlarged it, and a pair of carpets was made, one dated 946 of the Muslim calendar, 1539 to 1540, and signed by Maqsud Kashani. The larger carpet was bought by a London museum in 1893. Most of the bazaar was built or renovated in the Safavid and Zand periods.
ardahan: Ardahan lies in north-eastern Turkey near the border with Georgia, on the upper course of the Kura river and south of the Yalnızçam Mountains. The climate is humid continental, with brief, mild summers and very cold winters. Snow cover lasts from late October to mid April. In the 1640s the Ottoman traveller Evliya Çelebi described the fortress as sitting on an inaccessible cliff, with no gardens or orchards because of the cold.

Ardahan lay in the region of Gogarene, which Strabo calls part of an Armenia taken from the Kingdom of Iberia. In the Middle Ages it was a transit point for goods from the Abbasid Caliphate to the Black Sea region. From the 8th to 10th centuries Bagrationi princes of Tao-Klarjeti held it as Artaani, and it was part of the Kingdom of Georgia from the 11th to the 15th century. The Mongols took it in the 1230s, and the Georgian princes of Samtskhe recaptured it in 1266. By the Peace of Amasya in 1555 the Ottoman Empire annexed the western part of Samtskhe, and Ardahan became a formidable fortress-town.

Russia took the town after the Russo-Turkish War of 1877 to 1878. Its people were mostly Armenians, with Georgians, Pontic Greeks, Caucasus Jews, Russians, Kurds and others, and it prospered, exporting fruit, smoked lamb, wheat and wood. On 25 December 1914 the Ottoman army occupied it and massacred many Armenians, Pontic Greeks and Georgians; the Russians retook it on 3 January 1915. The Ottoman army regained it on 6 March 1918, the Democratic Republic of Georgia occupied it on 20 April 1919, and Turkish Nationalists took it on 23 February 1921, after which the remaining Armenians, Pontic Greeks and Georgians fled. A treaty then confirmed it as Turkish.

Ardahan is the seat of Ardahan Province and Ardahan District, a province it became in 1992 by separating from Kars. Its population was 22,927 in 2021, against 7,228 in 1960, when Kurds and Turks lived there. The walls of the fortress, Ardahan Kalesi, are of late antique or medieval origin and were rebuilt several times; in the 19th century they were adapted for small cannons.
ardashir-i: Accounts of Ardashir's ancestry differ. According to al-Tabari, he was the son of Papak, son of Sasan, and was born in a village near Istakhr in Pars, his grandfather Sasan being the trustee of the Temple of Anahita there. Another narrative, in the Shahnameh, makes him the child of Sasan, a descendant of Darius III, and the daughter of Papak, a local governor in Pars. A modern scholar, Daryaee, reads these claims as Ardashir tracing his lineage to whomever he could.

Al-Tabari reports that at the age of seven Ardashir was sent to the commander of Fort Darabgard, and on his death succeeded him there. When Papak and his son Shapur died, Ardashir became ruler of Pars.

Ardashir faced the army of Artabanus IV on the Hormozdgan plain, where the Parthian king was defeated and killed. W. B. Henning dates the battle and Ardashir's coronation to 28 April 224, but H. Taqizadeh calculates 6 April 227, and Josef Wiesehöfer places the coronation at Ctesiphon in 226. Ardashir took the title King of Kings and called his realm Ērānšahr, the realm of the Iranians.

Around 230 Persian forces attacked Roman territory in northern Mesopotamia and Ardashir besieged Nusaybin without taking it. The Roman emperor Severus Alexander campaigned against the Persians in 232, with some Roman victories in Armenia but nothing achieved in the south. His son Shapur probably became a royal partner on 12 April 240, probably so that Ardashir, who had other sons, could settle the succession without trouble.

Ardashir presented himself as a worshipper of Mazda and a descendant of the gods, and claimed to continue the Achaemenids, though the current belief is that the early Sasanians knew little of their history. He commemorated his victories with rock reliefs at Firuzabad, Naqsh-e Rajab and Naqsh-e Rustam. The name Iran, formerly a religious and ethnic term, was chosen for the region under Sasanian rule.

He founded the city of Ardashir-Khwarrah, later called Firuzabad, beside his former palace. Arabic and Persian literature attribute to him a testament of political advice for later kings, though its original Middle Persian text is lost and the surviving versions are Arabic translations.
ardeche: The department covers 5,550 square kilometres and is a land of great contrasts. It lies between 40 metres above sea level, where the Ardèche river flows into the Rhône, and 1,754 metres at Mont Mézenc. The Rhône valley borders it on the east for 140 km and the high plateaus of the Massif Central on the west. Its prefecture, Privas, is 140 km from Lyon, and the department's mountainous relief makes travel between its parts difficult, especially in winter. It has five natural regions: the western mountains, where the Loire has its source, the plateaus of the Haut-Vivarais and the Cévennes, the limestone Bas-Vivarais with its almost Mediterranean climate, the basalt plateau of the Coirons and the Rhône valley.

Humans have lived in the area since at least the Upper Paleolithic, as the cave paintings at Chauvet Pont d'Arc attest, and dolmens and menhirs stand on the river's plateau. The Vivarais takes its name from Viviers, capital of the Gaulish Helvii, and Auxonius moved the bishop's seat there in 430. Raids by Hungarians and Saracen slavers in the 9th century depopulated the region. It was part of the Kingdom of Burgundy-Arles, formed in 933, and was left to the emperor by its last king in 1032; it passed to the French crown in 1229, and by the treaty of 10 July 1305 Philip IV obliged the bishops of Vivarais to admit the sovereignty of the French king.

The Vivarais became a Protestant stronghold after Calvin's reformation, with over 75 Protestant churches by 1598 and eight pitched battles between 1562 and 1595. In 1629 Privas was burned to the ground by the forces of Louis XIII, and one fifth of the Protestant population emigrated. The Revocation of the Edict of Nantes in 1685 led to the Camisard revolt and to dragonnades by Louis XIV's dragoons; peace came only in 1715, and another 50,000 Protestants fled France. On 4 June 1783 the Montgolfier brothers, sons of a paper-maker, made the first hot air balloon ascent over Annonay.

The Ardèche was one of the 83 departments created on 4 March 1790. Its population rose from 273,000 in 1793 to 388,500 in 1861, a peak not since matched, while the silkworm industry collapsed after disease struck in 1855. The last blast furnace closed at Pouzain in 1929.

The department has 334,231 inhabitants, called Ardéchois. Its prefecture is Privas, and its largest city is Annonay. Rivers and gorges draw canoeists and kayakers, and the department holds part of the Cévennes National Park. The Ardèche chestnut, the châtaigne d'Ardèche, received appellation d'origine contrôlée status in 2006.
ardennes: The Ardennes is a natural region of extensive forests, rough terrain, rolling hills and ridges, lying mainly in Belgium and Luxembourg and extending into Germany and France. Its rocks are the remnants of a mountain range formed during the Hercynian orogeny, and the coal, iron and zinc beneath its low interior explain much of the geography and history of Wallonia. Hills average 350 to 400 metres and rise to 694 metres at the Signal de Botrange, and swift rivers, above all the Meuse, have cut steep valleys. The name comes from the ancient forest called Arduenna Silva in the Roman period.

In 881 and 882 Viking raiders used the old Roman roads of the Ardennes to attack the abbeys of Malmedy and Stavelot and to destroy Prüm Abbey in the Eifel. Much of the region belonged to the Duchy of Luxembourg, a state of the Holy Roman Empire. Revolutionary France annexed it in 1793, and the Congress of Vienna in 1815 restored most of it to the Grand Duchy of Luxembourg. In 1839 the Grand Duchy ceded its westernmost 63 per cent, including most of the Ardennes, to the new Kingdom of Belgium, where it is now Luxembourg Province.
Charcoal from the forests fuelled early furnaces, and after coal replaced it Wallonia became the second industrial power of the world after Great Britain, in proportion to its size and population.

Strategists judged the Ardennes unsuitable for large operations, yet Germany gambled on a rapid passage through it in both world wars. In 1940 German planners chose the forest as the route of their armour into France, since its size could conceal the divisions and the French thought an army would need at least 15 days to cross. The Germans did it in two days, and under General Heinz Guderian crossed the Meuse at Dinant and Sedan. France fell on 25 June 1940. In December 1944 the Germans launched a surprise attack there, the Battle of the Bulge, aiming to retake Antwerp; it was halted at the Meuse at Dinant.

The Ardennes is thinly settled. Its most populous cities, Verviers in Belgium and Charleville-Mézières in France, each exceed 50,000 inhabitants, and few other towns exceed 10,000. The terrain and climate limit agriculture, and the forests are rich in timber and game.
ardnamurchan: Ardnamurchan, in Scottish Gaelic Àird nam Murchan, is a peninsula of about 130 square kilometres, strictly the land beyond the villages of Salen in the south and Acharacle in the north, though the name is also used for the neighbouring districts of Sunart, Ardgour, Morvern and Moidart. Its main road is a single track for much of its length. A 36-metre lighthouse stands on Ardnamurchan Point. The north-western corner of the peninsula is an exposed lopolith, an intrusion of ancient magma whose rings show on satellite photographs and which draws university geology courses.

Adomnán of Iona records Saint Columba visiting the peninsula in the 6th century, when it seems to have been settled by Irish Gaels, and tells of three signs he performed there. The historian Donaldson identified Bourblaige, east of Kilchoan, with Muribulg, where the Annals of Tigernach record a battle between the Picts and the Dalriads in 731. Weapons and a coin of the reign of Edward I of England found at Cul na Croise may mark fighting between Alasdair Óg Mac Domhnaill and the brothers Lachlann and Ruaidhrí Mac Ruaidhrí.
