In 2011 a Viking ship burial, probably of the 10th century, was found at Port an Eilean Mhòir: a warrior buried with an axe, a sword with a decorated hilt, a spear, a shield boss, a whetstone from Norway and a ring pin from Ireland. The Clan MacDonald of Ardnamurchan held the area from the 1300s until 1618, when the Clan Campbell took control. Bourblaige was destroyed in the Highland Clearances of the early 19th century, which Dr John MacLachlan attacked in his poem Dìreadh a-mach ri Beinn Shianta.

About 2,000 people live on the peninsula, once part of the county of Argyll and now in the Lochaber ward management area of the Highland council. It has one of the highest shares of Scottish Gaelic speakers on the mainland and holds an annual Mòd. Its northern part lies in the Morar, Moidart and Ardnamurchan National Scenic Area.
arduin-of-ivrea: Arduin was born around 955 at Pombia, the son of Dado, Count of Pombia, a nephew of King Berengar II. When the German king Otto the Great conquered Italy in 961 and deposed Berengar, Arduin was still a boy. Northern Italy was then divided between bishops appointed by the emperor to rule the largest fiefs and minor nobles who held small rural fiefs. Arduin married Bertha, often said to be a daughter of Otbert II, Margrave of Milan, and from their three sons descended the later counts of Ivrea.

Arduin succeeded his kinsman Conrad in the March of Ivrea in 990. He backed the monastic orders and the minor nobles against the bishops. In 997, after Emperor Otto III granted the fief of Caresana to Pietro, Bishop of Vercelli, riots broke out in Vercelli in which the bishop was killed, and the cathedral where he lay was burned while Arduin intervened. Bishop Warmund of Ivrea excommunicated him, and in 1000 Pope Sylvester II confirmed the sentence and demanded that he abdicate in favour of his son. Arduin refused, expelled Warmund from Ivrea and took Vercelli and Novara.

After Otto III died on 23 January 1002, a diet in Pavia acclaimed Arduin king on 15 February, and he was crowned in the Basilica of San Michele Maggiore. The bishops, led by Frederick, Archbishop of Ravenna, opposed him. In the spring of 1003 he defeated Duke Otto I of Carinthia at Fabrica near the Brenta. In 1004 Henry II came south himself, was crowned in Pavia on 14 May and burned the city.

Arduin withdrew to the Orco Valley and later regained his former lands, though scholars now hold that many diplomas in his name are forgeries and that his power was limited to a small part of Italy. His coins, minted at Pavia, imitated those of Otto III. He died at the Abbey of Fruttuaria, which he had founded in 1003, on 14 December 1015.
ardys-of-lydia: Ardys was the son of Gyges of Lydia, whom he succeeded as the second king of the Mermnad dynasty. His name is the Latin form of Ardus, itself the Hellenised form of a Lydian name that was a cognate of either the Hittite bird-name ardus or the Hittite word for descendant, ḫardu-. In the 7th century BCE the Cimmerians, a nomadic people from the Eurasian Steppe who had invaded Western Asia, attacked Lydia several times, but Gyges repelled them. In 644 BCE they attacked a third time, led by their king Lygdamis. The Lydians were defeated, Sardis was sacked and Gyges was killed, and Ardys became king.

On taking the throne Ardys resumed the diplomatic activity with the Neo-Assyrian Empire that Gyges had ended. He attacked the Ionian Greek city of Miletus and captured Priene, which remained under the direct rule of the Lydian kingdom until its end. His reign fell in a period of severe crisis, caused by the Cimmerian invasions. In his seventh regnal year the Thracian Treres, who had migrated across the Thracian Bosporus and invaded Anatolia under their king Kobos, attacked Lydia in alliance with the Cimmerians and the Lycians. They defeated the Lydians again and for a second time sacked the capital, Sardis, except for its citadel.

Ardys's son Sadyattes succeeded him. Afterwards, with Assyrian approval and in alliance with the Lydians, the Scythians under their king Madyes entered Anatolia, expelled the Treres from Asia Minor and defeated the Cimmerians, who never again posed a threat. The Scythians then extended their domination to central Anatolia until the Medes expelled them from Western Asia. Strabo credits Madyes with expelling the Treres and Cimmerians. The final defeat of the Cimmerians was the work of Madyes and of Alyattes of Lydia, the son of Sadyattes and grandson of Ardys, whom Herodotus of Halicarnassus and Polyaenus claim finally defeated them.
arechis-ii-of-benevento: Arechis was born around 734, a descendant of the Lombards who had invaded Italy in the late 6th century. Their kingdom had its capital at Pavia and included two southern duchies, Spoleto and Benevento. He was the son of Duke Liutprand, whom he succeeded in 758. Around 757 he married Adelperga, a daughter of the Lombard king Desiderius, and kept friendly but largely independent relations with his father-in-law until Desiderius was deposed in 774. The couple had five children, three boys and two girls.

Arechis refused to submit when Charlemagne made himself king of the Lombards in 774, and Benevento was left largely alone. Taking the title of prince and issuing laws, which only Lombard kings had done before, were probably gestures of defiance. In 776 he was probably involved in a Lombard conspiracy against the Franks centred on Friuli, but gave it little practical support. He fought the Byzantine duchy of Naples for territory, then, perhaps in the mid-780s, made a pactum with its duke on landholding and the settlement of disputes.

In 787 Charlemagne marched south and besieged Capua. Arechis withdrew to Salerno and, according to Einhard, sent his sons Rumold and Grimold with a great sum of money as hostages, promising obedience on condition that he need not appear in person. Charlemagne kept the younger son. The Beneventan mint began striking silver coins like the Frankish ones, and coins and charters added Charlemagne's name and title to those of Arechis. Frankish influence was short-lived: after the deaths of Arechis and his elder son, Grimoald III was released and soon resisted the Franks.

Arechis and Adelperga were notable patrons of culture. Adelperga commissioned Paul the Deacon's Historia Romana, a textbook of Roman history widely used through the Middle Ages, and some historians argue that the couple also commissioned his Historia gentis Langobardorum. Arechis moved saints' relics to the new church of Santa Sofia, which survives, heavily restored, with rare 8th-century frescoes. He built a palace and castle at Salerno, which grew into an important port, and endowed Montecassino and San Vincenzo al Volturno.
areopagus: The council took its name from the Areios Pagos, the Hill of Ares, north-west of the Acropolis. The war god Ares was supposed to have been tried there by the other gods for the murder of Poseidon's son Halirrhothius. The institution's exact origin is unclear. Before the 5th century BCE it may have been a council of elders restricted to those who had held high office as archon, or it may have begun almost wholly as a homicide court. Homicide trials seem to have been held on the hill as early as the 7th century BCE, and possibly from the mid-8th.

In 594 BCE Solon restructured the council along with the rest of the Athenian state. Aristotle suggests that he confirmed its competence over treason and its guardianship of the laws. Cleisthenes enlarged the Boule to 500 men in 508/507 BCE, and there is little evidence that he changed the Areopagus. In 462/461 BCE Ephialtes may have put through reforms that left it almost nothing but a murder tribunal, in favour of the Heliaia. Most ancient authors say so, but this may be a later retrojection, since little suggests the council had done anything to provoke an attack. Aeschylus's Eumenides of 458 BCE sets the trial of Orestes there.

In the second half of the 4th century BCE the court grew in political influence and joined the anti-Macedonian faction. In 324 BCE it investigated charges of treason and bribery against Demosthenes in the Harpalus affair. In Roman times it remained a body of former archons, and after Sulla's capture of Athens in 86/87 BCE it became one of the most prestigious institutions of the city. Cicero remarked that to say the Athenian state is ruled by the council, the words 'of the Areopagus' are omitted. It had ceased to operate as a political council by at least the early 5th century CE, according to Theodoret of Cyrus.

The apostle Paul's sermon at the Areopagus is told in Acts 17, leading to the conversion of Dionysius the Areopagite. It is unclear whether he spoke before the council in a judicial setting or informally on the hill, since the council probably no longer met there by then but in the agora or the Stoa Basileios. After the council closed, houses, and a church and monastery dedicated to Dionysius the Areopagite, stood on the hill under Byzantine rule. The name is also used for the higher court of modern Greece, and John Milton's defence of press freedom, Areopagitica, takes its title from it.
arequipa: Arequipa extends along both banks of the Chili River, in a valley bordered by the Andes to the north and east and by low coastal hills to the south and west. The valley is a geographical corridor between the desert and the highland puna. The city stands 2328 m above sea level, and from almost any point in it the volcanic cones of Misti, Chachani and Pichu Pichu can be seen. Its position at a continental crossroads, on the silver route in colonial times and the wool route after independence, helped it accumulate administrative, commercial and industrial functions.

Until shortly before the rise of the Inca Empire, the area held nomadic groups who hunted, fished and gathered, then domesticated camelids and began to farm. Irrigation canals were built in the Chili valley, and the Yarabaya and Chimba groups settled where the city now stands.

The Spanish laid out the city on 15 August 1540 on a plan of 49 blocks, each 400 Castilian feet on a side. On 25 September 1541 a real cédula of Charles V made it the City of Arequipa. In the viceregal period its population was largely Hispanic and white, proud of the titles granted by the king of Spain and willing to cooperate with the Crown. The first known official census, in 1796, counted 37,241 inhabitants in the central area, among them 22,207 Spaniards, 5,929 Indians and 1,710 enslaved people.

After independence Arequipa acted as a counterweight to centralized power in Lima, a second capital. It saw more than seven uprisings or revolutions between independence and 1850 and twice housed the national government: President Luis José de Orbegoso installed his there in 1835, and during the war with Chile President Lizardo Montero declared it the capital on 31 August 1882. UNESCO inscribed 332 hectares of the historic centre as a World Heritage Site in 2000. Most of its heritage buildings were built in the 19th century on the foundations of colonial ones destroyed by the earthquake of 1868, mainly of sillar, a white volcanic stone.
ares: The name Ares is attested in Mycenaean Greek as a-re, written in Linear B. It is traditionally connected with the Greek word arē, meaning bane, ruin or curse, and Walter Burkert notes that it is apparently an ancient abstract noun meaning the throng of battle, or war. R. S. P. Beekes has suggested a Pre-Greek origin. In the Classical period Ares is given the epithet Enyalios, which seems to appear on the Mycenaean tablet KN V 52; Enyalios was sometimes identified with Ares and sometimes treated as another war god with a separate cult, even in the same town.

In the archaic tradition of the Iliad and Odyssey Ares is one of the Twelve Olympians. Many Greeks were ambivalent towards him. He embodies the physical valour needed for success in war, but also sheer brutality and bloodlust. In the Iliad Zeus tells him that he is the most hateful of all the gods on Olympus, yet will not see him suffer long, since he is his child. When Ares appears in myths he typically faces humiliation; in one tale, Hephaestus catches him with Aphrodite in a nearly invisible net and exposes them to the ridicule of the other gods.

Ares plays a central part in the founding myth of Thebes, as the progenitor of the Ismenian dragon killed by Cadmus. The dragon's teeth, sown in the ground, produced the armoured Spartoi, and Cadmus served the god for eight years to atone, then married Harmonia, a daughter of Ares and Aphrodite.

Only a few places in mainland Greece are known to have had a formal temple and cult of Ares. Pausanias notes an altar to him at Olympia. The Areopagus, the mount of Ares in Athens, was supposedly where Ares was tried and acquitted for killing Halirrhothius, a son of Poseidon, and the court that met there took its name from it. At Sparta an archaic statue of Ares in chains stood in the temple of Enyalios, which Pausanias took to mean that the spirit of war and victory was to be kept in the city.

His Roman counterpart Mars was originally an agricultural deity, and as father of Romulus he became a guardian of the Roman state. Roman writers reinterpreted the myths of Ares under the name of Mars, and in later Western art and literature the two figures became almost indistinguishable.
aretas-iii: Aretas, in Nabataean Aramaic Ḥārītaṯ, came to the throne on the death of his brother, Obodas I, in 87 BCE. His name, rendered in Arabic as Al-Ḥāriṯ, comes from Harith, meaning the collector, provider, ploughman or cultivator. During his reign Nabataea reached its largest extent, covering what is now northern Jordan, southern Syria and part of Saudi Arabia.

Damascus lay on the main trade route from the Mediterranean to India and the Middle East. Aretas took it from the weakening Seleucid Empire, styled himself Aretas Philhellen, friend of the Greeks, and had the Damascus mint strike silver coins in Hellenic style with his name in Greek rather than Nabataean Aramaic. He also brought Greek and Roman architecture to Petra and to new settlements such as Humayma, which received an aqueduct of 26.8 km. The Armenian king Tigranes II besieged and took Damascus in 72 BCE, but Aretas retook it in 69 BCE when Tigranes withdrew to meet a Roman attack.

In 67 BCE Aristobulus II overthrew his brother Hyrcanus II in Judea. Hyrcanus fled to Petra, and Aretas agreed to back him once Antipater the Idumaean promised to return the Arabian towns the Hasmoneans had taken. Aretas besieged Jerusalem for several months with 50,000 men, until Aristobulus bribed Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, deputy of Pompey, who ordered Aretas to withdraw. On the way home the Nabataean army suffered a crushing defeat by Aristobulus.

In 62 BCE Scaurus marched on Petra, but rough terrain and short supplies led him to seek the help of Hyrcanus, now High Priest, who sent Antipater to negotiate. The siege was lifted in return for several hundred talents of silver paid to Scaurus himself and recognition of Roman supremacy. Aretas kept all Nabataean territory and possessions and became a vassal of the Roman Republic.
aretas-iv: Aretas's Nabataean title, Ḥārītaṯ Rāḥem-ʿammeh, means Aretas, lover of his people. Josephus says he was first named Aeneas and took Aretas as his throne name, and an inscription from Petra suggests he descended from Malichus I. He came to power abruptly in 9 BCE after the sudden death of Obodas II, without seeking the approval of the Roman Emperor Augustus. Syllaeus, the minister of Obodas, made unfounded accusations against him in Rome; his second mission failed too and ended in his execution in 6–5 BCE.

Augustus recognised Aretas only after great hesitation. As the most powerful neighbour of Judea, Aretas often took part in its affairs, and he sent troops to support the Syrian governor Varus against the unrest that followed the death of Herod the Great in 4 BCE. His court was known for its lack of ceremony: Strabo, recounting an anecdote of Athenodorus, wrote that the king rendered an account of his kingship in the popular assembly. His first wife Huldu, a daughter of Obodas II, appeared on his coins until 16 CE; he later married Shaqilath.

When his daughter Phasaelis learned that Herod Antipas meant to divorce her to marry Herodias, she fled to her father. Aretas invaded the domain of Antipas and defeated his army, helped by soldiers from the lands of Philip the Tetrarch; Antipas escaped only with Roman help. Emperor Tiberius sent Lucius Vitellius the Elder, governor of Syria, against Aretas, but the march was halted at Jerusalem in 37 CE when news of the emperor's death arrived.

The Apostle Paul wrote that he escaped from Damascus in a basket let down through a window in the wall to evade the ethnarch of King Aretas. Whether Aretas then controlled the city is disputed: much evidence speaks against Nabataean control before 37 CE, and some scholars think Paul meant the official of a Nabataean community in Damascus, while others propose a brief annexation after 37 CE. Aretas died in 40 CE and was succeeded by his son Malichus II and his daughter Shaqilath II.
arezzo: Livy described Arezzo, Aritim in Etruscan, as one of the Capita Etruriae, and it is believed to have been among the twelve leading Etruscan cities. Etruscan remains include walls, a necropolis on Poggio del Sole and two bronzes, the Chimera of Arezzo of the fifth century BCE and the Minerva of the fourth, found in the sixteenth century and taken to Florence. The Romans conquered the city in 311 BCE, and as Arretium it became a military station on the Via Cassia. Gaius Cilnius Maecenas came of old Etruscan stock from the town, and in the Augustan period it was the third-largest city of Italy, well known for its exported Arretine ware.

Arezzo became an episcopal seat in the third or fourth century. The Roman city was demolished partly in the Gothic War and the Lombard invasion of the late sixth century, and only the amphitheatre remained. The commune threw off the bishop's control in 1098 and was an independent city-state until 1384, generally Ghibelline and opposed to Guelph Florence. Its university, the Studium, was founded in 1252. After the rout at Campaldino in 1289 its fortunes ebbed, and it yielded to Florence in 1384.

Arezzo is the capital of its province, about 80 kilometres south-east of Florence, at 296 metres above sea level. The upper town, with the cathedral, the town hall and the Medici Fortress, keeps its medieval appearance, which the city's decline after the Florentine conquest preserved. The church of San Francesco holds frescoes by Piero della Francesca, among its best-known works, and the Basilica of San Domenico a crucifix by Cimabue. Giorgio Vasari, Guido of Arezzo and Guittone d'Arezzo were natives, and the Giostra del Saracino, a game of chivalry, dates from the Middle Ages. It joined the Kingdom of Italy in 1860 and was liberated on 16 July 1944.
arg-of-karim-khan: When Karim Khan established his government in Shiraz he was influenced by Safavid architecture. After visiting Naqsh-e Jahan Square in Isfahan, he decided to build a large square in northern Shiraz, known as the Artillery Square. Around it stood Divan Karim Khan Square to the north, the Vakil Bazaar and several inns to the east, the Vakil Bathhouse and Vakil Mosque to the south, a garden to the south-west and the citadel to the west.

The citadel is rectangular and resembles a medieval fortress. It covers 4,000 square metres at the centre of a compound of 12,800 square metres, with four high walls joined by four round brick towers of 14 metres. Each wall is 12 metres high, 3 metres thick at the base and 2.8 metres at the top. Its design combines military and residential architecture, since it was both Karim Khan's home and the military centre of the dynasty. In 1827 James Edward Alexander described it as surrounded by a deep wet ditch.

After Agha Mohammad Khan Qajar conquered Shiraz, he set out to demolish Karim Khan's buildings out of hostility to him, and several Zand era buildings were pulled down, among them the wall Karim Khan had built around the city. The citadel was spared and served as the seat of the governors of Fars appointed by the central government. At times it was also used as a prison. Today it stands on Shahrdari Square and is a museum run by Iran's Cultural Heritage Organization.
argead-dynasty: The dynasty, also called Temenid, had King Caranus as its mythical founder. Herodotus tells in The Histories that three brothers of the lineage of Temenus, named Gauanes, Aeropus and Perdiccas, fled from Argos to the Illyrians and then to a town called Lebaea in Upper Macedonia, where they served the king. Dismissed by him because of an omen that something great would happen to Perdiccas, they settled near the garden of Midas below Mount Bermio and slowly formed a kingdom of their own. A Greek inscription relating to the belief in descent from Heracles was found by Manolis Andronikos in the royal palace of Aigai, near modern Vergina.

According to Thucydides, in the History of the Peloponnesian War, the Argeads came down from the highlands to Lower Macedonia, expelled the Pierians from Pieria, gained a narrow strip along the river Axios reaching to Pella and the sea, and added Mygdonia by driving out the Edoni, Eordians and Almopians. Another theory, held by the Greek historian Miltiades Hatzopoulos following the ancient author Appian, is that the dynasty came from Argos Orestikon rather than from the Peloponnese, its people completing their wandering from Orestis to Lower Macedonia in the 7th century BCE.

The Argeads were at first rulers of the tribe of the same name, which prevailed in early Emathia, later Lower Macedonia, with its capital at Aigai. Herodotus relates that when Alexander I of Macedon entered the Olympic Games, in 504 or 500 BCE, other competitors objected that he was not Greek; the judges, the Hellanodikai, examined his Argead claim and allowed him to take part. By the time of Philip II of Macedon the kingdom, now governed from Pella, included all the states of Upper Macedonia.

The death of a king almost invariably set off disputes among members of the family, and often a war of succession. A six-year interregnum from 399 to 393 BCE followed the death of King Archelaus, and wars of succession followed the deaths of Pausanias, Amyntas III and Perdiccas III, the last of which brought Philip II to power in 360 to 359 BCE after he deposed Amyntas IV. An established king could also face rebellion by a relative, as Perdiccas II did from his brother Philip. Modern historians disagree on a number of details of the family's genealogy.
argentina: Argentina covers a mainland area of about 2,780,400 square kilometres in southern South America, sharing borders with Chile across the Andes, Bolivia, Paraguay, Brazil and Uruguay. The highest point is Aconcagua, in Mendoza province, at 6,959 metres above sea level, the highest in the Southern and Western Hemispheres. The maximum north–south distance is 3,694 kilometres. Its major rivers, among them the Paraná and the Uruguay, which join to form the Río de la Plata, discharge into the Argentine Sea over the Patagonian Shelf. It is one of the most biodiverse countries in the world, with 15 continental zones, 2 marine zones and the Antarctic region.
Humans inhabited the region as early as 21,000 years ago, and the Cueva de las Manos, in Santa Cruz, holds stencilled handprints and hunting scenes made between 7,300 BCE and 700 CE.

Before European colonisation Argentina was sparsely populated by diverse cultures: basic hunters and gatherers such as the Selkʼnam and Yahgan in the extreme south, more advanced hunters such as the Tehuelche, and farmers with pottery such as the Guaraní in the northeast and the Diaguita in the northwest, whom the Inca Empire conquered around 1480. Europeans first arrived with the 1502 voyage of Amerigo Vespucci. Pedro de Mendoza founded Buenos Aires in 1536, but it was abandoned in 1541, and Juan de Garay re-founded it in 1580.

Argentina rose as the successor state of the Viceroyalty of the Río de la Plata, founded in 1776. The Argentine War of Independence (1810–1825) and the Declaration of Independence of 9 July 1816 were followed by an extended civil war that lasted until 1880 and ended in reorganisation as a federation. The name Argentina comes from the Latin argentum, silver, after the silver mountains legend among early explorers. Later came relative peace and mass waves of millions of European immigrants, mainly Italians and Spaniards, who greatly influenced its culture and demography.

The National Autonomist Party dominated politics from 1880 until the 1916 elections. The first coup, in 1930, began the Infamous Decade, and between 1930 and 1976 the armed forces overthrew six governments. The final coup, in 1976, was followed by a military junta that persecuted and murdered thousands of political critics in the Dirty War, which lasted until Raúl Alfonsín was elected president in 1983. Argentina is a federal constitutional republic of twenty-three provinces and one autonomous city, Buenos Aires. The 2022 census counted 46,044,703 inhabitants, and 92% live in cities.
argentine-national-anthem: In mid-1812 the ruling triumvirate ordered the Buenos Aires Cabildo to commission a national anthem. A Franciscan friar, Cayetano Rodríguez, wrote a text approved on 4 August, and the Catalan musician Blas Parera set it to music and conducted the premiere at the theatre on 1 November. Less than a year later the Assembly of Year XIII judged the song not effective enough, since recent triumphs of the Buenos Aires army had made the text obsolete. On 6 March 1813 poets were invited to submit lyrics, and the poem of the lawyer Vicente López y Planes was unanimously judged the best.

The words were designated the sole national march on 11 May 1813. Parera finished a new setting in a few days and conducted the official premiere at the theatre on 28 May, receiving 200 pesos. He possibly expressed his dislike of the new nation by quoting a negative gesture, in minor mode with dissonant chords, from an anti-Napoleonic war song.

Juan Pedro Esnaola's arrangement of around 1848 first used the title Himno Nacional Argentino. The full text, which López christened the Anthem of May, is ardently pro-independence and anti-Spanish, and its vision is Latin American as well as Argentine; a lion lying defeated at the feet of a new nation is an allegory of Spain itself. One line is disputed: an early song-sheet says Buenos Aires opone, opposes, the front of the peoples of the union, while a corrected sheet of the same date has pone, positions itself at the front. The first reading has been seen as centralist, and also as a misprint.

The song became popular at once. Within ten years it was performed throughout Argentina and in Chile, Peru and Colombia, where it was used until those countries had anthems of their own. In 1860 Esnaola was commissioned to make an official revision, with a slower tempo and richer harmony. A committee's version of 1927 was rejected after a heated public debate, and Esnaola's edition was confirmed as the official anthem in 1944.

The text was sung complete through the 19th century. On 30 March 1900 President Julio Argentino Roca abridged it by decree, so that only the first and last verses and the chorus are sung at official festivals and in public schools, since Spanish immigrants now shared national life. No anti-Spanish text is sung today. The anthem is performed at official events and has an anniversary on 11 May.
arghun: Arghun was the son of Abaqa Khan and a concubine, Qaitmish Egeci, and was born on 8 March 1258 near Baylaqan, though Rashid al-Din gives 1262, which is thought unlikely. He grew up in Khorasan and at twenty commanded an army against the Negudaris. Like his father he was a Buddhist, though favourable to Christians.

After Abaqa died in 1282 Arghun was talked out of contesting the kurultai, and his uncle Ahmad Tekuder was chosen. Arghun blamed the Juvayni brothers, who rose under Tekuder, for his father's death by poisoning, and he rebelled in 1283. He beat Tekuder's general Alinaq near Qazvin on 4 May but later surrendered to him. Buqa, a senior commander of Tekuder, freed Arghun, killed Alinaq and arrested Tekuder, who was handed to Arghun on 26 July 1284 and executed.

Arghun was informally enthroned on 11 August 1284. Kublai Khan confirmed him on 23 February 1286, and a second coronation followed on 7 April 1286. Buqa, to whom he owed the throne, became both sahib-i divan and amir al-umara and was named chingsang. Shams al-Din Juvayni was executed. Arghun grew to resent Buqa and his brother Aruq, who ruled Baghdad as his own appanage; he audited their finances, and when Buqa conspired against him, Prince Jushkab revealed the plot. Buqa was put to death on 16 January 1289, and King Demetre II of Georgia, who was implicated, was summoned to the capital and imprisoned.

Sa'd al-Dawla, a Jewish physician, became vizier and restored order. Jushkab was executed on 10 June 1289, and Hulachu and Qara Noqai were executed in October 1290 after Nawruz's revolt. Arghun also fought the Golden Horde, repulsing raids at Shamakhi in 1288 and Derbent in 1289, and founded the city of Arghuniyya near Tabriz.

Arghun sent four missions to Europe seeking a Franco-Mongol alliance against the Mamluks. The first, in 1285, carried a letter to Pope Honorius IV. In 1287 the monk Rabban Bar Sauma went to the pope and to Edward I and Philip IV, and returned in 1288 with friendly but vague replies. Buscarel of Gisolfe went in 1289, and Andrew Zagan in 1290. In 1290 he also began a shipbuilding programme in Baghdad, which failed after Genoese quarrels. The Mamluks took Acre on 18 May 1291, after his death.

Arghun became interested in alchemy, and after taking a concoction from a yogi fell ill. He died in Arran in March 1291, on 7 or 10 March, and was buried in a secret place in the mountains of Sojas. The missionary Ricoldo of Montecroce called him a man given to the worst villainy yet a friend of the Christians. Children in Italy were named Argone after him.
argo: In Greek mythology the Argo was the ship of Jason and the Argonauts, built with divine aid for the quest for the Golden Fleece from Iolcos to Colchis. Most accounts name the ship after her builder, Argus. Diodorus Siculus records that some thought the name came from an ancient Greek word for swift. Other Greek theories derive it from the builder Argos, son of Hestor or Alector, or from the city of Argos where she was supposedly built, and Cicero proposed that it came from the Argives, a name for the Greek people of Argos commonly used by Homer.

The best source for the myth is the Argonautica of Apollonius Rhodius. The ship was built in Thessaly around Mount Pelion, and Sextus Propertius, writing under Augustus, says she left from the port of Pagasae. Catullus wrote that she was the first ship to travel on the sea, while Dionysius Scytobrachion called her well made but not the first.

The Argo was built for the open sea and designed to move quickly with the aid of a sail. Apollodorus says she had fifty oars, all manned by the Argonauts, which would make her an early form of the penteconter. Euripides in Medea says the oars were of pine from Mount Pelion, and Catullus says the hull was fir. The prow held a piece of oak from Dodona, sacred to Zeus, which could speak and give oracles. The crew had the special protection of Hera.

Athena taught the steersman Tiphys to fix the sails to the mast, and Lynceus, with sharp sight by night and day, helped guide the ship. The Nereids and Triton were said to help her through dangerous moments. Herodotus says the Argonauts gave a bronze tripod to Triton when they were lost in Lake Tritonis, and that the ship had to be carried over land for twelve days to regain her course.

After the voyage the Argo was consecrated to Poseidon at the Isthmus of Corinth and kept as a monument. Years later a beam fell from the ship and killed Jason as he slept on the ground. He was then taken up into the sky, and the ship became the constellation Argo Navis.

Ancient authors, among them Apollonius Rhodius, Pliny and Philostephanus, discussed her probable shape, generally imagining a Greek warship or galley, and Aristotle used the story that the ship left Heracles behind because he was too heavy in a remark on ostracism in Athens. The ship has remained a motif in plays, books and films. In the 1963 film Jason and the Argonauts she is a warship with shields along the side, and her sacred oak appears as a speaking figurehead modelled on Hera.
argonauts: In Greek myth the Argonauts sailed in the years before the Trojan War, placed around 1300 BCE, and took their name from their ship Argo, named after its builder Argus. Their quest began at Iolcus in Thessaly, where Pelias had usurped the throne of his half-brother Aeson. An oracle warned Pelias against a man with one shoe, and when the young Jason arrived with a single sandal, Pelias sent him to fetch the Golden Fleece. The fleece hung in a grove of Ares in Colchis, guarded by a dragon that never slept. No definite list of the crew exists. Pindar names or implies Jason, Heracles, Castor, Polydeuces, Orpheus, Zetes, Calais and Mopsus among others,.

The voyage included a stay on Lemnos, where Jason and Hypsipyle had sons, and a night battle in which Jason killed King Cyzicus by mistake. Hylas was taken by a spring nymph in Mysia, and Heracles was left behind. In Thrace the blind seer Phineus told them the way in return for freeing him from the Harpies, and advised them to send a dove through the Symplegades, the clashing rocks. They passed, and the rocks never moved again.

At Colchis King Aeëtes set Jason tasks: yoking two fire-breathing bulls and sowing dragon's teeth from which armed men rose. Medea, his daughter, whom Hera and Aphrodite caused to love Jason, gave him a drug that protected him from fire and iron, and after he swore to marry her she lulled the dragon to sleep so that he could take the fleece. They fled by night. Medea killed her brother Apsyrtus, and Zeus sent a storm until Circe purified the crew. They passed the Sirens, whom Orpheus countered with song, and Talos on Crete, and reached Iolcus after about four months.

Ancient writers gave other routes home. Sozomen and Zosimus say the Argonauts founded the city of Emona on the way, part of modern Ljubljana, and Pliny the Elder reports that some writers say the ship was carried across the Alps on men's shoulders. Porto Ferraio on Elba was known in antiquity as the portus Argous, because the Argonauts were believed to have landed there while seeking Circe. The Slovenian town of Vrhnika shows a ship on its coat of arms, as it is believed to have been the starting point of the final journey on foot of the Argonauts.
argyll: Argyll, sometimes called Argyllshire, is a historic county and registration county of western Scotland. It is sparsely populated, with many islands and sea lochs along its coast and mountainous country inland. It is split into two mainland sections divided by Loch Linnhe, plus most of the Inner Hebrides, though not Skye or Eigg.

The northern section holds the peninsulas of Ardnamurchan and Morvern, and Ardnamurchan Point and Corrachadh Mòr are the westernmost points of the British mainland. The southern section is dominated by the Kintyre peninsula, whose end lies 21 kilometres from Northern Ireland across the North Channel. Bidean nam Bian near Glen Coe, at 1,150 metres, is the county's tallest peak. Its islands range from flat Coll and Tiree to mountainous Jura and Mull.

The Kilmartin Glen has standing stones and other monuments dating back to around 3000 BCE and is among the most significant areas for Neolithic and Bronze Age remains in mainland Scotland. Iona Abbey was founded in 563 CE and became one of the most important early Christian sites in Scotland.

The Gaelic kingdom of Dál Riata existed between the 5th and 9th centuries, with its main seat at the fortress of Dunadd in the Kilmartin Glen. It fragmented in the Viking Age: its Irish part was absorbed into the kingdom of Ulaid, the islands came under the Kingdom of the Isles, and the part on mainland Britain was united in 843 with the Pictish kingdom under Kenneth MacAlpin to form the Kingdom of Alba.

The name comes from Old Irish airer Goídel, 'border region of the Gaels', and airer can also mean 'coast', hence 'coast of the Gaels'. It came to be used for the former Dál Riata territory on mainland Britain, distinguishing it from the Innse Gall, 'islands of the foreigners', the Kingdom of the Isles ruled by Old Norse-speaking Norse-Gaels. Argyll was also a medieval bishopric with its cathedral at Lismore. Medieval lordships included Cowal, Kintyre, Knapdale and Lorn, and one central lordship called Argyll was an earldom, raised to a dukedom in 1701. From 1633 the shire covered all five provinces.

Argyll ceased to be used for local government in 1975, and most of it now forms part of the Argyll and Bute council area. Its historic county town was Inveraray, though the county council, which existed from 1890 to 1975, was based at Lochgilphead. Six towns held burgh status: Campbeltown, Dunoon, Inveraray, Lochgilphead, Oban and Tobermory.
ariadne: Ariadne's father was Minos, king of Crete and son of Zeus and Europa, and her mother was most commonly named as Pasiphaë, daughter of Helios and Perse; some authors name her mother as Crete, daughter of Asterius and Europa. Through Pasiphaë she was half-sister of the Minotaur, known in Crete as Asterion. Hellenistic lexicographers derived her name from Cretan elements meaning most and holy. Stylianos Alexiou and Robert S. P. Beekes argue instead that it is pre-Greek, and Beekes, noting the rare sequence dn, thought it a Minoan loanword.

Because the myths were transmitted orally, Ariadne's story exists in many variants. In the Athenian version, Minos attacked Athens after his son Androgeus was killed there, and the Athenians had to send seven young men and seven maidens to the Minotaur at intervals given as one, seven or nine years. When Theseus, son of King Aegeus, volunteered, Ariadne fell in love with him and gave him a sword and a ball of thread, Ariadne's string, so that he could find his way out of the labyrinth.

Most accounts say Theseus abandoned her on Naxos, where Dionysus found her sleeping and married her; some say Dionysus appeared to Theseus and demanded that he leave her. Many versions have Dionysus throw her jewelled crown into the sky as the constellation Corona Borealis. Other versions differ: in the Odyssey, Artemis kills her on the island of Dia, on Dionysus's testimony, and in another account Perseus kills her at Argos. Plutarch records a tradition that she hanged herself, after which Dionysus brought her and his mother Semele to Olympus.

Ariadne was honoured at festivals called Ariadneia on Naxos and in Cyprus. At Amathus in Cyprus, according to Paeon of Amathus as Plutarch cites him, she was worshipped as Aphrodite-Ariadne: she died in childbirth after Theseus's ship was swept out to sea, and on the second day of the month Gorpiaeus a young man lay on the ground and imitated labour. Plutarch also reports a Naxian belief in two Ariadnes, one married to Dionysus and one abandoned by Theseus.

Karl Kerenyi saw in her a Cretan Great Goddess, Mistress of the Labyrinth, citing a Linear B tablet from Knossos; Barry Powell suggested the Minoan Snake Goddess. In Etruscan she was called Areatha, and Hyginus identified her with Libera. Later works inspired by the myth include the opera Ariadne auf Naxos of 1912 and an 1820 oil painting, Bacchus and Ariadne.
ariane-rocket-family: France first proposed the Ariane project, and it was officially agreed at the end of 1973 after discussions between France, Germany and the UK. The name is the French spelling of Ariadne. The project was Western Europe's second attempt at its own launcher, after the unsuccessful Europa project, and was code-named L3S, the French abbreviation for third-generation substitution launcher. The European Space Agency charged Aérospatiale with developing all Ariane launchers and their test facilities, while Arianespace handled production, operations and marketing after its creation in 1980. Following the merger of 2000 that founded Airbus, its space branch and then ArianeGroup took over the duties of Aérospatiale.

Ariane 1 was a three-stage launcher derived from ballistic missile technology: the first two stages used hypergolic propellants and the third burned liquid hydrogen and liquid oxygen. Ariane 2 to 4 were enhancements with improved engines, stretched tanks and greater payloads, and the largest could launch two satellites mounted in the SPELDA adapter. Strap-on boosters, solid or liquid, are shown by suffixes, so an Ariane 42P has two solid boosters. Ariane 5 was a nearly complete redesign in which a single core stage with one Vulcain engine replaced the two hypergolic lower stages, with two solid-fuel boosters at the sides that can be recovered for examination but are not reused.

Ariane rockets are launched by Arianespace from the Guiana Space Centre at Kourou in French Guiana. By January 2006, 169 flights had boosted 290 satellites. In 1996 France's Cerise satellite, orbited by an Ariane 4 in 1995, struck a discarded Ariane stage, the first verified collision with catalogued space debris. On 4 May 2007 an Ariane 5-ECA set a commercial payload record by lifting two satellites with a combined mass of 9.4 tonnes. The 200th Ariane launch, on 16 February 2011, carried the Johannes Kepler supply craft to the International Space Station, and on 25 December 2021 an Ariane lifted the James Webb Space Telescope towards the Lagrange point L2. Ariane 5 flew its final mission on 5 July 2023.
arianism: Arianism is traditionally attributed to Arius, a presbyter who preached and studied in Alexandria, though modern scholars treat the fourth-century controversy as the result of deeper tensions already present among Christians and describe Arius as a theological conservative. They note that no single Arian party existed; those who opposed the Nicene Creed formed a loose coalition united by opposition to the term homoousios. The name Arian was a polemical term used by outsiders, not what the followers called themselves. In 321 a synod at Alexandria denounced Arius for teaching a heterodox view of the relation of Jesus to God the Father, and his followers' influence in the schools of Alexandria spread his views, especially in the eastern Mediterranean.

Little of Arius's own work survives except in quotations chosen by his opponents. His basic premise was that only God is independent of existing, so the Son, being dependent, must be called a creature. In his words, if the Father begat the Son, the one begotten had a beginning, and there was a time when the Son was not. The Logos was a divine being created by the Father before the world, serving as the medium of creation and subordinate to the Father.

In 325 the Emperor Constantine called the First Council of Nicaea, which condemned Arius and formulated the Nicene Creed, whose central term homoousios means of the same substance. Arius, not being a bishop, could not sit, and Eusebius of Nicomedia spoke for his position. After Constantine's death in 337 his son Constantius II encouraged the Arians and exiled Nicene bishops, including Athanasius of Alexandria.

Arianism was effectively wiped out among the ruling class of the Eastern Empire under Theodosius I, who held the Nicene faith. The missionary Ulfilas, an Arian bishop, translated the Bible into Gothic and converted the Goths, and Arianism spread to the Vandals, Langobards, Svevi and Burgundians. In the Germanic kingdoms of the 5th century separate Arian and Nicene churches existed side by side, the elites Arian and the Romance-majority population Nicene.

Organised Arianism survived in North Africa, Hispania and parts of Italy until suppressed in the 6th and 7th centuries. Visigothic Spain turned to Nicene Christianity under Reccared I at the Third Council of Toledo in 589, and the Lombard king Grimoald and his son Garibald, who reigned from 662 to 671, were the last Arian kings in Europe.
ariarathes-i-of-cappadocia: Ariarathes was born in 405 or 404 BCE to Ariamnes and had a brother named Orophernes. His family claimed descent from Cyrus the Great and from Anaphas, one of the seven Persian conspirators who killed the Pseudo-Smerdis. Under Artaxerxes II he and his family served as minor officials in the satrapy of Cappadocia, then governed by Datames. After the assassination of Datames, about 362 BCE, Cappadocia was divided into a northern and a southern satrapy, in response to the power Datames had amassed. By the 340s BCE Ariarathes had succeeded his father as satrap of Northern Cappadocia, a territory that later became part of the Kingdom of Pontus, and he sent provincial troops with Artaxerxes III on the campaign to pacify Egypt.

When Alexander the Great invaded Persian territory, Cappadocia and neighbouring Phrygia became rallying points for the Achaemenid resistance. Mithrobuzanes, governor of the southern satrapy, was killed at the Battle of Granicus in 334 BCE, and the Macedonian-appointed replacement failed to establish his authority. Ariarathes's own territory was largely unaffected by the invasion, and he commanded troops at the Battle of Gaugamela in 331 BCE. After the end of the Achaemenid Empire he kept resisting the Macedonians from his base at Gaziura as an independent monarch.

He minted coins at Sinope and Gaziura with legends in Aramaic, the imperial language of the Achaemenids. A coin from Gaziura shows a seated figure like Zeus with the inscription Ba'al Gazir, Lord of Gaziura. Mary Boyce and Frantz Grenet note that the figure could portray the Zoroastrian Ahura Mazda or Mithra.

After Alexander's death in 323 BCE, Cappadocia was granted to Eumenes, who could not dislodge Ariarathes. He turned to Perdiccas, regent for Philip III Arrhidaeus, who entered Cappadocia with the royal army in the summer of 322 BCE. Ariarathes mustered local troops and mercenaries but was defeated and captured, and he and most of his family were crucified that year. Antigonus I Monophthalmus later seized Cappadocia, and it passed to Lysimachus and then the Seleucids. About 301 BCE Ariarathes II restored Ariarathid control over Southern Cappadocia with Armenian help. The dynasty ruled the Kingdom of Cappadocia until 96 BCE, when Roman intervention replaced it with the Ariobarzanids.
ariarathes-v-of-cappadocia: Ariarathes V was a son of King Ariarathes IV of Cappadocia and Queen Antiochis, a noble Seleucid Greek woman who was the daughter of the Seleucid king Antiochus III. According to Livy he was educated in Rome, but that account may refer to another Ariarathes. He probably spent his youth studying in Athens, where he seems to have become a friend of the future king of Pergamon, Attalus II Philadelphus. His contemporaries distinguished him for the excellence of his character and his cultivation of philosophy and the liberal arts, and some historians rank him highest among the kings of Cappadocia.

At the wish of the Romans, Ariarathes rejected a marriage with Laodice V, the sister of Demetrius I Soter. Demetrius made war on him and put forward his brother Orophernes of Cappadocia, one of the supposed sons of the late king, as a claimant to the throne. Ariarathes lost his kingdom and fled to Rome around 158 BCE. The Romans restored him but allowed Orophernes to reign jointly with him, as Appian states and Polybius implies. The joint government did not last, and shortly afterwards Ariarathes was named sole king. In 154 he assisted Attalus II of Pergamon in his war against Prusias II of Bithynia, and sent his son Demetrius in command of his forces.

Ariarathes was killed in 130 BCE during the Roman war against Aristonicus of Pergamon. In return for his support, the Romans added Lycaonia and Cilicia to the dominions of his family. By his wife Nysa, daughter of King Pharnaces I of Pontus, he had six children, but all except one were killed by their mother so that she might obtain the government; the people put her to death for her cruelty, and her surviving son succeeded as Ariarathes VI of Cappadocia.

A strong philhellene, Ariarathes was honoured with Athenian citizenship and refounded the Cappadocian towns of Mazaca and Tyana under the Greek name Eusebia. He gave generously to Athens and its institutions, and an inscription survives in which an association of professional actors thanks him and his wife for their patronage. He corresponded with the philosopher Carneades, as Diogenes Laërtius attests.
arica: Arica lies only 18 km south of the border with Peru, at the bend of South America's western coast known as the Arica Bend, where the Azapa and Lluta valleys, which cut through the Atacama Desert, converge. These valleys provide citrus and olives for export. The climate is extremely dry, with an average annual rainfall of 0.76 mm, though maritime winds from the cold waters nearby make it mild. Because it lies close to the Peru-Chile Trench, it is subject to megathrust earthquakes.

Archaeological findings show that native groups lived at Arica 10,000 years ago, and these people were the first known culture to mummify their dead. Spaniards settled the land under Lucas Martinez de Begazo in 1541. By 1545 Arica was the main export entrepot for the silver coming down from Potosí, and the riches made it a target for pirates and privateers, among them Francis Drake and William Dampier. The population of the region shrank by 36% from 1540 to 1570 through disease, death in mining and emigration.

Arica became part of independent Peru in 1821, and in 1855 the Tacna-Arica railway, one of the first in Latin America, opened. An earthquake on 13 August 1868, estimated at magnitude 8.0 to 9.0, caused a tsunami measurable in Hawaii, Japan and New Zealand; estimates of its death toll vary greatly. Chilean troops captured the Morro de Arica on 7 June 1880 during the War of the Pacific, and the Treaty of Ancón in 1883 formally gave the region to Chilean control. The Treaty of Lima in 1929 restored Tacna to Peru, while Arica stayed Chilean. The Arica and Parinacota Region was created in 2007.

Arica is Chile's northernmost city and the capital of the Arica and Parinacota Region, with 241,653 people counted in the 2024 census. It is a port serving a large inland region and a free port for Bolivia, which it links by rail, as it does Tacna in Peru. The Morro de Arica, about 139 metres high, is where the Peruvian garrison made its last stand in 1880. The cathedral of San Marcos, designed by Gustave Eiffel, dates from the 1870s.
ariege-department: Ariège, named after the river Ariège, is a department in the Occitanie region of south-western France, and its capital is Foix. It covers 4,890 square kilometres and is divided into three arrondissements, Foix, Pamiers and Saint-Girons. To the south it borders Andorra and the Spanish province of Lleida. The north is plain, hills and low valleys given to agriculture; below the mountains lie the Pyrenean foothills; and the high country is dominated by the Pyrenees, with the Pica d'Estats at 3,143 m the highest point of the department. Its only true glacier is that of Mont Valier. Its inhabitants are called Ariègeois, and in 2023 there were 155,722 of them.

Ariège is one of the original 83 departments created during the French Revolution on 4 March 1790. It was formed from the counties of Foix and Couserans. A request to rename it Ariège-Pyrénées, to promote it better across France, was rejected. Foix has a fortress, the Château de Foix, on a hill above the town; it was attacked many times without being captured, including by Simon de Montfort, and was later used as a prison. Montségur stands on a rocky outcrop at 1,200 metres. During the Albigensian Crusade and the siege of 1244 the castle was largely destroyed, and more than two hundred Cathar priests were burnt at the stake as heretics.

In the early 17th century the Huguenot rebellions ravaged the area. In 1621 Huguenot forces ruined the church at La Tour-du-Crieu, and in 1629 Pamiers was sacked by Henry of Condé after uprisings that left several hundred dead. The abbeys at Foix, Tarascon-sur-Ariège, Saint-Girons, Saverdun and Le Mas-d'Azil were burned in the same period.

The 19th century brought strong industrial growth, supported by abundant water power and reserves of iron ore. A steel plant was established at Pamiers in 1817, and forges and blast furnaces followed at Montgaillard and Tarascon-sur-Ariège. Changes in forest laws in 1829 led to the War of the Maidens, a revolt of peasants who disguised themselves as women while resisting the loss of their rights to use the forests.

Ariège is known for its rural and mountainous landscape; more than half of it is mountainous and 490,965 hectares are forest. The Regional Natural Park of the Ariège Pyrenees, created in 2009, covers about 40 per cent of the department. Talc is mined in the Ax valleys, and the winter sports resorts include Ax 3 Domaines and Guzet-Neige. The patriotic song Arièjo O moun Pais, written by Father Sabas Maury, born in 1863, serves as its anthem.
ariovistus: Ariovistus is known only through Roman sources, chiefly books 1.31 to 1.54 of Julius Caesar's Commentarii de Bello Gallico, and no non-Roman account survives. Modern historians read Caesar's portrait of him as a violent, rash and angry barbarian with caution, since the commentaries served as political propaganda for the Senate and the Roman public. According to Caesar, Ariovistus spoke Gaulish fluently and had two wives, a Suebian and a sister of King Voccio of Noricum. Caesar styled him king of the Germani, though his authority probably extended only over the Germanic groups that had crossed into Gaul. In 59 BCE the Senate recognised him as king and friend of the Roman people.

The Arverni and Sequani asked Ariovistus to help them against the Aedui, Rome's allies, whom he had already defeated a few years earlier. At the Battle of Magetobriga his 15,000 men defeated the Aedui, took hostages and seized a third of their land, settling 120,000 Germanic people there. He then demanded more land for the Harudes, some 24,000 of them, and began to devastate Sequani lands. His forces were a migratory mix of peoples, among them the Harudes, Triboci and Marcomanni.

In 58 BCE the Aedui appealed to Caesar through Diviciacus. Caesar demanded that Ariovistus stop crossings, release hostages and respect Rome's allies, and Ariovistus refused. When they met with only cavalry, each accused the other of bad faith. Ariovistus manoeuvred around Vesontio to cut off Caesar's supplies, and the Germanic tribes, drawn up by tribe, finally faced Caesar's six legions. Germanic phalanx tactics briefly pushed the Romans back until Publius Licinius Crassus committed reserves. Ariovistus's line broke and fled toward the Rhine. He escaped, but both his wives were killed, one daughter was slain and another captured. The site of the battle is uncertain.

Caesar's victory broke the Suebi's ability to cross the Rhine for years, and defeating both the Helvetii and Ariovistus in one year was, in Adrian Goldsworthy's words, a massive achievement. Ariovistus disappears from history soon afterwards; by 54 BCE Caesar noted that his death had provoked indignation among Germanic warriors. In the early Empire the groups that had fought for him appear on both banks of the Rhine in Alsace, forming the basis of Germania Superior, and over time they integrated into Romano-Celtic society. His name is usually derived from Gaulish elements meaning noble and knowledge, giving noble sage.
ariq-boke: Ariq Böke was the seventh and youngest son of Tolui and Sorghaghtani Beki. After Genghis Khan died in 1227, leadership passed to Ögedei, and Ariq Böke peacefully attended the elections of both Ögedei and Ögedei's son Güyük. His eldest brother Möngke was enthroned in 1250, which made the family more powerful among the descendants of Genghis.

His mother was Christian, and he was known for sympathy towards Christianity. The Franciscan William of Rubruck, an envoy of Louis IX of France, wrote that he saw Ariq Böke make the sign of the cross and say that the Messiah is God. His brother Kublai Khan arranged a Confucian tutor for him, but Ariq Böke did not take to Chinese scholars as Kublai had.

While Möngke and Kublai conquered Southern China and Hulagu advanced west to Baghdad and Syria, the affairs of the Mongol heartland were left in Ariq Böke's hands. When Möngke died in 1259, Ariq Böke was elected khan in the absence of his brothers, with the support of most of the ministers and powerful families at Karakorum, including Möngke's family, and of the Oirats. In May 1260 Kublai was elected khan by his own supporters, and a civil war broke out between the brothers.

Ariq Böke had the Chagatai Khanate's candidate Abishqa, who was loyal to Kublai, captured and killed, and installed his own ally Alghu. Alghu later deserted him and killed his envoys, but Ariq Böke defeated him in a second engagement and forced him to flee west. Kublai, however, commanded Mongol cavalry and Mongolian, Manchurian, Han, Kipchak and Goryeo troops, and he blockaded trade from North China to Mongolia to cut the food supply. His supporter Kadan crushed Ariq Böke's force under General Alandar, and Karakorum twice slipped from Ariq Böke's control.

Ariq Böke submitted to Kublai in 1264 and was imprisoned. He died a few years later in unclear circumstances, which gave rise to rumours of poisoning. The scholar David Morgan sees him as the figurehead of a school of thought among the Mongols that opposed Kublai's attraction to settled civilisation and the Chinese way of life. In the traditionalist view the Mongol centre should remain in Mongolia and nomadic life be preserved, with China merely exploited. Kaidu continued this tradition. Some of Ariq Böke's descendants became important in the Ilkhanate and the Northern Yuan dynasty, and Yesüder, khan from 1388, can be traced back to him.
arirang: Arirang is believed to have originated in Jeongseon in Gangwon Province; according to Professor Keith Howard, the first mention is in a 1756 manuscript, and some Jeongseon locals trace it to the Goryeo era. The meaning of the word is ambiguous. Some linguists, among them Shin Yong-ha, suggest that ari meant beautiful and rang a beloved one, so that arirang meant my beloved one. A legend tells of a bachelor and a maiden who fell in love while picking camellia blossoms near the wharf at Auraji. In one version he cannot cross because the water is too high, and the two sing to express their sorrow; in the other he drowns attempting the crossing and sings after he dies.

Some believe the song spread to Seoul when workers from Gangwon were sent to rebuild Gyeongbok Palace under Prince Regent Heungseon. According to one theory, their families said arirang or ananri to the officials taking them away, phrases meaning that they could not be separated from lovers or families. The Maecheonyarok of the Joseon scholar Hwang Hyeon suggests that the song was widespread by then.

There are an estimated 3,600 variations of 60 different versions, usually titled by their place of origin. Jeongseon Arirang is generally considered the original, and Bonjo Arirang, the Standard Arirang of Seoul, is among the best known; it was popularised as the theme of Na Woon-gyu's 1926 film Arirang. Jindo Arirang and Miryang Arirang are other well-known variants. All versions include a refrain similar to arirang, arirang, arariyo. The word itself has no precise meaning in Korean, and most versions treat sorrow, separation, reunion and love.

The first known recording was made in 1896 by the American ethnologist Alice C. Fletcher in Washington, D.C., of three Korean students singing; it is held in the Library of Congress. During the Japanese occupation of Korea, singing patriotic songs became a criminal offence, and Arirang became an unofficial resistance anthem. Protesters sang it during the March First Movement of 1919, and several versions were banned in the 1930s for disturbance of public order. It reached Japan in the 1910s, and between 1931 and 1943 more than 50 Japanese versions were released.

South Korea submitted Arirang to the UNESCO Intangible Cultural Heritage list in 2012 and North Korea in 2014. It is sung in both North and South Korea and acts as a symbol of unity between the two. The U.S. Army's 7th Infantry Division adopted it as its official march song in May 1956.
aristagoras-of-miletus: Aristagoras was the son of Molpagoras and the son-in-law of Histiaeus, whom the Persians had set up as tyrant of Miletus but did not trust. After the general Megabazus complained about Histiaeus, Darius I summoned him to Susa and kept him there. On Histiaeus's recommendation the Persians appointed Aristagoras to rule Miletus in his place, around 500 BCE. Little else is known about him, and most information comes from Herodotus, who is virtually the only literary source.

Exiles from Naxos asked Aristagoras for troops to regain their homeland. He persuaded the satrap Artaphernes at Sardis to attack the island, promising to fund the expedition, and Artaphernes agreed to provide 200 ships. Aristagoras quarrelled with the Persian admiral Megabates, who secretly warned the Naxians. After a siege of four months the fleet ran out of supplies and sailed home. His position at risk, Aristagoras planned a revolt, and Histiaeus, still detained at Susa, sent him a message tattooed on a slave's shaved head telling him to rebel. In 499 BCE his council voted for revolt, against the objection of the historian Hecataeus.

Aristagoras gave up his own tyranny and convinced other Ionian cities to end theirs, and a joint government with a board of generals was created. At Sparta he showed King Cleomenes I a bronze tablet with a map of the world, but Cleomenes refused once he learned that Susa was three months' journey away. Athens sent twenty triremes and Eretria five. This force reached Sardis and burned it, and a fire destroyed the temple of Cybele. The Persians then drove the Ionians back and defeated them near Ephesus, after which the Athenians withdrew.

Before the revolt collapsed, Aristagoras left Pythagoras in charge of Miletus and sailed for Thrace, where he settled at Myrcinus, ignoring advice not to. While besieging a neighbouring town he was killed in battle. The Persians defeated the Ionian fleet at the Battle of Lade in 494 BCE, and Miletus fell. They killed the warriors, castrated the young men and sold the women and children into slavery. The revolt ended in 494/493 BCE, and the Persians then prepared the invasion of Greece, which began in 490 BCE. Herodotus's hostile portrait has shaped Aristagoras's reputation, and modern historians dispute how far Herodotus can be trusted on the revolt.
aristarchus-of-samos: Aristarchus was born on Samos in approximately 310 BCE. He likely moved to Alexandria and became a student of Strato of Lampsacus, who later headed the Peripatetic school in Greece. Ptolemy reports that Aristarchus observed the summer solstice of 280 BCE, and Vitruvius writes that he built two kinds of sundial, one a flat disc and one hemispherical.

His only surviving work, On the Sizes and Distances of the Sun and Moon, rests on a geocentric view. Aristarchus claimed that at half moon the angle between the Sun and Moon was 87 degrees, and with correct geometry but this inexact figure concluded that the Sun was between 18 and 20 times farther from the Earth than the Moon. The true angle is close to 89 degrees 50 minutes, and the Sun is about 400 times as far. Astronomers up to Tycho Brahe used the solar parallax that his figure implies. From a lunar eclipse he also worked out that the Moon's diameter is roughly one third of the Earth's.

His heliocentric work is lost and is known from a passage in The Sand Reckoner of Archimedes. According to it, Aristarchus supposed that the fixed stars and the Sun stay unmoved and that the Earth revolves around the Sun in a circle. Because no stellar parallax could be seen, he held that the stars were other suns, very far away, which implied a much larger universe. He drew on the central fire of Philolaus of Croton and recast it as the Sun.

Plutarch says that Aristarchus offered heliocentrism only as a hypothesis, while Seleucus of Seleucia, a century later, held it as a definite opinion. Plato, Aristotle and Ptolemy preferred the geocentric model, which was believed through the Middle Ages. According to Lucio Russo, the common notion that his contemporaries thought his view sacrilegious comes from a printing of a passage of Plutarch with words transposed. Nicolaus Copernicus knew that Aristarchus had a theory of a moving Earth, though he probably did not know it was heliocentric. A lunar crater, the minor planet 3999 Aristarchus and the telescope Aristarchos bear his name.
aristides: Aristides came from a family of moderate fortune, and his father was named Lysimachus. Early in life he became a follower of the statesman Cleisthenes. He probably first came to notice as strategos in command of his own tribe, Antiochis, at the Battle of Marathon in 490 BCE. Because of the distinction he won there, he is said to have been elected archon eponymos for the next year. He followed a conservative policy meant to keep Athens a land power, and he was one of the chief opponents of the naval policy proposed by Themistocles.

The conflict between the two leaders ended in the ostracism of Aristides, at a date given variously between 485 and 482 BCE. A story told of the vote has an illiterate voter, who did not recognise Aristides, ask him to write the name Aristides on his shard; he said he did not know the man but was irritated to hear him everywhere called the Just. Aristides wrote his own name. Early in 480 BCE a decree recalling exiles let him help defend Athens against the Persian invaders, and he was elected strategos for 480–479 BCE.

At the Battle of Salamis in September 480 BCE he gave loyal support to Themistocles and completed the victory by landing Athenian infantry on the island of Psyttaleia and destroying the Persian garrison there. Re-elected in 479 BCE, he commanded the Athenian forces at the Battle of Plataea in August with special powers. The Ionian allies, after revolting from the Spartan admiral Pausanias, gave him chief command and full discretion in fixing the contributions to the Delian League, formed in 478 BCE. His assessment was universally accepted as fair and remained the basis of taxation for most of the League's existence.

Some authorities say Aristides died at Athens and others that he died on a journey to the Black Sea; Nepos gives the date as 468 BCE. He lived to see the ostracism of Themistocles, to whom he always showed generosity, but died before the rise of Pericles. He apparently left too little to pay for his burial, and his descendants received state pensions even in the 4th century. Herodotus called him the best and most honourable man in Athens, Plutarch wrote his life, and Socrates praises him in Plato's Gorgias and Meno as an example of good leadership.
aristippus-of-cyrene: Aristippus was the son of Aritades and was born at Cyrene around 435 BCE. He is said to have come to Greece to attend the Olympic games, where he met Ischomachus and asked about Socrates. Ischomachus's description gave him a strong desire to see Socrates, and he went to Athens and made him his master.

Though a disciple, he departed in principle and in practice from the teaching and example of Socrates. He is also said to have been the first of Socrates's followers to take money for teaching. He sometimes sent it to Socrates, who often returned it, viewing it as an insult. There are indications that Aristippus has been conflated with his grandson, Aristippus the Younger.

Aristippus turned toward the court of Dionysius I of Syracuse, or of Dionysius the Younger, where he became a counsellor. Accounts say that he lived luxuriously there and kept the company of Lais. He told Socrates that he lived abroad to avoid involvement in the politics of his native city. He is also said to have been taken prisoner by Artaphernes, the satrap who drove the Spartans from Rhodes in 396 BCE.

Vitruvius tells that when Aristippus was shipwrecked on the coast of Rhodes he saw geometrical figures drawn on the shore and said, according to the story, that he saw the traces of man. He went to the gymnasium of Rhodes, discussed philosophy and received gifts. The message he sent home was that children should be given the kind of property that can swim out of a shipwreck. In old age he is said to have returned to Cyrene and to have died at 79.

Aristippus taught that pleasure is the supreme good, a view later called ethical hedonism, but that it should be moderated by self-restraint, and he warned his followers never to harm others. His best-known phrase is I possess, I am not possessed. Diogenes Laertius reports him as saying that the best course is not abstinence from pleasures but mastery over them without ever being worsted.

Plato and Xenophon accused him of straying from Socrates, who valued virtue above pleasure, and Aristotle called him a sophist. In Plato's Phaedo he is described as having been at Aegina, a pleasure resort, instead of attending Socrates's death. His daughter Arete, whom he named his intellectual heiress, and her son Aristippus the Younger turned his teaching into the system of the Cyrenaic school.

None of his works survives. Diogenes Laertius lists books ascribed to him on the authority of Sotion and Panaetius, but notes Sosicrates of Rhodes's statement that he wrote nothing. A book called On Ancient Luxury cannot be his, since its author mentions Theophrastus, who lived a generation later.
aristobulus-i: Aristobulus I was the eldest of the five sons of John Hyrcanus. His Hebrew name was Judah, and Aristobulus, a Greek name meaning best-advising, was an epithet he was the first Hasmonean to adopt. He was also called Philhellene, an admirer of Greek culture, though Josephus does not explain why. With his brother Antigonus he was entrusted by their father with the conquest of Samaria. The brothers besieged the city and defeated a relief army of the Seleucid Empire led by Antiochus IX Cyzicenus. They captured and razed Samaria near the end of John's reign and enslaved its inhabitants, then took Scythopolis and the whole region south of Mount Carmel.

John Hyrcanus had left the country to his wife, with Aristobulus to receive only the high priesthood. Instead Aristobulus had his mother imprisoned, where she starved to death, and so secured both the high priesthood and the kingship. He imprisoned all his brothers except Antigonus. Josephus states that he was the first Jew to establish a monarchy since the return from the Babylonian captivity. The Sadducees and Essenes were not troubled by his taking the title of king, but the Pharisees opposed it strongly, since they held that kingship belonged to the line of David.

He made war on the Ituraeans and took territory from them, compelling them to accept Jewish law and circumcision in order to stay on their land. Most scholars place their territory in northern Galilee, though its exact extent is unknown. Kenneth Atkinson finds no evidence of forced Judaization in Galilee during his reign. Aristobulus's coins carry the title of high priest and not that of king, in Hebrew, with the name Judah. Atkinson holds that the absence of a royal title does not show he was never a monarch.

Aristobulus fell ill with sudden abdominal pains and withdrew to his palace during the festival of Sukkot. According to Josephus, rumours spread by his wife and conspirators told him that Antigonus, who came to the Temple in armour, meant to seize the throne. The queen is said to have bribed the messenger so that Antigonus came armed to his brother, and Aristobulus killed him. He then grew rapidly worse and died soon after, in 103 BCE. The queen released his brothers and chose Alexander Jannaeus as the next king.
aristobulus-ii: Aristobulus was the younger of two sons of Alexander Jannaeus, king and high priest, and Salome Alexandra. After Alexander died in 76 BCE his widow became queen of Judea and installed her elder son Hyrcanus II as high priest in 73 BCE. Aristobulus shared his father's views on religion and politics and courted the nobles and the military by becoming the patron of the Sadducees. The fortresses the queen had placed at the disposal of the Sadducees were, in effect, a preparatory move for his seizure of the throne.

When Salome died in 67 BCE, Aristobulus directed his forces against his brother Hyrcanus, the legitimate heir. Many of Hyrcanus' soldiers defected to him in battle near Jericho. Hyrcanus gave up the throne and the high priesthood but kept the revenues of the office. Antipater the Idumaean then convinced Hyrcanus that Aristobulus planned his death, and Hyrcanus took refuge with Aretas III, king of the Nabataeans, whose army of 50,000 besieged Jerusalem for several months.

Both brothers appealed to the Roman deputy Marcus Aemilius Scaurus, who, moved by a gift of 400 talents, favoured Aristobulus and ordered Aretas to withdraw. When Pompey reached Damascus in 63 BCE, he favoured Hyrcanus, the elder and weaker brother, as a more reliable ally. Pompey captured Aristobulus and his sons Alexander and Antigonus and took Jerusalem after a three-month siege of the Temple Mount, in which about 12,000 Jewish defenders were killed. Judea became a client kingdom of the Roman Republic.

Aristobulus escaped in 57 BCE and led a rebellion against Rome until Aulus Gabinius besieged him in Machaerus, where Mark Antony helped subdue his forces. Taken prisoner again, he was released by Julius Caesar in 49 BCE to turn Judea against Pompey, and was poisoned on the way by Pompey's partisans. His son Alexander was beheaded by the Roman commander Scipio at Antioch. Another son, Antigonus, rebelled with Parthian help, became king and high priest in 40 BCE, and was defeated and killed by the Romans in 37 BCE.
aristophanes: Aristophanes was an Athenian citizen from the deme of Kydathenaion. His father was Philippus and his mother Zenodora, and his family is suspected to have been wealthy and well educated. Little is known of his life, and his plays are the main source. In Old Comedy the chorus spoke for the author in an address called the parabasis, but the facts found there concern almost entirely his career as a dramatist. Plato's Symposium shows him as a genial guest at a dinner with Socrates, but its reliability is open to doubt.

He wrote forty plays, of which eleven survive virtually complete. They were performed at the religious festivals of Athens, chiefly the City Dionysia and the Lenaia, and several won first prize. His second play, The Babylonians, now lost, was denounced by Cleon as a slander against the Athenian polis. Aristophanes then caricatured Cleon mercilessly, above all in The Knights, the first of many plays he directed himself.

His plays often dealt with real people, among them Euripides and Alcibiades, and with events such as the Peloponnesian War. Plato singled out The Clouds as slander that contributed to the death sentence of Socrates, although other satirical playwrights had also caricatured the philosopher. The Clouds was placed third at its first performance, and the text that survives is a later draft meant to be read rather than acted.

His plays are the only full-length examples of Old Comedy to survive, which makes them central to modern understanding of the genre. A typical plot has a prologue, the entrance of the chorus, a formal debate called the agon that decides the outcome, a parabasis in which the chorus addresses the audience, and an exodus of song and dance. He referred to rival comic poets and to the tragedians Aeschylus, Sophocles and Euripides, all three of whom appear in The Frogs. Ancient commentators valued his language as a model of the Attic dialect.
aristophanes-of-byzantium: Aristophanes of Byzantium, not to be confused with Aristophanes of Athens, was a Hellenistic scholar, critic and grammarian, born at Byzantium about 257 BCE. He soon moved to Alexandria, where he studied under Zenodotus, Callimachus and Dionysius Iambus. He succeeded Eratosthenes as head librarian of the Library of Alexandria at the age of sixty, and was himself succeeded by Apollonius the Classifier. His students included Callistratus, Aristarchus of Samothrace and perhaps Agallis. Aristarchus later became the sixth head librarian.

He devoted himself chiefly to the poets, above all Homer, who had already been edited by his teacher Zenodotus. He also edited Hesiod and the chief lyric, tragic and comic poets, arranged Plato's dialogues in trilogies and abridged Aristotle's Nature of Animals. He was the first to deny that the Precepts of Chiron was the work of Hesiod. As a lexicographer he compiled collections of foreign and unusual words and expressions, and special lists such as words denoting relationship and modes of address.

He is credited with reducing the Greek accents to a definite system as the pitched system of archaic and Classical Greek gave way to the stress-based system of Koine, at a time when Greek was becoming a lingua franca of the eastern Mediterranean. The accents were meant to help readers pronounce older literary works. Around 200 BCE he also devised one of the first forms of punctuation: dots that separated verses and showed how much breath was needed to read each fragment aloud. A dot at mid-level marked a short passage, a komma, the origin of the modern comma and its name.

Little of his large output survives: a few fragments quoted in the scholia of later writers, several arguments to Greek dramas, and part of a glossary. The most recent edition of the fragments was edited by William J. Slater. His pupil Aristarchus of Samothrace continued the work on Homer.
aristotle: The details of Aristotle's life are not well established, and ancient biographies are often speculative. He was born in 384 BCE in Stagira in Chalcidice, the son of Nicomachus, personal physician to King Amyntas of Macedon, and of Phaestis. His father was probably responsible for his early interest in biology and medicine. Both parents died while he was young, and Proxenus of Atarneus became his guardian.

At seventeen or eighteen Aristotle moved to Athens to study at Plato's Academy, where Plato called him the mind of the school. He stayed for nearly twenty years and left in 348 or 347 BCE after Plato's death. The traditional story is that he was disappointed when control passed to Plato's nephew Speusippus, though anti-Macedonian feeling in Athens may also have played a part. He went to Assos in Asia Minor at the invitation of Hermias of Atarneus, did research in botany and marine biology there with Theophrastus, and married Pythias, Hermias's adoptive daughter and niece.

Aristotle founded the Peripatetic school in the Lyceum in Athens and established a library there. Only around a third of his original output has survived, and most of it was probably edited by students and later lecturers. His logical works were compiled into the Organon around 40 BCE, and the Prior Analytics is credited with the earliest systematic study of logic.

In physics he added the heavenly aether to the four elements proposed by Empedocles.
