Until the male line of his dynasty died out in 1301, Hungary was ruled by a single line of princes, all descended from Árpád. Hungarians call him honalapító, the founder of our homeland.
arpad-goncz: Árpád Göncz was born on 10 February 1922 in Budapest into an upper-middle-class family of noble origin. His father, Lajos Göncz, worked as a post officer, and his mother, Ilona Haimann, was born in Transylvania. After the Soviet occupation of Hungary he joined the anti-communist Independent Smallholders' Party, which won the November 1945 election but had to accept a coalition in which the Communists kept the Interior Ministry and the police. He worked as personal assistant to the party's general secretary, Béla Kovács. After 1949, with the party absorbed into a communist-led front, he worked as a manual labourer and later as an agronomist.

During the revolution of 1956 Göncz was present at the demonstration of 23 October. He was arrested on 28 May 1957 with István Bibó, and on 2 August 1958 he was secretly tried and sentenced to life imprisonment, shortly after the execution of Imre Nagy. He was held in Budapest and then at Vác, where he learned to read and write English and translated John Galsworthy's The Forsyte Saga. Released in 1963, he made his living as a translator of more than a hundred literary works. His best-known translation is J. R. R. Tolkien's The Lord of the Rings, published in Hungary in 1981; Dezső Tandori translated its poems.

In 1988 Göncz co-founded the Historical Justice Committee, which demanded a proper reburial for Imre Nagy. He helped organise the reburial on 16 June 1989 and opened the ceremony. He was also a founding member of the Alliance of Free Democrats.

Göncz became Speaker of the National Assembly, the de facto head of state, and on 4 August 1990 the Assembly elected him president by 295 votes to 13. He was Hungary's first freely elected head of state, and the first in 42 years who was not a communist or fellow traveller. In his inaugural speech he said he would serve those who lacked the means to protect themselves. He served until 4 August 2000, when Ferenc Mádl succeeded him. He attended the signing of Hungary's accession to the European Union in Athens in April 2003 and died in Budapest on 6 October 2015, aged 93.
arpanet: Traditional telephone networks used circuit switching, in which each call is allocated a dedicated end-to-end connection. In the early 1960s Paul Baran at the RAND Corporation challenged this model, researching systems that could keep operating during partial destruction, but the telecommunication establishment rejected his work. Donald Davies at the National Physical Laboratory in the United Kingdom independently arrived at a similar concept in 1965.

In February 1966 Bob Taylor lobbied the director of the Advanced Research Projects Agency, Charles M. Herzfeld, to fund a network project, and Herzfeld redirected one million dollars from a ballistic missile defense program. Taylor hired Larry Roberts as program manager in January 1967. After an April 1967 design session, Wesley Clark proposed using minicomputers as interfaces, which Roberts named Interface Message Processors. In 1969 the contract to build them went to Bolt Beranek & Newman.

The initial configuration linked UCLA, the Augmentation Research Center at Stanford Research Institute, the University of California, Santa Barbara, and the University of Utah. The nodes were connected electronically in 1969, but applications became possible only with the Network Control Program, implemented in 1970 under the leadership of Steve Crocker, then a graduate student at UCLA. The network was declared operational in 1971, and by 1981 it numbered 213 host computers.

In 1971 Ray Tomlinson of BBN sent the first network email, and a study in 1973 found that three-quarters of the traffic consisted of email. The network was a research project, and because of its government funding personal and commercial use was discouraged or prohibited.

Bob Kahn and Vint Cerf formulated the Transmission Control Program for internetworking, which joined separate networks into a network of networks. TCP/IP became the standard for the ARPANET on 1 January 1983, after the Department of Defense had made it the standard for all military computer networking. The National Science Foundation funded the Computer Science Network in 1981 and NSFNET in 1986.

The ARPANET was formally decommissioned on 28 February 1990. Its packet switching, decentralised design and protocols laid the foundation of the Internet. Charles Herzfeld said the network was not begun to build a command system that would survive a nuclear attack, as many later claimed, but out of frustration that researchers were geographically separated from the few powerful computers.
arquebus: The word comes from the Dutch haakbus, hook gun, and was applied to many kinds of firearm. It first meant a handgun with a hook-like lug under the barrel, used to steady it against battlements. In their earliest forms these were defensive weapons mounted on German city walls in the early 15th century. The first certain use of the term dates from 1364, when Bernabò Visconti, lord of Milan, recruited 70 archibuxoli, though these were almost certainly hand cannon.

A shoulder stock was added in Europe around 1470, and the matchlock mechanism appeared a little before 1475, making the arquebus the first firearm with a trigger. The dating is disputed: some scholars have proposed that the matchlock was invented in Turkey by 1465, while others find the evidence for a European origin overwhelming.

In the matchlock, a length of smouldering rope soaked in saltpetre, the match, was held in a clamp. Squeezing the trigger lowered it into a priming pan, and the flash passed through the touch hole to ignite the powder in the barrel. A heavy version, later called the musket, appeared around 1521 to pierce plate armour. In the later 16th century the standardised caliver allowed faster loading, since bullets fitted its bore. The matchlock arquebus is seen as the successor to the hand cannon and the forerunner of the flintlock musket.

The Ottomans used arquebuses in the 1440s, and arquebusiers fought at the second battle of Kosovo in 1448. In Europe the Black Army of Hungary under Matthias Corvinus used them in unusual numbers, one infantryman in four, though by about 1500 only some 10 per cent of Western European infantry carried firearms. At Cerignola in 1503 they played a decisive role.

The Mamluks scorned gunpowder weapons, and in 1514 an Ottoman army of 12,000 arquebusiers devastated a much larger Mamluk army. The arquebus was cheap, since a helmet, breastplate and pike cost about three and a quarter ducats and an arquebus a little over one, and an arquebusier could be trained in two weeks.

It reached India by 1500, Southeast Asia by 1540 and China between 1523 and 1548. Portuguese traders introduced it to Japan in 1543 on Tanegashima, and within ten years upwards of three hundred thousand were reported made there. Arquebusiers needed protection while reloading, so pikemen, archers, artillery or fortified wagons were paired with them. At Nieuwpoort in 1600 Maurice of Nassau used the countermarch volley technique.
arras: Arras stands in northern France at the confluence of the rivers Scarpe and Crinchon, on a large chalk plateau, 182 kilometres north of Paris. Its chalk was quarried to build the most prestigious buildings and houses, so that residents once nicknamed it La ville blanche, the White Town, while its clay was used for bricks. The Crinchon flows through the city underground, and the Scarpe, two-thirds of it turned into canals, runs on through Douai to join the Scheldt.

Stone tools of the Mousterian culture mark prehistoric settlement in the Scarpe basin. The town was founded on the hill of Baudimont by the Belgic tribe of the Atrebates, who named it Nemetocenna after a nemeton that probably stood there. The Romans renamed it Nemetacum or Atrebatum and made it an important garrison town. In the 4th century it was known for its arts and crafts and its textile trade. Germanic invaders took and destroyed it in 406 or 407, and in 428 the Salian Franks under Clodion took control of the region.

After Clovis I became a Catholic, a diocese was created at Arras in 499 and given to Saint Vaast, who established an episcopal see and a monastic community. It was suppressed in 580 to found the diocese of Cambrai, from which Arras re-emerged five centuries later. By 843 Arras was the seat of the County of Artois, which joined the royal domain in 1191. Arras was once part of the Spanish Netherlands, controlled by Spain from 1556 to 1714; Louis XIII conquered it in 1640, and it officially became part of France in 1659.

Arras is the prefecture of the Pas-de-Calais department, and 42,621 residents were counted in 2022. The city centre is marked by two squares, La Grand'Place and La Place des Héros, surrounded by 155 Flemish-Baroque townhouses built in the 17th and 18th centuries, most of which were so badly damaged in 1918 that they had to be restored. The town hall and its 75-metre belfry date from the early 16th century and were rebuilt after the First World War; the belfry has been a UNESCO World Heritage Site since 2005. Beneath the city lies the Boves, tunnels 10 metres down that sheltered residents in both world wars. Arras was a centre of trouvère poetry, and Maximilien de Robespierre was born there.
arrian: Arrian was born in Nicomedia, the provincial capital of Bithynia, between about 85 and 90 CE. His full Roman name, Lucius Flavius Arrianus, shows that he was a Roman citizen, and his family belonged to the Greek provincial aristocracy, with citizenship probably going back several generations to the time of the Roman conquest. While in Epirus, probably at Nicopolis, he attended the lectures of Epictetus and became his pupil. In Athens he came to be known as the young Xenophon, because his relationship to Epictetus resembled Xenophon's to Socrates.

About 126 he was a friend of the emperor Hadrian, who appointed him to the Senate. He became consul suffectus about 130 and in 132, though one scholar gives 131, Hadrian made him governor of Cappadocia, a post he held for six years. According to Cassius Dio, after the Bar Kokhba revolt was suppressed in 135, King Pharasmanes II of Iberia caused the Alani to invade neighbouring lands, including Cappadocia, where Arrian's legions halted them. Dio adds that the Alani were also persuaded by gifts from Vologaesus and stood in dread of Arrian. Lucian called him a Roman of the first rank with a life-long attachment to learning, and Arrian himself used the title of second Xenophon.

Eight of his works survive; only the Anabasis and the Indica are wholly intact. The Anabasis of Alexander, in seven books, is considered the best source on the campaigns of Alexander the Great, modelled on Xenophon's account of the march of Cyrus. Scholars have generally preferred Arrian to other surviving primary sources, though modern study of his method has qualified this. The Indica draws on Megasthenes for India and on the journal of Nearchus for the voyage in the Persian Gulf.

He recorded the teaching of Epictetus in the Discourses, which he says he published because his notes were being circulated without authority, and in the Enchiridion, a short handbook of Epictetus's principles. Other works include a Periplus of the Euxine Sea addressed to Hadrian, the Techne Taktike on cavalry and tactics (136 or 137), and a treatise on hunting with hounds meant as an addition to Xenophon. His Parthica, on Trajan's Parthian war, his history of Alexander's successors and several biographies are lost or survive in fragments. Pliny the Younger addressed seven letters to him.
arris: Arris lies at an altitude of 1100 m in the highlands of the Oued El Abiod, between the Djebel Zellatou to the east, the Djebel Ichmoul to the north and the Djebel El Azreg to the west. Route Nationale 31 links it with Biskra and Batna through the Aïn Tinn pass, at 1800 m. In the Chaoui Berber language of the Aurès the name is said to mean white lands or lion cub.

In antiquity the town is said to have been a centre of the Gaetuli, Berbers who rose against Rome. After the fall of the Western Roman Empire Masties ruled the Kingdom of the Aurès as an independent ruler, and the inscription found at Arris, dated between the end of the 5th century and the middle of the 6th, proclaims his Christian faith and his title of Imperator. Masties escaped conquest by the Vandals, and the historian Jérôme Carcopino judged him inflexibly loyal to the Roman ideal and the forms of imperial government.

On 18 December 1886 the French created the mixed commune of the Aurès, with its seat at Arris, divided into douars under native assistants. The ethnologists Thérèse Rivière and Germaine Tillion, who worked in the Aurès from 1934 to 1940, described a town with a clinic and a primary school but no business, and a police force of six men for 60,000 people. Mostefa Ben Boulaïd, one of the nine founders of the National Liberation Front, was born in Arris and led the Aurès zone from October 1954 until his death in March 1956. On 1 November 1954, the day of the Toussaint Rouge, the insurgents cut the town off for several hours.

Arris is a commune of the Batna wilaya made up of 15 neighbourhoods. With Tighanimine it forms the daïra of Arris, one of 21 in the wilaya. A half-marathon named after Mostefa Ben Boulaïd is run in the town each year.
arrow-cross-party: Ferenc Szálasi founded the party in 1935 as the Party of National Will. It was outlawed in 1937 and reconstituted in 1939 as the Arrow Cross Party, modelled fairly explicitly on the Nazi Party, although Szálasi often criticised the Nazi regime. Its roots lay partly in the antisemitism that followed the Hungarian Soviet Republic and Red Terror of 1919 and the White Terror that answered them. Its ideology, which Szálasi called Hungarism, combined nationalism, the promotion of agriculture, anti-capitalism, anti-communism and an antisemitism that he called a-Semitism, which held that Jews could not belong in European society. It also drew on Turanism and a belief in Hungarian superiority. The arrow cross emblem was taken to be a symbol of the Magyar tribes.

During the 1930s the party came to dominate working-class districts of Budapest, defeating the Social Democrats. In the only election it contested, in May 1939, it won 15 per cent of the vote and 29 seats, though most Hungarians could not vote. Its claims to a Greater Hungary clashed with German ambitions, and Hitler delayed his endorsement for years; the Horthy government banned it at the outbreak of the Second World War. After Germany occupied Hungary in March 1944, the new prime minister Döme Sztójay legalised it. In the spring and summer of that year more than 400,000 Jews were deported from the countryside, with the help of the Interior Ministry and the gendarmerie, both linked to the party.

In October 1944 Miklós Horthy negotiated a ceasefire with the Soviets. Germany launched Operation Panzerfaust, took him into custody and forced him to abdicate, and Szálasi became Leader of the Nation and head of a Government of National Unity on the same day. Soviet and Romanian forces were already deep in Hungary, and the government's authority shrank to a narrow band around Budapest. Arrow Cross death squads murdered Jews in the streets and shot them at the Danube. The party helped Adolf Eichmann restart deportations and sent some 80,000 Jews out of the city. Most of Budapest's Jews were saved by a handful of Jewish leaders and diplomats, among them Raoul Wallenberg, Angelo Rotta, Carl Lutz, Ángel Sanz Briz and Giorgio Perlasca.

The government fell when the Soviet Army took Pest at the end of January 1945, though Arrow Cross and German forces fought on in the west until the war ended in April. Over 6,200 murder indictments were served on Arrow Cross men within months of the war, and Szálasi was hanged in March 1946 with three of his key associates. A memorial of 2005 on the Danube bank in Budapest commemorates Jews shot there by Arrow Cross militiamen.
arsaces-i: Literary sources on Arsaces are very scarce and come from contradictory Greek and Roman accounts written centuries after his death, and modern scholars once doubted that he existed until studies and archaeological finds in the 1960s confirmed him. The most accepted view, from the geographer Strabo, is that he was a Scythian chieftain who led the Parni, one of the three tribes of the Dahae confederacy of Central Asia. Ammianus Marcellinus calls him a bandit of low birth, and some modern historians argue that he was a native Persian. The Parni had moved into Parthia, then under Seleucid rule, and by the middle of the 3rd century BCE they had adopted the Parthian language and Zoroastrianism. Arsaces himself was probably born and raised in Parthia.

About 250 BCE Arsaces and his followers seized Astauene, and probably about 247 BCE he was crowned at Asaak, a city he had founded, which became the Arsacid royal necropolis. Andragoras, governor of the Seleucid province of Parthia, had declared his independence from Seleucus II Callinicus, and the Parni took the northern region from him and then the rest of Parthia, killing him. They also conquered Hyrcania. When Seleucus II led an expedition against him in 228 BCE, Arsaces made peace with the Greco-Bactrian ruler Diodotus II to avoid a war on two fronts, and withdrew to Central Asia among the Apasiacae. Seleucus II had to leave because of trouble elsewhere in his empire, and Arsaces regained his territory.

According to Justin, he 'settled the Parthian government, levied soldiers, built fortresses, and strengthened his towns'. He founded Dara and Nisa, which served as the Arsacid royal residence until the 1st century BCE. His coins, minted at Nisa, show a seated archer in Iranian dress in place of the Seleucid Apollo, and they bear the title kārny, once held by prominent Achaemenid military leaders, rather than the royal title basileus.

Arsaces died in 217 BCE and was succeeded by his son Arsaces II. Earlier scholars, following Jean Foy-Vaillant in 1725, held that his brother Tiridates also ruled, but numismatic data, a study by Józef Wolski and the discovery at Nisa of an ostracon bearing the name of Arsaces led to the conclusion that Tiridates is fictional. An everlasting fire in his honour was still guarded at Asaak more than two centuries after his death. His name became a royal honorific used by all the Arsacid kings, and his dynasty ruled for four and a half centuries until the Sasanian Empire overthrew it in 224 CE.
arsenio-martinez-campos: Arsenio Martínez-Campos y Antón was born on 14 December 1831. In 1860 he fought in the Tetuán War in Morocco, where he took part in 16 actions and won the Cross of San Fernando and the rank of lieutenant colonel. He then joined the second French intervention in Mexico under General Juan Prim. After the Revolution of 1868 he asked for a posting to Cuba and fought the rebels in the Ten Years' War, rising to brigadier general, until he was judged too soft and replaced by Blas Villate, Count of Balmaceda.

Back in Spain he supported the coup of Manuel Pavía and commanded brigades against the Carlists with little success, then fought the cantonal forces in Alicante and Cartagena. Although he hid his monarchism poorly, Marshal Serrano gave him a division in 1874, with which he took part in the relief of Bilbao on 2 May. Placed under watch in Ávila, he escaped to Madrid. After the rising at Sagunto he became Captain General of Catalonia, where he defeated the Carlists and ended the civil war.

As captain general of Cuba from 1876 he arranged the peace treaty of Zanjón (Paz de Zanjón), which granted more autonomy to the island and freedom to rebels who had been enslaved, and led a few years later to the abolition of slavery in Cuba. After heading a conservative government in 1879, regarded as Cánovas's puppet, he left the Conservative Party and joined the Liberals; as Minister for War under Sagasta he founded the General Military Academy. After Alfonso XII died in 1885 he supported the regency of Queen Maria Christina.

Sent back to Cuba against the new rising for independence, he faced troops struck by malaria and yellow fever and rebels skilled in ambush. After a defeat in July he proposed to the prime minister that hundreds of thousands of rural Cubans be reconcentrated behind trenches and barbed wire in Spanish-held towns, but refused to carry the policy out himself and resigned; Valeriano Weyler replaced him. He later presided over the Supreme War and Navy Council for a month, and died at Zarauz on 23 September 1900.
arsinoe-ii: Arsinoe was the first daughter of Ptolemy I Soter and his second wife, Berenice I of Egypt. She may have been born in Memphis but was raised in Alexandria, where her father had moved his capital. Her later reputation as a patron of scholars suggests a good education, and she corresponded with the thinker Strato of Lampsacus, who may have been her tutor.

Around the age of 15 she married King Lysimachus, who was then about 60, and bore him three sons: Ptolemy Epigonos, Lysimachus and Philip. To put her sons in line for the throne, she had Lysimachus's first son, Agathocles, poisoned on a charge of treason. She reportedly paid for a rotunda in the sanctuary on Samothrace.

After Lysimachus died in battle in 281 BCE, Arsinoe fled to Cassandreia and married her half-brother Ptolemy Keraunos, a marriage made for political reasons since both claimed Macedonia and Thrace. When she conspired against him with her sons, Keraunos killed two of them, Lysimachus and Philip, while the eldest, Ptolemy, fled to the Dardanians. Arsinoe took refuge on Samothrace and then went to Alexandria to seek the protection of her brother Ptolemy II Philadelphus.

In Egypt she is believed to have instigated the exile of Arsinoe I, the wife of Ptolemy II, though this is unproven. She then married her brother, and the pair were given the epithet Philadelphoi, sibling-lovers; estimates of the date run from about 275 to 272 BCE. Her role was unprecedented in the dynasty. She had towns named for her, appeared on coinage and contributed to foreign policy, including Egypt's victory in the First Syrian War. According to Posidippus she won three chariot races at the Olympic Games.

Arsinoe's rites of burial and deification took place at Mendes, where she had been a priestess, and are recorded on the Mendes stele with Ptolemy II's decree announcing her cult. Every temple in Egypt had to hold her statue beside the main god. An annual priesthood, the Canephorus of Arsinoe Philadelphus, was set up in Alexandria by 269 BCE, and its holder was named in the dating formula of official documents until the late second century BCE.

At Cape Zephyrium the admiral Callicrates of Samos built a sanctuary where she was worshipped as Aphrodite Euploia, and similar sanctuaries stood in ports such as Citium, Delos and Thera, linking her to protection from shipwreck. Her name became a naturalised Egyptian personal name.
arslantepe: Arslantepe, also known as Melid, was an ancient city on the Tohma River, a tributary of the upper Euphrates that rises in the Taurus Mountains. It has been identified with the archaeological site of Arslantepe near Malatya, Turkey. The mound covers about 4 hectares and rises about 30 metres above the plain. UNESCO named it a World Heritage Site in 2021 under the name Arslantepe Mound. A team from Sapienza University of Rome began excavating in 1961, later led by Marcella Frangipane.

A modest village of the Late Ubaid period occupied the site in the early fourth millennium BCE. In the Late Uruk period, dated about 3350 to 3000 BCE, four terraced and largely interconnected monumental buildings were built, two of them identified as temples, with many vases and clay sealings.

A palace complex of this phase held a hall of weapons with a cache of nine swords and daggers cast from arsenic-copper, three of the swords inlaid with silver. They date from about the 33rd to the 31st century BCE and are the earliest swords known. The phase ended in a violent fire.

Around 3000 BCE a large cist burial, the Royal Tomb, was built in a low-level settlement. It held two adolescent human sacrifices and a man of about 40, buried with metal goods, carnelian and rock crystal beads, and a sword. Kura-Araxes pottery then appeared. In the Late Bronze Age the city was the fortified centre of a region of the kingdom of Isuwa, and around 1350 BCE Šuppiluliuma I of the Hittites conquered it, using it as a base against the Mitanni king Tushratta.

After the Hittite empire it became the centre of the independent Luwian Neo-Hittite state of Kammanu, or Malizi, from the 12th to the 7th century BCE, with a palace and monumental stone lions and rulers. Tiglath-Pileser I made it pay tribute, and Sargon II sacked it in 712 BCE, after which the Cimmerians and Scythians invaded Anatolia and it declined.

Arslantepe is a source for early metalworking and trade. Its metal shows that it probably took part in the ore trade between the Black Sea coast and Upper Mesopotamia, and some objects from the Royal Tomb follow Kura-Araxes traditions, with metal traced to the northern Caucasus. Martina Massimino argues in 2023 that the Maikop-Novosvobodnaya kurgan group, rather than Kura-Araxes, built the tomb and ran this trade, citing recent finds at Basur Höyük.
arsuf: Arsuf was known in antiquity as Apollonia, in the Byzantine period as Sozusa, and to the crusaders as Arsur. It lay on a sandy area on the Mediterranean coast that ends towards the sea in a cliff, about 34 kilometres south of Caesarea. There is no archaeological evidence for a settlement before the Persian period, around 500 BCE, and the first record of the Greek name Apollonia comes from the mid-4th century BCE. A long-standing suggestion is that the Greek name came from reading the Canaanite god Resheph as Apollo, whose name would survive in the later Arabic Arsūf.

Under the Seleucids Apollonia was a port town, and by the mid-4th century BCE it was probably the main city and harbour of the southern Sharon Plain. Under Roman rule it prospered as the chief commercial and industrial centre between the Poleg and Yarkon rivers, though an earthquake partly destroyed it in 113 CE. The Roman proconsul Gabinius found it ruined in 57 BCE and had it rebuilt. By 449 it was called Sozusa and had a bishop, and it surrendered on terms to the Sasanian general Shahrbaraz in 614. The town fell to the Muslims in 640 and in 809 the Abbasids violently removed the Samaritans who lived there. Fear of Byzantine fleets led to its first fortified wall.

King Baldwin I took the town after a siege by land and sea, the crusaders rebuilt its walls and it became the Lordship of Arsur in the Kingdom of Jerusalem. The Muslims recaptured it in 1187, and it fell again to the crusaders on 7 September 1191 after the Battle of Arsuf, fought nearby between the forces of Richard I of England and Saladin. Balian of Arsuf built new walls, a large castle and a new harbour in 1241, and Louis IX of France repaired its ramparts in 1251. From 1261 the Knights Hospitaller ruled it. In 1265 the Mamluk sultan Baibars captured it after 40 days of siege; its inhabitants were killed or sold as slaves, and the town was razed.

The site was never again a city, and by the 14th century the geographer Abulfeda recorded it as without inhabitants. It lies within the municipality of Herzliya, just north of Tel Aviv, and was excavated intensively from 1994. Apollonia National Park opened to the public in 2002. Before the excavations the visible remains included the medieval city wall and moat, a crusader castle with a double wall and a port with jetties sheltered by a sandstone reef.
art-nouveau: The new style had its roots in Britain, in the floral designs of William Morris and the Arts and Crafts movement, which called for better treatment of the decorative arts and took inspiration from medieval craftsmanship and nature. Early prototypes include the Red House, with interiors by Morris and architecture by Philip Webb (1859), and Arthur Mackmurdo's chair and book cover of 1883.

The term Art Nouveau was first used in the 1880s in the Belgian journal L'Art Moderne to describe Les Vingt, twenty painters and sculptors seeking reform. The Franco-German dealer Siegfried Bing popularised it by opening the Maison de l'Art Nouveau in Paris in 1895, though he wrote in 1902 that it had been merely the name of a house meant as a rallying point for young artists.

Art Nouveau used the sinuous curves of plants and flowers, asymmetry and whiplash lines, and modern materials such as iron, glass, ceramics and later concrete. Early Belgian and French work took forms from lilies, vines and flower stems, and borrowed butterfly and dragonfly patterns from Japanese art. One aim was to break down the distinction between fine arts and applied arts.

The first Art Nouveau town houses, by Paul Hankar and Victor Horta, were built almost simultaneously in Brussels in 1892 and 1893, and Horta's innovation lay in the interior, where iron and glass opened up space and let in light.

The style took local forms. In Barcelona Antoni Gaudí's Modernisme used organic forms in the Palau Güell. The Vienna Secession was founded in April 1897 by Gustav Klimt, Koloman Moser, Josef Hoffmann and others. German Jugendstil took its name from the Munich journal Jugend, founded in 1896. In the United States the firm of Louis Comfort Tiffany played the central role.

The Paris Exposition Universelle of 1900 marked the high point of the style, attracting nearly fifty million visitors between April and November. By 1914 and the beginning of the First World War Art Nouveau was largely exhausted, and in the 1920s Art Deco and then modernism replaced it as the dominant style. It began to receive more positive attention from critics in the late 1960s, and a major exhibition of Hector Guimard's work was held at the Museum of Modern Art in 1970.
arta-greece: The first settlement in the area dates to the 9th century BCE. Ambracia was founded as a colony of Corinth in the 7th century BCE. In 294 BCE it was given to Pyrrhus, king of the Molossians and of Epirus, who made it his capital and a base for attacking the Romans, and adorned it with a palace, temples and theatres. In 146 BCE it became part of the Roman Republic. Arta is first attested under that name in 1082, when the Normans under Bohemond besieged it. In the Komnenian period it flourished as a commercial centre with links to Venice, and by 1157 it was a bishopric.

After the fall of Constantinople to the Fourth Crusade, the Partitio Romaniae of 1204 assigned the city to Venice, but in 1205 Michael I Komnenos Doukas came to Arta and founded the principality known as the Despotate of Epirus. The city remained its capital for most of its history, and it saw much building: the Church of the Parigoritissa and the Church of the Kato Panagia, and fortifications after 1227. Its exports to Venice and Ragusa included dried meat, lard, ham, furs and indigo.

Later the city changed hands often. Troops of the Empire of Nicaea took it after the Battle of Pelagonia in 1259, but John I Doukas soon recovered it. Andronikos II Palaiologos attacked it unsuccessfully in 1292, and the Angevins besieged it in 1303. Epirus passed to the Orsini family in 1318 and to Andronikos III Palaiologos in 1335. Arta fell to the Serbian king Stefan Dušan in 1347, was held by Albanian rulers from about 1367, and was captured by Carlo I Tocco in 1416. In 1449 it fell to the Ottomans, who called it Narda.

Arta lies on the Arachthos River, on the site of ancient Ambracia, whose remains include walls, the ruins of a temple of Apollo and a small theatre. The Castle of Arta was built by Michael I Komnenos Doukas in the early 13th century, though its present form is largely post-Byzantine. The palace of the Despots has vanished completely, but many churches survive, among them the cathedral Church of the Paregoretissa, built about 1290 by Nikephoros I Komnenos Doukas and his wife Anna Palaiologina Kantakouzene, and the Monastery of Saint Theodora, which holds the tomb of the city's patron, Theodora of Arta. The city was annexed to the Greek Kingdom in 1881.
artabanus-iv: Artabanus IV, also known as Ardavan IV, is incorrectly called Artabanus V in older scholarship. The name is the Latin form of the Greek Artábanos, from an Old Persian name meaning the glory of Arta. He was the younger son of Vologases V, who died in 208. His elder brother Vologases VI succeeded as king of the Parthian Empire around that year, and his rule was unquestioned for a few years, until Artabanus rebelled. The struggle between the brothers most likely began about 213.

Artabanus took much of the empire, including Media and Susa, while Vologases VI seems to have kept only Seleucia, where he minted coins. The Roman emperor Caracalla sought to exploit the conflict. He asked Vologases to send two refugees, a philosopher named Antiochus and a certain Tiridates, hoping for a pretext to invade, but Vologases sent them in 215 and denied him one. Caracalla's invasion of Armenia, led by the freedman Theocritus, ended in disaster. He then asked Artabanus to marry his daughter, and Artabanus declined; whether the offer was sincere is disputed. Artabanus contained Caracalla's forces at Nisibis in 217, and peace the following year left the Arsacids most of Mesopotamia. His brother continued to mint coins and challenge him.

Meanwhile the Sasanian family had risen in its native Pars, and its prince Ardashir I began conquering neighbouring regions such as Kirman. At first this did not alarm Artabanus. According to al-Tabari, whose work was probably based on Sasanian sources, the two agreed to meet at Hormozdgan at the end of April, but Ardashir arrived early, dug a ditch and took a spring. His 10,000 cavalry included men in flexible chain armour, while Artabanus's larger army was hampered by lamellar armour. The battle was fought on 28 April 224. Artabanus was defeated and killed, which ended the Arsacid era and began 427 years of Sasanian rule.

Ardashir had Artabanus's chief secretary, Dad-windad, executed and took the title shahanshah. He had two rock reliefs carved at Ardashir-Khwarrah, today Firuzabad, to celebrate his victory. The leading Parthian noble families, the Seven Great Houses of Iran, kept their power under Sasanian overlordship, and much of the early Sasanian cavalry was made up of Parthian nobles. Efforts to restore the Arsacid empire were made in the late 6th century by Bahram Chobin and Vistahm, but they failed.
artavasdes-ii-of-armenia: Artavasdes II, also called Artavazd II, was a member of the Artaxiad dynasty, the son and successor of Tigranes the Great, who had ascended the throne of a still powerful and independent state. Like his father, he used the title King of Kings, as his coins show. Plutarch described him as a well-educated man with a great fondness for all things Greek, an accomplished scholar who composed Greek tragedies and histories. He had two sons, Artaxias II and Tigranes III, and a daughter who possibly married King Archelaus of Cappadocia.

Artavasdes was king from 55 to 34 BCE. As an ally of Rome, he advised the proconsul Marcus Licinius Crassus, who was preparing to invade Parthia, to go through Armenia and offered 10,000 cavalry and 30,000 infantry, reasoning that Parthian cavalry would be less potent in the Armenian highlands. Crassus refused and took the direct route through Mesopotamia. The Parthian king Orodes II invaded Armenia and persuaded Artavasdes to a marriage alliance between the crown prince Pacorus I and Artavasdes' sister. News of Crassus' defeat and death at Carrhae reached the two kings during a performance of The Bacchae at the Armenian court.

In 36 BCE Artavasdes allied himself with Mark Antony in his Parthian campaign, supplying, according to Plutarch, six thousand horse and seven thousand foot. He persuaded Antony to attack his enemy Artavasdes of Atropatene, but when Antony left Armenia he abandoned the Roman cause, though he later gave refuge and supplies to the defeated Romans.

In 34 BCE Antony marched into Armenia and, after Artavasdes refused to come to Nicopolis, arrested him at Artaxata. His son Artaxias II was elected as successor but fled to the Parthian king after a lost battle. Artavasdes was taken to Alexandria and led in Antony's triumphal procession in golden chains; he refused to render homage to Cleopatra VII by proskynesis. In 31 BCE, after Antony's defeat at Actium, Cleopatra had him decapitated. An Armenian legend recorded by Movses Khorenatsi tells of him cursed by his father and imprisoned by spirits inside Mount Ararat, while the people of Armenia await his return.
artaxata: Artaxias I built the city on a peninsula of nine hills at the confluence of the Araks and Metsamor rivers, in the Ostan Hayotsʻ canton of the province of Ayrarat, perhaps on the remains of an older Urartian settlement. The name is of Iranian origin, a shortening of Artaxšas-šāt, the joy of Artaxias. Its citadel stood on the height later called Khor Virap, where Gregory the Illuminator was imprisoned by Tiridates III of Armenia. Strabo and Plutarch call it the Armenian Carthage and tell an apocryphal story that Hannibal chose the site.

Excavations show paved streets, bathhouses, markets, workshops and administrative buildings, with a treasury, a mint and a customs house; Armenia's first theatre was built here. Armenians, Greeks, Jews and Syrians lived in the city, which stood on trade routes linking Persia and Mesopotamia with the Caucasus, the Black Sea and Asia Minor. Tigranes II moved his capital to Tigranocerta, but Artaxata withstood Lucullus in 69 BCE and an assault by the Parthians. To save it from Pompey, Tigranes submitted to the Romans. Mark Antony marched on it in 34 BCE and took King Artavasdes II captive.

After Corbulo razed it, Nero sent architects to help Tiridates I rebuild it, and it was briefly renamed Neroneia. Trajan placed a Roman garrison there, and Roman forces under Statius Priscus destroyed it again in 163/64. The Sasanian king Shapur II ravaged it in the late 360s. After the partition of Armenia it was one of three authorised points of trade between Sasanian Iran and the Eastern Roman Empire. In 449 Armenia's leaders met there in council against the threats of Yazdegerd II, and the city was destroyed once more in the rebellion that followed. It then declined as Duin rose, and shifting rivers and floods probably led to its abandonment.

The site was identified in the 1920s, and excavations began in 1970. It lies 8 kilometres south of the modern city of Artashat in the Ararat Province, near the monastery of Khor Virap, and remains of the city walls and some buildings are still visible. In 2024 archaeologists from Armenia and Germany found there the remains of Armenia's oldest known church, an octagonal building dated to the mid-4th century.
artaxerxes-i: Artaxerxes I was the fifth King of Kings of the Achaemenid Empire, ruling from August 465 to December 424 BCE. He was the third son of Xerxes I. Greek sources surname him Long-handed, allegedly because his right hand was longer than his left. He came to the throne after Xerxes was murdered in 465 BCE by Artabanus, commander of the royal bodyguard, with the help of a eunuch, Aspamitres. Greek writers disagree on details, but after Artaxerxes discovered the murder he killed Artabanus and his sons.

From 460 to 454 BCE he faced a revolt in Egypt led by Inaros II, who with Athenian help defeated the Persian army of the satrap Achaemenes. Megabyzus defeated the Athenians in 454 BCE after a two-year siege, and Inaros was captured and taken to Susa.

After the Persian defeat at the Battle of the Eurymedon, around 469 BCE, fighting stopped. Artaxerxes adopted a strategy of weakening Athens by funding its enemies in Greece. Fighting resumed in 450 BCE at the Battle of Cyprus, and when Cimon achieved little, hostilities ceased. Later sources say that the Peace of Callias was agreed among Athens, Argos and Persia in 449 BCE, but the existence of a formal treaty is disputed.

Artaxerxes gave asylum to Themistocles, the victor of Salamis over his father, after his ostracism from Athens, and gave him Magnesia, Myus and Lampsacus. Themistocles learned Persian customs and language.

Josephus and several ancient traditions identify him as the Ahasuerus of the Book of Esther. In Ezra 7 a king Artaxerxes commissions the scribe Ezra to take charge of the religious and civil affairs of the Jews. The text does not say whether Artaxerxes I or Artaxerxes II is meant; most scholars hold that Ezra lived under Artaxerxes I. In his twentieth year Nehemiah, his cup-bearer, told him of the plight of Jerusalem, and the king sent him with letters of safe passage to rebuild the city walls.
artaxerxes-iii: Artaxerxes III, whose personal name was Ochus, was the legitimate son of Artaxerxes II and his wife Stateira. Before he became king he was a satrap and commander of his father's army. The Roman writer Justin tells how his eldest brother Darius, the heir, was executed for plotting against their father, and how Ochus, with the support of some eunuchs, drove another brother, Ariaspes, to suicide and had the favoured illegitimate son Arsames killed. Ochus was then appointed crown prince. After taking the throne he murdered much of the royal family to secure his position.

On his accession he ordered the satraps of western Anatolia to disband their mercenary forces, to consolidate royal power. In 356 BCE he tried to dismiss Artabazus II from his satrapy, and Artabazus revolted, defeated royal satraps with Athenian and Theban help, and fled to Macedonia in 354 BCE. About 351 BCE Artaxerxes invaded Egypt, but Nectanebo II, supported by Greek mercenaries, defeated him, and Phoenicia, Anatolia and Cyprus then declared independence. Idrieus of Caria reduced Cyprus, and Artaxerxes led a large army against Sidon, whose king Tennes tried to buy a pardon by betraying 100 citizens. The Persian king had them killed and then 500 more. Sidon was burnt and forty thousand people died.

After years of preparation Artaxerxes invaded Egypt again, led in person, with Greek mercenaries under Mentor of Rhodes. He created three divisions of shock troops, Pelusium and Bubastis surrendered, and Nectanebo abandoned the country. Egypt returned to Persian rule after about six decades. The king had city walls destroyed, looted temples and levied high taxes, and the native religion was persecuted. He also supported the city of Perinthus against the siege of Philip II of Macedon.

In late August or September 338 BCE the court eunuch Bagoas had Artaxerxes poisoned through his physician. Bagoas had most of the king's sons murdered and put the young Arses on the throne as Artaxerxes IV. His death proved a problem for Persia and may have weakened the country, which Alexander the Great later conquered. Artaxerxes had begun a building programme at Persepolis, with a new palace and the Unfinished Gate, and his tomb was cut into the mountain behind the platform, next to his father's. Silver coins issued while he was in Egypt carry an inscription in an Egyptian script reading Artaxerxes Pharaoh.
artaxiad-dynasty: The Artaxiad dynasty, also called Artashesian, ruled the Kingdom of Armenia until the Romans overthrew it. Its founder, Artaxias I, claimed kinship with the Orontids, the previous ruling dynasty. According to the geographer Strabo, Artaxias and Zariadres were Seleucid generals given Greater Armenia and Sophene by Antiochus III. After the Seleucid defeat at Magnesia in 190 BCE they made themselves autonomous kings, and the Roman Senate recognised them in the Treaty of Apamea in 188 BCE.

Scholars now think the two were local figures related to the Orontids. Their Irano-Armenian names and Artaxias's boundary stones, in which he calls himself an Orontid, point that way. Matthew P. Canepa regards the Artaxiads as Iranian dynasts. The later Armenian historian Movses Khorenatsi tells of a conflict in which Artaxias killed King Orontes.

Under Tigranes the Great, who reigned 95 to 55 BCE, Armenia was briefly the most powerful state east of the Roman Republic. He brought the largely autonomous nakharars under central control, took large territories from the Parthians and founded Tigranocerta as a new capital. In 83 BCE the Greeks of the Seleucid Empire offered him the Seleucid crown, and his realm then reached as far south as Acre. It stretched, for a short time, from the Caspian to the Mediterranean.

Tigranes had allied with Mithridates VI of Pontus. In 69 BCE a Roman army under Lucullus routed him outside Tigranocerta and Artaxata, and in 66 BCE Pompey forced his surrender, reduced Armenia to its former borders and let him keep the throne as an ally. His heir Artavasdes II was captured by Mark Antony in 35 BCE and later executed in Egypt. After Artaxias II was murdered, civil war between pro-Roman and pro-Parthian parties followed, and Armenia became a Roman protectorate under Augustus. The dynasty ended in chaos around 12 CE.

Hellenistic influence on Armenia peaked under the Artaxiads. Their coins followed Greek models with Greek inscriptions, and some call the kings Philhellenes. Cleopatra, the wife of Tigranes the Great, invited Greeks such as the historian Metrodorus of Scepsis to court, and Artavasdes II composed Greek tragedies himself. Their religion remained, in the words of James R. Russell, staunchly Zoroastrian. The Arsacid dynasty emerged only later as their undisputed successors.
artaxias-i: Armenia had been ruled since the 5th century BCE by the Orontid dynasty, probably of Iranian origin. At the end of the 3rd century BCE the Seleucid king Antiochus III the Great appointed Artaxias and Zariadres as military governors of Greater Armenia and Sophene. Strabo calls them Antiochus's generals, but boundary stones with Aramaic inscriptions show that Artaxias called himself an Orontid king and the son of Zareh, so that he and Zariadres were members of local branches of the dynasty and not outsiders. The later historian Movses Khorenatsi says Artaxias defeated and killed the preceding king Eruand, that is Orontes, in a war for the throne, though in one scholar's view his account adapts the battle of Alexander and Darius in the Alexander Romance.

After the Seleucid defeat at the Battle of Magnesia, Artaxias and Zariadres revolted and declared themselves independent kings in Greater Armenia and Sophene, and in 188 BCE the Roman Senate recognised them. They allied to expand their dominions, and the Seleucid king Seleucus IV did not fight them. Artaxias's kingdom, first centred on the Araxes valley, grew into Iberian land and especially Media Atropatene, and the Kura River became its northern and north-eastern border. According to Strabo, the union of these lands led their people to speak the same language, Armenian, though imperial Aramaic remained the language of court and government. Khorenatsi says he ordered the delimiting of villages and farmland, and about twenty boundary stones with Aramaic inscriptions found in modern Armenia confirm it.

He founded Artaxata, on the left bank of the Araxes, which served as capital until the 2nd century CE and became a major administrative and commercial centre. By 179 BCE he was strong enough to mediate in a war among the rulers of Asia Minor, but his plan to annex Sophene failed. In 165 or 164 BCE the Seleucid king Antiochus IV Epiphanes defeated and briefly captured him, apparently releasing him once he recognised Antiochus's authority, though his control of Greater Armenia seems not to have suffered.

Artaxias died around 160 BCE and was succeeded by his son Artavasdes I. His other known son was Tigranes I. He is regarded by modern scholars as the founder of independent Armenian statehood, and the historian Hakob Manandian called him the first true organiser of Greater Armenia. He features in the Armenian folk epic Vipasank', which Khorenatsi drew on; it places in his time an invasion by the Alans that actually belongs to the 1st century CE. In 2001 a statue of him was erected in the central square of Artashat.
artemis: In ancient Greek religion Artemis was the goddess of hunting, the wilderness, wild animals, transitions, nature, vegetation, childbirth, care of children and chastity. She was thought of as an unmarried maiden and as one of the three major virgin goddesses, alongside Athena and Hestia. She protected children, especially girls, and animal cubs, and was worshipped and feared as a goddess of childbirth and midwifery along with Eileithyia and Hera. She was believed to grant health or to send illness and death to women and children.

Classically she is a young huntress in a short skirt and hunting boots, with a quiver and a golden or silver bow, often roaming the mountains with a retinue of nymphs. Homer calls her Potnia Theron, mistress of animals, a title linked with images of a woman between two animals that go back to the Bronze Age. The deer was sacred to her, and the etymology of her name is uncertain.

Artemis was worshipped throughout ancient Greece with many local variations. Her best-known cults were on Delos, in Attica at Brauron and Mounikhia, and in Sparta, where the Spartans sacrificed to her before a campaign. The cult at Ephesus, where she was worshipped chiefly as a mother goddess like the Phrygian Cybele, eventually surpassed the others in fame. At Patras the Laphria festival centred on an annual bonfire into which domestic and wild animals were thrown alive.

Common practices included animal sacrifice, hymns, dances and processions, and votive offerings of jewellery, clothing or pottery. Her temples often stood outside city limits or between land and water. Her virginity may relate to her role as huntress, since hunters traditionally abstained from sex before a hunt.

Myths tell how the hunter Actaeon was turned into a stag and killed by dogs, in some versions for seeing Artemis bathing, and how she demanded the sacrifice of Iphigenia after Agamemnon killed her sacred deer. In the Trojan War she took the side of the Trojans. The Romans identified her with Diana and with the moon goddess Selene, although no record has been found of the Greeks calling Artemis a lunar deity. Her name survives in the genus Artemia, the brine shrimp.
artemisia-i-of-caria: Artemisia's father was Lygdamis I, satrap of Halicarnassus, and her mother came from Crete. She took the throne after the death of her husband because their son Pisindelis was still a youth. Besides Halicarnassus she ruled the nearby islands of Kos, Nisyros and Kalymnos. Her grandson, Lygdamis II, was satrap of Halicarnassus when Herodotus was exiled from the city. A later author, Thessalus, says that Xerxes gave her the island of Kos to be laid waste after it refused to give earth and water.

Artemisia fought as an ally of Xerxes I in the second Persian invasion of Greece and commanded ships at Artemisium and at Salamis in 480 BCE. At Salamis she led the forces of Halicarnassus, Kos, Nisyros and Calyndos and supplied five ships, which Herodotus says had the second-best reputation in the fleet after those of Sidon. Before the battle Xerxes asked his commanders whether to fight at sea. All advised it except Artemisia. In Herodotus's account she told Mardonius that the enemy's seamen were stronger than the Persians as men are to women, and she urged the king to wait, because the Greeks would soon disperse.

Xerxes was pleased but followed the others. During the Persian defeat an Athenian ship pursued Artemisia, and she rammed a friendly ship from Calyndos, commanded by Damasithymos, which sank. The Athenian captain Ameinias, thinking she had changed sides, turned away. Xerxes, watching, believed she had sunk a Greek vessel and said that his men had become women and his women men. Polyaenus adds that she carried two sets of colours, Persian and Greek. After the defeat she advised Xerxes to withdraw and leave Mardonius in Greece, and Xerxes sent her to Ephesus to look after his illegitimate sons.

A legend recorded by Photius thirteen centuries later says that she fell in love with a man from Abydos named Dardanus and, when he ignored her, blinded him while he slept. An oracle told her to leap from the rock of Leucas, and she died there. Her son Pisindelis succeeded her as tyrant of Caria.

Herodotus admired her decisiveness and intelligence, despite her support for Persia. Justin writes that one might see womanish fear in a man and manly boldness in a woman. Thessalus, in a speech, called her a cowardly pirate. A figure of Artemisia stood among the Persian figures in the Persian portico in the marketplace of Sparta.
artemisia-ii-of-caria: Artemisia was the sister and later wife of Mausolus, ruler of Caria. Mausolus was a satrap of the Achaemenid Empire who nevertheless held the status of king or dynast of the Hecatomnid dynasty. Her father is known to have been Hekatomnos, but the identity of her mother is less clear. One view makes her mother Aba, a daughter of Hyssaldomos and sister of Hekatomnos, but other scholars hold that the sibling marriages of the Hecatomnids were purely symbolic.

After the death of her brother and husband she reigned for two years, from 353 to 351 BCE. Her accession prompted a revolt in some island and coastal cities, which objected to a female ruler. She governed on the same principles as Mausolus and supported the oligarchical party on Rhodes. She is known as a commander of a fleet and played a part in the affairs of the Aegean after the decline of Athenian naval superiority.

According to the account of the Rhodian expedition, Rhodes sent a fleet against her without knowing that Mausolus had built a secret harbour. She hid rowers and marines and let the Rhodians into the main harbour. The Rhodian men who disembarked were killed in the marketplace, and she then sailed her own men back to Rhodes in the captured ships, where they were welcomed and took over the island. Polyaenus tells how she took Latmus by ambush while a procession drew its people out of the city, though he may have meant Artemisia I. Her monument at Rhodes was later called the Abaton, meaning inaccessible.

She became known for her grief at the death of Mausolus. She is said to have mixed his ashes into her daily drink and to have pined away during the two years she survived him. She induced the most eminent Greek rhetoricians to praise him, and she built at Halicarnassus the Mausoleum, which Antipater of Sidon listed among the Seven Wonders of the Ancient World. Boccaccio described her as a lasting example of chaste widowhood. Artists from the Renaissance on, among them Rembrandt, painted her drinking the ashes. According to Pliny, the plant genus Artemisia was named after her.
artemisinin: Sweet wormwood was an old remedy. In 1596 Li Shizhen recommended tea made from it specifically for the symptoms of malaria in his Compendium of Materia Medica. The modern search began in 1967, when the People's Liberation Army set up Project 523, a plant screening programme. According to the account given, it and its early clinical work were ordered by Mao Zedong at the request of North Vietnamese leaders, to help their malaria-ridden army. In the course of this research Tu Youyou found artemisinin in the leaves of Artemisia annua in 1972.

Named qinghaosu, or compound of green-blue wormwood, it was one of many candidates tested from a list of nearly 2,000 traditional medicines. Tu also found that a low-temperature extraction could isolate an effective substance, and she says she was influenced by Ge Hong's instruction of 340 CE to steep the herb in cold water. Her team's results were published in the Chinese Medical Journal in 1979.

Artemisinin and its derivatives are sesquiterpene lactones containing an unusual peroxide bridge, an endoperoxide ring responsible for their antimalarial action, and few other natural compounds have one. Because artemisinin itself is poorly soluble and poorly absorbed, semisynthetic derivatives were made: those of dihydroartemisinin from 1976, and artesunate, arteether and artemether in 1986. Project 523 also developed drugs to be used in combination with it, including lumefantrine, piperaquine and pyronaridine.

In the late 1990s Novartis filed a Chinese patent for the combination of artemether and lumefantrine, giving the first artemisinin-based combination therapy, Coartem, at reduced prices to the World Health Organization. In 2006 the WHO called for an immediate halt to single-drug artemisinin preparations, to lessen the risk of resistance, and clinical evidence of resistance in south-east Asia was first reported in 2008. Also in 2006, a team at the University of California, Berkeley reported yeast engineered to produce artemisinic acid, the basis of a semisynthetic route that Sanofi developed at Garessio in Italy; the WHO prequalified its artesunate on 8 May 2013.

Tu received the Lasker-DeBakey Clinical Medical Research Award in 2011, and on 5 October 2015 half of the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine. The other half went to William C. Campbell and Satoshi Ōmura for avermectin.
arthashastra: The Sanskrit title can be rendered as a treatise on political science, economic science or simply statecraft, since the word artha has a broad range of meanings. Artha, prosperity or material security, is one of the four aims of human life in Hinduism, beside dharma, kama and moksha. The text names two compilers, Kautilya (or Kautalya) and Vishnugupta, and a later interpolation and the traditions of the Gupta era and the Middle Ages identified Kautilya with Chanakya. Scholarship has questioned that identification, and the main studies since 1965 reject it.

Patrick Olivelle and McClish hold that the work grew in layers: earlier arthashastras dating from the 2nd century BCE to the 1st century CE were compiled in the 1st century CE, and a major redaction followed in the 2nd or 3rd century CE. Stylistic differences point to several hands, and some details fit the first centuries CE better than the Mauryan age.

The surviving text has 15 books, 150 chapters and 180 topics. It covers the training of a king, the work of the superintendents who ran mines, workshops, customs, agriculture and shipping, civil and criminal law, spying, diplomacy and war. It also deals with ministers, marriage and the remarriage of women, forests and wildlife, and taxation. The economy it describes is mixed: mines were owned by the state but leased to private parties, and private enterprise was taxed and regulated.

The ideal ruler is the sage king, who masters lust, anger, greed, conceit, arrogance and foolhardiness. On war, the text advises that where progress is equal, peace is to be preferred, since war brings losses, expense and absence from home. Books on foreign policy set out the sixfold strategy and the theory of the circle of states, and the text recommends a network of trained spies, including the use of women to sow quarrels among the chiefs of an enemy council.

The work was influential until the 12th century, when it disappeared from view. R. Shamasastry rediscovered a manuscript in 1905, published the Sanskrit text in 1909 and the first English translation in 1915. Verses of the work have also been found on fragments from Buddhist monasteries in north-west China, Afghanistan and north-west Pakistan, among them the Spitzer Manuscript, of about 200 CE.

In 1919 Max Weber wrote that Machiavelli's The Prince was harmless beside it. Later readers disagree about its character: Roger Boesche compared its state to a welfare-minded surveillance state, while Thomas Trautmann stresses that it recognises private property and land sales, though under rules of first refusal that do not make a free market.
arthur-conan-doyle: Arthur Ignatius Conan Doyle was born on 22 May 1859 at 11 Picardy Place, Edinburgh. His father, Charles Altamont Doyle, was born in England of Irish Catholic descent, and his mother, Mary, née Foley, was Irish Catholic. In 1864 the family was scattered because of Charles's growing alcoholism, and it came together again in 1867. His father died in 1893 in the Crichton Royal, Dumfries, after many years of psychiatric illness.

From 1876 to 1881 Doyle studied medicine at the University of Edinburgh Medical School and began writing short stories as a student. His first published piece, "The Mystery of Sasassa Valley", appeared in Chambers's Edinburgh Journal on 6 September 1879.

Doyle served as a doctor and surgeon on two sea voyages and then ran an unsuccessful medical practice in Portsmouth. His first Sherlock Holmes work, A Study in Scarlet, was written in three weeks and accepted by Ward Lock & Co on 20 November 1886 for £25. From "A Scandal in Bohemia" (1891) the Holmes stories appeared monthly in The Strand Magazine. Ambivalent about the character, he had Holmes killed in "The Final Problem" (1893), but public outcry brought him back in The Hound of the Baskervilles (1901), and he wrote Holmes stories until 1927. He also wrote The Lost World (1912), featuring Professor Challenger.

In 1900 he served as a volunteer physician at Bloemfontein during the Second Boer War and wrote a widely translated pamphlet defending the United Kingdom's role in it. He believed it earned him his knighthood from King Edward VII in 1902. He twice stood unsuccessfully for Parliament, in 1900 and 1906.

Doyle personally investigated two closed cases. The first, in 1906, concerned George Edalji, a lawyer of mixed British and Indian descent accused of threatening letters and animal mutilations at Great Wyrley; Edalji was exonerated, and the case partly led to the establishment of the Court of Criminal Appeal in 1907. Raised a Catholic, Doyle became agnostic as a young adult and later a spiritualist. His public support for the Cottingley Fairies, later confirmed as a hoax, led to a falling-out with the magician Harry Houdini. He died of a heart attack at Windlesham Manor, Crowborough, on 7 July 1930, aged 71.
arthur-evans: Arthur Evans was born on 8 July 1851 at Nash Mills, Hemel Hempstead, the first child of John Evans and Harriet Ann Dickinson. His father worked in the paper mill owned by the family of Harriet's father, John Dickinson, and profits from the mill later helped fund Evans's excavations at Knossos and his publications. He entered Harrow School in 1865 and matriculated at Brasenose College, Oxford, on 9 June 1870, where he read Modern History. His sight was blurry beyond a close distance, and he carried a cane he called Prodger to explore his surroundings.

Evans returned to Oxford with his wife Margaret in January 1883 and became Keeper of the Ashmolean Museum, then in a chaotic state of transition. He led the excavation of an Iron Age cemetery at Aylesford in Kent, published in 1890, and concluded that its culture was closely related to the continental Belgae, which remains the modern view. In 1898 he reported for the Manchester Guardian on the violence against Crete's Muslim minority and condemned religiously motivated violence from both sides.

The first excavation at Knossos was begun in 1877 by Minos Kalokairinos, until the Ottoman authorities stopped it. Evans bought the land with private funds and began work in March 1900, with Duncan Mackenzie and the architect Fyfe and 32 diggers. Within months they uncovered a large part of what he called the Palace of Minos, an intricate set of over 1,000 interlocking rooms that included workshops and wine presses and served as a storage, religious and administrative centre. He resigned as Keeper in 1908, became president of the Society of Antiquaries in 1914, and was knighted in 1911.

From what he found at Knossos and across the eastern Mediterranean, Evans concluded that he must distinguish the Minoan civilisation from Mycenaean Greece. He found about 3,000 clay tablets, which he transcribed and published in Scripta Minoa; some are now missing, so his transcriptions are the only record of their marks. He saw that the scripts were two separate systems, which he named Linear A and Linear B, with A the earlier, and he also defined an earlier pictographic writing. Linear B proved to be Greek, and Linear A has not been convincingly deciphered. His classifications and transcriptions have been of great value to scholars of Mycenaean Greece.

He was elected a Fellow of the Royal Society and a founding Fellow of the British Academy in 1901. He lived at Youlbury from 1894 until his death in 1941 and left part of his estate to the Boy Scouts.
arthur-i-duke-of-brittany: Arthur was born on 29 March 1187, the son of Duchess Constance of Brittany and Duke Geoffrey II, who died before his birth. Through Geoffrey he was a grandson of Henry II of England and Eleanor of Aquitaine. On 11 November 1190 he was named heir presumptive of his uncle Richard I and betrothed to a daughter of King Tancred of Sicily, a plan that came to nothing when Emperor Henry VI conquered Sicily in 1194. In 1196 Constance had him proclaimed Duke of Brittany and her co-ruler, at the age of nine, and he was spirited away to the court of Philip II of France to be raised with Philip's son Louis.

When Richard died on 6 April 1199 he named his brother John as heir, fearing that Arthur, aged twelve, was too young and under Philip's influence. Many Norman nobles preferred Arthur, who declared himself Philip's vassal, and Philip recognised his right to Anjou, Maine and Poitou. From 18 April Arthur styled himself Duke of Brittany, Count of Anjou and Earl of Richmond. John won over William des Roches, seneschal of Anjou, who took Arthur and Constance prisoner on 22 September. The Treaty of Le Goulet of May 1200 had Philip recognise John as Richard's heir and abandon support for Arthur.

In 1202 Arthur campaigned in Normandy with Philip's support, and Poitou rose in his favour. He besieged his grandmother Eleanor of Aquitaine in the Château de Mirebeau, but John surprised him on 31 July 1202 and Arthur was captured on 1 August and imprisoned at Falaise under Hubert de Burgh.

According to the chronicler Ralph of Coggeshall, John ordered two servants to blind and castrate Arthur, but de Burgh refused and spread word that the duke had died of natural causes. Arthur was later moved to Rouen under William de Braose and vanished in April 1203. Nothing is recorded of him afterwards, and it is generally believed that John killed him. The Margam Annals say John killed him with his own hand and threw the body into the Seine. William de Braose was also rumoured to be the killer, and his wife Maud later accused John of the murder. Neither the Bretons nor Philip knew what had happened.

Arthur left no known issue. His sister Eleanor remained John's prisoner for life, and he was succeeded in Brittany by his half-sister Alix of Thouars. In 1268 Henry III gave the manor of Melksham to Amesbury Abbey for the souls of Eleanor and Arthur. His death is central to Shakespeare's The Life and Death of King John.
arthur-iii-duke-of-brittany: Arthur was born on 24 August 1393 at the Château de Suscinio, a younger son of Duke John IV of Brittany and his third wife, Joanna of Navarre, and so a member of the ducal House of Montfort. After his father's death his mother married Henry IV of England and became Dowager Queen of England. He was called Richemont because he claimed the earldom of Richmond, which previous dukes of Brittany had held; the English never recognised his tenure and gave the title to John Plantagenet, Duke of Bedford, in 1414.

Arthur sided with the Armagnac faction against the Burgundians in their civil conflict of 1410 to 1414 and entered the service of the Dauphin Louis, Duke of Guyenne, whose widow he later married. He was wounded and captured at Agincourt on 25 October 1415. The English released him in 1420, and he helped persuade his brother Duke John to sign the Treaty of Troyes. In 1422 the English made him Duke of Touraine, but they refused him a high command and in 1424 he returned to the Dauphin's allegiance. With the support of Yolande of Aragon he became Constable of France in 1425, and he persuaded his brother, John V, to conclude the Treaty of Saumur with Charles VII on 7 October 1425.

His temper and the peace John made with the English in 1427 led to his expulsion from court, where Georges de la Trémoille stayed supreme for six years. As Constable he fought with Joan of Arc at the Battle of Patay on 18 June 1429. La Trémoille was overthrown in June of the following year, and Arthur resumed the war against the English and took action against the plundering bands known as routiers or écorcheurs. By 1435 he had regained influence and helped arrange the Treaty of Arras between Charles VII and Philip III, Duke of Burgundy.

After the Treaty of Tours in May 1444 he reorganised the army, creating the compagnies d'ordonnance and trying to organise the militia of the francs archers. In 1449 he reconquered nearly all the Cotentin with his nephew, and he commanded the French army at Formigny on 15 April 1450, which sealed the reconquest of Normandy, then besieged Caen. On the death of his nephew Peter II on 22 September 1457 he became Duke of Brittany, though he refused, like his predecessors, to do homage to the French king. He died on 26 December 1458, with no legitimate issue, and was succeeded by his nephew Francis II.
arthur-phillip: Arthur Phillip was born on 11 October 1738 in the parish of All Hallows, Bread Street, London. His father, Jacob Phillip, an immigrant from Frankfurt, is variously described as a language teacher, a ship owner, a merchant captain or a common seaman, and died in 1739. His mother, Elizabeth Breach, was the widow of a seaman. From 1751 to 1753 he attended the Greenwich Hospital School, a charity school for the sons of poor seafarers, where he learned literacy, arithmetic and navigation, including cartography. He then became an apprentice on the whaling ship Fortune, which hunted whales near Svalbard, before enlisting in the Royal Navy in 1755.

Phillip served under his mother's cousin, Captain Michael Everitt, on HMS Buckingham, HMS Union and HMS Stirling Castle during the Seven Years' War, including the Battle of Minorca in 1756 and the Siege of Havana. He became a lieutenant on 7 June 1761 and went on half-pay in 1763. He later served in the Portuguese Navy against Spain, was recalled to the Royal Navy in 1778 and, from 1784 to 1786, was employed by the Home Office official Evan Nepean to report on French naval arsenals such as Toulon.

In 1786 he was appointed to command the First Fleet of eleven ships, which was to found a penal colony in New South Wales. Finding Botany Bay unsuitable, he settled at Port Jackson. The flag was raised on 26 January 1788, and his government was formally inaugurated on 7 February. Phillip had asked for trained convicts but received only twelve carpenters and a few men with farming knowledge, and he faced severe problems of labour, discipline and supply. He set up civil courts that applied to everyone, convicts included, and clashed with marine officers under Major Robert Ross who refused any duty but guard duty.

His orders were to live in amity with Aboriginal people, and he treated them as under the protection of British law. The Eora avoided the settlement in its first year, attacked colonists who trespassed on their lands, and cultural differences led eventually to conflict. When Phillip sailed for Britain on 11 December 1792 for treatment of kidney stones, the colony had land grants, systematic farming and a water supply.

Phillip resigned the governorship on medical advice. After recovering he returned to naval duty in 1796, commanded the Hampshire Sea Fencibles, retired from active service in 1805 and rose to Admiral of the Blue on 4 June 1814. He died at Bath on 31 August 1814. Port Phillip, Phillip Island and Phillip Street in Sydney bear his name, and memorials stand in Bath Abbey, near Saint Paul's Cathedral in London and in Sydney's Royal Botanic Garden.
arthur-seyss-inquart: Seyss-Inquart was born on 22 July 1892 in Stannern, a German-speaking village near Iglau in Moravia, an area that formed a German linguistic island in a Czech-speaking region. His father, a school principal, was Czech and had changed his surname from Zajtich; his mother was German. The family moved to Vienna in 1907, and he studied law at the University of Vienna. In August 1914 he enlisted with the Tyrolean Kaiserjäger and served in Russia, Romania and Italy, and he was decorated for bravery several times. After the war he set up a law practice in 1921, and in 1933 he was invited to join the cabinet of Chancellor Engelbert Dollfuss.

Under Kurt Schuschnigg he became a State Councillor in 1937. He was not at first a member of the Austrian National Socialist party, but by 1938 he had become a respectable frontman for it. In February 1938 Schuschnigg made him Minister of the Interior after Hitler threatened military action. On 11 March Schuschnigg resigned in the face of a German invasion, and President Wilhelm Miklas reluctantly appointed Seyss-Inquart chancellor. German troops crossed the border the next day at his telegraphed invitation, a telegram drafted beforehand. Hitler chose full Anschluss over a puppet state; Seyss-Inquart drafted the act making Austria the province of Ostmark, joined the Nazi Party on 13 March and became its governor.

After the invasion of Poland he was deputy to Hans Frank in the General Government until 18 May 1940. After the Dutch capitulation on 15 May 1940 he became Reichskommissar for the occupied Netherlands, answering directly to Hitler. He authorized about 800 executions, some reports putting the total above 1,500, and imposed a collective fine of 18 million guilders after the strikes of May 1943. Around 530,000 Dutch civilians were forced to work for the Germans. Of about 140,000 registered Jews, only 30,000 survived the war.

He was arrested on 5 May 1945 on the Elbe Bridge in Hamburg. At the Nuremberg trials he faced four charges and was acquitted of conspiracy but convicted on the others and sentenced to death by hanging; the judgment stressed his reign of terror in the Netherlands. He denied knowledge of the shooting of hostages and said his conscience was untroubled. He was hanged on 16 October 1946.
arthur-st-clair: Arthur St. Clair was born in Thurso, Caithness, on 23 March 1737 by the modern calendar, probably the son of William Sinclair, a merchant, and Elizabeth Balfour. He reportedly attended the University of Edinburgh and was apprenticed to the physician William Hunter. In 1757 he bought a commission in the Royal American Regiment and served in the French and Indian War, at the capture of Louisburg under General Jeffery Amherst and under General James Wolfe at the Battle of the Plains of Abraham. He married Phoebe Bayard in 1760, resigned his commission in 1762 and settled in the Ligonier Valley of Pennsylvania, where his mills made him the largest landowner west of the Allegheny Mountains.

In January 1776 he became colonel of the 3rd Pennsylvania Regiment, fought at the Battle of Trois-Rivières and took part in George Washington's crossing of the Delaware on 25–26 December 1776; many biographers credit him with the plan that led to the capture of Princeton. Promoted major general in February 1777, he was given Fort Ticonderoga and on 5 July 1777 abandoned it to the larger army of General John Burgoyne. A court-martial in 1778 cleared him, but he never held a command again in the war.

Elected President of the Continental Congress on 2 February 1787, he presided while it passed the Northwest Ordinance. As governor of the Northwest Territory he named Cincinnati after the Society of the Cincinnati and issued Maxwell's Code, the territory's first written laws. The Treaty of Fort Harmar of 1789 was rejected by the tribes as illegitimate, and in the war that followed St. Clair, made senior officer of the army in March 1791, led the expedition that ended in his defeat of 4 November 1791, in which more than 600 American soldiers and scores of camp followers were killed.

Cleared by an investigation, he gave up his commission in March 1792 at Washington's request and remained governor. A Federalist, he angered the Ohio Democrat-Republicans, and President Thomas Jefferson removed him in 1802; the first Ohio Constitution gave the state a weak governor largely in reaction to his rule. He died in poverty in Greensburg, Pennsylvania, on 31 August 1818. St. Clair County in Illinois, Missouri and Alabama and St. Clairsville in Ohio are among the places named after him.
arthur-wellesley-1st-duke-of-wellington: Arthur Wellesley was born into an Anglo-Irish family of the Protestant Ascendancy, as the Hon. Arthur Wesley, the sixth of nine children of Garret Wesley, 1st Earl of Mornington, and Anne, Countess of Mornington. The exact date and place of his birth are not known; biographers mostly follow newspaper evidence that he was born on 1 May 1769, the day before his baptism at St. Peter's Church in Dublin.

The family was short of money, and on his mother's advice his brother Richard asked the Duke of Rutland, then Lord Lieutenant of Ireland, to consider Arthur for an army commission. He was gazetted ensign in the 73rd Regiment of Foot on 7 March 1787 and became aide-de-camp to successive lords lieutenant, in a post whose duties were mainly social. In 1798 he changed the spelling of his surname to Wellesley.

He reached Calcutta in February 1797, and his brother Richard, Lord Mornington, soon became Governor-General of India. In the Fourth Anglo-Mysore War against Tipu Sultan he ended the conflict with a victory at Seringapatam in 1799 and was appointed governor of Seringapatam and Mysore. As a major general he won a decisive victory over the Maratha Confederacy at the Battle of Assaye in 1803. In the Peninsular War he left Cork on 12 July 1808 and defeated the French at Roliça and Vimeiro. Recalled to face a Court of Enquiry after the Convention of Sintra, which he had not signed, he was cleared. He was promoted field marshal after the victory at Vitoria in 1813.

After Napoleon's first exile in 1814 he served as ambassador to France and was made Duke of Wellington. When Napoleon escaped from Elba on 26 February 1815, Wellington took command of a British-German and Dutch army in the Netherlands beside Blücher's Prussians. After Ligny and Quatre Bras he withdrew to a ridge south of Waterloo, where on 18 June he met Napoleon for the first time. He was prime minister from 1828 to 1830 and for under a month in 1834, oversaw the Roman Catholic Relief Act 1829 and strongly opposed the Reform Act 1832.

Wellington died at Walmer Castle in Kent on 14 September 1852, aged 83, of the after-effects of a stroke. He was given a state funeral in London on 18 November 1852, one of a small number of British subjects so honoured. The nickname Iron Duke relates to his political career, and its use is often disparaging; it may date from the iron shutters fitted at Apsley House in 1832 against rioters. Napoleon called him a Sepoy General, while Tsar Alexander I called him the conqueror of the world's conqueror.
