article-58: The first section defined a counter-revolutionary action as any act aimed at overthrowing, undermining or weakening the power of the workers' and peasants' Soviets and the governments of the Soviet Union and its republics, or the external security of the state and the main achievements of the proletarian revolution. Article 58-1 was updated with new sub-articles in force from 8 June 1934. The other Soviet republics had laws of the same kind: in Ukraine it was Article 54 of the penal code, in Belarus Article 63.

The sub-articles reached far beyond armed revolt. Contacts with foreigners for counter-revolutionary purposes, help to the international bourgeoisie and urging a foreign power to war or blockade were punished like an armed uprising. If a member of the armed forces fled abroad after treason, his relatives could be imprisoned for 5–10 years or exiled to Siberia for 5 years, even if they had only lived with him. Section 14, added on 6 June 1927, made counter-revolutionary sabotage, the careless or wilful failure to carry out defined duties, punishable by at least a year's loss of freedom and in aggravated cases by shooting.

Prisoners sentenced under Article 58 were often released without the right to settle within 100 km of large cities. Because one section made propaganda and agitation against the Soviet Union a crime and another punished those who failed to report it, the law gave the secret police a free hand to imprison anyone it suspected and became a political weapon. It was also applied to people outside the Soviet Union: in the Soviet occupation zone of Germany, people suspected of opposing the Stalinist regime, for example through contacts with organisations in the Western zones, were interned as spies under it, and 66% of the inmates of the NKVD special camp at Bautzen were held on this ground.

In The Gulag Archipelago of 1973 Aleksandr Solzhenitsyn mocked the breadth of the law, writing that there was no step, thought, action, or lack of action under the heavens which could not be punished by the heavy hand of Article 58. The code was largely rewritten after Nikita Khrushchev denounced Stalinism.
articles-of-confederation: The push for cooperation among the colonies began with the Albany Congress of 1754 and Benjamin Franklin's Albany Plan. On 12 June 1776, a day after appointing the Committee of Five for the Declaration of Independence, the Second Continental Congress resolved to appoint a committee of thirteen, one member from each colony, to draft a constitution for a union of the states. John Dickinson chaired it and presented its results on 12 July 1776. Long debates followed on state sovereignty, the powers of Congress, a judiciary, western land claims and voting, and Congress twice had to leave Philadelphia to evade British troops. It approved the Articles on 15 November 1777.

The Articles contain a preamble, thirteen articles, a conclusion and a signatory section. Article I named the confederacy The United States of America, and the second article declared that each state kept its sovereignty, freedom and independence and every power not expressly delegated. Congress could make war and peace, negotiate with foreign countries and settle disputes between the states, but it had no power of taxation and could only request money from the states. Most decisions, including changes to the Articles, needed the approval of all thirteen state legislatures, and there was no president, executive agency or judiciary.

Ratification took longer than expected. Virginia ratified first, on 16 December 1777, and twelve states had done so by February 1779. Maryland held out until the states with western land claims, especially Virginia, showed they would cede their claims west of the Ohio River, and it ratified on 2 February 1781. Congress was told on 1 March and proclaimed the Articles the law of the land.

Congress could not compel the states to supply troops or funds, and the Continental Army nearly starved in several winters of war. Too few delegates attended to form a quorum, so the 1783 Treaty of Paris waited months for ratification. The Confederation Congress did take two lasting actions, the Land Ordinance of 1785 and the Northwest Ordinance, which set rules for surveying land and admitting new states. After the Annapolis Convention of September 1786, a convention met in Philadelphia on 25 May 1787, and its delegates wrote a new constitution instead of amending the Articles. The federal government under the Constitution replaced the old one on 4 March 1789.
artificial-cardiac-pacemaker: In 1889 John Alexander MacWilliam reported in the British Medical Journal that an electrical impulse applied to a human heart in asystole caused a ventricular contraction, and that a rhythm of 60 to 70 beats a minute could be evoked by impulses at the same spacing. In 1950 the Canadian engineer John Hopps designed and built the first external pacemaker, working from observations by the surgeons Wilfred Gordon Bigelow and John Callaghan at Toronto General Hospital. It used vacuum tubes and mains power, was crude and painful in use, and carried a risk of electrocuting the patient. Paul Zoll and others made smaller devices from 1952, powered by a large rechargeable battery.

In 1958 the engineer Earl Bakken of Minneapolis made the first wearable external pacemaker, a transistorised device in a small plastic box, for a patient of C. Walton Lillehei. In 1959 Seymour Furman and John Schwedel first demonstrated temporary transvenous pacing, inserting the electrode through a vein of the arm.

A pacemaker keeps an even heart rate when the heart's natural pacemaker gives an inadequate or irregular beat or when its electrical conduction system is blocked. A permanent pacemaker is implanted under the skin below the collarbone, with one or more electrode leads passed along a vein into the chambers of the heart under X-ray guidance. Most modern devices are pacing on demand: they sense the heart's own rhythm and stimulate it only if no beat comes within a set interval, most commonly one second. They are programmable from outside the body. Biventricular pacemakers pace both sides of the heart in heart failure, and implantable cardioverter-defibrillators combine pacing with defibrillation.

The first implantable devices suffered from the short life of the available mercury batteries. In the late 1960s several companies, among them ARCO in the United States, developed isotope-powered pacemakers, and in early 1969 researchers at the National Heart Institute tested a nuclear-powered one that used heat from plutonium-238 in a titanium case. The lithium iodide cell developed in 1971 by Wilson Greatbatch overtook them, and lithium cells became the standard. In 1982 Anthony Rickards of the National Heart Hospital in London invented the first rate-responsive, or dynamic, pacemaker. In 2013 several firms announced capsule-sized leadless pacemakers, inserted through a catheter in the leg.
artsakh-historical-province: Artsakh lay on the easternmost edge of the Armenian Plateau, in the eastern part of the Lesser Caucasus, and was mostly mountainous and forested. Its area is estimated at 11,528 square kilometres. It bordered the Armenian provinces of Utik to the east, Gardman to the north-east and Syunik to the south-west, and the Arax river formed its southern boundary. Its two largest rivers, the Gargar and the Tartar, flow east to join the Kura. Important places, mostly fortified towns, included Parisos, Tigranakert, Sodk and Tsar, and in the early Middle Ages the castle of Khachen served for a long time as the centre of Artsakh. According to the 7th-century Ashkharatsoyts, the province had twelve cantons.

Strabo's "Orchistene", a region that supplied the most cavalry of the Armenian provinces, is believed to be a rendering of the name, and some scholars identify Artsakh with lands named in the inscriptions of Urartian kings. Many etymologies have been proposed, among them a derivation from a word for trees or bushes, from the Armenian word for grapevine, and from a root meaning rocky or mountainous.

Historians disagree on how early Artsakh belonged to Armenia. Robert Hewsen holds that it joined only after 189 BCE, when Artaxias I began to expand the Armenian kingdom, while many Armenian historians argue that it was ruled and populated by Armenians from the formation of the Armenian people. The early Armenian historian Movses Khorenatsi traces its ruling families to Aran, a descendant of the patriarch Hayk. After Armenia's conversion to Christianity in 301, Artsakh became a stronghold for missionaries, and around 410 Mesrop Mashtots opened the first Armenian school at Amaras.

By the Peace of Acilisene in 387 the Armenian kingdom was partitioned between the Roman and Sasanian empires, and Caucasian Albania, then a Sasanian ally, received Artsakh, Gardman and Utik. After the Battle of Avarayr in 451 it became a centre of resistance to Sasanian Iran.

From the 7th to the 9th century the Arab caliphates dominated the South Caucasus. In the early 9th century the Armenian princes Sahl Smbatian and Esayi Abu-Muse revolted against Arab rule and set up the principalities of Khachen and Dizak, and in 852 to 855 they fought the Abbasid commander Bugha, who failed 28 times to take Ktich Castle. From about 1000 the rulers of Khachen styled themselves Kings of Albania or of Artsakh, and later the principality split into smaller parts, the Khamsa Melikdoms of Karabakh. Artsakh then became a vassal of successive Turkic and Iranian powers, until it was ceded to Imperial Russia under the Treaty of Gulistan.
artuqid-dynasty: The Artuqids were a Turkoman dynasty rooted in the Döger branch of the Oghuz Turks and followed the Sunni Muslim faith. Their founder, Artuk, son of Eksük, was a general first under Malik-Shah I and then under the Seljuk emir of Damascus, Tutush I, who made him governor of Jerusalem in 1086. Artuk died in 1091, and his sons Sökmen and Ilghazi were expelled from Jerusalem by the Fatimid vizier al-Afdal Shahanshah in 1098. They established themselves in Diyarbakır, Mardin and Hasankeyf in al-Jazira, where they came into conflict with the Seljuk sultanate.

Sökmen defeated the Crusaders at the Battle of Harran in 1104. Ilghazi took control of Aleppo in 1118 at the request of the qadi Ibn al-Khashshab, and the next year defeated the Principality of Antioch at the Battle of Ager Sanguinis. After pillaging the County of Edessa he made peace with the Crusaders. In 1121 he marched into Georgia and was defeated by David IV of Georgia at the Battle of Didgori. He died in 1122, and in 1128 Aleppo fell under the control of Zengi, atabeg of Mosul.

After the death of Belek Ghazi the Artuqids divided into the branches of Harput, Hasankeyf and Mardin. Under Nur al-Din Zengi they became vassals of the Zengids. In a later settlement with the Seljuk sultan Kilij Arslan II, Saladin gained control of Artuqid territory, and the Artuqids stayed in nominal command of al-Jazira under Ayyubid rule. The Hasankeyf branch took Diyarbakır in 1198 and moved its centre there, but the Ayyubids destroyed it in 1231 after it tried to ally with the Seljuks. The Sultanate of Rum conquered Harput in 1234.

The Mardin branch lasted longest, as a vassal of the Ayyubids, the Sultanate of Rum, the Il-Khanate, the Timurids and the Qara Qoyunlu. Its ruler Qara Arslan, who reigned from 1260 to 1292, submitted to the Mongol Hulegu. The Qara Qoyunlu captured Mardin in 1409 and ended Artuqid rule.

Despite constant warfare the Artuqids left many monuments and commissioned mosques, bazaars, bridges, hospitals and baths. They made notable additions to the walls of Diyarbakır, including the towers Ulu Beden and Yedi Kardeş, commissioned in 1208 by Nasir al-Din Mahmud. A large caravanserai in Mardin and the Malabadi Bridge are still in use. The door of the Great Mosque of Cizre is a unique example of Artuqid metalworking, and their courts sponsored literature in Arabic. In 1206 Nasr al-Din Mahmud commissioned the earliest known manuscript of Ibn al-Razzaz al-Jazari's book on mechanical devices.
artur-gorgei: Görgei was born Johannes Arthur Woldemár Görgey at Toporc in Upper Hungary, now Toporec in Slovakia, on 30 January 1818. His family was impoverished and noble, of Zipser German descent, and had settled in the Szepes region under King Géza II of Hungary; it converted to Protestantism during the Reformation. He left the army on his father's death in 1845 and studied chemistry at the University of Prague under Josef Redtenbacher.

His research on coconut oil, begun in 1847 and sent to the Imperial and Royal Academy of Vienna on 21 May 1848, found lauric and decanoic acids in it and separated the fatty acids by the solubility of their barium salts. In March 1848 he married Adéle Aubouin, a French Huguenot, in Prague.

After the government called for officers on 17 May 1848, he joined the Hungarian army as a captain. At Ozora on 7 October 1848 his plans forced two Croatian forces to surrender, with almost 9,000 prisoners. He clashed with Lajos Kossuth over military operations and disapproved of the Declaration of Hungarian Independence, and Kossuth hesitated to name him commander-in-chief.

At the end of March 1849 Kossuth named him acting commander, since Vetter had fallen ill and the corps commanders György Klapka, Lajos Aulich and János Damjanich said he was the ablest. He led the victorious Spring Campaign, which freed almost all of Western Hungary, and he was made Minister of War.

When the Russians joined the Austrians in mid-June 1849 and advanced from all sides, he faced a far superior enemy. Promised reinforcements did not come, because Mór Perczel had been defeated at Káty on 7 June, and several experienced generals were unavailable. He was named dictator in the last days. After a council of officers on 11 August decided on surrender, in the hope of milder terms from the Russians, he surrendered his army to them at Világos on 13 August 1849.

Russian intercession spared him the executions that befell many of his generals. The Austrians took him to Klagenfurt, where he lived under strict police supervision, chiefly in chemical work, until the amnesty of 1867. After the Compromise he returned to Hungary, failed to find suitable work, and lived at Visegrád in a home provided by his brother István. Ferenc Deák helped him return, and each year he laid violets on Deák's grave.

Kossuth's Letter from Vidin, written after the surrender, bred a lasting hatred, and many Hungarians believed him a traitor, as he had foreseen at the council of 11 August. Research in the 20th century challenged this verdict and restored his reputation as one of the most talented Hungarian generals of the century. He died in Budapest on 21 May 1916, at the age of 98.
arturo-alessandri: Arturo Fortunato Alessandri Palma was born on 20 December 1868, son of Pedro Alessandri Vargas and Susana Palma Guzmán. His grandfather Pietro Alessandri Tarzi was an Italian immigrant from Tuscany who reached Chile from Argentina in 1821. He studied law at the University of Chile, graduated in 1893 and married Rosa Ester Rodríguez Velasco, with whom he had nine children. In 1897 he entered politics as a Liberal and represented Curicó for nearly twenty years. In 1915 he won a hard-fought Senate contest in Tarapacá against Arturo del Río and earned the nickname Lion of Tarapacá.

In 1920 Alessandri was the Liberal Alliance candidate and narrowly beat Luis Barros Borgoño of the Coalition Party. His speeches for the working class alarmed conservatives. Congress, controlled by the opposition, refused to pass his reforms, and Chile was politically paralysed for most of 1924. On 3 September 1924 a group of 56 officers protested over pay in the incident called ruido de sables, and on 5 September a military committee led by Colonel Marmaduque Grove and Major Carlos Ibáñez del Campo demanded his ministers' dismissal and a labour code. Congress passed the laws within hours, including sickness insurance, an eight-hour day and rights for labour unions. Alessandri resigned on 9 September, though Congress granted him leave instead, and left for Italy.

A coup in January 1925 led by Grove returned power to him, and he took office again on 20 March 1925. A new Constitution, approved by plebiscite on 30 August and promulgated on 18 September 1925, strengthened the presidency against the legislature. He also created a Central Bank. In his later period, from 1932 to 1938, the Treasury Minister Gustavo Ross led the recovery from the crisis of 1929 and public works followed, among them the National Stadium in Santiago. His government repressed a demonstration in the Marusia massacre, which was followed by the La Coruña massacre, and it put down the rural rebellion at Ránquil by force.

After the presidency Alessandri won a Senate seat in a by-election, was reelected in 1949 for Santiago and became President of the Senate. He influenced the elections of 1942 and 1946. He died in office as President of the Senate on 24 August 1950, aged 82, and his son Fernando succeeded him there. Another son, Jorge Alessandri, was president of Chile from 1958 to 1964.
arturo-toscanini: Arturo Toscanini was born in Parma, in Emilia-Romagna, the son of a tailor. He won a scholarship to the Parma Conservatory, where he studied the cello. Living conditions there were harsh and strict, and the menu consisted almost entirely of fish; in his later years he steadfastly refused to eat anything that came from the sea.

Toscanini's reputation as an operatic conductor of unusual authority and skill gradually supplanted his cello career. He was entrusted with the world premieres of Puccini's La bohème and Leoncavallo's Pagliacci. By 1898 he was principal conductor at La Scala, where he remained until 1908, returning as music director from 1921 to 1929. In December 1920 he brought the La Scala Orchestra to the United States and made his first recordings, for the Victor Talking Machine Company.

He had become disillusioned with Fascism before the March on Rome of October 1922 and repeatedly defied Mussolini, refusing to display his photograph or conduct the Fascist anthem Giovinezza at La Scala. In 1936 he resigned from the New York Philharmonic, and David Sarnoff, president of the Radio Corporation of America, proposed a radio orchestra for him. He conducted his first broadcast concert with the NBC Symphony Orchestra on 25 December 1937 in Studio 8-H at Rockefeller Center. Between 1948 and 1952 he conducted ten concerts telecast on NBC.

Toscanini conducted the world premieres of Pagliacci, La bohème, La fanciulla del West and Turandot, which have become part of the standard operatic repertoire, and the world premiere of Samuel Barber's Adagio for Strings. He was especially known for his performances of Beethoven, Brahms, Wagner, Richard Strauss, Debussy, Rossini, Verdi, Boito and Puccini.

At La Scala he pushed through reforms in the performance of opera, insisting on dimming the house lights during performances. His biographer Harvey Sachs wrote that he believed a performance could not succeed artistically unless unity of intention was first established among singers, orchestra, chorus, staging, sets and costumes. He disliked recording, especially the acoustic method, and began recording regularly only in 1938, at the age of seventy. He appeared three times on the cover of Time magazine, in 1926, 1934 and 1948.
artvin: Artvin stands on a hill overlooking the Çoruh River near the Deriner Dam, about 30 kilometres inland from the Black Sea. Above the town is a fortress that once lay within the medieval Georgian district of Nigali, with a single circuit wall around the summit, several rooms and a large donjon at the west.

Artifacts from the Bronze Age and earlier have been found. The area was part of Colchis and of Greater Armenia, and was invaded first by Scythians and then by Muslim armies led by Habib, son of Caliph Uthman, who held it from 853 CE until the Byzantines conquered it in 1023. The Principalities of Tao-Klarjeti arose in the 7th and 8th centuries and made the region one of the most important religious centres of Georgia. The Seljuk Turks conquered it in 1064, and the Safavids took it in 1502.

The Ottomans under Mehmed II defeated the Empire of Trebizond and brought the eastern Black Sea coast and its mountain hinterland under their control, and on 13 July 1551 their hold on Artvin was secure. After about 250 years the area was ceded to Russia following the war of 1828 to 1829, recovered, and ceded again after the Russo-Turkish War of 1877 to 1878. Much of the largely Muslim Georgian population moved west. British troops arrived in 1918, followed by the Democratic Republic of Georgia, and the Treaty of Kars in 1921 ceded Artvin to Turkey.

Artvin is the seat of Artvin Province and Artvin District, with 25,841 people in 2021, and the home of Artvin Çoruh University. The castle, also called Livane, was built in 937, and Ottoman buildings include the Salih Bey mosque of 1792 and the fountain of Çelebi Efendi of 1783. The Camili (Macahel) area is a UNESCO Biosphere Reserve. Artvin is also a former Armenian Catholic see, established in 1850 and listed as a titular see since 1972.
arunachal-pradesh: Arunachal Pradesh, meaning Land of the Dawn-Lit Mountains, has an area of 83,743 km2. It shares borders with Bhutan in the west and Myanmar in the east, and a 1,129 km border with China's Tibet Autonomous Region in the north at the McMahon Line. Its highest peak is Kangto, at 7,060 metres. Historical Indian texts describe its mountains, the Aruna Mountains, as the place where the sun rises. The state has among the highest diversity of mammals and birds in India.

Little is known of the ancient history of the region apart from the northwest, which came under the Monpa kingdom of Monyul, under Tibetan influence, between 500 BCE and 600 CE. In the 17th century the 5th Dalai Lama, Ngawang Lobsang Gyatso, who gained political supremacy over Tibet in 1642, imposed a tax called Khrey over Monyul and ordered fortresses called Dzong built in the Monpa area as centres of administration and tax collection. The tax was carried to Tawang Monastery and then to Lhasa.

After the annexation of Assam following the First Anglo-Burmese War, the British inherited the Ahom Kingdom's system of payments to the frontier tribes, known as posa, and set out to curb headhunting, civil wars and slavery. In the 19th century there was no urgency to demarcate the border. After independence in 1947, the People's Republic of China maintained that the McMahon Line was not valid. The North-East Frontier Agency was renamed Arunachal Pradesh on 20 January 1972 and became a union territory, and on 20 February 1987 it became a state.

Itanagar is the capital and largest town. The 2011 census counted 1,383,727 people, at 17 per square kilometre the least densely populated state of India. About 23 major tribes and 100 sub-tribes live there, among them the Nyishi, the largest group, and the Adi, Apatani, Galo, Tagin, Singpho and Nocte. China claims nearly four-fifths of the state as Southern Tibet.
arusha: Arusha stands at an elevation of 1,400 metres on the southern slopes of Mount Meru, on the eastern edge of the eastern branch of the Great Rift Valley. The height keeps temperatures relatively low, typically between 10 and 30 °C, and the region has two rainy seasons, the long masika rains from March to May and the shorter vuli rains in November and December. It lies close to the Serengeti National Park, the Ngorongoro Conservation Area, Olduvai Gorge and Mount Kilimanjaro.

The site was first settled in the 1830s by the agro-pastoral Arusha Maasai from the Arusha Chini community, south of Mount Kilimanjaro. They traded grain, honey, beer and tobacco with the pastoral Kisongo Maasai for livestock, milk, meat and skins, and demand grew in the 1860s when the Pangani Valley trade route was extended through Arusha to western Kenya. The Germans conquered it in 1896 and built a military fort in 1900, forcing many Africans from their land to dig lime or carry stones for it. The British took the town in 1916. The railway reached it from Moshi in 1928-29.

The United Kingdom signed the documents ceding independence to Tanganyika at Arusha in 1961, and the Arusha Declaration was signed there in 1967. The Arusha Accords, between factions in the Rwandan civil war, were signed on 4 August 1993. The United Nations Security Council decided on 8 November 1994 that the International Criminal Tribunal for Rwanda would sit in the city; it indicted 93 individuals and sentenced 62. Arusha received city status in 2012.

Arusha is the capital of the Arusha Region and the headquarters of the East African Community. It hosts the African Court on Human and Peoples' Rights and a branch of the International Residual Mechanism for Criminal Tribunals. The National Natural History Museum occupies the former German administrative outpost and holds models of Australopithecus.
arverni: The Arverni occupied the heart of the Massif Central, a territory centred on the valley of the Allier and the Limagne basin, which formed its economic core. The Limagne was settled more densely in the 3rd and 2nd centuries BCE than anywhere else in Gaul, and drainage ditches show intensive cultivation from the second half of the 3rd century BCE.

Ancient writers present the Arverni as a dominant power. Strabo, drawing on Posidonius, claims that their authority once reached as far as Narbonne. Historians regard this as heavily exaggerated, and the idea of an Arvernian empire is now generally seen as a construction of late-19th-century nationalist historiography. Christian Goudineau instead describes a hierarchical confederation under Arvernian leadership, in which client peoples such as the Vellavii and Gabali kept their own territory and institutions.

In the 2nd century BCE the Arverni appear to have been ruled by kings, Luernius and his son Bituitus. Bituitus was defeated in the Rhône valley in 121 BCE and, according to Livy, was captured and sent to Alba. In the first half of the 1st century BCE the monarchy gave way to aristocratic government.

In 52 BCE Vercingetorix led a coalition of Gallic peoples against Caesar. He won a victory at Gergovia, the chief Arvernian oppidum, but at Alesia Caesar besieged him and received his surrender. Caesar treated the Arverni leniently. Under Roman rule they kept the status of a free civitas and formed one of the largest civitates of Aquitania, with its capital at Augustonemetum. In the 5th century Sidonius Apollinaris, bishop of the Arverni from about 470, and Ecdicius led resistance to the Visigothic king Euric, but in 475 the emperor Julius Nepos ceded Auvergne to the Visigoths in exchange for Provence.

At the close of the Iron Age the civitas was, in Caesar's terms, a federation of pagi in which factions formed around great families with large followings. Wealth rested on the farming of the Limagne and on mining of silver-bearing lead and gold in the uplands. Coins spread from the later 2nd century BCE.

Their most important sanctuary was the temple of Mercury on the Puy de Dôme, where the god was called Mercurius Arvernus. Under the Empire the workshops of Lezoux produced terra sigillata that was exported well beyond the province.
arvids-pelse: Arvīds Pelše was born on 7 February 1899 into a peasant family on Mazie farm near Zālīte, in Bauska county of the Courland Governorate. As a worker in Riga he joined the Bolshevik Social-Democratic Party of the Latvian Region in 1915, and in 1916 he met Lenin in Switzerland. He worked in factories and ports from Riga and Vitebsk to Kharkov, Petrograd and Arkhangelsk, took part in the February Revolution and the October Revolution of 1917 as a member of the Petrograd Soviet, and joined the Cheka in 1918, when Lenin sent him to Latvia to carry the revolution there.

After the fall of Soviet Latvia he returned to Russia in 1919 and was a lecturer and political commissar in the Red Army until 1929. He graduated in history from the Moscow Institute of the Red Professoriat in 1931 and taught history in Moscow. In June 1940 he played a leading part in bringing Latvia into the Soviet Union, and from March 1941 he was secretary of the Latvian Central Committee for propaganda and agitation.

In 1959 about 2,000 party leaders and activists were stripped of their posts in a purge of nationalism, and on 25 November Pelše replaced the purged Kalnbērziņš as first secretary. Latvians came to regard him as a symbol of submission to Moscow. In 1963 he headed the Pelše Commission, which investigated the assassination of Sergei Kirov until 1967. He left the Latvian post on 15 April 1966, when the 23rd Party Congress made him a full member of the Politburo, and he chaired the Party Control Committee, which oversaw the discipline of party members, until his death.

Suffering from lung cancer and heart and lung failure, Pelše died on 29 May 1983. Yuri Andropov spoke at his state funeral, and his ashes were placed in the Kremlin Wall Necropolis. He wrote on the history of the Communist Party and of the revolutionary movement in Latvia, was twice made a Hero of Socialist Labour, in 1969 and 1979, and the Riga Polytechnic Institute was named after him.
aryabhata: In the Aryabhatiya Aryabhata says that he was 23 years old in the year 3600 of the Kali Yuga, which corresponds to 499 CE and implies a birth in 476 CE. He called himself a native of Kusumapura or Pataliputra, near present-day Patna in Bihar. His name is properly spelled Aryabhata, not Aryabhatta: every astronomical text spells it so, including Brahmagupta's references to him by name in more than a hundred places. His disciple Bhaskara I calls him āśmakīya, one belonging to the Aśmaka country, and some have argued for a Kerala origin.

He probably went to Kusumapura for advanced studies and lived there. A verse mentions him as head of an institution there, and it has been speculated that he headed the university of Nalanda, a link he never claimed himself. He is also reputed to have set up an observatory at the Sun temple in Taregana, Bihar.

He wrote several treatises, but only the Aryabhatiya survives. It has 108 verses and 13 introductory verses in four chapters, written in the terse style of sutra literature, so that commentators such as Bhaskara I and Nilakantha Somayaji (1465) explained its meaning. Its mathematics covers arithmetic, algebra, plane and spherical trigonometry, continued fractions, quadratic equations and a table of sines. The Arya-siddhanta, now lost, is known through Varahamihira, Brahmagupta and Bhaskara I.

He gave an approximation of π, 62,832 for a circle of diameter 20,000, accurate to two parts in a million. His kuṭṭaka method solved first-order indeterminate equations. In astronomy he stated that the Earth is round and rotates daily on its axis, so that the stars' apparent westward motion is relative, comparing it to a man in a boat who sees the shore moving backward. His model of the Solar System was geocentric, with epicycles. He explained eclipses by shadows, not by Rahu and Ketu, and calculated the sidereal rotation as 23 hours, 56 minutes and 4.1 seconds.

His work shaped Indian astronomy and, through an Arabic translation of about 820 CE, influenced the Islamic world. Al-Khwarizmi cites it, and the term sine descends from his jya. His calendar calculations are still used for the Panchangam.
as-salih-ayyub: As-Salih Ayyub was born on 5 November 1205, the son of the Ayyubid ruler Al-Kamil and a Nubian concubine, Ward Al-Muna, who served Al-Kamil's other wife Sawda bint Al-Faqih, the mother of Al-Adil. In 1221 he became a hostage at the end of the Fifth Crusade, while John of Brienne was held by Al-Kamil, until Damietta was rebuilt and restored to Egypt. In 1232 he was given Hasankeyf in the Jazira, which his father had taken from the Artuqids. In 1234 his father sent him to rule Damascus, which removed him from the succession in Egypt, after suspecting that he was conspiring with the Mamluks.

When Al-Kamil died in 1238, he left as-Salih his designated heir in the Jazira and another son, Al-Adil II, as heir in Egypt. As-Salih took Damascus in 1239 and used it as a base. His uncle Al-Salih Ismail captured Damascus from him in September 1239, and he was held prisoner at Kerak with Shajar al-Durr, who bore their son Khalil. In April 1240 An-Nasir released him and allied with him against the Egyptians, and in June 1240 they entered Cairo together, as Al-Adil was imprisoned by his own troops. As-Salih became the paramount ruler of the Ayyubid family.

He was insecure in Cairo, where the Ashrafiyya faction of emirs plotted to replace him with Ismail. He bought large numbers of Kipchak slaves, available in great numbers after the Mongol invasions, and formed two corps of up to 1,000 men each: the Bahriyya, garrisoned on Rawda Island in the Nile, and the smaller Jamdārīyah, who guarded him. The Mamluks later overthrew the Ayyubids.

In 1244, at his invitation, the remnants of the Khwarezmian army, routed by the Mongols, sacked Jerusalem. That year he defeated Ismail, allied with the crusader Kingdom of Jerusalem, at La Forbie. In 1245 he captured Damascus and the caliph al-Musta'sim in Baghdad awarded him the title of sultan. In 1246 he turned on the Khwarezmians and defeated them near Homs.

His capture of Jerusalem led to a call for a new crusade, and Louis IX of France took the cross. In 1249 Louis invaded Egypt on the Seventh Crusade and occupied Damietta. As-Salih was fighting Ismail in Syria, returned quickly and encamped at al-Mansourah. He died on 22 November 1249 after his leg was amputated because of an abscess.

He had kept his heir, al-Muazzam Turanshah, at a distance in Hasankeyf, and his widow Shajar al-Durr hid his death until Turanshah arrived. Turanshah's rule was brief and was followed by a long interregnum until the Bahri Mamluks took power. As-Salih was the last major Ayyubid ruler of Egypt and the last to combine rule of Egypt with effective rule of parts of Palestine and Syria.
asaba: Asaba, in Igbo Ahaba, is situated on a terrace of the lower Niger River, on its western bank in the historic midwest of Nigeria, immediately northeast of the point where the Anambra River joins the Niger. It lies across the river from Onitsha, and the two form in some respects a continuous metropolitan region, joined by the First and Second Niger bridges. The Niger's position here marks the geopolitical border between eastern and western Nigeria. Beyond the river banks the land rises as high plains and terraced hills to about 200 metres (660 feet), with secondary forest. The neighbouring towns of Ibusa and Okpanam stand on an escarpment to the west.

Asaba was originally made up of nine quarters, which internal strife, wars with other communities and the slave trade that followed reduced to five: Umuezei, Ugbomanta, Umuaji, Umuagu and Umuonaje. The name comes from the exclamation Ahabam, meaning I have chosen well, attributed to Nnebisi, the founding father of the town. The city was founded in 1884 and once served as the colonial capital of the Southern Nigeria Protectorate. Between 1886 and 1900 it hosted the Royal Niger Company, which the British authorities set up to stimulate trade and the export of goods to England.

The Anioma people are the native population, and most of them speak the Enuani dialect of Igbo. Asaba is culturally led by the Asagba of Asaba, to whom the leaders of the five quarters, each called a Diokpa, report on matters affecting the community. He is assisted by the Iyasele, the customary prime minister, and a council of chiefs and elders. Because of its history and position the town is generally regarded as the regional capital of the Anioma area.

Asaba is the capital of Delta State and the seat of the Oshimili South Local Government Area. It had a population of 149,603 at the 2006 census. The civil service leads its economy, and the Asaba Niger Bridge and the A232 road link it with Onitsha and Benin City. In October 2023 it joined the UNESCO Creative Cities Network and was named a UNESCO City of Film.
asaf-jah-i: Mir Qamar-ud-din Khan Siddiqi was born on 11 August 1671 at Agra, to Ghazi ud-Din Khan and his first wife Safiya Khanum. Aurangzeb gave him his name. His mother was the daughter of Sa'adullah Khan Chinioti, a Punjabi Muslim noble who was grand vizier of Shah Jahan from 1645 to 1656, while the Taj Mahal was completed. His paternal grandfather Kilich Khan came from Samarkand, travelled to India in 1654 on his way to the Hajj, settled there and joined Aurangzeb's army in the Deccan in 1657.

Mir Qamar-ud-din became governor of Bijapur in 1702 and survived the attacks during the siege of Wagingera Fort in 1705. For his performance in that siege he was raised to a rank of 5,000 zaat and 5,000 sowar. After Aurangzeb's death in 1707 he held a succession of provincial posts. He became Viceroy of the Deccan, with authority over six Mughal provinces, and received the title Nizam-ul-Mulk.

The Sayyid brothers, kingmakers at the Mughal court, grew powerful, and Nizam-ul-Mulk led a counter-movement of Turkic and Irani nobles against them. He captured the forts of Asirgarh and Burhanpur in 1720, and the Sayyid brothers were killed that year, Sayyid Hussain Ali Khan murdered and his brother poisoned. As a reward he was made grand vizier by Emperor Muhammad Shah, but he used his influence to extend his ambitions in the Deccan.

On 11 October 1724 he established autonomous rule over the Deccan and began the Asaf Jahi dynasty. He remained loyal to the Mughal emperor, took no imperial title and continued to acknowledge Mughal suzerainty. After his defeat by the Peshwa Bajirao I in 1728, the Deccan became in effect a tributary state of the Marathas. In 1739 he marched to Karnal against Nader Shah, but stayed passive with a third of the army while the Mughal force was beaten.

He dictated a last testament of 17 clauses and died at Burhanpur on 1 June 1748. He was buried at the shrine of Shaikh Burhan ud-din Gharib Chisti at Khuldabad, near Aurangabad, where Aurangzeb is also buried. His death brought unrest as his sons and grandson contended for the throne, with the backing of neighbouring states and foreign powers. The accession of Asaf Jah II, who reigned from 1762 to 1803, ended the instability. His descendants ruled as the Nizams of Hyderabad, and the state he founded became one of the largest and most prosperous of the princely states of the British Raj.
asaf-ud-daula: Born on 23 September 1748, Asaf-ud-Daula was the son of Shuja-ud-Daula and of Umat-ul-Zohra, better known as Bahu Begum. He became nawab at the age of 26 on his father's death in January 1775, with the aid of the British East India Company. His younger brother Saadat Ali led a mutiny in the army, which the British Colonel John Parker defeated decisively. Asaf's first chief minister, Mukhtar-ud-Daula, was assassinated in the revolt. His position as Nawab wazir was ratified by the Mughal emperor Shah Alam II.

After the revolt he restructured the government, appointing nobles favourable to him and British officers to his army. Hasan Riza Khan became chief minister, ably assisted by Haydar Beg Khan, and Tikayt Ray finance minister. His mother remained a challenge to his rule: she controlled much of the treasury, held her own jagirs and armed forces, and at one point sought the Company's help in appointing ministers opposed to him.

Shuja-ud-Daula had left two million pounds sterling in the vaults of the zenana, which his widow and his mother claimed under a will that was never produced. When Warren Hastings pressed the nawab for the debt due to the Company, Asaf obtained from his mother a loan of 26 lakh rupees against a jagir of four times the value, and later 30 lakh more in return for a full acquittal and the Company's recognition of her jagirs for life. The jagirs were afterwards confiscated on the ground of her complicity in the rising of Chait Singh.

The Bara Imambara, or Asafi Imambara, was begun as a charitable project to give employment in the famine of 1784, in which even nobles were reduced to penury. It is said that over 20,000 people worked on it, and that nobles were paid to pull down part of the work in secret at night so that their dignity was kept. The Rumi Darwaza, sixty feet tall, was modelled in 1784 on the Sublime Porte in Istanbul.

He died in Lucknow on 21 September 1797 and is buried at the Bara Imambara. A saying still known in the city records his generosity: to whom even God does not give, Asaf-ud-Daula gives. The painter Johann Zoffany portrayed him several times, and the Urdu poet Mir Taqi Mir was at his court.
ascanius: In Greek and Roman mythology Ascanius was the son of the Trojan prince Aeneas and Creusa, daughter of Priam. When Troy burned, Aeneas escaped to Latium in Italy with his father Anchises and his child Ascanius, though Creusa died in the flight. According to Dionysius of Halicarnassus, his original name was Euryleon and it was changed after the flight; according to Virgil he was also called Iulus or Julus. Another legend mentioned by Livy makes him the son of Aeneas and Lavinia, born in Latium and not in Troy.

After the death of Aeneas, Ascanius became king of Lavinium. The Etruscan king Mezentius besieged the city and made it surrender and pay a yearly tribute. Ascanius later fell on him and his army unawares and defeated him, killing his son Lausus. Exactly thirty years after the founding of Lavinium he founded Alba Longa and became its first king, leaving Lavinia in charge of Lavinium. He was succeeded by Silvius, who was either his younger brother or his son. Dionysius, however, makes Julus a son of Ascanius who disputed the succession with Silvius.

Virgil tells it differently. In the Aeneid, Aeneas kills Lausus and Mezentius, and Ascanius takes no part. Instead he is a teenager without war experience, besieged by the Italians, who prays to Jupiter and kills Numanus, husband of the youngest sister of Turnus, with an arrow. Apollo then speaks the words that became proverbial, sic itur ad astra, and orders the Trojans to keep the boy out of the fighting. The last part of Ascanius's prayer, audacibus annue coeptis, became the basis of the United States motto annuit coeptis.

Ascanius matters in Roman tradition through his descendants. Under the name Iulus he was claimed as ancestor by the gens Julia, the family of Julius Caesar, and so as progenitor of the Julio-Claudian emperors; some genealogies also make him an ancestor of Romulus and Remus. Virgil popularised the name Iulus, replacing Ascanius, to link the Julian family to earlier myth. Augustus, who commissioned the poem and could claim four Olympian gods in his family tree, encouraged poets to stress his supposed descent from Aeneas. Tradition places his death in the 28th year of his reign.
aschaffenburg: Aschaffenburg stands on both sides of the Main in north-west Bavaria, bordering Hesse, about 41 kilometres south-east of Frankfurt. The smaller Aschaff flows into the Main there and gave the town its name, originally "castle at the ash tree river". The Spessart hills separate it from the rest of Lower Franconia, so its inhabitants speak a local form of Rhine Franconian, not Bavarian or East Franconian.

The earliest settlement remains date from the Stone Age; the place was originally a settlement of the Alamanni, and Roman legions were stationed there. The Franks conquered the area around 550. A Benedictine monastery of St Michael, reportedly founded by Saint Boniface in the 8th century, became the collegiate church of St Peter and Alexander in 957. King Louis the Younger married Liutgard of Saxony there in 869. Archbishop Willigis, who reportedly built a stone bridge over the Main in 989, made it his second residence, and from 982 it belonged to the Archbishopric of Mainz for more than 800 years. A synod met there in 1292, and an imperial diet of 1447 approved a concordat sometimes called the Aschaffenburg Concordat.

The late-Gothic castle was destroyed in 1552 and replaced in 1605 to 1614 by the Renaissance Schloss Johannisburg. The town suffered greatly in the Thirty Years' War, being held in turn by the various belligerents. In 1803 it was made over to Archbishop Karl Theodor von Dalberg as the Principality of Aschaffenburg, which joined the Grand Duchy of Frankfurt in 1810, and in 1814 a treaty transferred it to Bavaria. From 1840 to 1848 King Ludwig I had the Pompejanum built, a Roman villa modelled on the house of Castor and Pollux at Pompeii. Allied bombing heavily damaged the town in the Second World War, and the Battle of Aschaffenburg from 28 March to 3 April 1945 destroyed much more.

The Schloss Johannisburg, completely restored after the war, holds a library with incunabula and a collection of engravings and paintings. The collegiate church of St Peter and Alexander dates mainly from the early twelfth century and preserves monuments by the Vischers and a painting by Matthias Grünewald. Across the river are the Park and Schloss Schönbusch. The town is the seat of a district but not part of it.
aschersleben: Aschersleben lies in the Salzlandkreis district of Saxony-Anhalt, near the confluence of the rivers Eine and Wipper, about 22 kilometres east of Quedlinburg and 45 kilometres north-west of Halle (Saale). Its municipality includes a number of villages incorporated between 2008 and 2010.

Aschersleben was first mentioned in 753, which makes it the oldest town of Saxony-Anhalt. The Latin name of its castle, Ascharia, gave the House of Ascania its name. The town obtained municipal status in 1266 and the right to build a city wall with defence towers in 1322. From 1252 to 1315 it was the capital of Anhalt-Aschersleben, after which it passed to the Bishopric of Halberstadt. In 1426 it joined the Hanseatic League, and the cultivation and trade of hops, for which a market place was laid out, brought an economic boom. After the Peace of Westphalia of 1648 it became part of the Principality of Halberstadt, and in 1815 it became part of the Prussian Province of Saxony.

In the 1930s a Junkers factory for aircraft fuselages was built there; the first fuselages were made in May 1935, and the works covered 564,000 square metres and employed about 6,000 people. From July 1944 about 950 prisoners from a subcamp of the Buchenwald concentration camp were forced to work there. The town was bombed from 1942 to 1945, and about 20 per cent of it was destroyed in nine raids, most heavily on 31 March 1945. U.S. forces occupied it on 17 April 1945, and it was handed to British forces on 23 May and to the Soviets on 1 July. It was part of East Germany until 1990, when it became part of Saxony-Anhalt.

Aschersleben is one of few German towns that keep large parts of their medieval city wall: 1.8 kilometres of an original 2.2, with 15 of 51 towers and bastions still standing, among them the Johannistorturm of 1380. The historic centre combines Romanesque (the Grauer Hof, of the 12th century, considered the oldest house in town), Gothic (the Protestant church of St. Stephani, of the 14th century), Renaissance (the town hall, built from 1517, and the Krukmannsches Haus of 1572) and Baroque buildings. A bronze statue of the polymath Adam Olearius (1599–1671), who designed the Globe of Gottorf, stands on a fragment of the city wall beside the Johannis gate tower.
asclepius: Asclepius is the son of Apollo and, in the earliest accounts, a mortal woman, Koronis, a princess of Tricca in Thessaly. When she slept with a mortal named Ischys, Apollo learned of it by his prophetic powers and killed Ischys, and Artemis killed Koronis, who was laid on a funeral pyre. Apollo rescued the child by cutting him from her womb.
Other traditions differ: a Phoenician tradition has him born of Apollo without any woman, and in a version set at Epidaurus Koronis exposed him on Mount Tittheion, where a goat gave him milk.

He was educated by the centaur Chiron. In one story a snake licked his ears clean and taught him secret knowledge; to the Greeks snakes were sacred beings of wisdom, healing and resurrection, and the rod wreathed with a snake became his emblem.

Asclepius is a hero and god of medicine in Greek religion, representing the healing aspect of the medical arts. He shared with Apollo the epithet Paean, "the Healer". He married Epione, and their daughters Iaso, Panacea, Hygieia, Aceso and Aegle personify aspects of health and healing. He was associated with the Roman and Etruscan god Vediovis and the Egyptian Imhotep. In myth he began to bring the dead back to life, and Zeus killed him with a thunderbolt, because Hades complained or because Zeus feared he would teach resurrection to other humans. At Apollo's request he was made immortal as a star, the constellation Ophiuchus.

From the fifth century BCE the cult grew very popular and pilgrims flocked to the healing temples, the Asclepieia. Strabo called the one at Trikala the most ancient. Others stood at Epidaurus, in the fourth century BCE, on the island of Kos, where Hippocrates may have begun his career, and at Pergamum. Ritual purification was followed by offerings, and the supplicant then spent the night in the holiest part, the abaton. Any dreams were reported to a priest, who prescribed a therapy by interpreting them.

Some temples used sacred dogs to lick the wounds of petitioners, and non-venomous snakes, now called Aesculapian snakes, moved freely in the dormitories where the sick slept. The original Hippocratic Oath begins with an invocation of Apollo the Physician and of Asclepius.
ascoli-piceno: Ascoli Piceno lies at the confluence of the River Tronto and the small River Castellano and is surrounded on three sides by mountains. The Sibillini National Park borders it on the northwest and the Monti della Laga National Park on the south. National Road 4, the Salaria, links it with Rome, following the Roman Via Salaria, the salt road that connected Latium with the salt-producing areas of the Adriatic coast.

Asculum in ancient Picenum was founded by the Italic Piceni and was originally a Sabine city. After its defeat by the Romans in 268 BCE it became a civitas foederata with nominal independence. One account describes its people as warlike and bearing a generations-old grudge against Rome for encroaching on their northern territories. Its siege in 89 BCE, after the Battle of Asculum, involved at least four Roman legions with Gallic and Spanish auxiliaries, as sling bullets found in the city show. It then became a municipium, and under the triumvirs or Augustus a colonia.

In the Middle Ages the Ostrogoths and then the Lombards of King Faroald ravaged it in 578. It was part of the Lombard Duchy of Spoleto from 593 to 789 and then ruled by vicars of the Franks, but the bishops gained the most influence. A free republican commune was established in 1189, but internal strife opened the way to outside rulers such as the condottiero Galeotto I Malatesta and Francesco Sforza, who was ousted in 1482. Ascoli then submitted again to papal suzerainty, and in 1860 it was annexed to the Kingdom of Italy.

Many buildings of the historic centre are of local travertine. Tradition holds that the city had some two hundred towers in the Middle Ages, and about fifty can still be seen. The Cathedral of Sant'Emidio houses an altarpiece by Carlo Crivelli. Roman remains include the Porta Gemina of the 1st century BCE, through which the Via Salaria entered the city, and the Ponte di Cecco over the Castellano. On the first Sunday in August a parade of more than 1,500 people in Renaissance costume honours Saint Emidio, protector of the city, and is followed by the Quintana, a tournament among knights of the six neighbourhoods.
ash-shihr: Ash Shihr, also written al-Shihr, is a walled town on a sandy beach in Hadhramaut. It has an anchorage but no docks, so boats are used. A dry riverbed, the wadi al-Misyal, divides the town in two: the western quarter is called Majraf and the eastern al-Ramla. It has several souqs, among them Suq al-Lakham, Suq al-Hunud and Suq Shibam. Fish oil was its main export.

Its history can be traced back to about 780 CE, and it was a major port on the incense trade route, exporting frankincense as far as China, and Ibn Khurradadhbih called the area around it the bilad al-kundur, the Land of Incense. It was also known for its ambergris. Pottery made at Yadhghat was exported through it, possibly as early as the 10th century. In 980 Persian exiles founded the rival port of Sharma up the coast, and medieval geographers from al-Muqaddasi in 985 to al-Dimashqi around 1300 mention the two together. It remained the main port of Hadhramaut until Mukalla replaced it in the 19th century.

Politically the town was held by the Ziyadids (818 to 981), the Banu Man in the 11th century, the Rasulids (1228 to 1454) and the Tahirids, and was taken in 1462 by the Kathiri sultanate under Badr ibn Tuwayriq. The Portuguese, who called it Xaer or Xael, attacked it several times in the 16th century, with battles in 1523, 1532, 1533 and 1548. In 1530 the Ottomans Mustafa Bey and Khoja Zufar advised Badr not to submit to the Portuguese and left cannon and 100 levends with him. In 1548 the Portuguese battered the fort with siege guns and stormed it on 7 April, slaughtering the Kathiri garrison. Later it became one of the three major cities of the Qu'aiti Sultanate, with Mukalla and Shibam.

Graves along the shore are said to be those of victims of the Portuguese. Carsten Niebuhr visited the town in the 18th century. Yemenis who emigrated to East Africa, and their descendants, are known as Shihiris, because most of them left through the port of al-Shihr.
ashanti-empire: The Asante Empire, Asanteman, also called the Ashanti Empire, was an Akan state in what is now Ghana. The name Asante means because of war, from the Twi ɔsa, war, and nti, because of, and comes from the state's origin as a kingdom created to fight Denkyira; Ashanti is the British transcription. The ancestors of the Asante moved north from Amansie, remembered by the Akan as their early homeland, to the Kumasi area as the Akan heartland broke up in disputes over succession and trade. Denkyira, which controlled much of the region's gold, made Oti Akenten, ruler of Kwaman, pay annual tribute and send a royal relative to its court, and he sent his nephew Osei Tutu.

Around 1680 leadership of the Asante union passed to Obiri Yeboa, whose death in battle with the Dormaa led to the rise of Osei Tutu. When the Denkyirahene Ntim Gyakari demanded heavy tribute and the Asante refused, war broke out around 1698. In tradition the Golden Stool, Sika dwa, became the central symbol of unity under Osei Tutu, with his adviser Okomfo Anokye.

After the Asante conquered Denkyira in 1701 they were the dominant inland power, with access to the coast and its trade with Europeans, and inland trade shifted toward Kumasi. The economy rested on gold and agricultural exports, slave trading, crafts and trade with markets further north. Osei Tutu was killed in 1717 in a war with Akyem, and the Aowin sacked Kumasi. In 1721 and 1722 the Asante defeated Aowin and Nzima, and Aowin prisoners were sold as slaves at Elmina, Cape Coast and Anomabo. By 1816, under Osei Bonsu, the Asante had absorbed the Fante Confederacy.

The Asante held their own against the British in the first two of the five Anglo-Ashanti Wars, killing General Sir Charles MacCarthy in 1824, but the British later burnt Kumasi. In the War of the Golden Stool, from March to September 1900, the court members not exiled, led by Yaa Asantewaa, Queen-Mother of Ejisu, attacked the British Residents at Kumasi Fort. The British won and exiled her and others to the Seychelles, where King Prempeh I already was.

The Asante state was centralised. The family, under its Abusua Panyin, was the basic political unit, and villages under an Odikro were grouped into divisions under an Ohene, which formed states under an Omanhene, and all the states formed the empire under the Asantehene. The Asante Kingdom survives today as a constitutionally protected traditional state within Ghana.
asherah: Asherah appears across the ancient Near East under related names. An Amorite goddess called Ashratum was worshipped in Sumer, where she was the wife of Mardu, or Amurrum, the supreme god of the Amorites, and a limestone slab from Sippar carries a dedication to her by Hammurabi. In Akkadian texts she appears as Aširatu, and one Amorite king of the 14th century BCE in the Amarna letters was named Abdi-Ashirta, servant of Asherah.

Among the Hittites she appears as Ašertu in the myth of Elkunirša, in which she tried to sleep with the storm god. In the Ugaritic texts she is Athirat, called Elat, holy, lady and progenitress of the gods, and the consort of El, with seventy sons.

In the Baal Cycle she champions her son Yam, the sea, against Baal. Her fullest title, rbt athirat ym, has traditionally been read as Lady Athirat of the Sea, though some scholars propose that ym means day. Her most common symbol is a tree, above all the date palm, and she is also linked with lionesses. Figures called Judean pillar figures show her with protruding breasts, and the Revadim figurine shows her suckling two smaller human figures. Scholars disagree about how far one can speak of her own iconography: one study concludes that there is no genuine Asherah iconography.

Whether Asherah was worshipped in Israel and Judah is debated. At Kuntillet Ajrud a jar bears inscriptions naming Yahweh of Samaria and his Asherah, and Yahweh of Teman and his Asherah, and another inscription comes from Khirbet el-Qom. Some scholars read these as evidence that she was venerated as Yahweh's consort, while others hold that the word means a cultic object or sanctuary. The noun appears forty times in the Hebrew Bible, mostly of a cultic object, usually understood as a wooden pole. Manasseh erected a statue of Asherah or perhaps a pole, Josiah is reported to have removed such items from the temple, and Deuteronomy 12:3 commands that the poles be destroyed.

The Septuagint renders the word as grove, and the King James Bible followed that through the Vulgate, so that English readers did not meet her name in it for over 400 years. The goddess, as Athirat, is also attested in inscriptions from south Arabia from the mid-first millennium BCE to the mid-first millennium CE.
ashgabat: Ashgabat lies on a highly seismically active oasis plain between the foothills of the Köpetdag mountains to the south and the Karakum Desert to the north, about 50 kilometres from the border with Iran. Most of the city stands between 200 and 255 metres above sea level. The climate is cold arid, bordering on semi-arid, with very hot, dry summers and cool, short winters, and the Soviet-era Karakum Canal runs through the city, carrying water from the Amu Darya.

The city grew on the ruins of Konjikala, a Silk Road city first mentioned as a wine-producing village in the 1st or 2nd century BCE and levelled by an earthquake in the 1st century BCE. Konjikala was rebuilt because of its favourable position on the Silk Road and flourished until the Mongols destroyed it in the 13th century. It then survived as a small village until the Russians took over in the 19th century.

Russian military engineers founded the city on 18 January 1881 as a fortified garrison on the western edge of the Turkmen village of Askhabad. Sixty-seven Turkmen families were compensated for the land taken. Until then buildings other than yurts were adobe and limited to one storey because of the earthquake risk, and in 1900 only the municipal museum had two.

Soviet rule was established in December 1917, but in July 1918 a coalition of Mensheviks, Social Revolutionaries and former Tsarist officers revolted and set up the Ashkhabad Executive Committee. After the British withdrew in April 1919 the Tashkent Soviet resumed control. From 1919 to 1927 the city was named Poltoratsk after the local revolutionary Pavel Poltoratskiy, and in 1924 it became capital of the Turkmen Soviet Socialist Republic. Much of it was destroyed by the earthquake of 1948.

Ashgabat is the capital and largest city of Turkmenistan, with about one million inhabitants, and is a multiethnic city with ethnic Turkmen as the majority. It stands apart from Ahal Province, which surrounds it. After the earthquake it was extensively rebuilt, and since independence its monumental buildings have been sheathed in white marble. It has been spelled Ashkhabad in English, from the Russian form, and in 2021 marked 140 years of its written history.
ashikaga-takauji: Ashikaga Takauji was born on 18 August 1305, and his childhood name was Matagorō. He was a male-line descendant of the samurai of the Minamoto Seiwa Genji line, who had settled in the Ashikaga area of Shimotsuke Province, in present-day Tochigi Prefecture. His father was Ashikaga Sadauji and his mother Uesugi Kiyoko, and his brother was Ashikaga Tadayoshi. The Zen master Musō Soseki, who enjoyed his favour, said that Takauji kept his cool in battle and was not afraid of death, was merciful and tolerant, and was very generous to those below him.

Takauji was a general of the Kamakura shogunate, sent to Kyoto in 1333 to put down the Genkō War, which had begun in 1331. Disillusioned with the shogunate, he joined the banished Emperor Go-Daigo and Kusunoki Masashige and seized Kyoto. Nitta Yoshisada then besieged Kamakura, and when the city fell the regent Hōjō Takatoki and his clansmen killed themselves, ending the shogunate and the Hōjō clan's power. Go-Daigo was enthroned again and began the Kenmu Restoration.

The samurai grew disillusioned with the restored court, which sought to return to the systems of the Heian period, and Takauji gained favour among those who believed he could restore feudal government. In 1335 he put down a rebellion by Hōjō Tokiyuki and took Kamakura for himself, claiming the title of Sei-i Taishōgun and allotting land to his followers without the court's permission.

Go-Daigo sent Nitta Yoshisada against him, and Takauji beat him and marched on Kyoto. He held it for a few days in February 1336 before being driven out to Kyūshū. He regained control there and defeated Yoshisada again at the decisive Battle of Minatogawa in 1336, killing Masashige, and seized Kyoto for good. He installed Emperor Kōmyō of the Northern Court in opposition to the exiled Southern Court, and the Nanbokuchō period began, in which two emperors fought each other for almost sixty years.

Takauji was appointed shōgun in 1338, which began the Muromachi period. He spent the last years of his rule in the struggle for Kyoto, which Southern forces took and Ashikaga forces retook several times between 1351 and 1358. His brother Tadayoshi, excluded from the administration in 1350, joined the Southern Court in 1351 and died in 1352. Takauji died on 7 June 1358 and was succeeded by his son Ashikaga Yoshiakira. His grandson Ashikaga Yoshimitsu united the Northern and Southern courts in 1392.

Because he rose by betraying the Kamakura shogunate and Go-Daigo, Confucian-minded historians have counted him among Japan's Three Great Villains. The Taiheiki, a 40-volume epic of the Muromachi period, tells the story from the Genkō rebellion to the establishment of the two courts.
ashikaga-yoshiaki: Yoshiaki was born on 5 December 1537, a son of Ashikaga Yoshiharu, the twelfth shogun, and a younger brother of Ashikaga Yoshiteru, the thirteenth. He entered the Kofuku-ji temple as a monk. By then the shogunate's authority was largely ignored across Japan, though factions still fought to control it for the prestige it kept. When the Miyoshi clan and Matsunaga Hisahide killed Yoshiteru in a coup, Yoshiaki returned to secular life. The Miyoshi installed Ashikaga Yoshihide as fourteenth shogun but could not hold Kyoto, and in November 1567 Yoshiaki moved to the An'yō-ji temple at Ichijōdani, the base of the Asakura clan.

The armies of Oda Nobunaga entered Kyoto in 1568 and set Yoshiaki up as shogun, while Yoshihide was deposed without ever entering the capital; historians date the start of the Azuchi–Momoyama period from this. Yoshiaki was in effect a puppet, and his Nijō residence, built in 1569, served as a symbol of his authority. Dissatisfied with Nobunaga's overlordship, in 1573 he asked Takeda Shingen for help. Shingen routed Tokugawa Ieyasu's army at Mikatagahara, and Yoshiaki raised troops against Nobunaga, but Shingen died of illness before reaching Kyoto. Yoshiaki surrendered, and Nobunaga spared his life but banished him from the city.

Yoshiaki shaved his head as a Buddhist monk but never formally gave up the title of shogun, so the empty shell of the shogunate could be said to have lasted some years longer. He served as a rallying point for Nobunaga's enemies and sent troops into the Ishiyama Hongan-ji War. In 1576 he sought the support of the Mōri clan, the largest daimyo of western Japan, and moved to Tomo, in present-day Fukuyama; the decade that followed is sometimes called the Tomo Shogunate. According to the historian Mary Elizabeth Berry, he was still resisting Toyotomi Hideyoshi in 1590. He died on 19 October 1597.
ashikaga-yoshimitsu: Ashikaga Yoshimitsu was born on 25 September 1358, the third son of Ashikaga Yoshiakira but the oldest to survive. His childhood name was Haruō. He was appointed shōgun in 1368 at the age of ten, the same year that Emperor Chōkei ascended the southern throne, and at twenty he was admitted to the imperial court as Acting Grand Counselor.

In 1379 he reorganised the institutions of the Gozan Zen establishment, and two years later he became the first person of the warrior class to host a reigning emperor at his private residence. In 1378 he built the Muromachi palace in Kyoto, from whose location the shogunate and the period take their name.

Yoshimitsu's chief political achievement was ending the fighting of the Nanboku-chō period. In 1392 he persuaded Go-Kameyama of the Southern Court to hand the Imperial Regalia to Emperor Go-Komatsu of the Northern Court, which firmly established the authority of the Muromachi shogunate and curbed regional daimyō. The commander Imagawa Sadayo was sent to subdue Kyushu in 1370, and the island was pacified by 1389.

In 1394 he gave the post of shōgun to his son Ashikaga Yoshimochi and became Grand Chancellor of State, the highest-ranking member of the court, but kept authority over the shogunate until his death. In 1395 he retired from all offices, took the tonsure and moved to his Kitayama villa, which had a pavilion two-thirds covered in gold leaf.

At Kitayama he received envoys from the Ming and Joseon courts at least six times. He accepted tributary relations with Ming China in 1401, and in 1402 or 1404 the title King of Japan, bowing three times to read a Ming document addressing him so. Many modern Japanese historians view this negatively, and Tsuji Zennosuke and Kuroita Katsumi called it a violation of Japan's tradition. His son Yoshimochi ended the embassies in 1411. Arai Hakuseki, by contrast, thought the title proper because the shōgun was the de facto ruler. In 1407 he began a plan to become Daijō tennō, a title of retired emperors.

Yoshimitsu died suddenly in 1408, aged 49, before the plan could be realised. His villa became Rokuon-ji, often called Kinkaku-ji, the Temple of the Golden Pavilion, where a statue of him stands. He was also the patron of Zeami Motokiyo, regarded as the founder of Noh theatre, whom he encouraged to give the art a loftier treatment. His posthumous name was Rokuon'in.
ashikaga-yoshinori: Yoshinori was born on 12 July 1394, a son of the third shogun, Ashikaga Yoshimitsu, and Fujiwara no Yoshiko; his childhood name was Harutora. He became a Buddhist monk at the age of ten. After the fifth shogun, Ashikaga Yoshikazu, died in 1425, Yoshikazu's father Ashikaga Yoshimochi resumed the headship of the shogunate but named no successor before his own death. The shogunal deputy Hatakeyama Mitsuie drew lots among the few Ashikaga candidates in the sanctuary of Iwashimizu Hachiman Shrine, and Yoshinori's name came out; it was believed that the god Hachiman had guided the choice.

Rebellions broke out during his rule: the Ōtomo rebellion and a rising of the monks of Mount Hiei in 1433, and the Eikyō Rebellion of the Kantō kubō Ashikaga Mochiuji in 1438, whose defeat strengthened the shogunate. In 1432 trade and diplomatic relations with Ming China, broken off under Yoshimochi, were restored after the Chinese emperor wrote through the Ryūkyū kingdom. The Ming title King of Japan let Yoshinori monopolise the China trade, and in 1434 an office, the Tosen-bugyō, was set up to guard trading ships and manage the trade.

In 1433 he began the compilation of the Shinshoku Kokinwakashū, the last imperial waka anthology, and in 1434 he dedicated the main hall of Ikkyu-ji. In 1441 he granted the Shimazu clan suzerainty over the Ryūkyū Islands.

Yoshinori was notorious for oppressive measures and unpredictable whims. Akamatsu Mitsusuke learned that the shogun meant to give three of his provinces to his cousin Akamatsu Sadamura, whose sister had borne Yoshinori a son. Mitsusuke invited Yoshinori to a Noh performance at the Akamatsu residence in Kyoto, where he was killed during the evening play at the age of 47, in what is called the Kakitsu Incident. His eight-year-old son Yoshikatsu was chosen to succeed him. The killing undercut the military ethic of loyalty, and the shoguns' power gradually eroded afterwards.
ashikaga-yoshiteru: Yoshiteru was born on 31 March 1536, the eldest son of the twelfth shogun, Ashikaga Yoshiharu, and of a daughter of Konoe Hisamichi; his childhood name was Kikubemaru. When his father was forced to retire in 1546 after a political struggle with Hosokawa Harumoto, Yoshiteru became shogun at the age of 11, invested at Sakamoto in Ōmi Province outside Kyoto. He was then called Yoshifushi and took the name Yoshiteru in 1554. His younger brother Ashikaga Yoshiaki later became the fifteenth shogun.

Harumoto's retainer Miyoshi Nagayoshi went over to Hosokawa Ujitsuna, and the war between the two Hosokawa drove Yoshiteru, his father and Harumoto from Kyoto; Yoshiharu died in Ōmi in 1550. Yoshiteru made peace with Nagayoshi in 1552, fought him again with the help of Rokkaku Yoshikata, and was driven out once more in 1558. Nagayoshi, fearing to be accused of killing a shogun, took him back under his influence and remained the real power in Kyoto.

Even so, Yoshiteru tried to make peace between daimyo such as Takeda Shingen and Uesugi Kenshin, Shimazu Takahisa, Ōtomo Yoshishige, Mōri Motonari and Amago Haruhisa, and gave the character teru of his name to samurai such as Mōri Terumoto. Oda Nobunaga and Uesugi Kenshin travelled to Kyoto to pay their respects.

After Nagayoshi died of illness in 1564, Matsunaga Hisahide and the Miyoshi Triumvirs sought to put Ashikaga Yoshihide in his place. In 1565 Matsunaga Hisamichi and Miyoshi Yoshitsugu besieged the buildings where Yoshiteru lived, later the site of Nijō Castle, and no daimyo came to his aid in time. The Jesuit Luís Fróis wrote that his squire Odachidono took his own life when his master died. Yoshiteru practised the sword regularly, and Tsukahara Bokuden, founder of the Kashima Shintō-ryū, was among his teachers, so he was called the Kengo shōgun. Many researchers regard him as the last effective holder of the office.
ashkelon: The name Ashkelon is probably Western Semitic and may be connected with the root š-q-l, "to weigh", perhaps pointing to the importance of the place as a centre of trade. It appears in the Egyptian execration texts in a form that suggests the earliest pronunciation was ʾaθqalānu. The ancient site, now called Tel Ashkelon, was the oldest and largest seaport in Canaan. It belonged to Philistia, the pentapolis of the Philistines, north of Gaza City and south of Jaffa.

Ascalon was an important city under Roman, Byzantine and early Muslim rule, and again in the time of the Kingdom of Jerusalem, because it lay near the coast and between the Crusader states and Egypt. The Battle of Ascalon was the last action of the First Crusade. After Baybars ordered the fortifications and harbour destroyed in 1270, the inhabitants moved to Majdal ʿAsqalān, which he established as a substitute 3 kilometres inland, with a congregational mosque, a marketplace and religious shrines.

Ottoman records of 1596 show Majdal as a large village of 559 Muslim households, the seventh most populous place in Palestine, helped by its position on the Cairo to Damascus road. In the late Ottoman and Mandatory periods it became the main weaving centre of the Gaza District. It had about 500 looms in 1909 and about 2,000 by the 1940s, often set up in private rooms, and made striped fabrics for abaya coats and regional dresses. In 1945 its population was 9,910, of whom 9,820 were Muslims.

Egyptian forces occupied Majdal early in the 1948 war, and Israeli forces captured it in early November 1948. All but about 1,000 residents had left by then. The remaining Palestinians were confined to a fenced area and deported in stages from 17 August 1950; Israeli records give 2,333 sent to the Gaza Strip, 60 to Jordan and 302 to other towns in Israel. Jewish immigrants and demobilised soldiers settled from July 1949. The town was renamed several times, the Afridar neighbourhood for South African immigrants was incorporated in 1953, and the name Ashkelon was adopted that year.

The ancient site is administered as Ashkelon National Park, where the city walls, Canaanite earth ramparts and Roman, Byzantine and Crusader ruins can be seen. The largest dog cemetery of the ancient world was found there. Majdal's Great Mosque, founded in 1300, now houses a museum. Ashkelon is the third largest city in Israel's Southern District.
ashkenazi-jews: Ashkenazi Jews are an ethnic subdivision of the Jewish diaspora. They emerged from Jewish communities that consolidated during the 10th century in the Rhineland and northern France, having migrated there from centres such as the Italian Peninsula and the Southern Levant. How the Ashkenazim came to exist as a distinct community is unknown and has given rise to several theories. The name derives from the biblical figure Ashkenaz, a son of Gomer in the Table of Nations; the biblical name is usually derived from the Assyrian Aškūza, a people identified with the Scythians.

After numerous massacres of Jews during the Crusades, the Ashkenazim began a gradual eastward migration, driven by mounting restrictions in the Holy Roman Empire and the favourable policies of Casimir III the Great of Poland and others. Expulsions from England in 1290, France in 1394 and parts of Germany in the 15th century pushed it further. In Poland, Jews received special protection from the Statute of Kalisz of 1264.

The migration increased after the persecution of Jews during the Black Death, and by the 16th century the bulk of Ashkenazi Jews lived in the Kingdom of Poland. By the 15th century the Ashkenazi communities of Poland were the largest in the Diaspora, and the area remained the main centre of Ashkenazi Jewry until the Holocaust.

From the late 18th century the communities were transformed by the Haskalah, or Jewish Enlightenment, and the struggle for emancipation. Maskilim advocated national languages in place of Yiddish and the revival of Hebrew. In the 19th century millions emigrated from Europe, to Ottoman Palestine and to the United States. Of about 8.8 million Jews in Europe at the start of the Second World War, mostly Ashkenazi, about 6 million were murdered in the Holocaust, including 3 million of 3.3 million Polish Jews.

The Ashkenazim adapted their traditions to Europe. They follow the German rite in the synagogue and until the Holocaust mostly spoke Yiddish, an offshoot of Middle High German written in the Hebrew script, with Hebrew, Aramaic and Slavic influence; it was spoken by over 11 million people before the Holocaust. Because Germany lay far from the Jewish religious authorities of Baghdad and Islamic Spain, Ashkenaz developed a minhag of its own. Joseph Karo's Shulchan Aruch of 1563, with the notes of Moses Isserles, became the normative code of law for Ashkenazic Jews.
ashoka: Information about Ashoka comes from his own inscriptions, other inscriptions that mention him, and ancient literature, especially Buddhist texts, which often contradict one another. His inscriptions concern mainly dhamma, and the American scholar John S. Strong suggests they are sometimes best thought of as the propaganda of a politician presenting a favourable image of himself. The Buddhist legends were composed long after his time and call for caution.

His inscriptions do not name his ancestors. The Puranas and the Mahavamsa state that his father was the Maurya emperor Bindusara and his grandfather Chandragupta, founder of the empire. His inscriptions mention rulers such as Antiochus II Theos and Ptolemy II Philadelphus, which places him in the 3rd century BCE. According to the Mahavamsa he was viceroy at Ujjain, which his own rock edict supports by mentioning a prince viceroy there.

Ashoka became emperor of Magadha around 268 BCE, with his capital at Pataliputra. His inscriptions show an empire covering almost the whole subcontinent except the far south, and reaching into Afghanistan. In Major Rock Edict 13 he states that he conquered Kalinga eight years after his accession; 100,000 men and animals were killed, many times that number perished, and 150,000 were carried away. He writes that remorse over this suffering led him to devote himself to dharma.

His edicts urge righteous conduct and respect for all sects, and mention medical facilities for people and animals, wells and roadside trees. Minor Rock Edict 1 shows him as a lay follower of Buddhism, though the inscriptions do not mention doctrines such as the Four Noble Truths. Buddhist legends credit him with 84,000 stupas, patronage of the Third Buddhist council and missions to Sri Lanka led by his son Mahinda, and the Ashokavadana also describes acts of violence after his conversion.

His last dated inscription is from his 26th regnal year, and the only source for his later years is Buddhist legend. According to the Sri Lankan tradition he died in his 37th regnal year, which suggests about 232 BCE. Twenty of his pillars survive. The Lion Capital of Ashoka was adapted for the State Emblem of India, and the Ashoka Chakra stands at the centre of its flag. His existence as a historical emperor had almost been forgotten until the decipherment of Brahmi in the 19th century.
ashot-i-of-armenia: Ashot was born around 820 to Smbat VIII Bagratuni and his wife Hripsime. Smbat VIII was sparapet, or supreme commander, and the son of Ashot Msaker, Prince of Armenia. The Bagratuni and the Artsruni were among the most powerful families, and both fought the Arab invaders. After the invasion of the Abbasid general Bugha al-Kabir, from 850 to 855, which sent many prominent nobles into captivity and exile, Smbat VIII was exiled to Samarra, where he died. Ashot rebuilt the ruined economy and consolidated the political authority of the Bagratuni house. In 856 the caliph al-Mutawakkil named him sparapet, as his father had been.

In 862 the Abbasid caliph al-Musta'in recognised Ashot as prince of princes of Armenia, of Georgia and of the Caucasus, hoping to protect himself against the local autonomous emirs. The title made Ashot a de facto king, though it gave him no administrative rule over a kingdom.
