He annexed Bagrevand, mediated between the Artsruni cousins Grigor-Derenik and Gurgen, and arranged marriages between his daughters and the Artsruni and Siunia houses.

His brother Abas, as sparapet, defeated the Kaysites of Manazkert at Karasunk. Emperor Basil I sought an alliance, and Patriarch Photius proposed a church union; the church council at Shirakavan in 869 rejected the union but did not refuse the alliance. Ashot was granted the right to collect taxes throughout the country, which sharply reduced the revenue reaching the caliphate.

Ashot was anointed and crowned by Catholicos Gevorg II Garnetsi in the cathedral of Shirakavan, before Armenian princes and representatives of foreign powers. Caliph al-Mu'tamid consented, and Basil I sent a royal crown with gifts and a letter calling him a beloved brother. Historians date the coronation differently, and the sources give his reign as four, five or seven years. He remained subordinate to the caliph, and the Armenian princes stood under him as first among equals.

The Byzantine emperor Constantine VII wrote that Ashot ruled over all the countries of the East. The first khachkar was made in 879 in honour of his wife Katranide. Ashot died in 890 while travelling to Gugark to put down a rebellion, at an inn at K'arsparn. His body was taken to Bagaran and buried in the cemetery of his ancestors. His son Smbat I succeeded him.
ashot-ii-of-armenia: Ashot II was the son of King Smbat I of Bagratid Armenia. Smbat had fought off an invasion launched by Yusuf Ibn Abi'l-Saj, the Emir of Atropatene, but when he surrendered he was tortured and beheaded by Yusuf at Yernjak. Ashot succeeded his father in 914. Yusuf had taken control of the central lands of Armenia and installed Ashot's first cousin, also named Ashot, at Dvin as anti-king. Ashot II married an unnamed daughter of Prince Sahak Sevada, the powerful ruler of Gardman, whom Ashot later had blinded after a failed revolt. Her name is sometimes given as Maria.

Harried by Yusuf's forces, Ashot went to Constantinople to seek help from Empress Zoe Karbonopsina. He was well received, and a Byzantine force under the Domestic of the Schools, Leo Phokas the Elder, marched along the Upper Euphrates the next year and entered Taron with little opposition. Winter halted the advance short of Dvin, but it had restored Ashot to a powerful position and inflicted heavy casualties on the Arabs. Civil war with the pretender went on from 918 to 920, when he conceded defeat. Ashot defeated other rebellions as well.
In 919 Yusuf instigated a failed rebellion against the caliph and was replaced by a more favourable Arab governor, Subuk. In 922 the Abbasid caliph in Baghdad recognised Ashot as ruler of Armenia.

The Byzantines, distressed by his close relations with the Arabs, sent John Kourkouas to support the rebels. He reached Dvin in 922 but failed to take it. In 923 the caliph released Yusuf, who returned to Armenia and demanded tribute, but Ashot defeated and routed the Arab armies sent against him for several years. A second failed attempt by Kourkouas in 927/8 coincided with Ashot's victories over an invading Muslim army near Lake Sevan and north of Dvin. For his success against rebellions and invasions he is remembered by the epithet Yerkat, the Iron.

When the Byzantine emperor Romanos I Lekapenos turned east to fight the Arabs in Syria, Ashot was left master of his domain. He died in 929 without sons or heirs and was succeeded by his brother Abas I. In 2012, on the 20th anniversary of the Armed Forces of Armenia, Catholicos Karekin II declared the cross that Ashot is said to have carried into battle the Guardian of the Armenian Army. He is a character in Muratsan's nineteenth-century historical novel Gevorg Marzpetuni.
ashot-iii-of-armenia: Ashot III was the eldest son of King Abas, and had two brothers, Atrnerseh and Mushegh. During his father's reign he held the office of Prince of Princes, which under the first four Bagratuni kings was mostly held by members of the royal house next in line to the throne. He succeeded Abas in 953. The Georgian Bagratids, who were related to the Armenian Bagratunis by marriage, recognised his suzerainty, as did the rulers of Vaspurakan, Kars, Khachen, Parisos and Shirvan, and he used the title Shahanshah of Armenians and Georgians.

In the first years of his reign Ashot gathered an army of 30,000 and tried to free the city of Dvin from Muslim rule. He was defeated near the city, and the Emirate of Dvin continued to exist in the heart of Armenia. Having failed there, he turned to Ani. The Bagratunis had earlier lived at Bagaran, Yerazgavors and Kars, none of which had Ani's natural defences. In 961 an assembly of the princes of Armenia, the catholicos Anania I Mokatsi and many bishops was held at Ani for Ashot's coronation, and the city was proclaimed capital. About 964 he built a wall across the narrowest part of its promontory, later called the Ashotyan walls, and he sponsored monasteries, hospitals, schools and almshouses.

In the late 960s and 970s Byzantium under Nicephorus Phocas and John Tzimiskes threatened Armenian lands, and Taron was seized in 968. In 974 Tzimiskes marched on Mush, but met Ashot's army of 30,000 and left Armenia; Ashot then supplied him with 10,000 soldiers for his campaign in Mesopotamia. A council he called at Shirakavan in 968 chose Bishop Vahan of Syunik as catholicos, but Vahan leaned to the Chalcedonian church and was deposed at Ani in 969.

Ashot sent his brother Mushegh to rule at Kars with the title of king, and in 966 gave the district of Dzoraget near Lake Sevan to his son Gurgen, ancestor of the Kyurikid line. Such sub-kingdoms continued under his successors, and served Armenia so long as the king at Ani remained strong. His wife Queen Khosrovanuysh founded the Sanahin Monastery in 966 and the Haghpat Monastery in 976. His epithet, the Merciful, is first found in documents after his death; his contemporary Anania Mokatsi does not use it, and a folk tradition from Akhaltsikhe links it to his punishing an overseer who withheld gold meant for the poor. He was probably buried at Ani or at Horomos.
ashraf-hotak: Ashraf was born in southern Afghanistan in the early 18th century into a prominent family of the Hotak tribe, which led the Ghilji Pashtun confederacy with the Tokhi tribe. He was the eldest son of Abdul Aziz Hotak and a nephew of Mirwais Hotak, the mayor of Kandahar who revolted against the Safavids in 1709 and ruled independently until 1715. Ashraf took part in the Ghilji invasion of Iran in 1721 and 1722, which ended in the capture of the Safavid capital Isfahan. Shah Soltan Hoseyn was overthrown and replaced by Ashraf's cousin Mahmud, with whom Ashraf had poor relations.

Ashraf returned to Kandahar, then went back to Isfahan and plotted against Mahmud, who grew unstable. Mahmud had him imprisoned, but on 22 April 1725 part of the Afghan army freed Ashraf and overthrew Mahmud, who was probably murdered soon afterwards. Ashraf was crowned shah on 26 April 1725. He blinded his own brother, executed most of the leaders of the coup that had put him on the throne and married a daughter of Soltan Hoseyn. The historian Michael Axworthy calls him as brutal and ruthless as Mahmud, but more calculating.

He tried to settle with the Ottomans, asking them to recognise him as a legitimate and independent Sunni ruler, but Sultan Ahmed III refused and ordered a campaign in 1726. The armies met at Khorramabad in November 1726 and the Afghans won. A peace agreement of October 1727 let the Ottomans keep their occupied lands while recognising Ashraf's rule. He lost a battle near Langarud against the Russians in 1727 but signed the Treaty of Rasht in February 1729. Most of the Iranian population still rejected Afghan rule, rebellions broke out and the Ghilji chiefs in Kandahar withheld support.

Tahmasp, Soltan Hoseyn's surviving son, rallied Qajar and Afshar chiefs, above all Nader Qoli Beg Afshar, later Nader Shah. Nader defeated Ashraf's force at Mehmandust near Damghan on 29 September 1729. Ashraf withdrew to Isfahan, where Afghan forces plundered the city and massacred part of its population. After a hard fight at Murche-Khort he fled on 13 November 1729, three days before Nader entered the city.

Nader beat him again at Zarqan and Pol-e Fasa. Ashraf failed to reach Basra by sea and set out for Kandahar overland. Near Sistan Baluchis attacked and killed him in early 1730, possibly sent by his cousin Hussain; another account says Hussain's son Ibrahim shot him after Ashraf stabbed him.
ashur-god: The name of the god Ashur is spelled exactly like that of the city of Assur, and some Assyriologists use different spellings to tell them apart. Little is known of the city in the 3rd millennium BCE. It had a temple of its own Ishtar, but no mention of Ashur as a distinct deity survives, and whether his cult existed then cannot be ruled out. Lambert suggested that the god was the deified hill on which the city stood, and the cliff over the Tigris near Assur was probably the original cult place.

In the Old Assyrian period the city's residents built and maintained his temple, and he appears in treaties and royal inscriptions. The rulers did not call themselves kings but governor (iššiak) or city ruler, keeping the title of king for Ashur. The earliest expression of this is the seal of Silulu, which opens: Ashur is king, Silulu is the governor of Assur.

Ashur is intrinsically tied to his city. He lacks characteristics, stock epithets and any early mythology, and represents the city and later the state and its power. His possible image on Old Assyrian seals is the bull altar. He also lacks original family: his only native relative is the goddess Šerua, whom Tukulti-Ninurta I called his daughter and Tiglath-pileser III his wife. Mullissu, identified with Ninlil, reflects his identification with Enlil, and Ninurta and Zababa were occasionally called his sons.

In the Assyrian version of the Enuma Elish, Ashur takes the place of Marduk and is written Anshar, so that two Anshars appear in the myth. Lambert blamed poor narrative skill; Frahm thinks it was intentional, to give Ashur both genealogical and political superiority. A text known as the Marduk Ordeal likewise has Marduk tried and imprisoned for crimes against Ashur.

From the Middle Assyrian period kings took the title of king and presented themselves as agents extending Ashur's rule over territory. The coronation ritual, performed in his temple, had a priest strike the king's cheek and proclaim: Ashur is king. Each province supplied food each year for the god's daily meal, showing that all Assyria cared for him jointly. The land of Assyria shared the god's name, so the country belonged to him.

In the Neo-Assyrian period royal actions were said to be done at Ashur's command, with the king as proxy, and oaths imposed on the defeated were sworn in his name. The king was chief priest of Ashur but was not considered a god. Edmonds cautions that the ideology of expanding the cosmos against a disorderly periphery appears only late in the sources, and was probably a later justification rather than the driver of expansion. After Assyria fell, a small sanctuary of Anshar is attested at Neo-Babylonian Uruk, probably founded by Assyrians.
ashur-nadin-shumi: Aššur-nādin-šumi, whose Akkadian name means "Ashur gives a name", was probably the firstborn son of the Neo-Assyrian king Sennacherib and his first crown prince, and so the designated successor to the Assyrian throne. Babylonia had been conquered by Tiglath-Pileser III (r. 745–727 BCE) less than thirty years before he became its king. In those years Babylonia repeatedly tried to become an independent kingdom again, and Babylonian revolts were an especially frequent nuisance during Sennacherib's reign, which required him to defeat numerous southern uprisings.

After defeating uprisings in 700 BCE, Sennacherib named his own son king of Babylon. Aššur-nādin-šumi was also titled māru rēštû, which can mean either the pre-eminent son or the firstborn son. The appointment and the title suggest that he was being groomed to follow Sennacherib as king of Assyria, as Assyrians in most cases followed the principle of primogeniture. Further evidence is that Sennacherib built a palace for him at Assur, as he would later do for the crown prince Esarhaddon.

His position as Assyrian king of Babylon was politically important and highly delicate, and would have given valuable experience to the intended heir of the whole empire. His tenure did not last long, however, and he was unable to handle the volatile political situation in the south.

In 694 BCE Sennacherib campaigned against Elam, in what is now southern Iran, to pursue Chaldean rebels who had fled there. In response to this incursion the Elamites invaded the southern parts of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. Probably encouraged by the Babylonians themselves, they captured Aššur-nādin-šumi at the city of Sippar. The prince was taken back to Elam and probably executed.
ashur-nirari-v: Ashur-nirari, whose name means Ashur is my help, was a son of Adad-nirari III and succeeded his brother Ashur-dan III as king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire in 755 BCE. He ruled during an obscure period from which few sources survive, so that apart from broad political developments his reign is poorly known. Assyrian officials were becoming powerful relative to the king. They accepted the monarch's authority but in practice acted with supreme authority and wrote their own cuneiform inscriptions about building and political activities, and such inscriptions are more common from this time than royal ones. Assyria's enemies were also growing more dangerous, and the decline coincided with the peak of the northern Kingdom of Urartu.

A contemporary inscription of Sarduri II of Urartu claims a victory over him in battle. A fragmentary treaty between Ashur-nirari and Mati'ilu, king of Arpad, survives, and almost all of what remains consists of curses against Mati'ilu. It probably followed his campaign against Arpad in 755 BCE. The only known inscription written under Ashur-nirari himself is a fragment recording a grant of lands and tax exemption to the official Marduk-sarra-usur after he distinguished himself in battle.

The list of eponyms shows the king staying in the land, not campaigning, in almost every year of his reign, except for three years. Besides 755 BCE he campaigned against the city of Namri in Urartu in 748 to 747. Since Assyrian kings customarily campaigned every year, this may point to domestic instability, and no building work under him is known.

Ashur-nirari is generally held to have died in 745 BCE, the year Tiglath-Pileser III came to the throne. The Assyrian King List calls Tiglath-Pileser his son, but Tiglath-Pileser's own inscriptions name Adad-nirari III as his father, which would make him a brother. Records survive of a revolt at Nimrud in 746 or 745 BCE, and Tiglath-Pileser credited his rise to divine selection, so he is typically assumed to have usurped the throne. In her 2016 doctoral thesis the historian Tracy Davenport suggested instead that the succession was legitimate and that the two were briefly co-rulers.
ashur-uballit-i: Ashur-uballit I was king of Assyria and the first king of the Middle Assyrian Empire. His father Eriba-Adad I had broken half a century of intermittent Hurrian-Mitanni influence over Assyria. Ashur-uballit's defeat of the Mitanni king Shuttarna III marks Assyria's full ascendancy over the Hurri-Mitanni civilizations, much of which it annexed, and the start of its emergence as a powerful empire.

With Assyrian power firmly established in Mesopotamia, the north-east Levant and south-east Anatolia, he began to make contact with other great powers, and two of the Amarna letters were sent by him. His messages to the Egyptians angered his Babylonian neighbour Burnaburiash II, who wrote to the pharaoh that the Assyrians were his vassals and that Egypt should send them back empty-handed.

Burnaburiash married Muballitat-Sherua, a daughter of Ashur-uballit, and they had at least one son, Prince Kara-hardash. Kurigalzu II may have been their son or grandson. After the death of Burnaburiash, disorder in Babylonia led Ashur-uballit to invade and install Kurigalzu II on the throne, the first of a series of Assyrian interventions in Babylonian affairs.

Kara-hardash succeeded his father, but a revolt soon showed how unpopular the Assyrians were. Ashur-uballit would not allow his grandson to be cast aside and invaded Babylon. Kara-hardash was killed in the rebellion, and the Assyrians placed Kurigalzu II on the Babylonian throne. The new king did not stay loyal and invaded Assyria, but Ashur-uballit stopped his army at Sugagu, not far south of Assur. He then counterattacked, took territory in central Mesopotamia and forced a treaty in Assyria's favour on Kurigalzu.
ashura: Ashura is an Aramaic word meaning tenth, and shares its root with the Hebrew asor. According to the traditions, fasting on Ashura was a Jewish practice that Muhammad adopted after his arrival in Medina in 622, and the hadith literature derives the observance from Yom Kippur. In a report in Sahih al-Bukhari, Muhammad finds the Jews of Medina fasting on the tenth of Muharram and says that Muslims have more right to observe the fast. The fast ceased to be obligatory after about a year, when relations with the Jews of Medina deteriorated, a change often associated with verses of the Quran that make Ramadan the main month of fasting. Other Sunni traditions describe fasting on Ashura as a pre-Islamic practice of the Quraysh.

For Shia Muslims, Ashura commemorates the death of Husayn ibn Ali, grandson of Muhammad and third imam, killed with most of his male relatives and his small retinue on 10 Muharram 61 AH (10 October 680) at the Battle of Karbala against the army of the Umayyad caliph Yazid ibn Mu'awiya. They had been surrounded for some days and deprived of the water of the nearby Euphrates. The women and children were taken prisoner and marched to Damascus. In Shia belief Karbala symbolises the struggle between good and evil, and mourning for Husayn is an act of protest against oppression and an act of worship.

Sunni Muslims also regard the killing of Husayn as a tragic event, but the ninth and tenth of Muharram are days of voluntary fasting, strongly encouraged by jurists. Ashura is also associated with the parting of the Red Sea by Moses and Noah's disembarking from the Ark.

Shia Muslims commemorate Karbala through the months of Muharram and Safar, most of all in the first ten days of Muharram. Gatherings called majalis centre on the narration of the Karbala story and the recitation of elegies, intended to move the audience to tears. Processions march in major Shia cities, carrying objects such as the alam, the ensign of Husayn. Mild self-flagellation, striking the face and chest, is common, while extreme forms with knives or chains have been condemned by many clerics. Ta'ziyeh, a dramatic reenactment of the martyrdom, is performed in Iran and elsewhere.

Sunni festivities on the day were established by the time of the jurist Ibn Taymiyya, who died in 1328, and may have grown up in response to Shia mourning: the Umayyad caliph Abd al-Malik ibn Marwan made Ashura a festive public holiday to counter the commemoration of Husayn. In the Maghreb the day is marked by fasting, almsgiving, special dishes, bonfires and carnivals.
ashurbanipal: Ashurbanipal was born c. 685 BCE, probably the fourth eldest son of King Esarhaddon. After the unexpected death of the first crown prince, Sin-nadin-apli, in 674, Esarhaddon named Ashurbanipal heir to Assyria and his elder son Shamash-shum-ukin king of Babylon, the two to rule as equal brothers. Ashurbanipal trained in hunting, riding, scholarship, archery and chariotry, and with his father often ill he managed the empire's intelligence network.

Ashurbanipal succeeded in 669 BCE. His early years went on rebellions in Egypt, which Esarhaddon had conquered. His largest campaigns were against Elam, defeated in 665, 653 and 647 to 646, and against Shamash-shum-ukin, who rebelled in 652 with a coalition of Assyria's enemies and died during the siege of Babylon in 648. His sack of Babylon weakened the empire and fed anti-Assyrian feeling in the south, perhaps contributing to the rise of the Neo-Babylonian Empire five years after his death. His destruction of Elam has been described as a genocide, and he boasted of massacres of rebellious civilians.

Little is known of his late reign, since the eponym canon ends in 649. He promoted eunuchs over the nobility. Whether his policies caused the fall of Assyria some two decades after his death is disputed among Assyriologists.

Ashurbanipal read Akkadian and Sumerian from his youth. He had scribes collect and copy texts from temple libraries across the empire for the Library of Ashurbanipal at Nineveh, which perhaps held over 100,000 texts, including omens, dictionaries, rituals and prayers. Around 30,000 survived the destruction of Nineveh in 612 BCE. Hormuzd Rassam found the North Palace in December 1853. Greek and Roman writers remembered a distorted figure, Sardanapalus, an effeminate, decadent last king of Assyria.
ashurnasirpal-ii: Ashurnasirpal II, whose name Aššur-nāṣir-apli means "Ashur is guardian of the heir", was the third king of the Neo-Assyrian Empire. He succeeded his father, Tukulti-Ninurta II, and reigned from 883 to 859 BCE. His queen was Mullissu-mukannišat-Ninua, and his son and successor was Shalmaneser III.

Ashurnasirpal began a vast programme of expansion. He conquered peoples to the north as far as Nairi, exacted tribute from Phrygia, and invaded Aram, subduing the Aramaeans and Neo-Hittites between the Khabur and the Euphrates. Like earlier Assyrian kings he campaigned along the Euphrates against the Aramaeans and in the Diyala against Babylon. His army was typically made up of infantry, including auxiliaries and foreigners, heavy and light cavalry and chariots. He installed Assyrian governors rather than relying on local client rulers who paid tribute, and where revolts recurred the local monarch was replaced by a governor loyal only to the Assyrian king.

His inscriptions record brutal treatment of rebels. After crushing a revolt in a two-day pitched battle, he states that he cut off the hands, feet, ears, noses and lips of prisoners, made heaps of their ears and heads, and burned children. After this victory he advanced without opposition to the Mediterranean and exacted tribute from Phoenicia. He did not destroy the Phoenician cities he conquered, and his siege of Tyre failed. Tribute from them supplied iron for weapons, Lebanese cedar for building, and gold and silver to pay troops. Of resettled populations he wrote that he imposed more tribute and tax than ever before, in horses, mules, oxen, sheep, wine and labour.

Ashurnasirpal moved his capital to Kalhu, modern Nimrud, using enslaved captives to build it. His palace there probably began about 878 BCE and was completed after around fifteen years, with the near-total rebuilding of the Middle Assyrian city. An inscription describing its inauguration records a ten-day banquet attended by 69,574 people. Its walls were lined with carved alabaster reliefs of the king with winged protective spirits, hunting lions and campaigning. Each bore the Standard Inscription, which traces his lineage, recounts his victories, defines his empire and tells how he founded Kalhu.

Austen Henry Layard rediscovered the palace in 1845 and sent many reliefs to Europe and North America, most to the British Museum; Max Mallowan re-excavated the site from 1947 to 1957. Bronze bands from the gates at Balawat, 6.8 metres high, show his reign; one set was found by Hormuzd Rassam in 1878.
ashvaghosha: Aśvaghoṣa is said to have been born at Saketa, today Ayodhya. His original name is unknown, and Aśvaghoṣa, meaning Horse-Cry, is a later nickname. According to his traditional biography, translated into Chinese by Kumārajīva, he began as a wandering ascetic who defeated all comers in debate. Challenged by the monk Pārśva, he lost, became Pārśva's disciple and was fully ordained as a bhikṣu. The same biography says that a Kuṣāna king besieged the central kingdom and took Aśvaghoṣa as part of the tribute. There he preached to seven horses that had been starved, and they listened in tears, so that he received his name. Other sources say all the horses of the country cried out at his birth.

His school is uncertain. He seems not to belong to the Mahayana period and may have been ordained in a Mahasanghika subsect, though research on the Saundarananda, which may draw on the Yogacarabhumi, raises the possibility of a link to the Yogacara or Sautrantika schools.

Much Buddhist literature before him was composed in Pāli and Prakrit, but Aśvaghoṣa wrote in classical Sanskrit. He is believed to have been the first Sanskrit dramatist and is considered the leading Indian poet before Kālidāsa. His Buddhacarita, or Acts of the Buddha, is an epic life of the Buddha. The monk I-tsing (Yijing) reported that it was read in all the five parts of India and in the countries of the South Sea, because it set out the doctrine in compact form. The Saundarananda, a kāvya poem, tells of the conversion of the Buddha's half-brother Nanda: the first half describes Nanda's life and the second sets out Buddhist doctrine and ascetic practice.

A fragment of his play, the Śāriputraprakaraṇa, survives in Sanskrit. Other works are attributed to him with doubtful authority. The Awakening of Faith in the Mahayana, once ascribed to him, is agreed by modern scholars to have been composed in China. The Vajrasuchi, a poem critical of class and inequity under Vedic religion, was first translated by Brian Houghton Hodgson in 1835.
ashvatthama: Ashvatthama is a major character of the Mahabharata, the son of Drona, royal preceptor to the Kuru princes, the Pandavas and the Kauravas, and of Kripi. His name derives from aśva, horse, and sthāman, strength or presence; at his birth he cried out like the celestial horse Uccaishravas, and a divine voice named him. He is mentioned as a combined incarnation of Shiva, Yama, Kama and Krodha, with a gem on his forehead. He grew up in poverty, was trained in warfare by his father alongside the Kuru princes, and was entrusted with celestial weapons including the Narayanastra and the Brahmashirastra. He became a close companion of Duryodhana, leader of the Kauravas.

In the Kurukshetra War he fought for the Kauravas and was one of three Kaurava warriors to survive. On the fifteenth day a false rumour of his death led Drona to lay down his weapons, and Dhrishtadyumna beheaded him. Enraged, Ashvatthama vowed vengeance and loosed the Narayanastra on the Pandava army; Krishna told the troops to discard their weapons, which nullified it.

After Duryodhana, mortally wounded, named him the last commander-in-chief, Ashvatthama went with Kripa and Kritavarman to a forest near the Pandava camp. Seeing an owl kill sleeping crows, he resolved to attack the sleeping camp, over Kripa's objections. He prayed to Shiva, who gave him a celestial sword and entered his body. He killed Dhrishtadyumna and Shikhandi, the five sons of Draupadi and other sleeping warriors, while Kripa and Kritavarman set the camp ablaze.

The Pandavas pursued him to Vyasa's hermitage, where he hurled the Brahmashirsha weapon. Arjuna countered with a similar weapon and retracted it; Ashvatthama could not, and redirected his into the wombs of the Pandava women, killing the unborn Parikshit, whom Krishna revived. Vyasa demanded the gem from his forehead, and Krishna cursed him to wander the earth for 3,000 years in suffering.

The Sapta Chiranjivi Stotram names him among seven immortals, and there is a shrine to him in the Ananthapadmanabhaswamy temple in Thiruvananthapuram. The historians R. Sathianathaier and D. C. Sircar propose that family legends of the Pallavas speak of an ancestor descended from Ashvatthama and a Naga princess.
ashvins: The name Ashvin, Sanskrit for horse possessors, comes from an Indo-Iranian stem for the horse. The Ashvins are Nasatya and Dasra, and in the Rigveda they are always referred to in the dual, though the texts distinguish the two. They are often called the grandsons of Dyaus, the sky-god, a formula that matches the Lithuanian Ašvieniai, the Latvian Dieva Dēli and the Greek Diós-kouroi, the boys of Zeus, who are Castor and Pollux. They are one instance of the Indo-European divine horse twins, which may also lie behind the English Hengist and Horsa and the Welsh Bran and Manawydan.

The name Nasatya appears 99 times in the Rigveda, and is probably related to a root for safe return home. The first mention of the Nasatya twins is in a treaty of about 1350 BCE between Suppiluliuma, king of the Hittites, and Shattiwaza of Mitanni.

The Rigveda mentions the Ashvins 398 times, with more than 50 hymns addressed to them. They are youthful twin horsemen who travel in a chariot drawn by tireless horses and who safeguard and rescue people. The chariot has three wheels and three chariot-boxes, and is drawn by horses, bulls, buffaloes and birds. They are linked with medicine, healing and the twilight, and they follow the dawn goddess Ushas, who is asked to awaken them. The Rigveda calls them slayers of darkness.

Their deeds of rescue are many. They drew the seer Rebha back from the waters after he had been bound and cast in for nine days and ten nights, and brought Bhujyu home from the sea. They freed Atri from a cleft in the earth, restored the eyesight of Rijrashva and gave Vishpala a metal foot. In the Shatapatha Brahmana they restore the youth of the old sage Chyavana, and the other gods at first refused them a share in the sacrifice because they spent too much time among mortals.

In ritual, honey is associated with the Ashvins, and they are the chief deities of the Pravargya rite, in which they receive hot milk. They are invoked at dawn, the time of their principal sacrifice. As a dual pair, with Indra and Vayu and with Mitra and Varuna, they share in the morning pressing of soma, and they are the last to receive soma in the overnight Atirātra rite.

Later texts keep them important. Sources vary, but they are generally said to be sons of the sun god and his wife Sanjna, who is said to have taken the form of a mare. The Mahabharata tells that Madri invoked the Ashvins and bore the twins Nakula and Sahadeva. A local tradition holds that the Ashvins first prepared the formulation behind chyavanprash for the sage Chyavana.
asia: Asia holds roughly 60% of the world's population. It shares the landmass of Eurasia with Europe, and its border with Europe is a historical and cultural construct, as there is no clear physical separation between them. Greek geographers such as Anaximander and Hecataeus used a threefold division of the Old World from the 6th century BCE, and the Ural River prevailed as the boundary in the mid-19th century. The boundary with Africa is the Suez Canal, the Gulf of Suez, the Red Sea and the Bab-el-Mandeb. Asia has the longest coastline of any continent, at 62,800 kilometres.

Researchers believe modern humans migrated to South Asia along the Indian Ocean about 60,000 years ago, and that they interbred with Denisovans in Southeast Asia. The history of Asia can be seen as the distinct histories of several peripheral coastal regions, East Asia, South Asia, Southeast Asia, Central Asia and West Asia.

The coastal periphery was home to some of the world's earliest known civilisations, each developing around fertile river valleys: those of Mesopotamia, the Indus Valley and the Yellow River shared many similarities and may have exchanged technologies and ideas such as mathematics and the wheel, while writing seems to have developed independently in each area.

Evidence of farming in West Asia dates back to around 9000 BCE. China and India traded places as the largest economies in the world from 1 to 1800 CE, and the Silk Road became the main east–west trading route in the Asian hinterlands, while the Straits of Malacca stood as a major sea route. Asia was the birthplace of most of the world's mainstream religions, including Islam, Judaism, Christianity, Hinduism and Buddhism.

Asia is subdivided into 49 countries, five of them transcontinental (Georgia, Azerbaijan, Russia, Kazakhstan and Turkey). The United Nations Statistics Division divides it into North Asia, Central Asia, West Asia, South Asia, East Asia and Southeast Asia, solely for statistical reasons. It has no single culture: various independent cultures coexist, and it varies greatly in ethnic groups, environments, economies and government systems. Asia is home to several language families, and more than 700 languages are spoken in Indonesia, over 400 in India and more than 100 in the Philippines.
asia-pacific-economic-cooperation: The inspiration for APEC came from the post-ministerial conferences of the Association of Southeast Asian Nations, launched in the mid-1980s, which showed the value of regular meetings between developed and developing economies. These led the Australian prime minister Bob Hawke to believe in the need for region-wide economic co-operation, and in January 1989 he called for more effective co-operation across the Pacific Rim. The first meeting took place in Canberra in November 1989, chaired by the Australian foreign affairs minister Gareth Evans and attended by ministers from twelve countries.

The organisation was at first an Australian initiative intended to secure greater Japanese engagement in the region. Its early years saw tension between members favouring a structured trade agreement and those, like the United States, who preferred a looser, consultative approach.

The first four annual meetings were attended by ministers. From 1993 they became Economic Leaders' Meetings, attended by heads of government from every member except Taiwan, which sends a ministerial-level official. In 1994 at Bogor the leaders adopted the Bogor Goals, aiming at free and open trade and investment by 2010 for industrialised economies and by 2020 for developing ones. In 1995 an Osaka meeting agreed to set up the APEC Business Advisory Council from 1996.

At Vancouver in 1997, Royal Canadian Mounted Police officers used pepper spray on protesters who objected to the presence of leaders such as Indonesia's president Suharto. At Shanghai in 2001 the leaders endorsed the Shanghai Accord, committing members to reduce trade transaction costs by five percent over five years. APEC began discussing a Free Trade Area of the Asia-Pacific in 2006, an idea traced to a proposal by the Japanese economist Kiyoshi Kojima in 1966.

APEC calls its members economies rather than countries, because the criterion for membership is being an independent economic entity rather than a sovereign state. Its 21 members include Taiwan, participating as Chinese Taipei, alongside the People's Republic of China, and Hong Kong. It has three official observers: the ASEAN Secretariat, the Pacific Economic Cooperation Council and the Pacific Islands Forum Secretariat. The Secretariat is based in Singapore, and the meeting rotates annually among members. In 1993 the United States president Bill Clinton insisted on informal attire and gave the leaders leather bomber jackets, which began the tradition of leaders dressing in the host's national costume for the group photograph.
asia-roman-province: Asia was a Roman province covering most of western Asia Minor. After the Romans crushed Antiochus III at Magnesia in 190 BCE, the Treaty of Apamea in 188 BCE gave most of the territory to the Attalid dynasty of Pergamum. King Attalus III, a close ally of Rome without a legitimate heir, bequeathed his kingdom to Rome. On his death in 133 BCE the pretender Eumenes III rebelled, and the consul Marcus Perperna defeated him. Manius Aquillius then formally established the province. It first took in Mysia, the Troad, Aeolis, Lydia, Ionia and Caria, and the Aegean islands except Crete.

A law of Gaius Gracchus in 123 BCE gave members of the equestrian order the right to collect taxes in Asia. Communities that could not pay borrowed from Roman lenders at exorbitant rates and often lost their land. By 88 BCE Mithridates VI of Pontus had conquered virtually all of Asia and ordered the slaughter of all Romans and Italians in the province, with estimates of the dead from 80,000 to 150,000. Sulla defeated him and in 85 BCE reorganized the province into eleven assize districts, among them Ephesus, Pergamum and Smyrna, which competed for dominance.

Under Augustus it became a proconsular province and the most prestigious senatorial one. It was a system of hundreds of largely self-governing Greek cities that competed for status through festival games, cults and oratory, and it had no full legions. In the 3rd century the Antonine plague and the Gothic invasions of the 250s and 260s brought decline. Diocletian divided the province into seven in the 4th century, and after the great plague of 543 many interior cities shrank to villages.
asilah: Asilah is a fortified town on the north-western tip of the Atlantic coast of Morocco, about 31 kilometres south of Tangier. Its ramparts and gateworks remain fully intact. The history of the area reaches back to about 1500 BCE, when Phoenicians occupied a site called Silis, Zili, Zilis or Zilil, which is being excavated at Dchar Jdid, some 12 kilometres north-east of the present town. That site was once taken for the Roman stronghold Ad Mercuri but is now accepted to be Zilil.

The town itself was first built by the Idrisid dynasty, and the Umayyad caliph Al-Hakam II rebuilt it in 966. Its walls were first built by the Almohads and restored by the Marinids and Wattasids. The Portuguese conquered it in 1471, rebuilt the walls to resist artillery and shrank the perimeter for easier control. In 1578 Sebastian of Portugal used Asilah as a base for his troops in a planned crusade that ended in his death, which led to the Portuguese succession crisis of 1580. The Saadians briefly regained the town in 1589, and then lost it to Spain.

Moulay Ismail took it for Morocco in 1692 and built the Grand Mosque in the former kasbah soon afterwards. In the 19th and 20th centuries it served as a base for pirates, and in 1829 Austria bombarded it as a punishment for Moroccan piracy. Moulay Ahmed er-Raisuni, a local pirate who rose to power and declared himself pasha of the region, built his palace there in 1909 and gained wealth partly through kidnappings and ransoms. From 1912 to 1956 Asilah was part of Spanish Morocco.

The old walled medina dates mostly from the Portuguese occupation of the 15th and 16th centuries and afterwards. It has two main gates, Bab Homar and Bab al-Qasaba, and a rectangular Portuguese tower called Borj al-Hamra. Its buildings are painted white and decorated with murals made during the International Cultural Moussem of Asilah, an art festival started in 1978 by the mayor Mohamed Benaissa and the painter Mohamed Melehi, which helped renew the town. Asilah is a seaside resort and a place of weekend visits from Casablanca. Its Kahal Synagogue, built in 1824, was restored and reopened in 2022.
asir: Asir lies on a high plateau that receives more rain than the rest of Saudi Arabia and holds the country's highest peaks, rising to almost 3,200 metres at Jabal Soudah near Abha. Average annual rainfall in the highlands probably ranges from 300 to 500 millimetres, falling in two seasons, chiefly in March and April. Daily temperature ranges are very large, with frosty mornings and afternoons often above 30 °C, and there is more natural vegetation than elsewhere in the country, including dense coniferous forest in sheltered areas. Farmers chiefly grow wheat and fruit, and historically the region produced coffee, barley, senna and frankincense.

The origin of the name is debated. Al-Masudi suggested that the region was first known as the Land of Azd; another view derives it from the Arabic ʿUsrah, hardship, for the rugged terrain; and Fuad Hamza links it to the prominence of the tribe of Banu Asir.

In 25 BCE the Roman commander Aelius Gallus marched south from Egypt on an expedition of some 1,300 miles to seize the overland trade routes towards Hadhramaut, hoping to capture Marib, capital of Saba, and the incense trade. The expedition was a disaster, and little information about Asir came of it.

After the Ottomans destroyed the First Saudi state in 1818, the Asiris went on fighting the forces of Ottoman Egypt. When the Ottomans withdrew in 1840, the dynasty of Al-Ayedh took control of the highlands. The Ottomans occupied them again after defeating and executing the Al-Ayedh leader in 1872 and set up a sub-governorate at Abha.

About 1906 Muhammad ibn Ali al-Idrisi began to establish control; he allied secretly with Great Britain in 1915, and after the First World War he ruled the Emirate of Asir, an internationally recognised state, until his death in 1920. Ibn Saud then began to annex the region, took Abha in 1920 and incorporated the rest by 1923. The Treaty of Taif of 1934 settled the claim of the Zaydi Imam of Yemen, and in 1935 Asir was made a separate governorate.

Asir is a province of Saudi Arabia of 76,693 square kilometres, with its seat at Abha. It borders the provinces of Mecca, Al-Baha, Riyadh, Najran and Jazan, and Yemen to the south. It has 17 governorates, and Khamis Mushait is its largest city. Asir National Park, established in 1981, extends from the Red Sea coast through the western foothills to the escarpment. King Khalid University, founded in 1998, has its main campus in Abha.
askold-and-dir: Nothing is known of the two men beyond the chronicles. They are named in the Primary Chronicle and in the Younger Redaction of the Novgorod First Chronicle, and their names are given in Old Norse as Haskuldr or Hǫskuldr and Dyr or Dýri. The Primary Chronicle was written about 250 years after their time; long credited to the monk Nestor, it may have been compiled in 1116 by Sylvester of Kiev, hegumen of St. Michael's Monastery at Vydubychi.

The historian Igor Danilevsky held the Scandinavian origin of the name Askold to be certain, while others proposed Slavic or Iranian roots. Late medieval writers, among them the 15th-century Polish historian Jan Dlugosz and the Kievan Synopsis of 1674, made Askold and Dir heirs of Kyi, a figure of legend. Vladimir Petrukhin traced this to Dlugosz's wish to support Polish claims to Kiev, and specialists rarely accept it.

In the Laurentian Codex of the Primary Chronicle, Rurik sanctioned their journey to Constantinople; travelling down the Dnieper, they settled at Kiev and took power over the Polans. The Slavonic chronicles link their names to the Rus' attack on Constantinople in June 860, which Patriarch Photios described as coming like a thunderbolt from heaven, but the connection remains tenuous, and most historians reject as apocryphal the story of Askold's later conversion.

The only foreign source to name either man is the Arab historian Al-Masudi, who called king al-Dir the first among the kings of the Slavs. If he is the same Dir, he may have ruled after Askold, mainly in the 870s and 880s. Boris Rybakov argued that the chroniclers had split one prince, Askoldyr, into two, a reading Danilevsky found to have no textual basis.

In the Novgorod First Chronicle it is Igor, not Oleg, who kills the two rulers and becomes prince in Kiev. Vasily Tatishchev and Boris Rybakov saw the killing as the reaction of pagan Varangians to Askold's baptism, and Tatishchev called Askold the first Rus' martyr. A Kievan legend places Askold's burial mound on Uhorska Hora, the Hungarian hill, where Olga of Kiev later built churches of Saint Nicholas and Saint Irene; a monument called Askold's Grave marks the place. In 2013 the synod of the Ukrainian Orthodox Church - Kyiv Patriarchate canonized Askold as a protomartyr.
asmara: Asmara stands at 2,325 metres on a rocky highland plateau, at the tip of an escarpment that forms the north-western edge of the Eritrean Highlands. The plateau separates the western lowlands from the eastern coastal plains, and the fertile land to the south is among the best farmland of the region. The climate is mild for the latitude, with most rain falling in July and August and frost extremely rare.

According to Tigrinya oral tradition, four clans lived on the Kebessa Plateau, named Gheza Gurtom, Gheza Shelele, Gheza Serenser and Gheza Asmae. Clans from the lowlands attacked their villages often, until the women of each clan decided that the four must unite for peace. The name Arbate Asmera means in Tigrinya that the four, feminine plural, made them unite. The first written mention is in a Latin itinerary from the reign of Emperor Dawit I (1382–1411). In the late 19th century the town was for a time the capital of Bahr Negash Gerada Zeray, and it then passed between several regional chiefs, the last of them Ras Alula.

Italian forces occupied the town in 1889, in coordination with local chiefs, and Governor Ferdinando Martini made it the capital of Italian Eritrea in 1897. The Eritrean Railway to the coast ran through Ghinda under the direction of Carlo Cavanna. By the 1939 census Asmara had 98,000 inhabitants, 53,000 of them Italian, out of 75,000 Italians in all Eritrea. Most of central Asmara was built between 1935 and 1941, a period when Benito Mussolini planned a second Roman Empire in Africa, and by the late 1930s it was called Piccola Roma, or Little Rome.

In 1952 the United Nations resolved to federate the former colony under Ethiopian rule, and the capital moved to Addis Ababa. In 1961 Emperor Haile Selassie I ended the federal arrangement and made the territory a province of Ethiopia, and the Eritrean War of Independence began. The city was home to the United States Army's Kagnew Station from 1943 to 1977. Asmara was left relatively undamaged in the war, which ended in 1991 with Eritrean independence, and it again became the capital.

Asmara is known for its early 20th-century buildings, among them the Art Deco Cinema Impero, which opened in 1937, the futurist Fiat Tagliero Building, the Cubist Africa Pension and the neo-Romanesque Church of Our Lady of the Rosary. In July 2017 UNESCO listed the city as a World Heritage Site, the first modernist city listed in its entirety. It is the see of the archbishop of the Eritrean Orthodox Tewahedo Church, which became autocephalous in 1993.
aspar: Aspar was the son of the magister Ardaburius and was of Alanic-Gothic descent. His name, in Iranian languages, means horse-rider. He rose as the general of a Germanic army in Roman service and held the rank of patrician and magister militum, master of soldiers. He played a crucial part in his father's expedition of 424 that defeated the Western usurper Joannes of Ravenna and installed Galla Placidia and her son Valentinian III, and he helped to negotiate a peace treaty with Geiseric after the Vandal invasion of Africa. He reached the consulship in 434 after campaigning in Africa.

Aspar could not become emperor because of his Arian religion, so he acted as a kingmaker. His subordinate Marcian became emperor by marrying Pulcheria, the sister of Theodosius II. When Marcian died on 27 January 457 the leading figures of the Eastern court took eleven days to choose a successor. Anthemius, Marcian's son-in-law and a magister militum, was a strong candidate, and Aspar was probably offered the throne by the senate but refused. He could have chosen his own son Ardabur but instead selected Leo I, an obscure tribune of one of his military units.

In 470, in a struggle for power between Aspar and the Isaurian general Zeno, Aspar persuaded the emperor to appoint his second son, Patricius, as caesar and to give him his daughter Leontia in marriage. The clergy and people of Constantinople did not think an Arian could become emperor, and riots broke out in the hippodrome, led by Marcellus, head of the Sleepless Monks. Aspar and Leo promised the bishops that Patricius would convert to Orthodoxy before he became emperor, and that the marriage would follow only after the conversion.

In 471 a conspiracy organised by Leo I and the Isaurians caused the death of Aspar and his elder son Ardabur. Patricius may have died on this occasion, though some sources report that he recovered from his wounds. Aspar's wife was an Ostrogoth, and the Ostrogoth King Theodoric the Great was her nephew. A cistern attributed to Aspar still exists in Istanbul. His death ended the Germanic domination of Eastern Roman policy, which he had influenced through the reigns of Theodosius II, Marcian and Leo I.
asparuh-of-bulgaria: Asparuh, also called Ispor or, rarely, Isperih, was a Bulgar khan of the second half of the 7th century. The Nominalia of the Bulgarian Khans says that he belonged to the Dulo clan. According to Byzantine sources he was a younger son of Kubrat, who had founded a spacious state, Great Bulgaria, in the steppes of modern Ukraine. Kubrat probably died in 665. The state broke up under Khazar attack in 668, and Asparuh and his brothers parted ways, each leading his people to seek a safer home.

Asparuh was followed by 30,000 to 50,000 Bulgars. He reached the Danube, and while the Arab caliph Muawiyah I besieged Constantinople, from 674 to 678, he and his people settled in the Danube Delta. In 680 the Byzantine emperor Constantine IV marched against the Bulgars and their Slav allies and drove them into a fortified encampment. The emperor then left the army to seek treatment for his ailments, and rumours that he had fled demoralised his troops. Some deserted, and the Bulgars broke through the blockade and routed their enemy at the Battle of Ongala in 680.

The victory led to the Bulgar conquest of Moesia and to some form of alliance with local Slavic groups. When Asparuh began raiding across the mountains into Byzantine Thrace in 681, Constantine IV made a treaty under which the empire paid the Bulgars an annual tribute. These events are seen in retrospect as the founding of the Bulgarian state and its recognition by the Byzantine Empire. Later tradition credits Asparuh with building Pliska and Drăstăr.

The length and dates of his reign are uncertain, and modern chronologies differ. A late tradition says he died fighting the Khazars on the Danube, and one theory, advanced by the historian Vaklinov, places his grave near Voznesenka on the Dnieper in Ukraine. Bulgarian historians have stressed that his state had a capital and a state tradition that could later be viewed as national, although in its first century or two it was plainly multi-tribal and hegemonic. The town of Isperikh bears his name.
assab-bay: Assab, also written Aseb, is a port city in the Southern Red Sea Region of Eritrea, on the western shore of the Red Sea. It lies about 50 kilometres north-west of the ancient city of Arsinoe Epidires. Its climate is the hot desert type of the Danakil Region: arid, with an annual rainfall of about 40 millimetres and a mean annual temperature approaching 31 degrees. Until the middle of the 19th century it was a tiny Afar fishing village of about 100 people and twenty huts, with little contact with the hinterland.

On 15 November 1869 the Italian missionary Giuseppe Sapeto bought the Bay of Assab on behalf of the Rubattino Shipping Company. He found two sultans, the brothers Hasan ibn Ahmed and Ibrahim ibn Ahmed, who agreed to sell for 6,000 Maria Theresa thalers. Sapeto argued that the bay suited Italy because of its nearness to the Bab-el-Mandeb and that, though nominally under the sultan of Aussa, it was an independent polity. The purchase was disputed in the Italian press and parliament, and Egypt declared the sale illegal.

The Italian government seized control in 1882 and opened a route inland to Shewa. Count Pietro Antonelli, envoy to Menelik II, agreed to supply the ruler with 2,000 Remington rifles imported through Assab, and by the end of 1884 had brought in 50,000 rifles and 10 million cartridges in exchange for camel loads of gold, ivory and civet.

The settlement declined after the Italian occupation of Massawa in 1885, which gave a larger port, and the arms trade broke down with the outbreak of hostilities with Menelik II. After the Battle of Adwa Assab was largely forgotten. Ethiopia preferred to trade through the French at Djibouti, and the Ethio-Djibouti railway cut trade further. The town lived on salt exports to Japan and nearby date plantations, with 1,000 to 3,000 people. After the Second Italo-Ethiopian War a road to Dessie and a rebuilt port gave it new impetus. The 3/15th Punjab Regiment captured Assab on 11 June 1941, taking its whole garrison.

Once Eritrea was federated with Ethiopia in 1952 and incorporated in 1962, Assab became an important port of entry. An oil refinery was begun in 1964 and opened in 1967, and Ethiopian migrants came to work at the docks and in the salt and fishing industries. By 1989 it had 39,600 inhabitants. The refinery closed in 1997, and the Eritrean-Ethiopian War of 1998 ended Ethiopia's trade through the port.

Assab is a port town whose people speak mainly Afar, Tigrinya and Arabic. It is served by an international airport. It began as Italy's first colonial foothold in Africa, and its purchase laid the foundations of the colony of Italian Eritrea.
assam: Assam lies south of the Eastern Himalayas along the Brahmaputra and Barak River valleys. The Brahmaputra, the lifeline of Assam, is an antecedent river older than the Himalayas, forming a flood plain 80 to 100 kilometres wide and about 1,000 kilometres long. The first dated mention of the region comes from the Periplus of the Erythraean Sea in the 1st century. Until the 12th century the region east of the Karatoya River was called Kamarupa. The name Assam, first used by the British in the Treaty of Yandabo in 1826, is associated with the Ahom people, originally called Shyam (Shan).

A rock-cut stupa at Sri Surya Pahar has been dated to 200 BCE. The region was a frontier of the Gupta Empire in the fourth century and was ruled by the Varmanas (c. 350 to 650), the Mlechchhas (c. 655 to 900) and the Kamarupa-Palas (c. 900 to 1100). After Kamarupa declined, authority was divided among the Kamata, Chutia and Kachari kingdoms, the Baro-Bhuyans and the Ahom kingdom of Upper Assam, with interventions from the Bengal Sultanate and later the Mughal Empire.

The Ahom kingdom, established in the 13th century, ruled until the early 19th century. The Moamoria rebellion (1769 to 1805) severely weakened it, and a rivalry between the Prime Minister Purnananda Burhagohain and the Ahom Viceroy of Western Assam, Badan Chandra Borphukan, led Borphukan to invite the Burmese. Three successive Burmese invasions followed, and King Chandrakanta Singha was defeated. The British then established tea estates, the region became part of the Bengal Presidency, and the Assam Province was created in 1912. Assam became a state of India on 26 January 1950.

Dispur is the capital of Assam, and Guwahati is the largest city. Assamese and Bodo are official languages. Assam is known for its tea and silk, and the Kaziranga and Manas National Parks are World Heritage Sites; more than half of the surviving wild population of the one-horned Indian rhinoceros lives in the state.
assassination-of-abraham-lincoln: John Wilkes Booth, born in Maryland into a family of prominent stage actors, was a national celebrity and an outspoken Confederate sympathiser. With Union victory imminent, he and conspirators including Lewis Powell, David Herold and George Atzerodt first plotted to kidnap Lincoln to aid the Confederacy. When that failed, they decided to kill Lincoln, Secretary of State William H. Seward and Vice President Andrew Johnson, hoping that removing the three most important federal officials would revive the Confederate cause.

Accounts of Booth's motives differ. In a letter to his mother he wrote of avenging the South. On 11 April he attended Lincoln's last speech, in which Lincoln promoted voting rights for emancipated slaves, and in anger urged Powell to shoot Lincoln on the spot. Powell refused for fear of the crowd.

On 14 April Booth learned at Ford's Theatre that Lincoln was to attend that evening's performance of Our American Cousin. Booth knew the theatre's layout and its staff. Major Henry Rathbone and his fiancée Clara Harris joined the Lincolns, and the president's usual protection was absent.

At about 10:25 pm Booth entered the presidential box and shot Lincoln in the head from behind. Rathbone struggled with him and was stabbed in the arm. Booth jumped to the stage, a drop of about twelve feet, and fled. Witness accounts conflict over what he shouted; most remembered Sic semper tyrannis. The surgeon Charles Leale found a wound behind the left ear and pronounced it mortal. Lincoln was carried to the Petersen House across the street and died the next morning. Elsewhere Powell attacked Seward at his home and wounded him, while Atzerodt got drunk and never approached Johnson.

Booth crossed into Maryland and, with Herold, was tracked by the largest manhunt in US history at the time, directed by Secretary of War Edwin Stanton. On 26 April they were found at a tobacco farm in King George County, Virginia, where Sergeant Boston Corbett shot Booth. A military tribunal tried the other accused. Powell, Herold, Atzerodt and Mary Surratt were hanged in July 1865. John Surratt, who fled abroad, was captured in Egypt in November 1866 and released after a mistrial in 1867.

Johnson was sworn in as the 17th president on 15 April. Lincoln was the first US president to be assassinated. A train carried his remains over 1,700 miles through seven states to burial in Illinois, with millions lining the route. Mourning spread to the South and around the world, and Walt Whitman wrote poems for him.
assassination-of-archduke-franz-ferdinan: Under the Treaty of Berlin of 1878, Austria-Hungary received the mandate to occupy and administer the Ottoman Vilayet of Bosnia, and it formally annexed Bosnia and Herzegovina in 1908. The assassins were members of a revolutionary movement later known as Young Bosnia, whose political aim was to free Bosnia and Herzegovina of Austro-Hungarian rule and establish a common South Slav state. All six were Austro-Hungarian citizens, and none came from Serbia.

In spring 1914 Gavrilo Princip, then in Belgrade, was shown a newspaper cutting announcing the archduke's visit to Bosnia in June. He asked Trifko Grabež to join the plot and wrote to Danilo Ilić in Sarajevo to recruit others. The conspirators were helped by the Black Hand, a Serbian secret nationalist group, and Major Vojislav Tankosić supplied bombs and pistols and trained them.

On the morning of Sunday 28 June 1914 Ilić posted six assassins along the motorcade route. Franz Ferdinand and his wife Sophie, Duchess of Hohenberg, rode in the third car, an open sports car, with Governor Oskar Potiorek. Two assassins failed to act, and Nedeljko Čabrinović threw a bomb. At the Town Hall the archduke interrupted the mayor's welcome to protest that he had come on a visit and was greeted with bombs.

Princip had moved to a position near the Latin Bridge. When the motorcade took a wrong turn and the driver stalled the car close to him, Princip stepped up to the footboard and shot the archduke and the duchess at point-blank range. He tried to shoot himself but was seized at once. At his sentencing he said that his intention had been to kill Potiorek, rather than Sophie.

Twenty-five people were indicted in the Sarajevo trial of October 1914. Five of the six assassins were under 20, and Princip, too young to be executed, was sentenced to 20 years in jail. Five of the older prisoners were sentenced to be hanged. Black Hand members were tried in Salonika in 1917 on charges later widely regarded as fabricated, and three of their leaders were executed.

The assassination precipitated the July Crisis, which led Austria-Hungary to declare war on Serbia and began the First World War. At first there was much sympathy across Europe for the Austrian position. Princip's legacy was re-evaluated after the breakup of Yugoslavia, and opinion of him in the successor states is largely divided along ethnic lines.
assassination-of-julius-caesar: After the Gallic Wars Caesar refused the Senate's demand that he disband his army, crossed the Rubicon and began the civil war of 49 BCE. In early 44 BCE he was named dictator perpetuo, dictator in perpetuity. Livy is said to have counted three incidents of 45 to 44 BCE as the last straws: Caesar's failure to rise for a senatorial delegation at the Temple of Venus Genetrix, his removal of the tribunes Gaius Epidius Marullus and Lucius Caesetius Flavus after a diadem was found on his statue, and the Lupercalia of 15 February, when Mark Antony offered him a diadem and he put it aside.

The plot began on the evening of 22 February 44 BCE, when Gaius Cassius Longinus and his brother-in-law Marcus Junius Brutus agreed that Caesar must be stopped from becoming king. The sources give sixty to eighty conspirators, among them Decimus Junius Brutus Albinus, Gaius Trebonius and Lucius Tillius Cimber. Cicero was not told. Brutus argued that only Caesar should die, and the plotters chose a meeting of the Senate on 15 March, the Ides of March, before Caesar left for a campaign against the Parthians.

Caesar nearly stayed at home after a nightmare of his wife Calpurnia, but Decimus Brutus persuaded him to come. In the Curia of Pompey, Cimber presented a petition for his exiled brother, and the conspirators crowded round. Publius Servilius Casca struck first, and Caesar was stabbed about 23 times. Plutarch says he pulled his toga over his head on seeing Brutus; Suetonius and Cassius Dio say he said nothing, though some reported Greek words to Brutus. An autopsy, the first recorded, found only one wound fatal.

Senators fled and the city went silent. Two days later Antony summoned the Senate and arranged a compromise: the assassins went unpunished and Caesar's appointments stood. Caesar's will, however, named his grandnephew Gaius Octavius as his heir, and as Octavian he gained much of the loyalty Caesar had held. The Second Triumvirate of Antony, Octavian and Lepidus was formed on 27 November 43 BCE, brought back proscription and defeated Brutus and Cassius at Philippi. Caesar was deified as Divus Iulius in 42 BCE.

The triumvirate then broke apart. Lepidus was exiled in 36 BCE, and Octavian defeated Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BCE. Restyled Augustus in 27 BCE, he established the Principate as the first Roman emperor.
assembly-of-experts: The Assembly of Experts is the deliberative body of Iran empowered by the constitution to appoint, supervise and dismiss the Supreme Leader. Its first election, on 3 August 1979, preceded the writing of the final system: as it drew near, Ruhollah Khomeini signalled which candidates Iranians should support and which they should avoid, characterising the opposition as Westernized intellectuals, Marxists and morally corrupt secular groups. The result fulfilled his aims, with clerics making up 68 percent of those elected.

The constitution leaves the first Assembly's law to the jurists of the first Guardian Council, with the Leader's approval, and later changes to the experts themselves. Elections for the Assembly proper were held in December 1982, 76 of its 83 members were chosen in the first round, and it first convened in 1983.

Under Article 107 the experts review the jurists who meet the qualifications of Articles 5 and 109 and elect the one found better versed in Islamic regulations or in political and social issues, or otherwise one of their own. Under Article 111 the Leader is dismissed if he becomes incapable of his duties or loses a required qualification. The Guardian Council supervises the Assembly's elections under Article 99, and vets the candidates.

The Assembly now has 88 members, who are mujtahids elected by direct vote for eight-year terms. It meets at least twice in every six months, and its meetings and notes are confidential. A commission handles the list of those eligible to succeed the Leader, and another monitors the sitting Leader. The 1989 referendum removed the requirement that the Leader be a marja'. Women are theoretically eligible, but the nine who applied in 1998 were rejected for lack of qualifications in fiqh.

Ali Meshkini chaired the Assembly from its first term until 2007. In 1985 it chose Ayatollah Montazeri as the successor to Khomeini, but on 26 March 1989 Khomeini dismissed him in a letter saying he was no longer eligible. After Khomeini's death on 3 June 1989 the Assembly chose Ali Khamenei as Supreme Leader in what proved a smooth transition: a leadership council of three was proposed and rejected, Mohammad-Reza Golpaygani lacked the votes, and Khamenei won two-thirds. Later chairmen included Akbar Hashemi Rafsanjani, who succeeded Meshkini in 2007, and Mohammad-Reza Mahdavi Kani.
asser: Asser was a Welsh monk who lived from at least 885 until about 909. Almost nothing is known of his early life. According to his Life of King Alfred he was a monk at St David's in what was then the kingdom of Dyfed, in south-west Wales, where he was brought up, tonsured, trained and ordained. He names Nobis, a bishop of St David's who died in 873 or 874, as a kinsman. The name Asser is likely to derive from Aser, or Asher, the eighth son of Jacob in Genesis, and may have been adopted when he entered the church.

Alfred recruited scholars from Britain and the continent for his court. Several Welsh kings, including Hywel ap Rhys of Glywysing and Hyfaidd of Dyfed, had submitted to his overlordship in 885, which may be how he heard of Asser, who most likely was recruited in early 885. Asser first met Alfred at the royal estate at Dean in Sussex. He asked for time, fell ill with a fever and was confined at Caerwent for twelve months and a week. When he recovered, in 886, he agreed to divide his time between Wales and Alfred's court, which his fellow monks supported in the hope of avoiding the assaults of King Hyfaidd on the monastery.

At Leonaford in 886 he read aloud to the king. On Christmas Eve 886 Alfred gave him the monasteries of Congresbury and Banwell, a silk cloak and incense, and between 887 and 892 the monastery of Exeter. Asser became bishop of Sherborne between 892 and 900; he first appears in the post as a charter witness in 900, and may earlier have been a bishop of St David's. He died around 909.

In 893 Asser wrote the Life of King Alfred, of fewer than twenty thousand words and the main source for Alfred's reign. About half of it is a translation of the Anglo-Saxon Chronicle for 851 to 887, with his own additions, and he drew on Bede, the Historia Brittonum and other works. It omits internal dissent and is one-sided, though written in Alfred's lifetime, and it ends abruptly, probably as an unfinished draft. It also records the submission of the south Welsh kings. Asser helped Alfred translate Gregory the Great's Pastoral Care.

The only known manuscript, Cotton MS Otho A xii, written about 1000, was destroyed in a fire in 1731, and the text is reconstructed from earlier transcriptions and from passages in other writers. A claim that Alfred founded the University of Oxford was interpolated by William Camden into his 1603 edition and is now known to be false. Doubts that the whole Life is a forgery are almost universally set aside.
assia-djebar: Fatima-Zohra Imalayen was born on 30 June 1936 in Cherchell, a small seaport near Algiers, to Tahar Imalhayène and Bahia Sahraoui, a family of Chenoua Berber origin. Her father taught French at the primary school in Mouzaïaville that she attended. She later went to a Quranic private boarding school in Blida, where she was one of only two girls, and studied at the Collège de Blida, where she was the only Muslim in her class. In 1955 she entered the École normale supérieure de jeunes filles, the first Algerian and Muslim woman educated at France's most elite schools. Her studies were interrupted by the Algerian War, and she continued them in Tunis.

In 1957 she chose the pen name Assia Djebar for her first novel, La Soif. Les Impatients followed in 1958. She taught at the University of Rabat from 1959 to 1962 and then at the University of Algiers, where she became head of the French section. She returned to Algeria in 1962 and published Les Enfants du Nouveau Monde; Les Alouettes naïves came in 1967. She lived in Paris from 1965 to 1974 and married the Algerian poet Malek Alloula in 1980. From 1997 to 2001 she directed the Center of French and Francophone Studies at Louisiana State University. She also made films, among them La Nouba des femmes du Mont Chenoua in 1977 and La Zerda ou les chants de l'oubli in 1979.

Most of Djebar's works deal with obstacles faced by women, and she is noted for a feminist stance. One critic describes her novels as focused on creating a genealogy of Algerian women, with a politics both anti-patriarchal and anti-colonial. In L'Amour, la fantasia of 1985, translated as Fantasia: An Algerian Cavalcade, she repeatedly states her ambivalence about language and about her identity as a Western-educated, Algerian, feminist, Muslim intellectual. She won the Neustadt International Prize for Literature in 1996 and the Peace Prize of the German Book Trade in 2000.
On 16 June 2005 she was elected to the Académie française, the first writer from the Maghreb to be so honoured and the fifth woman to join. She died in Paris in February 2015, aged 78.
assiniboine: The name Assiniboine is the French rendering of the Ojibwe asinii-bwaan, meaning stone Sioux. The people's own name is Nakoda, also written Nakota or Nakona. Their language belongs to the Mississippi Valley Siouan branch of the Western Siouan family. The Stoney of Alberta are closely related by language, and about 150 people speak Assiniboine today, most of them over forty.

Linguistic analysis shows the Assiniboine and Stoney sharing a common ancestry with the Sioux nation. Both Assiniboine and Sioux were gradually pushed westward from the woodlands of Minnesota onto the plains by the Ojibwe, who had acquired firearms from their French allies. The Assiniboine later obtained horses by raiding and trading with the Crow and the Sioux.

At the height of their power the Assiniboine dominated territory from the North Saskatchewan River to the Missouri River, hunting bison on horseback. The first European to describe them was Henry Kelsey of the Hudson's Bay Company in the 1690s. They became important trading partners and middlemen in the fur trade, exchanging beaver furs and bison hides for guns, metal pots, wool blankets and glass beads. They belonged to the Iron Confederacy with the Cree, an alliance in the fur trade that also sheltered its members from the Blackfoot.

Smallpox and other Eurasian diseases brought epidemics with high mortality, and the Assiniboine population fell from about 10,000 in the late eighteenth century to about 2,600 by 1890. On 1 June 1873 American wolfers killed at least 20 Assiniboine in the Cypress Hills Massacre, which led to the formation of the North-West Mounted Police.

Traditionally the Assiniboine were semi-nomadic and followed the bison herds in the warmer months. Women gathered and cultivated plants, made clothing and tools, and cured meat and skins; men hunted, traded and made war. The Sun and Thunder were held to be the most important manifestations of the Great Spirit, and the people held the Sun Dance and sought guidance in vision quests.

Today Assiniboine people live on reserves and reservations in Canada and the United States, often alongside other nations. In Montana these include the Fort Peck and Fort Belknap reservations. In Saskatchewan they include Carry the Kettle, White Bear, Ocean Man and Pheasant Rump; in Manitoba they hold no separate reserves.
assisi: Assisi is a town and comune of Italy in the Province of Perugia, in Umbria, on the western flank of Monte Subasio. The Romans built the municipium Asisium on a series of terraces on the mountain. Roman remains include city walls, the forum, now the Piazza del Comune, a theatre, an amphitheatre of the early 1st century CE and the Temple of Minerva, now the church of Santa Maria sopra Minerva. A Roman villa with frescoes and mosaics was discovered in 1997.

The earliest attested people of Assisi were the Umbri. The Romans took control of central Italy after the Battle of Sentinum in 295 BCE. The poet Propertius, born about 50-45 BCE, is generally regarded as a native. According to tradition Assisi was converted to Christianity in 238 by Bishop Rufino, who was martyred at Costano. The Ostrogoths of King Totila destroyed most of the town in 545, after which it came under the Lombard and then Frankish Duchy of Spoleto.

In the 11th century it became an independent Ghibelline commune, in constant struggle with Guelph Perugia. In a battle at Collestrada, Giovanni di Bernardone, better known as Saint Francis, was taken prisoner, which set in motion the events that led him to live as a beggar and found the Order of Friars Minor in the town in 1208. Clare of Assisi, with Francis, founded the Order of Poor Ladies. In the 13th century the city grew beyond its Roman walls and was under papal jurisdiction. It later fell to Perugia and a series of despots, and declined deeply with the Black Death of 1348. Two earthquakes in September 1997 damaged many historical sites.

UNESCO designated the Franciscan structures of Assisi a World Heritage Site in 2000. They include the Basilica of San Francesco, built between 1228 and 1253 after Francis's canonisation, whose lower church has frescoes by Cimabue and Giotto; the Basilica of Santa Chiara, begun in 1257, with the tomb of Saint Clare; the Church of San Damiano, given to Clare as the first home of the Poor Clares; and the Porziuncola, a chapel restored by Francis, inside Santa Maria degli Angeli.
association-of-southeast-asian-nations: The predecessor of ASEAN was the Association of Southeast Asia, formed on 31 July 1961 and made up of Thailand, the Philippines and Malaya. ASEAN itself was created on 8 August 1967, when the foreign ministers of Indonesia, Malaysia, the Philippines, Singapore and Thailand signed the ASEAN Declaration at Saranrom Palace in Bangkok. The Declaration aims to accelerate economic, social and cultural development, to promote regional peace and to maintain close cooperation with existing international organisations. Originally the association was founded to contain communism, but it gradually reoriented itself to economic development and to preventing foreign interference in Southeast Asia as a whole.

Brunei became the sixth member on 7 January 1984 and Vietnam the seventh on 28 July 1995, after the end of the Cold War. Laos and Myanmar joined on 23 July 1997. A Cambodian coup in 1997 and internal instability delayed Cambodia's admission until 30 April 1999. Timor-Leste joined on 26 October 2025 as the eleventh member. The first summit of heads of government was held in Bali in 1976, and the ASEAN Free Trade Area was signed in Singapore on 28 January 1992. A charter, signed in November 2007 and launched in Jakarta on 15 December 2008, formally established ASEAN as a legal entity.

ASEAN is an intergovernmental forum of all 11 states in Southeast Asia, with its headquarters in Jakarta. It operates on the principle of consensus and respect for national sovereignty, so that it cannot force a member state to change its domestic laws. The ASEAN Way, as scholars describe it, is an informal and personal working style that relies on compromise, consensus and consultation, and on quiet diplomacy that spares members public embarrassment. Every two years ASEAN organises the SEA Games, a sporting event meant to promote cultural exchange among its members.
assur: The remains of Assur lie on the western bank of the Tigris, north of its confluence with the Little Zab, in what is now the al-Shirqat District of the Saladin Governorate in Iraq. The city lies on a south-facing mountain spur with a triangular layout. Its higher northern area held the public buildings, including the palace and the temples of Ashur, Anu, Adad, Sin, Shamash and Ishtar.

Occupation lasted about 3,000 years, from the Early Dynastic Period to the mid-3rd century CE. In the Ur III period, about 2112 to 2004 BCE, it was governed from Ur. In the Old Assyrian period it was a hub of the karum trading network that reached through Mesopotamia, Syria and Anatolia, and a city assembly with legislative and judicial power ruled it. Shamshi-Adad I conquered it and made it his religious capital, and Hammurabi of Babylon took it around 1756 BCE. Ashur-uballit I later founded the Middle Assyrian Empire, and Tukulti-Ninurta I built a new temple to Ishtar there.

In the Neo-Assyrian Empire the royal residence moved elsewhere: Ashurnasirpal II made Kalhu the capital, Sargon II built Dur-Sharrukin, and Sennacherib chose Nineveh. Assur stayed the religious centre because of the temple of the national god Ashur, and many kings were buried beneath the Old Palace. It was sacked in the decisive battle of Assur against Median and Babylonian armies. It revived under the Parthian Empire, and Ardashir I of the Sasanian Empire sacked it about 257 CE, after which it was sparsely populated.

German archaeologists began regular exploration in 1898 and, between 1903 and 1914, under Robert Koldewey and later Walter Andrae, uncovered the temples, the ziggurat and the Old Palace, along with more than 16,000 cuneiform tablets now in the Pergamon Museum in Berlin. Assur is a UNESCO World Heritage Site, placed on the list of sites in danger in 2003 because of a proposed dam that would flood part of it.
assyrian-empire: Agricultural villages existed in the region by about 6300 BCE, and the earliest archaeological evidence from Assur dates to about 2600 BCE. The city was probably not independent until the collapse of the Third Dynasty of Ur, when a line of kings beginning with Puzur-Ashur I began to rule it. In the Old Assyrian period it was a city-state named for its god Ashur, governed in many respects as an oligarchy: the kings were stewards of Ashur and presided over a city assembly, probably of powerful merchant families.

Assyria rose as a territorial state under Ashur-uballit I in the early fourteenth century BCE. He was the first native ruler to claim the title of king, and soon claimed the dignity of a great king equal to the Egyptian pharaohs and Hittite kings. Its rise was linked to the decline of its former suzerain, the Mitanni kingdom. In the Neo-Assyrian period the army was the strongest in the world and the empire the largest yet assembled, from parts of Iran to Egypt.

In the late seventh century BCE, weakened by civil war, it fell to a coalition of Babylonians and its former vassals, the Medes and Scythians. The capitals Assur, Nimrud and Nineveh were nearly abandoned, and the region stayed sparsely populated.

At the top of society stood long-established families called houses, whose members held the most important offices, among them the vizier. Territory was divided into provinces, each under a governor responsible for order, public safety and the economy. The army was mostly levies called up for campaigns, with a small standing unit, the king's unit, in the Neo-Assyrian period. Assur remained the ceremonial centre even when the king ruled from elsewhere, since the king was Ashur's representative on earth.
