Assyria's success is attributed not only to its warrior-kings but to its ability to govern conquered lands efficiently, and later empires continued to use its methods of warfare and administration. Assyrian culture endured after the fall, and several Assyrian kingdoms emerged under Parthian rule. The Assyrian people, among the first to accept Christianity, developed the East Syriac rite and live today in their ancient heartland and in the diaspora.
astana: Astana lies in central Kazakhstan, on the Ishim River, in a very flat, semi-arid steppe region at an elevation of 347 metres. The city covers 722 square kilometres, with the older boroughs north of the river and the newer ones south of it. It is almost 1,000 kilometres from Almaty, the former capital, and the nearest big cities are Karaganda, 200 kilometres away, and Omsk in Russia, 450 kilometres away.

Many centuries ago the settlement of Bozok stood on the territory of modern Astana, a military fortress on the steppe section of the Silk Road and a large settlement of the twelfth to fourteenth centuries. The settlement of Akmoly was established on the Ishim on 18 June 1830 by Fyodor Shubin as the seat of an okrug. In 1832 it was granted town status and named Akmolinsk. In 1838, at the height of the liberation movement headed by Kenesary Khan, the Akmolinsk Fortress was burned; it was rebuilt after the movement was repressed. On 16 July 1863 Akmolinsk was declared an uyezd town.

Under Nikita Khrushchev the town was renamed Tselinograd, Russian for City of Virgin Lands. In 1989 it had a population of 281,000, of whom about 54.1 per cent were Russian and 17.7 per cent Kazakh. After Kazakhstan's independence the name was changed in 1991 to Akmola.

In December 1997 the city replaced Almaty as the capital of Kazakhstan, and in May 1998 it was renamed Astana, which means capital city in Kazakh. The decision to make it a modern, planned city was guided by Kisho Kurokawa, and its population more than doubled in the first decade as capital, passing 600,000 by 2007.

Astana is the capital of Kazakhstan and the seat of its government. Its landmarks include Akorda, the residence of the president, the Baiterek tower, 105 metres tall and built in 1996 to mark the transfer of the capital from Almaty, and the Astana Grand Mosque, the largest mosque in Central Asia, completed in 2022. The city hosted Expo 2017, the first world's fair held in Central Asia.
astarte: Astarte is the Hellenized form of the Ancient Near Eastern goddess ʿAṯtart, the Northwest Semitic counterpart of the East Semitic goddess Ishtar. Her name is first recorded at Ebla in the 3rd millennium BCE, in the forms Aštarta and Ištarta. Her main cult centre was Mari, and she was originally associated with Amorite cities such as Ugarit, Emar, Mari and Ebla. The meaning of her name remains unclear. She was worshipped from the Bronze Age through classical antiquity.

At Ugarit ʿAṯtartu had no astral aspect and played a minor role in myth, but she is often named in ritual and administrative texts, which suggests importance for the institution of kingship. She was regularly paired with the goddess Anat, with whom she shared beauty and a love of war, and the two are described hunting together. In the Baʿal Epic she is an ally of Baal against the sea god Yam.

Across cultures Astarte was linked with war, sexuality, royal power, beauty and healing, and at Ugarit and Emar with hunting. Her symbol was the lion, and she was associated with the horse and so with chariots, and perhaps the dove. The only images identified with certainty as Astarte show her as a combatant on horseback or in a chariot. In New Kingdom Egypt she was known as a West Semitic war goddess, with a cult attested from the reign of Amenhotep II in the 15th century BCE, and was sometimes paired with the god Resheph.

In the Iron Age the Canaanites worshipped her as ʿAštart. In Phoenicia in the 1st millennium BCE she overshadowed the other Semitic goddesses and became the main personification of a less warlike and more sensual vitality. As a fertility goddess she promoted love and presided over the reproduction of cattle and family growth, and was the consort of Hadad or Baal.

Her cult spread to Cyprus, where she may have merged with an ancient Cypriot goddess who may in turn have been adopted into the Greek pantheon to form Aphrodite. Phoenicians introduced her cult in their colonies on the Iberian Peninsula. At Memphis a temple of the goddess stood within the temple of Ptah, and from at least the 6th century BCE she was identified with Isis. Lucian of Samosata wrote that the temple of Astarte in the territory of Sidon was sacred to Europa, and Plutarch names her as the queen of Byblos in the story of Osiris.

The Masoretic vocalisation of her name in the Hebrew text, ʿAštōret, is thought by most scholars to put the vowels of the Hebrew word for shame on her consonants. In later kabbalistic and occult texts the name Astaroth was given to a male demon bearing little resemblance to the ancient goddess.
aster-revolution: In the second half of 1918 the war turned decisively against the Central Powers. Bulgaria capitulated on 29 September, and the Austrian military position became untenable. On 17 October the Wekerle government abolished the 1867 Compromise, keeping only a personal union with Austria, and the former prime minister István Tisza told Parliament the war was lost. Wekerle resigned on 23 October. Charles considered naming Mihály Károlyi, but changed his mind on the advice of politicians such as Gyula Andrássy, and Archduke Joseph August was named governor in the meantime.

On the evening of 23 October the Hungarian National Council was formed from opposition forces, led by Károlyi's Party of Independence and '48, with Oszkár Jászi's Radical Party and Ernő Garami's Social Democratic Party of Hungary, and set up its headquarters at the Hotel Astoria. A Soldiers' Council followed under Imre Csernyák. On 28 October crowds demanding Károlyi as prime minister tried to march on Buda Castle and were fired on by police on the Chain Bridge, leaving three or four dead and dozens injured. The general Géza Lukachich was to keep order, but his forces deserted him.

On 30 October the emperor named János Hadik prime minister. Soldiers gathered on Gizella Tér swore allegiance to the National Council and replaced the rose on their caps with an aster, which became the symbol of the revolution. The Soldiers' Council seized strategic points and arrested Lukachich.

At 3 in the morning of 31 October Hadik, prime minister for only 17 hours, resigned, and the emperor named Károlyi, who formed a cabinet that day. That afternoon soldiers killed Tisza, whom the crowds blamed for the war, at his villa. The revolution was relatively bloodless in Budapest, but violence and looting spread in the countryside as returning soldiers attacked the old order, and in non-Magyar areas the unrest took an ethnic character.

On 13 November Charles issued a proclamation recognising Hungary's right to decide the form of the state and withdrawing from state affairs without explicitly resigning. This opened the way to a declaration of independence and a republic on 16 November 1918, with Károlyi as provisional head of state.

The Hungarian army still had more than 1,400,000 soldiers when Károlyi took office, but his government disarmed it under the direction of the war minister Béla Linder, leaving the country without defence. Romanian, Franco-Serbian and Czechoslovak forces occupied it, and Hungary rapidly lost control of about 75 per cent of its former territory. In March 1919 a Communist putsch overthrew the republic and set up the Hungarian Soviet Republic.
astrakhan: Astrakhan lies on two banks of the Volga, in the upper part of the Volga Delta, on eleven islands of the Caspian Depression, about 100 kilometres from the Caspian Sea. At 28 metres below sea level it is the lowest city in Russia. The delta is rich in sturgeon. The name began as the Russian form of Hajji Tarkhan, from hajji, the title of a Muslim who has made the pilgrimage to Mecca, and tarkhan, a term in the Mongol states for a man not subject to taxation. A Tatar legend, first recorded by Ibn Battuta, says the settlement was founded by a Turkic pilgrim whose piety earned the future city exemption from taxation.

Travellers first mention the town in the early 13th century as Xacitarxan. Timur burned it to the ground in 1395 in his war with the Golden Horde, and from 1459 to 1556 it was the capital of the Astrakhan Khanate of the Astrakhan Tatars. Ivan the Terrible conquered the khanate in 1556 and had a kremlin built on a steep hill overlooking the Volga in 1558, traditionally taken as the foundation of the modern city. The Ottomans besieged it in 1569 and retreated, and a year later the sultan renounced his claims, opening the whole Volga to Russian traffic. In the 17th century merchants from Armenia, Safavid Persia, Mughal India and the Khivan Khanate settled there.

Stenka Razin and his Cossacks held the city for seventeen months in 1670 and 1671, and in 1717 it became the seat of the Astrakhan Governorate. Fires struck it in 1702, 1718 and 1767, and cholera killed much of the population in 1830. In March 1919, after a failed workers' revolt against Bolshevik rule, the Cheka executed between 3,000 and 5,000 people in less than a week. It became the seat of a Soviet oblast in 1943.

Astrakhan is the largest city and administrative centre of Astrakhan Oblast, in southern Russia, with 475,629 inhabitants at the 2021 census. For some 400 years it has been Russia's main centre of fish processing. The Kremlin has two cathedrals, consecrated in 1700 and 1710, built by masters from Yaroslavl, which keep traditional Russian features while their exterior decoration is baroque. The city has a large Muslim population, including Astrakhan Tatars, and the White Mosque dates from 1777.
astrakhan-khanate: The lower Volga lay at the crossing of the north-south trade route down the river to Persia and the east-west route north of the Caspian Sea. Turkic-speaking tribes lived there from the 6th century and formed Old Great Bulgaria and later the Khazars. After the Mongol conquest the western steppe became the Golden Horde, from which several khanates broke away in the 15th century: Kazan in 1438, Crimea in 1441, Astrakhan in 1466 and Russia in 1480. The Horde itself ended in 1502, and the steppe peoples around Astrakhan became the Nogai Horde.

The khans claimed descent from Toqa Temur, a thirteenth son of Jochi and so a grandson of Genghis Khan. When the Golden Horde ruler Küchük Muhammad died in 1459, power was divided between his sons Ahmed Khan bin Küchük and Mahmud bin Küchük, who was based around Astrakhan. The khanate was founded either by Mahmud or by his son Qasim I, and all its khans descended from Mahmud or Ahmed.

The khanate is poorly documented. Little survives beyond an imperfect list of khans with uncertain reign dates, a few military and diplomatic events and travellers' reports; Ambrogio Contarini visited in 1476. Its capital, Xacitarxan, which Russian chronicles call Astrakhan, stood 12 km north of the modern city. Its territory covered the lower Volga valley and the delta, bordered by the Caspian Sea to the south and the Nogai Horde to the east. The khans dealt regularly with Crimea, the Nogais and sometimes the Circassians, and Crimea briefly occupied the city twice, in 1523 and 1549.

Diplomatic contact with Moscow began in 1532 or earlier. Moscow conquered Kazan in 1552, and in 1551 Yamghurchi of Astrakhan made a nominal submission, then changed sides and allied with Crimea and the Nogais. Russia sent 30,000 troops against him. He fled in 1554, and Russia installed Dervish Ali Astrakhani, who soon intrigued with the Crimeans. Russia sent more troops and occupied Astrakhan in 1556, and destroyed the largest slave market on the Volga.

Most of the population were Astrakhan Tatars and Nogais, and merchants carried on a transit trade between Muscovy, Kazan, Crimea, Central Asia and the Transcaucasus. The nobility was ranked, from the top, as the khan, sultans, begs and morzalar. The rest of the people were the qara xalik, the standard Turkic term for commoners. The state religion was Sunni Islam.

After the Russian conquest the town and its name were moved 12 km south to the present site in 1558. Russian Orthodox Christianity largely replaced Sunni Islam, though a Sunni Muslim minority remains in the region, and the Kalmyks are largely Buddhist. In 1569 the Ottomans failed to take Astrakhan.
astrolabe: The word astrolabe comes from the Greek astrolabos, meaning star-taker. An astrolabe is essentially a flat version of the armillary sphere, which was invented in the Hellenistic period and had probably been used by Hipparchus to produce his star catalogue. The invention of the plane astrolabe is sometimes wrongly attributed to Hypatia, but it was known much earlier. The mistake arose from a letter by her pupil Synesius, which says she taught him how to build one but does not say she invented it. A treatise of the mid-7th century by Severus Sebokht shows that brass astrolabes were known in the Christian East before they appeared in the Islamic world or the Latin West.

An astrolabe has a disk with a raised rim, the mater, deep enough to hold one or more flat plates called tympans, each made for a particular latitude and engraved with a stereographic projection of the circles of azimuth and altitude. Above them turns the rete, a framework that bears a projection of the ecliptic and pointers for the brightest stars. The rete works as a star chart, and one full turn corresponds to a day. On the back are scales and an alidade, a sighting rule used to read the altitude of the sun or a star in degrees. Makers usually signed their instruments.

The tenth-century astronomer Abd al-Rahman al-Sufi wrote a text of 386 chapters reportedly describing more than 1,000 uses, from astrology and navigation to timekeeping and tide tables. Its religious uses included finding the times of prayer and the direction of Mecca. The geared mechanical astrolabe was invented by Abi Bakr of Isfahan in 1235. Gerbert of Aurillac, later Pope Sylvester II, almost certainly brought the instrument north of the Pyrenees, and Geoffrey Chaucer wrote a Treatise on the Astrolabe for his son. Mahendra Suri wrote the first Sanskrit manual, the Yantrarāja, in 1370. Sailors used a simplified form, the balesilha, to find latitude at sea.
asturias: Asturias, officially the Principality of Asturias, is coextensive with the province of Asturias and contains some of the territory of the larger medieval Kingdom of Asturias. It is bordered by Cantabria to the east, León to the south, Lugo in Galicia to the west and the Cantabrian Sea to the north. The Cantabrian Mountains form its natural border to the south, and in the eastern range the Picos de Europa National Park rises to 2,648 metres at the Torrecerredo peak. The region belongs to Green Spain, with a maritime climate and high rainfall all year round, since heat waves are rare because the mountains block southerly winds.

Asturias was inhabited first by Homo erectus and then by Neanderthals, and cave paintings in the eastern part date from the Upper Paleolithic. In the Mesolithic a native culture, the Asturiense, developed, and the Bronze Age brought megaliths and tumuli. In the Iron Age the territory came under Celtic influence. The local Celtic peoples, known as the Astures, were made up of tribes such as the Luggones and the Pesicos, who populated the entire area with castros, fortified hill towns. Their influence persists in place names, such as those of rivers and mountains.

For centuries the backbone of the economy was agriculture and fishing. In modern times the main industries were coal mining and steel production, and under the dictatorship of Francisco Franco the region was the centre of Spain's steel industry, which drew many migrants from Extremadura, Andalusia and Castile and León. The Statute of Autonomy of the Principality has been in force since 30 January 1982.

The communal capital is Oviedo, the largest city and seaport is Gijón, and Avilés is the industrial town. The region has about one million people and is divided into eight comarcas and 78 municipalities. Spanish is the only official language, but the Asturian language, also called Bable, is protected by law, and Eonavian is spoken in the west. Oviedo holds Santa María del Naranco and San Miguel de Lillo, a palace and a church built by the first Asturian kings on Mount Naranco, which form a World Heritage Site. The region's pre-Romanesque architecture also includes San Julián de los Prados, of the time of Alfonso II, and Santa Cristina de Lena. The traditional horreos, grain silos raised on stilts, are characteristic of its villages.
astyages: Astyages was the son of Cyaxares and succeeded him in 585 BCE, after the Battle of Halys ended a five-year war between the Lydians and the Medes. He inherited a large empire, which he ruled in alliance with his brothers-in-law Croesus of Lydia and Nebuchadnezzar of Babylon. His wife Aryenis, the sister of Croesus, had been married to him to seal the treaty between the two empires. The ancient sources report almost nothing about his reign. Herodotus portrays him as cruel and despotic, and Ctesias gives a favourable account, so both are regarded as biased.

Herodotus tells how Astyages dreamed that his daughter Mandane would bear a son who would destroy his empire. He married her to Cambyses I of Anshan, whom he took to be no threat, and after a second dream sent his general Harpagus to kill the child Cyrus. Harpagus gave the infant to a shepherd, and when Cyrus was found alive at ten, Astyages spared him on the advice of his Magi. Modern scholarship generally rejects Herodotus's claim that Cyrus was Astyages' grandson.

In Herodotus, Harpagus took revenge for a banquet at which Astyages is said to have fed him his own son, and he urged Cyrus to rebel in 553 BCE. After three years of fighting, Astyages' troops mutinied during the battle of Pasargadae. The contemporary Chronicle of Nabonidus names the mutiny as the cause of his overthrow. Cyrus then captured the capital, Ecbatana. Ancient sources agree that Astyages was treated with clemency, though they differ. Herodotus says he stayed at Cyrus's court for the rest of his life, while Ctesias says he became governor of a region of Parthia and was murdered by a political opponent. The circumstances of his death are not known.
asuncion: Asunción lies on the eastern bank of the Paraguay River, just north-northeast of the confluence where the Pilcomayo joins it. The river and the Bay of Asunción separate the city from the Occidental Region of Paraguay and from Argentina. The land around the bay was once covered with forests of the Humid Chaco, with trees often more than 40 m tall. The climate is humid subtropical, with very hot, humid summers and mild winters.

The conquistador Juan de Ayolas, who died around 1537, may have been the first to visit the site, on his way up the Paraguay River in search of a passage to the mines of Upper Peru. Juan de Salazar y Espinosa and Gonzalo de Mendoza were sent to look for him and failed to find him. Salazar stopped at a bay on the river to resupply his ships, found the people friendly, and decided to build a fort there in August 1537. He named it Nuestra Señora Santa María de la Asunción, after the Feast of the Assumption on 15 August.

Relations between the Spanish settlers and the Guaraní shaped the early town. They included the cuñadazgo, a Guaraní institution by which caciques gave women to newcomers to seal alliances, and later violent mass seizures of women known as rancheadas. Asunción became the demographic and economic centre of the colony, and in 1545 a priest called it the paradise of Muhammad, a phrase that became an epithet of the city. The mestizo population that grew from these unions gave rise to Paraguay's predominantly mixed society. Spanish expeditions set out from Asunción to found other cities, among them Buenos Aires for the second time, Villarrica, Corrientes, Santa Fe, Córdoba and Santa Cruz de la Sierra, which is why the city is called the Mother of Cities.

Under Gaspar Rodríguez de Francia, in office from 1813 to 1840, roads were built and streets named. Under Carlos Antonio López, president from 1844 to 1862, more than 400 schools, metallurgical factories and the first railway in South America were built. His son Francisco Solano López led the country through the Paraguayan War of 1864–1870. Asunción fell to Brazilian forces on 1 January 1869, and Brazilian troops occupied it until 1876.

Asunción is the capital and largest city of Paraguay and forms an autonomous capital district outside any department. It is the seat of the executive, legislative and judicial powers. Greater Asunción includes cities of the Central Department such as San Lorenzo and Luque. Spanish and Guaraní are both spoken in the city, together with the mixed Jopará, and about 90 per cent of its people are Catholic.
aswan-high-dam: The Nile's annual flood enriched the soil of its valley and delta, which made the valley ideal for farming since ancient times, but the flood varied: high-water years could destroy a whole crop, and low-water years could bring drought and famine. The earliest recorded attempt to build a dam near Aswan came in the 11th century, when the Fatimid Caliph Al-Hakim bi-Amr Allah summoned the engineer Ibn al-Haytham to Egypt to regulate the flooding. His field work convinced him the scheme was impractical, and, fearing the Caliph's anger, he feigned madness.

The British began the Aswan Low Dam in 1898, and it opened on 10 December 1902, but its small capacity let water pass largely unimpeded. In 1952 the Greek-Egyptian engineer Adrian Daninos began to plan a new dam. After the monarchy was overthrown, the Free Officers, including Gamal Abdel Nasser, were convinced the Nile's waters had to be stored in Egypt for political reasons, and accepted Daninos's plan within two months. The United States and the USSR were both at first interested in helping, but Cold War rivalry complicated matters.

The High Dam was built between 1960 and 1970, 7 km upstream of the Low Dam, with help from the Soviet Union. It was designed by Nikolai Aleksandrovich Malyshev of the Moscow-based Hydroproject Institute, with features new in the 1960s, including a very deep grout curtain below its base. It is 3,830 metres long and 111 metres tall, and when finished it was the tallest earthen dam in the world. Its reservoir, Lake Nasser, is 500 km long and covers 5,250 square kilometres. The dam releases on average 55 cubic kilometres of water a year, of which some 46 are diverted into irrigation canals.

The dam brought protection from floods and droughts, more agricultural production and employment, electricity and better navigation, which also benefits tourism. It flooded a large area, relocating over 100,000 people, and submerged many archaeological sites while others were moved. It is blamed for coastline erosion, soil salinity and health problems. Its costs and benefits remain controversial. One observer calls its impacts overwhelmingly positive, while another recommended tearing it down.
asyut: Asyut is the capital of Asyut Governorate in Upper Egypt. The modern city was built close to the ancient city of the same name. The name derives from the early Egyptian zꜣwtj, which became Coptic ⲥⲓⲟⲟⲩⲧ and means guardian of the northern approach of Upper Egypt. In Graeco-Roman Egypt it was called Lycopolis, wolf city. The climate is hot desert, and the city lies between two mountain ranges of about 600 metres.

Ancient Asyut was the capital of the Thirteenth Nome of Upper Egypt around 3100 BCE, on the western bank of the Nile. Its two most prominent gods were Anubis and Wepwawet, both funerary deities. In the First Intermediate Period its rulers supported the Herakleopolitan kings, and the conflict with the Eleventh Dynasty ended with the victory of Thebes and the decline of Asyut's importance. Mummies of wolves found in the rock chambers confirm the origin of the Greek name, and Osiris was worshipped there under the symbol of a wolf.

In the Christian era the city became the site of monasteries and churches, and a Byzantine treasure found near it in the early twentieth century, some of the most elaborate jewellery to survive from late antiquity, is now dispersed among museums in the West. Asyut stood at the end of the 40 Day Road that connected it to Darfur through the Selima and Kharga Oases. Its history goes back over 700 years, and caravans of up to 12,000 camels used it at its peak in the 14th century.

Asyut has around 528,000 inhabitants, and about half are Coptic Christian, one of the highest concentrations in Egypt. It has Assiut University, one of the largest in Egypt, and the Assiut Barrage, and the Asyut Dam, built in 1902, stands across the Nile at Al-Hamra. The city is one of the few in the world still making silver appliqué-work shawls, and it has a large textile industry, with pottery, inlaid woodwork and rugs.
atahualpa: Atawallpa, also written Atahualpa, was born about 1502, and sources disagree on where. Pedro Cieza de León and Juan de Betanzos place his birth in Cusco, with a mother of Inca lineage. Ecuadorian historians such as Enrique Ayala Mora favour Caranqui, in the present province of Imbabura. Most Peruvian historians hold that the Quito origin was invented by the side of his half-brother Huáscar to show him to the Spanish as a usurper and bastard.

He stayed with his father, the emperor Huayna Cápac, in Quito for more than ten years, helping to put down rebellions with the generals Chalcuchímac and Quizquiz. Huayna Cápac died in a smallpox epidemic, in 1527 or around 1525 by differing accounts, and Huáscar became emperor and appointed him governor of Quito.

The peace between the brothers deteriorated, and from 1529 to 1532 they fought the Inca Civil War. His generals Quizquiz and Chalcuchímac won the battles of Mullihambato, Chimborazo and Quipaipán, captured Huáscar and seized Cusco. Atawallpa reigned from April 1532.

Francisco Pizarro landed on Puná Island in January 1531 and in 1532 marched inland with 106 foot soldiers and 62 horsemen. Atawallpa, camped at Cajamarca with some 80,000 troops, judged them no threat and invited them to visit. They arrived on 15 November 1532 and prepared an ambush in the square. When Atawallpa entered in a litter, the friar Vincente de Valverde addressed him, and Atawallpa threw down the breviary he was handed. The Spaniards charged, killing a great number of his retinue, and Pizarro captured him. No Spanish soldier was killed.

Atawallpa offered to fill a room about 6.7 metres long and 5.2 metres wide to a height of 2.4 metres once with gold and twice with silver within two months. None of the early chroniclers mention any Spanish promise to free him. After months of fear of an attack by the general Rumiñawi, the Spanish tried him on charges of revolt, idolatry and murdering his brother and sentenced him to burning. Because the Inca believed the soul could not pass on if the body were burned, he agreed to baptism, and he was strangled with a garrote on 26 July 1533.
atal-bihari-vajpayee: Vajpayee was born into a Kanyakubja Brahmin family on 25 December 1924 in Gwalior. His father, Krishna Bihari Vajpayee, was a school teacher. He joined the Rashtriya Swayamsevak Sangh as a volunteer in Gwalior at the age of 12, in 1939, and became a full-time worker, a pracharak, in 1947. He gave up studying law because of the riots that followed Partition, and in Uttar Pradesh worked for newspapers edited by Deendayal Upadhyaya.

In 1951 the Sangh seconded Vajpayee to the newly formed Bharatiya Jana Sangh, and he became a follower and aide of its leader Syama Prasad Mukherjee. He was arrested during the Emergency imposed by Indira Gandhi in 1975. The Jana Sangh merged into the Janata Party, which won the 1977 election, and Vajpayee became minister of external affairs until he resigned in 1979. Former members of the Jana Sangh formed the Bharatiya Janata Party in 1980, with Vajpayee as its first president. He was elected ten times to the Lok Sabha and twice to the Rajya Sabha.

He was sworn in as the tenth prime minister in 1996 but resigned after 16 days without a majority. After the 1998 election he led the National Democratic Alliance, and the government lost a confidence vote by a single vote on 17 April 1999. The alliance won 303 of 543 seats in 1999, and he took the oath again on 13 October. His governments carried out nuclear tests at Pokhran in May 1998, fought the Kargil conflict in 1999, and launched the National Highways Development Project and, in 2001, the Sarva Shiksha Abhiyan education campaign.

Vajpayee announced his retirement from active politics in December 2005. He was a noted Hindi poet, whose works include Kaidi Kaviraj Ki Kundalian, poems written during the Emergency. He never married. He died at the All India Institute of Medical Sciences on 16 August 2018, aged 93, and seven days of state mourning followed. He received the Padma Vibhushan in 1992 and the Bharat Ratna in 2015. The Atal Tunnel at Rohtang and the Atal Setu over the Mandovi commemorate him.
ataturks-reforms: The reforms followed the Turkish War of Independence of 1919 to 1922, in which Mustafa Kemal Atatürk united much of the Turkish Muslim population and expelled the foreign forces occupying what the Turkish National Movement considered the Turkish homeland. In 1923 the Treaty of Lausanne ended the Ottoman Empire and recognised the Republic of Turkey. The Ottoman monarchy had been abolished by the Ankara government, and on 1 November 1922 the sultanate was abolished.

The reformers chose Ankara as the new capital in 1923, rejecting what they saw as the corruption of cosmopolitan Istanbul and choosing a more central site. Historians such as Erik-Jan Zürcher and Şerif Mardin stress continuities with the Tanzimat period, which began in 1839, with the schooling of Abdul Hamid II and with the Young Turks, rather than treating 1923 as the start of modernisation.

The republic was proclaimed on 29 October 1923, and the caliphate was abolished on 3 March 1924, the same day education was centralised. Sharia courts were abolished on 8 April 1924. The new Constitution of 1924 replaced that of 1921, and by 1928 the constitutional reference to Islam as the state religion had been removed. All medreses were placed under the Ministry of National Education.

Men's headgear was changed on 25 November 1925, and ashar, a tax in kind, was abolished on 17 February 1925. The Turkish Historical Society was founded in 1931 and the Turkish Language Association on 12 July 1932, and the Latin script was adopted, together with a purging of foreign loan words.

The Surname Law of 21 June 1934 required all citizens to adopt fixed hereditary surnames, and on 26 November 1934 titles and by-names were abolished. On 5 December 1934 women received full political rights to vote and be elected. State-owned factories and banks were founded, such as Türkiye İş Bankası in 1924, and the First Five Year Development Plan began on 1 December 1933. The literacy rate rose from 9% to 33% in ten years.

The Republican People's Party ruled as a one-party state from 1923 to 1945. After Atatürk's death in 1938 İsmet İnönü took over and extended the reforms, until the Democratic Party won the elections of 1950. Historians disagree about the reforms. Patrick Kinross held that most of the population accepted them, while Mustafa Tuna argued that they did not reach rural Turkey, where more than 80% of the population lived.

Critics point to the one-party regime, to the banning of the Progressive Republican Party in June 1925 after the Sheikh Said rebellion, and to the assimilation of Kurds that Uğur Ümit Üngör describes. The ideology that came to be known as Kemalism stayed central to the political system, and the military has seen itself as its guardian.
atbara-river: The Atbarah River, also called the Red Nile or the Black Nile, rises in north-west Ethiopia, about 50 kilometres north of Lake Tana and 30 kilometres west of Gondar. It flows roughly 805 kilometres to the Nile in north-central Sudan, joining it at the city of Atbarah, and is the last tributary the Nile receives before the Mediterranean. Its tributary the Tekezé, or Setit, is perhaps the true upper course, since it follows the longer course before the two meet in north-eastern Sudan. Other important tributaries are the Shinfa River, which rises west of Lake Tana, and the Greater Angereb, which has its source north of Gondar.

For much of the year the river is little more than a stream. In the rainy season, generally July to October, it rises some five metres above its normal level and forms a formidable barrier between the northern and central districts of Ethiopia's Amhara Region.

The earliest surviving mention of the river is by Strabo, who called it the Astaboras. Agatharchides and Ptolemy also name it. Richard Pankhurst and others argue that the name means River of the Boras people, linking asta to a Proto-Nubian word for water and the second part to a tribe named the Bora, who lived near Meroe. Pliny the Elder gives a different meaning, saying that in the language of the local people it meant water coming from the shades below.

In April 1898 a major battle was fought beside the river during the Anglo-Egyptian invasion of Sudan. An Anglo-Egyptian army under Lord Kitchener destroyed a Mahdist detachment of 20,000 men. In 1964 the Khashm el-Girba Dam, near Kassala in Sudan, closed the river to irrigate the newly built town of Halfa Dughaym and to resettle people displaced by the Aswan High Dam, which flooded 500 kilometres of the Nile Valley.
aten: The word aten appears in the Old Kingdom for anything flat and circular, and the sun was called the disc of the day, where Ra was thought to reside. The Aten was originally an aspect of Ra. It has no creation myth or family and is mentioned in the Book of the Dead. The first known reference to the sun disc as a deity is in the Story of Sinuhe of the 12th Dynasty. Under Amenhotep III the Aten was the pre-eminent creator deity of a pantheon and was shown as a falcon-headed god like Ra. Under his successor Amenhotep IV, who took the name Akhenaten, it became the sole god of the state religion, called Atenism.

In Atenism the Aten created all countries and peoples and cares for every creature. Its rays give life to the royal family, and others receive it from Akhenaten and Nefertiti in exchange for loyalty, so the royal family stands as intermediary in worship. The Great Hymn to the Aten shows the god as creator and giver of life. Whether this was monotheism is debated: some scholars speak of quasi-monotheism, others of monolatry, since Akhenaten did not deny other gods but did not worship them, and others of henotheism. The god was shown only as a disc with rays ending in human hands, because it was held to be beyond creation.

The cult centre was the city Akhenaten founded, Akhetaten, today called Amarna. Its temples were open and unroofed to let in the sun, and the larger covered about 800 by 300 metres. There were no statues, which were seen as idolatry; Akhenaten and his family were shown venerating the Aten and receiving the ankh from it. Offerings of meat, wine and fruit were set on open-air altars, and the daily rite of purifying and clothing the divine image was not performed.

After Akhenaten's death Tutankhamun, whose early name Tutankhaten meant "living image of the Aten", reopened the state temples and restored Amun as the pre-eminent solar deity. The Aten faded within about ten years.
atenism: Egyptian religion was traditionally polytheistic, with hundreds of deities, and the sun god Ra held a leading place in it. During the Middle Kingdom the rulers of Thebes joined their patron deity Amun to Ra as Amun-Ra, and under the Eighteenth Dynasty Amun gained still more importance, above all at Karnak. The word aten, originally a circle or disk, came to mean the disk of the sun and was increasingly treated as a deity. Amenhotep III, who reigned for 38 years in the early 14th century BCE, used the royal title aten-tjehen, the dazzling sun disk. His son Amenhotep IV was crowned about 1353 BCE and built a new temple at Karnak dedicated to the Aten, whom its inscriptions called both Ra-Horakhty and Aten.

About the fifth year of his reign the king took the name Akhenaten, roughly the effective spirit of the Aten, and founded a new capital, Akhet-aten, now known as Amarna. The Aten was shown as a sun disk whose rays end in hands, and its names were written in cartouches like a pharaoh's. Atenism was Egypt's state religion for about twenty years. It is described as monotheistic or monolatristic, though some Egyptologists call it henotheistic.

In about the ninth year, by one account, Akhenaten declared the Aten the only god and himself, as its son, the only intermediary between the god and the people. Workmen chiselled the names and images of Amun and other gods out of reliefs and inscriptions, and traditional temples were closed. The period also produced Amarna art, more emotional than conventional Egyptian art, which showed the king's family, above all his Great Royal Wife Nefertiti, in scenes of everyday life.

Akhenaten died in the 17th year of his reign. Under Tutankhaten, probably his son, who changed his name to Tutankhamun, a Restoration Stela denounced the decay of the traditional temples and proclaimed donations to restore them, and government moved back to Memphis and Thebes. Horemheb accelerated the demolition of Akhenaten's monuments, so that Amarna and the Aten temples elsewhere were erased within a few generations. Later king-lists ignored every ruler between Amenhotep III and Horemheb.
Because of its monotheistic character some writers have linked Atenism to Judaism, and Sigmund Freud, in Moses and Monotheism, took Akhenaten as the pioneer of monotheism and Moses as his follower.
athaliah: Athaliah is known only from the Hebrew Bible, in 2 Kings 8:16–11:16 and 2 Chronicles 22:10–23:15. The Deuteronomist calls her the daughter of King Omri of Israel, but she is usually considered the daughter of Omri's son King Ahab and Queen Jezebel. Some scholars think she was Omri's daughter who grew up as an orphan in Ahab's court. She was married to Jehoram of Judah to seal a treaty between the two kingdoms.

The biblical account says Jehoram killed his six brothers to secure his position, and that he turned from the worship of Yahweh practised by his father Jehoshaphat and grandfather Asa. In his reign Edom revolted, and a raid by Philistines, Arabs and Ethiopians carried off all his family but their youngest son, Ahaziah.

Ahaziah became king of Judah after Jehoram's death, and Athaliah became queen mother, gebirah. A year later Jehu, a general of Jehoram of Israel, killed Ahaziah and Jehoram of Israel on what the narrative calls Yahweh's secret command, and then killed Jezebel and the rest of Athaliah's extended family. On hearing of Ahaziah's death Athaliah seized the throne of Judah and killed all possible claimants, including Ahaziah's sons and perhaps Jehoram's children by another wife.

Some believe she acted so that David's descendants would not outlive her own kin, most of whom Jehu had already killed; others see the killings as divine judgment on Jehoshaphat for marrying his son to her. Her reign is dated about 841 to 835 BCE. The biblical writers say she established the cult of Baal in Judah.

Ahaziah's sister Jehosheba rescued an infant son of Ahaziah, Jehoash, from the killings, and Jehosheba's husband, the priest Jehoiada, raised him in secret. Six years later Jehoiada crowned Jehoash king in Solomon's Temple. Athaliah rushed to stop the rebellion but was killed by the captains outside the Temple, on Jehoiada's orders, since her blood would defile it. Her story was told by Boccaccio and Christine de Pizan, and it inspired Jean Racine's play Athalie in 1691, Handel's oratorio Athalia in 1733 and Mendelssohn's incidental music for Racine, first performed in Berlin in 1845.
athanagild: Athanagild, born around 517, was the Visigothic king of Hispania and Septimania. He rebelled against his predecessor Agila I in 551, and the armies of the two met at Seville, where Agila suffered a second defeat. After Agila's death in 554 Athanagild was sole ruler for the rest of his reign. Roger Collins argues that Isidore of Seville's account may be coloured by the hostility of later Visigothic kings towards Athanagild and his descendants. He died of natural causes in Toledo in December 567, according to Isidore, and after an interregnum of five months Liuva I became king.

During the conflict between the two men a Roman force sent by Justinian seized a large part of Hispania Baetica, or Andalusia. The reason for its arrival is unclear. Jordanes implies that Agila had summoned it. Isidore of Seville gives two conflicting stories: in the section on Agila, the Goths around him killed him from fear that Roman soldiers might invade Spain on the pretext of giving help, but in the next section Isidore says Athanagild asked Justinian for help and then could not remove the troops from the kingdom despite his efforts. Collins favours the account of Jordanes, since Justinian's other western interventions were also made in the name of legitimate monarchs.

Athanagild recovered a few cities, but the Romans kept most of their conquest, which was organised as the province of Spania and lasted long after his reign. Its exact extent is unclear. Scholars agree that it included New Carthage (Cartagena), and Collins names Medina Sidonia, Málaga and New Carthage as its principal strongholds; whether it included Corduba is disputed.

His queen, Goiswintha, bore him two daughters, Brunhilda and Galswintha, who married the Merovingian brother-kings Sigebert I of Austrasia and Chilperic, king of the Neustrian Franks. Gregory of Tours gave personal reasons for the marriages, but Ian Wood thinks the circumstances more complex. Since Athanagild had no sons, he may have meant to involve the Merovingians in the Visigothic succession, hoping for grandsons who could succeed him. His death in 567 changed the situation. Wood speculates that Galswintha's murder followed soon after, while Brunhilda became a central figure of Frankish history for the rest of the sixth century. Goiswintha survived the upheaval and became the second wife of Liuvigild, brother of Athanagild's successor Liuva.
athanasios-the-athonite: Athanasios was born in Trebizond to parents from Antioch and was patronised by Michael Maleinos. He studied at Constantinople, where he became known as Abraham, a fervent preacher who held great authority with Maleinos's nephew, Nicephoros Phocas. By the time Phocas ascended the imperial throne, Abraham was ill at ease with the lax morals of the monks in the capital. He changed his name to Athanasios and joined the monks at Mount Kyminas in Bithynia, in Asia Minor. In 958 he moved to Mount Athos.

On Athos Athanasios helped defend the hermits, who lived in sketes, against the Saracens, and began to bring the sketes already there into what became the Great Lavra, which he built with the financial help of Nicephoros. It was dedicated in 963, and three more foundations followed shortly after. He met considerable opposition from the hermits already on Athos, who resented his intrusion and his attempts to bring order and discipline to their lives.

When Nicephoros died, Athanasios's enemies prevailed and he had to leave Athos for Cyprus. He stayed there until the new emperor, John Tzimisces, resumed patronage of the Great Lavra and gave it its first charter in 972. That charter, kept at the Protaton in Karyes, is called the Tragos, meaning goat, because it was written on goatskin parchment. Moved by a divine vision, Athanasios returned at once to Athos as hegumen, or head monk, and introduced a typicon for cenobites based on those compiled by Theodore Studites and Basil of Caesarea.

Athanasios was killed when the cupola of his church collapsed, and after his death he was glorified as a saint. His feast day is 5 July. He is considered the founder of the monastic community on Mount Athos, which has since become a centre of Eastern Orthodox monasticism. The Saint Athanasius Bridge, 5 to 6 kilometres from the main compound of the Great Lavra, is traditionally attributed to him. Two lives of him survive: Vita A, written in the early 11th century by the monk Athanasios of the Panagiou Monastery in Constantinople, and Vita B, written by an anonymous author at the Great Lavra between 1050 and 1150.
athanasius-of-alexandria: Athanasius was born into a Christian family in Alexandria, or possibly in the Nile Delta town of Damanhur, between 293 and 298. His parents were wealthy enough to give him a fine secular education, though he was clearly not a member of the Egyptian aristocracy. He wrote most of his surviving works in Greek, but he was also fluent in Coptic, and some surviving copies of his writings are in Coptic. Rufinus tells a story that Bishop Alexander saw boys imitating baptism on the seashore, with Athanasius acting as bishop, and invited them to prepare for clerical careers.

About 319 the presbyter Arius, whose subordinationist teaching held that Christ the Logos was made and not begotten, came into conflict with Alexander and was excommunicated. He had the support of the powerful bishop Eusebius of Nicomedia. In 325 Athanasius, then a deacon and about 27 years old, took a leading part against the Arians at the First Council of Nicaea as Alexander's assistant. Alexander recommended him as successor on his deathbed, and according to the accounts Athanasius was elected by the bishops of Egypt amid the crowd's cries for him, probably in 326 or 328, his enemies later alleging that he was under the canonical age of 35.

His episcopate lasted 45 years, with interruptions. He faced repeated conflict with the Arians and with the emperors Constantine, Constantius II, Julian the Apostate and Valens, which brought five exiles totalling 17 years. His critics accused him of defiling an altar and of selling grain meant for the poor, and scholars note that he used the label Arian for many who did not consider themselves followers of Arius. He died on 2 May 373.

Athanasius was not a speculative theologian and held to the tradition proclaimed by the apostles and guarded by the fathers. He held that the Son and the Holy Spirit are consubstantial with the Father, which strongly influenced later doctrine of the Trinity. His two early treatises, Against the Heathen and On the Incarnation, were probably written about 318, before the Arian controversy. In the second he argued that the Word, through whom God created the world, entered it in human form to lead people back to the harmony from which they had fallen.

His Life of Antony, a biography of Anthony the Great, became his most widely read work and helped spread the ascetic ideal in East and West. His 39th Festal Letter, written in 367, is widely regarded as a milestone in the development of the New Testament canon.
atharvaveda: The Atharvaveda is a collection of 20 books containing 730 hymns of about 6,000 stanzas. Its language differs from that of the Rigveda and preserves older Indo-European archaisms. About a sixth of the text adapts verses of the Rigveda, mainly from its tenth book, and the 20th book is almost entirely borrowed from it. Its oldest name, given in its own verse 10.7.20, is Atharvangirasah. Michael Witzel dates the hymns to the early Indian Iron Age, because they name iron as black metal; no Vedic text can be dated absolutely.

Early Indian tradition recognised only three Vedas, and the early Buddhist Nikaya texts mention three. Acceptance of the Atharvaveda as the fourth probably came in the second half of the 1st millennium BCE. Its priests were counted among the lowest tier of Brahmins, and a stigma against them is recorded in Odisha into modern times.

The text was arranged by the length of its hymns, not by subject. Roughly, the first seven books hold charms for healing and sorcery, Books 8 to 12 speculate on a variety of topics, and Books 13 to 18 concern rites of passage. Many charms seek long life or recovery from illness, often with a plant or amulet, while others serve soldiers, lovers, farmers and households. Hymn 4.15 of the Paippalada edition deals with a fractured bone, and hymn 8.7 praises medicinal herbs. Diseases are taken to be caused by evil spirits.

It is sometimes called the Veda of magical formulas, a label many scholars reject. Jan Gonda points out that much of it is domestic ritual without magic, and some hymns are prayers for peace or speculation, such as hymn 10.7 on Skambha, the cosmic pillar, a synonym for Brahman. The text also includes a Brahmana, the Gopatha, and three principal Upanishads: the Mundaka, the Mandukya and the Prashna.

Two recensions survive, the Shaunakiya and the Paippalada, the latter the more ancient. Reliable Paippalada manuscripts were thought lost until Durgamohan Bhattacharyya found palm-leaf manuscripts in Odisha in 1957. Rudolf Roth and William Dwight Whitney published the Shaunakiya text in 1856, Ralph T.H. Griffith made the first complete English translation in 1895-96, and Whitney's nearly complete translation of 1905 is still cited.

The Caraka Samhita and the Sushruta Samhita direct physicians to the Vedas, especially the Atharvaveda, and Indian tradition links Ayurveda to it. Dominik Wujastyk notes, however, that the systematic medical literature begins with those two works. Verse 11.7.24 contains the oldest known mention of the Puranas as a genre.
athena: Athena, often called Pallas, was probably an Aegean goddess of the palace, who presided over household crafts and protected the king. A Linear B tablet from Knossos reads a-ta-na po-ti-ni-ja, which may mean Mistress Athena or the Lady of Athens, although any link to the city is uncertain. Scholars now generally agree that the goddess takes her name from the city, not the reverse. Similar city goddesses took their names from their cities elsewhere, such as Mykene at Mycenae and Thebe at Thebes.

Her epithets show her roles. Polias and Poliouchos mean of the city, Ergane the industrious, Parthenos the virgin, and Promachos she who fights in front. Homer's most common epithet for her is Glaukopis, usually translated bright-eyed. The little owl was associated with her from early on and became the mascot of the Athenians and later a symbol of wisdom.

In the classical Olympian pantheon Athena was the favourite child of Zeus, born fully armed from his forehead. As goddess of war she was the divine form of the heroic ideal, represented as the intellectual and civilised side of war, in contrast to Ares, who stood for mere bloodlust. She aided the heroes Perseus, Heracles, Bellerophon and Jason, and in the Odyssey she is the tutelary deity of Odysseus.

In a founding myth of Athens, reported by Pseudo-Apollodorus, she competed with Poseidon for the city's patronage. Poseidon struck the ground and raised a salt spring, and Athena offered the first olive tree. Cecrops, the king of Athens, judged hers the better gift. She was also one of the goddesses whose quarrel over a golden apple, settled by Paris, led her to side with the Greeks in the Trojan War.

In Athens her temples stood on the Acropolis, and the Parthenon was dedicated to her. Her main festival, the Panathenaia, was held in the month of Hekatombaion in midsummer and was the most important on the Athenian calendar. As Athena Ergane she was patron of crafts, especially weaving and metalwork, and in the late fifth century BCE her role as goddess of philosophy became a major part of her cult.

She was later syncretised with the Roman goddess Minerva and the Etruscan Menrva. Early Christian writers such as Clement of Alexandria condemned her, but in the Middle Ages some of her attributes passed to the Virgin Mary, and she was used as a Christian allegory. Since the Renaissance Athena has been an international symbol of wisdom, the arts and classical learning. Her cult is revived today in Hellenismos.
athenian-democracy: Athens was not the first polis to adopt a democratic constitution, and Aristotle points to other cities that did. Most accounts concentrate on Athens because it has the fullest record, including the only complete surviving constitution, compiled by Aristotle and his students in the 4th century BCE. Before democracy, Athens was ruled by archons and by the Areopagus, a council of former archons, whose members were generally aristocrats. In 621 BCE Draco replaced oral law with a written code to be enforced by a court. Cleisthenes later expanded the council, or boule, to 500 members chosen by lot each year.

Athenian democracy was direct rather than representative. Any adult male citizen over 20 could attend the assembly, the ekklesia, by right, and was expected to. Citizens made decrees, such as declaring war or granting citizenship, elected some officials and passed laws. Speakers argued for and against a motion, and the vote was usually by show of hands. About 1,100 citizens held office each year, most chosen by lot and about 100 elected, with strict term limits. Citizens had to be at least 30 to hold office or sit on a jury.

The courts gained power over time. From 416 BCE the graphe paranomon allowed any measure of the assembly to be challenged before a jury, which could annul it and punish its proposer, and from 355 BCE political trials were held only in the courts. Women, slaves, metics and minors were excluded. In the 4th century BCE there may have been 250,000 to 300,000 people in Attica, including some 30,000 adult male citizens.

Athenian democracy had critics in its own time, among them Thucydides, Aristophanes, Plato, Aristotle and the writer known as the Old Oligarch, who thought the common people were not the right people to rule and would make serious mistakes. The historian Samons notes that its practitioners left almost nothing but criticism of the system on a philosophical level. After the end of Athenian democracy few thought well of it. Plato and Aristotle saw it as rule by the poor, who plundered the rich, and well into the 18th century democracy was consistently condemned.
athens: Athens spreads across the central plain of Attica, the Athens Basin, which is bounded by Mount Aigaleo to the west, Mount Parnitha to the north, Mount Pentelicus to the north-east and Mount Hymettus to the east. The Saronic Gulf lies to the south-west. Lycabettus is one of the tallest of the many hills of the city. Ancient writers debated whether the city took its name from the goddess Athena or she from it, and modern scholars generally agree that the goddess took her name from the city. In the founding myth Athena and Poseidon competed for patronage of the city, and Athena won by offering the first olive tree.

The oldest known human presence is in the Cave of Schist, dated between the 11th and 7th millennia BCE, and Athens has been inhabited continuously for at least 5,000 years. By 1400 BCE it was an important Mycenaean centre, with a major fortress on the Acropolis. It is not known whether Athens was destroyed around 1200 BCE, as other Mycenaean centres were, and the Athenians always held that they were pure Ionians. After about 150 years of economic decline, its richly furnished Iron Age burials show that from 900 BCE it was again one of the leading centres of trade in the region.

Classical Athens was one of the most powerful city-states of ancient Greece and a centre of democracy, the arts, education and philosophy. It influenced the Hellenistic world and, above all, ancient Rome. Its chronology runs through Roman rule from 86 BCE, the Byzantine Empire from 395, the Duchy of Athens from 1205 to 1458, Ottoman rule from 1458 and Greece from 1833. Athens became the capital in 1834, after Nafplion, the provisional capital from 1829.

Athens is the capital and largest city of Greece and the capital of the Attica region. The monuments of the Classical age are still visible, the best known being the Parthenon, and the city also keeps Roman, Byzantine and a few Ottoman monuments. The Acropolis of Athens and the medieval Daphni Monastery are UNESCO World Heritage Sites. Athens hosted the first modern Olympic Games in 1896 and the Summer Olympics again in 2004.
atil: Atil, also spelled Itil, was the capital of the Khazar Khaganate from the mid-8th century to the late 10th century. It stood on the Silk Road, in the Volga Delta at the northwestern corner of the Caspian Sea, in what is now southern Russia. It became the capital after the defeat of the Khazars in the Second Arab-Khazar War. The name is often interpreted as coming from a Finno-Ugric word meaning river. Islamic sources such as Ibn Khordadbeh and Ibn Rustah called the Khazar capital Hamlikh or Hamlij, which may be a distorted form of the Hebrew ha-melekh, the king, so that the name Atil seems to have spread only in the 10th century. It is not known what the Khazars themselves called it.

At its height Atil was a major centre of trade, in three parts separated by the Volga. The western part held the administrative centre, a court house and a large military garrison. The eastern part, built later, was the commercial centre, with many public baths and shops. Between them lay an island with the palaces of the Khazar Khagan and the Bek, connected by a pontoon bridge. Arab sources of the 10th century say one half of the city was called Atil and the other Khazaran.

The city was multi-ethnic and religiously diverse, inhabited by Jews, Christians, Muslims, Shamanists and pagans, many of them foreign traders. Each group had its own places of worship, and seven judges settled disputes: two Christian, two Jewish, two Muslim and one for the Shamanists and other pagans. The Christians had their own bishop, and the minaret of the Friday mosque of the Muslims is said to have been higher than the castle.

Atil managed the Khazar slave trade, sending slaves west to the Black Sea port of Kerch or east across the Caspian Sea to Central Asia and the Abbasid Caliphate. Svyatoslav I of Kiev sacked Atil in 968 or 969. Ibn Hawqal and al-Muqaddasi refer to it after 969, which suggests it may have been rebuilt, but al-Biruni, in the middle of the 11th century, reported it in ruins again.

Its remains have not been positively identified, and one accepted hypothesis is that the rising level of the Caspian Sea washed them away. In 2008 Russian archaeologists announced that they had found Atil at Samosdelka, a village about 30 km south-west of Astrakhan, but a 2020 assessment by the Russian Geographic Society concluded that it had not been found there. A settlement from the Khazar period near the village of Semibugry, in the central Volga Delta, was being excavated in 2020 in the hope that it was Atil.
atisha: Atiśa was born as Candragarbha about 982, the second of three sons in a ruling family of Bengal, most probably in the village of Vajrayogini in Vikrampura, one of the capitals of the Pala Empire. His father was a king known as Kalyānaśrī and his mother was Prabhavati Sri. As a young man he began to study tantra in what is now Rajgir under a monk named Rāhulaguhyavajra, who initiated him into Hevajra. He then studied for seven years under a master named Avadhūtipā. According to Tibetan sources he was ordained at the age of twenty-eight by the abbot Śīlarakṣita at Bodh Gaya, and he studied almost all the Buddhist and non-Buddhist schools of his time.

Atiśa became a senior scholar at the monastery of Vikramaśīla when it had no more than one hundred ordained monks. Tibetan sources record that he spent twelve years in Sumatra in the empire of Srivijaya, and returned to India in 1025. He was appointed steward or abbot at Vikramaśīla, and he is also said to have nourished Odantapuri. The king of the Tibetan polity of Guge, Lha bla ma Ye shes 'od, sent missions to Vikramaśīla to invite scholars who could teach a pure form of Buddhism. Atiśa left Vikramaśīla in 1040, with the abbot Ratnakara's permission on condition that he return in three years.
He travelled through Nepal with Naktso and Gya Lōtsawa to Tolung, the capital of the Purang Kingdom, and spent three years there. In Tolung he met Dromtön, who became his main disciple.

At Tolung Atiśa compiled his most influential work, the Bodhipathapradīpa, or Lamp for the Path to Enlightenment. This short text of sixty-seven verses sets out the whole Buddhist path in terms of the three vehicles, Hīnayāna, Mahāyāna and Vajrayāna. It became the model for later texts of the Lamrim genre, the Stages of the Path, and was the basis of Tsongkhapa's writings on the subject. Atiśa and Dromtön are regarded as founders of the Kadam school, one of the New Translation schools of Tibetan Buddhism. In the 14th century the Gelug tradition adopted its teachings and absorbed its monasteries. His other writings include the Satyadvayavatara and the Madhyamakaratnapradipa.
atlantic-ocean: The Atlantic is the second largest of the world's five oceans, with an area of about 85,133,000 square kilometres, roughly 17% of Earth's surface. It occupies an elongated, S-shaped basin between Europe and Africa to the east and the Americas to the west. It connects to the Arctic Ocean in the north, the Pacific in the southwest, the Indian Ocean in the southeast along the 20° East meridian, and the Southern Ocean in the south. The Equator divides it into northern and southern parts.

A submarine mountain range, the Mid-Atlantic Ridge, runs down its length from 87°N to Bouvet Island at 54°S and divides it into two halves. It marks the boundary between the North American and Eurasian plates and between the South American and African plates. The break-up of Pangaea began in the central Atlantic, between North America and Northwest Africa, in the Late Triassic and Early Jurassic. The Gulf Stream and the North Atlantic Drift help keep the British Isles and northwestern Europe mild in winter.

The oldest known mentions of an Atlantic sea come from Stesichorus around the mid-sixth century BCE and from Herodotus around 450 BCE, where the name refers to the sea beyond the Pillars of Hercules, named for the Titan Atlas. Early Greek sailors believed it to be part of Oceanus, the great sea or river that surrounds all land. The southern Atlantic was called the Aethiopian Ocean as late as the mid-19th century, and English cartographers of the Age of Discovery called it the Great Western Ocean.

The Norse were the first known humans to cross the ocean, but the expedition of Christopher Columbus in 1492 proved the most consequential. It began an age of exploration and colonisation of the Americas by European powers, most notably Portugal, Spain, France and the United Kingdom.

From the 16th to the 19th centuries the Atlantic was the centre of the Atlantic slave trade and the Columbian exchange, and it occasionally hosted naval battles. Such battles and the growing trade of American powers such as the United States and Brazil increased in the early 20th century. Notable postwar conflicts include the Cuban Missile Crisis and the Falklands War.

The ocean remains a core component of trade around the world, with major transatlantic transport and communication routes. Its continental shelves hold petroleum and gas fields. They also include some of the world's richest fishing grounds, among them the Grand Banks of Newfoundland, Georges Bank and the Dogger Bank of the North Sea. Its marginal seas include the Mediterranean, the Baltic, the North Sea, the Caribbean and the Gulf of Mexico.
atlantic-slave-trade: Slavery existed in many parts of Africa, and in Portugal and Spain, long before the Atlantic trade. In 1444 six caravels docked at Lagos with 235 enslaved men, women and children captured in the Bay of Arguin, an episode historians have treated as the beginning of the Atlantic slave trade, although ships of Prince Henry the Navigator had brought enslaved people from West Africa since 1441. The Portuguese opened a trading post at Arguin in 1448.

In the Americas the Indigenous population was shrinking from European diseases, and Europeans were reluctant to emigrate. The solution was that used on the sugar plantations of Madeira and the Canary Islands around 1450: enslaved people brought from sub-Saharan Africa. From 1525 captives were carried directly from the Portuguese colony of Sao Tomé to Hispaniola.

Most of those transported came from Central and West Africa. Europeans generally bought their cargoes from African merchants rather than raiding, and mostly stayed in coastal forts or aboard their ships, because malaria and yellow fever made the coast the white man's grave. African rulers, traders and military aristocrats took part, selling captives taken in war in return for guns, gunpowder, alcohol and textiles. The three kingdoms of Loango, Kakongo and Ngoyo never allowed Europeans to build permanent forts.

In order of volume the main trading nations were Portugal, Britain, Spain, France, the Netherlands, the United States and Denmark. About 12.75 million Africans were loaded onto ships, and up to 2 million died on the voyage across the Atlantic, the Middle Passage, packed into unsanitary spaces for months. In the Americas they worked on plantations of sugar, coffee, tobacco, cocoa and cotton, in mines, and as skilled labourers and domestic servants.

Resistance began aboard ship: in 1729 the enslaved Africans on the Clare seized its firearms, drove out the crew and landed the ship near Cape Coast Castle. In Britain the Quakers began to campaign in the 1780s, and from 1789 William Wilberforce led the fight in Parliament. The Royal Navy's West Africa Squadron was established in 1808.

More than a quarter of those transported, some 3.2 million, embarked after British abolition in 1807. Brazil outlawed the trade in 1831 but ended it in practice only with the Eusébio de Queirós Law of 1850, and slavery there was abolished in 1888. Historians still debate its effects: the argument of Eric Williams that its profits financed British industrialisation has been strongly contested, and its demographic effect on Africa is disputed.
atlas-mountains: The Atlas Mountains stretch about 2,500 km through Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, separating the Sahara from the Mediterranean Sea and the Atlantic Ocean. They are associated with the Titan Atlas, and the Berber terms for mountain, Adrar and adras, are believed to be cognates of the name. The highest peak is Toubkal in central Morocco, at 4,167 metres. The mountains are primarily inhabited by Berber populations, and they are rich in iron ore, lead ore, copper, silver, mercury, rock salt, phosphate, marble, anthracite coal and natural gas.

The Anti-Atlas was formed in the Paleozoic Era, about 300 million years ago, as part of the Alleghenian orogeny, when Africa and America collided. In the Mesozoic Era the crust was extended and rifted, forming sedimentary basins whose rocks make up most of the surface of the High Atlas. In the Paleogene and Neogene Periods, between about 66 and 1.8 million years ago, the ranges were uplifted as Europe and Africa collided at the southern end of the Iberian Peninsula.

The range divides into four general regions. The Anti-Atlas, High Atlas and Middle Atlas lie in Morocco, the Tell Atlas in Morocco, Algeria and Tunisia, the Aurès Mountains in Algeria and Tunisia, and the Saharan Atlas in Algeria. The High Atlas has several peaks over 4,000 metres, including Toubkal and Ighil m'Goun at 4,071 metres, and its Berber people live in small villages and cultivate the high plateaus and valleys. The Middle Atlas receives more rain than the southern ranges and is home to most of the world's Barbary macaques.

The Tell Atlas, over 1,500 km long, parallels the Mediterranean coast; its eastern half has the most humid climate in North Africa. The Saharan Atlas marks the northern edge of the Sahara. The mountains hold Atlas cedar and several oaks, and animals such as the Barbary leopard and Barbary stag. The Atlas bear and North African elephant are extinct, and Barbary lions are extinct in the wild.
atomic-bombings-of-hiroshima-and-nagasak: The discovery of nuclear fission in 1938 made an atomic bomb a theoretical possibility, and fears that Germany would build one first prompted the Einstein-Szilard letter to Roosevelt in 1939. The work was placed under the U.S. Army Corps of Engineers as the Manhattan Project, eventually directed by Major General Leslie R. Groves. By July 1945 it had produced two types of bomb: Little Boy, an enriched uranium gun-type weapon, and Fat Man, a plutonium implosion-type weapon.

In the final year of the war the Allies prepared for a costly invasion of the Japanese mainland, after a conventional bombing and firebombing campaign that devastated 64 Japanese cities. The 509th Composite Group, commanded by Colonel Paul Tibbets, was trained and then deployed to Tinian. The Potsdam Declaration of 26 July 1945 demanded unconditional surrender, the alternative being prompt and utter destruction, and the Japanese government ignored it.

The United Kingdom's consent was obtained, as the Quebec Agreement required, and on 25 July General Thomas T. Handy issued orders for atomic bombs to be used on Hiroshima, Kokura, Niigata and Nagasaki, chosen as large urban areas that also held significant military facilities. An estimated 40,000 Japanese military personnel were stationed in Hiroshima. Nagasaki was a large seaport with shipbuilding and arms industries.

A Little Boy was dropped on Hiroshima on 6 August 1945, and a Fat Man on Nagasaki three days later. Until 9 August Japan's war council still insisted on four conditions for surrender, and the cabinet, which had to decide unanimously, reached no decision that day. Japan announced its surrender on 15 August, after the Soviet Union's declaration of war and invasion of Manchuria, and signed the instrument of surrender on 2 September.

The bombings killed 150,000 to 246,000 people, most of them civilians. An estimated 90,000 to 166,000 died in Hiroshima and 60,000 to 80,000 in Nagasaki within two to four months, roughly half on the first day, the rest from burns, radiation sickness and other injuries. The survivors are called hibakusha, and the Japanese government has recognised about 650,000 people as such. The Hiroshima Peace Memorial Museum opened in 1955.

The bombings remain the first and only use of nuclear weapons in an armed conflict, and scholars still debate their justification. Supporters argue they ended the war with minimal casualties; critics argue they were unnecessary and a war crime. In 1963 the District Court of Tokyo, in Ryuichi Shimoda v. The State, held that the bombings were illegal under the international law of the time, as indiscriminate bombardment of undefended cities, but denied the appellants compensation.
atomium: The name combines atom and aluminium, the metal in which the spheres were first clad. The monument was built as the main pavilion and symbol of the 1958 Brussels World's Fair. Its nine spheres, each 18 metres across, depict nine iron atoms in a body-centred cubic unit cell, such as an alpha-iron crystal, magnified 165 billion times. Faith in scientific progress was strong in the 1950s, and the subject was chosen to embody the enthusiasm of the Atomic Age and to promote the peaceful use of atomic research.

The choice also reflected Belgium's role in the field, since uranium from the Belgian Congo had become the dominant material for nuclear fission, including the fuel of the first nuclear weapons. The engineer André Waterkeyn, of the metal industry federation Fabrimétal, presented a first project in January 1955. The architects André and Jean Polak turned the concept into architecture. Work on the foundations began in March 1956, and the building was finished less than a month before the fair opened on 17 April 1958.

The Atomium stands 102 metres high on the Heysel plateau in Laeken, in the north of Brussels. Steel tubes 3 metres wide join the spheres along the twelve edges of the cube and from its eight corners to the centre. They hold stairs, escalators and a lift. The central lift was the fastest in Europe when built and carries 22 people to the top in 23 seconds. Only six spheres are open to visitors, and they hold exhibition halls and other public spaces, with a restaurant and panorama in the top sphere.
The original design had no supports under the three lower outer spheres, but wind-tunnel tests showed that the structure would topple in an 80 km/h wind, so support columns were added.

The Atomium was designed to last six months. Its popularity led the city to postpone its demolition year after year until the authorities decided to keep it, although for thirty years little maintenance was done. The Tour de France passed it in 1960, and the Brussels Motor Grand Prix was run nearby from 1960 to 1962.

A renovation by Jacques Delens and BESIX ran from March 2004, with the building closed from October 2004 until 18 February 2006. It replaced the faded aluminium sheets with stainless steel, added a new reception pavilion and fitted LED lighting. The cost was 26 million euros, two thirds paid by the Belgian government. Belgium's copyright society SABAM long claimed rights over images of the monument, until a law of June 2016 allowed pictures of the Atomium and other public buildings under copyright to be legally distributed.
atossa: Atossa was the eldest daughter of Cyrus the Great and his wife Cassandane. Her siblings included Cambyses II and Bardiya, and two sisters, Artystone and Roxane. She married her brother Cambyses II as his first consort. Marriages between close relatives were not uncommon in Achaemenid Persia, but those between brother and sister were frowned upon, and the sources are unreliable on this point: accusations of incest were a way to vilify Cambyses. She bore him no children, and his reign ended abruptly with his death in the spring or summer of 522 BCE.

A usurper, Gaumata, who claimed to be Cambyses' dead brother Bardiya, then seized power, and Atossa passed into his harem. Darius the Great overthrew him and took the harem and the throne. To legitimise his rule, he married Cyrus's daughters Atossa and Artystone, as well as Atossa's niece Parmys, and Atossa became his primary consort.

Atossa and Darius had four sons: Xerxes, Hystaspes, Masistes and Achaemenes. The marriage linked Darius, who belonged to a collateral branch of the Achaemenid line, to the family of Cyrus. Herodotus writes that Artystone was Darius's favourite wife, yet Atossa held far more influence at court. According to Herodotus, she urged Darius to launch an expedition against the Greeks because she wanted Greek maidservants. Her personal physician, Democedes of Croton, who had treated a tumour of her breast, guided the reconnaissance of the Greek coasts and then used the chance to escape.

Around 487 BCE Atossa secured Darius's support for the succession of Xerxes, though he was not the eldest of Darius's children, since the king had at least twelve sons. A frieze near the northern stairs of the Apadana at Persepolis showed Xerxes as crown prince. After Darius died in 486 BCE the transition was smooth, with only minor unrest in Egypt and Babylonia, which the sources attribute in part to Atossa's authority. During Xerxes' reign she was queen mother. She bore the honorific title Lady, previously given only to Anahita.

Nothing is known about Atossa's death. Aeschylus' tragedy The Persians shows her alive when Xerxes invaded Greece, and she is thought to have lived well into her seventies. She was buried at Naqsh-e Rustam, the royal necropolis where Darius and Xerxes also lie. In Aeschylus's play she enters with light in her eyes like that of gods, and the chorus calls her supreme among deep-girdled Persian women.

Herodotus's account of the excision of her tumour by Democedes is regarded as an early recorded case of a breast disease, sometimes interpreted as inflammatory breast cancer. She appears in Gore Vidal's novel Creation and in Siddhartha Mukherjee's The Emperor of All Maladies, and the minor planet 810 Atossa is named after her.
atropates: Atropates was a Persian nobleman who served Darius III, then Alexander the Great. Towards the end of the Achaemenid Empire he was satrap of Media. He was close to the royal family and was possibly of Achaemenid descent himself. At the Battle of Gaugamela in October 331 BCE he commanded the Achaemenid troops of Media and Sacasene. After his defeat Darius fled to the Median capital, Ecbatana, where Atropates gave him hospitality, until Darius was forced to leave in June 330 BCE. A month later Darius was killed by Bessus, and Atropates surrendered to Alexander.

Alexander first chose Oxydates as satrap of Media, but after about two years, in 328-327 BCE, he lost trust in Oxydates and reinstated Atropates. In 325-324 BCE Atropates delivered a sought-after rebel of the region, Baryaxes, to Alexander at Pasargadae. Alexander's regard for him rose so high that his daughter was married to the cavalry commander Perdiccas at the mass wedding at Susa in February 324 BCE. Later that year Alexander visited Atropates at Ecbatana with Hephaestion, who fell ill and died in October 324 BCE. Some authors related that Atropates once presented Alexander with a hundred women said to be Amazons, a story Arrian disbelieved.

Alexander died on 10 June 323 BCE, and Perdiccas, Atropates' son-in-law, was named regent for Philip III. In the Partition of Babylon in 323 BCE Media was divided in two. The larger south-eastern part went to Peithon, a general of Perdiccas, and a smaller north-western part, chiefly around the Araxes river basin, went to Atropates. At some point afterwards Atropates refused to give his allegiance to the Diadochi and made his part of Media an independent kingdom. Perdiccas was murdered by Peithon in the summer of 320 BCE.

The dynasty he founded ruled the kingdom for several centuries, at first independently or as vassals of the Seleucids, then as vassals of the Arsacids, into whose house they are said to have married. The Greeks called the region Atropatian Media, later Atropatia or Atropatene. The Arsacids called it Aturpatakan in Parthian, as did the Sasanians, and the name became Azerbaijan in New Persian, the source of the names of the modern nation of Azerbaijan and of the Iranian region of Azerbaijan, which is largely contiguous with the borders of ancient Atropatene. Medieval Arab geographers offered other explanations of the name, such as fire temple or guardian of the fire.
attack-on-pearl-harbor: War between Japan and the United States had been seen as possible since the 1920s. Japanese strategists believed that modern wars were protracted and required self-sufficiency, so that iron and oil unavailable in the home islands had to be secured. The attack followed months of negotiations in which Japan demanded an end to American sanctions, an end to aid for China, and access to the resources of the Dutch East Indies.

Planning began early in 1941 under Admiral Isoroku Yamamoto, who won the assent of Admiral Osami Nagano only after much contention, including a threat to resign. The planners studied the British air attack on the Italian fleet at Taranto in 1940.
