The aims were to destroy American battleships, to buy time before shipbuilding authorised by the Vinson-Walsh Act erased any chance of victory, and to undermine American morale.

On 26 November 1941 the Mobile Strike Force left the Kuril Islands with six aircraft carriers, two battleships, three cruisers, 11 destroyers and eight oilers. The destroyer Ward sank a midget submarine at 06:37 on 7 December in the first American shots in the Pacific. The first wave of 183 aircraft, led by Commander Mitsuo Fuchida, struck at 7:48 a.m. Hawaiian time, followed by a second of 171. The attack lasted ninety minutes. In all 2,403 Americans were killed, 2,008 of them sailors, and 1,178 were wounded. Eighteen ships were sunk or run aground. The battleship Arizona, hit by four armour-piercing bombs, exploded with 1,177 dead. Japan lost 29 aircraft and 55 airmen and nine submariners.

Yamamoto had intended that the attack begin only thirty minutes after Japan told the United States that negotiations were over. The 5,000-word message took too long to transcribe at the Japanese embassy in Washington and was presented more than an hour after the attack began. It neither declared war nor severed relations. Some accounts say Fuchida and Genda urged Nagumo to order a third strike, but historians doubt Fuchida's later claims, and Nagumo withdrew.

On 8 December Franklin D. Roosevelt delivered his Day of Infamy speech to Congress, which declared war on Japan less than an hour later. Germany and Italy declared war on the United States on 11 December, although the Tripartite Pact did not require it. The three American carriers were at sea, and the oil storage and repair facilities were not attacked. All but three of the damaged ships were repaired and returned to service. Rear Admiral Chūichi Hara said that Japan had won a great tactical victory at Pearl Harbor and thereby lost the war. Debate over why American intelligence was caught unaware began soon afterwards, and claims that officials knew in advance remain controversial.
attalus-i: Little is known of Attalus's early life. He was the son of Attalus and Antiochis. His father was a nephew of Philetaerus, founder of the Attalid dynasty, and won fame as a charioteer at Olympia. His mother was probably related to the Seleucid royal family. His father died before 241 BCE, and Attalus was adopted by the ruling dynast, Eumenes I, whom he succeeded on his death in that year.

The Galatians, Celts who had settled in central Asia Minor, had long exacted tribute from the region's rulers, and Eumenes I had probably paid it. Attalus refused, and around 238–235 BCE he defeated them decisively at the Battle of the Caecus River. He then took the surname Soter, meaning saviour, and declared himself king, which formally severed any tie to the Seleucid king as overlord. The victory was commemorated by a monument on the acropolis of Pergamon that included the sculpture The Dying Gaul.

In the First Macedonian War Attalus was allied with the Aetolian League and with Rome, and he took the island of Aegina as his base. In 205 BCE Rome, whose only friend in Asia he was, asked his help in bringing the cult of the Great Mother to Rome, and according to Livy he handed over a sacred stone. In 201 BCE he fought a large naval battle against Philip V of Macedon near Chios and escaped capture by spreading royal treasures on the decks of his stranded ships. In the Second Macedonian War he took Andros in 199 BCE and was honoured at Athens, which named a tribe after him.

In early 197 BCE, while addressing a Boeotian council at Thebes, Attalus collapsed with one side of his body paralysed. He was taken back to Pergamon and died around the time of the Battle of Cynoscephalae, at the age of 72. His kingdom was hardly bigger than at the start of his reign, since Antiochus III had seized much Pergamene territory. But he had made Pergamon a great centre of art and learning and earned Roman respect. Polybius notes that he settled the succession of his four sons so well that the crown passed to his children's children without a dispute. His eldest son Eumenes II succeeded him.
attalus-ii-philadelphus: Attalus II Philadelphus was the second son of Attalus I Soter and Queen Apollonis of Cyzicus. His epithet, Philadelphos, means "brother-loving". Before he held the crown himself he was an accomplished military commander in the service of his elder brother Eumenes II, and he served the kingdom of Pergamon both in the field and as an envoy.

In 192 BCE Eumenes sent Attalus to Rome to warn against Antiochus III. He was present at the Battle of Magnesia in 190 BCE, and around 189 BCE he led the forces of Pergamon alongside the Roman army of Gnaeus Manlius Vulso in Galatia. Between 182 and 179 BCE he defeated the Kingdom of Pontus under Pharnaces I and gained some territory.

On one occasion Eumenes was attacked near Cirrha on his way back from a visit to Rome and was believed to be dead. Attalus, on hearing this, married his brother's widow Stratonice of Pergamon and became king. When Eumenes returned, Attalus divorced Stratonice and handed back power without a fight. He also visited Rome often and sent envoys such as Andronicus of Pergamum, which won him the esteem of the Romans. They once offered him help in overthrowing his brother, but he declined.

When Eumenes died, his son was too young to rule, so Attalus took the throne as regent and married Stratonice a second time. Rome assisted him in his war against Prusias II of Bithynia in 156–154 BCE. In the summer of 152 BCE he joined Ptolemy VI, Ariarathes V and Rome in helping the pretender Alexander Balas take the Seleucid throne from Demetrius I, and in 149 BCE he helped Nicomedes II Epiphanes seize the throne of Bithynia from his father Prusias II.

With the help of his friend Ariarathes V of Cappadocia he expanded his kingdom, and he founded the cities of Philadelphia and Attalia. He was known as a patron of the arts and sciences and is said to have invented a new kind of embroidery. In old age he relied on his chief minister Philopoemen, and he repelled a raid by the Parthians. He was succeeded by his nephew Attalus III.
attica: Attica, or the Attic Peninsula, is a triangular peninsula projecting into the Aegean Sea. It is divided from Boeotia to the north by the Cithaeron and Parnes ranges and borders Megaris to the west. Mountains divide it into the plains of Pedias, Mesogeia and the Thriasian Plain, and four of them, Aigaleo, Parnitha, Penteli and Hymettus, enclose the hilly plain on which the Athens urban area now spreads. The mines of Laurion lie at the southern tip, near Cape Sounion. According to Pausanias the place was originally named Actaea and was renamed for Atthis, daughter of King Cranaus of Athens.

Traditions of the classical period held that during the Greek Dark Ages Attica became a refuge of the Ionians, and that many later left to found the twelve cities of Ionia. In the Mycenaean period the inhabitants lived in autonomous agricultural societies. Tradition said that twelve small communities were united under Theseus; many modern historians think they were incorporated progressively into an Athenian state, though they differ on when this happened.

Aristocratic families lived independently until the tyranny of Peisistratos and the reforms of Cleisthenes in 508/7 BCE, which divided Attica into about a hundred demes in three zones, the city, the coast and the inland, grouped into ten tribes. During the Peloponnesian war Lacedaemonian forces repeatedly raided Attica and fortified Decelea. The worship of Demeter and Cora at Eleusis lasted from the Mycenaean period to the late years of antiquity.

Attica later came under Roman, Byzantine, Venetian and Ottoman rule, and under the Franks in the 11th and 12th centuries; the Heruli raided it in 267 CE and the Goths under Alaric invaded in 396. Its peasants were the first to revolt in the Greek War of Independence, in April 1821, and Athens became the Greek capital in 1834.

Historical Attica encompasses the whole Athens metropolitan area. Refugees from Anatolia, and later the population exchanges under the Treaty of Lausanne, brought a surge of settlers. The modern administrative region is larger than the historical one: it includes Megaris as West Attica, the Saronic Islands, Cythera and the municipality of Troizinia.
attila: The Huns were Eurasian nomads from east of the Volga who migrated further into Western Europe around 370 and built a large empire there. Attila's father Mundzuk was the brother of Octar and Ruga, who reigned jointly over the Hunnic empire in the early fifth century. His family was noble, but it is uncertain that it formed a royal dynasty, and his birthdate is debated.

Nearly every complete source on Attila was written in Greek or Latin by the enemies of the Huns. The most important is Priscus, a Byzantine diplomat who went on the embassy of Theodosius II to the Hunnic court in 449 and is the only writer known to have recorded a physical description of him.

After the death of Rugila, Attila and his elder brother Bleda ruled jointly. Attila became sole ruler after Bleda's death in 445. In 447 he rode south again through Moesia, defeated the Roman army under Arnegisclus at the Battle of the Utus and rampaged through the Balkans as far as Thermopylae, though Constantinople was saved by its walls and by the Isaurian troops of Zeno. Callinicus wrote that more than a hundred cities were captured.

In 450 Honoria, sister of Emperor Valentinian III, sent Attila her ring in a plea for help to escape a forced betrothal. Attila took it as a proposal and asked for half the western empire as dowry. In 451 he crossed the Rhine and marched as far as Orléans before being stopped at the Battle of the Catalaunian Plains. In 452 he invaded Italy and razed Aquileia, and people fleeing his armies are said to have settled on islands of the Venetian Lagoon. He halted at the River Po, where Pope Leo I and two imperial envoys met him near Mantua and obtained his promise to withdraw.

Attila died in the early months of 453, after the Emperor Marcian stopped paying tribute. According to Priscus, he suffered a severe haemorrhage at a feast for his marriage to Ildico; Marcellinus Comes, eighty years later, reported that he was killed by his wife's hand, an account most scholars reject. His adviser Ardaric of the Gepids led a successful revolt, and the Hunnic empire quickly collapsed. Attila lived on in Germanic heroic legend and in a medieval story of his meeting with Leo I, which Raphael later painted.
attock: Attock lies east of the Indus River on the Pothohar Plateau, in the historical region of Gandhara. Its name is the romanised Punjabi aṭak, meaning blockade, barrier or obstruction, though it is also translated as skirt of the mountains. The Kala Chitta range lies south of the city and the Gandghar range north of it. The city is 80 km from Rawalpindi and 100 km from Peshawar.

Alexander the Great, Mahmud of Ghazni, Timur, Nader Shah and Babur crossed the Indus at or about the site of Attock Fort. The Mughal emperor Akbar founded the place as Atak-Banāras, and the fort was completed in 1583 under the supervision of Khawaja Shamsuddin, a minister of Akbar. Under the Mughals Attock belonged to the Lahore Subah. The Marathas occupied it in 1758, but Ahmad Shah Durrani came in person to recapture it and checked their advance by destroying their forces at Panipat. The phrase Attock se Cuttack was first used to describe the extent of the Maratha Empire after they took Cuttack in 1750 and Attock in 1758.

The Sikh Empire under Maharaja Ranjit Singh captured the fortress from the Durrani Nawab in 1813. In February 1849 the British East India Company conquered Attock Khurd, or Old Attock, and created Campbellpur District, and after the Indian Rebellion of 1857 the British established the Campbellpur Cantonment in 1857 to 1858. The new city's foundations were laid in 1908, several miles from the old town, and it was named after Sir Colin Campbell, commander-in-chief of British forces. Attock's first oil well was drilled at Khaur in 1915, and the region produced 350,000 barrels in 1928.

After the independence of Pakistan in 1947, Hindu and Sikh minorities emigrated to India and Muslim refugees from India settled in Attock. The government renamed Campbellpur as Attock in 1978. The city is the headquarters of Attock District and had 176,544 people at the 2023 census, most of them Punjabi speakers, with Pashto the second language.
auch: Auch is a commune in southwestern France, in Occitania, and the capital of the Gers department. It lies in the Gers valley, roughly in the centre of the department, 69 kilometres west of Toulouse. The commune covers 7,248 hectares, the third largest in the department, in a hillside landscape between 115 and 281 metres above sea level.

The Gers, a tributary of the Garonne, divides the town. The upper town on the left bank, built on a hill, is the site of the medieval city and most of the ancient monuments, and the lower town lies on the plain on the right bank. Narrow, steep medieval streets called pousterles link the upper town to the river, and a monumental staircase was inaugurated in 1863. The lower town was flooded several times, in 1897 and in 1952, before the course of the Gers was recalibrated after the floods of 1977.

Auch is a very ancient town, noted by the Romans during their conquest of the area in the 50s BCE, when it was settled by an Aquitanian tribe they called the Ausci. Its name for the town was Climberrum or Elimberris, tentatively explained from the Iberian iltir, meaning town, and a cognate of the Basque berri, new. The Romans renamed it Augusta Auscorum, Augusta of the Ausci. It was one of the twelve civitates of the province of Novempopulana and became the provincial capital after the Vandals destroyed Eauze in 409. The word Augusta was eventually dropped, and the name evolved into the Gascon Aush and the French Auch.

In 732, during Abdul Rahman's advance towards Bordeaux in the Umayyad invasion of Gaul, the town was supposedly moved across the river to much of its present site to avoid destruction. It became the seat of a Catholic archdiocese that lasted until the French Revolution, and its archbishops claimed the title of Primate of Aquitaine, Novempopulana and Navarre. The Hôtel de Ville was completed in 1778.
auckland: Auckland lies in the north of the North Island of New Zealand, on an isthmus less than two kilometres wide at its narrowest point, between the Manukau Harbour, which opens west to the Tasman Sea, and the Waitematā Harbour, which extends east to the Hauraki Gulf and the Pacific Ocean. The city straddles the Auckland Volcanic Field, which has produced at least 53 small volcanic centres over about 193,000 years. The most recent eruption, about 1450 CE at Rangitoto, was witnessed by Māori living in the area. Its Māori name is Tāmaki Makaurau, meaning Tāmaki desired by many.

Māori settled the isthmus around 1350 and valued its rich and fertile land. They built many pā, or fortified villages, mainly on the volcanic peaks. By the early 1700s a confederation called Te Waiohua was the main group, and from the 1740s Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei were the main tribe. The Māori population is estimated to have been about 20,000 before the arrival of Europeans. Firearms, introduced at the end of the eighteenth century, brought devastating intertribal warfare from 1807.

After a British colony was established in New Zealand in 1840, Lieutenant-Governor William Hobson chose Auckland as its capital, on land that Ngāti Whātua Ōrākei had given him. Wellington replaced Auckland as capital in 1865, but Auckland continued to grow, at first through its port and the logging and gold-mining of its hinterland, then through dairy farming nearby and manufacturing in the city. It has been the largest city in the country through most of its history. After the Second World War the motor vehicle dominated its transport, and suburbs such as the North Shore grew, especially after the Auckland Harbour Bridge was built in the late 1950s.

Auckland is New Zealand's most populous city and its leading economic hub, and the University of Auckland, founded in 1883, is the largest university in the country. Since the late 20th century the city has become multicultural. It is home to the largest ethnic Polynesian population of any city in the world, including many Pacific Islanders and Māori. Its landmarks include the Harbour Bridge, the Town Hall, the Ferry Building, the Sky Tower and the Auckland War Memorial Museum.
aude-river: The Aude rises at the Lac d'Aude, at 2,185 metres in the Massif of Carlit, in the commune of Les Angles in Pyrénées-Orientales. It flows parallel to the Tet, and the Col de la Quillane, at 1,713 metres, marks the edge of its watershed. In its upper course it runs through Capcir, feeding reservoirs such as Matemale and Puyvalador, and plunges into gorges, of which Saint-Georges is the most scenic. From Axat, where it is joined by the Aiguette and the Rébenty, it crosses limestone in the Pierre-Lys Gorges and passes Quillan, Espéraza, Couiza and Alet-les-Bains to reach Limoux.

Below Limoux the river turns east. This elbow results from stream capture: the Aude once flowed in the valley of the Hers. From Carcassonne it follows the great tectonic furrow between the Corbières and the Montagne Noire, receiving the Orbieu, the Argent-Double and the Cesse, and runs beside the Canal du Midi among vineyards to the plain of Narbonne. It reaches the Mediterranean at the Grau de Vendres, on the border of the departments of Aude and Hérault. Its catchment covers 6,074 square kilometres across six departments.

The Romans called the river Atax, and Polybius and other writers called it Narbôn. Medieval texts used forms such as Adice, Fluvium Atacis and Juxta Aditum fluvium, and a cartulary of 1342 calls it the Auda or Ribera d'Aude. The present name probably evolved from Atax, as given by Strabo, a word borrowed from the Gallic term atacos, meaning spirited or very fast. The river gave its name to the Aude department.

Its flow is mostly governed by rain, and it can rise suddenly in the Mediterranean autumn. On 12 and 13 November 1999 up to 620 millimetres of rain fell in two days at Lézignan-Corbières, more than the average annual total, while a storm in the Gulf of Lion raised the sea by 80 centimetres and held back the swollen river. The floods killed 35 people and ruined about 5,000 hectares of vineyards. In 2018 remnants of Hurricane Leslie fed a stalled cold front and caused flash floods; Carcassonne received 160 to 180 millimetres of rain within five hours, the Aude rose 7 metres, its highest level since 1891, and at least 14 people died, mainly at Villegailhenc.
augsburg: Augsburg lies in the Bavarian part of Swabia, about 50 kilometres west of Munich, at the convergence of the Alpine rivers Lech and Wertach and on the Singold. Its well-preserved old town stands on the northern foothills of a high terrace, and to the south extends the Lechfeld, an outwash plain left after the Ice Age. It is one of the oldest cities in Germany, and in 2019 UNESCO recognised its Water Management System, with its medieval canals and water towers, as a World Heritage Site.

The Romans founded the city in 15 BCE on the orders of Augustus, as Augusta Vindelicorum, the Augustan city of the Vindelici. In 120 CE it became the administrative capital of the province of Raetia. It was sacked by the Huns in the fifth century, by Charlemagne in the eighth and by Welf I, Duke of Bavaria, in the 11th. Augsburg received the status of a Free Imperial City on 9 March 1276, making it independent of the Prince-Bishop of Augsburg, though friction between them remained frequent. Its position at an intersection of trade routes to Italy made it a major trading centre.

In the 15th and 16th centuries the bank and metal businesses of the Fugger, Welser and Hochstetter families brought an economic boom. These families held a near-total monopoly in important industries. Monopolies were criminal under contemporary law and Martin Luther criticised the practice, but Emperor Charles V needed their financial help and cancelled the charge in the 1530s. Augsburg was also a major centre for textiles, armour, scientific instruments and gold and silver work, and its printers made it the largest producer of German-language books in the Holy Roman Empire. Jakob Fugger founded the Fuggerei, the oldest social housing complex in the world, in 1513.

Augsburg played a leading role in the Reformation as the site of the Augsburg Confession of 1530 and the Peace of Augsburg of 1555. In 1629 Emperor Ferdinand II issued the Edict of Restitution, which restored the legal situation of 1552, and it was revoked in April 1632 when Gustavus Adolphus of Sweden occupied the city. In 1686 Emperor Leopold I formed the League of Augsburg, called the Grand Alliance after England joined in 1689, to defend the Electorate of the Palatinate against France in the Nine Years' War. After the Holy Roman Empire was dissolved in 1806, Augsburg lost its independence and was annexed to the Kingdom of Bavaria.
augsburg-confession: Philipp Melanchthon, Martin Luther and Justus Jonas had drafted a statement of their views in the Articles of Schwabach in 1529. On 21 January 1530 Emperor Charles V invited the Imperial Diet to meet at Augsburg, to restore religious and political unity and rally support against the Ottoman advance after the Siege of Vienna. Some Protestants received the invitation with suspicion. Elector John of Saxony asked Luther, Jonas, Johannes Bugenhagen and Melanchthon to prepare a summary of the Lutheran faith, which became known as the Torgau Articles.

Luther was left at Coburg because he was an outlaw under the Diet of Worms. Melanchthon worked on a larger draft during the journey and sent it to Luther on 11 May, who approved it. The final text was adopted on 23 June. It was read in German by the Saxon chancellor Christian Beyer on 25 June 1530 in the small chapel of the episcopal palace, a venue chosen to exclude the public, and the reading lasted two hours. Neither the German nor the Latin copy handed to the emperor survives.

The Confession has twenty-eight articles, set out in positive statements and in negative ones. The first twenty-one describe the principles of Christian faith held by the Lutherans, and the last seven describe what they regarded as abuses in the Roman Catholic church. The signers included Elector John of Saxony, Margrave George of Brandenburg, Duke Ernest of Lüneburg, Landgrave Philip of Hesse and Prince Wolfgang of Anhalt, together with representatives of Nuremberg and Reutlingen. The cities of Weißenburg in Bayern, Heilbronn, Kempten and Windesheim also declared their concurrence. It states that in doctrine and ceremonies nothing had been received against Scripture or the Church Catholic.

Twenty Catholic theologians approved nine articles, approved six with qualifications and condemned thirteen. Their reply, the Confutation, was poorly prepared and never widely published. Melanchthon answered it in the Apology of the Augsburg Confession. The Lutheran princes formed the Schmalkaldic League, and the Schmalkaldic War of 1546 to 1547 was won by Charles V without settling the religious question. Eight years later the Peace of Augsburg gave Lutheranism legal status in the Holy Roman Empire.

In 1540 Melanchthon produced a revised edition, the Variata, signed by John Calvin; many Lutheran churches subscribe instead to the Unaltered Augsburg Confession. The Confession and the Apology are foundational documents of the Book of Concord of 1580. An English translation of 1536 influenced the Anglican articles of faith, culminating in the Thirty-Nine Articles of 1563. Felix Mendelssohn's Reformation Symphony marked its 300th anniversary.
august-hermann-francke: August Hermann Francke was born in Lübeck on 22 March 1663. He was educated at the Illustrious Gymnasium in Gotha and studied at the universities of Erfurt and Kiel, where he came under the influence of the Pietist Christian Kortholt, and finally at Leipzig. He made a special study of Hebrew and Greek and for a time took lessons in Hebrew from Ezra Edzardi at Hamburg. He graduated at Leipzig, where he became a Privatdozent in 1685, and a year later, with the approval of Philipp Jakob Spener, founded the Collegium Philobiblicum, where graduates met regularly for the systematic study of the Bible.

Francke returned to Leipzig in 1689 to give Bible lectures and became popular, but the university authorities opposed his teaching and before the end of the year forbade him to lecture on the grounds of alleged Pietism. In 1690 he became a deacon at Erfurt, where his preaching drew crowds, Roman Catholics among them, and angered his opponents; on 27 September 1691 the civil authorities ordered him to leave within forty-eight hours. Through Spener's influence he accepted the chair of Greek and oriental languages at the new University of Halle in December 1691 and was also made pastor of Halle-Glaucha. He later became professor of theology and held both offices for the remaining thirty-six years of his life.

Concerned for the underprivileged children growing up around him in ignorance and crime, Francke resolved in 1695 to found a "ragged school" supported by public charity. Within a year it needed a house, and another was added in 1697. By 1698 he had 100 orphans to clothe and feed and 500 day scholars, and the schools were later known as the Franckesche Stiftungen. Teaching was strictly religious, with Hebrew included and the Greek and Latin classics neglected, though he also taught natural science, physical exercises and manual trades. The institution ran an apothecary's shop and a press printing cheap copies of the Bible for mass distribution. In 1698 he founded the Gynaeceum, the first Protestant higher girls school, which lasted until 1730.

Francke married Anna Magdalena von Wurm in 1694, and they had three children. He died in Halle on 8 June 1727, when more than 2,300 pupils attended his schools. They provided a prototype that greatly influenced later German education, particularly women's education. Halle became a centre from which Pietism spread widely over Germany, and under Francke's influence Christian missionary efforts grew, with Halle the centre of the Danish-Halle Mission to India. Among his writings were Manuductio ad Lectionem Scripturae Sacrae (1693) and an account of his orphanage, Segensvolle Fußstapfen (1709).
august-revolution: The French ruled Vietnam from 1884 until the Japanese coup of March 1945. In 1887 they created the Indochinese Union from Tonkin, Annam, Cochinchina and Cambodia, adding Laos in 1893. In September 1940, months after France capitulated to Germany, Japanese troops entered northern Vietnam, and until March 1945 the French kept their administration and colonial army in exchange for letting Japanese troops pass. The Viet Minh, created in 1941, was an anti-imperialist front led by the Indochinese Communist Party and rallied support across political lines around Vietnamese independence. The Empire of Vietnam, backed by Japan, was led by the Nguyễn dynasty with Trần Trọng Kim's government.

On 13 August 1945, on news that Japan was about to surrender, the Party's Central Committee and the Viet Minh headquarters formed the National Uprising Committee, which issued Military Order No. 1 calling for a general uprising. A National People's Congress at Tân Trào on 16 August created the National Liberation Committee with Hồ Chí Minh as chairman. The Việt Nam Quốc Dân Đảng had seized power in Hà Giang on 13 August.

When Japan surrendered on 15 August, People's Revolutionary Committees across the countryside took over administration, and the Viet Minh took Hanoi on the morning of 19 August. The Japanese army was largely passive, though the Viet Minh besieged the garrison at Thai Nguyen on 20 August. On 22 August Field Marshal Hisaichi Terauchi pledged in Saigon that Japan would not intervene.

The Emperor Bảo Đại and his cabinet chose not to resist, so the transfer of power in major cities cost little blood. A telegram gave him twelve hours to abdicate, and he did so at Huế on 30 August. On 2 September Hồ Chí Minh declared the Democratic Republic of Vietnam in Hanoi.

The new state lacked international recognition, and the Allies still recognised French sovereignty. At Potsdam the Allies had divided Indochina at the 16th parallel, leaving the north to Chiang Kai-shek's China, whose 200,000 soldiers under Lu Han occupied it, and the south to the British. British forces arrived in Saigon on 13 September with French troops.

At a rally in Saigon on 2 September the French fired on protesters, killing 47, and a general uprising followed on 23 September. The Viet Minh also hunted down and executed leaders of rival militias, among them the Trotskyists Tạ Thu Thâu and Phan Văn Hùm. It repressed Trotskyists and non-communist nationalist parties, dividing Vietnam into hostile camps and beginning three decades of conflict, and the anti-communist State of Vietnam was established in 1949.
august-von-gneisenau: Gneisenau was born on 27 October 1760 at Schildau in the Electorate of Saxony, the son of a Saxon lieutenant of artillery, August William Neidhardt, and Maria Eva Neidhardt, née Müller. In 1782 he took the name Gneisenau from his family's lost estates in Austria and became an officer in the service of the Margrave of Bayreuth-Ansbach. With one of that prince's mercenary regiments in British pay he saw active service in the American Revolutionary War. On his return in 1786 he applied for Prussian service, and Frederick the Great gave him a commission.

In 1806 he served on Prince Hohenlohe's staff and fought at Saalfeld and Jena. In early 1807 he went to Kolberg as commandant. The small and ill-protected town held out against Napoleonic forces until the Peace of Tilsit in July 1807.

As chief of engineers and a member of the reorganising committee, he took a large part with Scharnhorst in rebuilding the Prussian army. Suspected by the French, he retired after the fall of Stein in 1809, visited Austria, Russia, Sweden and England on secret missions, and returned to lead the patriotic party in Berlin.

He then became quartermaster-general to Blücher, in what military history counts one of the best examples of harmonious co-operation between a commander and his chief of staff. The plan for the march on Paris, which led to Napoleon's abdication in April 1814, was specifically his. In 1815 he was again Blücher's chief of staff. When the old field marshal was disabled at Ligny on 16 June, Gneisenau took command, rallied the army and directed it towards Wavre.

Blücher decided there to support Wellington, a decision Gneisenau disagreed with, believing the British would soon be defeated. Part of the army marched to join Wellington at Waterloo on 18 June, and its flanking attack helped to decide the battle. Gneisenau led the pursuit, which took Napoleon's carriage, and saw that the Prussians reached Paris before Wellington.

He became governor of Berlin in 1818 and a member of the Staatsrath, and was promoted to field marshal in 1825. In 1831, after the Polish insurrection of 1830, he was given command of the Army of Observation on the Polish frontier, with Clausewitz as his chief of staff.

At Posen he was struck down by cholera and died in August 1831; Clausewitz died of the same disease in November. A statue by Christian Daniel Rauch was erected in Berlin in 1855, and in 1889 the Kolberg grenadier regiment received his name.
august-von-kotzebue: August Friedrich Ferdinand von Kotzebue was born in Weimar on 3 May 1761 to a respected merchant family and was educated at the Wilhelm-Ernst-Gymnasium, where his uncle, the writer Johann Karl August Musäus, was among his teachers. In 1776 he acted alongside Goethe in the premiere of Goethe's Die Geschwister. He studied law at Jena and at Duisburg, graduating in 1780, and practised first as a lawyer in Weimar. Through the Prussian ambassador at the Russian court he became secretary to the Governor General of Saint Petersburg, and in 1783 assessor to the high court of appeals in Reval, where he married a Russian lieutenant general's daughter. He was ennobled in 1785 and became president of the Magistrat of the Governorate of Estonia.

His novels of the 1780s and plays such as Menschenhass und Reue, 1790, were well received, but a satire, Doktor Bahrdt mit der eisernen Stirn, published in 1790 under Knigge's name, linked each of Zimmermann's opponents to a sexual perversion. Kotzebue denied authorship even when the police investigated, and the episode gave him a lasting reputation for dishonesty and lasciviousness. After his first wife died in 1790 he left Russian service. In 1798 he became court dramatist in Vienna but resigned after differences with the actors, and in Weimar he was uncomfortable, having attacked the romantic style Goethe was known for.

In 1800 he was arrested at the Russian border on suspicion of being a Jacobin and escorted to Tobolsk in Siberia, but a comedy flattering Emperor Paul I won him release, an estate and the post of director of the German theatre in Saint Petersburg. He returned to Germany in 1801 after Paul's assassination, edited Der Freimutige in Berlin from 1803 to 1807 and after the Battle of Jena-Auerstedt fled to his estate in Estonia, where he wrote satirical articles against Napoleon. From 1816 he worked for the foreign department in Saint Petersburg and in 1817 was sent to Germany as consul general for Russia. Some suspected him of spying, though he reported only matters already public.

In 1817 one of his books was burned at the Wartburg festival. In his weekly journal, the Literarisches Wochenblatt, he scoffed at Germans who demanded free institutions, and nationalist liberals detested him. Karl Ludwig Sand, a theology student, plotted to kill him, and on 23 March 1819, soon after Kotzebue had moved to Mannheim, attacked him at his house. Sand was nursed back to health after stabbing himself, convicted of the murder and executed later that year. The killing gave Prince Metternich arguments for the Carlsbad Decrees of 1819, which dissolved the Burschenschaften, curbed the liberal press and restricted academic freedom in the German Confederation.
augusta-raurica: Augusta Raurica, or Colonia Augusta Rauracorum, stands on the south bank of the Rhine about 20 km east of Basel, near the villages of Augst and Kaiseraugst. It is the site of the oldest known Roman colony on the Rhine. The city lay on a high plateau just south of the river, where the small rivers Ergolz and Violen carved a triangle whose apex pointed north to the Rhine and held the Roman castrum. Steep slopes defended it to the north, east and west.

The colony's territory is estimated at around 700 km2, covering much of the modern Canton of Basel, the Frick valley and the eastern Jura of the Canton of Solothurn. It was one of three colonies bearing Augustus's name, with Augusta Praetoria (Aosta) and Augusta Vindelicum (Augsburg), which marked the corners of a triangle across his Alpine conquests.

Lucius Munatius Plancus founded the colony around 44 BCE among the Rauraci, a Gallic tribe related to the Helvetii. No archaeological evidence of that date has been found, which suggests either that the civil war after the death of Julius Caesar disturbed the settlement or that Plancus's colony lay in the area of modern Basel. Successful colonisation waited for Augustus's conquest of the central Alps around 15 BCE, and the oldest find at the site is dated to 6 BCE by dendrochronology. The city was laid out from the temple of Jupiter as its high point, on a grid of rectangular blocks of about 50 by 60 metres.

In the 2nd century the city was a prosperous trading centre, and it flourished between the 1st and 3rd centuries, exporting smoked pork and bacon to other parts of the empire. A powerful earthquake damaged much of it in 250 CE. Around 260 Alemanni tribes or marauding Roman troops destroyed it. The Romans built a fortress on the Rhine, Castrum Rauracense, and resettled the city on a much smaller scale on its site. The two settlements are the centres of modern Augst and Kaiseraugst.

Augusta Raurica is an archaeological site and open-air museum. It had an amphitheatre, a main forum with a temple of Jupiter, an aqueduct, baths and the largest Roman theatre north of the Alps, seating 8,000 to 10,000. The site and Castrum Rauracense are heritage sites of national significance. Some 80 per cent of the built-up area has yet to be excavated, and it is the best-preserved Roman city north of the Alps not built over in medieval or modern times. The Roman Museum holds the silver treasure of Kaiseraugst, found in the fortress in 1961–1962.
augusta-savage: Augusta Savage was born Augusta Christine Fells in Jacksonville, Florida, on 29 February 1892, to Edward Fells and Cornelia Murphy. As a child she made figures, mostly small animals, from the red clay of her hometown. Her father, a poor Methodist minister, strongly opposed this, believing sculpture sinful because of the Bible's "graven images". She persevered, and the principal of her new high school in West Palm Beach, where the family moved in 1915, encouraged her and let her teach a clay modelling class. In 1921 she left for New York City with $4.60 and a letter of recommendation, was admitted to Cooper Union that October and completed its four-year course in three years.

After Cooper Union, Savage worked in Manhattan steam laundries to support her family. Her first commission was a bust of W. E. B. Du Bois for the New York Public Library. In 1923 she applied for a summer art programme at the Fontainebleau School of Fine Arts in France. She was accepted, but the American selection committee rescinded the offer when it learned she was Black. She wrote to the New York World, beginning the first of many public fights for equal rights. In 1928 she won the Otto Kahn Prize for Head of a Negro, and in 1929 she went to Paris with help from the Urban League, the Rosenwald Foundation and a Carnegie Foundation grant.

Savage returned to the United States in 1931. In 1934 she became the first African-American artist elected to the National Association of Women Painters and Sculptors. With a Carnegie Foundation grant she launched the Savage Studio of Arts and Crafts in a Harlem basement, open to anyone who wished to paint, draw or sculpt; her students included Jacob Lawrence, Norman Lewis and Gwendolyn Knight. In 1937 she became director of the Harlem Community Art Center, where 1,500 people took part in workshops.

For the 1939 New York World's Fair she created the 16-foot plaster Lift Every Voice and Sing, or The Harp, inspired by the song of James Weldon and Rosamond Johnson. It was one of the fair's most photographed works, but she had no money to cast it in bronze or to store it, and it was destroyed when the fair closed.

Depressed by her financial struggles, Savage moved to a farmhouse in Saugerties, New York, in 1945. Her best-known bust, Gamin, modelled on a Harlem youth, is at the Smithsonian American Art Museum. Much of her work was in clay or plaster because she could seldom afford bronze, and the location of much of it is unknown. She died of cancer in March 1962, in relative obscurity. The Augusta Fells Savage Institute of Visual Arts in Baltimore is named for her.
augusta-sicily: Augusta is a town and comune in the province of Syracuse, on the eastern coast of Sicily, facing the Ionian Sea. Its old town is an island, made in the 16th century by cutting through an isthmus. It is now joined to the Sicilian mainland by two bridges: one, built about the 12th or 13th century as part of the Frederick II of Swabia Viaduct, and an older one built when the city was founded, called the Porta Spagnola. The town has two ports.

The site lies near Megara Hyblaea, one of the oldest Greek colonies of Sicily, founded some 27 centuries ago. Syracuse destroyed it; it was raised from its ruins and later taken by the Romans together with Syracuse during the Second Punic War. Augusta itself was founded in 1232 by Emperor Frederick II on the ruins of one of its suburbs, Xiphonia. After Angevin rule it became part of Aragonese Sicily and, from 1362, a fief of Guglielmo Raimondo II Moncada. It returned to royal possession under Spain in 1560 and was extensively fortified against Turkish pirates.

In the later 17th century its harbour was the site of a naval battle between a Dutch and Spanish fleet and a French one, and in 1693 the town suffered a major earthquake and tsunami. In Operation Husky, the British and American invasion of Sicily in 1943, the British Eighth Army under General Montgomery captured Augusta on 13 July 1943, as planned, and moved north towards Catania.

Augusta is one of Italy's main harbours, especially for oil refining, with refineries in the Augusta-Priolo complex nearby. Megara Hyblaea remains an archaeological site that shows how a Greek colony of the Archaic period was organised. Among the town's buildings are the Castello Svevo, built about 1232 on a square plan 62 metres on a side, with eight towers, and the 17th-century Porta Spagnola.
auguste-comte: Auguste Comte was born in Montpellier on 19 January 1798, in the early years of the French First Republic. He attended the Lycée Joffre and the University of Montpellier and was admitted to the École Polytechnique in Paris, which held to the ideals of republicanism and progress. When the school closed for reorganisation in 1816 he continued at the medical school at Montpellier and did not ask to be readmitted. He came to see unbridgeable differences with his Catholic and monarchist family, having abandoned Catholicism under the influence of his first teacher, the Protestant pastor Daniel Encontre, and returned to Paris, earning money by small jobs.

In 1817 he became a student and secretary to Henri de Saint-Simon, who introduced him to intellectual society and greatly influenced his thought. He left Saint-Simon in 1824, again over differences, and historians still debate how much he drew on Saint-Simon's work. He failed to obtain an academic post and lived on sponsors and the help of friends. He married Caroline Massin in 1825. In 1826 he was taken to a mental hospital and left without being cured, only stabilised by the alienist Jean-Étienne Dominique Esquirol, and he attempted suicide in 1827. Before their divorce in 1842 he published the six volumes of his Cours.

The Course in Positive Philosophy, published between 1830 and 1842, set out positivism, and A General View of Positivism followed in 1848. Its first three volumes deal with the existing physical sciences, and the later ones with the coming of social science, the most complex of the sciences, for which Comte coined the term sociology. Because he classified the sciences and noted the mutual dependence of theory and observation, he is often regarded as the first philosopher of science in the modern sense.

He held that each branch of knowledge passes through three stages: the theological, in which the world is referred to supernatural powers, the metaphysical, an abstract stage rooted in the problems of French society after the Revolution of 1789, and the positive, or scientific.

In later years Comte developed the Religion of Humanity to give positivist societies the cohesion once supplied by worship, and proposed a positivist calendar in 1849. John Stuart Mill distinguished a good Comte, author of the Course, from a bad Comte, author of the secular-religious system. His English followers, including George Eliot and Harriet Martineau, mostly rejected the system but liked his injunction to live for others, vivre pour autrui, from which comes the word altruism.
auguste-de-marmont: Auguste Frédéric Louis Viesse de Marmont was born on 20 July 1774 at Châtillon-sur-Seine, the son of a former army officer of the petty nobility who adopted the principles of the Revolution. He entered the artillery and met Napoleon Bonaparte, whom he came to know better when he served at Toulon. He became General Bonaparte's aide-de-camp, accompanied him to Italy and Egypt and was promoted general of brigade. For commanding the artillery at Marengo he was made general of division.

In 1805 Marmont commanded a corps at Ulm and was then sent to take Dalmatia and occupy the Republic of Ragusa. For five years he was military and civil governor of Dalmatia. In 1809 he defeated an Austrian force there, defeated Ignaz Gyulai's corps at Graz and fought at the Battle of Wagram on 5 and 6 July. Napoleon made him a Marshal of the Empire, saying that he had not done enough to justify the choice entirely, and appointed him governor-general of the Illyrian provinces.

In May 1811 he was summoned to succeed André Masséna in command of the French army in northern Spain. At the Battle of Salamanca Wellington's cavalry charged his left flank and inflicted a great defeat, and Marmont was gravely wounded early in the battle. In 1813 he led a corps at Lützen, Bautzen and Dresden, and he fought through the defensive campaign of 1814.

Before Paris in 1814, believing that prolonging the war was pointless, he reached a secret agreement with the Allies. Together with marshals Mortier and Moncey he marched to a position where Allied troops surrounded them and they surrendered. The verb raguser, from his title, became a French word meaning to betray.

Marmont stayed loyal to Louis XVIII during the Hundred Days. As major-general of the Royal Guard he led the royalist troops in the July Revolution of 1830, but gave up when it became clear that they were outmatched. Charles X ordered him arrested, asking whether he would betray them as he had betrayed Napoleon. He went into exile, settled in Vienna, where he was tutor to the Duke of Reichstadt, and died in Venice on 22 March 1852, the last living Napoleonic marshal. His Mémoires, published after his death, are of great value for the military history of the period.
augustinas-voldemaras: Augustinas Voldemaras was born on 16 April 1883 in the village of Dysna, then part of the Vilna Governorate of the Russian Empire, to a family of modest means. He moved to Saint Petersburg in 1890 and in 1901 met Antanas Smetona, who became his close friend, political collaborator and eventually his political rival. He graduated in history and philosophy at the Saint Petersburg Imperial University in 1909 and later became a professor at its branch in Perm. He knew sixteen languages and wrote academic works in Lithuanian and French.

In 1918 Voldemaras joined the Council of Lithuania and, with Smetona, helped unite Lithuanian organisations behind it. After Germany's defeat and recognition of Lithuanian independence, the Council's Presidium chose him as the first prime minister. He took office on 11 November 1918 and kept the foreign and defence ministries for himself. On 21 December he left for Germany and the Versailles Peace Conference, which caused outrage, as he was seen as fleeing the Soviet advance. Mykolas Sleževičius replaced him on 26 December, but he stayed foreign minister until June 1920 and found little support at Versailles.

He was elected to the Seimas in 1926. With Smetona, as leaders of the Lithuanian Nationalist Union, he supported the military coup of 17 December 1926 against President Kazys Grinius and became prime minister again on condition that he uphold the constitution of 1922. Within a year the Seimas was dissolved without new elections, and in 1928 a new constitution replaced the old. In January 1928 he signed a border treaty in which Germany accepted Lithuanian possession of Klaipėda. He also helped establish the nationalist Iron Wolf organisation. After an attempt on his life on 6 May 1929 Smetona removed him from office on 19 September 1929.

Voldemaras was exiled to Plateliai and later Zarasai. In June 1934 officers linked to the Iron Wolf attempted a coup against Smetona with Voldemaras's involvement, but it failed, and he was imprisoned for four years until an amnesty on condition that he leave the country. He chose France. In June 1940, days after the Soviet occupation, he was arrested at the border and imprisoned, and he died in Moscow's Butyrka prison in 1942. His burial place is unknown, and a memorial stone was unveiled in Petrašiūnai cemetery in Kaunas in 2012.
augustine-of-canterbury: Augustine was prior of the Benedictine Abbey of St Andrew in Rome when Pope Gregory I chose him in 595 to lead a mission to Kent. Britain had been Christian under Rome, but after the legions left in 410 pagan Angles, Saxons and Jutes settled the south, and the native British Church in the west developed in isolation, with its own date for Easter and style of tonsure. Kent was ruled by Æthelberht, the leading Anglo-Saxon king, who had married a Christian Frankish princess, Bertha, and who allowed her freedom of worship. Gregory wrote to the Frankish kings for help, and the mission brought interpreters and priests from the Franks.

Augustine travelled with Laurence of Canterbury, his later successor, and about 40 companions. Soon after leaving Rome they halted, daunted, and Augustine went back to ask permission to return, but Gregory refused. In 597 they landed in Kent, and Æthelberht let them settle and preach in Canterbury, where they used the church of St Martin. The king's conversion probably took place in 597. Augustine founded the monastery of Saints Peter and Paul, later St Augustine's Abbey, on land the king gave. Gregory told the patriarch of Alexandria in 598 that more than 10,000 had been baptised, a number that may be exaggerated.

In 601 Gregory sent more missionaries with a pallium for Augustine and a plan for two metropolitan sees, at London and York, each with twelve suffragan bishops. The move to London never happened, probably because London lay outside Æthelberht's lands. In 604 Augustine founded bishoprics at London and Rochester for Mellitus and Justus, and a school. In 603 he met the British bishops south of the Severn, but according to Bede they refused to accept him as archbishop after he failed to rise at their entrance; differences over Easter, the tonsure and church organisation counted for more.

Before his death, on 26 May 604 or 605, Augustine consecrated Laurence as his successor. The mission then barely extended beyond Kent, but it introduced a more active missionary style to the British Isles, and much of its success came from his close relationship with Æthelberht. He was buried at what became St Augustine's Abbey, where a shrine was a place of pilgrimage until it was destroyed in the English Reformation. Later medieval writers, beginning with Goscelin around 1090, added miracles and invented stories to his life. St Augustine's Cross, erected in 1884 at Ebbsfleet in Thanet, marks the place where he is said to have first met Æthelberht.
augustine-of-hippo: Augustine was born in 354 in the municipium of Thagaste, now Souk Ahras in Algeria, in the Roman province of Numidia. His mother, Monica, was a devout Christian, and his father, Patricius, was a pagan who converted to Christianity on his deathbed. Scholars generally agree that the family were Berbers who were heavily Romanized and spoke only Latin at home. In his writings he mentions his identity as a Roman African.

At the age of 11 he was sent to school at Madaurus where he became familiar with Latin literature and with pagan beliefs and practices. His first insight into the nature of sin came when he and friends stole pears from a neighbourhood garden, a story he tells in the Confessions. In his youth he was drawn to the Manichaean faith and later to the Neoplatonism of Hellenistic philosophy, and Ambrose baptised him in 386.

Augustine was one of the most prolific Latin authors in terms of surviving works, with more than one hundred separate titles. They include works against the Arians, Donatists, Manichaeans and Pelagians, On Christian Doctrine, many sermons and letters, and the Retractationes, a review of his earlier works. The Confessions is a personal account of his earlier life and the first Western autobiography. The City of God, in 22 books, was written to restore the confidence of Christians shaken by the sack of Rome by the Visigoths in 410.

He is known as the Doctor of Grace for his views on the necessity of unmerited grace for salvation and on the nature of original sin. Against the Donatists he held that sacraments are valid regardless of the merit of the celebrant. In the City of God he imagined the Church as a spiritual City, distinct from the Earthly City. He coined the phrase just war.

Augustine died on 28 August 430. He is recognised as a saint in the Catholic Church, the Eastern Orthodox Church, the Lutheran churches and the Anglican Communion, and is one of the four Great Latin Church Fathers with Ambrose, Jerome and Pope Gregory I. He was the most cited author in the Summa Theologiae of Thomas Aquinas. Many Protestants, especially Calvinists and Lutherans, consider him one of the theological fathers of the Reformation, an interpretation the Catholic Church disputes. His analysis of time and memory in the Confessions influenced later philosophy, including Edmund Husserl and Martin Heidegger.
augusto-b-leguia: Augusto Bernardino Leguía y Salcedo was born on 19 February 1863 in Lambayeque and married into one of the distinguished families of the Peruvian oligarchy. He was educated in Valparaíso, Chile, and served in the Peruvian Army in the War of the Pacific. He then moved to the United States and became an insurance executive with the New York Life Insurance Company, and was very wealthy by the 1900s. He entered politics in 1903 at the urging of Manuel Candamo and José Pardo, serving as minister of finance until 1904, and then as prime minister under President Pardo until 1907.

Elected president in 1908 by an alliance of the Civil and Constitutional parties, Leguía pursued social and economic reforms; a law of 1911 introduced occupational accident protection for workers in mechanised private enterprises. On 29 May 1909 supporters of Piérola's Democratic Party forced their way into the Palacio de Gobierno and kidnapped him, and police had to rescue him in a fight that caused at least 100 deaths. He settled boundaries with Brazil and Bolivia, and was succeeded in 1912 by Guillermo Billinghurst.

In 1919, fearing that the Civilist Congress would not recognise his victory, he launched a military coup, dissolved Congress and was elected constitutional president by the new parliament. The constitution of 1920 allowed unlimited re-election, but he largely ignored it, suppressing opposition harshly. Víctor Raúl Haya de la Torre was exiled and founded APRA in Mexico in 1924.

Public works financed by loans included hospitals and drainage in Lima, the remodelled Palacio de Gobierno in 1926, the Banco Central de Reserva and over 800 new primary schools. The Treaty of Salomón-Lozano with Colombia was signed in 1922, and the Tacna-Arica compromise with Chile later drew criticism. His government was pro-American, with American advisers in customs and a contract in 1922 with the International Petroleum Company for the oilfields of the Sechura Desert.

The Great Depression drained foreign investment and halted public works, and the government was unpopular among both upper and lower classes. Luis Miguel Sánchez Cerro led a coup in Arequipa on 22 August 1930, and Leguía resigned on 24 August. He was arrested and charged with misappropriating government funds, was confined in the Panopticon of Lima and died on 6 February 1932. Critics treat his second term as a dictatorship, and the 1937 novel Pity the Tyrant by Hans Otto Storm depicts him as a tyrant.
augusto-cesar-sandino: Sandino was born on 18 May 1895 at Niquinohomo, in the Masaya Department of Nicaragua, the illegitimate son of Gregorio Sandino, a wealthy landowner, and Margarita Calderón, an indigenous servant of the family. At nine he went to live in his father's house and took his surname. In 1921 he shot and failed to kill a man who had insulted his mother, and fled, eventually to Mexico, where he worked at a Standard Oil refinery near Tampico and took in anti-imperialist, anarchist and spiritist ideas.

When Sandino returned, the Constitutionalist War had begun, in which Liberals under General José María Moncada rose against the Conservative president Adolfo Díaz. Sandino raised an army of gold miners and peasants. In May 1927 the Espino Negro accord, negotiated by the US envoy Henry L. Stimson, ended the fighting: both sides were to disarm and a National Guard would be formed. Sandino refused to disarm, returned to the mountains of Las Segovias, and in July declared war on the United States.

On 16 July 1927 his men attacked US Marines at Ocotal and were repulsed with the help of one of the first dive-bombing attacks in history; the Marine commander estimated 300 of Sandino's men dead, though the actual number was about 80. The Marines never captured him, and in November 1927 they found his headquarters at El Chipote abandoned and guarded by straw dummies. The Great Depression made overseas expeditions too costly, and the last Marines left in January 1933, after 130 of them had died. Sandino then met President Juan Bautista Sacasa and agreed to have his forces give up their weapons, but remained opposed to the National Guard.

On 21 February 1934, after talks with Sacasa, Sandino, his brother Sócrates and two generals were stopped at the gate of the presidential palace by National Guardsmen, taken to a crossroads and executed. General Anastasio Somoza García had ordered the killing without consulting Sacasa. Sandino's body has never been found. The Guard destroyed his army over the following month, and Somoza forced Sacasa to resign two years later and founded a dictatorship that ruled Nicaragua for four decades.

Sandino became a symbol of resistance to American imperialism across Latin America. The Sandinista National Liberation Front, founded in 1961, took his name and image and overthrew Somoza's son in 1979. In 2010 Nicaragua's congress named him a national hero.
augusto-pinochet: Augusto José Ramón Pinochet Ugarte was born in Valparaíso on 25 November 1915 to a middle-class family. His father, Augusto Pinochet Vera, descended from an 18th-century Breton immigrant, and his mother, Avelina Ugarte Martínez, was of Basque heritage. He attended schools in Valparaíso and Quillota and entered the Military School in Santiago in 1931. His records show an average student, and in 1935 he graduated as a second lieutenant in the infantry. After postings to regiments in Concepción, Valparaíso and Iquique, he entered the Chilean War Academy, and he later wrote two books on military subjects, Geopolítica (1968) and Campaña de Tarapacá (1972).

He became General Chief of Staff in early 1972 and was appointed commander-in-chief of the army by President Salvador Allende on 23 August 1973. On 11 September 1973 the combined armed forces, including the Navy, Air Force and Carabineros, overthrew Allende's government, and the presidential palace, La Moneda, was shelled. A junta of four commanders was established; it suspended the Constitution and Congress, imposed censorship and a curfew, and banned the parties of Allende's coalition and then all others. Historians differ on the part played by the United States, which tacitly supported the junta after the coup; some authors describe a covert campaign against Allende, while Sebastián Hurtado finds no documentary evidence of an active American role in the coup itself.

Pinochet was proclaimed Supreme Chief of the Nation on 17 June 1974 and officially titled President of the Republic on 17 December 1974. General Gustavo Leigh of the Air Force, who opposed him, was forced into retirement in 1978. The regime persecuted leftists and critics through executions, forced disappearances, internment and torture; a government commission report that took testimony from more than 30,000 people recorded at least 3,197 killed and about 29,000 tortured. Economists known as the Chicago Boys guided a programme of market liberalisation. A plebiscite in 1980 approved a new constitution, and on 5 October 1988 voters rejected a further presidential term, which led to elections.

Pinochet stepped down in 1990 but remained commander-in-chief of the army until 10 March 1998, when he became a senator for life. He was arrested in London in October 1998 on an international warrant, the first time a former head of government was arrested on the principle of universal jurisdiction, and was released on medical grounds by the Home Secretary Jack Straw in March 2000. Back in Chile, he faced about 300 criminal charges when he died of heart failure at the Military Hospital in Santiago on 10 December 2006, without having been convicted. A United States Senate investigation in 2004 found a network of accounts at Riggs Bank that he and his associates used to move money.
augustus-ii-the-strong: Augustus was born in Dresden on 12 May 1670, the younger son of John George III, Elector of Saxony, and Princess Anna Sophie of Denmark. As the second son he had no expectation of inheriting the electorate, which passed to his older brother John George IV when their father died on 12 September 1691. Augustus was well educated and toured France and Italy from 1687 to 1689; the court at Versailles impressed him deeply. He married Christiane Eberhardine of Brandenburg-Bayreuth on 20 January 1693, and their son, the future Augustus III, was born in 1696. John George IV died of smallpox on 27 April 1694, and Augustus became Elector of Saxony.

To be eligible for election to the Polish throne in 1697, Augustus converted to Roman Catholicism. The step shocked Protestant Europe, since Saxony had been a stronghold of German Protestantism, and he guaranteed its religious status quo. He won the election with the backing of Russia and Austria, although another candidate, François Louis, Prince of Conti, had received more votes. Contemporaries mocked the costly bribery of the Polish nobility as his Polish adventure.

He joined Frederick IV of Denmark and Peter I of Russia against Charles XII of Sweden in the Great Northern War. Charles defeated his armies at Riga in 1701 and at Kliszów in 1702, captured Warsaw, and in 1704 had Stanisław Leszczyński installed as king. After the Battle of Fraustadt on 1 September 1706 Charles invaded Saxony, and by the Treaty of Altranstädt in October 1706 Augustus gave up the Polish throne. Peter's victory at Poltava in 1709 allowed Augustus to return under Russian auspices. His attempts to build an absolute monarchy met resistance from the nobility, and in 1717 Peter forced him and the nobles to accept the Silent Sejm, an accommodation favourable to Russia.

Augustus died at Warsaw in 1733. His body was buried in Wawel Cathedral in Kraków, while his heart rests in Dresden Cathedral. He had not made the Polish throne hereditary, but his son Augustus III succeeded him, installed by the Imperial Russian Army during the War of the Polish Succession.

He is best remembered as a patron of the arts. In Dresden he began the Zwinger and built Pillnitz Castle, and he opened the Green Vault in 1723. In Warsaw he expanded the Saxon Palace and its Saxon Garden. He sponsored the alchemist Johann Friedrich Böttger, whose work led to the Meissen porcelain manufactory, founded in 1709, and in 1705 he founded the Order of the White Eagle. Contemporary sources claimed he fathered between 360 and 380 children; the number cannot be verified and is probably greatly exaggerated.
augustus-iii: Augustus was born on 17 October 1696 in Dresden, the only legitimate son of Augustus II the Strong. His mother, Christiane Eberhardine of Brandenburg-Bayreuth, remained a fervent Protestant and never set foot in Catholic Poland, which the Polish nobility took as a provocation. He was groomed from youth to succeed as king and studied Polish, German, French and Latin. Raised at first as a Lutheran by his grandmother, he was taken by his father on a tour of Catholic countries and converted to Catholicism in November 1712 in Italy. On 20 August 1719 he married Maria Josepha of Austria, daughter of Emperor Joseph I, and the wedding in Dresden was one of the most splendid of the Baroque era.

Augustus II died on 1 February 1733, and Augustus inherited the Saxon electorate without difficulty. His election to the Polish throne was harder. By the Löwenwolde Treaty with Austria and Russia, Russia would supply troops to ensure his election and he would recognise Anna as Empress and give up Polish claims to Livonia and Courland, while renouncing any claim to the Austrian succession. Stanisław Leszczyński was chosen at the election sejm with 12,000 votes to 3,000 for Augustus, but 30,000 Russian troops had entered Poland. The War of the Polish Succession followed, and Stanisław fled in 1734. The Pacification Sejm of 1736 confirmed Augustus.

He spent less than three years of his thirty-year reign in Poland, preferring hunting, opera and collecting art. The feuding of the Czartoryski and Potocki families paralysed the Sejm through the liberum veto. His adviser Heinrich von Brühl ran Saxony and in effect Poland, leaving Polish politics to the great magnates. Saxony joined Austria in the War of the Austrian Succession and again in the Seven Years' War, when Prussia invaded in 1756 and drained it. Under the Treaty of Hubertusburg of 1763 Saxony renounced its claim to Silesia.

Augustus died of a stroke in Dresden on 5 October 1763 and was buried at Dresden Cathedral, one of the few Polish monarchs buried outside Poland. His son Frederick Christian succeeded as elector and died two and a half months later. In 1764 Stanisław August Poniatowski was elected king with Russian support. Augustus was a patron of the arts. He enlarged the Dresden art gallery and founded the opera house in Warsaw in 1748, and Johann Sebastian Bach dedicated the Kyrie and Gloria of his Mass in B minor to him. Critics in Poland have long judged him lazy, though a historian found in the Dresden archives a description of him as honest and affectionate.
augustus-the-younger-duke-of-brunswick-l: Augustus was born on 10 April 1579 at Dannenberg Castle, the seventh child of Duke Henry of Brunswick-Lüneburg. His father had given up his share of the Principality of Lüneburg on marrying Ursula of Saxe-Lauenburg and was compensated with the small lordship of Dannenberg, keeping for his descendants a right to inherit should the Wolfenbüttel line die out. As the youngest child, Augustus had little prospect of ruling. He studied at Rostock, Tübingen and Straßburg, made a Grand Tour through Italy, France, the Netherlands and England, and from the age of 25 lived for three decades with a small court at Hitzacker.

When Duke Frederick Ulrich died without heirs in 1634, in the middle of the Thirty Years' War, long negotiations with his reluctant Welf relatives and an intervention by Emperor Ferdinand II settled the Wolfenbüttel principality on Augustus in the division of 1635. The war kept him at Dankwarderode Castle in Braunschweig until 1644, when he could move to his residence. He then carried out government reforms and founded the Bibliotheca Augusta, and after the Peace of Westphalia of 1648 his lands recovered quickly. He married three times, to Clara Maria of Pomerania-Barth, Dorothea of Anhalt-Zerbst and Elisabeth Sophie of Mecklenburg, and was succeeded by his eldest son Rudolph Augustus.

Augustus promoted German as a language of literature and in 1632 joined the Fruitbearing Society of Prince Louis I of Anhalt-Köthen. Under the pseudonym Gustavus Selenus, an anagram of his name joined to a play on Selene, the Greek goddess of the moon, he translated a book on rithmomachia by Francesco Barozzi, wrote a book on chess in 1616 and in 1624 a standard work on cryptography, Cryptomenytices et Cryptographiae libri IX, based largely on Johannes Trithemius. He employed the scholar Justus Georg Schottel as tutor to his sons and corresponded with Johannes Valentinus Andreae.
aukus: In 2009 the Australian Defence White Paper stated that the government had ruled out nuclear propulsion for the submarines that would replace the Royal Australian Navy's conventionally powered Collins class. In 2016 Prime Minister Malcolm Turnbull signed a deal worth A$50 billion with the French majority state-owned company Naval Group to design the Attack class under the Future Submarine Program. The design was based on the French Barracuda class, converted from nuclear to conventional propulsion, with a United States Navy combat system and torpedo.

According to press reports, in March the Australian navy chief Vice Admiral Michael Noonan asked his British counterpart for help in acquiring nuclear-powered submarines, and Australia approached the United States in April. Boris Johnson, Joe Biden and Scott Morrison discussed the matter at the G7 summit in Cornwall in June, without the knowledge of the French government or Naval Group. Morrison said Australia had been considering an alternative to the Attack class for the previous 18 months.

AUKUS is a trilateral security partnership between Australia, the United Kingdom and the United States, announced on 15 September 2021, with two lines of effort known as pillars. Pillar 1 concerns Australia's acquisition of nuclear-powered attack submarines and the rotational basing of American and British submarines in Australia. The United States and United Kingdom share nuclear propulsion technology with Australia, as they have done with each other since 1958 under the US-UK Mutual Defence Agreement. The Royal Australian Navy is to acquire at least eight such submarines armed with conventional weapons, with the basic design decided by a Nuclear-Powered Submarine Task Force headed by Vice Admiral Jonathan Mead.

Pillar 2 covers collaborative development of advanced capabilities in six technological areas, namely undersea capabilities, quantum technologies, artificial intelligence and autonomy, advanced cyber, hypersonic and counter-hypersonic capabilities, and electronic warfare, and in two functional areas, innovation and information sharing.

A direct result of the partnership was Australia's cancellation of the French contract, worth A$90 billion by then. The French government was notified only a few hours before the public announcement, and its foreign and armed forces ministers expressed disappointment. Australia later agreed a compensation settlement of €555 million with Naval Group. The Nuclear Nonproliferation Treaty allows non-nuclear-weapon states to produce highly enriched uranium for naval reactor fuel, but scholars such as Sébastien Philippe and James M. Acton criticised the transfer of the technology as a proliferation risk.
auld-alliance: After the death of the seven-year-old Margaret, the Maid of Norway, in 1290, Edward I of England moved to extend his authority over Scotland. The Council of Twelve, which governed Scotland for the time being, looked for allies abroad. France was a natural partner, since Philip IV had declared England's possession of Gascony forfeit in 1294. A Scottish embassy agreed the Treaty of Paris, signed on 23 October 1295.

Like every later renewal, the treaty favoured France. The French had only to continue their struggle against the English in Gascony, while the cost of any war between Scotland and England fell entirely on the Scots. Scotland was nonetheless allied to a major European power. The treaty gave no protection against Edward's invasion of 1296, and the Scots owed their survival chiefly to Robert the Bruce and to the mistakes of Edward II.

The alliance took on urgency after 1332, when Edward III set out to conquer Scotland and press his claims in France. In 1334 the young David II of Scotland and his court found refuge in France, at Château Gaillard, and the French paid an annual pension of £2000 for their upkeep. In 1346 David invaded England at Philip VI's urging and was captured at the Battle of Neville's Cross.

In 1418 the Dauphin, the future Charles VII, called on Scottish help against Henry V, and as many as 15,000 Scottish troops were sent to France between 1419 and 1424. French and Scottish forces won at the Battle of Baugé in 1421 but were defeated at Verneuil in 1424. Scots fought beside Joan of Arc at Orléans in 1429 and served in the Garde Écossaise, the bodyguard of the French crown.

The alliance was renewed in 1512, 1517 and 1548, but Scotland lost James IV and most of his nobles at Flodden in 1513. As Protestantism spread in Scotland, more people favoured links with England, and the Treaty of Edinburgh of 1560 ended the formal ties.

The alliance shaped Scottish life beyond war. Scots studied at French universities, and there were reciprocal dual nationality agreements, French privileges for Scottish vintners, and an influence on architecture, law and the Scots language.

Charles de Gaulle called it the oldest alliance in the world in a speech at Edinburgh in June 1942. Both countries marked its 700th anniversary in 1995. The historian Siobhan Talbott concluded that it had never been formally revoked.
auld-lang-syne: The text is a Scots poem written by Robert Burns in 1788 on the basis of an older Scottish folk song. Burns sent it to the Scots Musical Museum with the remark that it was an old song, of the olden times, which had never been in print nor even in manuscript until he took it down from an old man.

Some of the words were indeed collected rather than composed. A ballad, Old Long Syne, printed by James Watson in 1711, resembles the first verse and chorus closely and almost certainly derives from the same old song, so it is a fair supposition that the rest of the poem is Burns's own. The phrase auld lang syne also occurs in poems by Robert Ayton, Allan Ramsay and James Watson, and in older folk songs. The Scots title may be rendered as old long since, or less literally as days gone by.

The song opens by asking whether old times should be forgotten, which is generally read as a call to remember long-standing friendships. In George Thomson's Select Songs of Scotland of 1799 the second verse, about greeting and toasting, was moved to its present place at the end. The song originally had another melody, traced to about 1700 and judged mediocre by Burns. The first documented use of the tune now standard was in 1799, in Thomson's second volume. It is a pentatonic Scots folk melody, probably once a sprightly dance at a much quicker tempo, and there is some doubt that Burns intended it.

The composer William Shield seems to quote it in the overture to his opera Rosina of 1782, but both may have taken it from a common source, possibly a strathspey. In 1792 Joseph Haydn arranged it for George Thomson, and Beethoven later made an arrangement too.

Singing the song on Hogmanay, or New Year's Eve, quickly became a Scots custom that spread to other parts of the British Isles, and emigrants took it round the world. At Hogmanay in Scotland everyone joins hands in a circle and crosses arms at the last verse, while the tradition of singing it when parting with hands crossed arose in the mid-19th century among Freemasons and other fraternal organisations. It is also used at funerals, graduations, the closing of Scout jamborees and Burns suppers.

The melody has carried other words. In France the Jesuit Jacques Sevin translated the song in 1920 as Ce n'est qu'un au revoir. In Japan the tune serves for Hotaru no Hikari, played at school graduations. It was the tune of the Korean exile government's anthem from 1919 to 1945, and of the anthem of the Maldives until 1972. The first recording was made on a wax cylinder in 1898.
aulic-war-council: Emperor Maximilian I had already summoned permanent councils of war about 1500, and on 25 February 1531 Ferdinand I ordered from Linz an independent war council of four councillors. The Permanent War Council founded under Ferdinand on 17 November 1556 was a body of five generals and senior civil servants. It decided on fortress building, equipment, pay and the purchase of supplies, planned and conducted wars, and ran the civil and military administration of the border region of Croatia. On 31 December 1556 all military authorities were ordered to submit to it, and the title Hofkriegsrat was first used in 1564.

Once a standing Imperial Army existed in the 17th century, the council managed it as the central military agency and chancery, provided a staff for the emperor and directed the field armies. Its presidents included Raimondo Montecuccoli and Prince Eugene of Savoy. Every general except the generalissimo had to seek its authorisation for strategic decisions, a rule that kept action coordinated but proved a handicap against Frederick the Great of Prussia. Joseph II gave it supreme authority over every branch of military administration.

In 1799 its instructions, which called for trench warfare instead of lightning warfare, held up Field Marshal Alexander Suvorov in Italy. Archduke Charles, made president by Francis II in 1801, divided it into military, judicial and administrative departments. After the Napoleonic Wars it was one of the four parts of the State Council. Its business moved slowly through argument and circulating papers, the officer presidents clashed with civilian section heads, and the general staff remained a subordinate section of it.

In its last years the council investigated units of doubtful loyalty: in 1833 it ruled that soldiers belonging to Mazzini's Young Italy were guilty of high treason, and in the 1840s it judged that the South Slav Grenzer would obey orders. From 1 June 1848 it became the Austrian Ministry of War, which under the Austro-Hungarian Compromise of 1867 was one of the three common ministries. In Tolstoy's War and Peace the old Prince Bolkonski mocks it as the Hof-kriegs-wurst-schnapps-rat.
aulus-gabinius: Gabinius rose mainly thanks to the patronage of Pompey. As tribune of the plebs in 67 BCE he brought forward the Lex Gabinia, which gave Pompey command against the Mediterranean pirates, with control of the sea and of the coasts for 50 miles inland. Two of his other measures made loans of money to foreign ambassadors in Rome actionable, as a check on corruption in the Senate, and ordered the Senate to give audiences to foreign envoys on fixed days each year, from 1 February to 1 March.

From 66 to 62 BCE he served Pompey as a legate in the last phases of the Third Mithridatic War. In 65 BCE Pompey sent him with part of his army into northern Mesopotamia to pressure the Parthian king Phraates III into a treaty, and he then marched into Syria against pirates and brigands. Aristobulus, brother of Hyrcanus II, the high priest and king of Judea, bribed him to support his claim to the Judean throne and later accused Gabinius and Scaurus of taking bribes.

As praetor in 61 BCE he gave games of unusual splendour. He was elected consul for 58 BCE, though not without suspicion of bribery, alongside Lucius Calpurnius Piso Caesoninus. He helped Publius Clodius Pulcher bring about the exile of Cicero and secured Syria as his province.

As governor of Syria from 57 BCE he marched into Judaea, defeated the army of Alexander, nephew of Hyrcanus II, near Jerusalem and reinstated Hyrcanus as high priest. He suppressed revolts and rebuilt several towns.
