avarua: Avarua is a district and township in the north of Rarotonga, the largest island of the Cook Islands, and one of the island's five districts. The name means two harbours in Māori. The township is built around two harbours, Avatiu Harbour, where the main port is, and Avarua Harbour at Takuvaine, which used to be the main port and is now a small fishing port. The district is divided into 19 tapere, traditional sub-districts. The township is the central business district of Rarotonga and the location of government offices.

The Cook Islands were inhabited largely by indigenous Māori people until the late 19th century. Avarua was not the main centre of Rarotonga until missionaries of the London Missionary Society arrived in 1823 and set up their national headquarters there. Trading ships also based themselves there, and from the middle of the 19th century it was the religious and commercial centre of the Cook Islands. The islands became a British protectorate in 1888, and after the first British resident was appointed Avarua became the administrative and educational centre. The Cook Islands became part of New Zealand in 1901, and a Resident Commissioner governed until 1946, after which they began a transition to self-governance. In 1965 they achieved self-government in free association with New Zealand.

Avarua is the capital of the Cook Islands and an important commercial centre. Rarotonga International Airport and Avatiu Port, the main commercial harbour, are there. The township hosts the Sir Geoffrey Henry National Culture Centre, which includes the National Library and the Cook Islands National Museum. The coastal ring road Ara Tapu encircles the island, and the inner road Ara Metua, built in the 11th century, skirts the interior.
ave-maris-stella: The hymn's oldest known copies are 10th-century additions to two 9th-century manuscripts, one from Salzburg, now in Vienna, and the other still at the Abbey of Saint Gall. Its frequent place in the Divine Office made it popular through the Middle Ages, and other hymns were founded upon it. The title Star of the Sea is one of the oldest and most widespread titles given to Mary, and the hymn is often used as a prayer for the safe conduct of travellers.

The text, in seven short stanzas, greets Mary as the nurturing Mother of God, ever virgin and the happy gate of heaven. It plays on the Ave spoken by the angel Gabriel as the name Eva reversed, and asks her to loosen the chains of the guilty, bring light to the blind and drive away evil. Later stanzas ask her to show herself a mother, to make the singers meek and chaste and to prepare them a safe way to Jesus, and it closes with praise of the Father, Christ and the Holy Spirit. It was influential in presenting Mary as a merciful and loving mother.

The Roman Rite uses four plainchant tunes for the hymn, three for solemnities, feasts and memorials of Mary and a fourth in the Little Office of the Blessed Virgin Mary. These tunes served as the cantus firmus of polyphonic settings of the Mass by Josquin and Victoria. Renaissance settings include those of Guillaume Dufay, Giovanni Pierluigi da Palestrina, John Sheppard, William Byrd and Hans Leo Hassler, and Baroque ones Monteverdi's Vespro della Beata Vergine of 1610, a setting by Emperor Leopold I and four by Marc-Antoine Charpentier. Romantic settings include those of Dvorak, Grieg, Liszt and Elgar.

The melody also appears in the Irish plainsong Gabhaim Molta Bríde, in praise of Saint Brigid. In 1884 the second Acadian National Convention at Miscouche, Prince Edward Island, adopted it as the anthem of Acadia.
aventine-hill: The Aventine is the southernmost of the seven hills on which ancient Rome was built and belongs to Ripa, the modern twelfth rione of the city. It has two distinct heights, a greater one to the northwest, Aventinus Major, and a lesser one to the southeast, Aventinus Minor, divided by a steep cleft that carried an ancient road. Most Roman sources trace the hill's name to a king named Aventinus, a figure of tradition. In the founding myth, Remus takes his auspices on the Aventine and Romulus on the Palatine.

According to Roman tradition the Aventine lay outside the original city and its sacred boundary, the pomerium. Livy reports that Ancus Marcius, the fourth king, settled the Latins of Politorium there, and Strabo credits him with a wall to include the hill, while others credit Servius Tullius. It served as a staging post for foreign peoples and cults entering Rome. Servius Tullius built a temple of Diana there for the Latin League, and around 493 BCE the Senate provided a temple for Ceres, Liber and Libera, patron deities of the plebs, after one of the first plebeian secessions. Around 456 BCE a Lex Icilia gave the plebs property rights there.

In 392 BCE Camillus established a temple of Juno Regina, and later cults arrived, among them Summanus, Vortumnus and Minerva. In the imperial era the hill became an aristocratic quarter, with the private houses of Trajan and Hadrian before they became emperors and the Baths of Decius, built in 252. Its character probably led to its total destruction in the sack of Rome by Alaric I in 410.

The Aventine is now an elegant residential district with palaces, churches and gardens, among them the basilica of Santa Sabina and the Rome Rose Garden. In the Fascist period, many opposition deputies withdrew there after the murder of Giacomo Matteotti, an episode known as the Aventine Secession, which ended their presence in Parliament.
averroes: Averroes was born in Córdoba on 14 April 1126. His full name was Abu l-Walid Muhammad ibn Ahmad Ibn Rushd, and the nickname al-Hafid, the Grandson, is sometimes added to distinguish him from his grandfather, a noted judge and jurist. His family was well known for public service in legal and religious fields: his grandfather was chief judge of Córdoba and imam of its Great Mosque under the Almoravids, and his father was also chief judge until the Almohads replaced the Almoravids in 1146. By 1153 Averroes was in Marrakesh, the Almohad capital, making astronomical observations and supporting the building of new colleges, and he probably met the philosopher Ibn Tufayl there.

He wrote more than 100 books and treatises on philosophy, medicine, law, theology and linguistics. His commentaries on Aristotle fall into short, middle and long forms; the middle ones were probably written in response to the caliph Abu Yaqub Yusuf's complaints that Aristotle was hard to follow. He tried to return to what he considered the original Aristotle and rejected the Neoplatonist tendencies of al-Farabi and Avicenna.

In 1178 his Decisive Treatise argued that Islam and philosophy are compatible, and his Incoherence of the Incoherence of 1180 answered al-Ghazali's attack on the philosophers. As a Maliki judge he wrote the Bidayat al-Mujtahid, explaining why the schools of Islamic law differ. His General Principles of Medicine, known in Latin as the Colliget, was written around 1162. He might have been the first to see that the retina senses light, although scholars dispute what he meant.

Averroes's works survive chiefly in Hebrew and Latin translations; only a tiny handful of Arabic manuscripts of his long commentaries remain, and his legacy in the Islamic world was modest. In western Europe his commentaries entered in the thirteenth century and led him to be called simply the Commentator. His thesis that all humans share one intellect became the best-known and most controversial doctrine of Averroism, and his works were condemned by the Catholic Church in 1270 and 1277. Latin Averroism nonetheless attracted followers up to the sixteenth century.
aveyron: Aveyron, named after the river Aveyron, is a department in the Occitania region of southern France, and its prefecture is Rodez. It lies at the centre of a triangle formed by Toulouse, Clermont-Ferrand and Montpellier, in the south of the Massif Central, and approximately follows the outline of the former province of Rouergue. With an area of 8,735 square kilometres it is the fifth largest department in metropolitan France, yet largely rural, with 279,609 inhabitants in 2023. It consists of an ancient high rocky plateau, in which the Truyère, Lot, Aveyron and Tarn rivers have carved deep gorges. Its highest point is the Signal de Mailhebiau, at 1,469 m on the Plateau of Aubrac.

The earliest known inhabitants were the Rutenii tribe, though the area was inhabited before them, and the inhabitants of Rodez are still called Ruthénois after them. The department has many prehistoric monuments, including over a thousand dolmens, the most of any department in France. Until the 1790s the territory formed a province known as Rouergue. Aveyron is one of the original 83 departments created on 4 March 1790.

In 1797 Victor of Aveyron, a feral child, was found wandering the woods in the area, and his story is told in the film The Wild Child. In 1817 a local prosecutor, Antoine Bernardin Fualdès, was assassinated, and the sordid circumstances, in which his body was found floating in the river Aveyron, made the matter a cause célèbre. Recent studies indicate that he died at the initiative of a royalist organisation known as the Chevaliers de la Foi.

The regional dialect is Rouergat, a form of Languedoc Occitan. Several associations have asked the state for an ambitious language policy because of the risk of its disappearance. The department is known for Roquefort cheese, from the village of that name, and the couteau de Laguiole. Among its monuments are the medieval castle ruin of Najac and the abbeys of Conques, Sylvanès, Bonneval and Loc-Dieu. At Millau the Millau viaduct was opened in December 2004. Ten of its villages belong to the association Les Plus Beaux Villages de France, founded in 1901.
avgustyn-voloshyn: Voloshyn was born on 17 March 1874 in Kelecsény in Carpathian Ruthenia, then part of Austria-Hungary and now Kelechyn in Ukraine. His grandfather and his father, both named Ivan, were Greek Catholic priests of the Eparchy of Mukachevo, and his mother, Emilia Andriyivna Zombori, also came from a priestly family. His father spoke almost only Ukrainian with his children, then regarded as a peasants' language. At the gymnasium in Uzhhorod, which a classmate described as heavily Magyarized, he began in the preparatory class because he knew little Hungarian, but he graduated with distinction in 1892 and went on to study theology in Ungvár and Budapest.

Ordained a Greek Catholic priest, he taught mathematics at the Uzhhorod Teacher Institute from 1900 to 1917 and became a papal chamberlain, with the title of Monsignor, in 1924. In 1918 he became head of the Subcarpathian National Council, which in 1919 asked that Carpathian Ruthenia join Czechoslovakia. In 1925 he was elected to the Parliament in Prague as leader of the Ruthenian National Christian Party. He and his wife, Iryna Petryk, had no children, and from 1933 they raised 22 orphans in their own home.

On 26 October 1938 President Emil Hácha named him head of the government of the Subcarpathian Autonomous Region. As Czechoslovakia broke up, he proclaimed Carpatho-Ukraine's independence and offered Romania unification, which it refused. On 19 March 1939 he retreated to the border of Romania under the protection of the last Czechoslovak troops, then lived in Prague as a professor at the Ukrainian Free University.

When the Soviet army took Prague in May 1945, the NKVD arrested Voloshyn and took him to Moscow, accusing him of being a Ukrainian nationalist hostile to the Soviet Union, though he had never been a Soviet citizen. He died on 19 July 1945 in Butyrka prison, officially of heart failure; his grave is unknown. In 2002 he was named a Hero of Ukraine, and monuments to him stand in Uzhhorod, Kelecsény and, since 2021, at Askold's Grave in Kyiv, where a street was named after him in 2024.
avicenna: Avicenna was born around 980 in the village of Afshana in Transoxiana, to a Persian family. The village was near the Samanid capital of Bukhara, his mother's hometown. His father Abd Allah, a native of Balkh, was a Samanid official who had governed a village of the royal estate of Harmaytan during the reign of Nuh II. The family soon settled in Bukhara, a centre of learning, where Avicenna was educated, seemingly at first by his father. Under the Samanids Bukhara rivalled Baghdad as a cultural capital, and he had access to the great libraries of Balkh, Khwarazm, Gorgan, Rey, Isfahan and Hamadan.

At 17 Avicenna was made a physician of Nuh II. When he was at least 21 his father died, and he was given an administrative post, possibly succeeding his father as governor of Harmaytan. He later moved to Gurganj, the capital of Khwarazm, which he reports he did out of necessity, and served the Ma'munid ruler Abu al-Hasan Ali, who ruled from 997 to 1009.

He may have left in 999, when the Samanid Empire fell after the Kara-Khanid Khanate captured Bukhara and imprisoned the emir Abd al-Malik II; his close ties to the Samanids may have left him in an unfavourable position. While imprisoned in the castle of Fardajan near Hamadhan, he wrote the thought experiment known as the floating man.

Of about 450 works he is believed to have written, around 240 survive, including 150 on philosophy and 40 on medicine. He wrote mostly in Arabic and some in Early New Persian, notably the Danishnama. The Canon of Medicine, in five books, postulated that invisible tainted organisms were associated with disease and recommended isolating the ill. It served as a standard medical textbook in the Islamic world and Europe up to the 18th century. The Book of Healing, begun in 1014 and completed around 1020, treats logic, natural sciences, mathematics and metaphysics, not medicine.

His philosophy belongs to the Peripatetic school derived from Aristotle, though his commentaries often criticised Aristotle. In the floating man, a person suspended in the air and cut off from all sensation would still be self-aware, which he took to show that the soul is an immaterial substance. The historian of philosophy Peter Adamson calls his Proof of the Truthful, which identifies an entity that cannot not exist with God, one of the most influential medieval arguments for God's existence.
avidius-cassius: Avidius Cassius was born around 130 in the town of Cyrrhus in Syria. His father, Gaius Avidius Heliodorus, was of equestrian status and served Hadrian as secretary for correspondence before becoming prefect of Roman Egypt from 137 to 142. According to Cassius Dio, Heliodorus received that post, among the highest an equestrian could hold, through his oratory alone. His mother, Julia Cassia Alexandra, descended from Augustus through Junia Lepida and from Herod the Great through her father, and Cassius was also a distant descendant of Antiochus IV Epiphanes of Commagene.

Cassius probably began his career under Antoninus Pius and was a legionary commander by 161, perhaps in Moesia Inferior, which guarded against the Sarmatians. He rose quickly around 164 in the Parthian war of Lucius Verus as commander of Legio III Gallica. In 165 he led it down the Euphrates and defeated the Parthians at Dura-Europos, then crossed Mesopotamia to attack the twin cities on the Tigris.

At Ctesiphon he burned the palace of Vologases IV, and he destroyed Seleucia although it had surrendered, claiming that its people had broken their agreement. The first signs of the Antonine Plague appeared in his army that year. He was raised to the Senate, became suffect consul in May 166 and was appointed imperial legate of Syria late in 166.

Around 170 he was given the extraordinary title of Rector Orientis, with imperium over all the eastern provinces, to deal with the Bucolic War, a rebellion in Egypt centred on the Pentapolis of Middle Egypt and set off by a sharp rise in grain prices. The rebels came close to taking Alexandria before Cassius's troops halted them. He ended the revolt in 175 by dividing the rebel groups and then defeating them one by one.

Some accounts hold that Faustina the Younger, fearing that Marcus Aurelius would die while their son Commodus was still young, persuaded or tricked Cassius into rebelling. He claimed that Aurelius's troops in Pannonia had elected him. He had Egypt, Syria, Syria Palaestina and Arabia Petraea behind him, and perhaps seven legions, but the Senate declared him a public enemy and Publius Martius Verus of Cappadocia rallied support for Aurelius. Herodes Atticus is recorded as sending him a letter containing only the word emanes, meaning you are mad.

When Aurelius prepared to march east, a centurion killed Cassius and sent his head to the emperor, who refused to see it and had it buried. The revolt had lasted three months and six days, and no coins bearing his image were struck. Aurelius asked for no bloodshed against supporters, though one son, Avidius Maecianus, was killed and another, Avidius Heliodorus, was banished.
avignon: Avignon lies on the left bank of the Rhône, a few kilometres above its confluence with the Durance, about 580 km south-east of Paris, 229 km south of Lyon and 85 km north-north-west of Marseille. The river passes the western edge of the city in two branches, the Petit Rhône and the Grand Rhône, separated by the Île de la Barthelasse. The region is rich in limestone, and the present city walls, 4,330 metres long, were built of the soft limestone called mollasse burdigalienne. The climate is mediterranean, though sheltered inland, and the city is often windy, the strongest wind being the mistral. A medieval Latin proverb called it windy Avignon, pest-ridden when there is no wind and wind-pestered when there is.

The earliest forms of the name were reported by Greek writers, among them Strabo and Ptolemy. The Roman name Avennio Cavarum, in Mela and Pliny, shows that Avignon was one of the three cities of the Celtic-Ligurian tribe of the Cavares, with Cavaillon and Orange. Between 1309 and 1377, during the Avignon Papacy, seven successive popes resided in the city. In 1348 Pope Clement VI bought the town from Joanna I of Naples. Papal control persisted until 1791, when it became part of France during the French Revolution, which is why Avignon is also known as La Cité des Papes. Pope Gregory XI, born around 1329 and dead in 1378, was the seventh and last of the Avignon popes.

The medieval University of Avignon grew out of the schools already in the city and was formally constituted in 1303 by Boniface VIII in a papal bull. Boniface VIII and King Charles II of Naples were its first great protectors and benefactors. Its law department, covering both civil and ecclesiastical law, was the most important throughout the university's existence. Avignon absorbed Montfavet between 1790 and 1794, ceded Morières-lès-Avignon in 1870 and ceded Le Pontet in 1925.

Avignon is the prefecture of the Vaucluse department in the region of Provence-Alpes-Côte d'Azur, with 92,188 inhabitants in 2023. About 16,000 live in the ancient centre enclosed by the medieval walls, one of the few in France to have preserved its mediaeval city walls. The centre includes the Palais des Papes, Avignon Cathedral and the Pont d'Avignon, and was listed by UNESCO as a World Heritage Site in 1995. The Festival d'Avignon, founded in 1947, brings theatre, dance, music and cinema to the town's historic monuments each summer. The song Sur le Pont d'Avignon dates from the mid-19th century, when Adolphe Adam included it in an opéra comique first performed in Paris in 1853.
avila: Ávila lies in the centre of the Iberian Peninsula, north of the Sistema Central, on the right bank of the Adaja, a tributary of the Duero. At 1,132 metres above sea level it is the highest provincial capital in Spain. It is built on the flat summit of a rocky hill that stands above a brown, arid, treeless table-land strewn with grey boulders. Annual precipitation is 416 mm, and the Adaja is dry for several months of the year, so the town has historically had water supply problems.

In pre-Roman times, in the 5th century BCE, Ávila was inhabited by the Vettones, who called it Obila, meaning high mountain, and built one of their strongest fortresses there. Bronze Age stone statues of boars, known as verracos, stand nearby. The Roman town, called Abila or Abela, kept a rectangular plan with two main streets crossing at a forum. By tradition Secundus brought the Gospel to Ávila in the 1st century and became its first bishop.

After the fall of the Western Roman Empire Ávila became a stronghold of the Visigoths. The Moors conquered it, and as northern Christian kingdoms repeatedly attacked it, it became a virtually uninhabited no man's land. It was repopulated about 1088 after Raymond of Burgundy, son-in-law of Alfonso VI of León and Castile, definitively reconquered the area. Tradition holds that he employed two foreigners, Casandro Romano and Florin de Pontuenga, to build the walls that still stand. Ávila had a Jewish community, documented from 1144, which ceased to exist after the expulsion of 1492.

During the Revolt of the Comuneros the Santa Junta first met there on 1 August 1520, and in the summer it drafted in the cathedral the Proyecto de Ley Perpetua, a proto-constitutional draft that never came into force. A long decline from the 17th century reduced the population to just 4,000.

Ávila is the capital of the Province of Ávila in Castile and León, sometimes called the City of Stones and Saints. Its Old Town and the churches outside the walls became a UNESCO World Heritage Site in 1985. The walls, begun in 1090 and built between the 11th and 14th centuries, enclose 31 hectares with a perimeter of 2,516 metres, 88 towers and nine gates. Saint Teresa, the town's best-known resident and the first female Doctor of the Church, founded the Convent of Saint Joseph, the first of the Discalced Carmelite nuns, in 1562.
avitus: Eparchius Avitus was born at Avernia, the present Clermont-Ferrand, into a family of the Gallo-Roman nobility. His daughter Papianilla married the writer Sidonius Apollinaris, whose letters and panegyrics are an important source for his life. Avitus came to know the Gothic court: around 439 he met the future Theodoric II, whom he inspired to study the Latin poets. He served under the general Aetius against the Burgundians and defeated Hunnic raiders near Avernia in 437, and in 439 he became praetorian prefect of Gaul. In 451, when Attila invaded, he persuaded Theodoric to ally with Rome.

In 455 Emperor Petronius Maximus sent Avitus as an envoy to Theodoric II at Toulouse. While he was there news arrived that Maximus was dead and that Rome had been sacked by the Vandals under Gaiseric. Theodoric proclaimed Avitus emperor, and on 9 July the Gallic chiefs at Viernum did the same; about 5 August the Senate recognised him. He entered Rome on 21 September. He brought several Gallic senators into the administration, a policy opposed by the Roman aristocracy and people, and on 1 January 456 he took the consulate alone, which the Eastern court refused to recognise.

At his request Theodoric invaded Hispania, and on 5 October 456 the Visigoths defeated the Suebi on the Órbigo, but this left them unable to help him at home. Rome suffered from food shortages, and the treasury was so empty that Avitus melted down bronze statues to pay the Gothic guard he had been forced to disband. The generals Ricimer and Majorian rebelled, and the Senate deposed him. He fought them near Piacenza on 17 or 18 October 456, fled, and was spared on condition that he became Bishop of Piacenza.

The manner and date of Avitus's death are uncertain. Gregory of Tours says he died while travelling to Gaul to bring gifts to the basilica of Saint Julian; other sources have him strangled or starved on his successor's orders. He died in 457 or late in 456 and was buried at Brioude beside the tomb of Saint Julian.
avranches: Avranches is a subprefecture of the Manche department, at the southern end of the Cotentin Peninsula, where the E40 road links Saint-Lô with Brittany. The town was founded on high ground overlooking the dunes and coastal marshes of the bay between the Cotentin and Brittany, and from it Mont Saint-Michel can be seen. The mount was founded by Saint Aubert, Bishop of Avranches, in the 8th century. The inhabitants are called Avranchinais.

By the end of the Roman period the settlement of Ingena, capital of the Abrincatui, had taken the name of the tribe, which became Avranches. In 511 it became the seat of a diocese, suppressed in 1790, and later of a major Romanesque cathedral dedicated to Saint Andrew, dismantled during the Revolution. Around the turn of the 10th century the Avranchin was briefly held by Alan I of the Kingdom of Brittany, and in 933 Avranches and its territory were ceded to the Normans. Hugh d'Avranches, 1st Earl of Chester, a magnate under William the Conqueror, was the son of Richard le Goz, Vicomte d'Avranches.

A council was held at Avranches on 27 and 28 September 1172 after the murder of Thomas Becket. Henry II of England did penance there on 21 May 1172, swore fidelity to Pope Alexander III in the person of the papal legate and was absolved, reaching the Compromise of Avranches with the Church. The town was damaged in the Hundred Years' War and the Wars of Religion. On 8 August 1444 Henry VI of England made Álvaro Vaz de Almada the 1st Count of Avranches.

The town lost influence after the French Revolution, when the diocese was abolished and schools were closed, and it was occupied and raided by republican troops and by Chouans. The diocese was restored in 1802 as part of the Diocese of Coutances. Many English families settled there after the Treaty of Paris of 1814. The liberation of Avranches, led by General George S. Patton, began on 31 July 1944 and is regarded as the start of Operation Cobra, called La Percée d'Avranches in French.

Le Scriptorial museum houses the manuscripts of Mont Saint-Michel, deposited in the municipal archives during the Revolution, one of the largest collections of medieval illuminated manuscripts in France outside national and university libraries. A grassed terrace, La Plate-Forme, overlooking the bay, marks the site of the destroyed cathedral where Henry II did penance. The Gothic Revival church of Notre Dame des Champs was built in the 19th century, and the Basilica of Saint Gervasius and Protasius holds a treasury with the purported skull of Saint Aubert, probably a prehistoric trepanned skull. Botanical gardens were founded in the late 18th century in the grounds of a Franciscan convent.
avvakum: Avvakum Petrov was born about 1620 in Grigorovo, in what is now the Nizhny Novgorod region, to a priest named Pyotr and a nun, Maria. By his own account he became a deacon at twenty-one and an archpriest at Yurevyets at twenty-eight. In the late 1640s he and the future Patriarch Nikon belonged to the Zealots of Piety, a circle that aimed to purify religious life. When Nikon became patriarch in 1652, he began reforms intended mainly to bring Russian liturgy into line with other Eastern Orthodox churches, including changing the sign of the cross from two fingers to three. Avvakum rejected them as a corruption of the Russian Church.

For his opposition Avvakum was repeatedly imprisoned and exiled. In 1653 he and his family were sent to Tobolsk in Siberia, and later he went with Afanasy Pashkov's expedition to Dauria on the Chinese border, in which two of his sons died. Allowed to return to Moscow in 1664, after Nikon was no longer patriarch, he was exiled again, to Mezen. The Great Moscow Synod of 1666–1667 anathematised all who refused the changes, and Avvakum and his fellow Old Believers Lazar, Fyodor and Epifany were banished to Pustozersk, above the Arctic Circle. From 1670 they were condemned to a life on bread and water in a dugout. On 14 April 1682 they were burned alive in a log house.

During his imprisonment Avvakum wrote his autobiography, The Life Written by Himself. The first version was drafted in 1669–1672, with three more redactions to 1675. He called it a zhitie, a hagiography, and it tells of his struggle against the reforms, his sufferings in Siberia, his exorcisms and his love of nature. It circulated in manuscript for nearly two centuries before it was first printed in 1861. Viktor Vinogradov observed that it combines high literary language with vernacular, colloquialisms and profanity. Scholars such as Alan Wood regard it as a prototype of Siberian prison literature. Groups rejecting the liturgical changes survived his death and came to be called the Old Believers.
awa-province-tokushima: Awa was bordered by the provinces of Tosa, Sanuki and Iyo and was one of the provinces of the Nankaidō circuit. Under the Engishiki classification it was one of the 35 superior countries in importance and one of the middle countries in distance from the capital. Its provincial capital stood in what is now the city of Tokushima, and its short name was Ashū. People have lived there since the Japanese Paleolithic, and settlements and burial mounds of the Yayoi and Kofun periods have been found, above all in the fertile Yoshino River valley.

According to the Kogo Shūi the name was first written with the character for millet, which the province produced; in 713 Empress Genmei changed its spelling when the Ritsuryō codes standardised provincial names to two characters. The Sasaki and Ogasawara clans were its shugo in the Kamakura period and the Hosokawa in the Muromachi period, until the Miyoshi supplanted them and, under Miyoshi Nagayoshi, came to rule much of the Kinai region.

When internal conflict weakened the Miyoshi, Chōsokabe Motochika of Tosa invaded and by 1585 had united Shikoku. Hashiba Hideyoshi's armies defeated him within two months and forced him back to Tosa. Awa went to Hideyoshi's general Hachisuka Masakatsu, who handed it to his son Hachisuka Iemasa because of his age. Under the Tokugawa shogunate the Hachisuka ruled Awa and neighbouring Awaji from Tokushima Castle; the domain's nominal assessment of 257,000 koku made it the 17th largest. An early Meiji survey counted 584 villages.

After the abolition of the domains in 1871 the province passed through Myōdō Prefecture, Kagawa Prefecture and Kōchi Prefecture before it was separated in 1880 as Tokushima Prefecture, whose area it covers.
awadh: Awadh, known in British texts as Oudh, is a historical region of northern India that now forms the central part of Uttar Pradesh. Its name comes from the Sanskrit Ayodhya, meaning not to be warred against, and it is roughly synonymous with the ancient Kosala of Hindu, Buddhist and Jain scriptures. Known as the granary of India, Awadh mattered strategically for control of the Doab, the fertile plain between the Ganges and the Yamuna.

Humayun made the region part of the Mughal Empire around 1555, and under Akbar it was one of the subahs into which he divided the empire in 1590. Saadat Khan, a Persian adventurer, was appointed its governor in 1722 and laid the foundation of the Awadh dynasty as Mughal power weakened. The Nawabs were a Persian Shia Muslim dynasty from Nishapur, and Persian was used in government and at court. Shuja-ud-Daula fell out with the East India Company after aiding Mir Qasim of Bengal, and was defeated at the Battle of Buxar.

The British appointed a resident at Lucknow in 1773, and Asaf-ud-Daula moved the capital there from Faizabad in 1775. A treaty of 1801 with Saadat Ali Khan ceded half of Awadh to the Company and left the nawabs ceremonial kings, though the state remained part of the Mughal Empire in name until 1819. In that year Ghaziuddin Haidar began striking coins in his own name.

In 1856 the East India Company invaded and annexed the state under the Doctrine of Lapse. The Nawab, Wajid Ali Shah, was exiled to Calcutta. In the rebellion of 1857 his 14-year-old son Birjis Qadra was crowned ruler, and the rebels held the region until the British reconquered it after 18 months, including the Siege of Lucknow. In 1902 the new name United Provinces of Agra and Oudh was introduced.

The nawabs are remembered as patrons of arts, music and architecture. The Bara Imambara, the Chhota Imambara and the Rumi Darwaza survive at Lucknow, and the nawabs left a composite culture known as the Ganga-Jamuni Tehzeeb. Ayodhya, in the region, is one of the seven holy cities of Hinduism.
awaji-island: Awaji Island has an area of 592.17 square kilometres and is the largest island of the Seto Inland Sea. It is separated from Honshū by the Akashi Strait and from Shikoku by the Naruto Strait, where the Naruto whirlpools form. Since 5 April 1998 it has been connected to Kobe on Honshū by the Akashi Kaikyo Bridge, and the Kobe-Awaji-Naruto Expressway across the island has been the main eastern land link between Honshū and Shikoku.

Scholars such as Motoori Norinaga have claimed that the name means the road to Awa, the historic province across the Naruto Strait, although this etymology is disputed. Others, including Tsugita Uruu, read awa as millet, because of a story in the Kojiki and Nihon Shoki in which the kami Sukunabikona climbs a millet stalk on the island.

In the Shinto creation myth Awaji was the first of the ōyashima islands born from the kami Izanagi and Izanami. The Kojiki calls it Awaji no Honosawake no Shima and the Nihon Shoki Awaji-shima. Awaji formed a province, Awaji Province, between the 7th and the 19th century, and was part of Nankaidō.

Awaji Ningyō Jōruri, a form of traditional puppet theatre over 500 years old, is performed daily in Minamiawaji and is designated an Intangible Cultural Heritage of Japan. The puppets perform popular traditional dramas but have their origins in religious rituals. From the 1830s the local potter Minpei produced what became known as Awaji ware, or Minpei ware. In 1995 the island was the epicentre of the Great Hanshin Earthquake, which killed over 5,500 people and caused enormous damage in the north of the island, which experienced seismic waves of JMA intensity 7.

The island consists of three municipalities, Awaji, Sumoto and Minamiawaji, all part of Hyōgo Prefecture. The Nojima Fault, which caused the 1995 earthquake, cuts across the island. A section of it is preserved in the Nojima Fault Preservation Museum in the Hokudancho Earthquake Memorial Park, and the fault was designated a national natural monument in 1998 and an IUGS geological heritage site in 2022.

The architect Tadao Ando designed several structures on the island, including the Hompuku-ji water temple and the Awaji Yumebutai complex, both in Awaji City. The Onaruto Bridge Memorial Museum and the Uzushio Science Museum stand near Fukura.
awami-league: The party was founded on 23 June 1949 as the East Pakistan Awami Muslim League, a breakaway faction of the Muslim League formed within two years of the creation of Pakistan. Its founders were Abdul Hamid Khan Bhashani, Yar Mohammad Khan, Shamsul Huq and Sheikh Mujibur Rahman. The word Muslim was dropped in 1953 and it became a secular party, and after 1955 it was the East Pakistan Awami League, the provincial party of the All-Pakistan Awami League founded by Huseyn Suhrawardy as an alternative to the dominance of the Muslim League.

Awami comes from the Urdu word awam, meaning people, so the name can be translated as Bangladesh People's League. The party quickly gained wide support in East Pakistan and came to lead Bengali nationalism against the military and political establishment of West Pakistan.

The six-point demands proposed by Mujib in 1966 asked for greater autonomy for the provinces and were widely accepted in East Pakistan. In the elections of 1970 the Awami League won 167 of 169 East Pakistan seats in the National Assembly and none of West Pakistan's 138, which gave it a majority in the 313-seat house and the means to form a government without partners. This was unacceptable to West Pakistan's political leaders and led directly to the Bangladesh Liberation War. Mujib was arrested on 25 March 1971, and the war continued for nine months, until victory on 16 December 1971.

The party formed the first government of independent Bangladesh, which faced mine clearing, food shortages and a famine in 1974 in which 70,000 people died. In January 1975 the Awami League and other left-wing parties were merged into the Bangladesh Krishak Sramik Awami League. After the coup of 15 August 1975 the party was pushed to the political sidelines, and many senior leaders and activists were executed or jailed. In 1981 Mujib's daughter Sheikh Hasina became president of the party, and she united its rival factions. The party opposed the regime of Hussain Muhammad Ershad and emerged as a principal force after the restoration of democracy in 1990.
awash-river: The Awash is about 1,200 kilometres long and runs entirely within Ethiopia. It rises at an elevation of about 3,000 metres in the central highlands, west of Addis Ababa, then enters the floor of the Great Rift Valley, loops around Mount Zuqualla, passes the city of Adama and the Awash National Park, and is joined by its chief tributary, the Germama or Kasam. It ends in a chain of linked lakes that begins with Lake Gargori and finishes at Lake Abbe, on the border with Djibouti, at about 250 metres. It is the principal stream of a basin with no outlet to the sea, which covers about a tenth of Ethiopia.

The Awash Valley, and above all the Middle Awash, has a very high density of fossil hominins, dating from roughly 5.6 to 2.5 million years ago. They include many Australopithecines, among them Lucy, together with Ardipithecus and Homo erectus. The lower valley was inscribed on UNESCO's World Heritage List in 1980 for its palaeontological and anthropological importance.

In the 16th century the river was called the great Dir river and lay in the country of the Muslims. The valley from about 9° N downstream is the traditional home of the Afar people and the Issa Somali clan, and it has been counted as part of the historic regions of Fatagar, Ifat and Shewa. The first European to follow the river to its end, in the oasis of Aussa and Lake Abbe, was Wilfred Thesiger in 1933 and 1934.

The Koka Dam, completed across the river in 1960 about 75 kilometres from Addis Ababa, provides hydroelectric power and created Lake Gelila, also called the Koka Reservoir, which covers about 180 square kilometres. The river and its tributaries supply water to Addis Ababa and other towns and to irrigated farmland, including sugar-cane plantations. The lower valley is one of the last refuges of the African wild ass.
awjila: Awjila is an oasis town in the Al Wahat District of Cyrenaica in northeastern Libya. Since classical times it has been known for high-quality dates. With the adjoining oasis of Jalu it is isolated, the only towns on the desert highway between Ajdabiya, 250 kilometres to the northwest, and Kufra, 625 kilometres to the southeast.

An account of 1872 describes three oases, Awjila, Jalu to the east and Jikharra to the northeast, each with a small hill covered in date palms rising from a plain of red sand impregnated with salts of soda, and together holding 9,000 to 10,000 people. The people cultivate small gardens with water from deep wells. They are mainly Berber, and some still speak a language of Berber origin, the Awjila language.

Herodotus describes the nomadic Nasamones, who moved between the coasts of the Gulf of Sirte and the oasis of Augila, where they may have exacted tribute. In summer they left their flocks by the coast and went to the oasis to gather dates. Other people lived there permanently. Strabo notes that it resembled the oasis of Ammon in its palms and water. Procopius, writing around 562, reports that sacrifices to Ammon and to Alexander the Great continued in two Libyan cities called Augila, and that Justinian I turned the oasis's temples into churches.

The Arabs took Cyrenaica in 644, and the region around Awjila was conquered by Sidi Abdullah ibn Sa'ad ibn Abi as-Sarh, a companion of Muhammad, whose tomb was established there around 650. The chronicler Al-Bakri records several mosques by the 11th century. By the 10th century Awjila lay on the route between the Ibadi Berber capital of Zuwayla in the Fezzan and Cairo. In the early Mamluk era the route from Egypt ran through Awjila to the Fezzan and on to Kanem, Bornu and Timbuktu, and Awjila became the main market for slaves from those lands.

In 1639 it came under the Turkish ruler of Tripolitania. In the 18th century its merchants held a monopoly of the trade between Cairo and the Fezzan. From about 1809 a new route from Wadai through Kufra, Awjila and Jalu to Benghazi bypassed the Fezzan and Darfur. Muhammad ibn Ali as-Senussi stayed in Jalu and Awjila before opening his first lodge at al-Baida in 1843, and a Senussi centre was established at Awjila in 1872.

The Great Mosque of Atiq at Awjila is described as the oldest mosque in the Sahara, in a style whose rooms stay cool in summer heat and warm at night. The oasis remains known for its dates, which come from many varieties of palm, and for its tomatoes and cereals. From the 1960s the oil industry drove the growth of the once sleepy village.
axayacatl: Axayacatl, whose name means face of water in Classical Nahuatl, was born around 1449. He was a son of the princess Atotoztli II and her cousin, the prince Tezozomoc, and a grandson of the emperors Moctezuma I and Itzcoatl. His brothers were the later rulers Tizoc and Ahuitzotl, and he was the father of Moctezuma II and Cuitláhuac and an uncle of Cuauhtémoc. In his youth his military ability won him the favour of influential figures such as Nezahualcoyotl and Tlacaelel I.

On the death of Moctezuma I in 1469 Axayacatl was chosen to take the throne, to the displeasure of his two older brothers, Tizoc and Ahuitzotl. He ruled for twelve years and spent most of them consolidating his reputation as a warrior. The Great Sun Stone, also known as the Aztec Calendar, was carved under his leadership, and an earthquake in Tenochtitlan destroyed many homes during his reign.

In 1473, using the insulting behaviour of a few citizens of Tlatelolco as a pretext, he invaded the neighbouring city, killed its ruler Moquihuix and replaced him with a military governor. The Tlatelolcans lost any voice they had in forming Aztec policy. In 1474 he led a successful campaign against the Matlatzinca of the Toluca Valley.
He was then defeated by the Tarascans of Michoacan, the only major defeat the Aztecs had suffered up to that time. Despite some minor later successes, the defeat permanently damaged his image.

Although still young, Axayacatl fell gravely ill in 1480 and died a year later, in 1481. His brother Tizoc succeeded him. Axayacatl is also remembered as a poet who wrote two poems. The first, the Song of Axayacatl, is a defence against his brothers and critics. The second, the Song of the Ancients, is a lament written after his defeat in Michoacan.
axel-oxenstierna: Axel Gustafsson Oxenstierna was born on 16 June 1583 at Fånö in Uppland, the oldest of nine siblings. His parents, Gustaf Gabrielsson Oxenstierna and Barbro Axelsdotter Bielke, belonged to two ancient high noble families that had held high offices in the state and church for generations. He and his brothers studied at the universities of Rostock, Wittenberg and Jena, and on returning in 1603 he became a valet de chambre to King Charles IX of Sweden.

Oxenstierna undertook his first diplomatic mission in 1606 and joined the Privy Council during it. When Charles IX died in autumn 1611, the estates set aside the rules on age so that the 17-year-old Gustavus Adolphus could rule, and in return the king agreed to appoint Oxenstierna Lord High Chancellor, which he became on 6 January 1612. As principal Swedish plenipotentiary he negotiated the Treaty of Knäred with Denmark in 1613. From 7 October 1626 he was Governor-General of Prussia, governing from Elbląg.

After the death of Gustavus Adolphus at Lützen on 6 November 1632, the Swedish council commissioned him on 12 January 1633 as plenipotentiary legate in the Holy Roman Empire. He moved his headquarters to Mainz, headed the regency council for the six-year-old Christina, wrote the Instrument of Government of 1634, and argued that Sweden should stay in the war after the defeat at Nördlingen. He returned to Stockholm in 1636.

In 1643 the Privy Council decided to attack Denmark, a war that was largely Oxenstierna's work. It ended with the Treaty of Brömsebro, by which Sweden gained Gotland, Saaremaa, Jämtland, Härjedalen and, for thirty years, Halland. He blamed Queen Christina's interference for the modest Swedish gains at the Peace of Westphalia. At first he opposed her wish to abdicate, but he later helped her, and he died in Stockholm on 28 August 1654, two months after the accession of Charles X Gustav.

Oxenstierna is remembered for a uniform administrative system, and the boundaries of Sweden's administrative counties still largely follow those he set in the 17th century. He worked to open higher education to boys outside the noble families, which has led to his description as the father of Swedish meritocracy.
axis-powers: The Italian prime minister Benito Mussolini first applied the word axis to the Italo-German relationship in September 1923, writing that the axis of European history was passing through Berlin; he was then seeking an alliance with the Weimar Republic against Yugoslavia and France. After negotiations between Galeazzo Ciano and Ulrich von Hassell, Ciano and Konstantin von Neurath signed a Nine-Point Protocol in 1936, and on 1 November Mussolini announced a Rome-Berlin axis.

The Anti-Comintern Pact, an anti-communist treaty between Germany and Japan, was ratified in November 1936. Italy joined it in 1937, followed by Hungary and Spain in 1939. The Rome-Berlin Axis became a military alliance under the Pact of Steel, and the Tripartite Pact of 1940 formally integrated the military aims of Germany, Italy and Japan.

Six other countries signed the Tripartite Pact. Hungary was the first, on 20 November 1940, under Regent Miklós Horthy. Slovakia, Bulgaria, the Independent State of Croatia and Romania also took part in Axis military operations, while Yugoslavia's signatory government was overthrown in a coup days after it signed, and the membership was reversed. Japan set up puppet governments in occupied China, merged on 29 March 1940 into the Reorganized National Government at Nanjing under Wang Jingwei, which had no real power. A State of Burma was formed on 1 August 1943 under Ba Maw.

When Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on 7 December 1941, the Tripartite Pact required Germany and Italy to help only if Japan were attacked, yet Hitler ordered the Reichstag to declare war on the United States, and Italy also declared war. Ian Kershaw suggests this was a serious blunder, since it let the United States join the war in Europe and North Africa without limitation. At its zenith in 1942 the Axis presided over large parts of Europe, North Africa and East Asia, through occupation, annexation or puppet states. It ended with its defeat in 1945.

The Axis's primary goal was territorial expansion at the expense of neighbours, and it championed variants of fascism, militarism, conservatism and autarky. Unlike the Allies, there were no three-way summit meetings, cooperation was minimal, and at times the interests of the major powers were at variance. The Axis population in 1938 was 258.9 million, against 689.7 million for the Allies excluding the Soviet Union and the United States. Italy and Japan lacked industrial capacity, and their mobilisation remained low even by 1943.
ayacucho: Ayacucho lies in the south-central highlands of the Andes, in the valleys of the Huatatas and Chacco rivers. It is the capital of Huamanga Province and of the Ayacucho Region. Its older name, Huamanga, goes back to pre-Hispanic times, and its etymology is obscure. The linguist Rodolfo Cerrón-Palomino derives it from a colonial Quechua verb meaning to inaugurate or to come into the light. The name Ayacucho comes from Quechua aya, dead person, and kuchu, corner, and was a common place name in the Andes during the colonial period.

Traces of settlement more than 15,000 years old have been found at Pikimachay, about 25 km to the north. The Wari state, which came out of the interaction of the Huarpa and Nasca cultures, came to rule most of the highlands and coast of Peru from a centre near the present city, and was the dominant culture of the Andes before the Inca. After its collapse, cities were left and people dispersed into rural hamlets. Colonial chroniclers record a Chanca confederacy, which the Inca defeated.

Francisco Pizarro founded the Spanish city on 25 April 1540 as San Juan de la Frontera de Huamanga, a stronghold against the attacks of Manco Inca. A royal decree of 17 May 1544 titled it the most noble and loyal city. The city was an administrative centre and a stopping place between Lima and Cuzco, and a university was founded there in 1677.

General Juan Antonio Álvarez de Arenales declared independence in Huamanga on 1 November 1820. The Battle of Ayacucho on 9 December 1824, on the pampas of La Quinua nearby, was the last major clash of the Peruvian War of Independence, and the army led by Antonio José de Sucre won it. Simón Bolívar renamed the city Ayacucho by decree on 15 February 1825. In 1980 the Shining Path began its campaign in the region, and attacked the Ayacucho prison in 1982; its leader Abimael Guzmán was captured in 1992.

Ayacucho is known as the City of Churches for its 33 colonial churches and for mansions with balconies in the style of Spanish cities, and its Holy Week processions blend European and Andean traditions. The city is regarded as a capital of Peruvian popular art, with altarpieces, carvings in local alabaster known as Huamanga stone, and filigree work, and it has belonged to the UNESCO Creative Cities Network since 2019. Its music includes the yaraví and the huayno, and many songs are sung in Quechua.
aybak: Izz al-Din Aybak, the first of the Mamluk sultans of Egypt in the Turkic Bahri line, was an emir of Turkic origin who served in the court of the Ayyubid sultan as-Salih Ayyub with other Turkmens, and so was known among the Bahri Mamluks as Aybak al-Turkmani. His name means moon commander. He rose to emir and worked as a jashnkir, the sultan's taster and cupbearer, and held the rank of khawanja, the sultan's accountant.

After as-Salih died during the Frankish invasion of Damietta in 1249 and his son Turanshah was murdered in 1250, the widow Shajar al-Durr seized the throne with the help of her husband's Mamluks. The Ayyubids of Syria and the Abbasid caliph al-Musta'sim at Baghdad refused to recognise a sultana, and she appointed Aybak atabeg, commander in chief.

When the Syrian emirs refused homage and gave Damascus to an-Nasir Yusuf of Aleppo, Shajar al-Durr married Aybak and abdicated, after ruling for 80 days from 2 May 1250. From the end of July 1250 Aybak was sultan with the royal name al-Malik al-Muizz. To satisfy opponents in Syria and Baghdad, the Bahri Mamluks also installed al-Ashraf Musa, a six-year-old Ayyubid, as co-sultan, though real power stayed with Aybak. In October 1250 his emir Faris ad-Din Aktai defeated an-Nasir Yusuf's force at Gaza, and Aybak's army beat him near Al-Salihiyya. Through the caliph's mediation Aybak freed the Ayyubid prisoners and gained control of southern Palestine.

Aktai crushed a rebellion in Upper and Middle Egypt in 1253, but his growing power alarmed Aybak, who in 1254, with Qutuz and a few Mamluks, had him murdered in the citadel. The Bahriyya, among them Baibars al-Bunduqdari and Qalawun al-Alfi, fled to Damascus, al-Karak and the Seljuk Sultanate of Rum, and Aybak seized their property and deposed al-Ashraf Musa. In 1257 he decided to marry the daughter of Badr ad-Din Lu'lu', the emir of Mosul, seeking an ally against the exiled Mamluks. Shajar al-Durr felt betrayed and had him murdered after seven years of rule. He was about 60.

Aybak's 11-year-old son Ali was installed by the Mu'iziyya Mamluks under Qutuz as al-Malik al-Mansur Nour ad-Din Ali. The Egyptians neither liked nor respected Aybak, though historians remembered him as courageous and generous, and he built the Madrasah al-Mu'izzyah in Cairo. He ruled when Crusaders and Louis IX of France waited at Acre and the Mongols under Hulagu began to raid the eastern Islamic world. Before their deaths he and Shajar al-Durr firmly established the Mamluk Sultanate, which would repulse the Mongols, expel the Crusaders from the Holy Land and remain the most powerful political force in the Middle East until the Ottomans.
ayllu: Ayllu is a word of both the Quechua and Aymara languages. An ayllu is essentially an extended family or kin group with a defined territory, though it can include members who are not related. Its main purpose has been to meet the needs of subsistence and to settle how its families live together and with the wider community. Membership gave each family more variety and security in the land it farmed. Ayllu solidarity combines ties of kinship and territory with shared symbols, and the term also covers the people who live in a territory and feed its earth shrines.

How the ancient ayllu relates to the present one is unclear, because the Spanish chronicles never define the term precisely. In Inca cosmogony the ayllus descended from the stars, and as each star had its place in the sky, each ayllu had a place on earth defined by its paqarina, the mythical point where its lineage huaca emerged. An ayllu often had its own wak'a, a minor god usually embodied in a mountain or rock, and ayllus were named after a particular person or place. They educated their own children and owned their own parcel of land.

A married woman generally joined her husband's ayllu, as did her children, but she inherited land from her parents and kept her membership in the ayllu of her birth; most movement between ayllus came about in this way. A person could also join by taking on the duties of membership. The male head of an ayllu is called a mallku, literally condor, a title that can be freely translated as prince.

Ayllus continue to serve as a model of local Indigenous government across the Andes, as in the Andean community of Ocra. In Bolivia the ayllus send representatives to the National Council of Ayllus and Markas of Qullasuyu, Conamaq, which chooses an Apu Mallku as its head. The community labour of mink'a is known in Spanish as faena.
ayrshire: Ayrshire lies on the shores of the Firth of Clyde and is roughly crescent-shaped, a mostly flat county with areas of low hills that forms part of the Southern Uplands. The north holds the main towns and most of the population. In the south some rugged hill country, the Galloway Hills, runs from the Loch Doon area almost to the Solway Firth. The county is among the most agriculturally fertile regions of Scotland: potatoes are grown near the coast with seaweed fertiliser, and the region also produces pork, cattle and summer berries. Its small islands in the Firth of Clyde include Horse Isle, Lady Isle and Ailsa Craig.

The area was part of the land south of the Antonine Wall that the Romans briefly occupied under Antoninus Pius. It was inhabited by the Damnonii, who are presumed to have been Britons, and later formed part of the British Kingdom of Strathclyde, which was incorporated into the Kingdom of Scotland during the 11th century. In 1263 the Scots drove off a Norwegian army in a skirmish known as the Battle of Largs. Turnberry Castle, which dates from the 13th century or earlier, may have been the birthplace of Robert the Bruce.

The historic shire of Ayr was divided into Carrick, Kyle and Cunninghame. King's Kyle, the triangle between the Ayr and the Doon, is the birthplace and youthful home of Robert Burns. The area was long heavily industrialised, with steel making, coal mining and, in Kilmarnock, factory production, most notably of Johnnie Walker whisky. In the 17th century many people moved from Ayrshire to Ulster in the Plantation of Ulster, and the Ulster Scots dialect is largely an offshoot of the Lowland Scots spoken in Ayrshire.

Commissioners of Supply were created for each shire in 1667, and county councils followed in 1890. The county council was abolished in 1975 and its functions passed to Strathclyde Regional Council. Since 1996 Ayrshire has been divided between the council areas of East Ayrshire, North Ayrshire and South Ayrshire, though the historic boundaries are still used for land registration.
ayub-khan: Mohammad Ayub Khan was born on 14 May 1907 in Rehana, a village in the Haripur district of the North-West Frontier Province of British India, into a Hindko-speaking family of Pashtun descent. His father was a Risaldar-Major in the 9th Hodson's Horse, a cavalry regiment of the British Indian Army. Ayub entered the Royal Military College, Sandhurst, in 1926 and was commissioned a second lieutenant on 2 February 1928. He fought in the Second World War on the British side against the Imperial Japanese Army.

At the Partition of British India in 1947 he was among the most senior officers who opted for Pakistan. In 1951 he became the first native commander-in-chief of the Pakistan Army, succeeding General Gracey, and in October 1954 he entered the cabinet as defence minister.

On 7 October 1958 President Iskander Mirza abrogated the 1956 constitution and appointed Ayub Chief Martial Law Administrator. Three weeks later Ayub seized the presidency in a military coup, the first in the country's history. His foreign policy prioritised relations with the United States and Europe. He launched Operation Gibraltar against India in 1965, which led to an all-out war that ended in a stalemate and the Tashkent Declaration. In the 1965 presidential election he defeated Fatima Jinnah, in a contest that critics allege was rigged. Food price rises prompted demonstrations in 1967, and after protests in East Pakistan Ayub resigned on 25 March 1969, appointing General Yahya Khan as his successor.

Ayub Khan died of a heart attack on 19 April 1974 at his villa near Islamabad, aged 66. His administration moved the federal capital from Karachi to Islamabad in 1965, became party to the Indus Waters Treaty with India, and built irrigation canals, dams and power stations. In the decade of his rule the gross national product rose by 45%. Economists on the Planning Commission alleged that his policies rewarded elite families and major landowners, and in 1968, while his government marked a Decade of Development, mass protests broke out over the widening gap between rich and poor.

Critics blame him for not doing enough about the economic disparity between East and West Pakistan, and his centralised regime left East Pakistan feeling slighted, differences that ultimately led to the independence of Bangladesh.
ayurbarwada-buyantu-khan: Ayurbarwada was the second son of Darmabala and Dagi of the Khunggirat and a great-grandson of Kublai Khan. His name comes from a Sanskrit compound meaning the mountain of longevity. From his early teens he was tutored by the Confucian scholar Li Meng, who strongly shaped his political outlook. He could read and write Chinese and knew Chinese painting, calligraphy and history.

In 1305 Bulugan Khatun sent him away from court to Honan as prince of Huai-ning. When his uncle Temür Khan died without an heir on 2 February 1307, Bulugan tried to set up Ananda, governor of Ningxia. The chancellor Harghasun recalled Ayurbarwada and Li Meng to the capital Dadu, and together they imprisoned Ananda and Bulugan. Ayurbarwada then welcomed his elder brother Khayishan to the throne and was named Crown Prince in June 1307, the brothers promising that their descendants would rule in turn.

Khayishan died in January 1311, and Ayurbarwada succeeded him in April in a peaceful transition. He at once reversed his brother's policies: he disbanded the Department of State Affairs, which led to the execution of five high officials, abolished the Zhida paper notes and coins, trimmed the bureaucracy to its 1293 level and halted Khayishan's building projects. Mongols and Semuren, people from Central Asia and the west, were appointed beside Chinese advisers such as Li Meng.

His best-known reform was the examination system, based on Neo-Confucianism, with race-based quotas for Mongol and Han candidates; in 1315, for instance, 300 appointments went to the court, with an extra quarter reserved for non-Han people. He also had the laws gathered into a code, completed in 1316 and promulgated under his son as the Da Yuan Tong Zhi, and authorised translations of Chinese classics. A land survey in 1314 was carried out by corrupt officials, and a revolt broke out in Jiangxi in the autumn of 1315 and forced its abandonment.

He died on 1 March 1320. In 1316 he had made his own son Shidibala Crown Prince, breaking the promise to Khayishan's line. After Shidibala's assassination in 1323 none of his descendants ruled the empire, and the court saw two decades of turmoil in which the Khunggirat faction under Temuder and Dagi grew more powerful.
ayushiridara: Ayushiridara was the eldest son of Toghon Temür and Lady Gi, who came from a lower-ranked aristocratic family of Goryeo and had been a palace maid. Many Mongol noyans preferred another heir, and only after the purge of the family of Empress Danashiri and the death of Bayan were mother and son accepted at court. He began learning Chinese at ten in the house of the minister Toqto'a. In 1354 Ayushiridara, Lady Gi and the minister Hama accused Toqto'a of corruption while he was fighting the Red Turban Rebellion, and Toqto'a was exiled.

As crown prince from 1353 he drew the court into faction. With his mother he forced the first minister Tai ping to resign, and when the opposition leader Bolad-Temür occupied the capital in 1364 he fled to the general Köke Temür. After Bolad-Temür was murdered on the emperor's secret order, Ayushiridara pressed for his father's abdication, but the emperor only made him his lieutenant. In 1368 the Ming overthrew the Yuan and the court fled from Dadu to Shangdu. When Toghon Temür died at Yingchang in 1370, the Ming took the city, capturing Ayushiridara's son Maidarbal, and Ayushiridara escaped to Karakorum.

Enthroned as Biligtü, the Intelligent, he took the era name Xuanguang and made Köke Temür his commander in chief. In 1372 the Hongwu Emperor sent 150,000 men into Mongolia. The central division under Xu Da reached the Tuul River and was routed, the eastern division was beaten on the Kherlen and the Orkhon and near Karakorum, and the western one withdrew. Biligtü Khan asked King Gongmin of Goryeo for help, calling him a fellow descendant of Genghis Khan, but Gongmin refused. In 1375 the Mongol official Naghachu invaded the Liaodong Peninsula, and Köke Temür died that year. Biligtü Khan died in 1378 and his half-brother Tögüs Temür succeeded him.
ayutthaya-kingdom: Ayutthaya emerged in the late 13th and 14th centuries from a mandala of four port city-states of the lower Chao Phraya valley, Ayodhya, Lavo, Phrip Phri and Suphannaphum. In one scholar's account the merging polities were Lopburi, Suphanburi, Ayodhya and Phetchaburi, each of which had sent its own missions to China. Uthong V held Phetchaburi and Ayodhya by descent and gained Suphannabhum and Lavo through marriage, and 4 March 1351 is conventionally given as the foundation of the kingdom. Persian merchants knew the new centre as shahr-i naw, the new city. The name Ayutthaya comes from the Sanskrit Ayodhya, by way of the Ramakien.

The early kingdom was a maritime confederation, closer to the Malay trading polities than to inland states such as Sukhothai. It sent forces down the peninsula and drew tribute from the Malay principalities as far as Temasek and Sumatra. Its early chronology is probably fabricated by later elites, since early Ayutthaya kept no records. The 1430s to 1600 were an age of rising warfare, in which Ayutthaya fought for Tavoy, Mergui, Tenasserim and Martaban. From 1569 to 1584 it was a vassal of Toungoo Burma, then regained independence.

After the Portuguese and Dutch conquest of Malacca, Asian traders used portage routes across the peninsula that Ayutthaya controlled, and it became an intermediary between the great empires of the early modern world. Under Narai (r. 1657–1688) Persian and then European influence was strong, and an embassy went to Louis XIV in 1686.

Chinese trade kept the economy lively after the French and English left in 1688. Failure to settle the succession and the arrival of capitalism weakened the elite and the labour control on which its army and administration rested. The Konbaung dynasty of Burma invaded in 1759–1760 and 1765–1767. After a 14-month siege the city fell and was destroyed in April 1767, ending the 417-year-old kingdom. Within fifteen years the seat of authority had moved to Thonburi and Bangkok.

Ayutthaya followed the mandala system, in which the capital's control weakened with distance, and provincial governors were never fully brought to heel. The reforms of Borommatrailokkanat (r. 1448–1488) placed the king at the centre of a stratified hierarchy, and the king was regarded as the incarnation of Shiva or Vishnu. Ramathibodi II (r. 1491–1529) required every freeman to register as a phrai under a lord, owing corvée labour and military service. The state ran on a small service nobility, with the rest of the population serfs. The main religion was Theravada Buddhism, with Hindu rituals conducted by Brahmin priests. The court developed the classical dramatic forms khon and lakhon from the Ramakien.
ayyubid-empire: The Ayyubids were a Sunni Muslim dynasty of Kurdish origin, and medieval sources often called their state the Kurdish state. The progenitor, Najm ad-Din Ayyub ibn Shadhi, belonged to the Kurdish Rawadiya, a branch of the Hadhbani tribe. Later family members sponsored genealogies tracing a noble Arab descent, which are generally regarded as politically motivated. Saladin first served the Zengid ruler Nur al-Din, whose army he led against the Crusaders in Fatimid Egypt, where he was made vizier.

After Nur al-Din died in 1174, the Abbasid Caliphate proclaimed Saladin the first Sultan of Egypt, and he extended the sultanate over most of Syria, the Hejaz, Yemen, northern Nubia, Tripolitania and Upper Mesopotamia. After Saladin died in 1193 his sons contested the sultanate, and his brother al-Adil became sultan in 1200; all later sultans of Egypt descended from him.

In the 1230s the emirs of Syria tried to assert independence, and Sultan as-Salih Ayyub restored unity by 1247, except for Aleppo, though local dynasties had driven the Ayyubids from Yemen, the Hejaz and parts of Mesopotamia. In 1260 the Mongols sacked Aleppo and soon conquered the remaining Ayyubid lands. The Mamluks, who expelled the Mongols, kept the Ayyubid principality of Hama until they deposed its last ruler in 1341.

Saladin did not build a centralised empire. He gave his lands to kinsmen as semi-autonomous principalities under a family sultan. In Syria each major city was a relatively independent principality, while in Egypt the Ayyubids governed from Cairo. His army drew mainly on Kurdish and Turkic troops, with Kurds one third of it. The seat of government was Damascus from the 1170s to 1218.

The Ayyubids encouraged sugarcane and dug canals, and they traded with European states despite the war with the Crusaders. They built madrasas across the empire to strengthen Sunni Islam, and Ibn Shaddad counted 40 Shafi'i, 34 Hanafi, 10 Hanbali and three Maliki schools in Damascus in the mid-13th century. Saladin enclosed Cairo and al-Fustat within one city wall.
az-zahir-ghazi: Al-Malik az-Zahir Ghiyath ud-din Ghazi was the third son of Saladin. In 1186, when he was 15, his father appointed him governor of Aleppo, Mosul and the neighbouring areas recently taken from the Zengids, lands that had been under the control of Saladin's brother al-Adil. His two older brothers received Syria (al-Afdal) and Egypt (al-Aziz) at the same time. When he inherited in 1193 he was to owe suzerainty to al-Afdal in Damascus, but he conducted his affairs independently and for a while stayed out of his brothers' quarrels with their uncle.

In 1193 he called on al-Adil for troops to put down the revolt of the Zengid Izz al-Din in Mosul. The next year he received Latakia and Jableh in a settlement by which he recognised al-Afdal's authority, but in 1196 he joined al-Aziz and al-Adil in deposing and exiling that brother. In October 1197, with Bohemond III of Antioch threatening Latakia and Jableh, he destroyed the two ports; Bohemond took them, found them of no use and withdrew, and az-Zahir reoccupied them and rebuilt the fortress at Latakia. He kept many of his father's advisers and appointed Baha ad-Din as a judge in Aleppo.

After al-Aziz died in 1198, az-Zahir allied with al-Afdal, and with most of the other Ayyubid princes they besieged Damascus. The city held out for months, and he withdrew his troops. Al-Adil, having conquered Egypt, returned, reduced az-Zahir's territories to the area around Aleppo and forced him to recognise his suzerainty. In his last decade az-Zahir skirmished with crusaders and lent his army to other Ayyubid princes. King Leo of Cilicia defeated his forces at the Battle of Amq in 1206 but gained no lasting advantage against Aleppo, and in 1207 his troops lifted a siege of Homs.

In 1212 az-Zahir married Dayfa Khatun, the daughter of his old rival al-Adil, a match that ended the rivalry between the two branches of the family. Before his death he appointed his younger son al-Aziz Muhammad, born in 1213, to succeed him. He died on 8 October 1216. His lands had included northern Syria and a small part of Mesopotamia.
azad-kashmir: Azad Jammu and Kashmir covers 13,297 square kilometres in the western part of the larger Kashmir region. Its northern part lies in the lower Himalayas, with Jamgarh Peak at 4,734 metres and Sarwali Peak in the Neelum Valley, at 6,326 metres, the highest in the territory. The region receives rain in both winter and summer, and Muzaffarabad and Pattan are among the wettest places in Pakistan. Monsoon floods of the Jhelum and Leepa rivers are common. The southern districts of Bhimber, Mirpur and Kotli are extremely hot in summer. The north lies where the Indian plate underthrusts the Eurasian plate, and an earthquake in 2005 killed at least 100,000 people and displaced another three million.

The name comes from Azad Kashmir, "Free Kashmir", the title of a pamphlet issued in 1945 by the Muslim Conference at its 13th general session in Poonch. It is believed to have answered the National Conference's Naya Kashmir programme and to have declared that the Muslims of Jammu and Kashmir backed the Muslim League's struggle for Pakistan. The following year the party passed an Azad Kashmir resolution asking the maharaja for an elected constituent assembly; on the scholar Chitralekha Zutshi's account its aim was responsible government under the maharaja, tied to neither India nor Pakistan. On 19 July 1947 party workers meeting at the house of Sardar Ibrahim reversed this and demanded that the maharaja accede to Pakistan.

At the Partition of India in 1947 the British gave up their suzerainty over the princely states, which could join India or Pakistan or remain independent. The maharaja, Hari Singh, wanted independence, while Muslims in the western districts of Jammu province, which are now Azad Kashmir, wanted to join Pakistan. Since the ceasefire of 1949 Pakistan has exercised control over the territory without incorporating it.

Muzaffarabad is the capital. The territory has a parliamentary system modelled on the British Westminster system, with its own president, prime minister, legislative assembly, high court, supreme court and flag, though it is not represented in the Parliament of Pakistan. It is divided into three divisions and ten districts. Its people are almost entirely Muslim. Urdu is the official language, but most people speak Pahari-Pothwari, a dialect of Punjabi, with communities speaking Kashmiri, Gujari and Dogri. The Gujjars are estimated to be the largest community. Mirpur, Kotli and Bhimber are old towns of the Jammu region.
azai-nagamasa: Azai Nagamasa was the son of Azai Hisamasa, head of the Azai clan, whose seat was Odani Castle in northern Ōmi Province. Many of Hisamasa's retainers compelled him to step down in favour of his son, and Nagamasa took over the leadership of the clan in 1560. Between 1560 and 1565 he fought both Rokkaku Yoshikata and Saitō Tatsuoki with success, and he is remembered as a capable commander of troops in the field.

In 1564 he married Oichi, the sister of Oda Nobunaga. Nobunaga wanted peace with the Azai because their lands lay between the Oda domains and the capital, Kyoto. Oichi bore him three daughters, Chacha, later known as Yodo-dono, Hatsu and Oeyo, who all became prominent figures in their own right.

In 1570 Nobunaga declared war on the Asakura family of Echizen and besieged Kanegasaki castle. The Asakura had been allies of the Azai since the time of Nagamasa's grandfather, and the war is reported to have divided the clan: many retainers wished to honour the alliance, while Nagamasa himself is reported to have favoured neutrality. The clan chose to aid the Asakura, and Nobunaga's army at first fell back to Kyoto.

Within a few months Nobunaga and Tokugawa Ieyasu marched into northern Ōmi with an army estimated at 20,000 to 30,000 men. At the Battle of Anegawa the Azai and Asakura, between 15,000 and 20,000 strong, were forced back when part of the Tokugawa force struck the Azai flank, though the battle proved strategically indecisive. Over the next two years Nagamasa stood loosely aligned with the Asakura, the Miyoshi, the Rokkaku and several religious complexes against Nobunaga, who repeatedly besieged Odani.

In July 1573 Nobunaga laid siege to Odani Castle again. He defeated an Asakura relief force and destroyed that clan before returning to the siege. With no hope of winning, Nagamasa committed seppuku, having first entrusted Oichi and their daughters to Nobunaga; his father Hisamasa also took his own life. His infant son and heir, Manpukumaru, was later found and executed on Nobunaga's orders by Hideyoshi. A story that Nobunaga had the skulls of Nagamasa, Hisamasa and the Asakura leader lacquered as cups is of debated accuracy. His daughter Chacha married Toyotomi Hideyoshi, and Oeyo married the shōgun Tokugawa Hidetada.
azarmidokht: Azarmidokht was a daughter of the Sasanian shah Khosrow II, who was overthrown and executed on 28 February 628 by his son Kavad II. Kavad had all his brothers and half-brothers executed, including the heir Mardanshah; Azarmidokht and her sister Boran reportedly scolded him for it, and he became remorseful. The fall of Khosrow led to a civil war of four years, in which the most powerful nobles gained autonomy and the Persian (Parsig) and Parthian (Pahlav) noble families resumed their hostilities.

A plague swept the western provinces and killed half their population, Kavad among them. His young son Ardashir III was killed two years later by the general Shahrbaraz, who was murdered forty-three days later in a coup by the Pahlav leader Farrukh Hormizd, who helped Boran take the throne. Boran was deposed and replaced by her cousin Shapur-i Shahrvaraz, who was deposed in under a year by the Parsig faction led by Piruz Khosrow, who helped Azarmidokht ascend the throne.

On becoming queen, Azarmidokht stated that the country would be run as it had been under her father. Farrukh Hormizd asked her to marry him, to strengthen his authority and create a modus vivendi between the Pahlav and the Parsig; she declined. He then declared himself leader of the people and began to mint coins as a monarch would, at Istakhr and Nahavand. Azarmidokht supposedly allied herself with the Mihranid Siyavakhsh, grandson of Bahram Chobin, and with his help had Farrukh Hormizd killed.

Her coins followed the style of her father's: his portrait with the winged crown of Verethragna on the obverse, with the inscription khwarrah abzūd, increase in glory, and two attendants at a fire altar on the reverse. The portrait is read as a claim to legitimacy through Khosrow II, regarded as the last rightful king of Iran, and not as a response to her gender.

Farrukh Hormizd's son Rostam Farrokhzad, stationed in Khorasan, succeeded him as leader of the Pahlav. To avenge his father he marched on Ctesiphon, defeating every army of Azarmidokht that he met, then defeated Siyavakhsh and captured the capital. Azarmidokht was soon afterwards blinded and killed by Rostam, who restored Boran. The centre of power possibly drifted to the northeast, the Pahlav homeland, where Yazdegerd III later fled to seek aid against the Arab invasion. Islamic accounts depict Azarmidokht as beautiful and intelligent, attribute to her the building of a castle at Asadabad, and give her the title the Just.
azaz: Azaz lies in north-west Syria, roughly 32 kilometres north-north-west of Aleppo, near the border crossing into Turkey at Öncüpınar, south of Kilis. In ancient times it was known in Hurrian as Azazuwa, in Old Aramaic as Ḥzz, in Neo-Assyrian as Ḫazazu and in Medieval Greek as Azázion. Crusader sources call it Hazart.

Its topography and its position overlooking the surrounding region gave it strategic importance in the Crusader era. In Muslim hands it blocked communications between the Crusader states of Edessa and Antioch, and in Crusader hands it threatened the major Muslim city of Aleppo.

Excavations at Tell Azaz have yielded large quantities of ceramics from the early and middle Islamic periods, though the settlement is rarely mentioned in Islamic texts before the 12th century. The musician Ishaq al-Mawsili (767 to 850) visited it under Abbasid rule, and the Hamdanids of Aleppo built a brick citadel on the tell. On 10 August 1030 the Mirdasids defeated the Byzantine emperor Romanos III at nearby Tubbal. In December of that year the Byzantine generals Niketas of Mistheia and Symeon besieged and captured Azaz and burned Tubbal.

Around December 1118 Roger of Antioch and the Armenian prince Leo I took Azaz from the Turcoman prince Ilghazi of Mardin. In April 1125 Aqsunqur al-Bursuqi of Mosul and Toghtekin invaded the Principality of Antioch and surrounded the town. A Crusader coalition of 3,000 under King Baldwin II of Jerusalem confronted a Muslim coalition of 15,000 and defeated it at the Battle of Azaz, raising the siege. After the Zengid capture of Edessa in 1144 the fortresses of the County of Edessa were gradually neglected. Humphrey II of Toron sent sixty knights to reinforce Azaz in 1146, but the fortress fell to Nur ad-Din, the Zengid emir of Aleppo, in June 1150.

The Ayyubid emir al-Aziz Uthman rebuilt the Hamdanid structure in stone. Yaqut al-Hamawi called it a fine town in 1226, and it was the centre of a district that included Kafr Latha, Mannagh, Yabrin, Arfad, Tubbal and Innib. The Mamluk Sultanate ruled from the 13th century and the Ottomans entered the area in 1516, after the Battle of Marj Dabiq.

After the Ottoman Empire fell, the new border between Syria and Turkey ran just north of Azaz. The town was part of the French Mandate for Syria and the Lebanon and, from 1946, of independent Syria. The 2004 census gave it a population of 31,623. Rebels captured the town in July 2012 during the Syrian civil war, and from 2016 it lay in an area under Turkish control.
