azcapotzalco: Azcapotzalco lies in the northwestern part of Mexico City, in the Valley of Mexico, with its eastern half on the bed of the former Lake Texcoco and its historic centre on the old shoreline. The name comes from Classical Nahuatl and means the place of the anthills. A legend tells that ants helped the god Quetzalcoatl reach Mictlan, the realm of the dead, to recover the bones of men from the Fourth Sun and bring up grains of corn.

Hunter-gatherers reached the Valley of Mexico about 7,000 years ago, and permanent farming villages formed sometime between 5000 and 2000 BCE, growing corn, squash, chili peppers, avocados and beans. Around 200 BCE the Azcapotzalco area gained importance within the sphere of Teotihuacan, and when that city waned in 800 CE it remained an important ceremonial centre. When Tula rose, Toltec influence dominated the area, and Azcapotzalco was possibly a Toltec tribute city.

The town was the seat of the Tepanec dominion until the Aztec Triple Alliance overthrew it. In the centuries that followed it was a rural farming area. In the mid-nineteenth century it became part of the Federal District of Mexico City, and in the twentieth century the sprawl of the capital engulfed it. A pilgrimage from Azcapotzalco to the Basilica of Our Lady of Guadalupe, the Fiesta de los Naturales, has records of a first journey in 1532.

Azcapotzalco is a borough of Mexico City covering 34.5 square kilometres, fully urbanised and a centre of industry. Its population rose from 534,554 in 1970 to a peak of 601,524 in 1980 and was 441,008 in 2000. The historic centre, marked by Plaza Hidalgo, was designated a historical monument in 1986 and a Barrio Mágico in 2011. Many old neighbourhoods keep their own traditions, and the Azcapotzalco campus of the Universidad Autónoma Metropolitana was established in 1974.
azemmour: Azemmour lies in El Jadida Province, on the left bank of the Oum Er-Rbia River, about 75 kilometres south-west of Casablanca. Its name comes from the Berber word azemmur, which means wild olive tree. The town is generally identified with the Punic Azama, latinised as Asama. Historically it served as the capital of the Bedouin tribe of the Doukkala.

Before 1486 Azemmour was a dependency of the King of Fez. In that year its inhabitants became vassals and tributaries of João II of Portugal. In 1513 the governor, Moulay Zayam, refused to pay the tribute and gathered a large, well-equipped army. King Manuel of Portugal answered by sending a fleet of 500 ships carrying 15 thousand soldiers under Dom James, Duke of Braganza.

He took the city on 1 September without resistance from its inhabitants. Ferdinand Magellan, who later led the first circumnavigation of the earth, was among the Portuguese soldiers and lost his horse in skirmishes outside the city. Portuguese control was short. João III of Portugal abandoned the city in 1541 because of the economic difficulties of his court.

Among the people associated with the town is Estevanico, also called Esteban the Moor. He was enslaved and travelled with a Spanish expedition to North America in 1527. He was one of four men out of several hundred who survived shipwrecks on the Florida and Texas coasts, Native American slavery and attacks, and other setbacks over six years before reaching a Spanish colonial town.

Azemmour has a medina in three parts: a Jewish quarter or mellah, a kasbah and the old medina. Local artists have decorated sections of the Old City walls. The patron saint of the town is Abu Shuayb, whose mausoleum was built on the order of Mohammed ben Abdallah, and a moussem is held each year in his honour. The Sidi Boubeker lighthouse stands 8 kilometres to the north, and the beach at Haouzia, with its eucalyptus and pine, is used for surfing and kitesurfing.
azerbaijan: The name Azerbaijan derives from Atropates, a Persian satrap under the Achaemenid Empire who was reinstated as satrap of Media under Alexander the Great; the Greek name is a transliteration of an Old Iranian, probably Median, name meaning protected by the holy fire or the land of the holy fire. It evolved through Middle Persian Āturpātākān to the present form. The name was first adopted by the government of Musavat in 1918, when the independent Azerbaijan Democratic Republic was established. Until then the name designated the adjacent region of northwestern Iran, while the republic's area had been called Arran and Shirvan, and Iran protested.

The earliest evidence of human settlement dates to the late Stone Age and is related to the Guruchay culture of Azykh Cave. The Scythians settled in the 9th century BCE, and the Iranian Medes came to dominate the area south of the Aras river before it was integrated into the Achaemenid Empire around 550 BCE, which spread Zoroastrianism. The Sasanian Empire turned Caucasian Albania into a vassal state in 252, and King Urnayr adopted Christianity as the state religion in the 4th century.

In the first half of the 7th century Albania came under nominal Muslim rule, and the Umayyad Caliphate made it a vassal state after suppressing Christian resistance led by King Juansher in 667. Oghuz Turks seized the territory from the beginning of the 11th century, and the Seljuk Empire entered the area by 1067; under the Seljuks poets such as Nizami Ganjavi and Khaqani gave rise to a blossoming of Persian literature.

Until the 19th century the region remained part of Qajar Iran. The Russo-Persian wars of 1804–1813 and 1826–1828 forced the Qajar Empire to cede its Caucasian territories to the Russian Empire, and the treaties of Gulistan in 1813 and Turkmenchay in 1828 defined the border between Russia and Iran. An Azerbaijani national identity emerged by the late 19th century. The Azerbaijan Democratic Republic, proclaimed in 1918, became the first secular democratic Muslim-majority state in the world, and in 1920 the country was conquered and incorporated into the Soviet Union.

The modern Republic of Azerbaijan proclaimed its independence on 30 August 1991. The Nagorno-Karabakh region became de facto independent as the Republic of Artsakh with the end of the First Nagorno-Karabakh War in 1994. Azerbaijan is a unitary semi-presidential republic. About 97% of its 10,164,464 people are Muslim, and 94.8% are Azerbaijanis.
azores: The Azores lie in the North Atlantic in three groups spread over more than 600 km: Flores and Corvo to the west; Graciosa, Terceira, São Jorge, Pico and Faial in the centre; and São Miguel, Santa Maria and the Formigas islets to the east. Together the islands cover 2,346 km2, from São Miguel, the largest at 759 km2, to Corvo, the smallest at about 17 km2. Mount Pico, at 2,351 m, is the highest point in Portugal. The archipelago sits over a triple junction where three tectonic plates meet. The climate is mild, wet and often cloudy.

The discovery is poorly documented. A captain sailing for Prince Henry the Navigator, possibly Gonçalo Velho, may have found the islands in 1427, but this is not certain. From 1433 Gonçalo Velho Cabral gathered settlers, and in 1436 he sailed to establish colonies, first on Santa Maria. Many settlers came from Algarve and Alentejo. By 1490 some 2,000 Flemings lived on Terceira, Pico, Faial, São Jorge and Flores, so that the islands became known as the Flemish Islands.

In 1522 an earthquake and landslide devastated Vila Franca do Campo, then the capital of São Miguel, and killed about 5,000 people; the capital moved to Ponta Delgada.  After the death of Cardinal-King Henry in 1580, Philip II of Spain claimed the Portuguese crown, and Spain held the Azores under the Iberian Union from 1580 to 1642. The islands were the last part of the Portuguese Empire to resist him, until the Conquest of the Azores in 1583. In the Portuguese Civil War of 1828–1834 the liberals won at Praia da Vitória in 1829, and Terceira became the headquarters of the new regime.

The Azores are an autonomous region of Portugal, and Ponta Delgada is the largest city. The main industries are agriculture, dairy farming, livestock, fishing and tourism. The culture, dialect, cuisine and traditions vary considerably from island to island, because the remote islands were settled sporadically over about two centuries.
azov: At the start of the 3rd century BCE Greeks from the Bosporan Kingdom founded a colony nearby called Tanais. King Polemon I of Pontus burned it in the last third of the 1st century BCE, and the Goths practically annihilated it in the 3rd century CE. The Kipchaks seized the area in 1067 and renamed it Azaq, meaning lowlands. In the 13th and 14th centuries the Golden Horde claimed most of the coast, but allowed Venetian and Genoese merchants to settle on the site of modern Azov, where they founded a colony called Tana.

In the later 15th century the Ottoman Empire gained control and built the fortress of Azak, which blocked the Don Cossacks from raiding and trading in the Black Sea. In April 1637 three thousand Don Cossacks and four thousand Zaporozhian Cossacks besieged it, and it fell on 21 June. Tsar Mikhail ordered the Cossacks to leave after an ultimatum from Sultan Ibrahim, and the Turks reoccupied Azov in September 1642. Peter the Great, who wanted naval access to the Black Sea, recovered it in 1696, but the Pruth River Campaign forced him to hand it back in 1711. It was finally ceded to Russia by the Treaty of Kuchuk-Kainarji in 1774.

Azov stands on the Don River in Rostov Oblast, only 16 kilometres from the Sea of Azov, which takes its name from the town. The Powder Cellar Museum, built in 1799, is the only remaining fortress of Catherine's time in what was once southern Russia. The Azov Museum of History, Archaeology and Palaeontology, founded in 1917, holds one of the richest palaeontological collections in southern Russia.
aztec-empire: Nahua peoples descended from Chichimec peoples who migrated into central Mexico from the north in the early 13th century. Pictographic codices say their place of origin was Aztlán. The Mexica entered the Valley of Mexico as outsiders with limited resources, and military service was one of the few ways to win protection. They fought as subordinate allies of stronger city-states and allied with Azcapotzalco, paying tribute to its ruler Tezozomoc. Acamapichtli, son of a Mexica leader and a daughter of a king of Culhuacan, was enthroned as the first tlatoani of Tenochtitlan in 1372.

When Tezozomoc died in 1426, a succession crisis became a civil war. His son Maxtla usurped the throne and turned on the Mexica, whose ruler Chimalpopoca died soon after, possibly assassinated. Under Itzcoatl, Tenochtitlan joined Texcoco, whose king Nezahualcoyotl had fled into exile, the dissident Tepanec city of Tlacopan and Huexotzinco in war against Azcapotzalco, and won in 1428. The three cities formed the Triple Alliance.

Itzcoatl and Tlacopan carried out sweeping reforms of state and religion. It has been alleged that Tlacaelel ordered the burning of earlier books and rewrote Aztec history to give the Mexica a more central part. Moctezuma I replaced uncooperative kings with loyal rulers and set up tribute collectors who taxed people directly. Expansion reached the Gulf of Mexico and Oaxaca, and was briefly halted by a four-year drought that began in 1450. Axayacatl spent most of a thirteen-year reign consolidating, and Ahuitzotl, from 1486, put down rebellions and conquered the Oaxaca Valley and the Soconusco coast. He took the title huehuetlatoani to set himself above the rulers of Texcoco and Tlacopan.

Hernán Cortés landed in Yucatán in 1519 with about 630 men. He gained two interpreters, Gerónimo de Aguilar and the Nahua-Maya woman known as La Malinche, who became a key figure in his dealings with Nahua rulers.

The empire ruled indirectly. Local rulers were generally left in place so long as they paid tribute and sent troops, and in return received protection and a share in an integrated economy. At its height the state had 38 tributary provinces, supervised by high stewards called huecalpixque, with a separate official, the petlacalcatl, coordinating tribute at Tenochtitlan. A restive conquered city might receive a military governor, a cuauhtlatoani. Provinces were either tributary, with mandatory obligations, or strategic, client states acting by mutual consent. The empire was not continuous territorially: Xoconochco lay apart from the centre.

Nahua belief centred on teotl, a sacred power manifested in the supreme god Ometeotl and a large pantheon. The imperial cult was that of the Mexica war god Huītzilōpōchtli, whom conquered peoples had to add to their own gods, though they kept their traditions otherwise.
aztlan: Aztlán is the mythical home of the Aztec peoples. The word Aztec comes from the Classical Nahuatl aztecah, meaning people from Aztlán. Several ethnohistorical sources of the colonial period mention it. They list different groups as taking part in the migration to central Mexico, but the Mexica who later founded Mexico-Tenochtitlan appear in all of them. Mexica histories relate that seven tribes lived in Chicomoztoc, the Place of the Seven Caves: the Xochimilca, Tlahuica, Acolhua, Tlaxcalteca, Tepaneca, Chalca and Mexica. The Olmeca-Xicallanca and Xaltocamecas are also said to come from Aztlán. These tribes left the caves and settled near Aztlán.

The descriptions of Aztlán apparently contradict each other. Some legends describe a paradise, while the Codex Aubin says the Aztecs were subject to a tyrannical elite, the Azteca Chicomoztoca, and fled under the guidance of their priest. On the road their god Huitzilopochtli forbade them to call themselves Azteca and told them to be known as Mexica.

In one version a man heard a bird calling, Go now, and the people followed an idol of Huitzilopochtli carried by the priests, travelling until they came to a large lake and saw an eagle on a cactus holding a serpent. There they built Tenochtitlán. Cristobal del Castillo says the lake around the island of Aztlán was called Metztliapan, the Lake of the Moon. The meaning of the name is uncertain, and the Crónica Mexicáyotl's explanation of place of egrets is not possible under Nahuatl morphology.

Historians tend to place Aztlán either in northwestern Mexico or in the Southwestern United States, though whether it was a real or a mythological place is debated. Friar Diego Durán wrote that Moctezuma I sent an expedition to find it and that it located a place with the features of Aztlán, but he could give no precise location. From the 1960s Mexican intellectuals seriously considered Mexcaltitán de Uribe in Nayarit, an idea that Alfredo Chavero had raised late in the 19th century; the hypothesis is still debated. Some scholars argue that the true location cannot be found because of the conflicting accounts.

In 1969 the poet Alurista introduced the notion of Aztlán at the National Chicano Youth Liberation Conference in Denver, in a poem that became the preamble to El Plan Espiritual de Aztlán. For some Chicanos it refers to the Mexican territories the United States won in the Mexican-American War of 1846 to 1848, and many take it as a spiritual guiding force rather than a place.
azzone-visconti: Azzone Visconti was born in Ferrara on 7 December 1302, the sole legitimate son of Galeazzo I Visconti and Beatrice d'Este. In 1322 he was lord of Piacenza, but in the same year he and his father were forced to flee. In 1325 he commanded troops at the battles of Altopascio and Zappolino, both victories over the Guelphs. In 1327 Galeazzo and the other leading members of the family were arrested on suspicion of assassinating Galeazzo's younger brother Stefano. The Emperor confiscated their territories, local families took control of many cities long tied to the Viscontis, and Milan was ruled by a new imperial appointee and a council hostile to them. When Galeazzo died later that year, Visconti power was at a low point.

Azzone at once struggled with his uncle Marco for control of Milan. In 1329, with the support of another uncle, Giovanni, he bought the title of imperial vicar of Milan from the emperor Louis IV for 60,000 florins, or 125,000 by another account, of which he paid only 12,000, the feeble Louis being unable to force payment. Marco was killed the same year and Azzone was named as one of the assassins, but he was never condemned. Pope John XXII excommunicated him, placed Milan under interdict and threatened an invasion by his French allies. Azzone submitted and renounced the vicariate, but kept political power in Milan and on 15 March 1330 was appointed signore of Milan.

In 1331 he married Catherine of Savoy-Vaud and allied with Theodore I, Marquess of Montferrat, against King Robert of Anjou in order to capture his possessions in north-western Italy. He conquered Bergamo and Pizzighettone in 1332 and in 1335 went on to take Lodi, Crema and other Lombard lands that had ceded themselves to the Papal States, as well as Vercelli and Cremona. In 1339 Lodrisio Visconti revolted with a company of hired mercenaries, and Azzone, suffering from gout, had Luchino Visconti command the Milanese army, which defeated Lodrisio at the battle of Parabiago.

Azzone died on 16 August 1339 of an attack of gout and was buried in the church of San Gottardo, which he had commissioned some years before. His only child was a daughter, Luchina, and he had no male heir, so he was succeeded as lord of Milan by his uncles Giovanni and Luchino. Besides his political and military career, he is remembered for his great construction works in Milan and other cities of Lombardy.
